units.la: MIgraturus ad Dominū Ioannes Caluinus, quum de commodis Ecclesiæ ne tum quidem cogitare definiret, sua mihi ὑπομνήματα, id est schedarum ingentem aceruum commendauit, vt si quid in ijs inuenissem quo possent adiuuari Ecclesiæ, id quoque in lucem ederetur. Cogitanti autem hac de re mihi, eaque omnia peruolutanti, multiplices obstiterunt difficultates, quominus id tam citò præstaretur quàm ego volui, & fortasse etiam oportuit. Præterquàm enim quòd euoluendis tot schedis aliorum etiam operæ fuit adhibenda, & multum in eo temporis ponendum, eæ consequutæ sunt in hac ciuitate calamitates, pestis videlicet aliquot annos continuata, & tumultus illi ingentes in contiguo nobis regno excitati, quæ & me & illos institutum opus sæpissime abrumpere coegerunt. Magna quoque nobis in Epistolarum delectu difficultas, maligna præsertim ac peruersa huius seculi hominum ingenia reputantibus, oborta est, dum horum scriptorum editionem sic temperare studemus, vt quoad eius fieri poterit, sine cui usquam offensione quàm plurimis prosit. Multa quippe familiariter inter amicos dici scribique consueuerunt, præsertim ab ingenui spiritus hominibus, qualis fuit Caluinus si quisquam nostris temporibus alius, quæ minimè expediat emanare. Et habenda quoque nobis fuit non modò personarum, verùm etiam temporum & locorum ratio. Itaque ex plurimis non ita multa tandem edidimus, eaque expunctis interdum nominibus, ne cui præberemus expostulandi argumentum. qua in re etsi testari de nostra diligentia bonaque fide merito possumus, tamen non temerè metuimus, vt ne sic quidem omnium iudicijs perinde satisfecerimus. Fuerit enim hoc, præsertim in opere tam vario, & tàta sententiarum multis de rebus varietate, non modò perdifficile, verùm etiam ἀδύνατον. Omnibus quidem certè profuisse studuimus, & futurum speramus, vt illis quidem qui nullum ad hæc legenda præiudicium attulerint,
units.tr: When John Calvin was about to depart to the Lord, he had not yet decided on anything concerning the advantage of the Church, but he entrusted to me his hypomnemata [ὑπομνήματα], that is, a huge heap of notes, so that if I found anything in them by which the Churches might be helped, that too should be published. But as I considered this matter and went through all of it, many difficulties stood in the way, so that it could not be done as quickly as I wished, and perhaps it ought not to have been. Besides the fact that turning over so many notes required the labour of others too and a great deal of time, there came upon this city calamities: a plague that lasted for some years, and those great disturbances stirred up in the neighbouring kingdom, which often forced both me and them to interrupt the work we had undertaken. There was also a great difficulty for us in selecting the letters, especially when we reflect on the malicious and perverse dispositions of the men of this age. While we strive to shape the edition of these writings so that, as far as possible, it may benefit as many as possible without offence to anyone anywhere, we have had to take account of persons, times and places. Many things are customarily said and written between friends in familiar talk, especially by men of free spirit, such as Calvin was, if any man of our times was, and it is not expedient that such things should come out. So from very many letters we have at last published not very many, and in some cases we have removed names, so as not to give anyone grounds for complaint. In this matter, although we may rightly claim to bear witness to our diligence and good faith, we nonetheless fear, not without reason, that even so we have not satisfied everyone's judgments equally. For this, especially in a work so varied and with such great variety of opinions on many matters, would be not only exceedingly difficult but even impossible [ἀδύνατον]. Certainly we have striven to be of use to all, and we hope it will be, to those at least who have brought no prejudice to the reading of these things and are not of that kind of people of whom the comic poet rightly says that nothing is more unjust than they, provided at least that our purpose is approved; but as for wicked slanderers or open enemies of the truth, there is surely no reason for us to delay over them even a little.

units.la: A.ij. neque ex eorum genere fuerint, quibus verè dicit Comicus nihil quic-quam esse iniustius, nam strum saltem institutum probetur: improbos au-tem calumniatores, aut apertos veritatis hostes, non est profectò cur vel tantillùm moremur. Cæterùm Illustrissime Princeps, dum apud me ipsum reputarem quanti Celsitudinem tuam Calvinus ipse fecerit, venit & illud in mentem, si hanc tibi ultimam ipsius scriptorum partem consecrarem, hoc ipsum facturum me, quod ille si superstes esset, fa-cturus erat. Fuit enim hoc illi in more positum, & quidem ut aiebat, Apostoli exemplo, ut quos videbat dignos esse quorum virtutes reli-qui sibi proponerent imitandas, eos libenter operum saltem suorum ini-tiis nominatim appellaret. Sed & illud veritus est, ut ausim mihi singulari Celsitudinis tuæ humanitate fretus, pollicerer, fore ut qua benevolentia Calvi-num ipsum vivum tanquam excellentem servum Dei complexus es, eadem quoque scriptum illud utilissima nostris futurisque temporibus multa complectens, perinde atque auctoris ipsius manu oblatum accipias, quod quidem à Celsitudine tua vehementer etiam atque etiam peto. Bene Vale. D. Iesus Celsitudinem tuam heroicis omnibus donis magis ac magis locupletet, & singulari suarum Ecclesiarum bono quàm diutissimè conservet. Geneuæ, Calend. Februarijs, Anno temporis ultimi
units.tr: A.ij. Moreover, most illustrious Prince, while I was considering with myself how highly Calvin himself esteemed your Highness, it came into my mind that if I dedicated to you this last part of his writings, I would be doing what he himself, if he were still alive, was going to do. For it was his custom, and indeed, as he used to say, following the example of the Apostle, that he would gladly name by name those whom he saw to be worthy that others should propose their virtues for imitation, at least in the beginnings of their works. But he also feared, and I venture to promise, relying on the singular kindness of your Highness, that just as you embraced Calvin himself while he was living as an excellent servant of God, so you will receive this writing, which contains much that is most useful for our times and for times to come, as if it were offered by the author's own hand; and this I earnestly and repeatedly ask of your Highness. Farewell. May the Lord enrich your Highness more and more with all heroic gifts, and preserve you for as long as possible for the singular good of his Churches. Geneva, the Calends of February, in the year of the last time, 1575.

units.la: Admonitio ad Lectorem.
units.tr: Notice to the Reader.

units.la: QVÆ in huius operis editione à nobis requiri posse existimauimus,eorum nobis hic reddendam rationem putauimus,quæ tum nostri officij esse dicebamus,tum ad ipsam operis tractationem comparatiorem Lectorem redderent.
units.tr: We thought that the following points might be expected of us in this edition of the work, and we considered it right to give an account of them here, both because we said they were part of our duty and because they would prepare the reader better for working through the book itself.

units.la: Primum igitur quòd ad tempus attinet, ita equidé editionem hanc & seram fatemur, & posthumam, vt simul affirmare non dubitemus,si quis totius operis ex numerosis & perquam implicitis chartis extricandi summam aliquam apud se vel cogitando subduxerit,minùs fortasse nostram hac in parte cessationem esse reprehensurum.
units.tr: First, then, as to time: we freely admit that this edition is late and posthumous. We also do not hesitate to affirm that anyone who has himself reckoned, even only in thought, the labour of disentangling the whole work from its many intricate papers will perhaps find less reason to blame our delay in this respect.

units.la: In delectu ipso demum (omnia enim istiusmodi scripta emittere nunc quidem non potuimus) testamur, imprimis vnam publici commodi rationem nobis fuisse propositam: proinde si quibus nostrum hoc iudicium vbique non satisfaciet, postulamus,vt quod noluimus ad cuiusquam probi offensionem referri (absit enim illud à nobis) illud secius ne accipiant,& ex illo potius interpretentur,nempe
units.tr: As to the selection itself (for we could not now publish all writings of this kind), we testify that one consideration above all was set before us, namely the public good. Therefore, if our judgment does not satisfy some people everywhere, we ask that they not take it as an offence to any upright person (far be that from us), which we did not intend, but rather that they interpret it in the light of that consideration, namely: In so great a work it is permitted for sleep to creep in.

units.la: Opere in tanto fas est obrepere somnum. Interiecimus etiam insignium illorum in Ecclesia Dei virorum aliquot epistolas,quòd ad ipsorum pietatem, eruditionem, zelum pro domo Dei, sanctissimam denique inter se testandam coniunctionem tanquam illis auctoribus propitiis nobis id fas esse bono publico persuasum habueremus.
units.tr: We have also inserted some letters of several distinguished men of the Church of God, because we were persuaded that, given their piety, learning, zeal for the house of God, and finally the most holy fellowship among themselves, it was right for us to publish them for the common good, with these men favouring the undertaking.

units.la: Illud insuper addimus,quòd quum plerasque amicorum Calvini ad ipsum eruditas literas, ac non perinde Caluini ipsius ἀμνήστιας nancisceremur, non ante edendas à nobis illas iudicasse,quàm aliunde iflas Caluini quæ desiderantur (quod ab ipsis Lectoribus benignè postulamus si quas nobis conferre poterunt, vt nos hoc à multis quod sine ipsorum incommodo ac dispendio fiat,lubenter expectabimus) adiungere,ac reponere possemus.
units.tr: We add this as well: since we found most of the learned letters of Calvin's friends written to him, but not Calvin's own letters in the same abundance, owing to his forgetfulness [ἀμνήστιας], we judged that we should not publish the former until we could also add and restore those letters of Calvin's that are missing from other sources. We kindly ask the readers themselves to send us any they can contribute, and we will gladly await such help from many, provided it does not cause them inconvenience or expense.

units.la: Atque huius rei argumento hic agnoscimus,nec dimidiam quidé partem iflorum quæ nunc exeunt Caluini scriptorum saluâ futurâ ram penes nos fuisse, nisi vel aliunde remissa, vel ex ipsis αὐτογράφοις descripta quamplurima habuissemus: vt ad eam rem vnius præcipuè Caroli Ionuilæi studiosissimi iflarum rerum cu-stodis fidem,diligentiam, operam denique & operosam & sumptuosam nobis appositissimam fuisse profitemur.
units.tr: As evidence of this, we acknowledge that not even half of the writings of Calvin now coming out would have been safe in our hands, unless we had received very many from elsewhere or copied them from the autographs themselves. We therefore declare that the faithfulness, diligence, and finally the laborious and costly effort of Charles Jonvillier, most zealous keeper of these papers, were especially and most usefully available to us in this matter.

units.la: Alterum etiam adiiciendum putauimus,venisse nobis in mentem nempe, fieri posse vt quædam ex illis quæ hic reperiuntur, apud nonnullos fortasse manuscripta non perinde extent, siue apices singuli, siue dictiones, ac fortassis etiam sententiæ aliquæ
units.tr: We also thought it should be added that it came to our mind that some of the things found here may perhaps not appear in exactly the same form in the manuscripts held by certain people, whether single letters, words, or perhaps even some sentences.

units.la: A.iij.
units.tr: A.iij.

units.la: conferantur,tum q bonam hic fidem &ccertam diligentiam præ-stari à nobis satis esse duxerimus, tũ etiam q nonnulla subinde προσκαιρα,aut merè familiaria,aut deniq; minùs ad rem ipsam pertinentia quũ occurrerent,expugenda sine vlla fraude iudica remus,ne quid videlicet à vere seriis Lectore intentũ reu ocaret.
units.tr: We considered that we had shown good faith and sufficiently careful diligence here, and also that when some temporary matters [προσκαιρα], either merely personal or less relevant to the subject itself, came up, we judged they should be omitted without any deception, so that nothing would distract the truly serious reader from what he intends.

units.la: Postremò quũ non pauca ex Gallicis istius argumenti & exèpli scriptis occurrerent nobis,quæ cum nonnullo lectorum vsu adiungi Latinis natis si & ipsa Latina facta essent,videremus(dũ & ipsorum Gallicorũ,& Gallicæ Latinorum translationis edendæ occasio sese deinceps offerret)ad certum vsq; numerum nûc quidem Galliça Latinè exprimenda curauimus:in quibus bonā etiam fidem præstitam testamur, reliqua autem quæ in translationis exactiori opera desiderarentur,benignè condonari postu lamus: Translationes ipsas porrò hac ad marginem nota (Ex Gallico) designari voluimus.
units.tr: Finally, since we came across not a few French writings on this subject and these examples, which, we saw, would be useful to readers if added to the Latin works, and since the chance to publish both the French originals and the Latin translations of French works may present itself later, we took care for now to render a certain fixed number of the French writings into Latin. In these we also testify that good faith was kept, but we kindly ask that any remaining shortcomings in a more exact work of translation be pardoned. We wished the translations themselves to be marked in the margin with this note: (From the French).

To the truly learned and wonderfully eloquent man, Master John Calvin, outstanding restorer of purer Christianity, to be uniquely honoured as my brother and fellow-initiate. Calvin to Bucer. To the most illustrious man, Master John Calvin, faithful minister of the Church of Geneva, most dear brother. Calvin to Bullinger. To the outstanding minister of Christ, Master Henry Bullinger, faithful pastor of the Church of Zurich, most highly esteemed fellow-initiate and most upright brother. Farel to Calvin. To the reverend and most learned man, Master John Calvin, who teaches the Gospel of the Son of God at Geneva, his lord and brother in Christ, to be honoured. Calvin to Brenz. To the eminent servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, Master John Brenz, fellow-initiate and brother to be honoured in the Lord.

units.la: IOHANNIS CALVINI VITA A THEODORO BEZA GENEVENSIS ECCLESIAE Ministro accuratè descripta.
units.tr: The Life of John Calvin, accurately described by Theodore Beza, minister of the Church of Geneva.

units.la: SI QVIS erit qui me alio quàm tuendæ veritatis studio existimet ad hanc Ioannis Calvini vitam describendam accessisse, facilè me vt spero, ab hac calumnia præsens rerum humanarum status vindicabit. Vix enim vllum est breuius ad omnem calamitatem compendium, quàm virtutem laudasse: extremæ vero demetiæ fuerit, quod malum potsis vel vno silentio redimere id vltrò vbi accersere. Quòd si ne virtutem quidem vllam impunè prædicare patiuntur scelerati, quid iis expectandum est, quibus pietatem, id est quiddam ipsa virtute superius, prædicare propositum est? Qui non improbi tantùm homines aduersantur, sed etiam plerunque ij ipsi bellum indixerunt, qui maximè probi videri ac interdum esse studeant. Nec enim vllos habet pietas acriores inimicos, quàm eos ipsos qui falsam religionem pro vera seriò sunt amplexi. Sed ista me quantumuis in speciem terribilia minimè tamen perculerunt. Turpe enim fuerit malorum metu bonos silere, & superstitiosorum clamoribus oppressum Religionis vocem conticescere. Quòd si quis excipiat longè aliud esse Caluini vitam scribere, quàm veritatem defendere, fatebor equidem ego longè aliud esse homiminem quàm veritatem: sed hoc tamen dicere non erubescam, haud temerè dictum esse ab eo qui est ἀποστολος, Sicut misit me pater, ita & ego mitto vos, & Qui vos audit, me audit. Clamitent igitur homines tum qui id sibi per ignorantiam persuaserunt, tum qui per improbitatem sic loquuntur: Lutherum, Zuinglium, Caluinum à nobis prodiis haberi, qui tamen quoties libet Sanctorum cultores vt idololatras reprehendamus. Clament, inquam, isti quantum & quandiu volent. Habemus quod illis regeramus: nempe longè aliud esse verè sanctorum hominum labores pro Religione susceptos, dicta denique & facta commemorare (quarum rerum cognitione boni meliores euadant, improbi vero redarguantur, qui nobis vnus est scopus in hoc scriptorum genere) quàm, vt ipsi faciut, partim vere Sanctorum hominum vitam non minus impiis quàm ineptis narrationibus (vt quod Abdias ille nescio quis in Apostolorum historia fe cit) dedecorare, partim ex putidissimis mendaciis fabulosas historias (quas vulgò Legendas Aureas barbaro vocabulo, ego Ablegandas Stercoreas appello) conflare, ac tandem etiam veterum deorum idola mutatis tantum nominibus in vsum revocare. Tamigitur abfumusab istis mortuorum cultoribus, quàm tenebrae luci repugnant. Illud enim seuerissimis addiris comminationibus prohibet Dominus: nos Deo iubenti in ipsius opera corporis & mentis oculos intendere, obsequimur. Nemo enim est opinor, qui non hominesinter omnia Dei opera, & rursum inter caeteros mortales eos qui sanctitate simul ac doctrina pollent, maximè nobis cognoscendos & obseruandos esse fateatur.
units.tr: If anyone thinks that I have undertaken to write this life of John Calvin from some motive other than zeal for defending the truth, I hope the present state of human affairs will easily clear me of that charge. There is hardly any shorter way to bring every kind of calamity upon oneself than to praise virtue. It would be the height of folly to buy off an evil by silence when one could summon it freely. But if the wicked do not even allow any virtue to be praised with impunity, what must those expect who intend to proclaim piety, which is something above virtue itself? Not only wicked men oppose such people, but very often those very men who most want to seem and even be upright have declared war on them. For piety has no fiercer enemies than those who have seriously embraced a false religion as the true one. Yet these threats, however frightening they may look, have not in the least shaken me. It would be shameful for good men to keep silent out of fear of the wicked, and for the voice of religion to fall silent, crushed by the clamour of the superstitious. If someone objects that writing the life of Calvin is quite a different thing from defending the truth, I will indeed admit that a man is quite different from the truth. But I am not ashamed to say this: it was not said rashly by him who is the Apostle [ἀπόστολος]: "As the Father sent me, so I send you," and "Whoever hears you hears me." Let people, then, keep shouting: both those who have persuaded themselves of this through ignorance, and those who speak this way out of wickedness, that Luther, Zwingli and Calvin are held by us as prophets, although we constantly rebuke the worshippers of the saints as idolaters. Let them shout, I say, as loudly and as long as they like. We have this answer to give them: it is quite a different thing to record the labours undertaken for religion by truly holy men, their sayings and deeds finally (through knowledge of which good men become better and wicked men are refuted, which for us is the one aim of this kind of writing), from what they do themselves. They partly disgrace the lives of truly holy men with narratives no less impious than silly (such as that Abdias, whoever he was, did in his history of the Apostles), and partly cobble together fabulous stories out of the most foul lies, which are commonly called the Golden Legend in a barbarous name, but which I call the Dung Legends, and finally they bring back into use the idols of the old gods with only their names changed. We therefore keep far away from these worshippers of the dead, as darkness is opposed to light. For the Lord forbids this with the most severe threats, and we obey God when he bids us fix the eyes of body and mind on his works. For I suppose there is no one who does not admit that, among all God's works, and again among other mortals, those who excel at once in holiness and in learning are those we most need to know and to observe.

units.la: Non temerè certè Daniel stellis compatat sanctosDei homines, qui foelicitatis iter suo splendore caeteris commonstrent: quorum fulgorem qui totum extinguì morte patiuntur, digni sunt quos tenebrae rursum multò quàm antea densiores inuadant. Caeterùm ne illos quidem placuit imitari, qui dum ἐπιδεικτικὸν & συγκριτικὸν illud dicendi genus sectantur, veritatem non tam exornarunt, quàm suspectam nonnullis reddiderunt. Itaque non quàm ornatè, sed quàm verè scriberem laborans, simplici potius narratione vtendum putaui.
units.tr: Daniel did not compare holy men of God to the stars without reason, since they show others the way to happiness by their brightness; and those who suffer that light to be wholly put out by death deserve to be invaded by darkness again, far thicker than before. Yet it has not pleased us to imitate those who, while they pursue that epideictic and comparative [ἐπιδεικτικὸν, συγκριτικὸν] style of speaking, have not so much adorned the truth as made it suspect to some. And so, labouring not to write how elegantly but how truthfully, I thought it better to use a simple narrative.

units.la: ¶Natus est Ioannes Calvinus Nouioduni Veromanduorum aut certè proximorum Veromanduis finium oppido celebri, Anno à D natiuitate M. D. IX. V I. I D. Iulij, Patre Gerardo Caluino, matre Ioanna Franca, vtroque honestae fa mae & mediocribus facultatibus parente. Erat is Gerardus non pauci iudicii & consilij homo, ideóque nobilibus eius regionis plarisque charus: quod in causa fuit, vt inter Mommorios (quae familia illic fuit nobilitate praecipua insignis) liberaliter admodum paterno tamen sumptu Caluinus filius à prima pueritia educaretur. Eos deinde Lutetiam studiorum gratia secutus, praeceptorem habuit in Gymnasio Marchiano Maturinum Cordelium spectatae tum probitatis tum eruditionis virum, & insigne semper habitum in omnibus fere Galliae scholis iuuentutis erudiendae magistrum: Geneuae demum, eo ipso anno quo Caluinus, v I. Nonas Septembris mortuum: quum aunum agens octuagesimum quintum, eo docendi munere in hoc Gymnasio Geneuensi fungeretur. Translatus deinde in Gymnasium ab Acuto monte cognominatum, Hispanum habuit doctorem non indoctum: à quo exculto ipsius ingenio quod ei iam tum erat acerrimum, ita profecit, vt caeteris sodalibus in Grammatices curriculo culo relictis, ad Dialectices & aliarum quas vocant, artium stu-diû promoueretur. Destinarat autem eum pater ab initio Theo-logiæ studiis, ad quæ vltrò illum inclinare ex eo colligebat, qp in illa etiam tenera ætate mirum in modum religiosus esset, & seuerus omnium in suis sodalibus vitiorum censor: quod ex nō-nullis etiam Catholicis idoneistestibus multis post annis celebri iam eius nomine, audire me memini. Itaque quasi rebus sacris destinato, pater beneficium ab Episcopo Nouiodunen. impetra-uit in Ecclesia Cathedrali quam appellant, ac deinceps etiam Pa-rochiæ Curationem in pago vrbi vicino qui Pont. Episcopi dici-tur, ex quo ortus ipse Gerardus Calvinus pater in vrbem ipsam postea transferat: quo loco constat Ioannem ipsum Calvinum antequam Gallia excederet (nullis alioqui Pontificiis ordinibus initiatum) aliquot ad populum conciones habuisse. Sed hoc con-silium interrupit vtriusque mutatus animus. Patris quidem, quod Iurisprudentiam certius iter esse ad opes & honores videret: fili-j vero, quòd à cognato quodam suo Petro Roberto Oliuetano (cui Gallicæ Ecclesiæ conuersa ex Hebræo Biblia Neocomi im-pressa debent) de vera Religione admonitus, legendis sacris li-bris se tradere, à superstitionibus vero abhorrere, ac proinde se-se ab illis sacris seiungere coepisset. Profectus ergo iuris ciuilis au-diendi causa Aureliam, vbi tunc Iurisconsultorum Gallorum fa-cilè princeps Petrus Stella docebat, mirū quantopere breui tem-pore profecerit: adeò quidem vt quum sæpissimè obiret ipsorum Doctorum vices, Doctor potius quàm Auditor haberetur: eíque discedenti Doctoratus insignia absque vllo pretio, summo do-centium omnium consensu quasi optimè de Academia merito offerretur. Interea tamen ille sacrarum literarum studium simul diligenter excolere, in quo tantùm etiam promouerat, vt qui-cunque in ea vrbe aliquo purioris Religionis cognoscendæ stu-dio tangebantur, ad eum etiam percontādum ventitarent, eiús-que tum eruditionem tum ardorem magnopere admirarentur. Testantur autem nonnulli adhuc superstites, qui tum ei familia-res & contubernales fuerunt, consueuisse illum per id tempus, postquam frugaliter admodum coenasset, ad mediam vsque no-ctem lucubrare, manè verò experrectum quæ legisset in lecto a-liquandiu meditari, velutíque concoquere, nec facilè in ea me-ditatione passum interpellari. quibus cōtinuatis vigiliis ille qui-dem solidam eruditionem, & excellentem memoriam est con-secutus: sed illam vicissim vt verisimile est, ventriculi imbecilli-tatem contraxit, quæ varios ipsi morbos, & tandem etiam intem-pestiuam mortem attulit. Erat tum Academiæ Bituricensis ma-gna celebritas, quòd eò euocatus ex Italia Iurisconsultus ætatis suæ facilè princeps Andreas Alciatus venisset, quem sibi quoque
units.tr: ¶John Calvin was born at Noyon, a well-known town in the Vermandois or in a region very close to the borders of the Vermandois, in the year of our Lord's birth 1509, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July]. His father was Gerard Calvin, his mother Jeanne Franc, both of good reputation and modest means. Gerard was a man of no little judgement and good counsel, and therefore was dear to most of the nobles of that region. This was the reason why the young Calvin, from his earliest boyhood, was brought up quite generously among the Montmor family (a family especially distinguished there for its nobility), at his father's expense. Afterwards he followed them to Paris for the sake of his studies, and had as his teacher in the Collège de la Marche Maturin Cordier, a man of proven integrity and learning, who was always regarded as outstanding among almost all the teachers of youth in the schools of France. Finally, at Geneva, in the same year that Cordier died there on the sixth day before the Nones of September [2 September], at the age of eighty-five, he held that teaching office in the Geneva school. Then he was transferred to the college called Montaigu, where he had as teacher a Spaniard who was no unlearned man. Through him his cultivated mind, which was already then very keen, made such progress that, leaving his fellow students behind in the course of grammar, he advanced to the study of dialectic and the other arts, as they are called. His father had at first destined him for theological studies, and from this he gathered that the boy was inclined that way, since even at that tender age he was wonderfully devout and a strict censor of all the faults of his companions. I remember hearing this from some Catholic witnesses, competent men, many years later, when his name was already famous. So, as if he had been destined for sacred things, his father obtained for him a benefice from the Bishop of Noyon in the cathedral church, as they call it, and afterwards also the cure of a parish in a village near the city, which is called Pont-l'Évêque, from which place Gerard Calvin, the father, later moved into the city itself. At this place it is established that John Calvin himself, before he left France (though not initiated into any Catholic orders), gave several sermons to the people. But this plan was interrupted by a change of mind in both of them: in the father, because he saw that law was a surer road to wealth and honours; in the son, because he was admonished about true religion by a certain cousin of his, Pierre Robert Olivétan (to whom the French Church owes the Bible translated from Hebrew and printed at Neuchâtel), and began to devote himself to reading the sacred books and to shrink from superstitions, and therefore to separate himself from those rites. So he went to Orléans to hear lectures on civil law, where at that time Pierre de la Estoile, the chief of French jurists, was teaching. In a short time he made remarkable progress, so much so that, since he very often took the place of the professors themselves, he was regarded as a doctor rather than a listener; and when he left, the insignia of the doctorate were offered to him without any fee, by the unanimous consent of all the teachers, as one who had deserved very well of the university. Meanwhile, however, he diligently cultivated the study of Holy Scripture as well, in which he advanced so far that whoever in that city was touched by a desire to learn the purer religion came to consult him, and they greatly admired both his learning and his zeal. Some who are still alive, who were then his intimates and fellow lodgers, testify that at that time he used to sit up working until midnight after a very frugal supper, and in the morning, once awake, he would ponder for some time in bed what he had read, as if digesting it, and he did not easily allow himself to be interrupted in that meditation. By these continual night-watches he indeed obtained solid learning and an excellent memory; but in return, as is likely, he contracted a weakness of the stomach, which brought him various illnesses and at last an untimely death. At that time the University of Bourges was in great repute, because Andrea Alciato, the chief jurist of his age, had been summoned there from Italy; John, our man, thought it right to hear him too.

units.la: Ioannes nofler audiendum putauit. Itaque quum eò migrasset, amicitiam iniit & Religionis & literarum nomine cum Melchiore Vvolmaro Germano Rotuillensi, Græcarum literarum publico tum illic profeffore: cuius maxime viri eò libentius memini, quòd eundem ego à prima pueritia ad pubertatem vsque præceptorem vnicum habui: cuius doctrinam, pietatem, ceterasque virtutes, admirabilem denique in erudienda iuuentute dexteritatem nunquam satis possim prædicare. Hoc auctore & adiutore Caluinus Græcas literas didicit, cuius beneficij nemo riam omnibus postea testatam esse voluit, consecratis ipsius nomini Commentariis quos in alteram ad Corinthios Epistolam edidit. In his igitur studiis versantem, ita tamen vt sacras literas assiduè tereret, adeòque nonnullas interim concionesin agro Biturigum, in oppidulo quod Linerias vocant, præsente & probante illius domino habueret, repentina mors patris nuntiata in patriam reuocauit. Inde paulò post Lutetia trâsiens quum annum ageret vigesimumquartum, egregium illum commentarium scripsit in Senecæ libellum de Clementia: quo scriptore grauissimo, & ipsius Caluini moribus planeconueniente valde delectum eum fuisse constat. Ibi paucis mensibus innotuit omnibus purioris Religionis studiosis, inter quos frequenter postea non fine insigni pietatis testimonio commemoratem eum audiuimus Stephanum Forgeum celebrem mercatorem, postea pro Christi nomine crematum, cuius etiam nomen edito postea contra Libertinos libro celebrauit. Ab eo tempore sese Caluinus abiectis reliquis studiis Deo consecrauit, summa piorum omnium qui tum Lutetiæ occultos cœtus habebant voluntate, nec ei mox defuit, in quo sese strenuè exerceret. Erat tum Academiæ Parisiensis Rector, ita vt illic fit, designatus Nicolaus Copus Guillielmi Copi Basiliensis Regij medici filius: cui quum de more habenda esset Cal. Nouembris oratio, quo die à Pontificiis Panagia celebrantur, suggessit eam Caluinus, in qua purius & apertius quàm antea consueuissent, de Religione differebatur. Hoc vero Sorbona ferre non potuit, nec probauit Senatus quem Parlamentum appellant: à quo citatus Rector sese quidem in viam cum suis apparitoribus dedit, sed ab amicis in itinere admonitus vt sibi ab aduersariis caueret, domum reuersus, ex ipso postea Regno excedens Basileam se contulit. Itum est etiam in Gymnasium quod Fortretum vocant, vbi tum Caluinus sibi domicilium delegerat: quo forte domi non reperto, deprehensis inter schedas multis amicorum literis, nil propius factum, quàm vt plurimi in maximum vitæ discrimen incurrerent: ita tum erant actes illi admodum aduersus Ecclesiam iudices, & in his quidem præcipue Ioannes quidam Morinus, cuius adhuc nomen men ab insigni sæuitia celebratur. Sed hanc tempestatem Dominus Reginæ Nauarrensis vnicæ Regis Francisci sororis admirabili ingenio prædictæ mulieris, & piis tunc admodum fauentis intercessione dissipauit, missus in aulam, ibíque perhonorifice ab ea accepto & audito Caluino. Inde ille Lutetia relicta in agrum Santonicum demigrans, amico cuidam operam dedit, cuius rogatu breues quasdam admonitiones Christianas scripsit, quas Parochis nonnullis inter Sacra recitandas tradebant, vt populi ad veritatis indagandæ studium alliceren-tur. Eodem tempore Neracum Aquitaniæ urbem venit, Iacobum illum Fabrum Stapulensem senem salutatum, quem eadem illa Nauarrena Regina à Sorbonistis Mataeologis ob Mathematices & alia philosophiæ recta studia Parisiensi Academiæ non sine diuturno acerrimóque certamine restituta, & Scholasticam Theologiam exagitatam, in vitæ discrimen adductum liberarat, & in illa suæ ditionis urbe collocarat. Excepit autem iuuenem bonus senex, & libenter vidit, futurum augurans insignæ cœlestis in Gallia instaurandi Regni instrumentum. Rediit aliquanto post Lutetiam Caluinus, eo quasi Dei ipsius manu euocatus. Venerat enim illuc impius ille Seruetus, iam tum suum aduersus sacram Triadem virus dispergens: quem sese nihil magis appete re quàm eius colloquium simulantem, condicto loco & tempore Caluinus (idque non citra magnum vitæ periculum, quod tum latere propter accensam aduersariorum rabiem cogeretur) diutius quidem sed frustra expectauit, illo ne Caluini quidem conspectum ferente. Fuit au em is annus xxxiiii. supra fesquimillesimum horrenda in multos pios sæuitia insignis, Gerardo Russo Sorbonico Magistro sed pietatis studia magnopere tunc adiuuante, itémque Coraldo Augustiniani ordinis, (qui vnum & alterum iam annum fauore Nauarrenæ adiuti, negotium Christi in vrbe plurimùm promouerant) non modò ex pulpito deturbatis, sed etiam in carcerem coniectis: & eovsque inflammata fascinati Francisci regis ira obschedis quasdam aduersus Missam per vrbem sparsis, ipsiúsque regij cubiculi foribus affixas, vt publica decreta supplicatione, cui vnà cum liberis suis tribus nudo capite ardentem facem quasi expiationis causa gestans in terfuit, quatuor vrbis celebriotibus locis Οἰκονομίας Martyres vi-uos vstulari iuberet, atque adeò solenni iureiurando testaretur, se ne liberis quidem suis parsurum, si forte ceterri vis illis vt vocabat, hæresibus essent infecti. Eiusmodi rerum statum intuens Caluinus paulò post iuam Aureliæ insignem illum libellum edidisset, quem Psychopannychian inscripsit aduersus illorum errorem, qui dormire seiunctas à corporibus animas errore à vetustissimis vsque seculis repetito docebant,sec tuit, eoque consilio vnâ cum illo quicum eu aliquandiu vixisse diximus, iter Basileam ve giam ingressus,non procul vrbe Metensi in m tatem incidit, alterius ex seruis perfidia pec pta,qui altero exequis validiore strato tam r dedit,vt deprehendi nullo pacto potuerit, her ni viatico relictis imparatissimis: adeo vt ab uulo decem mutuo sumptis coronatis vix Ar Basileam peruenerint. Ibi praecipuos habuit los homines Simonem Grynaeum,&Vvolfga seseque Hebraïcis literis dedit: & quanuis late studeret,id quod ex Epistola quadam Buceri anno data liquet,tamen edere coactus est Christianae Religionis Institutionem quam vocauit, operis longè m Quum enim illam Francifci regis carnificina mani Principes qui Euangelio nomen dederant,& quorum ille tum amicitiam ambiebat, hoc vnum ille σοφὸν φαρμακον au- ctore Gulielmo Bellaio Langaeo repererat, vt sese non nisi in A- nabaptistas pro verbo diuino suum tantum Spiritum iactantes, & omnium Magistratuum contemptores animaduertisse dice- ret.Quod dedecus verae Religioni inustum nō ferens Caluinus, eius edendi libri occasionem arripuit, meo quidem iudicio in- comparabilis: addita excellenti ad Regem ipsum praefatione, quam si forte legisset ille,aut ego vehementer fallor,aiut magnū esset illi merettici Babylonicae iam tum vulnus illatum. Erat e- nim ille Rex non quales eum sunt consecuti postea: sed acerri- mus rerū aestimator,iudicij addignoscendum verū mon parui, eruditorum fautor,neque per se à nobis alienus. Sed illum haec audire nedum legere neque populi Gallici, meque ipsius regis peccata passa sunt, quibus ira Dei iam tum propinquā immine- bat. Edito hoc libro suaque veluti praestita patriae fidde, Calui- num visendae Ferrariensis Ducissae Ludouici x ii.Frarncorum re- gis filiae, cuius tum pietas celebrabatur, sinmúlque Italiae veluti procul salutandae desiderium incessit.Illam igitur viddit,simúlq; quantum id illum facere praesens rerum sta tus sinebaat, in vero pietatis studio confirmauit, vt eum postea viuum semper vnice dilexerit,ac nunc quoque superstes gratae in defunctuam memo- riae specimen edat luculentum. Caeterum ex Italia,in cuius fines se ingressum esse dicere solebat vt inde exir sus, rebus suis omnibus ibi compositis, abductoque quem vni- cum superstitem habebat Ant.Caluino frat gentinam reuerti cogitantem, interclusis ai brogum finesiter rfltitutum prosequi bella coëgerunt. Ita fa•́ctum vt Geneuanveniret, nihil ipse quidem de illa vrbe cogitans, sed vt mox pparuit, diuinitus eo perductus. Erat enim in illam vrbem pulò ante mirabiliter introducum Christi Euangelium duorum summorum virorum opera, Guillielmi Farelli Delphinatis on vt quidam commenti sunt ex cœnobio, sed ex schola Iacoi Fabri Stapulensis prodeuntis, & Petri Virteti Orbensis ex ago Bernensis ac Friburgensis ditionis, quorum postea laboribus opiofiffime Dominus benedixit. Eos igitur quum vtinter binos fieri solet, Caluinus transiens inuisisset, tum Farellus vt eit plane vir ille Spiritu quodam heroico afflatus, multis eunverbis frustra obtellatus, vt secum potius Geneuæ laboraret, uam longius excurreret, nec ei facile Caluinus assentiretur. At ego tibi inquit, studia tua prætexenti denuntio Omnipotentis Dei nomine, futurum vt nisi in opus iftudDomini nobcum incumbas, tibi non tam Christum quàm teipsum quærent Dominus maledicat. Hac terribili denuntiatione territus Caluinus sese Presbyterij & Magistratus voluntati permisit quorum suffragiis accedente plebis consensu delectus non Cocionator tantum (hoc autem primum recufarat) sed etiam acratum literarum Doctor, quod vnum admittebat, est dignatus anno Domini M. D. XXXVI. mense Augusto. Atque idem hic annus inito inter duas ciuitates Bernam & eneuam arctiori fœdere, & Laufannæ ad Christum accessione iabita aduersus Pontificios libera disputatione, cui Caluinu quoque interfuit, celebratus est. Tunc edita est à CaluincChriftianæ doctrinæ quædam veluti formula, vixdum emergenti e Papatus sordibus Geneuenfi Ecclesiæ accommodata. Addidit etiam Catechismum, non illum in quæstionis& reonsionesdiftributum quem nunc habemus, sed aliarum multoreuiorem, præcipua Religionis capita complexum. Aggrisus deinde cum Farello & Coraldo, plerisque ex collegistimicare turbas fugientibus, nonnulli s etiam quæ maxima Caluinfolicitudo fuit clàm opus Domini impedientibus, Ecclesiam componere, à ciuibus primum omnium contendit, vt coacti populus vniuersus, eiurato palàm Papatu, in Christiana Regionem acdifciplinam paucis capitibus comprehensam iurat. Quod etsi non pauci recusarent, vt in vrbe vixdum exibaudi Ducis rec bus, & Antichristi iugo liberata, & multadhuc factionibus æstuante, dedit tamen Dominus wigesim Iulij Anno M. D. XXXVII, vt palam prameunte publico Scriba, à Senatu Populoque Geneuensi in Christianæ Rigionis ac disciplinæ simul capita iuraretur. Istis vero exactus Satan & frustra, quod per externos
units.tr: Our John thought it worth hearing him. So when he had moved there, he formed a friendship, based on shared religion and learning, with Melchior Volmar, a German from Rottweil who was then public professor of Greek there. I remember this man with particular pleasure, because I had him as my only teacher from early boyhood until puberty, and I can never praise enough his learning, his piety and his other virtues, and above all his remarkable skill in teaching young people. Under his guidance and help Calvin learned Greek. Calvin later wished to bear public witness to this kindness, by dedicating to Volmar's name the commentaries he published on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. So while he was occupied with these studies, yet still wore himself out constantly over Holy Scripture, and meanwhile preached a few sermons in the countryside of Bourges, in a small town called Linières, with the approval and in the presence of its lord, the news of his father's sudden death recalled him to his homeland. Soon afterwards, passing through Paris in his twenty-fourth year, he wrote that outstanding commentary on Seneca's book On Clemency. It is well established that he was greatly delighted with that most serious author, whose character agreed very well with Calvin's own. In those few months he became known to all who cared for a purer religion. Among them, Étienne de la Forge, a well-known merchant, was often later mentioned by us with notable witness to his piety; he was afterwards burned for the name of Christ, and Calvin praised his name in a book he later published against the Libertines. From that time Calvin, leaving his other studies aside, devoted himself to God, with the warm goodwill of all the pious who then met in secret assemblies in Paris, and soon he found a field in which to exert himself vigorously. At that time the Rector of the University of Paris was, as is the custom there, Nicolas Cop, son of Guillaume Cop of Basel, the king's physician. When he was due, as usual, to deliver the oration on the first of November, the day the Papists celebrate All Saints, Calvin drafted it for him. In it religion was discussed more purely and openly than had been customary before. The Sorbonne could not tolerate this, and the Senate, which they call the Parlement, did not approve. Summoned before it, the Rector set out on his way with his attendants, but, warned on the journey by friends to beware of his enemies, he went back home, and afterwards, leaving the kingdom itself, he betook himself to Basel. There was also a raid on the college called Fortret, where Calvin had chosen his lodging. He was not at home when they came, and they seized many letters from friends found among his papers, so that many were brought into the greatest danger of their lives. The judges at that time were very hostile to the Church, and among them especially a certain John Morin, whose name is still famous for remarkable cruelty. But this storm was dispelled by the intercession of the Lady of Navarre, sister of King Francis, a woman endowed with admirable talent and then very favourable to the pious. Calvin was sent to the court, where he was received and heard with the greatest honour by her. Then, leaving Paris, Calvin moved to the Saintonge region, where at the request of a certain friend he wrote some short Christian exhortations, which were handed to certain parish priests to be read out during the sacred services, so that the people might be drawn to the search for truth. At the same time he came to Nérac, a town in Aquitaine, to greet the aged Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, whom the same Queen of Navarre had rescued from the Sorbonnist Mataeologists, who had restored the study of mathematics and other sound philosophical disciplines in the Paris Academy only after long and very bitter conflict, and who had been brought into danger of his life for attacking scholastic theology. She had settled him in that town of her domain. The good old man received the young man and gladly saw him, foretelling that he would be a remarkable instrument of heavenly restoration of the kingdom in France. Calvin returned to Paris some time later, summoned there as though by God's own hand. For that impious Servetus had come there, already then spreading his poison against the sacred Trinity. Calvin, intending to meet him by agreement at a set place and time, waited for him a long while, though in vain, since Servetus, pretending that he wished nothing more than a conference with him, did not dare to come into Calvin's sight. This was, however, not without great danger to Calvin's life, for he was forced to hide because of the fierce rage of his enemies. That year, 1534, was notable for a dreadful cruelty against many pious people. Gérard Roussel, a Master of the Sorbonne, who then greatly supported the cause of piety, and Coraud of the Augustinian order, who had for a year or two been aided by the favour of the Queen of Navarre and had greatly advanced the cause of Christ in the city, were not only thrown down from the pulpit but also cast into prison. The king Francis, inflamed to such a pitch of anger by placards against the Mass that had been scattered about the city and fixed to the doors of his own royal bedchamber, that, when a public supplication was decreed, at which he was present with his three children, bareheaded and carrying a burning torch as though for expiation, he ordered living martyrs to be burned in four of the most crowded places in the city. He even swore a solemn oath that he would not spare even his own children, if by chance they were infected with those heresies, as he called them. Seeing such a state of affairs, Calvin, shortly after publishing at Orléans his notable little book, which he entitled Psychopannychia, against the error of those who taught, with a doctrine repeated from the most ancient ages, that souls separated from bodies sleep, set out with the same purpose, together with that companion with whom we said he had lived for some time, to Basel. Not far from the city of Metz he fell into a danger, betrayed by the treachery of one of his servants, who, having put one of the other horses under a heavier load, so disturbed the fellow's mind that he could not be discovered in any way. Having left his travelling funds behind, they were quite unprepared, so that they reached Basel only with difficulty, having borrowed barely ten crowns. There he had as his chief friends Simon Grynaeus and Wolfgang Capito, and he devoted himself to Hebrew literature. Although he was studying in private, as is clear from a letter of Bucer dated that year, he was nonetheless compelled to publish the Institution of the Christian Religion, as he called it, a work far more substantial than was then expected. For when the butchery of Francis's king had been reported throughout Germany, the princes who had embraced the gospel, and whose friendship the king was then courting, had found this one remedy [σοφὸν φάρμακον], as Guillaume du Bellay de Langey reported, namely that he was punishing only the Anabaptists, who boasted of their own spirit in place of the divine word, and who despised all magistrates. Calvin, unable to bear this disgrace branded upon true religion, seized the occasion to publish this book, which in my judgment is incomparable, with an excellent preface addressed to the king himself. If by chance he had read it, or I am greatly mistaken, I think a grievous wound would already have been inflicted on that Babylonian harlot. For that king was not like those who came after him, but was a very sharp judge of things, not a poor judge of learning and a patron of the learned, and not by nature alien to us. But neither the sins of the French people nor his own would allow him to hear or read these things, and so the wrath of God, already near, hung over him. After publishing this book, and as it were fulfilling his promise to his fatherland, Calvin felt a desire to visit the Duchess of Ferrara, Renée, daughter of Louis XII, king of the French, whose piety was then celebrated, and at the same time to greet Italy as if from afar. So he saw her and, as far as the state of affairs at the time allowed, was confirmed by her in the true zeal for piety. Thereafter he always loved her with unique affection while she lived, and even now that she has died he gives a splendid example of grateful remembrance of her. Otherwise, intending to return from Italy, into whose borders he used to say he had entered only in order to leave again, and having settled all his affairs there, and having taken away with him his brother Antoine Calvin, whom he had as his only surviving brother, the wars that closed the borders of Savoy compelled him to go round by a longer route. So it happened that he came to Geneva, not at all thinking about that city, but, as soon became clear, led there by God. For shortly before, the gospel of Christ had been wonderfully introduced into that city through the work of two very great men, Guillaume Farel of Dauphiné, who came not, as some have invented, from a monastery, but from the school of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, and Pierre Viret of Orbe, from the territory of Bern and Fribourg. Afterwards the Lord blessed their labours most abundantly. When Calvin, as usually happens between two men, had visited them in passing, Farel, who was truly a man inspired by a certain heroic spirit, tried with many words, though in vain, to persuade him to labour with them in Geneva rather than travel further; and Calvin did not readily agree. But Farel said to him, as he pretended his studies: "I declare to you in the name of Almighty God that, unless you apply yourself to this work of the Lord with us, you will not seek Christ but yourself, and the Lord will curse you." Terrified by this fearful declaration, Calvin submitted himself to the will of the Presbytery and the Magistrate. Chosen by their votes, with the consent of the people also, he was accepted not only as preacher (though he had at first refused this) but also as teacher of Holy Scripture, which was the only office he would admit, in the year of the Lord 1536, in August. In the same year, after a closer alliance between the two cities, Bern and Geneva, and after the accession of Lausanne to Christ, a free disputation against the Papists was held, in which Calvin also took part. Then Calvin published a kind of formula of Christian doctrine, adapted to the Geneva Church, which had scarcely emerged from the filth of the Papacy. He also added a catechism, not the one divided into questions and answers that we now have, but a much older one, containing the principal heads of religion. Then, when he and Farel and Coraud had begun to set the Church in order, most of their colleagues fleeing the disturbances, and some, which was Calvin's greatest anxiety, secretly hindering the work of the Lord, he first of all required the citizens to be compelled, the whole people publicly abjuring the Papacy, to swear to a Christian religion and discipline summarised in a few heads. Although not a few refused this, in a city scarcely freed from the yoke of the Duke and the Antichrist, and still seething with many factions, nevertheless the Lord granted it, and on the twentieth of July, 1537, it was sworn publicly, with the public notary leading, before the Senate and people of Geneva, to the heads of Christian religion and discipline together. But Satan, thoroughly thwarted in this, since he had tried by foreign enemies in countless ways, thought he could bring about by a pretext of piety, first of all against the Anabaptists, and then against Pierre Caroli, of whom we shall speak soon, those who opposed that work of the Lord, whether because it was, however it then stood, very unwelcome to him, or because of what followed afterwards...

units.la: hostes infinitis modis tentarat, efficere sese pietatis obtentu ratus, primum omnium Anabaptistas, deinde Petrum Caroli de quo mox dicemus, oppositi, qui opus illud Domini, sive quod illud qualecunque iam erat, ei magnopere ingratum esset, sive quod ea quae postea consecuta sunt prosperaret, non interturbarent modo, verum etiam destruerent prorsus atque subverterent. Sed anteuerterat Satanam Dominus, quod ipse rei eventus docuit.
units.tr: Satan, who had tried in countless ways through external enemies, thought he could succeed under the cover of piety by first stirring up the Anabaptists and then Pierre Caroli, of whom we shall speak shortly. He wanted to oppose the work of the Lord, whatever it then was. Either that work was deeply unwelcome to him, or he foresaw that what followed would prosper, and so he meant not merely to disturb it but to destroy and overturn it utterly. But the Lord had anticipated Satan, as the outcome of events itself showed.

units.la: Anabaptistas enim Calvinus & Collegae publica, liberaque disputatione conuocatos, ea gravitate ex uno Dei verbo confutarunt decimo octauo Martij Anno M. D. XXXV II, vt quod rarae cuiusdam fuit felicitatis, ab eo tempore vix vnus aut alter in hac Ecclesia apparuerit. Alter Ecclesiae turbator P. Caroli nomine, maiores & diuturniores turbas dedit, quarum duntaxat summam recensebo, quod tota huius certaminis historia extet, & ex quadam Calvini ad Grynaeum epistola colligi potest. Ilum gnauiter impudentem Sophistam mater Sorbona quae peperierat, postea tanquam haereticum, non ita de ipsa merito ciecit.
units.tr: Calvin and his colleagues summoned the Anabaptists to a public and free disputation. On 18 March 1537 they refuted them from the Word of God alone, with such authority that, by a rare good fortune, after that time hardly one or two of that sect appeared in this Church. The other troubler of the Church, in the name of Pierre Caroli, caused greater and longer-lasting disturbances. I shall recount only the sum of them, since the whole history of this conflict survives and can be gathered from a certain letter of Calvin to Grynaeus. That shameless sophist, whom mother Sorbonne had brought forth, was afterwards cast out as a heretic, and he had done her little credit.

units.la: Venit igitur ille primum quidem Geneuam, inde Lausannam, postea Neocomum: Satanae Spiritu vsque adeo vbique comite, vt quocunque veniret, certa suae turpitudinis impressa vestigia relinqueret. Vbi se videbat a nostris argui, ad aduersarios trahebat: ab illis rursum ad nostros, vt illius artes aperte describitae extant prolixa quaedam Farelli ad Calvinum epistola. Tandem igitur aperte coepit optimum quenque, & quidem imprimis Farellum, Calvinum, Viretum, quasi de Sacra Triade minus recte sentientes criminari. Habita est ea de re Synodus Bernae valde frequens, in qua damnatus calumniae P. Caroli paulatim postea deccit, tandemque Mediomatrices subornatus venit, vt opus Domini quod feliciter illic Farellus inchoarat, impediret. Inde scripta epistola pios aperte lacessiuit, vt Apostasiae suae plena spe factae, beneficium aliquod canis famelicus obtineret. Romam autem nihilominus remissus, vt coram ipsi Beatiae satisfaceret, ibique cum ludibrio exceptus, premente inopia & Gallica scabie, vix in Xenodochium receptus, stipendium tandem peccati, mortem videlicet a filio peccati retulit. Et hic quidem fuit illius infaelicis exitus. Interea Calvinus, anno videlicet M. D. XXXVII, quod multos in Gallia videret veritatem quidem intus probe noscentes, sibi tamen indulgentes, quasi Christum animo colere satis esset, etiamsi Papistices sacris interessent, duas elegantissimas epistolas edidit: Vnam de fugienda idololatria Nicolao Chemino, quo amico & hospite vsus Aureliae plurimum fuerat, Officiali postea Cenomanensi designato: Alteram de Papisticis Sacerdotiis, Gerardo illi Russo cuius antea memini, quique Abbatia quadam ac deinceps Episcopatu post editum illum Parisien-
units.tr: He came first to Geneva, then to Lausanne, and afterwards to Neuchâtel, with Satan's spirit everywhere accompanying him, so that wherever he went he left the sure marks of his own baseness. When he saw himself being censured by our side, he went over to the opponents, and then back again to ours. His tricks are plainly described in a long letter of Farel to Calvin. At last he openly began to accuse the best men, and above all Farel, Calvin and Viret, of holding unsound views about the Holy Trinity. A very well-attended Synod was held at Bern on this matter, and Caroli, condemned for his slander, gradually sank afterwards. Finally he came, bribed by the Mediomatrici, to hinder the work of the Lord that Farel had happily begun there. From there he wrote a letter openly attacking the godly, hoping, full of his apostasy, to obtain some benefice as a famished dog does. He was nevertheless sent back to Rome to make satisfaction before the Pope himself, and there he was received with mockery. Pressed by poverty and French disease, he was barely taken into a hospice, and at last he received the wages of sin, namely death, from the son of perdition. Such was the unhappy end of that wretch. Meanwhile Calvin, in the year 1537, seeing that many in France knew the truth well inwardly but indulged themselves, as if it were enough to worship Christ in their hearts even while they attended Papist rites, published two most elegant letters. One, on fleeing from idolatry, was addressed to Nicolas Chemin, a friend and host with whom he had lived much at Orléans, later appointed Official of Le Mans. The other, on Papist priesthoods, was addressed to that Gérard Roussel I mentioned before, who was afterwards given an abbey and then a bishopric after the Parisian uproar.

units.la: Parisiensem tumultum donatus, non modo postea satis rectum cursum nom tenuit, verum etiam heram suâ Nauarrenam Reginam paulatim peflumdedit. Caeterum haec illum agente gravissimae domesticae seditiones exceperunt. Admissum fuerat in vrbe sicut antea diximus, Euangelium, & papatus eiuratus. Sed extrusa simulâ plerisque non fuerat indignâ multa flagitia, quae in ea vrbe Canonicis & impuro illi Clero tot annos addicta, dih viguerat: & veteres inter quasdam primarias familias inimicitiae bello Sab audito susceptae, adhuc exercebatur. Quibus leni primâ admonitione, deinde graviori aduersus refractarios increpatione tolledis, quum nihil proficeretur, & eovsque malum procef fiffet, vt Ciuitas priuatorum quorumdam factione in diuersas partes scinderetur, & non pauci sese in ordinem iuratum redigi nullo modo paterentur, eo tandem deueniendum fuit, vt magno heroico⁊ Spiritu praediti Farellus, & Caluinus cum Coraldo Collega, quê quum vt ante diximus, strenuè Lutetiae pro veritate depugnaffet, Caluins Bafileam, indeque Geneuam postquam illic ipse constituisset, perduxerat) aperte testarentur, sese Coenam Domini tam inter fe discordibus, & ab omni Ecclesiastica disciplina alienis ciuibus, ritè celebrate non posse Accedebat & aliud malum, quod videlicet in quibusdam ritibus Ecclesiae Geneuenf. à Bernenf. discreparet. Vtebantur enim Geneuenfes pane communi, & Baptisteria illa quae vocant tanquam ad Baptismi Miniftertiu minus necessaria, itemque dies festos excepto die Dominico sustulerant. quibus de rebus quum Synodus Laufannae à Bernenfibus coacta sic decidisset, vt Azymum pane illâq; restitui Geneuae postularet, collegium autem Ministrorum Geneuenfium fe prius audiri aequum duceret, eamque ob causam altera Tigurû Synodus effet indicta, his oblatis occasionibus, qui tum fuerat creati Syndici (annuus hic est fummufque in Republica Geneuenfi Magistratus) factionum ac discordiarum duces populum conuocant: eoque rem perducunt frustra sese Caluino cum eiusdem sententiae Collegis ad reddendum omnium rationem offerente, vt maiore parte meliorem superante, tresifti fidi Dei ferui intra biduum excedere vrbe iuberentur, quod Coenâ Domini celebrate tecufaffent. Hoc decretum quum effet Caluino renuntiatum, Certe, inquit, fi hominibus seruiuissem, mala mihi merces perfoluereatur, sed bene est quod ei inseruiui qui nû- quam non feruis suis rependit quod semel promisit. Et quis ista non exiftimaffet certâ perniciem Ecclesiae Geneuenfi allatura? Euentus tamen contrà ostendit diuina prouidentia id factum, partim vt alibi opera fidelis ferui fui vsus, variis eum experimentis ad res maiores instrueret, partim vt seditiosis illis suo ipforû impetu subuersis, Ecclesiam Geneuenfem à multis sordibus re‹.
units.tr: ...Parisian tumult, did not keep a fairly straight course afterwards, and gradually even betrayed his mistress, Queen Marguerite of Navarre. Meanwhile, while Calvin was at work, very grave domestic disorders arose. As I said before, the Gospel had been admitted in the city and Papacy abjured. But since it had been expelled, many shameful vices which had long been practised in that city by the canons and that impure clergy had not been removed, and old enmities between certain leading families, taken up in a war of Sabbath, still troubled the city. After a gentle first admonition and then a severer rebuke of the refractory had been tried, and nothing was gained, and the evil had advanced so far that the city was split into opposing parties by the faction of certain private men, and not a few refused in any way to be bound by a sworn order, it came to this: Farel and Calvin, with their colleague Coraud (who, as I said before, had fought bravely at Lutetia for the truth, and whom Calvin had brought from Basel to Geneva after settling there himself), openly declared that they could not celebrate the Lord's Supper properly among citizens so divided among themselves and alien to all ecclesiastical discipline. Another evil was added: in certain rites the Church of Geneva differed from that of Bern. For the Genevans used common bread, and they had abolished those baptismal fonts, which they called unnecessary for the ministry of baptism, and likewise the festival days other than the Lord's Day. When the Synod of Lausanne, gathered by the Bernese, decided these matters so as to demand that unleavened bread be restored at Geneva, and the college of Genevan ministers thought it fair that they be heard first, and for that reason a second Synod was summoned at Zurich, the factions and discord-leaders seized these opportunities. They had just appointed the Syndics (this is the annual and highest magistracy in the Genevan republic), and they called the people together and brought the matter to this point. Although Calvin, with his colleagues of the same view, offered to give an account of everything, the better party prevailed, and the three faithful servants of God were ordered to leave the city within two days, because they had refused to celebrate the Lord's Supper. When this decree was announced to Calvin, he said: "Certainly, if I had been serving men, I would have received a bad reward; but it is well that I have served him who never fails to repay his servants what he has once promised." And who would not have thought this would bring certain ruin to the Church of Geneva? Yet the outcome showed that it was done by divine providence, partly so that, using the faithful servant in another place, He might train him by various experiences for greater tasks, and partly so that, those seditious men being overthrown by their own violence, He might cleanse the Church of Geneva from many filths.

units.la: B.ii. purgaret. Vsqueadeo sese Dominus in cunctis suis operibus, ac praesertim in Ecclesiae suae gubernatione admiranda prębet. Sed haec omnia postea res ipsa patefecit. Tum vero magno cum bonorum omnium dolore tres illi edicto parentes, quum Tigurum primum venissent, ibique coacta Helveticarum Ecclesiarum aliquot Synodo, atque ex Synodi decreto per Bernensium intercessionem tentatis, sed frustra, Geneuensium animis, Calvinus quidem Basileam inde sese, ac mox Argentinam contulit. Illic igitur ex illius urbis Senatus voluntate, a summis illis viris quibus tanquam lucidis gemmis illa tum Ecclesia fulgebat, Bucero, Capitone, Hedione, Nigro & aliis eorum collegis ad Theologicam professionem propositio honesto stipendio evocatus, non modo Theologiam illic docuit magna cum doctorum omnium applausu, sed etiam ex Senatus consensu, Gallicam Ecclesiam constituta etiam Ecclesiastica disciplina plantavit. Sic expectatione sua frustratus Satan, pro Geneuensi Ecclesia Calvinum alibi exceptum, & aliam mox alibi nactam Ecclesiam conspexit: nihilo interea segnius laborans, ut aedificium Geneuense prorsus concussum penitus everteret. Itaque mox reperit male feriatos nonnullos, qui ut pietatis nescio cuius obtentu, iniquissimum illud defectum tegerent, panem communem quo antea in Coena vtebantur, in Azymum censerent conuenti oportere, scilicet ut nouis dissidiis ansam praeberent. Nequc hoc consilium Satanam fefellisset, nisi Calvinus bonos non nullos ista mutatione vsque adeo offensos, vt etiam a Coena sibi abstinendum putarent, serio monuisset, ne ob istud ἀδιάφορον litem moueret. Sic obtinuit panis Azymi vsus: de quo etiam postea restitutus Calvinus nunquam contendendum putauit, minime tamen dissimulans, quid alioqui magis esset probaturus. At ecce longe mox aliud periculosius malum, Anno videlicet M. D. XXXIX, exortum, simulque Calvini diligentia extinctum. Erat tum Episcopus Carpentoratensis Iacobus Sadoletus magna eloquentia homo, sed qua imprimis ad opprimendam veritatis lucem auteretur: nec aliam ob causam in Cardinalium numerum adscitus, quam vt vir alioqui vitae non flagitiosus, quos posset colores falsae religioni inducere, Is obseruata eius temporis occasione, destitutum tantis pastoribus gregem facile se interceptarum arbitratus, viciniam quoque praetexens (est enim Carpentoratensis Ciuitas Delphinatui, & hic rursus Sabaudiae continuus) literas dedit desideratissimis quos vocat, Senatui, Consilio, populoque Geneuatium inscriptas, in quibus nihil eorum praetermisit, quae ad eos in Rom illius meretricis gremium reuocandos pertinerent. Illis nemo tum erat Geneuae qui respondisset, opponeret: adeo vt nisi peregrino sermone scriptae fuissent, ma-gnum.
units.tr: B.ii. So wondrously does the Lord show himself in all his works, and especially in the government of his Church. But all these things the event itself later made plain. Then indeed, to the great grief of all good men, those three were sent away by the edict. When they first came to Zurich, and a Synod of several Helvetic Churches had been gathered there, and an attempt had been made through the mediation of the Bernese by a decree of the Synod, but in vain, Calvin withdrew from there to Basel, and soon afterwards to Strasbourg, while the Genevans' minds remained unchanged. There, by the will of that city's Senate, he was called to the theological professorship with an honourable stipend by those greatest men, who then shone in that Church like bright gems: Bucer, Capito, Hedio, Niger, and their other colleagues. Not only did he teach theology there with the great applause of all the learned, but also, with the consent of the Senate, he planted a French Church and established ecclesiastical discipline. Thus Satan was frustrated in his expectation: he saw Calvin received elsewhere in place of the Genevan Church, and soon found him a Church elsewhere, while he himself laboured no less diligently to utterly overthrow and destroy the Genevan building. So he soon found some ill-disciplined men who, under the pretext of some piety, wished to cover up that most unjust defection, and who judged that the common bread they had previously used in the Supper should be replaced by unleavened bread, no doubt so as to give new occasions for dissension. Nor would this plan have escaped Satan, had Calvin not seriously warned some good men, who were so offended by this change that they thought they ought to abstain from the Supper, not to stir up a quarrel over this indifferent matter [ἀδιάφορον]. Thus the use of unleavened bread prevailed. Calvin, when he was afterwards restored, never thought the matter worth contending over, though by no means concealing what he would otherwise have preferred. But behold, soon after, another, far more dangerous evil arose, in the year 1539, and was quenched by Calvin's diligence. At that time the Bishop of Carpentras, Jacopo Sadoleto, was a man of great eloquence, but he used it chiefly to suppress the light of truth. He had been admitted to the number of the Cardinals for no other reason than that, being otherwise a man of blameless life, he could lend colours to a false religion. Seizing the opportunity of that time, and judging that a flock deprived of such shepherds could easily be snatched away, and pretending also the nearness of his city (Carpentras belongs to Dauphiné, and Dauphiné in turn adjoins Savoy), he sent letters addressed to the most desired ones, as he called them, the Senate, Council and people of Geneva, in which he omitted nothing that might serve to recall them to the bosom of that harlot of Rome. At that time there was no one at Geneva who would reply or oppose him. So much so that, had his letters not been written in a foreign language, they would seem to have done great harm to the city in such a state of affairs.

units.la: M. D. XXXIX. cui etiam sequestrum proximè coiunguntur. gnum Ciuitati in eo rerum statu damnum daturæ fuisse videantur. At illa Caluinus Argentinæ quum legisset, omnium iniuriarum oblivius, sic statim & vere & eloquenter respondit, vt illemox totum illud negotium tanquam desperatum omiserit. Sed neque tamdiu expectauit Caluinus, vt legitimum illum pastoris affectum testaretur, quem aduersus Geneuenses ipsos tum apud suos gratissime pro communi pietatis causa laborantes retinebat: cuius demum affectus luculentum testimonium exhibent insignes epistolæ quas ad illos anno ipso quo reiectus est ac proxime consecuto Argentinæ dedit, quibus nimirum hoc unum agit, vt & ad resipiscentiam coram Deo, & ad toleran-tiam aduersus improbos, & ad pacem cum suis pastoribus fouendam, & ad Dei inuocationem imprimis exhortetur: atque ita illos comparat ad optatam illam lucem ex suis illis funestissimis tenebris iterum expectandam, vt etiam euentus mirifice comprobauit. Tum quoque Institutionem Christianam multo auctiorem, Commentarios in Epistolam ad Romanos Symoni Grynæo amicissimo suo dicatos, aureolum denique libellum edidit de Cœna Domini, in Gallorum suorum vsum, quem dein de latinum fecit Galasius: quod argumentum ita dextre simul ac erudite videtur explicasse, vt ea tot infœlicissimarum controuersiarum decisio in qua doctissimus ac optimus quisque merito acquieuit, illi potissimum secundum Deum accepta feratur. Nec minor fuit eius felicitas in multis in viam reuocandis Anabaptistis, inter quos duo præcipui fuerant, vnus Paulus Volsius, cui iam olim Erasmus suum illud Enchiridium militis Christiani dicauerat: quo pastore postea vsa est Argentinensis Ecclesia: Alter Ioannes quondam Storder Leodiensis, cuius postea pestę extin-cti viduam Idelletam nomine, grauem honestamque fœminam, Caluinus ex Buceri consilio vxorem duxit. Hæc tum Caluini studia fuerunt Argentinæ ad annum vsque M. D. XLI, quo anno fuerunt à Cæsare Vvormatiam primum, deinde Ratisbonam Comitia componendis Religionis dissidiis conuocata. Iis quod ita Theologorum Argentinensium collegio placuisset, Caluinus adfuit, minime quod constat Ecclesiis, ac suæ præfectum Galliæ inutilis, & Domino Philippo Melanchthoni, & Gasparo Crucigero beatæ memoriæ imprimis gratus, adeo vt eum ille sepe Theologum cognominarit, hic vero priuatum de Cœna cum eo colloquium habuerit, eiusque cognitam sententiam diserte coprobarit. Iam autem aduenerat illud tempus, quo constituerat Dominus Geneuensis Ecclesiæ miserteri. Itaque eorum Syndicorum vnus quorum opera factum fuerat decretum, vt fidi pastores eiiceretur, ita sese in Reipublicæ administratione gessit, vt seditionis teaus, dum per fenestram proripere se conatur, præceps ruens ut erat ingenti corporis mole,ita fcfe attribuerit,vt intra paucos dies ex illo casu sit extinctus. Alter homicidio perpetrato, capite multatus est. Reliqui duo malæ etiam administratæ in quadam legatione Reipublicæ accusati solum vererint,sintque absentes damnati.His veluti spumæ sordibus eiectis,Ciuitas Farellum suũ & Caluinum coepit requirere. Ac quum de Farello recuperando à Neocomensibus minimum spei affulgeret,enixè demũ in Caluinum intenta, Argentinam Legati adiuncta etiam Tigurinorũ intercessione mittuntur,qui ab Argentinensibus Caluinum repetant. Argentinenses præbent se difficiles. Caluinus ipse quanuis quæ improborum quorundam culpa sustinuerat,ipsius in Genevensis animum nihil immutassent,tamen à turbis abhorrens,& quòd Dominum videret ministerio suo in Argentinensi Ecclesia benedicere,plane se rediturum negare. Bucerus quoque & cæteri ægerrimè se illum dimisisse testati. Præstantibus tamen Genevensibus, censuit tandem Bucerus illorum precibus esse ad tempus concedendum:quodtamen à Caluino nonnisi interposita grauii diuini iudicij denuntiatione,& propositio Ionæ exemplo fuit impetratum. Sed quoniam in id tempus hæc inciderant,quo Caluino Ratisbonam ad Comitia(sic enim fuerat decretum)cum Bucero proficiscendum erat,dilata fuit eius discessio : & tamen per Bernensibus impetrarunt Genevenses,vt Petrus Viretus L aufanna Geneuam iret.Quò libentius in vrbem rediit Caluinus, cum videlicet habiturus collegam,cuius opera & consilio in instaurando Ecclesia plurimum adiuuari posset.Sic aliquot menses præcepto riere.quibus tandem elapsis Caluinus x i i i.Septembris Anno Domini M.D.XLI.Geneuam regressus est,summa cum vniuersi populi,ac Senatus imprimis singulare Dei erga se beneficiũ serio tũ agnoscentis congratulatione : vt Argentinenses vrgere nunquã destiterit,vt quod de certo illo temporis spatio cautum fuerat,ex pungeretur. Concesserunt id quoque tandem Argentinenses, ea tamen conditione vt ius ciuitatis honorarium quod in Caluinũ contulerant,saluum esset,& prebendæ quam vocant annuos reditus retineret. Quorum illud probauit Caluinus, siluerunt vero vt acciperet nunquam ab eo extorqueri potuit, vt qui nihil minus quàm opes curaret. Restitutus autem Ecclesiæ suæ flagitantì Caluinus,hanc in illius instauratione rationem tenuit,vt quoḋ eam vrbem videret omnino his frænis indigere, testaretur imprimis, se non posse ministerio suo rite fungi,nisi vnà cũ doctrina Christiana,Presbyterium quoque legitimũ cum ευταξία Ecclesiastica reciperetur.Tum igitur(qua de re mox plenius dicemus)& Presbyterorum deligendorum,& totius illius ordinis legees prelatæ sunt verbo Dei consentaneæ,& ciuibus ipsis gratiæ, quas postea miris modis Satan abrogare fustra est conatus.Scripsit quoque Catechismum Gallicè & Latinè,ab illo priore minimè discrepā-tem,sed multò auctiore,& in quæstiones ac responsiones distri-butum : quem merito nobis liceat admirandum quoddam opus vocare,tantopere plurimis etiam exteris populis probatū,vt non modò vernaculis plurimis linguis, vt pote Germanica, Anglica, Scotica,Belgica,Hispanica,sed etiáHebraicè ab Immanuele Tre-melio Iudeo Christiano, & Græcè ab Hérico Stephano legatur e-legātissimè conuersus. Qui deinceps fuerint ordinarii eius labo-res,ex reipsa diiudicari potest. Alternis hebdomadibus totis con-cionabatur,triduo vero docebat:singulis diebus Iouis Presbyteri] cognitionem regebat, diebus Veneris in communi collatione Scripturæ,quem Congregatione vocamus, iustam penè lestionē habebat:varios sacros libros doctissimis Commétariis illustrabat, modò Religionis hostibus respondebat, modò necessariis de re-bus vndiquēque scribebat. Quæ quisquis attentè legerit, mirabi-tur tot tantisque laboribus vnicū homunculum sufficere potuis-se. Vtebatur autem plurimùm Farello & Vireto, quibus tamen ipse multò plus conferebat. Sed eorum amicitia & coniunctionē non minus improbis inuisa,quàm piis omnibus iucunda mira-biliter delectabatur. Et sanè iucundissimum erat spectaculum,tres istos tantos in Ecclesia Dei viros vsque adeò in opere diuino consentientes, eósque diuersis donis florentes cernere & audire. Excellebat quadam animi magnitudine Farellus,cuius vel audire absq; tremore tonitrura,vel ardentissimas preces percipere nemo posset,quin in ipsum penè cœlū subuehi peretur. Viretus facundiæ suauitate sic excellebat, vt auditores ab ipsius ore necessariò pen-derent. Caluinus quot sonabat verba,tot grauissimis sententiis au-ditoris mentem explebat:vt sæpe mihi in mentem venerit,perse-ctum quodammodo videri posse pastorem,qui ex tribus illis esset conflatus. Vt ad Caluinum redeā,nō his modò curis,sed domesti-cis etiam externisq; aliis multis exercebatur. Sic enim Dominus benedicebat eius Ministerio,vt ex omnibus orbis Christiani par-tibus,partim eius consilium in causa Religionis effagitarēt,par-tim ad eum audiendum concurrent: adeò vt Italicam, Anglicā, Hispanicam denique Ecclesiam Geneuæ viderimus,neque tot ca-piendis hospitibus sufficere posse vna ciuitas videretur. Domi ve-rò etsi à bonis colebatur, ab improbis metuebatur,& optimè res erant constitutæ,non deerat tamen qui strenuè illum exerceret. Quæ certamina sigillatim explicabimus,vt habeát posteri singu-lare fortitudinis exemplum , quod pro viribus imitentur. Igitur vt ad historiam redeamus,simulatque in vrbem rediit, memor illius Sententiæ: Quærendum esse primùm regnum Dei, vt cæ-tera adiiciantur , nihil habuit antiquius , quàm vt Ecclesiasticæ politiæ legesverbo Dei consentaneæ Senatus consensu prescriberentur:à quibus postea discedere, neque Ministris ipsis neque ciuibus liceret. Id vero adeo ante probatum, nonnullis sensim ex vulgo, atque ex primariis ciuibus qui Papam quidem exuerât, Christum vero nomine tenus induerant, odiosum fuit. Nonnulli quoque ex iis Ministris, qui bonis illis eiectisi, vrbe mansferant (quorum tamen praecipui postea flagitiorum rei turpiter stationem deseruerant) etsi testimonio conscientiae conuicti repugnare non audebant, clanculum tamen obsisteb̃ant, sequeque in ordinem cogi non facile patiebantur. Neque vero deerat quod huic suae improbitati praetexerent, aliarum videlicet Ecclesiarum exemplum, in quibus nullus esset excommunicationi locus. Nō deerant denique qui Papisticam tyrannidem sic reuocari clamitarent. Sed has difficultates vicit Caluini constantia, cum insigni moderatione coniuncta: qui quum ex sacris literis non doctrinae modo, verum etiam administrationis Ecclesiasticae petendā esse rationem demonstraret, & doctissimorum eius seculi hominū, veluti OEcolāpadij, Zuinglij, Zuichij, Philippi, Buceri, Capitonis, Myconij sententiam ex ipsorū scriptis ostendisset, nec propterea damnari Ecclesias ipsas tanquam non Christianas, quae eovsque nondum promouissent, vel eos pastores qui suos greges eo fraeno non indigere exististimarent, denique demonstraret quantum inter papisticam tyrannidem & iugum Domini interesset, abstinuit facile, vt Ecclesiasticae politiae leges quibus etiamnum vtitur hęc Ecclesia, summo consensu conscriptae, perlectae, populique suffragiis probatae 20.Nouemb.recipererentur. Haec etsi foeliciter erant coepta, tamen quum non sine difficultate reipsa vsurpari posse considerarett Caluinus, totus in eo erat, vt & Viretum, quem ad tempus duntaxat aliquod concesserant Bernenses, & Farellum, quem Neocomenses eiectum excepterat, Collegas perpetuo habere; sed hoc frustra tentauit, Viretro mox Laufanna reuersō, Farello vero Neocomi permanente, vt restitutae huius Ecclesiae laude pene solus reportaret. Anno sequente Caluinū non pauca exercuerunt, vt enim quae domi vrgebat praeteream, instabat tum foris etiam inflammatus hostium Euangelii furor, multos ex Gallia, & Italia in vicinam & celebris iam nominis vrbem extrudens: quibus consolandis omnisque officij genere reficiendis, mirum quato studio sese iam tum impederit: vt eos omittā quos in ipsis leonū faucibus versantes, vndiquaque missis literis solabatur. Ac cessit eo anno duplex aliud maximū malū, annonae videlicet caritas, & pestis plerūque illius comes.
