Erat autē hęc iam tum Geneuae consuetudo, vt pestē laborātes suum extra vrbem Niofocomiū haberent: vbi quum pastoris constatis ac seduli operā requirereretur, plerisque contagionis periculū deterētatibus, tres ilfe obtulerūt, Caluinus videlicet, Sebastianus Castellio (de quo postea plura dictu)
units.tr: M. D. XXXIX. These also are closely joined with the sequestration, and they would seem to have caused great damage to the city in that state of affairs. But when Calvin read those letters at Strasbourg, forgetting all the injuries, he replied at once so truthfully and eloquently that the Genevans promptly abandoned the whole affair as hopeless. Nor did Calvin wait long to show that genuine pastoral affection which he kept, very pleasingly, toward the Genevans themselves, who were then labouring in their own cause for the common good of piety. The clearest evidence of this affection is found in the notable letters he sent to them in Strasbourg in the very year of his expulsion and the year after. Their sole aim is to urge them to repentance before God, to endurance against the wicked, to keeping peace with their own ministers, and above all to calling upon God; and in this way he prepared them to look again for that longed-for light out of their own most wretched darkness, as the outcome also wonderfully confirmed. At that time he also published the Christian Institutes, greatly enlarged, his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans dedicated to his very dear friend Symphorien Grynaeus, and finally a little golden book on the Lord's Supper, written for the use of his fellow Frenchmen, which Galasius afterwards turned into Latin. He seems to have explained this subject so skilfully and learnedly that the settling of so many unhappy controversies, in which every learned and good man has rightly acquiesced, may be credited chiefly to him, under God. His success was no less in bringing many Anabaptists back to the right way. Among them two were outstanding: one was Paul Volz, to whom Erasmus had long ago dedicated his Enchiridion of the Christian Soldier, and under whom the Church of Strasbourg afterwards made use of a pastor; the other was John Storder, once of Liège, whose widow, Idelette by name, a grave and respectable woman, Calvin married on Bucer's advice after the man's death by plague. These were Calvin's occupations at Strasbourg until the year 1541, in which the Emperor summoned first to Worms and then to Regensburg an assembly to settle the disputes over religion. Calvin attended there, as the college of Strasbourg theologians had decided: he was not at all useless to the Churches, and he was particularly dear to the late Philip Melanchthon and to Gaspar Cruciger of blessed memory, so much so that Melanchthon often called him "the Theologian," while Cruciger had a private conversation with him about the Supper and openly approved the opinion he knew. But by now the time had come when the Lord had decided to show mercy to the Church of Geneva. So one of the syndics, through whose efforts the decree had been passed to expel the faithful ministers, conducted himself in the government of the republic in such a way that, as a seditious man, he tried to escape through a window, and fell headlong; being of enormous bulk, he so injured himself that within a few days he died from that fall. Another was executed for committing murder. The remaining two, accused of mismanagement in a certain embassy of the republic, only fled and were condemned in their absence. With these dregs, like scum, thrown out, the city began to seek back its Farel and its Calvin. When there was little hope of recovering Farel from the people of Neuchâtel, the city turned earnestly to Calvin, and envoys were sent to Strasbourg, with the Zurichers also interceding, to demand Calvin back from the Strasbourgers. The Strasbourgers showed themselves difficult. Calvin himself, although the wrongs he had suffered at the hands of certain wicked men had not changed his feelings toward the Genevans, nevertheless shrank from the turmoil and, seeing that the Lord was blessing his ministry in the Church of Strasbourg, flatly refused to return. Bucer and the others also declared that they had let him go most reluctantly. Yet, since the Genevans pressed hard, Bucer at last thought he should be given up to them for a time, though Calvin agreed only after a grave warning of God's judgment had been announced and the example of Jonah set before him. But because these events fell at the time when Calvin was to set out with Bucer for Regensburg (for that was the decision), his departure was delayed. Still, the Genevans obtained from the Bernese that Peter Viret should go from Lausanne to Geneva. Calvin returned to the city all the more gladly, since he would have a colleague whose work and counsel could greatly help him in restoring the Church. So several months passed in this way, and when they had run out, Calvin returned to Geneva on the 13th of September, in the year of the Lord 1541, to the great rejoicing of the whole people and especially of the Senate, which truly acknowledged this as a singular benefit of God toward them. The Strasbourgers never ceased to press that the arrangement made about that fixed period of time should be cancelled. At last they also agreed, on this condition: that the honorary citizenship they had conferred on Calvin should remain intact, and that he should keep the prebend, as they call it, with its yearly income. Calvin approved the first point, but as to accepting the second, they could never extract that from him, since he cared nothing for wealth. Once restored to his Church, which demanded him, Calvin adopted this plan in restoring it: because he saw that the city utterly needed these bridles, he first declared that he could not discharge his ministry properly unless, along with Christian doctrine, a lawful presbytery and ecclesiastical order [εὐταξία] were also received. Then, as we shall explain more fully below, both the appointment of elders and the whole system of that order were laid down, in accordance with the Word of God, and granted to the citizens themselves as privileges, privileges which Satan later tried in vain to abolish by wondrous means. He also wrote a Catechism in French and Latin, not differing at all from his earlier one but much enlarged and arranged in questions and answers. We may fairly call it a remarkable work, approved so greatly by very many foreign peoples that it is read not only in many vernacular tongues, such as German, English, Scottish, Flemish, and Spanish, but also in Hebrew, translated most elegantly by Immanuel Tremellius, a Jewish Christian, and in Greek by Henri Estienne. What his continuing labours were may be judged from the facts themselves. Every other week he preached the whole week through, and on the third day he taught; on each Thursday he presided over the examination of the elders; on Fridays, at the common gathering for the study of Scripture, which we call the Congregation, he gave an almost complete lecture; he illuminated various sacred books with most learned commentaries; at one time he answered the enemies of religion, at another he wrote on necessary matters from every quarter. Anyone who reads these attentively will marvel that one little man could suffice for such great and numerous labours. He relied most on Farel and Viret, yet he himself contributed far more to them. Their friendship and partnership, hated by the wicked no less than enjoyed by all the godly, gave him wonderful delight. Indeed it was a most pleasant spectacle to see and hear those three great men in the Church of God so much in agreement in the divine work, and flourishing with such different gifts. Farel excelled in a certain greatness of spirit: no one could hear his thunder without trembling, or receive his most ardent prayers without feeling almost lifted up to heaven itself. Viret excelled in the sweetness of his eloquence, so that his hearers necessarily hung upon his lips. Calvin filled the mind of his hearer with the weightiest sentences, as many as the words he uttered; so that I have often thought a pastor could be seen to be, in some sense, made up of those three. But to return to Calvin: he was occupied not only with these cares but also with many domestic and foreign concerns. For the Lord so blessed his ministry that from every part of the Christian world some sought his counsel on matters of religion, and others came to hear him; so much so that we saw an Italian, an English, and even a Spanish Church at Geneva, and it seemed that no single city could hold so many guests. At home, indeed, although he was cherished by the good and feared by the wicked, and although affairs were very well ordered, there was no lack of people who vigorously harassed him. We shall explain these struggles one by one, so that posterity may have a singular example of courage, which they may imitate as far as they are able. So, to return to the story: as soon as he came back to the city, mindful of the saying that the kingdom of God must be sought first and the rest added to it, he had no more important aim than to have the laws of ecclesiastical polity, agreeable to the Word of God, prescribed with the consent of the Senate; and that neither the ministers themselves nor the citizens should be allowed to depart from them afterwards. This was so plainly approved beforehand that it was hateful to some of the common people, and to some of the leading citizens who had indeed cast off the Pope but had only put on Christ in name. Some of those ministers, too, who had remained in the city after the good men were expelled (though the chief of them later, guilty of shameful crimes, had disgracefully abandoned their post), although they dared not resist, convicted by the testimony of their own conscience, nevertheless secretly opposed it and did not readily suffer themselves to be brought into order. Nor were they lacking in pretexts for this wickedness, namely the example of other Churches in which there was no place for excommunication. Finally, there were those who cried out that this would restore Papist tyranny. But Calvin's steadfastness, joined with remarkable moderation, overcame these difficulties. For he showed from the Holy Scriptures that the rule must be sought not only for doctrine but also for the administration of the Church, and he displayed, from their own writings, the opinions of the most learned men of that age, such as Oecolampadius, Zwingli, Zwick, Philip Melanchthon, Bucer, Capito, and Myconius. He also showed that the Churches themselves were not to be condemned as non-Christian because they had not yet advanced so far, nor the pastors who thought their flocks did not need that bridle. In short, he demonstrated how great was the difference between Papist tyranny and the yoke of the Lord. Thus he easily secured that the laws of ecclesiastical polity, which this Church still uses, written with the greatest agreement, read out, and approved by the votes of the people, should be received on 20 November. Although these matters had begun happily, Calvin considered that they could not be put into practice without difficulty, and he was wholly intent on keeping as permanent colleagues both Viret, whom the Bernese had allowed to be lent for only a time, and Farel, whom the people of Neuchâtel had expelled and taken in. But this he attempted in vain: Viret soon returned to Lausanne, and Farel remained at Neuchâtel, so that Calvin almost alone won the credit for restoring this Church. In the following year many things troubled Calvin. I pass over what pressed him at home; abroad too the enemies of the Gospel raged with inflamed fury, driving many out of France and Italy into this neighbouring city, already famous. To console them and to restore them by every kind of service, he showed incredible zeal, not to mention those whom he comforted by letters sent from all sides while they were in the very jaws of lions. In that year there also came another double great evil: dearth of grain, and the plague which usually accompanied it. It was already the custom at Geneva that those suffering from the plague should have their own hospital outside the city. When the work of a faithful and diligent pastor was needed there, and most people shrank from the danger of infection, three offered themselves: Calvin, Sebastian Castellio (of whom more will be said later), and a certain Peter Blanchet. By lot, Castellio, to whom the lot had fallen, nevertheless changed his mind and shamelessly refused to undertake the burden; Calvin, against the wishes of the Senate, and Blanchet himself, taking this burden upon himself…

units.la: { } Vide: Sebastianus Castellio. ra diduri fumus (& Petrus quidam Blachetus: inter quos fortitio- ne facta, quum Castellio cui fors obtigerat, mutata nihilominus sententia subire hoc onus impudenter detrectaret. Caluinū inuitū Senatu, ipsequeadeo Blanchetus hoc onus in se recipiens ampliu̇s sortiti prohibuerunt. Tum quoque alia grauia inciderunt. Nā & Petrum Toffanum Monsbelgardensem Pastore exercebat controuersia de Cœna domini, & Basilex quoque non deerant qui Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ vix iacta fundamenta, frustra in contrarium laborante Myconio subruerent, qui duo consilia cum Caluino conferebā. Apud Mediomatricēs autem siue Metensēs etsi Farellus eo euocatus feliciter laborabat, opus tamē Domini partim per Apostatam P. Caroli cuius antea meminimus, valde impediebatur. Quibus in rebus quantum scribendo, monendo, hortando modis omnibus denique laborarit Caluinus, partim ex eius editis literis intelligi potest, partim vero qui sunt adhuc superstites testificantur. Sed & audaciorquām vnquam antea Sorbona P. Lifeti rum in Parlamento Parisiensi principis infaustæ infœlicisque memoriæ hominis fauore, ausa fuit facinus, quod mirum videri posset Episcopos, autipsum saltem Pontificē pati potuisse, nisi iampridem Ecclesiarū opibus inter se vt inter præ- dones fieri solet, dispertiendis occupati, suo præcipuo munere quod in administratione verbi posset esse vltrò bonis istis quos vocat, doctoribus cessissent: ea iamē cōditione, vt tanquā canes dominis suis illis subseruiāt, ex quorum mensis ossa tandē millies abligurita corrodūt. Ausa fuerat igitur Sorbona, nullo neq; diuino neq; humano iure fulta, fidei Christianæ articulos prescri bere, eiusmodi quidē, vt tum sua falsitate, tum illis summis ineptiis quæ sunt illi sodalitati familiares, omne sibi ipsis auctoritatem apud homines nō prorsus amentes merito derogare potuerint: quibus tamen alij metu, alij per imperitiā vltrò subscripserāt. Itaq; refpōdit iis Caluinus, ira vt& errores solidis rationibus praerudite refutaret, & eorundē stultitiā omnibus non penitus insulsis suauiter deridendā propinaret. Sic est annus ille exactus quem alius nihilo mitior excepit, iisdem malis caritate videlicet ac peste Sabaudiā infestantibus; & pergente vicissim Caluino domi quidem suos confirmare, foris vero Ecclesiarū hostes fortiter reprimere, editis præsertim libris quatuor de liberi arbitrij controuersia quos Philippo Melanchthoni dicauit, aduersus Albertum Pighium Campensem, sophistā illius ætatis facile principē, à quo etiā fuerat pro Antagonista delectus, ex quo videlicet reportata insigni victoria, galerum mox à Pontifice consequeretur. At ille hoc suo labore frustratus, id vnū assequutus est quod merentur veritatis hostes, nempe vt & doctis sanisque hominibus foeteret, & ab ipso Sathana deciperetur. Eos autem libro quàti facerèt testatus est suis literis Philippus,quas idcirco etiam edendas putauimus, vt habeat posteritas certum lucidentúmque testimonium,quod aduersus vtriusque calumniatorꝰs opponat. Sed & ex eiusdem Caluini literis eodé anno Ecclesiæ Monsbelgardensi scriptis,quid fit iis respondendum quibus cognoscet,qui de nimia ipsius seueritate in exercedis Ecclesiasticæ politiæ legibus querútur. Sequutus est annus supra sesquimillefimũ quadragesimus quartus, in quo Caluinus de Neocomensiũ ĩ Ecclesiasticis censuris instituto suam sententiã aperuit. Domi vero Sebastianus ille Castellio,cuius antea leuitatem notauimus vt erat quadam ταπεινοφροσυνης specie ineptissime ambitiosus,ac plane ex eorũ genere quos græci ιδιοτυφους apellant, indignatus quod suas ineptias in Gallica Noui Testamenti versione Caluino nõ probasset,eousque effebuit,vt exotica quædam doctrinã non contentus, palàm etiam Canticum Solomonis tanquam mpuram & obscœnam cantionem ex Canone expungi iuberet,& repugnates Ministros atrocissimis conuiciis proscinderet. Id illi vero sibi non ferendũ merito rati,hominem ad Senatum vocant: vbi pridie Cal.Iunij patientissime auditus, cognitaque causa calumniæ damnatus,ex vrbe excedere iussus est.Inde Basileam quum venisset,tandem ibi admissus,qualem se præstiterit,alibi à nobis dicetur.Ceterũ anno superiore quum Carolus quintus aduersus Gallũ totis viribus mouens Germanissic cauisset,vt tantisper dum Concilium vniuersale cogeretur,sese curaturum promittebat, neutri partium præiudicio facto inter quas de Religione disceptabatur, vtrinque pari inter se iure vterentur:plurimum ea re commotus Pontifex Romanus Paulus III i,grauissimam in ipsum Cæsarem expostulationem edidit, quòd Catholicis hæreticoscilicet exaquasset,& in alienam messem intecifse falcem videretur.Respondit Cæsar quod æquum censuit.Caluinus autem,quòd in iis literis grauiter læsa erat Euangelij veritas piorumq; innocentia, Pontificis audaciam repressit,Fuerunt tum Spiræ coacta imperij Comitia: qua accepta occasione Caluinus libellum edidit de Necessitate reformandæ Ecclesiæ,quo haud satis scio an aut meruosius, aut grauius eius argumenti scriptum nostro seculo editũ fuerit.Eodem anno Caluinus tum Anabaptistas tum Libertinos (in quibus veteres omnes quantumuis portentosæ renouatæ sunt hæreses)duobus libellis itã refutauit, vt neminem iis attente lectis arbitrer extitisse,qui vel ab istis nisi sciens & prudens decipi potuerit,vel si antea deceptus erat,non vlterius in rectam viam redierit, offensa tamen isto libro in Libertinos edito Nauarrena, quòd ab illius horrendæ sectæ Antesignanis duobus Quintino & Poscqueto quos nominatim Caluinus arguerat (rem pene incredibilem) eo vsque fuisset fascinata, vt quum alioqui illorum mysterium non tenerer,
units.tr: {} See: Sebastian Castellio. ...we were chosen, and Peter Blanchet with us. By lot, when Castellio, to whom the lot had fallen, changed his mind and shamelessly refused to take on this burden, Calvin being unwilling, the Senate and Blanchet himself undertaking the burden, they forbade any further casting of lots. Other grave matters also arose. Peter Toffanus, minister at Montbéliard, was troubled by a controversy about the Lord's Supper. At Basel too there were men who, while Myconius laboured in vain on the other side, undermined the barely laid foundations of church discipline; Myconius was conferring with Calvin on these two matters. At Metz, the Mediomatrici, Farel, though summoned there, was working successfully, but the work of the Lord was greatly hindered, partly by the apostate Peter Charles, whom we mentioned earlier. How much Calvin laboured in these matters by writing, admonishing and exhorting in every way may be understood partly from his published letters, and is partly attested by those still living. But the Sorbonne, with the favour of Peter Lizet, president of the Parlement of Paris, a man of unhappy and ill-starred memory, dared a deed more audacious than any before. It might seem remarkable that the bishops, or at least the Pope himself, could have tolerated it, had they not long since been busy dividing up the revenues of the churches among themselves, as robbers usually do, and had they not surrendered their chief office, the ministry of the Word, to those so-called good men, the teachers, on the condition that, like dogs serving their masters, they gnaw the bones from their tables, licked a thousand times. The Sorbonne, supported by no divine or human law, had therefore dared to prescribe articles of the Christian faith. They were of such a kind that, by their falsehood and by those supreme absurdities which are familiar to that fraternity, they deservedly stripped themselves of all authority among men who were not utterly mad. Yet others subscribed to them of their own accord, some from fear, some from ignorance. So Calvin answered them, both refuting their errors skilfully with solid arguments, and offering their folly for gentle mockery to all who were not wholly without wit. Thus that year passed, and another, no milder, followed, with the same evils, famine and plague, afflicting Savoy. Calvin, continuing meanwhile to strengthen his own people at home and to repress vigorously the enemies of the churches abroad, published above all four books on the controversy about free will, which he dedicated to Philip Melanchthon, against Albert Pighius of Kampen, the easily foremost sophist of that age, by whom he had himself been chosen as opponent. From this, that is, from which Pighius, having won a notable victory, would soon receive a cardinal's hat from the Pope. But Pighius, frustrated by this labour, achieved only what the enemies of truth deserve: he became a stench to learned and sound men, and was deceived by Satan himself. Philip testified in his letters how highly he valued those books, and we have thought these letters should be published too, so that posterity may have a certain and clear testimony to set against the calumniators of both. Also, from Calvin's letters written that same year to the church at Montbéliard, one may learn what should be answered to those who complain of his excessive severity in enforcing the laws of ecclesiastical polity. There followed the year 1544, in which Calvin set out his opinion on the institution of ecclesiastical censures among the people of Neuchâtel. At home, that Sebastian Castellio, whose lightness we noted earlier, was, under a certain show of humility [ταπεινοφροσύνη], most absurdly ambitious, and entirely of the kind the Greeks call self-conceited [ἰδιότυφοι]. Indignant that Calvin had not approved his absurdities in the French version of the New Testament, he was so inflamed that, not content with a strange doctrine, he openly ordered the Song of Solomon struck from the canon as an impure and obscene song, and tore to pieces the ministers who opposed him with the most savage abuse. The authorities, rightly judging that this could not be tolerated, summoned the man before the Senate. There, on 31 May, he was heard most patiently, the case was examined, he was condemned for calumny, and he was ordered to leave the city. When he came to Basel and was at last admitted there, what sort of man he showed himself to be will be told by us elsewhere. But in the previous year, when Charles V, moving with all his forces against France, had secured Germany by promising that, while a general council was being convened, he would see to it that neither party in the dispute about religion was prejudiced, and that both would enjoy equal right, the Roman Pope Paul III, greatly moved by this, issued a most severe complaint against Caesar himself, because he seemed to have made heretics equal to Catholics and to have put his sickle into another's harvest. Caesar replied as he thought fair. Calvin, however, because the truth of the Gospel and the innocence of the godly had been gravely injured in those letters, checked the Pope's audacity. At that time an imperial diet was held at Speyer. Seizing the occasion, Calvin published his book On the Necessity of Reforming the Church, and I scarcely know whether a more admirable or weightier work on this subject has been published in our century. In the same year Calvin refuted both the Anabaptists and the Libertines (among whom all the ancient heresies, however monstrous, have been revived) in two books, so effectively that I think no one who read them attentively could have been deceived by them unless knowingly and wilfully, or, if he had been deceived before, could fail to return to the right path. Yet the Queen of Navarre was offended by this book against the Libertines, because she had been so bewitched by two leaders of that dreadful sect, Quintin and Poquet, whom Calvin had named and refuted (an almost incredible thing), that, although she did not otherwise understand their mystery, she regarded them as good men, and so felt herself, as it were, pierced through the side by them.

units.la: M. D. XLIIII. ten eret, pro bonis viris illos haberet, ac proinde sese quodámo-do per eorum latus confossam arbitraretur. Quod quum intel-lexisset Caluinus, sic illi mira quadam moderatione respondit, vt & dignitatis, & collatorum ab hac Regina in Ecclesiam Christi beneficiorum memor, ingenue tamen & cordate vt fortem Dei seruum oportuit, nimiam illius in admittendis istiusmodi hominibus imprudetiam reprehenderit, & ministerij sui auctoritate asseruerit: effecerit denique vt horrendæ Libertinorū sectæ homines, qui in Gallia vsque sese effundere coeperat, postea sese intra Hollandiæ & proximarum regionum fines continuerint. Tot autem illius anni laboribus defunctum, noua rursum certamina sequentis anni eaque longe grauissima exceperunt. Nam quasi pestis diuinitus immissa exhauriendæ ciuitati totíque vicinIæ non sufficeret, vsque adeo apud pauperculos nonnullos auariá tum valuit, quorum opera ditiores in curadis ægrotis ac repurgandis ædibus vterentur, vt & horrenda coniuratione pestifero vnguine domorum postes ac limina atque alia quæuis obuia inficerent, vnde mox dira pestis sequebatur, & horrendo iureiurando solenniter cóepto inter se Satanæ se manciparent, si scelcris conscios vllis tormentis adacti prodidissent. Non pauci tamen partim in vrbe, partim in vicinis regionibus deprehensi, iustisque suppliciis sant affecti. Sed incredibile dictu est, quantam Geneuæ & ipsi imprimis Caluino inuidiam Satan hoc artificio conflarit, quasi scilicet ibi plane ille regnaret, vbi quàm maximè oppugnabatur. Fuit hic idem annus infamis illa plusquam immani carnificina, quam Aquenfe Parlamentum in fratres Vvaldenses Merindolæ, & Cabrieris, totóque illo tractu, non in vnum aut alterum quempiam, sed in populos ipsos nullo nec ætatis, nec sexus discrimine incensis etiam vicis exercuit. Hæc autem mala Caluinum refugientes Geneuam pauculos solante ac reficientem ea vehementius premebant, quod eosantea literis, summi isfq; pastoribus pure in Euangelio instituendos curarat, suaque apud Germaniæ Principes & Helueticas ciuitates intercessione periclitates antea seruarat. Glisc bat tum quoque rursum infoelix illa de Cæna Domini decertatio, Osiandro homine superbo monstrosique ingenij sopitam flammam fodiente: quod incendium quominus suppetur, per Caluinum certe non stetit, cuius ea de re ad Philippum vnam & alteram Epistolam edendam curauimus. Sed vtriusque sanis consiliis nullum locum tribuit eius hominis intemperies, quem vterque Periclem vocat. Interea pestis in vrbe defeuiés multos bonos tollebat. Caluinus autem ex suggestu in nonnullorū flagitia, ac præsertim aduersus scortationes quæ ne tum quidé desinere poterat, pro viribus detonabat, bonis quidem adsentientibus, sed paucis quibusdam
units.tr: M. D. XLIIII. When Calvin learned of this, he replied to her with a remarkable moderation: mindful both of her rank and of the benefits this Queen had conferred on the Church of Christ, yet frank and bold as a brave servant of God ought to be, he rebuked her excessive imprudence in admitting such men, and he asserted the authority of his ministry. In short, he brought it about that the men of the dreadful Libertine sect, who had begun to spread even through France, afterwards kept themselves within the borders of Holland and the neighbouring regions. Having got through so many labours that year, he was received again by new struggles in the following year, and far more grievous ones. For, as if a plague sent by God to drain the city and the whole neighbourhood were not enough, greed prevailed so much among some poor folk, whose services the wealthier used in tending the sick and cleaning houses, that in a dreadful conspiracy they smeared the doorposts, thresholds and whatever else lay in their way with a pestilential ointment, whence a dire plague soon followed. Having solemnly begun a dreadful oath among themselves, they handed themselves over to Satan, if, driven by any torture, they should betray their accomplices in the crime. Yet not a few, caught partly in the city and partly in the neighbouring regions, were punished with just penalties. But it is incredible to say how much hatred Satan kindled by this device against Geneva and especially against Calvin himself, as if of course he reigned there completely, where he was most assailed. This same year was also marked by that infamous, more than savage butchery which the Parlement of Aix carried out against the Waldensian brothers at Mérindol and Cabrières and throughout that whole district. It was not against one or two persons, but against whole peoples, without distinction of age or sex, and the villages were set on fire. These evils pressed upon the fugitives who had taken refuge in Geneva, and weighed all the more heavily on Calvin, who was comforting and restoring the few; for he had earlier taken care, by letters, that they should be purely instructed in the Gospel by excellent ministers, and had previously saved them, when they were in danger, by his intercession with the princes of Germany and the cities of Switzerland. At that time also that unhappy dispute about the Lord's Supper blazed up again, as Osiander, a proud man of monstrous intellect, stirred up the smouldering flame. That the fire should not be put out was certainly not Calvin's fault, and on this matter we have published one or two of his letters to Philip. But the intemperance of that man, whom both call Pericles, gave no room to the sound counsels of either. Meanwhile the plague raging in the city carried off many good people. Calvin, from the pulpit, thundered as far as he could against the crimes of some, and especially against fornication, which even then could not be stopped, with good men approving, but with a few others...

units.la: M. D. XLV. Σχισματικὸς bonorū conatus infringentibus, donec ipsi sese vi-trò sicuti suo loco dicetur, præcipites dederunt. Accedebat deni-que ad hæc mala, ᵹ tum quoque non deesse nt parum illæ quidē tempestiuæ de iure Ciuitatis disceptationes: nec pati possent a-liunde fideles pastores Ecclesiastica bona pontificiis erepta non sic vt oportuit plerisque locis administrari: Multi tunc clamo-res, multæ querelæ, multi denique scribendo ac loquendo labo-res, sed frustra plerunque suscepti: aperte quidem profitentes Cal-uino, fe quidem tot sacrilegiis minime fuere, quæ diuinitus tan-dem sciret seuerissime vindicanda, sed in eo tamen iustum Dei iudicium agnoscere, quod bona tam male prius à sacrificis ac-quisita, non sineret Dominus Ecclesiarum ærariis inferri. Alia præterea duplex solicitudo Caluinū eodem hoc anno domi si-mul & foris exercuit. Redierat tum Geneuam patriam suam ve-terator quidam quanuis adhuc inuenis, postquam aliquādiu E-remitam in Galliis simulasset. Eum pietatis speciem initio præ se ferentem Caluinus (homo si quisquam alius in deprehenden-dis aliorum ingeniis sagacis solertisque iudicij) quū mox agno-uisset, admonere primum ac mox liberius etiam, postea ambi-tiosè nimium in congregationis cœtu sese efferentem increpa-re cœpit. Hoc ille non ferens, reperit facile ex iis in quorum fce lera inuehi solitus erat Caluinus, quorum fauore & studio adiu-uaretur: adeo vt quum forte ageretur de pastore in mortui locū subrogando, palàm ille cum suis factum Ministerium ambiret. quid multis? interposita sua auctoritate iubet Senatus istius ra-tionem haberi. Obstitit cum suis collegis Caluinus, & quamtope te hic ambitus verbo Dei repugnaret, offenditque obstinuitque bo-na cum Senatus venia, vt scriptis Ecclesiasticis legibus statuetur. Erant tunc quoque in Galliis nonnulli qui persecutionum metu initio lapsi, eoque postea sibi placere cœperant, vt eos negaret peccare, qui in veram Religionē intenti, corpore duntaxat Pontificiis sacris interesse nt. Hunc igitur perniciosissimum errorem iam olim à patribus damnatum, Caluinus cuius illi fceueritatem nimiam esse causabantur, & scripto luculento refutauit, & adiunctis doctissimorum Theologorum Philippi Melanchthonis, Buceri, P. Martyris, & Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ sententiis ita coërcuit, vt ab eo tempore piis omnibus fœtuerit Nicodemitarū nomen: Ita enim illi vocabantur, qui errori suo sanctissimi viri illius exemplum prætexerent. Huc annum alius nihilo mitior excepit.
units.tr: M. D. XLV. Schismatics [Σχισματικὸς] thwarted the efforts of good men, until they themselves, as will be told in its place, rushed headlong to their ruin. To these evils was added the fact that at that time there were not lacking disputes about the rights of the city, rather ill-timed ones to be sure. Faithful ministers could not bear that church property taken from the Papists was, in many places, not administered as it should have been. There were then many outcries, many complaints, and in the end much labour in writing and speaking, though for the most part it was undertaken in vain. They openly declared to Calvin that they were by no means ignorant that so many sacrileges would at last be avenged by God most severely; but in this they acknowledged God's just judgment, that the Lord would not allow goods so wrongly acquired earlier by the sacrificers to be carried into the church treasuries. Another twofold anxiety exercised Calvin in this same year, at home and abroad. A certain old hand, though still young, had returned to Geneva, his homeland, after for some time feigning to be a hermit in France. At first he put on an appearance of piety. Calvin, a man as shrewd and keen of judgment as any in detecting the talents of others, soon recognised him. He began first to admonish him, then more freely, and finally to rebuke him when he made himself too ambitiously prominent in the assembly of the congregation. Unable to bear this, he easily found, among those whose crimes Calvin was accustomed to inveigh against, men whose favour and zeal would aid him. So it happened that, when by chance it was being discussed to appoint a minister in the place of one who had died, he openly sought the ministry for himself, together with his supporters. To make a long story short, by using his own authority he ordered the Senate to take account of him. Calvin resisted with his colleagues, and objected, as far as he could, how contrary such ambition was to the Word of God; he stood firm, with due respect to the Senate, that the matter should be settled by written ecclesiastical laws. In France at that time there were also some who, lapsing at first through fear of persecution, afterwards came to please themselves, so that they denied that those sinned who, while intent on the true religion, only attended Papist rites in body. Calvin, whose excessive severity they alleged, refuted this most pernicious error, long since condemned by the Fathers, in a brilliant writing. Adding the opinions of the most learned theologians, Philip Melanchthon, Bucer, Peter Martyr and the Church of Zurich, he so checked it that from that time the name of Nicodemites became odious to all the godly. For so they were called, who used the example of that most holy man as a pretext for their error. Another year, no milder, followed this one.

units.la: Præterquam enim ᵹ aduersus frequentes nuntios de Cæsaris ad-uersus Religione molitionibus, & Pontificis fraudes, à quo sum-missos incendiarios ferebant, confirmandus erat ciuiū animus, deplorandus erat in eo præcipuè ciuitatis statu, ᵹ tantum ab-esset vt improborum petulantia tot ferulis domari se paterètur, Vt contrà magis efferretur, adeoq; prorsus erüperet. Erant enim ducem nacti vanissimū quidem, sed audacem & ambitiosum im primis (quem idcirco Caluinus Comici Cæsaris nomine in suis Epistolis designat) Amedeum Perrinū nomine, hoc etiam iam-pridé consecutū, vt Generalis Capitaneus populi suffragiis crea-retur. Is ratus id quod res erat, statè se suisque similes vigentibus legibus, ac præsertim Caluino assiduè aduersus eorum lasciuiam detonante non posse, tandem quid vnà cum suis meditaretur, aperte hoc anno prodere cœpit. quod quū animadu-rsum simul ac repressum fuisset Senatorum auctoritate, tacuit ipse quidem, sed ita vt mox apertius improbitas sese proderet. Ecce enim pau lò post ex ipso Senatu quidam in hominum cœtu satis frequeti Caluinum vt falsa docentem corripit, à duobus ex pastorū col-legio (vt existimatur) clanculum impulsus, ebrioso vtroq;, nec minus quàm cæteri seueritatem legum metuente. Et hunc quidé latratum Caluinus nihil est moratus. Vocatur tamen ille in ius, cognitáq; causa ex SC. infamiç damnatur, coniunctíque duo illi falsi pastores exauctorantur, ipsáque adeo œnopolia interdicū-tur, tantùm abest vt malorum improbitas quicquam valuerit. Quod autem incendium hoc anno repressum fuerat, eo qui pro xime sequutus est, nēpe quadragesimo septimo supra sesquimil-lesimum prorsus erupit, nec aliud tempus eo seculo magis cala-mitosum incidit: Germaniæ Ecclesiis eò redactis, vt vnà cū pro-ceribus & vrbibus partim sese vltrò dedentibus, partim vi captis, vno momento euersum videretur, quicquid tot annis tantisq; la boribus extructum fuerat, iisque demum beati à plerisque habe-rentur, quos istis tumultibus tempestiua mors eripuisset. His pu-blicis tot Ecclesiarū calamitatibus quàtopere pium illud pectus cruciatum existimabimus, non aliter etiam in media pace in Ec clesias quantumuis remotas affectum, quàm si omnes illas hu-meris impositas gestaret? Quid verò? Quum summos illos viros quos amicissimos habuit, Philippum dico, Bucerū, Martyrem vi-deret ita periclitātes, vt morti quàm vitæ propiores essent, quàtis eum doloribus conflictatū putabimus? Fortissimo tamen animo Caluinū tempestates istas superasse, tum ipsius scripta tentantur, tum etiam res ipsa comprobauit: quū domi multò acrius ab im-probis vexatus, suo tamen ex illo gradu ipsis ne tantillùm qui-dem cesserit. Itaque vt ad domesticā certamina redeam, quum in eo totus esset, vt Euangelium quod annuntiabat, ostenderet non in speculatione quadam, sed in ipsa Christiana vita positū essa, hostes eos necessario expertus est, qui omni pietati ac honesta-ti, ipsi denique patriæ bellum indixerant. Eorū vt antè diximus, facile princeps erat Perrinus ille, quū ea tum esset & illius & suo-rum conditio, vt & ab ipsis extrema quæuis tentanda constarer. & improbi aperte inflarent, vt iftorum omnium cognitio à Præ fbyterio ad Senatum trásferretur. Prefbyterium exaduerfo vrge- re fancitas de ecclefiaftica difciplina leges verbo Dei confenta- neas, ipfiusque adeo Senatus opem implorare, ne quid detrimeti acciperet Ecclefia. Iudicauit Senatus ratas effe Ecclefiafticas le- ges oportere, illudque reipfa confirmauit. Ac tandem quum ille fua audacia fefe in extremum difcrimé coniecifiet, exitus totius rei istum quidem fuit, vt Senatu motus, abrogatoque Capitanei nomine priuatus viueret. Hæc autem omnia, etsi coram Magiftratu agebantur, dicitamen non poteft, quantopere Caluinum exercuerint: si quidé eovfque femel in ipfa Curia co acis Diacofiis deuentum eft, vt pené exertis iam enfibus, parum abfuerit quin mutuis cædibus Curiam ipfam cruentaret: quam fedicione Calvinus cum collegis fuperueniens, oppofito imprimis fuo ipfius capite inhibuit, quanquam fceleratorum factio in illum præcipue ferretur: ipso nihilominus eorum fcelera pergente grauiffi me deteftari, eofque grauiffime prout merebatur increpare. Neque vero vana fuit iudiciorum Dei denuntiatio. Siquidem per id tempus quidam famofum libellu fcripfiffe, & facro pulpito adfixiffe deprehenfus, in quo tum alia multa nefaria in facrum Miniftrerium, tum etiam illud fcriptum erat, Caluinum effe in Rhodanum præcipitandum, caufa dicta infinitarum aliarum blafphemiarum præter expectationem conuictus, capitis fupplicio affectus eft. Quinetiá poft eius interitum inuentus eft libellus ipfius manu aduerfus Mofen ipfumque adeo Chriftum profeffo fcriptus, quo impietatis fcelere dubium non erat, quin alio setiam aliquot infeciffet. Scripfit autem hoc ipfo anno in mediis illis certaminibus Caluinus Antidotum aduerfus tridentini cocilia- buli feffiones feptem: itemque Rotomagenfem Ecclefiam miffis literis aduerfus Francifcani cuiufdam fraudes renouatoru à Li- bertinis Carpocratis errorum venenum ibi fpargentem, confir- mauit. Anno fequente, id eft, quadragefimo octauo fupra fef- quimillefimum, erupit eiufdem illius factionis malum, iiis (quod pene incredibile eft) maxime abutete Satana, qui tame præcipue mederi malis iftis ftudebat, Farello nempe & Vireto. Quii ineute ftatim anno quum Geneuam venissent, & orationem in Senatu grauiffimam de componendis diffidiis habuiffent, Caluiino quidem nihil aliud quam emendationem morum poftulante, Perrino vero cum fuis nihil non fimulante, vt priftinum locu receperet, tum quidem vifa funt omnia compofita, fed bomis viris impofitum potius fuiffe, res ipfa mox comprobauit. units.tr: Besides, the spirit of the citizens had to be strengthened against frequent reports of Caesar's schemes against religion and the Pope's frauds, by whom, they said, incendiaries had been sent. And in that particular state of the city it was to be lamented that the wantonness of the wicked, far from allowing itself to be tamed by so many rods, was instead more inflamed and altogether burst out. For they had gained a leader, very vain indeed but bold and above all ambitious, whom Calvin therefore designates in his letters by the name of Caesar the Comedian: Amédée Perrin by name, who had already obtained this too, that he was created Captain General by the votes of the people. Thinking, as was the case, that he and his like could not stand under the laws in force, and especially with Calvin thundering constantly against their licentiousness, he at last began openly, this year, to betray what he was plotting along with his friends. When this had been noticed and checked by the authority of the Senators, he indeed fell silent, but in such a way that soon the wickedness revealed itself more openly. For behold, a little later, a certain man from the Senate itself, in a fairly crowded assembly, rebuked Calvin as teaching falsehoods, secretly prompted, it is thought, by two of the college of ministers, both of them drunkards, and fearing the severity of the laws no less than the rest. Calvin did not trouble himself at all about this barking. Yet the man was summoned to court, and after the case was heard he was condemned to infamy by decree of the Senate. Those two false ministers were removed from office together, and even the taverns were forbidden; so far was the wickedness of the bad from prevailing at all. But the fire that had been suppressed this year burst out entirely in the next, that is in 1547, and no other time in that century was more calamitous. The churches of Germany were brought to such a state that, with nobles and cities partly surrendering of their own accord and partly taken by force, whatever had been built up over so many years and with such great labour seemed overturned in a single moment. Many counted blessed those whom a timely death had snatched from those troubles. How greatly do we think that pious breast was tormented by these public calamities of so many churches, and was affected by churches however remote, even in the midst of peace, no differently than if he carried all of them on his shoulders? What then? When he saw those most eminent men whom he held as dearest friends, I mean Philip, Bucer and Martyr, in such danger that they were nearer to death than to life, how greatly do we suppose he was racked with pains? Yet that Calvin overcame those storms with a most courageous spirit is shown both by his writings and by the event itself: though harassed at home much more sharply by the wicked, he did not yield the least bit of his ground to them. So, to return to the domestic conflicts: since he was wholly bent on showing that the gospel he proclaimed lay not in some speculation but in the Christian life itself, he necessarily found as enemies those who had declared war on all piety and decency, and finally on the homeland itself. Of these, as we said before, that Perrin was easily the chief, since the condition of him and his people was then such that they would attempt any extremity, and the wicked openly puffed themselves up. The cognizance of all these cases was to be transferred from the Presbytery to the Senate. The Presbytery, on the other side, insisted on the laws of ecclesiastical discipline agreeable to the Word of God, and implored the aid of the Senate itself, lest the Church suffer any harm. The Senate judged that the ecclesiastical laws ought to be ratified, and confirmed this in fact. At last, when he had thrown himself into extreme danger by his boldness, the outcome of the whole affair was that, moved by the Senate, he lost the title of Captain and lived as a private man. All these things, though they were carried on before the magistracy, cannot be told in full, so greatly did they exercise Calvin. For once things came in the Senate chamber itself to such a point that, with swords nearly drawn, it lacked little that they would stain the Senate House with mutual slaughter. Calvin, arriving with his colleagues, checked this sedition, chiefly by interposing his own person, although the faction of the wicked was aimed especially at him. Nevertheless, while they persisted in their crimes, he detested them most gravely and rebuked them most severely, as they deserved. Nor indeed was the warning of God's judgments vain. For at that time a certain man was caught having written and fixed to the sacred pulpit a defamatory libel, in which many other wicked things were written against the sacred ministry, and also that Calvin should be thrown into the Rhone. His case being heard, he was convicted, beyond expectation, of countless other blasphemies, and was punished with death. Moreover, after his death, a little book was found, written in his own hand, against Moses and professedly even against Christ; there was no doubt that by this impious crime he had infected some others as well. In this same year, amid those conflicts, Calvin wrote the Antidote against the seven sessions of the Council of Trent. Likewise, by letters sent, he strengthened the Church of Rouen against the frauds of a certain Franciscan who was there scattering the poison of the errors of Carpocrates, renewed by the Libertines. The next year, that is 1548, the evil of that same faction burst out, Satan making most use (which is almost incredible) of those who nevertheless were especially eager to heal these evils, namely Farel and Viret. They came to Geneva at the very beginning of that year and delivered a most weighty speech in the Senate on settling the quarrels. Calvin asked for nothing but a reform of morals, while Perrin with his people pretended to agree to everything, so that he might recover his former place. Then indeed all seemed settled, but that good men had been imposed upon the event soon proved. For Perrin having been restored, the wickedness of the criminals rose so far that some even wore openly breastplates cut in the shape of a cross, by which they recognised one another, and others to their dogs

units.la: Caluini nomen imponerent, alij Caluinū in Cainū transformā-ret, non pauci denique illius odio abstinere se à Coena D. testa-rentur, quae omnia quum fortiter ille & collegae ipsius reprehen-derent, vocitis in Senatum, vicit quidem facile bonorum inno-centia: tandémque x v i i i. Dec. solenni iureiurando fancita rur-sum est ἀμνηστία. Sed haec omnia per simulationem facta fuisse, nec aliud tum quaesiuisse Perrinū, quàm vt Syndicatum adeptus, aditum sibi & suis ad omnia perdenda magis ac magis patefaceret, euentus comprobauit. Caluinus autem istis concertationibus non modò non cessit, verùmetiam quasi in otio sex Epistolas Pauli doctissimis commentariis illustrauit: & interim illud quod vocant, perfundandis Germanicis Ecclesiis editum, grauissimo scripto refutauit, veramque instaurandae Ecclesiae rationem ostendit: Astrologiae denique quam iudiciariam vocār, cui plusculum tribuere non pauci videbantur, falsitate atque vanitatem elegantissimo libello patefecit. Tùm quoque à Brentio Basiliae exulante literis salutatus, amicissimè illum consolatus est, in qua coniunctione vtinam perstare Brentius instituisset. Bucerū in Anglia exulante tunc quoque ingenue monuit, vt magis perspicuè de Coena Domini scriberet ac loqueretur, & amicissimè so latus est. Simulque Sommerfetum Ducem Angliae protectore indignissima postea morte affectum accuratè scriptis literis eorū admonuit, quae si tùm essent in illo regno animaduersa, multas fortasse tempestates Ecclesiae Anglicanae deuitassent. Crescebat in istis certaminibus mirabiliter Ecclesia Geneuensis, quod vt mirum in modum Satanam & malos angebat, ita Caluini excipiendis pro Christi nomine exulibus intenti studium vehementer acuebat: cui solitudini sic fauit anno consequente Dominus vt etsi non extincta prorsus, attamen ad tempus sopita furiosorum improbitas videretur. Et sanè induciis egebat ille, praesertim casu domestico grauiter afflictus: amissa videlicet vxore lectissima femina: quam tamen casum ita constanter tulit, vt hac etiam in re singulare fortitudinis exemplum toti Ecclesiae praebuerit. Eodem hoc anno exorta in Saxonicis Ecclesiis contentione de rebus Adiaphoris, quum à Caluino quoque consilium petereatur, sententiam hac de re suam liberè exposuit: Philippo etiam officij admonito, quem nonnulli vt in eo molliorem accusabat, immerito id quidem, vt accuratius postea Caluinus cognouit. Tùm enim erat ignotum quo animo malus ille genius & tota Flaccianorum cohors impelleretur: quae tot postea turbas dedit, & nunc quoque opus Domini labefactat, non aliter sanè, nec minùs impudenter ac furiosè, quàm si ab ipso Rom. Pont. magnis stipediis esset conducta. Caeterum hoc Ecclesiis Germanicis inflictū vulnus contrario beneficio Dominus apud Helvetios com-
units.tr: to give their dogs Calvin's name, others to change Calvin into Cain, and finally not a few to swear off the Lord's Supper out of hatred for him. When Calvin and his colleague resisted all this vigorously, they were summoned before the Senate, and the innocence of the good easily prevailed. On 18 December an amnesty [ἀμνηστία] was once again ratified by solemn oath. But the outcome proved that all this had been done by pretence, and that Perrin had sought nothing else than, once he had obtained the syndicate, to open up for himself and his people a wider and wider path to ruin everything. Calvin, however, did not give way to these contests. Rather, as if at leisure, he illustrated the six Epistles of Paul with most learned commentaries. Meanwhile he refuted in a very weighty writing the so-called Interim, issued to overthrow the German Churches, and showed the true way of restoring the Church. Finally, he exposed in a most elegant little book the falsehood and vanity of judicial astrology, which not a few seemed to value rather highly. Then too, greeted by letter from Brenz, who was in exile at Basel, he consoled him most kindly; would that Brenz had resolved to persist in that friendship. He also frankly advised Bucer, then in exile in England, to write and speak more plainly about the Lord's Supper, and was himself most warmly greeted by him. At the same time he carefully admonished the Duke of Somerset, Protector of England, who later suffered an most unworthy death, by letter. Had these things been noted in that kingdom at that time, they might perhaps have spared the English Church many storms. The Genevan Church grew wonderfully amid these conflicts. As this greatly vexed Satan and the wicked, so it fired Calvin's eager zeal for receiving exiles for the name of Christ. The Lord so favoured this quiet in the following year that the rage of the frenzied wicked seemed, though not wholly extinguished, lulled for a time. Indeed he needed a truce, especially as he was grievously afflicted by a domestic misfortune, namely the loss of his most excellent wife. Yet he bore this loss so steadfastly that in this too he gave the whole Church a singular example of fortitude. In this same year a dispute arose in the Saxon Churches over the adiaphora, and Calvin too was asked for counsel. He freely set out his opinion on the matter and also reminded Melanchthon of his duty, whom some accused of being too soft on this point, unjustly, as Calvin later learned more fully. For at that time it was unknown with what spirit that evil genius and the whole band of Flacians were driven. They later caused so many disturbances, and even now undermine the work of the Lord, no differently and no less shamelessly and furiously than if the Roman Pontiff himself had hired them with large pay. But the wound inflicted on the German Churches the Lord made amends for [com-]

units.la: M.D. cLIX. pensauit,Farello simul ac Caluino Tigurum profectis, vt,quum visus esset q ibusdam CaluinusConsubstantiationi nonnihil fa uere,de communi in eare omnium Helueticarum Ecclesiarum consensu omnibus liqueret. Neq; vero difficile factu fuit,vt inter bonos & veritatis amantes coueniret.Scripta est igitur summa omnium Helueticarum & Rheticarum Ecclesiarum appro batione consensio,quæ præsertim D.Bulingerum cum Caluino, Tigurinamque Ecclesiam cū Geneuensi arctissimo vinculo magis ac magis colligauit,in qua etiam omnes adhuc perstamus,& ad extremum vsque fauente Deo perstituros nos speramus. Hic annus ille fœlix nobis exactus est si cum cæteris conferatur: cuius eo libentius memini, quis mihi primæ ad Ecclesiasticas functiones vocationis meæ vocate me Laufannensi Ecclesia,impel- lente vero Caluino,initium fuerit.Scripsit quoque per id tempus binas eruditissimas epistolas Lælio Socino Senési Tiguri diu ver sato,ac tandem etiam mortuo.Ex iis vero quod fuerit illius ingenium,nempe plane Academicum, facile quiuis dignoscet,res autem ipsa scro ac nonnihil post eius obitum patefecit:quum Ec clefias peragrans,acdoctissimus quenque,ac in iis imprimis Phi- lippum,Caluinum,Ioach.deniq; Camerarium (à quo in Philip- pi vita perhonorifico testimonio contrà quàm mereretur,orna tus est)fefellisset.Siquidem illum postea Bellianæ de qua fuio lo co dicemus farraginis maxima ex parte auctorem fuisse,& Ser- ueti, Castellionis,Ochini denique furoribus fauisse compertum est,extante etiam illius in illud illustre primum caput Ioannis commentario,in quo facile omnium qui vnquam illum loscutn longe diuinissimum corruperunt, hæreticorum impietatem su- perasuit.Qui hunc excepit annus nempe quinquagesimus supra sesquimillesimum,fatis q ad Ecclesiam attinet tran quillus. fuit: eóque decretū est vt Ministri non tantum in concionibus, quas alij negligebant,alij non magno cum fructu audiebant,sedi etiam sigillatim perdomos & familias certo anni tempore adhibitto cu iusque regionis vrbis Decurione, itémque Presbytero, plebem i stituerent, & ab vnoquoque fidei rationem summatim exposcerent:qua ex re vix credibile est,quantus sit fructus confecquu tus. Alterum decretum vt in proximum diem referretur NNatalium D.celebratio, nec vlli alij sefti dies essent præter septimū quenque quem Dominicum vocamus:factu plurimos offerendit, adeò quidem vt non deessent,qui dies ipsos Dominicos à CCalui no sublatos confingerent,vt eum in inuidiam vocarent:quuum tamen non modo non postulante,sed etiam ignorate Ministro- rum collegio actu ea de re apud populu,decretumq; fuisse c con- staret, cuiustamen causa litem non esse mouendam Caluuinus existimauit. Offendiculu autem inde ả non nullis acceptu s Caluino præbuit libelli de Scandalis scribendi occasionem, Laurentio Normendio integerrimo veteriq; amico inscripti. Huius autem biennij tranquillitatem dissidia sequentis quinquagesimi- primi nempe supra sexquimillef facilè compensarunt. Nam præterquam q; toti Ecclesiæ ac Caluino nominatim luctuosus fuit Buceri morte, quem virũ summè dilexerat, itemque Ioach. Vadiani Consulis Sangallensis viri singulari tum pietate tum erudi tione præditi interitu, efferbuit factiosorum improbitas eò ardentius, quò diutius sopita delituerat: adeò ut palàm negarent cũ aduentatibus exulibus ius Ciuitatis communicandũ: nec eo contenti, Caluinũ ipsum ex concione trans Rhodanũ habita redeũtem per ludibrium pulsarint, & Raymundum eius Collegã nocte forte pontem Rhodani transeuntem, exempta furtim publica pene in subiectum fluuium præcipitarint. Denique in ipso D. Geruasij templo tumultum non paruum eo prætextu excitarint, q; Ministerinfanti ad Baptismum oblato indere Balthasaris nomen (quoniam id diserte leges scriptæ ob certam causam prohibebant) recusaret. Neq; tum aduersus hæc mala quicquã erat quod Caluinus opponeret, præter fortem inuidiamque patientiã. Sed & aliud nouũ malum Geneuensem Ecclesiam per id tempus inuasit. Dedit autem occasionem Hieronymus quidã Bolsecus ex Carmelitarũ societate Lutetiæ monachus, qui quũ aliquot ante annos cuculla quidè abiecta, sed monachismo retento profugisset, idem etiã decepta Ferrariensi Ducissa ab ea pulsus, ac tãdem triduo medicus factus Geneuæ venerat: vbi quum inter eruditos medicos nullo loco esset, vt sese Theologũ esse ostenderet, falsum & absurdũ quiddam de prædestinatione inter aliquos, ac tandè etiam in congregationis cœtu blateraurit. Eum Caluinus primum moderata reprehensione cõtentus refutauerat, deinde ad se vocatum docere meliora fuerat conatus. At ille siue ambitione mænastica percitus, siue ab illis factiosis, iampridè quærentibus per quem Caluinũ lacesserent, incitatus, palàm ausus est in ipso congregationis cœtu x v i. Octob. quum ille Ioānis locus explicaretur, Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit, & quia non auditis, ex Deo non estis, liberum arbitrium & operum præuisionem ad æternæ prædestinationis decretũ causis omnibus etiã ordine superius euertendũ, adiectis etiam in veram doctrinam cõtumeliis, fatuque mere seditioso proferre: idque eò vt existimatur. audacius, q; forte Caluinum suo loco non sedentem abesse crederet. Et aberat quidè ille initiò. Sed eo sermonem ingresso superuenientes, ponè alios nonnullos sese cõtinuerat. Finita monachi oratione, Caluinus repente apparens, quanuis planè nihil antea tale meditatus, tum certè si vnquam alias qui vir esset, ostendi. Siquidem illũ tot verbi diuini testimoniis, tot Augustini præscriptum locis, tot denique tamque grauibus argumetis confutauit, perculit, obruit, vt omnes praeter ipsummet perfridae frontis monachum ipsius vehementer puderet. Aderat in ipso audientium coetu Assessorum Praetoris vnus, quorum in vrbe ius prehensionis est. Is illum dimisso coetu tanquam seditiosum in custodia tradit. Quid plura? Causa multisdisputationibus agitata, Senatus Helueticarum etiam Ecclesiarum sententiam percontatus, illum tum vt seditiosum, tum vt merè Pelagianum xxii, Decemb. publicè damnatum vrbe expulit, fustuariam poenam minatus, si vel in vrbe vel in vrbis territorio effet deprehensus. Ipse postea in vicinum oppidum demigrans, multas magnasque turbas dedit, donec Bernensi quoque ditione bis expulsus, Ministerium in Gallicis Ecclesiis ambiens, quas tum pacificas fore putabat, Lutetiam primum, indeque Aureliam venit, poenitentiam miris artibus simulas vltroque cum Geneuensi Ecclesia reconciliationem petens, quod quum reipsa praestiturus videretur, vbi contra quam sperarat Ecclesias affligi animaduertit, repetita medicina, ad hostes Euangelii manifesta defectione (vxore quoq; Canonicis Augustodunensibus prostituta) transiuit, unde nunc etiam quibus potest maledictis vexitatem proscindit. At Geneuae interea Collegium Ministrorum in publico coetu veram de praedestinatione doctrinam asseruit, publicoque scripto deinceps a Calvino comprehensam comprobauit: hoc vnum iltis dissidiis confequuto Satana, vt caput hoc Christianae Religionis antea obscurissimum, dilucidum perspicuumque cunctis non cotentiofis euafirit. Anno vero deinceps sequuto magis apparuit quantam flammam accendisset impurus ille, licet communi tot Ecclesiarum iudicio damnatus. Etenim tum ipsa Quaestionis nondum antea satis a plerisque veteribus explicatae, nec eodem semper exitu agitatae difficultas, curiosa praesertim ingenia ad hoc ipsum disquirendum accendebat, tum factiosi praeclarum sibi oblatam occasionem ad omnia Calvino eiecto subuertenda putabant. Itaq; dici non potest quae non in vrbe tantum, verum etiam vltro citroq; veluti si classicum ipse Satan cecinisset, contentiones fiunt consequutae. Etsi enim pulchre inter praecipuarum Ecclesiarum pastores conueniebat, non deerant tamen qui in vicinis Bernensis ditionis Ecclesiis Calvino litem intenderent, quasi Deum facere peccati auctorem: parum certe memores hoc ipsum ppestilentissimum dogma fuisse a Calvino iampridem ex professo aduersus Libertinos refutatum. Basileae vero Castellio bonus ille & simplex homo, etsi clanculum fere agebat omnia, tamen non obscure Pelagianismum tuebatur. Quinetiam his de rebus ita scribere coeperat Philippus, vt quanuis antea Calvini aaduersus Pighium libro diserte subscripsisset, tamen Geneuenses quasi Stoicum
units.tr: M.D. cLIX. pensauit, with a contrary blessing among the Helvetians, when Farel and Calvin both went to Zurich, so that, since Calvin seemed to some to favour Consubstantiation somewhat, the common consent of all the Helvetic Churches on this matter might become clear to everyone. Nor was it difficult for agreement to be reached among good men who love the truth. Accordingly, a summary of consensus was drawn up with the approval of all the Helvetic and Rhaetian Churches. This especially bound Bullinger to Calvin, and the Church of Zurich to the Church of Geneva, more and more closely by the tightest bond, and in it we all still persist, and we hope, God favouring, to persist to the end. That year was a happy one for us compared with the others, and I remember it all the more gladly because it was the beginning of my first ecclesiastical functions, when I was called by the Church of Lausanne, Calvin urging it. At that time he also wrote two most learned letters to Lelio Sozzini of Siena, who had long lived at Zurich and had at last died there. From these letters anyone can easily tell what his talent was, namely purely academic. But the fact itself revealed it late, and somewhat after his death, when, wandering through the Churches, he had deceived all the most learned men, especially Melanchthon, Calvin, and finally Joachim Camerarius, by whom he was honoured in Melanchthon's life with a most flattering testimony, more than he deserved. For it was afterwards discovered that he was largely the author of Bellius's medley, which we shall discuss in its place, and that he favoured the frenzies of Servetus, Castellio and finally Ochino. His commentary on that famous first chapter of John survives, in which he surpassed in heretical impiety all who have ever corrupted that by far most divine passage. The year that followed, 1550, was quiet as far as the Church was concerned. It was therefore decreed that the ministers should instruct the common people not only in sermons, which some neglected and others attended without much profit, but also individually, house by house and family by family, at a fixed time of the year, together with the magistrate of each district or city and likewise an elder, and should demand from each a summary account of his faith. It is hardly credible what fruit resulted from this. A second decree was that the celebration of Christmas be transferred to the nearest day, and that no other festivals be kept except every seventh day, which we call the Lord's Day. This offended very many, to such an extent that there were those who invented that the Lord's Days themselves had been abolished by Calvin, in order to bring him into odium, whereas it was clear that the decree had been made about this matter with the people, not only without the College of Ministers requesting it but even without their knowledge. Yet Calvin thought that no dispute should be stirred over this cause. An offence taken from this by some gave Calvin the occasion to write his little book On Scandals, dedicated to Laurence Normand, a most upright and long-standing friend. But the quiet of these two years was easily made up for by the quarrels of the following year, 1551. For, besides the fact that Bucer's death was mournful to the whole Church and to Calvin by name, whom he had greatly loved, and likewise the death of Joachim Vadian, burgomaster of St Gallen, a man endowed with singular piety and learning, the wickedness of the factious blazed up all the more fiercely the longer it had lain hidden. So much so that they openly refused to share the rights of citizenship with the exiles who arrived. Not content with that, they jeered at Calvin himself as he returned from a sermon preached across the Rhône, and by chance pushed his colleague Raymond, who was crossing the Rhône bridge at night, having secretly removed the public railing, into the river below. Finally, in the very church of St Gervase they raised no small tumult on the pretext that the minister refused to give the name Balthasar to a child brought to baptism, since the written laws expressly forbade it for a certain reason. Nor was there then anything Calvin could oppose to these evils except brave patience in the face of hatred. But another new evil also attacked the Genevan Church at that time. The occasion was given by a certain Jerome Bolsec, a Carmelite monk of Paris, who, having some years before fled, casting off the cowl indeed but keeping his monkish ways, and then, having been expelled by the Duchess of Ferrara whom he had deceived, and having become a doctor after three days' training, had come to Geneva. There, since he had no standing among the learned physicians, in order to show himself a theologian he babbled some false and absurd thing about predestination among some people, and finally even in the assembly of the congregation. Calvin had at first been content to refute him with moderate rebuke, then, having summoned him, tried to teach him better. But he, either roused by monastic ambition or incited by those factious men who had long been seeking a way to harass Calvin, openly dared, in the very assembly of the congregation on 16 October, while that passage of John was being expounded, He who is of God hears God's words; and because you do not hear, you are not of God, to assert that free will and the foreseeing of works must be overturned, in all their causes and even in their order above, for the decree of eternal predestination, adding insults even against the true doctrine, and speaking with a purely foolish and seditious rashness. And he did this, it is thought, all the more boldly because he believed Calvin, who was not sitting in his place, was absent. And indeed at first he was absent. But when the monk had got into his discourse, Calvin arrived and had kept himself back behind several others. When the monk's speech was finished, Calvin suddenly appeared, though he had planned nothing of the kind beforehand, and then showed what kind of man he was, as never before. For he refuted, struck down and overwhelmed him with so many testimonies of God's Word, so many passages of Augustine, and finally with such weighty arguments, that all, except the monk himself of brazen face, were deeply ashamed for him. One of the assessors of the magistrate, who in the city have the right of arrest, was present in the assembly of hearers. He, the assembly being dismissed, handed him over to custody as a seditious man. To make a long story short: the case was debated at length, the Senate also sought the opinion of the Helvetic Churches, and then, on 22 December, publicly condemned him as seditious and as a plain Pelagian, and expelled him from the city, threatening him with flogging if he were caught either in the city or in its territory. He afterwards moved to a neighbouring town and caused many great disturbances, until, expelled twice also from the territory of Bern, seeking a ministry in the French Churches, which he then thought would be peaceful, he came first to Paris and thence to Orléans. There he feigned repentance by wonderful arts and sought reconciliation with the Genevan Church on his own initiative. Since he seemed ready to make this good in fact, when he noticed the Churches being afflicted, contrary to what he had hoped, he took his medicine again and by open desertion passed over to the enemies of the Gospel, having also prostituted his wife to the canons of Autun, whence now too he tears the truth with whatever slanders he can. Meanwhile at Geneva the College of Ministers, in public assembly, asserted the true doctrine of predestination, and afterwards confirmed it by a public writing drawn up by Calvin. This was the one result that Satan's quarrels achieved: this article of the Christian religion, previously most obscure, became clear and plain to all who were not contentious. In the following year it became clearer what a flame that unclean man had kindled, although he had been condemned by the common judgment of so many Churches. For the very difficulty of the question, not yet sufficiently explained by most of the ancients nor always discussed with the same outcome, especially kindled curious minds to investigate this very thing; and the factious thought they had been offered a splendid opportunity to overturn everything once Calvin was cast out. So it cannot be said what quarrels followed, not only in the city but also back and forth, as if Satan himself had sounded the trumpet. For although the ministers of the chief Churches agreed admirably, there were not lacking those who in the neighbouring Churches of the territory of Bern brought a charge against Calvin, as if he made God the author of sin, certainly little mindful that this most pestilential dogma had long before been expressly refuted by Calvin against the Libertines. At Basel, indeed, Castellio, that good and simple man, though he did almost everything secretly, nevertheless openly defended Pelagianism. Philip had begun to write on these matters in such a way that, although he had earlier expressly subscribed to Calvin's book against Pighius, the Genevans nevertheless seemed to some to be railing against the Stoic

units.la: M. D. LII. Stoicum Fratum inuehentes notare quibusdam videretur. Pontificios omitto, easdem calumnias millies refutatas nunc quoque repetentes. Pungebant illa grauissime sicuti par erat, illius animum, & eo quid am acerbius, quod ea fuit interdum per id tempus erroris efficacia, ut publica etiam auctoritate alicubi obstructum os veritati videretur. Neque haec fuit paucorum annorum controuersia: sed hoc anno imprimis bonus ille Eremita quem supra diximus cum Caluino disputaturus, prodiit, qui aliquot ante annis quum Ministerium ambiret repulsam passus, Iurisconsultus, & factiosorum patronus euaserat. Causa coram Senatu agitata est magna utrinque contentione: illo quidem impudetia & malorum fauore depugnante, Caluino vero sola veritatis auctoritate doctrinam suam tuente. Vicit ergo veritas, & Caluini scripta ipsorum etiam quod mirum est, aduersariorum suffragiis ut pia & orthodoxa rursum comprobata. Sed ne istius aduersarij aliquot post annis morientis reticenda est resipiscentia, cuius etiam testem Caluinum tanto studio adhibuit, ut non aliter sibi pacé conscientiae constare diceret, quam si Caluinum sibi conciliatum moribundus agnosceret, quem antea tam indigne a se impetitum fateretur: Cui etiam Caluinus tum nonmodo non defuit, sed benignissime consolatum erexit, & ad extremum usque confirmauit. Annus autem alter a superiore, nempe quinquagesimus tertius supra sexquimillesimum, ad exitum festinante factiosorum malitia tam fuit turbulentus, ut non Ecclesia modo, verum etiam Resp. extremum discrime adierit. Siquidem eo usque illi progressi sunt, clamoribus, & minis numero denique oppressa bonorum libertate, ut veteza de constitutiis Senatoribus Edicta (quo tamen argumento boni etiam sibi tanto melius deinde consuluerunt, ita illis etiam fauente Domino) refixerint, nonnullos Senatu moverint, peregrinis exulibus a quibus se metuere dicebant, arma omnia exceptis si quando urbe egrederentur, ensibus ademerint, adeo ut nihil aliud superesset: videretur, quam ut quum omnia in potestate haberent, quae toties agitauerat, facile exequerentur. Occasionem autem turbarum alteram quoque Satan tunc obiecit. Vetus enim ille sacrae Triadis, id est omnis verae Deitatis hostis, adeoque monstrum ex omnibus quantumuis rancidis & portentosis haeresibus conflatum, Michael Seruetus, postquam aliquot annis huc & illuc medicinam faciens oberrasset, teste quae Michaelis Villanouani nomine illas blasphemias parsisset, edito tandem Viennae Allobrogum spisso volumine (cuius excusor fuit Arnolletus quidam Lugdunensis Typographus. Corrector autem ut in illis officinis vocant, Gulielmus quidam Guerotius factiosus Geneuensibus pridem deditus, sed paucis ante menses ut scortationis & aliorum flagitiorum poenas vitaret Genetus
units.tr: In 1552, when some people seemed to find in the Stoic brothers a target for their attacks, I pass over the Papists, who kept repeating calumnies that had been refuted a thousand times. These charges pierced his spirit most painfully, as was right, and all the more so because at that time the power of error was sometimes so strong that, by public authority, the mouth of truth seemed to be stopped in some places. Nor was this a controversy of a few years. This year, above all, that good hermit whom we mentioned above came forward to dispute with Calvin. A few years earlier, when he had sought the ministry and been rejected, he had become a lawyer and a patron of the factious. The case was argued before the Senate with great contention on both sides: the hermit fought with shamelessness and the favour of the wicked, while Calvin defended his doctrine by the authority of truth alone. Truth won, and, what is remarkable, Calvin's writings were approved again as pious and orthodox, even by the votes of his opponents. But the repentance of that adversary, who died some years later, must not be passed over in silence. He called Calvin as a witness with such eagerness that he said he could not otherwise have peace of conscience unless the dying man acknowledged that he had been reconciled to Calvin, whom he confessed he had previously attacked so unworthily. Calvin not only did not fail him at that time, but most kindly consoled him, raised him up, and confirmed him to the end. The next year, that is, the fifty-third after the year one thousand five hundred, was so turbulent, as the malice of the factious hurried toward its end, that not only the Church but also the commonwealth faced the greatest danger. They advanced so far, with shouting and threats, and by finally overwhelming the liberty of good men, that they tore down the old edicts concerning the constitution of the Senators (though by this very occasion good men later provided for themselves all the better, the Lord thus favouring them as well). They moved some members of the Senate, and they took away from the foreign exiles, whom they said they feared, all their arms, except their swords when they might leave the city. So it seemed that nothing else remained but that, since they now had everything in their power, they should easily carry out what they had so often plotted. Satan also presented another occasion of disturbances at that time. For that old enemy of the holy Trinity, that is, of all true Deity, and so a monster compounded of all the most rancid and portentous heresies, Michael Servetus, after wandering about here and there for some years, practising medicine, and having published those blasphemies under the name of Michael Villanovanus, at last issued at Vienne in Dauphiné a thick volume. Its printer was a certain Arnollet of Lyon, a typographer; the corrector, as they call it in those workshops, was a certain William Guerot, a factious man long devoted to the Genevans, but a few months earlier had left for Lyon to escape the penalties of fornication and other disgraceful crimes.

units.la: C.i. Lugdunum profectus.) Eo inquam edito blasphemiarum pleno volumine Servetus, eòq; nomine in carcere Vienn̄ coniectus, ac inde mox nescio quibus artibus elapsus, Geneuā fare quodā venerat alio procul transiturus, nisi Dei prouidentia factū effet vt mox agnitus, Caluino, cui ille iampridem bene notus erat Magistratum admonente, carceri fuisset mancipatus. Quę certami- na tum, quaecunque de rebus suscepta fuerint, ex edito libro percipi plenissime poterat. Fuit autem horum omnium iste exitus, vt tandē perditus ille (cui etiam factiosorum vnus tum Praetoris Assessor in aurem insusurrasse quiddam credebatur, quo malum perdito hominis animum obstinaret) a vana illa sua confidentia prodi- tus, impietatis & infinitarum blasphemiarum ex omnium etiam Heluéticarum Ecclesiarum sententia damnatus, x x v i i Octob. nullo edito poenitentiae signo, infoelix viuus crematur. Sed & Farellus eodem anno eo vsque vi morbi fractus, vt a Caluino qui Neocomum ad eum visendum venerat, pro mortuo relinquē- retur, vitae postea praeter spem omnem restitutus, Ecclesiā mox recreauit. Ita plane inter spem & metum, terminante tamen dolorem laeteria, annum hunc eatenus exegimus. Ecce enim dum haec in Serueti causa aguntur, quidam ex factiosis Bertelerius non mine homo proiectae penitus impudentiae, cui ob multa flagitia Presbyterium mensa Domini interdixerat, in Senatum venit, postulárque ex auctoritate Senatus absolui: quod si factum esset, ambigi non poterat, quin mox solutis Ecclesiasticae disciplinae vinculis, omnia statim diffluerent. Itaque obstat sedulo fortiterque Presbyterij nomine Caluinus, ostenditque Magistratum sacrarum legum vindicem non destructorem esse oportere: nihil denique eorum praetermittit, quae tanti momenti continentio flagitabat. Vincebant tamen eorum falsi clamores, qui Presbyterium aiebant sibi in quibusdam Magistratus imperium arrogare, adeo vt in Diacosiorum consilio statueretur, vltimum excommunicationis iudicium ad Senatus cognitionem pertinere, vt quos vellet, absoluéret. In quam sententiam à Senatu parum tum ad eam rem attento obreptitie absolutorias literas sigillo Reipub. communitas Bertelerius obtinuit. Ac sperabat tum Perrinus cum suis, alterum sequuturum: nempe, vt vel Caluinum nisi mandato Senatus pareret, per tumultum opprimeret, vel si pareret, nullo postea negotio Presbyterij auctoritatem omnem, id est nequitiae ipsorum fraenum abrumperet. At Caluinus quanuis biduo duntaxat ante Coenam Domini mense Sept. de more celebrandam, de hoc facto commonefactus, inter concionandum elata voce ac manu, multa de sacris mysteriis in eorum contemptores loquutus: at ego, inquit, Chryfostomum sequutus occidi me potius patiar, quam haec manus Dei contemptoribus ptoribus iudicatis sancta Domini porrigat. Hæc vox (mirum dicitu) tantùm potuit apud illos quantumuis effræness, vt Perrinus statim clanculum Bertelerio mandaret, ne ad mensam accederet, sintque mysteria non sine tremore quodam, quasi numen ipsum in consperctu adesset, miro silentio celebrata.
