A prandio vero Caluinus locum illum insignem Actorum Apostolicorum forte tractans, in quo Paulus Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ vale dicit, testatus se eum non esse, qui aduersus Magistratum pugnare sciret aut doceret, coeúmque multis verbis cohortatus, vt in ea quam audiuisset doctrina perseueraret, tandem veluti postremâ hinc concionem Geneuæ habituras, & quandoquidem, inquit, ita se res habent, liceat mihi quoque Fratres apud vos hæc Apostoli verba vsurpare, Commendo vos Deo & sermoni gratiæ ipsius: quæ voces tum sceleratos illos mirificè perculerunt, tum bonos etiam tanto magis serio officij admonuerunt. Postridie Caluinus cum Collegis & Presbyterio à Senatu tum etiam à Diaconiis constanter postulauit, vt apud populum ipsum audirentur, quum de lege à populo lata abroganda ageretur. quamobrem in eam sententiam animis non mediocriter commutatis itum est, vt suspenso illo Diaconiorum decreto, staturetur, petendum esse à quatuor Ciuitatibus Helueticis iudicium, nec interea præsiudicium vllum fieri receptis legibus oportere. Sic discussa potius quàm sedata fuit hæc tempestas, quam illi præter spem omnem à Calnini capite auersam, in Farelli caput è re nata conuertere tentarunt. Farellus enim mense Martio morbo illo tam graui conflictatus, simulatque per valetudinem licuerat Geneuâ properans, peracerbe factiosos pro concione, partim causa ipsa, partim ætate & vetere sua quadam apud illos auctoritate fretus, increparat. Ipsi verò factam sibi iniuriam querentes, diem illi Neocomum reuerso dixerunt, impetratis à Senatu ad Neocomenses literis, vt Farellum addiem condictam adesse paterentur. Venit igitur Farellus, nec à periculo aberat, clamitantibus factiosis dignum esse qui in Rhodanum abiiceretur: quum ab vno ex ciuibus cordato iuuene admonito primùm Perrino videret etiam atque etiam, ne quid detrimenti communis veluti ciuium parens Farellus acciperet, tum adiuncto sibi altero etiam integro iuuene & socio, commonefactis cæteris quos bene affectos noueran, sese in Curia Farello sistente, ibique concurrente magna vrbis parte, attoniti ac de seipsis iam solliciti accusatores, audito Farello culpam ipsi sunt deprecati. Ita pene totus hic annus aduersus improbos, tum pro doctrina tum pro disciplina concertando consumptus fuit: prospero tamen vbique exitu, si vulnus excipias; quod non Anglia modò, sed Christianæ omnes Ecclesiæ Eduardi religiosissimi Regis intempestiua morte acceperunt.
units.tr: When that volume full of blasphemies had been published, Servetus was thrown into prison at Vienne, and from there he soon escaped by some arts I know not what, and came to Geneva, intending to pass on far away, had not Providence of God ensured that he was soon recognized, and, with Calvin, whom he had long known well, warning the magistrate, he was handed over to prison. What contests were then waged, and what matters were undertaken, could be fully learned from the published book. The outcome of all these things was that the lost man (to whom one of the factious, then assessor of the Praetor, was believed to have whispered something in his ear, by which he hardened the evil spirit of the lost man) was betrayed by his own vain confidence. Condemned by the judgment of all the Helvetic Churches as an impious man and guilty of infinite blasphemies, he was burned alive, unhappy, on the 27th of October, without showing any sign of repentance. And Farel, in the same year, was so broken by the force of disease that he was left for dead by Calvin, who had come to Neuchâtel to visit him; but afterwards he was restored to life beyond all hope and soon revived the Church. Thus, truly between hope and fear, though gladness ended our sorrow, we spent this year up to this point. For behold, while these matters were being handled in the case of Servetus, one of the factious, Berthelier, a man of utterly abandoned impudence, for whose many crimes the Presbytery had forbidden him the table of the Lord, came into the Senate and asked by the authority of the Senate to be absolved. Had this been done, there could be no doubt that, the bonds of ecclesiastical discipline being loosed, everything would at once fall apart. Therefore Calvin resisted this, earnestly and bravely, in the name of the Presbytery, and showed that the magistrate ought to be the guardian of the sacred laws, not their destroyer; in short, he omitted nothing that so grave a contest demanded. Yet the false outcries of those men prevailed, who said that the Presbytery was arrogating to itself the power of the magistrate in certain matters, so much so that in the council of the Deacons it was decided that the final judgment of excommunication belonged to the cognizance of the Senate, which might absolve whom it wished. The Senate, paying little attention to the matter at that time, was taken by surprise, and Berthelier obtained letters of absolution, sealed with the seal of the Republic, to that effect. Perrin and his followers hoped then for a second step: either to crush Calvin by tumult, unless he obeyed the Senate's mandate, or, if he obeyed, afterwards, without any trouble, to break all the authority of the Presbytery, that is, the bridle of their wickedness. But Calvin, though it was only two days before the Lord's Supper, which was to be celebrated in the month of September as usual, having been warned of this deed, spoke a great deal in his sermon, in a raised voice and with his hand raised, about the sacred mysteries against their despisers: "But I," he said, "following Chrysostom, would rather allow myself to be killed than give this holy hand of the Lord to judged despisers of God." This word (wonderful to relate) had such power over those men, however unbridled, that Perrin at once secretly ordered Berthelier not to approach the table, and the mysteries were celebrated in great silence, not without a certain trembling, as if the Deity itself were present in sight. After dinner, Calvin, happening to treat that remarkable passage of the Acts of the Apostles in which Paul bids farewell to the Church of Ephesus, testified that he was not one who knew how to fight or teach against the magistrate; and, exhorting them with many words to persevere in the doctrine they had heard, at last, as if it were to be the final sermon at Geneva, he said: "And since matters stand thus, let me also, brethren, use among you these words of the Apostle: I commend you to God and to the word of his grace." These words struck those wicked men with wonder, and warned the good all the more earnestly of their duty. On the following day Calvin, with his colleagues and the Presbytery, steadfastly demanded of the Senate, and also of the Deacons, that they be heard before the people itself, when the abrogation of the law passed by the people was under discussion. Therefore, with minds not a little changed toward that view, it was agreed that, the decree of the Deacons being suspended, it should be settled that judgment should be sought from the four Swiss cities, and meanwhile no prejudgment should be made against the laws received. Thus this storm was dispersed rather than calmed, which they, against all hope, tried to turn away from Calvin's head and onto the head of Farel, as the occasion arose. For Farel, who in March had been struggling with that grievous illness, as soon as his health allowed, hastening to Geneva, sharply rebuked the factious before the assembly, partly for the cause itself, partly relying on his age and a certain old authority he had among them. They, complaining that an injury had been done to them, named a day for him when he returned to Neuchâtel, having obtained from the Senate letters to the people of Neuchâtel so that they would allow Farel to appear on the appointed day. Farel therefore came, nor was he far from danger, the factious shouting that he deserved to be thrown into the Rhône. But when a sensible young citizen warned Perrin first, and then, with another upright young man as an associate joined to him, and having informed the others whom they knew to be well disposed, Farel presented himself in the Council Chamber, where a great part of the city gathered, the accusers, astonished and already anxious about themselves, heard Farel and begged pardon for their fault. Thus almost this whole year was spent contending against the wicked, both for doctrine and for discipline, with a prosperous outcome everywhere, except for one wound: the death, untimely, of the most pious King Edward, which not only England but all the Christian Churches received with grief.

units.la: Et tamen eo ipso Caluinus scribendo etiam intentus, egregios illos in Ioannem commentarios emisit. Liceat hic nobis & vtinam immerito testari de Serueto, quod de gemino monstro, Paulo Samosateno videlicet, & Ario Alexandrino, veteres illi patres experientia ipsa edocti scripserunt, ab iis nimirum primum orta incendia, quibus omnes orbis Christiani Ecclesiae postea penè deflagrarunt. Sumptum enim optimo iure Geneuae de Serueto supplicium non vt de sectario quodam, sed tanquam de monstro ex mera impietate horrendisque blasphemiis conflato, quibus totos annos triginta tum voce tum scripto coelum ac terra infecerat, ne nunc quidem dici potest quatopere Satanae rabiem exacerbarit, exorta flamma, quae Poloniam primum, inde Transylvaniam & Vngariam corripuit: & vtinam non longius perua serit. Quod & ipse Satanico plane spiritu praedixisse merito videri potest, quum hanc ex Apocalyp. sententiam ea qua caetera confuerat conscientia descriptam, illi suo libro praefari iberet: Factum est in coelo praelium magnum, Michael & Angeli eius pugnantes cum dracone. Verè id quidem, si Cum non pro κατά, sed pro συ accipias. Vix igitur desierant calere infoelicis illius cineres, quum de poenis haereticorum quaeri coepit: quibusdam coercendos quidem, sed victimo supplicio affici iure non posse opinantibus, aliis quasi de haeresi satis ex Dei verbo liquere non posset, & de Religionis capitibus omnibus in vtranque partem sentire Academicorum more liceat, existimantibus vnius Dei ef se iudicio relinquendos. Illam opinionem boni etiam nonnulli tuebantur, veriti nimirum ne si aliter sentirent, tyrannorum in pios saevitiam accendere viderentur. Istius autem auctores quorum principes erant Sebastianus Castellio, & Laelius Socinus, suo ipsorum causam agentes: illae quidem occultius, ille vero apertius, vt qui sua quadam in Sacrorum Bibliorum peruerfionem praefatione palam verbi diuini satis perspicuam auctoritatem conuellere studuisset, suisque in priorem ad Corinth. Epistolam adnotationibus, vt a verbo scripto tanquam imperfecto nos abducerent, diserte scripsisset, Paulum quandam Theologiam ea quam scriptis tradidisset reconditiorem, perfectos nescio quos, suos discipulos docuisse. Itaque quum anno M.D.LIII. incunte Caluinus subscribentibus Collegis omnibus copiosam Serueti doctrinae refutationem edidisset, adiectis etiam rationibus cur & quatenus a Magistratu quoque legitima praeunte cognitione puniri haereticos oporteret, opposuerunt istifarraginem partim ex scriptis piorum Doctorum depravatis, partim ex fanaticorum quorundam ignoti alioquin nominis schedis conscriptam, Martini cuiusdam Belli nomine (is ipse fuit Castellio, quanuis id postea eiurarit) praefationi inscripto, & emendatio Ciuitatis.
units.tr: Yet even while he was busy with his writing, Calvin also published those excellent commentaries on John. Here I may, and I wish I did not do so unjustly, bear witness concerning Servetus. The ancient Fathers, taught by experience itself, wrote of the twin monster, Paul of Samosata and Arius of Alexandria, that from these men first arose the fires by which almost all the churches of the Christian world were afterwards set ablaze. For the execution of Servetus at Geneva was rightly carried out, not as against some sectarian, but as against a monster compounded of sheer impiety and horrible blasphemies, with which for thirty years he had infected heaven and earth, both by voice and by writing. Even now it cannot be said how greatly that punishment stirred up Satan's rage. A flame broke out which first seized Poland, then Transylvania and Hungary, and would that it did not spread further. He himself can seem rightly to have foretold this with a truly satanic spirit, when he prefaced his book with this sentence from the Apocalypse, written down with the same conscience with which he had written everything else: "There was a great battle in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting with the dragon." Truly so, if you take "with" [σύν] rather than "against" [κατά]. Scarcely had the ashes of that unhappy man ceased to smoulder when the question began to be raised of how heretics should be punished. Some held that they should indeed be restrained, but could not rightly be put to death. Others said that on the points of heresy the Word of God did not give sufficiently clear light, and that on all the heads of religion one may hold opinions on either side in the manner of the Academics, leaving them to the judgment of God alone. Some good men also defended that opinion, fearing that if they thought otherwise they would seem to fuel the cruelty of tyrants against the godly. The authors of this view, of whom the chief were Sebastian Castellio and Laelius Socinus, pursued their own cause: the one more secretly, the other more openly. Castellio, in a certain preface to his translation of the Holy Bible, had tried openly to overthrow the authority of the divine Word, which is quite plain, and in his notes on the First Epistle to the Corinthians he had plainly written that, in order to lead us away from the written Word as imperfect, Paul taught some more recondite theology than he had committed to writing, to some perfect people, his disciples, I know not who. So when Calvin, at the beginning of the year 1553, with all his colleagues subscribing, had published a full refutation of Servetus' doctrine, adding also reasons why heretics ought to be punished by the magistrate too, after lawful examination, these men set against it a medley partly drawn from the corrupted writings of pious teachers, partly from the pamphlets of certain fanatics otherwise unknown, published under the name of a certain Martin Bellius (this was Castellio himself, though he later denied it), with a preface headed "Correction of the City," in which they claimed that this medley had been published.

units.la: M.D. LIII. mitatis nomine, in qua editam fuisse hanc farraginem mendi-bantur. Huic autem non tantum illo errore, sed multis etiā blas-phemiis scatenti libello postea respondi, ut ea molestia Caluinū longè melioribus curis, scribendis nimirum eruditissimis in Ge-nesim Commentariis intentum, & aliis itidem de quibus dice-mus Ecclesiæ suæ depellendis periculis occupatum, liberarem.
units.tr: ...in the name of the City, in which they falsely claimed this medley had been published. I afterwards replied to this booklet, which teems not only with that error but with many blasphemies as well, so as to free Calvin from that annoyance, so that he could give himself to far better cares: namely, writing his most learned Commentaries on Genesis, and warding off dangers from his own Church, which I will discuss in other places.

units.la: Pergebant enim rebus nouandis intenti factiosi: & quanuis rur-sum secunda Febr. coram Senatu solenni promisso sancita esset ἀμνηστία, tamen seipsis quotidie deteriores euadebant: vtrinque valde occupato Caluino, dum & illos pro suo more increpan-do ad meliorem frugem reuocare, & bonos aduersus illorum improbitatem confirmare studeret. Nam eo usque processerunt improbi, ut verbum Dei in obscoenas cantiones transformaret, & obuios vespere peregrinos pulsarent, ac interdum etiam spo-liarent. Ptiuatim vero ac proprie Rolseci, Castellionis, & aliorū quorundam de veritate scilicet valde solicitorum hominum o-pera vtebantur, controuersiæ de prædestinatione renouandæ: adeo vt famosum libellum conuitiorum plenum eūmque ano-nymon sparsisse non contenti, qu fidum illum Dei seruum mi-ris modis lacerabant, miserit Castellio Latinum alterum Lutetiæ clam excudendum: cui postea respondi, sicut & ipse Caluinus quasdam eiusdem argumenti ineptias certis capitibus compre-hensas refutauit. Incumbebat etiam eo tum temporis ex Anglia profugorum cura, quorum alij Vezaliæ, alij Emdæ, aliidenique Francofurti confederant, omnes à Caluino consilium subinde flagitantes: nec parum etiam angebatur quorundam in Gallicæ Argentinensis Ecclesiæ ab ipso olim plantatæ pastorum audacia, aliorum occulto fuore adiuta. Denique quantopere hoc anno pro variis Ecclesiis laborarit, testis est insignis literatum copia, quibus & Magnates multos ad amplectendum Euangelium ex-citauit, & fratres plurimos alios non procul ab extremis pericu-lis, alios in vinculis positos maximo cum fructu confirmauit. Diximus antea de doctrinæ Sacramentorum inter omnes Hel-ueticas & Rheticas Ecclesias consensu edito, maxima doctorum & bonorum omnium gratulatione. Displicuit haec concordia spiritui erroris, cuius iam pridem ea est quā cernimus efficacia. Itaque facile reperit qui sopitum ignem foderet, Ioachimum ni-mirum quendam Vvestphalum: cui claslicum canenti, succinuit postea Heshusius tunc verbi Minister, nunc etiam Episcopus, de quibus mox dicendum nobis erit. Ac tunc quidem Caluinus co sensionis illius explicationem edidit, quæ quò magis rabiem i-storum exacuit, eò magis omnibus veritatis amantibus profuit.
units.tr: For the factious men, intent on upsetting things, kept pressing on. Although, on the second of February, an amnesty [ἀμνηστία] had been confirmed by solemn promise before the Senate, they became worse every day. Calvin was greatly burdened on both sides: he strove both to call those men back to a better way, rebuking them as was his custom, and to strengthen the good against their wickedness. The wicked went so far that they turned the Word of God into obscene songs, and assaulted strangers they met in the evening, and sometimes even robbed them. Privately and especially, they used the efforts of Bolsec, Castellio and certain others, men who were truly very anxious about the truth, to renew the controversy about predestination. Not content with having spread a famous and anonymous libel full of insults, in which they tore that faithful servant of God in wondrous ways, Castellio sent another Latin one to be secretly printed at Lyons. I later replied to it, and Calvin himself also refuted certain absurdities of the same kind, gathered under definite heads. At that time the care of the exiles from England also weighed on him. Some of them had settled at Wesel, some at Emden, others finally at Frankfurt, and all of them repeatedly asked Calvin for advice. He was no less troubled by the boldness of some pastors of the French church at Strasbourg, which he had himself once planted, a boldness helped by the secret rage of others. Finally, how greatly he laboured this year for various Churches is witnessed by the remarkable number of his letters. By them he stirred up many nobles to embrace the Gospel, and he strengthened very many brothers, some who were not far from the greatest dangers, others who were in chains, with the greatest fruit. We have said before that the agreement on the doctrine of the Sacraments was published among all the Helvetic and Rhaetian Churches, to the great rejoicing of all learned and good men. This concord displeased the spirit of error, whose efficacy, as we see, has long been at work. So he easily found someone to stir up the smouldering fire, namely a certain Joachim Westphal. When he sounded the trumpet, Heshusius, then a minister of the Word and now also a bishop, joined in the chorus; of them we must speak shortly. Calvin, at that time, published an explanation of his view on this matter, and the more it inflamed the rage of those men, the more it benefited all lovers of the truth.

units.la: Annus vero proximè cōsecutus mirifico Dei beneficio Reipub. ac Ecclesiæ Geneuensi optatam quietem à domesticis certamisibus attulit: factiosis autem sua ipsorum opera perlitis, horren da coniuratione peropportune per ebriosorum quosrundam ex conscriorum numero petulantem audaciā detecta: & aliis quidē capitis supplicio affectis, aliis vero solum vertentibus: qui etsi aliquandiu postea ciuitate vexarūt, turpiter tamen omnes postea intereuntes, singulare seri quidem, sed iusti diuini iudicij exemplum praebuerunt. Sic liberata fuit ab his pestibus Respub. quum altero Dei beneficio paulo ante allato quatuor Hlucticarūm ciuitatum respōnso (quarum sententiam diximus ad annum superiorem vsum Senatui fuisse super Ecclesiastica Geneuensi disciplina percontari) vetera omnia Ecclesiasticae politiae edicta, contra factiosorum expectationem, communibus cuiam suffra giis rogata, perlataque fuissent. Non defuit tamen in quo tū quoque Calvinus strenue exerceretur. Nam foris quidem tum de Polonicis Ecclesiis voluntate Regis constituendis, tum de furiosa illa tempestate commutatis in Anglia rebus excitata, quae tres illos incomparabilis pietatis Episcopos & Martyres Ioānem Hopperum, Nicolaum Ridlæum, & Hugonem Latimerum inter tot alios fere innumerabiles, ac tandem etiam magnum illū Cranmerum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum in coelum vsque expulit, consolandis denique fratribus in Gallia vinctis, ac praesertim quinque fortissimis Martyribus hoc ipso anno Cameraci crudelissimè crematis, plurimum laborauit. Domi vero Seruetii cineres pullulare coeperunt: cuius blasphemiis fauere deprehensus Matthæus Gribaldus non incelebris Iurisconsultus, quum Geneuam forte venisset (erat enim Fargiarum dominus, qui pagus est in Geneuæ vicinia) deductus ad Calvinum à qu bufd am Italis, apud quos ille Patauij docuerat, recusante Calvino dextram illi porrigere, nisi prius de primario Christianæ fidei articulo, id est de sacra Triade & Deitate Christi inter eos conuenirent, nullum postea locum vllis admonitionibus vel argumentis reliquit. Itaque quod ei iam tum praedixit Calvinus, graue nimirum Dei iudicium pertinaci ipsius impietati imminere, ..hoc re ipsa postea expertus est. Tubinga primum profugus, quo fuerat Vergerij fauore introductus: Bernæ postea captus, simulaque abnegatione liberatus ad ingenium postea redi ens, Gentilis de quo mox dicemus fautor & hospes, superueniente demum peste correptus, paratum sibi supplicium praeuenit. Aliud dienique Calvinum huius anni solidum gaudium gaudere prohibuit. Patorum videlicet vicinorum pastorum f. ctio, qui sponte alio qui currentes, Bolseco praeterea instigante, vt sibi nomen aliquod ex tanti viri reprehensione quaererent, homines alioqui multis iam notis aspersi, non aliter in eum debacchabantur, quàm si Deum idcirco facerent malorum auctorem, quod ab externa æterna Dei prouidentia & ordinatione nihil excluderet. His calumniis de quibus antea nos quoque aliquid diximus, etsi nihil ille mouebatur, tandem tamen illorum maledicentia coactus, impetrauit à Senatu, vt vnà cum legatis Bernam profectus, veritatis causam coram Bernensibus ipsis ageret. Acta igitur illic causa est, & Sebastianus quidam infamia & exilio multatus: Bolsecus excedere finibus tum quidem iussus: neque tamen tum quicquam illis de re ipsa definire visum est, ita Domino Ecclesiæ suæ consulente. Visus enim fuisset Caluinus auctoritate vel gratia ob inuidiam, quod vtrò postea contigit. Nam & illæ omnes calumniæ nò ita multò post in fumos abierunt, & Andreas Zebedæus accusator acerrimus, Caluino iam mortuo, quum & ipse iam esset moriturus Neuiduni oppido quatuor milliaribus Geneua distante, accitis præcipuis, quibus, vltrò agnita quam oppugnarat veritate, & acta illa sua detestans, schedas omnes suas spectante se concremari iussit, iudicio certè meliore, quàm si hæc fuissent mille Senatus consultis imperata. Anno deinceps altero, Caluinum im prudentem tertiana in concione inuasit, ac tandem inuitum ex suggesto coegit descendere, multis indefalsis sequutis rumoribus, iisque vsque adeò Pontificiis gratis, vt de Caluini morte solenni supplicatione Nouioduni Caluini patriæ, Canonici suis idolis gratias egerint. Sed vicerunt bonorum preces: tantumque abfuit vt Caluinus ex eo morbo interiret, vt contrà veluti nouis auctus viribus, longum iter præter morem Francofurtum vsque videlicet ingrederetur, quo fuerat pacandis Ecclesiæ Gallicæ quæ iam tum illic erat, diuidiis euocatus. Hinc demum ille rediens, licet afflicta nonnihil valetudine, nihil tamen de quotidianis laboribus remisit, editis anno consequente in omnes Psalmos Commentarias longe doctissimis, quibus præfationem vere pretiosam adiunxit. Annum autem istum alioqui ob tumultus à Ministris illis factiosis nonnullis excitatos valde turbulentum, & tritici caritate infamem, cōsumpsit partim tuendæ aduersus Ioachimum Vvestphalum veritati: quùmque Vvestphalo postremum respondisset, nec ille tamen gratiendi fidem faceret, has partes in me recepi, eo per Dei gratiam cuius minimè pœnitere me posse euenit. Tunc quoq; tum ab illo, tum etiā à me refutatæ sunt Castellionis aduersus æterna Dei prædestinationem calumniæ, quas ille suppresso nomine spargendas curarat. Graui rer autem illū imprimis excruciauit sæuissima præsertim Lutetiæ orta piorum persecutio, intercepto illorum cœtu in vico Iacobæo, quò ad celebrandam cœnam Domini conuenerant. Ex eorum numero cæteris per noctis tenebras elapsis, capti sunt circiter octoginta, multíque cum opprobriis ac conuitiis prima luce in carceres perstracti, quanuis aliquot etiā primæ nobilitatis mu-
units.tr: The following year, by a wonderful gift of God, brought the Republic and the Church of Geneva the longed-for quiet from domestic strife. The factious men were ruined by their own efforts, and a dreadful conspiracy was most opportunely uncovered through the wanton audacity of some drunkards from among the Council of Sixty. Some were put to death, others fled from the city. Although some of these later troubled the city for a while, all of them afterwards perished in disgrace, providing a singular example, though a sad one, of the just judgment of God. Thus the Republic was freed from these plagues. At the same time, another gift of God came shortly before, namely the reply of four Helvetic cities (whose opinion, as we said, the Senate had the year before sought concerning Geneva's ecclesiastical discipline). All the old edicts of the ecclesiastical polity were, contrary to the expectation of the factious men, put to the vote and passed by the common suffrages. Nor was there lacking matter in which Calvin too was vigorously employed. Abroad, he laboured greatly both on the establishing of the Polish Churches according to the king's will, and on the affairs of England, which had been thrown into turmoil by the furious storm of changed circumstances there, a storm that drove into heaven those three bishops and martyrs of incomparable piety, John Hooper, Nicholas Ridley and Hugh Latimer, along with almost countless others, and at last even the great Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury. Finally, he laboured much to console the brothers imprisoned in France, and especially five most valiant martyrs who were most cruelly burned at Cambrai this same year. At home, the ashes of Servetus began to stir again. Matthew Gribaldi, a not unknown jurist, was caught favouring his blasphemies. When he happened to come to Geneva (for he was lord of Farges, a village near Geneva), he was brought to Calvin by certain Italians among whom he had taught at Padua. Calvin refused to give him his right hand unless they first agreed on the primary article of the Christian faith, namely the holy Trinity and the Deity of Christ. After that, Gribaldi left no room for any admonitions or arguments. So what Calvin had already foretold to him, that a grievous judgment of God hung over his obstinate impiety, he afterwards found to be true in fact. Gribaldi first fled to Tübingen, where he had been introduced through the favour of Vergerius; later he was taken at Bern, and, once freed by recantation, returned to his old disposition. Then he became a supporter and host of Gentilis, of whom we shall speak shortly. Finally, when the plague came upon him, he anticipated the punishment prepared for him. Another matter also prevented Calvin from enjoying the solid joy of this year. The faction of some neighbouring pastors, who of their own accord ran elsewhere, with Bolsec also egging them on, sought some name for themselves by reproaching so great a man. These men, already tainted by many known charges, raged against him in no other way than as if they were making God the author of evils because he excluded nothing from His external and eternal providence and ordination. Although Calvin was not moved by these calumnies, of which we too have said something before, he was at last compelled by their slander and obtained from the Senate that he should go to Bern with the envoys and plead the cause of truth before the Bernese themselves. The case was therefore heard there, and a certain Sebastian was punished with infamy and exile. Bolsec was then ordered to leave the territory, yet it did not seem right at that time to settle the matter itself, the Lord of His Church so providing. For Calvin would have seemed to act from authority or favour, out of ill will, which later did in fact happen. For all those calumnies vanished into smoke not long afterwards, and Andreas Zebedaeus, a most bitter accuser, when Calvin was already dead and he himself was about to die at Neuveville, a town four miles from Geneva, summoned the chief men, and freely acknowledging the truth he had attacked and detesting his former deeds, ordered all his pamphlets to be burned before his eyes. This was certainly a better judgment than if a thousand decrees of the Senate had commanded it. In the next year, Calvin was unexpectedly attacked by a tertian fever in the sermon, and at last compelled, against his will, to come down from the pulpit. Many false rumours followed, and they were so welcome to the Papists that, on the report of Calvin's death, the canons of Noyon, his native town, celebrated a solemn thanksgiving to their idols. But the prayers of the good prevailed, and so far was Calvin from dying of that illness that, on the contrary, as if renewed with new strength, he undertook a long journey, contrary to his custom, all the way to Frankfurt, to which he had been called by the parties to quiet the French Church there, which was already divided at that time. Returning from there, although his health was somewhat weakened, he relaxed nothing of his daily labours, and the following year he published commentaries on all the Psalms, most learned, to which he added a truly precious preface. That year, otherwise very turbulent because of the tumults stirred up by certain factious ministers and infamous for the dearness of wheat, he spent partly in defending the truth against Joachim Westphal. When he had given Westphal his final reply, and yet Westphal did not stop his clamour, I took up this part myself, by the grace of God, and it has turned out that I have never been sorry for it. At that time too, the calumnies of Castellio against the eternal predestination of God were refuted, first by Westphal and then by me, which he had secretly arranged to spread under no name. But a most cruel persecution of the godly, which arose especially at Paris, grieved him greatly: their assembly was broken up in the Rue Saint-Jacques, where they had come together to celebrate the Lord's Supper. Of their number, the others escaped through the darkness of night, but about eighty were taken and dragged, amid many insults and abuse, into prison at first light, although several women of the highest nobility were among them. The king's anger was inflamed not only by those who stood about him but also by the occasion of the times. For that signal defeat at Saint-Quentin had just been received, and the godly had gathered by night because they were in no way allowed to do so by day.

units.la: C.iiij. lieres in iis cernerentur. Accendebant Regis irâ non modò qui illum circunstabant, verum etiam ipsa temporum occasio. Hæc enim tum inciderùt, quum insignis illa clades ad Sanquinium esset accepta: & nocte conuenerant pii, quòd illis interdiu nullo modo licebat. Itaque veteris illæ & ramosæ calùniæ in Christianos olim excogitatæ, tunc quoque auctore quodam Demochare & Sorbonico Doctore repositæ sunt, quasi videlicet omnium malorum causa vnis verè Christianis esset tribuenda. Subortì nati etiam qui λυχνομυχῖται confirmarent, quibus credùli plerique assentiebantur. Producti sunt igitur ad flammas ad septem terrepetito exemplo: in quorum primo accesita est nobis quædam mulier, cuius demum vt & sex aliorum atque in his nouissimorum tuorum adolescentium constanti plane fuit admirabilis. Verùm partim detecta quidem, sed minime tamen coercita Sorbonicorum calumnia, matre nempe captiuas secum filias quæ constupratæ dicebantur, ad inspectionem iudicibus offerente, & optimo quodam doctissimoque viro pastore aliquot ante menses ibi agente, egregio libello cuncta illa mendacia facile reuincente, partim interuenientium Germanorum Priincipum legatione quam summa celeritate Calvinus procurauit, repressas illa nonnihil conquieuit. Annus hunc consequutus, Reipub. Genevensi felix illuxit perpetua inter Bernenses & Genevenses inita confœderatione, contra exulum illorum expectationem. Sed hanc felicitatem multa quoque aduersa aliunde comitata sunt, præter etiam exulum irritos vltimos conatus, de quibus plura dicere non constitui. Nam foris quidem recrudescebat in Gallia persecutio, domi vero ex Seruetii cineribus auctore quodam Valentino Gentili Cosentino, tetrerrima Tritheitarum hæresis pullulabat. Itaque vt illis malis occurreretur, missi sunt ad Germaniæ Principes cum Calvini literis, qui tot Ecclesiarum calamitatibus expositis, intercessionem eorum postularent dum assiduis literis interea laborantes Calvinus confirmabat. Cum Gentilis vero quid actum sit, quis denique fuerit istius monstri exitus, paucis commemorabo. Extat enim tota hæc historia partim ab ipso Calvino exactis publicis, partim à Benedicto Arretio Bernensi Theologo pastore fideliter descripta, a dicta que blasphemiarum ipsius refutatio, quæque omnia aliæque eodem congesta quæ ad illud argumentum pertinent, edita sunt in hac ciuitate anno Domini LXVII. supra sesquimillesimum. Ergo intæl x iste sagaci quidem sed vafro sophisticoque ingenio præditus, aliquan tò post sumptum de Seruet o supplicium, nactus illius librorum, itemque Calvini refutationem, facile animaduertit neque illius spectra & ideas quibus Samosateni hæresis ille colorauerat, neque inuectam à Sabellio personarum cum Essentia confusionem, Deitatatem denique Christi qualem impurus Arrius fictitiam esse docuiuit,cum verbo Dei conciliari posse.Et quum rursus quæ in Scriptpturis de vna Dei essentia, & tribus inter se te ipsa distinctis hypostasibus traduntur, intelligentiæ nostræ minimè quadrate videretur.fecit quod eiusmodi ingenia confuevuerunt,id est non se Dei sapientiæ submisit, sed id demum verum esse sibi persuasit quoad cum humana ratione consentiret.Itaque Monarchia ad unicam Patris personam transfusa, quem solum illum & unicum ἀνὰ τὸ ὁ Θεὸς esse voluit,Essentiationem,id est Essentiæ propagationem,n,tresque numero vt personas sic etiam Essentias, id est tres numero Deos,tres æternos,omnipotentes immensos aperte pro fiteri ci cœpit,eoque non modo sacrum Dei verbum, sed ipsius etiam Synodi Nicenæ (repudiato tamen Athanasij Symbolo) & voluminum scriptorum, videlicet Ignatij, Tertulliani,Irenæi & Lactantij auctoritatem inaudita quadam impudentia detorquere. Alios os enim omnes orthodoxos scriptores Nycenam Synodum sequuntur, non tantum repudiabat, sed etiam vt impios sugillabat. Hanc autem blasphemiam alixe quoque de hypostatica vnione sequebantur. Hæc clanculum initio inter paucos quasi disputationis causa agitata (quorum præcipui fuerunt Ioan. Paulus Alciatus Mediolanensis Miles, & Georgius Blandrata Salucienfis medicus) tandemque Italico presbytero nuntiata, caufifcim cogendo extra ordinem cœtui præbuerunt, vbi coram delectatis sanatoribus omnibusque Ministris ac Presbyteris, patientur auauditis, ac ex Dei verbo per Calvinum refutatis quæcunque illi profiteri voluerunt, ita res est composita, vt scriptæ orthodoxæ fidei ei omnes Itali statim subscriberent, sex duntaxat exceptis: qui tamen & ipsi postea seorsum vocati, manu quidem at corde non irem m vt postea apparuit,subscripserunt. Rediens igitur ad ingenium Gi Gentilis, eandemque blasphemiam rursum spargere deprehensus capitur,captus nihil dissimulat, auditus quandiu & quantum in voluit.Tandem veluti vitus(nec enim aliud habebat quam pertinaciā quod Calvino regeneretur) resipiscentiā incredibile simulatur,cuius etiam exemplum proprium ipsius manu scriptum extat. Quid id plura? abnegatione per compita civitatis fidem dimittitur præstitisse iureiurando sese portas vrbis no excessuri: mox tamen violata fide ad Matthæum Gribaldum in Subaudia fugit. Sequuntur aliquanto post Alciatus & Blandrata, Transylvaniæ & vicinarum regionum vastatores futuri. Gentilis autem iam tum in mineinente illi Dei iudicio apud Gribaldum manes (nam veteres illos alios os & imperitos & indoctos homines cotemnebat) ibique libellum aduersus Athanasium & Calvinum cudens, induxit ugdu numerum transiens, vbi excudendum illum (inscripta Gaienii Pre secto istorum scelerum profusa insciο præfatione) curauit, deinde Lugduni hescio quo modo à Pontificiis raptus, quum sese in Caluinum scribere dixisset, tanquam bene de Ecclesia Catholica meritus di mittitur. Inde in Morauiā ad Blandratam & Alciatum aliosque nihilo meliores discedit: vbi quū satis inter eos conuenire nō possent, à Tritheismo ad Samosatenum plerique trahuntur, veluti trahente illū ad poenam ipsius Christi manu, in Sabaudiā ad suū Gribaldūredit. At illam pestem alteram iam pestis fuisse ulterat. Eripitus etiam nobis iam erat Caluinus. Tum ille siue peni tus amés, siue q; mortuo Caluino, nemo nem superesse consideret à quo reuinceretur, recta ad Gaïensem ipsum Praefectum ipsi mei itò infestū venit: à quo mox agnitus, & Bernam iusto Dei iudicio ex superiori illa fluctuatione ad dicendū causam missus, tum per iuriorum, tum i probitas manifestae conuictus, frustra tentatis omnibus quibus in recta viam reuocaretur, capite multatus, dignas tandem tot scelicribus poenas persoluit. Hic igitur postea fuit illius causae exitus. Et tamen ne nunc quidem desunt egregij scilicet Christianismi assertores, tum ex Catholicis, tum ex bonis illis Vbiquitarijs, qui Caluinum audeant tanquam earum blasphemiarum auctorem, imò etiam vt qui Atheismo siue Mahumetismo aditum aperuerit, calumniari: quibus tamen ab illum stetentibus, easipsas blasphemias primus Caluinus, ac pene vnius toto tempore tanto labore coarguit. Lutetiae vero Cardinalis ex cuius nutu Rex cuncta administrabat, criminis haereseos cognitionem à iudicibus ordinariis & laicis quos vocant, ad Triumuiros Cardinales traducere conatus, repugnate diuinitus; potius quam humanitus Parisiensi Parlamento vtpote qui iam ipsius nō Christi causam ageret, totum illud nefariū consilium omnis fit. Sed extremus hic annus initiū nobis maioris lucis attulit, corrépto quattuor Caluino mense Octobri, quem morbum experti i tandé sumus nimium vere dicere medicos sentibus letalem esse. Etsi enim morbus ille Caluino octimestris tantum fuit, sic tamen cor pusculum illud macilentum, & laboribus ac viribus attritum, cón fecit, vt nunquam post a penitus conualuerit. Interim illud quatuor monentibus medicis & obtestantibus nobis vt ferre tandem aliquando respicere, abstinere quidem necessario à concio nib iis & praelectionibus interea vero literis vndiquaq; distantibus, & variis scribendis d[?] ac non ostes impendere, nec aliud habere frequentius in ore, quam sibi acerbum esse vitam vt ipse aliebat, otiosam: quia nos interim valentes pracillo ociosi videri possemus. Cuius rei testes sunt Christianae Institutionis vltima editio tum Latina tum Gallica, & Commentarij in Isaiam ab eo non tam emendati, quam nouis proctus emissi. Insignis fuit annus cosequentibus duo rum potentissimorum Regum pace arctissimā, cōtracta a assini tate,
units.tr: ...women were seen among them. The king's anger was inflamed not only by those who stood around him but also by the circumstances of the time. These events fell at the moment when that famous disaster at Saint-Quentin had just been received, and the godly had gathered at night because they were in no way allowed to meet by day. So the old and branching slanders once devised against Christians were revived then, under the authority of a certain Demochares and a Doctor of the Sorbonne, as if the one true Christians were to be blamed for all the country's misfortunes. Some even arose to affirm the λυχνομυχῖται [lychnomychitae, "lamp-creepers"], and many credulous people assented to them. Seven were therefore brought to the flames, following the same pattern. Among the first of them a certain woman was brought before us, and, after her, six others, and among these your youngest sons, whose constancy was truly admirable. Yet the Sorbonne's calumny was partly exposed but by no means checked. The mother offered to the judges the daughters she had kept with her, who were said to have been violated, for inspection. A certain excellent and most learned minister, who was then working there some months before, refuted all those lies easily in an outstanding little book. Partly, too, the attack was somewhat quieted by the embassy of the German princes, which Calvin arranged with the greatest speed. The year that followed shone happily upon the Genevan commonwealth, through the perpetual alliance entered into with the Bernese, contrary to the expectation of those exiles. But this happiness was also accompanied by many adversities from elsewhere, besides the futile last attempts of the exiles, about which I have decided not to say more. For abroad the persecution in France was breaking out again, while at home, from the ashes of Servetus, the most horrible heresy of the Tritheites was sprouting, under the leadership of a certain Valentine Gentilis of Cosenza. So that these evils might be met, men were sent to the princes of Germany with letters from Calvin, who, setting out the calamities of so many churches, were to ask for their intercession, while Calvin in the meantime strengthened them by his constant letters. As to what was done with Gentilis, and what finally became of that monster, I will briefly recount. For the whole story survives, partly in the public records which Calvin himself obtained, partly as faithfully described by Benedict Aretius, a Bernese theologian and minister, and the refutation of his blasphemies, together with all these and other materials gathered in that same matter, was published in this city in the year of the Lord 1567. So this man, endowed with a shrewd but crafty and sophistical mind, after the execution of Servetus, obtained his books and Calvin's refutation of them. He easily perceived that neither those phantoms and ideas with which the heresy of Samosata had coloured itself, nor the confusion of persons with essence brought in by Sabellius, nor finally the Deity of Christ, which the impure Arius taught to be fictitious, could be reconciled with the Word of God. And when, again, what the Scriptures hand down about the one essence of God and the three hypostases distinct among themselves seemed in no way to fit our understanding, he did what such minds are accustomed to do: he did not submit himself to the wisdom of God, but persuaded himself that only that was true which agreed with human reason. Therefore, transferring the monarchy to the single person of the Father, whom alone he wished to be the one [εἷς ὁ Θεός] God, he began to profess openly an "essentiation," that is, a propagation of the essence, and three essences in number as well as three persons, three eternal, omnipotent, immense gods. By this he twisted, with an unheard-of impudence, not only the sacred Word of God but also the authority of the Synod of Nicaea (though he rejected the Creed of Athanasius) and of the writings of Ignatius, Tertullian, Irenaeus and Lactantius. For he not only rejected all the other orthodox writers who follow the Synod of Nicaea, but also reviled them as impious. Other blasphemies about the hypostatic union followed this one. These matters were at first stirred up secretly among a few, as a matter for discussion (the chief of whom were John Paul Alciati of Milan, a soldier, and Giorgio Blandrata of Saluzzo, a physician). At last, when these were reported to an Italian elder, they provided the occasion for calling an extraordinary assembly, where, in the presence of the learned senators and all the ministers and elders, having been heard patiently, and refuted from the Word of God by Calvin, whatever they wished to profess was settled in such a way that all the Italians immediately subscribed to the written orthodox faith, except six only. These too, afterwards called aside individually, subscribed, though in hand rather than in heart, as later became clear. So Gentilis, returning to his nature and found again spreading the same blasphemy, was seized; when captured he concealed nothing, and was heard for as long and as much as he wished. At last, as if corrected (for he had nothing else than obstinacy, by which he might be refuted by Calvin), he feigned a repentance that was hard to believe, and an example of it, written in his own hand, survives. What more? After he had been dismissed with a recantation at the crossroads of the city, he swore an oath that he would not leave the gates of the city; yet soon, his faith broken, he fled to Matthew Gribaldi in Savoy. Shortly afterwards Alciati and Blandrata followed, destined to be the devastators of Transylvania and the neighbouring regions. Gentilis, however, already then, awaiting the just judgment of God, remained with Gribaldi (for he despised those old orthodox writers as unlearned and ignorant men), and there, forging a little book against Athanasius and Calvin, he passed over into the Grisons, where he had it printed, with a preface addressed to Gaiensis, the Prefect, unaware of these crimes. Then, seized at Lyon by the Papists in some way, when he said he was writing against Calvin, he was let go as one who had deserved well of the Catholic Church. From there he went to Moravia, to Blandrata and Alciati and others no better than they; where, since they could not agree well among themselves, most of them were drawn from Tritheism to Samosatenism, as if Christ's own hand were drawing them to punishment; and he returned to his Gribaldi in Savoy. But that other plague had already become a plague of another kind. Calvin had also already been snatched from us. Then Gentilis, either out of repentance, or because, Calvin being dead, he thought no one remained by whom he could be refuted, went straight to Gaiensis, the Prefect himself, who was hostile to him. Recognised by him at once, he was sent by the just judgment of God, from that former wandering, to Berne to plead his cause; there he was convicted by the judgment of the judges and by the clear proof of his own wrongdoing; after all means had been tried in vain by which he might be called back to the right way, he was condemned to death and at last paid the punishments due to so many crimes. This, then, was the outcome of that affair. And yet even now there are no lack of distinguished defenders of Christianity, both among the Catholics and among those good Ubiquitarians, who dare to slander Calvin as the author of those blasphemies, and even as one who opened the way to atheism or Mahometanism. Yet, while these people stand by their view, Calvin himself was the first, and well nigh the only one, who refuted those very blasphemies, with such labour through the whole time. At Paris, meanwhile, the Cardinal, at whose nod the king administered everything, tried to transfer the cognisance of the crime of heresy from the ordinary judges and the so-called laymen to the Cardinal Triumvirs; this was divinely, rather than humanly, resisted, and the whole wicked plan came to nothing, since the Parisian Parlement was acting not for Christ's cause but for his own. But this last year brought us a greater light, when in October Calvin was seized by a quartan fever, a disease which we have learned, too truly, that physicians call deadly to the senses. For although that illness lasted only eight months for Calvin, it so consumed that thin little body, worn down by labours and strength, that he never afterwards fully recovered. Meanwhile, the physicians advised him, and we begged him, at last to take some care of himself, to abstain of necessity from sermons and lectures, and in the meantime to devote himself to writing letters to all quarters and to various works. But he had nothing more often on his lips than that, as he said, it was bitter to him to live an idle life, since we, in the meantime, being well, might seem to him idle to a fault. The witnesses of this are the last edition of the Christian Institution, both Latin and French, and his commentaries on Isaiah, which he issued not so much corrected as newly produced. The year that followed was remarkable for the very close peace made between the two most powerful kings, and an alliance agreed upon...

units.la: M D. LIX. tate, extxtremus idem fortasse Geneuesi Ciuitati futurus, nisi Pontificiorum consilia qui regis Henrici simplicitate abutebantur, diuinitus fuissent impedita. Constat enim Henricū seucrissimis positis es edictis, adeoque in carcerem coiectis aliquot Senatoribus (qui tamen si per dnm Concilium vniuersale cogeretur, mitius in causa R Religionis agendum censebant) hoc vnum imprimis sibi proposuisse habuisse, vt restituta suo Duci Sabaudia, Geneuā fun-ditus euerteret: Geneuæ contrā laborāte imprimis Caluino quā-tuis valetudinario, atque tum grauissimè afflictis Ecclesiis cun-ctósque fratres confirmante, tum etiā precibus assiduis opem à Domino flagitante. Ecce autem in medio illo eminus iuxtà ac cominus vigente terrore, Rex ipse in ipso celebrandarū nuptia-rum apparatu, quibus pacem firmabat, ludicro hastarū concursu letale vt vulnus accepit: atque illud etiā eiusdē vnius hominis manu, cui ai regioru n stipatorum tunc Præfecto, Senatores illos comprehendendos paulò ante rex ipse mandarat: quam cædē postea Cardinalis Lotharingus x x Decemb. d Clarissimi Iurisconsulti, ac interregrimi Senatoris, sanctissimi denique Christi Martyris Annæ æ Burgij morte in quissima videri voluit expiasse. Geneua autē si singulari Dei beneficio in eam cōsilentiam illis quod vix credibile fit, temporibus erecta fuit, tanquam Domino ex densissimis tenebris limpidissimam lucem iterum atque iterū exci-tante, vt, vt quo anno & momento fere in ipsius exitium tam potē-tes Principes coniurarent, magnificis ad bos Gymnasij à fundamento toto nat atque Caluino extructis, scholam octo puerorum præceptorum, publicis Hebraicæ, & Græcæ linguæ, ac Philosophiæ, Theologiæ denique profesoribus ornatam Deo Optimo Maximo mo solemni ritu honorato & frequēti coetu in primario tēplo peperelessum primum atque expressis, quæ ad vilissimæ ac sanctissimæ institutionis usum & confirmationem perpetuā per tinerent, solenni quodam modo ritu consecraret. Anno proximo grauatiatus est invidia Caluinus à nonnullis, quasi quosdam aduersus Franciscum I I paterni regni heredem concitasset, eos videlicet, à quorum casu Ambrosiani tumultus nomē auditum est: quum Caluinus ipse quod certo scio, quicquid hoc fuit nunquam intellexerit, adeoque palam ore, & scriptis ad amicos literis impro-babarit. Eodem anno Stancarus quidam Mantuanus (fatali vi-delicet et Polonis Italia) asserere cœpit Christum non esse nisi secu-dum carnem Mediatorem; Arianismi insimulans quoque cunqui il-lum di dicerent, quatenus etiā Deus est, Mediatorem esse quasi fi-lium sui facerent patre minorem. Hanc calumniam, & retum hoc dogma, quū alij vt Philippus, & Martyr solide refutarunt, tum et-iam Ca Caluinus rogantibus Polonis perbreuiter quidē, sed nerno se admonuit coarguit: simulque prospiciens quod mox euenit, futurum videlicet, vt Stancari refutandi studio nonnulli impe- ritiores (nisi sibi cauetent) in errorem Tritheitarum inciderent, diserte praemonuit, vt à Blandrata, & alii eum sequutis sibi cauentes, ficaffererent Christum esse secundum vtraque naturam Mediatorem, vt interea Deitatem non multiplicarent: sed fru- ftra id factum, quod ad eos attinet quibus pereundum erat. Tum quoque Vvaldenses Boemi quos vocat, d uobus fratribus ad Cal- uinum missis, quaedam ab eo sunt de Religione percontati: qui- bus ille sicut par erat benigne satisfecit, eos etiam cohortatus, vt cum reliquis Ecclesiis sese prorsus coniungerent. Eodem tempo re quum non pauci pij Galli post Mariae reginae mortem, fingu- lari serenissimae reginae Elizabethae pietate & humanitate freti, in Angliam refugerent, peterentque reuerendi viri Edmundi Grin- dalli Episcopi Londinensis assensu, vt Geneua mitteretur, qui Ec- clesiam Gallicam illic constitueret, missus est eo Galasius. Cae- terum extremo anno M. D. L X. Francisci I I. regis obitu plane repentino, & quidem eo ipso momento quo iam erant ita de- sperata omnia, vt iis Deus vnus mederi posset, vix inierat regnum Carolus I x. adhuc puer, quo Geneuam per Caduceatorem allatae sunt eius nomine scriptae literae, quibus missos inde cuerebatur, qui regnum Galliae turbarent, petebatque vt mox reuocarentur, alioqui se iustissimas vlcisci endae iniuriae causas non praetermisi- surum. Vocatus à Senatu Caluinus, suo collega ümque nomine respondit, se, pertentibus Gallicis Ecclesiis, speciatae fidei & inte- gr vitae hominibus, quos eam ad rem idoneos forent sperabant, auctores hortatoresque fuisse, ne patriae opem suorum in causa tam sancta Ecclesiae videlicet pure instituedae flagitari, deesent: hoc illos praestitisse non vt regnum turbarent, sed vt Euangelii pacis docerent: q; si quid praeterea fecisse arguerentur, sese pa- ratos esse coram ipso Rege accusatoribus respondere. Necue lon- gius ista processerunt. Eodem anno Caluinus & ego Tilmanni Heshusij importunissimi hominis libro respondimus. Caluinus deinde Valentini Gentilis blasphemias Lugduni tum aluerfus Athanasij symbolum excusas refutauit. Edidit quoque suas in Danielem praelectiones Gallicis Ecclesiis inscriptas, ac in illis quidem Prophetae interpretet, in ipsa vero inscriptione Prophe- tam egit, imminentes tempestates praedices, quo tempore coacto Polliaci Episcoporum conuentu, & Regi in amplissimo regni con- sessu à me exhibita probatae; Galliarum Ecclesiarum Confessio- ne, plerique sibi Papatus profligationem quasi instantem pollicebantur. Tum quoque inter caeteros Francifcus Balduinus, Ecc- bolius postea propter Religionem ter minimum aut etiam quater mutatam cognominatus (nam & ante nouissimum Ecclesiarum Gallicarum casum ad x x x i i. Augusti. M. D. LXXII. nescio quo vt nobis
units.tr: In 1559 the same extreme danger would probably have fallen on the city of Geneva too, had not the Papists' plans, which were exploiting the simplicity of King Henry, been thwarted by divine providence. For it is well established that Henry, having issued the most severe edicts and thrown several senators into prison (although those senators thought that if a general council were convened, the cause of religion should be handled more mildly), had set himself this one aim above all: to restore Savoy to its duke and utterly overthrow Geneva. Geneva, meanwhile, was labouring under great anxiety, Calvin above all, though he was in poor health and was then sorely afflicted; he kept the brethren and the churches, which were very badly troubled, in their faith, and with constant prayers he sought help from the Lord. Then, in the midst of that terror, which was felt both far and near, the king himself was fatally wounded in a jousting tournament during the preparations for the wedding that was to confirm the peace. The blow came from the hand of the same man, then captain of the royal guard, to whom the king had shortly before given orders to seize those senators. The Cardinal of Lorraine later wished that slaughter to be atoned for by the death of the most distinguished jurist and senator, and of Anne du Bourg, that most holy martyr of Christ, who was put to death on 23 December. But Geneva, by a singular blessing of God, was raised up at that very time, which is scarcely credible, and the Lord, as it were, kindled again the purest light out of the thickest darkness. In the very year and almost the very moment when such powerful princes were conspiring for its destruction, the magnificent buildings of the Academy, built from the foundations up under Calvin, were completed. The school was adorned with eight boys' teachers and with public professors of Hebrew and Greek, of philosophy, and finally of theology. In the principal church, before a crowded assembly, it honoured God, most good and most great, with a solemn rite, and it consecrated in a solemn manner the first and the chief things that pertained to the use and the lasting confirmation of this most holy institution. In the following year Calvin was burdened with envy by some, as if he had stirred up against Francis II, heir to his father's kingdom, those men from whose fate the name of the Amboise tumult was heard. Yet Calvin himself, as I know for certain, never understood what this was, and he openly condemned it, both by word of mouth and in letters to his friends. In the same year a certain Stancarus of Mantua (by a fatal force, to be sure, for Italy belonged to the Poles) began to maintain that Christ is Mediator only according to his human nature. He also accused those who said that Christ is Mediator even as God of Arianism, since they made the Mediator, as it were, a son less than the Father. This slander and this doctrine were solidly refuted by others, such as Philip and Martyr, and Calvin too, at the request of the Poles, refuted and censured it very briefly, but with force. At the same time, foreseeing what soon happened, he clearly warned that, in their zeal for refuting Stancarus, some less skilled men (unless they took care) would fall into the error of the Tritheists. He warned them to beware of Blandrata and the others who followed him, who taught that Christ is Mediator according to both natures, so that they would not multiply the Deity in the process. But that warning was in vain for those who were doomed to perish. Then too the Bohemian Waldenses, as they are called, sent two brothers to Calvin, and asked him about certain points of religion. He kindly answered them as was fitting, and he also exhorted them to join wholeheartedly with the other churches. At the same time, when many godly Frenchmen, after the death of Queen Mary, had fled to England, trusting in the singular piety and kindness of the most serene Queen Elizabeth, and asked, with the assent of the reverend Edmund Grindal, Bishop of London, that someone be sent to Geneva to establish a French church there, Galasius was sent there. Finally, at the end of the year 1560, King Francis II died quite suddenly, at the very moment when all things were so desperate that God alone could heal them. Charles IX, still a boy, had scarcely begun his reign when letters were brought to Geneva in his name by a herald. They demanded that the men sent from there to disturb the kingdom of France be recalled at once, and they threatened that otherwise he would not neglect the most just causes for avenging the wrong. Calvin, summoned by the Senate, answered in his own name and in that of his colleagues. He said that when the French churches, which hoped to find men of proved faith and integrity fit for this task, asked for help, he and his colleagues had been the authors and encouragers of sending them, so as not to fail their country's help in so holy a cause, namely the establishment of the Church in its purity. They had done this not to disturb the kingdom, but to teach the gospel of peace. If they were accused of doing anything further, they were ready to answer their accusers before the king himself. Nothing further came of the matter. In the same year Calvin and I replied to the book of Tilemann Heshusius, a most troublesome man. Afterwards Calvin refuted the blasphemies of Valentine Gentile, published at Lyons, together with his attack on the Athanasian Creed. He also published his lectures on Daniel, dedicated to the French churches. In those lectures he interpreted the prophet, but in the dedication itself he played the prophet, foretelling the storms that were coming. At that time, when a meeting of bishops had been held at Poissy, and the Confession of the French churches had been presented by me to the king in the full assembly of the realm and approved, many were promising themselves that the overthrow of the Papacy was at hand. Then too, among others, there was Francis Balduin, later nicknamed Ecebolius because he changed his religion three or even four times. (For before the last destruction of the French churches, on 31 August 1572, I know not by what...)

units.la: M. D. LXI. vt nobis aliquādo etiam tum adiungeretur affectu mirificè duci, ab optimis ac sanctissimis viris testatū exhibitis ad eam rem boni ipsius Balduini ad Synodum literis, habuimus) ille inquam, à Cardinali subornatus, & Nauarreno malis artibus conciliatus libellum quendam siue àfe, siue potius à Cassandro quodam editum, qui sese pium & Moderatum Virum nuncupabat, in aula venditabat, Interimistico illo Cæsaris V. edicto eò etiam deteriorem, quòd moderatæ cuiusdā instaurationis specie, omnes Papatus corruptelas tueretur. Huius rei à me commonefactus Caluinus, refutationem libelli edidit, cui mox alia sunt adiuncta, quæ Balduini ingenium & instítutum quibusvis patefacerent. Hoc verò concoquere non potuit rabula, neque magis alterum meum responsum: nec ab eo tempore Caluinum & me meretricis conuitiis impetere destitit, donec anno superiore, Deo hominibusque alterutrius Religionis quos toties fefellerat, inuisus, Lutetiæ litem nescio quam persequens, siue liuore tabescés, quòd alium sibi prælatum videret, qui Henricum III. in Poloniæ regnum proficiscentem comitaretur, viuere simul ac maledicere desiit. Anno verò LXII. non modò pace, sed etiam libertate Gallicis Ecclesiis solenni Regio Edicto certis conditionibus concessa, mox autem Nauarreno Pontificiis artibus subornato, quum Guisius edita illa immani Vassiacena strage classicum cecinisset, & bellum illud ciuile his auspiciis coepisset, quo nunc totos xii. annos misera Gallia deflagrat, quot quantæquæ curæ Caluinum confecerint dici non potest: sic etiā ingrauescentibus eius morbis, vt iam tum illum diuinare liceret ad meliorem vitam citato gradu progredi. Nec tamen consolari & hortari vnum quenque, imò ne concionari quidè, & Theologiam in schola profiteri destitit: emisitque eo anno pulcherrimam Fidei Confessionem ad Status Imperii Francofurti tunc congregatos nomine Principis Condensis & piorum omnium, quos præter belli ipsis iniustissimè illati iniuriam, indignissimè etiam apud Germanos tuncsalsorum dogmatum nomine traductos auditum esset. Neque hic pigebit quiddam animaduersione non indignum commemorare. Iacebat ex podagra Caluinus in lecto xix. Dec. qui dies erat Sabbathi, & Boreas iam totum biduum flabat quàm vehementissimè. Tum Caluinus multis audientibus, Equidem inquit, nescio quid hoc rei sit, videbar mihi hac nocte audire tympana bellica quàm fortissimè personàtia, nec poteram mihi persuadere, quin ita se res haberet. Precemur obsecro, nam omnino magni aliquid geritur. Atqui hoc ipso die accidit ille apud Druydas acerrimus conflictus: de quo aliquot post diebus Geneuæ fuit renuntiatum. Anno consequente nempe LXIII. sic exacerbari funus eius morbi, iisque multiplices, vt plane fit incredibilem in corpusculo tam imbecillo, tot laboribus exhausto, tot denique morbis attrito, tam fortem ac generosum animum continueri diutius potuisse. Siquidem ne tunc quidem adducti potuit, ut sibi parceret. Imo si quando (quod nunquam nisi penitus inuitus fecit) publico suo munere abstinebat, domi interea vel consulētibus respondebat, vel amanuensēs dictando indefessus ipse fatigabat, atque eius rei fidem faciunt tum binae illae in ximae feriae ad Pa-lonos admonitiones adueršus blasphemos illos sacrae Triadis hostes: tum etiam quod fratribus ex Synodo Lugdunensi ad se missis abunde tum voce tum scriptis respondit, quod Commentarios in quatuor Moysis libros Latinos edidit, quod Gallicos ex Latinis ipse fecit, quod deniquae Commentarium in librum Iosuae qui fuit vltimus ipsius labor, iam tum inchoauit, quae tandem etiam moribundus absoluit. Annus autem Lxiiii supra sefquimillesimus, ipsi quidem perpetuae felicitatis, nobis autem longe maximi iustissimique doloris initium fuit. Siquidem v. Febr. Asthmate vocem eius praepediente vltimam habuit concionem: et ab eo tempore eo excepto quod aliquoties ad Congregationis coetum deportatus (quod illi vltimo Martij nouissimum accidit) paucula verba fecit, omni docedi munere abstinuit. Ipsius morbi incredibilibus animi corporisque laboribus contractis, variis multiplicēque fuerunt, vt sua quadam ad medicos Montpellienses epistola edita eos ipse percenset. Praeterquam enim quod corpore fuit natura imbecillo, macilento, et ad tabem vltro inclinante, dormiens pene vigilabat, magnam animi partem concionando, docendo, dictando cōsumebat per decem minimum annos prandio abstinuit, vt nullum omnino cibum extra statā coenę horam sumeret: vt eum mirum sit Phthisim effugere tamdiu potuisse. Fuit autem ei hemicranea familiaris, cui iffola illa inedia medebatur, adeo vt nonnunquam totas xxxvi. horas cibo abstineret. Sed et partim ex vocis cōtentione, partim quod fero nimis animaduertum est ex immodico aloes vsu, primum in haemorroidas easque tandem vlcerosas, deinde quinquie ante mortem annis in sanguinis excretionem aliquoties incidit. Quartana vero ipsum deserente, successeruntin dexterō cerure po-dagra, colici subinde recurrentes dolores, calculus demique, quem alioqui nunquam nisi aliquot ante mortem menses fefenserat. Medici quaecunque remedia poterant, adhibebat, nec quisquam hominum fuit, qui medicorum praecepta accuratius observauerat: caeteroquin quod adanimi labores attinet, valetudinis negligentissimus, adeo vt illum ne acerrimi quidem hemicraneę dolores à concionando vnquam prohibuerint. Tot autem ni rorbis oppressum, nemo ne vociam quidem audiuit emittentem, forti, ut dum Chrisiiano viro indignam. Tantum oculos illum ꝓ s-ælum at-tollens. tollens, Vsquequo inquiebat, Domine! hoc enim etiam valens tanquam symbolum in ore habeb at, agens de fratrum calamitatibus, quibus noctes ac dies magis etiam quam suis vllis malis afficiebatur. Admonentibus & obtestantibus nobis, ut saltem ægrotus ab omni dictandi, aut saltem scribendi labore abstineret, quid ergo in quiebat, vultis me otiosum a Domino deprehendi? Die Martij x. quum ut saepe consuevera mus ad eum una venisse mus, deprehendimus illum vedtitum, & suae mensulae ad quam scribere aut meditari solebat assidentem, unde cospectis nobis, post quam aliquandiu fronte in alteram manum, ut meditans consueverat, inclinata concicuisset, tandem voce subinde interrupta, sed blando & renidente vultu, Atego inquit, vobis Charissimi fratres, magnas gratias ago de vestra pro me sol citudine, & spero me intra quindecim dies (is autem morum censuris de more destinatus erat) vestro coetui postremum interfuturum. Tum enim opinor Dominum pacefacturum, quid de me statuerit, & fore ut me ad se recipiat. Interfuit igitur censuris ut ante consueverat, eiusdem mensis xxiiii, isque pacifice peractis, sentire se dixit nonnihil dilationis sibi a Domino concessum: ac ceptoque in minus novo Testamento Gallico, quaedam nobis in subiectis adnotationibus legit ipsemet, & de iis fratres consuluit, quod easquoque emendandas suscepisset. Postridie peius habuit, quasi pridiano labore fatigatus. xxvii, vero ad Curiae fores delatus, pedibus in Senatoriam vsque aulam comitibus duobus innixus ascendit, ibique novo Rectore Scholae Senatui oblato, aperto capite gratias egit pro acceptis ante beneficiis, ac nominatim quod in hoc suo ultimo morbo tantam sui rationem Senatus habuisset. Nam sentio inquit, me postremum in hunc locum venisse. Quae vix deficiente voce effatus, moestis ac lachrymantibus vale dixit. Secunda die Aprilis qui dies erat Paschae, quanuis prostratis viribus, tamen sellula in templum delatus, toti concioni interfuit, Coenam Domini ex mea manu accepit, eoque vultu hymnum cum aliis quanquam tremula voce cecinit, ut non obscura laetitiae signa in moribundi vultu elucerent. xxv. Aprilis Testamentum totidem verbis condidit.
units.tr: In the year 1561, when we still hoped that he might be won over to us, the best and most holy men had attested his goodwill in letters sent to the synod on his behalf. He, I say, was won over by the Cardinal and taken in by the Navarrese through foul arts. In the court he peddled a little book, put out either by himself or rather by a certain Cassander, who called himself a pious and moderate man. It was all the worse for the Interim of Emperor Charles V, since under the appearance of a moderate restoration it defended every corruption of the Papacy. Calvin, reminded of this by me, published a refutation of the book, to which other pieces were soon added that laid bare Balduinus's character and aims to anyone. The wrangler could not stomach this, nor could he stomach my second reply any better. From that time on he never ceased to assail Calvin and me with a harlot's insults, until last year, hated by God and by men of both religions whom he had so often deceived, he was pursuing some lawsuit or other at Paris. Whether wasting away with envy, because he saw another preferred to himself as the one to accompany Henry III on his journey to the kingdom of Poland, he stopped living and speaking ill at the same time. In the year 1562, peace and even liberty were granted to the French churches by a solemn royal edict on certain conditions. Soon afterwards, however, the Navarrese was won over by Papist arts, and when Guise had sounded the trumpet with that monstrous slaughter at Vassy, this civil war began under such omens, by which wretched France has now been burning for twelve whole years. How many and how great were the cares that wore Calvin down cannot be said. His illnesses grew so severe that one could already guess he was advancing at a quick pace toward a better life. Yet he did not cease to console and exhort each one, nor even to preach, and to lecture on theology in the school. In that year he also sent out a most beautiful confession of faith, addressed to the Estates of the Empire then gathered at Frankfurt, in the name of the Prince of Condé and of all the godly, who had been, besides the injury of the most unjust war waged on them, most shamefully slandered among the Germans as well with the name of false doctrines. Nor will it be tedious to mention here something not unworthy of note. Calvin lay in bed on the 19th of December, racked by gout, and that day was a Saturday. The north wind had been blowing as violently as possible for two whole days. Then Calvin said, before many listeners: "Indeed, I do not know what this means. It seemed to me last night that I heard war drums sounding most fiercely, and I could not persuade myself that matters were otherwise. Let us pray, I beg you, for surely something great is happening." And on that very day the most bitter battle took place at Dreux, which was reported at Geneva a few days later. In the following year, 1563, the affliction of his illness grew so severe, and so manifold, that it is truly incredible that a spirit so strong and noble could last any longer in a body so feeble, worn out by so many labours and finally broken by so many diseases. Indeed, not even then could he be persuaded to spare himself. Rather, if at any time he kept away from his public duty (which he never did except most reluctantly), at home he would either answer those who consulted him or, tireless himself, wear out his secretaries by dictating. The proof of this is the two most elegant sermons against those blasphemous enemies of the holy Trinity, delivered to the Poles, and also that he answered the brethren sent to him from the Synod of Lyon abundantly, both by voice and in writing. He published his Commentaries on the four books of Moses in Latin, he himself turned them into French from the Latin, and he had already begun the Commentary on the book of Joshua, which was his last labour, and which he finished even while dying. The year 1564, beyond fifteen hundred, was indeed the beginning of unending happiness for him, but for us the beginning of the greatest and most just grief. For on the 5th of February, his asthma impeding his voice, he gave his last sermon. From then on, except that he was carried several times to the assembly of the congregation (which happened for the last time on the last day of March), when he spoke a few words, he abstained from every duty of teaching. The manifold and varied troubles of his illness, which he had contracted through incredible labours of mind and body, he himself enumerated in a letter to the physicians of Montpellier, which was published. For apart from the fact that by nature his body was feeble and thin, and inclined to consumption, he kept almost sleepless nights, and spent a great part of his mind on preaching, teaching and dictating. For at least ten years he abstained from lunch, so that he took no food at all outside the fixed hour of the evening meal, and it is remarkable that he could escape consumption for so long. He was also troubled by hemicrania, which he treated with that very fasting, so that at times he would abstain from food for as many as thirty-six hours. But partly from the strain of his voice, and partly, as I have noticed, from the immoderate use of aloes, he first fell into haemorrhoids, and these at last became ulcerous, and then, five years before his death, he several times suffered bleeding from the blood. When quartan fever left him, gout settled in his right ankle, with colic pains recurring from time to time, and finally kidney stones, which, moreover, he had never felt until a few months before his death. The physicians applied whatever remedies they could, and there was no one who observed the doctors' precepts more carefully. Otherwise, as regards his labours of mind, he was most careless of his health, so much so that not even the sharpest pains of hemicrania ever kept him from preaching. Yet, oppressed by so many illnesses, no one ever heard him utter a groan, with a strong spirit, as is unworthy of a Christian man. He only lifted his eyes to heaven and said, "How long, O Lord?" For he had this phrase, as a kind of motto, always on his lips, when speaking of the calamities of the brethren, by which he was affected night and day even more than by any of his own ills. When we urged and begged him to abstain at least while sick from all dictating, or at least from all writing, he said, "What then? Do you want the Lord to find me idle?" On the 10th of March, when, as we often used to do, we had come to him together, we found him dressed, and sitting at his little table at which he was accustomed to write or meditate. When he saw us, after a while, with his brow bowed onto his other hand, as he used to do when meditating, he raised his head, and then, with his voice now and then interrupted, but with a gentle and smiling face, said: "And I, dearest brethren, give you great thanks for your care for me, and I hope that within fifteen days (this was the day appointed by custom for the censures of morals) I shall be present at your assembly for the last time. For then, I think, the Lord will settle what he has decided about me, and will receive me to himself." He therefore attended the censures as he had done before, on the 24th of the same month, and when they were peacefully concluded, he said that he felt a slight delay had been granted him by the Lord. Then, taking up the little New Testament in French, he himself read us some notes in the margins, and consulted the brethren about them, since he had undertaken to correct them as well. On the following day he was worse, as if worn out by the previous day's labour. On the 27th, however, he was carried to the doors of the Court, and, supported by two companions on foot, climbed as far as the senate hall. There, when the new Rector of the School was presented to the Senate, with head bared he gave thanks for the benefits received before, and especially that the Senate had shown such concern for him in this his last illness. "For I feel," he said, "that I have come to this place for the last time." Having spoken these words with his voice barely failing, he bade farewell to the sorrowing and weeping men. On the second day of April, which was Easter Day, although his strength was broken, he was carried in a little chair to the church and was present at the whole congregation. He received the Lord's Supper from my hand, and with such a countenance he sang the hymn with the others, though in a trembling voice, that no faint signs of joy shone in the face of the dying man. On the 25th of April he made his will, in exactly these words.

units.la: TO ANNIS CALVINI Testamentum.
units.tr: TO ANNIS: CALVIN'S TESTAMENT.

units.la: In nomine Domini, Amen. Anno M. D.
units.tr: In the name of the Lord, Amen. In the year 1564, on the 25th day of April.

units.la: LXIIII. die Aprilis XXV. Ego Petrus Chenalatus ciuis & Notarius Geneuensis testor ac profiteor me euocatum fuisse à Spectato viro Ioanne Caluino Ministro verbi Dei in hac Ecclesia Geneuensi, & eiusdem ciuitatis adscripto ciue, qui tum corpore quidem aegro, sed mente integra dixit sibi esse in animo testamentum suum conficere, & extremae voluntatis iudicium exponere: à meque petiit ut illud exciperem, & uti lingua nuncuparet, ac dictaret, ita conscriberem, quod confessim feci lle me profiteor, atque ad verbum ut nuncupare & dictare voluit, conscripsisse, neque quicquam ad illius verba adiecisse vel de iis detraxisse, sed hanc ab illo dictatam formulam sequutum esse.
units.tr: I, Pierre Chenalat, citizen and notary of Geneva, testify and declare that I was summoned by the honourable Jean Calvin, minister of the Word of God in this Church of Geneva and a citizen enrolled in the same city. Though his body was sick, his mind was sound, and he said that he intended to draw up his testament and set out his final wishes. He asked me to take them down, to write them out as he dictated and spoke them aloud, and I immediately did so. I declare that I wrote down his words exactly as he wished them spoken and dictated, adding nothing to them and taking nothing away, and that I followed the form he dictated.

units.la: In nomine Domini, Amen. EGO Ioannes
units.tr: In the name of the Lord, Amen. I, John
