units.la: Caluinus Minister verbi Dei in Ecclesia Geneuensi, variis morbis oppressus & afflictus, vt facile animum inducam, Dominum Deum statuisse me propediem ex hoc mundo educere, constituì facere meum testamentum, meámque vltimam voluntatem literis mandare, ea forma quae subsequitur: PRIMVM omnium gratias ago Deo, quòd misertus mei (què creauit & in hoc mundo collocaret) non solum me e profundis idololatriae tenebris in quas demersus eram, eripuit, vt me in Euangelij sui lucem adduceret, & doctrinae salutis participem faceret cuius eram indignissimus: neque solum eadem misericordia & benignitate multa mea vitia & peccata benignè & clementer toleravit, pro quibus tamen merebar ab illo reiici & exterminari: Verùm etiam tanti erga me clementia & mansuetudine est vsus, vt oppera mea dignatus sit vti in praedicanda & promulganda veritate sui Euangelii: testorque ac profiteor mihi esse in animo quod reliquum est vitae in eadem fide & religione transfigere, quam mihi per Euangelium suum tradidit: neque aliud praesidium aut poenam fugiendum salutis habere, quam gratuitam ipsius adoptionem: quae vna salus mea nititur: ac toto pectore ampletor misericordiam, quae propter Iesum Christum erga me est vsus: compensans mea crimina cum merito mortis & passionis ipsius, vt hac ratione pro criminibus & delictis meis omnibus satisfiat, eorumque memoria deleatur. Testor etiam ac profiteor me supplicitèr ab eo petere, vt ita me ablutum & mundatum velit sanguine sui summi illius redemptoris, effuso pro humani generis peccatiis, vt mihi
units.tr: Calvin, minister of the Word of God in the Church of Geneva, afflicted and worn down by various diseases, and so readily persuaded that the Lord God has determined to take me shortly out of this world, have resolved to make my will and to commit my last wishes to writing, in the form that follows. FIRST of all, I give thanks to God, who, having pity on me (whom he created and placed in this world), has not only snatched me from the deep darkness of idolatry in which I had been sunk, to bring me into the light of his Gospel and make me a partaker of the doctrine of salvation, of which I was most unworthy; but who has also, by the same mercy and kindness, graciously and patiently borne with my many faults and sins, for which I deserved to be rejected and cast out by him. Moreover, he has used such clemency and gentleness towards me that he has deigned to employ my labours in preaching and proclaiming the truth of his Gospel. I testify and profess that it is my intention to spend the rest of my life in the same faith and religion which he has delivered to me through his Gospel; and that I have no other protection for my salvation, and no other punishment to flee, than his free adoption, on which my one salvation rests. With my whole heart I embrace the mercy which he has shown towards me for the sake of Jesus Christ, setting my crimes against the merit of his death and passion, so that in this way satisfaction is made for all my sins and offences, and their memory is blotted out. I also testify and profess that I humbly ask of him that he will wish me so washed and cleansed in the blood of that highest Redeemer, shed for the sins of the human race, that

units.la: Bceat liceat apud tribunal ipsius consistere sub ipsius Redemptoris i-magine.Item profiteor me sedulò pro modo gratiæ & benignitatis qua Deus erga me vsus est;operam dedisse,vt cùm in concionibus,tum etiam in scriptis & commentariis purè & castè verbum ipsius prædicarem,& fideliter Sacram ipsius Scripturam interpretarer.Testor etiam ac profiteor me in contentionibus & disputationibus omnibus quæ mihi cum hostibus Euangelij habendæ fuerunt,nullis præstigiis,nullis malis artibus & sophisticis vsum esse,sed candidè ac syncerè in veritate propugnanda verfatu esse. Verùm,hei mihi,studium illud meum & zelus(si hoc nomine dignus est)adeò remissus & languidus fuit,vt innumera mihi ad munus meum præclarè fungendum defuisse fateor, ac nisi immensa Dei benignitas adfuisset,totum illud studium meum inane atque euanidum futurum fuisse:quinetiam agnosco nisi mihi eadem benignitas adfuisset, animi bona quæ mihi Deus largitus est,magis ac magis me culpæ atque ignauiæ reum apud eius tribunal fietura fuisse: quas ob res testor ac profiteor nullum me aliud præsidium salutis sperare,nisi hoc vnum, quum Deus Pater misericordiæ sit, vt sese mihi, qui me miserum peccatorem agnosco, patrem offendat. Quod reliquum est, volo post meum ex hac vita discessum, corpus meum terræ mandari eo ritu ac modo,qui in hac Ecclesia & ciuitate vsitatus est: dum beatæ resurrectionis dies adueniat. Quantum ad tenue patrimonium,quod mihi Deus largitus est,de quo in hoc testamento disponere statui, Hæres meus esto Antonius Caluinus, frater meus charissimus:sed honoris causa duntaxat:præcipitoque ac sibi habeto paterum argenteam quæ mihi à Varannio dono data est: qua eum contentum esse cupio. nam quæcunque in hæreditate mea reliqua sunt pero ab eo eiusque fidei committo,vt ea suis liberis, cùm morietur restituat. Ab eodem fratre & hærede meo lego scholæ puerili decem aureos scutatos: tantundem pauperibus peregrinis:tantundem pariter Ioannæ Caroli Costani & affinis meæ filiæ. Samueli verò & Ioanni eiusdem fratris mei filiis restituui volo ab hærede meo,cùm morietur quadragenos aureos scutatos : Annæ verò & Sufannæ & Dorotheæ, eiusdem filiabus aureos scutatos tricenos:Dauidi ipsorum fratri ad notam leuitatis & petulantiæ iuuenilis, scutatos aureos quinque & viginti. Hæc summa est totius patrimonij & bonorum , quæ mihi Deus largitus est,quantum quidem existimare possum:pretiū statuens & bibliothecæ,& mobilium,& vniuersi instrumenti domestici, rerumque ac facultatum mearum omnium. quòd si quid forte amplius reperiatur,volo id pro rata illis omnibus fratris mei filiis ac filiabus distribui,neq; Dauidem illum excludo: si pro Dei beni gratiæ ad bonam frugem redierit. Sed si quid erit quod supraescriptam summam excurret, credo nō magnum in ō negotium futurum: praesertim vbi alieno aeri satisfactū erit, cuius rei negotium diligenter mandaui eidem fratri meo, cuius fidei & beneuolentiæ confido: quae de causa illum esse volo ac tantum hu ius mei testamenti executorem: vnáque cum ipso spectatum virū Laurentium Normendium: poterit ille permittens conficien di bonorum meorum inuentarium, sine accuratiore forensi diligentia ac solennitate: permitto etiam ipsis vendere mea i mobilia, vt ex pecunia redacta, supra scriptam meam voluntatem exe quantur: quam expositi & dictui hoc xxv. Aprilis die: Anno M. D. LXIIII. Ioannes Calvinus, Po leaquam egc f pradictus notarius superius testamentum scripsi, continuo heri m Calvinus vsitati subscriptione sua & Chirographo illud confirmauit. Postero die qui fuit xxv i. Aprilis eiusdem anni, dum spectatus vir Caluinus me ad se vocari iussit, vnáq; mecū Theodorum Bezam, Raymundum Caluetū, Michaelem Copum, Ludouicum Enocum, Nicolaum Coladonium, Iacobū Bordesium Ministros & concionatores verbi Domini in hac Ecclesia Geneuensi, itemque spectatum virum Henricum Scrimgerum professorem artium cuius Geneuensis, & coram iis omnibus professus aut testatus est se mihi testamentum illud suum ea forma quasi uprà scriptum est, dictasse: simúlque me iussit illud ipsis audientibus & ea de causa aduocatis recitare, quod me clara voce & articulate fecisse profiteor. Et post illam recitationem testatus est ac c profes sus eam esse suam ultimam voluntatem, quam ratam esse c cupiat, in cuius rei testimonium & confirmationem petiit ab illis omnibus, vt eidem testamento manu sua subscriberent: quod continuo ab illis factum est anno & mense supradictis: Genuæ in vico vulgò dicto Canonicorum: & in eiusdem testatoris is domicilio. In cuius rei fidem & testimonium supradictum testamentum scripsi, & manu mea subscripsi, & vitato ligillo sui suprem i Magistratus nostri, obsignaui.
units.tr: I may be allowed to stand before his tribunal under the image of the Redeemer. Likewise I profess that, according to the measure of the grace and kindness with which God has dealt with me, I have diligently laboured both in sermons and in writings and commentaries to preach his Word purely and chastely, and to interpret faithfully his holy Scripture. I also testify and profess that in all the contentions and disputations which I had to engage in with the enemies of the Gospel, I used no tricks, no wicked arts or sophistries, but conducted myself frankly and sincerely in defending the truth. But alas, my zeal and eagerness (if it deserves that name) has been so slack and languid that I confess countless things were lacking to me in discharging my office well; and unless God's immense goodness had been present, all my effort would have been empty and vain. Indeed, I acknowledge that unless that same goodness had been with me, the gifts of mind which God has bestowed upon me would have made me, more and more, guilty of fault and idleness before his tribunal. For these reasons I testify and profess that I hope for no other protection of salvation than this one: that God is the Father of mercies, so that he may show himself a Father to me, who acknowledge myself a wretched sinner. As for the remainder, I wish that after my departure from this life my body be committed to the earth in the manner and rite customary in this Church and city, until the day of the blessed resurrection arrives. As for the modest patrimony which God has bestowed on me, and which I have resolved to dispose of in this will: let my heir be Antoine Calvin, my most dear brother, but only as a mark of honour. And let him take and keep for himself the silver goblet which was given to me as a gift by Varanne; I wish him to be content with it. For whatever else remains in my estate I entrust to him and to his good faith, that he restore it to his children when he dies. From the same brother and heir of mine, I bequeath ten gold crowns to the boys' school, the same amount to poor foreigners, and likewise the same to Jeanne, the daughter of Charles Costan and my kinswoman. But to Samuel and John, sons of the same brother of mine, I wish forty gold crowns to be restored by my heir when he dies; to Anne, Susanna and Dorothea, daughters of the same, thirty gold crowns each; and to David, their brother, as a mark of his lightness and youthful wantonness, twenty-five gold crowns. This is the sum total of the patrimony and goods which God has bestowed on me, as far as I can estimate, the value being set on my library, movables, all household equipment, and all my property and resources. If anything more is found, I wish it to be distributed in equal shares among all the sons and daughters of my brother, and I do not exclude David, if by God's grace he has come to good fruit. But if there is anything which exceeds the sum written above, I think it will not be a great matter, especially once the debt owed to others has been satisfied; I have diligently committed this business to the same brother of mine, in whose good faith and kindness I trust. For this reason I wish him to be the executor of this my will, and together with him the upright man Laurent Normand; he may permit the making of an inventory of my goods without more exact forensic diligence and formality. I also permit them to sell my movables, so that with the money raised they may carry out my wishes written above, which I have set out and dictated on this 25th day of April, in the year 1564. John Calvin. I, the aforesaid notary, wrote the above will; immediately Calvin confirmed it with his customary signature and handwriting.

units.la: Petrus Chenalatus.
units.tr: Peter Chenalatus.

units.la: HOc condito testamento, misit qui quatuor Syndicis cunctisque Senatoribus significaret, ut superpere se ante quam e vivis excederet, adhuc tunc eos omnes in Curia compellare, quo postridie se deportandum spectaret. Respondent Senatores se potius ad eum venturos, rogarunt que ut sua valetudinis rationem haberet. Postridie quum ad eum omnes e Curia venissent, mutuo data accepta, quesalute, post quam veniam petiisset quod ad ipsum vsque venissent, quum sibi potius ad eos accedem dum effet, & prefatus, iam pridem hoc cum ipsis colloquium expetiuisse, quod tamen eo vsque distulisset, dum paulo certius exitum suum praesentiret. Ego vero, inquit, honorandi Domini, ingetes vobis gratias ago, qp me plane nihil eiusmodi promeritum, tatis affectis honoribus, measq; plurimas infirmitates tam patienter saepe toleraftis, quod maximum semper apud me fuit vestrae in me singularis beneuolentiae argumentum. Et quanuis mihi munere meo defungenti varia subeunda certamina, variisque sustinendi fuerint insultus, qp sic oporteat optimum etiam quenque exerceri, scio tamen & agnosco nihil istorum vestra culpa accidit. Precor autem vos vehementer vt si quaecunq; oportuit, non praestiti, voluntatis meae potius quam facultatis habeatis rationem. Illud enim vere potuit testari, fuisse me Reip. vestrae ex animo studiosum, & vt officio meo plene non sim defunctus, publicis quidem certe commodis pro virili studuisse. Quod ni agnoscerem Dominum vicissim opera interdum mea non inutiliter voluisse, dissimulationis crimen non effugerem. Sed hoc a vobis etiam atque etiam peto, vt excusationem apud vos inueniam, qp ta exigua sint quaecunque publice vel priuatim praestiti, praeterea quae a me fieri oportuit: vltro certe agnosco me vobis hoc quoque nomine plurimum debere, qp vehementiam illam meam interdum immoderatam aequo animo tulistis: quae peccata mea confido mihi a Deo quoque ipso condonata. Caeterum quod ad doctrinam attinet quam ex me audistis, testor me non temere neque incerto, sed pure ac syncere verbum Dei mihi concreditum docuisse, cuius ira alioqui tam scirem huic capiti meo iam imminere, quam certus sum meos in docendo labores ei non diffiteri. Idq; coram Deo & vobis eo libentius testificor, qp minime dubitem Satanam prout consueui, improbos, leues, vertiginosos denique homines corrupendae quam ex me audiuistis, syncerae doctrinae excitaturum. Inde delapsus ad immensa illa beneficia quibus a Domino affecti fuerat, Ego, Ego, inquit, optimus sum testis, quot quantisque periculis Optimi Maximi Dei manus vos exemerit. Videtis porro quo loco sitis. Siue igitur secundae res vestrae fuerint siue aduersae, illud, quaeso, vobis ob oculos sem per obuersetur, illum vnum esse qui regna & ciuitates stabiliat, eoque nomine coli a mortalibus velit. Memineritis magnum illum Dauid iem testari se tum prolapsum esse, quo alta iam pace fuerit, nunquam certe resurrecturum, nisi Dominus bonitate sua manu ei porrexisset. Quid igitur tantillis homunculis fiet, quod ille tam potens & fortis ceciderit? Nempe magna vobis animi demissione opus est, vt magna cum Dei reuerentia solicite incedatis, illiusque vnius praesidio nitamini, certi nimirum Dei. ita futuru vt quod tam saepe reipsa sensistis, firmi illius ope perstetis, etiam si velut ex tenui filo suspensa vestra salus & incolumitas fuerit. Itaque si prospera vobis euenerint, cauete quasi, ne profanorum instar efferamini, sed Deo potius cum animi demissione gratias agite. Sin aduersa vobis acciderint, adeoque vos undique mortes circunsteterint, sperate tamen in eo qui mortuos etiam excitat. Imo tunc maxime cogitate sic vos ad Deo expergefieri, vt in eum vnum respicere magis ac magis discatis.
units.tr: Having made this will, he sent a message to the four syndics and all the senators, saying that before he departed this life he wished to address all of them in the Council chamber, where he hoped to be carried the following day. The senators replied that they would rather come to him, and asked that he consider his health. The next day, when they had all come to him from the Council, they exchanged greetings and asked after his health. He begged their pardon for coming all the way to him when he would rather have gone to them, and said that he had long wished for this conversation but had put it off until he could foresee his end more clearly. "I, honoured sirs," he said, "give you immense thanks, for you have never rewarded me with any such honours, yet you have often patiently borne my many infirmities, which has always been for me the greatest proof of your singular goodwill. Although in discharging my office I have had to undergo various struggles and endure various assaults, as it is fitting that even the best men should be tried in this way, I know and acknowledge that none of this came through your fault. I earnestly beg you, however, that where I ought to have done things and did not, you take account of my will rather than my ability. This much I can truly testify: I have been wholeheartedly devoted to your Commonwealth, and although I have not fully discharged my duty, I have striven, as far as I could, for the public good. If I did not recognise that the Lord had at times been willing to use my labours not without profit, I could not escape the charge of dissimulation. But this I ask of you again and again: that I may find pardon with you, since whatever I have done, publicly or privately, is so small, and there is much more that I ought to have done. I freely acknowledge that I owe you a great deal on this account too, that you bore my vehemence, at times immoderate, with an even mind. I trust that God himself has pardoned these sins of mine. As for the doctrine you heard from me, I testify that I did not teach it rashly or uncertainly, but taught the Word of God, entrusted to me, purely and sincerely. Otherwise I know that God's wrath would hang over this head of mine, just as I am sure that my labours in teaching do not deny it. I testify this before God and before you all the more willingly, because I have no doubt that Satan, as is his custom, will stir up wicked, fickle, and giddy men to corrupt the sincere doctrine you heard from me." Passing on from this to the immense benefits with which the Lord has favoured you, he said: "I, I am the best witness of how many and how great the dangers are from which the hand of God, the Best and Greatest, has delivered you. Moreover, you see where you stand. So whether your affairs be prosperous or adverse, let this, I beg you, always be before your eyes: that he alone establishes kingdoms and cities, and wishes to be honoured by mortals under that name. Remember that the great David himself testified that he had fallen when peace was deepest, and would never have risen again unless the Lord in his goodness had stretched out his hand to him. What, then, will become of such tiny little men, since that mighty and strong man fell? Surely you need great humility of spirit, so that you walk anxiously and with great reverence for God, and lean on the protection of him alone, the sure God. In this way it will come about that, as you have so often actually experienced, by the help of that firm one you will persevere, even if your safety and wellbeing hang as if by a thin thread. So if prosperity comes to you, take care not to be puffed up like the profane, but rather give thanks to God with humility of spirit. But if adversity comes upon you, and deaths surround you on every side, still hope in him who raises even the dead. Indeed, in that case above all, think of how you are awakened by God so that you may learn to look more and more to him alone."

units.la: Quod si firmam hanc Reipub. conseruandi cupiditatem videte etiam atque etiam, ne folium istud sanctum, in quo vos illi collocauit, sordibus conspurcetur. Hic enim vnus est summus Deus, Rex Regum, & Dominorum omnium Dominus, eos ad quibus honorabitur, honoribus afficiturus, & sui vicissim contemptores abiecturus. Hunc igitur ex ipsius praeceptis colite, & haec de re magis ac magis cogitate. Semper enim ab eo plurimum absumus, quod a nobis perfici decuit. Nouì ego singulorum ingenia & mores, & scio vos exhortatione egere. Nemo est ex iis etiam qui excellunt, cui multa non definit. Hic vnusquisque seipsum circumspiciat, & quae sibi decent intelligit, a Domino requirat. Videmus quot vitia in plerisque orbis terrarum Concilis regnent. Alij fri gent, publicoque neglecto rebus suis curandis incumbunt, alii priuatis affectibus indulgent, alij praeclaris Dei donis non vtuntur vt par erat, alij sese ostentant, & confidentia quadam quicquid censuerint a reliquis probari postulant. Senes commome facio ne iunioribus inuideant, quos a Domino comperierint aliquibus donis esse exornatos. Iuniores moneo vt procul ab omni elatione, sese modestos praebeant. Alius alium ne intercurbato. Vitae simultates, & omnes illas animi acerbitates, quae multos in gete da Repub. a recto instituto auerterunt. Haec autem vitabitis, si singuli quidem intra suum modulum sese continuerint, omnes vero bona fide committam sibi Reipub. partem administrent. In causarum vero ciuilium iudiciis, ne quis sit, obsecro, fauuori, vel inimicitiis locus. Nemo obliquis artibus ius peruertito. Nemo suis commendationibus quo minus leges valeant, obliftito. Nemo ab aequo & bono discedito. Si quem affectus simulterit, ritilla uerit, constanter ei resistito, & in eum respicito a quo fuuit in eo folio collocatus, & ab eodem sanctum Spiritu postulatato. Quod superest iterum precor, vt meas mihi infirmitates condonetis, quas ego coram Deo & Angelis, adeoque coram vobis Venerandi Domini, profiteor & agnosco. Haec vbi dixisset, Deum & Optimum Maximum precatus, vt eos suis donis magis ac magis cumulatos, sanctoque suo Spiritu ad totius Reipub. salutem gubernaret, prae bita singulis dextra, moestos oranes illos, nec aliter ab eo quam a communi parente cum lachrymis discedentes, dimisit. t. Die 28. Aprilis quum omnes, ipsius rogatu, Geneuensis ditionis Ministri conuenissemus. At vos, inquit, fratres, post obitum meum perstate in hoc opere, nec animo frangimini: Dominus enim hac Rempub. & Ecclesiâ aduersus hostium minas seruabit. Abstinet à vobis dissidia, mutuaque charitate vos complectimini. Cogitate etiam atque etiam quid huic Ecclesiæ debeatis, in qua vos Dominus collocauit: neque vos quicquam hinc abducat. Sin minùs, facile quidem fuerit nonnullis eius pertæsis quasi per cuniculos euadere: sed experientur illi Dominum decipi non posse. Quum primùm in hanc vrbem venirem, annuntiabatur quidem Euangelium, sed pertubatissimæ res erant, quasi nihil aliud esset Christianismus quàm statuarum euersio: nec pauci erant scelerati, à quibus indignissima multa sù perpessus. Sed Dominus ille Deus noster me, me, inquam, natura (dico quod res est) minimè audentem ita confirmauit, vt nullis illorum conatibus cederem. Argentina postea huc redij, vocationem hanc inuito animo sequutus, quòd infructuosa mihi fore videretur. Ignorabam enim quid statuisset Dominus, & res erat plurimarum maximarumque difficultatum plena. Sed pergens in hoc opere sensi tandem reipsa Dominum labori meo benedixisse. perstate igitur & vos in hac vocatione: instituturn ordinem retinete: Date simul operam vt populus in obsequio doctrinæ contineatur. Sunt enim nonnulli improbi & contumaces. Res, vt videtis, non male sunt constitutæ: quò magis coram Deo nocentes eritis, si vestra ignauia labefactentur. Testor vero me vobiscum fratres, vera syncerâque charitate coniunctissimum vixisse, & nunc à vobis discedere. quòd si quando me in hoc morbo morosiorem estis experti, veniam à vobis peto, & ingentes vobis gratias ago, quòd ægrotante me, onus mihi impositum sustinueritis, Hæc loquutus dextram singulis porrexit. Nos mœstissimis animis, ac minimè siccis oculis, ab eo tum discessimus. II. Maij quum ex Fatelli litteris cognouisset (Viretus enim longius aberat) statuisse illum iam octuagenarium & valetudinarium senem, iter ad se ingredi, sic ei Latinè rescripsit. Vale mi optime & integerrime frater, & quando te Deus superstitem manere vult in mundo, viue memor nostræ coniunctionis, quæ vt Ecclesiæ Dei fuit vtilis, ita nos eius fructus in cælo manet. Nolo te fatiges mea causa. Ægrè spiritum traho, & assiduè expecto, dum me anhelitus deficiat. Satis est quòd Christo viuo & morior, qui suis lucrum est in vita, & morte. Iterum vale cum fratribus. Geneuæ, II. Maij. M. D. LXIIII. Venit tamen Geneuam bonus ille senex, & quum vnà inter se locuti essent, postridie Neocomum rediit. Reliquos ad obitum vsque dies in perpetuis penè precibus consumpsit, voce quidem propter asthma fuspitiosa, sed oculis quales ad extremum vsque clare micantes habuit in coelum sublatis & ita compositio vultu, vt scse precantis ardor totum proderet, saepe Dauidis illud ingeminans in doloribus, Tacui Domine quia fecisti, & interdum illud Isaiae, Gemebam sicut columba. Audiui quoque quum diceret, Tu me conteris, Domine, sed abunde mihi sufficit, quod tua haec sit manus. Patere diem & noctem ipsius fores oportuisset, si admissi fuissent quotcunque officij causa illum adire cupiebant, quos cum, voce, vt diximus, praepedita, compellare se non posse videret, petierat vt vnusquisque potius pro ipso precaretur, quam de eo inuisendo laboraret. Saepe quoque mihi cuius conspectum alioqui nunquam iniucundum ei fuisse sum expertus, significauit, sibi religionem esse vel tantillum occupationes meas remorari, adeo fuit ille temporis parcus quod Ecclesiae impendi sciret, & in eo plus etiam aequo religiosus, ne amicos vel tantillum grauaret. Ita igitur se ipsum & amicos consolans vixit vsque ad x. i x. Maij quo die censuram intet nos Ministros exercere, & vna cibum capere amicitiae tessndae causa consueuimus, biduo post videlicet Pentecostes & coena Domini fequuturis. Eo die igitur quum nobis concessum esset vt apud ipsum coenam communis instruertur, & e lectulo, collectis vtcunque viribus, in proximum conclave esset delatus, postremum, inquit, ad vos accedo, fratres, nunquam posthac ad mensam accubiturus, quod nobis tristissimae coenae initium fuit. Concepit tamen preces, & paululum cibi sumpsit, sermone quantum licuit inter coenandum ad hilaritatem compositio. Inde coena nondum plane exacta, quum in contiguum cubiculum reporta rifc iussisset, renidenti plane vultu coetu compellans, paries hic, inquit, interiectus non impediet, quo minus corpore atbsens, vestro tamen coetui spiritu intersim. Contigit quod praedixerat. Siquidem ab eo die supinus semper iacuit, corpusculo (si vultum parum admodum immutatum excipias) ita emaciato, vt solus illi spiritus superest. Die quo decessit, nempe xx v i... Maij, visus est fortius & minore difficultate loqui. Sed hic errat extremus naturae conatus. Nam vespori circiter octauā, repente praesentis mortis certa signa apparuerunt: quod quum mihi paulo ante ab ipso digressio, & cuidam alij ex fratribus esset ad domesticis significatum, protinus accurrens, illum reperi vsque adeo tra quillē mortuum, nullōque pedum vel manuum cōcussisset, vt neque grauiorem spiritum antea duxerit, neque sensu & iudicio, imo ne voce quidem penitus, ad extremum vsque halitum fuerit destitutus, & dormienti quam mortuo multo similior videretur. Sic igitur eo die cum occidente sole splendida etiam haec lux nobis erepta est. Sequente nocte ac postero die in vrbe tota ingens fuit complorato. Requirebat enim vniuersa ciuitas sapien-
units.tr: Moreover, I urge you to take great care that this holy seat, on which the Lord has placed you, is not defiled with filth, for it is the sole and supreme God, King of kings and Lord of all lords, who will honour those for whom he is to be honoured, and will cast off those who despise him in turn. Worship him therefore according to his precepts, and think on these matters more and more. For we always fall far short of what ought to be done by us. I know the characters and habits of each of you, and I know that you need exhortation. There is no one among you, even among those who excel, whom many things do not displease. Let each one therefore look into himself, understand what becomes him, and seek it from the Lord. We see how many vices reign in most of the councils of the world. Some grow cold, and neglecting public business, devote themselves to their private affairs; others indulge their private passions; others do not use the excellent gifts of God as they ought; others show off, and with a certain confidence demand that whatever they have decided be approved by the rest. I warn the old not to envy the younger men whom they perceive to have been adorned by the Lord with certain gifts. I admonish the younger men to show themselves modest and far from all arrogance. Let no one provoke another. Avoid private quarrels and all those bitter feelings of mind which have turned many away from the right course in the government of the Republic. You will avoid these things if each of you keeps within his own measure, and if all, in good faith, administer the part of the Republic committed to them. And in the judgments of civil causes, I beg you, let there be no room for favour or enmity. Let no one pervert justice by crooked arts. Let no one, by his own recommendations, hinder the laws from having force. Let no one depart from what is fair and good. If any passion shall have stirred or provoked anyone, resist it firmly, look to him by whom you were placed in that seat, and ask for his holy Spirit. Finally, I beg you again to pardon my weaknesses, which I acknowledge and confess before God and the angels, and before you, honoured sirs. When he had said these things, having prayed to God, the best and greatest, that he would load them more and more with his gifts and govern them by his holy Spirit for the safety of the whole Republic, he gave his right hand to each, and dismissed them all, sorrowful, departing from him with tears as from a common father. This was on the 28th of April, when all the ministers of the Genevan territory had gathered at his request. "But you, brethren," he said, "persevere in this work after my death, and do not lose heart: for the Lord will preserve this Republic and Church against the threats of enemies. Keep yourselves from dissensions, and embrace one another in mutual charity. Consider again and again what you owe to this Church, in which the Lord has placed you; let nothing draw you away from it. If not, it will indeed be easy for some who are weary of it to slip away as if through tunnels, but they will learn that the Lord cannot be deceived. When I first came into this city, the Gospel was indeed proclaimed, but affairs were in great disorder, as if Christianity were nothing but the overthrow of statues; and there were not a few wicked men, from whom I suffered many most unworthy things. But that Lord, our God, so strengthened me, I say me, who by nature (I speak as the matter is) was least bold, that I yielded to none of their attempts. Afterwards I returned here from Strasbourg, following this calling with an unwilling mind, because it seemed to me it would be unfruitful. For I did not know what the Lord had decided, and the matter was full of very many and very great difficulties. But persevering in this work I at last felt in fact that the Lord had blessed my labour. Persevere therefore you also in this calling; keep the established order; take care together that the people are kept in obedience to doctrine. For there are some wicked and obstinate men. Affairs, as you see, are not badly arranged; the more you will be guilty before God if your negligence should weaken them. Indeed, I testify before you, brethren, that I have lived in true and sincere charity most closely united with you, and now depart from you. If at any time you have found me more peevish in this illness, I ask pardon from you, and I give you immense thanks, because while I was ill you have sustained the burden laid upon me." Having said these things, he gave his right hand to each. We, with most sorrowful hearts and with eyes by no means dry, then departed from him. On the 2nd of May, when he had learned from Fatio's letter (for Viret was farther away) that that old man, now eighty and in poor health, had resolved to set out to visit him, he wrote back to him in Latin as follows: "Farewell, my best and most upright brother; and since God wills you to remain alive in the world, live mindful of our union, which has been useful to the Church of God, and whose fruit remains for us in heaven. I do not want you to tire yourself on my account. I draw breath with difficulty, and I constantly expect that my breath will fail. It is enough that I live and die in Christ, who is gain to his own both in life and in death. Farewell again, with the brethren. Geneva, 2nd May 1564." Nevertheless that good old man came to Geneva, and after they had talked together, he returned to Neuchâtel the next day. For the rest of his days, almost to the end, he spent his time in continual prayers, his voice indeed hoarse because of asthma, but his eyes, which to the last were bright and clear, lifted up to heaven, and his face so composed that the ardour of his praying showed itself wholly, often repeating in his pains that saying of David, "I was silent, Lord, because you have done it," and at times that of Isaiah, "I mourned like a dove." I also heard him say, "You crush me, Lord, but it is quite enough for me that this is your hand." He ought to have been open to visitors day and night, if all who wished to visit him for the sake of duty had been admitted; and when he saw that, his voice being impeded as we have said, he could not address them, he asked that each one should rather pray for him than trouble himself to visit him. Often also he signified to me, whose sight I have always found not unpleasant to him, that it was a scruple for him to delay my occupations even a little; so sparing of time was he about what he knew was spent on the Church, and in this more than was fair scrupulous, lest he burden his friends even a little. So, consoling himself and his friends in this way, he lived until the 19th of May, on which day we ministers were accustomed to hold our censure among ourselves and to take a meal together to cement our friendship, two days before Pentecost and the Lord's Supper. On that day, therefore, when we had been granted leave to have the common meal prepared at his place, and he had been carried from his couch, gathering his strength somehow, into the next room, "I come to you for the last time, brethren," he said, "never again to recline at the table," which was the beginning of a most sorrowful supper for us. Nevertheless he offered prayers and took a little food, speaking as much as he could during the meal to keep the company cheerful. Then, when the supper was not yet quite finished, he ordered himself carried back into the adjoining chamber, and addressing the company with a plainly smiling face, "This wall that lies between us," he said, "will not prevent me, though absent in body, from being present in spirit with your company." What he had foretold came to pass. From that day on he always lay on his back, his little body (if you except his face, scarcely changed at all) so wasted that only his spirit remained to him. On the day he died, namely the 26th of May, he seemed to speak more strongly and with less difficulty. But this was the last effort of nature. For about eight o'clock in the evening, suddenly the certain signs of approaching death appeared; and when this had been reported to me, who had just left him, and to another of the brethren, and to the members of his household, I ran there at once and found him so quietly dead, and without any movement of hands or feet, that he had not drawn a heavier breath before, nor had he been wholly deprived of sense and judgment, nor even of voice, until his last breath, and he looked much more like one asleep than one dead. So on that day, with the sun setting, this bright light too was snatched from us. On the following night and the next day there was great lamentation throughout the whole city. For the whole city was seeking the wisest and most pious citizen.

units.la: piem. pientissimum ciuem, Ecclesia deplorabat fidi sui pastoris decessum, schola ereptum sibi talem doctorem lugebat, omnesque in communi secundum Deum parente ac consolatore orbati lamentabantur. Optabant multi cives eum spectare mortuum, quod ab eo ne mortuo quidem auelli possent. Quidam etiam peregrini qui videndi & audiendi ipsius causa procul venerant, inter quos etiam adfuit Clarissimus vir Reginae Angliae in Gallia legatus, auide admodum intueri saltem defunctum petebant. Ac initio quidem admittebantur. Sed quod haec nimia esset curiositas, vt calumniis aduersariorum occurreretur, placuit amicis vt postridie mane qui dies erat Dominicus, linteo de more inuolutum corpus ligneo loculo includeretur. Pomeridiana vero secunda, sequentibus funus Patritiis, vna cum pastoribus, professoribusque scholae omnibus, totaque pene civitate non sine vberibus lachrymis prosequente, elatus est, communique coemeterio quod planum palatium vocant, nulla penitus extraordinaria pompa, nulloque addito cippo (sic enim mandarat) conditus, cui propterea his versiculis parentau.
units.tr: The most wise and most pious citizen. The Church mourned the death of its faithful minister, the school lamented the loss of such a teacher, and all, orphaned of a parent and consoler under God, grieved together. Many citizens wished to see him even in death, since they could not tear themselves away from him even when he was dead. Some foreigners too, who had come from afar to see and hear him, among them the most distinguished envoy of the Queen of England in France, eagerly asked to look at him at least once he had died. At first they were admitted. But since this curiosity was excessive, and since it was thought necessary to forestall the slanders of his enemies, the friends decided that on the following morning, which was the Lord's Day, the body, wrapped in linen as is customary, should be enclosed in a wooden coffin. In the second hour after noon, the funeral was conducted with the patricians following, together with all the ministers and professors of the school and almost the whole city, weeping copiously. He was carried to the common cemetery, which they call the Plain Palace, with no extraordinary pomp at all, and was buried without any added monument, as he himself had instructed. For this reason the following verses were written in his memory.

units.la: Roma ruentis terrorille usaximus,
units.tr: The terror of falling Rome we have known,

units.la: Quem mortuum lugent boni, horrescunt mali.
units.tr: Whom the good mourn dead, and the wicked shudder at.

units.la: Ipsa a quo potuit virtutem discere virtus,
units.tr: Virtue itself, from whom virtue could learn to be virtuous,

units.la: Cur adeo exiguo ignotoque in cespite clausa
units.tr: Why, you ask, is he hidden in so small and unknown a turf,

units.la: Calumnus lateat, rogas?
units.tr: Where slander lies concealed?

units.la: Calumnum assidue comitata modestia viuum,
units.tr: Modesty, which constantly attended him living, despite slander,

units.la: Hoc tumulo manibus condidit ipsa suis.
units.tr: Has laid him in this tomb with her own hands.

units.la: O te beatum cespitem tanto hospite!
units.tr: O happy turf, with so great a guest!

units.la: O cui invidere cuncta possint marmora!
units.tr: O turf, at which all marble might envy!

units.la: Vixit annos quinquaginta quatuor, menses decem, dies decem & septem, cuius spatij dimidium in sancto Euangelij ministerio consumpsit. Statura fuit mediocri, colore subpallido & nigricante, oculis ad mortem usque limpidis, quique ingenij sagacitatem testarentur: cultu corporis neque culto neque sordido, sed qui singularem modestiam deceret: victu sic temperato, vt a foribus & ab omni luxu longissime abesset: cibi parcissimi, vt qui multos annos semel quotidie cibum sumpserit, ventriculi imbecillitate causatus: somni pene nullius, memoriae incredibilis, vt quos semel aspexisset, multis post annis statim agnosceret, & inter dicendum saepe aliquot horas interturbatus, statim ad dictata nullo commonefaciente rediret, & eorum quae ipsi nosse muneris sui causa interesset, quatumuis multiplicibus & infinitis negotiis oppressus, nunquam tamen obliuisceretur. Iudicij, quibuscumque de rebus consuleretur tam puri & exacti, vt pene vaticinari saepe sit visus, nec abertasse meminerim qui consilium ipsius esset sequutus.
units.tr: He lived fifty-four years, ten months and seventeen days, and he spent half of that span in the holy ministry of the Gospel. He was of medium height, of a somewhat pale and swarthy complexion, with eyes that remained bright until death and testified to the keenness of his mind. His dress was neither elegant nor slovenly, but such as suited a singular modesty. His diet was so moderate that he stayed far from delicacies and all luxury; he ate very little, and for many years took only one meal a day, blaming the weakness of his stomach. He hardly slept at all. His memory was incredible: those whom he had once seen he recognised at once after many years. While preaching he was often interrupted for some hours, yet he would return at once to the text dictated, without anyone reminding him. And though he was overwhelmed by very many and endless tasks, he never forgot those matters of his office which concerned him. His judgement, whatever matter he was consulted on, was so pure and exact that he often seemed almost to prophesy, and I cannot recall anyone who followed his counsel and was disappointed.

units.la: D.iij Facundiæ contemptor & verborum parcus, sed minime irritus scriptor, & quo nullus ad hunc diem Theologus (ablit erribo inuidia) putius, grauius, iudiciosius denique scripsit, quum tamen tam multa scripserit quàm nemo vel nostra vel patrum memoria. Erat enim hoc consequutus vigiliis iuuentutis, & quadam iu dicij acrimonia, dictandi exercitatione confirmata, vt iecque illi deesset vnquam quod appositè & grauiter diceret, neque e multo aliter scriberet quàm loqueretur. In doctrina quam initio o tradidit, ad extremum constans, nihil prorsus immutauit, quo od paucis nostra memoria Theologis contigit. Quòd ad ipsius mores attinet, quanuis illum natura ad grauitatem fiaxisset: taemo tamen illo in communi conuictu fuit suauior: in ferendis hominum vitiis quæ infirmitatis erant, mirè fuit prudens, vt iecque im portuna obiurgatione pudefaceret aut perterrefacere, timmbecillos fratres, neque vitia conniuendo vel adulando fouere. Adulationis autem & simulationis, improbitatis denique, s rarefertim si de Religione agebatur, tam fuit hostis acer & vehemens, quàm veritatis, simplicitatis, & candoris amans. Fuit omnino o naturæ ipsius temperamento ἐξυχολος, quod vitium etiam aixexerat laboriosissimum illud vitæ genus. Iræ tamen sic eum do:ucuerat Spiritus Domini moderari, vt ne verbum quidem fit ex to o auditu, quod viro bono indignum esset, nedum vt longius progrederetur: nec temere nisi tum commoueretur, quo de Religionis causa agebatur, aut aduersus præfractos homines ipsi nequotium erat. Tot tantasque virtutes domi & foris, tam multos aliudetfarios habuisse nemo mirabitur, qui vel eorum inter profanas gentes hominum historiam legerit, qui præ aliis aliquam virtutis speciem adamarint, tantùm abest, vt mirum cuiquam videri debeat fortissimum tum sanæ doctrinæ defensorem, cum puræ & vitæ fectatorem domi & foris tam acriter oppugnatum fuisse. Sed hoc potius admiratione dignum est, vnicum hominem tanquam Herculem quendam Christianum tot domandis monstris fuisse, nempe fortissima illa clava, id est Dei verbo vtentem. Itaque quot ei aduersarios Satan excitaui (nullos enim in tam multis hostes alios habuit), quàm qui pietati, & honestati bellum indixissent) tot feruo suo Dominus victoriarum trophæa defixit. Hæreticum isti faciunt Calvinum: quasi vero non sit hoc etiam nomine damnatus Christus ipse, & quidem ab ipsis Sacerdotibus. Expulsus est Geneua, adde & ab eadem reuocatus. Et quid Apostolis, quid Athanasio, quid Chrysostomo contigit? Exprobrant illi multa nonnulli alij, sed cuiusmodi? Ambitiosus fuit scilicet, imò etiam nouum papatum ambiuit, qui hoc vitæ genus, hanc Remp. hanc denique Ecclesiam, quam verè è possum paupertatis officinam appellare, rebus omnibus antepositum fuit. units.tr: D.iij He despised eloquence and was sparing of words, yet he was a writer by no means without result, and (let me say this without envy) no theologian to this day has written more purely, more weightily and more judiciously, although he wrote as much as no one in our time or in the memory of the Fathers. For he achieved this through vigils of youth and a certain sharpness of judgement, strengthened by the practice of dictating, so that he never lacked what he could say aptly and gravely, and he wrote no differently from how he spoke. In doctrine, he remained constant to what he had first handed down, and at the end changed nothing at all, which has happened to few theologians in our memory. As for his morals, although nature had made him rather serious, he was nonetheless more pleasant in ordinary company than anyone. In bearing with the faults of men, which were of weakness, he was wonderfully prudent, so that he neither shamed nor terrified the timid brothers with untimely rebuke, nor did he indulge their faults by overlooking or flattering them. But towards flattery and pretence, and indeed towards wickedness, especially when religion was at stake, he was as fierce and vehement an enemy as he was a lover of truth, simplicity and candour. Altogether, by the temperament of his nature he was quick-tempered [ὀξύχολος], a fault which that most laborious manner of life had also increased. Yet the Spirit of the Lord had taught him to restrain his anger so that not even one word was heard from him that was unworthy of a good man, let alone that it went any further; nor was he stirred lightly, unless it was when the cause of religion was at issue, or when he had to deal with stubborn men. No one will be surprised that he had so many and so great virtues at home and abroad, and so many enemies, if he has read the history of men among the profane nations, of those who most admired some appearance of virtue above others. So far is it from seeming strange to anyone that the most courageous defender of sound doctrine was so fiercely attacked at home and abroad, who was a pursuer of pure life. Rather, what is worthy of wonder is that this one man, like some Christian Hercules, subdued so many monsters, namely by using that most strong club, the Word of God. Thus, as many adversaries as Satan stirred up against him (for he had no other enemies among so many), as many as had declared war on piety and honesty, so many trophies of victory did the Lord fix for his servant. They make Calvin a heretic; as if Christ himself had not been condemned on this very charge, and indeed by the priests themselves. He was expelled from Geneva, and was also recalled by the same city. And what happened to the Apostles, to Athanasius, to Chrysostom? Some others reproach him with many things, but of what sort? That he was ambitious, indeed that he aspired to a new papacy, he who put this manner of life, this commonwealth and finally this Church, which I may truly call a workshop of poverty, before all things. ...

units.la: cumueumuladis scilicet opibus studuit, cuius bona omnia, carè etiam diuendita ipsius bibliotheca, vix trecentos aureos æquarant, vt non minus scitè quàm verè calumniam istam longè impudentissimam refellens hæc verba vsurparit, Me non esse pecuniosum si quibusdam viuus non persuadeo, mors tamen ostendet. Testari certè potest Senatus, quum perexigua essent eius stipendia, tum abfuisse vt in iis non acquiescceret, vt ampliora etiam obla ta pertinaciter recusarit. Exprobrat ei alij, quod illius frater Antonius Caluinus priorem vxorem suam ob adulterium, cognita causa, repudiarit. Quid ergo dicerent illi, si adulteram fouisset? Quod si in eum redundat hoc impudicæ mulieris dedecus, quod fiet Iacobi, Dauidis, ipsius denique filij Dei familiæ, in qua ipsemet Diabolum ex suis vnum diserte notauit? Delitiis scilicet illum & luxui indulsisse, tot ipsius laborum testes demonstrant. Quid quod nonnullos etiam dicere & scribere non pudet, regnasse illum Geneuæ tum in Ecclesia tum in Repub. atque adeo pro tribunali sedisse? Alij etiam illum nescio quem viuum pro mortuo cadauere excitando vniuerso etiam teste populo suppo suisse fabulantur, quod non minus putidum mendacium quàm si Romæ Papa fuisse diceretur, ausus est rapsodus ille Sorbonicus, Claudius Spensa maledicentissimo quodam libro inculcare. Quid enim istos pudeat? Sed ista neque apud eos qui tantum hunc virum norunt, neque apud posteros sani iudicij homines, qui mores hominis ex ipsius scriptis æstimabunt, refutatione indigent. Ego historiam vitæ & obitus ipsius, cuius spectator sedecim annos fui, bona fide persequutus, testari mihi optimo iure posse videor, longè pulcherrimum verè Christianæ tum vitæ, tum mortis exemplum in hoc homine cunctis propositum fuisse, quod tam facile sit calumniari, quàm difficile fuerit æmulari.
units.tr: ...He strove, of course, for a modest fortune, and when his goods were all valued, including his library, which was even sold cheaply, they barely amounted to three hundred gold pieces. Thus, refuting that slander, which is by far the most shameless, he used these words, no less wittily than truly: "I am not wealthy, if I do not persuade some while alive; death, however, will show it." The Senate can certainly testify that, although his stipend was very small, he was far from being content with it, and that he stubbornly refused even larger sums that were offered him. Others reproach him that his brother Antoine Calvin divorced his first wife for adultery, after the cause was examined. What then would they say if he had harboured an adulteress? But if the disgrace of this unchaste woman falls upon him, what will become of the family of Jacob, of David, and finally of the Son of God himself, in which the Devil himself was clearly noted as one of its members? That he indulged in pleasures and luxury, the many witnesses of his labours demonstrate. What of the fact that some are not ashamed to say and write that he ruled at Geneva, in both Church and Commonwealth, and even sat as a judge? Others, too, fabricate that he, by some arrangement, raised up I know not what living man in place of a dead body, before the whole people as witnesses; that is no less foul a lie than if one were to say he was pope at Rome. That Sorbonne rhapsodist, Claude de Saintes, dared to drive this home in a certain most abusive book. For what shame have such people? But these charges need no refutation, neither among those who know this man only slightly, nor among posterity, sane men of judgement, who will judge the man's character from his writings. I, who have been a witness of his life for sixteen years, have related in good faith the history of his life and death, and I seem to myself to be able to testify with the best right that in this man there was set before all the most beautiful example, truly Christian, both of life and of death; one which is as easy to slander as it is hard to imitate.

units.la: QVia nemo piorum reperietur, cuĩ pergratum non fit certo intelligere quosnam libros Ioannes Caluinus in lucem emiserit, quæque ab eo relicta fuerint scripta, & eo concionante excepta, ne quis etiam hac in parte posthac fallatur, sicuti satis notum est in scriptis magnorũ virorum vt plurimum accidisse, vt sub eorum nomine multa falsa obrepserint & adulterina, commodiss mum duximus huc attexere nominatim catalogum tum Scriptorum vel Librorum Caluini qui Latinè & Gallicè iam in publicum prodierunt: tum etiam eorum qui nondum editi sunt, quantum memoria complecti potuimus.
units.tr: Since there will be no godly person who would not be very glad to know with certainty which books John Calvin has published, and what writings were left by him, or taken down while he preached, so that no one may be deceived in this matter in future, (as is well known to happen in the writings of great men for the most part, that many false and spurious works creep in under their names), we have thought it most convenient to append here, by name, a catalogue both of the writings or books of Calvin that have already appeared in public in Latin and French, and of those that have not yet been published, as far as we have been able to recall them.

units.la: QVVM mihi ad manum sit rerum sylua, quæ argumentum amplissimum præbeat, temperabo tamé stylum, vt indices magis habeas quàm longam narrationem: cui si indulgeré, in iustum volumé propè excreuisceret. Ad Calend. Octob. quo anni tempore pueri qui à grammaticis ad Dialecticam demigrát, exerceri agendis fabulis solent, acta est in gymnasio Nauarræ fabula felle & aceto, vt ait ille, plusquam mordaci cōsperfa: inductæ sunt personæ, Regina muliebriter nendo intenta, & nihil aliud quàm colù & acus tractans. Tum Megæra illi faces admouens, vt acus & colum abiiceret. Illa aliquantulum reniti & obluctari, vbi verò Furiæ cessisset, Euangelia in manus accepit, ex quibus omnia quibus ante assueuisset, & penè seipsam dedidisset. Demum extulit se in tyrannidem, & omni genere sæuitiæ miseros & innoxios vexauit. Multa eiusmodi figmenta addiderunt, indigna prorsus ea muliere quam non figuratè nec obscurè conuitiis suis proscindebant. Res in aliquot dies suppressa est. Postea verò, vt est Veritas filia Temporis re ad Reginam delata, visum est statui pessimum exemplum eorum libidini qui rebus nouis inhiat, si impunitas daretur huic improbitati. Prætor stipatus centum apparitoribus gymnasium adiit, & suis iussis domum circunsidere, ne quis elaberetur, ipse cum paucis ingressus, comicum non reperit. Aiunt eum minimè id consilio prouidisse, sed quum forte in amici cubiculo esset, tumultu prius exaudisse quàm perspici posset, atque ita latebras quæsisse è quibus per occasionem effugeret. Prætor tamen pueris actoribus manum iniecit: cui dum vult obsistere
units.tr: Since I have at hand a forest of material that offers a very wide subject, I will nevertheless restrain my pen, so that you have an outline rather than a long narrative. If I indulged myself, the letter would almost grow into a volume of proper size. On the Calends of October, the time of year when boys who move from the grammarians to dialectic are customarily exercised in acting plays, a play was performed at the college of Navarre, seasoned, as the saying goes, with gall and vinegar, more biting than any before. The characters introduced were a queen, busy spinning in womanly fashion and doing nothing but handling her distaff and needle, and Megaera, who held torches to her so that she would throw away the needle and distaff. She resisted and struggled a little; but when the Fury had prevailed, she took up the Gospels, to which she had been accustomed, and had almost given herself over to them. At last she raised herself to tyranny and harassed the wretched and innocent with every kind of cruelty. They added many such inventions, utterly unworthy of that woman, whom they tore apart with their insults, not in figurative or obscure terms. The matter was suppressed for some days. Afterwards, however, as Truth is the daughter of Time, the affair was reported to the Queen, and it seemed that a most pernicious example would be set for those who gape after novelties if this wickedness went unpunished. The provost, attended by a hundred officers, went to the college and, ordering his men to surround the house so that no one could slip away, entered himself with a few others, but did not find the comedian. They say he had not planned this at all, but since he happened to be in a friend's room, he heard the uproar before he could be seen, and so sought hiding places from which he might escape by chance. Nevertheless the provost laid hands on the boys who had acted, and while he tried to resist them

units.la: Gymnasiarcha, inter eorū altercationes, lapides à nonnullis pue-ris cōiecti sunt. Ille nihilominus eos arripuit, & quod pro scena recitassent, iussit repetere. Omnia excepta sunt. Quando auctor sceleris deprehendi nō potuerat, proximum erat dei iis inquire-re, qui quū prohibere possent, permilissent, & tandiu etiam dissi-mulassent. Alter qui & auctoritate præcellit, & nomine (est enim magnus magister Lauretus) impetrauit vt haberet pro carcere honestiore custodiam domum cuiusdam (vt vocā Comitarij: alter Morinus ab illo secundus, iussus se domi continere dū in-quireretur. nunc quid copertum sit nescio: est tamen euocatus ad tres breues dies, vt nunc loquuntur. Hactenus de conœdiis. Alte-rum facinus ediderūt factiosi quidam Theologi æque malignū, etsi non vsqueadeo audax. Quum excuterent officias bibliopo-larum, libellum vernaculum, cuius inscriptio Speculum animæ peccatricis, retulerunt in numerum librorum à quorū lectione interdictum vellet. Regina vbi resciuit, quæsta est apud fratrem regem, profess se auctorem. Ille per literas magistris Academiæ Parisiensis imperauit sibi testirentur, an librum recensuissent in numero eorum quos iudicasserunt improbatæ religionis. Quod si ita haberet, sibi ratione sui iudicij redderent. De ea re Nicolaus Copus medicus nunc Rector retulit ad quatuor artium collegia, Medicinæ, Philosophiæ, Theologiæ, Iuris canonici. Apud magi-stros artium inter quos locum dicendi primum habuit longa & acerba oratione inuectus est in eorum temeritatē, qui ibi id iu-ris in maiestatem Reginæ vsurpassent. Dissi-mulauit ne se immisce-rent tanto discrimini, ne Regis iram experiri vellent, ie in Re-ginam virtutum omnium & bonarum literarum matrem arma sumerent. Postremo ne hanc culpam in se recipientes, improbi-tatem eorum alerent, qui parati sunt quiduis semper agere di sub prætextu huius nominis, vt dicant Academiam fecisse, quod ipsi iniussu Academiæ perpetrant. Omnium sententia fuit factum abiurandum. Idem censuerunt Theologi, Canonici, Medici. Re-ctor renuntiauit ordinis sui decretum, post Decanus Medicinæ, tertius Canonici iuris doctor, quartus Theologus, vltimus verba fecit Clericus Parochus Sancti Andreæ, in quem omnis culpa deriuabatur, aliis à se amolientibus. Primum magnificis verbis extulit Regis integritatem, qui Fidei se animosum protectorem hactenus gesserit. Esse aliquos finist os homines, qui hunc egre-gium animum conentur peruertere, qui etiam conspiauerint in exitium sacrę facultatis: sibi tamen certam spem esse nihil ob-tenturos aduersus talem constantiam, quam in Rege esse no-uisset. Quantum attineret ad negotium quod esset in nanibus, se quidem fuisse delegatum Academię decreto ad eam prouin-ciam, nihil tamen minus sibi in animo fuisse quam duerfus Reginam quippiam moliri, foeminam, tum sanctis moribus tum pura religione praeditam, cuius rei argumento esse poterant iusta, quę mattis suę manibus post mortem persoluisset: se pro damnatis libris babuisse obscœnos illos Pantagruelem, Syluam amorum, & eius monetę: hunc interim inter suspectos repo- suisse, quod si ie Facultatis consilio editus esset, magna fraude Aresti, quo vitium erat, inconsulta Facultate quicquam edere quod ad Fidem spectaret. Denique sibi hoc esse praesidium, mandato Facultatis factum quod in quaestionem vocabatur. Omnes esse culpę affines, si qua esset, quantumuis abnegarent. Atque hęc omnia Gallice, ut omnes intelligerent, si verum praefabatur: omnes tamen femebant eum obtendere ignorantiae suae hanc speciem. Aderant autem Episcopus Syluanectensis, Stella, & quidam ex praefectis aulae regiae. Vbi finem fecit dicendi Clericus, Paruus dixit lectum à se librum, nihil se dignum litura comperisse, nisi oblitus esset suae Theologiae. Demum postulauit ut ederetur decretum, quo Regi satisfieret Copus Rector pronuntiauit, Academiam non agnoscere censuram illam qualis fuisset, quo libellus censitus esset in libris aut damnatis aut suspectis, non probare neque in se recipere. Viderent qui id fecisset qua ratione se defensuri essent, paratas fore in tempore literas quibus se Academia Regi excusaret, ageret etiam gratias, quod sic tam benigne paterno more compellasset. Allatum est regium diploma, quo Parisiensi Episcopo permittitur praeficere quos velit singulis parochiis concionatores, qui prius pro libidine illorum eligebantur, ut quisque erat clamosissimus & stolido furore praeditus quem illi zelum vocant, quo nunquam arsit Helias, qui tamen zelo zelabatur super domum Dei. Vale. M. D. XXXIII.
units.tr: amid their quarrels with the head of the college, some boys threw stones. He nevertheless seized them and ordered them to repeat what they had recited on stage. Everything was taken down. Since the author of the crime could not be found, the next step was to inquire of those who, although they could have prevented it, had allowed it and had kept silent for so long. One of them, who excels both in authority and in reputation (for he is the great master Lauretus), obtained that instead of prison he should be kept under more honourable custody in the house of a certain man, called Comitarius; the other, Morinus, second after him, was ordered to keep himself at home while the inquiry went on. What has been concealed I do not now know; yet he has been summoned for three short days, as they now say. So much for the comedies. The factious theologians committed another deed, equally malicious, though not so bold. While they were searching the booksellers' shops, they put a little vernacular book, whose title is The Mirror of the Sinful Soul, among the books they wished to have forbidden. When the Queen learned of this, she complained to her brother the king, who declared himself the author. He ordered by letter the masters of the Paris Academy to testify whether they had listed the book among those they had judged to be of irreligious character; if so, they must give him an account of their judgment. About this matter Nicolas Cop, the physician who is now Rector, reported to the four faculties of arts: Medicine, Philosophy, Theology and Canon Law. Before the masters of arts, among whom he had the first place to speak, he inveighed in a long and bitter speech against the rashness of those who had there usurped this authority against the majesty of the Queen. They should have held back, lest they should entangle themselves in such danger, lest they should risk the king's anger by taking up arms against the Queen, mother of all virtues and of good letters. Finally, by accepting this blame they would only nourish the wickedness of those who are always ready to do anything whatever under the pretext of this name, so that they could say the Academy had done what they themselves commit without the Academy's order. The judgment of all was that the deed must be disowned. The theologians, canons and physicians gave the same opinion. The Rector announced the decree of his faculty; after him the Dean of Medicine spoke, then the third, a doctor of canon law, and the fourth, a theologian; last of all spoke the cleric, parish priest of Saint Andrew, on whom all the blame was laid, while the others moved it away from themselves. First he extolled with splendid words the integrity of the king, who had so far borne himself as the spirited protector of the Faith. There are some most wicked men, he said, who try to pervert this outstanding spirit, who have even conspired to the ruin of the sacred faculty; yet he had a sure hope that they would achieve nothing against such constancy as he had known in the king. As far as concerned the business in hand, he had indeed been delegated by decree of the Academy to that task, but nothing was further from his mind than to attempt anything against the Queen, a woman endowed with holy morals and pure religion, of which the proof could be the good works she had done with her own hands for his Majesty after his death. He had regarded as condemned those obscene books, Pantagruel, the Forest of Loves and their kind; meanwhile he had placed this one among the suspect, since, had it been published with the Faculty's counsel, it would have been by a great deceit of Aresti, whose fault it was, for he had published anything touching on the Faith without consulting the Faculty. Finally, this was his defence: he had acted by the Faculty's mandate in what was now being called into question. All who were involved in the matter, if there was any fault, would share the blame, however much they denied it. All this he said in French, so that everyone could understand, if he was speaking the truth; yet everyone felt that he was putting forward this pretence of ignorance as a cover. The Bishop of Senlis, Stella, and some of the officials of the royal court were present. When the cleric finished speaking, Parvus said that he had read the book and had found nothing deserving of erasure, unless he had forgotten his theology. At last he demanded that a decree be published by which the king would be satisfied. Cop the Rector declared that the Academy did not acknowledge that censure, whatever its nature, by which the little book had been judged among the condemned or suspect books, and that it neither approved nor accepted it. Let those who had done this consider by what reasoning they would defend themselves; in due time letters would be ready by which the Academy would excuse itself to the king, and would also give thanks that he had addressed them so kindly, in a fatherly manner. A royal letter patent was brought in, by which the Bishop of Paris is permitted to appoint to each parish whatever preachers he wishes, whereas before they had been chosen at the whim of those men, so that whoever was the most clamorous and endowed with foolish frenzy, which they call zeal, was chosen; with such zeal Elijah never burned, though he was consumed with zeal for the house of God. Farewell. 1533.
