units.la: PRiuilegia nouis libris impetrari nec abs re olim, nec sine publico bono constitutum fuit: atque utinam nullus hodie liber exiret non suo priuilegio ornatus: modo ne id esset vel gratia elicitum, vel pecunia redemptum Principis beneficium, quo temere commendaretur ad Typographi quaestum: sed graue praesumque testimonium, quo luce, & hominum oculis dignus ex vero pronuntiaretur. Hoc enim remedio decebat coerceri furiosam istam scripturientium libidinem, quae tot Anno 1535.
units.tr: It was never out of place, nor without public benefit, that privileges should be obtained for new books. I wish that no book appeared today without its privilege, provided that the prince's favour was not extracted by influence or bought with money, so that it could be rashly recommended for a printer's profit. Instead, it should be a serious and weighty testimony, by which a book worthy of the light and of people's eyes is declared true. This remedy would rightly restrain that mad lust of would-be writers, which every year, 1535, gives us so many examinations of books, with no method, no discrimination, and no shame. Such is the burning of an empty desire for fame that not a few would rather become known by any crime whatever than remain unknown in goodness. Now princes, by their excessive easygoing, give the Commonwealth very poor counsel: they not only permit good and bad books to be published, but also approve the very worst with their vote.

units.la: Epist.2. Praefatio Io.Calvini in Gallicā traslatione Bibliorū à Petro Roberto Olivetano edita Neocomi. librorum examina nullo modo, nullo delectu, nullo pudore, subinde nobis parit. Adeo vrit non paucos stolida nominis cupiditas, vt malint quouis facinore vtcunque innotescere, quàm bene latere. Nunc immodica sua facilitate pessime consulunt Reipub. Principes, qui non modo bonos malos libros edi permittunt, sed pessimos quosque suo suffragio comprobant. Hoc vero Sacrum Opus quod nec nuper natum est, nec ab homine profectum, ideo hominum testimonio minime indigere visum est. Et sane iniquissime comparatum esset, si talibus elogiis opus haberet, quorum sordibus nihil aliud quàm fœdarctur eius dignitas. Oraculum ergo, & æterna veritas summi Regis, cœli, terræ, marisque Domini, Regumque Regis, Diploma est priuilegij, quod nobis magnifice splendideque ipsum commendat: quod summa veneratione ab omnibus Gentibus, ætatibus, ordinibus publice ac priuatim excipi iubet. En edictum, cui omnes ad vnum obsequentes esse conueniat. Sed impiæ quorundam voces audiuntur, clamitantium rem esse indignam, vulgari hæc simplici plebeculæ mysteria: in quibus qui totam ætatem detriuerunt, magnis alioqui & ingenij & doctrinæ præsidiis adiuti, in medio tamen stadio sapius defecerunt: pauci aut forte omnino nulli reperti, qui vltimam lineam attigerint. Quid, inquiunt, præ istis asequi possunt miseri idiotæ, omnium bonarum artium rudes, & (si vsus quæritur) rerum omnium imperiti? Verùm cùm Dominus è pastorum caulis Prophetas, è piscatorum nauiculis Apostolos sibi coaptarit, cur non & nunc similes discipulos dignetur? Imò si iis Rabinis (qua sunt animi vel magnitudine vel ferocitate) pudenda est fors discendi cum plebeis & rudibus: quantum probrum est à talibus præceptoribus discere, qui nulla in parte vel abiectissimos excelluerunt, nisi quòd à Domino docti erant? Neque in eam partem hæc à me dicuntur, quò tollam ex Ecclesia docendi discendíque ordinem: quæ luculentam Dei benignitate agnoscere debet, dum à prophetis, doctoribus, interpretibus, qui ab eo missi sunt, probè instituitur. Sed hoc tàtum postulo, vt fideli populo Deum suum loquentem audire liceat, & à docente discere. Quando ille à minimo vsque ad maximum cognoscci vult, quando omnes θεοδίδακτους fore pollicetur, quando conqueritur in suis semper laborandum adhuc esse, quos vocat Ablactatos à lacte, auulsos ab vberibus: quando paruulis dat sapientiam, pauperibus εὐαγγελίσασθαι præcipit. Cùm ergo videmus ex omnibus ordinibus esse qui in Dei schola proficiant, agnoscimus eius veritatem, qui promisit effusurum se de Spiritu suo super omnem carnem. Isti contrà fremunt & indignantur. Quid hoc est nisi Deo suam largitatem exprobrare? O si eo seculo vixissent, quo Philippo erant quatuor filiæ prophetantes,
units.tr: Preface of John Calvin to the French translation of the Bible edited by Pierre Robert Olivétan at Neuchâtel, Epist. 2. But this Holy Work, which is neither recently born nor the product of a man, did not seem to need human testimony. And truly it would be most unjust if it needed such praises, by whose filth its dignity would only be defiled. The oracle, then, and the eternal truth of the highest King, Lord of heaven, earth, and sea, and King of kings, is the warrant of privilege, which commends it to us magnificently and splendidly. It orders that it be received publicly and privately, with the highest reverence, by all nations, ages, and orders. Here is an edict to which everyone without exception ought to submit. But the impious voices of some are heard, shouting that these mysteries are unworthy to be made common to the simple populace. Those who have spent their whole lives on them, though aided by great gifts of intellect and learning, have often failed in the middle of the course, and few or perhaps none have been found who reached the final line. "What," they say, "can wretched laymen, ignorant of all the good arts and (if experience is asked) inexperienced in all things, achieve beside these men?" But since the Lord has chosen prophets from the sheepfolds of shepherds and apostles from the fishermen's little boats, why does He not now deign to take similar disciples? Indeed, if the rabbis (who are proud either in greatness of spirit or in fierceness) are ashamed to learn with commoners and the untrained, how great a disgrace it is to learn from such teachers, who have excelled in no respect, not even the most humble, except that they were taught by the Lord! I do not say these things to abolish from the Church the order of teaching and learning. The Church ought to acknowledge with great thankfulness God's kindness, since it is properly instructed by the prophets, teachers, and interpreters whom He has sent. But I ask only this: that the faithful people be allowed to hear their God speaking and to learn from the teacher. For He wants to be known from the least to the greatest; He promises that all will be taught by God; He complains that among His own people there is always still work to be done, calling them those weaned from milk, torn from the breasts. He gives wisdom to little ones, and commands the poor to be evangelized [εὐαγγελίσασθαι]. Therefore, when we see that there are those from every order who make progress in God's school, we acknowledge the truth of Him who promised to pour out His Spirit upon all flesh. Those men, on the contrary, rage and are indignant. What is this but to reproach God for His generosity? Oh, if only they had lived in that age when Philip had four daughters who prophesied!

units.la: Ifa.28.9. phetantes,quàm indigne eas tulissent?nisi forte & indignis modis accepissent. Quando verò Dei verbum quoties libitum est, fortiter contemnunt, cur non Patrum saltem exempla imitantur,quibus tantùm se deferre simulant? Hieronymus non est dedignatus mulierculas studij confortes: Chrysostomus,& Augustinus quando non plebem hortantur ad hæc studia? quàm frequenter inculcant,ut domi relegant,quæ in Ecclesia audierunt? Quid quòd Chrysostomus plebeiis magis quàm Monachis necessariam esse Scripturæ sanctæ lectionem cõtendit: quòd variis curarum & negotiorum fluctibus iactati,in naufragium statim abriperentur seculi huius,nisi ad hanc ancoram hærerent? Laudatus est ab Eusebio Pamphilus Martyr, qui sacros codices paratos semper domi habebat, quos & viris & fœminis largiretur. Nec puriore illo seculo duntaxat,sed multis postea annis valuit hæc libertas:donec corruptum suisque cupiditatibus immersum vulgus,suapte nequitia,& ignauia hoc studij genus abiecit. Nùc vbi repeti cœpit,emersit hæc tyrannis,quæ populum à communi bono arceat. Id verò perinde est,acsi quis huic aqua & igni, communibúsque elementis interdicat, quia nondum iis vti visus sit.Quis cogitaslet tantam in Pastoribus crudelitatem,(nam Pastores & haberi & dici volunt)vt vitæ pabulum ex ouium fauicibus vi eripere non horreant? Sed periculum est, inquiunt, ne in multis sua simplicitate labatur vulgus,ne peruertat non intelecta,atque ita venenum pro alimento hauriat. Quàm hic impudenter ratiocinantur? Euangelium est odor mortis in morte iis qui pereunt, Iudeisscandalum ,Græcis stultitia: ergo ne legatur,ne audiatur. At est virtus Dei in salutem omni credenti, Iudæo simul & Græco:Christus est petra offensionis,in quam multi impingunt,& qua multi eliduntur:ergo ne sit Christus.Sed est vita æterna,vnica ad Patrem via & veritas. Quando hæc parum solida vident,addunt,inter tot hæreses quibus nunc orbis vexatur,contineri melius populum obedientia quàm doctrina. Sed tum quoque feruebant hæresibus omnia, cùm ij quos retuli& Chrysost. Augustt. suos ad studium cœlestis doctrinæ acriter stimulabant. Nempe tali eos pharmaco aduersus hæresesmunie-bant,talibus armis instruebant. Postremò miserè deplorant superbire ac ferocire vulgus, statim atque gustum aliquem sacrarum literarum concepit. Superbire autem vocant, non ex suo ore pendere, ac non quasi ex tripode profectum adorare, quidquid vel per somnium cogitauerint. Hinc hinc illæ lachrymæ. Sic quondam Rom.Pontif.& sacrificuli vix manus ab illo continuerunt, qui fastos populo describerat, quorum penes se esse arbitrium volebant. Ad hunc modum isti,cùm fumos suos nisi in tenebris vendere populo nequeunt,nihil mirû si hanc lucem
units.tr: Isaiah 28:9. How unworthily would they have borne it! Unless perhaps they would have received it with unworthy outrage. But when they bravely despise God's Word whenever they please, why do they not at least imitate the examples of the Fathers, to whom they pretend only to defer? Jerome did not disdain women as companions in study. When do Chrysostom and Augustine not exhort the common people to these studies? How often do they urge them to go over at home what they heard in the Church? What is more, Chrysostom contends that reading Holy Scripture is more necessary for ordinary people than for monks, since, tossed by the waves of various cares and business, they would at once be swept into the shipwreck of this world unless they clung to this anchor. Eusebius praised Pamphilus the martyr, who always kept the sacred codices ready at home, which he gave to both men and women. And this freedom flourished not only in that purer age, but for many years afterwards, until the common people, corrupted and plunged into their own desires, cast off this kind of study by their own wickedness and laziness. Now that it has begun to be sought again, this tyranny has emerged, which keeps the people from the common good. This is just as if someone were to forbid it water and fire, the common elements, because it has not yet seemed fit to use them. Who would have thought there was such cruelty in the ministers (for they wish to be both held and called ministers), that they do not shrink from violently snatching the food of life from the mouths of sheep? "But there is danger," they say, "that the common people, in their simplicity, may stumble in many things, that they may pervert what they do not understand, and so drink poison for food." How shamelessly do they reason! The Gospel is a fragrance of death to death to those who perish, a stumbling block to the Jews, foolishness to the Greeks. Therefore let it not be read, let it not be heard! But it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew as well as the Greek. Christ is a stone of offence, against which many stumble and by which many are crushed. Therefore let there be no Christ! But there is eternal life, the only way to the Father and the truth. When they see that these arguments are not very solid, they add that, amid so many heresies by which the world is now troubled, the people are better held in check by obedience than by doctrine. But then too, everything was seething with heresies, when those whom I have mentioned, Chrysostom and Augustine, were sharply stirring their people to the study of heavenly doctrine. Indeed, they were fortifying them against heresies with such a remedy, equipping them with such weapons. Finally, they wretchedly lament that the common people grow proud and fierce as soon as they have grasped some taste of the sacred letters. They call it pride not to hang on their mouth, and not to worship, as if from the tripod, whatever they have thought, even in a dream. Hence those tears! Thus once the Roman Pontiff and the little priests could hardly restrain their hands from him who had drawn up the calendar for the people, whose authority they wanted to keep in their own hands. In this way, since they cannot sell their smoke to the people except in darkness, it is no wonder that they cannot bear this light to approach.

units.la: a. iij. accedi non sustineant: pessime vero hoc eos habet, arcana sua quibus plus inclt obfcœni atis,quàm aut vllis bonæ Deæ sacris, autipfis etiam Bacchanalibus, sic palàm retegi ac traduci. Alij qui paulò volunt videri æquiores, causantur, tantùm vulgari vsu contentam debere esse promiscuam plebem: has versiones quæ non modò ad linguarum veri atem, sed ipsam loquendi proprietatem exiguntur in eruditorum Bibliothecis oportere magis versari,quàm rudium manibus passim volui: quorum vt aiunt,admodum pauci sunt qui aliquid inde allequantur,quàm plurimi vero nouitate offendantur. Hi quid spectent non video, nisi quod foli sapere volunt. Cùm enim negant vsum esse aliquem puriorisinterpretationis, quam quæ nunc habetur tot locisdeprauatiffima, in Spiritum S.non obscure sunt conzumeliofi: cuius donum esse linguarum interpretationem affirmat Paulus,& in Ecclesiæ ædificationem conferri postulat.Si donum ipfumfpernunt,sacrilegi: fi supprimi volunt, ne multis seruiat, inuidi & iniqui. Nouitatem quidem fateor plus fatis esse odiosam:quia multi sunt ventres qui non nisi glandeː pasci sustinerent, etiam reperta fruge. Sed ea demum nouitas odium mereretur, quam nullo opereprætio affectatam esse data opera, atque ascitam constat: quæ vero sepultam veritatem eruit, eam non omni fauore amplecti,turpissima ingratitudo est. Quòd fi ea est hominum barbaries, vt beneficiis etiam ipsis male afficiantur, omittendæ potius offensiones sunt & quæuisodia,quàm vt eorum gratia veritatis dispendio constet. Quanquam de populo securus sum,qui iampridem famelicus talibus epulis inhiat,tantùm abest vt à nouitate abhorreat.Sed hùc suæ malignitatis præ-textum quærunt,quibus non fatis eftin confertissimis theffauris volutari, nisi nummulos de meliore nota percussos populo inuideant,saluis etiam & integris suis thesauris. De interprete par cius loquor,ne quid cognationi quæ illi mecum intercedit, aut veteri uostræ familiaritati dare videar. Dicam tamen (quod & ipse mea fide polliceri ausim, nec liuor ipse inficiari possit) hominem nec ingenio tardum,nec eruditionis inopem,quantùm industria,studio, sedulitate adniti potuit,summa fide in hoc interpretandi officio versatum esse. Neque tamen quædam esse dubito, quæ vel pro iudiciorum varietate, vel quia operæ in longo interdum somnus irrepit, non omnibus placitura sint. Verùm lectores hortor, vt fi qua eius generis occurrant, nec hominem de sacris literis bene meritum mordere, profciiunde-re,& insectari malint,quàm modeste fui lapsus admonere. Hæc ingenuitas & Christianam pietatem, & liberalem doctrinam decet:nec peffimam gratia à Roberto nostro referent, qui multis aliis dotibus eximius,modestia tamé seipsum vincit:fi tamen eca est. ea est modestia ac non potius immodicus pudor, quo pene ab hoc tam sancto labore suscipiendo abstractus est, nisi hortatu ac etiam flagitatione sua victum sancti viri inuictique veri testes Chusemeth & Chlorotes tandem manus dare coegissent. Qui vero nulla ratione ab improbitate linguae cohiberi possunt, ij meminerint facillimam esse maledicendi artem, si quis ea certare velit: & quam mulierculae in triuiis melius exerceant, quam in scholis rhetores. Neque vero Comicum illud minor, male vicis sim audituiros pro sua maledicentia. Habet hominem quem impune lacessant, quantum ad procacitatis vices attinet. Sed ne magnam vitulerae huius fecunditae laudem expectent, moneo. Tam venum est illud quam vulgatum, cauillari omnia promptum esse, sed non item aemulari. Valete.
units.tr: a. iij. But this hurts them most terribly: that their secrets, which have more obscenity than any rites of the good goddess or even of the Bacchanalia, are so openly exposed and paraded. Others, who want to seem somewhat fairer, complain that the common and mixed populace should be content with the ordinary use of the vernacular, and that these translations, which are demanded not only for the truth of the languages but for the very propriety of speech, ought to be kept in the libraries of the learned rather than tossed about in the hands of the unlearned everywhere. Of these, as they say, very few gather anything from them, while very many are offended by the novelty. I do not see what they are aiming at, except that they alone want to be wise. For when they deny that there is any use in a purer interpretation than the one now held, which is most corrupt in so many places, they are not obscurely insulting the Holy Spirit, whose gift Paul affirms the interpretation of tongues to be, and whose purpose he demands to be the building up of the Church. If they despise the gift itself, they are sacrilegious; if they want it suppressed, lest it serve many, they are envious and unjust. I admit that novelty is in itself more than enough to be hateful, since there are many stomachs that could endure to be fed only on acorns, even when grain has been found. But only that novelty deserves hatred which is plainly affected and adopted on purpose, without any real worth. To embrace with no favour the one that digs up buried truth is most shameful ingratitude. If men are so barbarous that they are ill-disposed even towards benefits themselves, then offences and all hatred should rather be laid aside than that, for their sake, truth should suffer loss. Yet I am not worried about the people, who have long been hungering after such feasts, so far is the common folk from shrinking from novelty. But these men seek a pretext for their malice; it is not enough for them to wallow in the most crowded treasuries, unless they also begrudge the people some coins of better stamp, even while their own treasuries remain safe and intact. I speak about the translator in such a way as not to seem to give anything to the kinship that lies between him and me, or to our old friendship. Yet I will say this (and I myself dare to vouch for it on my own faith, and even envy itself cannot deny it): that he is a man neither slow of wit nor lacking in learning, and that, as far as industry, zeal, and diligence could strive, he has carried out the duty of interpreting with the greatest fidelity. Nor do I doubt that some things will please not everyone, either because of the variety of judgments or because sleep sometimes creeps into long labour. But I urge the readers that, if any such things occur, they rather admit to the modest correction of the lapse than bite, attack, and pursue the man who has deserved well of the Holy Scriptures. Such candour befits both Christian piety and liberal learning. Nor should they repay our Robert with the worst ingratitude, who, though distinguished by many other gifts, nevertheless surpasses himself in modesty, if indeed it is modesty, and not rather an excessive shame, which almost drew him away from undertaking this so holy labour, had not the witnesses of the holy man and the unconquered truth, Chusemeth and Chlorotes, at last forced him to give way, overcome by their exhortation and even urging. As for those who cannot in any way be restrained from the wickedness of their tongue, let them remember that the art of slander is very easy, if anyone wishes to compete in it, and that market-women in the crossroads practise it better than rhetoricians in the schools. Nor do I think that the saying of the comic poet is to be forgotten: that they will be badly treated for their slander. He has a man whom they can attack with impunity, as far as the turns of insolence go. But so that they do not expect great praise for the fertility of this bile, I warn them: it is as easy as it is common to carp at everything, but not equally easy to emulate. Farewell.

units.la: Gratia & pax augeatur tibi frater & Symmysta in Domino vnice colende. Orauimus nuper Basileae coram, nunc per literas, clarissimum & vere nobilem virum D. Maurum Musaeum, ate vt nobis impetraret, vti sustineres de religione nostra nobiscum coram commentari. Videmur nobis agnoscere, Dominum instituisse tui vsum Ecclesiis suis vberrimum concedere, eisque tuo ministerio latissime commodare. Proinde vt par est, optamus non nos modo, quorum nimirum non est apud Ecclesias tanta auctoritas, sed Ecclesias ipsas & qui ad illius ministerium iuuenes apud nos & alibi educantur, tecum per omnia conuenire. Quam multum siquidem parvae dissentiunculae praecipuorum ministrorum Ecclesiis obsint, haud dubie sat s perpesum habes. Atqui dedit Dominus, ni fallor, vt, si liceat tua omnia rite accipere, aliquid ad promouendum hunc tecum Ecclesiarum & ministrorum eius consensum possimus. Libenter itaque veniemus quo tu voles, vt in Domino summa cum obseruantia veritatis Christi, & tui, de tota administratione doctrinae Christi conferamus. Certe seculum hoc sic profecit, tam calumniando etiam quae recte dicta scriptaque sunt, quam exactissime seueriisimeque iudicando, quae secus, vt nos, quibus modis omnibus curandum est, vt ministerium nostrum adferat fructus plurimum, vituperetur a nemine, nihil ad summam diligentiam reliqui facere debeamus, quo nostra omnia, non solum vera sanctaque sint, quae vel scribimus vel dicimus, sed sic etiam depromantur, vt quae vera sanctaque sint, agnoscere valeant καὶ νῦν τισι in Ecclesia. Ad eam vero rem, quanti fecerit sanctorum conuentus & colloquia, D. Paulus, nosti mi frater, & symmysta in Domino venerande. Quantum huc fuit
units.tr: May grace and peace be increased for you, brother and fellow-minister in the Lord, to be honoured above all others. Lately we asked, in person at Basel and now by letter, the most illustrious and truly noble man, Master Maurus Musaeus, to obtain for us your consent to discuss our religion with us face to face. It seems to us that the Lord has willed that your service be granted in abundance to his churches and be lent most widely through your ministry. Accordingly, as is fitting, we wish not only ourselves (who certainly do not carry such authority among the churches) but the churches themselves, and those young men who are being trained for this ministry among us and elsewhere, to agree with you in all things. For you know well, brother, how greatly the small, petty disagreements among the leading ministers harm the churches. Yet the Lord has given us, unless I am mistaken, a means of advancing this agreement of the churches and ministers with you, if it is permitted for us to receive all your views rightly. We will therefore gladly come wherever you wish, so that in the Lord, with the utmost regard for the truth of Christ and for your own judgement, we may confer about the whole administration of Christ's teaching. Certainly this age has so advanced in calumniating even what has been rightly said and written, and in judging most exactly and severely what has not, that we, who must by every means take care that our ministry bears the greatest fruit and is blamed by no one, ought to leave nothing undone in the greatest diligence, so that all our words, whether written or spoken, may not only be true and holy, but may also be so set forth that those in the Church who are able to recognise what is true and holy may do so. As to that matter, my brother and venerable fellow-minister in the Lord, you know how highly the Apostle Paul valued holy assemblies and conferences. How much he...

units.la: 2. iiij. ter terras, per maria transcurrere ipsum, & suos, quos muerat vero aedificandi Ecclesias studio teneri, monere ad sanctum colloquium. Ergo in Domino suspiciendae frater, condic nos locum, siue Basileae siue Bernae, si aliter non poterit, Gebemis vt terrafte mus religiose, quae etiamsi tibi certa sunt, nobis am n pro nostra tarditate explicatione ampliore indigent. Etiam insipientibus debitores esse nolli, quaquam vere sapimus. Vinam vero nobis per Ecclesiarum negotia certe non negligen a, liceat breui nos Heluetiis videre, etiam inuocatos. Optime vale vir doctissime & sanctissime, & ne contemnas preces meas, doloremque eo super dolorem mihi adiicias. Nam quod non est datum te nosse & appellare cum hic essi s,dici non poteritvt dolat. Communicat mihi alioqui Capito omnia. Hic nesco quis sinister spiritus eum tam obliuiosum fecerit, vt omiserit, vel non meminerit te mihi prodere, quod & ipsi nunc dolet admodum. Argentorati Calend. Nouemb. M. D. XXXVI.
units.tr: ...2 Cor. 11, to run across lands and seas, and to urge his own people, whom he knew were moved by a true zeal for building up the churches, to a holy conference. Therefore, brother to be respected in the Lord, appoint a place for us, either Basel or Bern, if otherwise it cannot be done. ...(we ask you) to explain religiously; these matters, even if they are certain to you, need a fuller explanation for us because of our slowness. Nor do I wish to be a debtor to the unwise, although we are truly wise. Would that it might be allowed us, through the business of the churches which certainly is not to be neglected, to see you soon in Helvetia, even uninvited. Farewell, most learned and most holy man, and do not scorn my prayers, nor add grief upon grief to me. For that it was not granted for you to know and address me while you were here, cannot be said... Otherwise Capito shares everything with me. I do not know what sinister spirit has made him so forgetful that he omitted, or did not remember, to tell me of you, which he himself now greatly regrets. Strasbourg, Kalends of November 1536.
