units.la: Craldi morte ita sum consternatus, vt nullum ponere modim mœrori possim. Nullæ diurnæ occupationes animum meum sic retinere queunt, vt non in eam semper cogitationem reuoluatur. Miserrima dici tormenta excipiunt acerbiores nodis cruciatus. Non enim insomniis modo quibus ex consuetudine obduruì, diuexor, sed enecor etiam peruigiliis, quibus nihil valetudini meæ magis aduersum habeo. Præcipuè vero animum meu configit illa indignitas, fiquidé vera est suspicio, cui velim nolim, cogor locum aliquem dare. Quo tandem recident nostri posteri, cum in ipsis exordiis talia portenta iam emergăt? Quanti vereor ne scelus hoc magna aliqua Ecclesiæ clade breui luatur. Ad hæc non minimum est irę Dei indicium, in tanta bonorum paucitate, eo qui inter bonos postremus non erat, Ecclesiam orbari. Quid ergo aliud mi frater, quàm nostram calamitatem lugeamus? Quanquam neque validis solatiis deficimur. Magnum hoc, quod suo dolore & desiderio testantur omnes, quid de eius virtute ac integritate senserint. Sic enim ne in terris quidem latere patitur Dominus hostium nostrorum iniquitatem. Nec pilum lucri eo extincto fecerunt. Stat enim coram Domini tribunali testis & accusator eorum nequitiæ, cuius vox clarius sonabit in eorum perniciem, quàm si terram concuteret. Nos vero, quos ad tempus superstites reliquit Dominus, securè pergamus ea quam secutus est via, donec cursum nostrum peregerimus. Quamtalibet obiiciantur difficultates, nos tamen non impedient, quominus perueniamus ad eam quietem in quam ille iam receptus est. Nisi hæc spes nos retineret, quanta nos undique obsidet desperationis materia? Sed quoniam manet veritas Domini firma & inconcussa, in speculà nostra ad finem vsque perstemus, donec appareat quod nunc abscondituum est domini Regnum. Claricum porro iam cecinerunt aduersarij clarigatione in Mindam pronuntiata. Quoniam causa est religionis, omnes nostri necessario implicantur. Firmissimum & inuictum nobis præsidium erit, si Dominus exercituum sua nos virtute tuebitur. Alioqui vix tantum est nobis roboris, quod ad propulsandos hostium impetus valeat. Ad vnicum ergo illud asylum confugiamus, quod nunquam cömouebitur, etiamsi vniuersa concutiatur terra. Conuentum non definimus flagitare, donec fuerit impetratus. Onerius alteram à nobis quæstionem discuti voluit, an liceat sibi ac similibus Cœnam Domini cum ex eorum manibus accipere, tum etiam cum tanta hominum colluuie participare. Mihi cum Capitone nihil fuit in hac re dissentionis. Summa hæc fuit: Tantum debere inter Christianos esse odium schismatis,vt semper quoad licet refugiant.Tantum ministerij ac sacramentorum reuerentiam esse oportere vt vbicun que extare hæc cernunt,Ecclesiam esse censeant.Quando igitur Domini permiflu fit,vt per illos qualescunque tandem sint, Ecclesia administretur,fi Ecclesiæ signa illic conspiciunt,satius fore fi non fe à communione alienent.Nec obest quod impura quædam dogmata illic tradantur:reliquias enim ignorantiæ vix vlla est Ecclesia quæ prorsus nullas retineat.Nobis sufficit,fi doctri na qua Ecclesia Christi fundatur,locum habeat atque obtineat. Nec illud nos remoratur, quod legitimus haberi pastor nō debet, qui in locum veri ministri non tantum irrepserit fraudulenter,sed nefarie irruperit. Non enim est cur fe priuatorum vnuf-quisque istis scrupulis implicet: sacramenta cum Ecclesia communicant:pereorum manus dispensari sibi sustinet. quos enim tenere locum intelligunt, iure an iniuria, quanquam ad ipsos pertinet,de eo tamen iudicium suspendere vsque ad legitimam cognitionem possunt. Itaque fi eorum ministerio vtantur,non tamen periculum erit,ne aut agnoscere, aut approbare, autvllo pacto ratum habere videantur. Sed hoc vsu patientiæ suæ testimonium reddunt,dum scilicet eos tolerant,quos sentiant folen ni iudicio damnandos. Initio bonos fratres detrectaffe nec mirum est, neque nobis displicet. In eo siquidem feruore animorum quem necesse fuit tunc ebullire, nihil aliud quàm Christi fcin-dere fuisset. Deinde ambigebant adhuc quorsum tempestas vergeret, quæ tunc omnia permiscebat. Institit postea de fe agere, sed tanta contentione, vt viderretur nunquam desiturus, donec extorsisset quod petebat. Cur negaremus, erat manifesta ratio. Nam à ministro penes quem dispensatio est sacri huius mysterij, prudentia in delectu habendo requiritur. Ad hoc, non obscuré approbat eorum ministerium,fi quis eorum collegium non repudiet. Postremo cum huc quæstio recideret, satiusne foret cedere quàm recusare,hoc dilemmate vrgebamus:fi officium rite faceret,primo quoque die fequuturum exitum, fi nō faceret, flagitium esse quod nulla comprenfatione admitti fas eflet. Verum cum admonitus effet à me firmius obtentum quæri, facile præcidit quicquid illud erat.Experti fumus quàm difficile fit eos moderari, qui inani sapientiæ opinione deftipiunt. Cum omnes tempus hoc alienissimum iudicarent tractandæ fratrum causæ, Dominus spem omnem superauit.Impetratum quicquid petiimus.Videbatur initio tonerius ægre ferre,quod exigeretur confessionis formula:putabat hoc vno nostris satisfieri debere,quod à fe edocti erant. Postea tamen non adeo reclamauit, atque etiā qualem conscripsi eorum nomine, fine controuersia approbauit.Vereor ne tibi plurimū facessat negotij is, cuius partes sunt tte iute iuuare: sed patiendo tandem eluctaberis Quaesto te mi frater in tanta temporum iniquitate, animum adiicias ad retinendos omnes, qui vtcunque tolerabiles fuerint. De ceremoniolis effice apud fratres, ne eadem certent cum vicinis pertinacia. Ita fiet vt omnia nostra sint, nos ab omnibus liberi, serui simus pacis & concordiae. Si praetereo quae necessaria erant, eo fit, quod literae tuae mendum a Capitone, cui legendas dederam, mihi redditae sunt. Dominus te fruet, ac Spiritus sui robore ad omnia sustinenda confirmet, frater mi in Domino dilectissime. Admonet tua pro me solicitudo, vt tui curam vicissim tibi commendem. Valleenim attritum sibi te videri omnes narrant. Quaesto atque obscuro mi frater, sic de aliis cogita, simul vt memineris quod sis Ecclesiae Christi adhuc necessarius. Saluta millies mihi fratres omnes qui tecum sunt, Viretum, etiam Francisco cum aliis eos scribes. Capito, Sturmius Firmius te peramice salue-re iubent. Argentorati xxiiii. Octob. M. D. XXXVIII.
units.tr: The death of Craldi has so shaken me that I cannot find any limit to my grief. No daily occupations are able to hold my mind so that it does not keep turning back to that one thought. Torments more bitter than knots take hold of me, and they are most wretched. I am not only tormented by the sleeplessness to which I have grown accustomed, but I am worn out by sleepless nights as well, which do my health no good at all. Above all, that outrage pierces my heart. If the suspicion is true, I am forced, whether I like it or not, to give it some credence. Where will our descendants end up, when such monsters are already appearing at the very beginning? I fear that this crime will be paid for, soon, with some great disaster to the Church. Moreover, it is no small sign of God's anger that the Church is bereft of one who, among the few good men left, was not the least. What else, then, can we do, my brother, but mourn our calamity? Yet we are not without substantial comfort. It is a great thing that everyone bears witness, by their grief and their longing, to what they thought of his virtue and integrity. For the Lord does not allow even the wickedness of our enemies to remain hidden on earth. They have not gained a penny by his death. For he stands before the tribunal of the Lord as a witness and accuser of their wickedness, and his voice will sound out to their ruin more loudly than if it shook the earth. As for us, whom the Lord has left behind as survivors for a time, let us press on securely along the path he followed, until we have finished our course. However many difficulties are thrown in our way, they will not prevent us from reaching that rest into which he has already been received. If this hope did not sustain us, how much cause for despair surrounds us on every side! But since the truth of the Lord remains firm and unshaken, let us persevere at our post until the kingdom of the Lord, which is now hidden, appears. The enemies have already sounded the trumpet, having announced a formal declaration of war against Minden. Since the cause is one of religion, all of ours are necessarily involved. The Lord of hosts will be our firmest and invincible defence, if he protects us by his own power. Otherwise we have hardly enough strength to ward off the enemy's attacks. Let us therefore flee to that one refuge which will never be moved, even if the whole earth is shaken. We do not cease to beg for a council until it has been obtained. Onerius wanted another question discussed by us: whether he and others like him may receive the Lord's Supper from their hands, and also take part in it with such a crowd of people. Between Capito and me there was no disagreement on this matter. The sum of our view was this: among Christians the hatred of schism ought to be so great that they always avoid it as far as is lawful. The reverence due to the ministry and the sacraments ought to be so great that wherever they see these things existing, they judge that the Church is there. Therefore, since by the Lord's permission the Church is administered through those men, whatever they may be, if they see the signs of the Church there, it would be better not to hold themselves aloof from communion. Nor is it an objection that certain impure doctrines are taught there. For there is hardly any Church that retains no remnants of ignorance at all. It is enough for us if the doctrine on which the Church of Christ is founded has a place and holds its ground. Nor does it hold us back that he ought not to be regarded as the lawful minister, who has not merely crept into the place of a true minister by fraud, but has burst in wickedly. For there is no reason why each private individual should entangle himself in these scruples. They share the sacraments with the Church and allow themselves to be served by their hands. For although the question of whether those men hold their place rightly or wrongly belongs to them, they can nevertheless suspend judgment on it until it has been lawfully investigated. So if they make use of their ministry, there will be no danger that they appear to acknowledge, approve, or in any way ratify it. Rather, by this practice they bear witness to their patience, namely by tolerating those whom they know are to be condemned by their judgment alone. That the good brothers at first refused to recognise them is not surprising, nor does it displease us. For in that heat of spirits which had to boil over at the time, it would have been nothing other than tearing apart Christ himself. Then they were still uncertain which way the storm, which was then throwing everything into confusion, would turn. Afterwards they pressed to deal with the matter, but with such determination that they seemed never likely to stop until they had extorted what they were seeking. Why we should refuse was a clear reason. For prudence in choosing is required of the minister in whose charge the dispensing of this sacred mystery lies. Besides, their ministry is not obscurely approved if someone does not reject their college. Finally, when the question came back to this point, whether it would be better to yield than to refuse, we pressed this dilemma: if he performed the office properly, the outcome would follow on the very first day; if he did not, it would be a disgrace which could not be permitted by any allowance. But when he was warned by me that what had been obtained more firmly was being sought, he easily cut off whatever it was. We have found how difficult it is to restrain those who fall into the vain opinion of their own wisdom. When everyone judged this time most unsuitable for handling the brothers' cause, the Lord surpassed every hope. Whatever we sought was granted. At first Toneriusa seemed to take it badly that a formula of confession was demanded; he thought that our people ought to be satisfied with this one thing, that they had been taught by him. Afterwards, however, he did not object so strongly, and indeed he approved without dispute the form which I drew up in their name. I fear that he who has the part of helping you well will cause you much trouble, but by enduring you will at last struggle through. I beg you, my brother, in such a time of iniquity, to apply yourself to keeping all those who in any way are tolerable. Concerning the minor ceremonies, see to it among the brothers that they do not contend with their neighbours with obstinacy. So it will happen that all things are ours, that we, free from all, are servants of peace and concord. If I pass over what was necessary, it is because your letter was returned to me with a blunder made by Capito, to whom I had given it to read. May the Lord keep you safe, and strengthen you by the power of his Spirit to endure all things, my most beloved brother in the Lord. Your concern for me reminds me to commend your care to you in return. Farewell, for all report that you appear worn down. I beg you, my dear and afflicted brother, think of the others in the same way, and at the same time remember that you are still necessary to the Church of Christ. Greet all the brothers who are with you a thousand times for me, Viret too; you will write to Francisco and the others. Capito, Sturmius and Firmius greet you most warmly. Strasbourg, 24 October 1538.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: Quoniam verebar ne tibi molesta esset longior mearum litterarum expectatio, malui nuper abscissas praemittere, quam te differre in Michaelis aduentum. Nunc igitur reliqua cotexam. Prius vero quam veniam ad colloquium Philippi, breuiter tibi exponam quo progressus sit ex eo tempore rerum status. Tam iniquas conditiones ausus est tandem ferre Caesaris Legatus, vt parum abfuerit quin rursum ad gladios rediret. Volebat vt se a Sacramentariis nostri subduceret. Vides Satanae artes. Hoc scilicet captat, vt non modo vetera, quae olim seminauit, odia alantur: sed nouae quoque offensae, velut accensae facet ad maiora dissidia excitanda accedant. Atqui nostri nec Sacramentarios vllos recognoscunt, & coniunctionem sibi esse volunt cum Helueticis Ecclesiis. Ideoque illud omissum est a Caesare, factumque vt ad pacificendas inducias animi inclinarent: quae vtinam Ecclesiae Christi vtiles sint. Mihi certe nihil boni promittunt. Hoc quoque videt Elector Saxoniae, qui cum hactenus cunctator sit habitus, necessitatem belli impositam nobis putauit. Lantgrauius praeter omnium spem bellum dissuasit. Ac quamquam non detrectabat sequi, si aliter sociis videretur, emolliuit tamen eorum animos qui in eius alacritate plurimum reponebant. Nunc ergo res ad inducias vergit, inter quas de concordia vtrinque disputabitur. Verum aduersarij nihil aliud quam de belli opportunitate cogitabunt. Saxo ab hoc conuentu Cliuensem conueniet, cuius sororem habet in matrimonio. Si ad suscipiendam religionem illum adducere poterit, magnum erit regni Christi incrementum. Siquidem hodie non habet inferi̇ör Germania potentiorem principem, & qui latius dominetur nec superior etiam, excepto uno Ferdinando, qui amplitudine ationi tantum superat. De legatione ad Regem pro salute fratum a causa religionis commendanda, nihil dum erat decretum, cum Bucerus postremo scripsit. De legationibus enim vltimo loco agetur, quia ex rerum suarum conditione melius tunc deiberabunt, qua quidque ratione petere debeant. Ergo in id empus nos sustineamus. Cum Philippo fuit mihi multis de rebus colloquium: de causa concordiae ad eum prius scripseram, v bonis viris de ipsorum sententia certo possemus testari. Miseran ergo paucos articulos, quibus summam rei breuiter perstringeram. Iis line controuersia ipse quidem assentitur: sed fatetur esse in illa parte nonnullos, qui crassius aliquid requirant: atque ii tanta peruicacia, ne dicam tyrannide, vt diu in periculo fuerit quod cum videbant a suo sensu nonnihil alienum. Quanquam tamen non putat constare solidam consensionem, optat tamen vt haec concordia, qualiscunque est, foueatur, donec in vnitatem vnæ ve ritatis nos Dominus vtrinque adduxerit. De ipso nihil dubita, quin penitus nobiscum sentiat. De aliis rebus quales habuerimus sermones, longum esset enarrare: sed hæc erit aliquado materia iucundæ inter nos colloquutionis. Ad disciplinam dum venitur, ipse aliorum more ingemiscit. Magis enim deplorare miseram hac in re Ecclesiæ conditionem licet, quam corrigere: Ne vos istic solos laborare putes. Eduntur quotidie passim exempla, quæ omnes ad optandum remedium excitare merito debeant. Eiectus est non ita pridem Vima vir probus ac cœtus cum extrema ignominia, quod non sustineret magis vitiis indulgere. Dimissus est a collegis suis omnibus cum honorifi a commendatione, præsertim a Frechtho. Quæ Augusta nuntiantur, nihilo magis læta sunt. Ita posthac res lusoria erit, Pastores ministerio deturbare ac in exilium eiicere. Nec malum istud emedari potest, quia nec plebs, nec princeps iugum Christi a Papæ tyrannide discernunt. Censet ergo Philippus nihil melius esse, quam vt in tanta tempestate ventis aduersis aliquantum obsecundemus: sperque facit, vbi plus quietis ab externis hostibus erit, opportunitatem fore vt interioribus remediis oculos intendamus. Capito nunc Deum & homines obtestatur, perditam esse Ecclesiam, nisi mature succurratur rebus tam afflictis, nunc, quia profectum nullum videt, mortem precatur. Verum si vocatio no stra ex Domino est, vt esse non dubitamus, Dominus benedicet, vtcunque omnia aduersentur. Tentemus ergo remedia omnia, quæ si desunt, pergamus tamen ad vltimum vsque spiritu. Cum te video sic afflictari, interdum adesse cupio, vt nonnihil
units.tr: Since I feared that a longer wait for my letter would trouble you, I preferred to send you the fragments I had recently cut off, rather than have you put off everything until Michaelmas. Now, then, I will weave the rest together. Before I come to my conversation with Philip, I will briefly set out how the state of affairs has progressed since that time. The Emperor's envoy has at last dared to propose such unfair terms that he came close to taking up the sword again. He wanted Philip to separate himself from our Sacramentarians. You see Satan's arts. His aim, plainly, is not only that the old hatreds he once sowed should be kept alive, but that new offences should be added, as though kindled to stir up greater quarrels. Yet ours recognize no Sacramentarians at all, and they want to be in alliance with the Swiss Churches. So the Emperor dropped that demand, and this has made the minds of the parties inclined to arrange a truce. I wish it may prove useful to the Church of Christ. For my part, they promise me nothing good. The Elector of Saxony also sees this. Although he has hitherto been regarded as a hesitant man, he judged that war had been forced upon us. The Landgrave, beyond everyone's expectation, has argued against war. And although he did not refuse to follow if the allies thought otherwise, he has nevertheless calmed the spirits of those who placed great hopes in his eagerness. So now the matter is heading toward a truce, during which concord will be debated on both sides. But our opponents will think of nothing except the opportunity for war. At this assembly the Saxon will meet the Duke of Cleves, whose sister he has as his wife. If he can bring him to embrace the religion, it will be a great increase for the kingdom of Christ. For today Germany has no more powerful prince, nor one whose rule reaches more widely, nor even a superior one, except Ferdinand alone, who far surpasses him in the extent of his territory. Concerning an embassy to the King to commend the cause of religion for the safety of our brothers, nothing had yet been decided when Bucer last wrote. For embassies will be dealt with last, because then, from the condition of their own affairs, they will deliberate better about what each should seek and by what means. So let us hold out for that time. I had a long conversation with Philip on many matters. I had written to him earlier about the cause of concord, so that we could bear witness with certainty, from the good men themselves, to their opinion. I sent him a few articles, by which I had briefly summed up the substance of the matter. He himself assents to these on the main point, but he admits that there are some on that side who demand something rather crude, and these men are so obstinate, not to say tyrannical, that for a long time the matter was in danger, because they saw something a little alien to their own opinion. Although he does not think that a solid consensus exists, he nevertheless wishes that this concord, such as it is, be fostered until the Lord brings us on both sides into the unity of the one truth. Do not doubt about him that he thinks thoroughly as we do. To narrate the other things we discussed would take too long, but this will one day be a matter for a pleasant conversation between us. As for church discipline, while we are on it, he groans, as others do. For he says he laments the wretched condition of the Church in this matter more than he can correct it. Do not think that you alone there are labouring. Examples are published every day everywhere, which ought rightly to stir everyone to pray for a remedy. Not long ago a good man, Vima, was thrown out of his congregation with the utmost disgrace, because he would not tolerate indulging in vices. He was dismissed by all his colleagues with honourable commendation, especially by Frecht. What is reported from Augsburg is no happier. So from now on it will be a game to drive ministers from the ministry and cast them into exile. Nor can that evil be remedied, because neither the common people nor the prince distinguish the yoke of Christ from the tyranny of the Pope. Philip therefore thinks nothing better than that, in so great a storm, we should yield somewhat to the adverse winds. He hopes that when there is more quiet from external enemies, there will be an opportunity to turn our eyes to inner remedies. Capito now calls on God and men to witness that the Church is lost unless such afflicted affairs are speedily helped; now, since he sees no progress, he prays for death. But if our calling is from the Lord, as we do not doubt it is, the Lord will bless it, however much everything opposes us. So let us try all remedies, and if these fail, let us nonetheless press on to the last breath. When I see you so afflicted, I sometimes long to be with you, so that I may bring some

units.la: solatij afferam. Rursum dum succurrit nihil me tibi afferre posse, nisi materiam inuidię maioris, libenter absum, ne plus satis grauatum premam. Fratres Vvaldenses coronatum vnum mihi debebant, cuius partem à me mutuo acceperant, partem dederà nuntio qui cum fratre venerat, Sonerij mandato. Hunc vt tibi darent, iusseram. Si dederint, retinebis, quo tantundem ære tuo exonerer. Quod reliquum erit soluam cum potero. Ea enim mea est nunc conditio, vt assem à me numerare nequeam. Mirum quantum pecuniæ mihi effluat in extraordinariis sumptibus, & de meo præterea viuendum est, nisi velim fratribus oneri esse. Valetudinem quam mihi pro tuo in me amore solicitè comendas, non ita facilè curare licet. Sed nimis sum prolixus. Iniuriam enim talibus nūtiis facio. Bene vale optatissime frater. Dominus te ad hanc molestiarum molem sustinendam Spiritus sui virtute corroboret. Scripta mense Martio. M. D. XXXIX.
units.tr: comfort. Yet again, when it occurs to me that I can bring you nothing except more material for hatred, I gladly stay away, lest I press down on you with more than enough burden. The Waldensian brothers owed me a single crown, part of which they had received from me on loan, and part they had given to the messenger who came with the brother, on Sonnerius's instruction. I had told them to give this to you. If they have given it, you will keep it, so that I may be relieved of that amount of money you have spent on me. I will pay the rest when I can. My present condition is such that I cannot count out a single as. It is amazing how much money slips away from me on extraordinary expenses, and besides, I have to live on my own means, unless I want to be a burden to the brothers. As for my health, which you anxiously commend to me out of your love for me, it is not so easy to look after. But I have been too long-winded. I am doing wrong to such messengers. Farewell, most desired brother. May the Lord strengthen you by the power of his Spirit to bear this great mass of troubles. Written in March 1539.

units.la: POstridie quàm mihi reddita fuerat penultima tua epistola, dedi me in viam, vt Francfordiam peterem. Adeo autem tumultuarius fuit discessus, vt tibi respondere non vacauerit. Id quod in subitis consiliis fere euenire solet. Profectionem vero illam suscipere mihi nunquam in mentem venerat nisi pridie quàm exequutus sum. Verum cum literas à Bucero receperim, quibus indicabat se nihildum potuisse de fratrum cau sa agere: cupido mihi statim incessit eò vsque concedendi: partim ne fratrum salus negligeretur, vt fit in tanta rerum turba, tractare: partim vt cum Philippo de religione atque Ecclesiæ ratione commentarer. Vtraque nisi fallor ratio iusta tibi videbitur. Accedebant Capitonis ac omnium hortationes, præterea comitum opportunitas. Nam Sturmius & alij boni viri se mihi comitis adiungebant. De Domino de N. minus credendum est quàm feratur. Nosti enim quàm sit illud verum, famam eundo vires acquirere. Vnum tantùm concionatorem appetebat, qui hac Quadragesima plebe suam puriore doctrina imbueret. Domina R. illuc me initio inuitauit: sed quia via non satis aperta videbatur, excusaui me hic alia vocatione detineri, minutula quidem illa, sed quæ ad me obligandum sufficeret. Doctor Vlrichus iam secundum mensem procul abest, vt non possim cum eo de literis expostulare. Causatus est se eas depositu esse apud N. vnum nisi fallor, ex fratribus qui aliquando contra Solodorenses tumultuati sunt. Dolet mihi plurimum eas periisse: siquidem multa continebant, quæ magni interfuit non euulgari. De coniunctione quod suadebam non est quod tantopere aueserisite-stabar enim me nihil magis optare, quàm vt lògiflimde illinc pij omnes subducerent. Hoc vnum contendebam, ne foisfmate scinderent qualemcunque Ecclesiam: quę vtcunque esse corruptissima moribus, doctrinis etiam exoticis infecta, non tamen desciuerat penitus ab ea doctrina, qua Ecclesiam Christi fundari docet Paulus. Sed quia res est eiusmodi quam attingi non expediat, nisi prolixè & ordine excutiatur, nō vlterius prosequar: nisi quod testatum volo, me non aliam fratribus vnionem uasisse, quàm quæ nobis Christi exemplo monstratur, qui non lubitauit D. i mysteria cum deploratæ impietatis Iudæis participare. Atque vt intelligas qua prudentia consilio meum experdrint, ideos in primis exacerbauit, quòd Ministrum à Plebe dicernebam, illùmquedisp nsatorem esse asserebam à quo prudentia & fides requiratur. A priuatis minus quiddam & facilius dcebam exigi, vt fe vnufquifq; probaret. Verum id, si dabitur coràm colloqui, inter nos paruo negotio transigetur. Quòd video liculen ta Dei iudicia apparere in sonticas illas pestes quæ miserum Ecclesiam vexabant, partim me consolatur & recreat, partim autè animum meum perstringit, quia video non prorsus offendiculo carere. Est tamen omnino expetedum, vt quoquo molo Ecclesiam suam talibus excrementis purget Dominus. De Gastio mihi frater ad liquidum narrauerat. Male me habet illa Crynei facilitas in dandiscommendationibus: nec tam diu distulissem cum eo agere, nisi quo tempore literæ tuæ huc peruenerút, parcendum ei censuissem: quia tum vxor eius in vltimo vitæ periculo versabatur: nam grauida cùm esset, pœste correpta fuera. Quæso mihi significa, quo se bonus ille & infractus Christi martyr proripuerit. A N. video tibi non parum fore negotij, quandiu sic varicari perget. Sed quia tolli non potest, necesse erit tolerari. Puta tibi datum à Domino qui patientiam tuam exerceat. Habemus tibi non paruam gratiam, quòd nostro nomine Consulem salutaris: nam id quoque refert, vt intelligat vtrumque nostrum sic esse coniunctum cum Bucero & Capitone, vt omnia inter nos consilia communicemus. De bonis Ecclesiasticis vtinam tibi possem aliquid melius polliceri, quanquam non est res pessimo statu: Bucerus enim tanta constantia institit, vt videatur nonnihil promouisse. Philippus illum initio rei difficultate deterrebat: dimouerit tamen non potuit quin pergeret. Difficile autem videbatur impetrare, quoniam nihil id principes ad se pertinere putant, qui bona Ecclesiastica pro suo arbitrio administrant. Er alij quidem ægré ferunt sibi de manibus excuti lucrum cui iam assueuerunt. Alij tamèn si nihil iacturæ sensuri sunt, non facilè adducitur, vt inuidiam eius ordinis, quem magnum gnum esse in Germania nosti, in se concitent. Bucerus ex vetu- sta Ecclesiæ consuetudine modum protulit, quo & Ecclesiæ & pa- ci publicæ Imperij consulatur. Quoniam ea lege legata sunt bona, quæ hodie tenent Canonici primariæ Ecclesiæ huius ci- uitatis, vt à Comitibus administrentur, permittit vt sit collegium ex nobilibus familiis, à quo hæc possideantur: qui autem in il- lud collegium asciscentur, eos nec Sacerdotes esse vult, nec Ca- noniços: sed coniuges qui tantum fidem suam Ecclesiæ obliga- tam habeant, vt ad tutandam ipsius quietem impendat se ac sua omnia. Quoniam Episcopus est princeps Imperij, nec tolli po- test locus ille, quin magno cum motu Imperium concutiatur, putat expedire quod olim fiebat, vt in eius locum succedat ex collegio illorum Comitum, cui maneant falux possessiones, quæ sunt hodie penes Episcopum: vocetúrque Vicedominus, quod magis sit earum Oeconomu-, quàm proprietarius. Eius officium sit Ecclesiam tueri si alicunde impugnetur, atque in eam rem fi- dem suam solenni sacramento obstringat. Reliquæ facultates in vsum magis legitimum redigantur, vt sunt Præbendæ, Capellæ, Prioratus & reliqua. Vsum appello magis legitimum, vt mini- stris & scholis, pauperibus, aliisque Ecclesiæ oneribus destinen- tur. Id si obtinetur, erit vt in rebus adeo dissipatis tolerabilis cō- ditio. Aliqua & quidem iam magna spes est, quod Principes cœ- perunt animum inclinare, Ciuitates autem rem cordi habent, quæ vident Ecclesiarum suarum bona tam miserè dilapidari. De Basilio scripsit ad me Talcaris, illum petiisse nuper Geneuæ pu- blicam disputationem, sed repulsam passum esse: quod equidem libenter audio, ne in gente plus satis alioqui nouitatis cupida fa- fa dogmata eufulgentur, quibus refutandis nemo se opponat. Nunc ad secundam epistolam, quam ab ænigmatibus exordiris. Qui sint enim illi excubitores, ebriosi, fures, minimè assequor, nisi apertius exposueris. Proinde quæso vt mihi primis literis e- differas. De illa Comitis & Genani legatione nihil aliud potuit expectari, quàm vt irriti reuerterentur. Nescio an in fratribus tantum sit consilij, quantum animi esse nō dubito. Si Comitem fine formula certa dimiserunt, mihi factum eorum penitus im- probatur: scis enim quid parere nouerit illa inanis grauitatis af- fectatio. Teramus omnia tentari, ne per nos stetisse videatur quo minus Ecclesiæ melius haberent. Abs te hoc iure postulare ne- queunt, vt ministerium eorum approbes, quos Ecclesiasticè cen- sure relinquendos nemo non videt. Sed verissimum est quod ais, omnes qui sibi male conscij sunt nihil magis expetere, quàm vt omnia in obscuro demersa lateant, ne sua quoque fœditas dete- gatur. In tantis inuoluctis videndum quid possimus: cætera Do- mino permittenda. Cuperem sane vt malorum omnium sepulta eflet memoria quæ citra noxam retractari nō possunt. Sed quid prodest,odia, dissidia tum doctrinæ tum animorū, obtrectationes,cæteraque hæc mala in Ecclesiæ visceribus coclufa retineri, quæ tandem in pessimum vlcus erumpant? Optandum potius vt cum acerbitate aliqua discutiantur, si aliter fieri non potest. Sed quid vetat medium aliquod tenere,vt honor ministerio no stro suus restituatur, remedium Ecclesiæ illi miseræ ac perditæ adhibeatur,quæ inter fratres sunt offendicula collantur,dissimulatis acsuppressis malis, quæ nihil opus est de integro exagitari? Sunt enim quædam vulnera, quæ attactu magis recrudescũt: quiete melius & obliuione fanantur. Quid sibi obsecro volunt boni viri, quibus hoc venit in mentem, vt ego sine te redeam, qui tecum fumeiectus? Vtin operis communicatione manum præbeam iis, à quibus volo esse alienissimus,donec Ecclesiæ satisfecerint? Sic enim rem instituunt vt ex quatuor duo nobiscum remaneant: vt nullo Ecclesiæ iudicio quasi per veniam restitutus, locum sine vlla authoritate teneam? Quid enim facie-mus? vnde sumemus exordium, si res collapsas velimus instaurare?Si verbum fecero quod displicuerit, mox silentium imperabunt. Sed nolo apud te hæc & similia stylo prosequi,quæ me-liusipse reputas quàm dici queant. Rursum si id procedit, fratrũ iurgia vix potero sustinere:summam enim solo meo reditu con sedam existimabunt. Proinde optarim vt aliud potius quiduis agant ij qui hunc lapidem moliuntur. Nihil enim quàm magnam molestiam mihi accersunt,idque frustrà. Vt promisi breuiter tibi perscribam. Statum rerum Francfordiæ hunc compe-rimus.Aderant e domo Saxoniæ Electoreius frater,& nepos ex Henrico,quem Mauricium vocant. Hi tres in suo comitatu habebant equos quadringentos, Lantgrauius secum totidé equites adduxerat. Luneburgensis minore pompa. Aderat & Brande-burgensis iunior frater Electoris , Brunsuicensis iunior, aliíque tres quorum nomina non teneo. Hi omnes fœderatiːcæteri qui in fœdere continentur legatos miserant, vt Rex Daniæ, Dux Prussiæ aliíque nonnulli. De iis nihil mirum videbaur quod domi remanserant,quia rebus tam dubiis ac periculosis procul abesse tutum illis non erat. Verùm nemo erat qui non indigne acciperet,Vvirtembergésem malle venatione sua & nescio qui-bus lusoriis oblestamentis frui, quàm consultationi interesse,in qua & patria eius, & caput fortasse agatur, cùm biduo tantùm abesset.Qui volebant excusatum,dicebant non dubitasse curam in reliquos reiicere,quibus negotium cordi esse nouerat. A Ciui-tatibus,primarij viri insi fuerant.Primis deliberationibus bel-lum omnium suffragiis decernebatur, donec interuenerunt E-lectores duo, Comes Palatinus, & Ioachimus Brandeburgensis, cum Cæsaris literis,& legato Episcopo Hispano,quem Londen- sem appellant. Principio mandatum Cæsarisexpofuerunt, quo illis permittebatur vel pacem vel inducias cum aoftris pacisci, quibus rationibus ac legibus optimum fote exiftimarct.Deinde longa oratione ac validis argumetis conati sunt animos ad pa- cem inflectere: præcipue tamen caput hoc premebant, ꝯ Turca non quieturus fit,fi videat Germaniam intestinis bellis implica- tam. Etiam aditum habet patefactum, cum Vvalachias teneat, transitus illi à Polono exfoedere debeatur. Ita ergo iam nunc Germaniæ imminet.Pacis conditiones vt nostri excogitarent vo luerunt Si pax confici non posset,rogarūt vt ad inducias decur- reretur. Vtriusque fides ac fyncericas nostris est explorata. Nam Ioachimus in causam Euagelij omnino propensus est, Palatinus non iniquus. Verùm quia mandata quæ ab Hispania veniunt minus fidei habent,maluissent rem ab Electoribus vniuersis co- positam, penes quos summa in Imperio est potestas. Id impedi- tum fuit, quòd Maguntinus multas ob causas à Saxone repu- diatus est: Ioachimus in Comitia cosentire ausus non est,à qui- bus patruus excluderetur. Ergo nostri articulos obtulerunt,qui- bus fe inuitos ad belli cogitationem descendisse ostendebant:fi- quidem iniurias exponebant quibus fuerant ad id cofilium ne- ceffario adacti. Pacis leges dicebant, vt suas sibi Ecclesias admi- niftrare liceret, sub qua administratione,bonorum Ecclesiasti- corum dispensationem volebant contineri. Integrum deinde sibi seruabant, vt in fœderis societatem possent admittere qui adiungere fe vellent.Cum oblati iam effent articuli,discessimus. Postea significauit Bucerus Electores duos plus aliquanto con- cedere quàm Cæsaris legatum. Ratio est, quòd Cæsar,cùm ho- ftium nostrorum opibus indigeat aduersus Turcam perinde ac nostrorum, cupit vtrique parti fine alterius offensa gratificari. Summa tamen postulati eius est, vt citra præsentis status mu- tationem,viri docti ac probi & minimè contentiosi conueniât, inter quos de capitibus religionis controuersis disceptetur:post- ea res ad Comitia Imperij referatur, vt de sententia omnium ordinum Ecclesiæ Germanicæ reformatio transigatur. Inducias ad ea peragenda anni vnius paciscitur. Nostri nec breuibus ad- eo induciis contenti sunt, & aliquid certius sibi dari postulant. Ita omnia sunt adhuc in suspenso:nec extra belli periculum fumus, nisi Cæsar vlterius procedat. Iuliacenfis nuper patre or- batus, legatos misit cum huiusmodi mandato, Se ducatum Gueldriæ, cuius legitimus erat dominus, Dei beneficio recu- perandc: nunc sibi de eo controuersiam moueri tum à Cæsare, tum à Lotharingo, fine vllo fatis specioso prætextu. Lotharingū enim nihil iuris posse obtendere, nisi quòd fit hæres postremi ducis.Atqui illum per vim,contra ius & fas,ducatum possedisse, qui sententia imperij familię Iuliacensi adiudicatus erat. Cæsarem prætexere quidem emptionis titulum. Sed quam vel commentitiam, vel nimis fraudulentam esse appareat: nempe cum pretium fuerit 50.millium coronatorum,quo vel sola urbs æsti mari queat: certe eam summam infra anni vnius reditum esse. Rogabat ergo nostros vt apud Cæsarem intercederent, ne Principem Imperij line causa lacesseret. Quod si Cæsar nollet precibus acquiescere, auxilium eorum ad tuendam communem libertatem implorabat. Nihil adhuc responsi tulit: quando consilium capere ex rerum suarum inclinatione necesse habebunt. De fœdere tamen nulla fiebat mentio,etsi non est à religione alienus. Angli petitio fuit vt legatio ad se noua mitteretur, cui adiungeretur Philippus: vt haberet cuius consilio vti posset ad Ecclesiam melius constituendam. Non erat dubium quin legationem mitti vellent Principes. Melanchthonem mittere nō placebat,quod mollitiem animi eius suspectam habeant. Neque verò qua in opinione sit aut nescit, aut dissimulat: tametsi mihi sanctissime deierauit vanum esse hunc timorem. Et sane vt videor mihi eius animum perspicere, non minus illi fidere ausim quàm Bucero: dum negotium est cum iis qui sibi indulgeri aliquid volunt. Tanto enim studio propagandi Euangelij flagrat Bucerus, vt quæ præcipua sunt contentus impetrasse, interdum sit æquo lenior in iis concedendis, quæ minutula quidem ipse putat, sed habentamen suum pondus. Rex ipse vix dimidia ex parte sapit. Sacerdotes & Episcopos sucris sanctionibus non tantum ministerij priuatione,arcet à coniugio: Missas quotidianas retinet: septem Sacramenta vult saluæ esse: ita habet mutilum & semilacerum Euangelium, Ecclesiam vero multis adhuc nugis refertam. Iam quod sani cerebri non esse omnes vident, Scripturam vulgari idiomate haberi in regno non patitur: ac nouum interdictum nuper publicauit, quo ab eius lectione plebem arcebat. Atque vt intelligas illum non iocose insanire, nuper viru quendam probum & doctum exussit ob negatam præsentiam Christi carnalem in pane: cuius mors ab omnibus piis & eruditis valde comploratur. Non ritamen vtcunque eiusmodi facinoribus grauiter offendantur, eius regni rationem habere non desinent. Video de coniuratione nihil ad vos peruenisse præter obscurum & ambiguum rumorem. Cardinalis Polus fratrem habebat virum & primariæ nobilitatis & auctoritatis inter Proceres maximæ. Siquidem eorum familia Regem propinqua cognatione attingit: ipse vero rarę cuiusdam prudentię & grauitatis habebatur. Ita sibi in causa fratris moderatus erat, vt nihilo deteriore loco. Cùm Regi minime suspectus eil: r, effet,quii palam dissidium cum fratre præ fe ferebat:omnium opinionem sua calliditate fefellit.Ita inter fe pepigerant,vt Cardinalis exercitum duceret per Galliam : simulatque accederet ad finem regni, tumultum frater eius cum aliis coniuratis excitaret: quo Rex occupatus in placandis intestinis motibus, aduersus exteraum hostem defendere fe non posset. Cardinali facile erat armare militem Papæ sumptibus. Verum priusquam aduertaret,detegi est ab indice conspiratio. Nam quo fe rite instruerent,necesse habuerant coplures facere conscios. Nepos vir strenuus cum audiffet pactiones esse deprehensas, voluit sibi mortem consciscere. Sed cum impeditus fuisset, fequitiam quæstionis ferre non potuit.Sequuta est aliorum confessio:in omnes autores vindicatu est. Cum tot ac tantis Dei beneficiis tam male respondeat Rex, vereor magnopere ne tandem graues pœnas luat suæ ingratitudinis. Interim dum Francfordiæ habetur conuentus,moriuus est ex insperato filius Georgij,qui ob insaniam vinctus custodiebatur.Si fuisset patri superstes,tutela nouis motibus potuisset prębere causam.Nūc successor est non dubius ille Mauricius Henrici filius,quem in fœdere esse supra indicaui. Ita bona fpeseft, ditionem quam nunc tenet Georgius, statim Christi peculio accessuram.Nam Georgius ætatem excessit procreandæ soboli idoneam. Hac ratione vides, quantum ad summam rerum,pendere adhuc omnia, nec certam habere inclinationem. Quo magis rogandus est nobis Deus, vt faustum aliquem exitum rebus tam perplexis afferat. Quid profecerim in causa fratrum,simul quale fuerit, ac quibus de rebus meum cum Philippo colloquium, rescisces per Michaelem, qui ante nouem dies abire constituit. Cogor enim nunc præ tabellarij festinatione mittere dimidiatas literas. Alteram partem tunc excipies. Vale frater mihi amicissime.Thomam ac fratres omnes mihi saluta. Capito & Sturmius te millies salutant. Gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi tecum. Argentorati xvii.Calendas Aprilis. M. D. XXXIX.
units.tr: The day after I received your penultimate letter, I set out on the road to Frankfurt. My departure was so hurried that I had no time to answer you, which usually happens with sudden decisions. Indeed, I had never thought of making that journey until the day before I set out. But when I received a letter from Bucer saying that he had not yet been able to do anything for the brothers' cause, I immediately felt a strong desire to go there, partly to look after the brothers' safety, which could be neglected amid such confusion, and partly to discuss religion and the government of the Church with Philip. Unless I am mistaken, you will think both reasons sound. Capito and everyone else also urged me to go, and the opportunity of travelling with the counts added to my resolve. Sturmius and other good men joined me as companions. What is said about Lord N. should be believed less than it is reported; you know how true it is that rumour gains strength as it travels. There was only one preacher they wanted, one who would steep the people in purer teaching during this Lent. Lady R. first invited me there, but since the way did not seem open enough, I excused myself on the ground that I was held here by another calling, a small one indeed, but enough to bind me. Doctor Ulrich has now been far away for a month already, so I cannot question him about the letters. He said he had left them with N., one of the brothers who once rioted against the Solothurners, unless I am mistaken. I am very sorry they have been lost, since they contained much that it was important not to make public. As for the union I was urging, there is no need to take it so much amiss. I was saying that I wanted nothing more than for all the godly to withdraw from there. My only contention was that they should not tear apart, by schism, whatever Church there was. However corrupt it is in morals, and however infected with strange doctrines, it has not wholly departed from that teaching on which Paul says the Church of Christ is founded. But since the matter is of a kind that cannot be properly touched on without being examined at length and in order, I will not pursue it further, except to say that I wish it to be witnessed that I have sought no other union with the brothers than the one Christ shows us by his example, who did not hesitate to share the mysteries of God with Jews of deplorable impiety. And so that you may understand with what prudence they have taken my counsel, I was especially angered by this: I was distinguishing the minister from the people and asserting that it is the minister who needs wisdom and faith. From private persons, I said, less is required and it is easier to demand that each one prove himself. But if we are granted the chance to talk face to face, that matter will be settled between us with little trouble. That I see God's judgements appearing in the grievous plagues which were troubling the wretched Church partly comforts and refreshes me, but partly pierces my spirit, because I see that it is not entirely free of stumbling-block. Yet it is altogether to be desired that the Lord cleanse his Church of such refuse in whatever way he can. The brother had given me a clear account of Gastius. I am vexed by Crynaeus's readiness in giving recommendations. I would not have delayed so long in dealing with him, except that when your letter arrived here I judged that he should be spared, because his wife was then in mortal danger; she had been struck by the plague while pregnant. Please let me know where that good and unbroken martyr of Christ has taken himself. I see that you will have no small trouble with N. for as long as he continues to play the fool in this way. But since he cannot be removed, he must be endured. Consider it a trial sent by the Lord to exercise your patience. We owe you no small thanks for greeting the Consul in our name, for it also matters that he understands that the two of us are so joined with Bucer and Capito that we share all our counsels. I wish I could promise you something better about the Church's goods, although the matter is not in the worst state: Bucer has pressed it with such constancy that he seems to have advanced it somewhat. Philip at first discouraged him because of the difficulty of the business, yet he could not be turned aside from persevering. It seemed hard to obtain anything, since the princes think this has nothing to do with them, they who administer the Church's goods at their own discretion. Others indeed take it badly that the profit they have grown used to is being snatched from their hands. Others, if they are to feel no loss, are not easily brought to stir up against themselves the odium of that order, which you know is powerful in Germany. Bucer, following the ancient custom of the Church, has put forward a plan by which both the Church and the public peace of the Empire may be safeguarded. Since the goods which the canons of the chief church of this city now hold were bequeathed on the condition that they be administered by the counts, he permits there to be a college drawn from noble families, by which these goods may be possessed. Those who are admitted into that college he wishes to be neither priests nor canons, but married men who are so bound to the Church by their faith that they will devote themselves and all they have to defending its peace. Since the bishop is a prince of the Empire, and that position cannot be removed without great upheaval to the Empire, he thinks it advisable to do what used to be done: that someone from that college of counts should succeed him in that place, and that the remaining possessions, which are at present in the bishop's hands, should remain safe with him. He is to be called Vice-Lord, because he is more the steward of these goods than their owner. His duty will be to defend the Church if it is attacked from any quarter, and he will bind his faith to this by a solemn oath. The remaining resources are to be turned to a more lawful use, such as the prebends, chapels, priories and the rest. I call it a more lawful use if they are assigned to ministers and schools, to the poor, and to the other burdens of the Church. If this is secured, the condition will be tolerable among things so scattered. And there is now already some great hope that the princes have begun to incline their minds to it, and the cities hold the matter dear, since they see the goods of their Churches being squandered so wretchedly. Talcaris wrote to me about Basil, that he recently asked for a public disputation at Geneva but was refused; I gladly hear this, lest among a people otherwise eager for novelty, false doctrines be spread abroad with no one willing to oppose them in refuting them. Now to your second letter, which you begin with enigmas. I cannot at all grasp who those watchmen, drunkards and thieves are, unless you explain more plainly. So please defer this to your first letters. As for the embassy of the count and Genan, nothing else could have been expected than that they would return empty-handed. I do not know whether the brothers have as much good sense as I have no doubt they have zeal. If they dismissed the count without a set form, I totally disapprove of what they did, for you know what that empty affectation of gravity is capable of producing. Let us try everything, so that it may not seem that the fault lies with us if the Church does not fare better. They cannot demand of you that you approve their ministry, when everyone sees that they must be left to Church censure. But what you say is most true: all who are conscious of having done wrong desire nothing more than that everything be buried in darkness and lie hidden, lest their own foulness also be exposed. In such entanglements we must see what we can do, and leave the rest to the Lord. I would indeed wish that the memory of all the evils that cannot be recalled without harm were buried. But what good is it to keep hatreds, divisions both of doctrine and of minds, slanders, and these other evils locked in the bowels of the Church, which will at last break out into a most dangerous ulcer? It is rather to be wished that they be dealt with, with some sharpness, if this cannot be done otherwise. But what forbids us to hold some middle course, so that the honour of our ministry is restored, a remedy is applied to that wretched and ruined Church, the stumbling-blocks among the brothers are removed, and the evils, which there is no need to stir up afresh, are passed over and suppressed? For there are some wounds that break open more when touched; they are better healed by quiet and forgetfulness. What do these good men want, I beg you, who have come to the idea that I should return without you, who have been cast down together with you? That I should lend a hand in joint work to those from whom I wish to be most distant, until they have made satisfaction to the Church? For they arrange the matter so that out of four, two remain with us; so that, restored without any judgement of the Church, as though by pardon, I might hold a place without any authority? What, then, shall we do? Where shall we begin, if we wish to restore things that have collapsed? If I say anything that displeases them, they will at once command silence. But I do not want to pursue these and similar matters with you in writing; you yourself reflect on them better than they can be spoken. Again, if this goes forward, I will scarcely be able to bear the brothers' quarrels, for they will think the whole matter is settled by my return alone. So I would rather wish that those who are labouring to move this stone would do something else. For they are bringing upon me nothing but great annoyance, and to no purpose. As I promised, I will briefly write out for you the state of affairs we found at Frankfurt. There were present, from the house of the Elector of Saxony, his brother and his nephew from Henry, whom they call Maurice. These three had four hundred horses in their retinue; the Landgrave had brought with him as many horsemen. The Duke of Lüneburg came with less display. The younger brother of the Elector of Brandenburg was also present, the younger Duke of Brunswick, and three others whose names I do not recall. All these belonged to the alliance; the others who are included in the alliance had sent envoys, such as the King of Denmark, the Duke of Prussia, and some others. It did not seem at all surprising that these had stayed at home, since it was not safe for them to be far away in such doubtful and dangerous times. But there was no one who did not take it ill that the Duke of Württemberg preferred to enjoy his hunting and I know not what sorts of games and diversions, rather than take part in the consultation, in which his homeland and perhaps his own head might be at stake, when he was only two days away. Those who wished to excuse him said that he had not doubted that the care of the matter could be left to the others, to whom he knew it was dear. Leading men had come from the cities. In the first deliberations, war was decreed by the votes of all, until two electors arrived, the Count Palatine and Joachim of Brandenburg, with letters from the Emperor and with the Spanish bishop, whom they call of London, as envoy. At the start they set out the Emperor's mandate, by which they were permitted to make peace or a truce with our side, on whatever terms and conditions they should think best. Then, in a long speech and with strong arguments, they tried to bend the minds of the hearers towards peace; but above all they pressed this point, that the Turk would not be quiet if he saw Germany entangled in internal wars. He also has an open path, since he holds Wallachia, and passage through Poland is owed to him by the treaty. Thus, then, Germany is already threatened. Our side wished to devise the terms of peace themselves. If peace could not be made, they asked that recourse be had to a truce. The good faith and sincerity of both sides have been tested by ours. For Joachim is wholly inclined to the cause of the Gospel, and the Palatine is not unfavourable. But because the mandates that come from Spain carry less weight, they would have preferred the matter to be settled by all the electors, in whose hands is the supreme power in the Empire. This was hindered because the Archbishop of Mainz was rejected by the Saxon for many reasons; Joachim did not dare to agree to a meeting from which his uncle would be excluded. So our side offered articles by which they showed that they had come unwillingly to the thought of war, since they set out the injuries by which they had been driven of necessity to that counsel. They stated the terms of peace: that they be allowed to administer their own Churches, and they wanted the distribution of the Church's goods to be included under that administration. Then they reserved to themselves the right to admit into the alliance any who wished to join. When the articles had been offered, we left. Afterwards Bucer reported that the two electors had conceded somewhat more than the Emperor's envoy. The reason is that the Emperor, since he needs the resources of our enemies against the Turk just as much as of ours, wishes to please each side without offending the other. The sum of his demand, however, is that, without any change in the present state, learned, upright and least contentious men should meet, among whom the controverted heads of religion may be disputed; after that the matter is to be referred to the Imperial Diet, so that a reformation may be carried through by the judgement of all the orders of the German Church. He bargains for a truce of one year to carry this out. Our side are not content even with so short a truce, and demand that something more certain be given them. So everything is still in suspense, and we are not out of the danger of war unless the Emperor goes further. The Duke of Jülich, recently bereaved of his father, has sent envoys with a mandate to this effect: that he, by God's favour, is to recover the Duchy of Guelders, of which he was the rightful lord; now a dispute has been raised about it, both by the Emperor and by the Lorrainer, without any plausible pretext. For the Lorrainer can allege no right except that he is heir of the last duke. Yet that duke had held the Duchy by force, against law and right, although it had been adjudged to the house of Jülich by the sentence of the Empire. The Emperor puts forward the title of purchase. But how feigned or excessively fraudulent this is appears clearly: since the price was 50,000 crowns, a sum with which the city alone could be bought, and yet certainly that sum is less than one year's revenue. He therefore asked our side to intercede with the Emperor, so that he would not harass a prince of the Empire without cause. But if the Emperor were unwilling to yield to prayers, he begged for their help in defending common liberty. He has not yet received any reply; they will have to take counsel from the tendency of their own affairs. Yet there was no mention of an alliance, although it is not alien to religion. The English asked that a new embassy be sent to them, joined with Philip, so that they might have someone whose counsel they could use to set the Church in better order. There was no doubt that the princes wished to send an embassy. It did not please them to send Melanchthon, because they regard his softness of mind with suspicion. Nor indeed do they either not know or pretend not to know what opinion he holds, although he swore to me most solemnly that this fear is groundless. And truly, as far as I can see into his mind, I would dare to trust him no less than Bucer, provided we are dealing with men who wish some concession to be made to them. For Bucer burns with such zeal for spreading the Gospel that, content to have obtained the chief points, he is sometimes more lenient than is right in conceding things which he himself thinks trifling, yet which have their own weight. The King himself scarcely has half his wits. By sacred sanctions he forbids priests and bishops not only the exercise of ministry but also marriage; he retains the daily Mass; he wishes the seven sacraments to be kept safe. So he has a maimed and half-torn Gospel, and a Church still crammed with many trifles. Now, that he is not of sound mind everyone sees: he does not allow Scripture to be held in the vernacular in his kingdom, and recently he published a new prohibition by which he kept the common people from reading it. And so that you may understand that he is not raving in jest, he recently burned a certain upright and learned man for denying the carnal presence of Christ in the bread; his death is greatly lamented by all the godly and learned. Yet however gravely they are offended by such crimes, they do not cease to take account of the condition of that kingdom. I see that nothing certain about a conspiracy has reached you, only an obscure and ambiguous rumour. Cardinal Pole had a brother, a man of the first nobility and of the greatest authority among the nobles; for their family is closely related to the King. He himself was regarded as a man of rare prudence and gravity. He so moderated himself in his brother's cause that, though he was least suspected by the King, since he openly professed disagreement with his brother, he deceived the opinion of all by his cunning. They had agreed between themselves that the Cardinal should lead an army through France; as soon as he reached the borders of the kingdom, his brother with the other conspirators would stir up a tumult, so that the King, occupied in calming the internal disturbances, could not defend himself against the external enemy. It was easy for the Cardinal to arm soldiers at the Pope's expense. But before they could act, the conspiracy was revealed by an informer. For in order to arrange things properly, they had been obliged to make several accomplices. The nephew, a vigorous man, when he heard that the plots had been discovered, wished to take his own life. But when he was prevented, he could not bear the shame of the examination. A confession of the others followed; vengeance was taken on all the authors. Since the King responds so badly to such great benefits of God, I greatly fear that he will at last pay heavy penalties for his ingratitude. Meanwhile, while the assembly was being held at Frankfurt, the son of George, who had been kept in custody because of madness, died unexpectedly. If he had survived his father, his guardianship might have given cause for new disturbances. Now the undoubted successor is Maurice, son of Henry, whom I mentioned above as being in the alliance. So there is good hope that the territory which George now holds will soon come into Christ's possession. For George has passed the age suitable for begetting offspring. From this account you see how everything still hangs in the balance as far as the sum of affairs goes, and has no certain inclination. So much the more must we pray to God to bring some favourable outcome to affairs so entangled. What I achieved in the brothers' cause, and how it went, and about what matters my conversation with Philip was held, you will learn through Michael, who has decided to leave in nine days. For I am now compelled, because of the haste of the courier, to send you a half-finished letter. You will receive the other part then. Farewell, my dearest brother. Greet Thomas and all the brothers for me. Capito and Sturmius greet you a thousand times. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Strasbourg, 17 days before the Kalends of April, 1539.

units.la: Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CAL. FARELLO.

units.la: NON memini hoc toto anno fuisse diem vnum, quo magis obrutus fuerim variis negotiis.Nam cum hic nuncius voluerit principium libri mei secum auferre,circiter viginti folia relegere me oportuit.Adhæc legendum fuit & concionandum, scribendæ quaternæ literæ: transfigenda quædam controuersia,respondendum plus decem interpellatoribus. Excusabis ergo fi & breuiter & minus accurate scribo de omnibus rebus. Quid in conuentu deliberatum fuerit, non prius intelligemus ad liquidum quàm redierit Bucerus,quem ex eius literis expectamus ante septem dies. Scripsit tamen nobis nunquam fe vidisse paratiore animo principes nostros ad Euangelij defensionem. Certe Smalcaldiæ facinus in re non magna ediderunt, quo prodiderunt animi fui magnitudine. Erant enim illic impuræ quædam imagines, quas cum suis altaribus diruerunt. Sustulerunt etiam in Cœna eleuationem, quam haétenus retinuerant. Eant nunc qui moderationes nescio quas somniant, ad quas nos reuocent. Hoc tibi volui in gustum præbere, vt intelligas eos procul abesse à trepidatione. Senatus quoque noster cordatum fe præbet. Nuper Abbatissam, quæ dilapidare cœperat bona monasterij, in custodiam dedit. Camera imperij Episcopi rogatu eam dimitti iussit. Contemptum est mandatum. Socij fœderis factum approbarunt, & fe causam recepturos testati sunt. Missus inde nuncius ad Cameram qui denunciet non staturum Senatum illius iudicio, qualecunque tandem fuerit. Expectamus ergo dum lusorium suum fulmen iaculentur. Cura obsecro vt Ballio tus pecuniam mittat, vnde Vvendelino satisfiat. Non possum nunc vlterius pergere. Saluta omnes fratres diligenter. x x. Aprilis. M. D. XXXIX.
units.tr: I do not remember a single day in this whole year on which I was more overwhelmed by various business. When this messenger wanted to take the beginning of my book away with him, I had to re-read about twenty leaves. Besides, I had to lecture and preach, write four letters, settle a certain controversy, and answer more than ten objectors. So excuse me if I write briefly and less carefully about everything. We will not know clearly what was decided at the assembly until Bucer returns, whom we expect from his letter within seven days. He has written to us, however, that he never saw our princes more ready in spirit for the defence of the Gospel. Certainly at Smalcalden they did a deed, not great in itself, by which they showed the greatness of their spirit. There were some impure images there, which they destroyed along with their altars. They also abolished the elevation in the Supper, which they had kept until then. Let those now go who dream of I know not what moderation, to which they would call us back. I wanted to give you this as a taste, so that you understand they are far from trembling. Our senate too shows itself to be wise-hearted. Recently it put the abbess, who had begun to squander the monastery's goods, into custody. At the bishop's chamber's request, it ordered her released. The order was scorned. The allies approved the act and declared that they would take up the cause. A messenger was then sent to the Chamber to announce that the Senate would not abide by its judgment, whatever it might be. So we wait until they hurl their playful thunderbolt. Please see to it that Ballio sends the money, so that Wendelin may be satisfied. I cannot go on any further now. Greet all the brothers diligently. 10 April 1539.

units.la: Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CAL. FARELLO.

units.la: PLus iam boni ab ista qualicunque concordia sperare incipio quàm prius. Quoties reputabam quibuscum hominibus negotium nobis foret: simul quàm lubricam aç fluidam eorum fidem toties experti effemus, inde colligebam nos ista quo que reconciliatione aut nihil, aut quàm minimum profecisse. Ad quod leges vtrinque positæ, etiamsi nihil haberent maioris indignitatis, mihi tamen non omnino probabantur. Atqui unc fi verum est quod narras, sollicitari ad defectionem duos illos, necessarium profecto erat vel iniquis legibus inter nos tranfigen do, talibus malis occurrere. De firmiore autem constantia nonnullam spem concipio, quòd cum fidem suam omnibus istic Ec clefiis obligarint, validius tenentur, quàm vt adeo ex facili dissiliat. Iam aliqua ex parte fumus affequuti quod primo loco semper quæsiuimus, vt pessima illa inter fratres dissidia, quæ Ecclesias prorsus lacerabant, componeretur. Gratiam igitur Domino nunquam satis dignam habebimus, qui sua benignitate spem quoq; nostram ita superat. De reditu puto non procedere quod scripserat Talearis: nullum enim verbum ex eo tempore accepi. Nec dubito quin fratres rem illam tàquam superuacuam omiserint, ferint,cum viderunt aliunde contigisse remedium. Proinde quia totam actionem vel refrixisse, vel concidisse suspicor, ea cura mihi nimè iam me solicitum habet. Nuncium porro illum quem mihi attulerant literæ Talearis, non sine causa tantopere expauescebam. Non omnes causas tibi recensui: & paucas illas quas notabam, attigi tamen breviter, non exposui. Certè quod de te dicebam, momenti plurimum secum trahit. Nam aut ambos simul restitui, aut me per veniam restitutum videri oportet. Ita personæ indulgebitur restitutio, non causæ dabitur. Sed illa præcipuè cogitatio me consternat, dum ob oculos mihi pono in quatam voraginem ingrederer: nempe qua me absorberi totum sentiebam, cum tamen dimidio minor adhuc foret. Habeo, fateor, hic mea certamina, & ea quidem ardua: sed quibus exercear, non adobruar. Quanquam mihi non parum negotij futurum erat hoc Pafchate, si pettis illa de qua quæreris adfuisset. Aut enim ad rationem reddendam compulissem, aut ad Cœnam Domini admissus non fuisset. Vnus ex eius discipulis, ille quem voluit in Claudium Normanum stimulare, venturus erat, nisi præmonuisset ut mihi antea se purgaret, vel certè refipiscentiam promitteret. Toto mense concionem non audierat, publicum alex & ebrietatis veluti forum exercebat. De scortationibus etiam rumor susurrabat: & tamen prorupisset ad sacrosanctum illud mysterium, nisi viam præclusisset. Iocatus est apud eum qui denuntiabat quod voluerat illi indicari, se relinquere confessionem Papistis. Respondi esse quoque genus confessionis Christianæ. Si redierit Magister, erit iam mihi profestum cum eo bellum. Nec per me stetit, quominus iampridem cum eo congrederer. Ita eius impietatem palam & aperte etiam pro concione fugillabā, ut nihilominus aut ipsi, aut aliis dubius esset sermo, quàm si vel nominassem, vel digito demonstrassem. Nunc, quia Francfordiam petierat, Bucerum obsecraui ut ab eo non secus ac iurato hostē caueret. Vbi primum se ita tractari senserit, quales turbæ mihi præparantur? Ergo siue hic maneo siue migro, multæ fem per curæ, molestiæ, difficultates mihi instant. Gratum mihi esse fateor, quòd fratres tanta mei solicitudine teneri video, ut suppleuere nostram inopiam de suo parati sint. Non enim fieri potest quin tali amoris testimonio delecter. Verum tua & illorum beneficentia decreui abstinere, nisi quæ maior necessitas compulerit. Dabitur mihi à Vvendelino typographo, cui libellum nostrum commisi imprimendum, quantum ad extraordinarios sumptus sufficiet. In libris meis qui adhuc sunt Geneuæ, erit unde hospiti meo satisfiat vsque ad hyemem proximam: in posterum Dominus prouidebit. Cùm innumeros aliquando amicos in Gallia habuerim, nemo fuit qui assem mihi obtulerit: & tamè
units.tr: I already begin to hope more from that so-called concord than I did before. Whenever I considered what sort of men we had to deal with, and how slippery and fluid their good faith had repeatedly proved to be in our experience, I concluded that this reconciliation too had achieved nothing, or as little as possible. On this account, the terms laid down on both sides did not wholly please me, even though they contained nothing of greater unworthiness. But now, if what you report is true, that those two men are being solicited to defect, it was certainly necessary to meet such evils by settling matters between us, even on unfair terms. Yet I entertain some hope of firmer constancy, since they have bound their faith to all the Churches there, and are held too firmly to break away so easily. Now, in some measure, we have obtained what we always sought first: that those most wicked quarrels among the brothers, which were tearing the Churches apart completely, should be settled. We shall therefore never consider the grace of the Lord worthy enough of thanks, for by his kindness he surpasses even our hope. As to the return, I do not think what Talearis wrote will come to pass, for I have received no word from him since that time. Nor do I doubt that the brothers have dropped that business as superfluous, since they saw that a remedy had come from elsewhere. Therefore, since I suspect that the whole affair has either cooled or collapsed, that concern no longer troubles me very much. Moreover, I was not without cause so terribly alarmed by the news that the letter of Talearis brought to me. I have not recounted all the reasons to you; those few which I noted I touched on briefly, but did not explain. Certainly what I said about you carries very great weight. For either we must both be restored together, or I must appear to be restored through your indulgence. Thus the restoration would be granted to the person, and no ground would be given to the cause. But what most dismays me is the thought, when I set before my eyes into what an abyss I was entering: namely, one by which I felt myself wholly swallowed up, although it was still only half as deep. I have, I admit, my struggles here, and difficult ones indeed; but by them I am exercised, not overwhelmed. Yet I would have had no little trouble this Passover, if that matter about which you ask had been present. For either I would have compelled him to give an account, or he would not have been admitted to the Lord's Supper. One of his disciples, the one whom he wanted to goad against Claude the Norman, was about to come, unless he had warned me to clear himself beforehand, or at least promise repentance. For a whole month he had not heard a sermon, and he kept up a public market, as it were, of dice and drunkenness. Rumours also whispered of fornication; and yet he would have pushed himself up to that most holy mystery, had I not blocked the way. He joked with the man who announced what he had wanted to be told to him, that he was leaving the confession to the Papists. I replied that there is also a kind of Christian confession. If the Master returns, I shall then have a war with him at once. It has not been my fault that I have not long since come to grips with him. So openly and plainly did I rebuke his impiety even from the pulpit, that the talk was nonetheless ambiguous, either to him or to others, as if I had named him or pointed him out with my finger. Now, since he has made for Frankfurt, I have begged Bucer to beware of him no differently than of a sworn enemy. As soon as he feels that he is being treated thus, what storms will be prepared for me? So whether I remain here or depart, many cares, troubles and difficulties press upon me. I confess it is pleasing to me that I see the brothers held by such great concern for me, that they are ready to make up our poverty from their own resources. It is not possible that I should not be delighted by such a testimony of love. Yet, out of regard for your kindness and theirs, I have decided to refrain, unless some greater necessity compels me. Enough for the extraordinary expenses will be given to me by Wendelin the printer, to whom I entrusted our little book for printing. From my books, which are still at Geneva, there will be means to satisfy my host until next winter; in future the Lord will provide. Although I once had countless friends in France, there was no one who offered me a penny; and yet

units.la: c.j. si fecissent, poterant frui gratuita beneficentiae iactantia: nihilo enim illis constitisset offerre quod non acceptassent. Exciderat mihi Ludovicus, ille unus fuit qui obtulit: sed ipse quoque suam largitionem nimis magno vendicabat: si quidem me tantum no ad recantandum hortabatur. Certe clara voce fuisse me Ecclesiae transfugam pronuntiabat. Respondi quod debui talibus literis: vereor tamen ne literae interciderint. Tua igitur ac fratrum benevolentia in praesens contentus ero: facultates experiar, si quando erit necesse. Ac viciissim rogo ut pro illa in me vestra humanitate, animi gratitudine contenti sitis. Doleo mihi periisse coronatum: sed est cur socordiam hic meam accusem, nisi quod pudore retineri possem arbitrabar, ne sic abutererer. Placet maxime vestrum de Claudio consilium, ut antequam magis adoleverit, aut etiam induruerit barbaries, quae manent scintillae adhuc bonae institutionis in illa pueritia, eius opera excitentur. Sed quid fidem meam appellas in adiuvando fratrum conatu ad instaurandam disciplinam? Ad quos enim scriberem, aut quo stylo? Quare aut viam mihi aperi, aut ne expectes dum me temere ingeram. Nuper Philippo in faciem non dissimulavi, quin mihi admodum illa ceremoniarum copia displiceret. Videri enim mihi formam quam tenent, non procul esse a Iudaismo. Cum rationibus instarem, noluit mecum de eo contendere, quin nimis abundarent in ritibus illis aut ineptis, aut certe superfluis. Sed dicebat id dandum necessario fuisse Canonicatarum qui illic sunt obstinationi. Caeterum nullum esse in Saxonia locum qui non magis exoneratus esset Vvitemberga: et eam ipsam paulatim ex tanta farragine multa abscissuram. Clausula autem erat, Luthero non magis probari quas coactus retinuisset ceremonias, quam nostrani in illis parsimoniam. Vtinam vero perspectum optimo N. esset, quantum sit in Philippo f. nceritatis. Certe exuerat protinus omnem fraudis suspicionem. Quod Bucerus porro defendit Lutheri ceremonias, non ideo fit quod appetat, aut inuehere eas moliatur. Cantum Latinum adduci nullo modo poterit ut probet ab imaginibus abhorret. Alia partim contemnit, partim non curat. Sed non est timendum ut quae semel abrogata sunt, rursus postliminio reducat. Tantum non patitur, ut ob externas illas obseruatiunculas a Luthero dissungamur. Nec sane iustas esse puto dissidij causas. Foedus Germanicum nihil habet quod debeat pium pectus offendere. Cur enim quaeso quasdam dedit eis Dominus vires non coniungant ad communem Euangelij defensionem? Caeterum in societatem suam aut vi, aut quauis necessitate neminem pertrahunt. Quin potius sunt Ciuitates Euangelicae quibus magis placuit foedus cum Papistis, & ipsis adeo Episcopis, ut Norimberga. Vtinam sciret N. quibus attibus nuper tentati sunt in conuentu, & qua constantia resti-terunt. Nihil magis conabatur Caesaris legatus, quam vt eos ab Helueticis Ecclesiis diltraheret. Neque tamen eas nominabat: sed exigebat ne Sacramentariorum causam susciperent. Responderunt sibi fraternam tlle communionem cum iis quos ille Sacramentarios vocabat. Iam in vltimo actu quantum animi ostenderunt? Imponebat legem Caesar vt neminem reciperent in foedus inter eas quas cum ipsis paciscebatur inducias: consensu- runt: sed hac conditione, vt siqui reciperent Euangelium, esscnt tuti etiam extra foedus. Quod si impeterentur, profelli sunt se habituros pro foederatis qui causam Christi fultinerent. Id quoque mutuum petebant a Caesare, vt nulla inter id tempus foedera fierent aduersus Euangelium. Volebat Caesar vt Sacerdotibus manerent opes Ecclesiasticae vsque ad induciarum finem. Annuerunt nostri, modo Ecclesiis & scholis prospiceretur: atque illic ad extremum perstiterunt. Quid si referam insignem ciuitatis huius fortitudinem? Nam cum allatae essent Caesaris conditiones, vt irrita fierent foedera quae post Nurembergense conuentum inita fuerant, & ne posthac noua ferirentur inter nostros, vtque vtraque pars integra maneret vsq; dum habito colloquio Germanica Ecclesia reformaretur: factum est ex templo Senatusconsultum, quo edicebant se potius visuros vt liberi & vxores in conspectu suo necarentur, vt facultates omnes disperderentur, excinderetur vrbs, ipsi denique ad internecionem omnes caderent, quam admissuros eas leges, quibus Euangelio Christi via praecluderetur. Mi Farelle, cogita an non faciamus iniuriam talibus viris, qui otiosi eos criminamur, dum periculo aut terrore quouis dimoueri se a recta linea non sinunt. Itaque iam res proculdubio ad certamen vergit: & iam impreflio facta est in agrum Luneburgensem. Nostrum est, inquis, cauere diligenter omnia quibus in bonorum ac piorum offensionem incurramus: fateor: sed bonorum est viciflim cauere, ne temere ac citra rationem offendantur. Interim dum scribo, discipulus ille, cuius memini, redire in gratiam cupit, ac Claudium vltro sequestrem conflituit. Spero Dominum daturum vt contumaciam retundamus seuera lenitate. Bene est quod a Coena Domini absumus quindecim adhuc diebus, vt eius experimentum ante capiatur. Saluta mihi amicissime Thomam & reliquos fratres. Dominus vos omnes sibi conferuet diu incolumes & vnanimes. Date operam vt precibus intentae sint Ecclesiae, quando sic vrgent nos vndequaque discrimina. Scripta Aprili. M. D. XXXIX.
units.tr: ...if they had done so, they could have enjoyed the empty show of free generosity, since it would have cost them nothing to offer what they never had to accept. Ludovicus had slipped my mind. He was the only one who made an offer, but even he was asking too high a price for his largesse, since he only urged me to recant. He also declared loudly that I had deserted the Church. I replied to such letters as they deserved, though I fear the letters may have been lost. For now I will be content with your goodwill and that of the brothers, and I will try my resources if the need ever arises. In turn I ask that you be content with a grateful heart for your kindness towards me. I am sorry to have lost the crown, but I have reason to blame my own carelessness here, except that I thought shame would keep me from abusing it in this way. I very much approve your plan concerning Claude: before barbarism grows up further, or even hardens, the sparks of good training that still remain in that boyhood should be stirred up by his efforts. But why do you appeal to my faith in helping the brothers' attempt to restore discipline? To whom would I write, and in what style? So either open a way for me, or do not wait for me to thrust myself in rashly. Recently I did not hide from Philip to his face that I strongly disliked that abundance of ceremonies. I think the form they keep is not far from Judaism.
