When I pressed my arguments, he did not want to contend with me about it, except to say that the ceremonies were too numerous, either silly or at least superfluous, but that this had to be granted because of the obstinacy of the canons who are there. Otherwise, he said, there is no place in Saxony that is not more burdened than Wittenberg, and that Wittenberg itself would gradually cut away much of such a heap. The conclusion was that Luther does not approve of the ceremonies he retained under compulsion any more than of our sparing use of them. Would that our excellent N. understood how much sincerity there is in Philip! He at once laid aside all suspicion of deceit. As for Bucer's further defence of Luther's ceremonies, it is not because he aims at them or plans to introduce them. The Latin chant will in no way be brought in, since he shrinks from images. He despises some things and cares nothing for others. But there is no need to fear that what has once been abrogated will be restored by him through the right of return. He does not allow us to be divided from Luther over those trivial external observances. Nor do I think the causes of dispute are truly just. The German league contains nothing that ought to offend a devout heart. Why, I ask, has the Lord given some of them strength if they do not join it for the common defence of the gospel? Moreover, they do not drag anyone into their fellowship by force or by any compulsion. Indeed there are evangelical cities that prefer an alliance with the Papists, and even with the bishops themselves, such as Nuremberg. Would that N. knew with what attacks they were lately tested at the assembly, and with what constancy they resisted! The emperor's legate tried nothing more eagerly than to pull them away from the Helvetic churches. Yet he did not name them, but demanded that they not take up the cause of the Sacramentarians. They replied that for them there was fraternal communion with those whom he called Sacramentarians. And in the final act, how much courage did they show! Caesar imposed the condition that they receive no one into the league among those with whom they were making a truce; they agreed, but on this condition: that if any received the gospel, they would be safe even outside the league. And if they were attacked, they declared that they would hold as allies those who upheld the cause of Christ. They also asked Caesar for this reciprocal guarantee: that no treaties be made against the gospel in the meantime. Caesar wanted the Church's revenues to remain with the priests until the end of the truce. Our men agreed, provided that churches and schools were cared for; and there they held firm to the end. What if I mention the remarkable courage of this city? When Caesar's conditions were brought forward, that the agreements made after the Nuremberg assembly be annulled, that no new ones be struck among our people, and that each side remain intact until the German Church should be reformed by a colloquy held for this purpose, the Senate at once passed a decree declaring that they would rather see their children and wives killed before their eyes, all their goods destroyed, the city razed, and themselves all cut down to the last man, than admit those laws by which the way of Christ's gospel would be closed. My dear Farel, consider whether we are not doing an injustice to such men, when we accuse them of idleness while they refuse to be moved from the straight line by danger or terror of any kind. So now the matter undoubtedly moves towards conflict, and already an attack has been made on the territory of Lüneburg. It is our task, you say, to take diligent care that we do not fall into offence against good and pious people. I grant it; but it is also the task of good people to take care not to be offended rashly and without reason. Meanwhile, as I write, that disciple I mentioned wishes to return to favour, and he has voluntarily made Claude the mediator. I hope the Lord will grant that we crush his obstinacy with severe gentleness. It is well that we are still fifteen days away from the Lord's Supper, so that a trial of him may be made before it. Greet Thomas and the other brothers most warmly for me. May the Lord keep you all safe and united for a long time. Take care that the Churches are intent on prayer, since dangers press on us from every side. Written in April 1539.

units.la: Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: SAlue optime ac mihi dulcissime frater. Quæ mihi per literas fignificasti, intelligere mihi gratum fuit, etiamsi parum læta sint magna ex parte. Nam nec ignorare iuuat & scire vtile est. Ad singula tamen respondere nihil interest, De Claudio nihil audebam diuinare, ne me coniectura falleret. Nunc ex prin cipiis iudico qualis futurus sit in reformanda illa Ecclesia fuc- cessus, nisi Dominus ex insperato affulserit. Quod si bona fide ac gellerint nostri successores, intra exiguum tempus sentient plus inesse difficultatis quàm cogitarant. Fortasse & nobis red- dere testimonium cogentur bene ac fideliter gesti muneris. Quod zelo tuo moderantur, nihil mirum. Nondum enim ita incalue- runt, vt vel ignauiam tuam currendo assequantur. Tu autem vi- de quid temporis ratio ac necessitas postulet: atque ad eam amuf sim zelum tuum compone. De Paterniacensi Ecclesia Sonerio offerenda fuisse cogitatu, mihi nullo modo probatur. Peffimum enim exemplum est, vt à suis Ecclesiis abstrahantur fidi Pastores, quo aliis locus vacuus relinquatur. Si Richardus manet qualis erat, & tamen displicet, nescio quos amare debeamus. Ego certè pluribus Soneriis longè præferre ipsum non dubitem. Nunc quoque dum audio falso atque immerito ad te delatum, non possum facere quin suspicer aliquid maliciose atque ex composito hic esse factum. Multum nec sine causa hodie de ministerij contemptu querimur: & ipsi sæpe insanientem populum nostra vel stultitia vel cupiditate armamus. Nunquam mihi placuerunt artes illæ, vt alter in alterius locum arrogari affectaret: quod fieri his oculis palàm animaduerti in alia causa. Hæc mihi frater, tecum loquor, nedum omnia funcere fieri pro tuo candore putas, videaris conniuendo melis artibus suffragari. Neque etiam velim aliquem odiosius grauare dubiis mihi criminibus: sed pro nostra amicitia proferre liberè non dubito quæ timeo magis quàm credo. In eum locum assumptum esse placet, quem sine noxa potuit occupare. Zebedæum adeò inclementer tractari mihi plurimùm dolet. Neque, mihi crede magnam gratiam à Bucero ineunt, qui tanta tyrannide libros eius defendunt. Multò placidius fert ipse meam libertatem quoties ab ipso dissentio. Quanquam de iis mallem tecum potius coràm: quod futurum spero, nisi modicum laboré detrectaris. Indicaui Bucero tecum iniquissimè agi, quòd omnes eius amici tibi infesti esse perseuerarent: qui verò amici antea fuerunt, eius causa nunc abs te sint alienati. Ingemuit grauius quàm sperauerat. Cùm remedium quæreret, respondi vulnus esse ipso attactu periculosum: ergo sineret, donec melior ratio nobis appareret. De coniugio nunc apertius loquar. Ante Michaelis abitum nescio an mentionem aliquis forte intulerit istius de qua scripsi: verum semper memineris quid in ipsa quaeram: non enim sum ex insano amatorum genere, qui vitia etiam exosculantur, vbi semel forma capti sunt. Haec sola est quae me illectat pulchritudo, si pudica est, si morigera, si non saltuosa, si parca, si patiens, si spes est de mea valetudine fore solicitam. Ergo si putabis conducere, accinge te, ne quis alius anteuertat. Sin aliud censes, omittamus. Nihil posthac scribam donec veneris. Venies autem nobis omnibus exoptatissimus. Age, animum tuum hac profectione mirum in modum explicabis. Et tamen nihil obstat quominus scribas dum te comparas ad profectionem. Omnes te plusquam amice salutant, Capito, Bucerus, Sturmius, Pedrotus, Gaspar & Galli quos non nomino, quia nomina non tenes. Fratres omnes mihi saluta. Dominus vos omnes sibi suaeque Ecclesiae diu seruet incolumes. Argentorati, x i x. Maij M. D. XXXIX.
units.tr: Greetings, best and dearest brother. I was glad to learn from your letter what you signified, although for the most part it is not very cheerful. It is pleasant not to be ignorant, and useful to know. Yet it makes no difference to answer each point. I did not dare to divine anything about Claude, lest conjecture should mislead me. Now, from principles, I judge what success will attend the reform of that Church, unless the Lord appears unexpectedly. But if our successors act in good faith and with diligence, within a short time they will feel more difficulty than they had thought. Perhaps they will even be forced to give testimony against us for the good and faithful discharge of our office. That they restrain your zeal is no surprise: they have not yet grown so warm that they can overtake your sluggishness by running. But you see what the circumstances of the time and necessity require, and adjust your zeal to them. As for offering Sonerius for the Church of Paternay, I cannot at all approve the idea. For it is a very bad example when faithful ministers are drawn away from their own Churches, so that a vacancy is left for others. If Richard remains what he was and yet is displeasing, I do not know whom we ought to love. I, at any rate, would not hesitate to prefer him far above several Soners. Now too, since I hear that a false and undeserved report has been brought to you, I cannot help suspecting that something was done here maliciously and by design. Today we complain much, and not without cause, about the contempt for the ministry, and we ourselves often arm a raging people, either by our folly or by our greed. I have never liked those arts by which one man tries to claim another's place, which I have plainly seen happen in another case with my own eyes. I say this to you, brother, as to a friend; do not think that, because of your candour, you should appear to support such crooked arts by connivance. Nor would I wish to burden anyone with doubtful accusations, but for the sake of our friendship I do not hesitate to state frankly what I fear more than I believe. He has been assumed into the position that he could fill without harm. I am very sorry that Zebedaeus is treated so harshly. And believe me, Bucer does not win much favour by defending his books with such tyranny. He himself bears my freedom far more gently whenever I dissent from him. However, I would rather discuss these things with you in person; I hope this will happen, unless you shrink from a small effort. I told Bucer that you were being treated most unjustly, since all his friends kept on being hostile to you; and those who were friends before are now estranged from you on his account. He groaned more deeply than he had hoped. When he sought a remedy, I replied that the wound was dangerous to touch, so he should let it alone until a better plan became clear to us. Now I will speak more openly about marriage. Before Michaelmas departure, I do not know whether anyone perhaps mentioned to you that woman about whom I wrote; but always remember what I seek in her. For I am not one of that mad sort of lovers who kiss even faults once they have been captured by beauty. The only beauty that allures me is this: if she is chaste, if she is obedient, if she is not frivolous, if she is thrifty, if she is patient, if there is hope that she will be concerned for my health. So if you think it suitable, get ready, lest someone else get ahead of you. But if you think otherwise, let us drop it. I will write nothing more until you come. You will come, most desired by all of us. Come, you will explain your mind on this journey in a wonderful way. And yet nothing stops you from writing while you prepare for the journey. All greet you more than as a friend: Capito, Bucer, Sturm, Pedrotus, Gaspar, and the Frenchmen whom I do not name, because you do not know their names. Greet all the brothers for me. May the Lord keep you all safe for a long time for himself and his Church. Strasbourg, 19 May 1539.

units.la: Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: CAL. GENEVENSI ECCLESIAE.
units.tr: CALVIN TO THE CHURCH OF GENEVA.

units.la: Misericordia Dei nostri, & gratia Domini Iesu Christi vobis multiplicetur per Spiritus sancti communicationem.
units.tr: May the mercy of our God and the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be multiplied to you through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: NIhil mihi maiorem tristitiam attulit, dilectissimi fratres, Ex Gall. post eas turbas quae tam misere dissipauerant & penè euerterant vestram Ecclesiam, quàm vbi intellexi vestra iurgia & concertationes cum ministris ipsis qui nobis successerunt. Quanuis enim praeposteritas illa quae cum illorum primo aditu coniuncta etiamnum remanebat, merito vos posset offendere, quaecunque tamen occasio subiit, non possum sine magno & intimo horrore audire aliquod in Ecclesia schisma residere. Quare hoc mihi longe fuit acerbius quàm verbis aperire possim, quod audiui de vestris illis contentionibus quandiu in incerto statu versati estis: cum ea occasione non solum Ecclesia vestra scissa esset, aperte omnino, sed & ipsum ministerium Ecclesiasticum opprobrio & contumeliae expositum, quod est infiniti cuiusdam momenti. Cumque per illam ἀταξίαν quae nunc adhuc viget in Dei Ecclesia de remedio praesenti pro morbi ratione minus spei haberem, accepi cum summo gaudio malum illud in certam vnionem & consensum commutatum esse: cum statuerem ita factum iri vt quisque in viam rediret, atque ita regnum Domini nostri Iesu Christi promoueretur. Vbi enim sunt rixae & discordia, vix vlla spes est proficiendi in melius. Cum igitur fructum c.iij. certum ex illa conciliatione mihi sponderem, facile sum adduc-ctus vt ad illius quoq; confirmatione me adiungerem. Si enim in mediis ipsis grauissimis tempestatibus conscientiæ meq; iudicio & certo proposito semper ad Ecclesiæ communionem faciendâ & conseruandam studia mea contuli, tanto magis testificanda mihi erat propensio animi mei erga pios ipsos, vbi tam apposita ad eam rem se occasio offerebat. Ac videbam sane res ita tum dissipatas, vt mihi non ita procliue videretur eas in integrum statum reponi atque restitui. Vtcunque fit, optatissimam illam & valde opportunam occasionem iudicabam à Domino oblatam ad Ecclesiam veltram restituendam. Nunc vero, vbi contra mea illam expectationem, audiui conciliationem illam inter Pastores veltros & vicinas Ecclesias, à Farello etiam & à me ratam habitam, idoneam non fuisse ad vos syncero amicitiæ affectu & legitimæ coniunctionis vinculo cum veltris Pastoribus quibus animarum veltrarum cura mandata est, colligandos, coactus fui ad scribendum me conferre, vt conarer, quatum in me esset, medicinam huic malo facere, quod dissimulare sine graui erga Deum offensione non poslem. Et quanuis literæ meæ non valde amanter à vobis iâ accep ç fuerint, nolui tamen officio meo deesse, vt si nihil amplius assequerer, saltem animam meam liberarem. Nec tamen in dubium adduco quæ sit veltra mihi comperta propensa obedientia erga Deû & ministros ipsius, vt hanc meam exhortationem apud vos nullius ponderis futuram vereor, neq; etiâ vos latet mea erga vos syncerítas. Quod vero non est meum à vobis admissum consilium, tepori magis imputandum duco, cum res ita essent perturbatæ, vt quàm difficile esset statuere quid expediret. Nùc vbi res per Dei gratiam magis sunt sedatæ & copositæ, confido vos facile per spectaturos, nô aliud mihi esse propositum quàm vt vos perducam in rectam viam: vt ita de me persuasi reipsa exhibeatis quo affectu ducamini ad obediendum veritati. Imprimis expendite quæso seposito omni per sonarum respectu, quo honore affecerit & quid contulerit illis Dominus quos in Ecclesia sua instituit Pastores & verbi Ministros. Non modò enim iubet nos obsequentes præstare cum metu & tremore verbo ipsius dum nobis annunciatur: sed etiâ honore & reuerentia prosequendos mandat verbi ministros, tanquam ipsius legatione ornatos, & quos agnosci velit vt suos etiam Angelos. Sane, quandiu apud vos fuimus, non multum vobiscum contendimus de ministerij nostri dignitate, ne suspicioni vllam fenestram aperiremus: nunc verò extra illud periculum positus, liberius quod sentio proferam. Si mihi agendum esset cum ministris ipsis, docerem quæ esset muneris illorum ratio, & ad quid vobis suo ministerio teneantur. Cùm verò pro se singulis tum ministris tum priuatis ratio reddenda fit vitæ suæ tandem, magis est vt in sese quisque intueatur quid aliis debeat, quàm quid sibi debeatur ab alio diutius requirat. Vbi illa consideratio locum habebit inter vos, rum etiam hæc regula fixa hærebit, nempe eos qui locum ministrorum verbi tenent, quando regimen animarum vestrarum ipsis est commissum, agnoscendos esse vobis parentum loco, & in pretio habendos atque honorandos propter illud munus quo funguntur apud vos ex Domini vocatione. Nec tamen id co spectat vt auferatur ius illud vobis à Deo collatum (vt & suis omnibus) vt examini subiiciantur Pastores omnes, vt discernantur probi & improbi, atque reprimantur illi qui sub larua pastorum lupinam rapacitatem prodiderint. Tantum hoc volo apud illos qui partes Pastorum implent aliquatenus, vt finttolerabiles, vt vos etiam Christianæ gratis, ac proinde magis rationem habeatis eius quod à vobis debeatur aliis, quàm quod ipsis vobis alij debeant. Atque aperte hoc & paucis expediam. Duo hic vobis cogitanda sunt, Vnum, quod ministrorum vestrorum vocatio non accidit sine Dei voluntate. Quanuis enim mutatio illa quæ nostro discessu facta est, Diaboli artificio deputanda sit, vt quicquid eam est cosequutum vobis merito suspectū esse possit: in ea tamé singularis Domini gratia agnoscéda vobis est, cui deditui vos plane nō sustinuit: neq; vos relabi sub Antichristi iugum, à quo vos semel asse ruit. Sed potius & doctrinâ Euangelij apud vos extare adhuc voluit & aliquâ Ecclesiæ formâ vigere, vt pacata conscientia agere istic liceret. Admonuimus vos semper vt agnosceretis illâ Ecclesiæ vestræ euersionem vt visitationem Domini & vobis & nobis necessariam: neque tam attenderetis ad improbos & Satanæ instrumeta, quàm ad propria peccata, quæ non leuiore pœnam, imò longè etiā grauiorem commerita sint. Idem igitur vobis nūc etiam suggero. Præter quam enim quod illud est singulare remedium & appositum ad obtinendam à Domino misericordiā & relaxatione ab illius iusto iudicio quod incumbit vobis, alia etiam ratio subest, quæ huc vos debet adducere: ne videlicet obliuioni mandare videamini tātum illud Domini erga vos beneficium, quo factum est vt ædificium Euangelij plane non corrueret apud vos. Cum illud ita subsistit, vt miraculi loco habendum sit exēplum illud potētiæ ipsius, qua vna ab extrema calamitate tantum abfueritis. Quicquid sit, Dei prouidētiæ opus illud est q̃ extant ministri istic qui locum pastorum animarū & Ecclesiæ vestræ regimen tenēt. Accedit & illud quod serui Dei qui verbi ipsius ministerium exercent in vicinis Ecclesiis, vt moderentur tam perniciosis cōcertationibus, ipsi illorum vocationem comprobau. runt. Quorum etiam sententiæ subscripsimus,
units.tr: Nothing, dearest brothers, has caused me greater sorrow than the disturbances that scattered your church so wretchedly and almost overthrew it, and than learning of your quarrels and disputes with the ministers who have succeeded us. Although the irregularity which was joined to their first entry, and which still remains, might rightly offend you, whatever the occasion was, I cannot hear without great and inward horror that any schism lingers in the Church. So it has been far more bitter to me than I can express in words, to hear of those contentions of yours, for as long as you were unsettled. On that occasion your church was not only openly torn apart, but the ecclesiastical ministry itself was exposed to disgrace and insult, which is of the utmost importance. Since, in view of the disorder that still prevails in God's Church, I had little hope of a present remedy suited to the nature of the disease, I received with great joy the news that this evil had been changed into a firm union and agreement. I supposed this would happen so that each would return to the right way, and so that the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ would be advanced. For where there are quarrels and discord, there is scarcely any hope of progress towards better things. Since I therefore promised myself a sure fruit from that reconciliation, I was easily led to join myself also to its confirmation. For if, even in the most severe storms, I had always devoted my efforts, by my conscience's judgment and settled purpose, to making and keeping communion with the Church, then all the more ought my readiness of mind towards pious people to be made evident, when so fitting an opportunity for it presented itself. Indeed I saw that matters were then so scattered that it did not seem to me so easy to restore and re-establish them to their former state. However that may be, I judged that this most desired and very timely opportunity had been offered by the Lord for restoring your church. But now, contrary to my expectation, I have heard that the reconciliation between your ministers and the neighbouring churches, which was also approved by Farel and by me, was not suitable for gathering you together with your ministers, to whom the care of your souls has been entrusted, in sincere affection of friendship and in the bond of lawful fellowship. Compelled by this, I have turned to writing, so that I might try, as far as I am able, to apply a remedy to this evil, which I could not pass over without serious offence to God. And although my letter has not been received by you very kindly, I did not want to fail in my duty, so that if I achieved nothing further, at least I would free my own soul. Nor do I doubt how dutiful and obedient you are, as I have learned, towards God and his ministers, so I do not fear that this my exhortation will carry no weight with you; nor is my sincerity towards you hidden from you. That my counsel has not been acted upon by you I count rather to be imputed to lukewarmness, since matters were so disturbed that it was hard to decide what was expedient. Now that, by God's grace, things have been calmed and composed more, I trust you will readily consider that my only purpose is to lead you back into the right way, so that you may show, in fact, the same disposition by which you are moved to obey the truth as I have assumed of myself. First of all, I beg you to weigh, setting aside all regard for persons, what honour and what gifts the Lord has bestowed upon those whom he has appointed as pastors and ministers of the Word in his Church. For he not only commands us to obey his Word with fear and trembling while it is proclaimed to us, but he also orders that ministers of the Word be honoured and revered, as those adorned with his own commission, and whom he wishes to be recognised as his own angels. Indeed, while we were with you, we did not dispute much with you about the dignity of our ministry, lest we open any window for suspicion. Now, however, placed outside that danger, I will speak more freely what I think. If I had to deal with the ministers themselves, I would teach what the nature of their office is, and to what extent they are bound to you by their ministry. But since an account of his life must finally be rendered by each individual, both minister and private person, it is better for each to look into himself to see what he owes to others, than to demand for longer what is owed to himself by another. Where that consideration will hold sway among you, there this fixed rule will also remain: namely, that those who hold the place of ministers of the Word, when the government of your souls has been committed to them, are to be acknowledged by you in the place of parents, and to be esteemed and honoured on account of the office which they discharge among you by the Lord's calling. Yet this is not intended to take away from you the right that God has granted you (as to all his people) to have all pastors subjected to examination, so that the good and the bad may be distinguished, and so that those who, under the mask of pastors, have shown a wolfish greed may be restrained. I only want this to be understood concerning those who in some measure fill the role of pastors: that they should not be intolerable, so that you, as Christians, may have more regard for what you owe to others than for what others owe to you. And I shall set this out clearly and briefly. Two things are to be considered here. First, that the calling of your ministers did not happen without the will of God. For although that change which was made after our departure ought to be ascribed to the craft of the devil, so that whatever followed from it may rightly be suspected by you, yet in it you must acknowledge the singular grace of the Lord, who did not wholly abandon you to it, nor allow you to fall back under the yoke of Antichrist, from which he had once rescued you. Rather, he willed that the doctrine of the Gospel should still remain among you, and that the church should flourish in some form, so that you could act there with a quiet conscience. We have always urged you to recognise that the overthrow of your church was a visitation of the Lord, necessary both for you and for us; and not to attend so much to the wicked and the instruments of Satan, as to your own sins, which deserve a punishment not lighter, but indeed much heavier. Therefore I now suggest the same to you. Besides the fact that this is the unique and suitable remedy for obtaining from the Lord mercy and relief from his just judgment which weighs upon you, there is also another reason that ought to lead you here: namely, that you should not seem to consign to oblivion that great benefit of the Lord towards you, by which it came about that the building of the Gospel did not collapse among you altogether. Since it stands in such a way that that example of his power, by which you were kept only just short of utter calamity, must be regarded as a miracle. However that may be, it is a work of God's providence that there are ministers there who hold the place of pastors of souls and the government of your church. There is also this: the servants of God who exercise the ministry of the Word in the neighbouring churches have approved the calling of these ministers, in order to moderate such pernicious quarrels. We too have subscribed to their judgment, since no better plan appeared to us by which we might provide for your advantage and salvation.

units.la: c.iiij. cùm nulla nobis alia melior ratio appareret qua vestro commodo & saluti consuleremus. Quin integritas conscientiæ nostræ comperta sit vobis non dubito, vt statuere debeatis hic nihil non ex animo & syncerè factum esse. Præter affectum verò, ipsa etiam rei disquisitio perinde syncera ex me quidem fuit, vt nihil hic inuolutum à me habeatis. Quare vobis serio prospiciet dum est ne facilè improbetis quòd Dei serui ad vestrum & Ecclesiæ commodum & conseruationem esse necessarium iudicarunt. Alterum est vt inspiciatur quàm legitimè fungantur partibus suis, vt ministerium Ecclesiæ impleant. Atque hic, fateor, discretio plane requiritur (neque autor velim esse tyrannidis vllius in Ecclesiam inuehendę) vt pij homines habeant pro pastoribus qui vocationi suæ non insistant. Est enim illa indignitas non ferenda si certis personis illa reuerentia & obseruantia deferatur, quam Dominus ipse vnis verbi ministris adsignatam voluit. Proinde facilè vobis cõcedo de eo qui non docuerit verbum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quemcunque titulum vel prærogatiuam obtendat, indignum esse qui pro pastore habeatur, vt illi obedientia ministerio debita exhibeatur. Quia verò mihi constat de fratribus nostris qui apud vos hodie ministerij locum tenent, doceri vos Euangelium per illos, non video quid excusare liceat coram Domino dum illos negligetis aut reiicietis. Siquis respondeat hoc vel illud in eorum doctrina vel moribus sibi non placere, primùm à vobis contendo per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, vt quicquid esse potest serio expendatis primùm, & sine vlla iudicij præcipitatione. Cùm enim hoc singuli nobis vicissim debeamus ex officio charitatis, ne temerè in alios feramus sententiam, sed potius clementiam & æquitatem retineamus quantum in nobis erit, multo magis illa moderatio obseruanda est erga illos quos Dominus peculiariter eminere præ aliis voluit. Atque etiamsi non desit quod in illis requiri possit (de quo non possum pronunciare), cùm de eo mihi nō liqueat) vobis tamen succurrere debet, neminem adeò bene comparatum inueniri, in quo non sint etiam multa quæ desiderentur. Quare illa charitatis regula à nobis non præstatur, nisi sustineamus proximos cum ipsorum infirmitatibus, dummodo verum Dei timorem in illis agnoscamus, & syncerum affectum sectandæ ipsius veritatis. Postremò dubitare nō possum quod ad ipsorum doctrinam attinet, quin fideliter vobis tradant præcipua Christianæ religionis capita & quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria, ac simul administrationem Sacramentorum Domini coniungant. Hoc vbi locum habet, illic & substantia ipsa ministerij à Domino Iesu Christo ordinati viget, & legitima dignitas & obseruantia illi ministerio est deferenda. Nunc igitur, dilectissimi fratres, oro & moneo vos in nomine & virtute Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt auersis ab hominibus animis & mentibus ad vnicum illum Redemptorem nos attollamus, illúdque reputemus quantum sacris ipsius mandatis deferre teneamur. Ac si quicquid ille inter vos instituit, inuiolatum merito esse debet, nulla ratio vos poterit dimouere ab officio, vt ministerium, quod tam serio vobis commendat, sartum tectúmque non seruetis. Iam si disceptatis & contenditis cum vestris pastoribus ad rixas vsque & conuicia, vti accidisse audio, satis constat ea ratione ministerium ipsorum in quo elucere debuit splendor gloriæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi, opprobrio & contumeliis subiici, ac tantum non pedibus calcari. Vestrum est igitur attente illud cauere ne dum hominibus insultare videmini, Deo ipsi bellum reipsa indicatis. Neque porro illud leuis momenti videri vobis debet quod fiant & foueantur in Ecclesia schismata & sectæ, quod nullum pectus Christianum sine horrore etiam auribus haurire potest. Quin verò ita se res habeat vbi eiusmodi separatio est & quasi secessio inter pastorem & populum, res ipsa loquitur. Tandem igitur hoc accipite, si me à vobis pro fratre haberi vultis, vt solida sit inter vos quæ tanto nomini respondeat coniunctio, ne ministerium illud repudietis quod pro vestro commodo & Ecclesiæ salute coactus fui approbare sine vllo gratiæ vel metus hominum respectu. Quia verò totum illud tempus quo fidelis & pius collega meus in Domino hic fuit quia mihi per ordinarias occupationes licuit, colloquendo consumptum est, non potui vobis plenius scribere, vt volebam. Quare sic inter nos conuenit, vt ego quidem paucis traderem vobis rectam viam quam hic teneretis, ipse autem prout expedire iudicaret vos ad officiū coram adhortaretur. Hic igitur vobis amantissima salute à me adscripta, Dominum Iesum oro vt vos sancto suo præsidio protegat, vos suis donis magis ac magis cumulet, vestra Ecclesiam in rectum ordinem restituat, ac vos in primis Spiritu suæ mansuetudinis impleat, vt in vera animorum coniunctione omnes ipsius regno promouendo nos impendere possimus. Argentinæ. M. D. XXXIX. XXV. Iunij.
units.tr: c.iiij. since no other better course appeared to us by which we might look to your advantage and welfare. Indeed, I do not doubt that you have learned of the integrity of our conscience, so that you must judge that nothing here has been done except from the heart and sincerely. Apart from feeling, the examination of the matter itself was likewise so sincere on my part that you have nothing concealed by me here. Therefore, take care seriously that you not readily find fault with what the servants of God judged necessary for your benefit and the preservation of the Church. The second point is that you examine how lawfully they discharge their parts, so as to fulfil the ministry of the Church. Here, I confess, discernment is clearly required (and I would not wish to be the author of any tyranny brought into the Church): that godly men should regard as pastors those who do not keep to their calling. For that unworthiness is intolerable if that reverence and obedience, which the Lord himself wished to be assigned to the ministers of the Word alone, are given to certain persons. Accordingly, I readily grant you that whoever has not taught the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, whatever title or prerogative he puts forward, is unworthy to be regarded as a pastor, so that the obedience owed to the ministry is not shown to him. But since it is certain to me concerning our brothers who today hold the ministry's place among you, that you are taught the Gospel through them, I do not see what excuse may be allowed before the Lord while you neglect or reject them. If anyone answers that this or that in their teaching or morals does not please him, I first contend with you, through our Lord Jesus Christ, that you weigh carefully whatever can be said, and do so without any hasty judgment. For since each of us in turn owes this to the other by the duty of charity, not to pass judgment rashly on others but rather to keep clemency and fairness as far as lies in us, all the more must that moderation be observed toward those whom the Lord wished to stand out peculiarly above others. And even if there is not lacking what might be required in them (about which I cannot pronounce, since it is not clear to me), still it ought to come to your mind that no one is found so well made that there are not also many things in him that are wanting. Therefore that rule of charity is not practised by us unless we bear with our neighbours in their infirmities, provided we recognise in them the true fear of God and a sincere desire to pursue the truth itself. Finally, I cannot doubt that, as regards their teaching, they faithfully deliver to you the chief heads of the Christian religion and those things which are necessary for salvation, and join with this the administration of the Lord's sacraments. Where this obtains, there also the very substance of the ministry ordained by the Lord Jesus Christ flourishes, and its lawful dignity and observance must be paid to that ministry. Now therefore, most beloved brothers, I pray and admonish you in the name and power of our Lord Jesus Christ: let us turn our minds and hearts away from men, raise them to that one Redeemer, and consider how much we are bound to render to his sacred commands. And if whatever he has established among you ought rightly to be kept inviolate, no reason will be able to move you from duty, so that you do not preserve intact the ministry which he commends to you so seriously. Now, if you dispute and contend with your pastors even to quarrels and reproaches, as I hear has happened, it is quite clear that by such conduct their ministry, in which the splendour of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ ought to shine forth, is subjected to reproach and insult, and is all but trampled underfoot. It is therefore your task to take careful heed lest, while you seem to insult men, you in fact declare war on God himself. Nor should it seem to you of slight moment that schisms and sects are made and fostered in the Church, something no Christian breast can hear without horror. Indeed, when such separation, and as it were secession, exists between pastor and people, the thing itself speaks. Finally, therefore, accept this: if you wish me to be regarded by you as a brother, so that there may be a firm union among you corresponding to so great a name, do not reject that ministry which, compelled by concern for your benefit and the Church's welfare, I have been obliged to approve, without any regard to the favour or fear of men. But since the whole time during which my faithful and godly colleague in the Lord was here has been spent in conversation, as my ordinary duties allowed, I have not been able to write to you as fully as I wished. Therefore it was agreed between us that I should briefly set out for you the right way which you should hold here, while he himself would exhort you to your duty as he judged fit. Here, then, commending you with a most loving salutation written by me, I pray the Lord Jesus to protect you with his holy defence, to load you more and more with his gifts, to restore your Church to right order, and above all to fill you with the Spirit of his gentleness, so that in true union of minds we may be able to devote ourselves to advancing his kingdom. Strasbourg, 25 June 1539.

units.la: Vobis deditissimus I.C.
units.tr: Most devotedly yours, I.C.

units.la: LEO IVDAE CALVINO.
units.tr: Leo Jude to Calvin.

units.la: Gratiam & vitæ innocentiam à Deo Patre per Christum.
units.tr: Grace and innocence of life from God the Father through Christ.

units.la: Svperioribus annis, vir doctissime, epistolas duas dedisti non tantum doctas, sed etiam valde vtiles & necessarias, maximè præsenti rerum statu. Has ego ambas verti Germanice, vt & ij
units.tr: In recent years, most learned sir, you sent me two letters, not only learned but also very useful and necessary, especially in the present state of affairs. I translated both into German so that those who do not know Latin might also profit from them.

units.la: Epist. 18. fructum harum perciperent qui Latinè ignorant. Altera quam ad Episcopum scripsisti, Basileæ excusa est mea opera : alteram noluerunt excudere typographi, metu periculi fortasse deterriti. Nam in hac liberrime & pro Christiana παρρησία loqueris quo pacto se gerant qui sub Papæ tyrannide viuere ac degere cogun tur, damnans interim eos qui vtroque genu claudicant, & non tam Deo quàm Papæ seruire volunt, putantes satis esse fi Fidem corde veram & inconcussam seruent: etiamsi corpus sanguine Christi consecratum foris idolis prosternant & inclinent, con-fortes simul Satanæ & Christi, si fieri potest. Hanc ergo receptam Zuikio mihi Constantiensi, qui eam non fine gratulatione legit, iogans vt sibi per me liceret vt Augustam eam epistolam mit-tit excudendam: se scire quendam qui eam typis mandare velit, modo auctoris nomen (quod ego tuo bono in versione suppref-feram) permittatur præfigi. Hic ego pro te nihil dicere potui vel asserens vel negans: statui ergo expiscari literis tuam volun-tatem, eámque à te receptam Zuikio rescribere. Tu ergo frater, si consultum Reipub. Christianæ velis, & succursum multorum conscientiis, non negabis vt præfigatur nomen tuum, quum a-lea semel iacta sit. Non enim te eum puto qui ob declinandam in uidiam aut periculum, tantum fructum impedire velis. Non dubito si liber hic euulgetur, multos fore qui abiecto iugo Pon-tificio & excusso metu in castra Christi libero spiritu sint ad-uolaturi. Tu vale doctissime vir, & mentem tuam hac in re mi-hi literis significa primo quoque tempore. Tiguri, vltima Fe-bruarij. M. D. X L. Leo Iudæ tuus.
units.tr: Epist. 18. The one you wrote to the Bishop was published at Basel through my work. The other the printers refused to print, perhaps frightened off by the danger. For in that letter you speak most freely, with Christian boldness [παρρησία], about how those must conduct themselves who are forced to live under the tyranny of the Pope. Meanwhile you condemn those who limp on both knees, who wish to serve not so much God as the Pope, and who think it enough to keep the faith true and unshaken in the heart, even though they prostrate and bow outwardly before idols the body consecrated with Christ's blood, partners at once of Satan and of Christ, if that can be managed. I therefore showed this letter, which I had received, to my friend Zwick of Constance, who read it with no small delight. He asked that, through me, he might be allowed to send that letter to Augsburg for printing. He knew someone who was willing to have it printed, provided that the author's name were permitted to be placed at the front (which I would conceal in the translation for your own good). Here I could say nothing on your behalf, either affirming or denying. I have therefore decided to draw out your wishes by letter and to reply to Zwick with whatever you accept. So you, brother, if you wish to serve the Christian commonwealth and to help the consciences of many, will not refuse to have your name prefixed, since the die has been cast. For I do not think you are the sort of man who would hinder so much good in order to avoid envy or danger. I do not doubt that, if this book is published, many will flock to the camp of Christ with free spirit, having cast off the Papal yoke and shaken off fear. Farewell, most learned man, and let me know your mind on this matter by letter at the first opportunity. From Zurich, the last day of February, 1540. Your Leo Jude.

units.la: CAL. RICHEBVRCIO SVO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to his Richebourg, greetings.

units.la: CVM mihi primus de morte Claudij ac Ludouici filij tui al-latus esset nuntius, sic toto animo cófusus fui, vt multos dies nihil aliud potuerim quàm lugere. Ac tamen si coram Deo vt-cunq; me sustinebam iis administrulis, quibus in adueri-sis nos in-struit: apud homines tamen nullus fere erā. Certe ad omnia ossi-cia, non multò magis idoneus mihi videbar, quàm si fuissem fe-mimortuus. Hinc enim mœrebā optimum & fidelissimū amicū, mihi alienissimo tempore fuisse ereptum: cuius tanta mihi erat fa-miliaritas, vt nobis duobus nihil potuerit esse coniunctius. Inde subibat alius dolor, optimè spei adolescentē filium tuum primò ætatis flore esse sublatum: quem loco filij dilig bā, quia me, nō fe-cus ac patrē alterum, vicissim col bat. Hunc acerbissimū luctum excipiebat grauis, & anxia de iis, quos nobis superstites D. reli-querat, solicitudo. Domum huc illuc diffi-cta esse audiebā. Mal-herbij periculū cum ipsius causa me valde affligebat, tum etiam de reliquiis admonebat. Cogitabam fieri no posse, quin vxor effet vehementer consternata. Carolus vero tuus mihi assidue oculos versabatur. Nam qua præditus est ingenij bonitate, qua in fratre ac præceptorem non charitate modo, sed pietate quoq; semper fuit, minime dubium mihi erat, quin totus in squalore & lachrymis effet. Vna hæc cogitatio me nonnihil subleuabat, q; cum habebat fratre meum, quem illi in hac calamitate spetabā fore no minimo solatio. Verum id etiā non poteram reputare, quin simul in mente veniret, ambos nondum cuasiste periculū. Ita donec subsecutę sunt alterę literę quæ Malherbiū extra vitę discrimē laborare, Carolum, fratre meum, vxore, & alios saluos esse nunciaret, mœrore, & molestia tātum non oppressus fuit: nisi q; corā D. vt iam dixi, ne prorsus concideré, precibus & sanctis meditationibus quę nobis ab eius verbo suggerūtur, me fulcieba. Hęc ideo cōmemoro, ne ideo minoris tibi sint meę exhortationes, quibus nunc te solari cupio, quia facile esse cogites, in alieno dolore forte se exhibere: ego vero hic no iacto in alieno dolore fortitudiné, sed quū mihi singulari Dei beneficio datum sit, vt ab eo, qui mihi tecum pene ex æquo cōmunis fuit aliqua ex parte vel liberarer vel leuarer, quibus remediis vsus sum, quæq; mihi plurimum prodesse sensi, ea tibi, quoad per epistolā, & bre uem epistolam licet, cōmunico. Quanquā hac in re sic mihi habenda est tristitiæ tuæ ratio, vt interim mihi cum grauissimo ac cōstantissimo viro negotium esse meminerim. Neque enim me latet, quibus ad patientiā, moderationémq; perpetuo seruandam præsidiis fis instructus. Ne illas quidé consolationes, quæ inter ci uiles homines vsum habent, adhibere placet. Ne mortuum defleas, quæ mortale genueras: vt eam animi magnitudine præstes luctuoso casu, quam ingenium & natura præclarum, & optimis artibus excultū, quam ætas, quam multarum rerum peritia, quā denique existimatio postulat: vt vitæ anteactę recordatione te soleris. Illis, inquam, & aliis eius generis exhortationibus apud te supersedeo. Vnum enim certum est ac firmum consolationis genus, in quo te, ac tui similes acquiescere decet, quod ex interio re illo pietatis sensu manat, quo te abundare scio. Hoc ergo tibi omnino agendum est, vt mentem ad eas cogitationes reuoces, quę nobis ab optimo magistro in pietatis schola dictatur, ac fugeruntur. Eas hic recensere non est necesse, cum tibi sint perinde ac mihi familiares. Et tamen pro singulari tua pietate, & ea quā mihi defuerunt beneuolētia non illibeter forte in meis literis recognosces quę tibi alioquin spōte occurrunt. Filiū, quē apud te deposuerat. D. recepit. Hic sublatę sunt vanæ illę & prauę stultorū hominū querimoniæ, O cæca mors, o iniqua fata, o Parcę inexorabiles, o crudelis fortuna. Dominus qui in hac vitę statione ad tempus eum locauerat, euocauit. Quod à D.factum audimus, si-mul cogitemus non temere, non fortuito, non extraneo aliquo impulsu sed eo consilio, quo non modò nihil nisi quod rectum & iustum: sed nihil etiam nisi quod bonum, ac salutare nobis prouidet, statuit, ac facit. Vbi iustitia, & æquitas, illic nefas est reclamare. Vbi vero cum æquitate illa, nostra quoque vtilitas coiuncta est, cuius ingratitudinis foret, non placido, moderatóque animo suscipere, quicquid patri nostro placuerit? Quanquam in ipsa Dei prouidentia satis amplam leuationem habent fideles, quicquid acciderit. Nihil enim est quod nos magis exanimet, quàm dum his quæstionibus nos fatigamus. Cur non aliter? Cur in eum locum? bene hæc, & appositè dicerentur, si quid à nobis admissum esset reprehensione dignum. Verum vbi culpa nostra abest, eiusmodi querelis nullus est locus. Deus est igitur, qui filiū abs te repetiit, quem ea lege tibi educandum tradiderat, vt suus semper esset. Et ideo suffulsit, quia & illi è mundo emigrare: & hac orbitate vel te humiliari, vel tuam patientiam probare vtile erat. Hanc vtilitatem si non intelligis, primum rogādus Deus, vt tibi ostendat. Si celando vult te etiamnum magis exercere, permittendum vt plus sapiat, quàm mentis tuæ imbecillitas aequatur. Quantum ad filium attinet, si cum animo tuo reputes, quam difficile sit hoc d ploratissimo seculo rectum vitæ cursum tenere, beatum iudicabis, qui antequam tot discrimina, quę iam illi imminebant per ætatem obeunda essent, maturè liberatus sit. Perinde enim est, acsi quis turbulento, & tempestuoso mari, antequam in alium feratur, celeriter se in portum recipiat. Neq; enim sic Dei beneficium est longa vita, vt aliquid nobis depereat, si paucorum annorum spatio disiuncti ad meliorem vitam traducimur. Iam vero quia D.ipse, qui noster omnium Pater est, Ludouicum filij loco est volutrat: hoc tibi pro immensa sua benignitate largitus est, vt præclarum educationis tuæ fructum ante eius mortem caperes: vnde eam quoque benedictionem sci res ad te pertinere: Ergo Deus tuus, & feminis tui. Fuit à prima pue ritia, quantum anni ferre poterant optimis studiis institutus. In his iam mediocres progressus fecerat, vt magnam spem de se nobis in posterum faceret. Mores suos, & viuendi rationem bonis omnibus approbauerat, si quando lapsus erat non modò se patiebatur admoneri, & obiurgari, sed & quoque monitis prębebat docilem, & obsequentem. Erat quidem interdum vehementior ingenio, sed non vsque ad pertinaciam. Itaque impetus illi qui modum excedebant, paruo negotio frangebantur. Quod verò plurimi faciendum est nobis, pietatis rudimenta sic imbiberat, vt & veram Religionis intelligentiam haberet, & timore Dei nō siro fideliter erat imbutus. Hæc sanè tam præclara Dei beneficentia
units.tr: When the first news reached me of the death of Claude and of your son Louis, I was so utterly overwhelmed in my whole soul that for many days I could do nothing but grieve. Yet if I held myself up somewhat before God, by those aids with which he instructs us in adversity, before men I was almost nothing. Indeed, for every duty I seemed no more fit than if I had been half dead. I grieved that a most excellent and faithful friend had been snatched from me at the most unseasonable time, a friend with whom I had such close intimacy that nothing could have been more closely joined than the two of us. Then came another grief: that your son, of excellent promise, had been taken away in the first flower of his youth, whom I loved in place of a son, since he, no less than a second father, loved me in return. This most bitter sorrow was followed by a heavy and anxious concern for those whom the Lord had left us as survivors. I heard that the household had been scattered here and there. The danger to Malherbe distressed me greatly on his own account, and it also made me think of the rest. I thought it could not be that your wife was not greatly dismayed. But your Charles kept constantly before my eyes. For he is endowed with such goodness of character, and has always been devoted to his brother and his teacher not only with love but also with piety, that I had no doubt he was wholly in squalor and tears. Only one thought raised me up a little: that my brother was with him, and I hoped he would be a very great comfort to him in this calamity. But I could not even consider this without also remembering that both had not yet escaped danger. So, until other letters came announcing that Malherbe was out of danger of his life, and that Charles, my brother, your wife and the others were safe, I was almost crushed by grief and distress, except that before God, as I have said, I propped myself up, lest I collapse altogether, with prayers and holy meditations such as are suggested to us by his Word. I mention these things so that my exhortations, by which I now wish to console you, may not seem the less for that reason, as if you might think it easy to show courage in another's grief. I, however, do not here boast of courage in another's grief. But since by a singular blessing of God I have been granted to be freed or at least eased, in some part, from that sorrow which was almost shared between you and me, I pass on to you, as far as a letter and a short letter allow, the remedies I have used and which I have found most helpful to myself. Yet in this matter I must so weigh your sorrow that I remember I am dealing with a most grave and steadfast man. For it is not hidden from me with what defences you are equipped to keep patience and moderation always. Nor do I wish to apply even those consolations that are customary among ordinary people: not to mourn the dead, since you fathered a mortal; to show in this sad event the greatness of spirit that his talent and nature, distinguished and refined by the best arts, that his age, his wide experience of many things, and finally his reputation demand; to console yourself by recalling his past life. I set aside, I say, these and other exhortations of that kind with you. For there is one certain and firm kind of consolation, in which you and men like you ought to rest, which flows from that inner sense of piety of which I know you have an abundance. Therefore this above all you must do: call your mind back to those thoughts which the best teacher dictates to us in the school of piety, and which are handed down. There is no need to recount them here, since they are as familiar to you as to me. Yet, given your singular piety and the goodwill which I have not lacked, you will perhaps not unwillingly recognise in my letter what otherwise comes to your mind of its own accord. The Lord has taken back the son whom he had entrusted to you. Here are removed those vain and perverse complaints of foolish men: O blind death! O unjust fates! O inexorable Fates! O cruel fortune! The Lord, who had placed him in this station of life for a time, has called him away. Let us consider, when we hear what God has done, that it was done not rashly, not by chance, not by some outside impulse, but by that counsel by which he decides and does nothing except what is right and just, and nothing except what he provides for us as good and salutary. Where there is justice and equity, it is wrong to complain. But where our advantage also is joined to that equity, what ingratitude would it be not to receive calmly and temperately whatever has pleased our Father? Indeed, in God's very providence the faithful have ample relief, whatever befalls. For there is nothing that wears us down more than when we tire ourselves with these questions: why not otherwise, why in that place? These things would be said well and fittingly if something done by us deserved reproof. But where our fault is absent, there is no room for such complaints. It is God, therefore, who has taken back from you the son whom he had given you to bring up on the condition that he should always be his. And so he took him up, because it was useful both that he should depart from the world and that you should be humbled, or your patience be tested, by this bereavement. If you do not understand this usefulness, first you must ask God to show it to you. If he wishes to exercise you even more by concealing it, you must allow that he is wiser than the weakness of your mind can match. As for your son, if you consider in your mind how hard it is in this most lamentable age to keep the right course of life, you will judge him blessed who was released in good time, before the many dangers that were already threatening him as he grew older. For it is just as if someone, on a turbulent and stormy sea, before being carried to another place, quickly retreats into harbour. A long life is not so much a gift of God that we lose nothing when we are carried, after a few years, to a better life. And now, since God himself, who is the Father of us all, has taken the place of a father to Louis, he has granted you, in his immense kindness, to reap the splendid fruit of your upbringing before his death; so you should know that this blessing also belongs to you. Therefore, the God of you and of your wife. From earliest childhood he was trained in the best studies, as far as his years allowed. In these he had already made moderate progress, so that he gave us great hope of himself for the future. He had won approval from all good people for his morals and way of living. If he ever slipped, he not only tolerated being admonished and rebuked, but was also teachable and obedient to advice. He was indeed sometimes more vehement in temperament, but not to the point of stubbornness. So those impulses which went beyond due measure were easily checked. What we must value most is that he had so imbibed the rudiments of piety that he had both a true understanding of religion and was faithfully imbued with the fear of God. Truly, such a splendid kindness of God

units.la: centia in tuam sobolem merito plus valere debet ad leniedam mortis acerbitatem, quàm mors ipsa ad dolorem infligendum. Quantum ad me attinet, si nunquam huc se liberi tui contulis- sent, nullo nunc moerore ex Claudij, & Ludouici morte afflice- rer.Nunquam tamen efficiet grauissimus hic luctus,quem vtriuf que causa sustineo, vt me illius diei poeniteat, quo ad nos Dei manu appulsi, magis quam proprio consilio adducti, à me in a- micitiam recepti sunt, quæ non modò ad extremum perseuera- uit,sed aucta magis in dies fuit,ac confirmata. Quo igitur exem plo fuerunt,mecum vixisse gaudeo.Et quia moriedum illis fuit, apud me quoque mortuos esse gaudeo: vbi quietiores Deo ani- mas reddiderunt, quam si in his locis mori contigisset, vbi plus molestiæ ab eorum importunitate sensissent, à quibus iuuari o- portuisset, quàm ab ipsa morte. Nunc autem inter pias exhorta- tiones, in ipsa nominis Dei inuocatione sanctæ illæ animæ in Christi consortium euolarunt.Nec vellem iam omni vacare lu- ctu ea mercede,vt mihi fuissent incogniti.Eritenim mihi sancta vsque in finem eorum memoria: atque etiam vt confido,suauis. At quid prodest,inquies,filium optimæ speciextitisse,cùm in pri- mo ætatis flore correptus sit?Quasi verò nō hoc meritus sit Christus morte sua,vt viuis dominetur,& mortuis! Et si illius fumus, (vt esse nos oportet)cur non vitæ, & mortis habeat in nos arbi- trium?Qualibet ergo breui,opinione vel tua,vel mea,filius tuus vixerit, nobis satis esse debet, quòd cursum quem illi Dominus destinauerat,impleuit.Proinde ne putemus in flore periisse,qui coram Domino maturuerat. Dico autem ad maturitatem per- uenisse omnes,qui à Domino hinc euocantur:nisi forte cum eo litigare placet,quasi ante tempus aliquem rapiat.Hoc quidem de omnibus verum est: sed in Ludouico certior alia est, & magis propria ratio.Eò enim ætatis progressus erat, vt veris documen- tis sese Christi membrum approbare posset: hoc fructu edito,ex- tinctus est & nobis sublatus. Imò ex hac fluida, & euanidæ vitæ vmbra in veram immortalitatem receptus est. Neque te eum perdidisse exististimes, quem in beata resurrectione in regno Dei recuperabis. Sic enim vixerant, sic mortui sunt ambo, vt non dubitem apud Dominum esse:pergamus ergo ad hanc metam, quam attigerunt. Non dubium quin illos & nos simul indiuidua societate tunc colligaturus sit Christus, in illa incomparabili gloriæ suæ participatione. Caue igitur filium lugeas,vt perditum, quem agnoscis conseruari à Domino,vt perpetuo tuus manear, qui precario tantum fuerat tibi ad momentum temporis commodatus.Nec parum solatij ex eo accedet,si bene expedas, quid reliquum tibi sit. Habes superstite Carolum, de quo id iudicium habemus omnes, vt nemo sit nostrum qui non sibi talé filium
units.tr: ...the grace of God shown in your son ought rightly to count for more in softening the bitterness of death than death itself does in inflicting grief. As far as I am concerned, if your children had never come here, I would now feel no sorrow at the deaths of Claudius and Ludovicus. Yet this heavy grief, which I bear on behalf of both of them, will never make me regret the day when they were brought to us by God's hand, rather than by their own plan, and were received by me into friendship. That friendship has not only lasted to the end but has grown and been strengthened day by day. So I am glad they lived with me in whatever way they did. And since they had to die, I am glad they died among themselves too, where they gave up their souls more peacefully to God than they would have done had they died in those places where they would have felt more trouble from the unreasonableness of those from whom they ought to have had help than from death itself. Now, amid pious exhortations, in the very invocation of the name of God, those holy souls have flown into fellowship with Christ. I would not wish, even for that reward, to be free of all grief by having never known them. For their memory will remain holy to me until the end, and, as I trust, sweet as well. "But what good," you will say, "is it to have a son of the best character, when he is seized in the first flower of his age?" As if Christ did not merit by his death that he might be Lord over the living and the dead! And if we are his (as we ought to be), why should he not have the power of life and death over us? So, whatever the length of life your son had, whether it seemed brief to you or to me, it should be enough for us that he completed the course which the Lord had appointed for him. Therefore let us not think that he perished in his flower, when he had ripened before the Lord. I say that all who are called hence by the Lord reach maturity, unless perhaps one wishes to quarrel with him as if he snatched someone away before the time. This is indeed true of everyone, but in Ludovicus the reason is more certain and more particular. He had advanced to that age when he could show himself a member of Christ by true evidence; having produced this fruit, he was taken away and removed from us. Indeed, out of this fleeting and vanishing shadow of life he has been received into true immortality. Do not think you have lost him whom you will recover in the blessed resurrection in the kingdom of God. For both lived and both died in such a way that I do not doubt they are with the Lord. Let us then press on to the goal they have reached. There is no doubt that Christ will gather both them and us together at that time into an indivisible fellowship, in the incomparable participation of his glory. Take care, then, not to mourn your son as one lost, since you recognise that he is kept safe by the Lord, so that he may remain yours forever, when he was lent to you only for a moment of time. Nor will it bring little comfort, if you carefully consider what is left to you. You have Carolus surviving, of whom we all hold this judgement, that none of us would not wish such a son for himself.

units.la: cupiat. Ne putes hoc me dare tuis auribus: vel aliquid in tuam gratiam amplificare. Hoc nec mei ingenij, neque mei moris est. Simpliciter ergo dicam, quod reuera sentio, & quod apud extraneum quemlibet dicturus essem. Excellere adolescentem illum primo singulari pietate, ac vero Dei timore, qui est sapientiae nostrae summa: deinde humanitate ingenij, morum suauitate, rara modestia, & continentia. Neque hoc illi ex rumore vel auditu tribuo. Semper enim intentus fui, vt ipsius ingenium perspectum haberem. Hoc enim discriminis inter duos fratres, quum ambo viuerent, notaui. Ingenij celeritate praestabat Ludouicus, sed hic solida rerum intelligentia, & iudicio longe antecedebat. Promptior illeas proferendum quod legerat, vel audierat. Hic tardior, & verecundior. Paratior ille & expeditior, tum ad capessendas artes, tum ad omnes vitae actiones. Hic consideratior, & constantior: atque id etiam ferebat corporis constitutio. Siquidè Ludouicus, vt erat sanguineus, plus habebat hylaritatis, & alacritatis. Carolus qui in melancholia non nihil communicat, tanta facilitate se nō exerit. Modestiae & comitatis hic semper plus habuit, quae in eo etiam mirifice eluxit, q. potuit sua tolerantia fratris ferociam domare. Haec quoque in eo longe superiora: Moderatio, grauitas penè virilis, & in tota vita quaedam veluti aequabilitas. Talis ergo filius quantum valere debeat ad eleuandam orbitatis (qua te nunc Dominus afflixit) molestiam, tuipse iudicabis, & ita iudicabis, vtne in hac re fis Deo ingratus. At difficile est, inquies, patrium amorem, ita vel excutere, vel supprimere, vt nullum ex filij interitu dolore capiam. Ego vero id abste non contedo, ne doleas. Neq; enim hanc philosophiam didicimus in schola Christi, vt eam quam nobis Deus indidit, humanitatem exuendo ex hominibus lapides fiamus. Haec omnia eo duntaxat spectant, vt iustissimo tuo moerori modū & quasi temperamentum adhibeas. Vt persolutis quae naturae, & paternae pietati debentur lacrymis, tibi in lugendo minime indulgeas. Neq; tamen ideo me interpono, quo tuę prudentiae, constantiae, animique celsitudini diffidam. Sed tantum ne meum tibi officium hic deesse t. Quinquam si literae istę superuacuae erunt (q. mihi credibile est) pro tua tamē eximia humanitate boni consulēs, hanc meam felicitudine nimis fortasse anxiam: sed ideo venia non indignam, q. ab immodico meo erga te amore proficiscitur. Quinetiam Philippum, & Bucerum rogaui, vt meis literis suas quoque adiungerent: quia hoc tibi non ingratum f. re officium spectabam, si beneuolentię erga te suae testimonium aliquod tibi redderent. Vale clarissime vir, & mihi plurimum in Domino obseruande. Christus Dominus te, familiāmq; tuam conseruet, ac spiritu suo semper vos omnes dirigat, donec perueniatis quo Ludouicus, & Claudius praecesserunt.
units.tr: Do not think I say this to flatter your ears, or to magnify anything in order to win your favour. This is neither my nature nor my habit. I shall therefore speak simply, saying what I truly think, and what I would say to any stranger. That young man excelled first in singular piety and true fear of God, which is the highest point of our wisdom; then in gentleness of disposition, sweetness of manners, rare modesty and self-restraint. Nor do I attribute this to him from hearsay or report. For I was always intent on knowing his character well. I noted this difference between the two brothers while both were alive. Ludovicus excelled in quickness of mind, but this one far surpassed him in sound understanding of things and in judgement. The former was readier to bring forward what he had read or heard; this one was slower and more diffident. The former was more prompt and skilful both in taking up the arts and in all the actions of life; this one was more thoughtful and steadfast, and his bodily constitution also tended that way. For Ludovicus, being sanguine by temperament, had more cheerfulness and liveliness, while Carolus, who has some share in melancholy, does not show himself with such ease. In modesty and courtesy he always had more, and this shone forth in him wonderfully, since by his patience he was able to tame his brother's fierceness. In him these other qualities were also far superior: moderation, a seriousness almost manly, and a certain even temper throughout his whole life. How much such a son ought to count for in easing the distress of bereavement (which the Lord has now laid upon you), you will judge yourself, and you will judge so that you may not be ungrateful to God in this matter. But, you will say, it is difficult to shake off or suppress a father's love so completely that I feel no pain from the death of a son. I do not in fact ask you to do that, nor to grieve less. For we have not learned this philosophy in the school of Christ, that by putting off the humanity God has implanted in us we should turn from men into stones. All these things aim only at this: that you should apply a measure, as it were a restraint, to your most just sorrow; so that, having paid the tears owed to nature and paternal affection, you should not indulge yourself at all in mourning. Nor do I interpose this in order to distrust your prudence, steadfastness and loftiness of mind; only that I may not seem to fail in my duty here. Still, if this letter is superfluous (as I think it probably is), please take it kindly in view of your remarkable humanity, and pardon my perhaps too anxious good wishes, which are not unworthy of pardon since they arise from my immoderate love for you. Indeed, I have asked Philip and Bucer to add their own letters to mine, because I thought this would not be unwelcome to you, if they gave you some testimony of their goodwill towards you. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and one to be greatly honoured by me in the Lord. May Christ the Lord keep you and your household, and always direct you all by his Spirit, until you come to where Ludovicus and Claudius have gone before.

units.la: Gratia tibi & Pax à Domino qui tibi ac nobis saluum consilium & rectam voluntatem inspiret.
units.tr: Grace to you and peace from the Lord, who may inspire you with sound counsel and a right will, both for your salvation and ours.

units.la: MAllem huc te ad nos contulisses, de reconciliatione coràm nobiscum acturus quàm literis id expertus esses, præsertim quales tuę sunt. Vehementer ideo laboras ne videaris absq; iusta causa in Ecclesia turbas excitare: quasi villa turbandæ Ecclesiæ honesta causa obtendi possit. Demus non habitam fuisse tui rationem à fratribus quam oportuerat: an ideo tamen protinus itacumultuari fas fuit? Dicésne fuisse Spiritum Dei qui te impulerit ad denunciandum omnibus certamen? Neque hæc di co exprobrandi causa: vtinam passus fuisses me prorsus tacere. Verùm dum omnes eos qui tua saltem opinione nô satis æquos tibi se præbuerunt cum Satana coniungis, nimis certè stupidos arbitraris, si posse hoc silentio transmittere exiistimas. Dicis te indignatione fuisse percitum, vt Farellum & me traduceres, quoniam literis nostris effeceramus ne tibi fratres Neocomésés locum darent. Primùm id vel abs te confictum est, vel falsò ad te delatum: nihil enim vnquam mihi in mentem venit tale scribere Neocomensibus. In literis Farelli quantū audio (nihil enim habeo præter auditum) longè durius tractatus fuerat Michaël quàm tu. Cùm ergo neque verbo neque facto vnquam te læsisse m, imò cùm ne minima vnquam offensiuncula te pupugisset, cuius humanitatis fuit, me vsqueadeo atrociter lacerare? Quòd si qua in re priuato tuo commodo obstitisset, quàm alienata men homine Christiano illa ratio fuit, vt vindictæ cupiditate inflammatus in illud turbulentum consilium prorumperes? Cùm tibi semper antehac sine dubitatione fuisset frater, qui fieri potuit vt momento vno fierem hæreticus, à cuius communione abhorreres? Scilicet hoc non est sacrosancto Dei nomine abuti. Negas aliud tibi superfuisse, nisi vt nos irreconciliabiles proclamares (hoc enim est tuum verbum) sed paulisper quæso recum reputa, quàm te ridiculum facias, quem constat in media pace claficum cecinisse. Verùm fac tibi datam à nobis aliquâ occasionem: quid tamen sibi vult verbum illud quo veteris? Certè irreconciliabilis dicitur is quem cùm modis omnibus placare studueris, non potueris tamen ad vllam partem æquitatis inflectere. Quādo tam præstrictam ac pertinacè duritiem in nobis vnquā expertus es? De me quod conqueraris non habes: ego verò iustissimam rationem habeo, cur tecum expostulem, vt nihil dicam grauius. Neque tamen de vltione cogitaui: tantum abest vt facinus vllū hostile in te designauerim. De Farello velim scire, quam iniuriam tibi fecerit. Scripsit ne admitterentur ad minis- terium, qui Ecclesias sibi commissas deseruissent: an non debuit? Neque enim minor est perfidia si quis Ecclesiam reliquat, quam semel suscepérat in suam fidem, quàm si pater filios suos abiiciat. At te comprehendebat in eo numero, cùm tamen ab ea culpa esses alienus: si literas legeris, aliud comperies. Nihil enim postulabat a fratribus, quàm ut diligenter inquirerent: si cognitio tuæ causæ te purgabat, nonne idipsum optare debuisti? Metuim venisti deinde: quanta intemperies fuit apud Christi aduersarios iactare, te venisse instructum ut nos haereticos convincere? Et tamen retines interea illam gloriam quod nihil contra Euangelium moliaris. Sed quo exemplo hoc nobis probabis? Si quis ex professo bellum cum feruo Christi gerat, eúmque impediat quibus possit modis, quo minus Christi regnum promoueat, mirum si talem hominem dicas ab Euangelij partibus stare. Videte iterum frater atque iterum quò progrediare. Ministerium habemus à Christo minimè dissiundum: si dubi as habemus satis certum & fidele conscientiæ testimonium. Blandiaris tibi ut voles, senties demum in impetendo contra stimulum te calcitrare. Interea quid nobis nocere potes? Haereticos vocabis. vbi? Nempe inter eos qui te pro haeretico habebunt, etiamsi tua maledicentia ad tempus abutantur. Apud pios & doctos minimè vereor, ne quid mihi obtrectando proficias. Haec omnia in eam partem spectant ac ita accipi abs te volo, vt coram Deo recognoscas, quam viam sis ingressus: neque alios damnando immeritos, defensionem mediteris, quae non modo omni fundamento, sed etiam praetextu careat. Hoc si fuero consequutus, satis mihi est. Nolo tamen te propterea animum spemque abiicere. Nam si no bis vera & solida recti animi indicia ostenderis, parati sumus tecum mox in gratia optima fide redire, omnia obliuisci, ignoscere, & prorsus ex memoria delere. Vtinam pectus meum intueri posses, nihil enim magis cupio quàm Deo te reconciliare primum, vt inter nos fiat firma coniunctio. Sed crede mihi nunquam viliter Domino seruies, nisi istud supercilium de pofuceris, & linguae amarulentiam. Ergo si in gratiam nobis cum redire animus est: parati sumus ad te amplexandum, neque deerimus vllis officiis, quoad dabitur facultas. Verum in illam quam à nobis exigis pactionem, qui possimus descendere? vt tibi scilicet Ecclesiam iam despondeamus? Primum Ecclesiæ non sunt nobis ad manum sicut nosti, deinde qua conscientia id tibi pol liceremur, antequam de consensione doctrinæ constet? Non dissimulas te à nobis adhuc diffidere: & tamen vis locum tibi destinari ad docendum. Tu ipse perpende quantopere istud deceat. Nos vero plusquam stipites merito iudicares, si tibi obsequeremur. mur. Vt finem aliquando faciam,peto abs te,vt animo compo-sito ac sedato tecum disquisitas totam causam,vt has etiam literas non alia trutina,quàm iudicij ab iracundia penitus vacui,examines. Agnoscere certè nihil esse melius, quàm cursum male inchoatum reflectere. Si voles nos experiri,nullum amicitiæ officium tibi à me defuturum recipio:hoc etiam Farellus scrib pro fe promisit.Sed memineris eius charitatis, quam tanta seueritate ab aliis exigis,partem aliquam ergo alios exhibere.Si tibi pau lò asperior visus sum, quid literæ tuæ mereantur cogita: quanquam id quidem nequaquam respexi,sed tantum vt tibi prodesse:quod facturus mihi non videbar,nisi ad peccati tui recognitionem te adducerem. Vale frater mihi in Domino charissime: si modo diligi te, & fratris loco haberi pateris. Dominus Christus te Spiritu consilij & prudentiæ gubernet, vt ex istis periculosis scopulis, ad quos impegisti, & tempestuosa iactatione, in portum tecito recipias. Argentorati. x. Augusti. M.D. XL. Ioannes Caluinus ex animo tibi amicus. Farellus saluere te iubet,oratque vt scribo ad Dominum conuertaris,& tam sis paratus in amicitiam & fraternam coniunctionem nobiscum redire,quàm ipse te amplecti paratus est.
units.tr: I wish you had come to us here to seek reconciliation face to face, rather than trying it by letter, and especially by letters such as yours. You take great pains not to seem to be stirring up trouble in the Church without just cause, as if any honourable reason could be offered for disturbing the Church. Grant that the brethren did not show you the consideration they should have: was it therefore right to rush straight into an uproar? Will you say that it was the Spirit of God who drove you to declare war on everyone? I do not say this to reproach you; I wish you had allowed me to say nothing at all. But since you join with Satan all those who, at least in your opinion, have not dealt fairly with you, you must think them very stupid if you suppose they will let this pass in silence. You say you were so stung with indignation that you wanted to traduce Farel and me, because by our letters we had brought it about that the brethren of Neuchâtel would not give you a place. In the first place, this is either invented by you or was falsely reported to you: for it never once entered my mind to write anything of the kind to the people of Neuchâtel. In Farel's letters (for I have nothing but hearsay, as far as I hear) Michael was handled far more harshly than you. Since, then, I have never injured you either by word or deed, and since you were never even slightly offended by me, what sort of humanity is it to tear me to pieces so savagely? And if in some matter I had stood in the way of your private advantage, how far estranged from Christian feeling must you have been to break out into that turbulent plan, inflamed by a desire for revenge? Since hitherto you have always, without any doubt, been regarded as a brother, how could it happen that in a single moment I became a heretic, whose fellowship you shrink from? Clearly this is not to abuse the sacred name of God. You deny that anything was left for you but to proclaim us irreconcilable (for that is your word), but I beg you to pause a little and consider how ridiculous you make yourself, since it is well known that you sang the trumpet call in the midst of peace. But suppose we have given you some occasion: what then does that word you use mean? Surely a person is called irreconcilable when, although you have tried by every means to placate him, you have not been able to bend him to any measure of fairness. When have you ever found us so stubborn and obstinate? You have no complaint against me; I, on the other hand, have the most just reason to expostulate with you, not to say anything more severe. Yet I have not thought of revenge; so far am I from having planned any hostile act against you. I would like to know what injury Farel has done you. Did he write that those who had deserted the churches committed to them should not be admitted to the ministry? Ought he not to have done so? For there is no less treachery in a man who leaves a Church he once took under his care than in a father who casts off his sons. Yet you included yourself in that number, although you were free of that fault; if you read the letter you will find otherwise. For it asked nothing of the brethren except that they inquire carefully; if the investigation of your case cleared you, ought you not to have wished for this very thing? Then you came to us, and what a lack of restraint it was to boast among Christ's adversaries that you had come equipped to convict us of heresy! And yet in the meantime you keep the glory of having attempted nothing against the Gospel. But by what example will you prove this to us? If someone wages open war against a servant of Christ and hinders him by whatever means he can from advancing the kingdom of Christ, it would be strange if you called such a man one who stands on the side of the Gospel. Brother, look again and again to where you are heading. We have a ministry received from Christ, which must not be cast aside; and if we have any doubt, we have a sufficiently certain and faithful testimony of conscience. Flatter yourself as you will, you will at last feel that in attacking us you are kicking against the goad. Meanwhile, what harm can you do us? You will call us heretics. Where? Surely among those who will regard you as a heretic yourself, even if for a time they abuse your slander. Among the godly and learned I have no fear that you will gain anything by detracting from me. All these things I intend in this sense, and I want you to take them so, that before God you may recognise what path you have entered upon, and that you may not contrive a defence, by condemning others undeservedly, which lacks not only all foundation but even a pretext. If I succeed in this, it is enough for me. Yet I do not want you therefore to abandon your spirit and hope. For if you show us true and solid signs of an upright mind, we are ready soon to return with you into the best of grace and sincere faith, to forget everything, to forgive, and to blot it wholly from memory. I wish you could see my heart, for I desire nothing more than that you be first reconciled to God, so that a firm union may come about between us. But believe me, you will never serve the Lord rightly unless you lay aside that haughty pride and the bitterness of your tongue. Therefore, if you have a mind to return to favour with us, we are ready to embrace you, and we will not be wanting in any kindness, as far as opportunity allows. But to what agreement that you demand from us can we agree? Namely, that we should now betroth the Church to you? In the first place, the churches are not, as you know, within our reach; and secondly, with what conscience could we promise this to you before agreement in doctrine is established? You do not conceal that you still distrust us; and yet you want a place assigned to you for teaching. Consider for yourself how greatly this would be unbecoming. We, indeed, would deservedly be judged blockheads beyond all others if we gave in to you. To bring this to an end at last, I ask you to examine the whole matter with a calm and settled mind, and to weigh this letter too, by no other scale than that of judgement entirely free from anger. Surely you must acknowledge that nothing is better than to turn back a course badly begun. If you wish to test us, I promise you that no office of friendship will be lacking on my part; Farel also wrote that he promised this on his own behalf. But remember that you must show some part of that charity which you demand from others with such severity. If I have seemed to you a little too harsh, consider what your letter deserves; yet I have not looked to this at all, but only to what would help you, which I would not have seemed to do unless I led you to recognise your sin. Farewell, brother, most dear to me in the Lord, if indeed you allow yourself to be loved and regarded as a brother.
