May the Lord Christ guide you with the Spirit of counsel and prudence, so that out of those dangerous rocks on which you have run, and out of this stormy tossing, you may be brought at last into harbour. From Strasbourg, 10 August 1540. John Calvin, your friend from the heart. Farel bids you farewell and prays, as I am writing, that you may be turned to the Lord, and that you may be as ready to return to friendship and brotherly union with us as he himself is ready to embrace you.

units.la: GRYNAEVS CALVINO S.
units.tr: Grynaeus to Calvin, greeting

units.la: IVuenis hic apud nos dies aliquot fuit. Discere istic Religionem cupit.Est Nycçus:videtur esse simplex.Si qua istic est tibi hunc iuuandi spes,oro vt des operam. Diu non scripsi ad te: oro vt ne interpretetur secus, quàm est factum. Nam in istis occupationibus vestris nolebam cuiquam esse molestus.Spero amicitiam nostram esse in Christo Iesu indissolubilem.Vale,pridie Augusti. M. D. XL. Saluta omnes amicos.Subito hæc scripsi.
units.tr: This young man was with us here for some days. He wishes to learn religion there. He is Nycçus; he seems to be simple. If you have any hope there of helping him, I beg you to take the trouble. I have not written to you for a long time; I beg you not to read this as anything other than what it is. In your busy work I did not want to be a nuisance to anyone. I hope our friendship is indissoluble in Christ Jesus. Farewell, the day before 1 August 1540. Greet all friends. I wrote this in haste.

units.la: Simon Grynæus tuus.
units.tr: Simon Grynaeus, yours.

units.la: GRYNAEVS CALVINO S.
units.tr: Grynaeus to Calvin, greeting

units.la: ROgauit me N.vt se apud te excusarem diligenter. Hoc promittit de se mihi,& ego tibi de ipso,se de tuo scripto sentire vt par est.Nos enim te fratrem in Domino libenter ac cum gaudio agnoscimus,ac pro eximio ornamento Ecclesiæ non stræ amplectimur.Itaque noli hic tibi molestus esse amplius mi frater. De Lutheri super nostra confessione responso benignissimo credo te audiuisse. Spes est optima nobis cum recte procedurum. Vos istic in Domino Christo optimè valete.Saluta venerandum mihi Farellum. x 11.Februarij.
units.tr: N. asked me to make his excuses to you carefully. He promises this on his own behalf to me, and I promise you on his behalf that he feels about your writing as he ought. For we gladly and joyfully acknowledge you as a brother in the Lord, and we embrace you as an outstanding ornament of our Church. So do not trouble yourself any further here, my brother. I believe you have heard of Luther's very kind response to our confession. There is excellent hope for us that we shall proceed rightly. Farewell in the Lord Christ there. Greet my venerable Farel. 11 February.

units.la: Simon Grynæus tuus.
units.tr: Simon Grynaeus, yours.

units.la: NON dubito quin fratribus quicunque me ad redditum per literas hortati sunt, diligenter excusatis, quod nihil eis responderim. Nosti enim me eo biduo tanta animi perplexitate aestuasse, ut vix dimidia ex parte apud me esset. Postea tamen ut tibi morem gererem, aliquid ad eos in communi scripturam conatus sum: sed postea cum cogitarem quid euenire soleat communibus istis literis, mutaui consilium. Nam quod ad paucos missum est, volitat statim per multorum manus, donec passim fuerit euulgatum. Haec igitur mihi ratio fuit, ut tibi vni scriberem: ne alios adhibeas lectores quam a quibus videbis nihil esse periculi. Cur autem nolim latius dissipari, quod in finem tuum depono, intelliges vbi ad finem peruenetis. Tametsi animi mei sensum penitus tenere te confido, & aliis etiam bona fide exposuisse, breuiter tamen hic repetam qualiter hodieque sim affectus. Quoties memoria repeto, quam misere illic habuerim, fieri non potest quin toto pectore exhorrescam, vbi agitur de me reuocando. Illam inquietudinem omitto, qua sursum deorsum iactati perpetuo fuimus, ex quo tibi adiunctus sum collega: scio enim quocunque concedam mihi infinitas molestias esse propositas: si velim Christo viuere, hunc mundum mihi semper fore turbulentum: vitam praesentem certamini esse destinatam. Seddum cogito quibus tormentis excruciata tum fuerit mea conscientia, & quibus curis aestuarit, ignosce si locum illum velut mihi fatalem, reformido. Tu ipse mihi vna cum Deo optimus es testis, non alio vinculo me illic tandem retentum, nisi quod iugum vocationis, quod mihi a Domino impositum esse noueram, non audebam excutere. Tandiu igitur sic eram alligatus, malui extrema quaeuis perferre, quam in mentem recipere cogitationes mutandi loci, quae saepe alioqui mihi obrepebant. Iam vero vbi Dei beneficio semel sum liberatus, si in gurgitem quem mihi exitialem esse sum expertus, non ob libenter me immergo, quis mihi non veniam concedat? Imo vero quotusquisque erit, qui non me arguat nimiae facilitatis, si scies ac volens me praecipitem dedero? Quid autem quod etiam si nullo meo periculo absterrear, ministerium tamen meum illis vtile fore vix confido? Nam quo ingenio praediti sunt illic plerique? neq; ipsi mihi tolerabiles erunt, nec ego ipsis. Adde quod mihi maius ac difficilius certamen erit cum collegis quam cum extraneis. Quid vnius hominis opera poterit, tot vndique impedimentis fracta? atque vt verum fatear etiamsi omnia valde expedita mihi forent: nescio qua tamen desuetudine oblitus sum artes regendae multitudinis. Mihi hic cum paucis negotium est & quorum pars maior me non tantum vt pastorem audit, sed vt praeceptorem obseruat. Dices me nimis esse delicatum, qui his blanditiis delibutus nullam aspeciorem vocem nunc audire sustineam. Falleris vero si haec putas, sed cum paucis atque his nonnihil obsequentibus, bene praesse mihi arduum sentiam: ad tantum multitudinem continendam qui sufficerem? Quo autem consilio me revocent, vix audeo apud me aestimare: nam si syncero animo ducuntur, cur me potius quam eum cuius minisferium non minus necessarium ad instaurandam ipsorum Ecclesiam esset, quam principio ad eam fundandam fuit? Quid si me ideo vocant ne illis sint ludibrio, quod sint ab iis destituti, quorum subsidio freti nos ablegare ausi fuerant? Neque tamen ista omnia efficiunt, ne vocationi obtemperem. Nam quo magis ab illa provincia animus meus abhorret, eo magis mihi sum suspectus. Itaque nec mihi debere deliberare permitto, & a nostris peto ne me in consultationem adhibeant: ac quo liberius syncerius statuant, magna ex parte istos cordis mei astus dissimulo. Quid facerem? Malo enim protfus executire: vt me ab aliis regi patiar, quam lippitudini meae temere fidendo aberrare. Porro si te interrogem, quorum maxime arbitrio permittere me debeam: respondebis, nisi fallor, non alios esse ad consulendum mihi magis idoneos, quam Capitonem & Bucerum. Quid autem illi sentiant audisti ex ipsorum ore. Vtinam diligenter fratribus exponas: ac illi nullo praeiudicio occupati, serio expendant. Summa haec fit. Nihil hic astute me agere coram Domino testor, nec rimas scrutari quibus effugiam. Siquidem vt Geneuensi Ecclesiae prosperum cupio, ita malim vitam centies exponere, quam eam deserendo prodere. Sed quoniam ad reditum animus non sponte inclinat, paratus sum eos sequi, quos mihi fidos ac tutos duces fore bona spes est. Caeterum non est quod ante finem conuentus Vvormacienfis laborent de me recipiendo: quando legatum nondum miserunt. Die Dominico habebitur hic publica supplicatio per omnia templa: Lunae soluemus. Vos etiam sanctis precibus nos ad hoc certamen sustinendum adiuuate. Quid moliantur aduersarij nostri palam est. Nempe, vt omnes Imperij ordines in nostram perniciem armient. Quibus autem aribus nos adoriri instituerint incertum est. Quicquid tamen habent calliditatis in hac postrema explicabunt. Vale. Saluta omnes amicissime, Corderium, Thomam, Fatruum, Clericum & reliquos. Omnes nostri tibi & illis bene precantur. Argentorati, x xi. Octobr. M. D. X L.
units.tr: I do not doubt that the brothers who urged me by letter to return have been carefully excused for my not replying to them. You know that in those two days I was so tossed by mental turmoil that barely half of me was at my own disposal. Afterwards, however, to oblige you, I tried to write something to them jointly; but then, considering what usually happens to such common letters, I changed my plan. For what is sent to a few immediately flies through the hands of many until it is published everywhere. My reason, therefore, was to write to you alone, so that you do not bring in readers other than those whom you see to be free of danger. Why I would not want this to be scattered more widely, you will understand when you reach the end of what I am entrusting to you. Although I trust you fully grasp my feelings and have also explained them in good faith to others, I will briefly repeat here how I am still disposed today. Whenever I recall how wretchedly I was treated there, I cannot help shuddering to the depths of my heart when the question of my recall comes up. I pass over that restlessness by which we were constantly tossed up and down, ever since I was joined to you as colleague: for I know that wherever I yield, endless troubles are laid out before me; if I want to live for Christ, this world will always be turbulent for me; the present life is destined for struggle. But when I think by what torments my conscience was then racked, and with what cares it seethed, forgive me if I shrink from that place as if it were fatal to me. You yourself, with God, are my best witness that I was finally held there by no other bond than that I did not dare to shake off the yoke of the calling which I knew the Lord had laid upon me. So I was bound for so long that I preferred to endure any extremity rather than admit thoughts of changing place, which otherwise often crept upon me. Now, however, since by God's kindness I have once been freed, if I do not gladly plunge back into the whirlpool which I have found deadly to me, who would not forgive me? Indeed, how few will there be who would not accuse me of excessive ease if I knowingly and willingly threw myself headlong into it? Moreover, even if I were not frightened off by any danger to myself, I scarcely trust that my ministry would be useful to them. For many there are endowed with such talents that they will be intolerable to me, and I to them. Add that my struggle with my colleagues will be greater and harder than with outsiders. What can the work of one man accomplish, broken as it is by so many hindrances on every side? And to tell the truth, even if everything were very easy for me, I have forgotten, through I know not what lack of practice, the arts of governing a crowd. I have to do here with a few people, most of whom listen to me not merely as a minister but observe me as a teacher. You will say I am too delicate, having been steeped in such flattery, that I cannot now bear to hear any harsher voice. But you are wrong to think so; I find it hard to govern well even these few, and they are somewhat compliant; who would be sufficient to restrain such a multitude? As for the purpose for which they recall me, I can hardly bring myself to judge: for if they are led by sincere hearts, why call me rather than him whose ministry was no less necessary for restoring their Church than it was at the start for founding it? What if they call me only so that they will not be a laughing-stock, since they have been abandoned by those on whose help they relied when they dared to send us away? Yet all these considerations do not prevent me from obeying the call. For the more my mind shrinks from that province, the more I am suspicious of myself. So I neither allow myself to deliberate, and I ask our people not to bring me into the discussion; and so that they may decide more freely and sincerely, I largely conceal from them the turmoil of my heart. What should I do? For I prefer to be completely guided by others than to go astray by rashly trusting my own weak sight. Moreover, if I were to ask you whose judgment above all I should submit to, you will reply, unless I am mistaken, that there are no others more suitable to advise me than Capito and Bucer. You have heard what they think from their own lips. I wish you would explain it carefully to the brothers, and that they, free from any prejudice, would weigh it seriously. This is the sum. I call the Lord to witness that I am not here acting craftily, nor searching for loopholes by which to escape. For as I desire prosperity for the Church of Geneva, I would rather risk my life a hundred times than betray it by deserting it. But since my mind does not spontaneously incline to return, I am ready to follow those whom I have good hope will be faithful and safe guides for me. Otherwise, there is no reason for them to trouble over receiving me before the end of the Worms assembly, since they have not yet sent the envoy. On Sunday there will be a public supplication in all the churches here; on Monday we shall pay the dues. You too help us with holy prayers to sustain this struggle. What our adversaries are plotting is plain: namely, to arm all the orders of the Empire against us to our ruin. By what ears they intend to attack us is uncertain. Whatever cunning they have, they will reveal in this last affair. Farewell. Greet most warmly all of them, Corderius, Thomas, Fatruus, Clericus, and the rest. All our people wish you well, and they too. Strasbourg, 21 October 1540.

units.la: d.ij.
units.tr: d.ij.

units.la: QVod ad te hucusque non scripserim, praecipuè per Ludovicum du Four legatum Geneuensem, ne putes propterea factum venerande ac obseruande pater, quod aut dedigna tus sim, aut tua redintegratio mihi displiceret. Hanc idcirco nūc ad te dedi, vt certò scires primum metum non adfuisse Geneuæ: petieram enim Laufannam, consulturus D. Petrum Viretum su per nonnullis quæ ad Ecclesiæ nostræ statum pertinebant, ac praeterea quàm bono erga te sim ac Christiano animo & quātum mihi placeat quod videam te denuò à nostris agnosci bonum Pastorem ac fidelem: potissimum quòd hoc sciam via Spiritus sancti actum. Siquidem vna dierum Dominica quum haberem concionem apud Rippam, & viderem Ecclesiam nostræ desolatam (abierant enim qui curam ipsius suscepperant, Morentus videlicet & Marcutius: remanserat vero solus Henricus mecum. Sed qui sumus pro tanto populo soli regendo) continere me non potui quin populum in lacrymas effusum videns admonerem, vt conuersus ad Dominum Deum humili oratione per Christum Pastorum Pastorem ab eo imploraret Pastor m, & quidem talem qualem agnoscerent suæ profuturum Ecclesiæ. Et ne mentiar, tui non recordabar, nec te illum sperabam fore. Fecit hoc populus maxima vt dicitur cum deuotione. In crastinum verò Ducentorum congregatur consilium, & omnes petunt Caluinum: congregatur & generale sequenti die, itidem clamant omnes, Caluinum probum & doctum virum Christi ministrum volumus. Quod cum intellexissem non potui non laudare Deum aliterque iudicare quàm quod à Domino esset factum istud. & esset mirabile in oculis nostris: quóòq; lapidem quem reprobarant ædificantes in caput fieret anguli. Veni ergo venerande mi pater in Christo nostrum profectò. Te enim nobis donauit (vt audis) Dominus Deus. Suspirant etiam post te omnes, videbis quàm gratus fuerit aduentus tuus omnibus quòd benignè recipieris. Cognosces me insuper non qualem hactenus relationem quorundam, putasti (parcat illis Dominus) sed pium, syncerum ac fidelem fratrem ac amicum tuum. quid dicam in omnibus tuis votis obsequentissimum ac deditissimum. Ne ergo tarderis venire vt videas Geneuam, hoc est gentem nouam renouatam sanè opera, gratia Dei, D. Viretì. Faxit Dominus Iesus vt velox aduentus tuus sit ad nos. Vale, Ecclesiæque nostræ digneris succurrere. Alioqui requiret de manu tua sanguinem nostrum Dominus Deus, dedit enim te speculatorem domui Israel quæ apud nos est. Iterum vale. Salutabis nomine meo fi placeat, obsequentes illos Patres meos ac Dominos, D. Bucerum ac D.Capitonem, caeterosque Ecclesiae illius ministros.V i Ebr. anni M. D. XLI.
units.tr: That I have not written to you until now, especially through Ludovicus du Four, the Genevan envoy, do not think it was done, venerable and respected father, because I disdained you or because your reconciliation displeased me. I have sent this now so that you may know for certain that there was no fear at Geneva. For I had gone to Lausanne, intending to consult Master Peter Viret about several matters pertaining to the state of our Church. Besides, I want you to know how good and Christian my feeling towards you is, and how much it pleases me to see you acknowledged again by our people as a good and faithful minister; especially because I know this was done by the way of the Holy Spirit. For on a Sunday when I was preaching at Rippa, and saw our Church forsaken (for those who had taken up its care had gone away, namely Morentus and Marcutius, and only Henricus remained with me; but we are only two to rule so great a people), I could not help admonishing the people, who were dissolved in tears, that, turning to the Lord God, they should implore him with humble prayer, through Christ the Shepherd of shepherds, for a minister, and indeed one such as they would recognise would be useful to their Church. And, not to lie, I was not thinking of you, nor did I hope you would be he. The people did this, as is said, with the greatest devotion. On the next day the Council of Two Hundred gathered, and all asked for Calvin; a general assembly was gathered the following day, and likewise all cried out: we want Calvin, an upright and learned man, minister of Christ. When I heard this I could not help praising God, and judging that this had been done by the Lord, and that it is marvellous in our eyes, and that the stone which the builders had rejected has become the head of the corner. Come, therefore, my venerable father in Christ, to us indeed. For the Lord God has given you to us, as you hear. All long for you; you will see how welcome your arrival will be to everyone, since you will be received kindly. You will also find me, not the man some reports have described to you (may the Lord forgive those who made them), but your pious, sincere and faithful brother and friend, and, what shall I say, most compliant and devoted to all your wishes. So do not delay in coming to see Geneva, that is, a people renewed indeed by the work, by the grace of God, of Master Viret. May the Lord Jesus grant that your coming to us be swift. Farewell, and deign to help our Church. Otherwise the Lord God will require our blood at your hand, for he has set you as a watchman over the house of Israel that is among us. Farewell again. Greet, if it please you, in my name, those obliging fathers and masters of mine, Master Bucer and Master Capito, and the other ministers of that Church. 6 February 1541.

units.la: Tuus Iacobus Bernardus Minister Euangelicus Genevae.
units.tr: Yours, James Bernard, Evangelical Minister at Geneva.

units.la: CAL. VIRETO.
units.tr: Calvin to Viret.

units.la: CVM mihi literae tuae redderentur, iam eramus ad iter accinc̄ti, & non memini profectionem fuisse mihi in vita magis tumultuosam: itaq; cum non poslem ipse respondere, Claudio Ferrex, quem mecum vidisti Basileae, & fratri meo mandavi, vt Farello referiberent quid haberem animi. Nunc aliquantulum ocij nactus, scribere etiam tibi ex medio itineris cursu volui: excusabis autem quod confuse tibi & breviter respondeo, neque epistolam tuam habeo ad manum, vt singula capita possim ordine perspicere, & excutere, nec tantum temporis datur viatori in caupona, vt aliquid bene meditatum, & quasi conceptum liceat mandare literis: quantum autem memoria teneo, duae sunt praecipuae literarum tuarum partes. Priore ostendis mihi non esse deferendam Ecclesiam Genevensem, altera contendis maturandum quoque esse reditum, ne quid impedimenti, si longius, differamus Satan obiiciat. Ad illam non aliter respondeo quam quod semper solitus sum, Nullum esse locum sub coelo quem magis reformidem, non quia oderim, sed quoniam tot difficultates illic mihi propositas video, quibus superandis sentio me longe esse imparem. Quoties superiorum temporum subit recordatio, facere nequeo quin toto pectore exhorrescam, si cogar me iterum antiquis illis certaminibus obiicere. Si mihi cum Ecclesia illa tantum esset negocium, animo esset quietiore, certe minus terrerer: sed necesse est te multo plus intelligere quam dicam. Hoc habe uno verbo, dum multis signis intelligo, cuius qui plurimum nocere potest, inexpiabile in me odium manere, dum repeto quot circum circa pateant illi aditus ad malefaciendum, quot flabella semper inflata sint ad excitandos contentionum ignes, quot occasiones quae tunc a me prouideri minime possunt sese daturae sint, prorsus mirum exanimor. Sunt & plurima alia in ipsa urbe, quae mihi non parum solicitudinis iniiciunt. Quo plus progredior eo melius cerno quam arduum sit munus Ecclesiasticum gerere. Nequetamen haec omnia efficiunt, quin ad opem miserae Ecclesiae ferendam sim paratissimus si quid me valere intellexero. Quaecunque enim me hac in re turbant cogitationes, tamen etsi nonnihil afferunt remorae dum animum meum anxium tenet, mihi tamen excutere hoc nequeunt, quin facturus sim omnia, quae in eius salutem factura putauero. Testis d.iij. est Farellus me nunquam vno verbo detrectasse illam vocationem, sed deprecatum esse duntaxat ne male consulendo Ecclesiam semel perditam bis perderet. Interim satis ostendi, nihil mihi magis esse in votis quàm vel animam meam impendere vbi opus esset. Possem tibi coram luculentis argumentis planum facere quàm nihil hic simulauerim, sed hoc mihi certissimum videtur, quòd cum venissent legati Vvormaciam, nostros multis cum lachrymis per omnia sacra sum obtestatus, vt mei oblitì dispicerent, coram Deo, quid Ecclesiae fidem eorum implorantì, maximè esset salutare: vbi domum ventum est, quanuis nemo insisteret, non cessaui interpellare vt eam curam ferio susciperent, nec ipsi etiam, crede mihi, officio suo defuerunt: sed, quod suspicabamur, fere paulo post decretum est, vt Bucero adiungerer. hoc non videti mihi factum composito, vt antea Farello fciipsi, ita nunc tibi sanctè asseuero. Ita enim propemodū constitutum prius fuerat quàm Vvormacia rediremus, idque eorum consilio qui de Geneua minimè cogitabant. Equidem si me interroges non video causam cur mittar, verum vt minimè sim idoneus, non tamen fuit meum recusare. Necessario igitur veniendum erat nisi vellem passim audire pessimè. Proinde dum literae tuae venerunt, cum non esset integrum iam deliberare, putaui me tibi satis superque fore excusatum re bene intellecta. Habes nunc ad vtrunque tuum postulatum quo satisfiat, ad hūc vsque diem me scilicet nec venire vnquàm recusasse, nec potuisse hactenus. In posterum hoc tibi pro certo polliceor me consilium istuc proficiscendi nunquam mutaturum, nisi maior aliqua vis mihi viam praecluserit. Tangor enim illius Ecclesiae cura, vt par est, & iam nescio quid factum sit, vt animo incipiam esse inclinatiore ad capessenda eius gubernacula, siquidem ita res postularit. Sinautem inter nos conuenit vt statim postreditum ego cum Bucero istuc concedam, ex re praesenti in commune consultemus quid expediat, neque tantum de pastore constituendo sed de totius Ecclesiae instauratione, cogitemus. Ita plus authoritatis habebit sententia & certior erit in futurum, quoniam adhibebuntur hi à quibus postea timendum esset. Re semel constituta iam suo ipsi iudicio obstricti erunt ne reclament amplius, aut quicquam ad ordinem nostrum turbandum moueant. Interim mi frater per Christum te obsecro ne animo frangaris. Quo magis incertum est quandiu fumus hic futuri, eo minus conturbare te debet longioris morae cogitatio. Scio esse permulta quae tibi & anxietatem & taedium afferre queant, sed cogita tibi has partes nunc à Domino esse delegatas sustinedas exte vsque in aduentum nostrum eius Ecclesiae, cui vis consultum. Pridie quàm literas tuas reciperem senatui vestro excusatam
units.tr: When your letter was handed to me, we were already getting ready for the journey, and I do not remember any journey in my life being more full of commotion. So, since I could not reply myself, I entrusted Claude Ferrex, whom you saw with me at Basel, and my brother to report to Farel what I felt. Now that I have gained a little leisure, I wanted to write to you too, in the middle of my journey. You will excuse me for answering you in a confused and brief way. I do not have your letter at hand, so I cannot go through each point in order and examine it, and a traveller at an inn has no time to commit to writing anything carefully considered or, as it were, composed. As far as I remember, your letter has two main parts. In the first you show me that the Church of Geneva must not be abandoned; in the second you urge that my return should also be hastened, lest by delaying longer Satan put some obstacle in the way. To the first I reply only as I have always done: there is no place under heaven that I dread more. This is not because I hate it, but because I see so many difficulties laid before me there, and I feel that I am far too weak to overcome them. Whenever the memory of former times comes back to me, I cannot help shuddering from my whole heart, if I am forced to expose myself again to those old struggles. If my dealings were only with that Church, I would be more at peace and certainly less frightened. But you must understand far more than I can say. Take this in one word: I know from many signs that the man who can do the most harm to me bears an implacable hatred against me. When I go over how many approaches to doing harm lie open to him on every side, how many bellows are always blown to kindle the fires of strife, and how many opportunities may arise then that cannot at all be foreseen by me, I am utterly dismayed. There are also very many other things in the city itself that cause me no small anxiety. The further I go, the better I see how hard a task it is to undertake the ministry of the Church. Yet none of this prevents me from being most ready to bring help to the wretched Church, if I understand that I am of any use. For whatever anxious thoughts trouble me in this matter, though they cause some delay while they keep my mind uneasy, they cannot drive out of me the resolve to do everything that I think will be for its good. Farel is my witness that I never once refused that call in a single word; I only pleaded that by giving bad advice they should not destroy a Church a second time after it had already been ruined once. Meanwhile I have shown clearly enough that nothing is closer to my heart than to lay down my life wherever there is need. I could make this plain to you in person by convincing arguments of how little I have dissembled here. But this seems to me most certain: when the envoys came to Worms, I earnestly entreated our brethren, with many tears and by every sacred thing, to consider before God what would be most beneficial for the Church that implored their help. When we came home, although no one was pressing the matter, I did not cease urging them to take up that care seriously; nor, believe me, did they themselves fail in their duty. But, as we suspected, a decision was made shortly afterwards that I should be joined to Bucer. I do not think this was done by prior arrangement, as I wrote to Farel earlier, and so I now solemnly assure you too. For the plan had been more or less settled before we returned from Worms, and that by the counsel of men who were not thinking of Geneva at all. Indeed, if you ask me, I do not see why I should be sent, since I am by no means fit for it; yet it was not mine to refuse. I had to come, unless I wanted to hear the worst spoken of me everywhere. Therefore, when your letter arrived, since it was no longer open to deliberate, I thought that once the matter was properly understood, you would consider me more than sufficiently excused. You now have, for both of your demands, what would satisfy them: up to this day I have never refused to come, nor, so far, have I been able to. From now on I promise you this for certain: I will never change my intention to set out for there, unless some greater force blocks my way. For the care of that Church touches me, as it ought, and I do not know what has happened, but I am beginning to be more inclined to take up its helm, if the situation should require it. But if it is agreed between us that, as soon as I return, I should go there with Bucer, let us take counsel together on the present circumstances about what is expedient for the common good, and let us think not only about appointing a minister but about the restoration of the whole Church. In this way the decision will carry more authority and will be more secure in the future, since those will be included whom we would otherwise have to fear. Once the matter is settled, they will be bound by their own judgment and will not object any further or stir up anything to disturb our order. Meanwhile, my brother, I beg you through Christ not to lose heart. The more uncertain it is how long I shall be here, the less the thought of a longer delay should trouble you. I know there are very many things that can bring you both anxiety and weariness, but consider that these burdens have now been assigned to you by the Lord, to be borne until our arrival at that Church whose welfare you wish to promote. The day before I received your letter I had already sent my excuse to your senate.

units.la: uerant, ueram,quod in presens non possum istuc venire: excusationem meam acceptam esse confido. Bene vale frater suauissime & amice integerrime. Saluta diligenter meo nomine pios omnes. D.Spiritu suo vos confirmet ad omne opus bonum. Vlmæ, Calendis Martiis M. D. XLI.
units.tr: ...that I cannot come there at present; I trust my excuse has been accepted. Farewell, dearest brother and most sincere friend. Greet all the godly diligently in my name. May the Lord confirm you by his Spirit in every good work. Ulm, on the Calends of March, 1541.

units.la: FERAEVS FARELLO.
units.tr: Feraeus to Farel

units.la: PRofecturus Ratisbonam Caluinus mihi iniunxerat, vt ad te (quoniam tum ei non vacabat) de negotio Gebennensi scri berem: atque ille mihi conceptam quandam argumenti formulā illorum quæ tibi scribi volebat, reliquerat: quæ dum exequi volebam, ecce adferuntur ex illo literæ, quas ille Vlmæ scripserat, misit haud obsignatas atque ita mitti ad te iussit, propter illas ad Bernardum, quarum exemplar tibi scribi voluit. illas igitur sic omnes mitto. Ex illis poteris satis intelligere quid constituerit: quare nostro opus est toties repetere, nihil enim aliud mihi mandarat scribendum, præter id quod ex illius ad te & Viretum literis cognoscet, se scilicet post suum reditum vnà cum Bucero ad vos venturum, feque facturum quod e re illius Ecclesiæ vobis omnibus videbitur. Quare tu interim res omnes cura, vt certo expectasse te vbi aduenerit, comperiat. Illud interim addam, quod post acceptas tuas postremas literas, omnino suscipere illam prouinciam constituerit. Antehac enim licet non aperte ac plane reluctaretur, videbatur tamen inclinare potius in aliam sententiam: verum tuæ literæ omnino in hanc nostram sententiam confirmarunt, in illis enim periclis tonitrua mihi audire videbar. Gratulor itaque tibi ob illam tuam vehementiā, quia eff cisti quod vehementer cupiebam, vtilēq; toti reipublicæ Christianæ prouidebam. Vale tui Feræi in orationibus tuis memor. Nostra tota familia te saluū cupit. Argentinę v i i.Martij.
units.tr: Calvin, when he was about to set out for Ratisbon, had asked me to write to you about the Genevan business, since he himself had no time then. He left me a rough outline of the subject that he wanted to put to you, and while I was working on it, letters arrived from him. He had written them at Ulm, and he sent them unsealed with instructions that they be forwarded to you, along with the letter to Bernard, of which he wanted a copy sent to you. I am therefore sending you all of them. From them you will be able to understand well enough what he has decided, so there is no need for me to repeat it at length. He had instructed me to write nothing beyond what you and Viret will learn from his letters to you both: that after his return he will come to you together with Bucer, and that he will do whatever seems to all of you best for the good of that Church. Meanwhile, see to everything, so that you may know for certain that he is expected when he arrives. I will add this: after receiving your last letter, he has resolved to take on that task entirely. Before, although he did not resist openly and plainly, he seemed rather to lean toward another opinion; but your letter has fully confirmed him in our view. Indeed, I seemed to hear thunder in those dangers. So I congratulate you on that vehemence of yours, because you have brought about what I earnestly desired, and I foresaw that it would be useful to the whole commonwealth of Christians. Farewell. Remember Feraeus in your prayers. My whole household wishes you well. Strasbourg, 7 March.

units.la: Tuus Claudius Ferreus.
units.tr: Yours, Claude Feraeus.

units.la: BVCERVS ET ALII FRATRES GENEVENSI Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Bucer and the other brothers to the Church of Geneva.

units.la: GRatiam & pacē à Deo Patre, & Domino nostro Iesu Christo precamur vobis in dies magis confirmari & augeri, viri prudentissimi & cordatissimi, dominiqué obseruandi. Exhibuit nobis veltras ad se literas Caluinus fymmyfta & frater noster charissimus & colendus, quibus rogatis, vt Ecclesię veltræ desolatæ consilium salutare adferat, quo rite & ex sententia Christi restitui & confirmari queat. Gratulamur hunc animum vobis, quia hunc veltrum olim fidum ministrum respicitis eiusque d.ãij. vti consilio statuistis. vere enim Christus ipse contemnitur & iniuria afficitur vbi tales ministri reiiciuntur & indigne tractatur. Bene itaque nunc habent res vestræ,dum Christum in hoc præclaro eius organo rursus agnoscitis. In eo certe hic animus perpetuò illi constitit, vt saluti vestræ consulere cuperet, etiam & non labores modo maximi sed etiam sanguis insumendus ef-set. Nunc autem quid faciat non solum ille, sed nos quoque (quibus inconsultis, etiamsi id non oporteret, hactenus nihil ma gni fecit) non videmus. Cras aut post biduum abeundum ei no-bifcum Vvormaciam est ad colloquium de religione, quod Im-perator & Rex Ferdinandus cum Principibus Germanicis instituit ad quærendam concordiæ restituendæ inter Ecclesias viam & rationem. Sicque res comparatæ sunt, vt nisi hoc colloquio via ista & ratio inuenta fuerit, expectanda fit nobis fatis grauis rerum Germanicarum perturbatio. At religione in Germania profligata, verendum vt & alibi affligatur. Non videtur igitur confultum, vt Caluinus rescindat vocationem Domini, qua ad hoc colloquium deputatus est. Id speramus vos ipsos quoque expectaturos. Ne autem interim Ecclesiæ vestræ aliquid grauius accidat, visum est Caluino & nobis e re vestra fore fi opera Farelli & aliorum impetretis à Vireto viro vere pio, prudente & cordato, vt Laufannenfi Ecclesia fideli alicui vicario interim commissa, apud vos Ecclesiam Christi sustineret & instauraret, donec institutum illud Vvormacienfe colloquium finiretur. Tamen volente Domino hoc est fi non obstet grauius & quod in aliud tempus reiici nequeat negotium Ecclesiarum, aliqui ex nostris ad vos venire ipsi vellemus, & præfentes id consulere cum Caluino, & agere quod possemus cognoscere Ecclesiæ vestræ profuturum. Hoc est quod nunc dare vobis consilij, & opera quod offerre vobis in præfenti possumus. Id vt boni consu-latis rogamus. Nam certe Ecclesiam vestram maximi facimus: vt quæ recte constituta lucem Christi in Italiam & Galliam inferre fœliciter possit. Bene valete in Christo qui & Ecclesiam & rempublicam vestram tranquillet & beatam reddat. Amen.
units.tr: We pray that grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ may be increasingly confirmed and increased in you day by day, most prudent and wise men, and worthy of our respect. Calvin, the synmystes and our most beloved and esteemed brother, has delivered to us your letter addressed to him, in which you ask that he bring a saving counsel to your desolate Church, by which it may be rightly restored and strengthened according to the mind of Christ. We commend this attitude of yours, because you look to this man, your former faithful minister, and have resolved to act on his counsel. For Christ himself is truly despised and wronged when such ministers are rejected and treated unworthily. Your affairs are therefore in good order now, since you acknowledge Christ again in this excellent instrument of his. Certainly this man has always been resolved to care for your welfare, even at the cost not only of very great labours but of his own blood. But what he or we ourselves ought to do now we do not see; he has done nothing of great importance up to now without consulting us, which he ought not to have done even if he had wished. He must leave for Worms with us either tomorrow or the day after, for the colloquy on religion which the Emperor and King Ferdinand, with the German princes, have arranged to seek a way and means of restoring concord between the Churches. Things stand so that, unless this colloquy finds such a way and means, we must expect a very grave upheaval in German affairs. And if religion is overthrown in Germany, it is to be feared that it will be attacked elsewhere too. It does not seem advisable, therefore, that Calvin should renounce the calling of the Lord by which he has been appointed to this colloquy. We hope that you yourselves will also expect this. Meanwhile, so that nothing more serious may befall your Church, it has seemed good to Calvin and to us that, if you obtain through the efforts of Farel and others from Viret, a truly pious, prudent and wise man, that the Lausanne Church be entrusted meanwhile to some faithful vicar, he may sustain and restore the Church of Christ among you until the Worms colloquy is finished. Nevertheless, if the Lord wills it, that is, if no more serious obstacle stands in the way and the business of the Churches cannot be put off to another time, some of us would like to come to you ourselves, and, being present, consult with Calvin and do whatever we could recognise as useful for your Church. This is the counsel we can give you now, and the help we can offer you at present. We ask you to take it in good part. For certainly we hold your Church in the highest regard, since, being rightly constituted, it can happily bring the light of Christ into Italy and France. Farewell in Christ, who may make both your Church and your commonwealth peaceful and blessed. Amen.

units.la: EX quo hic sum nihil tibi scripseram, sed mãdaueram Claudio meo vt quicquid à me acciperet cutaret ad te perueni-renam nec erat dignum aliquid tua lectione: & ego abste literas prius expectabam, quas ea mercede remuneraret. Interim dum expecto, nuntiatur mihi grauis calamitas, Claudium nostrum quem vnice diligebam, peste absumptum esse, Ludouicu fratrem Caroli triduo post secutum, domum meam miserè dissipatam esse, fratrem meum cum Cardo in vicinum pagum concessisse vxorem se ad fratrem recepisse, minimum ex Claudij disciplinis decumbere. Ergo ad doloris acerbitatem accessit vehementer anxia pro iis qui superfuunt solicitudo, mihi dies ac noctes obuersatur vxor consilij inops, quoniam capite suo caret: cruciat me mirum in modum optimi Caroli orbitas, qui intra quatriduum fratre vnico, & praeceptore quem patris vice coluit priuatus est. Noui autem ipsum esse tenerrimo animo. De Malherbio cogitare non possum, quin simul in mentem veniant optimi iuuenes qui eum custodiunt. Quanquam autem haec mihi tantum afferunt moerorem, vt mentem prorsus obruere, & fragere animum possint, incredibile tamen est quanto luctu ob Claudij mei mortem conficiat: neque mirum tibi videri debet. His duobus annis quantum mihi opus fuerit certo & fideli amico, qui mecum tot tamque variis molestiis ac perturbationibus sustineret, potes cogitare. Ille vero se non modo fidelissimum sed per omnia obsequentissimum mihi exhibuit, adeo vt ipso aequè propemodum familiariter ac fratre meo vteretur. Cum animi suspensus, vt scis, nuper discessisset, sanctissima fide receperat se quocunque annui essem venturum: neque mihi vnquam defuturum. Ergo quo magis reputo quantopere indigeam bono consiliario, qui à latere meo nunquam discedat: ab altera parte quàm rarum sit hoc tempore exemplum talis beneuolentiae & fidei: non aliter possum iudicare quàm Dominum mihi huc ause-rendo, voluisse in peccata mea grauiter animaduertere. Sed dum obiter volo meas miserias attingere, vltra modum diffluo. Hoc facit cum optimi viri memoria (quae vtinam mihi tam suauis aliquando sit, quàm sancta semper erit) tum pia de reliquiis solicitudo. Caesar hactenus expectauit dum venirent Principes: adfuerunt ab initio duo Bauari, & latro Brunsuicensis, Germaniae dedecus simul & exitium: sensim venerunt legati, alius post aliud. Tandem secuti sunt ex Principibus, Fridericus Palatinus Electoris frater, Otho eius nepos, iunior Vvirtembergensis, Landgrauius, Moguntinus, Albertus Badensis, Princeps ab Anhalt, Saxonis legatus: Elector Brandeburgensis breui venturus est: alios non desinet folicitare Cæsar,donec protrahat. Saxo iustissim̃s causis absentiam suam excusauit per legatos. Duæ sunt vrbes in fœde-re,Coslaria,&Brunsuicum, quas Henricus sub prætextu Banni multis prædationibus & latrociniis aliquandiu infestauit. Nu-per nostri decreuerant, vt armis communibus defenderentur. Cæsar interea neimpedirentur Comitia, omnia iudicia in nos intentata suspendi:omnes etiam sententias contra nos latas irritas esse voluit, donec de tota summa hic cognosceretur. Eo e-dicto promulgato mandauit etiam Brunsuicensi nominatim,vt quæ rapuerat restitueret, & in posterum à vi abstineret. Quan-quam factûrum se omnia recepit, pergit tamen vt coeperat. di-cas cum Cæsare colludere.Quicquid sit,in tanta certè necessita-te deferre socios non potest Saxo:itaque manet in specula,vt si quid iste mouerit,statim se obiiciat.Deinde ex quo tempore de-nunciatæ erant illæ suspensiones,citatus fuit ad audiendam Ban-ni, hoc est clarigationis vel proscriptionis sententiam. Paucis post diebus idipsum nobis est factum. Cæsar nescio qua religio-ne, magna tamen asseueratione testatur hæc sibi magno peræ di-splicere:ac daturum operam vt in fumum abeant: siunt tamen non sine magno nostro periculo. Quid enim si cras pronuntia-rent? pedem hinc efferre non possumus, quin caput nobis ause-ratur. Excideret mihi Sabaudus qui huc se sistit ad sidem impe-rio obligandam,quo nostris opibus recuperet possessiones,quas cum teneret,Imperio nunquam accenseri voluit:seró igitur sed missus à Rege Galliæ legatus,aduocatus Raimūdus, qui pro Du-catu Sabaudiæ in fidem ac clientelam Imperij ipsum recipi pe-teret. L gationes exterarum gentium adsunt multæ ac magnifi-cæ.Contarenus Card.pro suo Pótifice, qui nobis primo ingr. slu tot cruces aspersit,vt biduo post brachium illi ex fatigatione la-borasse arbitrer.Mutinensis Episcopus filius Hieronymi Moro-ni sub Nuntij titulo separatim missus est.Cótarenus sine sanguine subig re nos cupit:proinde tentat omnes vias conficiendi ex sua vtilitate negocij citra arma.Mutinensis totus est sanguina-rius,& b llum subinde in ore habet. Vterque in hoc totus est,vt omnes amicas tractationes præcidat,sed hoc postea. Veneti suú habent legatum splendidum hominem. Anglus vero præter or dinarium quem habere solet,Vintoniensem misit magno appa-ratu, hominem ad malitiam nimis acutum. Omitto Portugal-lum & reliquos.A Rege quoque Galliæ est quidam Velius homo stolidus & importunus. Cum Principes nominarem, totam fa-cem ordinis Psaficì præterij excepto vno Moguntino. Adsunt tamen Episcopi s equentes, Ratisponensis, Augustanus,Spiren-sis,Bremensis,Saltzburgensis, Brixinensis, Vvormaciensis,Bam-bergensis,Hildesemensis,& aliquot alij:superest vt tibi scribam quid futurum suspicemur,si tamen vllo modo diuinare licet.Nā ego non satis certa indicia video, ex quibus sumi queant proba-biles coniecturæ. nostrorum omnium animi vehementer sunt exacerbati aduersus Henrichum, nam virulentissimis libellis eos proscidit nimis atrociter: itaque rogant Cæsarem,vt pro calumniatore censeatur, si compettum fuerit ipsum impudentissimis mendaciis eorum famam lacerasse. Nec video qualiter istud componi queat, nili ad ordinum cognitionem referatur. Iam enim Landgrauius negauit Cæsari se passurum vt transactione aut arbitrio controueʳsia hæc finiatur, ne Cæsarem quidem ipsum voluit arbitrum recipere.Hoc impedimentum tametsi minimè videtur ad rerum summam pertinere: quoniam tamen turbabit initia,verendum est vt multum officiat. Iam negocium religionis sic habet. Cæsar quia res suas plurimum impeditas cernit,non libenter nouas sibi molestias accersit.Timet impressionem Turcicam.A Rege Galliæ aut dubia pax aut aperti belli periculum. Quanquam de Turca varij rumores dissipantur. Cùm Hungaricus ille monachus,qui mortuo Ioanne rege pupilli tutelam arripuit, ægrè Ferdinandum sustineret, auxilium à Turca petiit : ille non nisi exiguas copias subsidio misit,quæ Pestam Ferdinandi vrbem aggressæ sunt. Vrbs est in ripa Danubij è regione Budæ:ad eam obsidionem soluendam miles colligitur. Iam alij Turcam ipsum aduentare ferunt magno exercitu & apparatu , alij hunc eius apparatum nescio quo domestico motu fuisse interpellatū asserunt:videbimus tamen breui quale illud sit: non enim dubium erit quin valde domi sit impeditus , si à Vvalachis abstineat. Post defectionem à suis tyrannis in eius potestatem,vt nosti, se tradiderant. Ille Palatinū ex eorum stirpe præfecerat, sed alumnum suum : nescio quí factum sit, vt eius sœuitiam experti extrema tentare maluerint, quàm sub eius dominio manere.Hac igitur hieme trucidato Palatino quicquid etiam Turcarum apud se fuit sustulerunt. Nouum sibi Ducem crearunt,quem iureiurando adegerunt ad promittendas cum Turca æternas inimicitias, arce occuparunt mu nitissimâ , quam ipse mira celeritate ædificauerat ad fines Poloniæ.Hanc contumeliâ si non vindicabit,sciemus alibi esse occupatum:& vtinam sit,vt ille dum curat sua vulnera,nos spatij aliquid ad colligēdas mentes ac vires habeamus. Polonus vicinos suos Vvalachos posset maximè adiuuare,nisi Tartari eius regno molesti essent:qui superiori hyeme magnas prædas subita incursione abegerunt,& videntur velle pergere vlterius.Quicquid sit, Cæsar compositam habere Germaniam cupit, donec ab illis se difficultatibus explicuerit,nec vllos motus hoc tempore excitabit, nisi magna hostium nostrorum importunitate, inuitus in aliquam necessitatem pertrahatur. Nostri semel audientiâ sibi fieri volunt: deinde quoniam nullam fidem aut diuturnam pacem foresperant, nisi constituta religionis concordia, & Ecclesiis in ordinem redu&tis, vrgebunt vt hanc a&ionem Ordines serio suscipiant. Alioqui nihil magis cupiunt quàm omnes dissensiones pacificare sine tumultu, nec bellum aliter horrent quàm certâ patriæ suæ perniciem. Itaque quoad poterunt se a turbulétis consiliis alienill. ess: ostendent. Alterius partis tria sunt genera: sunt enim qui classicum canunt, ac palam insaniunt, quod non primo die impetamur. Huius classis principes sunt Moguntinus, Bavari, Brunsuicensis Henrichus, & eius frater Episcopus Bremensis. Alij quoniam cófultum patriæ volunt, cuius interitum vel gravissimam calamitatem ac vastationem à bello prospiciunt, huc conterunt omnia sua studia, vt sine religionis constitutione qualiscunque pax fiat. Tertij tolerabilem aliquam & doctrinæ & disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ correctionem, libenter admitterent: sed quoniam vel nondum eousque progressi sunt, vt causam peni-tus cognitam habeant, vel sunt animo submissiore, quàm vt eius consilij authores se profiteri audeant, ita se gerunt vt videa-tur nihil, nisi publicam tranquillitatem quærere. In eo ordine sunt Coloniensis, & Augustanus, ex grege sacerdotali: ex Princi-pibus ambo fratres Palatini, Otho eorum nepos, & fortasse Dux Cliuensis. Qui turbare moliuntur, quoniam pauciores sunt nu-mero & omnes bonos sibi reclamantes habent, vix consequen-tur quod captant. Deinde Cæsaris animus vt dixi, omnino ad pa-cem inclinat si poterit obtinere, vt reiecto in aliud tempus religi-onis studio, hoc neruis omnibus contendet: sed nostri non facile acquiescent, & habebunt socios in flagitanda Ecclesiæ re-formatione: sic, tamet si exigua, nonnulla tamen spes est aliquid agendi. Legati Pont. pro solenni suo more, fortiter aduersantur, ne descendamus in aliquam a&ionem: a&um enim de regno suo putant, si vlla de religione disceptatio, si consultatio de Ecclesiæ reformatione, sine idoli illius authoritate instituitur. Palam simulant se promouere quam cupimus Collocutionem, sed clàm magnis cum pollicitationibus, tum minis nos oppugnat. Cæsarem parati sunt adiuuare grandi pecunia, si ad arma volet prorumpere, aut quod Contarenus mallet, si potest nos sine cæ-de reprimere: sin aliquid concedat Rom. sedis tyrannidi minus consentaneum, fulmina illa minantur, quibus totum orbem có-cutere solent. Propter res Italicas obnoxius est Cæsar. Ergo, si li-cebit, eò cófugiet, vt pace temporaria, vel paucorum annorum induciis, Germaniam componat intacta causa. Quod difficulter impetrabit. Vides nunc quod initio dixi, tam obscuras esse con-iecturas, vt ne diuinationi quidem relinquatur locus. Quid ergo agimus? Inuocabimus scilicet nomen Domini, precabimurque vt hanc maximam & grauissimam causam, in qua & ipsius gloria & Ecclesiæ salus continetur, sua moderatione gubernet, ac in tanto articulo ostendat, sibi nihil esse preciosius quàm cele-stem illa sapientiam, quam nobis in Euangelio reuelauit: & eas animas quas sacro filij sui sanguine redemit. Eóque intentioribus & animis & studiis nobis flagitandus est, quo sunt omnia ab omnibus incertiora. Si totam huius negotij progressionem ac seriem diligenter expendimus, reperiemus ipsum mirificis modis, sine hominum vel consilio vel auxilio, atque etiá praeter omnium spem, cuenta gubernasse. Ab hac igitur virtute quâ toties exeruit, nunc toti, rebus tam perplexis, pendeamus. Vnum me terret, quòd tantum inter nos video securitatis: id verò non me terret modò, sed consternat penitus, quòd noua quotidie offendicula excitatur, quale est εἰ τῆς ἐυγαμίας vel potius ἐυσγαμίας: neque tamen ideo deiicior. Nuper à Vireto literas recepi, quibus ideo breuiter respondeo, quòd nunc minimè integrum est nobis de ea re deliberare. Vtinam mi Farelle, concedere istuc primo die liceat: sed quid vis faciam? Teneor hîc constrictus, & vereor magnopere, ne tædio hîc contabescam. Vale optime & dulcissime frater. Saluta amantissime meis verbis omnes fratres, Thomam, Michaelem, cui magnum mœrorem afferent iste literæ, Corderium præceptorem meum, & reliquos. Ratisponæ iiii. Calendas Aprilis M. D.XLI.
units.tr: Since I last wrote to you, I had sent a message to my Claudius to see that whatever he received from me reached you, though nothing was really worth your reading. I was also waiting for your letter first, which you would have repaid with that kindness. While I was waiting, a grievous calamity was reported to me: our Claudius, whom I loved above all, has been carried off by the plague, and Ludovicus, Caroli's brother, followed him three days later. My household has been wretchedly scattered. My brother has withdrawn with Cardo to a neighbouring village, and he has taken his wife back to his brother's. Claudius's teaching has left him seriously ill. So, to the bitterness of my grief there has been added a deeply anxious concern for those who survive. Day and night my wife, bereft of counsel since she has lost her head, is before my eyes. The loss of the excellent Carolus torments me terribly. Within four days he has been deprived of his only brother and of the teacher whom he honoured in place of a father. I know him to have a very tender heart. I cannot think of Malherbius without at once remembering the excellent young men who look after him. Although these things bring me such sorrow that they can utterly overwhelm my mind and break my spirit, it is nonetheless incredible how greatly I am worn down by grief at Claudius's death. You ought not to find this surprising. You can imagine how much I needed, over these two years, a certain and faithful friend who would bear with me through so many and such varied troubles and disturbances. He showed himself not only most faithful but in every way most obliging to me, so that he treated me almost as familiarly as my own brother. When, as you know, he recently left me in some uncertainty, he pledged with most sacred faith that wherever I was going, he would come, and that he would never fail me. So the more I consider how greatly I need a good counsellor who never leaves my side, and on the other hand how rare an example of such goodwill and fidelity is in these times, the more I can only judge that the Lord, by taking him away from me here, has wished to punish my sins severely. But while I wanted to touch briefly on my miseries, I have run on beyond measure. This is caused both by the memory of that excellent man (I wish he could one day be as sweet to me as he will always be holy) and by my anxious concern for what remains. Hitherto the Emperor has waited for the princes to come. At the beginning there were present the two Bavarians and the brigand of Brunswick, a disgrace and a ruin to Germany alike. Envoys have come gradually, one after another. At last there have followed some of the princes: Frederick, Count Palatine, brother of the Elector; Otto, his nephew, the younger of Württemberg; the Landgrave; the Mainz envoy; Albert of Baden; the Prince of Anhalt; and the envoy of Saxony. The Elector of Brandenburg is soon to come. The Emperor will not cease to solicit the others, so as to delay matters. Saxony excused his absence through envoys, for most just reasons. Two cities are in the covenant, Goslar and Brunswick, which Henry, under the pretext of the ban, has for some time harassed with many raids and robberies. Recently our people decided that they should be defended by common arms. Meanwhile the Emperor, so that the Diet should not be hindered, wished that all lawsuits brought against us be suspended. He also wished that all sentences passed against us be made void, until the whole matter is examined here. When this edict was published, he also ordered the Brunswicker by name to restore what he had seized and to abstain from violence in future. Although he promised to do everything, he nonetheless continues as he began. You might say he is colluding with the Emperor. Whatever the case, Saxony cannot desert his allies in such great necessity. So he remains on watch, so that if the other moves anything, he may at once throw himself in the way. Then, from the time those suspensions were announced, the summons was issued for us to hear the sentence of the ban, that is, of outlawry or proscription. A few days later the same thing was done to us here. The Emperor, by I know not what scruple, yet with great assertion, declares that these things displease him greatly, and that he will take care that they vanish into smoke. Yet they are done not without great danger to us. For what if tomorrow they should pronounce? We cannot step out of here without having our heads taken from us. The Savoyard, who presents himself here to bind his allegiance to the Empire, has almost escaped my notice. He wants to recover by our resources the possessions which, while he held them, he never wished to be counted as part of the Empire. He is late, but he has been sent as envoy by the King of France, Advocate Raymond, who seeks that he be received into the allegiance and clientage of the Empire on behalf of the Duchy of Savoy. There are many and splendid embassies of foreign nations. Cardinal Contarini, for his Pontiff, who at first sprinkled us with so many crosses that I think his arm was weary from exhaustion two days later. The Bishop of Modena, son of Girolamo Morone, has been sent separately under the title of nuncio. Contarini wants to subdue us without bloodshed, and therefore tries every way of bringing the business to an end by his own advantage, without arms. The Modenese is wholly bloodthirsty and keeps war constantly on his lips. Both are wholly intent on cutting off every friendly negotiation, but of this later. The Venetians have a splendid man as envoy. The Englishman, besides the ordinary envoy he usually has, has sent the Bishop of Winchester with great show, a man too sharp for mischief. I pass over the Portuguese and the rest. There is also from the King of France a certain Velius, a stupid and troublesome man. When I named the princes, I passed over the whole flock of the Papist order, except for the one from Mainz. Nevertheless the following bishops are present: Regensburg, Augsburg, Speyer, Bremen, Salzburg, Brixen, Worms, Bamberg, Hildesheim, and several others. It remains for me to write to you what we suspect will happen, if indeed it is ever permitted to divine. For I see no sufficiently certain signs from which probable conjectures can be drawn. The minds of all our people are very much inflamed against Henry, for he has torn them to pieces too savagely in most virulent pamphlets. So they ask the Emperor that he be regarded as a slanderer, if it is proved that he has assailed their reputation with the most shameless lies. Nor do I see how this can be settled, unless it is referred to the judgement of the estates. For already the Landgrave has refused to allow the Emperor that this controversy be ended by compromise or arbitration; he did not even wish the Emperor himself to be accepted as arbiter. Although this obstacle seems in no way to affect the sum of the matter, since it will disturb the beginnings it is to be feared that it will do great harm. Now the question of religion stands thus. The Emperor, seeing that his own affairs are very much hindered, does not willingly bring new troubles upon himself. He fears a Turkish invasion. From the King of France there is either an uncertain peace or the danger of open war. Although various rumours about the Turk are circulating. When that Hungarian monk, who on the death of King John seized the guardianship of the infant, could barely hold out against Ferdinand, he sought help from the Turk. The Turk sent only small forces as aid, and these attacked Pest, a city of Ferdinand. The city lies on the bank of the Danube, opposite Buda, and soldiers are being gathered to raise the siege. Now some report that the Turk himself is coming with a great army and equipment; others assert that this preparation of his was interrupted by I know not what domestic disturbance. We shall soon see what it is. For there will be no doubt that he is greatly hindered at home if he refrains from the Wallachians. After their revolt from their own tyrants, as you know, they had surrendered themselves into his power. He had set over them a Palatine of their own stock, but one who was his own foster son. I do not know how it happened that, having experienced his cruelty, they preferred to attempt the utmost rather than remain under his rule. So this winter, after slaughtering the Palatine, they destroyed whatever Turks there were among them. They created a new leader for themselves, whom they bound by oath to pledge eternal enmity against the Turk. They occupied a most strongly fortified citadel, which he himself had built with wonderful speed on the borders of Poland. If he does not avenge this insult, we shall know he is occupied elsewhere. And I wish it may be so, so that while he tends his wounds, we may have some space to gather our minds and strength. The Pole could greatly help his neighbours the Wallachians, were it not that the Tartars harass his kingdom; they carried off great booty by a sudden raid last winter, and seem inclined to go further. Whatever the case, the Emperor wants Germany to be kept quiet until he has extricated himself from these difficulties, and he will stir no movement at this time unless, against his will, he is drawn into some necessity by the great importunity of our enemies. Our people want to be granted a hearing at once. Then, since they hope for no faith or lasting peace unless a settled agreement on religion is reached and the Churches are restored to order, they will press the Estates to take this business up in earnest. Otherwise they desire nothing more than to settle all dissensions peacefully and without tumult, and they dread war no less than the certain ruin of their homeland. So, as far as they can, they will show themselves aloof from troublesome counsels. The other party is of three kinds. For there are those who sound the trumpet and openly rage that we are not attacked on the first day. The leaders of this class are the Mainz man, the Bavarians, Henry of Brunswick, and his brother the Bishop of Bremen. Others, because they want the good of the fatherland, for whose ruin or most grievous calamity and devastation they foresee from war, devote all their efforts to bringing about some kind of peace without any settlement of religion. The third sort would gladly admit some tolerable correction of doctrine and of ecclesiastical discipline; but either they have not yet progressed so far as to have the cause thoroughly understood, or they are of too submissive a spirit to dare to profess themselves authors of that plan. So they conduct themselves in such a way that they seem to seek nothing but public tranquillity. In this group are the Cologne and Augsburg men from the priestly flock, and from among the princes both brothers of the Palatine, Otto their nephew, and perhaps the Duke of Cleves. Those who strive to stir up trouble, since they are fewer in number and have all good men protesting against them, will hardly achieve what they seek. Then, as I said, the Emperor's mind leans altogether towards peace, if he can manage it, by putting off the study of religion to another time, and he will strive with all his strength for this. But our people will not easily acquiesce, and they will have allies in demanding the reformation of the Church. So, although it is slight, there is some hope of achieving something. The Papal legates, as is their solemn custom, strongly oppose our taking any action, for they think their kingdom is finished if any debate on religion or consultation on reformation of the Church is set up without the authority of that idol. They openly pretend to promote the conference we desire, but secretly they assail us with great promises and also with threats. They are ready to help the Emperor with large sums of money if he wants to break out to arms, or, as Contarini would prefer, if he can restrain us without bloodshed. But if he concedes anything less agreeable to the tyranny of the Roman see, they threaten those thunderbolts with which they are wont to shake the whole world. The Emperor is under obligation because of Italian affairs. So, if he is allowed, he will take refuge there, so as to settle Germany by a temporary peace, or by a truce of a few years, with the cause left untouched. This he will obtain with difficulty. You now see what I said at the beginning, that the conjectures are so obscure that there is not even room left for guessing. What then are we doing? Surely we shall call upon the name of the Lord, and pray that he would govern this greatest and most serious cause, in which both his own glory and the salvation of the Church are contained, by his own moderation, and that in so great a matter he would show that nothing is more precious to him than that heavenly wisdom which he has revealed to us in the Gospel, and those souls which he redeemed with the sacred blood of his Son. Therefore we ought to press our demands with minds and efforts all the more intent, the more everything is uncertain to everyone. If we weigh carefully the whole course and sequence of this business, we shall find that he has governed it in wonderful ways, without the counsel or help of men, and even beyond everyone's hope. Let us therefore now hang wholly upon that power by which he has so often shown himself, in matters so perplexed. One thing frightens me: that I see so much complacency among us. This not only frightens me but utterly dismays me, namely that every day new stumbling blocks are raised, such as the question of "good marriage" [εὐγαμίας] or rather of "ill marriage" [δυσγαμίας]. Yet I am not on that account cast down. Lately I received a letter from Viret, to which I reply briefly, because it is now by no means open to us to deliberate on that matter. I wish, my dear Farel, that it might be permitted to go there on the first day. But what do you want me to do? I am held here bound, and I greatly fear that I shall waste away here from weariness. Farewell, best and sweetest brother. Greet all the brothers most lovingly in my words: Thomas, Michael (to whom these letters will bring great sorrow), my teacher Corderius, and the rest. From Regensburg, 29 March 1541.

units.la: A Datis proximis literis, nil quàm coitionibus in diuersoriis Electorum Saxonis & Brandeburgensis ac Lantgrauij faciendis (ad quas ex Imperatoriis & Regiis multi conuenerunt) operam dedimus. In die Paschæ etiam Cœnam in diuer forio Lantgrauij celebrauimus, communicante ipso quoque Lantgrauio. Hæc vsque ad x x. huius, quo die Imperator delectum colloquiorum enunciari fecit nostris, & legatis Electorum. Postridie indicatus is delectus est, & toti cœtui Imperij, & de eo consultatum vtrinque. Electores statim consenserunt, sed in cūfilio principum non potuerunt statim conuenire. Quidam enim etiam legatum Pontificis adhibendum esse contendebat: sed præualuit tamen sententia Electorum, vt Imperatori omnia relinquerentur. Nostri etiam biduo consultarunt quòd delecti nos sine arbitris congredi cum tribus alterius partis detrectabamus, & quidam nostrum differri negotium noua interceptione nolebant, ac metuebant ne à parte altera ineptiores adiunge- rentur. Tandem tamen vicit heri eorum sententia qui nostram supplicationem quam in Cancellaria inuenietis, Imperatori exhibendam iudicarunt. Ad vcsperam heri sub tertiam appellauit nos sex delectos Imperator apud se per Dominum Anaues astan tibus primis conciliariis, & negotium dedit vt omni studio vias quæreremus piæ & sanctæ concordiæ, eoque in negotio tantum Deum & Ecclesiarum salutem spectaremus, non dominos nostros aut vllum affectum. Nos post detrectationem modestam petiuimus adiungi quosdam, vt testes vtrinque. Id Imperator in deliberationem recepit, & rursus grauiter horta⸗ tus est, vt hanc causam optima fide ageremus. Dedítque dextram venientibus & discedentibus vt hoc non ignoretis scilicet. Inuenit tamen viam vt nobis satisfiat, quam post nostram appellationem Landgrauio aperuit. Vt adhibitis vtraque parte duobus testibus, per Præsidentem quem designauit Fridericum Palatinum. Orate Dominum: in horam expectamus vt initium fiat. Delecti sunt ab altera parte, Iulius Phlugius, Ioannes Eckius, & Gropcrus Coloniensis. A nostra Philippus, Pistorius & ego. Vigesima secunda Aprilis. M. D. XLI.
units.tr: Since my last letter I have been occupied only with the meetings held in the lodgings of the Elector of Saxony, the Elector of Brandenburg and the Landgrave, to which many came from the Imperial and royal side. On Easter day we also celebrated the Supper in the Landgrave's lodging, the Landgrave himself communicating too. This went on until the 20th of this month, when the Emperor had the choice of colloquists announced to our side and to the Electors' legates. The next day that choice was made known to the whole assembly of the Empire, and it was debated on both sides. The Electors agreed at once, but among the council of princes they could not agree straight away. Some insisted that a legate of the Pontiff should also be admitted, but the opinion of the Electors prevailed, so that everything was left to the Emperor. Our men also deliberated for two days, because we, the chosen men, refused to meet with the three from the other side without arbiters, and some of ours did not want the business put off by a fresh interruption, and feared that less capable men would be added from the other side. At last, however, yesterday the view of those prevailed who judged that our supplication, which you will find in the Chancery, should be presented to the Emperor. Yesterday toward evening, at about three o'clock, the Emperor summoned the six of us chosen men to him through Lord Anaues, with the leading councillors standing by, and charged us to seek with every zeal the ways of holy and pious concord, looking in this business only to God and the salvation of the churches, and not to our masters or any partiality. After a modest refusal we asked that some men be added as witnesses on each side. The Emperor took this under consideration and again earnestly urged us to conduct this cause in good faith. He also gave his right hand to those coming and going, so that you may know this, of course. Yet he has found a way to satisfy us, which he opened to the Landgrave after our appeal: namely, that with two witnesses from each side admitted, the matter be conducted through the President whom he has appointed, Frederick the Palatine. Pray to the Lord: we expect that the beginning will be made within the hour. Chosen from the other side are Julius Pflug, John Eck and Gropper of Cologne; from ours, Philip, Pistorius and myself. Twenty-second of April, 1541.

units.la: LVTHERVS MELANCHTHONI.
units.tr: Luther to Melanchthon.

units.la: ACcepimus iam alteras vestras literas, mi Philippe. Et licet dextræ tuæ constractæ me misereat, tamen ego neque tuis ominibus, neque meis credo. Res nostræ non casu, sed certo consilio, non quidem illo nostro tam fœlici, scilicet, immo solius Dei geruntur. Verbum currit, oratio feruet, spes tolerat, fides vincit vt palpare cogimur, & nisi caro essemus, dormire pos semus feriarisque, scilicet memores Mosaici illius, Vos quiescetis, Dominus pugnat pro vobis. Nam etiamsi omnia aliter velimus consulere, dicere, facere, vigilantissimi, si Deus non pugnarit, frustra vigilauerimus: illo vero pugnante, non frustra dormierimus. Et certum est ipsum pugnare, & paulatim & pedetentim descendere de throno ad iudicium illud expectatissimum. Multa sunt nimis signa quæ id mihi persuadent. Res in domibus vestris saluę sunt, gratia Dei. Nolite timere, Estote fortes & læti, nihil soliciti. Dominus prope adest. Agant quicquid possunt Henrici, Episcopi, a'que adeo Turca, & ipse Satan. Nos regni filij sumus, qui illum cósputum & occisum denuo ab istis Henricis, Saluatorem colimus & expectamus. XXII. Aprilis. M. D. XLI.
units.tr: We have now received your second letter, my Philip. Although I pity your right hand, which is cramped, I trust neither your omens nor mine. Our affairs are carried on not by chance but by a sure plan, not indeed by our own so-called good fortune but by God alone. The Word runs, prayer glows, hope endures, faith conquers, so that we are forced to flatter ourselves; and unless we were flesh we could sleep and take our rest, mindful of that saying of Moses: "You shall hold your peace, and the Lord shall fight for you." For even if we wish to plan, speak and act in every way with the greatest vigilance, if God does not fight, we shall have watched in vain; but with him fighting, we shall not have slept in vain. And it is certain that he is fighting, and gradually, step by step, he is coming down from the throne to that long-awaited judgment. There are very many signs that persuade me of this. Affairs in your houses are safe, thanks be to God. Do not fear; be strong and cheerful, anxious about nothing. The Lord is near. Let Henry, the bishops, and even the Turk and Satan himself do what they can. We are sons of the kingdom, and we worship and await the Saviour whom those Henrys spat upon and slew again. April 22, 1541.

units.la: ETsi hic adesse multis de causis piget, venisse tamen nunquā poenitebit.Delirare me putas?scio quid dicam.Et me non sine ratione loqui aliquando coràm audies. Nunc collige ex narratione,quantum poteris.Delecti nostri de peccato originali non difficulter transfegerunt:secuta est disputatio de libero arbitrio,quæ ex Augustini sententia composita fuit:nihil in utroque nobis decessit. De iustificatione acriores fuerunt contentiones.Tandem conscripta est formula,quam adhibitis certis correctionibus utrinque receperunt. Miraberis,scio,adversarios sātum cōceffille,cùm legeris exemplar, ita vt postrema manu correctū fuit,quod literis inclusum reperies.Retinuerunt etiā nostri doctrinę verę summā:vt nihil illic cōprehensum sit,quod nō extet in scriptis nostris: scio,desiderabis clariorem explicationem, & in ea re me tibi assentientem habebis. Verùm si reputes quibuscum hominibus negocium nobis sit,agnosces multum esse effectum. Ventum est deinde ad Ecclesiā: in definitione congruebāt sententiæ:in potestate diffidere coeperunt.Cùm nullo modo possint conciliari,visum est articulum illum omittere.In sacramentis rixati sunt nonnihil: sed cùm nostri suas illis cęrimonias, vt res medias permitterent,vsq; ad coenam progressi sunt. Illic fuit insuperabilis scopulus. Repudiata transsubstantiatio, repositio, circumgestatio,& reliqui superstitiosi cultus. Hæc aduersariis nequaquam tolerabilia. Collega meus qui totus ardet studio concordiæ, fremere & indignari,q; intempestiuç fuissent motæ eiusmodi quæstiones.Philippus in aduersam partem magis tendere, vt rebus exulceratis omne pacificationis spem præcideret.Nostri habita consultatione, nos conuocarunt. Iussi fumus omnes ordine dicere sententias:fuit vna omniū vox,transubstantiationem esse fictitiam,repositionem superstitiosam, idololatricā esse adorationem, vel saltem periculosam,cùm fiat sine verbo Dei. Mequoque exponere Latinè oportuit quid sentirem. Tametsi neminem ex aliis intellexeram,libere tamen sine timore offensionis,illam localem præsentiam damnaui:adorationem asserui mihi esse intolerabilem.Crede mihi,in eiusmodi actionibus opus est fortibus animis,qui alios cōfirment. Vos istic precamini Dominum diligenter, vt illo fortitudinis Spiritu nos sustineat. Scriptum deinde à Philippo compositum,quod vbi Granuellano oblatum est, asperis verbis repudiauit, q; illi tres delecti ad nos retulissent.Hæc cum fiant in ipso limine,cogita quantum adhuc superfit difficultatis,in missa privata,in sacrificio, in communicatione calicis. Quid si ad apertam præsentiæ confessionem vertetur? quanti tumultus effeturi sint? Literæ tuæ à Plumario altero mense quàm scriptæ fuerunt mihi redditæ sunt: mirabor, si non propediem aliæ non veniant. Salus fratrum mihi commendata est ut debet, sed heremus adhuc illo obice, quem nosti, Maurus qui ea de causa millus est, diligenter satagit in soluendo hoc nodo, ipsesolito maior affulget: Landgrauius enim aliquam sentire fructrationem unde omnia sperabat incipit: ergo inclinabit in illum nostrum. Id si fiet habebitur, ne dubita, singularis fratrum ratio, & Maurus pro sua virtute est virtus pius & cordatus incumbet. Crede mihi fideliter hactenus se gessit. Nihil tamen amplius impetratum quàm ut illis domum impune redire liceret, modo apud Episcopum abiurarent. N. nobis est modestissimus, Dominus eum vel tollat, vel emendet. Salutaamantissimè omnes fratres, Dominus Iesus vos conseruet. Philippus & Bucerus te salutant. nudiustertius cum praederemus cum Landgrauio, facta est metio tui amica. Ratisponæ x i. Maij.
units.tr: Although it grieves me to be here for many reasons, I shall never regret having come. Do you think I am raving? I know what I am saying, and some day you will hear me speak with good reason face to face. Now gather from this account as much as you can. Our delegates got through the matter of original sin without much difficulty. A disputation on free will followed, composed according to the view of Augustine; on both we conceded nothing. On justification the contentions were sharper. At last a formula was drawn up, which, with certain corrections on each side, they accepted. You will be surprised, I know, that the opponents conceded so much, when you read the copy as it was corrected in the final hand, which you will find enclosed in the letter. Our men also kept the sum of sound doctrine, so that nothing is included there that does not stand in our writings. I know you will long for a clearer explanation, and in that matter you will have me agreeing with you. But if you consider what men we have to deal with, you will recognise that much has been achieved. Then we came to the Church. In the definition the opinions agreed; over power they began to disagree. Since they could in no way be reconciled, it was thought best to omit that article. They quarrelled somewhat over the sacraments, but since ours allowed them their ceremonies as things indifferent, they advanced as far as the Supper. There was the insurmountable rock: transubstantiation, reservation, carrying about in procession, and the other superstitious forms of worship were rejected. These things are by no means tolerable to the opponents. My colleague, who burns wholly with zeal for concord, groaned and was indignant that questions of this kind had been raised out of season. Philip inclined rather to the opposite side, so that by exasperating matters he would cut off all hope of peace. Our men, after consultation, called us together. We were ordered to give our opinions each in turn. There was one voice of all: transubstantiation is fictitious, reservation superstitious, adoration idolatrous, or at least dangerous, since it is done without the Word of God. I too had to state in Latin what I thought. Although I had understood none of the others, I freely, without fear of giving offence, condemned that local presence; I declared that the adoration was intolerable to me. Believe me, in actions of this kind there is need of brave spirits who strengthen others. Pray to the Lord there diligently, that he may sustain us with that Spirit of fortitude. Then a writing composed by Philip was offered to Granvelle, and he rejected it with harsh words, as the three chosen men had reported to us. Since these things are happening on the very threshold, consider how much difficulty still remains: in private masses, in the sacrifice, in the communion of the cup. What if it turns to open confession of the presence? What tumults will it bring about? Your letter, written a month earlier, was delivered to me by Plumarius; I shall be surprised if others do not come soon. The welfare of the brothers has been commended to me as it should be, but we are still held up by that obstacle which you know of. Maurus, who has been sent on that account, is busily labouring to untie this knot, and the knot itself appears greater than usual, for the Landgrave is beginning to feel some frustration from the very quarter from which he hoped for everything; therefore he will incline toward our side. If this happens, it will be secured; do not doubt it. The brothers' case is unique, and Maurus, as far as his virtue goes, is a pious and sensible man and will apply himself. Believe me, he has so far acted faithfully. Nothing more has been obtained than that they might return home unharmed, provided they first abjure before the Bishop. N. is most modest toward us; may the Lord either take him away or correct him. Greet all the brothers most lovingly. The Lord Jesus keep you safe. Philip and Bucer greet you. The day before yesterday, when we were talking with the Landgrave, a friendly mention was made of you. Ratisbon, May 11.

units.la: M. D. XLI.
units.tr: M. D. XLI.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel.

units.la: NVntius die vno serius abiit quàm putabam, hic dies nobis aliquid peperit.
