Yet it is not yet a year since you were content with the Senate's first letter, and were already, in a way, girded for the road. Whence this new scruple? What of the fact that a motion was put to the people about you by name, when the people knew that those whom it had expelled were to be brought back into the city? For no mention was made of me or of anyone else, but only in these words: "Do you not declare here that an injury has been done to Farel and his companions?" What more do you ask of the people than that, by approving your innocence, it should make itself guilty? It was added: "Do you want Farel with his companions," and so on. You will pardon me, best of brothers, if I have spoken rather harshly; but this difficulty seems to arise from peevishness rather than from sound judgment. I am well aware of the sincerity of your mind, nor have I forgotten the many instances by which you have amply shown how little you regard yourself. But take care that those who do not know you thoroughly do not suspect anything of the kind; indeed, those who do not suspect will nonetheless seize the chance to carp. But the Church has by no means made satisfaction in proportion to the offence. Who denies it? Yet if you consider how delicate matters still are here, not to say anything harsher, you yourself would advise that this business should not be pushed any further. So I beseech you by Christ, my Farel, not to listen to just any advisers, but to yield to the counsel of those who lack neither prudence nor concern for the honour of your ministry, no less than you yourself have. But if you think that we know nothing, see nothing, judge nothing, then at least allow yourself, just once, to be won over by your friends. Farewell, best and dearest brother. Written on the third day before the Kalends of December, 1541.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CAL. TO FAREL.

units.la: POstridie aut saltem biduo postquam tibi scripseram, venit Carmelita Lugdunensis, à quo non frustra timuimus. Non fefellit nos diu: vultu, verbis, toto denique corpore, qualis esset prodidit. Neque tamen obstitit quominus cum eo humaniter ageremus. Omitto priuata beneuolentiae testimonia. Quantum ad ministerium ipsum attinet: vt obuiam iremus periculis omnibus, quae varia hinc inde instabant, contulimus cum Collegis nostris, quaenam erga eum ratio tenenda foret. Communiter censuimus eum ad nos vocandum esse, rogandumque vt nobis consilium suum exponeret. Condiximus in posterum diem. Ad primum postulatum respondit, se eo animo venisse vt Ecclesiae seruiret. Tum excusare coepi, quòd non statim eum reciperemus: ordinem enim esse nobis praescriptum à Domino, quem in vllius hominis gratiam violari nefas est: Id quoque ad exemplum pertinere, ne admitti se alij quoque eodem modo postularent. Hortatus sum vt cogitaret rem non esse in manu nostra sitam: cum aperto Dei Verbo conscientiae nostrae constrictae tenerentur. Quòd si timor Dei nos non impediret: ne per homines quidem licere: quia eius rei compositam formulam haberemus, cui stare nos oporteret. Deprecatus sum deinde, ne contemptu sui aut diffidentia nos differre existimaret. Addidi eius quoque imprimis interesse, ne ita subito onus subiret, satius fore multo, si aliquantulum adhuc temporis ad deliberandum sibi sumeret. Tota oratio cum erga eum honorifica erat, tum plena beneuolentiae ac humanitatis. Excepit breuiter, se petere, vt fides sibi exemplo daretur: duas esse causas cur nollet suspensus diutius manere. Nunc se habere idoneos comites à quibus deduceretur, & equo etiam ac viatico instrueretur: posthac non eam sibi commoditatem fore. Deinde si in Galliam sibi remigrandum foret, nihil esse melius quàm id citissime fieri, antequam rumor de eius ad nos aduentu latius manaret. Iussimus paulisper secedere ex communi consilio. Vitetus longam & grauem orationem de religione ac diligentia, quæ in vocandis ministris feruanda effet, habuit. Produxit tum ex Verbo Domini, tum ex veteris Ecclesiæ historiis exempla, rationes adhibuit quæ ad causam facere videbantur. Erat huiusmodi oratio, quæ hominem non lacefleret: & tamen ab importuna illa festinatione retrahere eum deberet: quæ denique, fi quid haberet pudoris ingenui, fine exprobratione aliqua permouere ad verecundiam posset. At jui adeo fractus non fuit, vt inde ceperit maiorem ferociendi audaciam. Si Domini, inquit, Spiritum vos habere putatis, ego eo non sum de ftitutus. Scio igitur quid liceat. Non hic sum quidem vt quæ à vobis obiecta sunt refellam: constat tamen Apostolos non fuisse vicissim probatos alios ab aliis. Hoc autem proferebat tanto fastu, vt videretur à refutatione abstinere, quoniam non eftemus digni, quibuscum experiretur. Addidit fe libenter id passurum fuisse, fi ante proximam Quadragesimam huc venisset: nunc cum in Ecclesia tam vicina specimen fui ediderit, notiorem fe debere esse, quàm vt noua probatione opus habeat. Respondi non esse illic Ecclesiam, ex qua iudicium de Pastoribus fumi oportéret. Quod fi aliquid nominis illi comparaffet, mirum non esse, quemadmodum enim Gallis quod ait Solomo, nempe animis famelicis etiam amara esse dulcia. Ad hæc magnam infirmitatem declarafle in suis concionibus. Nos quidem, non exprobrandi animo hæc commemorare, sed ineptis eius iactantiis cogi. Ita discessum est, nisi quod vnusquisque pauca verba subiecit, ad hominem mitigandum: scis quid profectum fuerit. Paulo post dixit in diuersorio, fe hic nullos reperire doctos homines: atque vt videas hominem plane furiosum, dixit nulla occasione. Cum vnus fortasse me & Viretum nominaffet, respondit fastuose, myriadem esse in Gallia multo doctiorum. Quid refert? inquies. Ego vero istas ineptias, vt par est, rideo. Animaduerto tamen esse certa argumenta maleuoli ac maligni animi. Rogabis quam fit doctus qui in alios omnes adeo seuerus est censor. Vidisti multos asinos, finge te vnum ex illis videre. Dum hæc scribo, literæ mihi tuæ afferuntur, quibus rursum flagitas vt alter nostrum ifthuc veniat. Atqui li scias quàm multa & necessaria nos hic detineant, facile excusatos habeas. Magnam fratrum multitudinem nunc habemus, quibus in singulas horas respondendum est. Inter eos duo sunt saltem, de quibus non modò bene speramus, sed splendidè nobis pollicemur. Alij sunt etiam non ineptı, sed illi duo excellunt. Nuncius tuus nondum colloquutus est nobiscum, sed post cacechifmum ad me veniet. Vale,frater integerrime. Viretus te plurimum salutat, cuius nomine hæc scripsi, longè plura additurus si ocium foret, sed iam alio vocor. Vtinam liceret chartam hanc implere: materia enim suppetit & animus non deest, sed abrumpere omnia cogor. Iterum vale. Geneuæ. x. Maij. M. D. X L I I.
units.tr: The day after I had written to you, or at least two days later, a Carmelite from Lyon came, and we had good reason to fear him. He did not keep us in doubt for long: by his face, his words, and indeed his whole bearing, he revealed what sort of man he was. Still, this did not prevent us from dealing with him courteously. I pass over the private expressions of goodwill. As for the ministry itself, to meet all the dangers that threatened from various quarters, we conferred with our colleagues about how we should deal with him. We agreed that he should be summoned to us and asked to set out his plan. We arranged a meeting for the next day. To the first request he replied that he had come with the intention of serving the Church. I then began to explain why we could not receive him at once: the Lord has prescribed an order for us, and it is wrong to violate it to please any man. This also bears on precedent, so that others would not demand to be admitted in the same way. I urged him to consider that the matter was not in our hands, since our consciences were bound by the plain Word of God. And if the fear of God did not restrain us, it would not be permitted even by human standards, since we have a settled formula in this matter to which we must abide. I then begged him not to think that we were delaying out of contempt for him or distrust of him. I added that it was especially in his own interest not to take on such a burden so suddenly, and that it would be much better for him to take a little more time to deliberate. The whole speech was both respectful towards him and full of goodwill and courtesy. He replied briefly that he asked for a written assurance to be given him, for there were two reasons why he did not wish to remain in suspense any longer. First, he now had suitable companions to escort him, and was also furnished with a horse and provisions; afterwards he would not have such an opportunity. Second, if he had to return to France, nothing was better than doing so as quickly as possible, before the rumour of his coming to us spread more widely. By common counsel we had him withdraw for a little while. Viret made a long and weighty speech about the piety and care that must be observed in calling ministers. He brought forward examples both from the Word of the Lord and from the histories of the ancient Church, and used arguments that seemed to bear on the case. The speech was of such a kind that it would not offend the man, and yet it ought to draw him back from that importunate haste; and finally, if he had any honest sense of shame, it could move him to modesty without any reproach. But he was so far from being subdued that he took from it greater boldness in swaggering. "If you think you have the Spirit of the Lord," he said, "I am not lacking in that. I know, therefore, what is permitted. I am not here indeed to refute what you have objected; yet it is well established that the apostles did not test one another in turn." He put this forward with such arrogance that he seemed to abstain from refutation, since we were not worthy for him to make trial of. He added that he would gladly have submitted to a test had he come here before the coming Lent; but now, since he had given a sample of himself in a church so near, he ought to be too well known to need a fresh test. I replied that there was no church there from which a judgement about ministers ought to be drawn. If he had won some reputation there, it is no wonder, for, as Solomon says, to hungry souls even bitter things are sweet. Besides this, he had shown great weakness in his sermons. We mention these things not with any desire to reproach him, but because we are compelled by his foolish boasting. So we parted, except that each of us added a few words to soothe the man; you know what came of it. Shortly afterwards he said in his lodging that he found no learned men here; and so that you may see the man is plainly mad, he said this without any occasion. When someone perhaps named me and Viret, he replied disdainfully that there were countless men in France far more learned. What does it matter, you will say? I for my part laugh at such foolishness, as is fitting. Yet I note that these are sure signs of an ill-willed and malicious mind. You will ask how learned a man is who is so severe a critic of everyone else. You have seen many donkeys; imagine you are looking at one of them. As I write this, your letter has been brought to me, in which you again demand that one of us come there. But if you knew how many and how pressing the matters are that keep us here, you would readily hold us excused. We now have a great multitude of brethren to whom we must reply every hour. Among them there are at least two of whom we not only hope well but promise ourselves splendid things. There are others too who are not without merit, but those two excel. Your messenger has not yet spoken with us, but he will come to me after the catechism. Farewell, most upright brother. Viret greets you warmly; I have written this in his name, and would have added far more had I had leisure, but I am already called elsewhere. I wish I could fill this paper, for there is matter enough and the will is not lacking, but I am forced to break off everything. Farewell again. Geneva, 10 May 1542.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel.

units.la: VTinam ita ad præsentis vitæ contemptum, ac sanctæ mortis meditationem erudiat vt hic annus multis piorum funeribus mihi luctuosus fuit. Poralis primus vrbis Syndicus ad Dominum migrauit: cuius mors nobis, vt par erat, tristis atque acerba fuit. Ipsius vero mortis species, vt nonnihil mihi solatij attulit, ita ex aduerso mihi dolorem auxit, dum cogito quantum in eo homine perdiderimus. Postridie quàm in morbum inciderat cùm essemus apud eum ego & Viretus, denunciauit se de vita periclitari: morbum enim quem patiebatur familiæ suæ esse fatalem. Habuimus deinde longum sermonem de rebus variis: sic loquebatur, quasi sana esset ac integra valetudine. Biduo quod proximè sequutum est acrius laborauit, sic tamen vt ingenio & loquendi dexteritate magis vigeret, quàm tota vita: quisquis ad eum visendi causa accesserat, audiebat præclaram aliquam exhortationem: ac ne putes futilem fuisse loquacitatem, quantum fieri potuit aptissimè singulis accommodabat, quod illis cõueniret ac prodesset. Cœpit inde meliuscule habere, vt spes optima esset restitutum propediem iri. Triduum durauit hic status: tandem iterum morbus ingrauescere, vt cõstaret maximum esse periculum. Quo tamen afflictior erat corpore, eo spiritus vividior fiebat. Taceo medium illud tempus. Quo die mortuus est, circiter nonam ante meridiem, illuc venimus ego & Viretus. Cum pauca verba fecissem de cruce, de gratia Christi, de spe vitæ æternæ, nolebamus enim prolixis sermonibus eum fatigare, excepit se accipere Dei nuncium vt par erat, se enim scire quam vim haberet Christi ministerium ad confirmandas conscientias fidelium. Illic de ministerio actoto illius vsu ita splendidè disseruit, vt nos stupore ambos afficeret: ac quoties mihi in mentem venit, adhuc obstupesco: sic enim loquebatur, vt videretur orationem ab aliquo nostrum diu ac diligenter meditatam referre. Hanc partem sic concludebat, vt diceret se remissionem peccatorum, quam ex mandato Christi pollicemur, non aliter accipere, quàm si Angelus sibi è cœlo apparuisset. Descendit postea ad vnitatem Ecclesiæ, quam miris elogiis commendauit, testatus nullum se habere melius nec certius solatium in certamine mortis, quàm quia in illa vnitate iam plane confirmatus esset.
units.tr: I wish this year had taught us to despise the present life and to meditate on a holy death, for it has been sorrowful for me on account of the many deaths of godly people. Porral, the first syndic of the city, has passed over to the Lord. His death was, as was fitting, sad and bitter for us. Yet the manner of his death, while it brought me some comfort, on the other hand increased my grief, as I think how much we have lost in that man. The day after he had fallen ill, when Viretus and I were with him, he declared that his life was in danger, for the illness he suffered was fatal to his family. We then had a long conversation on various matters, and he spoke as if his health were sound and whole. In the two days that followed he suffered more severely, yet he was more vigorous in mind and in skill of speech than he had ever been in his whole life. Whoever came to visit him heard some outstanding exhortation, and, lest you think his talkativeness was empty, he fitted it as aptly as he could to each person, so that it suited and benefited them. Then he began to be somewhat better, so that there was excellent hope he would soon be restored. This state lasted three days. At last the illness grew worse again, so that it was clear the danger was very great. Yet the more his body was weakened, the more lively his spirit became. I pass over that intervening time. On the day he died, about nine o'clock before noon, Viretus and I came there. After I had said a few words about the cross, the grace of Christ, and the hope of eternal life (for we did not want to tire him with long speeches), he declared that he accepted God's messenger as was right, for he knew what power the ministry of Christ had to confirm the consciences of the faithful. There he spoke of the whole use of the ministry so splendidly that he amazed us both; and as often as it comes to my mind, I am still astonished, for he spoke as if he were repeating an address that one of us had long and carefully meditated. He concluded this part by saying that he received the forgiveness of sins, which we promise on Christ's command, no differently than if an angel had appeared to him from heaven. Afterwards he came to the unity of the Church, which he commended with remarkable praises, testifying that he had no better or surer comfort in the struggle of death than that he was now fully confirmed in that unity.

units.la: Collegas autem nostros paulo ante vocauerat, ac redierat cum illis in gratiam, nec si in illo dissidio perstitisset, eo exemplo alij abuterentur. Dixerat autem nobis, Cùm publica Ecclesiæ æ dificatio vos cogat ad illos pro fratribus tolerandos, cur non eadé ratione pro pa storibus agnoscerem? Admonuerat tamen eos se- rio, ac illis quid peccassent in memoriam reduxerat: sed redeo ad illam postremam orationem. Conuersus ad eos qui adstabat, hortatus est omnes vt Ecclesiæ communionem haberent com- mendatas: eos vero qui in ceremoniis & diebus sunt superstitiosi admonuit, vt deposita peruicacia nobis acquiescerent: nos enim melius ac prudentius viderę quid expediret quàm illos: si quoq ; in illis fuisse magis obstinatum, sed datos sibi demum oculos, vt viderent quàm noxia esset contentio. Postea confessionem edidit breuem ac grauem ac luculentam. Inde nos hortatus est, cùm ad alias officij partes, tum vero ad constantiam: nec secus ac vates aliquis de futuris difficultatibus sermonem habuit. De Rep. mi- rum quàm sapienter dixerit quod ad rem pertinebat. Imprimis vt reconciliandis sociis vrbibus pergeremus operam studiúmq; impendere commendauit. Quicquid vociferentur clamosi ali- qui, dicebat, non oportet vos animis frangi. Non habeo tàtum temporis vt omnia persequar. Nos vbi aliqua subiecimus, con- cepimus orationem: sic discessimus. Secunda pomeridiana, cùm vxor mea venisset, iussit bono animo esse quicquid accideret: co gitaret se non temerè, sed mirabili Dei consilio huc adduɗtam, vt ipsa quoque Euangelio seruiret. Paulo post denunciauit, vo- cem iam tibi eripi. Cæterum etiam sine voce confessionem se retinere in animo, quàm prius ediderat, ac in ea morituram. Il- lic recitato Simeonis cantico, atque eius interpretatione ad se applicata, vidi, inquit, & manu tetigi salutare istud, atque ita se ad quietem composuit. Exinde sermone fuit destitutus, nutibus tamen indicabat, se nihil de animi vigore perdidisse. Sub horam quam veni illuc cum Syndicis. Cùm aliquoties erumpere in sermonem conatus est, & faucibus impediretur, iussi ne sibi molestus amplius foret, abunde eius confessione satisfactum. Cœpi tandem loqui vt potui, audiuit vultu admodum composi- to & tranquillo. Vixdum eramus egressi, cùm sandam animam Christo reddidit. Hæc narratio vix tibi erit credibilis, si expedas hominis naturam: verùm scito fuisse nouo prorsus spiritu tunc donatum. Nunc in deligendis nouis Collegis sumus valde oc- cupati, eòque magis, quòd dum putamus nobis contigisse ali- quem valde idoneum, postea deprehendimus nostræ expecta- tioni non satis respondere. Vbi aliquid constituerimus, intelli- ges. Neque enim, cùm absis, iuuare nos cùsilio potest. Vale, x v r. Iunij. M. D. X L I I.
units.tr: Our colleagues, however, he had summoned a little before, and he had been reconciled with them, and had not persisted in that dispute, lest others should take advantage of his example. He had said to us: "Since the public building of the Church obliges you to bear with those men as brothers, why should I not acknowledge them in the same way as pastors?" Yet he had admonished them earnestly, and had brought their faults back to their memory. But I return to that last address. Turning to those who stood by, he urged them all to keep communion with the Church, which he commended; and he admonished those who were superstitious about ceremonies and days to lay aside their obstinacy and yield to us, for we saw better and more wisely what was expedient than they did; and if any of them had been more obstinate, he said, they had now at last been given eyes to see how harmful contention was. Afterwards he published a brief, serious, and lucid confession. Then he exhorted us, both to our other duties of office and especially to constancy; and, like some prophet, he spoke of future difficulties. Concerning the state, it is wonderful how wisely he spoke on what pertained to the matter. Above all, he commended that we should press on with the work and zeal of reconciling the allied cities. "Whatever noisy men may cry out," he said, "you must not be broken in spirit. I do not have time to go through everything." When we had added a few things, we concluded the prayer, and so we departed. At two in the afternoon, when my wife had come, he bade her to be of good courage whatever might happen; she should consider that she had been brought here not by chance but by the wonderful counsel of God, so that she too might serve the Gospel. A little later he declared that his voice was now taken from him. Yet even without voice he kept in his mind the confession he had published earlier, and said he would die in it. Then, after the canticle of Simeon had been recited and its interpretation applied to himself, he said, "I have seen and touched that salvation," and so he composed himself to rest. After that he was deprived of speech, yet he indicated by nods that he had lost nothing of his vigour of mind. About the hour when I came there with the Syndics, as he several times tried to break into speech but was hindered by his throat, I bade him not to trouble himself further, since his confession had been amply satisfactory. At last I began to speak as well as I could, and he listened with a very composed and tranquil countenance. We had scarcely gone out when he gave his holy soul back to Christ. This account will hardly be believable to you if you consider the man's nature; but know that he was then endowed with a wholly new spirit. Now we are very busy in choosing new colleagues, all the more because, while we think we have found someone very suitable, we afterwards discover that he does not sufficiently meet our expectations. When we have settled something, you will know. For, since you are absent, he can not help us with counsel. Farewell, 15 June 1542.

units.la: VTinam mihi iam redditæ essent tuæ literæ quas in itinere esse non dubito. Nam etsi nihil læti in illis expecto, tamen hoc ipsum nonnihil me iuuaret, aliquid certi cognoscere de statu Ecclesiæ vestræ. Nunc scribere cogor de re mihi incognita: nec tamen mihi temperare queo, quin scribam. Audio euocatos fuisse in urbem classium omnium Decanos, ut audiant, quidnam de Cœna Domini statuerit Princeps. Nihil dicturus sum, quod tu non iam satis superque meditatum apud te habeas. Magnitudo tamen ipsa causæ tacere me ac quiescere non patitur. Duo hic spectanda esse vides, statum ipsum quæstionis, & ratio nem agendi, quæ partim ex circunstantiis pendet. De causa non opus est te monere, ut cum N. diligenter conferas. Hoc tamen velim tibi curæ sit, apud eum efficere, ut apud quoscunque loquatur, non dubitet hoc testatum relinquere, non modo figurari in Cœna communionem quam habemus cum Christo, sed etiam exhiberi: neque verba illic nobis dari a Domino, sed veritatem ac rem constare cum verbis. Hanc porro communionem non imaginariam esse: sed qua in unum corpus, vnámque substantiam cum capite nostro coalescamus. Excludat interim libera voce omnia absurda, excipiat, caveat, modo in illo capite tam necessario nihil extenuet. Neque enim ambiguis aut obscuris verbis implicare licet, quod summam lucem ac perspicuitatem requirit. In ratione agendi, hoc expendere oportet, quale exemplum edituri sint fratres, si doctrinæ iudicem habeant Principem, ut quicquid statuerit, amplectendum protinus sit atque habendum pro oraculo. Quale ac quantum sit hoc prætudicium ad posteros. Certe si ita patimur nobis iugum imponi, prodimus nostra dissimulatione sacrum ministerium. Neque hanc perfidiam, vel coram Deo, vel coram hominibus excusare poterimus. Verum minime necesse erit in hanc contentionem descendere: quando modesto ciuilique respondo declinare hunc scopulum fratres poterunt, si dicent maiorem esse causam, quam ut inconsultis suis Collegis aliquid recipiant. Habebunt autem speciosos ac fauorabiles prætextus, quibus illi satisfaciant. Illud quoque prætereundem non est, ut vbi bonam causam esse viderint, illuc serio se applicent: ne dum medij esse volunt, deserant veritatis defensionem. Non intelligo ut se adiungant ad vitia: vel si ambæ partes peccent, se implicent alterius societate. Hoc tantum volo, ut rectæ sanæque sententiæ palam nec dissimulanter adhæreant. Postremo fratri nostro expone, quid de hominibus ipsis sentias, & quid in illis deprehenderis: ut sciat quibus fidem habere ac dare debeat: sed inceptus sum, qui tam anxie te instruo, quasi non satis sit vno verbo signum dare.Finem igitur faciam. Vale optime ac suavissime frater. Dominus Iesus te Spiritu suo semper regat ac confirmet magis magisque.Saluta mihi omnes fratres. Geneuæ, xxiii.Augusti. M. D. XLII.
units.tr: Would that your letters, which I do not doubt are on the way, had already been given to me! For although I expect nothing cheering from them, yet this very thing would somewhat help me, to learn something certain about the state of your Church. Now I am compelled to write about a matter unknown to me, and yet I cannot restrain myself from writing. I hear that the deans of all the companies have been summoned to the city, to hear what the Prince has decided about the Lord's Supper. I am not going to say anything that you have not already considered more than enough in your own mind. Yet the greatness of the cause itself does not allow me to be silent and at rest. You see that two things must be considered here: the very state of the question, and the manner of acting, which depends partly on circumstances. You do not need me to warn you about the cause, so that you may diligently confer with N. Yet I would like you to take care that, wherever he speaks, he is not hesitant to testify that in the Supper not only is the communion we have with Christ figured, but also exhibited; and that the words are not given to us by the Lord in vain, but that the truth and the thing agree with the words. Moreover, this communion is not imaginary, but one by which we grow together into one body and one substance with our Head. Meanwhile, let him freely with his voice exclude all absurdities, accept, and guard against them, provided that in that most necessary head he diminishes nothing. For it is not permitted to entangle in ambiguous or obscure words what demands the highest light and clarity. As to the manner of acting, it is necessary to weigh what kind of example the brothers will set, if they have a prince as judge of doctrine, so that whatever he has decided must at once be embraced and held as an oracle. How great and how far-reaching this prejudgement is for posterity! Certainly, if we allow this yoke to be laid on us, by our dissimulation we betray the sacred ministry. Neither before God nor before men will we be able to excuse this treachery. Yet there will be no need at all to descend into this contention, since the brothers will be able to avoid this rock with a modest and civil reply, if they say that the matter is too great for them to accept anything without consulting their colleagues. They will, moreover, have specious and plausible pretexts by which they may satisfy them. This also must not be passed over: that when they see a cause is good, they should apply themselves to it earnestly, lest, while they wish to be neutral, they abandon the defence of the truth. I do not mean that they should join in vices; or, if both parties sin, that they should entangle themselves in the company of either. I only wish that they cling openly and without dissembling to a right and sound opinion. Finally, explain to our brother what you think of the men themselves and what you have found in them, so that he may know whom he ought to trust and to whom he ought to give faith. But I have gone on, I who instruct you so anxiously, as if it were not enough to give a sign with one word. I will therefore make an end. Farewell, most excellent and most sweet brother. May the Lord Jesus always rule and strengthen you more and more by his Spirit. Greet all the brothers for me. Geneva, 23 August 1542.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S.
units.tr: IO. CALVINVS N. S.

units.la: TErtio die ex quo tibi scripserã, venit ad me N.ac quid actum esset, breuiter exposuit. Mihi vero, vt simpliciter tibi quod sentio, fatear, summopere omnia displicent. De edicto dicam postea. Verum Decanus quis coegit respondere illud dare, quo praeiudicium Collegis suis omnibus afferrent? Vtinam vel abfuisset N. vel aliud cor, aliudque consilium ad hanc causam attulisset. Hoc ideo dico, quia N. mihi narrauit, eius culpa factum esse, vt Decani sic praecipitauerint. Video quid sit, Cui religio nō est, periculi metu per omnes sanctos deierare, is deinde hominum gratiæ hoc vel illud cocedere non dubitat: quia obnoxius, vt est, sibi videtur. Respondeant pro se alij quicquid volent: mihi tamen suam hanc facilitatem nunquam probabunt. Quantum ad summam ipsam spectat, vt tibi penitus assentiar, conscientia mea non patitur. Edictum nempe tolerabile esse censes, actutò à vobis posse recipi. Expendamus ergo id quod continet. Principio approbat N. formulam. At qualis illa est obsecro? Tu Buceri obscuritatem vituperas, & merito. At nihil est in Bucero adeò perplexum, obscurum, flexiloquum, atque, vt sic loquar, tortuosum. Exceptiouis tamen additur, vt tam haec confessio quam catechismus locum habeant, si certo modo explicentur. Quò remittimur? Hoc ergo à vobis quæritur, vt spondeatis vos nunquam discessuros à sententia vobis incognita. Deinde quid putas illic fuisse disputatum, nisi Christum non esse inclusum in pane? Id autem N. perinde accipit, ac si nihil aliud foret quam signum. Quicquid sit, nō ausim credere mysterium Cœnæ illic fuisse bene ac rite explicatum. At confessio N. adiungitur. Equidem non nego quin istud multum sit: sed mihi non sufficit, praesertim vbi omnia iterum ad disputationem illam & formulam quæ in Cœnæ administratione recitari solet, exiguntur. Atque vt hoc vnū mali sit, persuaderi nequeo, qui sententiam hac tulerunt, sanam de hac re sententiam tenere. Iam eius erit interpretari, cuius fuit pronuntiare. Ita periurij alligatus iudicabitur, qui secus docuerit, quàm ipsi iudices assequantur. Neque hac solaín parte erit periculum. Verat enim ne de vllo nouo ritu aut nouis ceremoniis verba posthac fiant. Quis autem nescit, illum & excommunicationem, tionem,& frequentiorem Coenæ vsum,& multa alia hoc nomi-ne comprehendere, quæ nos desideramus,ac restituta cupimus? Tacendum tamen erit.Cùm ita scientes ac volentes laqueum vo-bis induitis,cogitate non finem calamitatis hic fore,sed initium. Dominus enim vestrā mollitiem seueriore aliquo flagello corriget,si negligitis occurrere, cùm palàm iaciuntur fundamenta perniciosæ tyrannidis. At quid faceret Princeps,inquis?Nodum dico quid ille peccauerit in ipso ordine agendi:tantum demonstro,quàm non sit tutum vos astringere,nisi magna cautione adhibita.Quòd ad rationem modùmq; agendi pertinet,agnosco quod dicis, maiorem partem culpæ in ministris hæresre : hæreo tamen cùm lego edictum : tanta illic & ferocia & superbia se ostendit. Sententiam suam vocat definitiuum ἀρέστον, cui contradicere non liceat. Promulgat,non vt libertas sit ministris respondi:sed vt sequantur,teneant,obseruent,quod placuit. Agnosco etiam quod postea commemoras, N. iustas poenas dare suæ vel ambitionis,vel malignitatis, quòd in tam miseram seruitutem cogitur:quia pati non potuerit fratres secum esse liberos:sed nos simul plectimur,imò in totam Ecclesiam poena hæc redundat. Nam hoc exemplo edito,posthac necesse erit doctrinam non ftram,non modò potestati sed nutui vnius etiã hominis & quidem imperiti subiectam esse:vt loquendum sit aut tacendum,simul atque digito signum dederit. Neque tamen expedire censebam,vt fratres hac de re in certamen descéderent:sed videbantur mihi habere honestum prætextum declinandi, si cum excusatione ciuili & modesta confessionem suam offerrent. Atqui non postulatur ab illis confessio,inquis. Ego vero ideo dandam fuisse puto.Vale mifrater.Dominus semper te conseruet ac dirigat.Saluta omnes fratres: quibus tamen non communicabis omnia.Geneuæ,iii.Idus Septemb. M. D. XLII. Ioannes Calvinus suus.
units.tr: Three days after I wrote to you, N. came to see me and briefly explained what had happened. To be frank with you about what I think, I am extremely displeased with all of it. I will speak about the edict later. But what dean forced them to give that answer, by which they would prejudice all their colleagues? I wish N. had either stayed away or brought a different heart and a different plan to this business. I say this because N. told me that it was through his fault that the deans acted so rashly. I see what the matter is. A man who has no scruple about swearing by all the saints out of fear of danger will then not hesitate to concede this or that to the favour of men, since, being exposed as he is, he thinks himself vulnerable. Let others answer for themselves as they wish; they will never win my approval for this readiness of theirs. As far as the substance itself goes, my conscience does not allow me to agree with you fully. You think the edict tolerable and that you could accept it at once. Let us weigh, then, what it contains. To begin with, N. approves the formula. But what sort of thing is it, I beg you? You criticise the obscurity of Bucer, and rightly. Yet nothing in Bucer is so convoluted, obscure, equivocal and, if I may put it so, tortuous. However, a qualification is added: that both this confession and the catechism shall hold their place, provided they are explained in a certain manner. To what are we referred? So what is asked of you is that you promise never to depart from a view unknown to you. Next, what do you suppose was debated there, except whether Christ is not enclosed in the bread? N., however, takes this as though it were nothing but a sign. Whatever the case, I would not dare believe that the mystery of the Supper was properly and rightly explained there. But N.'s confession is added. I do not deny that this counts for a good deal; but it is not enough for me, especially when everything is referred back to that disputation and to the formula customarily recited in the administration of the Supper. And, to complete this one evil, I cannot be persuaded that those who passed this decision hold a sound view on the matter. Now it will be for the one who pronounced it to interpret it. Thus whoever teaches otherwise than the judges themselves understand will be judged bound by perjury. Nor will the danger lie in this part alone, for it forbids that from now on any word be spoken about any new rite or new ceremonies. Who does not know that under this name it comprehends that discipline and excommunication, and the more frequent use of the Lord's Supper, and many other things which we long for and desire to be restored? Yet we must keep silent. Since you knowingly and willingly put the noose on yourselves, consider that this will be not the end of the calamity but its beginning. For the Lord will correct your softness with some harsher scourge, if you neglect to resist while the foundations of a pernicious tyranny are openly being laid. But what would the prince do, you ask? I am not saying what he sinned in the very order of procedure; I only show how unsafe it is for you to bind yourselves unless great caution is employed. As for the manner and method of acting, I acknowledge what you say, that most of the blame lies with the ministers; yet I stick fast when I read the edict, for so much ferocity and pride shows itself there. It calls its own judgement a definitive decision [ἀρεστόν], to which it is not permitted to contradict. It promulgates it not so that the ministers may freely reply, but so that they follow, hold and observe what has pleased them. I also acknowledge what you mention later: that N. is paying a just penalty for his ambition or his malice, in that he is forced into such wretched servitude, because he could not bear that the brothers should be free alongside him. But we are punished at the same time; indeed this punishment overflows upon the whole Church. For once this example is published, doctrine will from now on necessarily be subject not only to the power but to the nod of a single man, and an unskilled one at that, so that one must speak or be silent as soon as he gives a sign with his finger. Yet I did not think it expedient that the brothers should enter into a contest over this matter; rather, they seemed to me to have an honourable pretext for evading it, if they offered their confession with a civil and modest excuse. But, you say, no confession is demanded of them. I, however, think it ought to be given for that very reason. Farewell, my brother. May the Lord always preserve and guide you. Greet all the brothers, though you will not share everything with them. Geneva, 3rd ides of September 1542. John Calvin, yours.

units.la: SVLTZERVS CALVINO S. Epist.45.
units.tr: SULTZER TO CALVIN, GREETINGS. Letter 45.

units.la: Binas ad te dedimus dierum non ita multorum interuallo. Itaque & tuas expectamus iam,idque eo auidius,quo magis tuum Ecclesiæque statum cupio cognoscere. Quanquam enim audiam non sine voluptate fœlicem istic Ecclesiasticæ reformationis disciplinæque communis successum,te tamen scribente & rectius liceat singula perspicere & animo meo magis exultare,quippe qui spem foueam,aliquando nostrā nobis ignauiam Ecclesiam istam vel exemplo tacito opprobraturam utiliter. Neque nos sane spem abiecerimus,reuocari aliquando ministerij sacri cum suis partibus auctoritatem, Ecclesiæ; vel alii. quam faciem conformari posse: si sublato fatali dissidio iiceat a-liquando ὁμοθυμαδὸν in communem causam incumbere, præ-sertim cum tu & tui similes velut lætæ aues præuolantes appa-reant, nec sinant despondere animum. Dominum itaque precor totius pacis charitatisq; Patrem, vt suum Spiritum impartire no bis dignetur, vt prodigiosa hæc lues tollatur è grege suo: nobisq; donet vt certis, moderatis ac salutaribus consiliis cuncta pera-gamus. Cæterum ex Argentorato heri Adrianus alumnus noster saufto nuncio significauit Coloniensem Episcopum, profligata Papismi impietate reformationem religionis per totam ditio-nem suam moliri D. Buceri auspiciis, qui denuo nunc serioque ab ipso accersitur, creditúrque eò profecturus veré sanctus Chri-sti Apostolus. Idem vero etiam Monasteriensem Episcopu me-ditari, ac vtrunque ad Protestantum fœdus aspirare. Nam de Ar-gentinensi nimirum accepisti, qui Argentinensium & quorun-dam suorum hortatibus impulsus, colloquium in Molsheim in-stituit, quod hoc ipso tempore DD. Bucero, Hedione, aliisque præsentibus peragitur, mox nimirum auspicatóque aperturum per eam quoque prouinciam Euangelio ostium. Dominus Iesus largiatur fœlicem progressum, non solùm propter horum ditio-nes amplissimas, verùm etiam propter exemplum quod haéte-nus inusitatum: ita nimirum etiam alios inuitaturum ad capes-sendam alacrius Euangelicam veritatem, qui per metum forte nihil sunt primi ausi tentare. De Farello nostro nimirum ex Buceri literis omnia intelliges: cuius angustiæ mirifice meum animum solicitum habent atque percellunt. Dominus & illius & Ecclesiæ misereatur, qui solus potest repressa tempestate, se-renitatem inducere, vt qui Verbo mare sedat quamlibet tre-mens exitiúmque minitans. Nos tantùm eum precibus excite-mus cùm nostrìstum Ecclesiarum nostrarum, & verorum Chri-sti membrorum συμπαθείας declaremus. Non desino expecta-re lætius aliquod nuncium, quod vtinam breui accipiamus. Vi-tebergæ, ne & hoc nescias, D. Lutherus Eucharistiæ subleuatio-nem, in Cœnæ sacræ administratione exercitam hactenus, su-stulit, tintinabulíque pulsum, propterea quòd & Gallos quos-dam & Germaniæ superioris studiosos ea cerimonia offendi intellexisset. Sed & in Ecclesia Leipsensi ipso consentiente his mensibus excepto vno, altaria omnia sunt confracta & simula-cra omnia sublata, vt plane declararit se non tam cerebrosum præstractúmque quàm vulgò habetur & audit. Id igitur nuncium mihi ab homine fidei exploratæ significatum eò me oblectauit impensius, quòd sperem plurimum pondérus ad Catholicam Ec-clesiarum consensionem habituram hoc factum, quando ritu vel copia vel diuersitate apud Saxonas non pauci offenduntur hactenus, maxime cum non desinत vbique artifices mire ad calumniam omnia detorquendi, & cauillandi. Paulus Fagius Isnefis D. Capitoni piæ memoriæ successurus fertur tum in ministerio Ecclesiastico tum Theologiæ professione, ilqe in horas expectatur. Hæc te scire volui. Quicquid erit te non celabo, quem ex animo & vere colo & diligo. Dominus te seruet cum vxore & symmystis, quos meo nomine amantes & diligenter salutabis. Salutant te Contzen, Beat. Gryn. & Telamon. Vale. Bernæ xxi. Octob. Anno M. D. XLII.
units.tr: We have sent you two letters within a short interval, and now we are eagerly awaiting yours, all the more because I long to learn how you and the Church are doing. Although I hear with real pleasure that the reformation of the Church and the common discipline there have been happily successful, I would still like to see the details more clearly, and to rejoice more fully in my mind, from your own letter. I cherish the hope that our Church, by its quiet example, will someday rebuke our own sloth to good effect. Nor should we give up hope that the authority of the sacred ministry, with its proper functions, may someday be restored in the Church, and that its face may be reshaped, once the fatal division is removed and we may at last set to the common cause with one accord [ὁμοθυμαδὸν]. This is especially so since you and men like you appear like joyful birds flying before us, and do not allow us to lose heart. I therefore pray to the Lord, the Father of all peace and love, that he deign to impart his Spirit to us, so that this monstrous plague may be removed from his flock, and that he grant us to carry out everything by sound, moderate and wholesome counsels. Otherwise, yesterday from Strasbourg our pupil Adrian brought the happy news that the Bishop of Cologne, with the impiety of Popery overthrown, is undertaking a reformation of religion throughout his whole territory under the auspices of Master Bucer, who is now being summoned again, and more earnestly, by the bishop himself; and it is believed that the man going there will be a truly holy apostle of Christ. The same report says that the Bishop of Münster is also planning this, and that both aspire to the alliance of the Protestants. You have heard about the Bishop of Strasbourg, who, urged on by the Strasbourgers and some of his own people, has arranged a colloquy at Molsheim, which is being held at this very time in the presence of Masters Bucer, Hedio and others, and which will soon, I trust, open a door for the Gospel in that province too. May the Lord Jesus grant a happy outcome, not only because of the very wide territories of these men, but also because of an example hitherto unheard of, which will likely invite others to embrace the Gospel truth more eagerly, since through fear they have perhaps dared to attempt nothing first. You will learn everything about our Farel from Bucer's letters; his distress greatly troubles and unsettles my mind. May the Lord have mercy on him and on the Church, he who alone can calm the storm and bring back serenity, as he who calms the sea with his word, however much it rages and threatens destruction. We only stir him up with our prayers, while we declare our sympathy [συμπαθείας] for the troubles of our Churches and of the true members of Christ. I will not cease to hope for some happier news, which I pray we may receive soon. Know also, lest you be ignorant of this, that at Wittenberg Dr Luther has abolished the lifting up of the Eucharist, which had hitherto been practised in the administration of the Lord's Supper, and the ringing of the bell, because he had learned that some Frenchmen and students from upper Germany were offended by that ceremony. Moreover, in the Church at Leipzig, with the consent of the pastor himself, all the altars have been broken and all the images removed in these months, except for one; so he has plainly shown that he is not as hot-headed and obstinate as he is commonly thought and reported to be. I was the more delighted by this news, which came to me from a man of proven faith, because I hope this deed will carry considerable weight toward the agreement of the Catholic Churches, since many among the Saxons have hitherto been offended by the rite, or by its abundance, or by its variety, especially as artisans everywhere never cease to twist everything to calumny and to carp at it. Paul Fagius of Isny is said to be going to succeed the late Dr Capito both in the ecclesiastical ministry and in the professorship of theology, and he is expected any hour now. I wanted you to know these things. Whatever happens, I will not hide it from you, whom I honour and love truly and from my heart. May the Lord keep you, with your wife and fellow-ministers, whom you will greet lovingly and diligently in my name. Contzen, Beat Gryn and Telamon greet you. Farewell. From Bern, 21 October 1542.

units.la: Tuus Sultzerus.
units.tr: Yours, Sultzer.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO.
units.tr: Bucer to Calvin.

units.la: Gratiam & pacem. Quàm infœliciter sibi consuluerint Mo-tenses, cum regnum Christi, non nisi certi de brachio carnis admittere voluerunt, in dies grauioribus calamitatibus patefit. Dominus corrigat quod à nobis peccatum est, & excitet regnum suum suo brachio. Colonia moliebatur aliquid pro Christo: d vereor vt nunc bello, quod Brabanti intulerunt Iuliacensi, etiam differatur. Noster quoque moliri cœpit aliquid, sed aduersarij dum non valet id aduertere, extrahunt etiam tempus quantum possunt. Vtinam sentiremus & bona & mala nostra, & conspirares rite in Domino, veris supplicationibus incumberemus. Pœnitentia vera, etiam apud Euangelicissimos, ignoratur. Christus nos excitet & suo Spiritu impleat. Res nostræ hic habent, vt solent, satius languidè pro donis nobis collatis: orate pro nobis vt magis inardescamus. Ludus literarius non incommodè habet. Aduenit ex Italia vir quidam Græcè, Hebraicè & Latinè admodum doctus, & in Scripturis feliciter versatus, annos natus quadraginta quatuor, grauis moribus & iudicio acri, Petro Martyri nomen est. Præfuit Canonicis regularibus Lucæ: adduxit tres, vnum Græcè doctissimum, reliquos duos iuuenes studiosos. Hic laborauimus iam ne in tantis Ecclesiæ nostræ opibus hi-furiant. Respice nos Domine Iesu. Hic te seruet & tuos: & habete nostram Ecclesiam, vt soletis in vestris precibus commedatam. Vale, Argent. xxviii. Octob. M. D. XLII.
units.tr: Grace and peace. How unhappily the Motensians have looked after their own interests, since they were willing to admit the kingdom of Christ only on terms of the arm of the flesh, is becoming clearer by the day through ever heavier calamities. May the Lord correct what sin we have committed, and stir up his kingdom by his own arm. Cologne was attempting something for Christ, but I fear that now, because of the war the Brabanters have waged on the Jülich territory, it too will be put off. Ours too has begun to attempt something, but since the adversaries cannot see how to prevent it, they drag out the time as long as they can. Would that we felt both our good and our bad fortunes, and that you agreed properly in the Lord, and that we devoted ourselves to true prayers. True repentance is unknown even among the most evangelical. May Christ rouse us and fill us with his Spirit. Our affairs here are, as usual, rather sluggish, so we have the gifts bestowed on us; pray for us that we may burn more fervently. The school is doing reasonably well. A certain man has arrived from Italy, very learned in Greek, Hebrew and Latin, and well versed in the Scriptures, forty-four years old, of serious character and keen judgement; his name is Peter Martyr. He was over the regular canons of Lucca, and he brought three companions: one very learned in Greek, and two young men devoted to study. Here we have already been labouring so that these men may not rage against the great resources of our Church. Look upon us, Lord Jesus. May he keep both himself and his people here, and hold our Church in your regard, as you are accustomed to commend it in your prayers. Farewell. Strasbourg, 28 October 1542.

units.la: M. Bucerus.
units.tr: M. Bucer.

units.la: MYCONIVS CALVINO.
units.tr: Myconius to Calvin.

units.la: Quia hactenus scribendi consuetudo non fuit inter nos, Caluine doctissime, potuissem & nunc supersedere, nisi legati Genevenses tam officiose tuo me nomine salutassent, & f.iiij.
units.tr: Since there has hitherto been no custom of writing between us, most learned Calvin, I could have let this pass even now, had the Genevan envoys not greeted you on my behalf so courteously and asked me to write something to you.

units.la: petiissent vt aliquid ad te perscriberem.Gaudeo igitur in primis, quod intelligo ex literis Bernatum, quàm bellè inter vos conueniat, id enim fuit vel primum quamobrem ego folicitus cum illis egerim,vt omni studio niterentur, vt in Domino foueretis concordiam. Videbatur ea res habitura momenti aliquid,vt fa- cilius inter ciuitates quoque fieret in posterum reconciliatio.Id quod etiamnum insidet,tantùm vos qui estis à concionibus,quod verum est,adhibere ne negligatis.Qui in Domino & eius doctri na sunt amici,non videntur indigere labore, vt in cæteris etiam fiant concordes.Quod illi scripserunt de te,idem scribunt de Fa- rello:itaque spes est,vt amicitia sic manete,propediem audituri fructum aliquem simus,quales ex eiusmodi radice solent suppul lulare.Gaudium illud eo maius est in me,quàm hactenus sensi, quantum sit malum in Ecclesiis dissidiû inter fratres.Bone Deus quàm ea res deuastauit nos! Nam etiam Carolo stadio defuncto, non video fierine queat,vt Ecclesia nostra coalescat aliquando: adeo semen odij ac inuidiæ à malo isto Satana seminatum est, qui haud nouit quiescere præsertim vbi Christi gloria per Eum gelij synceram prædicationem efflorescit. Quia cœpi, dicam, quod non institueraм, rem, imò dogma valde turbulentum ac pestilens,in quo se quidam miris versant modis laici,sed in po- testate positi,siquando possint nos,qui Verbo præsumus,auho- ritatemque nostram labefactare. Senatus inquiunt, Ecclesii est. Alij sic efferunt,Ecclesia super curiam est. Quæ ratio sit dorma- tis patet: libertatem nostram vellent opprimere cùm in docen- do,tum in corripiendo : nam etiam nunc excommunicationis vim omnem ad se rapuerunt.At quis sit auctor,etsi noui,l ben- ter hoc tempore in dubium verto. Non bene erit illi quoidam coram tribunali Christi. Quid animi verò putas,Caluine,inesse tali viro,nisi quòd hac ratione,quicquid prius vendicauit in mu nere Ecclesiastico sibi Papa,illud ipsum,quisquis ille tandem,co natur vendicare Magistratui? Consilium hoc tanto peius,quàto Magistratus hodie sunt à literis atque à cognitione rerum diui- narum & Ecclesiasticarum remotiores. Aiunt Mosem principe seculorem(sic didicerunt ab authore dogmatis)præscripsisse Aa- roni fratri omnia, Dauidem Regem sacerdotibus, aliosque re- ges pios:quidni igitur fieret idem in sacerdotio noui Testamen- ti? Quid si laicis huiusmodi argumentis fuerit persuasum? Hæc breuiter apud te dicta velim non etiam apud alios:& gratum fa- ceres,si per otium ad ea respondere aliquando mihi,par reddi- turo,vbiubi fuerit occasio & facultas.De Vireto scribam ad Bar- nates cum primum potero,sed fratrum nomine,vt auctoritassit maior,siquid impetrari valeat.Vellemus enim & nos istam Ec- clesiam esse,in bonum aliarum,quàm instrutissimam.Bucerus abiit,si nescis, Spiram ad Comitia, profecturus forsitan inde Coloniam. Quid illic negotij sit, nondum comperi. De Comitiorum actis ideo nemo quicquam nouit, quod adhuc non omnes sunt congregati. Spargitur dissensionem esse inter Principes & Ciuitates ob pecuniam, & milites dandos contra Turcam. Gaudeo quod Christus Dominus est, alioqui totus defperasset. Ille seruet Ecclesiam suam. Vale in Christo cum Vireto mihi charissimo, & cum tota Ecclesia tua. Basileae, x. Februarij anno M. D. XLII.
units.tr: I rejoice first of all, then, because I learn from your letters how well you agree with one another. This was indeed the main reason why I took trouble with those men, that they should strive with every effort to maintain harmony in the Lord. That matter seemed likely to carry some weight, so that reconciliation between the cities too might come about more easily in future. It still persists, provided that you who are the preachers, as is true, do not neglect to apply yourselves to it. Those who are friends in the Lord and in his teaching do not seem to need effort to be made agreeable in other matters as well. What they have written about you, they write about Farel too. So there is hope that, if friendship remains as it is, we shall soon hear of some fruit, such as usually springs from a root of this kind. That joy is greater in me than I have felt until now, by how great an evil discord among brothers is in the churches. Good God, how that thing has laid us waste! For even now that Carlstadt is dead, I do not see whether our church can ever be brought together. So deeply has the seed of hatred and envy been sown by that evil Satan, who knows not how to be quiet, especially where the glory of Christ shines forth through the sincere preaching of the Gospel. I shall say what I have not undertaken: a matter, or rather a doctrine, very troublesome and pestilent, in which certain laymen, though placed in subjection, busy themselves in wonderful ways, whenever they can, to weaken us who preside over the Word and to shake our authority. "The Senate," they say, "is the Church." Others put it more boldly: "The Church is above the court." What their aim is, is plain enough: they would wish to oppress our freedom both in teaching and in rebuke, for even now they have seized for themselves the whole power of excommunication. But who the author is, though I know him, I am reluctant at this time to name. It will not go well with that certain man before the tribunal of Christ. What spirit, do you think, Calvin, lies in such a man, unless that by this method he means to claim for the magistrate whatever the Pope formerly claimed for himself in the ecclesiastical office? This counsel is so much the worse, as the magistrates today are further removed from letters and from knowledge of divine and ecclesiastical matters. They say that Moses, as prince of the people (so they learned from the author of the doctrine), prescribed everything to his brother Aaron, David to the priests, and other pious kings likewise. Why, then, should not the same happen in the priesthood of the New Testament? What if laymen have been persuaded by arguments of this kind? I would like these things said briefly to you and not also to others. And you would do me a kindness if, at your leisure, you would at some time reply to these matters for me; I shall repay in kind wherever and whenever there is occasion and opportunity. I will write to the Bernese about Viret as soon as I can, but in the name of the brothers, so that the authority may be greater, if anything can be obtained. For we too would wish that church to be, for the good of the others, most thoroughly equipped. Bucer has left, if you do not know, for Speyer for the Diet, perhaps going from there to Cologne. What business he has there I have not yet learned. Nothing is known of the proceedings of the Diet for the reason that not all have yet assembled. It is rumoured that there is dissension between the princes and the cities over money and over soldiers to be given against the Turk. I rejoice that Christ the Lord is, otherwise he would have despaired entirely. May he preserve his Church. Farewell in Christ, with Viret, most dear to me, and with your whole church. Basel, 10 February, in the year 1542.

units.la: Of Myconius tuus.
units.tr: Yours, Myconius.

units.la: Melanchthon Calvino.
units.tr: Melanchthon to Calvin.

units.la: EX nundinis Francfordiensibus epistola ad me tua transmissa est, exempla vero editi scripti non sunt allata, tardius enim Francfordiam allata fuerant. Postea Bonnae apud D. Bucerum nactus exemplum, vidi τὴν ἀρχαῖον ψυχὴν ad me, & subito bonam partem disputationis euolui. Quod autem honorifico testimonio ornaris, & de tota re, non solum pie, sed etiam eloquenter disseruceris, de vtraque re, videlicet de mea gratitudine, & de ipsa disputatione coram nos, vt soliti sumus quoties vna fuimus, prolixe colloqui posse optarim: etsi enim tantum vel ingenij vel doctrinae mihi non arrogo quantum tribuis, & nos imprimis in Ecclesia agnoscete imbecillitatem nostram decet: tamen beneuolentia erga me tua vehementer delector, tibique gratiam habeo, quod in scripto luculento tanquam in illustri posita loco extare significationem amoris erga me tui volui. Gratum mihi & illud testimonium tuum esse ingenue fateor, quod me & amare & quaerere simplicitatem dicis. Nam praedicare bona conscientia potium fuisse hoc meum studium, cum initio harum contentionum, multa horridius & intricatius disputarentur, vt excerperem res vtiles, easque, ex illa caligine euolutas, quantum possem, plane & dextre recitarem, nec raro illud Euripidis mihi venit in metem, ἔσθλον τὸ σαφὲς, & ἀσφαλὲς τὸ μὴ σαφὲς: nec nihil periculi adijdum quaedam praecidi confragosiora: retinui vero & illustraui vtilia, quod tamen verecunde feci, ne irritatis vehementioribus ingeniis, discordias magis inflammarem. Fuit enim hoc quoque mihi curae, nostrum hoc est Ecclesiae consensum, in maioribus causis vt tueter. Vides enim quam multae aliae causae vtilissimae motae sint: vt autem ducum ars est leuiora & παρέργα interdum relinquere, ne impediantur in persequendis necessariis, ita nobis videndum est de quibus rebus maxime dimicandum sit. Pontifices maiori spe quam vnquam suas εἰς ψολομαχίας propugnant. Arbitratur enim stultitia
units.tr: Your letter to me was sent on from the Frankfurt fair, but the copies of the published writing were not brought, for they had been brought to Frankfurt more slowly. Afterwards, at Bonn, I obtained a copy from Dr. Bucer, I saw the Ancient Soul [τὴν ἀρχαῖον ψυχήν], and I suddenly unrolled a good part of the disputation. As for the fact that you honour me with an honourable testimony, and have discussed the whole matter not only piously but also eloquently, I would wish to be able to talk at length with you about both things, namely my gratitude and the disputation itself, face to face, as we have been accustomed to do whenever we were together. For although I do not claim for myself as much cleverness or learning as you attribute to me, and it is fitting for us especially in the Church to acknowledge our weakness, nevertheless I take great delight in your goodwill towards me, and I thank you that you wished to place in a brilliant writing, as on a conspicuous spot, a sign of your love for me. I frankly confess that your testimony is also welcome to me, in which you say that I both love and seek simplicity. For my aim in this has been rather to preach with a good conscience, since at the beginning of these disputes many things were argued in a very rough and tangled way, so that I might pick out the useful matters and, drawing them out of that fog, set them forth as plainly and skilfully as I could. Often the saying of Euripides came into my mind: "Clear is noble, and unclear is safe" [ἔσθλον τὸ σαφὲς, καὶ ἀσφαλὲς τὸ μὴ σαφὲς]. Nor was there no danger in it, since I had to cut off some rather rough points; but I kept and clarified what was useful, and I did this with restraint, so that I would not, by provoking the more violent wits, inflame discord further. For this too has been my concern: to defend our consensus of the Church in the greater matters. For you see how many other very useful causes have been raised. Just as it is the art of generals sometimes to leave aside lighter matters and side issues, lest they be hindered in pursuing what is necessary, so we must consider on which matters the struggle ought most to be fought. The Pontiffs defend their logomachies [εἰς ψολομαχίας] with greater hope than ever before. For they reckon, in their folly, that our doctrines will fall with our princes, whom they see entangled in civil wars and provoking Charles, who until now has been holding back and, as it were, shunning German wars.

units.la: Referenda ad annum 1543. nostrorum Principum nostra dogmata ruitura esse, quos videt implicari bellis ciuilibus, & irritare Carolum hastenus cessantem & quasi fugitantem bella Germanica. Etsi hoc tanto malo moueor, quod quidem sæpe prædixi vaticinans, [Greek] cùm principum [Greek] & alios morbos viderem: tamen scio Deum inter fatales Imperiorum tumultus Ecclesiam suam seruare mirabiliter. Non igitur frangamur animis, sed dum possumus, sonemus, vt cõuersus latro in cruce, doctrinam de Filio Dei, deque arcana sapientia, quæ est Ecclesiæ propria, de magnitudine humanæ infirmitatis, de pœnitentia, & fiducia promissæ misericordiæ propter Filium, de vera inuocatione & veris Ecclesiæ virtutibus, de mysteriis non polluendis, de Ecclesiæ politia, non illa quam singunt Pontifices, sed qualis fuit Prophetarum & Apostolorum, denique de vita æterna. Ad harum maximarum rerum doctrinam ornandam transferas velim eloquentiam tuam: quæ & confirmare nostros, & terrere aduersarios, & sanabiles iuuare poterit. Cuius est enim oratio hoc tempore in disputando, vel neruosior, vel splendidior? Nostra vel propter ingenij infirmitatem, vel propter eas ærumnas quibus consumpta est naturæ vis, si quia fuit, est squalidior. Magnopere igitur gaudeo Diuinitus te ad Euangelij explicationem excitatum esse, téque illa Apostoli voce adhortor quam scribit ad Timothæũ [Greek]. Etsi autem videor [Greek], tamen ad confirmados animos hæ mutuæ seu cohortationes, seu consolationes, præsertim in Ecclesia aliquid conducunt, vt Paulus se ait velle [Greek] aliorum piorum officiis ac commonefactione: satis vbique est hostium qui Domino bellum inferunt, qui nos delere conantur, eò sit firmior consensus noster, [Greek]. Fortassis nostra Germania paulò post à Turcis vastabitur, quod si fiet, eò magis vobis alibi in locis tutioribus studia literarum excitanda erunt, & pugnandum vehementius, vt in reliqua Europa Euangelij luce accendatis, & retineatis. Quod ad quæstionem de prædestinatione, habebam amicum Tubingę doctum hominem Francifcum Stadianum, qui dicere solebat, se vtrunque probare, euenire omnia, vt Diuina prouidentia decreuit & tamen esse contingentia: sed se hęc conciliare non posse. Ego cùm hypothesin hanc teneam, Deum non esse causam peccari, nec velle peccatum, postea contingentiam in hac nostra infirmitate iudicij admitto, vt sciant rudes Dauidem sua volun tate vltrò ruere, & eúdem sentio, cùm haberet Spiritu sanctum, potuisse eum retinere, & in ea lucta aliquam est voluntatis actionem. Hæc etiam si subtilius disputari possunt, tamen ad regendas mentes hoc modo proposita, accommodata videntur.
units.tr: To be referred to the year 1543. Although I am moved by this great evil, which I often foretold in prophecy when I saw the [Greek] and other diseases of princes, yet I know that God marvellously preserves his Church amid the fated tumults of empires. Let us not, therefore, lose heart, but while we can, let us sound out, as the thief converted on the cross did, the teaching concerning the Son of God and the hidden wisdom which is proper to the Church; concerning the greatness of human weakness; concerning repentance and trust in the promised mercy for the Son's sake; concerning true invocation and the true virtues of the Church; concerning the mysteries not to be profaned; concerning the polity of the Church, not that which the Pontiffs invent, but such as was that of the Prophets and Apostles; and finally concerning eternal life. I would wish you to turn your eloquence to adorning the teaching of these greatest matters, which can both confirm our people, terrify our adversaries, and help those who may be healed. For whose speech in disputation at this time is either more sinewy or more brilliant? Ours, whether because of the weakness of our wit or because of those hardships by which the strength of nature has been worn down, if it ever had any, is rather squalid. I therefore rejoice greatly that you have been roused by God to the explanation of the Gospel, and I exhort you with that voice of the Apostle which he writes to Timothy [Greek]. Although I seem [Greek], yet these mutual exhortations or consolations, whether by way of encouragement, especially in the Church, contribute something to strengthening minds, just as Paul says he wishes [Greek] by the offices and reminders of other pious people. There are enough enemies everywhere who make war on the Lord and try to destroy us; so much the firmer should our consensus be [Greek]. Perhaps our Germany will shortly be laid waste by the Turks; if that happens, all the more must the study of letters be stirred up for you elsewhere, in safer places, and you must fight more vigorously, so that you may kindle and keep the light of the Gospel in the rest of Europe. As for the question about predestination: I had a friend at Tübingen, a learned man, Franciscus Stadianus, who used to say that he held both things, that all things come about as divine providence has decreed, and yet that they are contingent; but that he could not reconcile these. For my part, while I hold this hypothesis, that God is not the cause of sin nor wills sin, I then admit contingency in the judgement of our weakness, so that the untaught may know that David rushed headlong by his own will; and I think likewise that, although he had the Holy Spirit, he could have held himself back, and that in that struggle there is some action of the will. Even if these things can be argued more subtly, yet as set forth in this way for guiding minds they seem well suited.

units.la: Accusemus ipsi nostram voluntatem cum labimur, non quaeramus in Dei consilio causam & contra eum nos erigamus, sciamus Deum & velle opitulari,& adeste luctatibus:μόνον Θέλησον, inquit Basilius,καὶ Θεὸς προσταυτά. Excitetur ergo cura in nobis,& laudetur Dei immensa bonitas, quum & promisit auxilium & praestat.Sed perentibus,vt inquit Dominus,hoc est iis qui promissionem intuentur. Nam a verbo Dei ordiendum est, nec repugnandum promissioni, sed ei assentiamur, nec disputemus antea,tunc nos adsensuros esse,cum arcanum decretum Dei nobis monstratum fuerit: adsentientem autem Deus adiuuat, qui per verbum est efficax. Haec non scribo vt tibi tradam quasi dictata,homini & eruditissimo ac peritissimo exercitiorum pietatis.Et quidem scio haec cum tuis congruere,sed sunt παχύτερα, & ad vsum accommodata. Haec Bonnae scripsi apud D.Bucerum, cum eo accersitus est vt Ecclesias in Diocesi Coloniensi, emendaret. Haec consilia Deo piis votis commendes. Rogo autem, vt mihi significes, an hanc epistolam acceperis. Nam si intelle xero certo ad te perferri meas literas,scribam saepius. Αντίδωρον tibi debeo,quare & grati animi significationem ostendam.Bene vale.x 1.Maij.
units.tr: Let us accuse our own will when we fall, and not look for the cause in God's counsel or set ourselves against him. Let us know that God is willing to help and to be present in our struggles: "Only will," says Basil, "and God will be at hand" [μόνον θέλησον, καὶ Θεὸς προσέσται]. Let the care in us be aroused, and let God's immense goodness be praised, since he has both promised help and gives it, to those who seek it, as the Lord says, that is, to those who look to the promise. For we must begin from the Word of God, not resist the promise but assent to it, and not dispute beforehand that we will assent only once the hidden decree of God has been shown to us. God helps the one who assents, for his Word is effective. I do not write these things as if to hand you a set of rules, you who are most learned and most skilled in the exercises of piety. I know that these things agree with your own, but they are cruder and adapted to practical use. I wrote this at Bonn, at the house of Master Bucer, who was summoned there to reform the churches in the diocese of Cologne. Commend these counsels to God with your pious prayers. I ask you to let me know whether you have received this letter. If I learn for certain that my letters reach you, I will write more often. I owe you an antidoron [ἀντίδωρον] in return, and so I will show you a sign of a grateful mind. Farewell well. 1 May.

units.la: Philippus Melanchthon.
units.tr: Philipp Melanchthon.

units.la: FARELLVS CAL.
units.tr: FAREL TO CALVIN

units.la: Vlde quae mentitur Carolus, dignus qui Pontifici seruiat: sed pudet Pontificios talem admittere, qui tam impudenter sit impudens. Et sane illi contigit quod inter sceleratos non raro euenit, vt sit aliquis adeo conscelleratus, vt scelesti ferre eum non possint. Venit primum Geneuam non expectatus neque expetitus,alios enim cupiebamus habere,vt pium Stapulensem, qui non sine lacrymis audiebat, gratias agens Deo, ordinem Ecclesiarum: & cupiebat,vt erat amans Galliae,ita videre compositas Ecclesias. Vbi venisset, dicebant omnes Episcopum Gallicum venisse, & erat apparatus, non pecunia ipsius Caroli,sed aliorum qui cum eo erant, quique quesiti tadem sunt de iniuria ipsis facta, vt is qui docuit apud D.Geruasium, Ioannes Tardiuus,qui aiebat se ab eo aliquot circunuentum coronatis. Nos hominem inuisimus in diuersorio, & post salutationem,agere coepimus de ratione dispensationis diuinae, quod vt geat ad confessionem sui nominis refugientes, & qui veritatem cognitam dissimulant: vt Carolo dicebamus euenisse, qui immerito pulsus esset, cum nihil egisset Pontifice indignum, nec Christo dignum. Gallia exierat,nunc absens scribendo praestaret ac resarciret, quod tacendo & dissimulando damni Ecclesiae.
units.tr: See what lies Charles tells, a man worthy to serve the Pope. But it shames the Papists to admit such a man, one who is so shamelessly shameless. And indeed what happened to him often happens among the wicked: someone is so utterly wicked that even the wicked cannot tolerate him. He first came to Geneva, neither expected nor sought, for we had wanted others, such as the pious Stapulensis, who listened to our ordering of the churches with tears, giving thanks to God, and who, since he loved France, longed to see the churches set in order in the same way. When Charles arrived, everyone said that a French bishop had come, and there was a display, not paid for by Charles himself but by others who were with him. These men were afterwards questioned about the wrong done to them, such as John Tardivus, who taught at the house of Master Gervase, and who said that he had been surrounded by several men with tonsures. We visited the man at his lodging, and after the greeting we began to speak about the plan of God's dispensation: how it leads those who flee to the confession of his name, and those who hide the truth they know, as we told Charles it had happened to him, since he had been driven out undeservedly, when he had done nothing unworthy of the Pope or worthy of Christ. He had left France; now, by writing from afar, he could make up for the harm he had done to the Church by silence and dissimulation.

units.la: Epist.49. dederat. Non fuit satis grata Carolo haec cantio, quae in prandio canebatur. Aliud erat consilium, nempe de remittendo in Galliam famulo, qui dum curaret aliquid emungere de sacerdotiis Caroli, apud nonnullos efficeret, ut erogarent pecunias in vsus pauperum Gallorum qui multi confluerent. Ego mirabar homines studium, quod statim anxius esset de pauperibus, edoctus quosdam monachos paria olim mouisse, & Lutetiae emunxisse aliquid pecuniae, de qua nihil resciui vnquam pauperibus datum: ac noui quosdam nolle quaedam pauperibus extstame ito relicta dispensare, nisi tam clam vt nemo resciat: & non l gantis nomine, sed ipsorum, si quid dent: & tamen plus videbantur illi in pauperes affecti quam Carolus. Ideo quod nunquam emendicaram, nolui suasu Caroli ordiri: sed dixi prius nobis agedum esse, vt panis verbi detur animo quam cibus corpori: eum qui haetenus prospexit pauperibus, nobis non defuturum neq; pauperibus. Cum dies aliquot egisset, ac tum ipse, tum alij qui cum eo erant non imminuerent famam quae spargebatur de Episcopo, & qui pro Euangelio laborabamus eam non minuetemus, quanuis modestius loqueremur aliis, rati non prorsus incommodaturum cursui Verbi (quod non prorsus contemnendi aliunde migrarent ad loca vbi Euangelium praedicatur) coepi rogare Carolum vt concionaretur, & id instantius: sed is multa causatus, nimirum quod nouus aduentaffet, vellétque plenius rationem tenere docendi, ferapi concionibus nostris, & id genus alia addens, petebat ne grauatè ferremus, si statim non concionaretur. Doluit id nobis, fateor, sed alius dolor hoc nobis in gaudium vertit. Siquidem intelleximus Magistrum nostrum theologice agere, hoc est vino theologico magistraliter & sorbonice vti, & quod sequitur, habere quae lectum eius sternerent, tibialia exuerent, ac familiarius dormituro adessent, vt alia taceam. Hic nos certiores facti hominem admonemus de iudicio Dei, de offendiculo omnium, & obtestamur propter Deum, vt frustra nō patiatur propter verbum pulsus Gallia, nec agat aliquid Christiano indignum. Videbatur non prorsus respuere quae primo dicebantur, & qui cum eo agebant, spem aliquam faciebant: quanuis dicerent hominem sui amantem, sibi vixisse & indulsisse genio: tamen pergendum: quod dum fit, incipit peccata sua tueri, & pergere. Nos admonemus si nobis adesse nolit, & prodest se non studeat, non aduertetur in tanto rerum discrimine, cum luctandum nobis sit cum tot monstris, vt nulla prorsus sit spes domari ea posse, nisi praesentissima virtute Dei id fiat: Non pergat sua improba agendi ratione cursum Euangelij impedire: is neque nos audiuit, neque tamen aperte ausus quicquam fuit: sed clam in deterius proficiens, palam videbatur cautius pergere.
units.tr: (Epistle 49.) He had given it. This caution, which was sung at dinner, was not very pleasing to Charles. Another plan was in view, namely to send back to France a servant who, while trying to extract something from Charles's benefices, would persuade some people to hand over money for the relief of the many poor French who were flocking together. I was surprised at the man's zeal, that he was at once so anxious about the poor, since I had learned that certain monks had once made the same display and had extracted some money at Paris, of which I never learned that anything reached the poor. I also knew that some people did not want to distribute to the poor what had been left to them in a public manner, but only so secretly that no one would find out, and in the name not of the one who was giving but of themselves, if they gave anything at all. Yet those men seemed more affectionate towards the poor than Charles was. For this reason, since I had never begged, I did not want to begin at Charles's urging. Instead I said that we must first see to it that the bread of the Word is given to the soul, before food is given to the body; he who had hitherto provided for the poor would not fail us or the poor. After some days had passed, and since neither he nor the others who were with him diminished the rumour spreading about the bishop, and since we who labored for the Gospel did not lessen it either, although we spoke more modestly to others, judging that it would not be at all harmful to the course of the Word (for those who were not at all to be despised were migrating from elsewhere to places where the Gospel is preached), I began to ask Charles to preach, and to do so more urgently. But he, offering many excuses, namely that he had only just arrived and wished to hold a fuller account of teaching, said that he would bear with our sermons, and adding other things of that kind, he asked that we not take it amiss if he did not preach at once. This grieved us, I confess, but another grief turned this into joy for us. For we understood that our Master was acting theologically, that is, using theological wine in the manner of a master and of the Sorbonne, and what follows, that he had people to spread his bed, to take off his stockings, and to be present for him as he went to sleep more intimately, to say nothing of other things. Here we, having been made aware of this, warned the man about God's judgment and about the stumbling-block to everyone, and we begged him, for God's sake, not to suffer in vain, having been driven from France on account of the Word, nor to do anything unworthy of a Christian. He seemed not to reject altogether what was first said to him, and those who dealt with him gave some hope. Yet they said the man loved himself, had lived for himself and indulged his own disposition; still, he had to be pressed on, and while this was being done, he began to defend his sins and to persist in them. We warned him that if he was unwilling to be present with us, and if he did not care to be useful, he would not notice in so great a crisis of affairs, when we have to struggle with so many monsters, that there is no hope at all of taming them unless this is done by the most present power of God. He should not, by his wicked manner of acting, go on impeding the course of the Gospel. He neither heeded us nor ventured openly to do anything, but, growing worse in secret, he seemed in public to proceed more cautiously.

units.la: Pontificiis inuidiosus cum effet, nihil commercij cum eis habe-bat: nostra consuetudine non multum oblectabatur, licet nos haberet familiariores. Interea Bernardus cogitabat de exuenda cuculla: quod vbi nobis indicauit, respondimus hoc parum esse, nisi cum aedificatione maiori id faceret, ita vt omnes factum probarent: quod sane fieret si poneret aliqua, quibus doceret se legitime id facere, & id omnibus apertis rationibus persuaderet, seque ad respondendum omnibus publica disputatione offerret: quod placuit Bernardo, &, vt suadebamus, Senatum adiit & disputationem impetrauit, quam nosdesperabamus, nostro nomine posse impetrari. Sed quia Bernardus ciuis erat, &, cum conuenissent Minores Gratianopoli, vbi Capitulum quod vocant (ita suos conuentus & Synodos nominant) celebrabant, di cebat se cupere illos ad disputationem vocari: annuit ad omnia Senatus Geneuensis: & quanuis Pontificiorum erat pars maior, tamen ita omnibus placuit, & missae fuerunt ad conuentum literae, vbi praerat a Cornibus. Satagebat per Bernardum Carolus vt praesideret in disputatione, & omnia resolueret. Nos rati nihil prosperè cessurum, quod tam arroganter fieret (videbamus enim inanis gloriae hominem appetentissimum) & Deo & Scripturae suum honorem saluum esse cupientes, Dominum tantum ex Scriptura omnia resoluentem diximus esse audiendum: cautum satis esse si essent qui curarent ne insolentius quis ferretur in disputatione, iuberentque vt partes pacatè inuicem audirent & loqueretur, idque liberè, quod & factum fuit: licet primus qui disputare coepit tergiuersando nollet alium respondere quam Bernardum qui proposuerat. Sed facile fuit ex iis quae proposita fuerant illi satisfacere.
