Actum est de libero arbitrio: nos abundè ex Scripturis satisfecimus, nec in eo plurimum laboris impendum fuit, nec praecipua erat controuersia nobis & Pontificiis, vt de merito Fideique iustificatione. Tamen super negotio liberi arbitrij non infeliciter locutus est Carolus, aperiens quid certaminis fuisset cum Pelagianis Augustino, & quod vidi abierint. Primò quod initium boni operis a nobis non esset, sed a gratia quae nos praeuenit: ita & progressus & consummationem boni operis gratiae deberi, & frustra hominem conari sine gratia nec ordiri, nec prosequi, nec perseuerare posse. Quod vbi fecisset, nosque grati commendaremus (quid enim aliud cupiebamus quam gloriam Dei & plebis aedificationem? quae cum cerneremus, laeti approbamus) tunc coepit Carolus argutari de successione regni terreni Christi, quod superstes Virgo post Filij mortem haeres fuerit. Bernardus nobis non adeo curantibus respondebat succedere matrem filio. Sed mox respondi non opus esse hic agere de terrena haereditate, cum Christi regnum non fit ex hoc mundo, bene conuenire inter virginem Christi matrem & filium, nec quenquam explebe adelle vt intelligat quo iure mater velit filio intentare actionem, & quid ex successione petat: sed in hoc omnes conuenisse vt intelligant an quæ Pontifex instituit & quæ seruant Pontificij ex Deo sint vel contra, vt de missa, cultu diuorum, & aliis traditionibus humanis. Hinc factum est vt ad alia se conuerterit, quæ in positis haberentur, & missam aggreslus est tueri: sed tamen ingenuè fassus est posita vera esse, pia & Christiana, sèque ea nolle impugnare quod falsa sint aut talia credat, cùm verissima essentiat: sed vt omnes intelligant rationem aduersariorum, daturum se operâ vt omnes ipsorum rationes & potiores etiam adducat, neq; omissurũ quicquam: quod & fecit diligenter. Et quanuis partem nostis impendiet in annotandis rationibus quibus pollet missa ferri, nos tamen vt nemo auditorum non potest hodie testificari, hominem memoria labentem & non satis tenentem quæ annotarat adiuuabamus vt sua formaret argumenta: sciebamus enim vnde desumpsisset. Cùmque id fieret, fatebatur se velle id dicere quod nos ab eo petebamus an vellet dicere, tantum abest vt argumenta ipsius effugeremus, aut timeremus, vt gratum esset etiá adiuuare. Aliqui ex Pontificiis, dum audirent rationes quæ ipsis placebant, non audita responsione abibant ad Canonicos, & Carolum commendabant: illi non ingrati vinum mittebant, & hortabantur vt strenuè se gereret. Is recipiebat se omnia effecturũ, iubens eos nihil moueri, si visus fuerit missam primò damnasse & inter disputandum nonnulla damnet in ea: se tamen ita rursus eam corroboraturũ, vt quàm firmissima maneat. Sed qui audierunt vtrosque, possunt referre quàm id effecerit. Nã & argumenta in fumum omnia abibat, nec poterat stare sacrificium & redemptio viuorum & mortuorum, non inuocatio diuorum, a-ctio quę peregrina fit lingua, adoratio panis & particularis sumptio Sacramenti, & id genus alia, quibus tota fœret missa. Cùmq; Viretus tam aperte dissoluere tomnia, vt adstantium nemo non assentiretur (scis quàm ille appositè & diserte possit aliquid explicare) Carolus armis exutus, nescius quid aliud afferret, cœpit o-re diducto insani more vociferari longum ba ba ba. Ego hominis dementiam taxans, quòd senex Theologus, & qui haberi velit ex numero eorum qui professi sunt Euangelium Christi, modestiam abiiceret, cùm iuuenem quem vt tyronem reputat, vixque censendum in numero aliquo Pastorum, ita suo exemplo formet, ea admittendo quæ nulla ratione in iuuene esse nt teren da. Si Christus & Apostoli ita cum Pharisæis, Scribis & aliis aduersariis egissent, an ita plantassent Euangelium? quid dicturi essent de nobis Euangelij hostes & aduersarij, si nos ita satisfacemus remus eorum rationibus?num tam impudens essetquòd coram plebe empta Christi sanguine, quæ conuenit vt intelligat quid sequi debeat,non rubore suffunderetur ita insanè agendo?Et sanè hominis amentiam tam potenter compescui,vt ipse,quanuis assuetus meretricia fronte omnia agere & pati,totus pudefieret, nec postea ausus fuerit tam temerè ferri.Quòd tam impudenter mentitur suis non fuisse satisfactum rationibus, vel vnam afferat cui non fuerit plus satis respònsum. Nolo hic interrogari eos qui non fuerant nobis aperti hostes, nec causæ æquiores, sed iuratissimos hostes ex familia Episcopi, qui cum nunquam antea nos audiuissent, & sperarent Carolum triumphaturum in tuendis sacris Pontificiis quæ diuinissima reputabant: cum audirent nos,tacti fuere intelligentes humana & impia esse quæ diuina sanctissimáque arbitrabantur. Et cum vellet suas significationes in vestibus & nescio quandam obseruantiam augustiorem in lingua peregrina & suis à magicis nihil euariantibus signis & actionibus & aliis quibus Cœna Domini prorsus sublata fuit & obscurata obtrudere: nos contrà proponebamus Christum qui purius docuit Patrem nem pe Spiritu & veritate,sublatis umbris adorandum vt iam non sit petendus Mons neque Ierosolyma. Cúmque sanctus Rex Ezechias serpentem æneum iussu Domini conflatum & erectum in quo Deus præsentissimam virtutem suam exeruit, fanatis, dum insplcerent serpentem, laesis à serpentibus: cuius beneficij seruatos serpens admonebat,& aliud longè maius præsagiebat,non fictum humano commento,sed quod Christus reuelauit, nempe Iesum ipsum ita exaltandum esse: & salutem daturum: hæc omnia cum diuina fuerint, nec fugerint sanctum Regem , non tamen ideo censuit tantum incumbendum vt tolleretur superstitio, quod aegrè sciebat se impetraturum, sed prorsus serpentem ignominiosè iussit comminuendum: quid Christianis ducibus & magistratibus non est faciendum in iis quorum superstitio & cultus omnem idololatriam Iudæorum superat? in iis quæ homines malè feriati erexerunt, quibus significationes ex arbitrio addiderunt, vnus sic , alter aliter? Vbi habemus purum Christi institutum , quem scimus omnium sapientissimum & considerantissimum: nec dubitamus fideliter fuisse conscripta à sacris scriptoribus Apostolis & Euangelistis , quæ faciunt ad rem. Hic scilicet potuit hisce re Carolus: qui ex iis quæ sensit in se Geneuæ quantum poterant occurrere , dum videbat locum esse in disputatione Laufannensi vtebatur , vt nos anteuerteret: quod sanè nobis non erat ingratum. Nam quid attulit Laufannæ quod contra eum Geneuæ non fuerit dictum , præter vnam de transubstantiatione,
units.tr: Since he was hated by the Papists, he had no dealings with them, and he took little pleasure in our company, although he regarded us as more familiar friends. Meanwhile Bernard was thinking of laying aside the cowl. When he told us this, we replied that it would be of little value unless he did it with greater edification, so that everyone would approve the act. This would indeed happen if he set out grounds on which he could show that he was acting lawfully, persuaded everyone of it by clear reasons, and offered himself to answer all comers in a public disputation. This pleased Bernard, and, as we urged, he approached the Senate and obtained a disputation, which we had despaired of obtaining in our own name. But because Bernard was a citizen, and the Minorites had gathered at Grenoble, where they held what they call the Chapter (for so they name their assemblies and synods), he said he wished them to be summoned to the disputation. The Senate of Geneva agreed to everything. Although the Papists were the greater part, it was nevertheless pleasing to all, and letters were sent to the assembly, which was presided over by Cornibus. Through Bernard, Caroli strove to preside over the disputation and settle everything. We thought nothing would go well if it were done so arrogantly (for we saw that the man was greedy for empty glory), and, wishing that the honour of God and of Scripture be kept safe, we said that the Lord alone, resolving all things from Scripture, was to be heard. It was enough of a safeguard, we said, if there were men who took care that no one should be borne along too insolently in the disputation, and who ordered that the parties listen to and speak with one another calmly and freely; and this was done, although the first man who began to dispute, evading the question, did not want to answer anyone but Bernard, who had made the proposal. But it was easy to satisfy him from the things that had been put forward. The question of free will was settled: we satisfied them fully from Scripture, nor was much labour spent on that point, nor was it the chief controversy between us and the Papists, as were merit and justification by faith. Still, Caroli spoke not unsuccessfully on the matter of free will, explaining what the dispute had been with the Pelagians against Augustine, and where they had departed. First, that the beginning of a good work does not come from us but from the grace that goes before us; so the progress and completion of a good work are likewise owed to grace, and man cannot begin, pursue or persevere without grace, and his efforts are in vain. When he had done this, and we, being grateful, commended him (for what else did we desire but the glory of God and the edification of the people? Seeing this, we gladly approved), then Caroli began to quibble about the succession to Christ's earthly kingdom, that the Virgin, surviving the Son's death, was his heir. Bernard, while we were not greatly concerned, replied that the mother succeeds the son. But I soon answered that there was no need to deal here with an earthly inheritance, since Christ's kingdom is not of this world; it agrees well enough between the Virgin, Christ's mother, and the Son, and no one is so foolish as not to understand by what right a mother would bring a suit against her son, and what she would seek by succession. Rather, all agreed on this: that they should understand whether the things the Pontiff has instituted, and which the Papists keep, come from God or are against him, such as the Mass, the worship of saints, and other human traditions. Hence it came about that he turned to other matters, which were regarded as settled, and undertook to defend the Mass. Yet he frankly confessed that the things laid down were true, pious and Christian, and that he did not wish to attack them as false or as things he believed to be such, since they were most true; but so that everyone might understand the reasoning of our opponents, he would take care to bring forward all their arguments, and the more important ones too, leaving out nothing. This he did diligently. And although you know he spent a part of his time in noting the arguments by which the Mass is supported, we nevertheless helped the man, who was slipping in memory and did not hold well what he had noted, so that he could shape his arguments (for we knew where he had taken them from). When this was done, he admitted that he was willing to say what we asked him whether he wished to say; so far were we from evading or fearing his arguments that it was pleasing even to help him. Some of the Papists, when they heard the reasons that pleased them, without hearing the reply went off to the Canons and commended Caroli; they, not ungratefully, sent him wine and urged him to acquit himself vigorously. He undertook to accomplish everything, bidding them not to be disturbed if he seemed to have first condemned the Mass and in the course of the disputation condemned some things in it; he would nevertheless so strengthen it again that it would remain most firm. But those who heard both sides can report how well he accomplished this. For all his arguments went up in smoke, and the sacrifice and redemption of the living and the dead could not stand, nor the invocation of saints, nor the action performed in a foreign tongue, nor the adoration of bread, nor the private reception of the Sacrament, and the other things of that kind by which the whole Mass is held together. When Viret dissolved all these so clearly that none of the bystanders failed to agree (you know how aptly and eloquently he can explain anything), Caroli, stripped of his weapons and not knowing what else to bring, began with his mouth wide open to shout "long ba ba ba," in the manner of a madman. I rebuked the man's madness, that an old theologian, who wishes to be counted among those who have professed the Gospel of Christ, should cast off his modesty, since he was training a young man, whom he regards as a novice and scarcely to be counted among any ministers, by his own example to admit things which in no way ought to be tolerated in a young man. If Christ and the Apostles had acted thus toward the Pharisees, the Scribes and their other adversaries, would they have planted the Gospel in this way? What would the enemies and adversaries of the Gospel say of us if we so satisfied their arguments? Would he not be so shameless as to blush before a people bought with the blood of Christ, who ought to understand what they must follow, by acting so insanely? Indeed I so powerfully curbed the man's folly that he himself, although accustomed to do and suffer everything with a brazen face, was utterly abashed, and afterwards did not dare to be carried away so rashly. As for his shameless lie that his arguments were not answered, let him produce just one to which a sufficient reply was not given. I do not want those questioned who were not open enemies to us, nor fairer in their cause, but the sworn enemies from the bishop's household, who, since they had never heard us before and hoped Caroli would triumph in defending the Papist rites, which they regarded as most divine, were moved when they heard us, understanding that what they thought divine and most holy was human and impious. And when he wished to force upon us his symbols in vestments, a certain more august reverence in a foreign tongue, and signs and actions taken from the magicians, which vary in nothing, and other things by which the Lord's Supper was utterly taken away and obscured, we on the contrary set forth Christ, who taught more purely that the Father is to be worshipped in spirit and truth, the shadows removed, so that the mountain and Jerusalem are no longer to be sought. And when the holy King Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent, which had been made and raised at the Lord's command, in which God displayed his most present power, because the fanatics, while they gazed upon the serpent, were wounded by serpents (the serpent, which had saved them from this benefit, was giving warning and foreshadowing something far greater, not feigned by human invention, but what Christ revealed: that Jesus himself was to be exalted in this way and would give salvation), although all these things were divine, and did not escape the holy King, he nevertheless did not think that he should devote himself so greatly to removing the superstition, since he knew he would hardly obtain it, but he ordered the serpent to be shamefully crushed to powder. What ought Christian leaders and magistrates not to do with those things whose superstition and worship surpass all the idolatry of the Jews? With things which ill-taught men have set up, to which they have added meanings at will, one this way and another that? Where we have the pure institution of Christ, whom we know to be the wisest and most thoughtful of all, and we do not doubt that the things pertinent to the matter were faithfully written down by the sacred writers, the Apostles and the Evangelists. Here Caroli could have answered, namely by those things which he felt in himself at Geneva, as far as they could occur to him, while he saw there was room in the Lausanne disputation, he used it to get ahead of us; which indeed was not unwelcome to us. For what did he bring at Lausanne that had not been said against him at Geneva, apart from the one deduction, as they call it, concerning transubstantiation? How adroitly he handled it, and the others not altogether clumsily! As for his writing that he was warned not to deal with us so precisely, was Caroli the man we feared? And did any fear ever hold us back from being conquered?

units.la: quam vocant, deductionem? quam dextre tractauit, vt alia non prorsus inepte? Quod scribit se admonitum ne tam praecise nobiscum ageret, scilicet Carolus erat quem timeremus? & aliquis aliquando metus nos tenuit ne vinceremur? Basileae vbi erat Esrasmus, Berus, Zicardus, Cantiuncula: theologi illi vt hi iurisperiti, in arenam descendimus, & sustinuimus argumenta non leuia nostrorum, vt Oecolampadij, Pellicani: sed Scripturis ita erant roborata, vt ne minimum quidem conuellere potuerint. Sed quis metus potest tenere eos qui certi sunt, dum stant pro veritate, ex promisso Dei, se habituros os & sapientiam cui omnes aduersarij non potuint resistere? & qui non propriam gloriam neque vt vincant quaerunt, sed gloriam Dei, & vt Christus & veritas vincat, & id petunt in priuatis & publicis precibus? At nouit Carolus nos ardentius precatos esse, & omnes ad preces inuitasse. Siquis forte nobis timens vt olim contigit, vbi primum vocabar ad praedicandum, & accurrissent aliqui magni vt videbantur, ego vero nullus videbar vt vere ex me sum: dicebant, quid faciet hic miser? vtinam nunquam venisset nec vocatus fuisset: non poterit subsistere, & omnes confundemur cum eo. Sed vbi collata fuerunt signa & vltro aduersarius ea quae volebamus tueri proponentes, in arenam aduersarium prouocaremus: ibi is quem tantopere nonnulli formidabant, dixit se nolle disputare, neque dignum esse qui librum posset mihi ferat. Si ita dictum fuerit Carolo non satis noui: sed quod ego neque Viretus vnquam cogitauerimus, hoc possumus certo affirmare: neque voluimus eum aliquid omittere eorum quae adduci possunt, imo potius, vt dixi, lapsum memoria & non satis tenentem quae dicenda erat, & vnde coepisset orationem, saepius in viam reducebamus. Quid tentarit sub finem disputationis, quam vt diximus, per Bernardum impetrauimus, non prorsus ignoramus: sed per D. effectu est vt illi non successerit. Recensita sunt quae tota disputatione fuerant tractata, ea fide vt intelligerent omnes rem ita habere: quid enim attinet in veritatis negotio, amanti veritatis aliud quam vera afferre? Inde ferio fuit admonitus Magistratus, vt officium faceret pro gloria Dei & plebis salute: fungeretur officio patris: non paterentur filios a D. sibi cocredito errare in iis quae tam aperte veritati diuinae repugnat, alioqui reus esset omnium quae admitterentur. Adducta exempla piorum qui praefuerunt populo, quod quam mouerit, ipsi norunt quibus dictum fuit. Carolus subinde cum Canonicis & cum aliis ex urbe tractabat. Quis metus hominem coegerit Geneuam deferere & montes circuire, nescio alium, nisi is fuerit qui contingit impio fugieti nemine persequente. Si dixisset Pontificios minatos fuisse Carolo, fortealiquibus, qui consuetudinem illius cum Pontificiis nescirent. Scirent,persuaderet:nā illi & multis minati sunt,& aggressi nonnullos,& varias coniurationes habuerunt: & saepius admonitus non timui, etsi viderim laedi & occidi nonnullos à Pontificiis: quod illis non bene cessit, nam aperta fuerunt eorum consilia. Sed quòd aliquis qui non esset Pontificius motum excitarit, vel aliquem ob religionem inuaserit, proferat si potest Carolus. Qui pacis tempore in urbe non ausus fuit agere neque aperta via ingredi, scilicet is est Carolus quem tam expectunt omnes perdere! tantus concionator! tam magnus disputator! ó quot plagas accepit! in quot discrimina incidit! quot & quanta passus est! Que Basileæ egerit, nonne pudet Gallos omnes referre tam stolidum è Gallia sese ita venditare in Germania? idque apud Grynaeum, cum quo si Carolum conferas, Therfiten conturleris Achilli. Inde secuta est vocatio in Ecclesiam Neocomensem: quàm cùm is non plantarit, nec aedificare adeo demum studuit, quàm fuerit legitima vocatio non dico. Quod nunc sentio vix potest impetrari, & quanuis, ut nofti, non sine magna anxietate data fuerit opera ut per optimos quosque iudicaretur quae sint partes Pastoris, quae Magistratus, quae plebis in debita vocatione Pastorū; quid non fit ut fixa non manent quae merito debent observari. Scilicet Carolus hac religione tenetur, ut caveat ne quid in vocatione desideretur, ut nosti quid oportuerit agere, ut is adducetur quem omnes Pastores praeter vnum exoptabant, & tota plebs cum Magistratu impensius rogabat. Sed ut intrant, boni scilicet, ita egrediantur. Quorsum attinebat Bernam mittere, & alibi interea herere, illinc ad Montem Bellegardium, & omnia dispicere ut locum haberet, tot precibus petere ut hominem adiuuaremus, & hesitasse quandiu potuit etiam cum vxore, e qua tuc genuit prolem. Sed quando finis esset? Cuperem te ex Vireto accipere ea quae non succurrunt mihi iam: nam vltra ea quae particulatim ipsum tangunt, potest fusius omnia persequi. Accedit quod hic nobis opportune sese obtulit cui libellum darem & omnia quae habeo. Et in primis est quod te rogem ut instes summa cura pro legatione ad Regem, quae si fieri potest, rotundè loquatur: nam literis minus fit quàm cantione. Sed si legatio mittatur & coram agatur mascule, non tantum iis pro quibus labo ratti succurretur, sed aliis qui passim periclitantur. Vale & precare D. pro nobis. Neocomi xi. Iunij M. D. XLIII.
units.tr: What of the deduction, as they call it, concerning transubstantiation, which he handled so skilfully that the rest was hardly clumsy at all? As for his writing that he had been warned not to press us so exactly: was Charles really someone we feared? Did any fear ever hold us back from being defeated? At Basel, where Erasmus, Berus, Zicardus and Cantiuncula were, we theologians, like those lawyers, went down into the arena and withstood the weighty arguments of our side, such as those of Oecolampadius and Pellicanus. But they were so fortified by Scripture that they could not shake the smallest part of them. Yet what fear can hold those who are sure, while they stand for the truth, on God's promise that they will have a mouth and a wisdom which none of their adversaries can resist? Those who seek not their own glory, nor even to conquer, but the glory of God, and that Christ and the truth may conquer, and who ask this in private and public prayers? But Charles knows that we prayed more fervently and invited everyone to prayer. Suppose someone, fearing for us as once happened, when I was first called to preach and some men of great standing, as they seemed, ran up, while I seemed to be nobody, as I truly am, and said: "What will this poor wretch do? Would that he had never come or been called! He will not be able to hold out, and we shall all be ruined along with him." But when the signs were compared, and the adversary of his own accord put forward the very things we wished to defend, and we challenged him into the arena, then he whom some had so greatly dreaded said that he did not wish to dispute, and that he was not worthy to bring me a book. If this was said to Charles, I do not know well; but what neither Viret nor I ever thought, this we can affirm with certainty: we did not want him to leave out any of the arguments that could be brought forward. Indeed, as I said, when he slipped in memory and did not hold firmly what was to be said, and did not know where to begin his speech, we often brought him back onto the road. What he attempted near the end of the disputation, which, as I said, we obtained through Bernard, we do not altogether ignore; but through D. it came about that he did not succeed. The points handled in the whole disputation were recounted, so that everyone might understand that the matter stands thus. For what is the use, in a matter of truth, of bringing anything to a lover of truth but true things? Then the magistrate was earnestly admonished to do his duty for the glory of God and the salvation of the people: to exercise the office of a father, and not to allow the sons entrusted to him by God to go astray in things which so plainly oppose divine truth, otherwise he would be guilty of all that was allowed to happen. Examples were cited of the godly who presided over the people; how much these moved them, those to whom it was said know themselves. Charles from time to time dealt with the canons and with others from the city. What fear compelled the man to leave Geneva and go round the mountains, I do not know, unless it was that which overtakes the impious fugitive when no one is pursuing. If it were said that the Papists had threatened Charles, perhaps some who did not know his association with the Papists would be persuaded. Those who knew would not be persuaded: for they have threatened him and many others, have attacked some, and have had various conspiracies; and though often warned, I was not afraid, although I have seen some harmed and killed by the Papists, which did not turn out well for them, since their plans were laid open. But let Charles produce, if he can, anyone who was not a Papist who stirred up a disturbance, or attacked anyone on account of religion. He who in time of peace did not dare to act in the city, nor to proceed by an open way: this is the Charles whom everyone is so eager to destroy! Such a great preacher! Such a great disputant! Oh, how many blows he has taken! Into how many dangers has he fallen! How many and how great things he has suffered! Are the French not ashamed to recount what he did at Basel, that such a fool should so exhibit himself in Germany, away from France, and that before Grynaeus, with whom, if you compare Charles, you would be setting Thersites beside Achilles? Then followed his call to the church of Neuchâtel. Since he did not plant it, nor even took pains to build it up, I will not say how lawful his call was. What I now feel can scarcely be obtained, and although, as you know, great pains were taken, not without much anxiety, to have it judged by all the best men what the parts of the minister, what of the magistrate, and what of the people are in the due calling of ministers, still, how is it that what ought rightly to be observed does not remain fixed? Clearly Charles is bound by this scruple, that he take care lest anything be lacking in his calling; as you know what ought to have been done, so that he would be brought in, the one whom all the ministers except one desired, and the whole people with the magistrate asked more urgently. But as they came in, good men of course, so they went out. What was the point of sending him to Berne and meanwhile lingering elsewhere, then to Mont-Bellegarde, and looking over everything so that a place might be had; of seeking with so many prayers that we might help the man, and of hesitating as long as he could, even with his wife, by whom he then had a child? But when would there be an end? I would like to receive from you what Viret has to say, which does not come to mind for me now; for beyond the things that touch him in particular, he can pursue everything more fully. Besides, a suitable opportunity has presented itself here for me to hand over this little book and everything I have. And first of all I ask you to press with the greatest care for an embassy to the King, which, if it can be done, should speak plainly; for things are gained less by letters than by caution. But if an embassy is sent and is conducted manfully, help will come not only to those for whom we labour, but also to others who are in danger everywhere. Farewell, and pray to the Lord for us. Neuchâtel, 11 June 1543.

units.la: Farellus tuus totus.
units.tr: Your Farel, wholly yours.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: Quod bene vertat Deus, hic retentus sum ut volebas: superest ut Viretum quoq; mecum retineam, quem à me auelli nullo modo patiar. Tuae quoque omniumque fratrum
units.tr: May God bless it. I have been kept here, as you wished. It remains for me to keep Viret with me as well, and I will not allow him to be taken from me in any way. Your part, and the part of all the brothers, is to help me here, unless you want me to be tormented in vain and to be most wretched, without any benefit.

units.la: §.j. partes me hic adiuuare, nisi vultis me frustra excruciari, ac sine commodo esse miserrimum. Vbi operam meam Senatui detuli, exposui non posse consistere Ecclesiam, nisi certum regimen constitueretur, quale ex Verbo Dei nobis praescriptum est, & in veteri Ecclesia fuit observatum. Capita deinde quaedam attigi, unde intelligerent quid vellem. Sed quia tota res explicari non poterat, petij ut nobis darentur qui nobis cognitum conferrent: sex nobis dati sunt. Conscribetur de tota Ecclesiae politia articuli, quos deinde Senatui exhibebimus. Collegae tres se nobis duobus consentire praestare ferunt: aliquid saltem obtinebitur. Qualiter cum vestra Ecclesia agatur, rescire cupimus. Quanquam speramus Bernatium & Biellensium auctoritate motus illos vel compositos in totum esse, vel nonnihil sedatos. Quando tibi cum Satana est certamen, & sub Chtifti vexillis militas, dabit victoriam is qui te armauit, atque in hanc pugnam perttraxit. Verum quoniam bona causa bono actore indiget, vide ne sic tibi indulgeas, ut fitaliquid, quod boni quoque merito desiderare in te queant. Non hortamur te vt bonam ac puram conscientiam hic praestes, de quo nihil ambigimus. Tantum cupimus vt quoad per officium licebit, te populo magis accommodes. Duq; sunt, vt nosti, species popularitatis: altera cum ambitione & placendi cupiditate fauorem aucupamur: altera cum moderatione & aequitate animos allicimus, vt se nobis dociles praebeant. Ignoscas, si liberius tecum agimus. Hac in parte videmus te bonis quoque ipsis non satisfacere. Etiam si nihil aliud sit, in eo tamen peccas, quod his non satisfacis, quibus te Dominus constituit debitore: scis quantum te amemus, quantum te colamus. Hic affectus, imo haec obseruantia nos impellit ad istam exactiorem ac rigidiore censuram: quia cupimus in illis eximiis dotibus quas in te Dominus contulit nullum extare naevum, qui maleuolis carpendi occasionem quam captant, praebeat. Haec scripsi ex Vireti consilio, ideo plurali numero vsus sum. Vale optime & amicissime frater. Geneuae, xvi. Septemb. M.D. XLIII.
units.tr: §.j. When I presented my work to the Senate, I explained that the Church could not stand unless a fixed form of government were set up, such as is prescribed for us by the Word of God and was observed in the ancient Church. Then I touched on some heads, so that they might understand what I wanted. But since the whole matter could not be explained, I asked that some men be given to us who would confer with us about what they knew. Six have been given to us. Articles will be drawn up covering the whole polity of the Church, which we will then present to the Senate. My colleagues say that three of them will agree with the two of us, so at least something will be secured. We wish to learn how things stand with your Church. We hope, though, that the disturbances have been either settled altogether or somewhat calmed, through the authority of the men of Berne and Biel. Since you are in a struggle with Satan and serve under the banners of Christ, he who armed you and drew you into this fight will give the victory. But since a good cause needs a good advocate, take care that you do not indulge yourself in such a way that there is anything in you which even good men might rightly find fault with. I do not urge you to show here a good and pure conscience, about which we have no doubt. I only wish that, as far as your duty allows, you would accommodate yourself more to the people. There are, as you know, two kinds of popularity: one wins favour by ambition and a desire to please; the other gently draws minds, by moderation and fairness, so that they become teachable toward us. Forgive me if I speak to you more frankly. In this matter we see that you do not satisfy even the good. Even if there were nothing else, you sin in this, that you do not satisfy those to whom the Lord has made you a debtor. You know how much we love you and how much we honour you. This feeling, or rather this regard, drives us to such a stricter and more severe judgment, because we want no blemish to remain in those outstanding gifts which the Lord has bestowed on you, a blemish which might give the ill-disposed the chance to find fault, which they are looking for. I have written this with Viret's advice, which is why I have used the plural. Farewell, best and most friendly brother. Geneva, 16 September 1543.

units.la: CAL. MONSBELGARDENSIBVS.
units.tr: CALVIN TO THE PEOPLE OF MONTBÉLIARD.

units.la: Gratia vobis & pax a Deo Patre nostro & Domino Iesu Christo fratres charissimi & obseruandi.
units.tr: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest and most esteemed brothers.

units.la: TAmetsi Neocomum duntaxat duo isti fratres missi a vobis fuerant, ad consulendos eius loci ministros: illorum tamen hortatu hucusque ad me profecti sunt, vt de quibus petebatis ab ipsis consilium meam simul sententiam ad vos perferrent. Ego vero non tantum mihi sumo, vt audeam non rogatus me in vestras consultationes medium ingerere, meamq; interponere opinionem. Sed quoniam nominatim adieceratin literis suis frater noster Toffanus,cupere vos meum & aliorum iu dicium audire, minime sum veritus ne mihi arrogantiæ aucte meritati daretur,si vobis simpliciter exponerem ac paucis,quid esset ipse facturus si personam vestram suftinetem. Iam quidem ante duos menses quid sentiam aliqua ex parte fratri nostro Toffano priuatim indicaui:nunc vero quoniam capita mihi recesserunt fratres de quibus ambiguitis, aut de quibus saltem non nihil est inter vos controuersiæ an recipi à vobis debeant: de singulis quid mihi videatur, breuiter respondeo. Vt se repræsentent ministro & offerant ad examen, qui Cœnæ dominicæ communicare volunt adeo non displicet: vt potius id sentiam vltro à nobis esse expetendum. Erit enim optimus piæ sanctæque in Ecclesia disciplinæ neruus. Verum quia procliuis inde lapsus foret ad corruptelam aliquam:vt obuiam eatur periculis omnibus,vtile erit simul præscribere limites,quibus legitimus vsus definiatur:primùm vt sit tanquam priuata cathechesis ad rudes faciliter edocendos,demum vt vsui sit ad eos monedos & obiurgandos,qui officio suo parum respondent:postremò vt ad trepidas conscientias erigendas & confirmandas valeat. De Cœnæ administratione ita sentio,libenter admittendum esse hunc morem,vt apud ægrotos celebretur communio,cum ita res & opportunitas feret. Nec magnopere etiá repugnandum est,quin maleficis detur qui plectendi sunt,fiquidé postulent, & ad receptionem satis comparatos esse appareat: hac tamen lege,vt sit vera communio: hoc est vt panis in coetu aliquo fidelium frägatur. Cœnam verò in ordinaria concione instituì extra ordine vnius rogatu nimis absurdum est: neque enim decet proponi coram omnibus sacrum illud epulum,quod omnium commune est,sine solenni denuntiatione, vt ad participationem se Ecclesia compareret. Eo autem modo fieri quo princeps iubet, quid aliud foret quàm subiicere vniuscuiusque libidini publicum Ecclesiæ ordinem? Quòd si necessitatem obiiciunt,non est cur recusetis frequentiorem vsum, ne quis amplius necessitatem obtendat, qui in coetum modo conuenire poterit. Baptismum obstetricibus permittere impia & sacrilega est Baptismi profanatio. Ergo hoc caput non tantum repudiandum iudico: verum, si vrgere vos princeps vltra modum pergat,vsque ad sanguinem resistendum potius quàm huic non tolerandæ superstitioni consentiatis. Rogabat Christus Pharisæos vndénam Ioannis Baptismus foret: é cœlo an ab hominibus. Nam si hoc secundum confessi essent,promptum erat colligere,vanum igitur esse & nullius momenti. Iam obstetricum Baptismus vnde erit? certè non ab eo qui hoc munus peculiariter Apostolis mandauit.Superest igitur vt à contrario auctore. Augustinus non de muliere sed de priuato viro mouet quæstionem, an si baptizetur in necessitate,peccet. Respondet deinde dubitanter, vt excuset magis quàm probet.Certè non asserit licere:quin potius fatetur subsse delictum. Verum si Christi regulam sequimur nullus restat locus dubitationi.In sepultura mortuorum hanc moderationem vellem adhiberi ne in templum funus deferretur, sed recta in cœmeteriû. Illic quoque exhortationem haberi vellem,vt in re præsenti suneris comites agnoscerent quod diceretur. Hæc ratio non admodum improbanda foret. De campanæ pulsu nolim vos pertinaciusreclamare,si obtineri nequeat vt princeps remittat:non quia probem,sed quia rem contentione non dignam arbitror. In festis non recipiendiscuperem vos esse constantiores, sic tamen vt non litigetis de quibuslibet, sed de iis tantùm quæ nec in ædificationem quicquam factura sunt,& superstitionem prima ipsa facie præ se ferant. Et habetis plausibilem recusandi materiam. Nam in Papatu magna celebritate Conceptionem & Assumptionem Virginis celuerunt. Quid habebit seruus Christi quod dicat, si suggestum conscenderit illis diebus, nisi vt eorum stultitiam rideat qui tales ferias excogitarunt? Breuiter & nudis verbis sensum meum explicaui. Argumentis agere vobiscum, vel superuacuum,vel non adeò necessarium visum est,quando pro vestra prudentia sine alio monitore quæ me rationes moueant, expendere potestis. Iam video quæ & quanta in exorando principe vos difficultas moueat. Verùm si modesta depreca- tione ostenderitis vos non posse aliter nisi velitis in eius gratiâ Christo illudere,non dubito quin tam æquo postulato ad extremum cessurus sit. Hanc ob causam suadeo ne vos nimis difficiles ac moriosos quoad licet,præbeatis. Nam vbi hanc vestra moderationem animadueꝛterit,facilius adducetur vt nonnihil vobis ipse quoque vicissim concedat,præsertim vbi viderit vos non absque causa pugnare. Quòd autem vos terret offendiculorum periculum,si quam nouam agendi formam receperitis quæ non sit nostris Ecclesiis vsitata,id quidem merito facitis:sed quia non eò ventum est perfectionis quin optemus adhuc progredi, hic timor vos impedire non debet ab iis ritibus admittendis ,quos alioqui non liceat penitus improbare. Valete optimi & mihi obseruandi fratres. Collegæ mei diligenter vos salutant , qui ab hoc meo iudicio nihil prorsus dissentiunt. Dominus Iesus vos emper Spiritu suo gubernet. Geneuæ. Nonis Octobris. M. D. XLIII.
units.tr: Although only those two brothers were sent by you to consult with the ministers of that place, nevertheless, at their urging, the matter has come to me, so that they might bring you my opinion along with the advice on what you asked of them. For my part, I do not claim so much for myself as to dare, unasked, to intrude into your deliberations and put forward my own view. But since our brother Toffanus expressly added in his letter that you wished to hear my judgment and that of others, I was in no way afraid that I would be thought arrogant, if I set out for you simply and briefly what I myself would do if I were in your position. Some two months ago I did indicate in part my opinion to our brother Toffanus privately; but now, since the brothers have brought me the heads about which you are uncertain, or at least about which there is some dispute among you as to whether they should be accepted by you, I reply briefly to each one, saying what seems right to me. As to the admission to the Lord's Supper of those who wish to communicate, after presenting themselves to the minister and submitting to examination, I am not so much opposed to this that I would rather think it should be demanded of us; for it will be an excellent sinew of pious and holy discipline in the Church. But since there would be a ready slide from this into some corruption, so that all the dangers may be met, it will be useful at the same time to prescribe limits by which lawful use is defined: first, that it serve as a private catechism for easily instructing the ignorant; second, that it serve to admonish and rebuke those who respond poorly to their duty; last, that it be effective for raising up and strengthening troubled consciences. As to the administration of the Supper, I think it should be readily admitted that the communion be celebrated among the sick, when circumstances and opportunity allow. Nor is it greatly to be resisted that those evildoers who ought to be punished be given the Supper, provided that they ask for it and it is evident that they are sufficiently prepared to receive it; yet only on this condition, that it be a true communion, that is, that the bread be broken in some gathering of the faithful. But to institute the Supper in the ordinary sermon out of order at one man's request is far too absurd: for it is not fitting that that sacred feast, which is common to all, be set before everyone without a solemn announcement, so that the Church may prepare itself for participation. And to act in that way, as the prince orders, what else would it be than to subject the public order of the Church to the whim of each individual? But if they put forward necessity, there is no reason why you should refuse a more frequent use, so that no one may further plead necessity, if he can come to the assembly at all. To allow midwives to baptize is an impious and sacrilegious profanation of Baptism. So I judge that this head must not only be rejected, but, if the prince presses you beyond measure, you should resist even unto blood rather than consent to this intolerable superstition. Christ asked the Pharisees whence John's baptism was: from heaven or from men. For if they had confessed the second, it would have been easy to conclude that it was vain and of no account. Now, where will the baptism of midwives come from? Certainly not from him who entrusted this office peculiarly to the apostles. It remains, then, that it comes from a contrary author. Augustine raises the question not about a woman but about a private man, whether he sins if he is baptized in necessity. He then answers hesitantly, so as to excuse rather than to approve. He certainly does not assert that it is lawful; rather he admits that a fault is involved. But if we follow the rule of Christ, no room for doubt remains. In the burial of the dead I would wish this moderation to be observed: that the corpse not be carried into the church, but straight to the cemetery. There I would also wish an exhortation to be given, so that in the present matter the companions of the funeral may recognise what is being said. This arrangement would not be greatly to be disapproved. As to the ringing of the bell, I would not have you object too stubbornly, if the prince cannot be persuaded to give it up; not because I approve of it, but because I think the matter is not worth a contest. As to festivals, I would wish you to be more firm in not receiving them, yet so that you do not quarrel over any at all, but only over those which will do nothing for edification and which at first sight display superstition. And you have a plausible ground for refusing. For under the Papacy the Conception and the Assumption of the Virgin were celebrated with great solemnity. What will a servant of Christ have to say, if on those days he mounts the pulpit, except to laugh at the folly of those who devised such holidays? I have explained my view briefly and in plain words. To argue with you at length seemed either superfluous or not very necessary, since by your own prudence, without any other adviser, you can weigh the reasons which move me. I see now what and how great the difficulty is that troubles you in dealing with the prince. But if you show, by a modest petition, that you cannot act otherwise unless you were willing to mock Christ in order to win his favour, I do not doubt that he will in the end yield to so fair a request. For this reason I advise you not to be too difficult or obstinate, as far as is permitted. For when he notices this moderation of yours, he will more easily be brought to concede something to you in return, especially when he sees that you are not contending without cause. As for your fear of the danger of stumbling-blocks, if you were to adopt some new form of action not customary in our Churches, you are right to do so; but since we have not reached such perfection that we do not wish to advance further, this fear should not prevent you from admitting those rites which in any case it would not be right to reject altogether. Farewell, best brothers, whom I esteem. My colleagues salute you warmly; they are in complete agreement with this my judgment. May the Lord Jesus always govern you by his Spirit. Geneva, the Nones of October 1543.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus vester.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: BVCERVS
units.tr: BUCER ## Grace and peace.

units.la: Gratia & Pax.

DE ipso Imperatore quid nobis pollicear, nec statuere ipse possum. Italorum & Hispanorum ei consuetudo placet. Imperij plenitudo aperte quæri videtur. Puerilibus vel animis potius superstitionibus inhæret. Dicit quotidie prolixas preces flexis genibus, dicit Rosaria decumbens in tetram, & defixo vultu in tabella coram virgine. Aperte nunc Christum vbiq; oppugnat. Meti depulit quod in ipso est. Edictum mittemus. Sic ergo cum habeat res, dubitare ipse incipio a te monitus an deceat ad ipsum scribi, quod tamen scribi velim. Martyrum exemplum qui Apologeticos suos scripserunt ad Principes palàm idololatras me mouet, & Maiestas Imperij, consideratióque mirabilium mutationum, quas effectas à Domino in magnis Regibus, vt Nabucadnezar, Cyro, & aliis legimus. Tu itaque iudica quid putes facto opus. Ad ipsum Imperatorem scriptus liber in plurium lectionem incidet, plus videbitur ponderis habere, & vrgeri æquitas scripto amplius poterit cum publice tum priuatim. Iam veritas clarè & incomprehensibiliter obiecta etiam hostibus suis, languere etiam facit eorum conatus contra ipsam, & mirabiliter consolatur & erigit studiosos sui, cum eius vident victoriam etiam in conscientiis aduersariorum. Ac si animus abhorret ab ipso Imperatore appellando, scribas ad Reges, vel ad Principes conuenturos in proximis Comitiis. Spero etiam edere librum si ad finem Decembris adsit: quanquam enim indicta sint Comitia ad finem: tamen vt adhuc apparent res, & belli negotium habet, videtur tempestiue id fore, si ad dimidium Decembrem vel finem Decemb. adsit. Explicari mihi velim illud de extirpatione masculæ virtutis in Gallia. Non intelligo: nihil enim audiui. Sed te per Christum rogo Ieremiam comitemur cum reliquiis populi sui gementem & verbo Dei illos persequentem, dum ipsum lapidarent. Semper aliquos lucrifaciemus, & ab isto incendio recipiemus. Dominus te & tuos confirmet. Bene vale. xxv, Octobris. M. D. XLIII. Vxor valeat, & quicquid apud te quàm optimè.
units.tr: As for the Emperor himself, I can promise nothing on our behalf, nor can I decide anything. He likes Italian and Spanish customs. His desire for full imperial power is plainly evident. He clings to childish or rather superstitious practices. Every day he says long prayers on bended knees, says the rosary lying prostrate on the ground, and fixes his gaze on a little picture before the Virgin. He now openly attacks Christ everywhere. He has driven out fear of what is in him. We shall send an edict. Since matters stand so, I begin to doubt, at your prompting, whether it is proper to write to him, though I would still wish to write. The example of the martyrs, who wrote their apologies to rulers who were openly idolaters, moves me, and so does the majesty of empire, and the consideration of the remarkable changes which we read the Lord brought about in great kings, such as Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus and others. So you judge what you think needs to be done. A book written to the Emperor himself will fall into the hands of more readers and will seem to carry more weight, and the justice of our cause can be pressed more strongly in writing, both publicly and privately. Moreover, truth set clearly and openly before its enemies also weakens their efforts against it, and wonderfully comforts and raises up its supporters when they see its victory even in the consciences of its opponents. But if your mind shrinks from addressing the Emperor himself, write to the kings or to the princes who will meet at the coming Diet. I also hope to publish the book if it is ready by the end of December. Although the Diet has been announced for the end of the month, yet, as matters now appear and the war has its business, it seems it will be timely if it is ready by mid-December or the end of December. I would like you to explain to me that point about the extinction of manly virtue in France. I do not understand it, for I have heard nothing. But I beg you through Christ: let us accompany Jeremiah, lamenting with the remnant of his people and pursuing them with the Word of God while they were stoning him. We shall always win some over and rescue them from this fire. May the Lord strengthen you and yours. Farewell. 25 October 1543. Let your wife be well, and whatever is with you, as well as possible.

units.la: M. Bucerus tuus in Domino.
units.tr: M. Bucer, yours in the Lord.

units.la: MYCONIVS CALVINO.
units.tr: Myconius to Calvin.

units.la: SCis quid egerit Cæsar in Germania inferiore contra Hildesheimenses, Antuerpiæ item contra bonos & doctos quosdam quos eiecit. Vt prohibuerit ne cibus detur aut hospitium insectis noua doctrina, sic enim vocat Euangelicam. Vt Coloniensem ciuitatem corroborarit aduersus Archiepiscopum: & tandem vt Euangelium ac Euangelicos homines Meti nuper profligarit, misso in hoc legato Carolo Boisot 1. Doctore, hoste nominis Christi truculentissimo: id quod reipsa probauit satis: eiecit enim D. Valtrinum Syluium (qui illic iussu Senatus & plebis aliquandiu praedicauit Euangelium) non sine ignominia vocauit enim haereticum, qui vi intrusus à Protestantibus, praedicarit Metensibus horum dogmata. De quibus, & de Coloniensi palam dixit, omnium impiorum & schismaticorum, & haereticorum esse pessimos. Amputauit praeterea linguam mulierculae quae inuecta erat in Missam Papae verius quàm petulantius, & haec poena fuit ex gratia, nam sententia lata mergi debebat. Hodie cum multis aliis exulibus Argentinae moratur. Articuli quos praeterea statuit seruandos, tales sunt, vt ministrum Antichristi & Satanae non obscure intelligas. Talem hostem ergo cum in Germania habeamus cum exercitu saeuissimo, quid non ad pacem omnibus viribus laboramus potius quàm ad discordiam? Obliti credo fumus Deum pacis esse Deum non dissensionis. Hoc enim si recto consideraremus animo, non dubium est quin postquam Euangelium eius profitemur, à nostris affectibus cessant paci nos deuouere mus. Oremus simul itaque, & imploremus Dominum, vt is finem contentioni tandem inueniat, postquam in nobis nihil eius reperiri licet. Ille adsit, quaeso, Verbo & Ecclesiae suae. Pergere dicitur Archiepiscopus Coloniensis plane sine terrore, similiter & Monasteriensis in proferendo Euangelio quàm latissime. Dominus adsit. Omnia praeterea nunc versantur in consultando, vt videlicet in annum futurum, Satanae frenis permissis, omnia miscentur. Equidem dico, Domine fiat voluntas tua. Vale in Christo cum piis fratribus omnibus. Basileae xxiii. Nouemb. anno M. D. XLIII.
units.tr: You know what Caesar has done in Lower Germany against the Hildesheimers, and likewise at Antwerp against certain good and learned men whom he expelled. He has forbidden that food or lodging be given to those infected with the new doctrine, for so he calls the Evangelical teaching. He has strengthened the city of Cologne against its Archbishop. And finally, he has lately crushed the Gospel and the Evangelical people at Metz, sending as his envoy in this business Charles Boisot, a Doctor and the most savage enemy of the name of Christ, as he has amply proved in fact. For he expelled Dr. Valtrinus Silvius, who had for some time preached the Gospel there by order of the Senate and people, and he did so not without disgrace: he called him a heretic, one who, thrust in by force by the Protestants, had preached their doctrines to the people of Metz. Of these people, and of the Cologne people, he declared openly that they were the worst of all impious, schismatic and heretical men. He also cut off the tongue of a little woman who had intruded into the Pope's Mass, more truly than wantonly; and this punishment was an act of grace, since the sentence pronounced should have been drowning. Today he lingers at Strasbourg with many other exiles. The articles which he has further laid down to be observed are such that you can clearly recognise in him a minister of Antichrist and Satan. Since we have such an enemy in Germany, with a most savage army, why do we labour with all our strength for discord rather than for peace? I think we have forgotten that God is the God of peace, not of dissension. For if we considered this with a right mind, there is no doubt that, since we profess his Gospel, we would cease to devote ourselves to our passions rather than to peace. Let us therefore pray together and implore the Lord to finally bring an end to this contention, since nothing of his can be found in us. May he be present, I beg, with his Word and his Church. The Archbishop of Cologne is said to be proceeding quite without fear, and likewise the Bishop of Münster, in spreading the Gospel as widely as possible. May the Lord be present. Moreover, everything is now being debated, namely that in the coming year, with the reins given to Satan, all things are being thrown into confusion. For my part I say: Lord, let your will be done. Farewell in Christ, with all the pious brothers. Basel, 23 November 1543.

units.la: Ofs.Myconius tuus.
units.tr: Yours dutifully, Myconius.

units.la: CALVINVS MYCONIO.
units.tr: Calvin to Myconius.

units.la: QVum huc primum appulissem, non potui, vt petieras, de statu huius Ecclesiae te facere certiorem: quia ne ipse quidem satisdum habebà compertum, qualis esset: ab eo quoque tempore non ausus sum certò aliquid asserere, rebus adhuc parum confirmatis: ne paulò post ante tempus laudasse poenitteret. Atque haec causa fuit, cur abstinuerim à scribendo, cùm reipublicae nostrae legati istuc proficiscerentur. Nunc quando in hac mea cessatione, pro tua humanitate antecuertisti, diutius iam differre non licet, quin tibi respondeā. De rebus nostris sic paucis habe. Primus mensis ex quo ministerium recepi, tātum mihi negotij ac molestiarum exhibuit, vt propemodum conficeret. Tantæ molis est collapsum ædificium instaurare. Quanquam enim Viretus multa iam restituere fœliciter cœperat, quia tamen totam ordinis ac disciplinæ formam in meum aduentum distulerat, fuit velut ab initio inchoandum. Cùm, superato hoc labore, respirandi otium mihi datum iri crederem: ecce nouæ curæ & illæ non multò aliis prioribus leuiores me subinde excipiūt. Hoc tamen me vtcunque solatur ac recreat, quòd non sine fructu laboramus: qui etsi non tam copiosus extat quàm optarim, non tamen ita est exiguus, quin appareat aliquam esse in melius factam commutationem. Et spes in posterum amplior affulget, si mihi relinquatur Viretus. Quo maiorem tibi gratiā & habeo, & ago, quia huius solicitudinis partem mecum suscipis, ne eum reposcant Bernates: ac te vehementer per Christi nomē obtestor, vt sedulò ac diligenter id facere pergas. Nā quoties de eius abitione cogito, totus exanimor. Fratres, vt spero, fideliter hac in re nos adiuuabunt (de ministris Bernensibus loquor) ita enim amamus inter nos, vt mihi de ipsis optima quæq; nō secus ac de me ipso, audeam polliceri. Sed vereor, ne Senatus parum se facilem præbeat. Quicquid erit, omni studio, diligentia, assiduitate in id incūbamus. Tūq; adeò ipse, quoad potes, enitere apud fratres, quemadmodum facturum te recipis. Quanquam enim voluntarios fore non dubito, proderit tamen vestram simul exhortatione accedere. Collegæ alij impedimento nobis sunt magis quàm subsidio: multum arrogantiæ & ferociæ habent, nihil zeli, minimū doctrinæ. Quod autem est pessimum, fidere illis nequeo, etiam si maximè velim: multis enim argumentis suam à nobis alienationem declarant: fidelitatis ac synceri animi nullum fere indicium præ se ferunt. Tolero tamen eos, vel foueo potius summa lenitate: à qua me abduci eorum improbitate non patiar. Quòd si tandē necessitas ipsa postulabit acrius remedium, dabo tamē operam, modisq; omnibus effectu curabo, ne disconcordiis nostris turbetur Ecclesia. Horreo enim factiones quas ex ministrorum dissensione semper emergere necesse est. Potui eos si voluissem, primo meo aduentu abigere: atque id nunc quoque in manu nostra est. Sed me huius quàm adhibui moderationis, nunquam pœnitebit: ne quis me nimis vehementem fuisse merito queratur. Hæc ideo tibi obiter refero, quo melius perspicias, quàm misér sim futurus, sublato Vireto. Quòd Ecclesiæ vestræ exemplo commemoras quàm noxia sit pestis ministrorum dissidium, id ego quoque superioribus annis expertus sum plus satis in hu-ius Ecclesiæ calamitate. Nobis, qui hīc eramus, nihil coniunctum esse poterat. Sed cum Satan infaustam illam simultatem inter fratres & nos excitaffet, nostri ipse quid fequutum fit. Itaq; hoc prorsus apud me statueram, nisi reconciliata cum illis gratia, hanc provinciam nunquam recipere: quia desperaveram posse vllo modo vtile esse hic meum ministerium, nisi manum illi mihi porrigerent. Interim multi in eorum coetu sunt mihi parum amici, alij etiam palam infensi. Sed hoc diligenter caueo, ne quid contentionis exoriatur. In vrbe, vt iam dixi, habemus intestinum semen dissidij: sed nostra mansuetudine & patientia efficimus, vt Ecclesia nihil incommodi inde sentiat, atque vt nihil perueniat ad ipsam plebem. Norunt enim omnes quàm placido humanoque ingenio sit Viretus: & ego nihilo sum asperior, hac sal tem in parte. Vix credes forsan: sic tamen res habet. Tanti enim mihi est publica pax & concordia vt manum mihi iniiciam: atque hanc laudem mihi adiuerfarij ipsi tribuere coguntur. Quinetiam ex inimicis nonnulli sponte in dies amici fiunt, alios comiter allicio, & proficere me nonnihil sentio: vtcunque non vbique succedat. Poteram cum veni magno plausu exagitare hostes nostros, & plenis velis inuehi in totam illam nationem, quos laeserat. abstinui: possem quotidie, si liberet, non modo impune, sed cum multorum approbatione perstringere. supersedeo: imo summa religione id fugio, ne verbulo vno infestari aliquem videar: nedum simul omnes. Hunc animum mihi Domi nus cōfirmet. Accidit tamen interdum vt necesse sit Collegis nostris resistere: sed nunquam id facimus, nisi vel sua importunitate nos cogant, vel aliqua grauior causa nos vrgeat. Referam tibi exemplum vnum, cuius me querimonia illa quae in literis tuis continetur, propter argumenti similitudinem, admonuit. Cum de erigendo Ecclesiastico iudicio cogitaremus atque id no bis Senatus detulisset, boni isti viri coram assentiebantur: quia scilicet contradicere in rebus tam apertis pudebat. Postea seorsum circumire, & prehensare singulos Senatores, ne quod haberent in manu ad pedes proiicerent (sic loquebantur) ne potestate, quam illis Deus contulisset, se abdicarent, ne darent occasionem seditionis: & eius generis permulta. Dissimulanter transire hanc perfidiam nullo modo licebat: & tamen dedimus operam, vt id sine contentione transfigeretur. Nunc habemus quaecunque presbyterorum iudicium & formam disciplinae, qualem ferebat tempor um infirmitas. Sed ne putes id nos sine maximo sudore fuisse consequutos. Vbique enim erumpunt profani illi spiritus, qui, vt disciplinam & ordinem effugiant, quem nullo modo ferre queunt, quo sibi libet quaerunt praetextus ad labefactandam Ecclesiae auctoritatem. Et mundus hoc habet solenne, quòd pro libidine regnare cupit, Christo autem imperium resignare non sustinet. Sed vtcunque plausibilem mundo & carni causam agant eiusmodi impostores, modo tamen coniunctis animi & studiis obuiam eamus, fortíque & inuicto zelo pugnemus pro sacra illa potestate, quam inuiolabilem esse decet, DominusChristus Spiritu oris sui eos conficiet. Illustrior enim est in hac re Dei veritas, quàm vt mendaciorum offuciis facile inducì queat. Mosem allegant & Dauidem. Quasi vero non aliud muneris habuerint illi duo, quàm vt populum ciuili potestate regerent. Dent igitur nobis insani isti similes magistratus, hoc est, singulari prophetiæ spiritu excellentes, & vtrâmque sustinetes persona, non proprio consilio, aut affectu, sed Dei mandato & vocatione: nos alibus id quod postulant, libenter largiemur. Quin Moses ipse ante consecratum Aaronem Sacerdotis munere fungitur: postea Dei iussu præscribit quod facto opus est. Dauid quoque non sine Domini permissu ad ordinandam Ecclesiam accingitur. Pij alij Reges constitutum ordinem tuentur sua potestate, vt decet: Ecclesiæ tamen suam iurisdictionem, & Sacerdotibus partes illis à Domino attributas relinquunt. Sed ego ineptus sum, qui in hanc syluam ingrediar, cùm tabellarius iamiam abituriat: quo fit, vt ad narrandam Albergij historiam non sit in præsens satis ocij. Incipiam tamen & sequar, donec veniat nuntius, qui literas semiplenas è manibus mihi abripiat.
units.tr: When I first arrived here, I could not, as you asked, inform you about the state of this Church, because I did not yet know for certain what it was like myself. Since then too I have not dared to assert anything with certainty, as matters were still little settled, lest I should soon regret having praised them before the right time. This was the reason I refrained from writing when the envoys of our commonwealth set out for your parts. Now, since by your kindness you have anticipated me in my silence, I can no longer delay replying to you. Concerning our affairs, take this brief account. Since the first month in which I accepted the ministry, it has given me so much business and trouble that it has nearly worn me out. It is a task of great difficulty to restore a collapsed building. For although Viret had already happily begun to repair many things, since he had postponed the whole form of order and discipline until my arrival, it was as if the work had to be begun from the beginning. When I believed that, once this labour was overcome, I would be given some leisure to breathe, behold, new cares, not much lighter than the former ones, keep seizing me one after another. Yet this consoles and restores me in some measure, that our labour is not without fruit. Although the fruit is not as abundant as I would wish, it is nonetheless not so meagre that no change for the better is apparent. And a more hopeful prospect for the future shines forth, if Viret is left to me. I am all the more grateful to you, and I thank you, because you share with me a part of this anxiety, so that the Bernese do not demand him back. I earnestly beseech you in the name of Christ to continue to do this diligently and faithfully. For whenever I think of his departure, I am quite undone. The brothers, as I hope, will assist us faithfully in this matter (I speak of the Bernese ministers), for we love one another so much that I dare to promise myself the best from them, just as from myself. But I fear the Senate may show itself less accommodating. Whatever happens, we are setting to work on it with all zeal, diligence and assiduity. And you yourself, as far as you can, exert yourself with the brothers, as you have undertaken to do. For although I do not doubt they will be willing, it will help if your exhortation is added to ours. My other colleagues are more of a hindrance to us than a help: they have much arrogance and ferocity, no zeal, and very little learning. What is worst, I cannot trust them, even though I would very much like to: for by many signs they declare their estrangement from us, and they show almost no evidence of fidelity or a sincere mind. Nevertheless I tolerate them, or rather I indulge them with the greatest gentleness, though I will not allow myself to be drawn away from this by their wickedness. But if necessity itself at last demands a sharper remedy, I will nonetheless take pains and see to it by every means that the Church is not disturbed by our dissensions. For I dread the factions which must always arise from disagreement among ministers. If I had wished, I could have driven them away at my first arrival, and that is still in our power. But I shall never regret the moderation I have shown: no one can justly complain that I have been too vehement. I mention these things to you in passing so that you may better see how wretched I shall be once Viret is removed. As for your remark, using your Church as an example, on how harmful the pestilence of disagreement among ministers is, I too have experienced this in the past years, more than enough, in the calamity of this Church. We who were here could have nothing in common. But when Satan had stirred up that unhappy enmity between the brothers and us, you know what followed for us. So I had firmly resolved in my own mind that, unless grace were restored with them, I would never accept this charge, because I had despaired of my ministry being in any way useful here unless they stretched out their hand to me. Meanwhile many in their company are little friendly to me, and some are openly hostile. But I take careful care that no strife arises. As I have said, there is in the city a hidden seed of discord; yet by our gentleness and patience we bring it about that the Church feels no harm from it, and that nothing reaches the common people. For everyone knows how placid and humane Viret's disposition is, and I am no harsher than he, at least in this respect. You may hardly believe it, but so it is. Public peace and concord are so important to me that I lay my own hand to them; and my opponents themselves are compelled to grant me this praise. Indeed, some of my enemies are becoming friends of their own accord every day, and I win others over by courtesy, and I sense that I am making some progress, although it does not succeed everywhere. When I came I could have roused our enemies with great applause and attacked that whole nation, which had wronged me, with full sails. I refrained. I could every day, if I wished, criticise them not only with impunity but with the approval of many. I hold back; indeed, out of the deepest conscientiousness I avoid even seeming to attack anyone with a single word, let alone all of them together. May the Lord confirm this disposition in me. Yet it sometimes happens that it is necessary to resist our colleagues; but we never do so unless either their own importunity compels us or some more serious cause presses us. I will relate to you one example, which, because of the similarity of the subject, reminded me of that complaint contained in your letter. When we were considering the setting up of an ecclesiastical court, and the Senate had referred this matter to us, those good men agreed with us to our faces, because of course it was shameful to contradict in matters so plain. Afterwards they went round privately and importuned the individual Senators, so that they would throw down to the ground whatever power they had in hand (so they put it), lest they should renounce the authority which God had conferred on them, and lest they should give occasion for sedition; and many things of that kind. It was by no means allowable to let this treachery pass unnoticed; and yet we took pains that the matter should be carried through without contention. We now have whatever judgment and form of discipline of the elders the weakness of the times allowed. But do not think we achieved this without the greatest sweat. For everywhere those profane spirits break out, who, to escape discipline and order, which they cannot in any way bear, seek whatever pretexts they please for undermining the authority of the Church. And the world has this customary trait: it wishes to reign at its pleasure, but cannot bring itself to surrender dominion to Christ. But however plausible a cause such impostors may make appear to the world and the flesh, let us nonetheless go against them with united minds and efforts, and fight with a strong and unconquered zeal for that sacred power which ought to be inviolable; the Lord Christ will destroy them by the Spirit of his mouth. For God's truth shines more clearly in this matter than that it can easily be led astray by the gloss of lies. They allege Moses and David. As if those two had no other office than to rule the people by civil power! Let these mad men, then, give us magistrates like them, that is, men outstanding in a singular spirit of prophecy, who sustain both persons, not by their own counsel or passion, but by God's command and calling: we will gladly grant them what they demand. Indeed Moses himself performed the office of priest before Aaron was consecrated; afterwards, by God's command, he prescribed what the deed required. David too did not set about ordering the Church without the Lord's permission. Other pious kings maintain the established order by their power, as is fitting; but they leave to the Church its own jurisdiction, and to the priests the parts assigned to them by the Lord. But I am foolish to enter upon this forest now, when the courier is about to leave at any moment; so for the present I have not enough leisure to relate the history of Albergatus. Still, I will begin and continue, until a messenger comes who snatches the half-finished letter from my hands.

units.la: Hoc principio habe, hominem istum iam multis annis nihil aliud quàm huc illuc curritare, ab aliis emungere pecuniam, vestes ab aliis: ita per impostu ras vitare: quemadmodum errones isti solent. Venerat huc sæpius ante nostram expulsionem locum petierat: sed non repertebatur idoneus, quia volebat scho lam celebrem, quæ in his regionibus nulla est, & magna stipendia. Paulò post rediit, deplorans suo more, spoliatum se fuisse à latronibus. Concedit in vicinum oppidulum, scholæ præfecturam ambit: non impetrat: hanc repulsam nobis imputat: qui adeò nihil illic vel auctoritate vel gratia poteramus, vt si cognitum fuisset nobis diffi licere, eo solo nomine impetraturus fuerit. Et tamen testis est nobis Deus, eo tempore nihil aliud conatos, quàm vt alicubi conditionem sibi aptam & commodam inueniret. Venit postea Argentinam, vbi viginti Batzios à me extorsit, quos ego aliunde mutuo accipere coactus sum. Nam libros tunc vendideram, & omnino eram exhaustus. Reddituram se intra paucos dies promiserat. Cistulam nullius precij apud me pignoris loco depositi. Reuersus aliquot post mensibus, petiit subridens, vel potius illudens, an non sibi mutuo aliquot coronatos dare vellem. Respondi me illa summula egere, quam habuerat. Nebulo interim cistulam clanculum à mea Bibliotheca subductam vxori Buccexi commendat: illa reuicit, ac me admoner: ego impudentiam eius coram aliquot testibus castigo. Dimidio anno post, aut integro anno scripsit ad me simplices literas, se obsideri Badenæ, totam regionis nobilitatem in se confspiratßse: non aliter posse euadere, quam si ego mitterem baiulum, qui eum in cista mercatoria asportaret. Bedrotus habuit se re similes: nos risimus: ego etiam paucis respondi. Nam multis coniecturis deprehendimus, ipsum in vrbe esse: ab eo tempore non comparuit: Iesquiannus elapsus interea est. Cum scire multas nugas inclusas esse in cistula, aperui coram multis testibus. Erant illic mala putrida, & omne genus scruta, libri semilaceri, & ij vulgares, ut Despauterius & similes. Reperi etiam literas, quas mihi subripuerat. Nouit hoc Sturmius, quem ego aduocaui. Reposuimus omnia, non sine multo risu. Cum Vvormaciam veniret sanctæ memoriæ Grynæus, nunciauit esse Basileæ. Mandaui mihi discedens, v' cistulam remitteret. Nebulo, ea accepta, clamitare me esse furem, sustulisse multos incomparabiles libros. Venit Laufannam: eadem retulit Vireto. Nuper cum huc se contulisset, decem circiter dies me inscio in vrbe fuit. Postea Vireti impulsu cum aggredior, rogo an non actionem furti mihi velit intentare: cum diceret se perdidisse praeclaros libros, vocaui impudentissimum nebulonem. Postridie aggressus est me domi meæ non modo contumeliosissimis verbis, sed furioso impetu: eam ob rem in custodiam datus est. Cum bona fide pro eo deprecarer magistratum, ac iam vocaretur sine vlla molestia dimittendus, nunciat custos carceris multo atrocius fuisse illic in me locutum: ita non passus est sibi benefieri: & tamen infra meritum poenas luit. Quod autem sublatum sibi aliquid queritur, vetus est eius cantilena. Non poterat olim tria passuum millia conficere, quin incideret in latrones. Vbique iactat se habere magnam librorum inestimabilium farraginem. Quemadmodum libros mihi oppignerabat, quos habebat Basileæ, cum meum auxilium in soluenda Badensi obsidione flagitaret: ita semel Bernæ, cum à me & Farello decem coronatos peteret, dicebat se habere domi tuæ magnum dolium librorum, & quinquaginta ducatos Bohemicos. Nuper etiam in cauponis nihil aliud prædicabat, quam nobilem bibliothecam, quam Basileæ reliquisset. Quanquam indignum est, ut de mea purgatione verbum faciā: puto enim sic me vixisse, ut sim extra furti suspicionem. Iam literæ iterum poscuntur. Vale optime, & mihi plurimum obseruande frater. Dominus Iesus te Spiritu suo ad opus suum semper dirigat, actuam familiam gubernet. Viretus te plurimum ac reuerenter salutat. Geneuæ x iii i. Mart.
units.tr: Keep this in mind: this fellow has for many years done nothing but run here and there, cadging money and clothes from others, and so getting by through cheating, as these vagabonds usually do. He came here often before our expulsion and sought a post, but none was found for him, because he wanted a famous school, which there is none of in these regions, and a large salary. Shortly afterwards he returned, lamenting in his usual way that he had been robbed by brigands. He withdrew to a neighbouring small town and sought the headship of a school; he did not obtain it, and blamed us for the refusal, although we had so little influence or favour there that, had he known it was impossible for us to help, he would have obtained it on that ground alone. Yet God is my witness that at that time we were trying for nothing else than to find him some position suited and convenient to him. Afterwards he came to Strasbourg, where he extorted twenty batzen from me, which I was forced to borrow elsewhere, for at that time I had sold my books and was utterly drained. He promised to repay it within a few days. He left a little box of no value with me as a pledge. Returning some months later, he asked me, smiling, or rather mocking, whether I would not lend him a few crowns. I replied that I needed that little sum which he had once had. Meanwhile the rogue secretly carried off the box from my library and entrusted it to Bucer's wife; she sent it back and reproached me, and I rebuked his impudence before several witnesses. Half a year later, or a full year, he wrote me a simple letter saying that he was besieged at Baden, that the whole nobility of the region had conspired against him, and that he could escape only if I sent a porter to carry him away in a merchant's chest. Bedrotus had a similar story. We laughed, and I replied to him briefly. For from many conjectures we gathered that he was in the city itself; from that time he has not appeared, and in the meantime a year has passed. Since I knew that many trifles were enclosed in the little box, I opened it before many witnesses. There were rotten apples in it, and all sorts of rubbish, half-torn books, and common ones such as Despauterius and the like. I also found letters which he had stolen from me. Sturm knows this, whom I called in. We put everything back, not without much laughter. When the late Grynaeus came to Worms, he announced that the man was at Basel. I instructed him as he left to send back the box. The rogue, having received it, began to shout that I was a thief who had taken away many priceless books. He came to Lausanne and told the same story to Viret. Recently, when he had come here, he was in the city for about ten days without my knowledge. Afterwards, at Viret's urging, I approached him and asked whether he did not wish to bring an action for theft against me, since he said he had lost excellent books; I called the most shameless rogue a rogue. The next day he attacked me in my own house, not only with the most abusive words but with furious violence; for this he was put in prison. When I earnestly pleaded for him before the magistrate, and he was about to be released without any penalty, the gaoler reported that he had spoken of me far more savagely there; thus he did not allow himself to be shown kindness, and yet he has paid a penalty below what he deserved. As for his complaint that something has been taken from him, that is an old song of his. He could never travel three miles without falling into the hands of brigands. Everywhere he boasts that he has a great heap of priceless books. Just as he used to pledge to me the books he had at Basel, when he was asking for my help in paying off the Baden siege, so once at Bern, when he sought ten crowns from Farel and me, he said that he had at home in your house a great cask of books and fifty Bohemian ducats. Lately, too, in the tavern he talked of nothing but the noble library he had left at Basel. Although it is unworthy that I should say anything in my own defence, I think I have lived in such a way that I am beyond suspicion of theft. Now the letter is being demanded again. Farewell, most excellent brother, and one to be most highly esteemed by me. May the Lord Jesus always direct you by his Spirit to his work, and govern your household. Viret greets you most warmly and respectfully. Geneva, 14th March.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus totus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, wholly yours.

units.la: CAL. NEOCOMENSIBVS.
units.tr: Calvin to the ministers of Neuchâtel.

units.la: Charitas Dei, & pax Christi, & communicatio Spiritus sancti vobis semper augeatur, fratres in Domino dilectissimi.
units.tr: May the love of God, the peace of Christ, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit always increase among you, most beloved brethren in the Lord.

units.la: CVm Enardus frater noster scriptum illud vestrum de modo exercendae disciplinae in fratres, & simul contrarium frattis cuiusdam attulisset, nemo fuit, qui non iudicaret, respoderi in promptu ad utramque posse. Sed quia non omnes adeGRANT, in hodiernum conuentum distulimus. Reiterum propositum hoc omnes uno consensu respondendum censuimus. Primum cum ministri certa quadam inter se disciplina opus habeant, non hoc quaerendum est qualiter sine legibus viuamus, sed inunda potius oeconomiae & ordinis ratio, quae apta sit ad nos in officio retinendos, & ad aedificationem seruiat. Nunquam autem sic cum paratae erunt res hominum, ut aliquid perfectum reperiatur. Ad hanc tamen scopum tendere semper debemus, ut coiunctis studiis, & communi, quantum fieri potest, consilio seruiamus Ecclesiae. Iā vero in hac nostra infirmitate fieri nequit, quin aliqua in nobis desiderentur, de quibus admoneri nos cogenit, & utile est. In aliis corrigeda sunt certa vitia: alij sunt anteuertendi, cum videmus periculum imminere, ne imprudentia labantur: alij ad maiorem zelum incitandi: alij obiurgandi, in alios inquirendu, si quis de illis sinister rumor, & tamé dubius, emersit. Nunc quaeritur, An omnino necesse sit, singulos a singulis priuatim admoneri, an vero interdum expediat, habita inter fratres deliberatio ne, hoc fieri a toto coetu. Atqui saepe contingit, ut a multis admoneri nos oporteat, de quo nemo vnus nos admonere potest. Exempli gratia, Erit, sicut nuper dictum est, exortus rumor aut querimonia de fratre quopiam: id vicini scient: non potest occurri meliore remedio, quàm si fratres, re inter se communicata, ipsum de quo agitur admoneant. Si falsa est criminatio, sic prouidebunt ne latius spargatur: sin vera, non ab vno tantum admoneri debuit ille, sed a fratrum coetu corrigi. Sit aliud exemplum, Erit aliquid in fratre quod disp licebit aliquibus vel ex plebe, vel ex collegis. Hic vertitur quaestio, num illud quod desideratur, pro vitio habendum sit & corrigedum?
