Ergo collatis capitibus, opus est iudicare. Multa quotidie incidunt eius generis. Atque huc spectabant ex parte Prouinciales Synodi, quae bis olim quotannis habebantur. Nam cum tractatum erat de doctrina, tum querimoniae de cuiusque vitiis audiebantur, & censura exercebatur in singulos. Vestrum ergo institutum, quale describitis, sanctum & legitimum indicamus. Et certè nimis esset impudentia
units.tr: When our brother Enardus brought us your writing on the manner of exercising discipline among the brethren, together with a counter-writing by a certain brother, no one present failed to judge that answers to both could readily be given. But since not everyone was present, we deferred the matter to today's assembly. Now we have all agreed, by one consent, to answer this proposition. First, since ministers need a fixed discipline among themselves, the question is not how we may live without laws, but rather what plan of order and arrangement is suited to keeping us in our office and serving edification. Human affairs will never be so arranged that something perfect is found. Yet we must always aim at this goal: that by united effort and common counsel, as far as possible, we serve the Church. Now in this weakness of ours it cannot be but that some faults are found in us, of which it is necessary and useful for us to be admonished. Some vices must be corrected in some; others must be anticipated when we see danger threatening that they may fall through imprudence; others must be stirred to greater zeal; others must be rebuked; and others must be inquired into if some sinister rumour, yet a doubtful one, has arisen about them. The question now is whether it is altogether necessary for individuals to be admonished privately by individuals, or whether it is sometimes expedient, after deliberation among the brethren, for this to be done by the whole assembly. Indeed it often happens that we must be admonished by many, about a matter on which no single person can admonish us. For example, as was just said, a rumour or complaint may arise about some brother; the neighbours will know of it. No better remedy can be found than for the brethren, having shared the matter among themselves, to admonish the very man concerned. If the accusation is false, they will thus take care that it is not spread more widely; but if it is true, that man ought not to be admonished by one alone but corrected by the assembly of the brethren. Take another example: there may be something in a brother that displeases some, either among the people or among his colleagues. Here the question arises whether what is found wanting should be regarded as a vice and corrected. Therefore, with heads brought together, a judgment is needed. Many such things happen every day. To this end, in part, looked the provincial synods, which were formerly held twice a year. For when doctrine was treated, complaints about each man's vices were also heard, and censure was exercised over individuals. We therefore judge your institution, as you describe it, holy and lawful. And certainly it would be too much impudence to disapprove in you the very thing we ourselves use as good and wholesome.

units.la: id ipsum improbare in vobis, quo nos tanquam bono & salu-tari vtimur. Adhibeatur modo æquitas primùm,& candor: de-inde prudentia & moderatio. Candorem cùm requirimus & æ-quitatem,hoc intelligimus, ne quis maligno animo fratrem su-gillare studeat. Prudentiam & moderationem sic accipimus, ne quis vitium arcanum deferat, quo nota fratri inuratur: neve quis immodica austeritate exaggeret quæ alioqui leuicula sunt. Quare si quando contingat, vel à morosis & importunis fratri-bus in medium proferri quæ tacenda potius erant, vel accusa-torio animo proferri arcana vitia, non modo nequaquam au-diendi sunt indices aut delatores, sed etiam seuere reprimendi. Quinetiam vt obuiam eatur his periculis, cùm agendæ sunt cé-surx, vtile est diligenter præfari, cauendum esse ab his omnibus, quæ salubrem censuræ medicinam vertunt in venenum. Nos certè statim ab initio præmonemus, vt si quę sint obscure simul-tates, aperiantur: si frater offensus à fratre fuerit, expostulet, antequam agantur censuræ, nec hæc simul permisceantur. His ergo initiis, quoad licet, præcludenda est via, ne obrepant: & si forte obrepserint, rescindenda sunt. Censuræ vero disciplina, quà non modo sanctam, sed etiam necessariam experimur, non est propterea negligenda aut omittenda. Fratrem verò illum qui ha-ctenus à vobis dissensit, obsecramus in Domino, ne vlterius pertinacia contendat ad repugnandum. Meminerit inter alia quæ Paulus in Pastore requirit, hoc esse non postremum, ne sit ἀνθά-λης, hoc est proprio iudicio addictus. Et certè hæc vna est ex præ-cipuis virtutibus boni Pastoris, sic exhorrere toto pectore con-tentiones, vt nunquam à fratribus, nisi ob causas maximè ne-cessarias, dissideat. Caueat etiam, ne qui hoc audiunt, suspicen-tur ipsum aut litigàdi studio, aut odio disciplinæ impedire, quo minus de nostris moribus fiat censura: non quia velimus hac eum inuidia grauare, aut vlla prorsus macula ipsum aspergere: sed ideo simpliciter hæc iudicamus, quia cupimus eius honori bene consultum. Quantum ad eius scriptum attinet, quo impu-gnare morem vestrum conatus est, quod bona eius venia dictu sit, cùm fraternam correctionem actum charitatis vocat, à quo nemo sit eximendus: non videtur nobis animaduertifle quod e-rat in primis cognitu necessarium, plures esse species fraternæ correctionis. Vt alias omittamus, hæc de qua disputatur, distin-ctam & propriam rationem habet. Est enim pars Ecclesiasticæ politiæ. Ergo cum illa generali correctione confundi non debet, quæ omnibus indifferenter mandatur. Proinde non concedi-mus illi esse simplicem & nudum charitatis actum: siquidem iu-dicium est ordinis & disciplinæ causa institutum, quod tamen vnam ædificationem pro fine propositam habet. Neque etiam conce-
units.tr: Let fairness and candour be applied first, and then prudence and moderation. When we require candour and fairness, we mean that no one should strive to disparage a brother with a malicious mind. We understand prudence and moderation thus: that no one should bring forward a hidden vice by which a mark is branded on a brother, nor magnify with immoderate severity things that are otherwise rather slight. Therefore, if it ever happens that things which ought rather to be kept silent are brought into the open, either by troublesome and importunate brethren, or hidden vices are brought forward with an accusing spirit, then not only must informers and accusers by no means be heard, but they must also be severely restrained. Moreover, to meet these dangers, when censures are to be carried out it is useful to preface them carefully with a warning that one must beware of all those things which turn the wholesome medicine of censure into poison. We, at any rate, admonish from the very beginning that if there are any hidden enmities, they should be brought out into the open; if a brother has been offended by a brother, let him seek redress before censures are carried out, and let these not be mixed together. From these beginnings, then, as far as is permitted, the way must be closed off, lest such things creep in; and if perhaps they have crept in, they must be cut away. But the discipline of censure, which we experience as not only holy but also necessary, is not therefore to be neglected or omitted. As for that brother who has hitherto dissented from you, we beseech him in the Lord that he no longer persist in obstinate opposition. Let him remember that among the other things Paul requires in a minister, this is not the least: that he not be ἀνθάδης, that is, addicted to his own judgment. And certainly this is one of the chief virtues of a good minister: so to abhor contentions with his whole heart that he never disagrees with the brethren except for the most necessary causes. Let him also take care that those who hear this do not suspect him either of a zeal for litigation or of hatred of discipline, which would hinder censure of our morals. We do not say this because we wish to burden him with that odium, or to stain him with any blemish whatever, but we judge these things simply because we desire his honour to be well consulted. As for his writing, in which he has tried to attack your custom, which, with his good leave, may be said, since he calls fraternal correction an act of charity from which no one is to be exempted, it does not seem to us that he has noticed what was especially necessary to know: that there are several kinds of fraternal correction. To pass over the others, the one now disputed has its own distinct character. For it is a part of ecclesiastical polity, and therefore must not be confused with that general correction which is enjoined indiscriminately on all. Accordingly we do not grant that it is a simple and bare act of charity, since it is a judgment instituted for the sake of order and discipline, which nevertheless has one edification set before it as its aim. Nor do we concede

units.la: concedimus, neminem ab eius obligatione eximi. Tametsi ambigua est loquutio haec, quia tam palfiue, quàm actiue accipi potest. Sed vtroque modo negamus omnes hac lege obstringi, quae specialiter est ministris destinata. Sicut enim quae ad ordinem habendi Senatus spectant leges, plebem non ligant: ita difcipli- nam inter nos obseruare conuenit, cui subiecti sunt foli ministri. Quod in eadem propositione habet, Sub praecepto Dei cadere fraternam correctionem, fi intelligit auctor, cuiusuis correctionis expresse Verbo Dei contineri: hoc verò nequaquam illi confitemur. Substantiam Ecclesiasticae disciplinae exprimit di fertis verbis Scriptura: forma autem eius exercendae, quoniam à Domino praescripta non est, à ministris constitui debet pro çdificatione. Qua ratione etiam negamus, solam delinquentis emendationem intuendam hic esse: respectus enim ordinis publici & communis aedificationis habetur. Cuius rei fumere exemplum ex Scripturis licet, Cùm Paulus Hierosolymam venisset, admonetur à Iacobo & Senioribus, quàm male audiat inter Iudaeos, simul etiam qualiter fe illis approbare debeat: non dubiù quin praeceffierit deliberatio inter fratres: & fuerit Paulo absente. Cur hoc? quia scilicet communis aedificationis intererat. Similiter cùm Petrum reprehendunt fratres, quòd ad Gentes diuertisset, non legimus quicquam illi in aurem clam fuisse ab vno dictu: quia scilicet offensio manarat ad plures, aequum fuit communiter ipsum àfratribus admoneri. Tametfiautem immeritò hac de cau fa arguebatur, non tamen peccaffe legimus fratres in modo agendi, sed in ipsa causa: modum enim tenebant vsitatum & ordinarium. Christi praeceptum, quod Matth.18. habetur, accipimus de occultis vitiis, quemadmodum etiam verba sonant. Ergo fi quid frater, te conscio, deliquerit, necalios habeatteftes, iubet Christus te ipsum priuatim conuenire: quanquam non vetat, quin idem facias, etiam fi qui alij tecum conscij sint. Fieri enim potest, vt tu hoc ignores, vel expedire non putes coram pluribus eum reprehendi. Quod postea subiungit, Si nihil hac via pro feceris, vt tecum duos aut tres testes adhibeas: hoc nostro iudicio intelligendum est non de testibus delicti, sed admonitionis, quo scilicet plus momenti habeat: porro hoc nihil ad impediendam censurae rationem, de qua nunc controuersia est. Neque enim hoc agitur, vt occulta delicta in medium proferantur, ad irrogandam fratribus infamiam, sed tàtum quae eiusmodi sunt, vt aliquid offendiculi genuerint, aut non procul absint à gignedo. Huius speciei exemplum habemus in Petri reprehensione: neque enim testes abegit Paulus, vt clam omnibus ipsum admonneret, sed hoc fecit coram Ecclesia. Nec tamen res omnibus nota erat: sed quia imminebat periculum, anteuertere voluit. Quintam propositionem recipere sine exceptione non possumus: pronunciat enim, nos scite facturos, si fratrem etiam peccato notorio laborantem admoneamus priuatim. Atqui Paulus, vbi prohibuit recipi aduersus presbyteros accusationem, nisi sub idoneis testibus: ex aduerso presbyteros peccantes coram omnibus argui vult, vt cæteri timorem habeant. Si interdum conueniit publice argui peccantes, etiam presbyteros, quibus habenda est maior reuerentia, idque pertinet ad exemplum, non scite neque prudenter faceret si quis abstinere vellet à tali reprehensione. Quid ergo? Certe quantum iudicamus, ex repraesenti & tempore capiendum est consilium. Semper autem haec duo sunt pro spicienda, ne à tristitia absorbeatur qui peccauit: & ne videamur ad peccata conniuere. Sextam propositionem cur addiderit frater mitamur: satis enim cöuenit, Ecclesiæ nomine, in Christi verbis, eam proprie designari, cuius membrum est ille, cuius contumacia denunciatur. Cæterum duo hic sunt obseruanda, sic publicandam esse contumaciam peccatoris obstinati coram vna Ecclesia, vt si ea per contemptum relicta, alio migret, illic quoque denuncietur. Atque hoc sibi volunt antiqui Canones cum extraneum ad communionem recipi prohibent, nisi testimonium attulerit. Vbi enim Ecclesiæ communio, si ab vna damnatus, ab altera recipitur? Vbi disciplina, si qui vnam Ecclesiam contempsit in aliam migrando, impune talem fert superbiam? Alterum quoque obseruandum est, vt vnius Ecclesiæ ministros esse sentiamus, qui in vnum collegium adunati, vnum corpus efficiunt. Quorsum enim Decanus? quorsum alia omnia? nisi tanquam vnius corporis membra inter nos coalescamus? Haec ab auctore propositionum in bonam partem acceptum iri, sicut syncero animo à nobis scripta sunt, confidimus. Nostræ sane omnium partes sunt, non tantum cedere veritati, sed vtrò eam, & obuiis, quod aiunt, manibus protrusisque accipere. Valete fratres in Domino dilectissimi. Dominus Spiritum sapientiæ & prudentiæ in dies vobis adaugeat in Ecclesiæ suæ ædificationem, & ministerium vestrum quam fructuosissimum reddat. Geneuæ, ex conuentu nostro. vii. Idus Nouembris.
units.tr: that no one is exempt from its obligation, although this phrasing is ambiguous, since it can be taken both passively and actively. But in either sense we deny that all are bound by this law, which is directed specifically to ministers. For just as laws concerning the order of holding the Senate do not bind the common people, so it is fitting that among us the discipline be observed to which only the ministers are subject. As to what he says in the same proposition, that fraternal correction falls under the precept of God: if the author means that every kind of correction is expressly contained in the Word of God, we by no means confess this to him. Scripture expresses the substance of ecclesiastical discipline in plain words; but its form of exercise, since the Lord has not prescribed it, must be established by ministers for edification. For this reason too we deny that only the amendment of the offender is to be considered here, since regard is had to public order and common edification. We may take an example of this from Scripture. When Paul had come to Jerusalem, he is admonished by James and the elders how badly he is spoken of among the Jews, and at the same time how he ought to show himself to them. There is no doubt that deliberation took place among the brethren beforehand, and that it was held in Paul's absence. Why so? Because, of course, common edification was at stake. Similarly, when the brethren rebuked Peter because he had turned aside to the Gentiles, we do not read that anything was said to him secretly, in his ear, by one man; because the offence had spread to many, it was right that he be admonished in common by the brethren. Although he was rightly accused in this matter, we do not read that the brethren sinned in their manner of acting, but in the cause itself, for they kept to the customary and ordinary way. The precept of Christ found in Matthew 18 we take to concern hidden faults, as the very words sound. So if a brother has sinned in your presence, and he has other witnesses, Christ bids you to meet him privately; yet he does not forbid you to do the same even if others also share your knowledge. For it may be that you are unaware of it, or do not think it expedient that he be rebuked before many. What he adds afterwards, If you have done nothing by this way, take with you one or two witnesses, in our judgment is to be understood not of witnesses to the offence but of the admonition, so that it may carry more weight; and this has nothing to do with hindering the method of censure, which is now under dispute. For the aim is not that hidden offences be dragged into the open to bring infamy upon the brethren, but only those of such a kind as have given rise to some stumbling-block, or are not far from giving rise to one. We have an example of this kind in Peter's rebuke: Paul did not dismiss witnesses in order to admonish him secretly before everyone, but did so before the Church. Nor was the matter known to all; but since danger was threatening, he wished to forestall it. We cannot accept the fifth proposition without exception, for it pronounces that we shall act wisely if we admonish privately a brother who is labouring under even a notorious sin. Yet Paul, when he forbade an accusation against elders to be received unless it was supported by credible witnesses, on the other hand wishes elders who sin to be rebuked before all, so that the rest may have fear. If it is sometimes fitting that sinners be publicly rebuked, even elders, to whom greater reverence is due, and this pertains to example, then one would not act wisely or prudently who wished to abstain from such rebuke. What then? Certainly, as far as we judge, counsel must be taken from the circumstances and the time. But always two things are to be kept in view: that the one who has sinned not be swallowed up by sorrow, and that we not seem to connive at sins. As for the sixth proposition, why the brother added, let him be to you as a publican, we grant it, for it is well agreed that by the name of the Church, in Christ's words, is properly meant that Church of which the one whose obstinacy is denounced is a member. Besides, two things are to be observed here: that the obstinacy of a stubborn sinner must be made known before one Church, so that if he, leaving it in contempt, migrates elsewhere, he is to be denounced there too. This is what the ancient canons mean when they forbid a stranger to be received into communion unless he brings a testimonial. For where is the communion of the Church, if one condemned by one is received by another? Where is discipline, if one who has despised one Church by migrating to another bears such pride with impunity? The other thing to be observed is that we regard ourselves as ministers of one Church, who, gathered into one college, form one body. For to what end is there a dean? To what end is anything else, unless we are joined together among ourselves as members of one body? We trust that these things, written by us in sincerity, will be taken in good part by the author of the propositions. It is indeed the part of all of us not only to yield to the truth, but to receive it of our own accord, with open arms, as they say. Farewell, brethren most beloved in the Lord. May the Lord daily increase for you the Spirit of wisdom and prudence, for the edification of his Church, and make your ministry most fruitful. Geneva, from our assembly, the seventh day before the Ides of November.

units.la: Salue mi amantissime frater. Res nostræ in ancipiti statu sunt, nec quid sperem magnopere, nec etiam quid desperem, habeo. In spem tamen magis propendeo, si quidem Synodo contro-uersia uerfia (vt par est) examinanda diiudicandáque committatur: eámquæ vt impetremus,studio acerrimo incumbemus:quanquâ reluctatutum pro virili Antagonistam elle coniiciam,qui ad cę-tera, omnem Ecclesiæ auctoritatem atque œconomiam ad tri-bunal tantum forense reuocat,corámque iis indubie hanc cupit ponfsimum decidi causam, quorum animos iam ante blandi-loquentia prærceupauit, aut prærceupasse videtur potius, actor futurus idcirco non ingratus,quod pro ipsorum placitis,ceu pro aris ac focis depugnet.pro disputationis habitæ auctoritate,tan quam Dianæ illius magnæ Ephesiorum, clamoribus indefinen-tibus vociferetur.Nos quanquam bonorum voluntates à nobis non alienas esse cognoscimus, tamen Domini beneficio nullus adeò applausus humanus sic nobis oculos perstrinxit, vt non potius causæ bonitatem, quàm suffragia potentum respicia-mus. Neque vllorum mortalium reformidamus iudicium: do-net modo nobis Christus,vti qua par est,æquanimitate,pruden-tia, constantiáque stare pro veritate atque pugnare possimus. Statum controuersiæ hunc nobis vrgebimus.Primùm vt quę sit Scripturæ Canonicæ prę omnibus omnium mortalium scriptis, auctoritas intelligatur, deinde vt prophetiam religionisque dogmata non vllis hominum pronuntiatis, sed Canonis solius lydio examinari conueniat:postremò quàm non fuerimus nos ha-ctenus, neq; nùc simus vllius non necessariæ nouationis auctores.Qua in relicet abunde nobis & Scripturæ,& veterum auctoritas exemplaq; suffragentur, tamen negotij erit non exigui esi veritatem etiam probabilem auditori efficere,pręposterámq; & nimiam placitorum humanorum admirationem,& affectatio-nem constatiæ animis eximere, maximè quâdo eam φιλαυτίαν noster ille mirabili lenocinio incendit & auget.Quocirca te ro-go mi amantissime frater, vti tuo nos consilio velis instruere, idque copiose & prolixè, quibúsque hęc potissimum rationibus agi à nobis placeat docere : eo enim officio nec gratius, neque magis necessarium præstare nobis potes. Scribas autem rogo quamprimum, ne intempestiua actione obruamur prius,quàm tuo aliorúmque consiliis præparemur. De Eucharistia déque ministerij sacri auctoritate & vsu , œconomia item Eccle-siæ, quatenus agendum differendúmque sit, in ipsa (arbitror) arena discemus : sed de his satis. De Philippi & Lutheri re-conciliatione , déque noua apud Brabantos hæresi , mitto, quę ad me ex Wittebergà Ambrosius noster Blaurerus scripsit, quòd sciam ea non ingrata fore tibi. Dominum laudo eos motus salubriter consopitos,nec dubito sanitatem aliquam Ec-clesiæ allaturos esse, adeò nouit is etiam mala nostra ad sui nos minis gloriam vlectorumque salutem conuertere:De pace inter Cæsarem & Gallum varia narrantur. Sunt qui dissimilisse rursum putent, quanquam id vix verisimile mihi fit. Helvetios non reuerti mitamur, adeoque nec nuntiis nec litetis significari, vbi sint & quid agant. Fama tristis licet non publica fert ab Anglorum Rege caesos esse memorabili grauissimaque strage, eámque nonnihil probabilem facit repentinus & improuisus legati Regij à Salodoro discessus. Sed iam vale: & nos precibus consiliisq; tuis iuuare perge. Salutat te amanter & reuerenter Beatus charus & venerandus Collega. Symmystas tuos vtriusque nomine saluere iube. Bernæ, v i i. Nouemb. Anno M. D. XLIIII. Tuus Sulzerus.
units.tr: Greetings, my dearest brother. Our affairs are in a precarious state. I have neither great hope nor great despair about them. Still, I lean more towards hope, provided the controversy is committed to a synod to be examined and judged, as is fitting. We will work with the utmost zeal to obtain this. Yet I expect that our opponent will resist with all his might. In other matters he reduces all the authority and government of the Church to a purely forensic tribunal, and he undoubtedly wants this case decided chiefly before those whose minds he has already won over with flattering speech, or rather seems to have won over. He will be a welcome advocate for them, since he fights for their opinions as if for altars and hearths. As for the authority of the disputation that was held, he will shout with tireless clamour, like the crowd for that great Diana of the Ephesians. We know that the goodwill of good men is not alien to us. Yet by the Lord's kindness no human applause has so dazzled our eyes that we look to the merit of the cause rather than to the votes of the powerful. Nor do we fear the judgment of any mortal. Only let Christ teach us to stand for the truth and fight for it with the proper equanimity, prudence and steadfastness. This is the state of the controversy we will press. First, that the authority of canonical Scripture above all the writings of all mortals be understood. Second, that prophecy and the doctrines of religion should be examined not by any human pronouncements but by the touchstone of the canon alone. Last, that we have not hitherto been, and are not now, authors of any unnecessary innovation. Although both Scripture and the authority and examples of the ancients support us abundantly in this, it will be no small task to make even the truth plausible to the hearer, and to remove from minds their perverse and excessive admiration for human opinions and their affectation of constancy, especially since that self-love [φιλαυτία] our friend kindles and increases with wonderful flattery. So I ask you, my dearest brother, to instruct us with your counsel, and to do so fully and at length, and to teach us which methods you think we should chiefly pursue. No service you could render us would be more welcome or more necessary. Please write as soon as possible, so that we are not overwhelmed by an untimely action before we are prepared by your counsel and that of others. About the Eucharist, the authority and use of the sacred ministry, and likewise the government of the Church, we shall learn, I think, in the arena itself, how far we must act and how far defer. But enough of this. Concerning the reconciliation of Philip and Luther, and the new heresy among the Brabanters, I send what our Ambrosius Blaurer wrote to me from Wittenberg, since I know it will not be unwelcome to you. I praise the Lord that those disturbances have been wholesomely quieted, and I do not doubt they will bring some healing to the Church, for he knows how to turn even our evils to the glory of his name and the salvation of his people. Various reports circulate about the peace between the Emperor and the Frenchman. Some think it was again a pretence, though this seems hardly likely to me. We wonder that the Swiss have not returned, and that neither messengers nor letters report where they are or what they are doing. An unofficial but sad rumour reports that they were cut down by the King of the English in a memorable and very grievous slaughter. The sudden and unexpected departure of the royal envoy from Soleure makes this somewhat credible. But now farewell. Continue to help us with your prayers and counsel. Our dear and venerable colleague Beatus greets you warmly and respectfully. Please greet your fellow initiates on behalf of us both. From Berne, 7 November 1544. Yours, Sulzer.

units.la: AB hoc fratre, qui meas tibi literas reddidit, coronatum & duos capitatos argenteos accipies. Hæc enim summa, nisi memoria me fallit, restabat. Peto vt me excusatū habeas, quòd non citius miserim. Caeterum qua de causa mittatur istuc frater hic à Neocomensibus, ipse coràm referet. Nihil aut parum, meo iudicio, difficultatis est in causa. Sed vnius hominis peruicacia & importunitas eos cogit, vobis & nobis molestos esse. Habent in suo coetu vnum ex eo Doctorum grege, ex quo nemo haćtenus vir bonus prodiit, qui non cessat aliquid subinde illis negotij exhibere. Sunt autem duæ causæ, quæ ipsum im pellunt. Nam & natura factus est ad contradicendum: & quia nō tanti æstimatur ab aliis, quanti seipsum facit, hoc se modo vlcif citur. Si esset in hac Ecclesia, facile cohiberetur. Ratio enim eius domandi nobis esset ad manum. Illic verò habet Principis Legatorum, à quo sustinetur. Sic enim hominum se præsidiis muni re solent eiusmodi fuci, vt impune noceant. Quod vos omnes sponte factu ros scio, peto tamen à vobis, vt in causa tam san ćta fratribus porrigatis manum. Hoc est, vestra aućtoritate ad iuuetis eos & instruatis, quò Ifmaëlem illum compescant. Hoc, non quia putarem esse necessarium, sed vt fratri morem gere rent, scripsi.
units.tr: From this brother, who is delivering my letter to you, you will receive a crown and two silver coins with heads on them. This, if my memory serves, was the only sum still outstanding. I ask you to excuse me for not sending it sooner. As for why this brother is being sent to you by the Neuchâtel people, he will explain in person. In my judgement the case involves little or no difficulty. But the obstinacy and importunity of one man is forcing them to trouble both you and us. In their congregation they have one of that group of teachers from whom no good man has yet come forth, and he never stops causing them some trouble. There are two causes that drive him on. He was made by nature for contradiction, and since others do not value him as highly as he values himself, he takes revenge in this way. If he were in this Church, he could easily be restrained, for we would have a ready means of taming him. But over there he has the support of the Prince's envoys, and he relies on them. Such impostors are accustomed to fortify themselves with the protection of men, so that they can harm with impunity. I know you would all do this willingly, yet I ask you to lend a hand to the brothers in a cause so holy. That is, by your authority, help and instruct them, so that they may curb that Ishmael. I write this not because I think it necessary, but so that I may humour the brother.

units.la: Est aliud præterea, quod te summopere oratum velim. Sunt in Prouincia fratres pro quibus scis nos semper laborarle. Neque id immerito. Sunt enim ea pietate innocentiáque præditi, vt bonis omnibus commendata ipsorum salus esse debeat. Ante triennium iam eo visque progressi fuerant, vt Curiç Aquensi confessionem ediderint puram ac simplicem: qualis inter nos edere tur. Ac ne subito feruore, qui statim euanuerit, factum id putes: quoties fuerunt interpellati, constanter in ea perstiterunt. Inter ea crudeliter suerunt vexati. Cùm sæuam hostium tyrannidem pertupertulissent, tandem impetrarunt à Rege, vt iudices darer, qui de tota causa verius cognoscerent. Rex duobus inquirendi partes mandauit: cognoscere ipse ac pronuntiare voluit. Hoc contisnent literæ, vt de eorum doctrina & moribus publicè & clàm diligenter sciscitentur, qui mittendi sunt. Hoc fratres non reformidant. Nam ita se gesserunt apud omnes, vt singulare probitatis testimonium habeant etiam ab aduersariis. Quòd ad doctrinam spectat, confessionem Regi edituri sunt, sicuti postulauit, claram & synceram: quæ distinctè plus complectitur, quàm dici in eos possit. Nunc totis viribus renituntur & Episcopi, & Præfecti, & Curia ipsa, ne Regio diplomati sit locus. Si non admittitur, expositi erunt leonibus & lupis, vt efferatam rabiem in eos exerant. Hoc enim captant illi, vt sibi impune aduersus miseros grassari liceat. Si admittitur, nec sic quidem euaserint periculum. Nam & in oppidulis tribus, & in compluribus pagis puram Euangelij doctrinam profitentur. Et in oppidulo vno templum inquinamentis omnibus repurgarunt: Cœnámque illic & Baptismum nostro more celebrant. Quò præsentius illis vtrinque periculum imminet, eò maiore studio adiuuandi sunt à nobis: præsertim in hac admirabili constantia, cui nos deesse, summo flagitio non careret. Addè quòd hic eorum causa non agitur sed aut patefacta per eorum cladem erit via crudelitati impiorum in toto regno: aut Euangelium hoc modo perrumpet. Quid ergo superest, nisi vt neruos omnes intendamus, ne cessantibus nobis, pij fratres opprimantur, & occludatur Christo ianua in longum tempus? Huius rei volui te præmonitum, vt si quando ad vos cófugerint, paratos habeas vestrorum animos ad opem illis ferendam. Alterum autem ex his duobus agendum erit. Vel enim petendum erit à Rege, vt concedo semel beneficio frui eos sinat: vel mitigandus eius animus, si aduersus eos excanduerit.
units.tr: There is also something else that I very much want to ask of you. There are in the Province brothers for whom you know we are always labouring, and not undeservedly. For they are endowed with such piety and innocence that their safety ought to be commended to all good men. Three years ago they had advanced so far that they published at Aix a confession that was pure and simple, of the kind published among us. And lest you think this was done in some sudden fervour that would soon fade, whenever they have been challenged they have stood firm in it. Meanwhile they have been cruelly harassed. Having endured the savage tyranny of their enemies, they at last obtained from the King that judges should be appointed to examine the whole case more truthfully. The King committed the inquiry to two men, but wished to hear the case and pronounce judgement himself. The letters state this: that those who are to be sent should carefully investigate, both publicly and privately, the doctrine and morals of these men. The brothers do not fear this, for they have so conducted themselves before everyone that they have a singular testimony of integrity, even from their adversaries. As to doctrine, they are going to present the King with the confession he asked for, clear and sincere, which sets out distinctly more than can be said against them. Now the bishops, the governors and the court itself are striving with all their strength that the royal decree may find no place. If it is not admitted, they will be exposed to lions and wolves, so that these beasts may vent their savage rage upon them. For that is what those men are aiming at, that they may be free to rage against the wretched with impunity. If it is admitted, even so they will not escape danger. For they profess the pure doctrine of the Gospel in three small towns and in many villages, and in one small town they have cleansed the church of all defilements, and there they celebrate the Supper and Baptism after our manner. The more immediate the danger threatening them on both sides, the more eagerly they must be helped by us, especially in view of this admirable constancy, in which to fail them would be a most shameful crime. Moreover, their cause is not being decided here, but either through their ruin a way will be opened for the cruelty of the impious throughout the whole kingdom, or the Gospel will break through in this manner. What remains, then, but that we strain every nerve, lest, if we are idle, the godly brothers are crushed and the door to Christ is shut for a long time? I wanted you forewarned of this, so that if ever they flee to you for refuge, you may have your people ready to bring them aid. Of the two courses, one will have to be pursued: either we must ask the King to allow them to enjoy the favour once, or his feelings must be softened, if he has flared up against them.

units.la: Audio Lutherum tandem cum atroci inuectiua non tam in vos, quàm in nos omnes prorupisse. Nunc vix audeo à vobis petere, vt taceatis: quia neque squum est, sic vexari immerentes, & illis negari sui purgandi locum: & statuere difficile est, num id expediat. Sed hæc cupio vobis in mentem venire: primùm quæstus sit vir Lutherus, & quàtis dotibus excellat, quanta animi fortitudine & constantia, quanta dexteritate, quanta doctrinæ efficacia hactenus ad profligandum Antichristi regnum, & simul propagandam salutis doctrinam incubuerit. Sæpe dicere solitus sum: etiam si me diabolum vocaret, me tamen hoc illi honoris habiturum, vt insignem Dei seruum agnoscam: qui tamé vt pollet eximiis virtutibus, ita magnis vitiis laboret. Hanc intemperiem, qua vbique ebullit, vtinam magis frenare studuisset.
units.tr: I hear that Luther has at last burst out with a savage invective, not so much against you as against all of us. Now I can scarcely bring myself to ask you to keep silent, because it is neither fair that innocent men should be harassed in this way and denied a place to clear themselves, and yet it is hard to decide whether this is expedient. But I wish these points to come to your mind. First, consider what a man Luther is, and with what gifts he excels: what courage and steadfastness, what skill, what effectiveness of doctrine he has devoted to overthrowing the kingdom of Antichrist and at the same time spreading the teaching of salvation. I have often been accustomed to say that even if he were to call me a devil, I would still pay him this honour, that I acknowledge him as an outstanding servant of God, who, though he is strong in remarkable virtues, nevertheless labours under great vices. Would that he had striven more to bridle this intemperance, which boils over everywhere.

units.la: Vehementiam autem,quæ illi est ingenita,vtinam in hostes veritatis semper contulisset, non etiam vibrasset in seruos Domini.Vtinam recognoscendis suis vitiis plus operæ dedisset.Plurimum illi obfuerunt adulatores, cùm ipse quoque natura ad sibi indulgendum nimis propensus esset. Nostrum tamen est, sic reprehendere quod in eo est malorum, vt præclaris illis donis aliquid cócedamus.Hoc igitur primùm reputes,obsecro,cum tuis collegis, cum primario Christi seruo, cui multùm debemus omnes,vobis esse negotium. Deinde nihil vos,confligendo,profeturos,quàm vt lusum impiis præbeatis, vt non tam de nobis quàm de Euangelio triumphent.Si mutuò nos proscindimus,plus satis habent nobis fidei. Cùm autem vno consensu & ore vno prædicamus Christum,eo abutuntur ad fidem nobis derogandā, in quo plusquàm par sit,nobis credunt.Hæc potius intueri & cogitare te velim,quàm quid sua intemperie promeritus sit Lutherus. Ne ergo nobis euenit quod denuntiat Paulus, vt inuicem mordendo nos & lacerando,consumamur,etiam si ille nos provocauerit,abstinendum potius à certamine,quàm vt communi Ecclesiæ iactura vulnus augeamus. Vale frater mihi in Domino plurimum honorande, & amice charissime. Saluta reuerenter Symmystas omnes meo nomine.Dominus vos conseruet,& sua in vobis dona magis ac magis augeat.Geneuæ,xxv.Nouemb M.D.XLIIII. Collegæ mei vos plurimum salutant.
units.tr: Would that he had always directed the vehemence that is ingrained in him against the enemies of the truth, and had not also lashed out at the servants of the Lord. Would that he had given more effort to recognising his own faults. His flatterers did him great harm, since he himself was also by nature too inclined to indulge himself. It is our duty, however, to rebuke the evils in him while still granting something to those outstanding gifts. Therefore, I beg you, first weigh this: that you, together with your colleagues, have to do with the foremost servant of Christ, to whom we all owe much. Next, in contending with him you will gain nothing except to offer the impious a spectacle, so that they triumph not so much over us as over the Gospel. If we tear each other apart, they have more than enough reason to distrust us. But when we preach Christ with one consent and one voice, they abuse that to take away credit from us, and they believe us more than is fitting in whatever they can use against us. I would rather you looked at and considered these things than what Luther has deserved by his intemperance. Let it not happen to us, then, as Paul warns, that by biting and tearing one another we are consumed; even if he has provoked us, we should refrain from strife rather than widen the wound by a common loss to the Church. Farewell, brother, most honoured by me in the Lord, and dearest friend. Greet all our fellow ministers reverently in my name. May the Lord preserve you and increase his gifts in you more and more. Geneva, 25 November 1544. My colleagues send you their warmest greetings.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: PRAEFATIO IOAN. CALVINI IN EDITIONEM Gallicam Noui Testamenti Neocomi Anno M. D. XXXV. Cuius hæc summa est:
units.tr: PREFACE OF JOHN CALVIN TO THE FRENCH EDITION OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, NEUCHÂTEL, 1535. Its summary is this:

units.la: CHRISTVM ESSE LEGIS FINEM.
units.tr: CHRIST IS THE END OF THE LAW.

units.la: Omnibus iis qui Iesum Christum & Euangelium ex animo diligunt.
units.tr: To all who love Jesus Christ and the Gospel from the heart.

units.la: CVM Deus Optimus Maximus absolutissimus omnium opifex,in illa vniuersi creatione plusquàm admirandum sese exhibuisset,tum verò in hominis creatione,ita operi summam apposuit,vt in eo singularis quædam supra omnes alias res conditas tanti auctoris Excellentia emineret. Vnum videlicet ad imaginem suam & similitudinem effformauit,vt gloriæ ipsius notæ in nouissimo illo ipsius opere expressæ emicarent.Fœlix ni mirum homo,& nunquam non fœlix futurus,si priuilegij supra alias creaturas in seipsum erogati non immemor, cù plena demissione missione sese coram vno Creatore perpetuò deie—tum sisteret: si ipsum vnum continua gratiarum actione prædicaret: si nihil in sese repositum statuendo, tot illa cœlitus accepta dona ad Dei vnicam(vt quæ tota illius esset)gloriam referenda cogitaret.Infœlix verò, dum suam fœlicitatem illam non capit, ac in semet-ipso gestit acquiescere: dum ipsi excidit tantus ille singularis erga se liberalitatis auctor, contumeliosè ingratus in ipsum attollens sese, superbire etiam ausus est aduersus factorem suum. Hinc ille præceps letho datus est: hinc à natiua illa ingenuitate in pudendam seruitutem deiectus, à creationis excellentia detrusus cœpit iacere. Hinc illum excipere pro gloria nuditas, pro tot & tantis Dei donis miseranda abdicatio, vt in sua illa superbia confusus vel inuitus disceret, quod syncero affectu præ se ferre paulò ante dedignatus erat. Ergo hæc illius schola & studium esse tum debuit, vt & seipsum meram vanitatem esse agnosceret, & nihil aliud extitisse prius ex sese quàm vanitatem etiam peisentiret: quod præterea accessisset, peculiari Dei indulgentiæ acceptum ferri debuisse. At verò Dominus tam indignum creaturæ nobilissimæ casum auersatus, & ipsam exosam habere cœpit, atque vt pro tali merito dignum erat, ne opus quidem suum censere: ex quo & imago illa atque expressio ipsius plane iam induƈta esset, & tam præclara bonitatis ipsius erga hominem testimonia conuulsa. Sic demum illius cuiusdam delectationis loco, quam ex creatura illa singularem percepisset Dominus, vt non secus atque in filij dilecti amore acquiesceret, despectus & abominatio Domini ipsius successit: vnde & si quid aliàs gratum ab homine extitisset, si paterno intuitu illum Dominus prosecutus esset, totum illud ipsi tædio, diuidiæ, abominationi fuerit: & non secus atque de perduellionis reo, pronuntiarit, pœnitere se quod hominem creasset. Enimuero neque in eo etiam vnde primùm cœperat, stetit hominum prauitas, quin potius vt quidam appositè expressit, Ætas parentum peior auis tulit se nequiores, mox daturos progeniem vitiosiorè. Quid igitur? Nempe cùm fœcunda illa culpæ sæcula extremam aduersum se manum Dei prouocassent, Deus ipse non tam in misericordiam & paternam indulgentiam propensus, quàm ipsamet misericordia atque indulgentia, cùm amore non prosequi nollet, quòd amari in sese adeo esset indignum, humanum genus tamen interire prorsus, & meritissimo exitio absorberi non sustinuit: resipiscendi tempus & rationem si forte ad sese aliquo modo redirent, prorogauit: & quanuis aperte quidem indignationem quasi oculis conniuentibus dissimulaꝛet, sibíque itaipsos permitteret, vt nulla vox eius, nulla lex ac directio expressa exaret, quæ argueret peccati: nunquam se tamen adeo apud ipsos Dominum celauit,quin illa exhiberet quę & officij commone-facerent, & ad ipsum quærendum ac tantumnon palpandum veluti manu duceret:vt vel pro illius modi cognitione,ab ipsis agnosci etiam,& agnitum legitimo honore coli oportuerit. Nâ quo se verteret quisquam cum non vocalia quædam testimonia veritatis & gloriæ tanti opificis occurrerent,quæ non alte,sonore,ac splendide summi vnius Dei Maiestatem in sublime sub tato,tot rerum admirabilissimo paratu euectam circunferrent? Sic adeo in singulis partibus illius vniuersi sursum ac deorsum insculptas reliquit atque expressas gloriæ, potentiæ, bonitatis, sapientiæ, æternitatis significantissimas inscriptiones! Vnde illud Pauli, apud ipsos etiam hominesapud quos Dei veri notitia ex Verbo non extitit,non ideo tamen ... reliquisse. Ergo quot exiterunt vbique Dei creaturæ, totidem remanserunt præcones humano generi,immensæ gloriæ sui auctoris:ac proinde ex illatum rerum agnitione ad Deum ipsum peruenire debuit, vt & ipsi agnito, fides omnis atque obsequium deferretur, quod tanti illius beri bonitati,sapientiæ,potentiæ,æternitati cogrueret.Quid quod ipsemet alioqui non vocales creaturę,homini ipsi etiam hac in parte quasi verba præiuisse dicerentur?Nempe & volucrum moduli Deum personabant, & bruta ipsa mugientia auctorem illum inclamabant, & elementorum series ad ipsum stupebat,& montes illum intonabant, & fontes fluuiique ipsimet oculis quasi nictabant,& gramina ac flores ipsi adblandiebantur. Sed neque etiam extra sese quemque adeo illum requirete opus erat: quin cum in semetipso cuique beneficium ipsius conlataret, quę deinde iusta celebrationis excusatio, quin ad ipsum continuo ferrentur omnes, in quo vno omnes viuimus & mouemur & sumus? Atque vt certior extaret ipsius erga homines propensionis demonstratio, satis illi non fuit commune illam exterum naturæ pædagogiam constituisse vniuersis: sed quod longe præstantissimum, ipsemet ore suo certum quendam populum, Israelem nempe compellare dignatus est, quem primum mera & gratuita benignitate vnum ex omnibus populis sibi selegisset. His demum tum verbo suo seipsum manifestum reddidit,cum etiam operibus stupendis potentiæ illius suę documenta protulit. Hos ex Ægypti fornace ferrea eductos, in qua viui ac videntes atterebantur, in optatissimam libertatem asser-uit. His se tanquam exilij participes ducem interdiu & per noctem præcutit.Pauit in deserto in promissę regionis possessionem intulit: victorias ac triumphos quasi in finum effudit. Ex his vnis, quasi ad ipsum aliæ Gentes minus pertinerent, nomen ipse ducere, illos populum ac gentem suam vicissim nominare voluit. Atque hęc omnia sub illa tantum conditione, vt nullum aliud
units.tr: When God, the best and greatest, the most perfect maker of all things, had shown himself more than admirable in the creation of the whole universe, he set the crown on his work in the creation of man. In man a singular excellence of so great an author stood out above all other created things. He fashioned one creature alone in his own image and likeness, so that the marks of his glory might shine forth, expressed in that last work of his. Man would indeed be happy, and would always remain happy, if he did not forget the privilege bestowed on him above other creatures; if he presented himself before the one Creator continually, with full humility and submission; if he praised him alone with unceasing thanksgiving; and if, setting nothing down to himself, he thought that all those gifts received from heaven were to be referred to the sole glory of God, since they were wholly his. But man is unhappy when he does not grasp this happiness and delights to rest in himself; when that great and singular giver of his liberality slips from his mind, and, lifting himself up in shameless ingratitude, he dares to be proud against his maker. Hence he was given over headlong to death. Hence, cast down from his native nobility into shameful servitude and thrust out of the excellence of creation, he began to lie prostrate. Hence nakedness received him in place of glory, and a pitiable disowning in place of so many and great gifts of God; so that, confused in his pride, he learned against his will what he had a little before scorned to profess with sincere feeling. This ought therefore to have been his school and his study: both to recognise that he himself is pure vanity, and to perceive that nothing had ever come from himself except vanity; and whatever else had come to him should have been counted as received by the special indulgence of God. But the Lord, turning away from so unworthy a fall of the most noble creature, began to loathe it, and, as such a deserving required, not even to regard his own work as worth anything. By this the image and expression of himself was now utterly torn down, and such clear testimonies of his goodness towards man were overthrown. Thus, in place of that delight which the Lord had taken in that singular creature, so that he rested as in the love of a beloved son, scorn and abomination of the Lord himself succeeded. Whence, if anything pleasing had ever come from man, and the Lord had regarded him with a fatherly gaze, all of it became to him a weariness, a displeasure and an abomination; and, as with a man accused of treason, he declared that he repented of having made man. Indeed the wickedness of men did not stop even at the point where it began; rather, as someone aptly put it: "The age of the parents, worse than the grandfathers, brought forth children more wicked, who were soon to produce an offspring more vicious." What then? Namely, when those fertile ages of sin had provoked the extreme hand of God against themselves, God himself, not so much inclined to mercy and fatherly indulgence as mercy and indulgence itself, since he was unwilling not to love them, though it was so unworthy of them to be loved, yet did not endure that the human race should perish utterly and be swallowed up by its deserved ruin. He deferred the time and the means of repentance, in case they might somehow come back to themselves. And although he dissembled his indignation openly, as if with eyes half-closed, and let them go their own way, so that no express word, no law or direction of his, should accuse them of sin, yet he never hid himself from them so completely that he failed to set before them things which both reminded them of their duty and, as it were, led them by the hand to seek him, and almost to touch him. So, even for the sake of such knowledge, they ought to have recognised him, and having recognised him, to have honoured him with the worship that was his due. For where could anyone turn, when there were no vocal testimonies of the truth and of the glory of so great a maker, which did not proclaim far and wide, loudly, deeply and splendidly, the majesty of the one supreme God, lifted up on high beneath the heavens, in the most admirable array of so many things? So he left his glory, power, goodness, wisdom and eternity inscribed and expressed in the parts of the whole universe, above and below, in the most significant lettering! Hence that saying of Paul, that even among those men with whom the knowledge of the true God did not arise from the Word, ... he nevertheless did not leave himself without witness. Therefore, as many creatures of God as exist everywhere, so many heralds of the immense glory of their author remained for the human race; and accordingly, from the knowledge of these things men ought to have come to God himself, so that, he being known, all faith and obedience might be rendered him, fitting to the goodness, wisdom, power and eternity of so great a Lord. What of the fact that the creatures, though otherwise not vocal, were said to have anticipated words even for man himself in this respect? Indeed the songs of birds sounded forth God, the dumb beasts bellowed out their maker, the series of the elements stood amazed at him, the mountains thundered him forth, springs and rivers winked as it were with their eyes, and grasses and flowers fawned upon him. But neither was there any need for each person to seek him far outside himself. When his benefit was conferred on each person within himself, what just excuse was there, that not all were carried straight to him, in whom alone we all live and move and have our being? And so that a clearer demonstration of his inclination towards men might stand, it was not enough for him to have set up that common outward schooling of nature for all. Far more outstanding, he himself, with his own mouth, deigned to address a certain people, namely Israel, whom he had first chosen out of all peoples for himself by pure and free kindness. At last he made himself manifest by his word, when he also brought forth proofs of his power in stupendous works. These, led out of the iron furnace of Egypt, in which they were ground down while living and seeing, he delivered into most desired liberty. As fellow exiles with them, he went before them as their leader by day and by night. He fed them in the desert, brought them into possession of the promised land, and poured out victories and triumphs as it were into their bosom. From these alone, as if the other nations were less concerned with him, he chose to take his name and in turn to call them his people and nation. And all this under this one condition alone: that they should acknowledge no other

units.la: Act.14.17. aliud numen admittendo,in ipso vno singulariter acquiescerét. Hoc porrò Fœdus appositis benevolentiæ suæ testimoniis amplissimis, tum apud ipsos fanciuit, tum confectis & editis ea de re publicis tabulis,in perpetuum rei monumentum confirmauit. Scilicet illa hærens lateri Lethalis arundo natiua corruptio nempe peruicit: neque magis ipsi Israëlitæ Dei monitis parere sustinuerunt,neque ad illam doctrinam,quæ tam opportunè revocaret in viam, attenderunt. Ac proinde uti reliqui passim populi vagi ac palantes ad rerum naturæ magisteriū, cæci ac surdi constanter oberrarunt:ita etiam Iudæos nihilò melius,& Lex & Prophetæ affecerunt: & seruus Dei cæcior ad lucem Dei,& admonitiones surdior,& ad mandata præfractior deprehensus est. Enimuerò neque etiam tenebræ illæ reliquum orbem eo vsque occupauerunt ,quin homines adhuc ad tot illa bona quæ ipsos circumfluerent attoniti, arcano quodam animi motu ad tātum illorum largitorem reuocarentur. Veruntamen iidem in sale-bris hæserunt omnes ,ac præterito illo Creatore cuius omnis erat ista gloria,cōfinxerunt sibi falsa numina,atque post somnia, & inanissima cerebri sui commenta abrepti sunt. Demum vbi semel extra viam currere coeperunt, non iam vno aliquo illo ementito numine contenti,innumera deinde pro sua temerita-te atque vanitate præfixerunt: ac nulla gens aut natio extitit, quæ non hic sibi peculiares Deos pro suo arbitrio instituerat. Et hi sunt primi idololatriæ natales. Hæc illa lœna improba, quæ homines à Deo prorsus auersos atque simulachris affixos mancipauit.cum eadem simulachra ipsis hominibus & originem suam, & suum illud esse, acceptum ferre debebant. Iudæi vero, vnius quidem Dei mandata quæ per Prophetas continuò destinabantur,vtcunque non repudiarent, aperte tamen in ipsum fœdifragi, non minus temere ab eo defecerunt legem à se aperte violatam despectui habere,ac quicquid simularent,odiose ex animo coeperunt.Nam & ad falsos deos profiliierunt,& in cultu idolorum, quantumuis obnitente Domino nihilò leuius reliquis etiam gentibus insanierunt. Quod cùm ita esset,vt demum tam Iudæi,quàm Gentes à Deo alienatę, ad ipsum reuocarentur,nouo plane fœdere opus fuit, quod ipsum firmum atque inuiolatū maneret. Vt fœdus illud certò coiret & sanciretur,requirebatur Mediator, qui ipse intercederet atque sese medium sisteret inter Deum & homines, vt pacem conciliaret. Sine hoc Mediatore, homo maledictioni Dei obnoxius ex quo se præcipitem in peccatum dederat,inexcusso iugo premebatur, miseriç & opprobrio æterno addictus,propter iram & indignationem Dei aduer sus ipsum accensam. Atq; Mediator ille D.N.Iesus Christus erat, vnus verus æternus Dei Filius,quem missurus erat Pater in mundum. h.iij. dū,vt omnes ex horrēda dispersione, & vastitate colligeret: illè vna spes piorum omnium,per quē à primi parentis seruitute in veros natales essent tandem restituendi.Sic enim ad ipsum Adamum iamprimum collapsum à se aliquando exigendum cœperat Dominus: Futurum, vt semen mulieris conterereret serpentis caput, id est per Christum nasciturum ex Virgine, distinctum ac conuulsam iri Satanæ tyrannidem. Sic deinde eandem promissionem apud Abrahamum renouauit,quod in ipsius semine benedicendæ essent omnes Gentes. Sic nempe prænuntiabatur idē Christus exoriturus ex Abrahamo, à cuius benedictione ad vniuersas Gentes sanctificatio emanaret. Sic cum Isaaco egit Dominus. Sic continuis seculis eadem promissio ex ore Prophetarum apud Israelitas audita,repetita,confirmata est.Quod vt certius esset, & iam quasi oculis subiiceretur, ipsas vsque nascituri Christi peculiares notas:Matrem videlicet,locum,tempus,mortem ipsius ac resurrectionis gloriam, regnum mox secuturum, & quæ spes inde piorū existere deberet, Dominus ipse prœsigna-uit.Nam de matre quidem eadémq; Virgine extabat insignis ille locus apud Isaiam : Ecce virgo concipiet & pariet filium, & vocabis nomen eius Immanuel.Apud Mosen vero,tempus à Iaco bo ipso animam agente notatum discerte fuerat. Non auf-ferretur sceptrum de Iuda, neque Dux de femore eius, donec veniat qui mittendus est:& ipse erit expectatio gentium.Hoc autem reipsa constitit sub illud tempus,quo natus est Dominus.Iam enim triginta septem anni circiter elapsi erant, ex quo Iudæis mero illo ac supremo Imperio spoliatis,Romani H rodè Idumæum expa-tre,ex matre Arabem regè constituerant:cum nunquā prius antea res Iudæorū ita concidissent,quin si ex sua gente regem non haberent, ex eadem tamen præfectos saltem ac rectores & con-siliarios quosdam retinerent. Apud Danielē vero tempus idem nascituri Christi post certas hebdomadum periodos dispunctū extabat. Natalis locus etiā apud Michæā aperte signatus erat his verbis:Et tu Bethlehem Ephrata,minima non es in millibus Iuda, ex te enim egredietur qui dominabitur in Israële,& exitus ipsius à diebus æternis.Passiones autem & quicquid nostro nomine,vt perfectum Mediatorem præstaret, Dominus ipse subiturus erat, Isaias & Zacharias aperte & indubitate prædixerāt: iidemq; cum Ieremia luculenti testes extiterant tā gloriōsæ ipsius resurrectionis, quām venturi regni,& salutis omnibus piis asserendæ. Atque illa tot testimonia & denuntiationes sanctorum Dei hominū, sulcra demum & statumina fidei Patrum extiterunt: sic ipsi ex-xerunt & confirmarunt seipos, ac quodammodo pauerunt certissima illa spe atq; expectatione tantę redemptionis, à Domino tempore suo exhibendæ,Vnde etiā præ summo illo desiderij ardore,
units.tr: Act.14.17. admitting no other deity, they might rest in him alone with singular devotion. This covenant he both established among them, with the most ample tokens of his goodwill, and confirmed for a perpetual memorial by public tablets drawn up and published concerning it. Yet the deadly arrow of innate corruption clung to their side and prevailed. Nor did the Israelites themselves submit to God's warnings any more, or attend to that teaching which might so opportunely have recalled them to the way. Accordingly, just as the other peoples, wandering and straying everywhere, constantly went astray, blind and deaf to the teaching of nature, so the Law and the Prophets dealt no better with the Jews. The servant of God was found more blind to the light of God, more deaf to admonitions, and more stubborn towards the commandments. Indeed, those darknesses did not occupy the rest of the world so completely that men, astonished at the many good things flowing around them, were not still called back by some secret stirring of mind to the great giver of them. But all of them stuck in the mire, and, forgetting the Creator to whom all that glory belonged, they fashioned for themselves false deities and were carried off after dreams and the most empty figments of their own brains. Finally, once they began to run outside the way, no longer content with that one invented deity, they set up countless others through their own rashness and vanity. There was no nation or people that did not establish for itself peculiar gods at its own pleasure. These are the first origins of idolatry. This is that wicked mother of all, which handed men over, utterly turned away from God and fastened to images, although the images themselves ought to have owed their origin and very existence to men. The Jews, indeed, though they did not repudiate the commandments of the one God which were continually sent through the Prophets, nevertheless openly broke faith with him. No less rashly they revolted from him, holding in contempt the law they had openly violated, and whatever they pretended, they began to hate from the heart. For they both leapt to false gods, and in the worship of idols they went mad no less than the other nations, though the Lord resisted. Since this was so, when at last both Jews and Gentiles, estranged from God, were to be recalled to him, a wholly new covenant was needed, one that would itself remain firm and inviolate. For that covenant to be surely brought into being and ratified, a Mediator was required, who would himself intervene and set himself between God and men to make peace. Without this Mediator, man, subject to the curse of God from the moment he cast himself headlong into sin, was pressed down under an unbreakable yoke, given over to misery and everlasting reproach, on account of the wrath and indignation of God kindled against him. This Mediator was our Lord Jesus Christ, the one true and eternal Son of God, whom the Father was going to send into the world, so that he might gather all people out of the dreadful dispersion and waste. He is the one hope of all the godly, through whom they would at last be restored from the slavery of our first parent to their true birthright. For so the Lord had begun to deal with Adam himself, when he had first fallen, promising that the seed of the woman would crush the head of the serpent, that is, that Christ would be born of a Virgin and that the tyranny of Satan would be broken and overthrown. So, afterwards, he renewed the same promise to Abraham, that in his seed all the nations would be blessed. Thus it was foretold that this same Christ would arise from Abraham, from whose blessing sanctification would flow out to all nations. So the Lord dealt with Isaac. Through the following ages this same promise, heard from the mouths of the Prophets among the Israelites, was repeated and confirmed. And so that it might be more certain, and set before their very eyes, the Lord himself marked out the particular signs of the Christ who was to be born: his mother, namely, his place, his time, his death and the glory of his resurrection, the kingdom that would soon follow, and the hope which should thence arise for the godly. Concerning the mother, who was also a Virgin, that famous passage in Isaiah stood: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Immanuel. In Moses the time had been clearly noted, when Jacob was dying: the sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations. This indeed came to pass about the time when the Lord was born. For about thirty-seven years had already passed since the Jews, stripped of their sovereign power, had been ruled by Herod the Idumaean, who had been made king by the Romans, the son of an Arabian mother. Never before had the affairs of the Jews so collapsed that, if they did not have a king from their own nation, they still kept governors, rulers and certain counsellors from it. In Daniel, the same time for the birth of the coming Christ was set out after certain periods of weeks. The place of birth was also plainly marked out in Micah, in these words: And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are least among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth one who will rule in Israel, and his going forth is from everlasting days. His sufferings, and whatever he himself was to undergo for our sake, so that he might be a perfect Mediator, Isaiah and Zechariah had foretold clearly and without doubt. These same prophets, together with Jeremiah, had been bright witnesses both of his glorious resurrection and of the kingdom to come, and of the salvation to be asserted for all the godly. And those many testimonies and announcements of the holy men of God became at last the foundations and supports of the faith of the Fathers. Thus they nourished and strengthened themselves, and in a way fed upon that most certain hope and expectation of so great a redemption, which the Lord would reveal in his own time. Hence, too, with that supreme ardour of desire,
