Eodem etiam referedum,q; diuersis temporibus ac vicibus excitati sunt à Domino,Duces,Reges ac Iudices, qui Israelem ab hostiū iugo liberarent,in bona pace regerent, ruinas sarciret,cumulatè prosperarent, ac non vulgarium virtutum nomine apud reliquos populos extollerent.Sic nempe gustum aliquē fouere inter suos voluit mirabilium Messiæ exhibendi operum Dominus,vt in eo extatura speraretur solida virtus ipsius, atque fœlicissimi regni præsens Maiestas. Tandem igitur,vbi adfuit plenum illud tępus ac dies à Domino præordinata, adstitit coràm Messias ille tot retro seculis exoptatissimus:atq; idem illa omnia cumulatè præstitit,quæ erat ad omnium redemptionem necessaria.Neq; verò intra vnum Israelem tantum illud beneficium stetit,cum potius ad vniuersum humanum genus vsque porrigendum esset: quia per vnumChristum vniuersum humanum genusreconciliandū erat Deo, vti his Noui Fœderis tabulis continetur, & amplissimè demonstratur.Atque vt huius Dei beneplaciti plena fides ac perpetua extaret, Dominus Iesus ipse qui Fœderis istius sponsor est, atque ipsamet illius substantia,Apostolos sibi designauit,quibus hoc munus mandauit, vt ipsius beneficium per orbem vniuersum prędicarent. Ipsi vero non tantum dederunt omnem opetam,vt mandatum Domini prestarent,dum verbo & voce testimonium ipsius circunferrent : sed etiam Mosis & Prophetarum exemplo eandem illam doctrinam ad perpetuam, & indubitatæ ipsius perceptionem in hos libros contulerunt. Horum autē hęc summa est,quod primùm quidem traditum est ab illis,tum quid fecerit,& quę passus sit pro nobis Dominus:tum verò quis istius veritatis vsus ac fructus ad nos peruenire t, acquo modo nobis applicandus esset.Atque huic volumini inditum est Noui Fœderis seu Testamenti nomen, ratione Veteris illius ,quod nempe cum Nouo coalescere oporteret, & in illo impleri. Nam & in sese infirmum erat Vetus illud & minus perfectum , vnde & abrogatum est Nouo adueniente, & abolitum. At vero Nouum istud æternum est,quod nunquam aut consenescat, aut deficiat, cùm illius Mediator Christus sit, qui sua morte illud fanciuit,
units.tr: Gen.3.15 · Gen.22.18 · Gen.26.4 · Ifa.7.14 · Gen.49.10 · Dan.9.24 · Mich.5.2 · Ifa.53.49 · Ier.23.5.31 · Zach.2 · Zach.9 ardour, many kings and prophets long ago earnestly desired that the day should be present to them, with their eyes fixed upon it, although by faith they could already anticipate in their minds what it was not yet granted to perceive with their eyes. To this same purpose also belonged that law given to them in writing, by which so many and such varied ceremonies, expiations and sacrifices were handed down, as so many figures and shadows of better things, which were to be brought by Christ, who himself was the body of which these were the shadow, and the substance and truth. For the law brought nothing to perfection; it only directed and led, like a tutor, to Christ, who is, as the Apostle teaches, the end and fulfilment of the law. To the same purpose belongs also that at different times and in turns the Lord raised up leaders, kings and judges, who were to free Israel from the yoke of its enemies, keep it in good peace, repair its ruins, make it prosper abundantly, and raise it, by the name of no ordinary virtues, above the other peoples. Thus the Lord wished to foster among his own a certain taste of the wonderful works that the Messiah was to perform when he came, so that in him was hoped for a solid strength and the present majesty of a most happy kingdom. At last, therefore, when that fullness of time and that day ordained by the Lord had arrived, that Messiah, so longed for through so many past ages, stood before them. He indeed fully accomplished all those things which were necessary for the redemption of all. Nor did that benefit stop within Israel alone, since it was rather to be extended to the whole human race: for through the one Christ the whole human race was to be reconciled to God, as is contained and amply demonstrated in these tablets of the New Covenant. And so that the full faith in this good pleasure of God might stand firm and perpetual, the Lord Jesus himself, who is the surety of this covenant and its very substance, appointed the Apostles for himself and entrusted them with this task: to proclaim his benefit throughout the whole world. They indeed did not merely give every effort to carry out the Lord's command, bearing witness to him by word and voice, but also, after the example of Moses and the Prophets, committed that same teaching to these books, for its lasting and unshaken preservation. The sum of these books is this: first, what the Lord did and suffered for us was handed down by them, and then what fruit and benefit of this truth reaches us, and in what way it is to be applied to us. This volume has been given the name of the New Covenant or Testament, in relation to the Old, which was bound to join with the New and be fulfilled in it. For that Old covenant was weak in itself and less perfect, and therefore it was abrogated and abolished when the New came. But this New covenant is eternal, which never grows old or fails, since its Mediator is Christ, who ratified it by his death,

units.la: h.iiij. atque irrefixum constituit, cum per illam attulit summam ac perfectam expiationem omnium praeuaricationum, quae sub veteri Foedere temanebant. Huic Foederi Euangelij nomen etiam adscribitur, quod bonum & laetitiae illud nuntium significat: quia nempe offendit Christum Filium Dei viui vnicum atque aeternum, hominem factum esse, vt per ipsum Filij Dei adoptionem efficeremur. Ac proinde vnus hic ille seruator nobis statuitur, in quo vno sita est nostra omnis redemptio, pax, iustitia, sanctificatio, salus, vita, qui mortuus est propter peccata nostra, resurrexit propter iustificationem nostram: qui in coelum ascendit, vt illuc aditum nobis patefaceret, ac nostro nomine hereditatem cerneret: qui se perpetuo coram Patre nobis Aduocatum sisteret ac Sacerdotem exhiberet: qui vt Rex, Dominus, ac summus Heres designatus ad dexteram Patris sedet, vt semel vniuersa tum in coelo tum in terra in suum ordinem ac statum reponeret. Hoc vero penes nullum vnquam Angelorum, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum fuit, neque vllus ex ipsis ad tantum munus destinatus fuit. Atque vt venturi Christi in veteri Foedere apud Prophetas sparsa extabant testimonia quamplurima: ita etiam Dominus Iesus manifestis indiciis atque indubitatis argumentis Ecclesiae sese exhibens, is ipse Christus esse demonstratus est. Siquidem Dominus Deus, tum vocem suam, tum Spiritus sancti, tum Angelorum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, adeoque omnium rerum conditarum in testimonium Filio suo adhibuit, vt iam repugnandi locus non esset, nisi quis sponte Dei veritati obliteret auderet. Extat enim coelestè illud ac solenne oraculum
units.tr: And he fixed it firmly, since by it he brought the full and perfect expiation of all the transgressions that remained under the old covenant. This covenant is also called the Gospel, a word that signifies good and joyful news: namely, that Christ, the only and eternal Son of the living God, has become man so that through him we might be made the adopted sons of God. Accordingly, this one Saviour is set before us, and in him alone lies all our redemption, peace, righteousness, sanctification, salvation and life. He died for our sins and rose again for our justification. He ascended into heaven to open the way there for us and to take possession of the inheritance in our name. He stands constantly before the Father as our Advocate and presents himself as our Priest. As King, Lord and appointed chief Heir, he sits at the Father's right hand, so that he may finally set all things in heaven and on earth in their proper order and state. No Angel, Patriarch, Prophet or Apostle has ever held this power, and none of them was destined for so great an office. Just as many testimonies to the coming Christ lay scattered among the Prophets in the old covenant, so the Lord Jesus, presenting himself to the Church by clear signs and indubitable proofs, has been shown to be that very Christ. For the Lord God called upon his own voice, the Holy Spirit, the Angels, the Prophets, the Apostles, and indeed all created things, as witnesses to his Son, so that there is no room left for resistance, unless someone dares wilfully to close his eyes to the truth of God. For there is that heavenly and solemn oracle, greater than any objection: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him" (Matt. 17.).

units.la: omni exceptione maius: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo acquiescui, ipsum audite. Spiritus S. vero in nostris cordibus testis est veritatis Christi locupletissimus, vt passim inculcat Apostolus. Angeli vero e iam non semel. Sic enim Gabriel Angelus ad Virginem matrem futuram: Ecce concipies in vtero, & paries Filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum. Ipse enim erit magnus & Filius Altissimi vocabitur, & dabit illi Dominus sedem Dauid patris sui, & regnabit in domo Iacob in aeternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Idem prorsus ab Angelo Iosephus Mariae sponsus accepit. Idem ab Angelo denunciate audierunt Pastores: natum ipsis Seruatorem, qui est, inquit, Christus Dominus. Cui etiam Angelo statim accessit tot aliorum coniunctus & vnanimis concentus, cum illo natiuitatis Domini argumento, Gloriam in Excelsis Deo, pacem hominibus in terra, decantarent. Nec minus Simeon iustus ille in Spiritu propheticò Christū salus est, dum passis vlnis adhuc tenellum in templo complexus, excepit his verbis ad Dominum: Nunc dimittis seruum tuum Domine secundum verbum tuum in pace, quia viderunt oculi mei salutem tuam, ruam,quś parafli ante faciem omnium populorum. Perinde e- tiam Ioannes Baptista de illo testimonium insigne tum maxi- me edidit,cùm ad Iordanem illum intuens, Ecce, inquit,Agnus ille Dei:Ecce qui tollit peccatum mudi. Hoc ipsum deinde tum Petrus, tum alij omnes Apostoli fassi & testati sunt, & aperte prædicarunt: impleta esse nimirum in Christo Dei Filio illa omnia, quæ de illo extarent apud Prophetas, atque ad nostram salutem pertinerent.Atque hoc ipsum testimonium per vniuer- sas Gentes ab ipsis omnium nationum & conditionum homi- nibus, quos ad illum excitare Domino placuit, constanter etiam editum atque confirmatum est ad ista vsque tempora, vti ex le- ctione auctorum facile cuiuis constabit. Quæ quidem omnia cùm eodem plane recidant, atque inter se omnino conueniant, euincitur manifeste contineri illic certissimam veritatem: cùm vbi falsum subest, perpetuus ille consensus constare non ita pos set. Ettamen præter illa augustissima testimonia, Patris ipsius, Filij,Spiritus sanctitum deinde Angelorum,Prophetarum,Apo stolorum Christi Domini, ipsa etiam illius opera, ipsæ virtutes incomparabiles veritatem illius non minus aperte oculis sub- iecerunt. Quid enim quòd nullo non morborum genere affli- ctos restituit? quòd claudos,cæcos,surdos,mutos,paralyticos,le- prosos, lunaticos, dæmoniacos sanauit, quòd mortuos reuoca- uit in vitam? quis vero legitimos etiam illos virtutis ipsius ac bonitatis præcones ac testes necessarios eleuabit? Quid quòd sua ipsius potestate sibi ipsi vitam reddidit, quòd peccata remisit? Quare non immerito ad sua illa opera Iudæos relegabat quæ à Patre accepisset, vt quæ de ipso verissimè testaretur. Quid quòd ipsis etiam impiis atque ipsius osoribus certissimis, vis ipsa veritatis testimonium aliquod Maiestatis ipsius expressit, vt de Caya- pha de Pilato,de ipsius vxore & aliis etiam constat? Non attin- go dæmonum etiam extortas confessiones, quas nempe Domi- nus ipse repudiarit. Ipsa vero rerum vniuersitas huius quoque laudis partem quam semel edidit, conferat.Iubente Christo ven- ti ponunt, mare commotum placidum redditur, os piscis di- drachma profert,illum moriétem dissractæ petræ ac monumen ta,illum dississum à summo in ipso Templo velum,illum obscu ratus sol, illum sepulchra reclusa, illum resurrecta mortuorum corpora, illum adeò sursum omnia & deorsum Deum suum ac Dominum & supremum herum, illum cœlestem Legatum ad hominum salutem à Patre demissum agnouerunt, tetiata sunt, inclamarunt.Horum omnium autem verissimæ tabulæ hoc no uo fœdere exhibentur. Hic regni paterni hæredes instituit. Hic apud hæredes designatos suam metem testatus est, cuius plenum effectum suo tempore sortiantur. Ad istam hereditatem in vocamur omnes fine personarum acceptione, masculi, fœminæ, sum-mi, infimi, heri, ferui, magistri, discipuli, doctores, idiotæ, ludæi, Græci, Galli, Romani: nemo hinc excluditur, qui modo Christum qualis offertur à Patre in salutem omnium admittat, & admif-sum complectatur. Agite igitur Christiani & Christianæ necum omnes, ac ne Testamenti illius tabulas celari, vel corrumpi li-namus, quod tam firmo iure nostrum est, fine quo cœlestis Regni spes omnis frustra concipitur: omnisque verorum bonorum, promissionum Christi, incomparabilis beatitudinis ab info de-ftinatæ nobis expectatio concidit atque interuertitur. Nam quò nos conuertemus vno hoc singulari lumine destituti, vt quod fit boni & mali discrimen, quid Dominus iubeat, quid vetet, quid lux, quid tenebræ, quid e cœlo fit, quid ex hominibus ftatuete possimus? Tolle Euangelium, diuitiæ egestatem spirant, sapientia stultitiam sapit coram Domino, potentia imbecillitatis conuincitur, omnis humana iustitia apud Dei tribunal damnata corruit. Rursus Euangelij notitia efficimur filij Dei, fratres Christi, communicipes sanctorum, cœlorum ciues, Dei cum Christo cohæredes. Sic egeni cumulamur, debiles viribus donamur, stulti sapimus, iniusti iustificamur, mœrentes consolationem percipimus, trepidi ad confidentiam erigimur, feruï ad libertatem vocamur. Euangelium est verbum vitæ, verbum veritatis, potentia Dei ad salutem cuiuis credenti, clauis scientiæ salutis. Hac Regni cœlorum fores credentibus patefiunt, dum à peccatis absoluuntur. Hac incredulis obserantur fores, dum in peccatis constringuntur. Fœlices qui audiunt, qui custodiunt, qui veras filiorum Dei notas ita in sese exhibent. Infœlices qui respuunt audire, qui obseruare negligunt, qui sese eo modo Diaboli filios produnt. Huc huc Christiani omnes attendite, hic sapere audete: ignorans enim ignorabitur: ac fi cæcus cæcum ducat, ambo in foueam cadent. Vna est Euangelij ad vitam & salutem via: vna fides & certitudo promissionum Dei, quæ vno Euangelio constant. Euangelij auditus & intelligentia conferunt fidem viuam, spem fixam, fynceram erga Deum dilectionem, feruentem erga proximum charitatem. Quænam igitur spes vlla vestra est, fi Euangelium contemnitur a vobis, fi dedignamini audire, inspicere, legere, atque animo recondere? En qui huius seculi vanitatem consectantur, vt ea summo studio atque indefesso captant, quæ ad suam illam fœlicitatem pertinere existimant! Ad illud inquam tam insano studio abripiuntur, vt neque fe respiciant, neque laboris vllius, aut periculi, aut nominis fui etiam rationem habeant: adeo puden-dum istud seruitium eos delectat, vt ad corpus vnum omnia referant, cuius tam vana est vita, tam misera, tam instabilis.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit too is the most abundant witness of Christ's truth in our hearts, as the Apostle repeatedly urges. The Angels have borne witness more than once. Thus the Angel Gabriel spoke to the Virgin who was to be his mother: "Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end" (Luke 1.). Joseph, Mary's betrothed, received the very same message from an Angel. The shepherds heard from an Angel the announcement that a Saviour had been born to them, "who is Christ the Lord" (Luke 2.). And straightaway, joined to that same Angel, came a great company of others in harmonious chorus, singing the praise of the Lord's birth: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men" (Luke 2.). Likewise Simeon, that righteous man, filled with the prophetic Spirit, embraced the tender child in the temple with outstretched arms and spoke these words to the Lord: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word; for mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people" (Luke 2.). Likewise John the Baptist bore a remarkable testimony to him, most of all when, looking upon him at the Jordan, he said: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1.). Afterwards Peter and all the other Apostles also confessed and attested this very thing, and openly preached that all those things which stood written about him among the Prophets and pertained to our salvation had been fulfilled in Christ, the Son of God. This same testimony has been steadily given and confirmed among all nations, by people of every nation and condition whom it has pleased the Lord to stir up to it, down to our own times, as anyone can easily ascertain from reading the authors. Since all these testimonies come to the same point and agree entirely with one another, it is clearly proved that the most certain truth is contained here; for where falsehood lay underneath, such a continuous consensus could not stand. Yet besides those most august testimonies of the Father himself, of the Son, of the Holy Spirit, and then of the Angels, the Prophets and the Apostles, the works of Christ the Lord, and his incomparable powers, have set his truth before our eyes no less plainly. For what of the fact that he restored those afflicted with every kind of disease, that he healed the lame, the blind, the deaf, the dumb, the paralytic, the lepers, the lunatics and the demoniacs, and that he called the dead back to life? And who would count those as anything but lawful and necessary heralds and witnesses of his power and goodness? What of the fact that by his own power he restored his own life, and that he forgave sins? Rightly, therefore, he referred the Jews to those works which he had received from the Father, so that they might bear true witness concerning him. What of the fact that even his impious enemies and most certain haters were compelled by the force of truth to give some testimony to his majesty, as is attested of Caiaphas, of Pilate, of his wife and of others too? I do not touch on the confessions wrung even from demons, which the Lord himself rejected. Let the whole of creation, indeed, contribute its share of this praise, which it once gave. At Christ's command the winds are stilled, the sea, troubled, is made calm, the mouth of a fish brings forth the didrachma, rocks are split and tombs opened when he dies, the veil of the Temple is torn from top to bottom, the sun is darkened, the dead bodies of the saints rise again. Thus all things, above and below, acknowledged him as their God, Lord and supreme master, and recognised him as the heavenly envoy sent by the Father for the salvation of men; they bore witness to him and cried out. Now the true record of all these things is set forth in this new covenant. Here he appoints heirs to his Father's kingdom. Here, among the heirs he has designated, he has left his will, whose full effect they will receive in due time. We are all called to this inheritance without regard to persons: men and women, high and low, masters and servants, teachers and disciples, the learned and the unlearned, Jews, Greeks, French, Romans. No one is excluded from it, provided only that he admits Christ, offered as he is by the Father for the salvation of all, and embraces him once admitted. Come then, Christians, men and women, all together with me, and let us not allow the tablets of that testament to be hidden or corrupted, since our right to them is so firm; without them all hope of the heavenly kingdom is vainly conceived, and every expectation of true goods, of the promises of Christ, and of the incomparable blessedness destined for us from the beginning collapses and is overturned. For where shall we turn, deprived of this single light? How could we determine, from ourselves, what is the distinction between good and evil, what the Lord commands, what he forbids, what is light, what is darkness, what is from heaven? Take away the Gospel, and riches breathe poverty, wisdom savours of folly before the Lord, power is convicted of weakness, and all human righteousness, condemned before the tribunal of God, collapses. Conversely, through the knowledge of the Gospel we are made sons of God, brothers of Christ, fellow-partakers of the saints, citizens of heaven, and co-heirs of God with Christ. So the needy are enriched, the weak are endowed with strength, the foolish become wise, the unrighteous are justified, the sorrowing receive consolation, the trembling are raised to confidence, and slaves are called to liberty. The Gospel is the word of life, the word of truth, the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, the key of the knowledge of salvation. By it the gates of the kingdom of heaven are opened to believers, as they are absolved from their sins; by it the gates are shut against unbelievers, who remain bound in their sins. Happy are those who hear it, who keep it, who thus display in themselves the true marks of the sons of God. Wretched are those who refuse to listen, who neglect to observe it, who by that very means betray themselves as sons of the Devil. Come hither, all you Christians, give heed here, dare to be wise here: for "the ignorant will be left in ignorance," and "if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch." There is one way to life and salvation through the Gospel: one faith, and one certainty of the promises of God, which rest on the Gospel alone. Hearing and understanding the Gospel bring a living faith, a firm hope, a sincere love of God, and a fervent charity towards one's neighbour. What hope, then, can you have, if you despise the Gospel, if you disdain to hear it, to look into it, to read it, and to store it in your mind? See how people pursue the vanity of this age, seizing with the greatest zeal and tireless effort those things which they think pertain to their own happiness! They are carried off, I say, by such a mad eagerness that they have no regard for themselves, for any toil, danger or reputation of their own; so much does that shameful servitude delight them that they refer everything to a single body, whose life is so empty, so wretched and so unstable.

units.la: Nos vero vbi de immortali, incorrupta, æterna, incomparabili beatitudine, de thesauris cœli adipiscendis agitur nobiscum tanta liberalitate, tanta fide, tanto nostro compendio, non enitentur per obiecta quæquis impedimenta, vt potiora illa consectentur? Qui operantur mechanicis, rebus nempe vilioribus, summo labore artem addiscunt, vt periti euadant: qui artes liberaliores sectantur, tantumnon seipsos conficiunt, vt aliquid eo in studio promoueant, ex quo sapientiæ ac virtutis nomen acquirant: quæ tamen ipsa aliud non sunt, quàm fumus apparens, & euanidus vapor. Nos vero quantum interiori studio rapi decerbat ad cœlestem illam sapientiam, quæ videlicet supra mundum ipsum fertur, quæ ad Regni Dei mysteria pertingit, quæ eadem Euangelio nobis ita dignante Domino reuelatur. Ecquid igitur erit quod à sancto Euangelio nos abducat, & ab illo alienet? Contumeliæ nempe, maledictiones, probra, imminutiones, dignitatum præsentium mulctationes? Atqui hic ipse Dominus Iesus præit nobis, cuius vestigia carpere nos decet, si veri ipsius discipuli esse & haberi volumus: neque porro vila eiusmodi molestiarum impressio repudiada est, quæ nempe cum incomparabilis beatitudinis, gloriæ, exaltationis fide apud Dominum commutanda sit. An igitur exilia, proscriptiones, amissiones facultatum nos dimouebunt? Atqui illud non minus constat, etiamsi ex certa regione adeoq; natali ipso solo, migrare videbimur, Domini esse terram & orbem: imo, & terra etiam pulsos, & omni hospitio prohibitos, extra Dei Regnum nihilo magis futuros. Si exuimur & ad egestatem redigimur, Pater ille non deest, cui ad nos alendos nihil deest. Christus seipsum pauperem reddidit, vt & ipsum per vestigia paupertatis subsequeremur. Insitabunt afflictiones, carceres, aculei, & omnes illud carnificinæ erga Dei seruos instrumentum. Atqui ipsius Christi exemplo, iter illac ad gloriam nobis commonstrari certò scimus. Tandem nempe vna mors perterrefaciet. Atqui ne illa quidem eripere vitam poterit, quæ per illam etiam vnicè erat expetenda. Des modo Christum præsentem, & quicquid maledictissimum haberi potest, summæ benedictioni cedet, quicquid execratissimum sanctificationi, quicquid funestissimum summo bono. Vt igitur vniuersi mundi vires nobis insultent, stet nobis mens oportet. Neque enim excidere poterit illa promissio: Dominus ex allo subsannabit eos. Conuenite & conspirate & non erit. Sic autem à Tertulliano appositè traditum est iam olim, Sanguinem Martyrum semen esse Ecclesiæ. Neque deest etiam nobis certissima illa consolatio, quod oculis à mundo & rebus præntibus ad Dei tribunal conuertis, illud ipsum patienter ex pectamus, quo demum extante momento corruet totus illo. paratus impiorum, & quicquid tanto opere aduersus tremen-dum iudicem sibi moliti sunt,dicto citius euanescet.Hoc autem extabit,cum Regnum Dei,quod spe tantum iam percipinus,re-ipsa tandem reuelabitur.Cum Dominus Iesus Christus cum Angelis Maiestatis suæ visendus apparebit Cum vniuersi sig llatim ad illius Magni Regis lorum & cognitionem sua illa de sistetur. Atque tum demum qui constanter in hoc fœdere perstiterint, & ad Patris Cœlestis voluntatem rebus omnibus insuperhabitis attenti fuerint, collocabuntur ad dexteram, percipient scopum fidei, benedictionem cum vita æterna coniunctam. Quemadmodum ipsos non puduerit Christum agnouisse,& cōfessum esse,dum in hominum opprobrio & contemptu uceret: ita etiam gloriæ ipsius tum reuelatæ fient participes, ctemamq; per illum coronam percipient. Contrà impij,prefracti,reprobi, ac contempti Euangelij rei,qui item vt locum suum ac dignitatem retinerent, cum Christo humiliari atque deiici non sustinuerint,qui in metu hominum sepulti,à timore Dei defecerint, vt & spurij & illegitimi,ac tanto parente indigni statuerunt ad laxuam, in maledictionem pestundabuntur, ac proinfidelitatis mercede pœnis æternis addicti conflagrabunt.Quare vbi audimus Euangelio nobis Christum offerri in quo omnes Dei promissiones sint Etiam & Amen : vti Christus ipse illic significat se à Patre missum esse, versatum cum hominibus, perfecisse quic quid ad nostram salutem opus esset, vti hoc totum in Lege & Prophetis comprehensum ante extabat, illud dubitandum non est, patere etiam per illum nobis cœli thesauros, Dei ipsius inquam diuitias omnes illic exhiberi : denique vitam æternam in illo cumulate esse reuelatam. Siquidem hæc est vita æterna,vt agnoscant te verum Deum & Iesum Christum quem misisti : in quo sunt singulæ salutis nostræ partes repositæ. Hic noster Isaacus oblatus in sacrificium, vt potestati mortis non succubuerit. Hic Iacobus ille vigilantissimus, nunquam non in gregis sibi commissi salutem intentus. Hic Iosephus ille, pius frater ac misericors,in summa sua dignitate,indignissimos atque abiectissimos fratres non dedignatus. Hic Melchizedek summus Sacerdos vnico æterno sacrificio perfunctus semel, quo simul vniuersis finem imponeret. Hic Moses summus Legislator, legis ipsius in cordis tabulis inscribendæ singularis auctor. Hic Iosua fidus deductor, qui suos in promissam hæreditatem intulit. Hic Dauid inclytus ac semper inuictus potestatem omnem aduersariorum perfregit atque subiecit sibi. Hic Solomo splendidus triumphator populum in pace prosperrima gubernauit.Hic Samson fortissimus, in media morte infenfissimos illos ac numerosissimos hostes semel prostrauit. Denique quicquid salutare hominibus aut
units.tr: But when the matter concerns immortal, incorruptible, eternal and incomparable blessedness, and the obtaining of the treasures of heaven, offered to us with such generosity, such faithfulness and at such little cost to ourselves, shall we not strive, whatever obstacles stand in the way, to pursue those better things? Those who work at mechanical crafts, things of lesser worth, learn the trade with the greatest labour so that they may become skilled. Those who pursue the liberal arts all but wear themselves out so that they may advance in that study and win the name of wisdom and virtue. Yet these very things are nothing but apparent smoke and a vanishing vapour. How much more ought we to be carried off by inner zeal to that heavenly wisdom, which is borne above the world itself, which reaches to the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, and which the Lord, deigning to do so, reveals to us in the Gospel. What then will there be that could draw us away from the holy Gospel and estrange us from it? Reproaches surely, curses, insults, diminishments, the loss of present dignities? But this same Lord Jesus goes before us, and it befits us to follow in his footsteps if we wish to be and be counted his true disciples. Nor should any impression of such troubles be rejected, since they are to be exchanged for the faith of incomparable blessedness, glory and exaltation before the Lord. Will exiles, proscriptions and the loss of property then drive us away? But it is no less certain that even if we seem to migrate from a certain region, indeed from our very native soil, the earth and the whole world belong to the Lord. Even if we are driven from the land and denied all hospitality, we shall be no less outside the Kingdom of God. If we are stripped and reduced to poverty, that Father is not lacking, who lacks nothing for feeding us. Christ made himself poor, so that we too might follow in the footsteps of his poverty. Afflictions, prisons, goads, and every instrument of torture for God's servants will assail us. But from the example of Christ himself we know for certain that the way to glory is shown to us through these. Finally, a single death will terrify. But not even that can snatch away life, which by that very death was to be sought alone. Only grant Christ present, and whatever can be deemed most accursed yields to the highest blessing, whatever is most loathsome yields to sanctification, and whatever is most deadly yields to the supreme good. So, though the powers of the whole world insult us, our mind must stand firm. For that promise cannot fail: "The Lord will laugh at them; they will plot together, and it will come to nothing." Tertullian long ago rightly said that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church. Nor do we lack that most certain consolation: when we turn our eyes from the world and present things to the tribunal of God, we patiently await that moment at which the whole edifice of the impious will collapse, and whatever they have so eagerly contrived against the dread Judge will vanish more quickly than a word. This will come to pass when the Kingdom of God, which we now grasp only in hope, is at last revealed in fact. When the Lord Jesus Christ appears, to be seen with his angels in his majesty, all things will at once be summoned before the tribunal and the knowledge of that great King. Then at last those who have persevered steadfastly in this covenant, and have been attentive to the will of the heavenly Father, setting aside all other things, will be placed at his right hand and will attain the goal of faith, the blessing joined with eternal life. Just as they were not ashamed to acknowledge and confess Christ while he lived in the reproach and contempt of men, so they will also become partakers of his glory, then revealed, and will receive through him the eternal crown. On the contrary, the impious, the stubborn, the reprobate and the despisers of the Gospel, who, so as to keep their place and dignity, would not endure to be humbled and cast down with Christ, who, buried in the fear of men, have failed through fear of God, and who have judged themselves bastards and illegitimate, unworthy of so great a Parent, will be cast out into the darkness and the curse. Consigned as the wages of unbelief to eternal punishments, they will burn. Therefore, when we hear that Christ is offered to us in the Gospel, in whom all the promises of God are Yea and Amen, and when Christ himself signifies that he was sent by the Father, dwelt among men, and accomplished whatever was needful for our salvation, as all this was previously contained in the Law and the Prophets, there is no doubt that the treasures of heaven, indeed all the riches of God himself, are set forth to us through him, and that eternal life has been revealed in him in abundance. For this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent; in him the several parts of our salvation are laid up. Here is our Isaac, offered in sacrifice, who did not yield to the power of death. Here is that most watchful Jacob, never not intent on the safety of the flock committed to him. Here is that Joseph, pious and merciful brother, who in his high dignity did not disdain the most unworthy and abject brothers. Here is Melchizedek, the highest priest, who, having once performed the single eternal sacrifice, put an end to all sacrifices at once. Here is Moses, the supreme Lawgiver, the unique author of the law to be written on the tablets of the heart. Here is Joshua, the faithful leader, who brought his people into the promised inheritance. Here is David, renowned and ever unconquered, who broke through all the power of his adversaries and subdued it to himself. Here is Solomon, the splendid triumphant king, who governed the people in most prosperous peace. Here is Samson, most strong, who in the midst of death once laid low those most hostile and most numerous enemies. Finally, whatever salutary thing for men you can either grasp by thought or express in prayer, all of it is found in Christ and is in fact established.

units.la: Ie.17.3 aut cogtando assequi, aut ex voto proferre possis, totum illud in Christo obuium est,ac reipsa constat. Christus humiliatus est vt nos sattolleret, seruituti subiectus vt in libertatem assereret, pauper factus vt ditaret,venditus vt redimeret, captus vt liberaret, damnatus vt absoluerct, factus maledictio in nostram benedictionem, oblatio pro peccato ad nostram iustitiam, deformatus vt reformaret,mortuus vt viuificaret.Per Christum nem pe distorta omnia complanantur, atque inaudita rerum omniū transformatio producitur. Per Christum , etiam emollita duritics,plagata ira,illustratæ tenebræ,iustificata iniustitia,roborata infirmitas,erecta desolatio,occupatum peccatum,calcatus contemptus, confidens trepidatio, inductum debitum , leuatus labor,recreatus mœror, fortunatum infortunium, explicata perplexa, ordinata confusa,scissio resarta, ignobilitas nobilitata, contumacia peruicta,comminatio perterrefacta,retectæ infidiç, infultus inuasi,vim vis patitur,pugna impugnatur, prælium impetitur,vltio vindicatur,tormentum torquetur,damnatio damnatur,abyssus absorbetur, infernus deprimitur, mors emoritur, mortalitas immortalitate commutatur. Vno verbo per Christū misericordia miseriam sustulit,bonitas infœlicitatem exhausit. Et quæ teli erant Diaboli ad nos inuadendos, qui ad pungendos aculei, illa eadem exercitamenta iam supersunt, ex quibus fructum insignem percipiamus.Nunc inquam,gloriari cum Apostolo ita audemus,Vbinam ó inferne tua victoria?Vbinam ó mors aculeus tuus? Nunc per Christi Spiritum, quem promisit suis,non iam viuimus ex nobis,sed ex fide Filij Dei, ac per eundem Spiritum iam cœlestibus assidemus : In mundo agentes, à mundo peregrinamur. Et quocunque sub axe versemur,quocūque loco simus , quocunque modo accipiamur, perinde illa omnia sunt nobis. In afflictionibus præsenti animo sumus , in mœrore exultamus, in vituperio exaltamur,in inopia abundamus,in nuditate contegimur,in malis duramus, in morte viuimus. Hæc illa est nimirum vera & non fucata sapientia, quam ex hac vita assequamur , & cui neque Angeli , neque homines, neque vita , neque mors quicquam addant vel detrahant. Hæc est statio in qua nobis consistendum est. Nimirum illud est in tota Scriptura à nobis quærendum , vt Christum vere agnoscamus, & quas in illo præsentes diuitias offerat nobis Pater. Neq; vllus est apex in Scriptura apud Mos n & Prophetas,qui non illuc nos deducat. Etenim cum in Christo reconditi sint omnes scientiæ & intelligentiæ thesauri, frultra ab illo nos abduci sinamus , nisi sponte à veritatis luce ad mendacij tenebras transuerti cogitamus. Quamobrem apposite Apostolus 1.Cor.2 2.nō aliam scientiam sibi tribuit, quàm quòd Christum cognoscàr,
units.tr: Ie.17.3 Whatever you can either attain by thinking or express in prayer, all of it is ready to hand in Christ and is in fact established. Christ was humbled to lift us up, made subject to servitude to set us free into liberty, made poor to enrich us, sold to redeem us, taken captive to deliver us, condemned to absolve us, made a curse for our blessing, an offering for sin for our righteousness, disfigured to reform us, dead to make us alive. Through Christ, indeed, all crooked things are made straight, and an unheard-of transformation of all things is brought about. Through Christ, hardness is softened, wrath appeased, darkness illumined, unrighteousness justified, weakness strengthened, desolation raised up, sin overcome, contempt trampled underfoot, trembling made confident, debt imposed is cancelled, labour lightened, sorrow refreshed, misfortune made fortunate, the perplexed made plain, the confused put in order, the torn sewn together again, lowliness ennobled, obstinacy overcome, threats made to tremble, hidden snares uncovered, assaults on the invaded, force suffers force, battle is fought against battle, war is waged against war, vengeance is avenged, torment is tormented, damnation is condemned, the abyss is swallowed up, hell is cast down, death itself dies, and mortality is exchanged for immortality. In a word, through Christ mercy has taken away misery, and goodness has drained away unhappiness. And the weapons the Devil used to attack us, and the stings with which he pricked us, these same things are now our exercises, from which we gather remarkable fruit. Now, I say, we dare to glory with the Apostle: "O death, where is your victory? O grave, where is your sting?" Now, through the Spirit of Christ, whom he promised to his own, we no longer live from ourselves, but live by the faith of the Son of God, and through the same Spirit we now sit with the heavenly ones. Living in the world, we are pilgrims from the world. And whatever part of the sky we dwell under, whatever place we are in, however we are received, all those things are the same to us. In afflictions we are of good courage, in sorrow we rejoice, in dishonour we are exalted, in want we abound, in nakedness we are clothed, in evils we endure, in death we live. This, surely, is that true and unfeigned wisdom which we should seek from this life, and to which neither angels, nor men, nor life, nor death can add or take away anything. This is the standing-place on which we must stand. Surely this is what we must seek throughout all of Scripture, to recognise Christ truly, and what present riches the Father offers us in him. Nor is there any summit in Scripture, among Moses and the Prophets, that does not lead us there. For since all the treasures of knowledge and understanding are hidden in Christ, we would be in vain to let ourselves be led away from him, unless we willingly choose to turn from the light of truth into the darkness of falsehood. Therefore the Apostle aptly claims for himself no other knowledge than that he knows Christ, 1 Cor. 2.2, and him crucified.

units.la: 1.Cor.1.55 atque illum crucifixum. Quanuis enim caro aliter iudicet, cuiusta cognitio vilis & vulgaris sit, est tamen illa nobis abunde, quam perpetua vita meditemur. Neque vero operae nos poenitebit, vbi noltrum omne studium ac mentem ad illius vnius noticiae perceptionem contulerimus. Nam quid quisquam nostrum iure requirat ad doctrinae coelestis cumulum, quàm vt Deum ita cognoscat, vt in ipsum trasformemur: facratiffimam ipsius imaginem in sese iam infculpiam habeat, vt iustitiae ipsius particeps euadat? vt Regni haeres fiat, ac tandem cumulate illud possideat? Atqui illud constat, & iam olim ipsum Dominû sese ita intuen dum praebuisse ac nunc demû quàm appositissime in facie Christi sui. Quare ab ipso vel tantillum deflectere, vel quouis modo diuertere sit nefas. Quin potius in eo vno consistat nobis animus, vt ex Scriptura cognoscere discamus Christû vnum, vt per ipsum recta deducamur ad Patrem, in quo demû cumulata extat omnis perfectio. Hi sunt inquam, verae hominum sapientiae termini, quam vnam sapientiam in hac vita summo studio perquirendam tantum singuli sibi proponant: & cui neq; Angelus neque mortalis quisquam, neque viuus neque vita functus appo nere vel detrahere audeat. Hic mens nostra coquiescat, vt de suo ne tantillum quidem admiscat, aut vllam additiciam doctrinâ admittat. Quod si quis doctrinae huic vel minimum apicem superaddiderit, is sese anathematî coram Deo & Ecclesia ipsius obnoxium iam iam agnoscat. Ad vos autem Reges, Principes viri & Christiani Magistratus ad hoc à Deo inflituti, vt delinquentes coerceatis, probos aute tueamini, & à noxa immunes conseruetis, prout iubet Dei verbum: ad vos inquâ, speetat, officiiq; veltri ratio exigit, vt hanc sanctam doctrinam, vti iliimam proculdubio & in primis necessariam praedicari, doceri, explicariq; iubeatis in omni ditione vestra, vt quàm longè lateq; veltrûm singulis patet imperium, regnum, principatus & dominatus, vbiq; illustretur, ac amplificetur Dei nomen, suûsque Euangelio coftet honos, quippe quum aequissimum sit, Reges omnes, regnâque ite omnia, summa cum fui demissione, ei parere & obedire, eiúsque gloriae inseruire. Videte vero vos etiam, qui vobis Episcoporum & Pastorum nomen apud miseram plebem tribuere soletis, videte etiam atque etiam ne Christi Iesu oues suo illo pabulo destituantur: neve hinc arceantur, prohibeantur, aut ratione vlla impediantur Christiani vlli, quin liberum sit sua singulis lingua, legere, reuerenter tractare, audire & intelligere hoc sanctum Euangelium, quando ita vult Deus, praecipitque ipse Iesus Christus. Ideo enim per vniuersum terrarum orbem misit suos Apostolos & seruos, singulari etiam & mirifica liberalitate, omnium linguarum facultate eos instruens, diuinóque dono ornans, vt omnibus linguisac omni creaturæ euangelizarent: voluitque debitores esse Græcis & Barbaris, tum sapientibus, tum insipientibus, ne quis ab eorum doctrinæ perceptione excluderetur. Enimuero si vere estis tantorum virorum vicarij successores & imitatores, vobis hæc cura incumbit, vt quemadmodum illi exemplo prærierunt, sic & ipsi faciatis, sic, inquam, vos comparetis, inuigilantes gregi, omnique ratione dantes operam & elaborantes vt nemo non ex toto grege recta cognitione, & fide Iesu Christi imbuatur ex puro Dei verbo. Sin minus, statiam lata in vos sententia, & sacris literis, tanquam publicis commentariis authenticisque tabulis consignata, fore certissime, vt animas eorum omnium e manu vestra repetat Dominus Deus Pater lumi-num, sancto suo Spiritu velit ignaris omnibus affulgere huius sancti Euangelij salutari intelligentia infirmos corroborare, cæcos illuminare, detque suæ veritati regnare in omnibus populis & nationibus, vt vniuersus mundus, nonnisi vnum Deum, vnumque Seruatorem Iesum Christum, vnam Fidem, & vnum Euangelium agnoscat. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1.5 and him crucified. For although the flesh judges otherwise, and his knowledge seems cheap and common, it is nevertheless enough for us to meditate on it throughout life. Nor will we regret the effort when we have directed all our zeal and mind to grasping that one knowledge. For what should any of us rightly seek as the sum of heavenly teaching, but to know God in such a way that we are transformed into him, that he already has his most sacred image engraved within us, that we become partakers of his righteousness, that we become heirs of the kingdom and at last possess it in full? It is certain that the Lord himself has already shown himself to be gazed upon in this way, and now at last most fittingly in the face of his Christ. Therefore to turn aside from him even a little, or to deviate from him in any way, is wrong. Rather let our mind rest in this one thing: to learn from Scripture to know Christ alone, so that through him we may be led straight to the Father, in whom all perfection is at last found in full. These, I say, are the true limits of human wisdom, which each one should seek with the greatest zeal in this life alone; and to which neither angel nor any mortal, neither living nor dead, may dare to add or subtract. Here let our mind find rest, so that it mixes in not even the smallest part of its own and admits no added doctrine. But if anyone adds even the slightest point to this teaching, let him acknowledge that he is already liable to anathema before God and his Church. But to you, kings, princes, and Christian magistrates, instituted by God for this purpose, that you may restrain wrongdoers, protect the upright, and keep them free from harm, as the word of God commands: to you, I say, this task belongs, and the nature of your office requires that you command this holy doctrine, which is undoubtedly the most useful and especially necessary, to be preached, taught and explained throughout your dominions, so that wherever your rule, kingdom, principality and lordship extend far and wide, the name of God may be made known and magnified, and honour be given to his gospel. For it is most right that all kings and all kingdoms should submit and obey him with the greatest humility and serve his glory. But see also you, who are wont to claim for yourselves the names of bishops and pastors before the wretched people: see again and again that the sheep of Christ Jesus are not deprived of this pasture, nor that any Christian be kept away from it, forbidden, or hindered in any way, but that it be free for each person to read in his own tongue, to handle reverently, to hear and understand this holy gospel, since God wills it and Jesus Christ himself commands it. For he sent his apostles and servants throughout the whole world for this purpose, equipping them also with a singular and marvellous generosity, giving them the ability of all tongues and adorning them with a divine gift, so that they might preach the gospel to all tongues and every creature; and he wished them to be debtors both to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, so that no one should be excluded from perceiving their teaching. Indeed, if you are truly the successors and imitators of such great men, this care falls to you: that, just as they went before you by example, you also should act, and so prepare yourselves, keeping watch over the flock and taking pains by every means that no one in the whole flock be left without right knowledge and faith in Jesus Christ, drawn from the pure Word of God. But if not, know that a sentence has been pronounced against you, and it is most certainly written in the holy letters, as in public records and authentic tablets, that the Lord God, the Father of lights, will require the souls of all those from your hand. May he, by his holy Spirit, deign to shine upon all the ignorant, to strengthen the weak with the saving understanding of this holy gospel, to enlighten the blind, and to let his truth reign among all peoples and nations, so that the whole world may acknowledge one God, one Saviour Jesus Christ, one faith and one gospel. Amen.

units.la: Quoniam Claudio nostro mandaui vt tibi copiose omnia exponat, de quibus per alium scripturus essem, non vt ar longiore Epistola. Si tibi prima specie displicebit meum in ipso mittendo consilium, scito me hac ratione adductu esse, quod cum scirem, aut saltem suspicarer, eos à quibus rogatus fui hoc facturos, nisi eorum voluntati morem gererem, anteuertere malui. Si tuas ad Bucerū literas meis adiungere placuerit, faciet rem meo iudicio perquam vtilem. Tamen si enim respõsum neque ab illo neque ab aliis spero quale optandum foret, danda est tamé opera, vt inter nos quam minimum differentionis appareat. Ego hac causa, quominus magis insistam, impedior, ne vrgere & propemodum velle cogere videar, vt mihi assentiatur. Tibi hac in parte maior erit libertas. Quid moliatur in Gallia Christi hostes, & qualiter primas eorum insidias discussit Dominus, intelliges ex Roberti literis, quibus acceptis protinus ad Bucerum scripsi, & quanta potui vehementia obtestatus sum vt ne vllis se illecebris irretiri pateretur. Huius nunc quoque Philippum admoneo, ac illi in memoriam reuoco, qualiter pridem à Langæo similibus technis sit tentatus. Vide tamen vt omnia clā suppressa contineas: scis enim vt quæcunque duobus tribúsve dixeris,
units.tr: Since I have instructed our Claudius to explain to you fully everything about which I would otherwise have written through another, I shall not write a longer letter. If at first sight my plan in sending him displeases you, know that I was led to it by this reason: since I knew, or at least suspected, that those by whom I was asked would do this, I preferred to forestall them rather than to refuse their wishes. If you think fit to add your letter to Bucer to mine, you will, in my judgement, do something very useful. Yet, even though I hope for no answer from him or from others such as would be desirable, care must still be taken that as little difference as possible appears between us. I am held back from pressing the matter further, lest I seem to urge and almost to want to force him to agree with me. You will have greater freedom in this matter. You will learn from Robert's letters what the enemies of Christ are plotting in France, and how the Lord has frustrated their first snares; on receiving them I at once wrote to Bucer and urged him, as earnestly as I could, not to allow himself to be snared by any allurements. I now also warn Philip of this and recall to his memory how Langeus was tried some time ago by similar tricks. Take care, however, to keep all these things hidden, for you know that whatever you say to two or three people soon spreads further.

units.la: Epist.59. statim latius manent. His diebus cum Anabaptista quidam Hebellos illos ineptos palam venum exposuisset, meo impulsu captus fuit. Expertus es quale fit hominum genus. Ego vero tam barbaram atrocitatem haftenus in nullo videram.Cum ego humaniter pro linguae meae more eum compellarem, nunquam aliter dignatus est mecum loqui, quamin ficum cane sibi negocii fuisset.Cum introductus fuisset in curiam: voluit primo Syndico assidere: inde repulsus, caput oculo que torquedo, Prophetica maiestatem simulans, tribus verbis ad rogata respondebat, fi liberet, saepius tacebat.Dehinc nobis exortum est de iureiurando certamen. Cum rogarem nunquid Lex Domini viam vitae nos doceret, axioma illud execrabile protulit, Abolitum esse vetus Testamentum. Tum ego ex Pauli citaui, vtilem esse ad reddendum Dei hominem perfectum in bono opere. Vrgebam, vt ad hoc responderet: sed verbum nullum exprimere potui. Sic explicaui rem totam, vt omnes praefractam hominis inscitiam cum pari impudentia agnoscerent. Cum se vrgeri sic videret, ad solitam illam sectae petulantiam descendit, nullum esse hominum genus, quod commodius viueret ministris. Refpodi paucis, non tam vt causae nostrae patrocinium susciperem, quam vt refutare beluae insolentiam. Postea me auarum vocauit. Risi tut omnes: sciebant enim quantum hoc anno ab ipsis recusaffem atque id tam ferio, vt iureiurando assererem, me nunquam concionem habiturum nisi desisterent. Sciebant me non tantum extraordinariam munificentiam recusasse, sed remisifie etiam aliquid de iusto stipendio, nec minus viginti coronatis. Itaque omnia probris fuit impetitus. Respondi modeste, si meo loco essem, ipsum fore diuitem: hoc non esse, signum auaritiae, qui esset pauper in media ditescendi facultate. Verum ipsum a me capitaliter accusari furti: si negaret, caput meum ad calumniae poenam offerre. Constabat enim ipsum duobus solidis & dimidio vendidisse quatuor folia, quae quatuor denariolis illi constiterant. Neque per indicarram steterat, quominus pluris venderet. Vrgebam, si bene sibi esset conscius, innocentiam suam tueretur. Cum tace ret pro more suo, corpide ipsorum perfectione differere. Cum suam obstinationem satis prodidisset, in exilium eiectus fuit. Biduo post, cum in vrbe deprehensus foret, virgis caesus est, libri coram exulti, ac denuntiatum sub poena suspendij, ne rediret. Homo est, vel pecus potius desperatae nequitiae. Literas, quas pridem ad vos scripseram, remittendas stat im curabis. Vellem Toffanum admoneres, vt vnius mrae ad ipsos Epistolae, & alterius ad Schnepfium exemplaria, sicut rogaueram, ad me remitteret: ut ocium haberes ad nos inuisendos, quam nobis iucundum officium omnibus faceres? Quaeso aliquando te ad iter tandem coniicenec tantum laetus esset nobis,sed vtilis quoque aduentus tuus:sicuti ex re praesenti agnosces,& te laboris,scio, non poenitebit:festina ergo. Saluta fratres omnes, quos ego magis amabo,si te huc extrudant. Dominus vos omnes conseruet.Ignosce meae lassitudini.Familiae tuae plurimam salutem.x x i.Ianuarij. M. D. XXXVI.
units.tr: Epist. 59. A few days ago a certain Anabaptist openly put on sale those foolish little booklets, and he was seized at my instigation. You have experienced what sort of men they are. Indeed I had hitherto seen no such barbarous savagery in anyone. When I addressed him courteously, in keeping with my manner of speaking, he deigned never to speak with me otherwise than as if he had dealings with a dog. When he was brought before the council, he first wished to sit beside the syndic; rejected from there, he twisted his head and eye, mimicking prophetic majesty, and answered questions with three words, and when it pleased him, he was more often silent. Then a dispute arose between us about the oath. When I asked whether the Law of the Lord did not teach us the way of life, he put forward that execrable axiom: that the Old Testament had been abolished. Then I cited from Paul that it is profitable for making the man of God perfect for every good work. I pressed him to answer this, but I could not get a single word out of him. I explained the whole matter so clearly that everyone recognised the stubborn ignorance of the man together with equal impudence. When he saw that he was being pressed in this way, he fell back on that customary petulance of the sect, that there is no class of men who live more comfortably than ministers. I replied briefly, not so much to take up the defence of our cause as to refute the beast's insolence. Afterwards he called me a miser. Everyone laughed, for they knew how much I had refused from them this year, and so firmly that I swore an oath that I would never preach again unless they desisted. They knew that I had not only refused their extraordinary generosity but had even remitted something of my just stipend, and not less than twenty crowns. So he was assailed with insults on every side. I answered modestly that if I were in his place he would be rich; that it was not a sign of avarice for someone to be poor in the midst of the means of growing rich. But I said that he himself was openly accused of theft, and if he denied it I would offer my head to the penalty for slander. For it was established that he had sold four sheets for two and a half shillings, which had cost him four pennies, and it was not for lack of an opportunity that he did not sell them for more. I urged him, if he was conscious of being innocent, to defend his innocence. When he kept silent, as was his custom, he began to discourse on their perfection. When he had sufficiently revealed his obstinacy, he was cast into exile. Two days later, when he was caught in the city, he was beaten with rods, the books were burned before his eyes, and it was announced under penalty of hanging that he was not to return. He is a man, or rather a beast, of hopeless wickedness. See that you have the letters which I wrote to you some time ago sent back to me at once. I would like you to warn Toffanus to return to me, as I asked, one copy of the letter to them and another to Schnepfius. Would you not perform a most pleasant service for all of us, if you had leisure to visit us? I beg you at last to set out on the journey, for your arrival will be not only most pleasant to us but also useful, as you will recognise from the present situation; and I know you will not regret the labour. Hurry, then. Greet all the brothers, whom I shall love all the more if they push you here. The Lord keep you all. Forgive my weariness. Very many greetings to your household. 21 January 1536.

units.la: CAL. MELANCHTHONI.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON.

units.la: CVM hic nobilis & pius adolescens profectionem hac, meo rogatu, ad vos susceperit, paucis exponam. Libellum ediderani lingua vulgari, quo eorum simulationem reprehendebam, qui quum Euangelij luce donati sint, non tamen abstinent ab vllis Papistarum sacris, quae sciunt sacrilegij & anathematis plena esse. Malles forte me aliquid de tam praecisa seueritate remittere. Verum quam iustam causam habuerim, re bene perpensa & cognita,iudicabis. Cum audirem multos de meo rigore cóqueri,at praesertim ex eorum genere,qui tanto sibi plus sapere videntur, quanto diligentius vitae suae cauent,excusationem compositi,quae illis aures aliquanto durius vellicauit quam prior libellus. Multi, quibus religio pro philosophia est,secure hoc totum contemnunt.Quicunque serio Deum timent,eo saltem vsque sunt promoti,vt sibi displicere incipiant. Sed quoniam perplexa illis res videtur, adhuc haerent dubij, donec tua & D. Lutheri auctoritate confirmentur. Et quidem vereor,ne ideo vos consulant, quod sperent vos sibi fore mitiores. Quocunque tamen id faciant animo, quia certo persuasus sum vos fideles ipsi pro vestra fynceritate & pro vestra etiam singulari prudentia salutare consilium daturos,libenter me facturum recepi quod petebant, vt hominem data opera ad vos mitterem.Quoniam autem magnopere referre arbitrabar,non modo sententiam meam vobis perspectam esse,sed rationes etiā quibus adductus ita sentirem, non esse incognitas,libellos in linguam Latinam statim vertendos curaui. Tametsi autem improbe hoc facere videri possim, tamen per nostram amicitiam te rogo, vt legendi taedium subire ne recuses. Tanti iudicium tuum facio, sicuti par est, vt mihi sit molestissimum quicquam me suscipere,quod tibi minus probetur. Te quidem pro eximia tua humanitate multa aliis in dulgere scio, quae tibi non permitteres. Sed videndum quid nobis liceat:ne relaxemus vbi Dominus adstringit. Neque vero vt mihi a sententiaris rogo,quod nimiae impudentiae foret,vel in mea gratiam vllo modo a libera simplicique sententiae tuae expositione deflectas : sed tantum vt legendi molestiam deuorare ne grauerius. Equidem cupio sic penitus inter nos conuenire, vt ne
units.tr: Since this noble and pious young man has undertaken this journey to you at my request, I will set out the matter briefly. I had published a little book in the vernacular in which I rebuked the pretence of those who, though they have been given the light of the Gospel, still do not abstain from any of the Papists' rites, which they know to be full of sacrilege and anathema. You would perhaps prefer that I relax something of such uncompromising severity. But you will judge how just my cause was once you have weighed and understood the matter well. I have heard many complain of my rigour, especially people of that sort who seem to themselves so much wiser the more carefully they guard their lives. They have written an excuse for themselves, which has grated on their ears rather more harshly than my first booklet did. Many, for whom religion is a kind of philosophy, scorn all this with complete indifference. Those who fear God in earnest have at least advanced so far that they begin to be displeased with themselves. But since the matter seems perplexing to them, they still hang in doubt until it is confirmed by your authority and that of Dr. Luther. I fear indeed that they consult you because they hope you will be gentler with them. Whatever their intention, I am firmly persuaded that you, being faithful and, by your sincerity and singular prudence, wise, will give sound counsel, and so I gladly agreed to what they asked, namely to send the man to you on purpose. Since I thought it greatly mattered not only that my opinion should be clear to you but also that the reasons which led me to hold it should not be unknown, I arranged for the booklets to be translated into Latin at once. Although I may seem to be acting shamelessly in doing this, I ask you, by our friendship, not to refuse to endure the tedium of reading them. I value your judgement as highly as is fitting, so it would be most distressing to me to undertake anything that you did not approve. I know that, in your remarkable kindness, you grant many things to others which you would not allow yourself. But we must consider what is permitted to us, lest we relax where the Lord binds us. Nor do I ask, as though from a sympathiser, anything that would be excessively shameless; nor do I ask you in any way to turn aside, for my sake, from the free and simple statement of your own opinion. I ask only that you bear the tedium of reading. Indeed I long to agree so thoroughly with you that not even the slightest trace of disagreement should appear between us. But it is for you rather to lead me than for me to watch what pleases me. You see how familiarly I deal with you, yet I do not fear that I am going beyond due measure, for I know how much my standing with you allows me because of your singular goodwill towards me.

units.la: in verbulo quidé vno dissensionis vlla species appareat. Sed tuū est mihi potius præire,quàm spectare quid mihi placeat. Vides quàm tecum agam familiariter:neq; tamen vereor, ne modum excedam: scio enim quantum mihi apud te pro singulari tua in me beneuolentia liceat. In D. Martino plus aliquanto difficultatis erit:quantum enim ex rumore & quorundam literis intelligere potui vix dum bene placatus hominis animus leui de cau sa exulcerari posset. Proinde quas ad eum literas scripsi,nuntius tibi ostendet: vt illis inspectis, totum negotium tuo consilio regas. Ne quid ergo perperam aut inconsulte tentetur, quod infeliciter postea cedat, tuum erit prouidere: quod te, pro summa tua dexteritate, probe factypum scio. Cæterum quales istic contentiones vos exercuerint, & qualis fuerit exitus, nondum certò re scire potui: nisi quòd atrocem libellum exiisse audio, nouo incendio excitando instar facis futurum, nisi ab alia parte Dominus animos retineat, alioqui plus iusto feroces & inflatos, sicut nosti. Quid autem vbi sic prouocantur? Dum reputo quàm nùc alieno tempore intestinæ concertationes nos abripiant, propemodum examinor. Nuper mihi ostendit Nurembergensis mercator hac iter faciens, apologiam quandam Osiandri: cuius me vehementer eius nomine pudui t. Quorsum enim attineba, Zuinglianos tertio quoque versu lacess re ac Zuinglium ipsum vexare tam inhumaniter? ac ne sancto quidem Dei seruo Oecolampadio parcer? quem vtinam dimidia ex parte ref rret. Mihi certè longè maiori stet in pretio. Neque verò postulo, vt famam suam impunè traduci tacitus sinat: sed vellem ab eorum virorum contumelia abstinere, quorum memoria piis omnibus in honore esse debet. Itaque sicut mihi displicet illius petulentia, cuius elegis se infamarum fuisse queritur, ita in ipso & moderationem, & prudentiam, vel sanitatem potius desidero. Deus bone, quales & quàm iucundos lusus præbemus Papistis? quasi illis locauerimus nostram operam. Sed ego importunè facio, qui malis istis recensendis, quibus mederi non potes, moerorem tibi fructu augeo. Gemamus tamen, quoniam Ecclesiæ incommodis affici nos decet: sed hac spe interea nos sustentemus, quod vtcunque premamur ac vexemur inter magnos fluctus, non tamen opprimemur. Magna Concilij expectatione erecti sunt omnium animi in Gallia: nec dubium quin rex ipse, saltem initio, spem aliquam & voluntatem Concilij cogendi habuerit. Nam à Cæsare reuersus Cardinalis Tornonius illi persuaserat, Cæsarem id in animo habere. Interea consulebat Cæsaris nomine, vt duos aut tres ex vobis Rex ad se accerseret: idque scorsum: quo à singulis aliquid per blanditias eliceret, vel quo- uis modo extorqueret, quod ab omnibus non posset simul impetrari.Pollicebatur Cæsar idem se facturum. Hic porrò finis erat,vt illis quasi præiudiciis obstricti, eo minus posletis cum ad feriam disceptationem ventum esset. Nam quia frangi nos in rebus & simplici causæ actione desperant, nullum vident melius compendium,quàm si principes habeant obnoxios,& quasi vinctam ac alligatam teneant eorum libertatem. Hoc consilium cùm Regi placeret,negauit Castellanus,committendos vobis ad disputationem Gallos Theologos, nisi bene ante instructi essent ac comparati. Vos homines esse in hoc pugnæ genere exercitatos:nec tam facile posse labefactari.Cauendum esse,ne Rex pro dita suorum inscitia, totum regnum magno ludibrio exponeret.Ambitio Regis fecit vt præualeret hæc sententia.Duodecim sunt delecti, qui Meloduni decapitibus controuersis disputent: & tandem ad Regem referant quid censuerint. Silentium iureiurando promiserunt.Sed illis tacentibus certò scio,nihil nisi de opprimenda veritate açturos,se qualemcunque reformationem quærere vtcunque simulent:certo certius est hoc vnum agitare, qualiter sepulta sanæ doctrinæ luce suam tyrannidem stabiliat. Ego Cardinalis Turnonij consilium à Deo fuisse discussum interpretor: ne quem ex nostris incautum & nihil tale suspicantem irretirent.Meminis.ti iisdem attribus te tentatu fuisse à Langeo. Verùm si in Dominum respexerimus,frustra nos adorientur omnibus machinis. Vale,clarissime vir & amice mihi semper obseruande. Dominus ibi semper adsit, diúque Ecclesiæ suæ incolumem te seruet.x i i.Calendas Februarij. M. D. XLV.
units.tr: With Dr. Martin there will be rather more difficulty, for as far as I could gather from rumour and from some men's letters, his mind, not yet well settled, could easily be inflamed again over a slight cause. Therefore the messenger will show you the letters I wrote to him, so that, once you have read them, you may direct the whole business by your counsel. It will be your task to foresee that nothing is attempted rashly or unwisely, which might turn out badly later; I know you will do this well, given your great skill. As for the quarrels that have troubled you there, and what the outcome was, I have not yet been able to learn for certain. I only hear that a bitter pamphlet has been published, which will be like fuel for a new fire, unless the Lord restrains the minds of the other side, which are otherwise more fierce and swollen than is right, as you know. But what can be done when men are provoked like this? As I reflect how inopportunely these internal contentions now carry us away, I am almost at a loss. Recently a merchant of Nuremberg, passing through here, showed me a certain apology by Osiander, and I was deeply ashamed on his account. For what was the purpose of attacking the Zwinglians at every turn and treating Zwingli himself so inhumanely? Nor has he spared even the holy servant of God, Oecolampadius, whom I wish he had praised by half as much. To me, at least, he is worth far more. I do not demand that he let their reputation be slandered with impunity in silence, but I should like him to refrain from insulting those men whose memory ought to be honoured by all the pious. So, just as I dislike the petulance of the man who complains that he was defamed in his elegies, so I wish for moderation, prudence, or rather sanity, in Osiander himself. Good God, what sport and what delight we furnish for the Papists, as if we had hired out our labour to them! But I act unseasonably, since by recounting these evils, which you cannot remedy, I only add to your sorrow. Yet let us groan, since it is fitting that we be affected by the troubles of the Church; but meanwhile let us sustain ourselves with this hope, that however we are pressed and harried amid great waves, we shall not be overwhelmed. The minds of all in France are lifted up by a great expectation of a Council, and there is no doubt that the king himself, at least at first, hoped for and wished for the convening of a Council. For Cardinal Tornonius, returning from Caesar, had persuaded him that Caesar had this in mind. Meanwhile, in Caesar's name, he advised that the king should summon two or three of you to himself, and do so separately, so that by flattery he might draw something from each, or extort by whatever means what could not be obtained from all together. Caesar promised that he too would do the same. The aim of all this was that you, bound by such prejudgments, would be the less able to resist when the time for the public disputation came. For since they despair of breaking us in matters and in the plain pleading of our cause, they see no better device than to hold the princes under obligation and keep their freedom, as it were, bound and fettered. When this plan pleased the king, the Chancellor (Castellanus) refused to commit the French theologians to a disputation with you unless they were first well instructed and prepared. He said that you were men exercised in this kind of combat and not so easily shaken, and that care must be taken lest the king, through the ignorance of his own people, expose the whole kingdom to great ridicule. The king's ambition brought it about that this opinion prevailed. Twelve men have been chosen who are to dispute at Melun on the controverted heads, and finally report to the king what they judged. They have promised silence under oath. But while they keep silent, I know for certain that they will do nothing but suppress the truth; whatever reformation they pretend to seek, it is most certain that they are pursuing only this, how to establish their own tyranny by burying the light of sound doctrine. I interpret the Cardinal Tornonius's plan as having been frustrated by God, so that they might not ensnare any of ours who was unwary and suspected nothing of the kind. You will remember that you were tested in the same way by Langeus. But if we look to the Lord, they will attack us in vain with all their machines. Farewell, most distinguished man and friend, whom I shall always honour. May the Lord be ever present with you there and keep you safe for his Church for many years.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: MYCONIVS CALVINO.
units.tr: MYCONIUS TO CALVIN.

units.la: AGo tibi gratias, doctissime Caluine, pro libro tuo quæ scripsisti ad Carolum Quintum,vt maiores nequeam.Profuerit,nécne perinde est,quasi ipsis non fuerit scriptus:aliis tamen proderit. Nam crede mihi, habere tuam inuentionem saltem,quæ pie studiosis plurimum valet prodesse.Vnum dolet mihi quòd qui attulit, primum quaternionem fecit illegibilem, adeò madore nescio quo literæ penitus sunt abrasæ. Cæsar si legit,in contrarium motus est, adeò persequitur in Belgis sanctos.Maria regina, Imperatoris soror, non potuit tueri Sacellanum suum Carmelitam,quin fuga consulere sibi sit coactus. Et postquam iam periculo liberatus erat, condemnatus est vt hæreticus:& quia ipse non aderat,libri eius combusti sunt publicè. Sic accidit filio Margrauij Antuerpiensis,& aliis bonis ac piis viris sine numero.Conatur vir ille sic recociliare sibi Papa indignan-
units.tr: I give you thanks, most learned Calvin, for your book which you wrote to Charles V, so that I cannot give greater thanks. Whether it will help them or not is much the same as if it had not been written for them; yet it will help others. For believe me, it is at least a good thing to have your work, which is very useful to pious students. One thing grieves me: the man who brought it made the first quire illegible, for the letters have been utterly rubbed away by some dampness or other. If Caesar read it, he was moved to the contrary, so much does he persecute the saints in the Low Countries. Queen Mary, the Emperor's sister, could not protect her Carmelite chaplain, so that he was forced to flee to save himself. And after he had already been freed from danger, he was condemned as a heretic; and because he was not present, his books were publicly burned. So it happened to the son of the Margrave of Antwerp, and to countless other good and pious men. That man tries in this way to reconcile himself to the indignant Pope-

units.la: i.ij. tem: quidni conatus idem est ad Deū, à cuius manu grauius premitur! dicitur enim laborare grauissimis diuerfiffimisque moribus. Schola Louanienfis per Brabantiam eiicit ex ludis minoribus omnia quæ Christi sunt.Iulianica vt ita dicam,reformatio. Dominus confirmet Ecclesiam suam.Misi ad te lit ras D.Bucceri, & cum tuis literas Papæ ad suos, & eas quas scripsit ad Cæsarem, dignas certe quæ ab omnibus legantur, & scholiis adiciis intelligantur.Obsequutus es nimirum consilio Buceri. Quod si sic habet, velim nos, staruto pretio, tuo labore non priues. De Concilio,veluti per somnium audiui, reuocatum est. Comitia non procedunt. Hactenus solus Episcopus Augustanus, nuper Cardinalis factus,Vvormaciæ fuit, & eas nugas egit quæ in more sunt inferiorum ciuitatum, & Romæ nunquam cessant. Laruati,vt non cognoscantur,domos intrant ciuium: ibi edunt, bibunt ludunt,saltant,libidinantur, & quicquid esse potest iucundum faciunt, aliquoties ingenti cum damno, & ignominia pa-trisfamilias.Et non est,vt audio,qui vel mutire audeat.Præparationes dignæ, liue ad Comitia, siue ad Concilium. Exurgat Dominus,rogemus,ad iudicadum causam suam de gente non sancta: sic enim in diris flagitia magnorum hominum crescunt, vt mihi videatur iram Dei propiorem esse quàm putemus.Largitur is nobis, vt diem eius expectemus cum gaudio. Volui te,mi Caluine,sic salutare,boni consulas rogo. Vale cum familia in Domino.Ministros Christi pios nomine meo salutabis.Basilez, v i.Martij,anno M. D. XLV.
units.tr: i.ij. him, the Pope is trying in the same way to win back the favour of one he has offended. Why should his attempt not be the same toward God, by whose hand he is pressed more heavily? He is said to be labouring under the gravest and most diverse ills of character. The Louvain school is driving out of the lower schools everything that belongs to Christ. It is, so to speak, a Julianic reformation. May the Lord strengthen his Church. I have sent you the letters of Mr. Bucer, along with yours to the Pope's men, and those he wrote to the Emperor. They are certainly worth reading by everyone and understanding by the scholars. You have of course followed Bucer's advice. If that is so, I would like us not to be deprived of your labour, for a fixed price. As for the Council, I have heard, as if in a dream, that it has been called back. The diet is not moving forward. So far only the Bishop of Augsburg, lately made a cardinal, has been at Worms, and he has gone through those trifles that are customary in the lesser cities, and that never cease at Rome. Masked so as not to be recognised, they enter the houses of citizens; there they eat, drink, play, dance, indulge their lusts, and do whatever can be pleasant, sometimes to the great loss and disgrace of the head of the household. And, as I hear, there is no one who dares even to murmur. Preparations worthy of the diet, or of the Council, are being made. Let us pray that the Lord arise to judge his own cause against a people that is not holy; for the crimes of great men grow so monstrous that it seems to me God's wrath is nearer than we think. He grants us to await his day with joy. I wanted to greet you thus, my Calvin; I ask you to take it in good part. Farewell, with your household, in the Lord. You will greet the faithful ministers of Christ in my name. Basel, 6 March, in the year 1545.

units.la: Of.Myconius tuus.
units.tr: Of. Myconius tuus.

units.la: CAL. REGINAE NAVARRAE.
units.tr: TO QUEEN CATHERINE OF NAVARRE.

units.la: Accepi à certo homine literas, quas tuo mandato à fe scripras te stat ur: quibus mihi plane cōstat librum quem de Libertinis edidi, tibi minime probari. Ac dolet mihi tibi tristitiam attulisse, nisi ea ad tuam salutem pertineat. Illa siquidem est non poenitenda tristitia, vt ait Apollolus, cuius neminem causam dedisse poenitere debeat. Et tamen vix mihi liquet, cur liber ille tibi tantum displicuerit. Causam is qui ad me scripsit exprimit, quod liber ille scriptus sit,inquit, in te ac tuos domesticos. Atqui,quod ad te attinet,nunquam mihi in animum venit tuum nomen attingere, aut quicquam detrahere illi obseruantiæ, quam tibi debent pij omnes: vt non accedat regia illa Maiestas, ad quam te euexit Dominus, domus illa regia ex qua edita es, totum denique illud summæ nobilitatis fallagiū, quod te in mundo conspicuam reddit.Nam quibus non sum ignotus, non ignorant etiam quam ab illa inhumanitate alienus sim, vt domi-
units.tr: I have received a letter from a certain man, which he wrote, as you state, at your command. From it I learn clearly that the book I published on the Libertines does not please you at all. I am sorry to have caused you sadness, unless that sadness serves your salvation. For it is a sadness not to be repented of, as the Apostle says, one which no one should have reason to regret. And yet it is hardly clear to me why that book displeased you so much. The man who wrote to me gives the reason: the book, he says, was written against you and your household. But as far as you are concerned, it never occurred to me to touch your name or to detract in any way from the reverence which all the godly owe you: not to mention that royal majesty to which the Lord has raised you, that royal house from which you come, and in short all that splendour of the highest nobility which makes you conspicuous in the world. Those who know me do not fail to know how far I am from that inhumanity of despising earthly dominion and principalities and whatever else belongs to human government.

units.la: {y} Epist.61. dominationes ac principatus terrenos despiciam, & quæ alia ad humanam politiam pertinent. Mihi vero ignotæ non sunt etiam eotes illæ quas in te Dominus contulit, & quomodo te vsus fuerit atque adhibuerit ad Regnum suum promouendum: quæ quidem omnia satis iustum argumentum mihi & tui obser uandi præbent, & affirmandi tui nominis. Atq; hic tibi persuadeat velim, qui te ita aduersum me accendunt, neque tibi valde consulere, neque mihi quicquam inde priuatim decidere, sed inde captare occasionem tui dimouendi à syncero affectu quo Dei Ecclesiam prosequeris: & vt sensim animum abducas ab illo obsequio, quo te hactenus Domino Iesu Christo atque ipsius etiam membris impendisti. Quod ad domesticos tuos attinet, non puto videri tibi posse domum tuam digniorem ipsa familia Domini Iesu Christi, cuius certum membrum Diaboli nomen retulit: seruus inquam ipsius, mensæ eiusdem assessor, & in eum gradum euectus, vt vnus ex Filij Dei legatis designaretur. Etli non ita præceps fui vt etiam notarem domum tuam, cum potius ipsam rei veritatem ita expresserim vt coram Domino, vt simul non attigerim quicquam illos ad te pertinere. Iam videndum est vltro ne & animi causa illos ita perstrinxerim, an vero adactus magnis & iustis rationibus, adeoque ipsa necessitate, illos ita acceperim: ac si res vt se habet probetenes, ita mihi persuadeo, vt non excusatione modo tibi dignum videatur quod hic admisi, sed & laude digna à te iudicanda sit mea simplicitas. Sic igitur de illa recta audio & sentio, vt nihil inter homines perniciosius ac magis execrandum audiri possit.
