Sic illam nocere video, vt facem ardentem iudicem, qua omnia statim conflagratura sint, luem certissimam qua nihil non inficiendum sit, statuam, nisi obuiam eatur quamprimum. Iam cum ad illud munus à Deo vocatus sim, vrget me conscientia mea vt pro virili resistá præsenti malo. Eò accedit quod à tot piis eo nomine in dies interpeller, qui fidem meam & officium implorare non desinant, & totum fere Belgium eo malo circumseptum queratur, vt saltem remedium adhibere studeam. Et tamen tot occasionibus inductus totum annum me continui, vt viderem an silendo potius consopiretur malum. Si quis obiiciat integrum mihi fuisse scribere aduersus prauum dogma, vt personis simul parcerem, non deesset legitima excusatio. Cum enim mihi compertum sit quantum damni dederit Artesis & vicinæ Henaultiæ Antonius Pocquetus, vti à fide dignis perlatum est ad me: Quintinum porro non alio spectare quam vt ad brutum istud sectæ genus infirmos & simplices perducat, non alieno testimonio, sed meipso aurito teste mihi constet satis: cum, inquam, toti in eo illi sint vt sanam doctrinam euertant, miseras animas in exitium immergant, in orbem terrarum Dei contemptum inuehant, an mihi teftius agere integrum fuerit,te iudicem appello.Canis fi quis herum im petat,saltem latratu absterreat.Quis igitur me ferat dum veritatem Dei impeti audio, fi tandiu os mihi occludi sinam? Neque vero dubito non expectare te vt in gratiam tuam,in defensione Euangelij prœuaricer,quando illa mihi mandata est.Peto igitur ne moleste feras,fi adaftus necessitate pro meo munere,nisi Deu in me prouocare vellem, illi certo homini ex tuis non peperce- rim,cum in te omnino interea nihil protulerim.Quod epiftolę auctor ait tuo nomine, parum tibi gratos futuros tales seruos qualis ipse sim , ita etiam de me iudico vt non magno vsui esse me tibi posse agnoscam.Neque enim facultas adest,neque tu eo homine eges. Et tamen neque propensio animi erga te deest, neque dum viuam per Dei gratiam alium me esse aut haberi su ftinebo.Atque vt ipsa meum obsequium auerseris, illud non faciet quin eandem mentem & affectum erga te constanter retineam. Quod reliquum est, probe tenent qui me norunt quàm alienus sim à captando ad principes aditu, cùm nunquam honorum studio titillatus fuerim.Neque etiam vt hoc conatus effem mihi fortasse successi ffet. Sed est quod Deo gratias agam, cùm ab illo studio animus mihi integer constiterit.Est enim abundefatis in quo acquiescam, quod illi Hero addiftus sim,qui me admisit & habuit inter suos,adeoque munus illud mihi com miserit quod tanti est apud ipsum ponderis,vtcunque apud homines vile & despectum iaceat. Ego vero omnium mortalium ingratiffimus sim, nisi meam illam conditionem omnibus honoribus atque diuitiisanteferrem. Quod ad notam inconftatiæ quam mihi inuris, ita tibi cofirmo plane tibi impositum fuisse. Nunquam enim eo etiam adductus sum vt fidei meæ confessionem à me quisquam posceret Atque fi eo mihi deneniendum fuisset,nihil habeo quod de me iactare audeam:neque tame diffido quin cum ita me dominus sustinuerit aliquando vt propter ipsius verbum alterius nomine vitæ periculum adire non dubitaueiim, idem ipse mihi sua virtute manum porrecturus fuisset, vbi mea confessione nomen ipsius glorificandum fuisset.Arqui beneficio illius ita mihi constiti vt nemo habeat quod mihi veritatis negatæ aut paliuodiæ notam directè vel obliquè inurat. Ac quod magis cit, semper mihi horroriffuit illa vecordia, vt quis ad Christum abnegandum adducatur vt capiti & facultatibus consulat (idque iam inde cum effem in Gallia) quod idoneis testibus confirmare possum. Sed tamen vt tibi certius confiet,qui me ita apud te detulerunt, humanitate tua pessime vsos fuisse, testem apud te appello D.Cleracum,à quo certissimè cognosces quam falsa fit ciufmodi calumnia quæ mihi imponi-turtur & quam nullo modo ferre possum, ne per illam blasphemetur nomen Dei: quanuis enim nihil omnino ipse sim, quando tamen Domino placuit vti me vt instrumento ædificandæ domuisuæ, satis cum aliis video quam caudam traheret probrum illud si in me hæreret, vt ad Euangelij infamiam redundaret. Benedictus vero Dominus qui non tantum in me Satanæ licere voluit, mēque adeo in mea infirmitate sustinuit; cùm nūquam ad examen vsque fidei vel ad vincula me probatum voluit. Breuitatem Epistolæ & quandam pertur bationem mihi condones velim, cùm acceptis illis literis statim ad hanc responsionem me contulerim, ut ea tibi nomine à me satisfactum curarem, ne quid de eo affectu remitteres, quem erga pios hactenus abundē præ te tulisti & reipsa exhibuisti. Dominus noster Iesus Christus præsidio suo te protegat, ac Spiritu dirigat ad vocationem ipsius syncero zelo & prudentia ad extremum vsque prosequendam. x x.April. M. D. XLV.
units.tr: Epist. 61. I am not unaware of the gifts the Lord has bestowed on you, nor of how he has used you and employed you to advance his kingdom. All of this gives me a sufficiently just reason both to observe you and to affirm your name. Here I would have you believe that those who so inflame you against me are not truly serving your interests, nor do they gain anything privately from it for themselves. Rather, they are seeking an occasion to draw you away from the sincere affection with which you cherish the Church of God, and to lead your mind gradually away from that obedience with which you have hitherto devoted yourself to the Lord Jesus Christ and to his members. As for your household, it does not seem to me that you can regard your house as more worthy than the very family of the Lord Jesus Christ, from which a certain member bore the name of the Devil: a servant of his, I mean, a table-companion of the same, raised to such a rank that he was designated one of the envoys of the Son of God. Although I was not so rash as to mark your household, I set out the truth of the matter as in the sight of the Lord, and I did not touch on anything as pertaining to you. Now it must be considered whether I wrote about them of my own accord, out of spite, or whether I was driven by great and just reasons, and indeed by necessity itself, to treat them as I did. If the matter stands as it is, I am persuaded that what I have done here deserves not merely excuse but praise, and that my simplicity ought to be judged worthy of your approval. So I hear and think of that doctrine of yours in such a way that nothing more pernicious or more to be execrated can be heard among men. I see it doing such harm that I judge it a burning torch by which everything will at once be consumed, and I reckon it a most certain plague by which nothing will not be infected, unless it is checked as quickly as possible. Now, since I have been called to that office by God, my conscience urges me to resist the present evil with all my strength. Added to this, I am petitioned daily by so many godly people on this account, who never cease to implore my faith and duty, and nearly the whole of Belgium, surrounded by that evil, complains, so that I may at least strive to apply a remedy. And yet, moved by so many occasions, I kept silent for a whole year, to see whether the evil might rather be quieted by silence. If anyone objects that I could have written against the perverse doctrine while also sparing persons, there would be no lack of a legitimate excuse. For since it has been reported to me by trustworthy men how much harm Antonius Pocquetus has done in Artois and neighbouring Hainaut, and since Quintinus aims at nothing else than to lead weak and simple people into that brutish sect, I am sufficiently assured of this not by another's testimony but as an ear-witness myself. Since, I say, they are wholly intent on overturning sound doctrine, plunging wretched souls into ruin, and bringing contempt of God into the world, I appeal to you as judge whether it would have been right for me to act with restraint. If someone attacks a master, a dog should at least frighten him off with its barking. Who, then, would tolerate me, when I hear the truth of God being assailed, if I let my mouth be shut for so long? Nor do I doubt that you do not expect me, to win your favour, to betray the defence of the gospel, since it has been entrusted to me. I therefore ask you not to be annoyed if, compelled by necessity in the discharge of my office, unless I wished to provoke God in myself, I did not spare that man from your household, since in the meantime I have said nothing at all against you. As for the writer of the letter saying, in your name, that such servants as I am would be of little pleasure to you, I judge of myself in the same way, that I know I cannot be of great use to you. For I have neither the ability, nor do you need such a man. And yet there is no lack of goodwill towards you, and as long as I live, by the grace of God, I will not allow myself to be or be thought otherwise. Even if you reject my service, that will not prevent me from keeping the same mind and affection towards you constantly. As to the rest, those who know me well are aware how far I am from seeking access to princes, since I have never been stirred by the desire for honours. Nor, perhaps, would I have succeeded had I tried. But I have reason to thank God, since my mind has remained free from that desire. For I have enough to rest content in, that I am attached to that Master who has admitted me and counted me among his own, and has entrusted to me an office which is of such great weight in his sight, however cheap and despised it may lie in the eyes of men. Indeed I would be the most ungrateful of all mortals if I did not prefer that condition of mine to all honours and riches. As for the mark of inconstancy with which you brand me, I assure you that it has been plainly falsely imposed on me. For I was never so driven that anyone demanded a confession of my faith from me. And if I had been obliged to make one, I have nothing I could dare to boast of about myself. Yet I do not doubt that, just as the Lord has sustained me at times so that I did not hesitate to face danger to life for the sake of his word, so he himself would have stretched out his hand to me by his own power, when my confession was to glorify his name. But by his blessing I have so stood that no one has cause to brand me, directly or indirectly, with the mark of denying the truth or of cowardly flattery. And what matters more, that madness by which someone is led to deny Christ in order to care for his head and property has always horrified me, from the time I was in France, as I can confirm with suitable witnesses. Yet so that it may be more certain to you that those who reported me to you so badly misused your kindness, I call on Monsieur Cleracus as witness before you, from whom you will learn most certainly how false is the calumny that is imposed on me, and how little I can bear that the name of God be blasphemed through it. For although I am nothing at all, since the Lord has been pleased to use me as an instrument for building his house, I see well enough, along with others, how far that disgrace would drag if it clung to me, so as to redound to the infamy of the gospel. Blessed be the Lord, who has not only allowed Satan so much in me, but has sustained me in my weakness, since he has never willed me to be tested to the point of trial of faith or of chains. I would ask you to pardon the brevity of this letter and a certain agitation of mine, since, as soon as I received that letter, I set about this reply, so that I might have it sent to you in my name, lest you should relax at all that affection which you have hitherto shown abundantly towards the godly, and in fact displayed. May our Lord Jesus Christ protect you with his help, and direct you by his Spirit to pursue his calling to the end with sincere zeal and prudence. 20 April 1545.

units.la: Tibi addictissimus & ad obsequium paratissimus Io.Calvinus.
units.tr: Your most devoted servant, ready for your service, John Calvin.

units.la: CAL. MELANCHTHON.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON.

units.la: VTinam vt me angit, adeoque excruciat mœroris tui συμ-πάθεια: sic aliqua eius parte subleuare te possem. Si ita est, vt dicunt Tigurini, habuerunt iustam scribendi causam. Vester autem Pericles quanta intempestie ad fulminandum rapitur? præsertim cùm eius causa nihilo sit melior. Multū illi debemus omnes, fateor. Nec ego inuitus patiar, vt summa authoritate posseat, modò sibi ipsi moderari sciat. Quanquam in Ecclesia semper videndum est, quousque hominibus deferamus. Actū enim est, vbi vnusquispiam plus potest reliquis omnibus: præsertim vbi hoc ipsum non dubitat experiri, quantum possit. In tanta quidem dissipatione, quantam nunc cernimus, difficile est res turbatas componere. Verum si in nobis omnibus esset is animus qui esse debet, aliquod forsan remedium posset inueniri. Et certè fœdum exemplum transmittimus ad posteros, dum omnem libertatem sponte malumus proiicere, quàm vt hominis vniusanimum offensiuncula aliqua pungamus. At est vehemens ingenium, & impetus habet violētos. Quasi verò hæc vehementia non magis exultet, dum omnes illi indulgent, atq; omnia permittunt. Si inter prima renascentis Ecclesiæ initia iam emergit hoc tyrānidis exēplum: quid breui, rebus in deterius col lapsis, fiet. Defleamus ergo Ecclesiæ calamitatem, neq; modò taciti apud nos hunc mœrorē deuoremus: sed audeamus aliquando li berum gemitum edere. Quid si etiam Domini permissu in has angustias fis redactus,ne plenior tandem de hac re confessio tibi extorqueatur?Verissimum equidem fateor esse quod doces:& quòd placido genere docendi haftenus studuisti animos à contentione reuocare, prudentiam moderationémque tuam laudo. Sed dum locum hunc tanquam scopulum aliquem refugis, ne in quorundam offensionem incurras,plurimos,qui aliquid certius in quo acquiescant,abs te requirunt,suspensos perplexófq; relinquis. Est autem, vt me aliquando tibi dicere memini, non satis nobis honestum , eam doctrinam , quàm plerique sancti proprio sanguine testatam relinquere non dubitant, ne atramento quidem consignare. Ad hanc ergo plenam & solidam mentis tuæ explicationem forte viam tibi patefacere nunc vult Deus,ne perpetuo hæreant dubij, qui ab authoritate tua pendét, quosfcis esse quamplurimos.Neque hoc tam incitâdi quàm consolandi tui causa dico. Nisi enim ex hac turbulenta concussione aliquid hinc exoriturum sperarem, multo acerbiore luctu conficerer. Quanquam exitum quieti expectmus qualem dare Dominus voler:interea cursum nostrum infractis animis persequamur.De responso tuo,magnam tibi habeo gratiam,simul etiam de humanitate non vulgari, quam sibi abs te exhibitam fuisse Claudius mihi testatur.Qualis erga me futurus effes inde conjecturam facio quòd meos tam benigne comiterque accipias. Deo autem maximas gratias agere non desino,qui dedit,vt in eius quæstionis summa, de qua rogati eramus , sententiæ nostræ congruerent. Tametsi enim paululum est discriminis in particulis quibusdam , de re tamen ipsa optimè inter nos conuenit. XXVIII.Iunij. M. D. XLV.
units.tr: Would that I could relieve some part of your sorrow, which tortures me with its sympathy (συμπάθεια), as it does you! If it is as the Zurich men say, they had a just reason for writing. But your Pericles, how untimely is he hurried into thundering, especially when his cause is in no way better? We all owe him much, I confess. Nor would I unwillingly allow him great authority, provided he knows how to restrain himself. Yet in the Church we must always consider how far we should yield to men. It is all over when one man has more power than all the rest, especially when he does not hesitate to test how much he can do. In such a scattering as we now see, it is hard to settle troubled affairs. But if all of us had the spirit we ought to have, some remedy might perhaps be found. Certainly we hand down a shameful example to posterity when we prefer to throw away all freedom rather than sting one man's spirit with some small offence. But he has a vehement nature and violent impulses. As if this vehemence does not exult all the more while everyone indulges it and grants it everything! If this example of tyranny already emerges in the first beginnings of the reborn Church, what will happen soon, once things have slid into worse? Let us then lament the calamity of the Church, and not merely swallow this grief in silence among ourselves; let us dare at last to utter a free groan. What if, by the Lord's permission, you have been driven into these straits, so that a fuller confession on this matter may at last be wrung from you? I freely confess that what you teach is most true, and I commend your prudence and moderation, in that you have so far striven with a gentle manner of teaching to call minds back from contention. But while you shun this place as if it were a rock, lest you incur the offence of certain people, you leave very many, who ask from you something more certain on which to rest, held in suspense and perplexed. It is, as I remember telling you once, not honourable enough for us to leave unsealed in ink even that doctrine which many saints have not hesitated to attest with their own blood. So perhaps God now wishes to open for you a way to this full and solid explanation of your mind, so that those doubters who depend on your authority, whom you know to be very many, may not cling to doubt forever. I say this not so much to urge you on as to console you. For unless I hoped that something good would come out of this turbulent upheaval, I would be worn down by a much more bitter grief. Yet let us await a peace of whatever kind the Lord wills to give, and meanwhile pursue our course with unbroken spirits. For your reply I owe you great thanks, and also for the uncommon kindness which Claudius tells me you showed him. What sort of friend you would be to me I can guess from the fact that you receive my people so kindly and courteously. I do not cease to give the greatest thanks to God, who has granted that our opinions agree on the main point of that question about which we were asked. For although there is a little difference in certain details, on the matter itself we agree very well. 28 June 1545.

units.la: CALVINVS MYCONIO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MYCONIUS.

units.la: NVnc instandi tempus est,ne frustra tantum laboris pro miseris fratribus exhauserimus. Et nunc opem ipsi nostram vel tacentes implorant, fi vnquam antehac. Rex enim, vt ex Germania intellexi,moderationem aliquam fe adhibituru simulat:iam enim profectum esse commissarium, qui de rebus eorum inquirat,Verum nihil inde leuationis expectandû.Com missionis,vt loquuntur,sibi infestissimi hostes erunt conscij.Nemo est qui mutire ausit pro veritate. Miseri fratres vel in sentinis nauium & subterraneis carcerum fossis vincti tenentur, vel fuga dispersi procul absunt, vel latent apud amicos. Rogandus ergo erit Rex,vt vinctos primùm dimittat,& omnes restituat in integrum : deinde commissarios mittat homines æquos & humanos:rabiosis istis cognitionem adimat. Tu igitur in hac rem totis neruis enitere. Crimé quo grauantur ne illis noceat,effice.
units.tr: Now is the time to press on, lest we have spent so much labour in vain on behalf of our wretched brothers. And now they implore our help, even in their silence, as never before. The king, as I have learned from Germany, pretends that he will show some moderation; for a commissioner has already set out to inquire into their affairs. But we should expect no relief from this. Those most bitter enemies will be aware of the commission, as they put it. No one dares to make a sound for the truth. The wretched brothers are held bound either in the bilges of ships or in the underground pits of prisons, or they are scattered in flight and far away, or they lie hidden among friends. The king must therefore be asked first to release the prisoners and restore everyone to his former state; then to send commissioners who are fair and humane, and to take the investigation away from those raging men. You, then, must strive with all your strength in this matter. See to it that the charge with which they are burdened does not harm them.

units.la: Est enim impudenter confictum: & suspicor in qua officina: Mirortantum habuerifidei nihili hominibus, quorum mendaciis aures vestrorum hominum occalescere iampridem debuerunt. Fingut allatum esse hunc à mercatoribus rumorem. Atqui nunc quam id hostes obtendere ausi sunt: quia facturi erant absque colore. Grynianus Regis legatus, qui perpetratae stragis auctor fuit sua perfidia, praetextu hoc non abutitur. Obsiste ergo quantum potes, ne falsis delationibus alienentur bonorum animi ab illis iuuandis. Vale, mi frater & amice honorande. Dominus te vnà cum symmystis conseruet, quos salutabis diligenter meo nomine. Collegae mei vos etiam reuerenter salutant. Geneuae XXIIII.Iulij. M. D. XLV.
units.tr: For it is shamelessly fabricated, and I suspect from what workshop. I am amazed that men's word counts for so little, when their lies should long ago have hardened your people's ears. Let it be pretended that this rumour was brought by merchants. But consider how the enemies have now dared to put it forward, since they were going to act without even a pretext. Grynaeus, the king's envoy, who was the author of the slaughter through his treachery, does not make use of this pretext. Therefore resist as much as you can, lest the minds of good men be turned away from helping them by false accusations. Farewell, my brother and honoured friend. May the Lord keep you together with your fellow initiates, whom you will greet diligently in my name. My colleagues also greet you respectfully. Geneva, 24 July 1545.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: ERgo tibi vtilis coeperat esse Collega, vt statim abs te discederet. Sed haec ingens erga eum Domini misericordia, & beneficium etiam in vos non paruum quod eum hinc ad se recipere noluit, nisi correctum: & prouidet ne quod vobis praeiudicium apud improbos afferret eius obstinatio. Si Tollanus succedet, aliquanto plus tibi erit ab eo leuamenti. Marcurtius paralysi correptus decumbit. Antonius Armentiacus nobis ablatus est summo bonorum omnium dolore. Ioannes quoque Camerius Biturix in eadem classe. Intellexi ex hoc fratre vos litiga re adhuc cum sacrilegis. Hic scortatores & huius notae homines nos exercent. Sudamus autem non magno profectu. De bonis Ecclesiae in verum vsum hic restituendis, ego despero. Concedunt quidè satis liberaliter: sed nihil efficitur. Iam saepius frustra magnos labores exhausi. Dico: denuntio. Hoc tantum consequor, ne videar silentio approbare. De fratre Ganspero expectabimus Dei voluntatem. Egeram tuo nomine gratias Bucero, & iterum stimulaueram, vt iusseras. Hoc praecipuum est, quod vita eius est in manu Domini: nec expositae erit libidini impiorum, donec ille volet. Si verus est rumor ille de nouis Delphini nuptiis, idem nobis breui imminet. Neque enim multum relaxationis hic nobis dabitur, si semel nefanda conspiratio coierit. Ego de vita mea nō sum solicitus: modò Ecclesiae suae Dominus prospiciat. De Brusuicensi audieram, sed iamdiu nihil ex Germania litterarum venit. Vale frater integerrime & mihi amicissime cum tota tua familia, quam meo nomine diligenter salutabis. Dominus vos istic seruet ac regat Spiritu suo. Salutant te omnes amici, Copus, Abel, Galasius, Nicolaus cum domo sua, vxor mea.
units.tr: So my colleague had begun to be useful to you, only for him to leave you at once. But this is a great mercy of the Lord towards him, and no small benefit to you as well, that he was unwilling to receive him back here unless he was first corrected. The Lord also takes care that his obstinacy does not bring any harm upon you among the wicked. If Tollanus succeeds him, you will have considerably more help from him. Marcurtius has been struck with paralysis and is bedridden. Antonius Armentiacus has been taken from us, to the great grief of all good people. Also John Camerius of Bourges is in the same condition. I have learned from this brother that you are still wrangling with the sacrilegious. Here, fornicators and men of that stamp trouble us. We sweat, but without much result. As for restoring the goods of the Church here to their true use, I despair. They do concede quite generously, but nothing is achieved. I have already often spent great labour in vain. I speak out; I give warning. This is all I gain: that I do not seem to approve by my silence. As for Brother Gaspard, we shall wait for the will of God. I have given thanks to Bucer in your name and have pressed him again, as you had asked. The chief thing is that his life is in the hand of the Lord, and it will not be exposed to the lust of the impious as long as he himself wishes. If that rumour about the new marriage of the Dauphin is true, the same danger hangs over us shortly. For we shall not be granted much respite here if that accursed conspiracy once comes together. As for my own life, I am not anxious, provided only that the Lord looks after his Church. I had heard about the man from Brusuicum, but for a long time no letters have come from Germany. Farewell, most upright brother and dearest friend, with all your household, whom you will greet diligently in my name. May the Lord keep and rule you there by his Spirit. All your friends greet you: Copus, Abel, Galasius, Nicolas with his household, and my wife.

units.la: Epist.65. Fratribus salutem plurimam. Geneuæ, v i. Nonas Octobr. M. D. X L V.
units.tr: Epist. 65. Greetings to the brothers. Geneva, the sixth day before the Nones of October, 1545.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: IOuis sub cœnam mihi ruæ ad Viretum literæ redditæ fuerãt: vt postridie cum fratribus posse m capere consilium, siid tibi placere intellexissem. Sed à me tantum & Vireto scribi volebas. Itaque nullam facere mentionem ausus sum. Cùm verò mihi oblatæ fuerunt tuæ posteriores, iam fratres discesserant. Itaque iam amissa est illa opportunitas. Sed quid profuisset me de tua voluntate in tempore fuisse admonitum? Ego enim consilium vos petere à nobis nequaquam puto, quo non indigetis, nec verisimile est, cupere vobis exponi quid de illa re sentiamus. Tenetis enim haud dubie, sed literas petitis, vt interpretor, quæ vobis adiumento sint ad vestros homines coarguendos. Speratis enim mehus fractum iri eorum contumaciam, si complures Ecclesias vobis suffragari viderint. Et certe vix vnquam hoc vitium, quocum vobis certamen nunc est, corrigetur, nisi Ecclesiarum consensu. Atque vtinam ad hanc sanctam conspirationem animum adiicerent, quos duces aliis esse oportet: sed vides vt res nostræ sint dissipatæ. Quod ad nos sp{s}ctat, libenter vobis morem geremus. Neque enim dubito pro Symmystis etiam spondere. At timendum est ne ridiculi simus vestris hominibus, ab illis exigendo quod nondum impetrauimus à nostris. Docebimus quis rectus sit vsus bonorum Ecclesiæ, & qui legitimi sint eorum œconomi, vt auctoritate nostra vrgeamus Neocomenses. Cur non potius exordium à nobis facimus? videte ergo ne dum iuuare vos studemus, magis obsimus causæ vestræ. Quod si tamen manes in sententia, præscribe quid vtile sentias, ego statim obsequar. Quanto plus ponderis ei fuerit in eo libello, quem adhuc Argentinæ cum essem, curaui imprimendum? Loquuntur enim illic Principes, quo quoque Euangelium amplexi sunt: promittunt restitutionem omnium quæ occuparunt, si quando ad piam aliquam concordiam ventum fuerit. Admonendi essent vestri vt principum exemplo, saltem ad id tempus, omnia sibi integra seruarent. Rogabis quidnam igitur cessem, si eadem hic cœno vitia, quæ vos istic excruciant, & tantum facessant negotij. Ego verò non celso palam in concionibus quoties opportunitas ira tulit, contestor Deum & homines, graue nobis imminere iudicium: in Senatu idem aliquoties egi: neque tamen hoc modo mihi defunctus videor, dum nihil me profecisse video. Verum sequor Ambrosium, qui doctrinam locum pastoris sibi reRinens, ita vt pro illis vindicandis paratus esset vitam opponere, agros tyrannidi Imperatoris Valentiniani sinebat. Sic enim suspicantur Magistratus nostri, de æmulatione esse certamen, quia ægrè seramus excusatum esse nobis de manibus quod illi sibi sumpserunt: nisi forte hoc simulant, quò fidem studio nostro derogent. Neque tamen ita vitanda est nobis suspicio, vt ad sacrilegia conniueamus. Tantum cogitare operæ pretium est, quousque contendere expediat: quanquam in præsentia longiorem disceptationem ingredi non est animus: ideoque finem faciam. Nostri omnes te salutant, præsertim Symmystæ, Nicolaus, frater, vxor, quæ ipsa tuis & familiæ tuæ precibus se commendatam esse cupit, nam adhuc cum morbo difficulter luctatur: sed hoc habemus solatij, quod pedem vnum videtur à sepulchro retraxisse, sed necdum vires colligit: & magnis doloribus infestatur. Vale optime frater & amice integerrime. Collegis tuis plurimam salutem. Geneuæ, xiii. Octobr. M. D. XLV.
units.tr: I received your letter to Viret at supper-time on the evening of the day before yesterday, so that I might be able to take counsel with the brothers the next day, had I understood that this pleased you. But you wished only that I and Viret should write, and so I did not dare to mention it. When your later letters were brought to me, the brothers had already left, and so that opportunity is now lost. But what would it have profited me to have been reminded in time of your wishes? For I do not think you seek counsel from us at all in a matter where you have no need of it, nor is it likely that you want us to set out what we think about that business. You undoubtedly hold the position yourselves, but you ask for letters, as I interpret it, which may serve as support for convicting your men. For you hope that their obstinacy will be broken more easily if they see several Churches giving you their backing. And indeed this vice with which you are now contending will hardly ever be corrected except by the agreement of the Churches. Would that those whom it behoves to be leaders for the others would apply their minds to this holy common cause! But you see how our affairs are scattered. As far as we are concerned, we shall gladly comply with you. Indeed I do not doubt that I can even promise this on behalf of my fellow-workers. But we must fear lest we become ridiculous to your men, demanding from them what we have not yet obtained from our own people. We shall teach what the proper use of the goods of the Church is, and who are the lawful stewards of them, so that we may press the people of Neuchâtel with our authority. Why do we not rather make a beginning with ourselves? See, then, that while you are eager to help, you do not rather harm your own cause. Yet if you remain of your opinion, prescribe what you think useful, and I shall obey at once. How much more weight would there be in that little book which I, while I was still at Strasbourg, took care to have printed? For there the princes speak, who have also embraced the Gospel: they promise the restitution of all that they have seized, if at any time some pious agreement is reached. Your people ought to be admonished, following the example of the princes, at least until that time, to keep everything intact for themselves. You will ask why, then, I am slow to act, if the same filthy vices that torment you there trouble us here and cause just as much trouble. But I do not keep silent openly in the sermons whenever opportunity has prompted me, calling God and men to witness that a grave judgement hangs over us. I have done the same several times in the Senate. Yet I do not seem to have discharged my duty in this way, since I see that I have accomplished nothing. But I follow Ambrose, who, holding the teaching office as his place, and being ready to lay down his life to defend those things, nevertheless allowed the fields to be given up to the tyranny of the Emperor Valentinian. For our magistrates suspect that this contest is one of rivalry, because we bear it with ill grace that what they have taken into their own hands has been excluded from our reach; unless perhaps they only pretend this, in order to undermine the credit of our zeal. Yet we must not so avoid suspicion as to connive at sacrilege. It is only worth considering how far it is expedient to press the matter; though at present I have no intention of entering on a longer dispute, and so I shall make an end. All our people salute you, especially my fellow-workers, Nicolas, the brother, and my wife, who herself wishes to be commended to your prayers and those of your household, for she is still struggling with difficulty against illness; but we have this consolation, that she seems to have drawn one foot back from the grave, though she does not yet gather her strength, and she is troubled by great pains. Farewell, best of brothers and most upright friend. Greet your colleagues most warmly. Geneva, 13 October 1545.

units.la: THEODORVS CAL.
units.tr: Theodorus to Calvin

units.la: SAlutem in Domino. Gratissimum mihi fuit, Caluine doctissime, quod per ciuem eúmque vt intellexi vicinum tuum me iusseris salutari. Etsi autem longe plus voluptatis attulissent literæ, tamen cum mihi de tuis occupationibus constet, facilè patior te id quod tibi commodius & facilius fuit, fecisse. Ego vocatus à Principibus ad colloquium Ratisbonæ, & additus Domino Philippo socius cum iam quasi in procinctu essem, ab articulorum morbo oppressus, domi mee decumbo: ac per alienam manum ad te scribo, vt tu quoque intelligas & amari te impensè à me, & voluntatem neutiquam deesse tibi gratificandi. Philippus quoque, propter periculum valetudinis domi se continuit, & profectus eius loco est D. Georgius Maior ac 27. Ianuarij victriusq; partis Theologi, qui ibi non magna frequentia sunt à præsidentibus Episcopo Aistetensi & Comite à Fuistenberg iunt co uocati, & recitatæ quædam sententiæ eis sunt Cæsaris nomine, quæ & forma & conditiones huius colloquij esse debeat. Cuiusmodi autem exfuerint nondum licuit rescisscere: coniicio autem plus habituras dubitationum & periculorum quàm ipsum colloquium: intelligimus enim hoc à Cæsare Pontifici promissum, vt de quibus non conueniat inter collocutores, concilium Tridentinum pronunciet. Ex nostra parte sunt Ratisponæ, M. Bucerus, Erhardus Schepphius, Ioannes Brentius, Martinus Frechtus, Ioannes Piftorius, D. Georgius Maior. De aduersariis vt inquirerem diligentius nondum libuit, nisi quod constat de auditore sordium Caesaris, de Maluendo, Pelargo, Cochlaeo. Principes nostri adhuc sunt Francfordiae ac strenue hoc agunt, ut foedus suum & confirment & propagét: hoc autem dignum laude factum est, quod omnes qui per totam Germaniam Euangelium Christi amplexi sunt, pollicentur Episcopo Coloniensi auxilium, fi propter religionem eum oppugnet Caesar. De Tridentino concilio puto te omnia nostr. Bene vale in Domino, & quod peramanter rogo, rescribe quoque. Hoc pene excideret. Legi conciunculam tuam de Sacramento Coenae, ac probo quod panem & vinum sic signa vocas, ut signata re vera adsint: vtinam possint à te in eam sententiam deduci, qui nuda tantum signa relinquunt. Iterum vale. Datae Noribergae postridie Purificationis. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: Greetings in the Lord. It was very welcome to me, most learned Calvin, that you had me greeted through a citizen and, as I understand, a neighbour of yours. Although a letter would have given me far more pleasure, since I know how busy you are I am content that you did what was more convenient and easier for you. I have been summoned by the princes to the colloquy at Regensburg and attached to Master Philip as his companion. When I was already more or less ready to set out, I was overcome by a gout attack and am now lying ill at home. I am writing to you through another's hand so that you may know both that I hold you in great affection and that I lack no willingness to do you a kindness. Philip also stayed at home because of the danger to his health, and in his place went Dr. Georg Major. On 27 January theologians of the victorious party, who are not many in number there, were summoned by the presiding Bishop of Eichstätt and Count von Fürstenberg, and certain articles were read to them in the Emperor's name, setting out what the form and conditions of this colloquy should be. What these articles were I have not yet been able to learn. I suspect, however, that they will raise more doubts and dangers than the colloquy itself, for we understand that the Emperor has promised the Pope that whatever the participants do not agree upon will be decided by the Council of Trent. On our side at Regensburg are Master Bucer, Erhard Schepp, Johannes Brenz, Martin Frecht, Johannes Pistorius and Dr. Georg Major. I have not yet cared to inquire more carefully about our opponents, except that it is certain about the auditor of the Emperor's ... , Malvenda, Pelargus and Cochlaeus. Our princes are still at Frankfurt and are working energetically to both confirm and extend their alliance. It is commendable that all those throughout Germany who have embraced the Gospel of Christ have promised the Bishop of Cologne aid, should the Emperor attack him on account of religion. As for the Council of Trent, I think you know everything about it. Farewell in the Lord, and, as I earnestly ask, please write back. I nearly forgot this: I have read your little sermon on the Lord's Supper, and I approve of your calling the bread and wine signs in such a way that the things signified are truly present. I wish that those who leave only bare signs could be brought by you to that opinion. Farewell again. Given at Nuremberg, the day after the Purification, 1546.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel

units.la: PArum abfuit quin ludi nostri versi fuerint in tragoediam. Cum meam sententiam rogasset Senatus, negaui me respon sui um nisi de communi fratrum consilio. Auditis fratribus, respondi multas ob causas nobis non videri expedire ut agerétur, & simul causas exposui: nos tamen nolle contendere, si Senatus contenderet. Cum instaret dies, N. pro concione iterum inuectus est in actores (semel enim id fecerat) verum haec fecunda inuectiua tam fuit vehemens, ut protinus concursus ad me factus fuerit, magni clamores, minae, & quid non? Quod nisi interperiem quorundam grauiter comp scuissem, manu pugnaturi erant. Conatus sum in fecunda concione mollire iratos animos, moderatione adhibita, nam imprudentem fuisse iudicabam qui extra tempus tali declamatione vsus foret. Verum magis displiceabat excellus, nullo enim modo approbare poteram quod dixerat. Ille verum esse tuebatur, ego constanter negabam. Erant ex fratribus qui hominis obstinationem fouebant. Circiter nonam vespertinam mihi renunciatum est centum autcirciter postridie conuenturos in curiam. Extemplo fratres vocaui: decreuimus eundum esse cum N. Vix illi fuit permissum ut mecum egrederetur: deduco illum, alios accersi interea iubeo. Accusatores renuunt nobis praesentibus se verbum facturos, sibi enim nihil esse mecum negocij, nisi quod reuerenter de me sentirent, ideoque nollet mecum litigare. Ego acriter instito communem esse causam, donec appareat, N. in officio peccasse: iubemur vtrinque secedere. Ab aduersa parte seditiosi clamores minantur se fuisse N. occisuros, nisi me reuerit fuisset. Ad cohibendum tumultum detentus fuit in Curia, sed honorifice. Secundo die omnes turbas Domini auspiciis composuimus. Abel enim gratia valebat, ego auctoritate apud actores. Senatus vero erat nostcr. Hoc tantum male me habebat quod non esset fortior & animosior: nam pro more suo nimium timide se gessit. hic finis. Nunc ludi aguntur: adest Virtus spectator, qui ex composito iterum rediit, et furiosum nostrum ad sanam mentem reducat. De fratribus suis nihil prorsus audio. Est apud vos Helias Lemouicus cognomine, natione Rupellensis, qui me tertiis iam literis rogavit, ut vobis testarer quid de superiore eius vita intellexerim. Pij qui illinc veniunt, affirmant probum fuisse virum & honestae vitae, atque etiam coelibem fuisse, cum illinc migraret ad nos. Itaque non est quod haec suspicio impedimentum coniugio afferat. Excusabis quod illi non respondevrim: atque etiam quod tibi adeo breviter perstrinxerim, quod longiorem forte orationem postulabat. Vale frater in Domino charissime & integerrime amice. Saluta diligenter omnes fratres. Nemo hic te vel illos salutat, quoniam nemo scripturum me sciebat, praeter Nicolaum fratris socerum qui interuenit. Dominus vobis perpetuo adsit ac sanctis vestris laboribus benedicat. Geneuae 1111. nonas Iulij. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: We came close to our games being turned into a tragedy. When the Council asked for my opinion, I replied that I would answer only with the common consent of the brothers. After hearing the brothers, I replied that for many reasons it did not seem to us expedient that the matter be pursued, and at the same time I set out the reasons; yet we did not wish to contend, if the Council chose to contend. As the day approached, N. again inveighed against the actors in the sermon (for he had done so once before), but this second invective was so vehement that a crowd immediately gathered around me, with great shouting, threats, and everything else. Had I not, with considerable effort, restrained some of them, they would have come to blows. In the second sermon I tried to soften the angry spirits by exercising moderation, for I judged that he had been imprudent to use such a declamation out of season. Yet the man's obstinacy displeased me more, for I could in no way approve what he had said. He maintained that it was true; I steadfastly denied it. Some of the brothers were encouraging the man's stubbornness. About nine in the evening I was informed that about a hundred men, or thereabouts, would gather the next day in the Council chamber. At once I summoned the brothers, and we decided that we must go with N. He was scarcely permitted to leave with me. I took him away and ordered others to be summoned in the meantime. The accusers refused to speak in our presence, saying that they had no quarrel with me except that they thought of me with respect, and so they did not wish to dispute with me. I insisted sharply that this was a common cause, until it should become clear that N. had sinned in his office; we were ordered to withdraw from each other. From the opposing side, seditious shouts threatened that they would have killed N. had I not returned. To check the tumult he was detained in the Council chamber, but with honour. On the second day we settled all the disturbances under the Lord's auspices: Abel, indeed, had influence through his favour, and I had authority with the actors. The Council was truly on our side. This alone troubled me, that it was not braver and more spirited, for in its usual way it acted too timidly. That is the end of it. Now the games are being performed; Virtue is present as spectator, who, by arrangement, has returned again to bring our madman back to sound mind. I hear absolutely nothing about his brothers. Among you there is Élie of Limoges by surname, a native of La Rochelle, who has asked me in three letters now to attest to you what I have learned of his earlier life. Pious people who come from there affirm that he was an upright man of honest life, and that he was also unmarried when he migrated to us. So there is no reason for this suspicion to stand in the way of his marriage. You will excuse my not having answered him, and also my having touched on your matter so briefly, when perhaps it called for a longer letter. Farewell, brother most dear in the Lord and most upright friend. Greet all the brothers diligently. No one here greets you or them, since no one knew I was writing, except Nicolas, the brother-in-law of the brother, who happened to come in. May the Lord be with you always and bless your holy labours. Geneva, 4 July 1546.

units.la: CAL. VIRETO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET.

units.la: NVper spurius ex domo Fabrorum, cui nomen est ab Orba, uxorem duxit spuriam cuiusdam Nantuatis. Triginta aut circiter prodierunt obuiam sponsae. Vides quam ridicula fuerit pompa, nosti enim maritum hominem nihili & nullius honoris: & tamen eius causa strepitus audiebatur tota urbe valde intempestiuus. Egressi sunt cum haberetur prima concio: inter secundam concionem sunt reuersi. Quid secutum est? Dominus stercore asperso totam illam pompam. Abel coniugio benedicebat. Cum stipularetur fidem coniugalem, nebulo alibi habebat animum: iussus ut saltem annueret, caput concussit. Magna populi obmurmuratio. Abel perrexit, cum deberet actionem abrumpere. Verum se nequaquam animaduertisse ierat. Quod ridebat noster, seuere punitum fuit a Senatu: nam cotemptor ille per dies octo in arcum carcerem inclusus hodie coram Ecclesia culpam deprecatus est. Patruus uxoris Ioannes nunc est in carcere. Seuere prohibitum insulario nequid praeter aquam & panem illi det: neque exiturus est nisi cum publica ignominia: nam cum Deum palam abnegaret, atque a fratre nostro Raymundo reprehenderetur, repetita execrabili Dei iuratione, dixit sibi dolere quod non abrepta barba eum in terram illisum pedibus calcasset. Proserpina etiam pridie quam sponsam exciperent tam honorifice, socrum ita vulnerauit, ut largus illi sanguis ex occipitio flueret, facies autem laceratione foeda esset, torum caput luto & puluere conspersum. Nofti qualis fit tempe-ries vetulæ: audiebatur toto vico inclamans Dei & hominum fidem. Proferpinam ad Confi-lorium vocauimus, sed ad sororem euolauerat. Proximè iterum vocabitur. Quid facerem? filetione redimerem vnius hominis gratiam, vt à tota Ecclesia proditionis damnarer: dabo tamen operam, ne iure excandescat. Penthesilea certè breui nobis reprimenda erit: nam malas omnes causas suscipit & furiose def-nit: deniq; ue fronte meretricia agit omnia & loquitur. Vale frater & amice integerrime. Saluta Symmyftas omnes diligenter. X i. Augusti. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: Recently a bastard from the house of the Smiths, called from Orbe, married the bastard daughter of some Nantuatan. About thirty people went out to meet the bride. You see how ridiculous the procession was; you know the husband is a man of no standing and no reputation, and yet on his account a very ill-timed uproar was heard throughout the whole city. They went out while the first sermon was being preached and came back during the second. What followed? The Lord splashed that whole procession with dung. Abel was blessing the marriage. When the marriage vows were being exchanged, the scoundrel had his mind elsewhere; ordered at least to give his assent, he shook his head. Great muttering from the people. Abel went on, when he ought to have broken off the action. But he claimed he had not noticed at all. Because our man laughed, the Senate punished him severely: that contemner was shut up for eight days in the Arc prison, and today before the Church he asked pardon for his fault. The wife's uncle John is now in prison. The jailer was strictly forbidden to give him anything but water and bread, and he will not come out except with public disgrace. For when he openly renounced God and was rebuked by our brother Raymond, he repeated his execrable oath against God, and said he was sorry he had not seized his beard, thrown him to the ground and trampled him under foot. Also Proserpina, the day before they received the bride so honourably, wounded her mother-in-law so that a copious stream of blood flowed from the back of her head, and her face was disfigured by the laceration; her head was smeared with mud and dust. You know what sort of temper the old woman has: she was heard all over the neighbourhood crying out for the faith of God and men. We summoned Proserpina to the Consistory, but she had flown off to her sister. She will be summoned again soon. What am I to do? I would buy the favour of one man by silence, only to be condemned as a traitor by the whole Church. Still, I will take care that she does not become justly angry. Penthesilea, too, must soon be restrained by us, for she takes up every bad cause and defends it madly; in short, she does and says everything with a whore's brazenness. Farewell, brother and most upright friend. Greet all the fellow-members diligently. 11 August 1546.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: TAmetsi literæ non omni ex parte mihi placebant, q; vere-bar ne asperitate nimia stomachum tam delicatum offen-derent: reddendas tamen curaui, sed ita vt nesciret à me fuisse visas. Hic enim quasi abs te sibi commissas in eius domum pertulit. Si tonabit suo more, tandem eius fulmina euanescent in crepitus. Ego me illi non offero tantum sed propemodum obtrudo: duntaxat modo adhibeo, vt meminerim quem locum teneam: n q; id mea causa, sed quia homo adulationibus assuetus modestia mea abuteretur in Christi ludibrium. Despero itaque, nisi Dominus remedium adhibeat. Vxor eius prodigiosa est furia. Vidua N adeo procaciter lasciuit, vt dicas esse iuuenculà. Deinde male sibi conscia verbis omnibus, quæ pro concione prose-runtur, incitatur ad rabiem domi quicquid veneni habet, in nos euomit: quanquam erga te mire fe præbuit beneuolam. Duos enim n potestuos, cum periculose ægrotarent in fe recepit, neq; aliter tractat quam filios. Hoc officium dignum est liberali gratiarum actione, quam non omittes, vbi fe nuncius obtulerit. Nobis omnibus adeo est infesta, vt credam Cæsarem ipsum nihilo magis esse inimicum. Etiamen si causa dicenda fit, fateor me nescire, nisi quod impudenter criminum omnium defensionem suscipit. Narrabo hic iocosam historiam. Nuper huc venit Frumetivxor. Per omnes tabernas per omnia fere compita declamitauit aduersus longas vestes. Cum id mihi fuisse indicatum sciret, excusauit se ridendo dixisse, aut nos indecenter vestiri cum magno Ecclesiæ offendiculo: aut vos falsum docuisse, cum diceretis à longis vestibus dignoscì posse falsos prophetas. Cùm tam puridam calumniam refutarem, coepit etiam Spiritui sancto adscribere, quod vobis impegerat. Quid sibi vult, dicebat locus ille Euangelij? Venient ad vos in longis vestibus. Respondi me nescire, vbi esset illa sententia, nisi forte inueniretur in Euangelio Manichæorum. Sic enim extat locus Lucæ. 20. 45. Cauete à Scribis qui volunt ambulare in stolis. Non autem venient ad vos,&c. quod ex Matth.7. interpolauerat.Cum sentiret se vrgeri,conquę sta est de nostra tyrannide,quòd non cuiuis liceret quiduis garrire. Trastaui mulierem vt debui. Statim ad Michaelis viduam perrexit,quæ eam hospitio recepit, non mensæ tantum sed lecti sociam,quia ministris maledicebat. Hæc vulnera, quod insanabilia mihi videntur,intacta relinquo, donec manum Dominus admoueat. Cœnam proximo die dominico sumus celebraturi. Hinc cogita quibus angustiis nunc constringar.Vtinam me absente posset celebrari, hac conditione,vt ad vos vsque vel manibus reptarem. Fratribus tuis vtinam illud Terentianum veniret in mentem,Perdere in tempore lucrum facere est.Admonui,sed non festinant quantu vellem. Paulisper tamen adhuc hanc moram quanuis nobis ingratam, sustineant. Vale frater & amice integerrime.Saluta meo nomine diligenter fratres omnes,fami liam,& pios ciuss. Dominus te conseruet ac semper regat suo Spiritu,Amen.Genevæ,Calend.Septemb. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: Although your letter did not altogether please me, since I feared that its excessive harshness would offend a stomach so delicate, I nonetheless saw to its delivery, but so that he would not know I had read it. He brought it to his house as if it had been entrusted to him by you. If he thunders in his usual way, his thunderbolts will at last dissolve into crackling. I do not merely offer myself to him, I almost force myself on him; I only take care to remember what position I hold, not for my own sake, but because a man accustomed to flattery would abuse my modesty to mock Christ. I despair, therefore, unless the Lord applies a remedy. His wife is a prodigious fury. The widow N. has played the wanton so shamelessly that you would call her a young girl. Then, being conscious of guilt, she is inflamed to rage at home by every word that is spoken from the pulpit, and vomits out at us whatever poison she has; although toward you she has shown a remarkably kind disposition. For when two of her nephews were gravely ill, she took them into her care and treats them no differently than her own sons. This service deserves a generous expression of thanks, which you must not neglect when an opportunity for a messenger presents itself. She is so hostile to all of us that I believe Caesar himself is no more hostile. As for a cause to be pleaded, I confess I do not know, except that she shamelessly undertakes the defence of all crimes. I will relate a comic story here. Recently Frumet's wife came here. Through all the shops and almost every crossroad she declaimed against long robes. When she learned that this had been reported to me, she excused herself by saying, laughingly, that she had said either that we dress indecently, to the great scandal of the Church, or that you taught falsely, since you said false prophets could be distinguished by their long robes. When I refuted such a filthy calumny, she began also to ascribe to the Holy Spirit what she had thrust upon you. "What," she said, "does that passage of the Gospel mean? 'They will come to you in long robes'?" I replied that I did not know where that saying was, unless perhaps it could be found in the Gospel of the Manichaeans. For the passage of Luke stands thus: "Beware of the scribes, who want to walk about in long robes" (Luke 20:46). "But they will not come to you," etc., which she had interpolated from Matthew 7. When she felt herself pressed, she complained of our tyranny, because it was not permitted to everyone to chatter about whatever he liked. I treated the woman as I ought. Immediately she went to the widow of Michael, who received her into her house, making her a companion not only at table but also in bed, because she was cursing the ministers. These wounds, which seem incurable to me, I leave untouched until the Lord applies his hand. We are to celebrate the Lord's Supper next Sunday. Think, then, what straits I am now confined in. Would that it could be celebrated in my absence, on condition that I could crawl to you even on my hands! Would that your brothers might remember that Terentian saying, "To lose time is to make gain"! I have admonished them, but they do not hurry as much as I would like. Yet let them endure this delay, however unwelcome to us, for a little while longer. Farewell, brother and most upright friend. Greet diligently all the brothers, your household, and the pious citizens on my behalf. May the Lord keep you and always rule you by his Spirit. Amen. Geneva, Kalends of September 1546.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: ADiscessu vestro choreæ nobis plus exhibuerūt negocij,quâ putaueram.Omnes ij qui interfuerant vocati ad Consistoriū duobus exceptis Corneo & Perrino, impudêter Deo & nobis mentiti sunt.Excandui,vt rei indignitas postulabat & gra uiter in illum Dei contemptum inuectus sum , q. pro nihilo ducerent sanctas obtestationes, quibus vsi fueramus ludibrio habere.Perstit rūt in sua contumacia. Egocūm res mihi comperta esset,nihil aliud poteram quàm Deũ testari pœnas tantę perfidię daturos:simul tamen denunciaui,me vel proprię vitę dispendio factūrū,vt veritas patefiret,ne quid se lucrifcisse mentiendo putarent. Francisca etiam Perrini grauiter conuiciata est nobis q. adeo infesti essemus fabris.Respondi vt visum fuit atq; vt merebatur. Rogaui nūquid sacrosanctæ esset domus,nunquid legibus soluta?Patrem iam vnius adulterij conuistū tenebamus:alteri ius probatio propè ad manū erat:de tertio magnus erat rumor: frater senatum & nos palam contemplerat ac deriserat : tandè adieci fabricandam illis esse nouā vrbem, in qua seorsum viuerēt, nisi vellent nobis hîc sub iugo Christi continerī:quādiu Geneuę essent,eos frustra nihil ne legibus parerent. Nam si tot essent diademata in domo fabrorū, quos sunt furiosa capita, id non fore impedimento quin Dominus foret superior. Maritus Lugdunū interea concesserat,sperans rem tacitè sepultum iri. ensui,vt iu reiurādo ad veri confessionē adigērētur. Corneus illos monui, fe nequaquam passurum vt peierarent.Non modò confessi sunt quod volebamus sed se eo die saltasse apud Balthazaris viduam. Omnes in carcerem coniecti,Syndicus insigne moderationis exemplum fuit. Nam in se & totum gregem seuerius est concionatus,quàm vt oportueritcum eo multa verba facere.Admonitus tamen grauiter in Consistorio fuit, loco suo deiectus,donec pœnitentiæ testimonium edidisset. Perrinum Lugduno reuersum aiunt:quicquid agat,pœnam non effugiet.Henrichus abdicatus fuit nobis consentientibus: illic altercatio incidit non illepida. Confessus fuerat verum esse quicquid à testibus scriptum fuerat. Interim confugiebat ad illud præsidium, Aduersus præsbyterum accusationem ne admittas, nisi sub duobus aut tribus testibus. Rogaui,cuiùsnam esset sententia hæc. Ex ore tuo te iudico seruę nequam. Iam enim causam in testium fide non consistere, sed in eius confessione. Cum testes adhuc repudiaret, dilemmate institi. Aut veram esse eius confessionem,aut falsam:si vera esset, nihil amplius hæsitandum esse: sin falsa, cum teneri reum periurij quòd iuratus aliter quàm res habebat,dixisset.Eousquequeprorupit,vt diceret se falso & nequiter locutum esse.Cùm iniquum esse diceret ab eo se premi,qui deberet eum defendere, rogaui quo iure illi astrictus essem ad malam causam tuendam, nunquàm enim meiurasse in factionem Francifcanam. Multa homini vltro citróque dicta fuerunt , sed ita vt probro ac odio omnium plenus diceretur.Abdicatus ministerio simul retrusus fuit in carcerem,vnde tamen triduo post fuit liberatus.Illic stte nuus fuit saltationum patronus: vtquoad potuit exacerbarit in me eorum odia, qui iam ante plus fariserant alienati. Verùm quicquid per eius similes moliatur Satan: exemplum valde proderit.Duo enim iam vulgò dicuntur,nullam spem esse impuni tatis cùm primariis non parcatur,& me nihilo magis amicis quàm alienis fauere. Perrinus cum vxore fremit in carcere: vidua prorsus insanit,alij pudore confusi silent.Diazius Hispanus quem apud Gallasium hic vidisti, Virete, & qui Neocomo Germaniam proficiscens transierat cum duobus Senarclenis,crudelissimè fuit interfectus:cùm Cæsar appropinquare diceretur,Neoburgum se contulerat, quod oppidum est sub ditione Othonis Henrici ducis.Indeadme scripserat,13.Martij. Fratrem habebat Romæ nomine Alphonsum,qui data opera illuc venit, vt pium virum tolleret è medio.Collocuti sunt aliquot diebus. Cùm Ioânes nihil se proficere intelligeret,Alphonsum reliquit.Hic simulans sibi aliquid excidisse,famulum mittit qui fratrem reuocet, ac domi interficiat.Subsecutus est domum vsque:de cæde perpetrata fidem non habuit famulo , donec cadauer spectasset ipse. Tum equis celeribus in comitatum Tirolensem se proripuit.
units.tr: Since your departure the dances have given us more trouble than I had expected. All who had been present, except two, Corneille and Perrin, were summoned to the Consistory and shamelessly lied to God and to us. I was indignant, as the enormity of the matter demanded, and I spoke sharply against this contempt of God, because they treated as a joke the holy appeals we had made to them. They persisted in their obstinacy. Once the facts had been established for me, I could do nothing but call God to witness that they would pay the penalty for such treachery. At the same time I declared that I would, even at the cost of my own life, see that the truth was brought out, so that they would not think they had gained anything by lying. Francisca, Perrin's wife, also heaped abuse on us, saying that we were so hostile to the craftsmen. I answered as seemed fitting and as she deserved. I asked whether the house was perhaps sacrosanct, perhaps exempt from the laws. We already had the husband convicted of one adultery; for another, the proof was almost in hand; about a third there was great rumour; and the brother had openly looked down on and mocked the Council and us. Finally I added that a new city would have to be built for them, where they could live apart, unless they chose to be held here under Christ's yoke; as long as they were in Geneva, they would not obey the laws in vain. For however many furious heads there are in the house of the craftsmen, this would not hinder the Lord from being superior. Meanwhile the husband had withdrawn to Lyons, hoping the matter would be quietly buried. I urged that they be bound by oath to confess the truth. I warned Corneille that I would in no way allow them to commit perjury. Not only did they confess what we wanted, but they also admitted that they had danced that day at the widow Balthazar's house. All were thrown into prison. The Syndic was a notable example of moderation, for he preached more severely against himself and the whole flock than there was any need to say much to him. Nevertheless he was sharply admonished in the Consistory and removed from his post until he gave a sign of repentance. They say that Perrin, now back in Lyons, will not escape punishment whatever he does. Henri was dismissed with our consent, and there an altercation arose that was not without wit. He had confessed that whatever the witnesses had written was true. Meanwhile he took refuge in that defence: "Do not admit an accusation against an elder unless it is supported by two or three witnesses." I asked whose opinion this was. "I judge you, worthless slave, from your own mouth," I said, "for the case no longer rests on the trustworthiness of witnesses but on his confession." While he still rejected the witnesses, I pressed him with a dilemma: either his confession was true or it was false. If true, nothing more was to be doubted; if false, he was held guilty of perjury, since under oath he had said otherwise than the facts were. At last he burst out so far as to say that he had spoken falsely and wickedly. When he complained that it was unfair for him to be pressed by one who ought to defend him, I asked by what right I was bound to him to defend a bad cause, since I had never sworn allegiance to the Franciscan faction. Much was said on both sides, but in such a way that he was described as full of disgrace and hated by all. Deprived of the ministry, he was at the same time thrown into prison, from which, however, he was freed three days later. There he became the patron of the dances, and so far as he could he stirred up their hatred against me, among those who had already been alienated before. But whatever Satan contrives through men like him, the example will be of great use. For two things are now commonly said: that there is no hope of impunity, since the leading men are not spared, and that I favour my friends no more than strangers. Perrin frets in prison with his wife; the widow is quite mad; others, confused with shame, keep silent. Diazius the Spaniard, whom you saw here at Gallasius's, and who had passed through Neuchâtel on his way to Germany with the two Senarclenses, was most cruelly murdered. When the Emperor was said to be approaching, he had betaken himself to Neuburg, a town under the rule of Duke Otho Henry. From there he wrote to me on 13 March. He had a brother in Rome named Alphonsus, who came there on purpose to remove the pious man from the midst. They talked for several days. When Joannes understood that he was getting nowhere, Alphonsus left him. Pretending that something had slipped his mind, Alphonsus sent a servant to recall his brother and kill him at home. The servant followed him right to the house. Alphonsus would not believe the servant about the killing until he had seen the corpse himself. Then he hurried away on swift horses into the Tyrolese county.

units.la: Dux Otho praefectum palatij misit, qui eum ad supplicium postularet. Nisi Ferdinandus humana omnia diuinaque miscere volet, necesse est tam indignum & abominabile facinus vindicet. Nam praefectus in carcerem se vnâ dedit. Valete fratres charissimi. Dominus Iesus vos semper tueatur. Salutate amicos omnes. Tu Farelle plurimam salutem dices ciuium magistris. Vtinam aliquando istud adrepere quoquomodo liceat. Nostri omnes vos salutant. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: Duke Otho sent the prefect of his palace to demand him for punishment. Unless Ferdinand wishes to confound all things human and divine, he must avenge so unworthy and abominable a deed. For the prefect himself gave himself up into prison along with him. Farewell, dearest brothers. May the Lord Jesus always keep you. Greet all our friends. You, Farel, will give my warmest greetings to the magistrates of the citizens. Would that at some time it might somehow be possible to creep in there. All of ours greet you. M.D.XLVI.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO.
units.tr: BUCER TO CALVIN.

units.la: Mihi vero valde probatur optime & colende atque charissime Caluine, quòd fratres inuisis. Nosti enim quàm graviter deplorem, istud charitatis & pietatis officium, vt fratres & Symmystae sese inuicem inuiserent, monerent, consolarentur, adeò hoc tempore nostro negligi, imò etiam à plerisque damnari. Quanto enim plus piae & salutaris consensionis & mutuae instaurationis retineri inter nos poterat, si libuisset frequentius conuenire, & in Domino inter nos omnia communicare. Dominus tibi adsit, vt quod piè instituisti, sit etiam fratribus suorum. Multa est lentitudo vitae Christi in membris eius, magnamque ipse in illis saepe infirmitatem sustinet. Quòd initio belli tam multi, & cum his etiam gens vestra, finxerunt se credere bellum hoc non esse motum religioni, prodiderúntque adeò fratres & socios, & quod nunc gesto bello, vt geri potuit, à geretibus sine aufspicio Domini quisque pro se & nescio quam pacem contra iurisiurandi religionem petit & accipit, quidam etiam se hostes deinde profitentur sociorum, hinc regni Christi apud nos (quid dicâ intelligis) quid dici res ipsa ferat, neglectus. Quantum putas dedisse causam quòd communio Christi, & vitae ac spiritus eius mutua subministratio inter alios plane rescissa & prohibita, inter alios ignorata & neglecta, inter nullos, vt oportuit, excitata & agitata fuit? Modò hic peranxiè laboratur, deliberando quid nos facere Dominus velit. Offerunt quidam spem pacis, quae libertatem & religionem nobis relinquat salvam, sed quam pacem defertis sociis amplecti oporteat. Socij vero in superiori Germania omnes iam defecerunt à nobis, praeter Constantiam: quanquam nunc quidam etiam de Augusta affirmant nondum esse deditam. Horrent itaque omnes corda tiones admittere, quo vel violetur religio societatis iurata, vel circumscribatur vllo modo libertas seruiendi Deo. Horrent etiam humiliationem refugere, quam infert Dominus & intulit toti prope Germaniae dum etiam non vident iustam in populo poenitentiam. Ora Dominum vt nostris det spiritum consulj, k.j. quo id statuant quod probet ipse & salutare velit facere Ecclesiæ. Optarim cuique potestati, quam Dominus imposuerit, prolixè deferri quę oporteat, tantum ne quid detrahatur Deo. Cùm antea fœdere nostro vigente & multis formidabili, pax solida religioni obtineri non potuit, haud fine causa metuunt multi grauem religionis circumscriptionem subsequuturam, fœdere dissoluto, & tam fractis & humiliatis sociis: sed ita frangi humiliariq; meruimus. Orandus igitur Dominus, ut hoc firmius ipsius nitamur brachio, quibus adeo concidit brachium carnis. In Comitiis Augustanis anno ɔo. nullū erat fœdus, & liberè tum confitebantur multi, & condemnationem grauissimam fortiter excipiebant. Nouit Dominus qui sunt eius. Initia multorum tetra sunt, ita aperta blasphemia & pietatis charitatisque abiuratio admiscetur: paucorum est certa fides, & eò res recidit. Cùm venerit Filius hominis, putas inuenturum fidem in terris? Hoc verò magis orandus Dominus, quò nos conseruet in solida & constante confessione ac prædicatione Euangelij sui, ac donet vitā quoque illud exornare aliquanto quàm fecimus plerique hactenus studiosius. Sed quis nostrum non quotidie ob hanc remissionem disciplinæ exrruciatur, quod fratres & Collegæ primarij adeo nullam admittunt disciplinæ, non dico seueritatem, necessariam tamen mediocritatem, ut in Papatu factum est? ita plerique hominibus prospectum volunt, nó Ecclesiis: & Ecclesiarum damnis auertere damna impiorum Collegarum putant humanum. Cùm etiam tot malis non desinut patroni, propter Ecclesiam noluunt in offensionem incurrere potentum & gratiosorum hominum. Vale in Domino Iesu cum sanctissimo collegio Farello & Vireto, quibus quæ scribo opto esse communia. XVIII. Martij. M. D. XLVII.
units.tr: I entirely approve, most excellent, honoured and dearest Calvin, that you are visiting the brethren. You know how deeply I lament that this duty of love and piety, that fellow-brethren and colleagues should visit, admonish and console one another, is so neglected in our time, and indeed condemned by many. How much more of that holy and wholesome agreement and mutual renewal could we have kept among ourselves, if we had been willing to meet more often and share everything with one another in the Lord! May the Lord be with you, so that what you have piously undertaken may also be of service to his brethren. The life of Christ in his members is very sluggish, and he himself often bears great weakness in them. At the beginning of the war, many, and among them your nation too, pretended to believe that this war had not been stirred up over religion. They thus betrayed their brethren and allies. And now that the war is being waged, as it could be waged, by those waging it without the auspices of the Lord, each man seeks for himself, and accepts, some peace or other against the sanctity of the oath, in violation of the faith they swore. Some even now declare themselves enemies of their allies. Hence, here among us, the kingdom of Christ (you understand what I mean, and what the matter itself compels one to say) is neglected. How much, do you think, has contributed to this: that the communion of Christ, and the mutual supplying of his life and Spirit, has been utterly cut off and forbidden between some, ignored and neglected among others, and among none has been stirred up and pursued as it ought to be? Right now people are labouring anxiously here, deliberating what the Lord wills us to do. Some offer the hope of a peace that would leave us our liberty and religion safe, but it is unclear how one ought to embrace such a peace while abandoning one's allies. In upper Germany, all the allies have already defected from us, except Constance, although some now affirm that even Augsburg has not yet surrendered. Hence everyone shrinks from admitting any terms by which either the religion of the sworn alliance would be violated or the liberty of serving God would be curtailed in any way. They also shrink from avoiding the humiliation which the Lord inflicts, and has inflicted on almost all of Germany, since they do not yet see a just repentance among the people. Pray the Lord to give our people a spirit of counsel, so that they may decide what pleases him and what he wills to make salutary for the Church. I would wish that whatever is fitting be fully laid before each authority that the Lord has set over us, provided nothing is taken away from God. Since before, while our league was in force and formidable to many, a solid peace could not be secured for religion, many fear, not without reason, that a grievous curtailment of religion will follow, now that the league is dissolved and the allies so broken and humbled. But we have deserved to be broken and humbled in this way. The Lord must therefore be entreated that we may lean more firmly on his arm, since by it the arm of flesh has so utterly fallen. At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 there was no alliance, and many then confessed freely and bravely endured the most grievous condemnation. The Lord knows who are his. The beginnings of many are foul, since open blasphemy and the renunciation of piety and love are mixed in. Sure faith belongs to a few, and it comes down to that. When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth? Yet the Lord must be entreated all the more that he would preserve us in a firm and constant confession and proclamation of his gospel, and grant that we also adorn our life with more zeal than most of us have so far shown. But which of us is not tormented every day by this slackness of discipline, that the brethren and our chief colleagues admit so little discipline, I do not say severity, but at least the necessary moderation, as happened under the Papacy? So most men want provision made for themselves, not for the Churches, and they think it is humane to turn aside the losses of the Churches by the losses of impious colleagues. Since the patrons also do not cease to be troubled by so many evils, for the sake of the Church they are unwilling to incur the displeasure of powerful and influential men. Farewell in the Lord Jesus, with the most holy college of Farel and Viret, to whom I wish that what I write be common property. 18 March 1547.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS VIRETO S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Viret, greetings

units.la: DE aduentu ad nostuo ego dubius sum consilij. N. quàtùm audio, in exponèda tibi necessitate modum excessit. Quanquam non solus ipse in hac re peccat. Adeo pueri iunt ple rique, ut ridicula capitis concussione terrentur, dum vnus homo nihili suam insaniam prodit. Ego non meam causam, sed publicam tueor: quæ me absente acta est. Si desistam, totum Cœ-sistorium ruat, necesse est. Quinetiam ita se gerunt, ut quotidianos in concionibus clamores extorqueant. Caeterum patrum me N. preces mouissent. Nunc frater noster S. Pand. mihi indicauit, Comicum nostrum Cæsarem & quosdam eiusdem factionis diligenter scisscitatos esse, annon statim venturus esse. Video igitur à multis te desiderari: ab aliis expectari, quia te accitum nonrunt. runt.N.egregiè fe offert, ἀλλ' ἐσὶν υγιὲς. Praeter illos nemo est qui me adierit.Vnum mihi suspectum reddiderunt quaedam nō leues coniecturae.Amo quidem hominem,sed non patitur fidem sibi haberi.Timidus est primùm,deinde suspicax:postremò vm-bram istam vel laruam adorat.Qui rem cupiut fine motu compositam, fperanttè idoneum fore pacificatorem. Factio ipsa te cupit, vt tua intercessione nonnihil subleuetur. Nos te petimus & cupimus:ac ego imprimis,vt videas,iudices, agas quicquid ex re Ecclesiae est cognoueris.Sed agnosce miserum statum.Nuper audiit Farellus, incommodè accidisse, quòd ad me diuertisset: quia nihil posset agi, nisi effet à me separatus. Mihi certè nihil gratius quàm fi omnia feliciter hic abs te peracta effent, me ad Garamantas relegato.Sed haec tibi ratio non minus quàm mihi displicebit.Eam dico quae tibi à moderatiffimis,vt videri volunt, praescribitur. Vt tamen habeas, quid sentiam in re perplexa : fi post s hic esse proximo die martis,& manere vsque ad diem lunae,faceres,vt videtur,operaepretium. Vale igitur,frater & amice Chariff.vnà cum vxore & fratribus, quos salutabis omnes meo nomine.xxvii.Mart. M. D. XLVII.
units.tr: I am uncertain about your coming to us. As far as I hear, N. has gone beyond due measure in setting out his need to you, though he is not the only one at fault in this matter. Most men are so childish that they are frightened by a ridiculous shaking of the head, while one worthless man displays his madness. I am defending not my own cause but the public one, which was decided in my absence. If I give up, the whole Consistory must collapse. Indeed, they behave in such a way that they wring out daily outcries during the sermons. Otherwise, the entreaties of N.'s friends would have moved me. Now our brother S. Pand. has told me that our comedian Caesar and certain men of the same faction have been asking carefully whether you will come at once. I see, then, that you are missed by many and awaited by others, since they have not summoned you. N. offers himself splendidly, but it is sound [ἀλλ' ἐστιν ὑγιές]. Apart from them, no one has approached me. One man has been made suspect to me by certain not slight conjectures. I do indeed love the man, but he does not allow himself to be trusted. First he is timid, then suspicious; lastly he worships that shadow or specter. Those who want the matter settled without disturbance hope that you will be a suitable peacemaker. The faction itself wants you, so that by your intercession it may be somewhat relieved. We seek and desire you, and I especially, so that you may see, judge, and do whatever you learn belongs to the cause of the Church. But recognize our wretched condition. Recently Farel heard that it had been inconvenient that you lodged with me, since nothing could be done unless he were separated from me. Certainly nothing would be more welcome to me than if everything were happily completed here by you, with me banished to the Garamantes. But this course will displease you no less than it displeases me, I mean the course prescribed to you by the most moderate men, as they wish to appear. Still, so that you have my view on this tangled matter: if you were here the day after next, Tuesday, and stayed until Monday, you would, it seems, do a worthwhile thing. Farewell, then, brother and dear friend, together with your wife and brothers, whom you will greet all in my name. 27 March 1547.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: Bvcervs Calvino S. D.
units.tr: Bucer to Calvin, greetings

units.la: ORate Dominum ardenter pro hac republica & Ecclesia,vt discat animà suam perdere,quò feruet eam.Caetera ex hoc optimo fratre.Dominus feruet vos & erigat contra mala omnia.Vxor tua & domus tua tecum salueat.Idem petit & mea. Pridie Calendas Aprilis. M. D. XLVII.
units.tr: Pray to the Lord fervently for this commonwealth and Church, that he may learn to lose his soul in order to save it. The rest from this excellent brother. May the Lord keep you and raise you up against all evils. Your wife and your household fare well with you. My wife asks the same. The day before the Kalends of April 1547.

units.la: Cal. Vireto S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Viret, greetings

units.la: IN causa Sonnerij feci quantùm fides primùm mea,deinde pudor etiam sinebat.Cùm nemo effet fratrum,cui non venirent in mentem eadem illa omnia, quae nos illi obieceramus, visum est mature occurrere. Atque vt plus auctoritatis haberet mea oratio,literas etiam tuas recitaui.Clausula haec fuit:quia vnum hoc remedium perfpiciebà, ne frater qui hactenus strenuè laborafset in vinea Domini,& virtutibus non continendis polleret, inutilis in posterum redderetur : mihi non displicere migrationem quam petebat. Nam ex malis compluribus, quae timerem,hoc esse minimum. Postquam ad consultationem venturum est,multorum sermonem aliquoties abrupi,vt in mitiorem sententiam quoquo modo adducerentur. Sed erant firmiores,
units.tr: In the affair of Sonnerius I have done as much as my faith first, and then my sense of shame, allowed. Since there was not one of the brothers to whom those same objections we had raised against him had failed to occur, I thought it best to meet them early. And so that my speech might carry more weight, I also read out your letter. Its closing clause ran: because I saw that this was the one remedy, that the brother, who has hitherto laboured vigorously in the vineyard of the Lord and excels in virtues that cannot be held back, should not be rendered useless in future, I was not displeased by the migration he sought, for of the many evils I feared, this was the least. When we came to the consultation, I broke off the speeches of many of them several times, so that they might somehow be brought to a milder opinion. But they were too firm to be bent.
