Nosti qui sint & quales, & quantum detrimenti afferant Ecclesiis quæ nos merito ad misericordiam fui inuitare debent: sed potissimum Christi sanguis quo redemptæ fuerunt, qui tam scelesté àtam impiis in domo Dei conculcatur:rependat illis iu dex iustus idque cito, prout egerunt, tam obstinatis animis, & tanta improbitate: & piis perfecte det pergere,vota eorum exaudiens qui Christi gloriâ,Ecclesiarum ædificationem & omnium salutem studio multo exoptant.
units.tr: I think you have heard that the Synod has at last been granted and admitted, although no day has yet been fixed. May Christ grant that the churches and the holy ministry be properly looked after, and that what needs correcting be corrected as it ought to be. Please see for yourself what is lacking in the teaching of many and in their lives, so that the Epicureans do not take so many others down with them. This must be dealt with at the right time by suitable men, with great fear of God and constant prayers, lest Satan, who nurses and drives these men, hide them behind his tricks and pretences, so that they are not recognised and escape punishment. You know who they are and what sort they are, and how much harm they do to the churches, which ought rightly to invite us to pity. Yet above all the blood of Christ, by which they were redeemed, is trampled on so wickedly and so impiously in the house of God. May the just Judge repay them, and quickly, as they have deserved, given how obstinate their minds are and how great their wickedness. And may he grant the godly perfect perseverance, hearing the prayers of those who with great zeal desire the glory of Christ, the building up of the churches and the salvation of all.

units.la: Farellus tuus totus.
units.tr: Yours wholly, Farel.

units.la: CALVINVS BVCERO S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BUCER, GREETINGS.

units.la: Literæ tuæ tamen fi gaudio & tristitia mixtæ erant, mihi tamen perquam gratæ fuerunt. Vtinam animi tui mœrorem & eas curas, quibus te cruciari video, posset aliqua ex parte subleuare. Omnes tamen etiam atque etiam obsecramus,ne te absq; professu conficias: vt lætus sis atque hilaris in tam varia & multiplici lugendi materia, neque tuæ est pietatis,neque expedit,neque optandum nobis est. Danda est tamen opera,vt te quoad licebit Domino & Ecclesiæ seruies. Amplum quidem stadium cucurristi: sed nescis quantum adhuc tibi restet. Ego fortassis qui paulum à carceribus sum progressus iam propior sum metæ. Sed in manu Dei est cursus nostri moderatio & finis. Vt tamen maxime esset vegetus, dum pericula quæ ex multis partibus impedent circumspicio, multæ mortes quotidie versantur ante oculos. Sicut ergo isthic vos pugnæ exercent ita hic lentos timores fouemus: quanquam & tumultus iam intus sedatos esse confido, & rumor est vobis esse à Gallis inducias. Vtinam & firmæ pacis ratio iniri posset: iamiam enim qui hæc duo regna inter se committit, videmus interea ociosum ridere, & vtramvis captare fortunam, vt viribus integris adoriatur victorem, & victis spolia absque sudore & sanguine legatiadeo que de ambobus triumpher, ac prædam rapiat. Sed dum mecum reputo quàm prauis consiliis regatur Gallia, de hac re fere desperò. Illum quidem plus satis timent: sed alios superbè despicendo, non cauent sibi ab eius astutia. Et sane Dominus hac cæcitate atrocem eorum in sanctos sæuitiam, & quæ in dies magis glisceit (vt ego quidem interm.j. pretor)iure vlciscitur. Vrinam ficu+ illic vires colligit impietas, & augescit semper in peius, i'a Angli contraria aemulatione ad solidam Christianismi puritatem contendat: donec ad vnicam Christi regulam omnia illic constituta cernantur. Dominum Protectorem, vt volebas,conatus sum hortari,vt flagitabat prae-fens rerum status: tuum quoque erit modis omnibus instare, fi modo detur audientia (quod te facere sum persuasus) praesertim vero, vt ritus qui fupe-rftitionis aliquid redolent tollantur e medio. Hoc tibi nominatim commendo,vt te inuidia liberes,qua te falso grauari apud multos non ignoras: nam mediis consiliis vel authorem,vel approbatorem semper inscribunt. Scio hanc quorundam animis suspicionem altius infixam esse, quam vt eam reuellere facile fit,etiam fi nihil omittas.Et sunt qui te ma-ligne nullo errore inducti calumniantur. Denique fatale quo-dammodo hoc tibi malum est,quod fugere vix possis. Cauendu tamen ne imperitisdetur male suspicandi occasio,improbi vero obloquendi praetextum arripiant. N. tibi fine causa molestum esse valde dolo. Vtinam aliquando humanitatem discat.Ego fa-cilius ignosco,quod tam malitia impelli ipsum quam caeco im-petu ferri animaduertifie mihi videor. Non credas quam nos a-liquando atrociter lacerarit,& absentes & innoxios & amicos. In Viretum praesertim, cum praeter meritum summa quorunda iniquitate aliorum vero perfidia prope effet opprefus, non mi-nus violenter inuectus est quam in sceleratissimum Ecclesiae proditorem. Certe masuetudini assuesceret,fi sciret quam noxia fit praeferuidi fui zeli & immodicae austeritatis intemperies.Ti-bi haec indignitas cum aliis malis qua soles aequitate deuoranda est.Nec vero Tigurinis causam suam probaret.Hac in parte no-nihil abste dissentio,quod putas aduersae parti fieri iniuriam.Na dum eos nunquam tam crafle hallucinatos putas, vt Christum vbique diffusum imaginarentur,non tenesquid interalios feri-pferit Brentius, Christum cum in praesepi iaceret gloriosum in coelo fuisse,etiam fecundum corpus. Atque vt apertius loquar, feis doctrinam Papistarum modeftiorem magisqu sobria esse, quam Ampfdorphij & similium fuerit qui tanquam Apollinis Phoebades insanierunt. Scis quam inhumaniter vexatus fuerit Dominus Philippus quia modum aliquem teneret.Deliria quo-que secum idololatriam trahebat.Quorsum enim illud Lutheri adorabile sacramentum, nisi v: idolum in templo Dei erigatur? Ego tamen sepulta esse haec omnia cuperem.Summa quidem con-tentione semper apud vicinos nostros institi,vt ab inf statione abftineren::vtiamen illis fatisfieret, errores omnes quibus mi-nime consentiebam damnare suppressis nominibus non dubi-taui.De loco tu certe nimis subtili: rdifferere mihi videris.Alios grauius offendit, obscuritas quam astutè data opera accersi abs te putant.Atq; hos quidem errare scio. Sed non video cur tanto- pere refugias quod docemus cum in cœlum ascendisse Christus dicitur,hac loquutione exprimi locorum distantiam. Neq; enim an in cœlesti gloria sit locus,hîc disputatur,f-d tantum an Christi corpus sit in mundo.Id cum scripturis clare testatum si ,pro Fidei articulo amplecti non dubito. Et tamen cum in scripto no stro reperies,quorundam morositati non absque certamine datum fuit: nam ego aliter verba temperauerā. Cæterum quia hac quam vsurpauimus forma nihil continebatur, nisi quod sentiebam,aliis eam concedere non fuit religio. Effectum sacramentorum & quid per ea nobis Dominus conferat luculentius & vberiusexplicari,quàm multi patiantur, piè & prudenter optas. Neque verò per me stetit,quin pleniora quædam essent. Gemamus ergo ferentes ea quæ corrigere non licet. Exemplar scripti quod mihi remiserunt,hîc habebis.Capita duo quę verebaris ne admitterent, perlibenter sunt amplexi.Si Bullingeri mansuetudinem reliqui sequuti essent,facilius omnia impetrassent: bene tamen habet quòd in veritatem consensimus,& tenuimus summam rei.Si theses tuas duobus tantum in locis aliquantum flecteres,faceres appositissimè,nempe vt clarius exprimeres te locorum distantia Christum à nobis qui in mundo sumus,disiunge- re:deinde,vt commenta omnia quibus hactenus ad superstitionem induxæ sunt hominum mentes clarius reiiceres, præsertim vt Spiritui sancto Christóque suam gloriam vindicares, ne quicquam ad ministros vel elementa transferatur. Initia actionis in consensione ineunda meram desperationem præ se ferebant. Subita lux affulsit. Voluerunt priores cum aliis Ecclesiis communicare.Non ægrè concessimus.Quod autem N.dissentit, æquo animo ferendum est. Farellus tibi scribit copiose,vt videbis,Viretus non audet: non enim credas quàm iniquè tractetur. Et tamen quàm potest officiosissimè te salutat,petítque vt se habeas excusatum. Collegæ etiam mei omnes te reuerenter salutant. Nihil hic novi, nisi quod Tigurum & Bernas spem omnem fœderis Gallo abscesserunt.Vale clarissime vir & Pater in Domino mihi plurimum obseruande.
units.tr: Your letter, though it was mixed with joy and sadness, was nonetheless most welcome to me. I wish I could relieve, in some part, the grief of your mind and those cares by which I see you are tormented. Yet we beg you again and again not to wear yourself out without any restraint: it is neither becoming to your piety, nor expedient, nor to be wished by us, that you should be cheerless and gloomy amid such varied and manifold causes for mourning. Still, care must be taken that you serve the Lord and the Church for as long as you are able. You have indeed run a long course, but you do not know how much of it still remains for you. As for me, who have advanced a little from the starting-gates, I am perhaps now nearer the goal. But the direction and the end of our course lie in the hand of God. Yet, however vigorous I might be, while I look round at the dangers that threaten from many quarters, many deaths present themselves before my eyes every day. So, just as the battles keep you busy there, so here we nurse anxious fears, although I trust that the disturbances within are now calmed too, and there is a rumour among you that the French have agreed to a truce. I wish a basis for a firm peace could be found. For we see that the man who sets these two kingdoms against each other sits idly by in the meantime, laughing, and seeks to seize whichever fortune he likes, so that he may attack the victor with his strength unimpaired, and take the spoils of the conquered without sweat or blood, and so triumph over both and carry off the prey. But when I consider with myself how unwise the counsels by which France is governed are, I almost despair of this matter. They fear that man greatly enough, yet by scornfully despising the others they do not guard themselves against his cunning. And indeed the Lord, by this blindness, rightly avenges (as far as I can judge in the meantime) their savage cruelty against his saints, which grows greater day by day. I wish that impiety there were not gathering its strength and always growing worse, and that the English, in a rival zeal, were striving toward the solid purity of Christianity, until everything there is seen to be set up according to the one rule of Christ. I have tried to exhort the Lord Protector, as you wished, as the present state of affairs demanded; it will be yours too to press this in every way, if only a hearing is granted (which I am persuaded you will do), and especially that the rites which smack somewhat of superstition be removed from the midst. This I commend to you by name, so that you may free yourself from ill will, which you know you are falsely burdened with among many: for they always ascribe to you as author or approver whatever counsels they dislike. I know this suspicion has been fixed more deeply in the minds of some than it can easily be torn out, even if you leave nothing undone. And there are some who slander you, led by no error but out of malice. In short, this is a kind of fated evil for you, which you can scarcely escape. Yet care must be taken that the inexperienced are not given an occasion for evil suspicion, and that the wicked do not seize a pretext for railing. I am very sorry that N. is troublesome to you without cause. I wish he would at some time learn gentleness. I more easily pardon him, since I seem to see that he is driven as much by malice as carried by a blind impulse. You would not believe how savagely he has at times torn us to pieces, both absent and innocent, and our friends too. Especially against Viret, although he was almost overwhelmed by the great injustice of some and the treachery of others, undeserved, he inveighed no less violently than against the most wicked traitor of the Church. Certainly he should accustom himself to mildness, if he knew how harmful is the intemperance of his overheated zeal and immoderate severity. You must bear this indignity, along with his other wrongs, with the equanimity you are wont to show. Nor would the Zurich men approve their own cause on this point. In this part I dissent somewhat from you, in that you think an injustice is being done to the opposing side. For while you think they were never so grossly deluded as to imagine Christ diffused everywhere, you do not grasp what Brenz wrote among others, namely that Christ, although he lay in the manger, was in heaven in glory, even according to his body. And to speak more plainly, you know that the doctrine of the Papists is more moderate and more sober than that of Amsdorf and the like, who raved as if they were Apollo's Phoebades. You know how inhumanly Master Philip was harassed, merely because he kept some measure. Their delusions also drag idolatry along with them. For to what end is that adorable sacrament of Luther's, unless an idol is set up in the temple of God? Yet I would wish all these things to be buried. I have always insisted, with the greatest effort, with our neighbours, that they abstain from the outward observance; yet, so that they might be satisfied, I did not hesitate to condemn all the errors to which I did not consent in the least, while suppressing names. As for the place, you seem to me to argue too subtly. Others are more gravely offended by the obscurity which they think you have deliberately sought by a cunning device. And these I know are mistaken. But I do not see why you so strongly shrink from what we teach, that when Christ is said to have ascended into heaven, this expression signifies the distance of places. For the question here is not whether there is a place in heavenly glory, but only whether the body of Christ is in the world. I do not hesitate to embrace this as an article of faith, since it is clearly attested by the Scriptures. And yet, when you find it in our writing, it was granted with contention to the peevishness of certain men; for I had softened the words otherwise. Moreover, since nothing was contained in the form we have used except what I myself felt, it was not a matter of conscience for me to concede it to others. That the effect of the sacraments, and what the Lord bestows on us through them, be explained more clearly and fully than many allow, you wish piously and prudently. Nor has it been my fault that some of the statements were not fuller. Let us therefore groan as we bear those things which it is not permitted to correct. You will have here a copy of the writing which they sent back to me. The two chapters which you feared they would admit, they most willingly embraced. If they had followed the gentleness of Bullinger, they would have obtained everything more easily; yet it is well that we have agreed to the truth and held to the substance of the matter. If you bent your theses a little in two places only, you would do it most fittingly: namely, so that you might more clearly separate Christ, who is distant from us who are in the world, by the distance of places; and then, so that you might more clearly reject all the inventions by which hitherto men's minds have been led into superstition, especially so that you might vindicate for the Holy Spirit and for Christ their own glory, lest anything be transferred to the ministers or the elements. The beginnings of the action on reaching agreement showed nothing but sheer despair. Then a sudden light shone forth. The former men wished to communicate with the other Churches. We did not grudgingly concede this. But that N. dissents must be borne with an even mind. Farel writes to you at length, as you will see; Viret does not dare, for you may not believe how unjustly he is treated. Yet he greets you as respectfully as he can, and asks that you hold him excused. All my colleagues also greet you with reverence. Nothing new here, except that Zurich and Bern have abandoned all hope of an alliance with France. Farewell, most distinguished man and Father, most to be honoured by me in the Lord.

units.la: CALVINVS BVCERO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BUCER.

units.la: VEritatem rem esse pretiosissimam, vt est, omnes fatentur. Atqui cum bonorum omnium fons sit vnus Deus, quic quid vspiam veri tibi occurret, nisi bis Deo ingratus esse veliis, ab ipso profectum esse ne dubites, nec secus ac vocem è cœlo delapsam excipias. Nam & dona Dei contemptim præ-m.ij.
units.tr: Everyone admits that truth is a most precious thing, as it is. Since God is the one fountain of all good things, whatever truth occurs to you anywhere, do not doubt that it has come from him, unless you wish to be ungrateful to God, and you should receive it as if a voice had fallen from heaven. For it is wrong to despise the gifts of God, and it is an even greater impiety to ascribe to man what belongs to God alone.

units.la: Epist.94. terire nefas est : & quod proprium est ipsius adscribere homini, maior etiam num impietas. Ergo & philosophia praeclarum est Dei donum: & qui omnibus seculis extiterunt docti viri, eos Deus ipse excitauit, vt ad veri notitiam mundo praelucerent. Verum inter eorum scripta & eam doctrinam quam Deus suo numini dedicauit, vt generi humano sacrosancta est, magnum est discrimen : illic enim tenuem quandam veri atis particulam tibi praelibari comperias, vnde gustum capias modo quam amoena sit ac suauis cognitu, hic vero plenam tibi copiam affluere quae animum tuum penitus reficiat: illic vmbram & imaginem tibi ob oculos subiici, quaeque ad amorem eius exciter modo, non ea tibi familiarem reddat, hic solidum corpus tibi sisti ex quo non familiariter tantum cognoscere, sed quodammodo attrectare liceat: illic semen quasi praefocatum, hic frugem habeas, & quidem in sua maturitate. Illic denique exiguas tantum scintillas emicare, quae sic viam demonstrent, vt in medio cursu deficiant, vel potius quae viam demonstrare nequeant, sed tantum retinere, ne longius abeatis: hic vero Spiritum Dei instar lucidissimae facis, vel potius instar Solis ipsius, plenofplendore affulgere, vt & vitae tuae cursum usque ad vltimam metam regat, & in beatam immortalitatem perducat. Hinc collige vbinam peregrinari, & vbi velut fixis sedibus acquiescere debeas.
units.tr: Epist. 94. Philosophy too is an excellent gift of God, and God himself raised up the learned men who have existed in every age, so that they might shine a light on the knowledge of the truth for the world. Yet there is a great difference between their writings and that doctrine which God has dedicated to his divine majesty, which is holy to the human race. For in the former you will find only a slender particle of truth, offered in a taste, so that you may sample how pleasant and sweet it is to know; but in the latter a full abundance flows to you, which thoroughly refreshes your soul. In the former a shadow and an image is set before your eyes, which stirs up love of God but does not make him truly familiar to you; in the latter a solid body is presented to you, from which you may not only know him intimately but, in a manner, handle him. In the former you have seed, as it were choked, in the latter the fruit itself, and indeed in its ripeness. In the former only tiny sparks gleam, which point out the way so feebly that they fail in the middle of the course, or rather cannot point out the way at all but only hold you back from going further; but here the Spirit of God shines forth like the brightest torch, or rather like the Sun itself, with full splendour, both to guide the course of your life to its final goal and to lead you to blessed immortality. From this, gather where you ought to be a wanderer, and where you ought to rest as if in a fixed abode.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL, GREETING.

units.la: DE rebus nostris vix habeo quod scribam : quia mihi adeo sunt obscurae, vt de exitu valde sim perplexus. Fracti sunt eorum animi, qui se aliquos esse iactabant. Multum se consequutos esse putant, si ille non posset omnia, qui nisi eorum ignauia nihil posset. Quotidie nouae occasiones eius domandi offeruntur: adeo omnes negligunt, vt dicas sponte sibi iugum accersere. Nam quia sibi mutuo non fidunt: quisque de retinenda sua statione est solicitus. Interea nulla vox est libera. Nobis liceret tranquillis esse, si nihil moneremus. Sed dum videre cogimur, quae si Romae audiremus fieri, sua indignitate reprehensionem aliquam exprimerent, tacere qui possumus? Ego tamen, vt hortaris, dum retinendae Ecclesiae studeo, ipse retineor, ne prosiliam vltra quam expediat. Vix octo dies nobis effluent absque conflictu. Spero Dominum ita mihi adfuturum, vt tibi moderatio & aequitas, vel potius tolerantia mea probetur. Omnia enim obiiuione deuorabo, modo ne cur… quibus nunquam erit postulandum, vt adiuuent: quando eo prolapsi sunt, vt refipiscentiae nulla spes appareat. Libelli editio, cum pudorem multis incussit, tandem permisa. Quinetia exemplar plar ad me fuit allatum, vt fide mea iudicioque excutleretur. Sed cum repuIo quales insultusfratribus nosiris sustinendi sint, videor mihi propemodum sub umbra certare lusorium certame. Argentinensibus hoc modo reliquum erat, vt ab Episcopo inducias impetrarent. Bonus Tollinus post discessum principis adhuc cum Symmysiis haeret, ne locum deserant. Vale frater & amice integerrime. Dominus I sustibi adsit perpetuo, te sustineat, tuos labores benedicat. Saluta diligenter fratres nostros, Christophorum, Michaelem, Satonum, Gasparum & reliquos, totamque familiam. Collegae mei vos salutant, & vxor, quae se vestris precibus commendat. Geneuae, xi 1. Decembris. M. D. XLVIII.
units.tr: I hardly have anything to write about our affairs, because they are so obscure to me that I am very perplexed about the outcome. The spirits of those who used to boast that they were somebody have been broken. They think they have achieved much if he, who could do nothing except through their cowardice, cannot do everything. Every day new opportunities to tame him are offered, yet everyone is so careless that you would say they are voluntarily fetching a yoke upon themselves. For since they do not trust one another, each is anxious about keeping his own position. Meanwhile no voice is free. We could be at peace if we said nothing. But while we are forced to see things done which, if we heard of them being done at Rome, would wring some rebuke from us by their unworthiness, how can we keep silent? Yet I, as you urge, while I strive to keep the Church intact, am myself held back, lest I leap forward more than is useful. Scarcely eight days slip by for us without conflict. I hope the Lord will so stand by me that your moderation and fairness, or rather my patience, may be proved to you. For I will swallow up all things in forgetfulness, provided that ... (to those from whom there will never be a need to ask for help, since they have slipped into such a state that no hope of repentance appears). The edition of the little book, since it has caused shame to many, has at last been permitted. Moreover a copy was brought to me, so that it might be examined by my faith and judgment. But when I consider what sort of assaults our brothers must endure, I seem to myself to be contending almost in the shade, as in a mock contest. For the people of Strasbourg this was the only course left, to obtain a truce from the Bishop. Good Tollin, after the prince's departure, still clings to the Symmysians, so that they do not abandon their place. Farewell, brother and most upright friend. May the Lord Jesus be with you always, sustain you and bless your labours. Greet diligently our brothers, Christopher, Michael, Satonus, Gaspar and the rest, and the whole household. My colleagues greet you, and my wife, who commends herself to your prayers. Geneva, 11 December 1548.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BUCER TO CALVIN, GREETING.

units.la: SAL. & annum seuumque omne quam foeliciffimum precor. Ingentes vero tibi gratias ago de literis tuis, ita praeter tuum morem vberibus Volebam hanc tibi vbertatem compensare, sed intempestiua hora moneor de his mercatoribus. Est enim dies hic vt recordari potes, quo ciuitas solenniter iurat, & distrahunt misere permulta alia. Vtinam sicut istud foedus ciuile, hic aliquando redintegrafsemus atque sanxisemus foedus vitae aeternae: quomodo vos conati soli praestitistis. Verum qui spiritus istam tam apud vos Religionem per necessariam dissoluit, idem obstat nec ea hic persuaderi vnquam potuerit. Sic igitur fumus modo scopae non dissolutae tantum, verum etiam disiectae. Dominus colligat seruetque sibi suos. Te stupefacit animos cortus illius tam cordati adeo subito concidisse. O optime, non idem est corpus illud. Robora eius erepta sunt, quaedam pridem, quaedam nuper. Superiunt & qui velint libenter redimere vitam suam Reipublicae pristinam colendi Christi libertatem. Ardum alij non videntur velle pro Christo periclitari, imo ditiores quique minantur palam se hinc commigraturos, (id quod antea fecerunt supra quinquaginta num ro) nisi gratia retineatur Imperatoris, & hic non creditur posse exorari, vt remittat quod edixit, res labuntur eo quo labuntur. Ah mi frater, temporibus Martyrum cum Ecclesiae seuera disciplinae Religione erant coiunctae, quam multi tum defuientibus persecutionibus, à Domino defecerunt? Quid igitur miramur si in ista nostra dissolutione pauci perstent? Nemo sane, nisi firma Christi fide sit obfirmatus, poterit crucem eius rem exfistimare sibi expetendam. At vbi fides in Dominum vera, ibi homines non magis promptis animis praeceptis eius obsequuntur in pace, quam offerunt animas suas pro illis in persecutione. Summum est hoc praeceptum Domini iij. mini,quòd à nobis poscit, vt orauit Patre pro nobis, vt in ipso vnum simus, ac nos ipsi omnes in vita noua, vita Dei perpetuis ministeriis instauremur. Ex hypocrisi nimis alte insita in Papatu, ad qualemcunque Christi professionem nostri traducti sunt: ea hypocrisis perpaucis est plane excussa. Maluerunt itaque videri quàm esse Christi. Cùm autem & videri ipsorum obest cupiditati & hoc quoque abiiciunt. Placebat liberatio à superstitionibus & tyrannide Papae, & viuendi pro arbitrio licentia: at quia venter Deus eorum in extremum adduceretur periculum, nisi in aliquam fe rursum Papae traderent seruitutem, malunt hanc subire praesertim per nos non parum mitigatam, quàm periculi tari de summo suo bono. Mendaciis tantum opus est, & pauca illa stipe, quibus extrema omnium scelerum ac flagitiorum redimitur licentia. Oremus igitur & satagamus, mi frater, vt fratres quorum res adhuc consistere videntur, ex nostrorum casu & de suo sint foliciti. Nisi enim Christo Domino penitius insiti, eius quoque disciplinam inter se restituant, & ipsis misere metuo. Nam nisi semen verbi Dei hac ceu occetur, & subnascens herba cum repurgetur, tum fultentetur, video quàm facile vel æstu persecutionis exarescat, vel praefocetur vnà subcrefcétibus carnalium cupiditatum spinis. Sed quid ista ad te, qui ipse haec sicut exactius consideras, ita maiore pridem religione vrges? Verum libet apud te vel hoc modo deplorare nostram miseriam & per uerfitatem, qui ista non pertinatiore pridem studio fumus persecuti. Nunc permulti hic iugo Domini commodissimo sese libenter submitterent totos, sed vereor ferum esse. Quanquam etiam in hac ipsa perditione nostra non desunt & in omnibus ordinibus, qui restitutioni solidae communionis & disciplinae Christi strenuè aduersantur, tametsi velint non in postremis Euangelij fedatoribus numerari. Tam istud adhuc male notum est nostris Mysterium corporis Christi. Oretis, vt facitis, diligenter pro hac Ecclesia, in qua profecto sunt quamplurimi granarij Christi, quos bonus Pastor omnino sibi conseruabit: hisq; Antiochaeis temporibus moderabitur & potentius & citius, quàm multorum ferat opinio. De scripto quod D. Ant. M. attulit, maximas ago tibi gratias Ecclesiae nomine: suum feret fructu indubie vberrimum. Seditione in Galliis sedatam gaudeo & opto vt in animis quoq; fit sedata. Terret tamè me omen, praesertim cùm non sit sedata ea clementia, qua veteres sapientes Imperatores vti soleabant. Responsum Tigurinorum probo. N. sapientia & nos prodidit Antichristi mancipia appellant populum Christi, num velint sui Concilij decretis acquiescere. Dent qui vere Christi sunt, dignum Christo Concilium, & veniant ad illud vltro, Christum iuicunq; amplectuntur. Meminisfi quantopere apud nostros ftros institerim, vt Ecclesiæ Christi aliquando causam suscipe-rent contra summos eius hostes & pestes,&Ecclesiam ab illis iusta simpliciter reperirent. At sicuti nostri Christi leges nunquā voluerunt in se ipsi simpliciter suscipere, ita nec ausi sunt eas adueriariis Christiana fortitudine obiicere. Merito itaque nostro illi reposcunt à nobis quæ Christi sunt,& eius Ecclesiarū omnia. Oro autem Dominum, vt quæ nunc fideliter & constanter respondent istic pro Christi regno,periculum dum non est in oculis & in manibus,postea quoque cum ea quæ caro metuit, in conspectum venerint aut etiam nonnihil afflixerint,retineant. Et nostri enim , quandiu aliquod habere carnis brachium sibi videbantur,responsa dabant plerunque satis fortia,quorum fracto eo brachio pessime meminerūt. Dominus exerat vel alicubi suum brachium. Hunc plurimum oro,vt tibi vxorem tuam sanet,imò Ecclesiæ ipsi Christi magis quàm tibi,quò tu possis agere pro illa quæ agis expeditiùs,& lubentius. Collega & vxor inuicem precantur tibi optanda omnia in annum ingredientem & omnia secula,Amen.1x.Ian. M. D. XLIX.
units.tr: Greetings. I pray that the new year and every season after it may be as happy as possible. I give you immense thanks for your letter, so full beyond your usual manner. I wished to repay you in kind for this fullness, but an untimely hour reminds me of these merchants. For today, as you may recall, is the day on which the city solemnly swears its oath, and many other matters distract me wretchedly. Would that, just as we renew this civil covenant, we might one day here also renew and ratify the covenant of eternal life, as you alone have striven to do. But the spirit that dissolves that religion among you, though it is so necessary, is the same spirit that stands in the way, so that it could never be persuaded here. So we are now not merely unbound but scattered, like a broom. May the Lord gather and keep his own. It astonishes you that that gathering, so sensible, has collapsed so suddenly. My dear friend, that body is no longer the same. Its strength has been taken away, some of it long ago, some of it lately. Some remain who would gladly buy back, at the cost of their lives, the republic's former liberty of worshipping Christ. Others, however, seem unwilling to risk danger for Christ. Indeed the wealthier ones openly threaten to emigrate from here (as more than fifty of them did before) unless the emperor's favour is kept; and since it is not believed that he can be prevailed upon to revoke what he has decreed, affairs slide to where they are sliding. Ah, my brother, in the times of the martyrs, when true religion was joined with the strict discipline of the Church, how many fell away from the Lord once the persecutions ceased? Why then do we wonder if few persevere in this dissolution of ours? Indeed no one, unless made firm by a sure faith in Christ, can regard his cross as something to be desired. But where faith in the Lord is true, people obey his commands in peace just as readily as they offer their souls for them in persecution. This is the highest command of the Lord, which he asks of us, as he prayed to the Father for us: that we be one in him, and that we all be renewed in a new life, the life of God, through continual ministries. Our people have been brought to some profession of Christ out of a hypocrisy too deeply implanted by the Papacy, and very few have plainly shaken off this hypocrisy. So they have preferred to seem rather than to be Christ's. But since even seeming hinders their desires, they cast this off too. They liked deliverance from the superstitions and tyranny of the Pope, and freedom to live as they pleased. But since their belly, which is their god, would be brought into extreme danger unless they gave themselves again into some servitude to the Pope, they prefer to undergo this, especially as it has been by us not a little softened, rather than be put in danger concerning their highest good. They need only lies, and a little small coin, by which the utmost licence of every crime and shameful deed is bought. Let us therefore pray and labour, my brother, that the brethren whose affairs still seem to stand may be anxious, from our fall, about their own. For unless they are deeply implanted in Christ the Lord and also restore his discipline among themselves, I fear wretchedly for them. For unless the seed of God's word is, as it were, harrowed, and the springing herb is weeded and then supported, I see how easily it will wither in the heat of persecution, or be choked by the thorns of carnal desires growing up alongside it. But why say these things to you, who considers them more exactly yourself and have long pressed them with greater scruple? Still, it pleases me to lament before you, at least in this way, our misery and perversity, we who have long pursued these things with no stubborn zeal. Now many here would gladly submit themselves wholly to the Lord's most convenient yoke, but I fear it is too late. Yet even in this very ruin of ours, there are not lacking, in all ranks, those who strenuously oppose the restoration of sound communion and of Christ's discipline, although they wish not to be counted among the least of the Gospel's peacemakers. So far the mystery of the body of Christ is still poorly understood by our people. Pray for this Church, as you do, diligently; in it there are indeed very many grains of Christ's harvest, whom the good Shepherd will surely keep for himself. In these Antiochene times he will govern them both more powerfully and more quickly than many suppose. For the writing which Master Antony brought, I give you the greatest thanks in the Church's name; it will undoubtedly bear most abundant fruit. I rejoice that the sedition in France has been quelled, and I wish it may be quelled in men's minds too. Yet an omen frightens me, especially since that clemency which the wise emperors of old used to employ has not been applied. I approve the reply of the Zurich people. Our own wisdom too has betrayed us: the minions of Antichrist call the people of Christ to ask whether they will submit to the decrees of their council. Let those who are truly Christ's demand a council worthy of Christ, and let all who embrace Christ come to it of their own accord. You remember how strongly I pressed among our people that they should at some point take up the cause of Christ's Church against its greatest enemies and plagues, and plainly find the Church's claims just. But just as our people never wished simply to take Christ's laws upon themselves, so they have not dared to set them against their adversaries with Christian fortitude. Rightly, then, those of ours demand back from us what belongs to Christ and all of his churches. I pray the Lord that those who now answer faithfully and steadfastly there for Christ's kingdom, while danger is not before their eyes and in their hands, may keep this faithfulness afterwards too, when what the flesh fears has come into view or has even somewhat afflicted them. For our people too, as long as they seemed to have some arm of flesh to rely on, gave answers mostly quite bold; but once that arm was broken, they remember those answers very poorly. May the Lord stretch out his own arm, somewhere at least. I pray most earnestly that he heal your wife, for your sake, or rather for the Church of Christ itself more than for yours, so that you may be able to do more readily and willingly what you do for it. My colleague and wife pray in turn that all things to be wished for you may come in the year now beginning and in all ages. Amen. 9 January 1549.

units.la: Tuus totus Bucerus.
units.tr: Wholly yours, Bucer.

units.la: CAL. MONSBELGARDENSIBVS.
units.tr: Calvin to the Monsbelgard Church

units.la: Fidelibus Christiservis ministris Monsbelgardensis Ecclesiæ, fratribus & Symmystis charissimis.
units.tr: To the faithful servants of Christ, the ministers of the Monsbelgard church, my brothers and dearest fellow-ministers.

units.la: GRatia vobis & Pax à Deo Patre nostro & Domino Iesu Christo.Charissimi & ex animo colendi fratres,tandem accidit quod diu timuimus, vt isthic quoque constitutum à Domino Ecclesiæ ordinem Satan per suos ministros cuerteret. Hoc tamen solatij, quoad in retristissima fi ri potest, literæ vestræ attulerunt quod inde intelleximus vos omnes in officio ad extremum perstitisse.Nam sp grauiter testati estis vobis improbari istas corruptelas quæ ad inquinandam sanæ doctrinæ puritate ingerebantur,digna ministris Christi fuit constantia: quòd nunc etiam perfidedissimulationi exilium præoptaris,in eo specimen editis luculentum syncerę vestræ fidei. Nam vbi vos abdicat docendi munere qui hactenus & Ecclesiæ Christi hospitium præbuerat in ditione sua,& vobis permiserat Christi prædicandi libertatem,vlterius nostro iudicio progredi non expedit:præsertim vbi nulla profectus spes apparet,neq; oues quibus vos Christus Pastores præfecerat,operam vestram amplius defiderant.Nam vt proditor est qui volens cedit ac stationem vltrò deserit suam, sic resistere vbi coginur nostrum nō est nisi forte nos ad subeundum discrimen nominarim vocaret Ecclesiam m.iiij. nam tunc centies mori præstaret, quàm frustrari eorum vota qui Christum sequi parati essent. Vestra autem ratio longè diuersa est: quandiu enim fuistis Pastores, non defuit gregi vestra sedulitas aut solicitudo. Nunc cùm perseuerandi studium nihil profuturum sit, ac ne oues quidem ipsę quibus obstricta est vestra fides, sibi vtile esse censeant vos vltrà tendere, perfuncti sane estis. Restat igitur vt gubernacula vobis tradita commendetis Christo, vt solus ipse Spiritu suo regat, quando iam labori vestro non datur locus. Cæterùm satis reputamus quanto mœrore sitis oppressi, quibus nihil præter exilium & egestatem propositum est: sed præcipuus mœror est ex ipsa Ecclesiæ clade, cuius maiorem vos habere rationem comprobastis quàm vestri. Et nos qui dem malis vestris tam publicis quàm priuatis afficimur vt par est: atque vtinam liceret manum vobis porrigere. Nùc quod residuum est, vos hortamur vt in hoc Christianæ syncer/ itatis testimonio pergatis ad finem usque. Beatior erit quamlibet misera vestra conditio, quàm si locum & nomen retineretis unde Filius Dei exulat. Quanquam breui sentiemus ipsum ita regnare in cœlo, vt virtutem suam in terra quoque exerere velit. Nos interea ad militiam paratos esse oportet quando nondum tépus est triumphandi. Valete optimi & integerrimi fratres. Dominus Iesus vobis adsit, vos consoletur, & in sancta perseuerantia confirmet. Geneuæ xv Ianuarij. M. D. XLIX.
units.tr: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Dearest brothers, whom I cherish from my heart, what we have long feared has at last happened: Satan has used his ministers to overturn there too the order that the Lord established in the Church. Your letter, however, has brought some comfort in this most sorrowful matter, because from it we understand that all of you have held to your duty to the end. You have solemnly declared that you disapprove of the corruptions that were being forced in to defile the purity of sound doctrine, and that is the steadfastness that befits ministers of Christ. Now too you prefer exile to treacherous silence, and in this you have given a clear example of your sincere faith. For when the one who had hitherto offered the Church of Christ a home in his lands, and had allowed you the freedom to preach Christ, dismisses you from your teaching office, in our judgement it is not expedient to go any further, especially since no hope of progress appears and the sheep, over whom Christ set you as shepherds, no longer need your labour. A man who gives way when he is pressed and abandons his post of his own accord is a traitor; so it is not for us to resist when we are compelled, unless perhaps the Lord were to call us by name to face the danger. In that case it would be better to die a hundred times than to disappoint those who are prepared to follow Christ. Your situation, however, is quite different. As long as you were pastors, your diligence and care did not fail the flock. Now that persistence will profit nothing, and since not even the sheep to whom your faithfulness was bound think it useful for you to go on further, you have indeed fulfilled your task. It remains, therefore, that you commit the reins entrusted to you to Christ, so that he alone may rule by his Spirit, since there is now no room for your labour. Yet we fully recognise how great your grief is, when nothing lies before you but exile and poverty. But the chief sorrow is the ruin of the Church itself, whose welfare you have shown you value more than your own. We too are grieved by your troubles, both public and private, as is right; and would that we could stretch out a hand to you. For the rest, we urge you to persevere to the end in this witness of Christian sincerity. Your condition, however wretched, will be happier than if you kept the place and name from which the Son of God is in exile. Yet before long we shall see him reigning so in heaven that he will also wish to display his power on earth. Meanwhile we must be ready for battle, since it is not yet time to triumph. Farewell, most excellent and upright brothers. May the Lord Jesus be with you, comfort you, and confirm you in holy perseverance. Geneva, 15 January 1549.

units.la: Fratres vobis in Domino vere coniuncti Ministri Genevensis Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Brothers truly joined to you in the Lord, the ministers of the Geneva church.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus omnium nomine.
units.tr: John Calvin, on behalf of all.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO S.D.
units.tr: Bucer to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: INtendite preces, Optimi viri & fratres, pro reliquiis Ecclesiæ nostræ & ministerij. Iam enim Episcopo promissum est, hīc non permittendum prædicari contra Interim. Vel hodie itaque vel intra perpaucos dies obsignabitur meum & præcipuorum Collegarum ministerium. Sic verò res meæ sunt comparatæ, vt quo vel primùm, vel postea Dominus mihi nondum certò mó-strauerit, vt monstret, & ducat, mecum ores ab ipso religiose. Annos & familiam meam nostri tum etiam inuidiam fa-calem. Re-sta ad Dominum quouis genere transitus optimum. Proximus exilium, non plane otiosum & strenuè. Nisi Dominus intercedat potenti brachio suo, expectanda est hortibilis sicut Ecclesiarum vastatio, ita etiam Ministrorum persecutio. Vacant enim ministeriis iam innumeræ parochiæ: huius pudet tamen auctores calumniæ. lamitatis: ideo forsan recipient consiliu Spirensis ἀραρσχόπου, vt qui noluerint ordinari ab Episcopo, aut ordinati Ecclesiis suis secundum Interim ministrare, mittantur ad remos. Et iam Moguntinus in sua Synodo constituit, omnes eos qui cœnobiticam vel sacerdotalem vitam professi sunt, ad eandem vi reducantur, quacunque in vitæ conditione fuerint. Quid? Antichristus vult id, quod auder, sibi restituere, vt imperet omnia omnibus. Cótra Christus, nec perdet ex suis quenquam. Dominum itaque arden ter & assidue oremus, vt hunc Spiritu suo conficiat quâprimùm, aut deprimat nonnihil, alioqui non fieret salua omnis caro. At teneri in Domino non caro, sed Spiritus sunt, & in his triumphabit crucifixus. Aliquoties nunc scribitur Landgrauium miserrimum à Domino esse respectum, deflereque amare suum lapsum: nullúmque velle iam Papisticum sacrum audire: atq; scripsisse ad suos de nullo se vnquam facto suo doluisse, & dolere acerbius, quàm quod salutarem Christi doctrinam negarit: rogasque illos, & esse obtestatos, vt quantùm vllo modo valeant sanæ doctrinæ patrocinentur. Se miserum sperasse sua defectione à Domino liberationem posse impetrare ab immanissimis custodibus suis. Confido hæc vera esse. Vnà itaque miserrimo Principi gratulamur hac Domini misericordiam, per quem iam ante hoc bello Dominus pro suo populo multa præclara fecit. Optime valete. VII Febr. M. D. XLIX.
units.tr: Pray earnestly, most excellent men and brothers, for the remnants of our Church and ministry. For it has already been promised to the bishop that preaching against the Interim will not be permitted here. Today or within a very few days my ministry and that of my chief colleagues will be sealed up. My circumstances are such that I do not yet know with certainty where, or when, the Lord will show me the way; I ask you to pray to him devoutly that he may show it and lead me. Our people [...] also feel hostility toward me. Every route is open to the Lord by whatever means he chooses. The exile before me is not altogether idle, and I shall be vigorous in it. Unless the Lord intervenes with his mighty arm, we must expect the destruction of the churches, and also the persecution of the ministers. Already countless parishes stand without ministers, and the authors of this calamity are not ashamed of it. Therefore they will perhaps adopt the counsel of the Speyer [ἀραρσχόπου]: that those who refuse to be ordained by the bishop, or who, once ordained, refuse to minister in their churches according to the Interim, be sent to the galleys. And already the Mainz bishop has decreed in his synod that all who have professed the monastic or priestly life should be brought back to the same state, whatever their condition in life. What then? Antichrist wants to restore to himself what he dares, so as to rule over all things. Christ, on the contrary, will lose none of his own. Let us therefore pray to the Lord ardently and constantly that he may bring this man to an end by his Spirit as soon as possible, or at least humble him somewhat; otherwise "all flesh" would not be saved. But those who are held in the Lord are not flesh but spirit, and in these the crucified one will triumph. It is now repeatedly written that the most wretched Landgrave has been regarded by the Lord, that he mourns his fall bitterly, that he no longer wishes to hear the Papist mass, and that he has written to his people that he has never regretted any deed of his, and regrets none more bitterly than that he denied the saving doctrine of Christ; and that he begged and urged them to defend sound doctrine in every way they can. He wretchedly hoped that by his defection he could obtain deliverance from the Lord from his most savage guards. I trust these reports are true. Therefore we rejoice together with the most wretched prince at this mercy of the Lord, through whom, even in this war, the Lord has already done many splendid things for his people. Farewell, most excellently. 7 February 1549.

units.la: Tuus Bucerus.
units.tr: Yours wholly, Bucer.

units.la: RESPONSVM AD QVÆSTIONEM D. TOSSANI Ministri Monsbelgardensis.
units.tr: RESPONSE TO THE QUESTION OF D. TOSSANUS, Minister of Montbéliard.

units.la: Si Sacramentorum administratio Ministro interdicetur.
units.tr: Whether the administration of the Sacraments may be forbidden to a minister.

units.la: Quod de re rogati sumus à fideli Christi seruo & optimo nostro Symmystia D. Tossano, nos invocato Domini Spiritu ita respondendum censuimus. Primò videmus duas potissimùm rationes esse, quæ Tossanum solicitant ad migrandum. Nam quia Sacramentorum administratio illi eripitur, quæ pars est Ministerij, quo hactenus functus est in Ecclesia Monsbelgardensi, ita se munere abdicatum existimat. Deinde quia dimissi sunt reliqui fratres, quos in eadem functione habuit collegas, veretur ne locum docendi retinedo, multis offensionem pariat: acsi se ab illis disiungat, quibusque tum fuit illi vocatio communis, ac multi interpretentur priuatis eum rationibus potius consulere, quàm publico Ecclesiæ bono. Cum ante mensem nos consuluissent omnes simul fratres, quidnam sibi agendum esset, ita
units.tr: You have asked us about this matter, as a faithful servant of Christ and our most excellent colleague, Tossanus. Having invoked the Spirit of the Lord, we have judged that the answer should be as follows. First, we see that there are mainly two reasons that trouble Tossanus and move him to leave. Because the administration of the Sacraments is taken from him, and that is part of the ministry he has so far discharged in the Church of Montbéliard, he thinks he has been stripped of his office. Then, because the other brothers, whom he had as colleagues in the same function, have been dismissed, he fears that by keeping his place as teacher he will give offence to many. He fears that if he separates himself from them, with whom his calling was held in common, many will interpret his action as serving private interests rather than the public good of the Church. When all the brothers consulted us a month ago about what they should do, we replied in this way:

units.la: Epist.99.
units.tr: Epist. 99.

units.la: respondimus Vt proditor est qui volens cedit, ac stationem suam deserit: sic resistere vbi vi cogimur, nostrum non est, nisi forte nos ad subeundum discrimen nominatim vocaret Ecclesia. Vestra autem ratio longe diuersa est. Nam quandiu fuistis Pastores, non defuit gregi vestra sedulitas, ac folicitudo. Nunc cum perseuerandi studium nihil profuturum fit, ac ne oues quid m ipsæ quibus obstricta est vestra fides, sibi vtile censeant vos vltra tendere, perfundi sane estis. Hæc exceptio fi recipitur, soluta erit priordifficultas. Flagitatur enim Toffani opera, tum ab Illuftriff. Principe Chriftophoro, tum ab ipsa plebe. Ergo quandiu Ecclesiam habet cui prodesse queat, sicam deferat, nō videtur rite neque ex officio facere. Si hac conditione retinererur, vt liberam pure fyncereque docendi facultatem nefaria aliqua pactione, vt alij permulti fecerunt, sibi minueret, centies mori prætiatur, quàm dicendi locum tanti redimere. Sed nunc vbi integra Christi confitendi libertas permittitur, nulla est causa cur fe eximat. Quòd autem ministerij fui parte aliqua priuatur, tamen fi dolenter ferendum est, non tamen ideo in totum liberata est eius fides erga Ecclesiam: sicut nec penitus abdicatus est suo munere. Nam fi Pastoris munus omni ex parte explere nequeat, magnū tamen est, fi Doctorem præstet. Et cum Sacramenta veluti accessiones verbi sint, illis sublatis verbum etiam cuius præcipuę sunt partes vltrò abiicere, nimis absurdum eflet. Prudenter itaque verandi fratres nostri Ecclesiæ Argentinenfis Pastores admonent, Ecclesiam ad tempus foueri verbo posse, vtcunque Sacramentis careat. Si Toffino hactenus nulla cum Ecclesia Monfbelgardenfi necessitudo fuisset, magnopere illi optandum foret, vt ad liberum docendi munus, nullo adhuc concesso Sacramentorum vsu admitteretur. Imo suum illic Ministerium hac ratione auspicatus est, & aliquandiu Doctoris personam sustinuit, priusquam obtineret quæcunque sunt ex Pastoris officio. Nunc quia potestas tenebrarum eovsque inualuit, vt per suos eripiat Satan, quod hactenus habuit Christi beneficio, quid fuperefi nisi vt ad priorem illum cursum redeat, fideleque in docendo & monendo operam impendat, donec quæ nunc collapsa sunt, rursum Dominus instauret? Olim cum tyrannorum sæuitia expulsi effent ex suis Ecclesiis sancti Pastores, clam tamen eas visitabat, ac interdum etiam habitu militari, vt refert Eusebius. Quare hæc facultas quæ Tofli no datur, multò minus repudianda est, vt quibus hactenus fuit Pastor, nunc fe Doctorem exhibeat. Ita munus obibit Deo probatum, & Ecclesiæ salutare, vtcunque dimidia parsfolitæ administrationis fit ablata. Huc pertinet Prophetarum exempla, qui templo euerso, & erepto ad tempus fa-crificandi ritu, docendi tamen partes exequi non defiterunt. Hæc fuit quidem ipsorum querimonia, Quomodo cantabimus canticum Domini in terra aliena? cum tamen hoc populo carmen dictarent, ita obibant docendi munus. Ita vbi violenter spoliamur Sacramentorum vsu, adeo nō debet Pastor relicta statione abiicere docendi curam, vt hic maxime instare debeat, & quodammodo docendi studium & assiduitatem duplicare, si liceat. Sic ergo statuimus. Dum ita priuatur Toffanus Sacramentorum ministerio, vt tamen Illustriss. Princeps docendi locum illi offerat, & populus flagitet eius operam: non esse hoc genus missionis, quod fidem eius liberet, quin Doctoris officio incumbere debeat, quandiu docendi libertas illi concessa fuerit. Nec tantum iudicamus hoc expedire, sed etiam omnino necessarium ducimus, nisi à Dei vocatione cui hactenus paruit, subducere se volet. A quo consilio quia certò persuasi sumus eum toto animo abhorrere, non difficulter adductum iri confidimus vt maneat. Porrò quod timet, ne improbi iactent ventris potius cura retineri eum, quàm aedificandę Ecclesiae studio, ea sane suspicio quātum in nobis est, sedulò est cauenda. Verùm si eum adstrictū tenet iustæ vocationis Religio, sicuti nos sentimus, qualisacunque futura sit hominum opinio: constanter tamen pergere in eo debet, quod intelligit Deo probari. Nos quidem satis experimur quanta sit seculi nostri ingratitudo. Quanquam hoc quoque incōmodum senserunt omnes Dei serui, vt benefaciendo male au dirent. Sed hodie magis quàm aliàs vnquam regnat hoc vitium. Itaque non debet expectare frater noster Toffanus, vt omnibus probet ¶ summa Religione instituerit, etiam si nullum mortis periculum recusct. Erunt semper ignaui & nihili hominȩs, qui dēsidiæ suę ʿtedium fallent eum calumniando. Nec verò, si ædificandæ Ecclesiæ occasionem sibi oblatam non repuit, ideo se difiun git à fratribus suis, qui ea priuantur. Quin potius eum hortari fratres debent, ne quod residuum st lucis, patiatur sua culpa extingui. Hoc enim seruos Christi decet, quò magis os sibi obstruendum videant, studere modis omnibus atque adniti, vt in aliorum linguis resonet pura Euangelij doctrina, & eorum voce ipsorum silentium quasi farciatur. Nunc Deum oremus, vt quemadmodum fi delíter cōfulimus fratri nostro Toffano, quod arbitramur ex re Ecclesiæ esse, vt eius animū confirmet ad subeunda fortiter certamina quæ illi proposita esse cernimus. Non miramur si in rebus tam impeditis animo perplexus hæreat. Nō miramur etiam, si in hac subita Ecclesiæ dissipatione, varię eum cogitationes agitent. Non miramur postremò, si in hac temporum iniquitate, tamque peruersis ac malignis hominū iudiciis æstuat atque alternat in hac deliberatione, lum satisfacere omnibus cupit. Sed illi gratulamur, quòd suas omnes cogitationes, omniaq; studia in vnum hunc finem dirigit,primùm vt Deo obsequatur, deinde vt se totum Ecclesiæ impendat.Hoc singulare est Dei donum,quòd nihil aliud speɛtat vel cupit,quàm vt conscientiæ suæ tranquillitati sit consultum. Quòd autem sibi proprióque iudicio diffidens,fratrum consiliis permittit se regendum, in eo pia ipsius modestiam, vt par est exosculamur. Et nos certè hic non aliud secuti sumus,quàm quod Dominus ipse Spiritu verbóque suo dictauit: quemadmodum hunc sumus auspicati, vt mentes linguásque nostras gubernaret. Atque huius modestiæ fructum vt speramus, non pœnitendum feret, quòd vocationis suæ certior factus,ad sustinendos quosuis impulsus lögè erit instructior: & fretus piorum auctoritate,minus erit obnoxius calumniis im proborum.Infirmis certè satisfactum erit vbi intellexerint,ideo stetisse ipsum in sua Ecclesia, vt fratrum consiliis acquiescerent. Iam præter Ecclesiæ respectum,nos quàm plurimum mouet cor datissimi Principis Religio,quem sic videmus affectum, vt nihil omittat, quò saltem pars aliqua regni Christi salua in ipsius ditione maneat. Hæc heroica animi magnitudo, cùm illi cœlitus data sit, eam pro sua virili adiuuare Tossani officium est. Nos quoque breui fore speramus,vt viam aliquam per quæcunq; ob stacula inueniat Dei benedictio,ad promouendum tam præclari instituti cursum,ne successu tandem careat.Geneuę,x i.Calend. Martij. M. D. XLIX.
units.tr: Whoever yields and deserts his post willingly is like a traitor; but it is not for us to resist when we are compelled by force, unless the Church should call us by name to face the danger. Your case, however, is quite different. As long as you were pastors, your diligence and care did not fail the flock. Now that the wish to persevere would be of no use, and the sheep to whom your faith is bound might judge it not useful for you to go further, you are certainly excused. If this exception is accepted, the earlier difficulty is resolved. Tossanus's work is demanded both by the most illustrious Prince Christoph and by the common people themselves. Therefore, as long as he has a Church he can serve, it does not seem right, nor consistent with his duty, for him to abandon it. If he were to keep his place on condition that a wicked bargain, as many others have made, diminished his freedom to teach purely and sincerely, he ought to prefer a hundred deaths to buying the right to speak at such a price. But now, when full freedom to confess Christ is granted, there is no reason why he should withdraw. That he is deprived of some part of his ministry is, however grievous, no reason for his faith towards the Church to be wholly released, any more than he has been completely stripped of his office. For if he cannot fulfil every part of the pastor's office, it is still a great thing if he provides the teacher's. And since the Sacraments are, as it were, additions to the Word, it would be far too absurd to cast away the Word itself, of which they are the chief parts, merely because the Sacraments are taken away. Accordingly, our wise brothers, the pastors of the Church of Strasbourg, rightly advise that a Church can for a time be sustained by the Word, however much it may lack the Sacraments. If Tossanus had had no bond with the Church of Montbéliard until now, it would be greatly to be wished for him to be admitted to the free office of teaching, even without any use yet granted of the Sacraments. Indeed, he began his ministry there in this way, and for some time sustained the person of a teacher before he obtained whatever belongs to the pastor's office. Now, since the power of darkness has prevailed so far that Satan, through his agents, snatches away what he had until now by the grace of Christ, what remains but that he should return to that former course, and labour faithfully in teaching and admonishing, until the Lord restores what has now fallen? Long ago, when holy pastors were driven from their Churches by the savagery of tyrants, they nevertheless visited them secretly, and sometimes even in military dress, as Eusebius reports. Therefore this opportunity which is given to Tossanus must be all the less rejected: since he has been a pastor to them until now, he should now present himself as a teacher. In this way he will discharge a office approved by God and salutary for the Church, even though half of the customary administration has been taken away. To this belong the examples of the Prophets, who, when the Temple had been overthrown and the ritual of sacrificing had been taken away for a time, did not cease to carry out the duty of teaching. Indeed this was their complaint: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a strange land?" Yet while they dictated this song to the people, they thus discharged the office of teaching. So when we are violently deprived of the use of the Sacraments, a pastor ought not to abandon his post and give up the care of teaching; rather he ought especially to press on, and in some way, if it be lawful, double his zeal and assiduity in teaching. So we determine this. While Tossanus is deprived of the ministry of the Sacraments, yet the most illustrious Prince offers him a place of teaching, and the people demand his work, this is not the kind of dismissal that releases his faith, so that he ought not to devote himself to the duty of teaching for as long as the freedom to teach has been granted to him. We judge this not only to be expedient, but we also consider it wholly necessary, unless he wishes to withdraw from the calling of God which he has obeyed until now. Since we are firmly persuaded that he utterly abhors such a plan, we trust he will without difficulty be brought to remain. Moreover, as for his fear that wicked men will boast that he is kept back by concern for his belly rather than by zeal for building up the Church, such a suspicion must certainly be carefully guarded against, as far as lies in us. But if the obligation of a lawful calling holds him fast, as we think it does, then, whatever the opinion of men may be, he ought steadfastly to persist in what he understands to be approved by God. We indeed learn well enough by experience how great is the ingratitude of our age. Yet all the servants of God have felt this inconvenience too, that by doing good they are ill spoken of. But today this vice reigns more than it ever has. Therefore our brother Tossanus should not expect that he will prove to everyone that he has acted with the greatest piety, even if he refuses no danger of death. There will always be idle and worthless men who, by slandering him, will cover up the weariness of their own sloth. Nor indeed, if he does not reject the opportunity offered him to build up the Church, does this mean he is separating himself from his brothers, who are deprived of it. Rather, the brothers ought to exhort him not to allow, through his own fault, whatever light remains to be extinguished. For it befits the servants of Christ, so that they may see their own mouths being stopped the more, to strive and labour by every means that the pure doctrine of the Gospel may resound in the tongues of others, and that by their voice their own silence may, as it were, be made good. Now let us pray to God that, just as we have faithfully advised our brother Tossanus, which we think is for the good of the Church, he may strengthen his spirit to bear bravely the struggles which we see are set before him. We do not wonder if in such difficult circumstances his mind hangs in perplexity. Nor do we wonder if, in this sudden dispersion of the Church, various thoughts stir him. Nor, finally, do we wonder if in this iniquity of the times, and amid such perverse and malicious judgments of men, he wavers and goes back and forth in this deliberation, while he longs to satisfy everyone. But we congratulate him that he directs all his thoughts and all his efforts to this one end: first, that he may obey God, and then that he may devote himself wholly to the Church. This is a singular gift of God, that he seeks and desires nothing else than that the tranquillity of his conscience be cared for. As for his submitting himself to the counsels of the brothers, distrusting his own judgment and his own opinion, we kiss his pious modesty, as is right. And indeed we have followed nothing else here than what the Lord himself dictated by his Spirit and his Word, just as we began this in order that he might govern our minds and tongues. And we hope that the fruit of this modesty will not bring him any regret: having been made more certain of his calling, he will be better equipped to withstand whatever assaults come, and, relying on the authority of the godly, he will be less exposed to the slanders of the wicked. Certainly the weak will be satisfied when they understand that he has stood firm in his Church for this reason, that he might acquiesce in the counsels of the brothers. Moreover, apart from regard for the Church, we are greatly moved by the religion of that most worthy Prince, whom we see so disposed that he omits nothing by which at least some part of Christ's kingdom may remain safe in his dominion. Since such heroic greatness of spirit has been given to him from heaven, it is the duty of Tossanus to help it to the best of his strength. We also hope that before long the blessing of God will find some way, through whatever obstacles, to advance the course of so noble an undertaking, so that it may not in the end lack success. Geneva, 19th February 1549.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO S.
units.tr: BUCER TO CALVIN, GREETING.

units.la: Sanete salus nostra Iesus Christus.Nam hic Ecclesiæ tue alūnus dixit te cum istinc discederet,cum duo morbo fuisse cōflictatum. Nos verò multò perniciosiore capitum & membrorum nostrorum maximæ partis malo consicimur incredulitatis.Eò enim hominum metus,Dei reuerentiam hic exclusit, vt Episcopo permissum sit Religionem Christi Interimicæ commutare. Et huic atque Imperatori promissum, dandam operam possibilem, ne quid hic doceatur contra Interim : Idque vt nos verbi Ministri præstemus, à nobis petierat, atque etiam nobis mandarunt:ad un to tamen si qui id non possent aut nollent,vt causas huius ipsis exponerent. Hoc factum est: causas reddidimus omnes curæ pastorali deseruientes,cur religiosum nobis sit non reprehendere manifestas doctrinæ Christianæ & Sacramentorum corruptelas:maximè cùm hic Papistæ restituti sint,verbis & factis pro omni virili sua hominibus commendaturi, & obtrusuri,tandemque etiam imperaturi. Qui Remp.administrant, statuerunt se non posse hic plus recipere purę Religionis,quam Imperator velit concedere,vel tolerare.Interea misit Episcopus huc,&c
units.tr: Holy Jesus Christ, our salvation. For this foster-son of your Church told me, when he left there, that you had been struggling with a twofold illness. We, however, are afflicted by a far more destructive evil, the unbelief of most of our heads and members. Fear of men has so shut out the reverence of God here that the bishop has been permitted to change the religion of Christ into the Interim. He also promised this to the Emperor, that every possible effort would be made to ensure nothing is taught here contrary to the Interim. He asked us, the ministers of the Word, to guarantee this, and has also ordered us to do so. But if any of us could not or would not, they were to set out their reasons to him. This has been done. We have given all our reasons, as those committed to pastoral care, why it is a religious duty for us not to fail to denounce the plain corruptions of Christian doctrine and the sacraments, especially since the Papists have been restored here, who will commend them to people by word and deed with all their strength, and force them upon them, and finally even command them. Those who administer the commonwealth have decided that they cannot here allow more of pure religion than the Emperor is willing to concede or tolerate. Meanwhile the bishop sent here,

units.la: huc,& petiit à collegiis,heri à nostro vt omnia iuxta Interim re-ftituamus, & statim respondeamus, quomodo, qua ratione, & quando id velimus præstare.Sc in iis quç omnino non aduerfan tur suo muneri & iuramento (ficilli suo Romano cauent fidelius,quàm nos nostro cœlesti Domino) nobis adfuturum. Reliqua tolerantur. Quç ista?vt vxores retineant qui habent,& Eucharistiam totam dispensent. Verùm vt ne reprehendant qui eâ dispensant,aut sumunt dimidiam. Nofti autem scholam totam sustineri à nostro collegio.Collegia petierunt spatium deliberandi per mensem. Dimidius mensis concessus est. Tantillo igitur tempore feretur hic pura Religionis administratio. Et à nobis expectatur,vt Imperator iubeat nos, dum ei obtemperemus,detineri. Vrit enim indubie desolatio Ecclesiarum tanta, non qui eius auctores sunt : nam hi per fefanç doctrinæ Christi hostes sunt. Tantum tenent nos fufpitia & lacrymæ sanctorum, quorum ingens adhuc hic numerus est, ne priusquam iubeamur, hinc nos moueamus. Obsignare enim non abrumpere miniflerium nostrum,fi vel it Dominus,optamus. Videsvt res nostræ habeant, & quàm opus fit, vt vestris miserrimam hanc Ecclesiam, & nos precibus adiuuetis. Quò fi id concedatur, euolare, vel vbi primum debemus,nondum liquet. Si dabitur,spero Dominum id quoque cöceffurum, vtibi coràm valedicam,priusquam profugiam longius. Manet enim certè nos sæua persecutio,& est iam horribilis Ecclesiarum vastatio: nec enim possunt Episcopi suis Ecclesiis Ministros, quanquam quoslibet admittant, imò conquirant, inuenire. Spirenfis capularis Episcopus iam decreuit ad remos quicunque nolintex nostris suæ ministe-ria r tinere,& ad Interim conformare. Non autem huic, nec tot huiusmodi Filij Dei hostibus,sed ipsi suo Filio Pater tradidit potestatem omnem in cœlo & in terra. Hicque Pastor noster bonus est,qui suas oues facilè tuebitur suo brachio,suáque virga & baculo:vt nec quicquam eis boni defit,nec noceat mali aliquid. Is velit nos hoc ipso suo baculo & virga sic consolari,ne etiam mali quicquam metuamus. Id nobis & vos precemini.& dum potes scribas. Etiamsi enim hic non fuero, mei tamen hic erunt,& mittent ad me quç scribes. Dominus Iesus maneat apud vos firmius, quàm retineamus eum hic: quod faciet cùm dabit doctrinam suam vinculis disciplinæ suæ in animis alligari.x x. Februarij. M. D. X L I X. Vxor mea tibi salutem precatur. Idem faciunt Collegæ.
units.tr: Here he asked the colleges, yesterday, on our behalf, that we restore everything according to the Interim, and reply at once how, by what means, and when we are willing to do so. And in those matters which do not at all conflict with his office and oath (they guard their Roman one more faithfully than we guard our heavenly Lord), he will stand by us. The rest is tolerated. What are these? That those who have wives may keep them, and that they may distribute the whole Eucharist. But that they should not reprove those who distribute it, or those who take only half. You know that the whole school is supported by our college. The colleges asked for a space of a month to deliberate, and half a month was granted. So the pure administration of religion will be carried on here for such a short time. And it is expected of us that the Emperor orders us to be detained, while we obey him. For the desolation of the Churches will certainly burn, though not on those who are its authors, for they are enemies of the sound doctrine of Christ. Only the suspicions and tears of the saints hold us back, and their number here is still huge, so that we do not move from here before we are ordered to. For we wish to seal our ministry, not to break it off, if the Lord so wills. You see how our affairs stand, and how much need there is for you to help this most wretched Church and us with your prayers. If that is granted, where we should flee as soon as we are able is not yet clear. If it is granted, I hope the Lord will also grant that I may bid you farewell in person before I flee further. For a savage persecution certainly awaits us, and the horrible devastation of the Churches is already upon us. The bishops cannot find ministers for their churches, though they admit whomever they can, indeed they search them out. The Bishop of Speyer has already decreed that whoever will not hold their ministries from ours shall be sent to the galleys and conformed to the Interim. But the Father has given all power in heaven and on earth not to him, nor to so many enemies of this kind of Son of God, but to his own Son. And this Shepherd of ours is good, who will easily protect his sheep with his arm, with his rod and staff, so that nothing good is lacking to them and no evil harms them. May he wish to console us with this very rod and staff, so that we fear no evil. Pray this for us, and you may write while you can. For even if I am not here, my people will be here, and they will send me what you write. May the Lord Jesus remain with you more firmly than we hold him here, which he will do when he binds his doctrine in men's minds with the chains of his discipline. 20 February 1549. My wife sends you her greetings. My colleagues do the same.

units.la: Tuus Bucerus.
units.tr: Yours, Bucer.

units.la: TAmetsi valde mihi acerba fuit mors vxoris: mœrorem tamen meum, quoad possum, cohibeo. Et amici certatim officium faciunt. Me quidem & illos minus proficere fateor. quàm optandū sit: hoc tamen ipsum quod cōsequor, dici vix potest, quantùm me iuuet. Nosti animi mei tenacitudine, vel molli tempotius. Quare nisi valida moderatio adhibita fuisset, nō ita hactenus steti sem. Et certè non vulgaris est doloris materia. Priuatus sum optima socia vitæ: quæ, si quid accidisset durius, non exilij tantum ac inopiæ voluntaria comes, sed mortis quoq; futura erat. Quoad vixit, fida quidem ministerij mei adiutrix fuit. Ab ea nec minimum quidem impedimentum vnquam sensi. Atque vt de se nunquam fuit anxia, sic de liberis, toto morbi decursu, nunquam mihi molesta fuit. Quia timebam ne intus curam premendo se frustra cruciaret, triduo ante mortem, ego mentionem vitro iniecti, promisique me partibus meis nō defuturum. Excepit illa protinus. Iam eos commendaui Domino. Cum dicerem, id non obstare, quominus & mihi curæ esset, respondit: Scio te non neglecturum quod scias Domino commendatum esse. Heri quoque primum resciui, cum instaret quædam mulier, vt mecum de illis ageret, præcisè ita loquutam esse; hoc vero præcipuum est, vti pie sanctèque viuant. Maritus meus vrgedus non est, vt eos in casta disciplina & timore Dei instituat. Si pij erunt, confido illis sponte fore patrem: sin alij, indigni sunt pro quibus à me rogetur. Hæc animi magnitudo plus apud me valet quàm centum commendationes. De amica tua consolatione magnam tibi habeo gratiam. Vale, optime & integerrime frater. Dominus Iesus te cum vxore tueatur, ac gubernet. Illi & fratribus plurimam salutem dices meo nomine. VII. Aprilis. M. D. XLIX. Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Although the death of my wife has been very bitter to me, I restrain my grief as far as I can, and my friends compete in offering their services. I admit that I and they accomplish less than is to be wished, yet what I achieve, even this, can hardly be told how much it helps me. You know the stubbornness of my spirit, or rather its tenderness. Therefore, had not a strong self-control been applied, I would not have held out so far. And certainly the matter of my grief is no ordinary one. I am bereft of an excellent companion in life, who, had anything harder befallen, would have been not only a voluntary companion in exile and poverty, but would also have been one in death. As long as she lived she was indeed a faithful helper in my ministry, and I never felt the least hindrance from her. And just as she was never anxious about herself, so, throughout the whole course of her illness, she was never troublesome to me about the children. Because I feared that she, by keeping her care to herself, would torment herself to no purpose, three days before her death I myself mentioned the matter and promised that I would not fail in my part. She took it up at once: "I have already commended them to the Lord." When I said that this did not prevent me from caring for them too, she replied: "I know you will not neglect what you know has been committed to the Lord." Only yesterday did I first learn, when a certain woman pressed her to discuss them with me, that she had said precisely this: "But the chief thing is that they live piously and holily. My husband need not be urged to bring them up in chaste discipline and the fear of God. If they are godly, I trust he will be a father to them of his own accord; but if they are otherwise, they are unworthy that I should ask him on their behalf." This greatness of spirit means more to me than a hundred commendations. I am very grateful to you for your friendly consolation. Farewell, best and most upright brother. May the Lord Jesus keep and guide you and your wife. Give my warmest greetings in my name to her and to the brothers. 7 April 1549. Your John Calvin.

units.la: VIRETVS CALVINO. S.
units.tr: Viret to Calvin. Greetings.

units.la: QVæ mihi vno mul orum ore, eorumq; grauiss. testium, de tui animi constantia ac fortitudine nunciantur, in hoc tam acerbo familiæ tuæ vulnere, luctuque domestico, faciunt vt mihi apud te opus esse gratulatoriis quàm consolatoriis literis potius exiftim: m, atque eò magis, quò penitius noui animi tui, vt ipse appellas, tenerit udinem. Hoc enim potius nomine, quàm molliti ici, esse appellandam censeo. Nam id neutiquam mollis animi opus est, quod præstas. Quò fit vt magis mirer vim in te agentem diuini illius Spiritus, qui se verè consolatoris dignum cognocognomine, in te palam facit. Annon merito illius in te vim agnoscam, tam forti ferente animo domesticos casus, quibus nihil tibi acerbius priuatim contingere potuit aut propius attinge re, qui ad alienas calamitates ita commoueri soleas, earumque sensu haud secus afficiare, atque si tua ipsius res ageretur? Non est vulgaris, crede mihi, haec tua virtus, neque vulgare testimonium diuinae erga te beneuolentiae. Quo fit vt me mei vehementer pudeat, quod olim in consimili casu, non praestiterim eandem animi fortitudinem, aut saltem vmbram ipsius sim aliquâ assequutus. Adeò totus abiectus & prostratus fui eo calamitatis telo, vt totus orbis nihil mihi nisi mera solitudo videretur. Nihil erat suaue, nihil quod animi dolorem lenire posset. Ego me frequenter apud memetipsum accusabam, quòd mihi mollius longè ferre viderer meum dolorem, quàm deceret, non dico câ duntaxat personam quam sustineo, sed virum qui vel à primo limine philosophiam illam caelestem saluutarit, cuius me non solùm discipulum, sed aliorum doctorem profitebar, quòdque iis nescirem, in illo meo morbo, remediis vti, quae aliis suppeditare soleo, quos iis video indigere. Tu verò contrà, tantùm abest vt frangaris debili erisque animo, vt potius caeteros longè reddas tuo exemplo fortiores, quando quod aliis praecipere consueuisti, te quoque facere posse testaris, vtpote qui non solùm cùm valeas, noris certa aegrotis consilia dare, sed ab iis quoque æger remedia petere, ac idem sentire quod valens & sanus. Mirificè & incredibiliter me recrearunt, non inanes tantùm rumores, sed tam multi nuncij, qui narrarunt te tam infracto pectore, actam dextrè, imò & foelicius quàm hactenus vnquam omnia procurasse quę tui sunt officij, ac tam vbique semper fuisse praesenti animo in conuentibus, vestris, in concionibus, in omnibus denique negotiis cùm priuatis tum publicis, vt omnes magna coepit admiratio, idque eo potissimum tempore, quo recentior ac proindè acerbior tuum animum dolor lancinare ac prosternere debuit. Perge igitur quò coepisti pede, ac tu te ira gerito, vt hanc omnibus de te confirmes opinionem, hoc luctu adeò de sua sen animum non deturbari tuum, quin semper tibi adsit praesentissimè: neque sic te dolore impediri, quin ea omnia facilè perspicias, quę ad te consolandum aliquid possunt habere momenti. Hoc autem vt efficias, vtque subinde constantius in hoc perseueres propositò, & magis atque magis confirmere, maiùsque in dies percipias solatium, ardentissimis votis Dominum exposco. Quid enim aliud conferre possum? Nam neque tanta est mea auctoritas, neque tam acuta ratio, quibus te à maerore luctúque deterrere possim, autreuocare, nisi hoc tibi sua spon te sua suppeditaret institutio, & confirmatus in ferenda cruce animus, & diuinæ bonitatis exuberantissimus in te fauor, cuius reliqua omnia munera sunt, quibus te affatim Dominus cumulauit. Quamobrem non ero hac in parte longior. Quin potius metuo ne hæc nimis sint apud te multa. Salutat te vxor officiosissime, quæ non vulgarem concepit dolorem ex charissimæ sororis obitu, quæ mecum eam calamitatem nobis omnibus communem exististi mat. Mihi vehementer dolet, quod mihi non datur tuo præsenti frui conspectu. Quæcunque me rationes impediant, si te cupere intellexero, crede mihi, tua soluis voluntas, omnes difficultates, vt superem facile efficiet. Salutant te Collegæ & reliqui omnes fratres officiosissime, inter quos & Francisci um Viuiacensem annumera, qui nunc hic est, & qui tibi suo nomine salutem quoque adscribi iussit. Saluta domesticos & reliquos amicos nostros, meo præsertim nomine Gallasium, Bezam, Ottomannum: cui & Franciscus salutem dicit. Vale. Laufannæ. x. Aprilis. M. D. XLIX.
