units.tr: What is reported to me, in one voice by many and most weighty witnesses, about the constancy and courage of your spirit under this so bitter wound and domestic sorrow to your family, makes me think that I have more need to write to you with congratulations than with consolation. This is especially so because I know more intimately the tenderness of your heart, as you yourself call it. For I think it should be named tenderness rather than softness, since what you show is by no means the work of a soft spirit. So I marvel all the more at the power of that divine Spirit working in you, who makes himself plainly visible in you as a truly consoling Spirit. Should I not rightly recognise his power in you, when you bear domestic misfortunes with such a brave spirit, though nothing could have come to you more bitterly or closer to home in private, you who are usually so moved by other people's calamities and feel them no less than if your own affairs were at stake? Believe me, this virtue of yours is not common, nor is it an ordinary sign of God's goodwill towards you. Therefore I am deeply ashamed of myself, because in a similar case long ago I did not show the same courage of spirit, or at least did not reach even a shadow of it. I was so utterly cast down and prostrated by that blow of misfortune that the whole world seemed to me nothing but bare desolation. Nothing was sweet, nothing could soothe the pain of my spirit. I often accused myself inwardly that I seemed to bear my grief far too softly, not to say unbecoming the part I play, but unbecoming a man who from the very threshold had taught that heavenly philosophy, whose pupil I professed myself, and not only that but a teacher of others; and that in that sickness of mine I did not know how to use the remedies that I usually supply to others, whom I see in need of them. You, on the contrary, are so far from being broken or weakened in spirit that you rather make all the others far braver by your example, since you testify that you can do what you are accustomed to advise others to do. For you not only, while in health, know how to give sure counsel to the sick, but when sick you also ask for remedies from them, and feel the same as one who is well and sound. I was wonderfully and incredibly refreshed, not only by empty rumours but by so many messengers who reported that with so unbroken a heart you have carried out all your duties more skilfully and even more happily than ever before, and that you have always been so ready and present in spirit everywhere, in your meetings, in your sermons, and finally in all business, both private and public, that everyone has begun to marvel, and this especially at the very time when your sorrow, fresher and therefore more painful, ought to have been tearing at your heart and laying you low. So go on as you have begun, and bear yourself in such a way that you confirm this opinion of you in everyone's eyes: that your spirit is not so shaken by this grief as to fail to be fully present to yourself, nor so hindered by sorrow that you cannot clearly see all that might have some weight in consoling you. To bring this about, and so that you may persevere ever more steadfastly in this purpose and be increasingly strengthened and daily receive greater comfort, I pray to the Lord with my most ardent wishes. For what else can I contribute? My authority is not so great, nor my reasoning so keen, that I could turn you back from grief and sorrow, unless your own instruction, a spirit strengthened to bear the cross, and the most abundant favour of divine goodness towards you, of which all the rest are gifts, supplied this for you, and with which the Lord has heaped you full. Therefore I will not be longer on this point. Rather I fear that these things are already too many for you. Your wife greets you most dutifully; she has conceived no ordinary grief at the death of her dearest sister, a calamity which has become common to all of us along with me. It grieves me greatly that I am not allowed to enjoy the sight of you in person. Whatever reasons prevent me, if I understand that you desire it, believe me, your wish alone will make it easy for me to overcome all difficulties. Your colleagues and all the other brothers greet you most dutifully, among whom please count Francis of Vivier, who is here now, and who has asked that greetings also be added to you in his name. Greet your household and our other friends, especially in my name Gallasius, Beza, and Ottomannus, to whom Francis also sends greetings. Farewell. Lausanne, 10 April 1549.

units.la: Tuus Petrus Viretus.
units.tr: Yours, Peter Viret.

units.la: CALVINVS ZOZINO S.
units.tr: Calvin to Zozinus, Greeting

units.la: LIteras tuas paucis post reditum meum diebus accepi. Ex eo tempore catharrus mihi valde fuit inf. stus: necdum molestiam exhibere desinit. Vt breuiter ad quæstiones tuas respondeam. Cum vxor non alia lege ducenda sit homini Christiano, nisi vt sei illi ad omnia piæ vitæ officia adiutricem præstet ac sociam, vbi ab hoc scopo vel minimum aberratur, non dubito quin vitiosum sit coniugium. Is porro qui vxorem ducit impiis Papatus superstitionibus adhuc implicitam, quid aliud quàm prophanationem in domum suam inducit? Nam si corpus viri est vxor, excusari certe non potest, qui mulieri se adiungit quotidie ad peruersos cultus se prostituenti, vt ipse quodammodo dimidia sui parte inquinetur. Superstitioso dicere, quod si quis talem ducat vxorem, consecrare magicis auspiciis nuptias cogetur. Cæterum puellam alioqui recte sentientem, quæ tamen carnis metu in idololatriæ simulatione detinetur, prorsus cum religionis hoste conferre non ausim. Quanto enim quisque est alienior à Christo, ab eo nos quoque magis abhorrere decet. Quam autem mihi describis, certum est à professis hostibus longo interuallo distare. Qui ad Baptismum Papalem tot prauis superstitionibus fœdatum, liberos suos offert, culpa non vacat. Atque id, ni fallor, inter incommoda recito, quibus pij homines stimulari debent ad migrandum. At Melachthon & Martyr non prohibent: modo detestetur ille quisquis erit, quæ pugnant cum Christi institutione. In eo nihil esset absurdi: nisi quod ad certam mortem paratum esse oportet, qui hoc audebit. Et tamen sic eorum, quos nominas, respofa probo, vt in singulis partibus non subscribam. Lusoriam Baptismi imitationem pro mero ludibrio, vt est, habendam censeo. Baptismus tamen Papistarum, vtcunque mille ludibriis scateat, efficaciam suam retinet: quatenus in hunc finem administratur, vtex Christi mandato recipiant fidelium liberi signum adoptionis. Video enim Circuncisionem multis superstitionibus vitiatam, nihilominus pro gratiae symbolo habitam fuisse. Quod obiicis in conuentu piorum, debere Baptismum celebrari, non obstat, quominus in idololatrarum coetu administratus, valeat. Nacum docemus quid fieri deceat, vt purus sit Baptismus omnique inquinamento vacuus, non abolemus Dei institutionem, etiamsi eam idololatrae corrumpant. Porro inter illas Papalis Baptismi corruptelas, manet aliquid Dei proprium. Deinde sic Papistis detrahimus Ecclesiae nomen, vt tamen illic quasdam manere reliquias Ecclesiae, non negemus. Certe cum Iosias & Ezechias ex toto Israele colligerent qui defecerant a Domino, ad alteram Circuncisionem eos minime vocarunt. Et cum templum ipsum variis sacrilegiis pollutum foret, Circuncisio tamen valere non desiit. Ergo vtcunque eos pecare dicam, qui illic suos liberos ad Baptismum offerunt: non tamen Baptismum protinus nullum esse sentio, in quo nota aliqua diuinae institutionis, etsi multis alioqui maculis foedata apparet. Qui ab externa idololatriae professione non abstinent, non audeo simpliciter damnare, etiamsi fidem suam dissimulent periculorum metu. Nam cum videamus pios qui inter persequutiones latuerunt, probatos fuisse Deo, plus a nobis exigi fas non est. Neque tamen is sum qui torpori eorum indulgeam. Quin potius hortabor, vt in omnes profitendę sux fidei occasiones intenti sint: neque impiorum apertas in Deum blasphemias sic taciti audiant, vt annuere videantur. Legem tamen imponere non audeo, quatenus progredi necesse habeant. Qui vero interim dum sacra peraguntur, in tepis animi gratia obambulant, quoscunque praetextus obtendant, nullam excusationem merentur. Pręquam enim quod ipsa delectatio quam ex tali spectaculo capiunt, parum eos Dei probris affici ostendit: in hanc offensionem temere incurrunt apud multos, quasi religionis potius quàm superstitionis contemptu id faciant. Quare hanc licentiam merito improbo, quae cum a simulatione idololatriae non multum distat, tum prophanum nescio quid magis, quàm Christianum sapit. Vltima quaestio de carnis resurrectione quam tibi a me expediri cantopere desideras, etsi apud me non multum habeat difficultatis, plus tamen temporis & operae requiritur. Colligedi enim
units.tr: I received your letter a few days after my return. Since then a catarrh has been very troublesome to me, and it has not yet stopped troubling me. To answer your questions briefly: since a Christian man ought to take a wife on no other condition than that she be a helper and companion to him in all the duties of a godly life, I do not doubt that a marriage is faulty where there is even the slightest departure from this aim. Moreover, the man who takes as his wife a woman still entangled in the impious superstitions of the Papacy, what else does he bring into his house but profanation? For if the wife is the body of the man, he certainly cannot be excused who joins himself to a woman who daily prostitutes herself to perverse worship, so that he is in some measure defiled in half of himself. One might say to a superstitious person that if anyone takes such a wife, he will be compelled to consecrate the marriage with magical rites. But a girl who otherwise thinks rightly, yet is held back by fear of the flesh from feigning idolatry, I would by no means dare to compare with an open enemy of religion. For the further anyone is from Christ, the more we ought to abhor him. The case you describe is certainly far removed from that of professed enemies. He who offers his children to Papal baptism, defiled by so many wicked superstitions, is not free from fault. And I count this, unless I am mistaken, among the disadvantages by which godly men ought to be spurred to migrate. But Melanchthon and Martyr do not forbid it, provided that whoever it is detests what conflicts with Christ's institution. In this there would be nothing absurd, except that whoever dares it must be prepared for certain death. Yet I approve of the answers of those you name in such a way that I do not subscribe to every part of them. I think the sportive imitation of baptism should be regarded as mere mockery, as it is. Nevertheless the baptism of the Papists, however full of a thousand mockeries it may be, retains its efficacy, insofar as it is administered for this end: that by Christ's command the children of believers receive the sign of adoption. For I see that circumcision, though it was vitiated by many superstitions, was nonetheless regarded as a symbol of grace. That you object that baptism ought to be celebrated in an assembly of the godly does not prevent it from being valid when administered in an assembly of idolaters. When we teach what ought to be done so that baptism may be pure and free from all pollution, we do not abolish God's institution, even though idolaters corrupt it. Moreover, among those corruptions of Papal baptism, something of God's own remains. Again, we so deny the name of Church to the Papists that we do not deny that some remnants of the Church remain there. Certainly when Josiah and Hezekiah gathered from all Israel those who had fallen away from the Lord, they by no means called them to a second circumcision. And when the temple itself had been polluted by various sacrileges, circumcision nevertheless did not cease to be valid. Therefore, however much I say that those sin who there offer their children to baptism, I do not judge that baptism is altogether null, in which some mark of divine institution appears, though otherwise stained with many blemishes. Those who do not abstain from outward profession of idolatry I do not dare simply to condemn, even if they conceal their faith for fear of dangers. For since we see that the godly who lay hidden during persecutions were approved by God, it is not right to demand more of them than that. Nor am I one who would indulge their sluggishness. Rather I would exhort them to be intent on every occasion of professing their faith, and not to hear the open blasphemies of the impious against God so silently that they seem to assent. Yet I do not dare to impose a law as to how far they must go. But those who, while the sacred rites are performed, stroll about with a lukewarm spirit, whatever pretexts they put forward, deserve no excuse. For the very pleasure they take in such a spectacle shows how little they are moved by reproaches against God; they rashly incur offence in the eyes of many, as if they did it out of contempt for religion rather than superstition. Wherefore I rightly condemn this licence, which, since it is not far from feigning idolatry, savours of something profane rather than Christian. The last question, concerning the resurrection of the flesh, which you earnestly desire me to settle for you, though it presents me with not much difficulty, nevertheless requires more time and effort. For many passages of Scripture that pertain to that matter would have to be gathered and carefully explained, if the subject were to be thoroughly examined.

units.la: n.j. & accuratè explicandi essent plurimi Scripturæ loci qui ad eam rem pertinent, si argumentum penitus excutiendum sufc pere. Ego verò non tam vitandi laboris causa, quàm q; curiosi magis quàm utilis hæc quæstio videtur, breuitate ipsa testari malo, nihil magis quàm sobriam eius tractationem placere. Manichæorum delirium refutandum obiter: qui carnem resurrectu-ram negant, quia immunda est. Quòd res tibi incredibilis videtur huius carnis resurrectio, nihil mirum. Quòd autem hac ratione permotus, sufficere statuis, si credas nouis corporibus aliquando nos esse induendos, hoc à Scripturæ doctrina est alienum. Principio vox ipsa resurrectionis, præsertim cum carni adscribitur, aliud sonat. Hæc enim est promissio. Qui suscitauit Christum à morte, viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra, propter Spiritum Christi in vobis habitantem: sic alibi, Reformabit Christus abiectum corpus nostrum vt fiat conforme corpori suo glorioso. Certè his corporibus nunc putredini obnoxiis, nomínatim promittitur immortalitas. Frigidæ sunt voces istæ! corruptibile hoc induet incorruptionem. Non posset expressius loqui, inquit Tertullí. nisi cutem suam manibus teneret. Argumentum à contrariis, Si mors huius carnis ab Adam: Ergo eiusdem carnis resurrectio à Christo: quia nos à corruptione inflaurat. Citandus Ezechielis locus, qui continet resurrectionis typum. Occidit Deus & viuificat: quid, nisi quod erat mortuum? Quod ridênt Athenienses resurrectionem à Paulo prædicatam, hinc colligimus, qualis fuerit prædicatio. Risus ille sanæ intelligentiæ confirmatio est piis. Metuite eum, qui potest animam & corpus perdere in gehenna. Quod corpus? Nempe quod occidunt tyranni. Ab vsu sacramentorum ritè probatur carnis resurrectio. Baptismus non animam tantum, sed carnem quoque sanctificat. Cœnæ participatio ad cœlestis vitæ fiduciam nos inuitans ad sensus etiam corporales dirigitur. Locus ex 8. ad Rom. capite conueniet, præcipuè vbi loquitur de redemptione corporis. Mortificationem Christi circunferentes, vt & vita Christi in corpore nostro manifestetur. Tertull. Arrhabonem resurrectionis nostræ in cœlum vexit. Ergo negent eum in cœlo esse, qui nos resurrecturos negant. Nisi nos corpore suscitat Deus, mortuos non suscitat. Enoch & Eliam corpore & anima seruatos vocat Tertull. candidatos futuræ immortalitatis. Deinde fideles, nō tantum vocantur Dei templa: sed hoc honore eorum corpora insigniuntur. Similiter dicuntur & membra Christi. Porrò templa Spiritus & membra Christi sine spe in staurationis in putredinem abire nimis absurdum est. Quinetiam eodem loco satis declarat Paulus hæc esse corpora, quibus cœlestem æternamque gloriam destinauit Deus. Præterea citantur homines ad tribunal bunal Christi, vt referat quisque secundum ea quæ per corpus gessit. Atqui minime conuenit rependi nobis in aduentitiis corporibus præmium operum, quibus peragendis hæc quæ nunc gestamus, fuerunt instrumenta. Pauli scilicet corpus in quo illustratum fuit Dei non onen honore priuabitur, & corpus aliunde conflatum martyrij gloria coronabitur? Huc accedit quod Christus in quo non vnuam modo imaginem habemus futuræ nostræ resurrectionis, sed etiam pignus, corpus quod exuerat, resumpsit. Ad hoc exempla conformari nos oportet. Alioqui non diceretur proprie, sicut dicitur, primitiæ resurgentium. Et certè quos superstites inueniet dies ille, subita immutatione in iisdem corporibus resurgent. Si diuersam esse nostri rationem excipias, illud Pauli tibi regeret, Non omnes quidem dormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur. Si in omnes competit immutatio, certè hæc ipsa caro renouabitur. Et quid clarius his verbis desideres? Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem. Neque repugnat, quòd aliam forte carnem ibidem Paulus docet: ad qualitatem enim hoc refert. Neque aliud sibi vult, quàm quod aliis verbis postea tradit: vt absorbeatur quod mortale est à vita, ideo dicuntur corpora sanctorum è sepulchris resurrexisse. Quomodo illi exierunt è monumentis, nos quoque proculdubio Dominus educet. Itaque Isaias cùm sub resurrectionis imagine populi restitutionem depingit. Surgite, inquit, habitatores pulueris. Neque aliter Christus: Mortui qui in sepulchris sunt, vocem filij Dei audient. Quod non fuisset, nisi receptis cadaueribus, resurgerent. Quod etiam exprimit illic Isaias, cùm dicit, Viuent mortui tui, cadauer meum resurget. Vnde & dormitionis nomen fluxit: quod significatione carerent, nisi velut è somno corpora expergefiant. Falsum enim est, quæ humo conduntur corpora, dormire, si noua illis consumptis creanda sunt. Quinetiam si corpora quibus nunc circumdamur, non resurgunt, superstitiosus fuit ab initio mundi sepelendi ritus: quem tamen diuinitus fuisse traditum extra controuersiam esse debet, vt symbolum esset futuræ resurrectionis. Et sanè si creatio noui corporis sperenda foret, non huius quod nunc incolimus instauratio: frustra optaret Paulus, vt spiritus & anima, ac corpus inculpata sint in diem Domini. Eodem & altera exhortatio pertinet, vt nos mundemus ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus. Nam si hæc caro peccati sordibus inquinatur, sordium suarum pœnam sustineat, necesse est. His testimoniis sic acquiesco, vt diuersis cogitationibus ad quaendam fidem meam aditus non pateat. Atque hæc tibi satisfactura spero, nisi mentem tuam nimis occupatam reperiant: quod & à pietate & modestia tua procul abest. Sed tamen leniter pro nostra amicitia monendum te cesui, quia nuper cum te audirem, subuerebar, ne altiores apud te radices egisset haec opinio, quam ut facile eam abiceres. Ceterum ingenii tui dexteritate confisus, ea digito monstrare satis habui, quae apud hominem minus acuta um aut exercitatu vlterius prosequutus essem. Vale eximie vir & frater mihi in Christo Domino charissime. Saluta meo nomine diligenter, hospitem tuum D. Pellicanum & reliquos. Dominus Iesus tibi semper adsit tEque Spiritu suo gubernet.
units.tr: Yet I, not so much to avoid the labour as because this question seems more curious than useful, prefer to show by its very brevity that nothing pleases me more than a sober treatment of it. The delirium of the Manichaeans should be refuted in passing: they deny that the flesh will rise because it is unclean. That the resurrection of this flesh seems incredible to you is no wonder. But that, moved by this reasoning, you decide it is enough to believe that we shall at some time be clothed with new bodies, this is foreign to the teaching of Scripture. First, the very word resurrection, especially when it is ascribed to the flesh, means otherwise. For this is the promise: "He who raised Christ from the dead will also quicken your mortal bodies, because of the Spirit of Christ dwelling in you"; likewise elsewhere: "Christ will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body." Certainly immortality is expressly promised for these bodies, which are now subject to putrefaction. Those words are cold! "This corruptible shall put on incorruption." Tertullian says that he could not speak more expressly unless he were holding his own skin in his hands. Here is an argument from contraries: if death came to this flesh from Adam, then the resurrection of the same flesh comes from Christ, because he restores us from corruption. The passage of Ezekiel which contains a type of the resurrection must be cited: "God kills and makes alive": what else is made alive but what was dead? That the Athenians laughed at the resurrection preached by Paul, from this we gather what kind of preaching it was. That laughter is, for the godly, a confirmation of sound understanding. "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell." What body? Surely the one that tyrants kill. The resurrection of the flesh is also rightly proved from the use of the sacraments. Baptism sanctifies not only the soul but the flesh too. The participation in the Supper, which invites us to confidence in heavenly life, is directed also to the bodily senses. The passage from the eighth chapter of Romans will fit here, especially where he speaks of the redemption of the body: "bearing about the mortification of Christ, so that the life of Christ may also be made manifest in our body." Tertullian: Christ carried the pledge of our resurrection into heaven. Therefore let those who deny that we shall rise also deny that he is in heaven. Unless God raises us in body, he does not raise the dead. Tertullian calls Enoch and Elijah, preserved in body and soul, candidates for future immortality. Moreover, the faithful are called not only temples of God, but their bodies are marked with this honour. Similarly they are called members of Christ. And it is surely too absurd that the temples of the Spirit and the members of Christ should go to putrefaction without hope of restoration. Furthermore, in the same place Paul sufficiently declares that these are the bodies for which God has destined heavenly and eternal glory. Besides, men are summoned to the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive what he has done through the body. Yet it is by no means fitting that the reward of works be repaid to us in other, borrowed bodies, when the bodies we now bear were the instruments of performing those works. Shall the body of Paul, in which the glory of God shone, be deprived of honour, and a body made from some other stuff be crowned with the glory of martyrdom? Add to this that Christ, in whom we have not only an image of our future resurrection but also a pledge, resumed the body he had laid aside. We ought to be conformed to this example. Otherwise he would not properly be called, as he is, the firstfruits of those who rise. And surely those whom that day finds still alive will rise in the same bodies by a sudden change. If you except a different condition for us, Paul's words will answer you: "We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed." If the change applies to all, then certainly this very flesh will be renewed. And what could you desire clearer than these words? "This corruptible must put on incorruption." Nor does it conflict that Paul elsewhere teaches another flesh, for he refers that to quality. Nor does he mean anything other than what he later hands down in other words: that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Therefore the bodies of the saints are said to have risen from the tombs. As they came out of the graves, so without doubt the Lord will lead us out too. So Isaiah, when under the image of resurrection he depicts the restoration of the people, says: "Arise, you who dwell in the dust." Christ speaks no differently: "The dead who are in the graves will hear the voice of the Son of God." This would not be so unless the corpses were received back and rose again. Isaiah also expresses this where he says, "Your dead shall live; my corpse shall rise." Hence the name "sleep" also arose, which would have no meaning unless the bodies were awakened as from sleep. For it is false that bodies laid in the earth sleep, if new ones are to be created for them once these have been consumed. Moreover, if the bodies with which we are now surrounded do not rise, the rite of burial from the beginning of the world would have been superstitious; yet it must be beyond controversy that it was divinely handed down, to be a symbol of future resurrection. And indeed, if the creation of a new body were to be hoped for, and not the restoration of the one we now inhabit, Paul would pray in vain that spirit and soul and body be found blameless at the day of the Lord. The other exhortation also pertains to this, that we cleanse ourselves from every pollution of flesh and spirit. For if this flesh is defiled with the filth of sin, it must necessarily bear the punishment of its filth. I acquiesce in these testimonies in such a way that no access is opened to varying thoughts in my faith. And I hope these things will satisfy you, unless they find your mind too much occupied, which is far from your piety and modesty. Yet I thought I should gently admonish you, for the sake of our friendship, because when I recently heard you, I feared this opinion had taken deeper roots in you than you could easily cast out. Yet trusting in the keenness of your wit, I thought it enough to point at it with a finger, whereas with a man less sharp I would have pursued it further by argument. Farewell, distinguished man and brother most dear to me in the Lord Jesus Christ. Greet diligently in my name your host, D. Pellicanus, and the others. May the Lord Jesus always be with you and govern you by his Spirit.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS ELIO ZOZINO ITALO.
units.tr: John Calvin to Elio Zozino, an Italian.

units.la: IDeo serius quàm optabas, respondeo, quia inuitus, vt verum fateat, quò me vocant literæ tuæ protrahor. De resurrectione carnis, video tibi minimè esse satisfactum. Atqui si plus à me postulas, ne scire quidem vltra quàm docui, appeto. Si excusem non esse mihi plus datum à Domino, æquum non esset, me prætera vrgeri. Tenenda enim nobis est regula, Credidi, ideo loquar. Verum dico in hac fide, quam a, ut te professus sum, sic me acquiescere, vt longiùs tendere fas mihi esse non arbitrer. Audio quid tu contrà. Quum hoc præcipuum sit fidei nostræ caput, cum in eo posita sit felicitatis nostræ summa, non videri superuacuam eius inquisitionem. Et sunt istæ quidem speciosæ illecebræ. Sed quod Spiritus Dei per os Ioannis admonet nondum apertius, & noticiam in diem vltimum differri, modum mihi præscribi sentio. Quæ tibi scripsi, adeo firma apud me sunt, & Dei verbo comprobata, vt nulla me dubitatio sollicitet. Sic porrò sufficiunt, vt eorum fiducia, mortem securè contemnam. Si plura desideras, aliunde petenda sunt. Quoniam nunquam à me impetrabis, vt obsequendi tibi studio, fines à Domino positos transiliam. In aliis quoque si parciores ero, quàm optes, ignoscé. De vxore ducenda si quis à me consilium petat, non aliud suadebo, nisi eam ducat, quæ parata sit Christum cum marito sequi. Idque non ore tantum profitetur, sed re ipsa demonstret. Nam quæ alioquin rectè sentiens, ab impietatis tamen professione discedere non vult, eam quisquis ducet vxorem, pessimum sibi laqueum induet. Nimis sæpe expertus sum in multis, quantùm à Christo recedant, qui se implicant talibus coniugiis. Verum vt sigillatim tibi respondeam. Quod rogas an à coniugio Papistico, non secus atque à Turcico sit abstinendum: Ego qui superstitiones Papatus, in quibus educati sunt penitus retinent, non ausim tamen in eodem gradu cum Turcis locare. Nam aliquanto propius ad nos accedunt. Verum omissa comparatione, homini Christiano fas esse nego, se vxori adiungere, quæ sit à Christo aliena. In eo autem numero scimus esse omnes Papistas. Qui licitum sibi esse putat eam accipere, quae adhuc multis erroribus tenetur implicita, modo iustitiam in Christo suam quaerat, non animaduertit, quantis postea in rebus futurum sibi cum illa sit dissidium. Nemo igitur, me auctore, hoc periculum adibit: quin potius haec mea sententia est, nec pie, nec in Domino matrimonium contrahere, qui aliam sibi sociam ascisci, quam quae diuortium prius cum Papa fecerit. Scio no lemper dari optionem ex voto, verum difficultas culpam non purgat. Solennis Papatus abnegatio si accedat, laudanda quidem erit: sed ego eam quasi necessariam exigere non audim: sicuti nec certum modum finire, quousque in pietatis doctrina progressam est oportet, quae ducenda est vxor, nisi quod velim relicto Christi hoste & manifesta impietate valere iuslu, Christo nomen dedisse. Quod rogas an ratum vel irritum eiusmodi coniugium habere Ecclesia debeat, quorsum pertineat non satis adquor. Nam sicuti mutuus vtriusque partis consensus requiritur, vt rite Dei nomine & auspiciis consecrentur nuptiae: ita si quis ab officio declinet, non definit tamen legitimum esse coniugij vinculum, quo alter alteri obligetur. Leuitatem merito quidem improbabit, fidem tamen datam non soluit. Ego si ex duobus malis eligendum sit leuius, facere aliter non posse arbitror, qui sub Papatu degit, quam vt liberos suos ad Baptismum quanuis adulteratum offerat. Si corruptelas, quae cum Dei mandato pugnant detestetur, pie & ex Christiani hominis officio faciet. Praesens sane mortis periculum: sed eo plus laudis merebitur constantia, quod nullo metu frangetur quisquis erit, quominus confessionem pietate sua dignam edat. Liberos siquis Baptismo priuet, plus duplo pariet offensionis. Itaque hoc non consulerem. Iam cum mollities animi omnes fere qui viuunt sub Antichristi tyrannide, impediat ne liberè testentur se ab inquinamentis Papistarum esse alienos, hinc monendi sunt, vt ego ipsos moneo, quam miseri sint, & quantum in labyrinthum demersi, qui Dei offensam nisi altera offensa fugere nequeunt. Hoc vero est inter sacrum (vt loquuntur) & saxum premi, non posse Christo liberos suos offerre quin ad inquinamenta Antichristi prostituant: & tamen non posse vsum Baptismi praetermittere, quin contempti Christianismi no tam in se suscipiant. Hunc si minimum iis qui illic sibi blandiuntur, admoneo: vt suam infoelicitatem in suis quoque liberis agnoscant. Cum Papistarum Baptisma à lusorio distinguo, fingis tibi respondsum, quod tanquam à me datum impugnes. Non reperies in meis literis, scio, pendere illius vim ab intentione consecrantis. Tantum, nisi fallor, ideo dixi efficax quatenus in hunc finem administratur, vt in Christi corpus nos inserat, vel vt noftrx fit renouationis symbolum.Iam nihil mea refert,fit ne ho-mo Lucianicus qui baptizat,fit ne Diabolus.Tantùm enim res-picienda est institutio,& continuus vsus, qui à Christi mâdato, tanquam ex fonte fluxit.Certè non heri primùm cœpit baptizâ-di ritus.Eum nec Papistæ,nec idololatræ alij excogitarunt.Per-peram itaque cum æstimas, nisi ad originem suam reuocetʃ. Vt-cunquè autem multis prauis acceflionibus vitiatus fuerit, sem-per tamen stetit hoc fixum baptizari Christi mandato,in nomi& Patris,Filij,& Spiritus fanctiʃvt fit regenerationis testimonium. Hic est finis quem considerandum doceo.Nec alia fuit ratio,cur olim Circuncifionem Deus in media sacrorum omnium prosa natione ratam nihilominus habuerit:nisi quòd in illum primùm finem dirigebatur,vt fi-gillum effet diuini fœderis:Ero Deus tuus, & feminis tui post te. Itaque cum populus sub Iofia fœdus de integro feriret, ac folennem suæ defectionis pœnitentiam age-ret,non tamen iterata fuit Circuncifio:quæ non infidelitate mo-do, sed impiis multis superstitionibus polluta erat.-Tanti enim est sancta Dei institutio , vt inter multiplices hominum corru-ptelas,ad vim suam retinendam præualeat.Antiftrophon,quòd in me torquere vis, nullum est. Neque enim lufloria Baptismi i-mitatio,vt credis,in populum Dei inferebat:sed instituti diuini-tus traditi obseruatio.Et tamen degeneres erant filij,qui fœdus cum patribus initum violauerant. Quòd Ecclesiæ reliquiæ ma-nere in Papatu dico, non restringo ad electos, qui illic dispersi sunt:sed ruinas diflipatæ Ecclesiæ illic extare intelligo.Ac ne mi-hi longis rationibus disputandum fit,nos Pauli auctoritate con-tentos esse decet,qui Antichristum in templo Dei sessurum pro-nuntiat. Quanquam & hoc rationibus fatis validis me probasse puto,Ecclesiam licet femiruptam,imò fi lubet,diruptam ac de-formem,aliquam tamen manere in Papatu. Atqui non patior, vt in priuatis pij hominis ædibus Baptismus purè iuxta Christi regulam administretur. Facilis refponfio est. Nam huiusmodi Baptismum, qui apud nos non permittitur, ac iure quidem ve-titus est, facilius tolerarem , quàm Papalem illum tot sordibus infectum. Verùm hic non agitur,quid ego probem. Quòd au-tem Baptismum pro nihilo me duoturum putas, quem è fratri-bus meis quispiam forte intra priuatos parietes administraue-rit, hoc nunquam mihi venisse in mentem, Deum & homines testor. Longè enim aliud est præscribere,quid rectum fit ac fyn-cerum,& quid inter exoticas accessiones residuum fit ex Dei in-ftitutis. Si Turca in Ecclesiam folenni fidei professione receptus fuerit, quin baptifandi quoque sint eius liberi,non dubito. Vi-get enim promissio illa:Ero Deus tuus & tuorum. Timiditatem, qua fit, vt cautius viuant quidam, quàm vt in fuspitionem, ve-niant
units.tr: I am answering later than you wished, because I am reluctantly drawn to it, to tell the truth, by your letter. Concerning the resurrection of the flesh, I see that you are not at all satisfied with what I have said. Yet if you ask more of me, I do not even aspire to know beyond what I have taught. If I should plead that the Lord has not given me more, it would not be fair for me to be pressed further. For we must hold to this rule: "I believed, therefore I spoke." I tell the truth when I say that in this faith, to which, as you know, I hold, I rest in such a way that I do not think it right for me to reach further. I hear what you say in reply: since this is the chief article of our faith, and since the sum of our happiness rests on it, its investigation should not be thought superfluous. Those are indeed attractive enticements. But I feel that a limit is prescribed for me, because the Spirit of God, through the mouth of John, has not yet admonished us more clearly, and has deferred the knowledge of it until the last day. What I have written to you is so firm with me, and so confirmed by the word of God, that no doubt troubles me. Indeed it is enough for me that, trusting in it, I may despise death securely. If you want more, it must be sought elsewhere. You will never obtain from me that, out of eagerness to comply with you, I should leap over the bounds set by the Lord. If I am more sparing than you would like in other matters too, please forgive me. If anyone asks my advice about taking a wife, I would advise only this: that he take a wife who is ready to follow Christ along with her husband. And let her profess this not only with her mouth, but demonstrate it in fact. For whoever takes as his wife a woman who, though otherwise of sound judgment, is unwilling to renounce the profession of impiety, will tie a most wretched noose for himself. I have too often seen in many cases how far from Christ those people withdraw who entangle themselves in such marriages. But to answer you point by point. As to your question whether one should abstain from a Papist marriage no less than from a Turkish one: I, who would not dare to place the superstitions of Papacy, in which they have been brought up and which they still deeply retain, on the same level as the Turks, for they come somewhat closer to us. Yet setting comparisons aside, I deny that it is lawful for a Christian man to join himself to a wife who is alien to Christ. We know that all Papists belong to that number. Whoever thinks it permissible to take as wife a woman who is still entangled in many errors, provided he seeks his own righteousness in Christ, does not notice how great will be the disagreement between them afterwards in matters of the greatest importance. Therefore no one, on my authority, will undertake this danger. Rather this is my opinion: that a man who takes for himself as companion a woman who has not first divorced the Pope contracts marriage neither piously nor in the Lord. I know that the choice according to one's wish is not always given, but difficulty does not excuse the fault. If a solemn renunciation of Papacy follows, it will indeed be praiseworthy; but I do not dare to demand it as though it were necessary, just as I do not dare to fix a certain measure of how far a woman who is to be taken must have advanced in the teaching of piety, except that I would wish a man, having cast off the enemy of Christ and manifest impiety, to have given his name to Christ. As to your question whether the Church ought to hold such a marriage valid or void, I do not quite understand what it pertains to. For just as the mutual consent of both parties is required so that a marriage may be duly consecrated under God's name and auspices, so if one party shrinks from his duty, the bond of marriage by which each is bound to the other does not on that account cease to be lawful. He will rightly be condemned for his fickleness, but he does not thereby release the pledge given. If, of two evils, I had to choose the lesser, I think that a man who lives under Papacy cannot do otherwise than offer his children to baptism, though it is corrupted. If he detests the corruptions which conflict with God's command, he will act piously and in accordance with the duty of a Christian man. There is indeed a present danger of death; but the steadfastness will deserve so much more praise, because whoever he is, he will not be broken by any fear so as to fail to make a confession worthy of his piety. If anyone deprives his children of baptism, he will produce more than double the offence. Therefore I would not advise this. Since a softness of spirit prevents almost all who live under the tyranny of Antichrist from openly bearing witness that they are free from the pollutions of the Papists, such people must be warned, as I warn them, of how wretched they are, and how deeply they are sunk in a labyrinth, when they cannot escape offending God except by another offence. This is indeed to be pressed between the "sacred" (as they say) and the rock: they cannot offer their children to Christ without prostituting them to the pollutions of Antichrist; and yet they cannot omit the use of baptism without taking upon themselves the contempt of Christianity. I admonish those who flatter themselves there, if only a little, that they should recognise their own unhappiness also in their children. When I distinguish the baptism of the Papists from a mockery, you invent for yourself an answer which you then attack as though it were given by me. You will not find in my letters, I know, that its force depends on the intention of the one who consecrates it. I have said only, if I am not mistaken, that it is effective insofar as it is administered for this purpose: that it may graft us into the body of Christ, or that it may be a symbol of our renewal. Now it makes no difference to me whether the man who baptizes is a Lucianic man or the Devil. For one must look only to the institution and the continuous practice, which flowed from Christ's command as from a fountain. Certainly the rite of baptizing did not begin only yesterday. Neither the Papists nor idolaters devised it. Therefore you judge wrongly, unless you refer it back to its origin. However much it has been corrupted by many depraved additions, this has always remained fixed: that one is baptized by Christ's command, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that it may be a testimony of regeneration. This is the end which I teach must be considered. Nor was there any other reason why God long ago kept circumcision valid in the midst of the whole nation of holy things, except that it was directed to that one end: that it might be a seal of the divine covenant: "I will be your God, and the God of your seed after you." Therefore when the people under Josiah renewed the covenant, and performed the solemn repentance of their defection, circumcision was nevertheless not repeated, though it had been polluted not only by unfaithfulness but by many impious superstitions. For the holy institution of God is so great that, amid the manifold corruptions of men, it prevails to retain its force. The retort which you try to turn against me is nothing. For the imitation of baptism which you believe was introduced among the people of God was not a mockery; it was the observance of an institution handed down by divine command. And yet the sons were degenerate who had violated the covenant made with their fathers. As to my saying that remnants of the Church remain in Papacy, I do not restrict this to the elect who are scattered there; I understand that the ruins of the dispersed Church still stand there. And so that I need not dispute at length with reasons, it is fitting for us to be content with the authority of Paul, who declares that Antichrist will sit in the temple of God. Although I think I have also proved this by reasons strong enough, that the Church, though half-broken, or even, if you like, shattered and deformed, still remains in some measure in Papacy. But I do not allow baptism to be administered purely, according to Christ's rule, in the private houses of a godly man. The reply is easy. For I would more readily tolerate that kind of baptism, which is not permitted among us and is indeed rightly forbidden, than that Papal one, infected with so much filth. But what I approve is not the issue here. As to your thinking that I would count for nothing the baptism which one of my brothers may perhaps have administered within private walls, I testify before God and men that this never came into my mind. For it is quite another thing to prescribe what is right and sincere, and what remains from God's institutions amid foreign accretions. If a Turk were received into the Church by a solemn profession of faith, I do not doubt that his children too should be baptized. For that promise holds: "I will be your God and the God of your children." That some people live more cautiously than they should, for fear of falling into suspicion of tyranny, it is not mine simply to condemn. For there is one lawgiver and judge, whose ... I do not see condemned. But as for those who think that their cunning pretence in attending the Masses is a useful aid for advancing the glory of God, would that they considered that it is not so poor…

units.la: 2. Thess. 2. 4. niant tyrannis, simpliciter damnare non est meum. Vnus enim legislator & iudex, cuius orenon video damnari. Qui vero aflutam suam simulationem in adeundis missis vtile promouendae gloriae Dei subsidium esse putant: vtinam cogitarent non ita inopem esse Deum, vt nostris mendaciis indigeat. Certum quidem est, hac occasione interdum quosdam Christo lucrifieri. Id quoties euenit, exemplo Pauli gaudeo. Quouis enim modo propagetur regnum Dei, lucro apponere nos decet. Sed nunc disputatur, an tale probetur Deo obsequium: quod ipse negat. V II. Idus Decembris. M. D. XLIX.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 2. 4. To condemn them outright, as tyrants, is not my business. For there is one lawgiver and judge, and I do not see anyone condemned by his mouth. As for those who think their crafty pretence in approaching the envoys is a useful aid to advancing the glory of God: would that they considered that God is not so needy that he depends on our lies. It is certain that on this occasion some are sometimes gained for Christ. Whenever that happens, I rejoice with the example of Paul. However the kingdom of God is spread, it is fitting that we should add to its gain. But the question now is whether such obedience is pleasing to God, and he denies that it is. V II. Ides of December, 1549.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL.

units.la: DE Carmelita cum ego cofultus essem a Vireto, statim quid sentirem respondi: ne amplius fratribus molestus esset. Alia omnia frustra mihi tentari videbantur. Nam vt accerseretur fide publica, neque expedire censebam: nec vnquam Bernatibus fuisset persuasum. An tu illis consuleres, vt tam proiectae impudentiae cani darent maledicendi impunitatem? Nam si addita aliqua exceptione vellent restringere eius licentiam, negaret sibi esse tutum. Quinetiam non petit quia venire cupiat. Verum si posset obtinere, circumferret hoc & illuc, & se iactaret apud imperitos, qui inde coniecturam facerent eum esse aliquem. Si nofles eius impudentiam, statuerec etiam proculdubio, magis hinc arcendum esse, quam fide publica euocandum, vt impune cum magno supercilio Christum blasphemaret. Nam centies victus, sine fronte tamen triumphum canet. Insistere, vt fide publica tutum illi accessum cures, nimis est ridiculum. Quo enim loco talem nebulonem esse putas? Haec in meis ad Vireium literis & similia longius sum prosecutus. Facile autem fuit in meam sententiam eum adducere, cum iam sponte huc propenderet. Fratres etiam omnes libenter assensi sunt. Caeterum quid Carmelitam moramur? cum nihilo mitius se gerat Capunculus vester. Cum hostes tam procul quaeris, videris nullos habere domi. Atqui potius hoc contenderem, vt iste insanus alio abigeretur. Tales si sint hostes profecti, non adeo nocent. Nunc vero cum bellum intus gerant, hac laboramus difficultate, quod illis resistere non possumus, quin concutiatur Ecclesia. Scripsit ad me nuper epistolam, cuius exemplar breui, vt spero, ad vos mitteretur, vna cum fratrum nostrorum expostulatione: vnde intelliges nihilo mitius me ab eo prouocari quam a Carmelita. Verum ea epistola nihil ad libellum, quem tandem e manibus emisit, vt me vlciscetur, quod non ex eius
units.tr: When I was consulted by Viret about the Carmelite, I at once replied what I thought: that he should no longer trouble the brothers. Every other course seemed to me to be tried in vain. I did not think it advisable that he be summoned under a public safe-conduct, and it would never have been persuaded to the Bernese. Would you advise them to give such a brazen impudence a licence to slander with impunity? For if they wished to restrain his freedom by adding some exception, he would say that it was not safe for him. Moreover, he does not ask to come because he longs to come. But if he could obtain it, he would carry it about here and there and boast of it among the unlearned, who would infer from it that he was someone of importance. If you knew his impudence, you would also decide without doubt that he should be kept away from here rather than summoned under a public safe-conduct, so that he might blaspheme Christ with impunity and with great arrogance. For though beaten a hundred times, he will still sing of triumph without shame. To labour to secure him safe access under a public guarantee is far too ridiculous. For what place do you think such a scoundrel should have? I have pursued these points at greater length in my letters to Viret and similar ones. It was easy, however, to bring him to my opinion, since he was already inclined to this of his own accord. I also readily agreed with all the brothers. But why do we dwell on the Carmelite, when your little Capuchin behaves no more gently? When you seek enemies so far off, you seem to have none at home. Yet I would rather contend that this madman should be driven elsewhere. If such enemies go abroad, they do not do much harm. But now, since they wage war within, we are troubled by this difficulty: that we cannot resist them without the Church being shaken. He wrote to me recently a letter, a copy of which, I hope, will shortly be sent to you, together with the complaint of our brothers. From it you will understand that I am provoked by him no more gently than by the Carmelite. Yet that letter has nothing to do with the little book which he has at last put out into the hands of the public, to take revenge on me because I had not given you counsel according to his opinion.

units.la: n.iiij. sententia vobis consilium dedissem. Non exponam tibi fusius quale sit argumentum, & quanta dexteritate tractetur. Tantum proponne tibi Capunculum illic loqui: nam tibi iam notus esse debet. Ego certe nunquam credidissem tam insulsum hominem esse, nisi ipse testimonium & quidem reipsa, de se reddidisset. Si é clausstro suo veteri ficineptiret, ego suauiter riderem, quod profesi Christi hostesfuam stoliditatem pueris quoque ipsis ita proderent. Nunc vero cum cogito, eiusmodi non stra incubare Ecclesiae Dei, & quasi in sinu nostro dormire, temperare stomacho meo non possum, quin ebulliat. Quanquam priusquam aliquid aggrediar, tuum consilium super ea re audire optarim: num expediat querimoniam deferre ad fratres. Cette eiusmodi probris eo scripto continentur, de quibus si iure egero, nemo tam iniquus erit iudex, qui non vindicandam publica ignominia tale petulantiam censeat. Vtinam daretur colloquendi facultas, sed quia hoc non est, rescribas mihi quam primum velim, num censeas expedire, vt ego fratrum literis meas priuatim adiungam. Iam communes illae scriptae sunt. In conuentu decreuimus mittendas esse. Ego meas incoepi. Quanquam ego acriter pungo, fratres tamen nihilo sunt blandiores: sic tractandus est ille asinus. Nisi enim bene pungatur, qui est stupiditate, non sentiet: si tibi non contigerit fidus nuntius, nos tamen prima occasione mittemus. Tuum poltea erit consilium, num illo praesente recitari debeant Libellus meus de Coena in Latinam linguam versus est a Collega nostro Parisino. Ioannes Giradus eum excudere statuit. Ego tamen nondum annui, amabo te, significes, num vtile censeas hoc tempore publicari. Scis vt prudens nominatus ita incedam ne graviter impingam in hanc aut illam partem. Fieri poterit, vt neutris satisfaciat. At causa non erit, cur asperius quisquam accipiat, quae scribo. Omnes nostri reuerenter te salutant, Collegae, familia nostra, & Nicolai quae aucta est nuper fratris mei filiola. Bernardinus quoque. Dauid nosser scire cupit, num vetus sodalis redierit: & quid de coniugio sperretur. Vale frater mihi amicissime. Saluta meo nomine fratres & amicos omnes cum tota familia. Genevae, x iii. Decembris.
units.tr: n.iiij. I shall not explain to you at length what sort of argument it is, or with how much skill it is handled. I only set before you that Capunculus speaks there, for he must already be known to you. I certainly would never have believed him to be such a foolish man, had he not himself given testimony of it, and indeed by his actual deeds. If he were playing the fool out of his old cloister, I would laugh gently, since enemies of Christ reveal their stupidity so plainly even to children. But now, when I reflect that men of this kind hatch plots against the Church of God, and sleep as if in our bosom, I cannot restrain my stomach from boiling over. Yet before I undertake anything, I would like to hear your counsel on this matter: whether it is expedient to lay a complaint before the brothers. Since in that writing there are contained such abuses that, if I proceed rightly against them, no judge will be so unfair as not to judge that such insolence should be avenged by public disgrace. I wish an opportunity for talking together were given, but since it is not, I would like you to reply to me as soon as possible, whether you think it expedient for me to add my letters privately to the brothers' letters. Those common letters have already been written; we decided in the assembly that they should be sent. I have begun my own. Although I sting sharply, the brothers are no gentler; such an ass must be handled this way. For unless he is pricked sharply, he who is dull will not feel it. If you do not find a trustworthy messenger, we will nevertheless send them at the first opportunity. It will then be your decision whether my book on the Supper should be read in the presence of that man. It has been translated into Latin by our colleague in Paris. John Girard has decided to print it. I have not yet consented, however; please let me know, I beg you, whether you think it useful to publish it at this time. You know that, as a cautious man, I proceed so as not to strike too heavily against this or that party. It may be that it will satisfy neither side. But there will be no reason for anyone to take what I write too harshly. All our people greet you respectfully: the colleagues, my household, and the little daughter of my brother Nicolas, who has recently been added to the family. Bernardin too. David wishes to know whether our old companion has returned, and what hope there is of his marriage. Farewell, my dearest brother. Greet all the brothers and friends in my name, with the whole household. Geneva, 13 December.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO.
units.tr: CAL. FARELLO.

units.la: DE moite vxoris meae iam forte istuc rumor peruenit. Ego, ne prorsus moerore conficiar, quoad possum, admitor. Adsunt etiam amici, nec quicquam reliquum faciunt, vt aliquid leuationis afferant animi mei aegritudini. Cum hinc frater tuus discessit, iam fere de vita erat desperatum. Cum die Martis fratres cuncti adessent, censuerunt optimum fore, si communis inter nos precatio conciperetur. Id factum est. Cum Abel omnium nomine eam hortatus ad fidem & patientiam esset, breviter (ut iam valde fracta erat) testata est quid haberet in animo. Postea exhortationem, quae tempori congruere, videbatur, adieci. Porro quia nunquam de liberis suis verbum fecerat, veritus ne pudore impedita, in animo solicitudinem aleret, quae eam magis cruciaret quam morbus ipse, coram fratribus testatus sum, eos mihi ita curae futuros acsi mei essent. Respondit illa, iam eos Domino commendavi. Cum exciperem non obstare illud quominus agerem ipse quoque meas partes, respondit protinus, si Domino curae erunt, scio tibi fore commendatos. Tanta animi fuit magnitudo, ut videretur e mundo egressa. Quo die animam Domino reddidit, frater noster Borhonius, circiter horam sextam, pias exhortationes attulit: inter quas illa exclamabat: ut omnes animaduerterent cor eius supra terram longe elevatum. Nam haec voces erant, O resurrectio gloriosa! Deus Abraham & omnium Patrum nostrorum, iam a tot seculis in te sperarunt fideles, nemo frustratus est. Ego quoque expectabo. Sententias tas les concisas iaculabatur potius quam pronunciabat. Neque id ex aliorum verbis, sed ut in animo cogitationes agitabat, sic paucis verbis restabatur, quid secum meditata esset. Sexta hora domo abstractus sum. Post septimam, cum in alium locum exportata esset, coepit statim deficere. Cum subito vocem sibi eripi sentiret, oremus, inquit, oremus, vos omnes pro me orate. Eadem hora domum ingressus sum. Non potuit vocem ullam edere, signa ostendit animi commoti. Ego pauca loquutus de Christi gratia, de spe vitae aeternae, de vitae nostrae contubernio, & de migratione, abdidi me ad precandum. Integra mente & preces audiuit, & attenta fuit ad doctrinam. Ante octavam placide expiravit. Ut vix inter vitam & mortem discernerent qui aderant. Nunc moerorem sic deuoro, ut a munere meo nullam intermissionem habuerim. Quinetiam Dominus aliis certaminibus me interea exercuit. Vale frater & amice integerrime. Dominus Iesus te Spiritu suo confirmet, & me etiam in hac tanta calamitate quae certe me fregisset, nisi manum e coelo porrexisset is, cuius officium est erigere prostratos, debiles confirmare, lassos reficere. Salutat fratres omnes, totamque tuam domum. Genevae, 1 Aprilis.
units.tr: My wife's death has perhaps already reached you by now. I am not utterly crushed by grief; I hold myself together as best I can. Friends are with me as well, and they leave nothing undone that might bring some relief to my sorrowful spirit. When your brother left here, she was already almost despaired of. On Tuesday, when all the brothers were present, they thought it best that we should together offer a common prayer. This was done. When Abel, on behalf of all of us, exhorted her to faith and patience, she briefly declared (for she was by then very weak) what was in her mind. Afterwards I added an exhortation that seemed suited to the moment. Moreover, since she had never said a word about her children, and I feared that, held back by shame, she would nurse anxiety in her heart which would torment her more than the illness itself, I declared in the presence of the brothers that they would be as much my care as if they were my own. She replied that she had already commended them to the Lord. When I objected that this did not prevent me from doing my own part as well, she answered at once: "If they are under the Lord's care, I know they will be commended to you." Such was the greatness of her spirit that she seemed already to have gone out of the world. On the day she gave up her soul to the Lord, our brother Borhonius, about the sixth hour, brought devout exhortations; among them she cried out that all should notice that her heart was lifted far above the earth. For these were her words: "O glorious resurrection! God of Abraham and of all our fathers, the faithful have hoped in you through so many ages, and none has been disappointed. I too will wait." She flung out such brief sentences rather than speaking them. And she did not say these things in the words of others; rather, as her thoughts stirred within her, so in a few words she gave expression to whatever she had been pondering in her mind. At the sixth hour I was drawn away from the house. After the seventh, when she had been carried to another room, she began at once to fail. When she felt her voice being snatched from her, she said: "Let us pray, let us pray; all of you pray for me." At that same hour I went back into the house. She could not utter any sound; she showed signs of a troubled spirit. I spoke a few words about the grace of Christ, the hope of eternal life, the fellowship of our life, and our departure, and then withdrew to pray. With her mind intact she heard the prayers and was attentive to the teaching. Before eight o'clock she passed away peacefully, so that those who were present could hardly tell between life and death. Now I swallow my grief in such a way that I have had no break from my duties. Indeed the Lord has in the meantime exercised me with other struggles. Farewell, brother and most upright friend. May the Lord Jesus strengthen you by his Spirit, and me too in this so great calamity, which would certainly have broken me, had he not stretched out a hand from heaven, he whose office it is to raise up the prostrate, to strengthen the weak, and to refresh the weary. He greets all the brothers and your whole household. Geneva, 1 April.

units.tr: John Calvin.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS VIRETO S.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO VIRET, GREETING.

units.la: SAtis coniicio, quantopere nunc angaris, sed quid facias? Necesse est istos abire in locum suum: vtcunque totus mundus conspiret, non ad retinendos tantum ipsos, sed etiam altius prouocandos. De literis, quas N. scripseram, nihil te respondisse miror. Nondum scio an ad eum fuerint perlatae. Mandaueram enim, vt si tibi displicerent, suppprimeres. Expectabam simul vt de coniugali negotio aliquid certi renuntiares. Fac vt aliquid breui de vtroque rescisceam. Michael Aromatarius celeriter istuc se profecturum mihi dixit, Celij causa. Vno verbo respondi, tam malas causas nunquam bene tuendas suscipi, tractari saepius infeliciter: exitum semper perniciosum: etiā dum obtinetur quod quaesitum fuerat. Permisi tamen, vt affinis sui causa aliquid experiretur. Consulo, vt medium te geras: neque te admisceas vllo modo. Nam & Varrotio denuntiaui, si malam causam esse sciret, ne sciens ac volens pugnaret aduersus Deum. Sine Comitem & similes satagere. Tantum eatenus te interpone, vt appareat te nihil aliud optare, quam vt recte habeant omnia. Vale, frater & amice integerrime. Dominus tibi propitius sit semper, ac tuas lacrymas vertat in gaudium. Geneuae, x x IIII. Octobris. M. D. XLVI.
units.tr: I can well guess how hard pressed you are at present, but what can you do? Those men must go to their own place. However much the whole world conspires, the aim is not only to hold them back but to provoke them more deeply still. I am surprised that you have not replied to the letter I wrote to N. I do not yet know whether it reached him. I had instructed you to suppress it if it displeased you. I was also expecting you to tell me something definite about the matrimonial business. Please arrange that I learn something about both matters soon. Michael Aromatarius told me that he would set off for your part of the world quickly, on Celius's account. I replied in a word that such bad causes are never well defended, and that when they are taken up they are very often handled unsuccessfully, and the outcome is always ruinous, even when what was sought is obtained. Nevertheless I allowed him to try something for the sake of his relative. My advice is that you take a middle course and not mix yourself into it in any way. I have already warned Varrotius that if he knew the cause was bad, he should not fight knowingly and willingly against God. Let Comes and others like him bustle about. Interpose yourself only so far that it appears you wish nothing except that everything turn out well. Farewell, brother and most upright friend. May the Lord always be gracious to you and turn your tears into joy. Geneva, 24 October 1546.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO. S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET. GREETING.

units.la: IN quanta anxietate tibi scribam, narrabit hic frater. Vxor enim parturit, non sine extremo periculo, quod nondum vterus partui maturus erat. Sed Dominus respiciat nos. Nostri omnes iam fecerunt periculum. Primus spectimem ad populum dedit, quale semper expectauimus. Petrus multo aptior ad docendum. Geniftonio foeliciter ceflit prima concio, quartus spem nostram superat. In stipendiis horum non fumus consecuti, quod volebamus. Nam duobus aliis Senatus sine magna disceptatione decreuit, quantum priores habebant: hoc est Henricus & Champerellus. Permiserant de diaconis consultationem Syndico Cornuensi, Ioanni Paruo, & mihi. Verum postquam retulimus, non sunt obsecuti nostro consilio: spem tamen melioris statu interea fecerunt. Cum viderem difficiliores in hac re, acri ter aurem illis vellicaui de administratione bonorum Ecclesiasticorum: in tempore cogitandum illis esse, qualiter Deo & hominibus rationem redditur forent: Papam fuisse furem & sacrilegum, videndum ne simus successores. Vsus sum autem praefatione, satione, quæ attentionem excitaret, Meliora esse vulnera amici &c. Item, Ne quærerent Balaam, qui illis in maledictione benediceret. Res in aliud tempus dilata fuit. Dixi enim omnino oportere breui eius tractationem seriam suscipere. Domum tuam vo lebant relinquere vacuam, sed ego distuasi, non malis rationibus. Itaque Philippo Ecclesiastico data est. Vale.
units.tr: How anxious I am as I write to you, the brother who carries this will tell you. My wife is in labour, and not without extreme danger, since the womb was not yet ready for delivery. But may the Lord look upon us. All our men have now made their trial. The first has given the people a specimen of the kind we always hoped for. Petrus is much better suited to teaching. Geniftonius's first sermon went happily, and the fourth surpasses our hope. We have not obtained what we wanted regarding the stipends of these men. For without great dispute the Senate decreed to the other two as much as the former men had received: that is, Henricus and Champerellus. They had allowed the consultation about the deacons to the Cornuan syndic, John Parvus, and to me. But after we reported back, they did not follow our advice, though meanwhile they have held out hope of a better state of affairs. Seeing them more difficult in this matter, I sharply tugged at their ears about the administration of the Church's goods: they should consider in good time how they will have to render account to God and to men; the Pope was a thief and a sacrilegious man, and they should see to it that we are not his successors. I used a preface and a comparison meant to arouse their attention: "Better are the wounds of a friend," etc. Likewise: "Let them not seek Balaam, who would bless them while cursing." The matter was put off to another time, for I said it was entirely necessary to take up its serious treatment soon. They wished to leave your house empty, but I dissuaded them, for reasons that were not weak. So it has been given to Philip Ecclesiasticus. Farewell.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO s.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL. GREETING.

units.la: PErgunt scilicet aduersarij suo more, cum tam impudenter in nos retorquent quicquid peccarunt. Sed bene habet, quod ad fingendum sint tam parum acuti. Quid enim ea, quam recitas, fabula puerilius? Video quidem esse qui recipiant: adeo iuuat eos sinistri aliquid de nobis subinde audire. Sed momento hoc euanescet, ut reliqua eiusdem notæ: imo quæcunque in officina sua fabricant tales artifices. Mecum ita bellum geritur, ut te ad opem ferendam nolim frustra accersere. Palam enim non pugnant hostes: quia hactenus non successit. Sed clandestinis fusuris conantur multorum animos paulatim a me alienare. Qua in re nonnihil proficiunt. Trollietus ille, qui ministerium ambiebat, repulsæ vindictam quam poterit, exequitur. Primus illi astus fuit in suscipiendo cruciatorum patrocinio. Tunc a me exceptus, ut decuit, & magno cum ludibrio etiam factionis suæ vexatus: nunc literas, quas Petro famulus est furatus, per cauponas circunfert. Aiunt autem scriptas ante quinquennium fuisse. Ego, ut ostendam nos non nisi ingenue agere, breui in lucem protraham. Hoc pessimum, quod non libenter modo, sed auide audiuntur, qui nos totumque nostrum ordinem perstringunt. Fuit tempus, cum nemo aduersus ministros mutire auderet. Nunc nulla prope oratio magis fauorabilis. Et Satan nouas semper occasiones excudit. In coniugio Macrini coacti sumus eos qui parum alias amici erant, valde exacerbare. Pronuntiauit Senatus nullum esse coniugium, in quo solennis sponsio intercesserat: partibusque liberam fecit alibi contrahendi facultatem. Praetextus est in affinitate satis remota: nam vxor quæ illi mortua est, consobrina erat matris puellæ, de qua nunc agitur. Rogaui, quo iure tantum sibi permisissent. Et de tota causa habita est a nobis in curia grauis oratio: nihil tamen impetratum. Interea regerunt nos in hominis gratiam importunius contendere. Sed hæc cum aliis sunt deuoranda. Hoc boni saltem habemus, quod quicquid moliantur, sacræ conciones si quando fuerunt frequentes, nunc sunt frequentissimæ. Si quando tibi commodu erit nos inuisere, gratissimus erit tuus aduentus. Vt venias, nisi pro tua opportunitate instare non audeo. Si tamen vel minima se offerret occasio, nolim eam praetermittas. Vale frater mihi in Domino charissimo cum familia tua, Christophoro, Satono, & reliquis Symmystis nostris. Dominus vos omnes tueatur perpetuo, vestrisque sanctis laboribus benedicat. VIII. Septemb.
units.tr: Naturally our adversaries carry on in their usual way, shamelessly turning back upon us whatever wrongs they themselves have committed. But it is well that they are so clumsy at inventing. For what could be more childish than the tale you recount? I see there are some who believe it: so much do they enjoy hearing something unfavourable about us from time to time. But this will vanish in a moment, as have the other things of the same kind, indeed whatever such craftsmen fabricate in their workshop. My quarrel with them is being waged in such a way that I would not wish to summon you to bring help in vain. Openly the enemies are not fighting, because so far it has not succeeded for them. But by secret intrigues they try gradually to alienate the minds of many from me, and in this they make some progress. That Trolliet, who was seeking the ministry, is pursuing the revenge that he can after his rejection. His first trick was taking up the patronage of the malefactors; I received him then as he deserved, and he was attacked with great mockery even by his own faction. Now he is carrying around, through the taverns, letters which his servant stole from Peter. They say these were written five years ago. I will bring them into the light soon, to show that we act only in good faith. This is the worst of it: those who disparage us and our whole order are heard not only willingly but eagerly. There was a time when no one dared to murmur against the ministers; now there is hardly any speech more popular. And Satan forges new occasions all the time. In the marriage of Macrinus we were forced to exasperate greatly those who were otherwise not very friendly. The Senate declared that there is no marriage where a formal betrothal has taken place, and it gave the parties freedom to contract elsewhere. The pretext is an affinity that is rather remote: for the wife who died to him was a cousin of the girl's mother, the girl about whom we are now concerned. I asked by what right they had granted themselves such power. And we delivered a weighty speech in the court about the whole case, but nothing was obtained. Meanwhile they bid us contend more insistently for the man's favour. But these things must be swallowed along with the rest. This at least is a good thing for us: whatever they attempt, the sacred sermons, whenever they have been well attended, are now very well attended indeed. If at any time it will be convenient for you to visit us, your coming will be most welcome. I do not dare to press you to come, unless it suits your convenience; yet if even the slightest opportunity should present itself, I would not want you to let it pass. Farewell, brother most dear to me in the Lord, with your family, Christopher, Satonus, and our other fellow-workers. May the Lord keep you all forever and bless your holy labours. September 8.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINUS VIRETO. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET. GREETING.

units.la: NON peto ut ignoscas; si breuius & perturbatius tibi scribam, quàm res postularet. Habes enim meam excusationem, quâ tibi sufficere confido. Respondebo tamen ad singula epistolae tuae capita paucis verbis. De Farello idipsum mihi nuntiauerat Tossanus quod scribis. Itaque iam quietiore sum animo. Quod autem de profectione cogitabam, non alio spectabat, nisi ut in Germaniam causam promouerem, & Metensibus ipsis adderem a nimium, ne in bona causa adeo timidos se ostenderent. Sed nunc expectabimus, quid illis Dominus dederit. De Iacobo mihi non placet, quòd tam molliter acceptum dimiseris. Nam si nolebas causam tuam facere, cur non simpliciter obiiciebas eum nimis impudenter facere, quòd rem ita contestatam negarer, impleuisse cum totam vicinitatem suis querimoniis? Cùm plus quingentis testibus conuinci queat, audetne adhuc tergiuersari? Tu autem tua dissimulatione videtis mihi audaciorem posthac reddidisse ad negandum. Ego vero stanteram nisi memoria excidisset, litteris adscribere: Legas Iacobe, & si quem habes humanitatis sensum, fleas. Si causam ex me quaesiisset, multo asperius exposuisse quam Farellus. Sic tractandi sunt isti ἀλλάζοντες. De Neocomensibus patienter ferro, quòd nuntio, ut hucvsque meis saltem sumptibus veniret, non mandarunt. Sed iampridem nouit vt sapiant. Negotiū vero κακολογίᾳ sic tractari oportuit, nisi quod vestram constantiam in postremo actu nunc desidero. Ego si vestro loco essem, ac vellem summa lenitate cum eo agere, sic rationes mas instituerem. Causam totam haberem instructam, acti iudici vellem demonstrare, unde pronuntiaret. Darem post ea optionem, mallétne missionem hoc praetextu petere, quòd Dominus multis de causis eum a ministerio excluderetur cum fratrum praeiudicio Bernam ablegari: hoc est, omnibus sentetiis damnati. Atque habito eius respondo, virgerem ad fidem praestandam. Sicubi detrectaret, tunc palàm in apertum campum eum retraherem. Neque enim aequum est, vt totius Ecclesiae dedecore vnius hominis, non dico qualis, existimatio redimatur. Non est autem cur hanc conditionem recusat. Dominus non patitur me amplius hoc ministerio fungi.Impedimenta autem non exprimat:sed ita dissimulet aut silentio transmittat,ne qua suspicio in Ecclesiam deriuetur, sed in eius familia potius tota resideat. Bene vale, frater charifl. cum tua familia & fratribus. Vxor mea te plurimùm salutat. Dominus omnes vos conferuet. Vale iterum. Geneuæ.
units.tr: I do not ask you to forgive me if I write to you more briefly and more hurriedly than the matter required. You have my excuse, which I trust will be enough for you. Still, I will answer each point of your letter in a few words. Tossanus had already told me about Farel what you write, so I am now more at ease in mind. As for my plan of departure, it aimed at nothing else than to advance the cause in Germany, and to add a little spur to the people of Metz themselves, so that they would not show themselves too timid in a good cause. But now we will wait to see what the Lord may give them. I am not pleased about James, because you dismissed him so gently. For if you did not want to make his case your own, why did you not simply object that he was acting too shamelessly, in denying a matter so attested, and in filling the whole neighbourhood with his complaints? When he can be convicted by more than five hundred witnesses, does he dare still to evade? But by your dissembling you have, it seems to me, made him bolder in denying from now on. As for me, I would have written in the margin, unless it had slipped my memory: "Read this, James, and if you have any sense of humanity, weep." If he had asked my opinion of the case, I would have set it out far more harshly than Farel did. Such people must be dealt with in this way. About the Neocomenses I am patient, since they did not commission the messenger to come at least at my expense so far. But they have long since known to be wise. The affair, however, had to be handled with abuse in this way; only I now miss your steadiness in the final act. If I were in your place and wanted to deal with him with the greatest gentleness, I would arrange matters thus. I would have the whole case prepared, and I would want to show the presiding judge the grounds on which he should pronounce. Then I would give him a choice: whether he would prefer to request dismissal on the plea that, for many reasons, the Lord excludes him from the ministry, to the prejudice of the brethren, and that he is sent away to Berne: that is, condemned by every vote. And when he has an answer, I would press him to give security. If he refused, then I would drag him openly into the field. For it is not right that the disgrace of the whole Church be redeemed by the reputation of one man, I do not say of what sort. Nor is there any reason for him to refuse this condition. The Lord does not allow me to continue in this ministry any longer. But he should not state the obstacles; instead let him pass over them in silence or dissemble, so that no suspicion arises against the Church, but rests rather entirely on his own household. Farewell, dearest brother, with your family and the brethren. My wife greets you warmly. May the Lord preserve you all. Farewell again. From Geneva.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS VIRETO S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Viret, greetings

units.la: HActenus nuntium expectaui,qui præfationem, quam à me petebat Bucerus,ad Myconium rectà perferret. Poteram citius Bernam mittere,nisi frustra sperando diem de die traxissem. Ergo danda erit opera,vt prima quaque occasione perferatur.Festinatione opus esse admonebat Myconius.Per me nō stetit. Si Toffanus mihi diem vnum concessisset, eram illi daturus. Nam quo die attulit,me impeditum tenuit capitis dolor.Postridie abire voluit. De rebus nostris non mirum est si varia audias. Tota enim vicinitas, cùm de nobis sine occasione libenter mentiatur,nunc qualemcunque oblatam materiam libentius arripit. Nec desunt in vrbe flabella. Magnificus cùm absolutus semel fuisset omnibus sententiis,iterum in carcerem retrusus fuit. Nisi Dominus mare & ventos increpet, graues nobis imminere procellas video:quas commouent,à quibus sedari potius decuerat.Te accersere non audeo multas ob causas.Vna præcipua est, quòd vereor ne tandem istis cedendum sit, qui nullum se finem ostendunt facituros,donec omnia perdiderint. Huic te flammæ opponi iniquum esset. D.Sulcero scripturus eram,si non obstitissent variæ & assiduæ interpellationes. Ages tamen illi gratias meo nomine,quòd me in istis angoribus consolatus est. Gratissimum in ea re mihi officium præstitit.Illi & fratribus omnibus plurimam salutem. Dominus te cùseruet actibi adsit. Vxor mea te plurimùm salutat.Nos ambo tuam. Geneuæ.
units.tr: Until now I have been waiting for a messenger who would carry the preface that Bucer asked of me to Myconius directly. I could have sent it to Berne sooner, but I kept hoping for a day and so let the time slip from one day to the next. So I must take care to have it delivered at the first opportunity. Myconius kept reminding me that there was need for haste. The delay is not my fault. If Toffanus had granted me one day, I would have given it to him. As it was, when he came on the day he brought it, a headache kept me from work, and the next day he wanted to leave. It is no wonder that you hear various reports about our affairs. The whole neighbourhood is glad to lie about us without any cause, and now it eagerly seizes on whatever material is offered. Nor are there lacking fans to stir the fire in the city. Magnificus, after being fully acquitted by every vote, was thrown back into prison. Unless the Lord rebukes the sea and the winds, I see heavy storms hanging over us, stirred up by men who should rather have been calming them. I dare not summon you here, for many reasons. The chief one is that I fear we may at last have to give way to those who show no sign of stopping until they have ruined everything. It would be unfair to expose you to this flame. I had meant to write to Sulzer, but various and constant interruptions prevented me. Still, please thank him on my behalf for consoling me in these troubles. In this matter he has done me a most welcome service. Give my most hearty greetings to him and to all the brothers. May the Lord keep you and be with you. My wife greets you warmly. We both are yours. From Geneva.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel, greetings

units.la: PArû abfuit, quin priuignus meus sine vllis ad te literis istac transiret. Tempus enim scribendi inter concionem & prandium mihi constitueram. Atqui certamen nobis fuit in Senatu,leuc illud quidem & momenti instar caducum:sed tamen in quo tempus illud,quod literis meis destinauerâm,consumpsimus.Factio, quam nofti,calumniâ struxerat, Antonio Pigneto duce, quæ nostram libertatem in concionibus valde minueret. Vtscias, quid sit consilij & animi apud nos: decretum erat, vt nos omnes admonerent τισσαράκοντα τει, ne in vehementia pérgeremus. Vicerat pars deterior, nisi in arenam progressi essemus. Ita causam egimus Christi nostri auspiciis, vt hostium quoque nos puderet: hoc negotium me vltra decimam exercuit. Quod si mihi liber fuisset totus dies, nescio tamen quid scribere debeam.
