Vale frater & amice integerrime. Dominus tibi adsit ac benedicat sanctis tuis laboribus perpetuò. Saluta diligenter nostro omniū nomine fratres, & familiam. x i x. Martij. Quód ad nostram velitationem, prospere successit. Pignetus ex vrbe eiicitur. Senatus ad scortationum licentiam coercendam egregiè animatur. Fracti aduersarij non sine magna ignominia.
units.tr: It was a near thing that my stepson did not go to you without any letter from me. I had set aside the time between the sermon and dinner for writing. But we had a contest in the Senate, a trifling matter and, one might say, of little consequence, yet it used up the time I had set aside for my letter. A faction, which you know of, had devised a slander under the leadership of Antoine Pignet, which would greatly curtail our freedom in the sermons. So that you may know the state of affairs and of mind among us: it was decided that they should all warn us to avoid vehemence for forty days [τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας]. The worse party would have won unless we had entered the arena. So we pleaded the cause of Christ our Lord under his auspices, so that even our enemies were ashamed of themselves. This business took up more than ten hours. Even if I had had the whole day free, I still do not know what I ought to write. Farewell, brother, and most upright friend. May the Lord be with you and bless your holy labours always. Greet the brothers and your household diligently in the name of all of us. 19 March. As for our skirmish, it has turned out well. Pignet has been driven out of the city. The Senate is strongly roused to restrain the licence of fornication. The beaten adversaries are in great disgrace.

units.la: GASPAR CARMELVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Gaspar Carmel to Calvin, greetings

units.la: Salutem per Iesum Christum seruatorem nostrum unicum.
units.tr: Greetings through Jesus Christ, our only Saviour.

units.la: VTinam tecum præceptor obseruande, nuper Neocomi cum esses, coràm colloqui mihi licuisset. Quod certè, Deo iuuan te, fecissem, si certi aliquid de aduentu tuo habuissem. Sed id cùm factum non sit, superest vt tecum per literas colloquar, téque mihi in consilium adhibeam super ea re, de qua iam subinde mentionem in cœtu nostro feci, sed frustra. Nam quanuis fratres videant & sciant me in Eccl sia, quæ mihi comm sta est, obrui magnitudine negotij, tanquam fluctu, nullus tamen adhuc mihi adiunctus fuit, qui velut in parte laboris esset. Cùm itaque hac via non successisset, tentaui aliam, rogando fratres classis nostræ efficerent, vt aliquis vicarius muneri meo succederet. Verùm nec id quoque ab eis impetrare potui. Nouem iam annos onus omnino humeris meis impar, cui etiam succumbere incipio, solus sustinui. Præsum duabus Ecclesiis, quarum templa disiunctissima sunt, Iter, hyeme potissimùm, ob iniuriam temporis permolestè conficitur. Non raro mihi accidit, vt equo insidens frigore penè astrictus fuerim, & quandoque aqua pluuiali totus madens suggestum conscenderim. Mira est quoque loci totius vastitas. Patet enim millia passuum quatuor in longitudinem, & in latitudinem totidem. Certè me totum hic penè confício. Si rationem mei fratres habere nolint, ero posthac inutilis Ecclesiæ Domini: nam literis operam dare, præ multitudine negotiorum, non possum. Accedit hoc ad labores reliquos, quod mihi feré, verum fateor, mortis instar est, hoc est me ostiatim, quæ ad victum necessaria sunt, tota hyeme quærere necesse sit, cogárque cogârque sæpe nunc eandémque domum huius rei gratia,haud semel,sed decies,adire. Re nonnunquam infecta,vexatus multorum maledictis discedo. Te per Dominum oro,ut mihi tuis consiliis adsis: nescio enim quid mihi in hac re amplius faciendum sit. Pestis nuper Neocomi graßari cum coepisset,consilio nonnulorum factum est,ut posthac si graßari pergat, alter ex ministris teneatur pestë laborantes inuisere, aut diaconum aliquem conducere,qui id onus assumat. Multi hoc pacto, quantum ex bono aliquo viro intelligere potui, sperant brevi futurum, ut pestë pereant, quorum opera Ecclesiæ Domini adhuc valde egent. Dominus suis adsit,& impiorum conatus dissipet. Vale.Monasterij rx.Iunij. M. D. L.
units.tr: I wish, revered teacher, that I had been able to speak with you face to face when you were recently at Neuchâtel. With God's help I would certainly have done so, if I had had any definite news of your coming. But since that did not happen, it remains for me to confer with you by letter and to ask your counsel on a matter which I have already raised from time to time in our assembly, but in vain. For although the brothers see and know that I am overwhelmed by the magnitude of the work in the Church committed to me, as if by a flood, no one has yet been joined to me who might share the labour. Since this way had failed, I tried another: I asked the brothers of our classis to arrange for some assistant to succeed me in my office. But I could not obtain even this from them. For nine years now I have borne alone a burden far too heavy for my shoulders, and I am beginning to sink under it. I preside over two churches whose buildings are very far apart. The journey, especially in winter, is extremely wearisome because of the harshness of the weather. It often happens that, while sitting on my horse, I am nearly frozen with cold, and sometimes I climb into the pulpit soaked through with rain. The sheer vastness of the district is also remarkable. It stretches four thousand paces in length and as much in breadth. Truly, I am almost worn out here. If my brothers will not consider my situation, I shall henceforth be useless to the Church of the Lord, for I cannot give time to writing because of the press of business. To this, among my other labours, is added something that is for me almost like death: I must go from door to door all winter seeking what is necessary for living, and I am often compelled to go to the same house for this purpose not once but ten times. Sometimes I leave with nothing achieved, and I go away worn out by the abuse of many people. I beg you through the Lord to help me with your counsel, for I do not know what more I should do in this matter. When the plague recently began to spread in Neuchâtel, it was decided on the advice of some that if it continues to spread, one of the ministers should be bound to visit those suffering from the plague, or else some deacon should be hired to take on that burden. Many people, as far as I could gather from a certain good man, hope that these men will soon perish of the plague, though the Church of the Lord still greatly needs their work. May the Lord be with his own and scatter the attempts of the wicked. Farewell. From Münster, 9 June 1550.

units.la: Ns Calvino.
units.tr: To Calvin.

units.la: GRatiam & Pacem à Domino. Desidero plurimùm literarū vestrarum consolationem. Quanquam enim hîc non desint mihi certi in Domino amici,& fratres:attamen nescio quo pacto,perquàm anxiè cupiam rescire, quid veteres amici & probatiores Collegæ agât, quomodo opus Domini per eos procedat, vtque etiam me admoneant,consolentur & exhortentur. Subinde scribuntur ex patria,& ex aliis locis Germaniæ, quæ animum meum magnopere excruciant:tum resChristi hîc quoque geritur,vt nisi Dominus innocentissimum & religiosissimum Regem & alios aliquot pios homines singulari respiciat clementia,valde verendum sit ne horrenda Dei ira,breui&in hoc regnum exardescat. Inter Episcopos hactenus de Christi doctrina conuenire non potuit, multò minus dedisciplina. Paucissimæ Parochiæ idoneos habet Pastores,pleræque venundatæ sunt nobilibus,sunt etiam ex Ecclesiastico ordine, atque ex iis quoque qui Euangelici videri volunt,qui tres aut quatuor atq; plures Parochias tenent, nec vni ministrant, sed sufficiunt sibi eos qui minimo se conduci patiuntur, plerunque qui nec Anglicè legere possunt,quíque corde puri putidi Papistæ sunt. Et primores quidem regni multis Parochiis præfecerunt eos, qui in coenobiis fuerunt,vt pestione eis persoluenda se liberarent,qui sunt indoctissimi, & ad sacrum ministerium ineptissimi. Hinc inuenias Parochias in quibus aliquot annis nulla fit habita concio. Quid autem nudis edictis & remotione instrumentorum superstitionum profici queat ad regni Christi restitutionem,nó ignoratis. Vtraque hîc Academia habet permulta egregia collegia,magnis opibus & multis optimis legibus instructa, qualia in nulla Academia orbis habetur:non solum enim egregiè aluntur in iis collegiis quamplurimi, in plerisque vltra centum studiosi,
units.tr: Grace and peace from the Lord. I long greatly for the comfort of your letters. For although I do not lack certain faithful friends and brothers in the Lord here, I nonetheless long, with an intense anxiety I cannot explain, to learn how my old friends and more approved colleagues are doing, how the work of the Lord is advancing through them, and whether they also admonish, console and encourage me. Letters keep coming to me from home and from other places in Germany, and they greatly torment my mind. Meanwhile the cause of Christ is also being pursued here, so that unless the Lord looks with singular mercy upon the most innocent and devout King and some other pious men, we have every reason to fear that the dreadful wrath of God will soon blaze up against this kingdom. Until now the bishops have not been able to agree on the doctrine of Christ, much less on discipline. Very few parishes have suitable ministers. Most have been sold to nobles. Among the clergy, and among those who wish to be thought evangelical, some hold three, four or more parishes and minister to none of them. Instead they find substitutes who will accept the smallest wage, most of them men who cannot even read English, and who are pure-hearted only in the sense of being stinking Papists. The leading men of the realm have set over many parishes those who had been in the monasteries, so that they might be rid of paying them a pension; these men are most unlearned and utterly unfit for the sacred ministry. Hence you may find parishes in which no sermon has been preached for some years. You are not unaware what bare edicts and the removal of superstitious furnishings can accomplish toward the restoration of Christ's kingdom. Both universities here have many excellent colleges, richly endowed and well governed by many good statutes, such as no university in the world has. In these colleges not only are very many students supported handsomely, in most of them more than a hundred scholars,

units.la: Epist.114. verum honestas etiam pro vestibus & libris habent inde pensiones pecuniarias. Ex his debebant ad Ecclesias subinde extrudi fidelium ministrorum examina: Nam omnes artium Magistri theologiæ discendæ deputati sunt, quatuor tantum, in quolibet collegio exceptis, quorum duo medicinæ, duo peritiæ legum debent operam nauare. Sed ea prid~m inoleuit conniuentia, &hoc maximè tempore ita est corroborata, vt multò maxima pars collegarum, sint vel acceribissimi Papistæ, vel dissoluti Epicuræi, qui quantum possint iuuentutem ad sua studia pertrahunt, & odio imbuunt sanæ Christi doctrinæ atque disciplinæ. Atque nostri quoque adeò sunt parci concionum suarum vt per totam quadragesimam excepto vno aut altero dominico die, quam tamen adhuc volùt videri obseruare in die ipso memoriæ mortis Christi ac etiam resurrectionis, neque hodie vllam populo concionē dederint. Interim plerique Parochorum sic sacra recitant & administrant, vt populus statundem de Christi mysteriis intelligat, atque si adhuc Latina & non vernacula lingua vterentur. Cum vero de hac tam hoc renda Ecclesiarum deformitate querelæ deferuntur à sanctis hominibus ad regni proceres, dicunt his malis mederi esse Episcoporum: cùm des runt ad Episcopos Euangelium pridem prosessos, respondent illi, se ista emendare non posse nisi publica regni constitutio de eo fiat. Dum autem magna illa regni concilia habentur quotannis, tot ingeruntur cauſę prophanç, vt hæc Christi causa locum non inueniat. Tum com mittunt deliberationè de his rebus hominibus tam multis, tam-que animis dissentientibus, vt nè semel adesse omnes & ad hoc negotium possint congregari, nedum aliquid rectum & solidũ de tantis rebus constituere. Ad quam causæ Christi procrastinatione, quibus otium & fastu Antichristi magis cordi est quàm crux Christi, Episcopis, haud impigri adsunt plerique ex nobilibus bonis Ecclesiasticis ditati, qui & ipsi præsertim, Ecclesiarum vastationem magis lucrosam sibi existimant, quàm earum piam reformationem. Accedit his malis quòd non pauci omni veræ pœnitentiæ, fidei, bonorum operum, communionis & disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ cura reiecta, vnum hoc agitent ac contendant, ac sæpenumero admodum irreligios vt de ea Christi per Sacramenta participatione tradant, quæ veræ pietatis sensum non satis sesipiant. Atque hi maximè sequuntur eos magistros qui ardét publicè scribere, & adserere, conatum esse fanaticum, moliri Ecclesiæ & pœnitentiæ discipli-nam, vt qui palàm peccauerunt ad a-gendam pœnitentiam ligentur, eàque perac-ta ab eo vinculo absoluantur & nominatim peccatorum cum scandalo coniunctorum absolutionem ab Ecclesia percipiant. Adeò permittunt sibi in quæuis Dei verba & quantumuis clara eas inserre inter-pretapretationes, quas illis suggerit ipsorum prudentia, aut etiam fa-ftidium, ne dicam odium eorum qui recte docent, aut vtrunq; simul malum. Haec vero tibi, optime Caluine, ideo tam libere scribo, vt preces pro iis Ecclesiis amplius intendatis, & cum ad ducem Somerfeti scribis, eum grauissime de illa Ecclesiarum vastatione, & proditione admoneas: quod illæ paucissimis exceptis permittuntur, quæ nihil vel Christi norunt vel quærunt. Rogo proinde te vt has nemo nisi Farellus & Viretus legant. Nosti enim quàm non conducat, istafpargi, & minime omnium per nos. Pro sereniffimo rege qui ad miraculum vsque in pietatis & literarum studiis proficit, preces vestras accumulate. Etenim in quanto versetur humanitus discrimine inde facile agnoscas, q; Papistæ passim tantopere ferociant, cum videant & sciat tamen, regem totis viribus incumbere in regni Christi restitutionem. Sed vident maiorem natu sororem, Papistica pertinacissimè tue ri & vsurpare, siue quod ita ferat ingenium eius, siue quòd de consobrino tantùm confidit. Sed tam frigida regni Christi molitio meretur ista pericula, & aduersarios conatus. Agas mecum gratias Domino qui me morbis meis magna ex parte liberauit, qui me ad medium Martij iterum acerbissimè inuaserat. Possum enim qualitercunque rursum munus meum obire, quanquam multa adhuc hæreat debilitas in cruribus, brachiis & manibus quibus nondum ad scribendum recte vti possum. Orate Dominum pro me vt si fieri potest, me quamprimum hinc liberet, aut aliqua ex parte Ecclesiæ suæ vtilem faciat, imò vt sanctificet no men suum in me quocunque ipse vult modo. Optime vale cum tuis omnibus, optimo Farello, Vireto & huius monetæ collegis tuis aliis. Cantabrigiæ die Pentecostes. M. D. L.
units.tr: Epist. 114. but the honourable fellows also receive monetary pensions for their clothing and books. From these colleges, men examined for faithfulness should from time to time have been sent out into the churches as ministers, for all the masters of arts are assigned to the study of theology, except four in each college, of whom two are to devote their labour to medicine and two to the law. But this laxity first took root, and at this present time it has been so strengthened that the great majority of the fellows are either most bitter Papists or dissolute Epicureans, who draw the young as far as they can toward their own studies and steep them in hatred of the sound doctrine and discipline of Christ. Our own men are also so sparing of their sermons that throughout the whole of Lent, except one or two Sundays, though they still wish to appear to keep even that day for the memory of Christ's death and resurrection, they have given the people no sermon at all. Meanwhile most of the parish priests recite and administer the sacred rites in such a way that the people understand the mysteries of Christ hardly any better than if they were still using Latin rather than the vernacular. When complaints about this shameful deformity of the churches are brought by holy men to the nobles of the realm, they say that the bishops must remedy these evils. When they go to the bishops, who once professed the gospel, the bishops reply that they cannot correct these things unless a public constitution of the realm is made concerning them. Yet while those great councils of the realm are held every year, so many profane matters are thrust in that this cause of Christ finds no place. Then they entrust deliberation on these matters to so many men, with minds so divided, that they can scarcely all be gathered together once for this business, let alone settle anything right and solid about such great matters. To this postponement of Christ's cause contribute the bishops, who are not idle in it, most of them enriched with church revenues from the nobles, who are themselves more concerned with the ruin of the churches, which they consider more profitable to themselves, than with their pious reformation. To these evils is added that not a few, having cast aside all care for true repentance, faith, good works, communion and ecclesiastical discipline, aim at this one thing and contend for it, and very often, quite irreligiously, teach that participation in Christ through the sacraments is to be had without that sense of true piety which they scarcely perceive. And these men most of all follow those teachers who openly write and assert that it is a fanatical undertaking to set up church discipline of repentance, by which those who have sinned openly are bound to perform penance, and, once it is done, are released from that bond and receive from the Church absolution of their named sins that are joined with scandal. So freely do they allow themselves to insert into any words of God, however clear, those interpretations which their own prudence suggests, or even their distaste, not to say hatred, for those who teach rightly, or both evils together. I write these things to you, excellent Calvin, so freely for this reason: that you may direct your prayers more earnestly for those churches, and when you write to Duke Somerset, admonish him most seriously about that devastation and betrayal of the churches, since they are handed over to men who, with very few exceptions, know nothing of Christ and seek nothing of him. I therefore ask you that no one read these things except Farel and Viret; you know how unhelpful it is for such things to be spread abroad, and least of all by us. Pour out your prayers for the most serene King, who advances in the study of piety and letters almost to a miracle. From this you may easily perceive in what peril of human affairs he stands, since the Papists everywhere rage so fiercely, seeing and knowing that the king is bending all his strength to the restoration of Christ's kingdom. But they see that his elder sister holds fast to Papistry most stubbornly and usurps it, whether because her temperament bears her that way, or because she trusts only in her cousin. Yet so cold an undertaking for Christ's kingdom deserves these dangers and the opposition it provokes. Thank the Lord for me, who has freed me in large part from my sicknesses, which had attacked me again most bitterly until the middle of March. I am able, in whatever measure, to resume my duties, although much weakness still clings to my legs, arms and hands, so that I cannot yet use them properly for writing. Pray the Lord for me, that if it can be done, he may free me from here as soon as possible, or make me in some part useful to his Church, and indeed that he may sanctify his name in me in whatever way he himself wills. Farewell, best of friends, with all your people, with excellent Farel, Viret and your other colleagues of this coinage. From Cambridge, on the day of Pentecost, 1550.

units.la: VALENTINO PACAEO DOCTORI LYPSICO.
units.tr: TO VALENTINUS PACAEUS, DOCTOR OF LEIPZIG.

units.la: QVod me dignum existimasti, cuius amicitiam vltrò appe-teres: in eo me tibi valde obstrictum esse sentio, ac libenter profiteor. Nunc quod mearum est partium, saltem in mutuo amoris affectu paria tecum facere conabor. Scripta vero mea tibi probari, cum ego mihi gratulor, tum Ecclesiæ nomine gaudeo. Nam & quia tali viro placent, non poenitenda esse statuo: & simul futurum spero, vt multi iudicium tuum sequuti, aliquem ex lectione fructum capiant. Nec vero hoc à me vel am bitiosè vel arroganter dictum accipias. Nam sicuti vel nullo haberi loco, vel nomen meum penitus sepultum latere facile patiar: ita certè non alio consilio scribo, nisi quia profuturos spero meos labores. Quòd si quis inde prouenire fructus poterit, eum quàm latissimè spargi cupio. Verùm de me plus satis. Quoniam Satanæ minis tros nò dubitamus sedulò conatus suos isthic persequi, anxiè veremur, ne iam à priore ftaru Ecclesiæ vestiæ deflexerint. Præterquam enim quod improbos videmus mirisartibus pollere, & pugnando non sa igarinin parte nostra nihil fere prudentiæ, animorum etiam minus. Vtinam in retinenda saltem doctrinæ puritate aduerfariij nos ingenuos, vt decebat, & cordatos sentirent. Sed tantum abest, quin hæc in vulgo constantia appareat, vt in ipsis quoque ducibus fœda perfidæ defectionis exempla vbique appareant. Quanquam si fidelitër pattibus nostris defungi velimus, vltrà progredi necesse est. Quorsum tédant adulterini isti ritus, quos nobis ingerunt professi Christi hostes, nemini est obscurum: nempe vt claram doctrinæ lucem obruant, vt vitient syncerum Dei cultum, vt quædam sint oppressæ veritatis trophæa. Cùm olim clandestinas insidias piorum libertati struerent astuti homines, Paulus ne ad momentum quidem illis cedere sustinuit. Gloriatur Paulus, ne in vnius quidem hominis circuncisione quicquam se decli- improbis, quò liber tas apud Gentes integra maneret. Nos hodie taciti & amentibus similes innumera superstitionum colluuie Ecclesiam Dei optimi obruique feremus? sed περὶ τῶν ἀδιαφόρων pertinaciter litigandum esse, negant graues & pij homines. Mi frater, quàm vereor, neque abs te, ne ista ἀδιαφορία magnam ac luctuosam nobis διαφορὰν breui pariat. Et sanè dolendum est, homines quosdam ita in rebus mediis sine delectu ac modo extendere libertatem, vt fidei vnitatem lacerët: sic promiscua facere omnia, vt sacrum Dei cultum exoticis quibuslibet corruptelis secure corrumpant. Vt liberè dicam, quod pro tua prudentia nò ignoras, iam istic plus satis fœcium erat in ceremoniis. Vnde, ante hac nihil refectum fuisse apparet, nisi quod hominibus plus æquo ad indulgentiam propensis tolerabile non fuerat visum. Vt concedam fœtidas illas sordes, quibus purgatæ fuerunt vestrae Ecclesiæ, in rebus mediis posse censeri: earum tamen restitutio eritne res media? Quanquam paucum verecundè facere mihi videntur illi, qui res omnes externas sic indifferentes habent, vt cœlestibus Dei oraculis, & sanctæ Christianismi professioni indifferenter ferant quæuis misceri ludibria. Si mihi cum rudi aliquo & gregario homine est negotium, exemplis quàm id absurdum sit ostenderem. Apud te verò genus ipsum attigisse, suffi-cit. Huc accedit quòd doctrinam ipsam, licet dissimulanter, his strophis inuoluunt. Nam vbi baptismum & sacram Cœnam fœdarunt indignis corruptelis, vt parum ab hiftrionicis ineptiis differant: conformationem & extremam vnctionem admittunt. Quorsum? Vt septem numerentur sacramenta. Alias species apud hominem peritum non enumero. Verùm, vt solis ceremoniis agatur, delectum tamen adhibendum censeo, ne quid admittamus vel à recto Dei cultu alienum, vel quod Euangelij claritate obscuret: deinde ne facilitas nostra hostibus insultandi malitiam præbeat. Hîc standum est, meo iudicio, etiam fi decé mortes nunc sint oppetendæ. Quò turpior est multorum ignauia, qui antequam instet vitæ dimicatio, vel illecebris deliniti, vel cæco metu perculsi, vel nescio quibus minis territi, stationem suam flagitiosè deserunt: & tamen non desinunt suggestum occupare, vnde Christum eiusque doctrinam & Ecclesiæ salutem scelerata perfidia, doctorum nomine larvati prodant. Vides, eximie vir, vt beneuolentia erga me tua fretus non minus familiariter in finum tuum quæcunque sentio, deponere audeam, quàm fi interior longíque temporis consuetudo tecum mihi intercederet. Atque hinc iudicium facere potes, quantam habuerim literis tuis fidem. Vale eruditissime vir, frater & Symmysta mihi ex animo colende. Dominus te Spiritu suo regere pergat, tuósque labores benedicat in Ecclesiæ suæ ædificationem. Saluta reuerétèr meo nomine D. Erasmum Sarcerium, D. Ioachimum Camerarium, D. Rheticum & alios amicos. Collegæ mei & reliqui fratres vobis plurimam salutem dicunt, vestri in precibus suis memores. Geneuæ, xi ii. Calendas Iulij. M. D. L. D. Philippi ideo nullam fici mentionem, quia illi scorsim scribo. Si habes qui Argentoratum veniant, illuc tuo poteris literas tuas destinare. Aut Vvendelinus Richclius typographus, aut Ioannes Sturmius libenter mihi reddendas curabit. Si tibi quispiam Augustæ fidelis amicus erit, is Bernam commodè mittere poterit ad Musculum. Inde ad me perferentur.
units.tr: That you thought me worthy of your friendship, seeking it of your own accord, makes me feel that I am greatly bound to you, and I gladly confess it. Now, as far as lies with me, I will try to match you at least in mutual affection. As for my writings being approved by you, I rejoice on my own account, and I rejoice in the name of the Church. For since they please such a man, I judge that they need not be regretted; and at the same time I hope that many, following your judgment, will gain some fruit from reading them. Nor should you take this as said by me either ambitiously or arrogantly. For just as I can easily bear either being held in no regard or my name lying wholly buried, so certainly I write with no other purpose than because I hope my labours will be useful. If any fruit can come from them, I wish it to be spread as widely as possible. But enough about me. Since we do not doubt that the ministers of Satan diligently pursue their designs there, we anxiously fear that they have already turned aside from the former state of your Church. For besides seeing that the wicked are strong in wonderful arts, and that in fighting our side has almost no prudence, and even less courage, we would wish that our opponents, at least in keeping the purity of doctrine, might find us, as is fitting, frank and wise. But so far is this steadfastness from appearing among the common people, that shameful examples of treacherous desertion are to be seen everywhere, even among the leaders themselves. Yet if we wish to discharge our duty faithfully, we must go further. To what end these adulterated rites tend, which the professed enemies of Christ force upon us, is clear to everyone: namely, to overwhelm the clear light of doctrine, to corrupt the pure worship of God, and to set up trophies of oppressed truth. When of old crafty men laid secret snares against the liberty of the godly, Paul would not yield to them even for a moment. Paul glories that he did not yield, not even for the circumcision of one man, so that the liberty among the Gentiles might remain intact. Shall we today, silent and like madmen, endure the Church of God being buried under an endless filth of superstitions? But grave and godly men deny that concerning things indifferent we must contend stubbornly. My brother, how I fear that this "indifference," not from you alone, will soon bring forth among us a great and mournful "difference"! And indeed it is to be lamented that some men extend liberty in matters intermediate so without discrimination or measure that they tear the unity of faith; they make everything promiscuous, so that they securely corrupt the sacred worship of God with whatever foreign corruptions. To speak frankly, as you, in your prudence, do not fail to know, there was already more than enough filth in the ceremonies there. Hence it appears that nothing was reformed before, except that what seemed tolerable was not seen to be so by men inclined more than is fitting to indulgence. Granted that those foul filths, by which your Churches were purged, can be judged among things indifferent: is their restoration, however, a matter indifferent? Yet those seem to me to act with little modesty who hold all external things so indifferent that they bear, with indifference, any mockeries whatever being mingled with the heavenly oracles of God and with the holy profession of Christianity. If I had to deal with some rude and common man, I would show by examples how absurd this is. With you, however, it is enough to have touched upon the matter itself. Add to this that they wrap up the doctrine itself in these trappings, although covertly. For when they have defiled baptism and the holy Supper with unworthy corruptions, so that they differ little from theatrical follies, they admit confirmation and extreme unction. To what end? So that seven sacraments may be counted. I do not enumerate other species to a learned man. But even if the matter concerns only ceremonies, I still judge that a selection must be made, lest we admit anything either alien to the right worship of God or obscuring the clarity of the Gospel; and then, lest our readiness to yield give our enemies an occasion for malice to insult us. Here, in my judgment, we must stand firm, even if death must now be faced honourably. How much more shameful is the cowardice of many, who, before the struggle of life presses on, either soothed by allurements, or struck by blind fear, or terrified by I know not what threats, shamefully desert their post; and yet they do not cease to occupy the pulpit, whence, under the name of teachers, they betray Christ and his doctrine and the salvation of the Church with wicked treachery, masked. You see, distinguished man, how, relying on your goodwill towards me, I dare to lay open to your bosom whatever I feel, no less familiarly than if there were between us an intimate acquaintance of long standing. And from this you can judge how great a confidence I have placed in your letters. Farewell, most learned man, brother and fellow-sacramentarian, whom I cherish from my heart. May the Lord continue to guide you by his Spirit, and bless your labours for the building up of his Church. Greet respectfully in my name Dr. Erasmus Sarcerius, Dr. Joachim Camerarius, Dr. Rheticus and other friends. My colleagues and the remaining brethren send you their warmest greetings, and are mindful of you in their prayers. At Geneva, 12th of the Kalends of July, 1550. I make no mention of Philip here, because I write to him separately. If you have people who are going to Strasbourg, you may send your letters there. Either Wendelin Rihel, the printer, or John Sturm will gladly take care to have them delivered to me. If there is some faithful friend of yours at Augsburg, he can conveniently send them to Bern to Musculus. From there they will be carried to me.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus ex animo tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours from the heart.

units.la: BVLINGERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BULLINGER TO CALVIN, GREETINGS

units.la: Didici à N. nostro te, Caluine colendiffime & charissime, reste valere, quo nomine tibi gratulor, optóque vt fit diuturnum. Nos quoque recte valemus hic omnes Deo gratias. Curiæ intra 9. septimanas extinxit pestis 1100 homines. Mirum est in tam angusto oppido & breuissimo tempore tot esse sublatos. Cum his migrauit & D. Ioan. Blafius. Decubuit & D. Ioan. Commander, sed reualuit per Chriftu. In vicinia Curiæ plurimi moriuntur. Nos adhuc liberi sumus ab illa lue. Cæsar Augustę cupit modis omnibus emulgere ex Principibus & ordinibus Imperij cosensum in continuatione Concilij Tridetini ite auxilium contra rebelles. Vrget & alia quædam capita, nec audio esse quenquam qui ei fe opponat.14.Augusti milites Hispani domû, vt vocant, concionum sacrarum pone ædem S.Vlrichi diripue- runt. Capti sunt ex iis aliquot,sed plurimi arbitrantur ex carce- re impune dimittendos. Ferociunt Papistæ & minantur extre- ma. Aiunt Cæsarem totum in eo esse vt Magdeburgum omni- bus rebellibus faciat exemplum. Cæterum ignorat viuere & vi- ribus pollere eum qui custodit Israelem. Nostrum erit in hisce turbis ardentes Domino preces offerre, & pro periclitantibus & pro nobilisipfis:deinde & constanter facere nostrum officium di- cendo & scribendo.Mitto tuæ pietati 111.Decadem quam hac ætate conscripsi, non vt putem te illa indigere, sed vt beneuo- lentiam erga te meam testarer. Salutant te fratres. Saluus sit D. Nic.Gallasius cum omnibus bonis. Vale cum tuis omnibus. Ti- guri,xxx.Augusti. M. D. L.
units.tr: I have learned from our friend that you, Calvin, most honoured and dearest, are in good health. I congratulate you on this and pray that it may long continue. We here are all in good health, thanks be to God. In Chur, within nine weeks, the plague has carried off 1,100 people. It is astonishing that so many have been taken in so small a town in so short a time. Mr. Johann Blasius has died among them. Johann Commander also fell ill but recovered through Christ. In the neighbourhood of Chur very many are dying. We are so far free from that plague. Caesar Augustus wishes by every means to draw from the princes and estates of the Empire their consent to the continuation of the Council of Trent, and their help against the rebels. He presses some other points as well, and I hear of no one who opposes him. On 14 August Spanish soldiers plundered the house, as they call it, of the sacred sermons behind the church of St. Ulrich. Some of them were taken prisoner, but many think they will be released from prison unpunished. The Papists are growing fierce and threaten the worst. They say that Caesar is entirely intent on making Magdeburg an example to all rebels. But he does not know that the one who keeps Israel lives and is mighty. In these troubles it will be our task to offer ardent prayers to the Lord, both for those in danger and for the nobles themselves, and then to do our duty steadfastly by speaking and writing. I send your piety the 111th Decade, which I have written in these times. I do not think you need it, but I send it to bear witness to my goodwill toward you. The brothers greet you. May Mr. Nicolas Gallasius be safe with all good things. Farewell, with all your people. Zurich, 30 August 1550.

units.la: CAL. MELANCHTHONI.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON.

units.la: Icebat olim Satyricus ille:Si natura negat,facit indignatio versum. Mihi nunc longè secus accidit. Adeo enim me di- fertum non facit præsens dolor, vt fere elinguem potius reddat.Præterquam enim quod me verborum facultas ad expri- mendum animi affectum deficit,sola rei de qua scriptutus sum, cogitatione fractus prope obmutesco. Mei aque gemere potius quam loquiexistimes,velim. Quandoquidem christi hostes exhila- rent vestra cum Magdeburgensibus certamina, ex illorum lu- dibriis ac sannis,plus satis notum est.Fœdum certe ac detestabi- le,Deo primum & Angelis, deinde toti Ecclesiæ spectaculum præ- bent.Hic,mi Philippe,etiam si nulla in te culpa hæreret,prudé- tia tamen atque æquitatis tuæ foret,vel fanando malo remedium, vel mitigando leuamen saltem aliquod excogitare Sed ignosce, si ego non omnite prorsus culpa libero.Atque hinc cóiecturam facere potes,quàm grauia sint aliorum de te iudicia,& quàm si- niftri odiosique sermones. Patere interea, mi Philippe, vt in li- bera admonitione veri amici officio fungar: acri paulò acrius tecum agam, ne quicquam ideo ex veteri mea in te benevolen- tia atque obseruantia imminutum putes. Etsi istud tibi nouum vel insolens non erit, me rustica potius simplicitate offendere, quàm adulatorie in vllius hominis gratiam loqui. Ego etiam quia vicissim expertus sum, tibi nihil esse ingenuitate gratius, minus anxiè laboro,ne mol- ftè feras à me reprehendi,fi quid iu re displicet.Cupio equidem tua omnia sine exceptione,& mihi probare,& aliis.Sed ego te nunc apud reipsum accusò,ne iis qui absentem damnant, cogat subscribere. Hæc tuæ defensionis summa est,modò retineatur doctrinæ puritas,de rebus externis non esse pertinaciter dimicādum. Atqui si verum est,quod pro certo passim asseritur, tu res medias & indifferentes nimis longè extendis. Cultum Dei mille modis apud Papistas adulteratum non ignoras. Corruptelas,quæ minimè tolerabiles erant,sustulimus. Nunc impij,ut de subacto Euangelio triumphum agant, eosdem iubent restituere. Si quis recusare non dubitet, hoccine pertinaciæ adscribes? Id verò à tua modestia quàm alienum sit, noui. Tu si ad cedendum fuisti mollior,id tibi vitio à multis verti,non est quod mireris. Adde, quòd eorum quæ tu media facis, quædam cum Dei verbo manifestè pugnant. Nimis præcisè fortassis quædam alij urgent, atque ut in contentionibus fieri solet, odiosè quædam exagitant,quibus non inest ratum mali. Verùm si quid in rebus diuinis intelligo,tam multa Papistis abste concedi non oportuit: partim quia laxasti quæ verbo suo Dominus adstringit, partim quia proterue Euangelio insultandi materiā dedisti. Cùm Circuncisio adhuc licita esset,annon videsPaulum, quia versuti ac malitiosi aucupes insidias piorum libertati tendebant,illis profectam à Deo ceremoniam pertinaciter negare? Itaque ne ad momentum quidem se illis cessisse gloriatur, quò Euangelij veritas integra maneret apud Gentes. Hodie verò nō de circuncisione nobis molesti sunt hostes: sed ne quid syncerum nobis relinquant,putidis fuisfermentis & doctrinam & omnia pietatis exercitia inficiunt. Quòd Magdeburgenses dicis tantùm de linea vestè rixas mouere,quorsum pertineat,non video. Lineæ enim vestis vsum cum multis ineptiis, tam apud vos quàm apud illos hactenus retentum fuisse arbitror. Sed profectò crassioribus e corruptelis manum dedisse,quæ aperte ad vitiandam totius doctrinæ puritatem & labefactandum Ecclesiæ statum tenduntpassim fremunt boni & religiosi homines. Si forte quod tibi aliquando dixi, oblituses, nunc in memoriam revoco:nimis charum esse nobis atramentum,si ea literis testari dubitemus, quæ tot ex medio grege martyres quotidie sanguine suo obsignant. Atque ita quidem loquebar, quo tempore longius à telorum iactu abesse videbamur. Nūc cùm nos in arenam Dominus protraxerit,eò virilius nos eniti decebat. Alia,ut nosti,tua est,quàm multorum conditio. Plus enim ignominiæ ducis vel antesignani trepidatio, quàm gregariorum militum fuga sustinet. Ergo ut aliorum timiditati parcatur,nisi æquabile inuictæ constantiæ exemplum ostendas, vacillationem in tanto viro non ferendam est: omnes dicent. Itaque plures tu vnus paulum cedendo,querimonias & gemitus excitasti, quàm cetum mediocres aperta defectione. Quanquam autem certò persuasus sum, te mortis formidine nunquam compulsum fuisse, vt ad aliam linea vel minimum vnquam deflecteres: fieri tamē
units.tr: That satirist of old said: "If nature denies, indignation makes verse." With me now it is quite the reverse. My present grief does not make me eloquent but rather almost struck dumb. For apart from the fact that my ability with words fails to express the feeling of my mind, I am so broken by the mere thought of the matter I am writing about that I almost lose my voice. You may think I should groan rather than speak, and I would like that. Since Christ's enemies are rejoicing in your disputes with the Magdeburgians, we know well enough from their jeers and sneers how it stands. Certainly they present a foul and detestable spectacle, first to God and the angels, then to the whole Church. Here, my Philippe, even if no blame clung to you, it would still be the part of your prudence and fairness to devise either a remedy to heal the evil or at least some relief to soften it. But forgive me if I cannot altogether acquit you of blame. And from this you may judge how grave the judgements of others about you are, and how sinister and odious their talk. Meanwhile, my Philippe, allow me to discharge the duty of a true friend in a frank admonition. I will deal with you rather sharply, so that you do not think my old goodwill and esteem toward you has been diminished by it. Although this will not be new or unusual for you, that I offend by a rustic plainness rather than speak flatteringly to win anyone's favour. And since I have in turn found that nothing is more pleasing to you than candour, I worry less anxiously that you will be annoyed at being reproved by me if something in your work displeases me. Indeed I wish all your works to please both me and others, without exception. But I now accuse you before yourself, so that you are not forced to subscribe to what those who condemn you in your absence say. This is the sum of your defence: provided the purity of doctrine is kept, one should not contend stubbornly over external matters. Yet if it is true, as is everywhere confidently asserted, that you extend indifferent and intermediate matters too far, then... You are not unaware how the worship of God has been corrupted in a thousand ways among the Papists. We removed the corruptions which were quite intolerable. Now the wicked, to triumph over the subdued Gospel, order them to be restored. If anyone hesitates to refuse, will you ascribe this to obstinacy? I know how far that is from your modesty. If you were too soft in yielding, you should not be surprised that many have blamed you for it. Add that some of the things you call indifferent clearly clash with the Word of God. Some men press certain points too strictly, perhaps, and, as usually happens in disputes, bitterly attack certain things that contain no real harm. But if I understand anything of divine matters, you ought not to have conceded so much to the Papists, partly because you loosened what the Lord binds by his Word, and partly because you gave them shamelessly an occasion to insult the Gospel. While circumcision was still lawful, did you not see that Paul stubbornly denied that this ceremony, which came from God, was to be yielded to those men, since crafty and malicious fowlers were setting snares for the liberty of the godly? Therefore he boasts that he did not yield to them even for a moment, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain whole among the Gentiles. Today our enemies are not troubling us about circumcision, but in order to leave us nothing pure, they infect both doctrine and all the exercises of piety with rotten leaven. As to your saying that the Magdeburgians are quarrelling only about the linen garment, I do not see what this has to do with it. For I think that the use of the linen vestment has hitherto been retained, along with many silly things, both among you and among them. But that you should have given a hand to cruder corruptions, which clearly tend to spoil the purity of all doctrine and to undermine the state of the Church, good and religious men everywhere murmur. If perhaps you have forgotten what I once said to you, I now call it back to your memory: our ink is too precious to us if we hesitate to bear witness in writing to those things which so many martyrs seal daily with their blood from the midst of our flock. Indeed I spoke thus at a time when we seemed further from the throw of the weapons. Now that the Lord has dragged us into the arena, it becomes us to strive the more manfully. Your position, as you know, is different from that of many. For the wavering of a commander or standard-bearer brings more disgrace than the flight of common soldiers. Therefore, unless you show an even example of unconquered constancy, so that the timidity of others may be spared, a wavering in so great a man will not be tolerated; everyone will say so. Thus you alone, by yielding a little, have provoked more complaints and groans than the mediocre crowd would by open desertion. Yet although I am firmly persuaded that you were never driven by fear of death to bend the least bit from the line, I suspect that some other kind of fear may have struck your spirit.

units.la: o,iij.potuisse suspicor,vt animum tuum alia timoris species percelleret. Scio enim, quantopere inhumani rigoris crimen horreas. Sed memineris oportet, non maiorem Christi seruis famae quam vitae rationem esse habendam. Neque enim Paulo meliores fumus, qui per infamiam & probra secure perrexit. Nos censeri praefractos ac tumultuosos homines, quibus magis libet in totius orbis exitium ruere, quam ad moderationem aliquam descendere, acceperunt id quidem & durum est. Sed iam pridem ad voces illas occalluisse aures tuae debuerant. Nec vero vel mihi tu ita male notus es, vel ego tibi adeo sum iniquus, vt te ab aura populari, ambitiosorum more pendere arbitrer. Sed non dubito, quin te illae interdum functiones debilitent: quid? an prudentis & considerati hominis est, Ecclesiam scindere ob res minutas & prope friuolas? An non tolerabili aliquo incommodo pax redimenda? Cuius dementiae est, sic ad extremum tueri omnia, vt totius Euangelij summa negligatur? Olim cum haec & similia ab aflutis hominibus spargerentur, te plus iusto moueri solitum, animaduertisse mihi videor, ac ingenue tibi aperio: ne quid vere diuinam animi tui magnitudinem impediat, qua te alioqui abunde instructum esse scio. Huius meae vehementiae non obscura tibi ratio est, q; tecum mori centies malim, quam traditae abs te doctri nae videre te superstitem. Neque hoc dico, quasi vel periculu sit, nec vnquam tuo ministerio patefacta Dei veritas intereat, vel tuae perseuerantiae vllo modo diffidam: sed quia nunquam satis solicite cauebis, ne quam captant impij cauillandi occasionem, ex tua facilitate arripiant. Dabis veniam quod miserabiles istos quanuis irritos gemitus in finum tuum exonero. Vale clarissime vir, & mihi semper ex animo obseruande. Dominus te Spiritu suo regere pergat, virtute Spiritus sui fultetet, praesidio suo tueatur, Amen. Saluta quaeso meo nomine amicos, si qui istic erunt. Hic plurimi sunt qui te reuerenter salutant. Multi enim vitandi idololatriae causa ad nos in voluntarium exilium ex Gallia profugiunt. M. D. LI.
units.tr: For I know how greatly you dread the charge of inhuman harshness. But you must remember that the servants of Christ ought to have no more regard for reputation than for life. For we are no better than Paul, who went on securely through infamy and reproach. That we should be considered stubborn and turbulent men, who would rather rush to the ruin of the whole world than descend to any moderation: they have heard this, and it is indeed hard. But your ears should long ago have grown hardened to such voices. Nor am I so badly acquainted with you, nor so unfair to you, as to think you hang on popular applause like the ambitious. But I do not doubt that such things sometimes weaken you. Well, is it the part of a prudent and considerate man to split the Church over trifling and almost frivolous matters? Should peace not be bought at some tolerable cost? Whose madness is it to defend everything so stubbornly that the whole sum of the Gospel is neglected? Once, when such things were being spread by crafty men, I seem to have noticed that you were accustomed to be moved more than was right, and I frankly tell you so, lest anything hinder that truly divine greatness of your spirit, with which I know you are otherwise amply endowed. The reason for my vehemence is not hidden from you: I would rather die a hundred times with you than see you survive the doctrine you have handed down. I do not say this as if there were any danger that the truth of God, once revealed through your ministry, would perish, or as if I distrusted your perseverance in any way; but because you will never be cautious enough, lest the wicked seize an occasion to carp from your easygoing nature. You will forgive me for unloading these wretched, though futile, groans into your bosom. Farewell, most distinguished man, and always to be esteemed by me from my heart. May the Lord continue to rule you by his Spirit, strengthen you with the power of his Spirit, and keep you under his protection. Amen. Please greet the friends in my name, if any are there. Here there are very many who respectfully greet you. For many are fleeing from France to us in voluntary exile, to avoid idolatry. 1551.

units.la: CAL. HALLERO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Haller, greetings.

units.la: Quod tibi nuper ac Musculo nostro ad leuandum vtriusq; domesticum moerorem, nullae a me literae venerunt, peto abs te, mi Hallere, ne meum inde erga vos studium aestimes. Ex quo enim domos vestras pestte tactas esse audiui, qua anxie de vestro periculo cogitauerim, non est quod laborem multis verbis exprimere. Haec porro memoria non piis & cordatis hominibus gratior esse debeat, quam literarum officium: tibi ac illi plane satisfactum iri confido, vbi intellexeritis meum silentium tium ex neglectu minime profectum esse. Cur autem scribendi partes omiserim hæc fuit causa, quod sero huc fama perlata est, nec scire tunc certò poteram, quousque grassata esset calamitas. Itaque rebus dubiis nihil tentare ausus, ad preces me conferre malui, quas & vobis esse magis necessarias, & magis optari scie-bam. Cæterū cum festi dies hic abrogati grauiter ex vestris quos-dam offenderint: illic quoque multos spargi odiosos sermones credibile est. Atque ita statuo me totius rei auctorem non à ma-le uolis tantùm, sed ab imperitis quoque adscribi. Ego autem vt sanctè testari possum, me inscio ac ne optante quidem hac rem fuisse transfactam, ita ab initio in animum induxi, inuidiam po-tius tacendo leuare, quàm excusationes quærere nimis folicitas. Priusquàm vrbem vnquam ingrederer, nullæ prorsus erant fe-riæ præter diem dominicum. Quæ apud vos celebrantur, eodem plebiscito acceptæ sunt, quo ego & Farellus fuimus expulsi: idq; improborum violentia tumultuose extortum magis fuit, quàm legitimo ordine decretum. Ex quo sum reuocatus hoc tempe-ramentum quæsiui, vt Christi natalis celebraretur vestro more, aliis autem diebus extraordinariæ supplicationes tabernis ma-ne clausis, fierent: à prandio ad suas operas aut res agendas quif-que rediret. Erant tamen interea præfracti quidam, qui præpo-stera quadam malitia à communi more dissiderent. Et varietas cum in Ecclesia riè compositæ tolerabilis non foret, atque etiā apud exteros suspitionem gigneret, non bene ciuibus inter se conuenire, Senatum hortatus sum, vt commodo remedio in po-sterum hoc dissidium tolleretur. Verùm simul illa, quam hacte-nus coluerā, moderatio disertis verbis ac nominatim à me lau-data est. Aliquanto post tanquam nouus aliquis hospes, de abro-gatione audiui. Atque vtinam N. olim minus ambitiosè egisset. Nam in hac rota prouincia abolita fuerat dies festi. Quatuor isti, vt postliminio redirent, ille non minus pertinaciter contendit aduersus omnes Gallicæ linguæ Pastores, quàm fi de Ecclesiæ falu-te agerentur. Dixit s Victore aduersus Oiietales pro suo Pascha-te dimicare. Cùm olim ex ipso scisciraretur quo iure Circuncisio plus haberet honoris quàm mors Christi, obmutescere coactus est. Sed præerita omittamus. Mihi satis fuit breuiter indicasse, vt de hęc tam repentina apud nos mutatio. Ego tametsi neq; suasor neq; impulsor fui, sic tamen accidisse non molestè fero. Quòd si statuth nostræ Ecclesiæ esque compertum haberes, non dubitares meo iudicio subscribere. Hoc tamen testatum esse volo, si mihi delata optio fuisset, quod nunc constitutum est non fuisse pro sententia dicturum. Nec tamen est cur homines adeò exasperen-tur, si libertate nostra vt Ecclesiæ ædificatio postulat, vtimur: què admodū nec vicissim præiudicio esse morem nostrū æquum est. Vale eximie vir ac frater mihi ex animo colende. Saluta quæ-fo meis verbis collegas tuos & D.Nicolaum Zer. Fratres mei te & illos plurimum salutant.Dominus vos Spiritu suo regat,tuea-tur,in omnibus benedicat,Amen. Geneuæ iiii.Nonas Ianuar. M. D. LI.
units.tr: You have had no letter from me since your recent loss and Musculus's, when you were both comforting each other over your domestic grief. I ask you, my dear Haller, not to judge my goodwill towards you by that. Since I heard that the plague had struck your households, I have been anxious about your danger, and there is no need for me to spell out my worry at length. Yet this remembrance ought to be more welcome to pious and sensible men than any letter would be. I am confident that you and he will be fully satisfied once you understand that my silence did not come from neglect. The reason I did not write was that news of the disaster reached me late, and I could not then know for certain how far the calamity had spread. So, not daring to attempt anything in such uncertain circumstances, I preferred to turn to prayer, which I knew was more needed by you and more to be wished for. Moreover, since the holidays recently abolished here have deeply offended some of your people, it is likely that many spiteful rumours are circulating there too. I believe that I am being held responsible for the whole affair, not only by the malicious but also by the ignorant. I can honestly testify that this was done without my knowledge and not even at my wish. From the beginning I resolved to lessen the ill feeling by keeping silent rather than by making overly anxious excuses. Before I ever entered the city, there were absolutely no holidays apart from the Lord's Day. Those now observed among you were adopted by the same vote by which I and Farel were expelled, and that vote was extorted by the violence of wicked men in a tumultuous manner rather than decreed by lawful order. After I was recalled, I sought a compromise: the birth of Christ would be celebrated in your manner, while on other days extraordinary prayers would be held with the shops closed in the morning, and after dinner each person would return to his own work or business. Meanwhile, however, there were some stubborn men who, from a perverse malice, dissented from the common custom. Since such variety was not tolerable in a church so well ordered, and since it also gave outsiders the impression that the citizens did not agree among themselves, I urged the Senate to remove this dissension by a suitable remedy for the future. At the same time, I openly and by name praised that moderation which I had hitherto observed. Some time later, like a new guest, I heard about the abolition. Would that N. had acted less ambitiously at some earlier time! For in this whole province the holidays had been abolished. To have those four men restored, he contended as stubbornly against all the pastors of the French tongue as if the salvation of the Church were at stake. He said that he was fighting for his Easter against Victor and the Quietists. When once he was asked by what right circumcision had more honour than the death of Christ, he was forced to fall silent. But let us pass over past matters. It was enough for me to have briefly indicated the cause of this sudden change among us. Although I was neither its advocate nor its instigator, I do not take it badly that it has happened. If you knew the statutes of our Church and were aware of them, I do not doubt that you would, in my judgement, approve them. I wish it to be attested, however, that if the option had been offered to me, I would not have spoken in favour of what has now been decided. Nor is there any reason why men should be so exasperated if we use our liberty as the building up of the Church requires; just as it is not fair that our custom should in turn be prejudged. Farewell, distinguished man and brother, whom I hold dear from my heart. Please greet your colleagues and Master Nicolaus Zerkinder on my behalf. My brothers send their warmest greetings to you and to them. May the Lord rule you by his Spirit, keep you, and bless you in all things. Amen. Geneva, 2nd January 1551.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO S.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel, greetings.

units.la: Petrus Forneletus literas mihi tuas ostendit, quibus ad fusci-piendum apud vos diaconi munus, eum inuitas. Quia me quoq; sciebat abs te literas accepisse: putabat in illis aliquid, quod ad se pertineret,cōtineri.Respondi quod res erat, te ne ver bo quidem meminisse. Consilium petiit. Non potui aliud dare, nisi vt vos inuiseret quasi hoc tantum acturus, vt vobis salutatis,ad munus suum rediret. Ex quo ad nos rediit,nonnihil me peccasse fateor, quod non familiarius eum de anteactis admonui. Multa quidem obstiterunt: sed nihil magis,nisi quod verebar ne sibi iniuriam fieri putaret,si partes monitoris apud eum suscipere auderem. Ergo peccatum agnosco, quod multa verecundia impeditus, fratris officium omisi. Ex quo ad nos reuersus est, placidè & modestè segessit. Aliud quod scribam in præsentia non habeo. Si esset vnà, multa narrarem. Petrus tibi de misero quodam Britone narrabit, qui phrenetide correptus, multum nobis molestiæ fecesset. Fuit hic Pedemontanus quidam, valde sibi placens, qui sibi Dominum apparuisse dicebat: vt Mosesipse fceret, ego Aaron. Cum die Natalis, concione habita, inspectioni priuatæ per vnam decuriam operam dedisset, sesus domum redeo. Ille me ita excepit, vt micam panis gustare non sineret. Dominum sibi apparuisse: habere in mandatis, quæ ieiuno ieiunus exponeret. Cum me animus deficeret, post meridiem scilicet, obsecraui, vt mihi paululum quiddam ederé permitteret. Non desiit inde me fatigare, donec heri seuerè repudiatus fuit à fratribus. Tametsi ridiculè insanus est: in hoc tamen subornatus est à Satana, vt friuolis allegoriis admirabilem illam virtutem,quæ in redemptione populi exerta fuit, obscuret, adeóque in nihilum redigat. Verùm hæc colloquiis magis conueniunt, quàm literis. Aliunde nihil suppetit scriptione dignum. Vale frater & amice integerrime,mihíque ex animo semper amande & colende. Dominus Iesus te semper regat,feruet,benedicat, & modis omnibus per te glorificetur. Geneuæ, pridie Nonas Ianuar. M. D. LI.
units.tr: Peter Fornelet showed me your letter, in which you invite him to take up the office of deacon among you. Knowing that I too had received a letter from you, he thought that something in it concerned him. I replied that the matter stood as it was: you had not even mentioned it. He asked for my advice. I could give him no other, except to visit you as if he were going only to greet you and then return to his duty. As for his return to us, I confess I was somewhat at fault in not admonishing him more intimately about his past conduct. Many things stood in the way, but above all I feared he would think himself wronged if I dared to take on the role of admonisher towards him. So I acknowledge my fault: hindered by excessive shyness, I neglected a brother's duty. Since he came back to us, he has behaved calmly and modestly. I have nothing else to write at present. If we were together, I would tell you much. Peter will tell you about a wretched Briton who, seized by frenzy, caused us considerable trouble. There was a certain Piedmontese, very pleased with himself, who said that the Lord had appeared to him, and that he was to be Aaron while he himself was Moses. On the day of the Nativity, after he had preached and had given attention to a private inspection by one decury, I returned home. He received me so that he would not let me taste a crumb of bread. The Lord had appeared to him, he said, and had given him commands which he would explain to me while I was fasting. When I was growing faint, that is after midday, I begged him to allow me to eat something small. From then on he did not cease to pester me until yesterday, when he was sternly rejected by the brothers. Although he is absurdly insane, he has nevertheless been suborned by Satan to obscure, by frivolous allegories, that admirable power which was displayed in the redemption of the people, and so to reduce it to nothing. But these things are better suited to conversation than to letters. Otherwise I have nothing worth writing. Farewell, brother and most upright friend, whom I shall always hold dear and honour from my heart. May the Lord Jesus ever rule you, keep you warm in spirit, bless you, and be glorified through you in every way. Geneva, 4th January 1551.

units.la: CAL.
units.tr: CAL.

units.la: NVper cùm irem Neocomum, nuncius cum tuis literis in itinere mihi occurrit. Alteras postea domum reuersò quidam Italus obtulit cum quinta Decade. Quòd te librostuos non ideo mittere excusas, vt abstedifcam:ego verò vt meos labores piis omnibus cupio prodesse, ita vicissim libenter ex aliorum scriptis proficio. Atque hæc verè fraterna est communicatio, vbi sic inter nos distributa esse Spiritus dona agnoscimus, vt nemo vnus sibi sufficiat. Gratum ergo mihi tuum munus fuit. Plurimum etiam gaudij attulit, non mihi solùm, sed etiam Farello & reliquis fratribus consensionis nostræ editio. Vtinam quindecim diebus citius venissent tuæ literæ. Nam his nundinis Francfordianis exiisset. Quantùm ad Galliam nostram tempestiua erit publicatio. Valde quidem, vt spero, vtilis. Nuper excusi sunt mei in Iesaiam & Epistolas Canonicas commentarij. Vtrôsque Regi Angliæ dicare visum est. Exemplar præfationis vnius, quod Vergerio misi, abs te legi potuit. Addidi & priuatas literas, quibus generosam pueri indolem acuere conatus sum. Interea allatus est tristis nuncius, Hopperum in carcere teneri. Hoc pridem subueritus fueram. Nunc vereor, ne Episcopi quasi victores ferociùs multò insolescant. Itaque sicuti in recusanda vnctione eius constantiam laudo: ita de pileo & veste linea maluissem (vt illa etiam non probem) non vsque adeo ipsum pugnare: idque nuper suadebam. Multos & potentes habet aduersarios: nec dubito quin acriter ad eum opprimendum insistant. Sed Dominum illi adfuturum spero: & quidem eò magis, quòd perfidè, vt audio, nonnulli eum oppugnant, qui alioqui simulant Euangelio se fauere. Vobis tranquillum Ecclesiæ statum gratulor. Hic sunt improbissimi nebulones, qui non parum molestiæ & turbarum nobis facessunt: quibus tamen exitum, quem meriti sunt, instare confido. Consilia Imperatoris multos anxios reddunt. Quòd nonnullæ eius copiæ nunc Alpes traiiciunt, merito suspitiosum est. Si hanc regionem inuadat, non alia spe me consolor, nisi quòd me Dominus ex misera hac vita eripiet. Interea gregem suum cuius me cura præcipuè excruciat, non negliget. Vale ornatissime vir, & Symmysta plurimum mihi obseruande, vnà cum fratribus quos nostro omnium nomine diligenter salutabis. Gallasius etiam priuatim te salutat. Dominus te regere pergat suo Spiritu, manu sua protegere, ac benedicere tuos sanctos labores. Amen. Genevæ, 1111. Idus Martias. M. D. LI.
units.tr: Recently, when I was going to Neuchâtel, a messenger met me on the road with your letter. Later, on returning home, a certain Italian delivered the second letter together with the fifth Decade. You apologise for not sending your books so that I might learn from them; but I, just as I desire that my labours benefit all pious people, so in turn gladly profit from the writings of others. This is truly a brotherly sharing, when we recognise that the gifts of the Spirit are so distributed among us that no one is sufficient for himself. Your gift was therefore welcome to me. The publication of our Consensus also brought great joy, not only to me but also to Farel and the other brothers. Would that your letter had come fifteen days sooner, for it would have gone out at these Frankfurt fairs. As for our France, the publication will be timely and, I hope, very useful. Recently my commentaries on Isaiah and the Catholic Epistles have been published. I have thought fit to dedicate both to the King of England. You were able to read a copy of the preface to one of them, which I sent to Vergerio. I have also added some private letters in which I have tried to sharpen the noble disposition of a boy. Meanwhile sad news has arrived that Hooper is held in prison. I had long feared this. Now I fear that the bishops, like victors, will become far more insolent. So, just as I praise his steadfastness in refusing the anointing, I would have preferred (though I do not approve even of this) that he not contend so stubbornly over the cap and the linen vestment; and I recently urged him to this. He has many powerful adversaries, and I do not doubt that they will press hard to crush him. But I hope the Lord will stand by him, all the more because, as I hear, some who otherwise pretend to favour the Gospel are attacking him treacherously. I congratulate you on the peaceful state of the Church among you. Here there are most wicked scoundrels who cause no little trouble and disturbance for us; yet I am confident that the end they deserve is at hand. The Emperor's plans make many people anxious. That some of his forces are now crossing the Alps is rightly suspicious. If he invades this region, I comfort myself with no other hope than that the Lord will snatch me from this miserable life. Meanwhile he will not neglect his flock, whose care weighs on me most heavily. Farewell, most distinguished man and my fellow initiate, whom I greatly honour; along with the brothers whom you will diligently greet on behalf of all of us. Gallasius also greets you privately. May the Lord continue to rule you by his Spirit, protect you by his hand, and bless your holy labours. Amen. Geneva, 12th March 1551.

units.la: BInas abs te paucis diebus literas accepi: vtrasque singulares erga me benevolentiae plenas atque eo nomine mihi gratissimas. Bene habet, quod non eundem modo animum Deus nobis contulit, vt Regem Angliae & eius consiliarios incitare-mus ad pergendum: sed fecit etiam vt consilia nostra tam apte inter se congruerent. Hoc certe ad eorum confirmationem nihil, vt spero, valebit. Reditum nunc j, qui libros illuc meos cum literis tulit, indices iam expectare incipio. Simul ac reuersus erit, si quid dignum afferet relatu, dabo operam vt tibi fit comune.
units.tr: I received two letters from you within a few days, both full of exceptional goodwill towards me and therefore most welcome. It is good that God has given us not only the same purpose, to urge the King of England and his counsellors to go forward, but has also made our plans agree so closely. Certainly, I hope, this will do nothing to harden them. I am now beginning to look for the return of the man who carried my books and letters there. As soon as he comes back, if he brings anything worth reporting, I will take care that you hear of it.

units.la: Interea scripsi ad illustrissimum Sommerfeti Ducem, oftedique fieri non posse, quin Papista superbius insolescerent. Nisi mature compositum esset diffidiu de ceremoniis. Hortatus ergo sum hominem, vt Hoppero minus potius corrigeret. Qui cquid simulet Papa non ex ultimo consilium Tridentinum ferio cogi. Cóiecturae meae ratio est, quod Rex Gallia Episcopis omnibus suis mandauit, vt sedulo quisque diocesin suam perlustret: acta vistationis singuli ante sex menses confecta ad Metropolitans referant. Sibi esse in animo nationale totius regni concilium celebrare Illic Tridenti & Papae nulla mentio. Neque tamen dubito, quin res inter eos de compositio geratur. Nempe vt Gallus in Papae gratiam, obiecto concilio nationis fuco, Tridentinum illud dissoluat. Prudentes accensum bellum in Italia iudicant. Turcicus legatus nunc in aula Gallica est qui Regem ad bellum stimulet. Maxime classis Italiae vel Hispaniae imminet. Ergo Domini s. stes, nec Ecclesiae tamen sint molesti, occupabit. Cum mihi Tridentum petenti iter fore ita noueris: nam ses inhuminus, qui nobis falsam vnus hospitium nō offers. Sed expectas forte nouam bullā quae nos admittat. Neque enim ex eorum numero, qui de iure, vel consuetudine, vel priuilegio sanctae sedis Apostolicae locum obtinent. Licebit ergo nobis domi quiescere. Quāquam est etiam quod domi agimus. Nam & Christus laboris materiam suppeditat: & Satan ociosos sedere nō patitur.
units.tr: Meanwhile I have written to the most illustrious Duke of Somerset and shown him that the Papists cannot fail to grow more insolent unless the dispute over ceremonies is settled soon. So I urged the man to be less ready to give Hopper a correction. Whatever the Pope may pretend, the Council of Trent is not being seriously convened. My reason for this conjecture is that the King of France has instructed all his bishops to survey their dioceses carefully, and that each of them is to send the records of the visitation, completed six months ago, to the metropolitan. He intends to hold a national council of the whole kingdom there, and there is no mention of Trent or of the Pope. Nevertheless I do not doubt that the matter is being arranged between them: namely, that the Frenchman, to win the Pope's favour, will dissolve that Trent council under the pretext of a national one. Wise men judge that war has been kindled in Italy. A Turkish envoy is now at the French court to spur the King on to war. A fleet threatens Italy or Spain above all. So may the Lord restrain them, yet without troubling the Church. You know that the road to Trent will be difficult for me, since a certain inhospitable fellow offers us no lodging. But perhaps you are waiting for a new bull admitting us. For we are not among those who hold a place by right, custom or privilege of the Holy Apostolic See. So we may rest at home. Yet there is also work for us at home: Christ supplies material for labour, and Satan does not allow the idle to sit still.

units.la: Dabis festinationi meae venia. Nam cum Germanici adolescentes operam mihi suam offerrent, horam tantum ad scribendum dederunt, quae propere effluxit. Vale ornatissime vir, & frater mihi ex animo obseruande & charissime. Collegae mei te reuerenter salutant. Meo & illorum nomine plurimum salutem dicesD. Bibliandro, D. Pellicano, Galthero, & reliquis fratribus, Dominus vos omnes tueatur suo praesidio, Spiritu gubernet, labores vestros prosperet. Cosenso nostra minus diligenter Latinè hic impressa fuit, quam vellem. Sed breui rursum excudetur.
units.tr: You will pardon my haste, for when the young Germans offered me their services, they gave me only an hour to write, and it slipped away quickly. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and brother whom I honour and love from my heart. My colleagues greet you respectfully. In my name and theirs, give many greetings to Dr Bibliander, Dr Pellicanus, Gualther and the other brothers. May the Lord keep you all under his protection, govern you by his Spirit, and prosper your labours. Our Consensus was printed here in Latin less carefully than I would have wished, but it will soon be reprinted.

units.la: Interea Gallicum exemplar Latino adiunxi, in quo te mendum nullum
units.tr: Meanwhile I have added the French copy to the Latin, in which you will find no error.

units.la: Epist. 121. nullum offendet. Geneuæ x.Aprilis. M. D. LI.
units.tr: Epist. 121. You will find no error in it. Geneva, 10 April 1551.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus vere tuus.
units.tr: Yours truly, John Calvin.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET. GREETINGS.

units.la: QVod n hil iam à multis diebus literarum accepisti, scito nim s assiduam & simul anxiam vestri memoriam in cau si fuisse. Mœror quem ex Buceri morte concepi, solicitudinem ac metum auget. Iam & mors Vadiani nouum vulnus inflixit: cuius opera etiam non tam longè se proferre, & per omnes Ecclesi s spargi poterat, maximo tamen vsui erat in ciuitate magni ponder s, imo apud Helvetios & Rhetos. Quàm multiplicem in Bucero iacturam fecerit Dei Ecclesia, quoties in me tem venit, cor meum prope lacerari sentio. Faxit Dominus, vt reliquos omnes, qui mihi lugendi essent, superstites relinquam, vt lætior moriar. Vale frater integerrime. Dominus te conserueat, cum vxore & familia. Omnes plurimum salutabis meo nomine. Geneuæ, x Maij M. D. LI.
units.tr: Since you have received no letter from me for many days, know that your memory has been constantly in my mind, and at the same time anxiously so. The grief I have felt at Bucer's death increases my anxiety and fear. Now the death of Vadianus has also inflicted a new wound: his work could have spread not so far only, but throughout all the churches, and yet it was of very great use in his city, and of great weight even among the Swiss and the Rhaetians. How great a loss the Church of God has suffered in Bucer, whenever I think of it, I feel my heart almost torn apart. May the Lord grant that I leave behind all the rest, whom I would have to mourn, still alive, so that I may die the more cheerfully. Farewell, most upright brother. May the Lord preserve you, with your wife and household. Greet all of them most warmly on my behalf. Geneva, 10th May 1551.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO S.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel, greetings

units.la: REdiit tandem ex Anglia Nicolaus, aduersis ventis retentus ad dies vndecim: postea iactatus tam sæua tempestate, vt vix naufragium effugerit. Se tam amanter ac benigne exceptum fuisse narrit, vt iure mihi gratuler laborem optimè collocatum. Cum Duci Sommerseti literas meas dedisset, atque alteras quoque ad Regem dixisset se habere: ipse offerendi partes vltrò suscepit: ac postridie in aulam profectus est. Nisi mihi verba dantur, cum Regio consilio perplacuit munus, tum vero Regem ipsum mira lætitia perfudit. Cantuariensis nihil me vtilius factumm admonuit, quàm si ad Regem sæpius scriberem. Hoc mihi lögè gratius, quàm si ingenti pecuniæ summa ditatus forem. In statu Regni multa adhuc desiderantur. Est inter alia malum quoddam incurabile, donec Rex sui iuris esse cœperit: toti Ecclesiæ proventus à Proceribus vorantur: interea vili mercede nihili hominės cõducunt, qui Pastorum vices obeant, vel saltem locum occupent. Ego tamen omnes pungere nõ desinam. De Buceri obitu nihil attigeram, ne vulnus meum scinde rem. Dum enim mecum reputo, quantâ in vnius hominis morte iacturam fecerit Dei Ecclesia: fieri non potest, quin nouo subinde mœrore excrucier. Angliæ multùm profuisset. Plus aliquantò in posterum sperabam ex eius scriptis, quàm hactenus præstiterat. Huc accedit, quòd Ecclesiam nunc fidis doctoribus nudatam esse video. Apud Helvetios plurimum valebat auctoritas Vadiani. Eum Dominus abstulit. Oflander prorsus insanit. Colligemus tamen animos, donec confectum sit, quod nobis ad metam vsque restat. Vnum vereor, ne inter cursores locum occupans, aliis sim tarditatis exemplū. Hoc tamen non parum me solatur, quod tu, qui alios omnes strenuitate vicisti, mihi tam clementer ignoscis & indulges. Satis est, si vagis aliorum erroribus non abducti in recta via pergamus: etiam si alij longo spatio praecedant, alij procul sequantur. Quod ad nostrum amicum ϭεο-παλαιὸν spectat: ego vero eum, vt mones & hortaris, sedulo fovebo, & Collegis meis auctor ero, vt idem faciant. Sed crede mihi, nihil syncerum apparet. Quid captaret, ab initio olfeci. Id me iam deprehendisse, & quasi manu tenere dissimulo. Improbos in deliciis habet, vt solebat. Malis causis aeque patrocinatur. Nihil e fastu & ferocia remittit. Cohors eius liberius etiam foli o exultat. Ego tamen sic mihi moderabor, vt facile agnoscat sibi fuisse ex animo reconciliatum. Audifti opinor, quam funestam pompam nuper egerint. Et tamen ciuis optimi tam indigna trucidatio eorum lasciuias non cohibuit. Quod me rogat Chriftophorus, vt ad eorum coenas accedam: ego vero hactenus nemini eorum negaui: sed cum Amblardo Corneo mandatae essent vices, procrastinando, feriem constitu am abrupit. Interea hospitibus, qui multi quotidie hac transeunt, vel qui ad nos habitandi causa demigrant, me impendo. Inter alios Marchio a Vico Neapolitanus nuper appulit. Subsequetur mox alter. Si nos proximo Autumno inuisas, auctam aliquo numero vrbem reperies. Spectaculum mihi iucundum, nisi quod obruor concursu. Viretus nuper hic fuit. Sed euolauit citius, quam optassem. Bellum iam aperte inter Pontificem & Gallos geritur. Cardinales quicunque Regis partibus fauebant, Roma fugisse rumor est. Si implicabitur huic bello Cæsar, aliquid saltem laxationis dare Magdeburgo & sociis cogetur. Vale frater integerrime, & mihi Collegam tuum aliosque Symmystas & amicos plurimum saluta. Nostri quoque tibi plurimam salutem dicunt. Collegae mei, Normandius, Budæus, Trierius, Sanlaurentius, Colladonij ambo, & frater meus. Dominus te seruet diu nobis incolumem, Spiritu suo fulciat, benedicat sanctos conatus tuos, & Ecclesiam tibi commissam suis auspiciis regat. Geneuæ, x v. Iunij. M. D. LI.
units.tr: Nicolas has at last returned from England. Contrary winds held him back for eleven days, and afterwards he was tossed about by such a violent storm that he barely escaped shipwreck. He reports that he was received so warmly and kindly that I may rightly congratulate myself on a task well spent. When he had given the Duke of Somerset my letters, and mentioned that he also had another for the King, he volunteered himself to deliver them, and the next day he went to court. Unless I am being deceived, the Council was greatly pleased with the business, and the King himself was filled with remarkable joy. The Archbishop of Canterbury advised me that nothing I could do would be more useful than to write to the King more often. This pleases me far more than if I had been enriched with a large sum of money. Much is still lacking in the condition of the kingdom. Among other things there is an incurable evil, which will last until the King begins to govern in his own right: the revenues of the whole Church are devoured by the nobles, while meanwhile worthless men are hired for a paltry wage to fill the place of ministers, or at least to occupy the position. I, however, will not cease to sting them all. I had said nothing about Bucer's death, lest I tear open my wound. For when I reflect on how great a loss the Church of God has suffered in the death of this one man, I cannot help being tormented by fresh grief again and again. It would have greatly benefited England. I had hoped for considerably more from his writings in the future than he had yet achieved. Added to this, I see that the Church is now stripped of faithful teachers. Among the Swiss the authority of Vadian carried great weight. The Lord has taken him away. Osiander is completely mad. Yet let us gather our courage until what remains for us to reach the goal is finished. I fear one thing only: that while occupying a place among the runners, I may become an example of slowness to others. Nevertheless, it comforts me not a little that you, who surpassed all others in energy, are so gentle in pardoning and indulging me. It is enough if, not led astray by the wandering errors of others, we keep to the straight path, even though some go far ahead and others follow at a distance. As for our old friend, I will indeed cherish him diligently, as you advise and urge, and I will be an advocate among my colleagues that they do the same. But believe me, nothing about him appears sincere. I smelt from the start what he was aiming at. I pretend that I have now detected it and, as it were, hold it in my hand. He keeps the wicked in his favour, as he used to. He defends bad causes just as readily. He does not lay aside any of his arrogance and fierceness. His faction exults even more freely in the open. Yet I will so conduct myself that he easily recognises that he has been reconciled to me in good faith. I suppose you have heard what a deadly procession they recently staged. And yet the shameful slaughter of that excellent citizen did not restrain their wantonness. Christopher asks me to attend their dinners. I have so far refused none of them, but since the turns had been assigned to me along with Amblardus Corneus, by putting it off I broke off the sequence. Meanwhile I am devoting myself to the guests, who pass through here in great numbers every day, or who migrate here to settle. Among others, the Neapolitan Marquis of Vico has recently arrived, and another will soon follow. If you visit us next autumn, you will find the city enlarged by some numbers. The spectacle delights me, except that I am overwhelmed by the crowds. Viret was here recently, but he flew away sooner than I wished. War is now openly being waged between the Pope and the French.
