There is a rumour that all the cardinals who favoured the King's side have fled from Rome. If Caesar becomes entangled in this war, he will at least be compelled to grant some relief to Magdeburg and its allies. Farewell, most upright brother, and greet warmly your colleague and the other fellow-workers and friends. Our people also send you their warmest greetings: my colleagues Normandy, Budé, Trie, Saint-Laurent, the two Colladons, and my brother. May the Lord keep you safe with us for a long time, strengthen you by his Spirit, bless your holy endeavours, and rule the Church committed to you under his auspices. Geneva, 15 June 1551.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to N., greetings

units.la: QVum mihi fe nuntius hic cum tuis ad Bezam literis obtulit, ego & recenti metu perculsus, & simul graui moerore oppressus eram. Pridie enim nuntiatum mihi fuerat, peste correcorreptum esse. Itaque non tantum periculo anxius, sed prope attonitus, pro singulari meo in illum amore, quasi iam mortuū lugebam: etsi non tam priuati amoris erat hic luctus, quàm ex publica Ecclesiæ cura oriebatur. Equidem inhumanus sim, nisi eum redamem, qui me plusquàm fraternè diligit, & colit non secus ac patrem. Sed me vehementius cruciabat Ecclesiæ iactura: cùm hominem, ex quo amplissimos fructus expecto, subita mors te ab ipsis stadij carceribus nobis præripi viderem: quem & ingenij suauitas, & morum elegantia, & ingenuus animi candor nō minus antea amabilem bonis omnibus reddiderint. Verùm, si huc semel furtim aduolaris: quod te magnoperè hortor vt facias, longè seipso etiam superiorem reperies. Quòd tibi perditum esse dicis, infaustum illud omen procul faceflat. Hoc magis consentaneum, vt suo discessu te vere & in solidum recuperet. Quid enim nobis est extra Christum, quo fruamur? Spero autem tem hominis vitam nostris precibus concessam. Quanquam enim nondum periculum euasit: heri tamen lætior nuntius allatus est. Cras, vt spero, audiemus quod omnem dubitationem eximat. Vale, eximie vir, & officium hoc meum boni consulle, quòd tam familiariter ad hominem ignotum scribo. Dominus te Spiritu suo gubernet, ac præsidio tueatur. Pridie Calendas Iulij. M. D. L I.
units.tr: When this messenger brought me your letter, along with the one for Beza, I was both struck by a fresh fear and weighed down by deep grief. For the day before I had been told that he had been seized by the plague. So I was not only anxious for his danger but almost stunned, and out of my special affection for him I was already mourning him as if he were dead, though this grief sprang less from private affection than from concern for the public good of the Church. Indeed I would be inhuman if I did not love in return a man who loves me more than a brother and honours me as a father. But what tormented me more violently was the loss to the Church, since I saw that a man from whom I expect the richest fruits was being snatched from us by sudden death, just as he was coming out of the very starting-gates of the race. His sweetness of mind, his refinement of manners and his open candour had already made him no less lovable to all good men. Indeed, if you slip here secretly once, which I earnestly urge you to do, you will find him far better than even himself. As for your saying that he is lost to you, may that ill-omened word be far away. It is more fitting that by his departure he should restore him to you truly and wholly. For what do we have apart from Christ to enjoy? I hope, however, that the man's life has been granted to our prayers. Although the danger is not yet past, a more cheerful report was brought yesterday. Tomorrow, I hope, we shall hear something that will remove all doubt. Farewell, distinguished sir, and take my action kindly, since I write so familiarly to a man I do not know. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit and keep you under his protection. The day before the Kalends of July, 1551.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO. s. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Viret, greetings.

units.la: STatueram ad te nunc venire, & iam ad iter propemodum accinctus eram. Sperabam aduentu nostro aliqua eius moleftię parte leuatum te iri, qua te improbi isti nebulones afficiunt. Quanquam enim ad te non pertingunt eorum latratus, fieri tamen non potest, quin te vel mordeat vel saltem pungat tam indigna malignitas. Libenter etiam cum D. Zerkinte collocutus essem, quem istic forte audierā. Velim interea, vt cum illo agas, num tam importuna Francisci Maurisij petulantia compesci queat. Mea certè non magni refert. Cur enim scarabeum in sua palude frementem securè contemnere non liceat? Sed me exem plum mouet. Indoctus monachus mihi in pago ignobili detrahit. Ridiculum. Sed esse concionatorem, qui pro suggestu declamitet, nos esse Papistis deteriores, quiin Consistorio scriptā manu sua schedam proferat, vbi me nominatim arguitfalsa & Dei verbo contraria docere, vbi me impostorem vocat, vbi impiè sentire blaterat, qui mihi assentiuntur: mihi valde acerbum est, alios etiam magis cruciat. Non videt miser ille, nihil se proficere aliud, nisi quòd se detestandum plebi sibi commissæ propinat. Ego iamillic Papista existimor. Eo nomine me amant ac mihi fauent.Verum interea laceratur Christus, improborum maledicentiæ exponitur eius veritas, infirmæ cósciétiæ labefactátur: & tandem longius spargetur flamma,iam nos intestinis discordiis flagrare.Quamquam hactenus quieui: fratres tamen mei instât, nò vlterius ferendum esse,vt publicè nobis videntibus & scien-tibus damnetur cómunis Ecclesiæ nostræ doctrina. Etiâ nim's præfractos & morosos placauit nostra cum Tigurinis cocordia. Narrabat enim Theobaldus Toquerus quē nolti, nuper hic trâ-siens,Nubergenses mihi applaudere.Sed nebulo hic in suis latebris tumultuando,vult aliquid famæ acquirere.Ego vt lité mo-ueam,nondum persuadeor.Sed quid censeat Zerkintes,magno-pere scire expedit:& tu cum venies simul consilium tuum asse-res.Vale frater optime & integerrime. S luti vxorem & filiolas meo nomine. Dominus vos omnes tuè itur,vobis adsit,vos gu-bernet.Nostri te plurimum salutant.Fratribus quoq; istic plu-rimam ex me salutem dicēs.Geneuæ,v Idus Augusti, M. D. L I.
units.tr: I had resolved to come to you now and was already nearly ready for the journey. I hoped that by our coming you would be relieved of some part of the annoyance that those wicked scoundrels cause you. For although their barking does not reach you, such unworthy malice cannot fail to bite you, or at least prick you. I would gladly have talked with Mr. Zerkinte, whom I happened to hear of there. Meanwhile, I would like you to deal with him and see whether such troublesome impudence on the part of Francis Maurisius can be restrained. For my own part, it matters little. Why should it not be permitted to despise calmly a beetle buzzing in its own swamp? But one example moves me. An ignorant monk slanders me in an obscure village. It is ridiculous. But that a preacher, who declaims from the pulpit that we are worse than the Papists, should produce in the Consistory a written paper in his own hand, in which he charges me by name with teaching things that are false and contrary to the word of God, calls me an impostor, and babbles that those who agree with me think impiously: this is very bitter to me, and it torments others even more. The wretched man does not see that he achieves nothing except to present himself to the people committed to him as someone to be detested. I am already considered a Papist there, and on that account they love and favour me. Meanwhile Christ is torn apart, his truth is exposed to the slanders of the wicked, and weak consciences are shaken; and at last the flame will spread further, since we are already burning with internal discords. Although I have kept quiet until now, my brothers insist that it can no longer be endured that the common doctrine of our Church should be publicly condemned while we look on and know. Our agreement with the Tigurines has placated even the stubborn and peevish. For Theobald Toquerus, whom I do not want, passing through here recently, reported that the people of Nuremberg applaud me. But this scoundrel, making a racket in his hiding places, wants to win some fame for himself. I am not yet persuaded to stir up a dispute. But it is very important to know what Zerkintes thinks, and when you come, you will at the same time set out your own counsel. Farewell, best and most upright brother. Greet your wife and little daughters on my behalf. May the Lord go with you all, watch over you and govern you. Our people greet you most warmly. Give my very warm greetings to the brothers there too. Geneva, the fifth day before the Ides of August, 1551.

units.la: CALVINVS CRAMMERO ARCHIEPISCOPO CANTVARIENSI S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, greetings.

units.la: TV quidem, illustrissime Domine, verè & prudenter n hoc tam confuso Ecclesiæ statu, nullum aptius afferri posse re-medium iudicas,quàm si inter se coëuntes pij, cordati,& in Dei schola probè exercitati homines,qui suum in pietatis do-ctrina cósensum profiteantur. Videmus enim quàm variis arti-bus Satan,Euangelij lucem,quæ mirabili Dei bonitate nobis ex-orta passim refulget conetur obruere. Cōductitij Papæ canes la-trare nō desinunt,ne purus Christi sermo exaudiatur. Tanta li-centia passim ebullit & grassatur impietas, vt parū à manifestis iudibriis absit religio.Qui professi nō sunt veritatis hostes,ea ta-men proterua lasciuunt, quæ breui sn si obuiam eatur, fœdam nobis cósusionem pariet. Neque solum in hominum vulgo re-gnat hic tum stultæ curiositas,tum intéperantis audacię mor-bus:sed quod magis pudendum est,in ordine quoque pastorum nimis iam grassatur. Quibus deliriis seipsum deludat & quosda alios safcinet Ofiander,plus satis notum est.Et Dominus quidè, vt ab initio vsq; mundi solitus est syncerā fidei vnitatem,ne la-ceretur hominum dissidiis,mirabiliter,& modo nobis incogni-to,seruare poterit. Quos tamen ipse in excubiis locuit, mini-mè torpere vult: quando & eosdem sibi destinauit Ministros, quorū opera sanam in Ecclesia doctrinā ab omnibus corrupte-lis purget,ac incolumē ad posteros transmittat.Tibi præsertim, ornatiss.Præsul, quò altiore in specula sedes, in hanc curam,vt facis,incumbere necesse est.Quod nō ideo dico,quasi tibi addé-dum dum esse nouum calcar existimem:qui nó modò sponte præcur-ris,sed aliis quoque instas voluntarius hortator.Verû vt te in tâ fausto præclaróque studio, mea gratulatione confirmè. Lætum quidem est in Anglia Euangelj successum audimus. Sed istic quoq; vsu venire,quod suo tempore expertus est Paulus,nó dubito:vt ostio ad recipiendam puram doctrinam aperto,multi repente aduersarij cóera insurgunt.Etsi vero me non latet, quàm multi sint vobis ad manû,idonei ad refellenda Satanæ mędacia vindices:sacit tamen eorum improbitas, qui ad tuibådum satagunt,vt bonorum sed litas hac in parte nunquam n mia sit,aut superuacua. Deinde scio nó ita vnius Anglię haberi abste ratione m,quin orbi simul vniuerso cósulas.Regis quoque serennissimi nó modò generosi indoles,sed rara eti im pietas merito exscu-landi,qʒ sanctum consilium de habendo eiusmodi conuentu s.a uore suo prosequitur,& locum in regno suo offert. Atque vtinam impetrari posset, vt in locum aliquem docti & graues viri ex præcipuis Ecclesiis coirent,ac singulis fidei capitibus diligenter excussis,de cómuni omnium sententia cert in posteris trade rent Scripturę doctrinam.Cæterū in maximis secul: nostri malis hoc quoque numerandum est, qʒ ita aliæ ab aliis distractæ sunt Ecclesiæ,vt vix humana iam inter nos vige it societas,nedū emi neat sanctā mes broru Christi cómuni cátio,quà ore proficentur omnes,pauci re ipsa syncerè colunt. Quòd si frigidius,quàm par esset,se gerunt doctores:grauissima penes ipsos Principes est culpa,qui vel prophanis suis negotiis implicit,Ecclesiæ silutem & totam pietatem negligunt:vel singulì priuata pace contenti, aliorum curá non tanguntur. Ita fit,vt membris dissipitis,laceru iaceat Ecclesiæ corpus. Quantum ad me attinet,si quis mei vsus fore videbitur ne decernit quidem maria,si opus sit,ob eâ rem traiicere pigeat.Si de iuuando tantum Anglię regno ageretur,iam mihi ea satis legitima ratio foret. Nunc cùm quæratur grauis & ad Scripturæ normam probè compositus doctorum hominum consensus,qua Ecclesiæ procul alioqui dissitæ,inter se coalescát, nullis vel laboribus,vel molstiis parcere, sas mihi esse arbitror. Verùm tenuitatem meam factuAfter spero, vt mihi parcatur. Si votis prosequar, quod ab aliis susceptum erit, partibus meis defunctus ero. D.Philippus longius abest, quàm vt vltrò citróque commeare breui tempore literæ queant. D.Bullingerus tibi forte iam rescripsit. Mihi vtinam par studij ardori suppeteret facultas.Porrò quod me facturum principio negauì,ipsa rei quàm sentis, difficultas tentare me cogit: non vt te h rter modo, sed etiam obtisterad pergedum:donec aliquid saltem effectũ fuerit, si non omnia ex voto successint.Vale ornatissime Præsul,& mihi ex animo reuerède.Dominus te Spiritu suo regere,sanctósque tuos conatus benedicere pergat. Geneux.
units.tr: You, most illustrious Lord, rightly and wisely judge that in this so confused state of the Church no more suitable remedy can be offered than if pious, sensible men, well trained in the school of God, came together and professed their agreement in the doctrine of piety. For we see by how many arts Satan tries to overwhelm the light of the gospel, which by the wonderful goodness of God has risen among us and shines everywhere. The hired dogs of the Pope do not cease barking, so that the pure word of Christ may not be heard. Impiety boils up and rages everywhere with such license that religion is scarcely distant from open mockery. Those who have not professed themselves enemies of the truth nevertheless wantonly indulge in such shameless things that, unless they are quickly met head on, they will bring foul confusion upon us. This disease of foolish curiosity and intemperate audacity reigns not only among the common people but, what is more shameful, rages too much even among the order of ministers. How Osiander deludes himself with these delusions and fascinates some others is more than sufficiently well known. The Lord indeed, as he has always been accustomed to do from the beginning of the world, will be able to preserve the sincere unity of faith wonderfully and in a manner unknown to us, so that it is not torn by the quarrels of men. Yet he does not want those whom he has set on watch to grow sluggish at all, since he has also destined for himself the same ministers, by whose work he cleanses sound doctrine in the Church from all corruptions and transmits it intact to posterity. Especially you, most distinguished Prelate, since you sit on a higher watchtower, must necessarily apply yourself to this care, as you do. I do not say this as if I thought a new spur had to be added to you, you who not only run ahead of your own accord but also, as a willing exhorter, urge others. Rather, I want to confirm you in such a happy and outstanding undertaking with my congratulation. It is indeed joyful that we hear of the success of the gospel in England. But I do not doubt that what Paul experienced in his own time happens there too: that when a door is opened to receive pure doctrine, many adversaries suddenly rise up in opposition. Although I am not unaware how many suitable defenders you have at hand to refute the lies of Satan, the wickedness of those who labour to wound them makes it so that the care of good men in this matter can never be excessive or superfluous. Next, I know that the matter must not be regarded as concerning England alone, so that you consult only the English and not the whole world at the same time. The most serene King's noble disposition, and his rare piety too, deserve to be praised; he favours with his good will the holy plan of holding such a gathering and offers a place in his kingdom for it. And would that it could be obtained that learned and grave men from the principal Churches should come together in some place and, after each article of faith has been carefully examined, hand down to posterity, by the common agreement of all, the doctrine of Scripture with certainty. Moreover, among the greatest evils of our age this must also be counted: that the Churches have been so separated from one another that human fellowship hardly flourishes among us, much less does the holy communion of Christ's brothers shine forth, which all profess with their mouths but few truly cultivate in fact. But if the teachers act more coldly than they should, the greatest blame lies with the princes themselves, who either are entangled in their profane affairs and neglect the safety of the Church and all piety, or, each content with private peace, are not moved by the concerns of others. Thus it happens that, with its members scattered, the body of the Church lies torn. As far as I am concerned, if anyone thinks my service would be of use, I would not hesitate even to cross seas for this purpose, if need be. If the matter concerned only helping the kingdom of England, that would already be a sufficiently legitimate reason for me. Now, since what is sought is a serious consensus of learned men, carefully composed according to the rule of Scripture, by which Churches otherwise far apart may come together, I think I am bound to spare no labour or trouble. But I hope that my meagre ability will be overlooked. If I pursue with my prayers what is undertaken by others, I shall have discharged my part. Philip is too far away for letters to pass back and forth in a short time. Bullinger has perhaps already written back to you. Would that I had an ability equal to the ardour of my zeal. Moreover, as to what I said at the beginning, that I would not do, the very difficulty of the matter, which you yourself feel, compels me to try; not only to urge you on, but also to press forward, until at least something is achieved, even if not everything succeeds as we wish. Farewell, most distinguished Prelate, and believe me to be sincerely devoted to you. May the Lord continue to guide you by his Spirit and bless your holy efforts. Geneva.

units.la: CALVINUS CRAMMERO ARCHIEPISCOPO CANTVARIENSI S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, greetings.

units.la: QVando hoc tempore minimè sperandum fuit, quod maximè optandum erat, vt ex diuersis Ecclesiis, quæ puram Euangelij doctrinam amplexæ sunt, conuenirent præcipui quíque doctores, ac ex puro Dei verbo certam de singulis capitibus hodie controuersis ac dilucidam ad posteros cōfessionem ederent: consilium quod cœpisti, reuerende Domine, vehementer laudo, vt mature apud se religionem Angli constituant: ne diutius rebus incertis, vel minus rite compositis quàm decebat, suspensi hæreant plebis animi. In quam rem ita omnes qui gubernacula istic tenét, communibus studiis incumbere oportet, vt tamen præcipuæ sint tuæ partes. Vides quid locus iste postulet, vel magis quid pro muneris quod tibi iniunxit ratione abs te suo iure exigat Deus. Summa est in te auctoritas, quam non magis tibi honoris amplitudo conciliat, quàm concepta pridé de tua prudentia & integritate opinio. Coniecti sunt in te bonæ partis oculi, vel vt tuum motum sequatur, vel vt cessationis tuæ prætextu torpeant. Atque vtinam te duce aliquanto logius iam ante triennium progressi forent, ne tantum hodie negotij crassis superstitionibus tollendis ac certaminum restaret. Fateor equidem ex quo sciò refloruit Euangelium in Anglia, intra breue tempus non paruas acceßiones esse factas. Verum si reputas, & quid adhuc desit, & quàm nimis fuerit in multis rebus cessatum, non est quòd remissius ad metam, quasi magna stadij parte confecta properes. Neque enim quasi te videam in opere assiduum, monendus videris, netibi quasi defunctus indulgeas. Sed, vt liberè loquar, magnopere vereor, nec definit metus hic recurrere, ne tot cunctando transigantur autumni, vt perpetuæ tandem hyemis frigus succedat. Iam ætas quò magis ingrauescit, acrius ad stimulare debet: ne si rebus confusis e mundo sit migrandum, magna te ex conscientia tarditatis, anxietas constringat. Res confusas appello: quia siccorrectæ sunt externæ superstitiones, vt re sidui maneant innumeri surculi, qui assiduè pullulent. Imò ex corrupt lis Papatus audio reliquam esse congeriem, quæ nō obscuret modò, sed propemodum obruat purum & genuinum Dei cultum. Interim totius ordinis Ecclesiastici anima non spirat, vel saltem non viget, vt par erat: doctrinæ scilicet prædicatio. Certè nunquam integra florebit religio, donec Ecclesiis melius prospectum fuerit, vt idoneos habeant Pastores, & qui docendi munus serió obeant. Id quominus fiat, occultis quidem artibus obstitit ebsistit Satan. Vnum tamen apertum obstaculum esse intelligo, quod praedae expositi sunt Ecclesiae reditus. Malum sane intolerabile. Sed praeter illam dissipationem, quae nimis crassa est: non multo leuius mihi videtur aliud vitium, quod ex publico Ecclesiae prouentu aluntur ociosi ventres, qui lingua incognita vespere cantillent. Nihil dico amplius, nisi quod te approbatore esse eius ludibrij, quod palam cum legitimo Ecclesiae ordine pugnat, plusquam absurdum est. Quanquam autem non dubito, quin haec tibi subinde veniant vltro in mentem, & ab optimo & integerrimo viro D. Petro Martyre, cuius te consilio vti plurimum gaudeo, suggerantur: tot tamen ac tam arduae difficultates quibuscum luctaris mihi visae sunt sufficere, ne superuacua foret mea exhortatio. Vale clarissime Praesul, & mihi reuerende. Dominus te diu conseruet incolumem, Spiritu prudentiae & fortitudinis magis ac magis locupletet, tuosque labores benedicat. Amen.
units.tr: At a time when it was hardly to be hoped for, though it was greatly to be wished, that the leading teachers of the churches which have embraced the pure doctrine of the Gospel should meet and, from the pure Word of God, publish a sure and clear confession for posterity on each of the points disputed today, I warmly commend the plan you have begun, reverend Sir: that the English establish their religion without delay, so that the minds of the people do not hang in suspense for longer on uncertain matters or on matters less properly settled than they ought to be. For this purpose, all who hold the helm there must apply themselves to the common task, though your part should be the chief one. You see what this place requires, or rather what God demands of you by right, for the office he has laid on you. The authority you hold is great, and it is won for you not so much by the dignity of your rank as by the opinion already formed of your prudence and integrity. The eyes of the better part of the people are fixed on you, either to follow your lead or to grow sluggish under the pretext of your inaction. And would that under your leadership they had advanced much further already, three years ago, so that such a great task of clearing away the gross superstitions and of settling disputes would not remain for us today. I admit that since I learned that the Gospel had revived in England, no small additions have been made within a short time. But if you consider both what is still lacking and how much has been neglected in many matters, there is no reason for you to slacken your pace and hurry towards the goal as if you had already covered the greater part of the course. For I do not see you as idle in the work, so that I need to exhort you, nor do I think you should indulge yourself as if you had finished. But, to speak frankly, I greatly fear, and this fear does not cease to return, that so many autumns may pass in delay that the cold of endless winter will follow. As your age advances, it ought to spur you on more sharply, lest, if the time should come to depart from a world still in confusion, anxiety over the great guilt of your slowness should weigh upon you. I call these matters confused because, although the outward superstitions have been corrected, there remain countless shoots that keep sprouting again. Indeed, I hear that from the ruins of the Papacy there is left a heap which not only obscures but almost buries the pure and genuine worship of God. Meanwhile the soul of the whole ecclesiastical order does not breathe, or at least does not thrive as it should: I mean the preaching of doctrine. Certainly religion will never flourish in full until the churches are better provided for, so that they have suitable ministers who discharge the office of teaching diligently. Satan has by hidden arts hindered this from being done. I recognise, however, one open obstacle: the revenues of the Church have been exposed to plunder. That is indeed an intolerable evil. But apart from that dissipation, which is all too gross, another fault seems to me hardly less serious: out of the public income of the Church, idle bellies are fed, who chant in an unknown tongue in the evenings. I say no more, except that for you to approve of this mockery, which openly conflicts with the lawful order of the Church, would be more than absurd. Yet although I do not doubt that these thoughts often come to you unbidden, and that they are suggested by that excellent and most upright man, Peter Martyr, whose counsel I rejoice greatly to use, still, the many and very grave difficulties with which you wrestle seemed to me enough, so that my exhortation would be superfluous. Farewell, most distinguished Prelate, and reverend to me. May the Lord keep you safe for a long time, enrich you more and more with the Spirit of prudence and fortitude, and bless your labours. Amen.

units.la: CAL. MINISTRO BVRENSI S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to the minister of Bourges, greetings.

units.la: Quod friuolis illis sermonibus de abrogato apud nos die Dominico fidem non habueris, prudenter abs te factum est. Nam eiusmodi fabularum portentis sua absurditas fidem omnem derogat. Quod autem fiducia nostrae modestiae fretus grauiter repulisti calumniam quae nobis inurebatur, in eo amici & fratris officium nobis praestitisti. Nam certe plusquam insanus essem, si inepta haec & friuola nouitate turbarem bonos, improbos armarem, omnium me exponerem ludibrio. Et quid de me loquor? Hominem hic ex turba nullum esse adeo importunum arbitror, qui hoc vnquam somniauerit. Ego tamen iam longo vsu contemnere rumores iitos didici, vel saltem aequiore animo ferre: quod mihi hactenus propemodum fatale fuit, putidis his calumniis quotidie onerari. Fortassis res vna fabulae materiam praebuit quod festus dies, qui Christi natali dicatus erat, in proximum diem Dominicum translatus est. Rectene an secus, non meum est pronuntiare. Ac per me licet, vt liberè, tuo id iudicio improbes. Quando enim factum est me nec auctore, nec conscio, mihi imputari non debet. Miraberis, nostros, inconsultis Pastoribus, receptum in Ecclesia ordinem ita subito mutasse. Verum id quoque inaduertentia potius quam peruicacia accidit. Antequam vrbem hanc primo aduentu ingressus essem, abrogati erant dies festi omnes, praeter Dominicum. Farello & Vireto hoc vtile visum fuerat. Ego receptae consuetudini libenter acquieui. Eandem quoque ratione noua haec Bernatium prouincia secuta initio fuerat. Surrexit N. nec minus tumultuose
units.tr: That you did not give credence to those frivolous stories about the abolition of the Lord's Day among us was a wise thing to do, for the sheer absurdity of such monstrous fables destroys all belief in them. As for your firm rejection of the slander being fastened on us, relying on the confidence of our modesty, in this you have performed the duty of a friend and brother. For I would certainly be more than mad if I were to disturb good people with this silly and frivolous novelty, arm the wicked, and expose myself to the ridicule of everyone. And why do I speak only of myself? I think there is no one in this crowd so thoughtless as to have dreamed of such a thing. Yet by long practice I have learned to despise such rumours, or at least to bear them with a more even mind, though until now it has almost been my lot to be burdened daily with these foul calumnies. Perhaps one thing gave material for the fable: the feast day dedicated to Christ's birth was transferred to the following Sunday. Whether that was right or wrong is not mine to pronounce; you may freely disapprove of it by your own judgment. Since it was done without my authority or knowledge, it should not be imputed to me. You will be surprised that our people changed the order received in the Church so suddenly, without consulting the ministers. But this too happened through inadvertence rather than obstinacy. Before I first entered this city, all feast days except the Lord's Day had been abolished. This had seemed useful to Farel and Viret, and I willingly acquiesced in the custom received. In the same way, the new province of Bern had at first followed this practice. Someone N. arose, no less tumultuously

units.la: p.j. pro diebus festis, quàm olim Victor Romanus pro suo Pascha te pugnauit. Ex quo autem fuimus expulsi, quatuor festi dies cum aliis quibusdam ritibus institutis sunt. Reuersus, cùm momento possem quicquid me absente actum erat, magnæ partis applausu conuellere, placidè quieui: nisi q; dissimulare non poteram, præposterè celebrari Christi circuncisionem, præterito mortis die: id inscite ac perperam ab indoctis hominibus fabricatum est. Iam q; diem conceptionis Christi sub Mariæ nomine plebs colebat, acriter in eam superstitionem quotannis inuectus sum. Galli enim sua lingua festum nostræ Dominæ in Martio appellant. Ac proinde dies illi sacer esse vulgò creditur. Sic tamē mihi temperaui, vt compescerem ex aduerso, qui dies illos prorsus tollendos clamitabant. Nam qui inter principio nomen Euangelio dederant, adeò ægrè tulerant nouationem posteà inductâ, vt mihi interdum non pepercerint, q; nimis tepidus videbar. Quinetiam ad gladios semel ventum erat. Cùm vtrinque immodicus cōtentionum feruor præualeret, media ratio nobis placuerat, vt mane clausis tabernis feriæ agerentur, à prandio conferrent se ad operas ordinarias. Idante annos nouem statutû fuit; neq; tamen hoc modo sedata fuerunt certamina. Varietas enim in clausis vel apertis tabernis turpe diffidiū prodebat. Cùm nec finis nec remedium inueniretur, anno proximè elapso veni in curiā: rogaui Senatum vt modum aliqué pro sua prudentia excogitaret, quo populus in meliore cōsensu retineretur. De abrogatione nominatim locutus nō sum. Quin potius laudaui, q; hæc nus foueda pacis studio, se ad Bernatium more accomodaffent. Cùm plebiscito audiui abrogatos esse dies illos, adeò res erat inexpectata, vt propemodum obliturim. Certè li sententia rogatus essem, nihil aliud dico, nisi q; vix ausus est im ita statuere. Vides in toto historiæ contextu nihil fuisse recens inductum: sed Ecclesiæ consuetudinem quæ malo exemplo euersa fuerat, reuocatam: & tamen id præter opinionem meam accidisse. Nec verò hæc sola fuit Ecclesia, quæ nullas, præterquàm diei septimæ feriàs retinuerit. Argetoratí enim idem olim institutum erat. Ego adueniens ordinem bene cōpositum turbare non debui. Quod nunc etiam quasi postliminio reuocatus est, mihi non videtur esse tanta offensionis causa. Si quid tamen culpæ esset, iniquè faciunt, qui me subiiciunt alieni facti reum. Vale.
units.tr: for the feast days than Victor of Rome once fought for his Easter. After we were expelled, four feast days were instituted along with certain other rites. When I returned, I could in a moment have overturned whatever had been done in my absence, with the applause of the greater part, but I quietly kept still. Yet I could not pretend not to notice that the Circumcision of Christ was being celebrated out of order, before the day of his death; this had been clumsily and wrongly devised by unlearned men. Since the common people were celebrating the day of Christ's conception under Mary's name, I attacked that superstition sharply every year, for the French call the feast of Our Lady in March in their own language, and so that day is commonly believed to be sacred. Yet I so restrained myself that I checked those on the other side who loudly demanded that these days be abolished altogether. For those who had first professed the Gospel were so displeased with the later innovation that they sometimes did not spare me, as if I seemed too lukewarm. Indeed, things had once come to swords. When the immoderate heat of the contention prevailed on both sides, we agreed on a middle course: the holidays would be kept in the morning with the shops closed, and after lunch people would return to their ordinary work. This was established for nine years, but the disputes were not settled in this way, for the variation between closed and open shops revealed a shameful division. When neither end nor remedy could be found, last year I went to the council and asked the Senate to devise, in its prudence, some way by which the people might be kept in better agreement. I did not speak of abolition by name. Rather, I praised them for having, out of zeal for peace, adapted themselves to the custom of Bern. When I heard by plebiscite that those days had been abolished, the thing was so unexpected that I almost forgot it. Certainly, had I been asked for my opinion, I would have said nothing else than that the matter was hardly to be decided in this way. You see that in the whole course of the story nothing new was introduced, but the custom of the Church, which had been overturned by bad example, was restored, and yet this happened contrary to my expectation. Nor was this the only Church which retained no feast days except the seventh day's rest; at Strasbourg the same arrangement had once been in place. Coming there, I ought not to have disturbed an order well arranged. That it has now been restored, as it were by right of return, does not seem to me to be so great a cause of offence. If there is any fault, however, they act unfairly who make me answerable for a deed that was not mine. Farewell.

units.la: BVLINGERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BULLINGER TO CALVIN, GREETINGS.

units.la: Vlx meas illas occluseram, tradendásq; Italo illi Cremonési curauerâ, cùm tuæ mihi per hunc tabellionem redduntur, Caluine coledif.frater, & quidem expectatæ & gratissimæ. Non
units.tr: I had scarcely sealed my letters and handed them to that Italian from Cremona when yours were brought to me by this messenger, Calvin, most honoured brother, and they were indeed both welcome and gratefully received.

units.la: Epist.129. Non aliud expectauerā de te, mi frater, respónsum, quàm quod exhibes. Scio enim in huiusmodi rebus parum pietatem promo uentibus, multum autem inuidiæ conflantibus, te nunquâ fuisse morosum. Ego quidem in his eam libertatem seruari cupio, quā video apud Ecclesias viguisse ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus. Nostra Ecclesia ante annos, ni fallor, x 11. plura habuit festa: sed abrogatis hisfolum retinuit diem Dominicam, & festa Christi, Natiuitatis videlicet, Circūcisionis & Ascensionis D. Adiecit & missionem Spiritus S. superioribus propter celebrationē Cœnæ D. Abrogauit autem festa alia, q̃ vicini interpretarentur nos ferias agere diuis. Ergo vt palā profiteremur nos non colere diuos cultu soli Deo debito, omnia in vniuersum abrogauimus. Multa quidem erat altercatio in innouationis initio, modò autē summa est inter nos tranquillitas. Certum est D. Bucerum migrasse ad D. in Anglia & D. Hopperum episcopatui suo restitutū esse, qua de re tibi dudum scripsi, si literæ tibi sunt redditæ. Addo his aliud non lætum nuntium D. Vadianum nostrum excessisse 6. Aprilis magno cum mœrore totius vrbis & Ecclesiæ Sangall. Seruamur nos, mi frater, sæuiori certamini, cui si nos D. immiscuerit, certò non deseret. Ipse vires conferat, vt ipsum & confessionem doctrināque & in corpore nostro semper glorificemus. Si quando dabitur occasio, scribe obsecro. Nam nihil mihi tuis est gratius literis. Vale æternū cum Gallasio & omnibus fratribus. Tigurì x x i x. Augusti. M. D. LI.
units.tr: Epist. 129. I expected no other answer from you, my brother, than the one you have given. For I know that you have never been tiresome in matters of this kind, which bring little credit to piety but much ill will to those who handle them. For my part, I wish to see preserved in these matters the freedom which I see flourished among the Churches from the very times of the Apostles. Our Church, some eleven years ago, if I am not mistaken, had several feasts. But with these abolished, it kept only the Lord's day, together with the feasts of Christ, namely his Nativity, Circumcision and Ascension. It also added the feast of the sending of the Holy Spirit, which had been part of the earlier observances because of the celebration of the Lord's Supper. It abolished the other feasts, since our neighbours would have interpreted our keeping holidays as a way of honouring the saints. So, in order to declare openly that we do not give to the saints the worship owed to God alone, we abolished them all together. There was indeed much dispute at the beginning of the reform, but now there is complete calm among us. It is certain that Bucer has migrated to the Lord in England, and that Hooper has been restored to his bishopric; I wrote to you about this some time ago, if my letter reached you. To these I add another unhappy piece of news: our Vadian has departed this life on 6 April, to the great grief of the whole city and the Church of St Gall. We, my brother, are kept for a harder struggle, and if the Lord engages us in it, he will certainly not desert us. May he himself grant strength, so that we may always glorify him, both in his confession and doctrine and in our own body. Whenever an opportunity is given, please write, I beg you, for nothing is more pleasing to me than your letters. Farewell for ever, with Gallasius and all the brethren. Zurich, 29 August 1551.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. N. S. D.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN to N. N., greetings.

units.la: Cùm Ministri Veterani contemptu turbæ incommodè in Ecclesia subortæ essent.
units.tr: When the veteran ministers had been brought into disrepute by a disturbance that had arisen in the church.

units.la: PLurimùm dolet, fratres dilectissimi, non offerri potius occasionem gratulandi vobis de prospero Ecclesiæ vestræ statu, quàm significandi vobis quàm molestè tulerim, quòd tristia ad me de vobis perlata sint. Iam enim acerbus fuit de optimi fratris N morte nuntius, cùm in illo vobis oblatus esset à Domino Pastor opportunissimus & verè fidelis: quod est rarius his temporibus maximè, cùm qui se syncerè Domini operi impendant, pauci reperiuntur. Ac iam vobis exploratum esse non dubito, & quàm vtilis esset illius opera, & quàm integrè se inter vos gereret. Et tamen spero illum qui à vobis iam electus est, fidelem etiam operam præstaturum, pro Dei gratia in ipsum collata, vt vos destitui non contingat: modò etiam videatis ne alij interea exuti maneant, vt omnino vos facturos spero, cùm ista inter vos & illos fratres ex communi consensu tractari exstimem: &c
units.tr: I am deeply sorry, dearest brothers, that I have no occasion to congratulate you on the prosperous state of your church, and must instead tell you how painful it was to hear the sad news that has reached me about you. The news of the death of our excellent brother N. was already bitter, since in him the Lord had offered you a most timely and truly faithful minister. Such men are rare in these times especially, when few are found who devote themselves sincerely to the work of the Lord. I do not doubt that you already know how useful his labour was and how blamelessly he conducted himself among you. Yet I hope that the man you have now chosen will also render faithful service, by the grace of God bestowed upon him, so that you are not left destitute. Provided, of course, that you see to it that the others meanwhile are not also left without their ministers, which I hope you will certainly do, since I think these matters are being handled between you and those brothers by common consent: etc.

units.la: ꝑ.ij. ipsorum angustiae fidem vestram implorent. Illud vero me ad scribendum impulit, aegritudo nempe animi mei, quam vestrae contentiones & iurgia mihi conciliant, quorum nullum finem video. Putabam enim omnia consopita esse, ac Deo eo nomine gratias egeram, maxime vbi ab optimo fratre N. idoneo, ita se rem habere accepissem. Atque illud vulneris illius mei acerbitatem parit, cum vigere malum audio, quod extincta audirem. Agebatur ante de quibusdam, quae in fratre N. desidera-batis, quibus illa medicina adhibita fuerat, qua vobis idonee, vt existimo, satisfactum esse oporteret: cum & ipse nominatim censura sese submisisset. Nunc nouam litem exortam audio, quod plerique illum pro Pastore habere detrectant, nisi abire ministerio iussus, nouae electioni subiiciatur. Ego vero tacere non possum videri mihi illos mali consiliji auctores, qui omnia ita ad vi-uum resecant, quod ad Ecclesiae aedificationem nullo modo faciat. Equidem non teneo quomodo illic primum fit institutus Pastor & ministerio fungi coeperit. Si electio in forma sua locu habuisset, nullus esset hodie controuertendi locus. Sed demus re non carere defectu aliquo. Expendite interea, cum aliquis exstitit in regione extranea qui postulet sibi dari locum & facultatem colligendi gregis Domini, annon qui illic adsunt, & in ministerium primum consentiunt, reipsa illum elegisse dicendi sint, etiamsi nulli tum ritus accedant? Illud vero mihi ingratitudinis plenum videtur, si successu temporis ille reiicitur, cuius opera ercta fuerit Ecclesia: aciam illius ratio non habeatur, qui viam ipse & modum aperuit, quo Ecclesia primum colligeretur in Domino per suum ministerium. Fateor vero vbi ordo semel stratus est, fixum & immotum re inlendum esse: sed longe alia est ratio, vbi ne tenuissima quidem Ecclesiae initia extant. Quid enim dicemus de plurimis illis Ecclesiis, quae Domino per Germaniam erectae sunt? An qui primum illis Euangelio praedicando nauarunt operam, non sine vllo ritu admissi sunt pro veris Pastoribus? Neque vero cogito vos hominum auctoritati subiicere: sed exemplum illud profero, quod ad confirmandum illud quod posui, facia: nimirum non requirit vt electio in eadem forma locum habeat rebus nondum constitutis, atque vbi Ecclesia suam quandam formam & ordinem iam admisit. Quare nulla mihi constare potest illarum difficultatum ratio, nisi quod accersi occasiones a remotis iudicio. Expendite praeterea vbi vos demergatis, si hoc semel perfringatur. Quod enim ius erit statuendum de tot Baptismis intermedij temporis? Quid de Coena vobis perinde administrata? Plura non addam, cum vel illa sint plus satis, vt frenum inducant immoderatis contentionibus. Quod si neque ista satisfaciunt fratribus, qui zelo ducti nimis sunt opinionibus suis addicti,peto ab illis per Dominum,vt cogitent etiam atque etiam in quod discrimen Ecclesiam adducant. Habitatis istic vt precario. Vbi hoc notabitur,tam esse difficiles in multis rebus, annon vestra morositas tædium aliquod & animi alienationem allatura sit bonis illis & piis, S natoribus,à quibus tam humaniter excepti estis? Deinde annon vobis liquet,nos omnes in illius quo de agitur persona semel periab illis,qui vnum hoc captat, vt vos omnes opprimant? Mirum sane,cum Guelfæ & Gibellini sese coniungere sustineant aduersus nouum hostem emergentem,vos vero non eorum exemplo duci, qui in vnam veritatis Euangelij professionem vocati sitis Qui vobis aduersantur in certo articulo, iam vos lacessere incipiunt vt tandem euertant. Frater ille stat paratus ad illos repellendos,ac primos impetus suos stiner. Quam igitur indignum est illum porro etiam à vobis vexari. Atqui vel illa afflictio qua constringitur, idonea erat ad emolliendam etiam illorum pectora, qui essent in illum exacerbatissimi: maximè cum & pestem vobis à Deo immissam attendistis,& alterum ex Pastoribus iam ereptum esse: quasi iam & pastum vobis plane subducendum comminatur Dominus,vbi nullam rationem admittitis qua vobis satisfiat. Hæc ad vos scribo, vt ignem accensum extinguam. Et tamen si quis nondum potest acquiescere,saltem à vobis peto per Dominum, vt extra vllum motum & contentionem, sustineatis modò aurem præbere rectis cõsiliis, quibus deinde placide manus detis. Spero equidem quam hic à me habetis admonitionem vobis factura satis : nec tamen ab illo vltimo remedio vos prohibere volui. Atqui longè magis optarim,vt quam primum quicquid est mali emendetur sine mora, vt omnes in veram concordiam coalescant. Hoc si continuat,iam vobis significo,magnum vos gaudium allaturos plurimis fratribus vestris,quibus ita vestra salus & tranquillitas est cordi, vt ad illam procurandam vobis si opus erit, paratissimos habituri sitis. Valete dilectissimi fratres. Dominus vos Spiritu suo regat cum vera prudentia, mansuetudine & constantia. Collegæ vos ex animo salutant. Geneuæ,x x i i. Decembris. M. D. L I.
units.tr: Sig. ij. Their distress implores your loyalty. What has moved me to write is the sickness of my own mind, which your quarrels and wranglings cause me, and of which I see no end. For I had thought that everything had been quieted, and I had given thanks to God for it, especially when I had heard from the excellent brother N. that matters stood so. The bitterness of my wound comes from hearing that an evil which I had heard was extinguished is flaring up again. Earlier there was talk of certain faults you had found in brother N., to which that remedy was applied, by which you ought, I think, to have been adequately satisfied, since he had himself submitted by name to censure. Now I hear that a new dispute has arisen, because many refuse to regard him as minister unless, after being ordered to leave the ministry, he is subjected to a fresh election. I cannot keep silent: it seems to me that those who cut everything so brutally to the quick, in a way that in no sense serves the edification of the church, are authors of bad counsel. For my part, I do not see how the first appointment of this minister was made, or how he began to exercise the ministry. If the election had been held in its proper form, there would be no ground for dispute today. But let us grant that the matter lacks nothing beyond some defect. Meanwhile consider this: when someone in a foreign region asks to be given a place and opportunity to gather the flock of the Lord, should not those who are there and agree to his ministry at the outset be said to have truly chosen him, even though no rite was added at that time? It seems to me full of ingratitude if he is rejected later, once the church has been built up through his labour, and no account is taken of the man who first opened the way and method by which the church was gathered in the Lord through his ministry. I admit that once an order has been established it must be kept fixed and unmoved. But the case is very different where not even the faintest beginnings of a church exist. For what shall we say about the many churches that the Lord has raised up throughout Germany? Were not those who first laboured to preach the gospel to them admitted as true ministers without any rite? I do not mean that you should submit to human authority; I bring forward this example to confirm what I have said, namely that an election in the same form is not required when matters are not yet settled, as when a church has already adopted some fixed form and order. Therefore I can see no ground for those difficulties, unless occasions are being drawn from remote judgments. Consider also where you will plunge, if this one principle is once broken. For what rule will be laid down about so many baptisms performed in the meantime? What about the Lord's Supper administered in the same way? I will add no more, since these alone are more than enough to bridle immoderate contention. But if these considerations do not satisfy those brothers who, led by zeal, are too attached to their opinions, I ask them through the Lord to think again and again what peril they are bringing the church into. You live there only on sufferance. When it is noted that you are so difficult in many matters, will your obstinacy not bring some weariness and alienation of mind to those good and pious senators by whom you were received so kindly? Moreover, is it not clear to you that we all, in the person of the man in question, have been ensnared by one who seeks only this, that he may crush you all? It is indeed astonishing that the Guelphs and Ghibellines can join forces against a new enemy that has emerged, while you, called into the one profession of the truth of the gospel, are not led by their example. Those who oppose you on a certain article are already beginning to harass you, so that they may finally overthrow you. That brother stands ready to repel them and to resist their first onslaughts. How unworthy it is, then, that he should be harassed by you too! Yet even the affliction that now binds him ought to have been enough to soften the hearts even of those who were most embittered against him, especially since you have seen the plague sent by God, and one of your ministers already snatched away. As if the Lord threatened to take away your pasture altogether, when you admit no reasoning by which you might be satisfied. I write these things to you to put out a fire that has been kindled. Yet if anyone still cannot consent, I ask you at least through the Lord to make every effort to avoid all movement and contention, and only to lend your ear to sound counsel, to which you will then gladly yield. I trust indeed that the admonition I have given you here will suffice, and I did not wish to bar you from that last remedy. But I would far rather wish that whatever evil there is be corrected at once, without delay, so that all may be united in true concord. If this happens, I tell you now that you will bring great joy to many of your brothers, who hold your salvation and tranquillity so dear that they will be most ready to help you in securing them, should it be needed. Farewell, most beloved brothers. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit with true prudence, gentleness and steadfastness. Your colleagues salute you from their hearts. Geneva, 22 December 1551.

units.la: Io. CALVINVS N. N. S. D. Eiusdem fere cum superiore argumenti.
units.tr: John Calvin to N. N., greeting. On nearly the same subject as the previous letter.

units.la: VTinam nunquam aliud mihi scribendi ad vos argumentu suppeteret, quàm vt Domino pro suis in vos donis ipsi gratias agerem, vósque eadem opera vt ad continuum profectum exhortarer Sed facit Satanæ nequitia,vt optatum illud at-
units.tr: I wish another subject for writing to you had never presented itself to me, other than to thank the Lord for his gifts to you and at the same time to urge you toward continual progress. But the malice of Satan has snatched that welcome subject from me.

units.la: Epist. 131. Ex Gall. gumentum mihi nunc ereptum fcntiam. Sic enim accepi illum vos inhalasse quodammodo, vt nisi vos Dominus respexisset, atque opem attulisset singulari sua benignitate, totum Ecclesiæ ædificium extremam ruinam minitaretur. Et vero malum diutius non fuit, sed a quo fletjt? Quis enim est ignis semel accensi extinguendi modus? Nunc igitur cum flamma consopita fuerit a Domino ipsius gratia, atque opera fidelium ipsius ministrorum: ne tamen idem vobis deinceps contingat, induxi in animum vobis admonitione apposita cauere in posterum, dum etiam culpam quæ a vobis admissa est, ob oculos ponerem. Vos autem obtemperastis, vt æqui & boni hoc officium consulatis, neque fi aspe-rior vobis visus fuero, vt res feret, eo minus admittatis reprehensionem: ne si secus fiat, malum duplicetur a vobis. Qui sim, & quo salutis vestræ affectu ducar, quicunque vere ad gregem Domini pertinent, facile agnituros confido: cum & vos in sinu & corde ipso gestem, non secus ac mihi charissimos liberos. Neq; hoc ab vlla ambitione proficiscitur. Nam & satis mihi est, vt pro fratre a vobis habear, & Christi seruum me profiteri non pœnitet, quin vestrum quoque esse ex animo agnoscam. Hoc igitur ad vestram vtilitatem pertinet, vt mea hæc admonitio qua salutí vestræ consultum volui, non pereat, aut cótemptu vobis inutilis reddatur. Ac primum quidem inaudita illa mihi est agendi ratio, vbi sic loquimini, Placere vobis vt ille concionetur, atque vt Cœnam vobis ministret. Sane oportet ministrum a populo approbatum esse, antequam in ministerij possessionem mittantur. Quod si quis scipsum intrudit alia via, vbi in Ecclesia ordo iam constitutus est, legitima vocatione destituitur. Ex eo tamen nego sequi, populum electioni fui Pastoris præesse debere. Tenatur Scriptura, institutos fuisse per oppida ac vicos ab Apostolis Pastores cum populi consensu. Sed illinc constat præfuisse ipsos sua prudentia & auctoritate tanto negotio, vt populum regendo, omnia decenter fierent & absque tumultu. Viguit porro eadem politia in Ecclesia Christiana, quandiu ordini ac disciplinæ locus remansit. Quare si hoc ius vobis arrogatis, vt pro arbitrio asciscatis vobis Pastores, hoc nihil aliud est quàm ordinem a Deo positum cum honestate Christiana cóuellere. Accedit alterum malum, quod temerariæ illæ mutationes & perpetuæ nouationes, non possunt non certissimum periculum, & peffimam causam secum trahere: ac vitium illud plane damnandum est. Scio natura hoc quæri, quia placeat: sed tantò consultius est illum natiuum pruritum semel extinctum esse. Hoc verò cum in vita humana perpetuum vsum habeat, tum imprimis ea in re qua de agitur. Fit enim Satanæ artificio, vt de die in diem huius & illius Pafi oris tædium nos corripiat, vt tandem sapor
units.tr: Epist. 131. From the French. For I have heard that he breathed upon you in such a way that, unless the Lord had looked upon you and brought help by his singular goodness, the whole building of the Church would have threatened final ruin. Indeed the evil did not last long, but from what did it spring? For what is the way to put out a fire once it has been kindled? Now, therefore, since the flame has been quenched by the grace of the Lord himself and by the work of the faithful ministers, yet so that the same thing may not happen to you again, I have resolved to set before you an admonition, so that you may take care in future, while also setting before your eyes the fault you have committed. You, however, have obeyed, so that you may take this duty as fair and good people do. If I seem rather harsh to you, as the matter requires, do not on that account accept the rebuke any less, lest, if it turns out otherwise, the evil be doubled by you. I am confident that all who truly belong to the flock of the Lord will readily recognise who I am and with what affection toward your salvation I am moved, since I carry you in my bosom and heart no differently than my dearest children. Nor does this proceed from any ambition. For it is enough for me to be regarded as a brother by you, and I am not ashamed to profess myself a servant of Christ, nor do I fail to acknowledge from my heart that I am yours as well. Therefore it serves your advantage that this admonition of mine, by which I wished to provide for your salvation, should not perish or be rendered useless to you through contempt. First, indeed, that manner of acting is unheard of to me, when you speak thus: that it pleases you that he should preach and that he should administer the Supper to you. Surely a minister ought to be approved by the people before they are sent into possession of the ministry. But if anyone thrusts himself in by another way, where an order is already established in the Church, he lacks lawful calling. Yet from this I deny that it follows that the people ought to preside over the election of their pastor. Scripture testifies that pastors were appointed by the Apostles in towns and villages with the consent of the people. But it is clear from that same passage that the Apostles themselves presided, by their own prudence and authority, over so great a matter, so that by governing the people all things were done decently and without tumult. Moreover, the same polity flourished in the Christian Church for as long as room remained for order and discipline. Therefore, if you claim this right for yourselves, to take pastors to yourselves at your own discretion, this is nothing other than to tear up the order established by God, together with Christian decency. There is also a second evil: those rash changes and perpetual innovations cannot fail to bring with them a most certain danger and a very bad cause, and that vice is plainly to be condemned. I know that nature seeks this because it pleases; but it is far more advisable that this innate itch be extinguished once and for all. Now, while this has a constant hold in human life, it has especially a hold in the matter we are discussing. For by Satan's artifice it comes about that from day to day weariness of this or that minister seizes us, until at last the savour and taste of the Word of God fades away in us,

units.la: Ad.14.24 sapor & gustus verbi Dei in nobis euanescat: cumque appetitus incerto & immoderato feremur, nihil quod rectum sit & saluta- te ampliùs admittamus. Iam vt non defuerit vobis ratio quæ- dam & apparentia, vt vocant, tamen non definit vitiosus esse agendi modus: Quæ tamen ratio subesse potuit? Cùm vnus ex vestris ad certas Ecclesias visitandas profectus esset, alter illius loco submissus est cum vestro iudicio & approbatione, ignotus vobis esse non poterat qui iam multò ante concionatus fuerat apud vos. Neque coniectutis actum fuit, cùm & de doctrina & de vita constaret. Si quis illum despicit, arrogantiam cum superbia in Deum prodit. Quid igitur sibi hoc vult, cùm idem ille & legitimè electus, & fideliter defunctus Pastoris inter vos munere, vt etiam appolita ad eam rem Dei dona in ipso extant, iam verò minus vobis adlubescat? quem verò illi præferetis? Homi- nem incognitum. Quis verò superest à temeritate apertissima vos nunc purgandi locus? Regeritis scilicet, istum multò orna- tius dicere. Sic nempe meminisis illius Pauli sententiæ: Quòd Regnum Dei non sit in sermone, sed in virtute? Proinde vt ipse alibi confirmat: Ille vnus in pretio nobis sit, qui est in Christo noua creatura: neque hæreamus in carne & apparentia illa exter- na, quæ nobis oculos hebetet ne syncerè, vt par est, iudicare possimus. Cauendum inquam, à laruis, id est, ab omni eo quod extra se se ostentat, vbi vt plurimum fucus latet: sed ad id quod præcipuum & verum est intendamus, atque illic pedem figamus. Atqui bene iudicandum, vbi malum non apparet. Concedo, vbi de aliquo pro fratre agnoscendo agitur: sed cùm de insti tuendo Pastore agitur, longè aliud examen requiritur. Interea verò meis istis verbis præiudicium cuiquam fieri nolim, cùm qui sit nobis incognitus, eò deteriorem non sit in sese. Tantùm hoc damno vt leuitatis & temeritatis plenum, quòd eo loco & ad talem munus hominem adhibere audemus, quem minus idoneè explorauimus, vt legitimum de illo testimonium præcedat. Scriptura enim ita Pastorem probum esse vult, vt & talem agnosci haberiq; præscribat. Enimvero si quis scipsum ita immittat atq; ingerat, vti iste à vobis inductus est, iam ipse ambitionis notam sibi inuflit, vt non inquiratur vlterius. Ego sanè malim pugnum mihi præcidi, quàm ferre vt aut ea ratione intromitterer, aut intromissus Cœnam ministrarem, vt ierga ipsum à vobis hac in re per tumultum gesta sunt omnia. Tanti momenti est vel vnum exemplum. Pertinet omnino ad Pastoris veri munus Moisis exemplum, cùm neminem ex Domini populo non Prophetam esse optaret. Agnoscere etiam oportet, adeóque locum cedere quantùm est in nobis, illis, qui dona illa acceperunt à Domino quæ ad Ecclesiae ædificandam conferant: quod & fratrem nostrum
units.tr: Acts 14:24 savour and taste of the Word of God fades away in us, and, since we are carried away by an uncertain and immoderate appetite, we no longer admit anything that is right and wholesome. Even if you had some reason and what they call an appearance, the manner of acting is nonetheless faulty. But what reason could there have been? When one of yours had set out to visit certain churches, another was sent in his place with your judgment and approval. He who had already preached among you long before could not be unknown to you. Nor was the matter undertaken without conjecture, since both his doctrine and his life were well attested. If anyone despises him, he betrays arrogance and pride against God. What, then, does this mean, since the same man was both lawfully elected and faithfully discharged the office of minister among you, as the gifts of God bestowed for that purpose are still evident in him; and yet now he is less pleasing to you? Whom, then, will you prefer? A man unknown to you. What place now remains for you to clear yourselves of this most manifest rashness? You will say, of course, that he preaches much more elegantly. Surely you remember that saying of Paul: that the Kingdom of God is not in speech but in power? Therefore, as he himself affirms elsewhere, let that one alone be prized by us who is a new creature in Christ; and let us not cling to the flesh and that external appearance, which dulls our eyes so that we cannot judge sincerely, as is fitting. We must beware, I say, of masks, that is, of everything that presents itself outwardly, where for the most part deceit lies hidden; but let us aim at what is principal and true, and plant our foot there. Yet one must judge well where evil does not appear. I grant this where it is a matter of acknowledging someone as a brother; but when a pastor is to be installed, a far different examination is required. Meanwhile, I would not wish any prejudice to be done to anyone by these words of mine, since one who is unknown to us is not for that reason worse in himself. I only charge this: that it is full of levity and rashness that we dare to put a man into that place and into such an office whom we have examined too little, without a lawful testimony about him going before. For Scripture wills that a pastor be so proved that it prescribes he be recognised and held as such. Indeed, if anyone thrusts and forces himself in, as this man was introduced by you, he himself brands himself with the mark of ambition, so that no further inquiry is needed. I would surely rather have my fist cut off than endure being admitted in that way, or, once admitted, administering the Supper, just as everything was done toward him by you in this matter, amid tumult. One single example is of such weight. The example of Moses certainly pertains to the true office of a pastor, when he wished that none of the Lord's people should not be a prophet. We must also acknowledge, and yield place as far as lies in us, to those who have received from the Lord those gifts that serve to build up the Church; which I do not doubt our brother also looks to, as he clearly showed when he admitted him even more readily than he himself would have done.

units.la: p.iiij. spectare non dubito, vt aperte ostendit, cum illum admisit etiam promptius quam ipse fecisset. Sed vt resipsa per se excruciatur, quis vobis suggesssit penes populum esse, vt Pastorem temere mutetis, prout hic potius quam ille, huius vel illius oratio aut ornatus in dicendo vos plus minus vce ceperit: aut penes populum esse pronunciare, placere sibi vt Coenam ministret? Quin telegamus potius huiusmodi ambitum ad claustra monachorum, cum Dei Ecclesiam alia moderatio prorsus deceat! Vos vero plus etiam audetis, quam par sit, ii ex vna concione statim fertis sententiam. Non pertinet, vt puto, ad omnes huius vitij notatio. Nam vel vnum susurronem huius turbae auctorem esse potuisse mihi persuadeo. Cum tamen ita vos humiliauit Dominus, vt ista tentatione abrepti fueritis, ego sane vobis vehementius obstitisse, quam a fratre nostro factum sit. Vt enim laudo ipsius modestia, ita etiam motum illum insolentem maiori seueritate mihi refrenandum esse duxisse. Accedunt & circumstantiae quae malum exaggerant. Habetis Pastorem in carcere detentum. Illo ita absente, tales motus excitare, an excusationem vllam admittit? Inter extraneos ita tumultuari, vt cum illos vobis vna moderatione conciliare debueritis, iam ipsorum iudicio obnoxios reddatis, qui in vestrae Ecclesiae administratione tam praecipitanter vos geritis. Neque vero offendi vos oportet mea ista acerbitate. Si enim essem apud vos, vehementius multo vrgerem istud publicum delictum, cuius momentum fortasse vt & causam ego eminus exactius expendo, quam vos in medio illo contentionis strepitu & pulvere cernatis. Ac sperO omnino de vobis sic ista a vobis acceptum iri, vt & mihi ad Deo gratias agendum vestro nomine os aperiatis. Quod si vobis modicam tristitiam attuli, me quidem non poenitet, vt Paulus loquitur, dummodo ista sit tristitia secundum Deum: vbi nempe ita vos admisse culpae poenitebit, vt consultius deinceps agatis. Scitis quam ipse cupiam meipsum consolari, dum vobis simul gaudij materiam obiulero. Cum vero aliquid mali subortum est, illic sese vera amicitia exerit, vbi ad vitia non conniuemus, sed libere coarguimus, vt nullus prauus affectus aut carnalis intermistus sit. Si quis de me hic quereretur, vidisset imprimis an suum reatum ferio excusit, cui censura adeo molesta sit. Atqui longe me melior de vobis spes sustinet, vt habeas enus vestri experimentum habui. Qui enim Deo vos obsequeres praestatis, docilesetiam exhibituros statuo, & aequo ac pacato animo admissuros reprehensiones, quae ex ipsius verbo ad vos ita diriguntur, vt quae in illis amaritudo subest, ad interiorem sanitatem & animae salutem plurimum faciat. Valete amantissimi fratres. Dominus vos omnes foueat in timore nominis sui & veritatis dilectione, det vobis continuum incrementum mentum in omni bono & gratia Spiritus sui, vt glorificetur in vobis nomen ipsius magis ac magis. Amen.
units.tr: p.iiij. But how can the matter itself be racked by its own nature? Who suggested to you that it lies with the people to change their pastor rashly, according as this man's rather than that man's speech or ornament in speaking has moved you more or less; or that it lies with the people to pronounce that it pleases them that he should administer the Supper? Rather let us banish such ambition to the cloisters of monks, since a different moderation altogether befits the Church of God! You, however, dare more than is proper, and you pass judgment at once on the strength of a single sermon. The censure of this fault, I think, does not apply to all of you. For I am persuaded that even a single whisperer could have been the author of this uproar. Yet since the Lord has humbled you so that you were carried away by this temptation, I surely resisted you more vehemently than our brother did. For just as I praise his modesty, so I thought that the insolent commotion had to be restrained by me with greater severity. Circumstances also add to the evil. You have your pastor held in prison. With him thus absent, can such commotions be excused in any way? To riot among outsiders in such a way that, when you ought to have won them over to yourselves by one moderation, you now make yourselves liable to their judgment, you who conduct yourselves so headlong in the administration of your Church. Nor should you be offended by this harshness of mine. For if I were among you, I would press this public offence much more vehemently; its weight, and perhaps its cause, I weigh more exactly from afar than you can discern them in the midst of that clamour and dust of contention. And I hope altogether that these things will be received by you in such a way that you will open your mouths to give thanks to God on my behalf. But if I have brought you a modest sadness, I am not sorry, as Paul says, provided that this sadness is according to God: namely, where you so regret the fault you have admitted that you act more wisely thereafter. You know how much I wish to console myself, while at the same time offering you matter for joy. When some evil has arisen, true friendship shows itself there, where we do not connive at faults but freely rebuke them, so that no depraved or carnal feeling is mixed in. If anyone complained about me here, he would first have seen whether he had excused his own guilt, for whom the censure is so burdensome. But a far better hope sustains me concerning you, since I have had experience of your character. For I judge that you who render obedience to God will also show yourselves teachable, and will receive with an even and calm mind the rebukes directed at you from his own Word, so that whatever bitterness lies in them contributes greatly to inner health and the salvation of the soul. Farewell, most beloved brothers. May the Lord cherish you all in the fear of his name and in love of the truth, give you continual increase in every good thing and in the grace of his Spirit, so that his name may be glorified in you more and more. Amen.

units.la: VIRETVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: VIRETUS TO CALVIN, GREETINGS

units.la: COgnoscesex Farelli literis quid egerit, quomodo sit excep-tus & quid à nobis requiratur, quid item velit ad te scribi suo nomine. Non dubito quin tibi saepe illud veniat respolum D. in mentem, quod fecit Paulo deprecanti illum carnis stimu-lum quo assiduè & tam acerbè pungebatur. Nosti quas ob cau-sas D. servuis suis aduersa immittat, & quam in partem Paulus interpretetur. Non vos tot artibus & tam malis ac toties Sa-anas impetteret, nisi hoc vestrum propugnaculum quod habet apud vos Christi Ecclesia, sibi ad nodum sentiret aduersarium & suo regno inimicum. Sit igitur vobis hic eius insultus tanquam Sacramentum, quo magis atque magis confirmemini in s. hoc certamine ad quod estis vocati. Si ex mundo essetis vos mundus diligeret, vobis faueret. Certissime igitur notae vobis esse debent sanctae vestrae vocationis impiorum prava studia, quibus alij clam alij palam sanctis vestris conatibus resistunt, & pia studia remorari conantur. Memento eius fiduciae qua sese Dauid eri-gebat aduersus Goliath pugnaturus, memor victoriae illius quam ex dilaniato à se vrso & leone reportarat. Qui te hactenus cum tuis fratribus inuictum seruauit, perficiet opus quod coepit in vo-bis Impij proficient in peius, quandiu volet D. Sed interea eo-rum interitus nec dormitat, n c cunctatur. Non vident caeci iu-dicia D. tam illu tria quorum fulgor omnibus perstringit ocu-los. Atque eò testantur se esse deploratiores, & à Deo magis alie-nos. Oportet esse sectas, vt qui probati sunt, fiant manifesti. Opor-tet iam re ipsa experiri, sinne coetus electorum & reproborum, quando D. i veritati hoc credere nolunt tam aperte docenti. Soli-citi expectamus exitum huius turbationis. Scripsisti nuper te nolle scribere quid facturus esses, si nostro esset loco. Scribe. Nam crede mihi si quod facturus esses, cum à nobis fieret, gloriam Dei promouere posset, nullo nostro deerimus muneri. Hoc tamen nos male haber, quod nondum satis prospicere potuimus, quid magis in rem Eccl. sit futurum esset. Vale. Collega te salutat. Laufannae X X I I I I. Decemb. M. D. L I.
units.tr: From Farel's letter you will learn what he has done, how he has been received, and what is required of us, and likewise what he wishes written to you in his own name. I do not doubt that you often recall the answer the Lord gave Paul when Paul asked to be rid of the thorn in the flesh with which he was so constantly and so painfully pricked. You know why the Lord sends adversities to his servants, and in what sense Paul interpreted them. Satan would not assail you with so many arts and such wicked attacks, so often, unless he felt that this bulwark which the Church of Christ has among you was a thorn in his side and an enemy to his kingdom. Let this assault of his therefore be to you like a sacrament, by which you may be more and more strengthened in this holy struggle to which you have been called. If you were of the world, the world would love you and favour you. Therefore the wicked endeavours of the ungodly, by which some secretly and others openly resist your holy efforts and try to hinder your pious undertakings, must be very well known to you. Remember the confidence with which David rose up against Goliath, mindful of the victory he had won over the bear and the lion he had torn apart. He who has kept you and your brethren unconquered until now will complete the work he has begun in you. The wicked will grow worse for as long as the Lord wills. But meanwhile their destruction is neither asleep nor delayed. The blind do not see the judgments of God, which shine so brightly that they strike the eyes of all. And by this they testify that they are more desperate and more alienated from God. "There must be sects, so that those who are approved may be made manifest." It is now necessary to test in fact whether there is any fellowship between the elect and the reprobate, since they are unwilling to believe this truth which God teaches so plainly. We await anxiously the outcome of this disturbance. You wrote lately that you did not wish to write what you would do if you were in our place. Write it. For believe me, if what you would do, when done by us, could advance the glory of God, we shall not be wanting in any of our duty. Yet this troubles us, that we have not yet been able to foresee sufficiently what would be most useful for the good of the Church. Farewell. Your colleague greets you. Lausanne, 24 December 1551.

units.la: MINISTRIS HELVETICIS FRATRIBVS ET Symmystis plurimum obseruandis. S.
units.tr: TO THE SWISS MINISTERS, OUR BRETHREN AND FELLOW PRESBYTERS, TO BE MOST HIGHLY RESPECTED. GREETINGS.

units.la: E S T hic Hieronymus quidam, qui abiecta monachi cuculla, vnus ex Circunforaneis medicis factus est, qui fallendo, & fruštrando tantum sibi impudentię acquirunt, vt ad quiduis audendum propti sint,ac parati. Is iam ante octo menses in publico Ecclesiæ nostræ coetu doctrinâ de gratuita Dei electione, quam ex verbo Dei acceptam vobiscum docemus, labefactare conatus est. Ac tunc quidem qua fieri potuit moderatione sedata fuit hominis protervia. Postea non destitit locis omnibus obstrepere, ut simplicibus hoc fidei caput excuteret. Tandem virus suum nuper aperto gutture euomuit. Nă cum pro more nostro unus e fratribus illum Ioannis locum exponeret, ubi pronunciat Christus ex Deo non esse, qui verba Dei non audiunt, dixisset quotquot Spiritu Dei renati non sunt, peruicaciter vsq; in finem Deo resistere: quia peculiare sit obedientiæ Donum, quo Deus suos electos dignatur. Surrexit nebulo ille, ac dixit falsam & impiam opinionem, cuius auctor fuit Laurentius Valla, nostro seculo exortam esse: quod Dei voluntas rerum omnium sit causa. Hoc autem modo peccata, & malorum omnium culpa in Deum transcribi, & illi affingi tyrannicâ libidinem, qualem Poëtæ veteres in suo Ioue comminenti sunt. Postea ad alterum caput defecit, non ideo salutem cófequi homines, quia electi sint, sed ideo eligi, quia credant: nec reprobari quenquam nudo Dei placito, sed cos tătum, qui se communi electione priuant. In hac quæstione agitanda multis, & atrocibus conuitiis in nos inuectus est. Præfectus vrbis re audita eum duxit in carcerem, præsertim quia tumultuose plebem hortatus fuerat, ne se decipi à nobis sineret. Nunc ad Senatum delata est causæ cognitio: vbi errorem suum nō minori obstinatione quâ audacia tueri perrexit. Interea cum iactaret se in aliis Ecclesiis cóplures habere à sua parte ministros, postulauimus à Senatu nostro, ne prius de tota summa pronunciaret, quàm habito Ecclesiæ vestræ responso, cognosceret nebulonem illum improbe suffragij vestri titulo abuti. Ille initio pudore victus Ecclesiarum iudicia non abnuere, sed cauillari vos merito propter familiarem cum fratre nostro Caluino vsum vi deri suspectos. Senatus tamen sicuti à nobis rogatus erat, vos consuluit consulendos. Huc quoque accessit, quæ vestram Ecclesiam im plicabat. Zuinglium enim præ aliis omnibus damnas, Bullinge rum eiusdem fecerit esse sententiam mentiebatur. In Ministrisetiam agri Bernensis alute dissidij animam captauit. Nos verò sic Ecclesiam nostram cupimus hac peste purgari, ne indi fugata vicinis noceat. Tametsi autem nostra, & publicæ tranquillitatis magnopere interest, quâ profitemur doctrinam, vestro consensu appro bari: non est tamen, quæ fidem vestram multis verbis implore mus. Non ignota est vobis fratris nostri Caluini Institutio, quâ hic præcipue suscipit oppugnădam. Quàm reuerenter, ac sobrie illic de arcanis Dei iudiciis differat, prædicare nihil attinet: quia satis luculentus per se testis est liber. Nec verò quicquam hic do-
units.tr: There is a certain Jerome here, who, having cast off the monk's cowl, has become one of the travelling quacks. Such men acquire so much impudence through deceiving and cheating that they are ready and prepared to dare anything. This man, eight months ago, in the public assembly of our Church, tried to shake the doctrine of God's free election, which we teach with you as received from the Word of God. Then the fellow's wantonness was calmed with as much moderation as possible. Afterwards he did not cease to clamour in every place, so as to shake this article of faith among the simple. At last he has recently vomited his poison with open throat. For when, according to our custom, one of the brothers was expounding that passage of John where Christ says that those who do not hear the words of God are not of God, and had said that as many as are not born again by the Spirit of God resist God stubbornly to the end, because perseverance in obedience is a peculiar gift with which God honours his elect, that scoundrel rose up and declared that a false and impious opinion had arisen in our century, whose author was Laurentius Valla: that the will of God is the cause of all things. In this way, he said, sins and the guilt of all evils are transferred to God, and a tyrannical lust is ascribed to him, such as the ancient poets invented for their Jupiter. Afterwards he turned to the other point, that men obtain salvation not because they are elect, but are elected because they believe; and that no one is reprobated by the bare pleasure of God, but only those who deprive themselves of the common election. In debating this question he launched many atrocious insults against us. The prefect of the city, when he heard of it, led him into prison, especially because he had stirred up the common people tumultuously, urging them not to let themselves be deceived by us. Now the case has been referred to the Senate for examination, where he has persisted in defending his error with no less obstinacy than audacity. Meanwhile, since he boasted that he had several ministers on his side in other Churches, we asked our Senate not to pronounce on the whole matter until it had learned, from the response of your Church, that this scoundrel was wrongly abusing the title of your suffrage. At first, overcome by shame, he did not refuse the judgments of the Churches, but jeered that you were rightly held suspect because of your familiar intercourse with our brother Calvin. The Senate nevertheless, as we had asked, consulted you as those to be consulted. To this was added what implicated your Church: for he claimed that you condemn Zwingli above all others, and falsely asserted that Bullinger held the same opinion. He also tried to catch the spirit of a harmful division among the ministers of the Bernese territory. We, indeed, wish our Church to be purged of this plague, lest, once driven out, it harm its neighbours. Although it greatly concerns our own and the public tranquillity that the doctrine we profess be approved by your consent, there is nonetheless no need for us to implore your faith with many words. The Institutes of our brother Calvin, which this man especially undertakes to attack, are not unknown to you.
