How reverently and soberly he discourses there on the hidden judgments of God, there is no need to preach: the book is in itself a sufficiently clear witness.

units.la: cemus, emus, nisi quod sacro Dei verbo proditum, in Ecclesia vestra iam inde à restituta Euangelij luce obtinuit. Satis conuenit, fide nos iustificari: sed in eo apparet solida Dei misericordia, cum fidem intelligimus gratuitæ adoptionis esse fructum. Adoptione vero ex æterna Dei electione fluere. Hic autem impostor cum electionem ex fide pendere fingit, tum fidem ipsam nō minus ex proprio motu hominis, quam ex cœlesti inspiratione oriri. Rursum extra cōtrouersiam est, ꝙ pereunt homines, ipsorum malitiæ imputandum esse. Sed in reprobis, quos Deus arcano suo consilio tanquam indignos præterit, ac deserit, illustre se profert hu militatis documentum. Hieronymus autem iste nihil iustè à Deo fieri concedit, nisi cuius ratio posita iaceat sub oculis. Hoc denique inter nos fixum est, ac cōcessum: Deum in hominum pecca tis culpę socium adscribi fas nō esse: nec vllo modo in eum cōpetere peccati nomē. Id tamen nō obstat, quò minus miro quodam, & incōprehensibili iudicio per Satanam, & reprobos tanquam iræ suæ organa manus suæ potentiam exercens, nunc fideles ad patientiam erudiat, nunc hostibus suis pœnas infligat quales merentur. Hic profanus nugator Deum reatu inuolui clamitat, cum eius prouidentiam rerum omnium arbitrā facimus. Denique omne discrimen inter causam remotam & abscondi tam, & propinquas tollens, erumnas sancto Iob impositas Dei opus censeri nō patitur, quin pariter cum diabolo, & Caldæis, & Sabæis latronibus reus fiat. Proinde quod mutua inter nos coniunctio postulat, vestra subscriptione Christi doctrinam sacrilegiis proterui, & male feriati hominis grauatam leuare, & assere re ne grauemini. Quòd quia vos vltrò, & libenter facturos confidimus, anxiis vel accuratis precibus vobiscum agere superuacuum est. Nos vicissim sicubi vsui erit vobis nostra opera, ad fraternum omne officium semper paratos habebitis. Valete charissimi, & obseruandi fratres. Dominus vos Spiritu suo regat, labores vestros benedicat, & Ecclesiam vestram tueatur. Geneuæ.
units.tr: Nor do we teach here anything except what has been handed down in the sacred Word of God and has held sway in your Church since the restored light of the Gospel. It is agreed well enough that we are justified by faith; but the solid mercy of God appears in this, when we understand that faith is the fruit of free adoption, and that adoption flows from God's eternal election. But this impostor, while he feigns that election depends on faith, also holds that faith arises no less from the man's own motion than from heavenly inspiration. Again, it is beyond controversy that men perish through their own malice. Yet in the reprobate, whom God, by his secret counsel, passes over and forsakes as unworthy, a remarkable proof of his justice is displayed. This Jerome, however, concedes that nothing is done justly by God unless its reason lies open before the eyes. Finally, this is fixed and agreed between us: that God may not be counted a partner in the guilt of men's sins, and that the name of sin can in no way apply to him. Yet this does not prevent him, by a certain wonderful and incomprehensible judgment, exercising his power through Satan and the reprobate as instruments of his wrath, now training the faithful to patience, now inflicting on his enemies the punishments they deserve. This profane trifler cries out that God is implicated in guilt, since we make his providence the arbiter of all things. Finally, by abolishing every distinction between remote, hidden and proximate causes, he does not allow the afflictions laid upon holy Job to be counted the work of God, unless God is made equally guilty with the devil, and with the Chaldeans and the Sabaean robbers. Therefore, as the mutual fellowship between us requires, please do not hesitate, by your subscription, to lift the burden that this shameless and ill-behaved fellow has laid on the doctrine of Christ. Since we trust that you will do this readily and willingly, it is superfluous to deal with you by anxious or elaborate prayers. We in turn, wherever our labour may be of use to you, will always have our fraternal service ready at hand. Farewell, most dear and honoured brothers. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, bless your labours, and protect your Church. Geneva.

units.la: CAL. MINISTRIS BASILIENSIBVS S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to the ministers of Basel, greetings.

units.la: Gratia vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro & Domino Iesu Christo charissimi & plurimùm fratres honorandi.
units.tr: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, beloved and most honoured brothers.

units.la: ETsi responsum de quæstione vobis propositā dedistis minus plenum ac liquidum quàm res forte postulabat, certè quàm spes votaque nostra ferebant: vestrum tamen candorem iuuandíque studium gratis animis amplexi sumus. Cæterum nihil illic nisi pium & orthodoxum cōtineri sentimus. Vtinā talis confessio impetrari à Bolseco potuisset. Nulla enim causa fuisset exhibēdę vobis molestię. Sed quod de ipso testati sumus, plusquā ferreæ esse frontis hominem, verum esse comprobat, cum e vestro iudicio subscribere mentitur. Nec vero eum puduit coram Senatu nostro idem iactare. Sed valida refutatione quæ in promptu erat, confusus, tandem obmutuit. Porro an quicquam vestrę doctrinæ affine habeat, non est difficile iudicium. Literis nostris actestimonio ne habeatur fides: descriptas ex actis publicis eius responsiones Senatus nostor vobis misit, in quibus reperiens ad verbum fidem ab electione non pendere: item electionem esse ex fide: item neminem in sua cæcitate manere ob naturæ corruptionem: quia rite à Deo illuminantur omnes: Deum vero contumelia afficiGi, si quis dicat deseri aliquos in sua cæcitate à Deo: quoniam illi sic visum est. Item trahi à Deo rationales omnes creaturas: nec quenquam ab initio deseri, sed qui sæpius Deo recludatus est. Item ex lapideo corde fieri cor carneum, nihil esse aliud quàm dari cor intelligentiæ capax. Hanc vero gratiam generalem esse: item non esse hos potius quàm illos ad salutem prædestinatos. Cum illi ex primo ad Ephesios capite obiectus esset locus, pro desperata sua impudentia respondit, non illic de communi piorum salute tractari: sed quod Paulus cum suis collegis in munus Apostolicum electus foret. Cum rursum à nobis exceptum esset, solos igitur Apostolos adoptionis gratuitæ esse compotes, solos Deo reconciliatos esse, solos remissione peccatorum donatos, adeo non motus est, ut canino risu fulmina illa exciperet. Conferre hæc delirii cum vestro iudicio: quid magis dissentaneum? Absit ergo ut vos impiis eius erroribus dicamus fut-tragari: à quibus vos esse alienissimos epistola vestra distincte clamat. Imo cum tentaret impostor vos sibi implicare, detecta eius fraude proteruiam strenue compescuimus. Cuius rei Senatum nostrum habemus locupletissimum testem. Et cum in exilium actus est, publice ex solenni more pronuntiatum ex sci ipso fuit, iudicia Ecclesiarum, quibus staturum se receperat, contumaciter spreuisse. Scribat Fallesius hominem esse non malum, & in gratiam ignoti nebulonis famam suam ludibrio proditurat. Breui maiore quàm vellemus Ecclesiæ damno constabit, quàm noxia fuerit pestis. Nam alia quoque errorum monstra alere multi sunt idonei testes. Et nunc cum fidem vestram aperte oppugner, fallaci cosenfusus simulatione, à vobis literas elicere conatus est, quarum præextextu apud rudes & simplices abuteretur. Vos autem & amicè erga nos, ut fratres decebat, quod respofum distulistis, vsque dum facti estis de tota re certiores: atque ut vestra prudentia dignum erat, scitè & rectè quod impij & perfidi nebulonis astutia vos circumuenire passi non estis. Vt vestra moderatio non vulgari laude digna est: ita vos eius fructum sensurosspe-ramus. Pro ista, qua erga nos vsi estis humanitate, non vulgares habemus.
units.tr: Although the answer you gave to the question put to you was less full and clear than the matter perhaps required, and than our hopes and wishes looked for, we have nonetheless gladly accepted your candour and your zeal to help. Moreover, we find nothing in it but what is godly and orthodox. I wish Bolsec could have been brought to make such a confession. There would then have been no need to trouble you. But what we testified about him, that the man has more than iron forehead, is proved true, since he lies in claiming that he subscribes to your judgement. Nor was he ashamed to boast of the same thing before our Senate. But when a strong refutation was at hand, he was confounded and at last fell silent. As for whether his teaching has anything in common with yours, the judgement is not difficult. Let no faith be given to our letter as testimony. Our Senate has sent you his answers, copied word for word from the public records, and in them you will find that: faith does not depend on election; election is from faith; no one remains in his blindness because of the corruption of nature, since all are duly illumined by God; but God is insulted if anyone says that some are left by God in their blindness, because it so seemed good to him; all rational creatures are drawn by God; no one is abandoned from the beginning, but only one who has often rejected God; a heart of flesh is made from a heart of stone, which is nothing else than being given a heart capable of understanding; this grace is general; and some are not predestined to salvation rather than others. When the passage from the first chapter of Ephesians was put to him, he answered, in his desperate impudence, that it does not treat of the common salvation of the godly, but of Paul and his colleagues being chosen for the apostolic office. When we countered that therefore the apostles alone are partakers of free adoption, alone are reconciled to God, alone are granted forgiveness of sins, he was so far from moved that he met those thunderbolts with a dog's laugh. Compare this raving with your judgement: what could be more contrary? Far be it, then, from us to say that you are infected by his impious errors, from which your letter clearly proclaims you are most remote. Indeed, when the impostor tried to entangle you with himself, we vigorously checked his impudent deceit once it was exposed. Our Senate is a most ample witness of this. And when he was driven into exile, it was publicly announced, according to the solemn custom, that he had stubbornly scorned the judgements of the Churches, to which he had pledged himself to submit. Let Fallesius write that the man is not bad, and for the sake of some unknown rascal expose his own reputation to ridicule. Before long it will become evident, at a cost to the Church greater than we would wish, how harmful this pest has been. For many are capable witnesses that he also nourishes other monstrous errors. And now, since he openly attacks your faith, he has tried, with a deceitful pretence of humility, to extract letters from you, under whose pretext he might deceive the untaught and simple. You, however, both kindly towards us, as brothers should be, have postponed your reply until you were fully informed of the whole matter, and, as your prudence deserved, wisely and rightly have not allowed yourselves to be taken in by the cunning of that impious and treacherous rascal. Your moderation is worthy of no ordinary praise; and we hope you will reap its fruit. For this kindness which you have shown towards us, we give you no ordinary thanks.

units.la: Eph. 1. 5. & deinceps.
units.tr: Eph. 1. 5. & deinceps.

units.la: habemus gratias. Valete eximij viri,& fratres nobis ex animo colendi. Dominus vos cum Ecclesia vestra conseruet ac benedicat.Mense Ian. M. D. LII.
units.tr: We give you thanks. Farewell, distinguished men and brothers, whom we cherish from our hearts. May the Lord keep and bless you together with your Church. January 1552.

units.la: CALVINVS CHRISTOPHORO LIBERTETO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO CHRISTOPHER LIBERTET, GREETINGS.

units.la: TV vero, mi Christophore longe falleris, si aeternum Dei cōsilium ita posse discerpi putas, vt quosdam elegerit in salutem, neminem mexitio destinarit.Nam si aliquos elegit,sequitur certe non omnes esse electos. Porrò quid de his dicendum erit,nisi eos sibi relinqui vt pereant? Mutua igitur inter reprobos & electos relatio sit oportet. Verbo quidem fatetur Hieronymus Bolsecus, certum aliquem numerum à Deo electum esse, sed cū propius vrgetur,ad vniuersos homines delabi ipsum necesse est. Dicit enim palam ex aequo gratiam omnibus offerri quae ad salutem sit illis efficax:quod alij recipiunt,alij respuunt,discrimen in libero eorum arbitrio esse, qui Deum vocantem motu proprio sequuntur. Neque enim dissimulat sic libero arbitrio praeditos esse omnes,vt in medio omnibus posita sit obtinendae salutis facultas. Hoc modo totam praedestinationem ab ipsa radice conuelli vides:statui liberum arbitrium,quod salutem aliqua ex parte nobis acquirat. Atque hoc plus quam ridiculum est, q; Hieronymus liberum arbitrium cofessus,à meriti voce abhorret. Quisquis enim ideo censetur in Dei filiis, quia oblatae sibi adoptionis gratiae se aptauit, quomodo merito spoliandus est? Hunc sibi sensum, vel potius hoc se delirio implicitum teneri, iam satis prius ostenderat:sed nuper rursus ad nos venit. In coetum nostrum vocatus, cauillando nihil profecit, quin eum ex suis latebris in lucem protraherem. Praeter quindecim verbi Ministros aderant & alij testes idonei. Negarunt omnes,si vel vnam pudoris guttam habuisset,potuisse statim ad sanam mentem reuerti. Sed initio puerilibus cauillis ludebat:sed tertio verbo cum premeretur,frontem penitus abiecit. Subinde enim,quod bis & ter concesserat,negare:quod negauerat,rursus concedere:vacillare à suis principiis,interdum etiam excidere:fine fine & modo in eosdem reuolui circuitus. Nec fieri aliter potuit.Nisi enim tractos à patre fuisset,qui ad Christum venient,fatemur,& hoc peculiare est: Spiritus sancti opus in electis, vel omnes promisceue electos esse constat,vel causam electionis in cuiusque merito sita est. Si reprobationis exordium in secunda hominis cōtumacia statuitur, sequitur nihil apud Deum esse constitutum, sed suspensum esse eius consilium,quid de singulis actarus sit.Fatetur Hieronymus natura omnes prauos esse, gratia Dei omnibus offerri, quæ ingenitam à natura prauitatem corrigat. Quosdam fingit liberi arbitrij sui motu correctionem admittere, vt sit efficax: alios, quibus idem liberum esset, respuendo bis fieri contumaces: inde fictitiam reprobationem elicit. Ita æternum Dei consilium subiici hominum arbitrio, quis non videt? Et tu elegantiam nescio quam in tanta insulsitate videre te putas? Atqui, si quid in diuinis intelligo, hoc multò ineptius ac crassius commentum est, quàm Papistarum fuit. Iam si fructus electionis est, bona & recta in homine voluntas, reprobos sequitur toto cordis affectu ad malum ferri. Nec verò Paulus, cum volentis esse negat, aliquam tribuit reprobis voluntatem, quæ per se sit irrita: quin potius ex Dei misericordia fluere docet, quòd bene velle & recte currere incipiant, qui prius erant ab omni rectitudine auersi. Desinant ergo fontem & primam causam discretionis inter electos & reprobos in humano arbitrio locare, si quem electioni Dei locum relinquere volunt.
units.tr: You are greatly mistaken, my Christopher, if you think the eternal counsel of God can be torn apart in such a way that he has chosen some for salvation while appointing no one to destruction. For if he has chosen some, it certainly follows that not all are elect. What then must be said of the rest, except that they are left to perish? There must therefore be a mutual relation between the reprobate and the elect. Hieronymus Bolsec indeed admits in words that a certain fixed number has been chosen by God, but when he is pressed more closely, he must slide down to all men without exception. For he openly says that grace is offered equally to all, and that it is effective for salvation: some accept it, others reject it, and the difference lies in the free choice of those who follow God calling them by their own motion. Nor does he conceal that all are so endowed with free will that the ability to obtain salvation is placed before everyone alike. In this way you see that the whole doctrine of predestination is uprooted from its very foundation: he sets up a free will that gains salvation for us in some measure. And this is more than ridiculous, that Hieronymus, while confessing free will, shrinks from the word merit. For whoever is counted among the sons of God because he has fitted himself to the offered grace of adoption, how can he rightly be stripped of it? He had already sufficiently shown that this was his view, or rather that he was entangled in this delirium; but lately he came to us again. Called before our assembly, he gained nothing by his quibbling, except that I dragged him out of his hiding places into the light. Besides fifteen ministers of the Word, other fit witnesses were present. All of them denied that, if he had possessed even one drop of shame, he could have returned at once to sound mind. At first he played with childish quibbles; but when, at the third word, he was pressed, he cast off all shame. Thereafter he kept denying what he had twice and thrice conceded, conceding again what he had denied, wavering from his own principles, sometimes even slipping out of them, and rolling endlessly round the same circuits. Nor could it have happened otherwise. For unless those who come to Christ had been drawn by the Father, we would admit that, and this is peculiar: it is the work of the Holy Spirit in the elect, and it is agreed that either all are promiscuously elect, or the cause of election lies in each one's merit. If the beginning of reprobation is placed in the second stubbornness of man, it follows that nothing has been settled with God, but that his counsel is left in suspense as to what will become of each individual. Hieronymus admits that all are evil by nature, and that the grace of God is offered to all, to correct the depravity born in them by nature. He imagines that some admit correction by the motion of their own free will, so that it becomes effective; while others, to whom the same free will was given, become doubly stubborn by rejecting it: from this he draws out a fictitious reprobation. Who does not see that in this way the eternal counsel of God is made subject to the will of men? And do you think you see some elegance in such utter silliness? Yet, if I understand anything of divine matters, this invention is far more foolish and crude than any the Papists have devised. Further, if the fruit of election is a good and right will in man, then the reprobate, with their whole heart's affection, are carried toward evil. Nor indeed when Paul denies that it is of him who wills, does he ascribe to the reprobate any will that is in itself ineffective; rather he teaches that it flows from God's mercy that those who were previously turned away from all rectitude begin to will well and to run rightly. Let them therefore cease to place the source and first cause of the distinction between elect and reprobate in human choice, if they wish to leave any place for the election of God.

units.la: CAL. FARELLO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL, GREETINGS.

units.la: CVM his mensibus assiduo concionum onere supramodum grauatus fueris: iam tempus esse arbitror, vt tibi aliquantu- lum quietis indulgeas. Frater noster Christophorus interea se paulatim colliget. Neque enim salubre foret, tam cito à morbo longam profectionem suscipere. Ergo si consilio meo obtem peras, breui nos inuises. Si videbitur, in itinere comitem assumes Viretum. Nisi faciurum te cõsiderem quòd suadeo, haberesà me longiores literas, etsi in rebus nostris nihil est quod te exhilaret: qua etiam ratione à scribendo impedior, ne bis tibi sim molestus. Caue tamen ne miseros fugias. Vale integerrime frater & præstantissime Christi seruc. Dominus tibi perpetuò adsit, te guberner, labores tuos benedicat. Collegam, fratres, amicos & familiam saluta. Geneuæ x. Iulij, M. D. LII.
units.tr: Since you have been greatly burdened these months by the constant load of preaching, I think the time has come for you to indulge yourself in some rest. Our brother Christopher will meanwhile gradually gather his strength, for it would not be wholesome to undertake a long journey so soon after his illness. So if you obey my advice, you will visit us shortly. If it seems good, you may take Viret with you as a companion on the journey. Unless I thought you would do what I advise, you would have a longer letter from me, although there is nothing in our affairs that could cheer you; and this is also the reason I am prevented from writing, lest I be a burden to you twice over. Take care, however, not to flee from the wretched. Farewell, most upright brother and most excellent servant of Christ. May the Lord be with you always, govern you, and bless your labours. Greet the colleagues, brothers, friends and your household. Geneva, 10 July 1552. Your John Calvin.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: MELANCHTHON CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: MELANCHTHON TO CALVIN, GREETINGS.

units.la: REuerende vir, & charissime frater, sæpe ad te scriberem, si ta bellarios certos haberem. Colloqui etiam mallem de rebus grauissimis multis: quia & iudicium tuum magni facio: & scio integritatem animi, & candorem in te summum esse. Nunc ita viuo ὡσπερ ὀρνεος ἐν σφηκίας. Sed fortassis ex hac mortali vita ad collegium in cœlo candidius breui accedam. Audio Francisfcum Dryandrum hac æstate apud te fuisse. Mihi, si viuam noua exilia expectanda sunt. Quare si cedendum erit ex his locis, colloqui tecum decreui. Studia doctrinarum in his regionibus mediocria fuerunt. Nunc lue, & bellis impediuntur. Ac saepe gemens deploro causas horum furorum in gubernatoribus. Oro etiam Filium Dei, ut has calamitates leniat, & auferat causas. Si voles mihi saepius scribere, poteris literas Francisco Dryandro mittere. In pagella, quam inclusi breuiter scripsi historica huius Autumni. Bene vale. Calend. Octob. M.D.LII. Iam respondeo ad Gorgonem Osiandri. In Pannonia Turcici Bassae tres sunt qui habent duos exercitus & recens occuparunt quaedam oppida insignia, & trucidauerunt exercitum Regis Ferdinandi. Nunc profectus est in Austriam Dux Saxoniae Mauricius, ut ducat exercitu contra Turcos. Interea Marchio Albertus vastata vicinia circa Noribergam, & vexata Francfordia, diripit oppida in dioecesibus Moguntina & Treuirensi. Gallici Regis exercitus accessit ad Leodiensem dioecesim. Imperator Carolus Spirae exercitum colligit, ut Gallicum Regem & Marchionem reprimat. In Saxonia filius Comitis Alberti Mansfeldensis colligit exercitum circa Bremam, & nunc ad haec loca nobis vicina accedit, recuperaturus suam patriam, & turbaturus totam regionem. Ita sunt in Germania passim vastationes. Ecclesiae sunt in luctu & moerore: & doctrinarum studia conticescunt. Crescit robur seditiose clamantium de libertate. Vobis tranquillitatem gratulor, & Deum oro, ut nobis quoque nostras miserias leniat.
units.tr: Reverend man and dearest brother, I would often write to you if I had such certain messengers. I would also prefer to talk with you about many most weighty matters, since I greatly value your judgment and know that your integrity and candour of mind are very great. Now I live like a bird in a cage [ὡσπερ ὀρνεος ἐν σφηκίας]. But perhaps I shall soon pass more brightly from this mortal life into the college in heaven. I hear that Francis Dryander was with you this summer. For me, if I live, new exiles are to be expected. Therefore, if I must withdraw from these places, I have decided to speak with you. The studies of learning in these regions have been middling; now plague and wars hinder them. And often, groaning, I lament the causes of these frenzies in the rulers. I also pray the Son of God to soften these calamities and remove their causes. If you wish to write to me more often, you may send your letters to Francis Dryander. In the little page which I enclosed I have briefly written the history of this autumn. Farewell well. Kalends of October 1552. Now I reply to the Gorgon of Osiander. In Pannonia three Turkish pashas have two armies and have recently seized certain notable towns, and they have slaughtered the army of King Ferdinand. Now Duke Maurice of Saxony has set out for Austria, to lead an army against the Turks. Meanwhile Margrave Albert, having laid waste the neighbourhood around Nuremberg and harassed Frankfurt, plunders the towns in the dioceses of Mainz and Trier. The army of the French king has moved into the diocese of Liège. Emperor Charles is gathering an army at Speyer to check the French king and the Margrave. In Saxony the son of Count Albert of Mansfeld is gathering an army near Bremen, and now approaches these places near us, intending to recover his homeland and to disturb the whole region. Thus there are devastations everywhere in Germany. The churches are in mourning and sorrow, and the studies of learning fall silent. The strength of those who clamour seditiously about liberty grows. I congratulate you on your tranquillity, and I pray God to ease our miseries too.

units.la: Philippus.
units.tr: Philip.

units.la: SI PIA MVLIER A MARITO PROPTER Religionem durius tractabitur.
units.tr: IF A PIOUS WIFE IS TREATED MORE HARSHLY BY HER HUSBAND ON ACCOUNT OF RELIGION.

units.la: A D speciem propositam de muliere quae Religionis vere no mine durissime tractatur a marito, & in seruitute quadam acerbissima habetur, rogatus an illi mulieri liceat, derelicto tali marito, si se huc recipere vel alibi, vbi sit Ecclesia, in qua pacata conscientia victura sit. Respondi satis nos quidem videre aerumnas & angustias fidelis mulieris, cui & nos mutuo cogemisceremus, & Deum ut ipsam respiciat precaremur. Cum vero quaeritur quid ei facere liceat ex Dei verbo, merum hoc ac simplex responsum a nobis reddi posse sine vllo alio respectu: quod ei molestum esse nolimus, etiam si nostra sententia ad illius affectum plane non faciat: quando & illam & nos etiam ab vno Magistro ita pendere oportet, ut nullus sit nostris affectibus locus, vbi de eius voluntate praestanda agitur. Hic igitur respicere oportet quodnam sit vinculum matrimonii: eiusmodi nempe, ut non liceat fideli per se & sponte relinquere in fidelem, vt docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 7. 11. Et certum est Paulum eo vsque separationem negare, etiamsi fideli ab infideli plurima eaque grauissima toleranda sint. Neque enim Ethnici vel Iudæi tum æqui fuerunt Christianis, quàm nunc sint Papistæ. Iubet tamen Paulus, vt fidelis perstet in officio constanter erga Deum, neque tamen defert partem infideli quæ Dei veritati aduersetur. In summa ita vni Deo postponi debent mundus, parentes, liberi, maritus & vxor, vt vbi illa simul retinere non licebit, tum omnibus abrenuntiatis, vni Domino adhæreamus. Ex quo non consequitur, Christianismo tolli omne naturæ ius & ordinem, vbi nulla vis maior adegerit. Tum enim debet pia mulier eniti tanto magis, vt officio fungatur erga virum qui veritati resistit, vt illum lucretur quantum in ipsa erit, vt docet Pet. 1. 3. 1. Atque vt resfunt in Papatu, partis fidelis officium est studere & eniti, vt comparem in viam salutis perducat. Quòd si obstinatum animum experiatur, non tamen discef sionem à pietate simulet vllo modo, quin potius de sua integritate & constantia testetur quicquid accedat, vel sibi obiectû habeat. Iam vbi pars fidelis ita officio functa, persecutione premetur eo nomine, licebit tum illi fuga sibi consulere. Vbi inquam fidelis vir siue mulier fidei confessionem ediderint: ac si expediet ostenderint, fas non esse sibi consensum præbere abominationibus Papisticis, ac tum persecutio illis imminebit ea occasione, vt instet ipsis certum periculum, licebit tum illis cuadere, si Dominus viam ipsis aperuerit. Neque hoc diuorti in spontaneum appellari potest, cùm vi quis ad fugiendam persecutionem adigitur. Quod autem ad speciem proposicam attinet, illa huic nostræ sententiæ non respondet. Constat enim mulierem qua de agitur tacere & dissimulare pietatem, atque sincere sese polluisse perstitionibus, adeòq; sese ad arbitrium mariti inflectere: quia nullo iure à marito abscedere potest, nisi & plenioram fidei confessionem ediderit, & vi maiore coniuncta. Iilla tamen obtinerit. Petat igitur à Domino vt ipsam confirmet: deinde ad pugnam sese animosius accingat Spiritus 5. virtute freta quàm hactenus, vt maritum educeat cum omni mansuetudine & modestia quam fidem profitetur, vtque ei fas non sit in mariti gratiam Deum offendere. Expendiatur quidem illa asperitas mariti à nobis quà mulier attingit. Verùm illud non impedit, quominus vires ipsa colligat, atque exitum Domino commendet. Constat enim infidelitate fieri, vt metu præpediti, quod vocationis nostræ est agredi non audeamus. Non est igitur idoneum eiusmodi fundamentum, cui nos innitamur. Tandem vbi officio functa, periculum sibi imminere intellexerit, adeò vt maritus in vitæ discrimen ipsam adducat, tum demum patebit ei libertas illa quam omnibus piis offert Dominus,vt luporum fauces euadãt.x xii. Iulij. M. D. LII.
units.tr: You ask me about the case proposed of a woman who, truly on account of religion, is treated most harshly by her husband and kept in a very bitter kind of servitude. You ask whether it is lawful for her, leaving such a husband, to withdraw here or elsewhere, where there is a Church in which she may live with a quiet conscience. I answer that we certainly see the troubles and distress of this faithful woman, with whom we grieve in turn, and we pray that God will look upon her. But when the question is what she may lawfully do according to God's Word, a plain and simple answer can be given by us without any other consideration, and we would not wish to trouble her with it, even though our opinion does not fully accord with her inclination. For both she and we must depend so entirely on the one Master that there is no room for our affections when the question is what his will requires. Here, then, we must consider what the bond of marriage is: namely, of such a kind that a believer may not leave an unbelieving spouse by his or her own choice and will, as the Apostle teaches (1 Cor. 7:11). And it is certain that Paul denies separation to such an extent, even though the believer must bear very many and very grievous things from the unbeliever. For neither the Gentiles nor the Jews were then more fair to the Christians than the Papists are now. Yet Paul bids the believer to persevere steadfastly in duty towards God, and yet he does not yield to the unbeliever any part that opposes the truth of God. In sum, the world, parents, children, husband and wife must be placed so far beneath the one God that, when it is not lawful to keep both, we renounce all and cling to the one Lord. It does not follow from this that all natural right and order is abolished by Christianity, when no greater force has compelled it. For then the pious wife ought to strive all the more to fulfil her duty towards her husband who resists the truth, so that she may win him as far as lies in her power, as 1 Peter 3:1 teaches. And, as things stand under the Papacy, it is the duty and effort of the believing partner to lead the other into the way of salvation. But if she experiences a stubborn mind, she must nevertheless in no way feign a departure from piety; rather, whatever befalls her or is thrown in her face, she should bear witness to her own integrity and constancy. Now, when the believing partner has so performed her duty and is pressed with persecution on that account, it will then be lawful for her to look to her own safety by flight. When, I say, a believing man or woman has made confession of the faith, and, if it is expedient, has shown that it is not right for them to give consent to the Papist abominations, and then persecution threatens them on that occasion, so that a certain danger presses upon them, it will then be lawful for them to withdraw, if the Lord has opened the way for them. Nor can this be called a voluntary divorce, since someone is compelled by force to flee persecution. As for the case proposed, however, it does not agree with this our opinion. For it is clear that the woman in question conceals and dissimulates her piety, and has sincerely polluted herself with superstitions, and so bends herself to the will of her husband; because she cannot lawfully withdraw from her husband unless she has made a fuller confession of the faith, and that together with greater force. Let her therefore ask the Lord to strengthen her; then let her gird herself more boldly for the struggle, trusting in the power of the Spirit more than hitherto, so that she may lead her husband, with all gentleness and modesty, to the faith which she professes, and so that it may not be right for her to offend God for the sake of her husband's favour. We indeed consider the harshness of the husband as far as it touches the wife. But that does not prevent her from gathering her strength and committing the outcome to the Lord. For it is plain that it is through unbelief that, hindered by fear, we do not dare to undertake what belongs to our calling. Therefore this is not a suitable foundation on which we should rest. Finally, when she has performed her duty and understands that danger is hanging over her, so that the husband brings her into peril of her life, then at last that freedom will be open to her which the Lord offers to all the pious, so that they may escape the jaws of the wolves. 22 July 1552.

units.la: BVLINGERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BULLINGER TO CALVIN, GREETING

units.la: DIv iam nihil tuæ pietati scripsi,frater in Domino colende & dilecte,præsertim q; feriam aliquam occasionem obser uarem. Ea cum modo sit oblata, scribendi volui officium repetere. Retulit haud dubie frater ille Laufinnensis è Comitiis Badensibus rediens quid actum sit ab vrbibus Tiguro, Basilea, Schaffusio in causa vinctorum propter verbum Dei in Gallia:& quòd V.C. Ioannes Habius vrbis nostræ Cos. ad Regem missus sit legatus.Is ergo hodie scriptis ad amplissimum vrbis Senatum literis exposuit, quomodo legationem iniundam obierit, quid responsi à Rege ex ore ipsius proprio acceperit. Nempe q; post diligentem supplicationem factam, Rex non comunicato cum suis consilio postularit diserte,ne vrbes illæ in hoc negotio pergant ipsi esse molestæ: cum non ita pridem scriptis ad iiii. vrbes literis idem negotium scripto agentibus animi sui sententiam explicarit,de quo nihil cesserit: liberum se facere vrbibus, vt pro suo beneplacito res suas gubernent: id ipsum omnino velle in regno suo, quod prorsus cogitet purum seruare à seditiosis illis hominibus. Hæc est illius Regis responsio,quæ ita vti meretur à nostris accepta est. Hoc nescire te nolui,vt hoc ardentiores preces Domino offerre vnà pergeremus. Viuit qui populum suum ex Ægypto liberauit.Viuit qui captiuitatem ex Babylone reduxit. Viuit qui Cæsaribus,Regibus ac Principibus profligatis Ecclesiam suam asserruit.Oportet nos quidem per multas afflictiones ingredi in regnum Dei. Væ autem illis qui tangunt pupillam oculi Dei. Pergamus nos constanter docere verbum Dei, prædicare Euangelium Christi, & cum omnibus sanctis,in cælum oculos attollere. Non deferet nos qui dixit,Ero vobiscũ vsque ad consummationem seculi. In mundo afflictionem habebitis,confidite,ego vici mundum,Christus seruet nos & suam Ecclesiam.Saluta fratres omnes.Salutant te fratres. Tiguri,x v. Augusti. M. D. LII.
units.tr: I have written nothing to your piety for some time now, dear brother in the Lord, and I particularly wished to renew my duty of writing since I was seeing some occasion for it. Now that such an occasion has been offered, I wanted to resume the office of writing. Without doubt, that brother from Lausanne, returning from the Diet of Baden, has reported what has been done by the cities of Zurich, Basel and Schaffhausen on behalf of those imprisoned in France for the sake of the word of God, and that our fellow citizen, the honourable Johannes Haller, consul of our city, has been sent to the King as an envoy. Today, then, he has set out in writing for the most honourable Senate of the city how he carried out the mission entrusted to him, and what answer he received from the King in his own words. Namely, after a diligent petition had been made, the King, without consulting his council, demanded plainly that those cities should not persist in this business, since they were being troublesome to him; although not long before, when four cities had written to him about the same matter, he had explained his opinion in writing, and had yielded nothing on that point: he makes the cities free to manage their affairs at their own pleasure, and he wishes this very thing to hold throughout his kingdom, since he fully intends to keep it free of those seditious men. This is the King's reply, and it has been received by our people as it deserves. I did not want you to be ignorant of this, so that we might go on offering more fervent prayers to the Lord together. He lives who led his people out of Egypt. He lives who brought back the captivity from Babylon. He lives who, having overthrown Caesars, Kings and Princes, has vindicated his Church. We must indeed enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions. But woe to those who touch the apple of God's eye. Let us continue steadfastly to teach the word of God, to preach the Gospel of Christ, and, together with all the saints, to lift our eyes to heaven. He who said, "I will be with you until the end of the age," will not desert us. "In the world you will have tribulation; take courage, I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). May Christ keep us and his Church. Greet all the brothers. The brothers greet you. Zurich, 15 August 1552.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL, GREETINGS.

units.la: ADiscessi vestro rursus in curiam vocatus sum.Neque enim comicus noster Cæsar legationis obeundæ causa ante voluit pedem vrbe mouere, quàm negotium hoc transfactum esset:quia timebat,ne se abscente aliquid grauius decerneretur in cognatum. Non tamen vocatus sum per apparitorem,sed venit
units.tr: I had scarcely left you when I was summoned back to the council. Our comic Caesar did not want to leave the city on his embassy until this business was settled, because he feared that something more serious would be decided against his kinsman in his absence. I was not summoned by a messenger, however. One of the senators came to my house to escort me.

units.la: q.j. domum vnus ex senatoribus, qui me deduceret. Illic Balthasar ex more conquestus est de iniuria sibi facta. Respondi quod visum est. Senatus deliberatio nec difficilis, nec longa fuit. Nisi quod omnes, ac si non iudices, sed voluntarij arbitri sederent, nihil statuere audebant, quod non utrique parti scirent gratum fore. Balthasar cum suo patrono semel atque iterum vocatus, feroci-ter calcitrauit. Tandem vitus est, qui sua intemperie omnia turbare solet, illius lasciuiam domare: vel saltem sedare nimium feruorem: necogeretur Senatus in eum esse durior. Etsi autem simulabant ambo, se grauiter vri ob inustam infamiae notam, nihil tamen malebant, quam tota litem placide componi. Quia nullo modo elabi poterat miser iste, quin poenam daret eius conuitij, quod ebrius in me effutuerat, tandem quasi precibus cognati sui victus, staturum se arbitrio Senatus promisit. Multa praeterea, quae vltro citroque agitata sunt. Quia transactionem mihi negaui ratam fore, nisi publicis literis testata esset: recitatur ex scripto Senatusconsultum, in hanc formam. Recte me & ex officio fecisse, quod illum a sacra Baptismi sponsione depulerim. Nihil esse causae, cur se laesum queratur, cum suo merito repulsam illam passus sit. Illi mandari, ut me in posterum reuereretur colat, abstineat ab omni contumacia. Et quia sparsus esset rumor, illum mihi absenti maledixisse, quod sibi nunquam venisset in mentem dicere, locum illi fui purgandi dari. Haec autem purgationis species palinodia erat, honesto praetextu velata, quo dedecus effugeret. Additum etiam, Senatum haec omnia sibi integra seruare: & fore vindicaturum, si quando ille insolesceret. Sed quia laqueo se constrictum teneri cernebat, eius veniam extorsit. Caeterum affinis eius, qui materteram habet uxorem, quasi mea facilitate liceret sine modo abuti, de suo addidit, ut ego vicissim pro bono & honesto cum homine haberem. Ostendi breuiter quam absurdum & indignum illud foret. Ita sine mora & absque vlla disceptatione, quod perperam addiderat, expungere iussus est. Ego primo illo capite contentus, quo magna mihi & Collegis libertas parta est, in reliquis me exorabilem praebui. Nobis enim dabatur, quod sanguine meo redemptum optaf-fem. Nam etsi aliquoties rationibus nostris succubuerant, nihil tamen adhuc certi pronuntiatum fuerat. Porro vt sentiret ille quanuis indignus, me salutis ac quietis suae esse cupidum, consului vt ad veniam deprecandam sponte se consistorio offerret. Facturum promisit, & venit quidem: sed minime animatus vt decebat. Superbe enim iactauit se nullius culpae sibi esse conscium, & parum aberat, quin alios impeteret. Ego meo officio defunctus exęufaui, quod paterna indulgentia eum ad bonam frugem reuocare frustra conatus essem. Dimissus est cum tristi responso, respondo, excommunicari eum & sodales, donec resipiscerent. Mirabili Dei prouidentia hoc totum gubernatum fuit, quòd pri uata venia fretus, in animo habebat paucis pòst diebus infantem mihi afferre, vt maiorem apud rude vulgus inuidiam conflaret, si reiiceremmihi vero religio fuisset admittere, qui publico Ecclesiae iudicio damnatus, nondum poenitentiam suam professus erat. Nunc non facilis modò nobis victoria, sed plausibilis etiam causa erit. Quanquam de exitu, qualem prospicio instare, non admodum mihi gratulor. Fida enim confessione nos eludet, quae tamen ipsa ad exemplum proderit. Seniores omnes habemus optime nobis coniunctos, valde etiam cordatos in asserendo Ecclesiae iure, & coercenda improborum proteruia. Vnum duntaxat excipio, qui tamen perfidis suis blanditiis nemi-nem hactenus potuit flectere. Perendie hac transiit filius Iusti Ionae per equos celeres ad Regem properans, à Comite Mansfeldensi legatus. Nescio quid dicam, nisi quod iusta Dei vindicta vbique mundus turbatur, qui sub illius obsequio quiescere non poterit. Plura literis non licet committere. Quum Ecclesiae Saxonicae facta essent mentio: inter alia narrauit, Melanchthonem male audire, quòd non magis ingenuè professus sit, sibi nobiscum in causa sacramentaria bene conuenire. Ipse autem de tota re ita prudenter & scitè disseruit, vt nihil in eius sermone futile animaduerterim, cum tamen satis acriter ad eum obseruandum essem intentus. Non dubito quin iam audieris me patriae esse su-perstitem. Ita vrbem mortuam lugere cogor, quę superiore anno ob falsum mortis meae rumorem solennes habuit supplicationes, vt de Christo triumpharet. Vale integerrime frater, & fidelis Christi serue, cuius praesidio te commendo. Geneuae, 1111. Nonas Decembris. M. D. LII.
units.tr: There Balthasar, as is his custom, complained of the wrong done to him, and I gave the answer that seemed right. The council's deliberation was neither difficult nor long, except that all of them, as if they were not judges but voluntary arbiters sitting in judgment, dared to decide nothing that they did not know would please both parties. Balthasar was summoned together with his patron once and again, and kicked out fiercely. At last he was brought to heel. He is a man who usually throws everything into confusion through his own lack of restraint, and it was needful to tame his wantonness, or at least to calm his excessive heat, lest the council be forced to be harsher with him. Although both of them pretended to be deeply stung by the stain of infamy inflicted on them, they actually preferred nothing more than that the whole quarrel be settled peaceably. For this wretched man could in no way escape without paying the penalty for the insult he had hurled at me while drunk. At last, as if overcome by the entreaties of his kinsman, he promised to abide by the council's judgment. Much else was also argued back and forth. Since I had declared that I would not regard the settlement as binding unless it was attested by a public document, a decree of the council was read out in writing, in this form: that I had acted rightly and in accordance with my office in barring him from the sacred pledge of baptism; that he had no cause to complain of being wronged, since he had suffered that rejection through his own fault; that he was ordered to show me respect in future, to honour me, and to refrain from all insolence. And because a rumour had spread that he had spoken evil of me in my absence, something he said he had never even thought of saying, an opportunity was given him to clear himself of this charge. This form of purgation, however, was a recantation, veiled under a respectable pretext so that he might escape disgrace. It was also added that the council would keep all these matters intact and would take vengeance if he should ever grow insolent again. But since he saw himself held fast in a noose, he wrung a pardon out of them. Moreover, a relative of his, who has an aunt as his wife, added on his own initiative a clause, as if my good nature allowed him to abuse me without limit, that in return I should treat the man with kindness and honour. I showed briefly how absurd and unworthy that was. So, without delay and without any dispute, he was ordered to strike out what he had wrongly added. I was content with that first point, by which great freedom has been won for me and my colleagues, and in the remaining matters I showed myself willing to be persuaded. For we were granted what I would have wished to buy with my own blood. Although on several occasions they had given way to our arguments, nothing certain had yet been pronounced. Furthermore, so that he might understand, however unworthy he is, that I desire his salvation and peace, I advised him to offer himself voluntarily to the consistory to beg pardon. He promised to do so, and indeed he came, but in no way with the spirit that was fitting. For he boasted arrogantly that he was conscious of no fault, and it was a near thing that he did not attack the others. I discharged my duty and, having tried in vain to call him back to sound conduct by a fatherly indulgence, I sent him away with a grim answer: that he and his associates were to be excommunicated until they repented. By a wonderful providence of God the whole affair was so managed that he, relying on a private pardon, intended within a few days to bring an infant to me, so as to stir up greater hatred among the common people if I refused him. But it would have been a scruple for me to admit someone who had been condemned by the public judgment of the Church and had not yet professed his repentance. Now our victory will be not only easy but also well founded. Yet I do not greatly rejoice at the outcome, which I foresee is at hand in the form I expect. For he will mock us with a faithful confession, which will nevertheless serve as an example. We have all the elders most closely united with us, and very sensible in asserting the right of the Church and in restraining the arrogance of the wicked. I make one exception, who has so far been unable to bend anyone with his treacherous flatteries. The day before yesterday the son of Justus Jonas passed through here, hastening on swift horses to the King, sent as envoy by the Count of Mansfeld. I do not know what to say, except that by the just vengeance of God the world is everywhere in turmoil, and it will not be able to rest under his obedience. I may not commit more to a letter. When the churches of Saxony were mentioned, among other things he related that Melanchthon is ill spoken of because he has not more openly professed that he agrees well with us on the sacramentarian question. He himself, however, discussed the whole matter so prudently and skilfully that I noticed nothing frivolous in his speech, although I was attending to him quite keenly. I do not doubt that you have already heard that I am still alive in my homeland. So I am forced to mourn a city that is as good as dead, which last year, on a false rumour of my death, held solemn supplications that it might triumph over Christ. Farewell, most upright brother, and faithful servant of Christ, into whose protection I commend you. Geneva, 2 December 1552.

units.la: Literis tuis quas altero postquam datae fuerant, mense accepi, nihil potuit accidere hoc tempore gratius. Nam ad ingentes molestias, quibus satis duriter conficior, nullus fere est dies quo non aliquid noui doloris, vel curae accedat. Itaque sub qua premor malorum congerie brevi tabescerem, nisi eorum acerbitatem Dominus suis remediis leniret: in quibus hoc mihi nō leue fuit, quòd & te mediocriter valere cognoui, vt salte fert aetas, & tenera corpusculi tui valetudo: & de amore in me tuo nihil prorsus esse mutatum, ipsis literis factus sum certior. Relatu mihi fuerat, sic te mea quadā nimis libera admonitione, quae tamen longè aliter afficere te debuerat, fuisse offensum, vt epistolam coram aliquot testibus conscinderes. Etsi autem pi-rum credibilis erat nuncius, ex quo tamen longo tempore fuc-cessu variis signis confirmatus est, aliquid tandem sspicari co-ctus sum. Quo nunc libentius cognoui, saluam adhuc inter nos manere coniunctionem: quam certe, vt ex concordi pietatis af-fectu coaluit sanctâ perpetuò, & inuiolabilem esse decet. Quum autem magnopere nostra interfit, quam Deus nominis sui au-spiciis sacrauit amicitiam, bona fide, constanterque ad extremum colere: totius etiam Ecclesiæ magna hic agitur vel utilitas, vel iactura. Vides enim quam multorum in nos conuersi sint oculi: vt improbi maledicendi ansam ex dissidiis nostris capiant: vt obscuris tantum simultatibus infirmi turbentur. Nec vero parui refert ne qua ad posteros exeat vllius inter nos exortæ discordiæ suspicio. Plusquam enim absurdum est, postquam discessio-nem à toto mundo facere coacti sumus, inter ipsa principia alios ab aliis dissilire. Porro etsi me procul abs te distare agnosco, libenterque fateor; quia tamen non ignoro, in quem theatri sui gradum me Deus extulerit: non est cur dissimulem, sine magna Ecclesiæ iniuria non posse amicitiam nostram violari. Atque vt nulla sit nobis aliorum ratio: ex tuo ipsius sensu æstima, quam mihi acerbum foret, ab eo homine alienari, què & vnicè amo, ac reuereor, & Deus vt toti suæ Ecclesiæ conspicuum redderet, non modò singularibus donis magnificè ornauit, sed adhibuit ad res summas gerendas primarium ministrum. Et certè mirus hic ac prodigiosus est stupor, quòd inter nos tam facile contemnitur sicer ille consensus, quo cœlestes Angelos referre in mundo decebat. Interea non desinit Satan discordiarum semina passim spargere: & sit nostra socordia, vt multam materiam coaceruet. Tandem excitandis ignibus reperit sua flabella. Referam quid nobis in hac Ecclesia, summo piorum omnium cruciatu acciderit. Ac iam annus integer elapsus est, ex quo inter has pugnas iactamur. Quidam nebulones, quum nobis de gratuita Dei electione, & misera humani arbitrij seruitute litem mouerent, & publicè tumultuarentur, nihil ad nos grauandos habuerunt magis plausibile nominis tui prætextu. Quum experti essent, quàm nobis promptum esset, quæcunque ingerebant commenta refellere, hoc scilicet artificio nos obruere tentabat, nisi vel-lemus palàm abs te discedere. Et ea quidem seruita fuit à nobis moderatio, vt minimè extorserint, quod astutè captabant. Profesti ergo sumus ego, & collegæ omnes mei, eundem, quo tendis, in doctrina scopum nobis esse propositum. Nec verbum in tota disceptatione excidit, vel in te minus honorificum quàm par erat, vel quod tibi fidem derogaret. Nec tamen fieri potest, quin me interea vehementer vtat tacita ista cogitatio: improbis post mortem nostram, vexandæ Ecclesiæ occasionem, quoties libuerit, relinqui, dum pugnantes eorum sententias in certamé committent, quos velut vno ore, vnum idémque loqui decue-rat. Quòd se Osiander nobis subduxit, imò nō sine violento impetu se proripuit, nō mirum, nec tantopere dolendum. Tu enim expertus pridem es, ex eo esse ferarum genere, quæ nunquam circumtantur: & ego semper inter nostra dedecora eum numeraui. Quo certè die mihi primùm visus est, profanum hominis ingenium, & fœdos mores suum detestatus. Quoties suaue, ac generosum vinum laudare vellet, has in ore habebat voces, Ego sum qui sum: Item, hic est Filius Dei viui: quæ manifesta Dei ludibria proderent. Quò magis sæpe miratus sum vestra omnium indulgentia talem belluā tolerari. Præcipuè verò, quum locum in præfatione quōdam tuo legerem (vbi post Vvormaciense infinitæ specimen plufquam liberaliter abs te laudatur) obstupui. Sed facessatille, quem alienissimum à nobis esse expedit. Quosdam alios retentos mallem. Vt tamen hos quoque omittam: me non leuiter pungit, quæ in nostra docendi ratione nimis palàm cõspicitur repugnantia. Equidem non ignoro, si quid detur homi-num auctoritati, longè æquius esse, vt tibi subscribam, quàm vt tu in sententiam meam descendas. Verùm id non agitur: neque etiam à piis Christi ministris optandum est. Hoc scilicet quæri vtrinque decet, vt consentiamus in puram Dei veritatem. Me autem, vt ingenuè fatear, religio impedit, ne tibi in hac doctrinæ parte accedam: quòd nimis philosophicè de libero arbitrio disputare videris in electione tractanda nihil aliud habere propositum, nisi vt te ad communem hominum sensum accommodes. Neque enim hallucinationi tribui hoc potest, quòd homo acutus, & prudens, & in Scriptura probè exercitatus, electioné Dei cum promissionibus confundis, quæ sunt vniuersæ. Nihil enim magis notum est, quàm verbi prædicationem omnibus promiscuè esse communem, sed fidei Spiritum solis electis singulari privilegio donari. Vniuersæ sunt promissiones. Quî fit igitur vt nō peræque apud omnes vigeat earum efficacia? Nempe quia non omnibus brachium suum Deus patefacit. Nec verò apud homines mediocriter in Scriptura versatos earum disputatione indiget: cùm pariter omnibus Christi gratiam offerant promissiones: & externa voce inuitet Deus quoslibet in salutem: peculiare esse fidei donum. Et mihi videor totam hanc quæstionem, quanuis impedita sit ac spinosa, proximè edito libello dilucidè explicasse. Cùm res adeò plana sit, te ex animi sensu prorsus diuersum tradere, nemo erit sani iudicij, cui persuadeas. Curam simul & dolorem mihi auget, quòd te video hac in re propemodum esse tui dissimilem. Audio enim, cùm tibi oblata esset for-
units.tr: Your letter, which reached me in the month after it was written, could not have come at a more welcome time. I am worn down by heavy troubles, and hardly a day passes without some new sorrow or anxiety being added. Buried under this mass of evils, I would soon have wasted away, unless the Lord had softened their bitterness with his remedies. Among these, one thing was no small comfort: I learned that you are reasonably well, as well as your age and your fragile health allow, and the letter itself assured me that your love for me has not changed at all. I had been told that you were offended by a certain rather free admonition of mine, which should have affected you very differently, and that you tore up my letter in front of several witnesses. Although the report was hardly credible, it was confirmed by various signs over a long time, and at last I was forced to suspect something. I am now all the more glad to learn that our fellowship still remains intact among us. It ought certainly to be kept holy and inviolable forever, as it grew from a harmony of godly feeling. Yet it matters greatly to us both that the friendship which God consecrated under the auspices of his name be cherished in good faith and steadfastly to the end. Indeed, the welfare or the loss of the whole Church is at stake here. You see how many eyes are turned upon us, so that wicked men may seize an occasion to slander us because of our disagreements, and so that the weak may be troubled by even obscure enmities. Nor is it of small importance that no suspicion of any discord arising between us should pass to posterity. For it is more than absurd that, after we have been forced to withdraw from the whole world, we should leap apart from one another over the very first principles. Now, although I acknowledge, and gladly admit, that I am far away from you, yet, since I am not unaware of the stage in the theatre to which God has raised me, I see no reason to conceal that our friendship cannot be violated without great injury to the Church. And so, setting aside any consideration of others, judge from your own feeling how bitter it would be for me to be estranged from that man whom I love and revere above all, and whom God has not only adorned with outstanding gifts, to make him conspicuous to his whole Church, but has also employed as the chief minister for carrying out the highest tasks. Truly, it is a remarkable and monstrous stupor that among us that agreement, which ought to have marked us out in the world as heavenly angels, is so easily despised. Meanwhile Satan does not cease to scatter the seeds of discord everywhere, and our negligence allows him to heap up abundant material. At last, to kindle the fires, he has found his bellows. I will relate what has happened to us in this Church, to the supreme torment of all the godly. A full year has now passed since we have been tossed about amid these conflicts. Certain scoundrels, when they stirred up a quarrel with us over the free election of God and the wretched bondage of the human will, and made a public uproar, had nothing more plausible to use for burdening us than your name as a pretext. When they found out how ready we were to refute whatever inventions they put forward, they tried to overwhelm us by this trick, unless we were willing to break openly with you. Yet we showed such moderation that they never extorted what they craftily sought. Therefore I and all my colleagues have professed that the same aim in doctrine which you pursue is set before us. In the whole dispute not a word fell from us that was less honourable to you than was fitting, or that would detract from your credit. Nevertheless, I cannot help being greatly troubled meanwhile by this silent thought: that after our death the wicked will be left an opportunity, whenever they please, to harass the Church, while those whose opinions ought to have spoken as with one mouth, and as one and the same voice, set their conflicting views against each other. That Osiander has withdrawn from us, or rather, has torn himself away not without violent assault, is no surprise and need not be lamented so much. For you have long since experienced that he belongs to that kind of wild beast which are never tamed, and I have always counted him among our disgraces. On the very day when I first saw him, I thought his character profane and his manners foul. Whenever he wished to praise a sweet and noble wine, he had these words on his lips: "I am who I am," and likewise, "This is the Son of the living God," which would expose manifest mockeries of God. So much the more often have I wondered that such a beast is tolerated by all of you. Especially when I read a certain passage in your preface, where you praise him far more than generously after the Worms colloquy, I was astonished. But let him go, the one whom it is best to keep as far from us as possible. I would rather have some others retained. But, to pass over these also, what troubles me not lightly is the contradiction that is too plainly visible in our method of teaching. Indeed, I am not unaware that, if any weight is given to the authority of men, it would be far more fair for me to subscribe to you than for you to come down to my opinion. But that is not the question at issue, nor should it be desired by the godly ministers of Christ. Rather, it is fitting that both sides seek this alone, that we agree in the pure truth of God. As for me, to be honest, my conscience holds me back from coming to you on this part of doctrine, because you seem to dispute about free will too philosophically when treating election, and to have no other aim in doing so than to accommodate yourself to the common sense of men. For this cannot be attributed to a slip of the mind, that you, a man who is keen, prudent, and well trained in Scripture, confuse the election of God with the promises, which are universal. For nothing is better known than that the preaching of the Word is common to all without distinction, but that the Spirit of faith is given as a singular privilege to the elect alone. The promises are universal. Why then is their efficacy not equally present in all? Plainly because God does not reveal his arm to all. Nor does the matter need lengthy disputation among men who are moderately versed in Scripture, since the promises equally offer the grace of Christ to all, and God invites whomsoever he pleases to salvation by an outward voice, while faith is a peculiar gift. And I think I have explained this whole question clearly in the little book I recently published, though it is so intricate and thorny. Since the matter is so plain, no one of sound judgment will be persuaded that you hold a view quite different from what you really feel. What increases both my care and my grief is that I see you in this matter almost unlike yourself. For I hear that, when the formula of our consensus with the Church of Zurich was put before you, you immediately seized your pen and pierced through one opinion, which discerns sparingly and soberly the elect of God from the reprobate. Which, to say nothing of other things, is very far from the gentleness of your disposition.

units.la: q.iij. mula nostræ cum Tigurina Ecclesia consensionis, protinus arrepto calamo sententiam vnam,quæ Dei electos à reprobis parcè,& sobriè discernit,abs te fuisse confossam. Quod certè ab ingenij tui mansuetudine,vt alia taceam, valde abhorret. Itaque vt meum libellum legere, vel saltem gustare sustineas, non rogo:quia id frustra mihi facturus videor.Vtinam his de rebus coram aliquando colloqui liceret. Notus est mihi tuus candor, perspecta ingenuitas, & moderatio : pietas vero Angelis,& toti mundo testata est.Ergo facile,vt spero,tota ea res inter nos expediretur. Quare fi vnquam fe daret opportunitas, nihil magis optarem,quàm ad te accurrere : sin vero contigerit quod times, erit hoc mihi in rebus miseris & luctuosis non leue solatium, videre te prius,& amplecti, quàm ex hoc mundo migrandum fit.Hic minimè fruimur ea quiete,quam existimas. Intus multum negotij,molestiarum atque etiam turbarum.In conspectu sunt hostes, à quibus noua subinde pericula ceruicibus nostris imminent. A Burgundia quinque horarum itinere distamus.A ditione Gallica intra vnius horæ spatium ad portas nostras venitur.Sed quia nihil beatius est,quàm militare sub Christi vexillo,non est cur te ista incommoda à nobis visendis deterreant. Interea gratum officium præstabis,tuum & communem Ecclesiæ statum indicando. Vale clarissime vir,& mihi ex animo honorande frater. Dominus te præsidio suo tueatur, Spiritu regat, & benedicat sanctos labores tuos.Collegæ mei,& multi pij,cordatíque homines te reuerenter salutant.Geneuæ,ııı Calendas Decembris. M. D. LII.
units.tr: The formula of our agreement with the Church of Zurich was offered to you, and you immediately seized your pen and tore apart one sentence, the one that distinguishes God's elect from the reprobate carefully and soberly. Certainly, to say nothing of other things, that is far removed from the gentleness of your character. So I do not ask you to read my little book, or even to glance at it, since I think I would be wasting my effort. I wish we could talk about these matters face to face sometime. I know your frankness, your honesty and your moderation well, and your piety has been witnessed to angels and the whole world. So, I hope, the whole affair could easily be settled between us. Therefore, if ever an opportunity presents itself, I would wish for nothing more than to run to you. But if what you fear happens, it will be no small comfort to me in these wretched and sorrowful circumstances to see you and embrace you before we must depart from this world. Here we do not enjoy the quiet you imagine. Inside there is much business, many troubles and even disturbances. Enemies are in sight, and fresh dangers from them constantly hang over our necks. We are five hours' journey from Burgundy, and within the space of one hour one can come from French territory to our gates. But since nothing is more blessed than to serve under Christ's banner, there is no reason for these inconveniences to deter you from visiting us. Meanwhile you will do a welcome service by informing us of your own state and that of the Church in general. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother whom I honour from my heart. May the Lord protect you with his help, rule you by his Spirit, and bless your holy labours. My colleagues and many godly and sensible men greet you respectfully. Geneva, 3 days before the Calends of December 1552.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: PRæfectum vrbis vestræ libenter vidi: tum quòd se hominem pium atq; integrum esse nobis probauit: tum mihi familiariter exposuit vt valeres, & quo in statu restuæ nunc effent.Fuit hic circiter dies quindecim.Quanquam autem cupit in patria suam operam Domino impendere, quia tamen munus suum variis difficultatibus implicitum esse videt, quibus se parem fore minimè confidit:testatus est in difcefiu,placere sibi mi grandi consilium. Quàtum ad rationes tuas domesticas spectat, nihil arbitror fore melius,quàm si primo quoq; dic laqueos expedias,quibus istic teneris.Frater tibi iniquus est,magisque pertinax, quàm vt sponte,quod etiam sine eius fraude fieret, subsitutionis suæ iure cessurus sit. Tu verò remedij quærendi studio, malum duplicare cogites. Ne posthac imprudentia te lapsum fuisse queraris,tibi iam denuntio,fi vxore duxeris,nihil fore tua fequitute miserius. Iam vt tibi obsequens,& morigera aliqua cötigat,& quo ad solum vertendum parata fit,nihildum tamen ha ratione profectum fuerit. Liberi procreādi sunt,qui frattem à substitutione depellāt. Quousque tandem,obsecro,libertatem tuam differs,ad quam præcipiti fere cursu properandum erat?de indequibus auspiciis nuptias tuas celebrabis? Quo genere con fecrationis Domino liberos ab ipso tibi datos offeres?qualis erit familiæ tuæ religio? An non cernis nouos te laqueos induere, quibus ne ftrangulerismagnopere timendum est? Imò inexplicabilm labyrinthum te ingredi?Vt nihil fit incommodi praeter biennij moram:est tamen ὑπο-στόλεισον,tempus ita extrahendo, vacatonem interea à Domino petere.Sed ego aliter iudico:te in hoc lucum,vnde nunc emergere conaris,penitus demersum iri, fi te emel coniugio inuoluas. Iam quid mætre tua fiet cuius ætas singulis diebus ingrauescit? Sanè hoc singulare est Dei donum,quod cum Dominus illi per te manum porrigat,nihil magis cupit,quàm cito à vinculis liberari. Nunc eam per flexuosas ambages circumducere,neque effet humanum,& à pietate etiam tua magis abhorret. Praeterea falleris,fi te solutum fore speras, fimuac fueris pater.Quis enim cauebit,liberos patri fore superstites?ergo nctum quidem libera erit agrorum venditio.Quare nihil melius quàm vt transfigas quouis modo cum fratre. Atqui tertia,vel dimidia pretij parte, vt nimium tenax est,ac cupiens, te frauabit?Crede mihi non parum lucri feceris,fi dimidium itā ftæ æstimationis recipiàs. Qua in re non mediocriter tibi vtilis erit Præ. eti opera.Et fe bona fide ac sedulò factuum pollicitus est quicquid iniunxeris. Quòd fi hæc te nondum satis afficiunt, ad obtefutiones me conuertam. Te igitur per incomparabile illud redemptionis beneficium obsecro, quo nos dignatus est Filius Dei: ne quid te impediat,vel remoretur, quominus te illi totum adacas.Nec tibi suspectum est: decet desiderij mei ardorem. Quiafcis in quem finem tantopere aduentum tuum expectam. Et magni interest,celeriter te ad opus illud accingi,quod Ecclesiae Dei plusquam necessarium esse cognoscis. Quare omnes morarum nexus vel dissue,vel abrumpe: vt te nobis quamprimum sitas. Hanc epistolam, cum mihi tempus sesquihorae nuntius dare,ex lecto dictare coactus sum. Excusa igitur,quòd non mea potius manu Vale exiinie vir,& frater ex animo colede. Dominus te spiritu consilij,& fortitudinis gubernet,ne quid tibi aliud propositum fit,quam illustrare sanctum eius nomen.
units.tr: I was glad to see the prefect of your city. First, because he proved to us that he is a pious and upright man. Second, because he explained to me in detail how you were and what your affairs were like. He was here about fifteen days. Although he wishes to devote his efforts to the Lord in his homeland, he sees that his office is entangled in various difficulties, and he is by no means confident that he will be equal to them. On leaving, he declared that he was pleased with my advice. As for your domestic affairs, I think nothing will be better than if you untie, as soon as possible, the snares in which you are held there. Your brother is unfair to you and rather obstinate, so he will not willingly give up his right of substitution, even though this could be done without fraud on his part. But you, in your eagerness to find a remedy, are planning to double the evil. So that you cannot later complain that you fell through lack of foresight, I now warn you: if you take a wife, nothing will be more wretched than your situation. Even if some woman should turn up who is compliant and obedient to you, and ready to move away with you, nothing would yet have been gained in this way. Children must be born, who will keep your brother away from the substitution. How long, I beg you, will you put off your freedom, toward which you ought to be hastening at almost headlong speed? With what auspices will you celebrate your marriage? With what kind of dedication will you offer to the Lord the children he has given you? What will the religion of your household be like? Do you not see that you are putting on new snares, by which you have great reason to fear being strangled? Indeed, are you not entering an inextricable labyrinth? You may say that there is no harm beyond a delay of two years, and that it is a kind of shrinking back [ὑποστολή], prolonging the time and meanwhile asking the Lord for leave. But I judge otherwise: you will be utterly sunk in the very pit from which you are now trying to climb out, if once you entangle yourself in marriage. Now, what will become of your mother, whose age grows heavier every day? Surely this is a unique gift of God: since the Lord holds out his hand to her through you, she wants nothing more than to be freed quickly from her chains. To lead her round through winding detours now would be inhuman, and it is even more contrary to your piety. Besides, you are mistaken if you hope to be released as soon as you become a father. For who will guarantee that the children will survive their father? Then, of course, the sale of the fields will be free. Therefore nothing is better than that you come to terms with your brother by any means. But will he, as tight-fisted and as eager as he is, cheat you out of a third or half of the price? Believe me, you will have made no small gain if you recover half of this valuation. In this matter the efforts of Prévost will be of no small help to you, and he has promised, in good faith and diligently, to do whatever you direct. But if these arguments do not yet move you enough, I will turn to entreaties. So I beg you by that incomparable benefit of redemption, by which the Son of God has deigned to save us: let nothing hinder or delay you from devoting yourself wholly to him. Nor should you be suspicious of this: it befits the ardour of my longing. You know for what purpose I so eagerly await your coming. It matters greatly that you set yourself quickly to that work, which you know is more than necessary for the Church of God. Therefore loosen or break off all the knots of delay, so that you may be with us as soon as possible. I was forced to dictate this letter from my bed, since the messenger gave me only an hour and a half. So pardon me that it is not written in my own hand. Farewell, distinguished man and brother, whom I cherish from my heart. May the Lord guide you with the spirit of counsel and fortitude, so that nothing else may be set before you than to make his holy name shine forth.

units.la: Nonis Decembris. M. D. LII.
units.tr: Nones of December, 1552.

units.la: CVM hoc bono viro loquutus sum. Quinam inter nos habi ti fuerint vltrò citroq; sermones, referre nihil attinet. Monui cum & hortatus sum, vt par erat: sic tamen, ne qua illi sinistra obreperet suspicio. Vides enim pro tua prudentia, quàtopere in hac bonorum paucitate cauendū sit, ne à nobis prorsus alienentur, qui sunt vtcunque tolerabiles. De fratribus qui Lugduni in vinculis tenentur, nihildum noui allatum est. Tributunt ad nos sexptimo quoque die, & vicissim aliquam à me exhortationem recipiunt, magis officij causa, quàm pro necessitate. Admirabilis enim Spiritus Dei virtus pleno fulgore in illis se profert. Neque tamen dubito, quin meis literis magis animentur. In aliis quibusdam partibus Galliæ ignes ef se accensosferunt: nec alia res magis sedat hostium rabiem, quàm frigus & ignavia eorum, qui volunt Christum sine cruce possidere. It fit, vt cessante scruiendi materia, nullæ sint aut raræ in multis pœnis persecutiones. Sed misera pax, quæ tam perfido silentio redmitur. Parisiis tamen Regis ipsius mandato in carcerem conductus est nobilis ille vir, qui nos ante biennium tam propenso studio excepit, non multò post Pentecostem. Homo erat valde fictus, sed non minus cordatus: nec ab eo tempore illustria suæ potentatis documenta edere destitit. Paulò antequam iniecta illi esset manus, mihi scripserat, se iam totum in eo esse, vt rebus suis expeditis ad nos mare graret. Sic autem statuerat decidere cum tyrannis, vt tertia parte suarum facultatum contentus, duplum illi relinqueret. Inter alia narrabat, quod te latere nolo, sibi in vrbis nostræ ruinis oblatum fuisse mirum spectaculum, quòd domus patris mei, aliis omnibus in cinerem redactis, integra stet. Tandem subiicit: Je ne doute pas que Dieu n'ait voulu laisser quelque signe contre tous ceux de vostre ville, lesquels huict ou dix ans auparauant auoyent brusle en peincture Monsieur de Normandie, & la reste. Porrò hoc postremum quod refert, ex curia Parisiensi decreto factum erat, quæ ridiculum suum stuporem in prodidit, quòd sepulta mei mentione Abelem citari iussit in foro Noviodunensi: ac nisi se listeret, pronunciauit habendum esse pro conuicto. Res mihi incredibilis foret, nisi arestum nobis in memorabile illud fuit: quòd cùm in turri quadrata, quæ in medio foro erat, tabulam æneam ad perpetuum Normandij decus ex eodem curiæ decreto figendam locasset, turris illa qm priuatis ædibus incendio consumpta fuit. Nunc dicit Normandius, exequutioni se intercedere, donec suâ arcem restituerit ciues nostri. N. qui infœliciter, magna nostra inuidia cum morando ratus est. itus est, fateor bonam pecuniæ summam hinc inde corrasisse. Verùm à me adeo hac in re adiutù fuisse nego, vt potius diffua-serim, si quis me consuluit. Sed tanta erat hominis improbitas, vt ignotissimum quenque aggredi nunquam veritus fuerit. Vix autem quenquam dimisit, quem non emungeret. Socer fratris mei homo interdum satis tenax duobus coronatis multatus fuit. Quinta vero importunitate conatus sit me adigere, vt illi conciliarem quindecim coronatos, referre nihil attinet. Ego verò tandem animadvertit hominis impudentia, & mendacii sessus, non minus præcise & auditæ quam ingenuè negaui quod petebat. Ex ærario quidem pauperum nihil fuisse erogatum, sanctè affirmo. Atque hoc mihi acceptum ferri debet, quòd nostros diaconos non decepit. Nam instabat eius nomine Vernolius, in quem ego excandui, quòd stultè se impostori ministrum præbe-ret. Iam verò cùm de me privatim desperans communiter à fra-tribus auxilium rogasset, ac me inuito irrupisset in cœtum nostrum, breuiter in conuentu respodi: non solùm fratres eius præ cibus non concederet, sed ne deliberationem quidem velle suscipere: quia nimis odiosum & iniquum foret, dubio adhuc iudicij euentu, & pendente causæ actione, præiudicio nostro damnare aduersum eius partem. Habeo vltra decem idoneos testes, qui meo consensu affuerunt illi mutuò non fuisse datum afferent. Nec per simulationem apud te profectus fuerit dum hic eras, nullo modo me posse adduci, vt me commendatione cum iuuas, bonos viros fraudarem. Imò memoria tenes, aliquanto durius me tunc loquutum esse. Si ne hoc quidem modo falsas criminationes effugere licet, quid facerem? Nisi quòd leniendus est patientia dolor. In quo etsi laboro, minus tamen proficio, quàm vellem. Neq; enim leuiter me excruciat, quòd video cum plausu recepi, quicquid improbis calumniarum in me euomere libuerit. Sparguntur isti falsi quidam rumores, non tamen absque aliquo colore: quia vulgò coniciunt friuolum & nihili hominem, sine meo suffragio, aureos triginta & amplius non fuisse repertum. At Graucrius hinc iactare non dubitat, sibi datos fuisse à Sena-tu nostro Apparitores, qui domum meam excuterent. Mihi sane difficile est, homini plus satis pathetico non efferuescere. Hactenus tamen me nemo vociferantem audiuit. Sed quod omnium erat caput, mihi deest, vt istis Domini ferulis ad veram hæ militatem erudiar. Quò magis necesse est liberis fratrum castigationibus domari. Qui in parte esse mihi tuum officiū. Neq; enim timidè solùm me admones, sed quasi demulces, acsi nihilò plus tibi liceret in me, quàm precario concessum fuerit. Equidem video quid speres. Morositati enim quàm ex assiduis molestiis cotraxi, parcendum esse iudicas. Etsi autem mihi iucundá est tua humanitas, quæ ex amore nascitur: pudet tamen, quod me libertate tua offendere metuis. Vale frater integerrime. Dominus te suis donis indies magis locupletet, ac benedicat sanctos labores tuos. Saluta fratres & amicos meo nomine. Collegę mei & plurimi fratres tibi plurimam salutem dicunt. Genevæ, x V. Februarij. M. D. LIII.
units.tr: I have spoken with this good man. There is no point in reporting what conversation passed between us in either direction. I admonished and exhorted him, as was fitting, yet in such a way that no unpleasant suspicion might creep into his mind. For you see, with your prudence, how carefully we must guard, in this scarcity of good men, against those who are at least tolerable being entirely alienated from us. Nothing new has yet been reported about the brothers who are held in chains at Lyon. They send messages to us every sixth day, and in turn receive some exhortation from me, more as a matter of duty than of necessity. For the wonderful power of God's Spirit shows itself in them in full brightness. Yet I do not doubt that they are encouraged all the more by my letters. In certain other parts of France, they say, fires have been kindled, and nothing calms the rage of the enemies more than the coldness and cowardice of those who want to possess Christ without the cross. So it comes about that, with the matter of persecution ceasing, there are no persecutions, or only rare ones, in many places. But it is a wretched peace, which is bought at the price of such treacherous silence. Yet at Paris, by the king's own order, that noble man who received us so eagerly two years ago has been cast into prison, not long after Pentecost. He was a man very shrewd, yet no less prudent, and from that time he has not ceased to give illustrious proofs of his power.
