units.la: QVod de bello Sacramentario apud Saxonas restaurato scri bis,cum dolore certè accipio:vt qui nihil nisi grauia offen dicula,ex intestinis eiusmodi conflictibus oritura sperare possim. At enim iam ante plus satis aerumnarum erat in Ecclesia & regnans triumphansque adhuc Antichristus, merito nisi studio insensati esse velimus, ad mutuam in Domino οµόνοιαν excitare & permouere debeat. De Castalione miror vehementer, si pergit nomen tuum ministeriumque arrodere, qui adeo se pacis charitatisque studiosum simulat. Monebitur autem grauius, quando, ex nihilo esse non possunt quae significas, nimirum a viris fide dignis nunciata tibi. Et indicium quidem est capitis egregiè cerebrosi perditique & deplorati in eo quisquis est, qui epistolam nomine suppositicio contra te ad Senatum vestrum est architectatus. Neque enim gloriam inde sperare potest, quod te virum Dei celebriorem in certamen prouocet: & vt apud Gelium habetur, inimicitias obscurus cum eminente suscipiat, neque magnum prouentum ad atterendam existimationem tuam apud cordatos saltem expectare, nomine suppresso, quando tale genus famosorum libellorum naturæ quodam instinctu, exosum habetur mentibus ingenuis. Sed deteget aliquando hanc Satanicam praui tatem Dominus Iesus, & vt hactenus reprimet fraudulenta consilia. Caeterum de annotationibus Castalionis in Epist.ad Rom.cap.9.ex praesentium latore omnia cognosces, & si quae sunt, quae de rebus Germanicis cupis cognoscere. Nam apud nos nouï nihil est, nisi quod attrito Matchione Alberto Episcopi criflas tollunt cum suo Ioue Henricho Brunsuicense, qui Principibus nobis vicinis aliquot, motus dedisset, nisi Caesaris auctoritate, adeius necessarios vsus fuiflet in Germaniam inferiorem reuocatus. Sic nos pergit hortari ad poenitentiam Dominus Deus, quem prote tuisque nō desinam ferio precari. Vale in Christo Iesu. Basileae xiiii. Iulij. Anno M. D. LIIII. Salutant te tuosque collegas mei symmystae.
units.tr: I receive with real grief what you write about the Sacramentarian war being revived among the Saxons, since I can expect from such internal conflicts nothing but serious troubles. There was already more than enough misery in the Church, and Antichrist still reigns and triumphs; unless we wish to be deliberately senseless, this ought to rouse and move us toward mutual concord in the Lord [ὁμόνοιαν]. I am greatly surprised if Castalio goes on gnawing at your name and your ministry, when he pretends to be so keen on peace and charity. He will be rebuked more severely, since what you report cannot have arisen from nothing, being told to you by trustworthy men. Indeed, whoever it is that devised a letter under a false name against you to our Senate shows the mark of a thoroughly deranged, lost and hopeless mind. He cannot hope for glory from it, by challenging to a contest a man more famous than yourself, nor, as is said in Gellius, does an obscure person take on enmity with an eminent one. Nor can he expect any great gain for damaging your reputation among sensible people, when the name is suppressed, since this kind of defamatory pamphlet is, by a certain natural instinct, hateful to honourable minds. But may the Lord Jesus one day expose this satanic wickedness, and restrain fraudulent schemes as he has done until now. For the rest, you will learn everything from the bearer of this letter about Castalio's annotations on Romans chapter 9, and anything else you wish to know about German affairs. For there is no news here, except that, with Margrave Albert worn down, the bishops are raising their crests again, together with their Jupiter, Henry of Brunswick, who would have stirred up several princes neighbouring us, had he not been recalled to Lower Germany by the Emperor's authority, for whose necessary services he was needed. Thus the Lord God continues to call us to repentance, and I shall not cease to pray earnestly for you and yours. Farewell in Christ Jesus. Basel, 14 July 1554. My fellow-initiates salute you and your colleagues.

units.la: t.iij.
units.tr: t.iij.

units.la: VIRETVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: VIRETVS CALVINO S. D.

units.la: IAM gratias nobis cum agite Domino omnes, & gratulemini nobis de foelici Orbanae causae successu Vicerun nostri 18.fuf fragiis. Eodem ipso die iussi sunt sacrificuli cum Francifcanis & Claranis à suis sacris desistere, non sine magnorotius populi Papistici & publico ludu. Is autem dies ille ipse erat, qui diem sefum praecedit Germani quem pro Deo suo tutelari colunt. Laudetur Do.qui hanc nobis dedit victoriam aduersus Antichristu: atque eo gloriosiorem & laetiorem, quo diutius prorogata est. Rogant me fratres vt si commode fieri possit ad proximum Dominicum diem eo me conferam. Tussis mea sese remisit,ac me infestare desiit.Erat enim valde infesta & frequens. Vix eo accedam ante aliam hebdomadem,tum propterea quod iam totis tribus hebdomadibus nullam hic concione habui,tum propterea quod nescio,an adhuc satis tutum sit mihi me nimis aperto caelo committere,donec paulo diutius vires confirmauero. Salutat te fratres omnes. Salutat te vxor & tota familia. Vale optime ac doctissime. Laufannae 1 1.Augusti. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Now give thanks to the Lord, all of you, and congratulate us on the happy outcome of the Orbe cause: our men have won the victory over the eighteen... (the Latin reads "Vicerun nostri 18.fuf fragiis"; the sense is that our side has prevailed, by eighteen votes). On that very day the little priests, along with the Franciscans and the Clarisses, were ordered to give up their sacred services, not without great mockery from the Papist people and public amusement. Now that day itself was the one that comes just before the Sabbath of the German whom they worship as their guardian god. Let the Lord be praised, who has given us this victory over Antichrist, and all the more glorious and joyful for having been delayed so long. My brothers ask me to go to them on the coming Lord's day, if it can conveniently be done. My cough has eased off and has ceased to trouble me, for it had been very troublesome and frequent. I shall scarcely come before another week, both because for three full weeks now I have held no sermon here, and because I do not know whether it is yet safe enough for me to trust myself to the open air too much, until I have strengthened my strength a little longer. All the brothers greet you. My wife and the whole household greet you. Farewell, most excellent and most learned man. Lausanne, 11 August 1554.

units.la: CALVINVS SVLCERO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO SULZER, GREETING.

units.la: QVum tumultuari non desinant indocti & praefracti homines,qui bellum Sacramentarium in Saxonia renouant: ineunda erit aliqua ratio, quae illorum intemperiem mitiget, vel clamores saltem compescat, & simul pios & graues doctosque nobis conciliet. Mihi nihil aliud in mente venit,quam in breui libello testatum facere,quanto rectius & syncerius sentiat nostrae Ecclesiae,quam illi calumniantur. Simulac plus ocij nactus fuero,tale aliquid meditor. Nunc excuditur mea in Genesin praefatio,ad filios Ioannis Friderici Saxoniae Ducis, in qua pacis & concordiae studium obiter commendo. Caftallio,mihi crede, nō minus virulenta est bestia,quā indomita & perinicax. Charitatem simulat: nempe vt modestiā:quum tamen nihil arrogantius fingi queat. Libellum illum atrocibus in me probris refertū ipse & alij confarcinarant eo consilio, vt subitus in me impetus cōsurgeret. Lōge decepti sunt. Nam decreuit Senatus,vt mihi legendus daretur. Mihi vero no modo promptum fuit, calumniarum nebulas discutere:sed etiam couertere in meam laudem, quicquid odiose obiectum fuerat. Mihi vero magis tolerabile est priuatim impeti, quam videre subinde miseros, qui hic degunt Christi exules, quotidie nouis molestiis vexari. Quanquam Dominus hac quoq; in parte haetenus manum nobis porrexit, ne frageremur. Verum,de statu nostro si plura scire cupies,nuntius tiii fideliter referet. Filius est Scribæ Senatus,iuuenis probus & ineger.Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi obseruande frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit,te gubernet,ac tueatur. Collegæ mei te reuerenter salutant.Tuis nostro omnium nomine plurimam salutem dicces.Geneuæ v I i.Idus Augusti. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Since the unlearned and unruly men who are reviving the Sacramentarian war in Saxony will not stop their brawling, some plan must be devised to moderate their intemperance, or at least to silence their clamour, and at the same time to win over to us the pious, serious and learned. I can think of nothing better than to show, in a short book, how much more correctly and sincerely our Church thinks than those men slander it. As soon as I have gained a little more leisure, I am planning something of this kind. Meanwhile my preface to Genesis is being printed, addressed to the sons of John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, in which I briefly commend the pursuit of peace and concord. Castellio, believe me, is no less venomous a beast than he is untamable and obstinate. He feigns charity, as he feigns modesty, although nothing more arrogant could be invented. He and others stuffed that little book, crammed with savage insults against me, in order that a sudden attack upon me might arise. They were far mistaken. For the Senate has decided that it be read to me. For my part, it was not only easy for me to scatter the clouds of slanders, but also to turn to my own praise whatever had been maliciously thrown at me. Indeed, it is more bearable for me to be attacked in private than to see from time to time the wretched men who live here as exiles for Christ being vexed daily by new troubles. Yet the Lord has so far stretched out his hand to us in this matter too, so that we do not perish. But if you wish to learn more about our situation, your messenger will report it faithfully. He is the son of the Secretary of the Senate, a young man of upright and blameless character. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and my brother to be respected. May the Lord always be with you, govern you and keep you. My colleagues greet you respectfully. Convey our most hearty greetings to yours, in the name of us all. Geneva, the seventh day before the Ides of August, 1554.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: I. CAL. D. DOCTORI MARPACHIO, ARGENTINENSIS ECCLESIÆ PASTORI.
units.tr: I. Calvin to Doctor Marpach, minister of the church at Strasbourg.

units.la: IA Mfere fesquiannus est,ex quo multa de Ecclesiæ Gallicanç, quæapud vos est,dissidiis subinde audire non sine magno dolore cogor. Nam dum pauci homines improbi, ac proterui mdeftiam fratri nostro N. exhibere volunt,factum est illorum intemperie, vt prauis contentionibus vexata fuerit Ecclesiola, cui Dominus apud vos quietum hospitium concessit. Mihi vero hunc nuntium tristem acerbumque fuisse mirum non est: cuia non secus me torqueret dissipatio eius gregis,quem Dominus meo labore,olim colligi,& ad tempus foueri voluit, ac vincerum meorum laceratio. Quanquam autem remedium aliquod maturè adhiberi vehementer cuperem, quia tamen speraban quicquid turbarum excitatum fuerat, tua & fratrum nostrorum prudentia,ac moderatione facilè sedatum iri:satius mihi visum est quiescere, ne vel frustra vobis molestus forem,vel diffidere æquitati vestræ viderer. Sed quum rem quotidie in deterius collabi rumor esset, statui mihi esse scribendum aliquid. Nec vero me diutius silere patiebatur dolor. Id dum mecum agito,ecce lætior nuntius affertur, rationem à clarissimo Senatu iniam esse,quæ proferuiam quinq; nebulonū frænaret:nūncq; sedaros esse motus,vt saltem tolerabilis sit status. Vtinam omnia sic essent ex voto composita,ne quid mihi præter gratulationem restaret,eamque puram & solidam.Verum,quia subesset adhuc in futurum tristis quædam suspicio & metus, studium huic malo purgando adhibere officij mei esse duxi. Duo autem,quantum intelligo, fuerunt totius mali capita, delatus est initio N.quod de sacra Domini Cœna aliter quàm vos sentiret,& doceret.Non dico à quibus,vel quo animo ratio concordiæ habenda fuit. Suscepta cognitio est. Verùm, si bona fide res tunc agebatur, transfacta esse debuit. Qui accusatus fuerat,fidei suæ confessionem edidit. Quàm vera,quàm liquida,quàm plena fuerit,nō disputo. Hoc mihi vnum sufficit,non esse improbatam. Itaque sic apud me antehac cogitaui,sentétiam fratris,& symmystæ vestri,si nō prorsus silentio vestro probata fuit, tolerabilem fuisse indicatā. Clàm interim obliquis artibus vos quicquam esse machinatos ne suspicari quidem libet. Quid ergo restabat, nisi vtquinque rebulonibus ad turbandam Ecclesiam longe plus quam par erat, dari existimarem? Hoc enim debuit a vobis omnibus rite expedi, an fas sit, an deceat, an denique rectum sit atque humanum, quinque homines turbuletos, palam a reliquo corpore dissidentes, foueri contra suum Pastorem. Sed quia hoc quoque vnus nunc sanatum est, ad illud prius redeo. Quid vltra fl. gitteturà N. quàm praestiterit, mihi non satis compertum est. Vos quidem operam dare conuenit, ne nimis praecise vrgeatur. Si hodie viuret eximius ille Dei seruus, & fidelis Ecclesiae Doctor Lutherus, non tam esset acerbus, vel implacabilis, quin liberer admitteret hanc confessionem: nobis vere praestari, quod figurant Sacramenta: ideoque in sicra Coena corporis & sanguinis Christi nos sicri participes. Quoties enim professus est, non aliam ibi esse pugnandi causam, nisi vt constaret, Dominum in nnibu signis non ludere nobiscum, sed intus implere quae oculos proponit, ac proinde effectum signis esse coniunctum? Hoc inter nos conuenit, nisi magnopere fallor: Coenam Christi non theatrici esse spectaculum spiritualis alimenti, sed re ipsa dare quod figurat: quia illic piae animae Christi carne & sanguine pascantur. Quanquam autem deprecatoris hic vicespotius quam monitoris suscipio: libere tamen dicendum est, nimis foremorosos, si qui hac moderatione non contenti fratrem suo ministerio leiciant. Adde quod turpe exemplum est, qui rite & ordine vocatus est ad munus Pastoris, sine legitimo Ecclesiae iudicio, mero Senatus nutu abdicari. Fieri quidem passim incipit: sed iam aliquoties vidi in eorum capita recidere, qui scientes, & volentes ius Ecclesiae prodiderant. Sancti, quae apud omnes pios adhuc viget, diuque, vt spero, vigebit, Capitonis, & Buceri memoria, quorum perspecta fuit & fides & prudentia & eruditio & integritas, instar lampadis locum istum collustrat, vt notius sit, a que adexemplum notabilius quicquid a vobis in vtranque partem geritur. At certe, quae in feruando Ecclesiae ordine eorum erat religio, decies mori malui, sed nunc, quam violentam Pastoris deiectio nem, non dico suo consensu, sed etiam silentio probare. Equidem si quid opera pretium ex meo aduentu cui tuis Collegis speraret, laborem non recusarem. Imo eo libentius ad vos venire, quia me quoque in hanc controuersiam inuolui video. Mihi autem valde acerbum est, doctrinae genus, quod liberè istic olim tam in Schola, quam in templo professus sum, nunc repudiari. Sed ne importune satagere videar: non vltra mihi progrediendum esse duxi, quàm vt te & rogando, & monendo, & obsecrando, & hortando pij fratris, deinde miserae Ecclesiolae quietem tem procurem. Si me impetrasse audiam, quod summopere cupio, erit cur nobis omnibus gratuler. Vale eximie vir vnà cum symmystis fratribus mihi charissimis, quibus tecum Ecclesiam istam gubernant, quibus ego meas literas communes esse volo, si ita censueris. Dominus vos omnes tueatur suo praesidio, Spiritu prudentiae, rectitudinis, aequitatis & constantiae dirigat, laboresque vestros benedicat. Amen. Geneuae VII I. Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIII.
units.tr: For a year and a half now I have been forced, from time to time, to hear of the quarrels in the French church among you, and not without great grief. While a few wicked and insolent men wished to bring disgrace upon our brother N., their intemperance caused the little church, to which the Lord granted a quiet refuge among you, to be troubled by wicked contentions. To me it is no wonder that this news was sad and bitter. The scattering of that flock, which the Lord once wished to be gathered and cherished for a time through my labour, and the tearing of my own bowels, tormented me no less. Although I greatly wished some remedy to be applied early, yet because I hoped that whatever disturbances had been stirred up would be easily calmed by your prudence and moderation and that of our brothers, I thought it better to keep quiet, lest I be a nuisance to you to no purpose, or seem to distrust your fairness. But when there was daily rumour that the matter was sliding for the worse, I decided that I must write something. Nor could my grief let me keep silent any longer. While I was turning this over, behold, a happier message was brought: that a plan had been adopted by the most distinguished Senate which would curb the audacity of five scoundrels, and that the disturbances were now calmed, so that at least the state is tolerable. Would that everything had been arranged so according to my wish, so that nothing remained for me but congratulation, and that a pure and solid one. But since some sad suspicion and fear still lingered for the future, I judged it my duty to apply myself to purging this evil. As far as I understand, there were two heads of the whole evil. First, it was reported at the start that N. felt and taught about the Lord's Supper differently from you. I do not say by whom, or with what intention, a plan of agreement had to be taken up. The inquiry was undertaken. But if the matter was then handled in good faith, it ought to have been brought to an end. The man who had been accused published a confession of his faith. How true, how clear, how full it was, I do not dispute. This alone is enough for me, that it was not rejected. So I have thought hitherto that the opinion of our brother and your fellow-minister, if it was not wholly approved by your silence, was judged tolerable. Meanwhile I do not even like to suspect that you have plotted anything by oblique arts. What then remained, except that I should think too much had been granted to five troublemakers for disturbing the Church, far more than was fitting? For this ought to have been properly settled by all of you: whether it is lawful, whether it is seemly, whether finally it is right and humane, that five turbulent men, openly dissenting from the rest of the body, be fostered against their own minister. But since this too has now been remedied, I return to the earlier point. What more N. should have done is not sufficiently clear to me. You should indeed take care that he is not pressed too precisely. If that outstanding servant of God and faithful teacher of the Church, Luther, were alive today, he would not be so harsh or implacable as not to freely admit this confession: that what the sacraments figure is truly given to us, and therefore in the holy Supper we are made partakers of the body and blood of Christ. For how often did he profess that there was no other cause for contention there, except to establish that the Lord does not mock us with signs, but inwardly fulfils what they set before our eyes, and so the effect is joined to the signs? This, unless I greatly err, is agreed among us: that the Supper of Christ is not a theatrical show of spiritual food, but really gives what it figures, because there pious souls are fed with the flesh and blood of Christ. Although in this I take on the role of an intercessor rather than an admonisher, I must speak freely: they would be too stubborn who, not content with this moderation, harass a brother in his ministry. Add that it is a shameful example that one who was rightly and orderly called to the office of minister should be removed by the mere nod of the Senate, without a lawful judgment of the Church. Indeed this has begun to happen here and there, but I have several times seen it fall back upon the heads of those who, knowingly and willingly, had betrayed the right of the Church. The memory of Capito and Bucer, whose faith, prudence, learning and integrity were well known, and which still flourishes among all the godly and, I hope, will long flourish, lights up that place like a lamp, so that whatever is done by you on either side is better known and more notable as an example. Certainly, in keeping the order of the Church they were so scrupulous that I would rather die ten times than approve, even by silence, such a violent deposition of a minister, not to speak of giving consent. Indeed, if anything worthwhile could be hoped for from my coming to your colleagues, I would not refuse the labour. I would come to you all the more willingly, since I see that I too am being drawn into this controversy. But it is very bitter to me that the kind of teaching which I once professed there freely, both in the school and in the church, is now rejected. Yet lest I seem to meddle unseasonably, I have thought I should go no further than to secure the peace of the pious brother and then of the poor little church, by asking, admonishing, beseeching and exhorting you. If I hear that I have obtained what I most earnestly desire, there will be cause for me to congratulate us all. Farewell, distinguished man, together with the fellow-ministers most dear to me, with whom you govern that church; I wish my letter to be shared with them, if you think fit. May the Lord keep you all under his protection, direct you by the Spirit of prudence, uprightness, fairness and steadfastness, and bless your labours. Amen. Geneva, 25 August 1553.

units.la: Io. CALVINVS D. GASPARI LISERO, ECCLESIAE NVRLINGENSIS PASTORI. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Dr. Gaspar Liserus, minister of the church at Nurlingen. Greetings.

units.la: EGO vero, optime frater, nimis agrestis forem, ac inhumanus, si tuum in scribendo officium, quod vt a summa erga me beneuolentia profectum esse video, ita grato animo, hilarique amplecti decet, audaciae, vel temeritatis damnarem Itaque & libenter intellexi, te meam amicitiam expetere (quo nomine tibi deuinctum esse profiteor) & ex tuis literis alterum gaudium accessit, dum permultos esse significas, qui fructu ex meis laboribus non poenitendum colligant: in quorum numero te quoque esse asseris. Haec enim Dei benedictio mihi non parum addit animi: hoc tam maligno saeculo, esse tamen pios & eruditos homines, qui non modo priuatim ex meis lucubrationibus proficiant, sed vtilitatem quam sentiunt, fideli opera studeant latius quasi de manu quod acceperunt, in manum proferre. Pergamus igitur hoc cursu, mi frater: ac inter nos sincere vigeat donorum Dei communicatio, quae Ecclesiam, inuidia & ambitione proculi valere iussis, aedificet. Meum quoque studium in sedanda discordia, quae nimis infeliciter initio renati Euangelij exarsit, tibi probari gaudeo. Vtinam eadem vbique regnaret modestia. Sed iam denuo surgunt turbulenti homines, non minus quam indocti, quos nulla de causa nescio quae intemperies ad bellum reparandum exagitat. Noltrum vero est talibus flabellis placide occurrere, ne incendium longius grassetur. Tranquillum Ecclesiis vestris statum gratulor: sed non simul coniunctos esse disciplinae neruos, qui eum contineant, dolendum est. Nec alia corrigendi vitij ratio apparet, quàm si Pastores, quos scria regni Christi cura tangit, inter se consentiant. Nam vt vnus, aliis in consilium non adhibitis, quicquam tentes, auctor esse non audeo. Adde quòd nunquam vtile putaui, ius excommunicandi permitti singulis Pastoribus. Nam & res odiosa est, nec exemplum probabile, & facilis inde in tyrannidem lapsus, & alium vsum Apostoli tradiderunt. Strenuè verò vt ad fymmystas tuos incſ-tandos labores, non tantùm consulo, sed vehementer hortor. Brentio nondum scripsi: breui tamen, vt spero,melior dabitur opportunitas,quam non præтermittam. Libellus de necessitate reformandæ Ecclesiæ,supplex est exhortatio ad Cæsarem,& Ordines imperij: quem inter opuscula reperies. Vale integerrime frater. Dominus te regat Spiritu suo, virtute sustentet, laboremque tuum benedicat. Geneuæ v 1.Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Indeed, best of brothers, I would be too rustic and inhuman if I condemned as rash or reckless your letter, which I see comes from great goodwill towards me and which deserves to be embraced with a grateful and cheerful heart. So I was glad to learn that you seek my friendship (I confess myself bound to you by that bond), and your letter brought me a second joy, when you report that there are very many who gather from my labours a fruit they need not regret, and you say that you are among them. This blessing of God adds no little courage to me: that in so wicked an age there are still pious and learned men who not only profit privately from my writings but, feeling the usefulness of them, take pains by faithful work to pass on more widely what they have received, as if from hand to hand. So let us press on along this course, my brother, and let the sharing of God's gifts flourish sincerely among us, to build up the Church, with envy and ambition left far behind. I am glad that my effort to calm the discord, which broke out all too unhappily at the beginning of the renewed Gospel, has met with your approval. Would that the same moderation reigned everywhere! But now turbulent men rise again, no less untaught than restless, whom I know not what intemperance stirs up to renew the war for no cause. It is our task to meet such fans calmly, so that the fire does not spread further. I congratulate you on the peaceful state of your churches, but it is to be lamented that the sinews of discipline that would hold that peace together are not also bound tightly. Nor does any other way of correcting the evil appear than for the ministers, whom the concern for the kingdom of Christ touches, to agree among themselves. For I dare not advise that one man attempt anything without taking others into counsel. Add that I have never thought it useful for the right of excommunication to be granted to individual ministers. For the matter is invidious, the example is not a sound one, the slide into tyranny is easy from there, and the Apostles handed down a different practice. But I not only advise, I earnestly urge you to devote your labours to inciting your fellow symmystae. I have not yet written to Brenz; yet a better opportunity will soon be given, I hope, and I shall not let it pass. The little book on the necessity of reforming the Church is a suppliant exhortation to the Emperor and the estates of the empire; you will find it among my opuscula. Farewell, most upright brother. May the Lord guide you by his Spirit, sustain you by his strength, and bless your labour. Geneva, the sixth day before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINUS MELANCHTHONI S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON, GREETING

units.la: QVanquàm meis vltimis literis abs te non fuisse responsum doleo & valde miror: fastidio tamen vel contemptu id ef-se factum, quum nihil minus in naturam morèsque tuos cadat, suspicari nequeo. Itaque nuntium hunc nactus, qui suam mihi in literis tibi reddendis operam obtulit, tentandum rur-sus putàui, num forte quid possem elicere. Ego verò non de tuo erga me amore dubitans, qui semper immodicus fuit, ita loquor: sed quia silentium tuum, vt Ecclesiæ Dei noxium esse iudi-co, itâ merito triste, molestúmque mihi esse debet. Scribebam nup-er de illo doctrinæ capite, in quo magis sensum tuum dissi-mulas, quàm à nobis dissentis. Quid enim aliud de homine a-cerrimi iudicij, cœlestisque doctrinæ peritissimo arbitrer: quum neminem mediocriter in sacris verisatum lateat,quod ipse quasi ignotum tegis? Et tamen funditus perit gratuitæ Dei misericor-diæ cognitio, nisi hoc tenemus, mero Dei beneplacito à repro-bis discerni fideles,quos in salutem eligere voluit: nisi & hoc de-inde constat, fidem ab arcana Dei electione manare: quia Spiri-tu suo illuminat, quos eligere, antequam nascerentur, ei visum est,& adoptionis gratia in familiam suam inserit. Hanc doctri-nam à summo theologo conuelli quàm absurdum sit, pro tua prudentia expende. Manifestum certè dissidium in scriptis no-stris notari,pessimi exempli esse vides. Net verò hanc tollendæ discrepantiæ legem præscribo,vt tu mihi assentiaris: sed ne pu-deat nos sacris Dei oraculis subscribere. Querendæ verò conci-liationis quæcunque tibi placuerit ratio, eam libenter amplec-tar. Ecce nunc homines indocti,& turbulenti, bellum Sacra-mentarium à parte vel ra innouant: quos etiam ipsos tua taci-turnitate foueri boni omnes gemunt & queruntur. Quantum-uis enim audax sit inscitia: nemo tamen dubitat, si liberius prosi-teri quod sentis, in animum induceres, quin tibi facile sit eorum interimintemperiem aliquà saltem ex parte sedare.Nec vero ita humanitatis oblitus sum,quin & mecum reputem, & alius quoque ostendam,quo cum hominum genere tibi negocium sit: quàm te anxium,perplexúmq; teneat ista rerum perturbatio:quàm mul ta circunspicere tibi necesse sit,quæ tuum cursum impediunt,ac morantur.Sed nihil tanti est,ut furiosis hominibus tua dissimulatio ad turbandas & dissipandas Ecclesias fraenum laxet. Taceo iam, quàm pretiosa nobis esse debeat ingenua sanæ doctrinæ professio. Scis annis plus triginta defixos in te fuisse innumeras multitudinis oculos, quæ nihil magis cuperet,quàm se tibi docilem præbere. Quid? an hodie ignoras, plurimos ab ambigua illa,in qua te nim s timidè continesdocendi forma dubios pendere? Quòd si tibi syncerè,solidéque testari quod esset vtile cognitu,liberum non est, saltem danda erat opera, ut fraenares istorum intemperiè,qui de nihilo importunè tumultuantur. Quid enim,obsecro,sibi volunt?Clamauit tota vi a Lutherus, nō alia de re se cōtendere, nisi vt suam Sacramentis virtutem assereret. Conuenit, non inanes esse figuras,sed te ipsa præstari quicquid figurant:In Baptismo adesse Spiritus efficaciam,vt nos abluat,& regeneret. Sacram Coenam spirituale esse epulum, in quo verè Christi carne & sanguine pascimur. Ergo in sedando tumultu, quem denuo concitant præposteri homines, causa magis videtur fauorabilis, quàm vt inuidiæ metu cessandum sit: cuius tamen varias agitationes in isto gradu effugere non potes. Danda solùm opera est, vt aheneus ille bonæ conscientiæ murus non eas modò, sed quamlibet violentos totius mundi impetus fortiter sustineat. Nam dum ab Osiandri patronis & flexibilem, & profanæ magis philosophiæ deditum, quàm cœlesti doctrinæ, vocari audio, grauius me vulnerat probrum illud, quàm si vel maleuoli,vel proterui homines obiicerent,quod non modò fa teri honestum esset,sed etiam magnificè iactare gloriosum.Vale clarissime vir, & frater mihi imprimis obseruande.Dominus te præsidio suo tueri,Spiritúque regere pergat vsque in finem. Geneuæ, v i Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Although I am sorry and greatly surprised that you have not answered my last letter, I cannot suspect that this was done out of disdain or contempt, since nothing is further from your nature and character. So, having found this messenger, who offered to carry my letter to you, I thought I should try again to see whether I could draw something out of you. I do not doubt your love for me, which has always been immoderate, when I say this. But I judge your silence to be harmful to the Church of God, and so it must rightly be sad and troubling to me. Recently I was writing to you about that point of doctrine on which you hide your real opinion rather than openly dissenting from us. For what else am I to think of a man of the sharpest judgment and the greatest skill in heavenly doctrine, since it is known to anyone who has at all studied sacred matters that you are concealing what you yourself know? And yet the knowledge of God's free mercy perishes utterly, unless we hold that the faithful are distinguished from the reprobate by God's mere good pleasure, whom he chose to salvation; unless it is also established that faith flows from God's hidden election, because he enlightens by his Spirit those whom he decided to choose before they were born, and grafts them into his family by the grace of adoption. Consider for yourself, in your prudence, how absurd it is for this doctrine to be torn up by so great a theologian. You can see that the open disagreement noted in our writings is a most dangerous example. Yet I do not prescribe this law for removing the discrepancy, that you should agree with me, but only that you should not be ashamed to subscribe to the sacred oracles of God. As for the means of seeking reconciliation, whatever method you prefer, I will gladly embrace it. Now, uneducated and turbulent men are renewing the sacramentarian war, from one side or the other, and all good people groan and complain that your silence fosters them. However bold their ignorance may be, no one doubts that if you resolved to profess more freely what you think, it would be easy for you to calm, at least in part, the frenzy of these men. Nor have I forgotten human kindness to such an extent that I do not myself consider, and also show you, what kind of men you are dealing with, and how anxious and perplexed you must be by this disturbance of affairs, and how many things you must look around at that hinder and delay your course. But nothing is worth allowing your dissimulation to loosen the bridle of furious men for disturbing and scattering the Churches. I say nothing yet of how precious the open profession of sound doctrine ought to be to us. You know that for more than thirty years the countless eyes of the multitude have been fixed on you, and that they desire nothing more than to show themselves teachable by you. What? Do you not know today that very many are left in doubt by that ambiguous manner of teaching in which you timidly restrain yourself? But if it is not free for you to testify sincerely and solidly what would be useful to know, you should at least have taken care to restrain the frenzy of those who rush into tumult without cause. For what, I beg you, do they want? Luther cried out with all his might that he was contending about nothing other than to assert the power of the sacraments. It is agreed that the figures are not empty, but that whatever they figure is really given by you: that in Baptism the efficacy of the Spirit is present to wash and regenerate us; that the Holy Supper is a spiritual feast, in which we are truly fed with the flesh and blood of Christ. Therefore, in calming the tumult which these absurd men are stirring up again, the cause seems more favourable than that one should cease for fear of hatred; yet you cannot escape its various agitations at this stage. You must only take care that that brazen wall of a good conscience bears up bravely not only against these, but against the most violent assaults of the whole world. For when I hear that you are called by the supporters of Osiander pliable and given more to profane philosophy than to heavenly doctrine, that reproach wounds me more severely than if malicious or shameless men were to throw it at me, a reproach which it would not only be honourable to confess, but glorious even to boast of. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother especially to be honoured by me. May the Lord continue to protect you with his help and guide you by his Spirit to the end. Geneva, the sixth day before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CAL. VALERIANO POLANO s. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VALERIAN POLANUS, GREETING

units.la: QVod ex longa & infesta iactatione tandem in portum appulisti, vbi saltem animum colligere liceat,gaudeo. Quod verò istic statio tibi oblata est,in qua te vtiliter exercitas, & pusillo gregi, qui tua opera, & sedulitate collectus est, operam tuam impendas, non tibi solum priuatim, sed etiam multis piis fratribus, ad quos fructus peruenient, gratulor. Triste quidem miserumque spectaculum est, dispersas, quasi laceri corporis membra Ecclesias videre. Sed quid si haec dissipatio admonet instare tempus, quo Dominus filios suos in coelum colligat, qui exilio vix locum in terris reperiunt? interea assuescant profugi fratres, vbi & corpore & animo peregrinati fuerint, ad vltimam migrationem. Porro, vt se placide in precario hospitio contineant, te illis & modestiae & moderationis exemplar esse conuenit. Atque in eam rem non parum adiumento fore tibi spero symmystam tuum D. Morellum, cui non minus praeclarum synceri animi, & mansueti spiritus, quam doctrinae testimonium boni viri reddunt. Eum meo nomine plurimum saluere iubebis. Collegae mei vobis ambobus salutem optant. Vale charissime frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit, te Spiritu suo regat, laboresque tuos benedicat. Geneuae, VI. Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: I rejoice that after a long and troubled tossing you have at last reached harbour, where at least you may have leisure to collect your mind. I congratulate you that a post has been offered to you there, in which you are usefully employed and devote your labour to the little flock gathered through your work and diligence, to the benefit not only of yourself privately but of many pious brothers, to whom the fruit will come. It is indeed a sad and wretched sight to see the Churches scattered like the limbs of a torn body. But what if this dispersal is a warning that the time is near when the Lord will gather his sons into heaven, who scarcely find a place on earth in their exile? Meanwhile let the exiled brothers learn, wherever they have wandered in body and mind, to prepare for their final migration. Moreover, that they may calmly keep themselves in a borrowed dwelling, it becomes you to be an example of modesty and moderation to them. And in this matter I hope your fellow-initiate, our dear Morellus, will be no small help to you, whose good men bear witness to his sincere mind and gentle spirit no less than to his learning. You will give him my warmest greetings. My colleagues wish you both health. Farewell, dearest brother. May the Lord always be with you, guide you by his Spirit, and bless your labours. Geneva, the sixth day before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: CAL. PERRVCELIO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO PERRUCEL, GREETINGS

units.la: Tibi locum obtigisse, vbi operam impendas Dei Ecclesiae, gaudeo: ac Dominum precor, vt ad stationem, in qua te locauit, fideliter tueatur Spiritu suo gubernet. Porro, quia in ceremoniis tibi non datur quae optanda esset, libertas dabis opera, vt te ferre omnes intelligant magis quam probare, quicquid superfluum erit. Ego quid sentirem, meis ad fratres literis, de te nihil cogitans, palam & ingenue sum testatus. Quibus non placebit meum consilium, nihil apud eos te iuuabit mea auctoritas. Apud alios plus habebit poderis, vt arbitror, testimonium illud, quam si quid priuatim tibi scriptum ostenderes: quia facile obreperet suspicio, gratia, & precibus esse elicitum. Semper quidem tibi duo haec imprimis erunt spectanda: ne quid tibi plus imponi sinas, quam ferat Ecclesiae aedificatio, & tranquilla puraque conscientia suscipere tibi liceat. Spero etiam a Senatu & Pastoribus nonnihil impetratum iri, modo absit contentio. Nihil enim magis eos exacerbat, & ad repugnandum acuit, quam vbi se, & sua damnari putant. Tu vero ex re praesenti melius quid ex pediat, disputes. Quare nihil praescribo. Vale eximie vir, & frater mihi charissime. Dominus te Spiritu suo regat, laboremque tuum benedicat. Collegae mei te amanter salutant. Fratribus gratiam Dei, & omne benedictionis genus ex animo precor. Geneuae VI. Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: I rejoice that you have been given a place where you may labour for the Church of God, and I pray the Lord that He may faithfully keep you at the post in which He has placed you and guide you by His Spirit. Furthermore, since you are not given the freedom in ceremonies that would be desirable, you will take care to let everyone understand that you tolerate, rather than approve, whatever is superfluous. I have stated openly and frankly, in my letters to the brethren, what I think, without thinking anything of you in particular. Those who do not approve my counsel will not be helped by my authority in any way. Among others, I think that testimony will carry more weight with them than if you showed them some private letter written to you, since suspicion would easily creep in that it had been drawn out by favour and entreaties. You must always keep two things chiefly in view: that you do not allow more to be imposed on you than the building up of the Church can bear, and that you may take it on with a calm and pure conscience. I also hope that something will be obtained from the Senate and the ministers, provided there is no contention. For nothing so irritates them and sharpens them to resist as when they think they and their own are being condemned. You, however, should discuss what is more advantageous from the present situation. So I prescribe nothing. Farewell, excellent man and brother most dear to me. May the Lord guide you by His Spirit and bless your labour. My colleagues salute you affectionately. I pray from my heart for the grace of God and every kind of blessing for the brethren. Geneva, 6th before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: CALVINVS
units.tr: CALVIN

units.la: ETsi communis amicus noster Sturmius consilium mihi suum de Commentariis dicandis perscribens, te quoque idem sentire addiderat: hoc tamen ipsum ex tuis literis intelligere, longe mihi fuit gratius. Vnum vereor, ne labor meus, quem tibi curae esse ostendis, non tanti aestimandus fuerit. Qui fit autem, vt de tuis in eundem librum Commentariis sileas? Nam quum adhuc esses in Anglia, ex responsione quam Roberto Stephano dederas, breui exituros sperabam. Quare eorum fructu, quem non dubito vberem fore, diutius fraudari Dei Ecclesiam molestè fero. In hac enim confusa librorum sylua graues, eruditas, & solidas piorum, rectéque sentientium hominum & qui pari auctoritate, iudicióque praediti sunt, lucubrationes extare imprimis necesse est, tum ad puritatem doctrinae asserendam, vt ad posteros salua integráque perueniat, tum ad refutandam eorum qui omnia permiscent, insulsam leuitatem. De Philippo, valde mihi dolet. Ergo ei nom satis est, vel quocunque tulerit hominum gratia, flexibilem nutare, vel silentio prodere veritatem, nisi cordatos Dei seruos, ad quorum imitationem potius ipsum eniti decebat, inflectere ad suam mollitiem conetur. Praeclare vero abs te factum, quod te liberum veritatis doctrinae defensorem fore professus es. Sic enim tuo exemplo praescripta est ei regula, quatenus pax foueuda sit, vt scintillam aliquam virilis animi, spirare tandem discat. Ad collegam tuum, cui nimis seruiliter ille gratificari voluit, D. Sturmii hortatu scripsi, vt eum N. placarem: vt cunque tamen succedat, nunquam me poenitebit aliquid tentasse. Verum, si qui collapsi sunt, tuum est impositum tibi onus eo animosius sustinere. Quod cum plane te facere intelligo, magis ac magis in ea sententia confirmor, te mirabili Dei prouidentia, qui laborantı Ecclesiae succurreres, istic fuisse retentum. D. Zankum meo nomine salutare cupio. D. Marchio noster te plurimum salutat. Vale praestantissime vir & mihi obseruande frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit, et gubernet, laboréque tuos benedicat. Si maturius venissent tuae literae, copiosior ad Principes, tuo admonitu, fuisset exhortatio. Sed post dimidium Augustum mihi fuerunt redditae. Collegae mei te salutant. Geneuae v Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Although our common friend Sturm, writing out his plan for dedicating the Commentaries, had added that you also thought the same, it was much more pleasing to me to learn this from your letter itself. I fear only that my labour, which you show you care about, will not be thought worth so much. But why is it that you are silent about your own Commentaries on the same book? For while you were still in England, I hoped from the answer you had given to Robert Estienne that they would soon come out. So I am grieved that the Church of God is kept for too long from the fruit of them, which I do not doubt will be abundant. For in this confused forest of books it is above all necessary that the weighty, learned and solid labours of godly men who think rightly, and who are endowed with equal authority and judgement, should exist, both to assert the purity of doctrine so that it may reach posterity safe and whole, and to refute the silly levity of those who mix up everything. I am very sorry about Philip. It is not enough for him, whatever favour of men he has won, to waver in pliancy or to betray the truth by silence, unless he tries to bend the upright servants of God, whose imitation he ought rather to strive after, to his own softness. Indeed you have acted admirably in professing yourself a free defender of the doctrine of truth. For by your example a rule has been set before him as to how far peace is to be cherished, so that he may at last learn to breathe some spark of a manly spirit. I wrote to your colleague, whom he wished to please far too servilely, at the urging of Sturm, to appease N.; however it turns out, I shall never regret having attempted something. But if some have fallen, it is your burden, laid upon you, to bear with more courage. Since I understand that you are doing exactly this, I am more and more confirmed in the view that by the wonderful providence of God, who would help the Church in its distress, you were kept there. I desire to greet Master Zanchi in my name. Our Marquis salutes you warmly. Farewell, most excellent man and brother whom I must honour. May the Lord be always with you and guide you, and bless your labour. If your letter had come earlier, the exhortation to the Princes at your suggestion would have been fuller. But it was delivered to me after the middle of August. My colleagues salute you. Geneva, 5th before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: CAL. IOAN. SLEIDANO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Sleidan, greetings

units.la: QVum ex fratris nostri N. literis nuper intellexissem extribus,quos regendæ Gallicæ Ecclesiolæ Senatus præfecit, teesse vnum, vehementer, vt par erat, gauisus sum: & hoc mihi gaudium fore diuturnum cōsido. Sic enim statuo tibi diuinitus magis quàm humano consilio prouinciam hanc fuisse iuncta̱m, qui tua fide & prudentia componas, quicquid hactenus turbarum mouit Satan: præcaueas deinde, ne qua improbis detur tumultuandi occasio. Ergo ex animi mei voto cōsultum est pusillo gregi. Te verò quò minus ad officium exhorter, nullus tibi mor impedit: sed quia superuacuum esse existimo. De Philippi consensu quantopere vna in re mihi gratulari debeam, nescio: quādo in summis capitibus vel philosophis se venditans sanam doctrinam aperte oppugnat: vel ne in se quorundam irritet odia, sensum suum astute saltem parum ingenue, regit. Dominus cum fortiore Spiritu instruat, ne grauem ex eius timiditate iacturam sententiæ posteritas. A tribus mensibus in Aquitania quinque aut sex fuerunt exusti, in quorum morte Christus magnificè triumphauit. Nuper etiam in oppido Venetæ ditionis, aulò ultra Vulturinam admirabili constantia ad vltimum vsq; Spiritu, pius vir mihi probè notus, Christum cōfessus est. Noui hic nihil fertur, quod non peræque vobis notum sit. Vale eximie vir, & mihi plurimùm honorande. Dominus te cum familia tueatur perpetuò, & benedicat. De classe Turcica cætior allatus est nunc tius, exusto quodam oppido, vastata regione maritima, captis hominum quinque millibus in Græciam rediisse. Genevæ v i. Calendas Septembris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: When I learned from the letter of our brother N. recently that one of the three whom the Senate has set over the little French church to govern it is you, I rejoiced greatly, as was fitting, and I trust this joy will be lasting. For I judge that this charge was joined to you by God's providence rather than by human counsel, so that by your faith and prudence you may settle whatever disturbances Satan has so far stirred up, and then take care that the wicked are given no occasion for tumult. So my heart's wish has been granted for the little flock. As for urging you to your duty, no delay hinders you, but I think it would be superfluous. How much I ought to rejoice over Philip's agreement on one point, I do not know, since on the chief articles he sets himself up as a philosopher and openly opposes sound doctrine, or else, so as not to stir up the hatred of certain people against himself, he conceals his opinion cleverly, though at least not very candidly. May the Lord equip him with a stronger Spirit, so that posterity does not suffer a grave loss from his timidity. Within the last three months five or six have been burned in Aquitaine, and in their death Christ triumphed gloriously. Recently too, in a town a little beyond Vulturina in the territory of Venice, a pious man, well known to me, confessed Christ with remarkable constancy, right to his last breath. Nothing new is reported here that is not equally known to you. Farewell, most excellent man and most honoured by me. May the Lord keep you and your family always and bless you. A messenger has now brought more certain news that a Turkish fleet, after burning a certain town and laying waste the coastal region, has returned to Greece with five thousand people taken captive. Geneva, six days before the Kalends of September, 1554.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN sends greetings to N.

units.la: Si infans sine Baptismo per occasionem decesserit.
units.tr: If an infant dies without Baptism through some chance circumstance.

units.la: PErlatum est ad me de tua orbitate ex morte filij, cui & alter dolor accessit, quòd nonnulli ex piis fratribus offendiculum ex eo conceperint, quòd sine Baptismo infans e vita excesserit, cùm tibi per tempus hoc præstare licuisset. Quòd ad primum attinet, non est quòd diutius insistam vt te consoler propter illius thesauri amissionem, cuius diuturnam fruitionem sperare poteras. Sic enim de te existimo, vt teipsum per te remedia illa adhibere dolori tuo non dubitem: adeóque iam eo vsque illa tibi applicando profecisse, vt ad Dei nomen glorificandum te cōparaueris, ex quo didicisti nihil nobis accidere posse melius, quàm vt voluntatem nostram illius arbitrio simpliciter subiiciamus. ciamus. Maxime vbi ipse nos ea gratia dignatus est,vt pro suis agnoscat in vita & morte,qui ipsi & viuunt & moriuntur.Quòd ad alterum verò, fateor oblatam scandali occasionem piis omnibus, si tua cessatione vel neglectu infans sine Baptismo excessit.Baptismus enim res magis sacra est & augusta, quàm vt vllo modo contemni debeat. Quare non modò ij ferendi non sunt, qui Baptismum negligunt,sed & illi nò probandi, qui iactatione quadam & ostentationis causa,rei sanctæ administrationem in multos dies protrahunt. Tuum est igitur aperire consilium & mentem tuam fratribus,vt scandalum ipsis oblatum tollas. Neque verò dubito, quin re ita percepta , habeant in quo acquiescant.Si tibi fuisset propositum diutius illic viuere vt alij faciunt, peccatum à te fuisset,nisi infantem ad Baptismum quamprimù offerres.Etsi verò illi etiā non sunt excusandi,qui istic offerunt ad Baptismum liberos, vbi super stitionibus Papisticis polluantur:non possunt tamen reiicere notam illam Christianismi,qualis etiam istic extat, quin hoc ad Dei ipsius contemptum pertineat. Tibi autem longè aliud erat propositum. Cùm enim hoc ante præcepisses cogitabas de vxore adhuc prægnante in veram Ecclesiam deducenda: aut si parturitio prius interuenisset de matre cum partu abducéda,vt ex Dei ordinatione pure infans tingeretur. Atque illud fuisset luculentum testimonium non contemptus Baptismi,sed legitimæ reuerentiæ,cùm illum syncerum ex Domini ordinatione filio tuo ita procurasses.Illa igitur dilatio cùm pars quædam fit Confessionis fidei tuæ, vbi à fidelibus aut dira fuerit,illos amplius non offendet:cùm si res ex voto succeßt, nihilò magis dilatio illa,quàm tua ipsius profectio coiuncta damnari potuisset. Fieri posse quidem existimo vt nō desint qui nō approbent illam demigrationem à natali solo,qu a se talibus exemplis perstringi sentiant:qui si in eo peccant,temere alios tentant exemplo suo subiicere, quasi legem illis viuendi ex suis moribus figant.Ab illis verò,qui ea quæ recta sunt,probant, neq; adhæret malo,facilè existimo hoc etiā probatum iri,vt perinde liceat Christiano homini cōsulere filio suo,vt ad syncerum Baptismum in Ecclesia Christi percipiendū abducatur à Papa, atq; vt pater ipse illinc emergat.Tatum tibi Dominus licere noluit.Causam ipse nouit.Sanè ita te humiliare illi placuit.Nec tamé factum per se damnationem meretur quum propositum tuū sanctum fuerit & laudabile. Atqui infans ita priuatus est signo salutis,Baptismo nempe.Nego tamen illius coram Deo deteriorem esse conditionem.Quanuis enim Baptismus sit sigillum adoptionis nostræ:inscripti sumus tamen in libro vitæ,tū mera gratia Dei nostri,tū illius promissione.Cedo enim quo nomine Filij nostri seruantur,nisi ex illo verbo,Ego sum Deus feminis tui. Ac nisi illud verbum ad eos pertineret,ne ad Baptismū quidem admittendi essent.Iam si eorum salus Dei promissione nititur,& fundamentum illud idoneum est ex seipso, non est existimandum perire omnes pueros,qui sine Baptismo è vita excedunt.Sic enim sub commendatione signi illius gratiæ Dei, Deus ipse afficeretur iniuria & cōtumelia,& eius veritati derogaretur,qui sali filius nostra ipsius fulta promissione non satis confirmaret. Cum igitur nullus in te neglectus Baptismi deprehendatur, priuatio illius infanti nocere nō potuit,quum ante excesserit, quàm tibi commodè ad Baptismum offerre liceret. Quare nulla scandali occasio supereret, nisi qui sibi ipsis vitro molestiam inde accersent. Tu verò piis omnibus hoc ita se habere significabis, vnde sibi satisfactum nouerint. Dominus te & vxorem præsidio suo tueatur,Spiritu sancto confirmet,atque in bonum magis ac magis promoueat.v i.Septemb. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: I have heard of your bereavement in the death of your son, and a second grief has been added to it: some of our pious brothers have taken offence that the infant passed from this life without Baptism, when it would have been possible for you to provide it at this time. As to the first point, I need not dwell long on consoling you for the loss of that treasure, whose long enjoyment you might have hoped for. I think so well of you that I do not doubt you are applying those remedies to your own grief, and indeed you have advanced so far in applying them that you have prepared yourself to glorify the name of God. From this you have learned that nothing better can happen to us than to submit our will simply to his decision, especially since he has deigned to grant us this grace, that those who live and die by him should acknowledge in life and in death that they belong to him. As to the second point, I admit that an occasion of offence has been given to all the pious, if the infant died without Baptism through your delay or neglect. For Baptism is a thing too holy and too weighty to be despised in any way. Therefore not only must those be borne with who neglect Baptism, but those too must not be approved who, out of a certain showiness and for the sake of display, put off the administration of a holy thing for many days. It is your duty, then, to make your plan and your mind clear to the brothers, so that you may remove the offence given to them. I have no doubt that, once the matter is understood in this way, they will have something to rest in. If it had been your purpose to go on living there, as others do, you would have sinned, unless you offered the infant for Baptism as soon as possible. Although those also are not to be excused who there bring their children to Baptism where they are polluted by Papist superstitions, yet they cannot reject that mark of Christianity which also exists there, without this amounting to contempt of God himself. But your purpose was quite different. For you had already decided beforehand, as you were thinking, to bring your wife, who was still pregnant, into the true Church; or, if labour had come on first, to take the mother away with the child so that the infant might be purely baptized according to God's ordinance. That would have been a clear proof not of contempt for Baptism but of lawful reverence, since you had thus arranged for your son to receive the pure sacrament according to the Lord's ordinance. That delay, therefore, since it is part of the confession of your faith, will not offend the faithful, even if it has been harshly received by some; for if the matter had turned out as you wished, that delay could no more have been condemned than your own departure. I think it is quite possible that there will be some who do not approve of that emigration from one's native soil, since they feel themselves pricked by such examples. If they are wrong in this, they rashly try to make others submit to their example, as if they were fixing a rule of living for them from their own customs. But from those who approve what is right and do not cling to what is wrong, I easily expect that this too will be approved: that it is equally lawful for a Christian man to consult for his son, so that he may be taken away from the Pope to receive pure Baptism in the Church of Christ, and that the father himself may come out from there. The Lord did not wish you to have this freedom; he knows the reason. Certainly it has pleased him to humble you in this way. Yet the deed in itself does not deserve condemnation, since your purpose was holy and praiseworthy. But the infant has thus been deprived of the sign of salvation, namely Baptism. I deny, however, that his condition before God is worse. For although Baptism is the seal of our adoption, we are nonetheless written in the book of life, both by the mere grace of our God and by his promise. For I ask by what name our children are kept, except by that word: I am the God of your seed. And if that word did not pertain to them, they ought not even to be admitted to Baptism. Now if their salvation rests on God's promise, and that foundation is in itself sufficient, we must not think that all children perish who depart from this life without Baptism. For in that case God himself would be wronged and insulted under the pretext of that sign of his grace, and the truth of him who has promised our salvation by his own word would be derogated from, as if it were not sufficiently confirmed. Since therefore no neglect of Baptism can be found in you, the lack of it could not harm the infant, since he died before it could conveniently be offered to Baptism by you. Therefore no occasion of offence remains, except for those who bring trouble on themselves for no reason. But you will make it clear to all the pious that this is how matters stand, so that they may know they have been satisfied in this. May the Lord keep you and your wife under his protection, confirm you by the Holy Spirit, and advance you more and more in goodness. 6th September 1554.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D. Vtrinam Baptismus recte administrari possit.
units.tr: CALVIN TO THE LORD'S SERVANT, GREETINGS. Would that Baptism could be rightly administered.

units.la: ROgatus sententiam de pueris ad Baptismum Ecclesiæ veræ offeredis,vbi Ecclesia ipsa latet adhuc,& vix potest pro locorum iniquitate & temporum conuenire, dixi: Cùm quis sub Papatus tyrannide non modò ipse ab illius pollutionibus abstinet,sed etiam liberos suos Domino offerre,& baptizandos iuxta Domini institutum curare studet,zelum illum & sanctum esse & laudabilem.Magna est enim indignitas,vbi tam singularis thesaurus, liberi nempe à Domino nobis donantur, ita illos pollui sinere apertis superstitionibus quas homines in sacru Baptismum inuexerunt. Imprimis autem obseruandum est,cùm istud Sacramentum complectatur sacram & solennem introductionem in Ecclesiam Dei, sitque testimonium cœlestis nostri municipatus,in quem adscribuntur illi quos Dominus adoptat sibi,fas non esse administrare Baptismum , nisi in cœtu fideliū. Non quidem,vt templum requiratur,sed vt vbiuis numerus aliquis fidelium conueniat,qui Ecclesiæ corpus efficiat, & qui baptizat pro Pastore agnoscatur. Si enim infans clám baptizetur & nullis adhibitis testibus,illud neque respónderet ordini à Domino posito,neque Apostolorum exemplo. Oportet igitur infantem baptizari in cœtu aliquo, qui quidem cœtus profiteatur sibi nihil esse commercij cum Papistic is pollutionibus.Cum il-li,de quibus relatum est,sic conuenire poterunt in nomine Domini, etiamsi exiguus sit illorum numerus qui ita conuenient, oramus Deum vt rectum illum zelum ipsis adaugeat,quem iam contulit, vt se & suos Deo Patri consecrent & Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Qua in re nos etiam illis quibuscunque modis dabitur, defuturi non sumus. 1. Octob. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: When I was asked my opinion about bringing children to baptism by the true Church, where the Church itself still lies hidden and can scarcely be assembled because of the wickedness of the places and the times, I said this: when someone under the tyranny of the Papacy not only keeps himself free of its pollutions, but also takes care to offer his children to the Lord and to have them baptized according to the Lord's institution, that zeal is both holy and commendable. For it is a great disgrace, when such a singular treasure, namely children, is given to us by the Lord, to allow them to be polluted in this way by the open superstitions which men have introduced into holy Baptism. Above all, it must be observed that, since this sacrament embraces the holy and solemn introduction into the Church of God, and is a testimony of our heavenly citizenship, in which are enrolled those whom the Lord adopts as his own, it is not lawful to administer Baptism except in an assembly of the faithful. Not indeed that a temple be required, but that some number of the faithful gather wherever they may be, which forms the body of the Church, and that the one who baptizes be acknowledged as minister. For if an infant were baptized secretly and with no witnesses present, that would conform neither to the order instituted by the Lord nor to the example of the Apostles. It is necessary, therefore, for the infant to be baptized in some gathering, which gathering professes that it has no fellowship with the pollutions of the Papists. As for those of whom mention has been made, if they can come together thus in the name of the Lord, even though the number of those who so gather be small, we pray God to increase in them that right zeal which he has already bestowed, so that they may consecrate themselves and their own to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ. In this matter we will not be wanting to them in whatever ways it is given to us. 1 October 1554.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus.
units.tr: John Calvin.

units.la: SVLCERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: SULCERUS TO CALVIN, GREETINGS.

units.la: A Mercatu Francofurtensi cum scribere per bibliopolas constituissem, profectione improuisa impediebar. Laborabat Ecclesia Argentinensis haud leui iam periculo implicita: quod Ministri excessuri plerique viderentur nisi idololatriae omnimodam abrogationem obtinerent. Augebat metum nostrum, intestina inter ipsos fratres discordia, quia duo ex illis se non solum reliquis abiunxerant, sed priuatim & publice eorum qui sunt x iiii. studiis repugnabant. Accurrimus ergo pro fraternae coniunctionis officio, & quantum potuimus, his instituimus, vt pientissimis Symmystirum conatibus fauerent, vtcunque se nollet periculo illigari, suis quibusdam ductirationibus. Illis vero, sic vt zelum moderarentur, ne temere lupis prodérent laniandam Ecclesiam Benigniter ab vtrisque auditi sumus, & eo vsque videntur profecisse optimi Dei serui, vt si non impetrentur quae velimus omnia: gradum tamen vt fecerint, ad demolitionem Papatus, siquidem quod omnino sperant, capita reliqua concedantur. Verum de eventu scribet proximis ad me Marpachius. Agit officium strenue Dux Christophorus cum patruo Comite Georgio, cum erga eum ipsum quem dixi Senatum Argentinensem, tum Marchionem Badensem vicinum nobis, qui nuper est illi pollicitus, se exactis sacrificulis veram religionem instauratarum. Rogemus Dominum, vt Regni sui pomoeria dignetur misericorditer extendere. Albertus Bauarus cum Salisburgensi & Aichstetensi Episcopis crudeliter contra veram pietatem furit instituta inquisitione, quae etiam cum Hispanica certet. Nec secus apud Viennam Austriae sancti vexantur. Verum & haec impiorum molimina nouit Dominus ad Ecclesiae incrementum nominisque sui gloriam conuertere. In Anglia nouos subinde motus excitari accipio, sed astibus atque potentia regiorum opprimi partem meliorem, rerumque potiri pro voto Hispanos licet coronationem Rex nondum sit consequutus. Vale in Christo Iesu, cuius gratiae te cum tuis omnibus vnice commendo. Basileae, 1 11. Octobris. Anno M. D. LIII 1.
units.tr: I had decided to write to you through the booksellers at the Frankfurt fair, but an unexpected journey prevented me. The Church of Strasbourg is caught in no slight danger, since most of its ministers seem ready to leave unless the idolatry is completely abolished. Our fear is increased by the internal discord among the brothers themselves. Two of them have not only separated themselves from the rest but also oppose, both privately and publicly, the views of the fourteen others. So, out of duty to our fraternal fellowship, we ran to them and did what we could to persuade them to favour the most devoted efforts of our fellow-workers, even if they did not want to be entangled in danger, and to moderate their zeal by some of their own considered measures, so that they would not carelessly hand over the Church to the wolves to be torn apart. Both sides heard us kindly, and the excellent servants of God seem to have advanced so far that, even if not everything we wish is obtained, they have at least taken a step towards the demolition of the Papacy, provided that the remaining points, which they hope for entirely, are granted. Marpach will write to me about the outcome in his next letter. Duke Christopher is working vigorously on this, together with his uncle Count George, both with the Strasbourg senate, which I mentioned, and with the Margrave of Baden, our neighbour, who recently promised him that once the sacrificing priests were expelled he would restore the true religion. Let us pray that the Lord will mercifully extend the borders of his kingdom. Albert of Bavaria, together with the bishops of Salzburg and Eichstätt, rages cruelly against true piety by setting up an inquisition which rivals even the Spanish one. The saints at Vienna in Austria are harassed no differently. But the Lord knows how to turn these machinations of the impious to the increase of the Church and the glory of his name. I hear that new disturbances are being stirred up from time to time in England, but the better part is being crushed by the zeal and power of the kings, and the Spanish, although the king has not yet obtained his coronation, are gaining control as they wish. Farewell in Christ Jesus, to whose grace I commend you and all yours above all. Basel, 11 October, in the year 1553.
