units.la: MELANCHTHON CALVINO.
units.tr: MELANCHTHON TO CALVIN.

units.la: Euerède vir,& charissime frater,legi scriptum tuum in quo refutasti luculenter horrendas Serueti blasphemias, ac Filio Dei gratias ago,qui fuit ἐρασιστὴς huius tui agonis.Tibi quoque Ecclesia & nunc & ad posteros gratitudinem debet, & debebit.Tuo iudicio prorsus assentior. Affirmo etiam vestros magistratus iuste fecisse,quòd hominem blasphemum, re ordine iudicatà,interfecerunt.Quòd vero in proximis literis me hortaris, vt reprimam ineruditos clamores illorum, qui renouant certamen περὶ ἐρωτολατρείας,scito quosdam praecipuè odio mei eam disputationem mouere,vt habeant plausibilem causam ad me opprimendum. Cum doctis & bonis viris multa colloquutus sum de multis disputationibus, quas haec vna continetur, de diuinarum personarum proprietatibus, de patefactione Dei διὰ λόγου καὶ πνεύματος in vera conuersione, seu consolatione. De his tantis rebus maximè tecum loqui cuperem,quem scio amantem veritatis,& non habere animum occupatum odiis,aut aliis stultis affectibus.Sic ait Nazianzenus ἐκ φωτὸς τοῦ πατρὸς φῶς κατακλαμέντος τὸν υἱὸν ἐν φωτὶ τῷ πνεύματι ἀγίῳ. Etsi pauca sunt eius Scriptoris dicta de illa agni tione Dei, quae lucet in vera consolatione, tamen hoc dicto delectatus sum, quod inserui huic Epistolae, quia tibi quoque gratam fore eius mentionem arbitrabar.Haec nihil πρὸς τὴν ἀρτολατρείαν. Nō despero nos colloquuturos esse,antequam ex hoc mortali carcere mens discedat. Etsi enim propter senectam a meta huius curriculi non procul absum,tamen quotidie noua exilia expecto. Oro autem Filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum crucifixum pro nobis, & resuscitatum, custodem Ecclesiae suae, vt te & nos omnes gubernet. Bene vale charissime frater.Die xiiii.Octobr. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Excellent man and dearest brother, I have read your writing in which you have brilliantly refuted the horrible blasphemies of Servetus. I give thanks to the Son of God, who was the [ἐραστής] supporter of this struggle of yours. The Church both now and in future generations owes you, and will owe you, gratitude. I entirely agree with your judgment. I also affirm that your magistrates acted justly in putting to death that blasphemer, after the case had been heard in due order. As for your urging me in your last letter to restrain the uneducated outcries of those who revive the dispute concerning [ἐρωτολατρεία], know that some are stirred up to that debate chiefly out of hatred for me, so that they may have a plausible pretext for crushing me. I have talked at length with learned and good men about the many disputations contained in this one question: about the properties of the divine persons, and about the revelation of God [διὰ λόγου καὶ πνεύματος] through Word and Spirit in true conversion, or consolation. I would very much like to speak with you about these great matters, since I know you love the truth and do not have a mind occupied with hatreds or other foolish passions. Nazianzen says: [ἐκ φωτὸς τοῦ πατρὸς φῶς καταγλαζόμενον τὸν υἱὸν ἐν φωτὶ τῷ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ], the Son, a light shining from the light of the Father, in the light of the Holy Spirit. Although that writer says little about that knowledge of God which shines in true consolation, I was delighted by this saying and have inserted it into this letter, since I thought its mention would be pleasing to you as well. These things have nothing to do with [ἀρτολατρεία]. I do not despair that we shall converse with one another before the mind departs from this mortal prison. For although on account of old age I am not far from the goal of this course, I nonetheless expect new exiles every day. I pray that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us and raised again, the guardian of his Church, may govern you and all of us. Farewell, dearest brother. On the 14th of October, 1554.

units.la: P. MARTYR CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: PETER MARTYR TO CALVIN, GREETING.

units.la: Circa festum Paschę literas ad te,vir clarissime,dederam,sed adolescenti Hungaro,& quidem nobilissimo,qui non longe a Seleftadio est interfectus: quare cùm tam mœstus interuenerit casus,ad te perferri non potuerunt,& quae tum noue ram atq; scribebam, cùm te aliunde iam resciuisse nō dubitem minime repetenda censeo. Huc verò tristissima ex Anglia sunt allata,nimirum ibi parlamentum (vt vocant) esse assensum, vt Papae sua restituat tyrannissima. Et Philippus Rex Angliae sit & habeatur: bonorum virorum qui abire possunt vndiq; fit fuga. Atque tanta est rerum perturbatio,vt nullo pacto explicari queat.
units.tr: Around the feast of Easter I had written to you, most distinguished sir, but the letters were entrusted to a young Hungarian, and a most noble one, who was killed not far from Sélestat; because of that sad event they could not be delivered to you. I do not think I should repeat what I then wrote and was writing, since I have no doubt you have already learned of it from elsewhere. But sad news has come here from England, namely that Parliament (as they call it) has consented that the Pope should restore his most tyrannical power, and that Philip is to be and be considered King of England. Good men who are able to leave are fleeing from every quarter. And such is the confusion of affairs that it cannot be explained in any way.

units.la: Iámque hîc sunt apud nos tres præclarissimi equites, nempe Morisinus, Chæcus, & Cuccus, non minus pietate quàm eruditione insignes quos intra paucos dies puto venturos. Hæc ideo scribo, vt rebus illis propemodum perditis, neduum afflictis, velis precibus vnà cum tua Ecclesia subuenire. Certè iam Cantuariensis, & reliqui Episcopi, qui vnà captiui detinentur, in extremo versantur discrimine. Nos hic iam satis quiete agimus quo ad externa. Etiâ de nostra Gallica Ecclesia liberati metu videmur, quod multi antea suspicabantur fore, vt aliquid in doctrina & Sacramentorum administratione mutaretur. Id neque factum est, & vt confido, non fiet. Vtinam quorundam contentio aduersus Pastorem tolli queat. Eam tamen spero tandem quieturam, vtque iudico facilius dissimulando consopietur, quàm si vi & potentia contrà eatur. Et hoc quoque malum precum indiget. Nec te postremò latere velim, me vnà cum reliquis bonis viris id vehementer dolere, quòd aduersus ver tatem, ac tuum nomen, adeò inepta & falsa spargant de æterna Dei electione, atque de hæreticis extremo supplicio non afficiendis. Sed bene habet quòd in his quæ scribunt (vt audimus) nomen suum profiteri non audét. Vt audimus, dixi, quoniam huc Argentinam ne vnus quidem allatus est ex illis anonymis libris. Nos hîc quoties rogamur, cùm publicè tum priuatim, partes & veri & tuas pro virili tuemur, præsertim Zancus & ego. Quomodo verò D. Allasco sit per Daniam & Saxonicas Ecclesias male acceptus, ex isto qui tibi meas reddet, poteris cognoscere. Vale atque pro nobis ora. Zancus te plurimùm salutat. Vicissim quæso Martinengo necnon Galeatio Marchioni & N. salutem meo nomine dixeris. 1 x. Maij. Argentinæ.
units.tr: Now there are three most distinguished gentlemen here with us, namely Morisinus, Chæcus and Cuccus, no less remarkable for piety than for learning, whom I think will arrive within a few days. I write this so that you may help, with your prayers together with your Church, these affairs which are almost ruined and by no means without distress. Certainly the Archbishop of Canterbury and the other bishops, who are being held captive together, are now in the greatest danger. We here are now living quite quietly as far as external matters go. We also seem to be freed from the fear, which many earlier suspected, that something would be changed in our French Church in doctrine or in the administration of the sacraments. That has not happened, and, as I trust, will not happen. I wish the contention of certain people against the Pastor could be brought to an end. Yet I hope it will finally be quiet, and, as I judge, it will be more easily quieted by being ignored than if it is opposed by force and power. This evil too needs prayers. Nor would I wish to conceal from you that I, together with the other good men, grieve greatly that they spread such foolish and false things about eternal election of God and about not inflicting capital punishment on heretics, against the truth and your name. But it is well that, in what they write (as we hear), they do not dare to profess their name. As we hear, I say, since not even one of those anonymous books has been brought here to Strasbourg. Here, whenever we are asked, both publicly and privately, Zanchi and I defend the cause of the truth and your part to the best of our ability. How Lord Alasco has been badly received through Denmark and the Saxon Churches you will be able to learn from the man who will deliver my letters to you. Farewell, and pray for us. Zanchi greets you most warmly. In turn I ask you to give my greetings in my name to Martinengo, and also to the Marquis Galeazzo, and to N. 1 May, at Strasbourg.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN, TO N., GREETING

units.la: EGo verò, mi frater, non adeo sum morosus, quin amicis facile ignoscam, etiam si nihil ad me toto anno scribant. Nam quia in hoc officij genere minus sum sedulus, vel saltè dum me alieni occupant, summis amicis interdum quod debetur non persoluo, libenter de mutua silentij venia cum ipsis paciscor. Ergo nisi aliâ suspicio animum meum pupugisset, nullas abs te literas mihi venire, nunquam ægrè tulissem. Cæterum multa fuerunt, quibus me offensum fuisse non dissimulo. De vestris dissidiis nemo fratrum tuorum priuatim ad me scripsit. Per alios delatæ sunt querimoniæ. Ego nō me vltrà interposui, quàm vt per eosdem nuntios suaderem, quæ pacis, & cōcordiæ erant. Certè eius generis fuerunt mea consilia, vt non minus habita fuerit à me amicitiæ nostræ ratio, quàm fides Christo & Ecclesiæ v.ij. præstita. Quare non est cur me eorum pudeat, vel tu mecum expostulcs. Inquire obsecro, reperies nihil à me profectum, quod non tibi summopere placere debuerit. Atque vtinam magis familiaris tuis symmystis fuisses: Rex, vt opinor, momento transfata foret. Interea tuas ad Fatellum literas legi, ex quibus olfeci animum tuum vel in me esse exulceratum, vel obliquis suspicionibus infectum. Excandescentiæ vero & stomachi in eos, quibus, vt nunc scribis suffragari me putabas, plenæ erant. Cur si amicitiam nostram laesam putabas, non statim conquestus es? Verum hæc apud me occulta sunt nunc: ac ne minimæ quidem offensionis signum dedi. Tantum doluebat, quod te à fraterna communione subduceres. De tolerandis hæreticis quanam esset tua sententia, ex quibus sdam sciu. Tu quidem licet in umbra iudicas. At si tibi ferio hic fuisset certandum, forte consilium mutasses. Sciunt tamen amici, quàm placidè, & comiter tunc excusaue rim, quod nobis parum esses propitius. Quanquam à nobis hodie dissentiat N. quia tamen & syncerus est Christi minister, & pietatis affectu regitur, deinde homo est probus, & moderatus, nobis amicus esse non desinet. Ego illi propterea molestus no ero. Nunc tamen lecta nostra excusatione, siquidem eam in manus sumere dignatus es, te non fuisse mitigatum, nonnihil miror. Sed vt vero te esse disciplinam, quis vnquam somniauit? Quiduis potius mihi esset credibile, quàm eò vsque animi te esse abreptum. Nec vero arbitror, famam tuam verbulo attactam fuisse. Quod autem Diaconum tuum passus fueris, non tantum mihi & sanæ doctrinæ obloqui, sed in alterendis Serveti deliriis palàm bacchari, quis non vitio tibi verteret? Iam vt ingenuè omnia fatear, de æterna Dei prædestinatione te nō recte sentire, mihi dictum est. Ego etsi verebar ne quid esset, semper tamen minus esse credidi, quàm audire cum acerbissima molestia cogebar. Porrò, quum multis modis iniuriam mihi fieri putarem, non tamen sum tumultuatus: sed illas indignitates tacito mœrore devorare malui, quàm vel amicitiæ nostræ veteris, vel coniunctionis fraternæ vinculum scindere. Atque nunc te rogo, vt mihi saltem ta cere liceat, dum indignè non minus, quàm hostiliter vexor. Si decima tantum ex parte scias, quàm atrocibus probris lacerer, pro tua humanitate ingemiscas miserius, ad quas obdurui. Vndique me canes allatrant. Haereticus passim vocitor. Quicquid fingi calumniarum potest, in me congeritur. Denique me inuidi, & maleuoli ex grege nostro infestius oppugnant, quàm aperti hostes ex Papatu. Non tamen itafum meritus vel de Ecclesia Dei, vel de ipsis, vt tam iniquâ mercedem rependere debeant. Auctarium vt isthinc accederet, non timui. De Diacono tuo loquor, quem tua conniuentia minimè ali oportuit, quum non minus impiè cōtra puram religionem insurgeret, quàm improbè homini innoxio maledicebit. Et tamen non aliud postulo, nisi vt mihi permittas eius contumelias leniter ferre. Quanta fide & integritate Christo seruieris, quâ cordatè functus fis tuo officio, quàm constanter & labores, & certamina quibus te exercuit Dominus, sustinueris, ego tibi testis sum: ac te in posterum perpetuò tui similem fore confido. Itaq; nihil magis cupio, quàm saluam inter nos benevolentiam manere, quò alacrius, & synceriore studio nos vltrò citròque iuuare pergamus. Vale eximie vir, & colende frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit, te gubernet ac tuos labores benedicat. Collegæ mei te plurimum salutant. Geneuæ x v. Octobris. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Indeed, my brother, I am not so touchy that I cannot readily forgive friends even if they write nothing to me for a whole year. Since I am rather lax in this kind of duty, and sometimes fail to pay what is owed to my closest friends, especially when other business keeps me busy, I willingly come to a mutual agreement with them to overlook each other's silence. So, had some other suspicion not stung my mind, I would never have taken it hard that no letter from you had come to me. Yet there were many things by which I do not hide that I was offended. No one of your brethren wrote to me privately about your disagreements. Complaints were brought to me through others. I did not interpose myself any further than to urge, through those same messengers, what would serve peace and harmony. Certainly my counsels were of such a kind that I held our friendship no less dear than the faith I had pledged to Christ and to the Church. So there is no reason for me to be ashamed of them, nor for you to remonstrate with me. Inquire, I beg you, and you will find that nothing came from me that should not have pleased you greatly. Would that you had been more familiar with your fellow-mystics: the king, I think, would have been changed in a moment. Meanwhile I read your letter to Fatellus, from which I sensed that your mind was either exasperated against me or infected with oblique suspicions. Indeed, it was full of anger and bile against those whom, as you now write, you thought I was supporting. Why, if you thought our friendship had been harmed, did you not complain at once? But these things are now hidden from me, and I have given not the slightest sign of offence. I was only grieved that you were withdrawing from fraternal fellowship. As to your opinion on tolerating heretics, I know some of it. You indeed judge in the shade. But if you had had to fight here in the open, perhaps you would have changed your mind. Yet my friends know how calmly and courteously I then excused it, that you were not very favourable to us. Although N. differs from us today, nevertheless, since he is a sincere minister of Christ and is governed by a zeal for godliness, and since he is moreover an upright and moderate man, he will not cease to be a friend to us. I will therefore not trouble him. Now, however, having read our excuse, since you deigned to take it in hand, I am somewhat surprised that you were not softened. But who ever dreamed that you were so lacking in discipline? I would rather believe anything than that you had been carried away to such a degree of mind. Nor do I think your reputation was touched by a single word. But who would not blame you for allowing your deacon not only to speak against me and sound doctrine, but to rave openly in spreading the delusions of Servetus? To speak frankly about everything: I have been told that you do not think rightly about the eternal predestination of God. Although I feared there might be something in it, I always believed it to be less than I was forced to hear with most bitter distress. Moreover, although I thought I was being wronged in many ways, I did not make an uproar; I preferred to swallow those indignities in silent sorrow rather than sever the bond of our old friendship and our fraternal union. And now I ask you at least to let me keep silent, while I am tormented no less unworthily than hostilely. If you knew even a tenth part of how savagely I am torn by shameful insults, you would groan more pitifully for my humanity, at how hardened I have become. Dogs bark at me from every side. I am called a heretic everywhere. Whatever calumny can be invented is heaped upon me. Finally, envious and ill-disposed men from our own flock attack me more fiercely than open enemies from the Papacy. Yet I have not so deserved, either of the Church of God or of these men themselves, that they should repay me with such an unjust reward. I did not fear that this would be added as a further sweetener from your side. I am speaking of your deacon, whom your connivance ought by no means to have fed, since he rises up no less impiously against pure religion than he wickedly curses an innocent man. And yet I ask for nothing else than that you allow me to bear his insults calmly. With what faith and integrity you have served Christ, with what wisdom you have discharged your office, and how steadfastly you have endured the labours and conflicts with which the Lord has exercised you, I am a witness; and I trust you will be forever like yourself in the future. Therefore I desire nothing more than that goodwill between us remain safe, so that we may continue to help one another, willingly and in both directions, with more eagerness and more sincere zeal. Farewell, distinguished man and honoured brother. May the Lord always be with you, govern you, and bless your labours. My colleagues greet you warmly. Geneva, 15 October 1554.

units.tr: CALVIN TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF POLAND. GREETING.

units.la: ETsi ego ante annos quinque, Serenissime Rex, quandam librorum meorum partem vestræ Maiestati publicè dedicaueram, vt pietatis semen, quod iam tunc cordi vestro diuinitus insitum audieram, magis ac magis excitarem: nunc tamen minimè auderem homo ignobilis, priuat s tam inclyto Regi literas offerre, nisi venerar dus frater noster cui hoc debeo, &c, cuius vt fidelis erga M.V. obseruantia mihi nota est, ita non dubito quin sensus vestros probè compertos habeat me suo consilio & hortatu animassIer. Quia ergo spopondit non ingratum M.V. fore hoc meum officium: temeritatis culpam non sum amplius veritus. Iam verò quia absurdum foret, ab Euangelij Ministro in conspectum tanti Regis vacuas literas venire: illud idem argumentum, quod continet publica mea in Epistolâ ad Hebræos præfatio, quia nullum vel melius, vel Regia persona dignius, vel tempori aptius occurrit, mihi sumendum putaui. Sic enim persuasus sum, proea, quam Filio Dei communi magistro defertis, reuerentia, ab eius seruo moneti, vobis nō fore graue, aut molestum. Et certè hæc modestia decet omnes Christi discipulos, à summo vsque ad infimum à Regibus ipsis ad plebem vsque, cœlesti eius doctrinæ libenter, & placida animi mansuetudine se submittere. Nam & hoc modo secundum Dauidis præceptum osculantur regnorum omnium Principem & caput terreni Reges dum per homines, quibus dicendi munus iniunxit, loquentem audire non respuunt. Cæterum, quòd mearum partium vicissim esse arbitror, operam dare studebo, ne vobis fastidio sit mea prolixitas. Ac primùm horribiles tenebras, quę passim gras-
units.tr: Although, most serene King, I publicly dedicated a part of my books to Your Majesty five years ago, so that I might stir up more and more the seed of piety which I had already heard was divinely planted in your heart, yet now I would hardly dare, as a man of humble rank, to offer a letter to so illustrious a King, unless our honoured brother, to whom I owe this, etc., had urged me. His faithful regard for Your Majesty is known to me, and I do not doubt that he understands your feelings well. He has counselled and encouraged me, and since he has promised that this duty of mine will not be unwelcome to Your Majesty, I no longer fear the charge of rashness. Now, it would be absurd for a minister of the Gospel to come into the sight of so great a King with empty letters, so I have thought fit to take up the same subject that my public preface to the Epistle to the Hebrews contains. No subject is better, none more worthy of a royal person, none more suited to the times. For I am persuaded that the reverence you pay to the Son of God, our common Master, will not be burdensome or troublesome to you when you are admonished by his servant. Indeed, this modesty becomes all Christ's disciples, from the highest to the lowest, from kings themselves down to the common people: to submit willingly and with a calm gentleness of mind to his heavenly teaching. In this way, according to David's precept, kings of the earth also kiss the Prince of all kingdoms and head of all, when they do not refuse to hear him speaking through the men to whom he has entrusted the office of speaking. As for my part, which I think I must in turn perform, I will take care that my lengthiness is not tedious to you. And first, I will not touch upon the horrible darkness spread everywhere, the flood of errors that overwhelms almost the whole world, nor upon the abuses and corruptions by which religion is defiled, lest I waste Your Majesty's time in a superfluous treatment of a matter already known. For I am not addressing some rude person ignorant of sincere piety, but a King endowed with the light of purer doctrine, who can judge rightly not only that he himself is freed from the crude superstitions of the common people, but also how deadly is that labyrinth in which the greater part of the human race is entangled.

units.la: Epist. 190. fantur:errorum colluuiem,qua obruitur totus fere mudus:abu-sus & corruptelas, quibus foedata est religio, non attingam,ne in superuacua rei cognitae tractatione M. Vestram frustra occu-pem.Neque enim ad rudem quempiam,& fyncerae pietatis igna-rum mihi habendus est sermo:sed apud Regem purioris doctri-nae luce praeditum, vt non modo a crassis vulgi superstitionibus fit ipse liber,sed etiam quam exitialis fit labyrinthus ille, quo ma-ior pars generis humani tenetur implicita, recte iudicet. Nam quu gregarios quoque discipulos lucernis similes esse velit Chri-ftus,quae in sublimi positae fulgorem suum longe emittunt:quid a Rege exiget,quem in summo dignitatis ftigio locauit, vt a-liis omnibus praeluceat? Nam quo magis honorifica est folij cui praeftis,altitudo,eo difficilius est, parem gerere animum,vt lo-cus hominis virtute ornetur: & de reddenda apud Deum ratio-ne magis folicite cogitandum. Quod fi obscuris hominibus ti-mendum est,ne hoc viuificum femen torpore suffocatum dege-neret,vel prorsus interear, quid M. Vestrae agendum est,cui non fatis est, vt erem ex fe fructum proferre, nisi eandem sementem ad multa hominum millia propagare studeat. Memineritis ergo,praestantissimae Rex,in persona vestra lucem toti Poloniae di-uinitus esse accensam, quae fine graui culpa diutius latere ne-quit.Itaque haec prima fit cura, & hoc primum studium, fubie-ctas vobis ditiones ex foeda Papatus dissipatione ad Christi obse-quium colligere. Erumpat tandem heroica illa, quae nimis diu intus sopita iacuit virtus,& in re tam praeclara, memorabile fui documentum praebeat.Neque vero me fugit,aut quam arduae fit molis opus,aut quam multiplices & magnae difficultates instet, quas suo more ingeret Satan. Sed quum hic pro gloria Dei de Christi regno,pro sacrorum puritate,pro humani generis salute pugnetur,ea est causae excellentia,quae & molestias omnes ab-sorbeat sua laude,& obstacula facile superet.Imo quid agendum fit,ipsi veritatis hostes suo exemplo praescribant. Nam quo acrius ad eam opprimendam eniti eos videt. M. Vestra, eo turpius ef-set, insanum eorum ardorem non saltem corda strenuitate aequare. Ruant igitur,quam maximo poterunt impetu, machi-nas omnes admoueant, ignea quae Satan illis suppeditat, & vi-ruleta iacula torqueant,tam insidiis denique,quam aperto Mar-te grassentur,adeo ad frangendum generosum pectus,& coelesti Spiritus Dei virtute praeditum haec omnia valere non debent, vt totidem sint potius ad piam contrarij studij,& conatus aemu-lationem stimuli. Huc accedit, quod quum Deus proprium o-pus suum esse afferat,collapsam Ecclesiam,cuius est vnicus fun-dator, restituere,haud dubie statuendum est,eum nobis laboran-tibus minime defore.
units.tr: Epist. 190. For if Christ wants even ordinary disciples to be like lamps, which, set on high, send their light far, what will he require of a King whom he has placed on the highest step of dignity, that he should shine before all others? For the higher the seat you preside over is honoured, the harder it is to keep an equal spirit, so that the man's place is adorned by virtue; and one must think more anxiously about giving account before God. But if obscure men must fear lest this life-giving seed, smothered by torpor, degenerate or perish altogether, what must Your Majesty do? It is not enough for you that the seed should bring forth fruit by itself, unless you also strive to propagate the same seed to many thousands of men. Remember therefore, most excellent King, that in your person a light has been divinely kindled for all Poland, and that it cannot remain hidden for long without grave guilt. So let this be your first care and first zeal: to gather the lands subject to you out of the foul dispersion of Papacy into obedience to Christ. Let that heroic virtue, which has lain too long smothered within, break out at last and give a memorable proof of itself in so noble a matter. Nor am I unaware either how arduous a work it is, or how many and great difficulties Satan, after his manner, will heap up. But since here the battle is fought for the glory of God, for the kingdom of Christ, for the purity of the sacred things, and for the salvation of the human race, the excellence of the cause is such that it swallows up all troubles in its own praise and easily overcomes obstacles. Indeed, the enemies of the truth themselves prescribe what must be done by their example. For the more eagerly Your Majesty sees them striving to crush it, the more shameful it would be if you did not match their frenzied ardour with courage of heart. Let them rush forward with the greatest force they can, let them bring up all their machines, the fiery darts and poisoned javelins that Satan supplies them, and let them rage with ambushes as much as with open war. All these should not avail to break a generous breast endowed with the heavenly virtue of God's Spirit; they should rather be so many spurs to a pious emulation of the opposite zeal and effort. Moreover, since God declares that the work is his own, namely to restore the fallen Church, whose sole founder he is, we must undoubtedly conclude that he will by no means fail us as we labour.
