units.la: Quod ad te aperte & liberè scribere instituì, omnem in modum a te peto, vt illud boni consulas, atque sic existimes, si quid hic simplicius egisse visus fuero, illud non a temeritate vel audacia, sed ab vno & certo obsequij tibi secundū Dei praestandi affectu profectum esse. Vt enim meipsum nimis inutilem seruum in heri mei domo apud me sentio, ita tamen abstinere omnino nō possum, quin pro gratiae ab ipso in me collatae modulo, aliquid ad te vsq; transmittam: adeo vt non parū mihi ipse defuturus videar, nisi te quamprimum isto ad te scribendi officio adeam, atq; compellem. Neque vero in eo me deficiunt satis idoneae rationes. Vna est, eaque vna iusti per se momenti, q non tuae minus quam aliorum salutis, pro Domini vocatione qua fungor, habendam mihi rationem existimem. Altera, quod cum tu in illam celsitudinem & supereminentiam intueor, quae ad regni Dei incrementum, vti ab illo est, ita etiam nō mediocriter conferre possit, sic mihi persuadeo, à nobis qui ministerio fungimur, peculiarem quandam vestrum curam, eo nomine habendam esse. Mea vero quod ad te sic est ratio, vt cum à tua illa Excellentia discesserò, eum in te tamen Dei timorem, & ferium illi obsequendi affectum agnoscam, vt ferendus omnino non sim, nisi ad omnem occasionem procurandae salutis tuae intentum me praebeam. Quod ita me testante mea conscientia procul à fuco vel adulatione tibi testificari, nouit ille cui aperta sunt occulta & intima cordium & cogitationum. Accepi à multis iisq; fide dignis de N. quem concionatorem habes, q cum ad tempus & pro suo modulo, aliquid non poenitendum praestiterit, idem nunc tibi auctor sit, quod id nullum incommodum habere dicar, vt post Missam auditam, aliqua comunionis species subiungitur, quae Coenae Domini loco sit. Illud porro à quadam ex tuis probari non potuisse, quod verita sit, ne quid hic fieret non ex Dei verbo, quod aperte malum esse sentiret. Te autem bono illo N. auctore non tantum erga illam vulgum tuum immutatas, sed & in eam sententiam adducam, ut minime ferendam illam multieris & similium morositatem existimes, quae sua importunitate scandalum infirmis sine causa adferat. Ego vero cum istius rei tale momentum esse viderem, ut dissimulari nullo modo posset, tibi etiam ea proponi quae longe aliter se haberent, apud me decreveram, quid ipse sentirem, si quid ex Dei verbo percepi, scri pto tibi aperire. Cumque in ea cogitatione defixus haererem, comodissime a N. mihi significatum est te hoc ipsum a me expetere, ut quid in re perplexa tibi sequendum esset, semel & serio intelligeres. Inde igitur animus etiam creuit huius apud te fungendi officii, quo ut spero rem ipsam ita tibi ob oculos ponam, ut quid de ea statuendum sit, non ita difficile colligas. Fac igitur ut cum Dei veritas in medium prodibit, sic illam agnoscas, ut zelus iste tuus tam ab omni contumacia absit, quam te Dei timentem & Verbi ipsius auditioni reverenter subiectam mihi hactenus agnovisse visus sum. Et quod ad illas occasiones quibus factum est, ut rumor iste primum ad me pervenisset, noli in illis exquirendis haerere, cum & qui illa referebant, non putarent, te a me iustorum admonendam vnquam esse. Ego vero centies pe rire malim, quam ut villius mortalis gratia vel occasione, D. i verbum inflexile aut protulisse etiam dici possim. Summa causa igitur haec vna est, quod ferre non potuerim verbum Dei ita sepeliri, inuerti, corrumpi, depravari in rebus tanti momenti, & ab illis ipsis quibus fidem adhibes, & quos apud nō vulgari loco esse vis. Quod igitur ad N. attinet, si tibi aperiam quid de illo mihi compertum sit, ut deinceps tibi prospicias, neque ipsius doctrinam confidentius admittas, timendum mihi non putem, ne in siniistri affectus opinionem apud te incidam, cuius causas procul habeo. Ac si quod meum in hominem odium notari potest, illud eo uno letit, quod hominem vrgere nunquam desierim, ut sese serio ad Ecclesiae aedificationem in verae doctrinae syncera professione applicaret. Qui vero verbum Dei malo animo conuellat, & veritatem ipsius extinguere conetur, non si meo mihi parente coiunctior sit, parcat illi oculus meus, quin ut instrumentum Satanae accipiam. Istius porro hic fuit semper scopus, quantum ex certa experientia percepi, ut quantulumcumque intelligentiae Scripturae a Domino accepisset, illud totum ad quaestum & ambitionem conferret. Sic igitur & quod verum esse sciebat, non reticuit, vbi illinc aliquod emolumentum captauit, & vbi vel minimum molestiae subolfecit, non minus strenue recantauit. Illa conscientia praeditus, cum sibi coram hominibus alicuius nominis, vel bene nummatis concionem habendam praecepit, & qui apud ipsum vt Deo gloriam darer, instarent, ita illis quidem satisfacere studuit, vt simul nom gratuitam à se locatam operam satis indicaret. Cùm verò aliud theatrum succederet, noster homo ad palinodiam appositè instructus sibi perinde consuluit. Quare de illo iudicari aliter non potest, quàm de eo cui verbum Dei fit profabula: & qui persona quadam parasyti indutus in theatrum prodeat, vt sese his vel illis venditet. Priuatos mores non attingo, qui vtinâ concionatoris nomini minus male respondercnt. Alienum est, scio, ab homine Christiano, alteri detrahere. Hoc si quaererem, nimis idoneas occasiones praetermisi. Sed illud me vrget, quod clamat Dominus, ne lupos toleremus sub Pastorum larua gregem ipsum dispersuros: quòd iubet istorum improbitatem retegi, qui praesentissimae sint pestes ad ipsius familiam & inficiendam, & enecandam. Et tamen si mihi hominem ipsum appellare integrum fuisset, illum potius quàm te primùm nunc officij admonendum duxisse cùm satis cogitem quàm irreconciliabile istorum mihi odium conciliem. Nulla enim hoc tempore mihi acerbior est contentio, quàm cum istiusmodi, qui sub Euangelij nomine principum animos fermento suo illaqueant, atque illos suis artibus & dolis semper quasi ex nebulis suspensos tenent, neque vnquam ad veram lucis fruitionem adduci sustinent. Quid igitur facerem cum illis, quos Dei timore ita vacuos noui, vt & ipsius iudicij nomen ipsis futurum sit pro cantione vel naenia? Quod vnum superest igitur ne igno ti deinceps fallant, & plus damni dent, depingendos mihi apud illos statuo, qui ad ipsorum technas magis sumt expositi. Haec via mihi consultior visa est, vt quibus maximè timendum est, opportunè quoad possum non desim. Istum porrò semel in viam reducere conatus sum, vt ad suae prauitatis agnitionem hominé adegerim. Atqui ille nihilo minus in eo perstabat, vt se non reiecturum aut ab eo recessurum diceret, quod impium esse ipsi constabat. Semel tamen cùm in meum quendam tractatum incidisset, ferò & non sine grauibus imprecationibus protesiatus est, cùm Mille abominationem plane explorati am haberet, illi se nunquam interfuturum. Scilicet iuranti credidissem, quem non minus futilem quàm gracculum garrientem iudicarem. En quae meae huius ad teipsam admonitionis causam plane necessariá: nam & apud istum operam lusisset, & tibi certius consulere aliter quod sentirem, nō potui. Sed quod de illo testificatus sum, fac non satis esse mihi compertum, vt tuipsa periculum facias. Si enim penitus inspexeris sic colliges, hominem in tractando Dei verbo hoc vnum sibi propositum habere, vt ita gratiam apud te ineat, vt & inde beneficia & eiusmodi lucra captet, & in
units.tr: Since I have decided to write to you openly and frankly, I earnestly ask you to take it in good part and to judge that if I seem to speak too plainly here, this comes not from rashness or boldness but from a single and sincere desire to show you the respect I owe to God. I know myself to be a very useless servant in the house of my master, yet I cannot altogether refrain from sending you something, according to the measure of the grace that he has bestowed on me. Indeed, I would seem to myself to fall short in a great measure if I did not hasten to approach you and urge you by this letter. Nor am I without sufficient reasons for doing so. One is, and it is of weight in itself, that I think I must have regard, in accordance with the calling of the Lord which I discharge, for your salvation no less than for that of others. The other is that when I look upon you in that high and eminent position, which can contribute no little to the growth of the kingdom of God, as it comes from him, I persuade myself that we who serve in the ministry ought to have a special care for you on that account. My own reason for writing to you is this: when I depart from your Excellency, I nevertheless recognise in you the fear of God and a earnest desire to obey him, so that I would not be fit to live at all unless I showed myself eager to seize every opportunity of securing your salvation. God, who knows the secrets and inmost thoughts of hearts, knows that I bear witness to you of this, with my conscience as my witness, far from pretence or flattery. I have heard from many, and from trustworthy men, concerning N., whom you have as preacher, that although for a time and according to his ability he has accomplished something not to be regretted, he now advises you that there is no harm in adding, after the Mass has been heard, some kind of communion that will take the place of the Lord's Supper. Moreover, some of your people have been unable to approve of this, because they feared that something was being done here that was not from the word of God, which they judged to be plainly wrong. Yet by that good N. as your adviser, you will be led not only to change your attitude towards your people, but also to think that the peevishness of such men as the Moderator and others like him is in no way to be tolerated, since by their importunity they cause scandal to the weak without cause. Indeed, when I saw that this matter was of such importance that it could in no way be passed over, I had decided in my mind to set before you also the things that were entirely otherwise, and to make clear to you in writing what I myself think, if I have grasped anything from the word of God. And while I was stuck fast in this thought, it was most conveniently signified to me by N. that you yourself were asking this of me, so that you might understand once and for all, and seriously, what you ought to follow in a perplexing matter. Hence my spirit grew also in the office which I undertake with you; by it, as I hope, I will so place the matter itself before your eyes that you may not find it difficult to gather what must be decided about it. Do therefore, when the truth of God comes forward, acknowledge it in such a way that your zeal is as free from all obstinacy as I seem hitherto to have recognised you to be one who fears God and reverently submits to the hearing of the Word itself. And as for those occasions through which this rumour first came to me, do not dwell on searching them out, since neither those who reported them thought that you would ever need to be admonished by me about them. For my part, I would rather perish a hundred times than be able to be said to have uttered a word of God that was inflexible, or wavering, through the favour or occasion of any mortal man. The sum of the matter, therefore, is this one thing: that I could not bear that the word of God should be so buried, perverted, corrupted and depraved in matters of such great weight, and by those very people in whom you put your trust and whom you wish to hold in no ordinary place. Therefore, as far as N. is concerned, if I disclose to you what I have learned about him, so that you may look out for yourself from now on and not admit his teaching too confidently, I do not think I need fear that I shall incur an impression in your mind of ill feeling, the causes of which are far from me. And if any hatred of mine towards the man can be noted, it is outweighed by this one thing: that I have never ceased urging the man to apply himself seriously to the building up of the Church in the sincere profession of true doctrine. But as for one who tears up the word of God with an evil mind and tries to extinguish its truth, even if he were more closely joined to me than my own parent, my eye would not spare him, and I would not regard him otherwise than as an instrument of Satan. Moreover, the aim of this man has always been, as far as I have perceived from sure experience, that whatever small understanding of Scripture he had received from the Lord, he would turn all of it to gain and ambition. Thus, when there was profit to be had from it, he did not keep silent about what he knew to be true, and when he sensed even the slightest trouble, he recanted no less briskly. Endowed with this conscience, when he was ordered to preach before men of some standing, or well-off men, and those who urged him to give glory to God were pressing him, he took care so to satisfy them that at the same time he made it sufficiently clear that his work was not offered to them for free. But when another stage followed, our man, well trained for a recantation, provided for himself in the same way. Therefore one cannot judge of him otherwise than of one for whom the word of God is a fable, and who, dressed up in the character of a parasite, comes out on the stage so as to sell himself to this man or that. I do not touch on his private morals, which I wish corresponded less badly to the name of preacher. It is foreign, I know, to a Christian man to detract from another. If I wanted to do this, I have passed over far too many suitable occasions. But what urges me is what the Lord cries out: that we should not tolerate wolves that will scatter the flock itself under the mask of ministers; he commands that the wickedness of those who are most dangerous pests, both for infecting and for killing his household, be exposed. And yet, if it had been permissible for me to name the man himself outright, I would have thought it right to give you this warning now rather than him first, though I consider well enough how irreconcilable the hatred of such men towards me would become. For at this time no contention is more bitter to me than with men of this kind, who under the name of the Gospel ensnare the minds of princes with their leaven, and keep them always suspended as if in mists by their arts and tricks, and never allow them to be brought to the true enjoyment of the light. What then should I do with those whom I know to be so empty of the fear of God that the very name of judgement will be for them a matter of mere charm or lullaby? What remains, therefore, so that the ignorant may no longer be deceived by them and do more harm, is that I resolve to portray them before those who are more exposed to their snares. This way seemed to me the more advisable, so that I may, as far as I can, be present opportunely where the danger is greatest. Moreover, I have tried once to lead him back to the right way, so that I might bring the man to recognise his own depravity. Yet he nevertheless persisted in saying that he would not reject it or depart from it, which he himself knew to be impious. Once, however, when he had come across one of my treatises, he protested, not without heavy curses and with much hesitation, that since he held a thousand abominations to be plainly known, he would never be present at them. Certainly I would have believed the man swearing, whom I judged to be no less trifling than a chattering jackdaw. Here is the plainly necessary cause of this admonition of mine to yourself: for I would have been wasting my labour with him, and I could not otherwise counsel you more reliably about what I think. But as for what I have testified about him, do not suppose it is not sufficiently established for me, so that you may put it to the test yourself. For if you examine him thoroughly, you will conclude that in handling the word of God he has this one aim before him: to win such favour with you that he may thereby catch benefits and such gains, and never incur the offence of anyone at all.

units.la: x.iij. aullius offensionem vnquam incurrat. Nunc omisso homine, rem ipsam aggrediar. Hoc est igitur illius consilium: quòd Missa non ita abominanda sit, quin & ipsi illam facere, & aliis qui fideles sint, Missæ interesse liceat: quibus vero hoc agere religio sit, illos perturbare Ecclesiam, esse infirmis scandalo, quorū praecipuam causam apud nos esse voluerit Dominus. Quòd ad illud attinet, quid Missa valeat, vix scio operæprețium ne facturus sim, si quid ad illud apud te praesertim regeram. Sic enim mihi persuadeo illam à te non alio quàm horrendi sacrilegij loco haberi, si quid aliud eo nomine censendum sit. Verendum igitur ne ridiculus apud te sim, si illud probare contendam, de quo te non dubitare non magis ipse dubitem. Breuitas etiam epistolæ vix ea completi posset, quæ iustum volumen caperet. Quare vt obiter aliquid attingam, vt minus adhuc perplexa hæreas, sic habe. Missa est sacrificium ab hominibus institutum, pro redemptione viuorum & mortuorum, vt certo loco Canon Missæ perhibet. Missa igitur execranda est blasphemia, qua passio Domini conuellitur, atque vis ipsius euanida & inanis prorsus reddi- tur. Cùm enim dicimus fideles effuso Christi cruore redemptos, peccatorum remissionem, iustitiam, vitæ æternæ spem adeptos esse, hoc non aliter accipi potest, quàm quatenus bonus Redemptor noster Patri seipsum offerens, atque victimam immolandam sistens, semetipsum illo ipso actu obtulit in sacrificium æternum, quo nobis constat purgatio & emundatio ab iniquitatibus nostris, ac proinde nostra in gratiam apud Patrem cœlestem receptio, cum Regni etiam cœlestis speranda participatione, vti pluribus ostendit disertè & manifestè euincit Apostolus ad Hebræos à 7. ad 11. Quò pertinet hæc illius appositissima exhortatio, quam ex doctrina de efficacia vnius Sacerdotij & sacrificij Christi in æternum colligit. Quum habeamus, inquit, per Christi carnem, viam illam & recentem ac viuam, accedamus corde puro ad Dominum. Nam si vna Christi mors vnicum illud sacrificium non completitur, quod peractum semel, perpetuam causam habeat, vt vis illius æterna sit, inducatur nempe & pro nullo habeatur. Respondent sacrificuli praestigiatores, se nō offerre nouum sacrificium, sed ipsissimum Christi sacrificium. Sic magis blasphemiis sese inuoluunt. Quis enim prodibit ad offerendum sacrificium Christi præter Christum ipsum idoneus? Quid verò Apostolus de vnico illo sacrificio incomparabili? Si inquit, vt per Christum peccata aboleantur, vnicum illius sacrificium non sufficit, sed iterum illud offerendum sit, iterum etiā sit ipsi moriendum. Quare duorum alterum hîc statuendū est, vt aut horrenda Missæ blasphemia aperte execranda habeatur, aut si retinetur, vt crux Christi (quod absit) pedibus conculcetur.
units.tr: x.iij. ...that he never incurs anyone's offence. Now, setting the man aside, I will take up the matter itself. This, then, is his position: the Mass is not so abominable that he himself may not celebrate it, and that those of the faithful who wish may attend it; but that for those for whom it is a matter of conscience to do so, they disturb the Church and are a stumbling block to the weak, and the Lord has willed that these be the chief cause among us. As for what the Mass is worth, I hardly know whether it is worth my while to undertake this, especially as I would be explaining it to you. For I am persuaded that you regard it as nothing other than a place of horrible sacrilege, if anything else is to be judged under that name. I fear, therefore, that I would seem ridiculous to you if I labored to prove what I myself am no more in doubt about than you are. Nor could the brevity of a letter contain what would fill a substantial volume. So, that I may touch on something in passing, and so that you may be less perplexed, take this: the Mass is a sacrifice instituted by men, for the redemption of the living and the dead, as a certain passage of the Canon of the Mass declares. The Mass is therefore an execrable blasphemy, by which the passion of the Lord is overthrown and its power rendered utterly empty and void. For when we say that the faithful, redeemed by the blood of Christ poured out, have obtained the remission of sins, righteousness, and the hope of eternal life, this can be understood only in this way: our good Redeemer, offering himself to the Father and presenting himself as the victim to be slain, offered himself by that very act as an eternal sacrifice, by which cleansing and purification from our iniquities is secured for us, and consequently our reception into favour with the heavenly Father, together with the hope of sharing in the heavenly kingdom. The Apostle shows this plainly and clearly, at length, in Heb. 7 to 11. To this belongs his most fitting exhortation, which he draws from the doctrine of the efficacy of the one priesthood and sacrifice of Christ for ever: "Since we have," he says, "through the flesh of Christ, that new and living way, let us draw near with a pure heart to the Lord." For if the one death of Christ does not complete that unique sacrifice, which, once accomplished, has a perpetual cause so that its power is eternal, then it is brought down and counted as nothing. The sacrificing juggler-priests reply that they do not offer a new sacrifice, but the very sacrifice of Christ. Thus they entangle themselves all the more in blasphemies. For who would come forward fit to offer the sacrifice of Christ, apart from Christ himself? And what does the Apostle say about that unique and incomparable sacrifice? If, he says, the sacrifice is not sufficient to abolish sins through Christ, but it must be offered again, then he must again suffer death. Therefore one of two things must be decided here: either the horrible blasphemy of the Mass is openly held as execrable, or, if it is retained, the cross of Christ (which God forbid) is trampled underfoot.

units.la: Quàm bellè vero Missæ conueniat cum Cœnæ Domini, ipsa Cœ-næ à Domino institutio me tacente tibi suggereret. Cumulus autè abominationis ipsa quæ ibi primas tenet elementi adoratio est. Hoc enim nullum colorem habet. Quæ cum ita se habeant, qua fronte ille affirmare audeat Missam esse quid medium, & nō ita intolerabile, nisi conuictus fateatur tot horrenda in Deum peccata, ipsamque abominationem quæ illic capiut attollit, res perè inde etiam esse leuis alicuius momenti? Quid enim quis obtendat, quominus tam horrendæ impietatis societate teneatur, qui illam se supra verbum Dei reuereri, & magis impese obseruare conuictus sit? Quàm vero illud D. placeat testatur ipse apud Ezec. 20. cap. 39. vers. Agite, inquit, & merum idolorum cultum profitemini gentium ritu, neq; sanctum nomen meum cum vestris idolis permiscete. Sic enim ipsi cogitabant conciliandam esse obedientiam legis Dei, cum vanissimi gentium superstitionibus, quas sibi ascisc endo, à Dei lege se prorsus auerte bant. Hoc alibi confirmat, vbi ait, illos se perditurum qui iurarent per nomen suum vt Dei veri, ac nihilominus alios simul Deos sibi affingerent. Neque valet illa responsio, præcipuè à Deo mentem requiri, vt illa pura sit, quicquid externo gestu quis præ se ferat. Nempe hoc refutat Dominus, cùm testatur eodem illo corpore se glorificari velle, pro quo non minus quàm pro anima seipsum impenderit: sic oris confessionem requirit: sic nullam nostri partem non sibi consecrari iubet. Hoc verò locum habere non potest, quin illis omnino vt le dicamus, quæ à se reprobari non minus aperte testatus sit. Hic verò ne sermonem magis intendam, quod Epistola non ferret, reliqua facilè erit petere extra-ctatu à me edito. Quid pio homini cum Papisticis superstitionibus commune esse possit, vtq; se illic gerere debeat. Illic te reperturam confido, quò tibi plenius satisfactum agnoscas. Superest altera quæstio, an dicendum sit tubari infirmorum conscientias, si quis fidelis à Missa penitus & omnimodo abhorreat: ille hoc asserit. Ego verò videre non possum, quomodo hoc illi excidè-rit quod tam securè præterg reditur, estque præcipui momenti in hac quæstione. Primum enim illud est in Dei cultu, & irrefixum stare oportet, quicquid Dominus iubet aut vetat verbo suo, ab eo obseruando ne latum vnguen discedere fas esse. quamcunq; in partem hoc alij interpretentur. Iam res quasdam non eo loco esse cōcedo, sed quæ mediæ sint, quòd ad ipsum vsum vel abstentionem: cúmque illæ quasi nostro delestui reliquæ sint, videdum quid captus proximorum ferat, ne nostra libertate ad illorum infirmitatem iis in rebus non temperata, periculose offen-dātur. Ac nominatim Apostolus Rom. 15. ver. 2. scopum euitan-dæ proximi offensionis statuit, vt illum in bonum ædificemus. Ex quo sequitur nihil nocentius à nobis ad proximum pervenire posse, quàm quod non ad ipsius ædificationem, sed ad destructionem pertineat. In Epistola verò ad Cor.1. 8. & 10. cap.difertius etiam hoc exequitur ut ostendat, ficius nostrum & illius apud nos sensum adfratrum & proximorum captum temperandum esse, ne plus audendi quàm sibi licere considerent sibi sint exemplum à nobis ducant, quod non aliud est quàm exitium proximo quantùm in nobis sit accersere. Iam ad rem. Fac interesse Mistæ aliquem ex iis qui pij habentur, & cui Missæ impietas explorata sit, tantum ut ignorantiæ aliorum adstantium fortasse sese, ut loquuntur, accommodet. An non verò qui illic adstant cum sua ad Missam deuotione, dum nostra præsentia illam nobis quoque probari non temere colligunt, in malum à nobis confirmantur? quàm grande scelus à Paulo illud pronunciandū existimamus, (quicquid de illius magnitudine nostra peruicacia subducat) quum rerum illarum vsum attingens, quæ per se fidelibus promisçuæ esse poterant. tamen destrictè tamen monet, ut nobis non addicti, proximorū præcipua potius causa sit, propter conscientiam inquit non tuâ sed alterius, quo vel offenditur & in malo confirmabitur, vel quasi fractis repagulis exemplo tuo in exitium ille abripietur. Vide igitur imprimis, ne isto offendiculi & scandali nomine tibi imponatur. Vtenim grauissimum illud est offendiculi genus, vbi nostro exemplo fratter in præceps mittitur, ac corruit qui erigendus erat nostra moderatione: ita etiâ si omnia scandala in vtramuis partem euitare cogitamus, vnum compendium illud est, facessat Christus à nobis. Etenim ille per petuus est offendiculi lapis, ad quem hominum maxima pars impingit. Et in populo Iudaico perinde hoc olim extitit, cùm ad illos primùm missus sit Dominus. Imò Deus ipse iam ante offendiculo illi suæ genti maxima ex parte fuerat. Iterum igitur regulam quam suprà posui repeto, quod quicquid iubet aut vetat verbo suo Dominus, ab eo ne latum vnguem discedere fas est, vel cum totius mundi offensione. Cùmque Christus impiis sit semper offendiculo, non est expectandum, vt iidem minus offendantur, cùm nos Euangelium profiteri animaduerterint. Quòd verò ad illa attinet quæ quod ad vsum media sunt, vt à nobis vsurpari omittive possint integra conscientia, in illorum vsu videndum, ne nihil non fratribus concedamus, vt libertas illa nostra charitatis legi perpetuò inseruiat. Et tamen ista infirmorum susceptio seu tolerantia eò referri debet, vt ipsi sensim ad ea quæ recta sunt, promoueantur, & ad Deum propius accedant. Nam si exemplo nostro ipsorum conscientia quasi vim patitur, nos illorum exitio causam damus. Et quòd ad illos attinet, qui nunc aliquo pietatis gustu imbuti sunt, cùm paucissimi sint quibus Missa
units.tr: How well the Mass agrees with the Lord's Supper, the institution of the Supper itself would suggest to you, even if I said nothing. The greatest abomination, however, which holds the first place there, is the adoration of the element. For this has no colour at all. Since these things stand as they do, with what brazenness does he dare to affirm that the Mass is something middling and not so intolerable, unless, when convicted, he confesses so many horrible sins against God, and, in raising up the abomination that is there, admits that the matter is therefore of some slight importance? For what can he allege why he should not be bound by fellowship in so horrible an impiety, when he has been convicted of revering that rite above the word of God and of observing it more zealously? How well the Lord's approval of this is shown by his own words in Ezek. 20:39: "Go," he says, "and serve every one his idols, and profess the pure worship of idols in the manner of the nations, and do not mingle my holy name with your idols." For they thought that obedience to the law of God could be reconciled with the most empty superstitions of the nations, which, by adopting them, they turned utterly away from the law of God. He confirms this elsewhere, where he says that those will perish who swear by his name as the name of the true God, and at the same time fashion other gods for themselves. Nor does that answer hold, that God chiefly requires the mind to be pure, whatever outward gesture one displays. The Lord refutes this when he testifies that he wishes to be glorified in that same body for which he gave himself no less than for the soul; thus he requires the confession of the mouth; thus he bids no part of us to be left unconsecrated to him. But this cannot hold without our wholly rejecting those things which he has testified no less plainly to be reprobated by himself. But I do not wish to extend this discussion further here, as a letter would not bear it; the rest will easily be sought in the treatise I have published, on what a godly man has in common with Papistic superstitions and how he ought to conduct himself there. I trust you will find there what you may acknowledge as more fully satisfying to you. There remains another question: whether it must be said that the consciences of the weak are disturbed if a believer utterly and in every way shrinks from the Mass. He asserts this. But I cannot see how this slipped from him, which he so confidently passes over, and which is of chief importance in this question. For first of all, in the worship of God, this must stand fixed and unshaken: whatever the Lord commands or forbids by his word, it is not lawful to depart from it by so much as a hair's breadth in obeying it, in whatever direction others may interpret it. Now I grant that some things are not of this kind, but are indifferent as to their use or abstention; and since these are, as it were, left to our judgment, we must consider what the capacity of our neighbours can bear, lest, with our liberty not tempered to their weakness in such matters, they be dangerously offended. And specifically the Apostle, in Rom. 15:2, sets as the aim of avoiding the offence of a neighbour that we build him up for good. From this it follows that nothing more harmful can come from us to a neighbour than what does not serve his edification but his destruction. In the Epistle to the Corinthians, chapters 8 and 10, he works this out even more clearly, to show that our own feeling and the feeling of our brethren and neighbours must be tempered in such matters, lest they, considering that they may dare more than is permitted them, take us as their example, which is nothing other than to bring about, as far as in us lies, the ruin of our neighbour. Now to the matter. Suppose someone who is counted among the godly, and who has clearly recognised the impiety of the Mass, attends the Mass, only accommodating himself, as they say, perhaps to the ignorance of the bystanders. Do not those who stand there, with their own devotion to the Mass, while they rashly conclude from our presence that it is also approved by us, become confirmed in evil by us? How great a sin we must judge that to be which Paul pronounces (whatever our stubbornness may detract from its magnitude), when, touching on the use of those things which in themselves could be common to believers, yet he warns strictly that we should not be given to them, for the chief cause of our neighbours, saying: not your conscience, but that of the other, by which he is either offended and confirmed in evil, or, as if the barriers were broken, is snatched away to destruction by your example. See, then, above all, that you are not deceived by the name of stumbling block and scandal. For this is the most grievous kind of stumbling block, when by our example a brother is sent headlong and falls, who was to be raised up by our moderation. So, even if we intend to avoid all scandals in either direction, there is one sure way: Christ must be removed from us. For he is the perpetual stone of stumbling, against which the greater part of mankind strikes. Among the Jewish people this was once exactly the case, when the Lord was first sent to them. Indeed God himself had already, before that, been a stumbling block to his people for the most part. Therefore I repeat the rule I laid down above: whatever the Lord commands or forbids by his word, it is not lawful to depart from it by so much as a hair's breadth, even with the offence of the whole world. And since Christ is always a stumbling block to the impious, it is not to be expected that they should be less offended when they perceive that we profess the gospel. As for those things which are indifferent as to use, which may be taken up or omitted by us with a clear conscience, in using them we must see that we do not concede everything to our brethren, so that that liberty of ours may always serve the law of charity. And yet this receiving or tolerating of the weak must be directed to this end, that they may gradually be advanced toward what is right, and draw nearer to God. For if their conscience is, as it were, forced by our example, we give cause for their ruin. And as for those who now are imbued with some taste of piety, since there are very few for whom the Mass...

units.la: Missa iam in idololatriæ suspicionem saltem nō veniat: nostro tamen illo exemplo ducuntur vt ab illa non abstineant, cum iam assistendi scrupulus conscientiam pungens reuellitur. Illud vero deterrimum est scandali genus, quo infirmæ conscientiæ & à spe sanationis non remotæ, transfuerfæ nostro exemplo ab omni sensu pietatis, ad nostri facti perniciosum argumentum semel abripiuntur. Audio postremò bonum nostrum N. scandali istius de Missa adeunda grauitatem eleuare velle Germanicarum Ecclesiarum exemplo, quæ inquit liberum cuique faciunt Missas adire vel non adire. Cedo vero auctorem istius impostura & contumeliç aduersus tot Dei Ecclesias: Res aperta est, si vel minimum inquiri iust ris. Ego vero tibi confirmo, hoc ita receptum esse, non tantum apud omnes quæ istic sunt Ecclesias, sed & apud vnumquemque ex fidelibus, Missam abominationem esse non ferendam. Et Capito ipse qui moderationis studiosior habitus est, scripsit librum ea de re ad Regem Angliæ non ita priuum, quo docet Principum esse in illud incumbere imprimis, vt munus suum præstent, vt execrandam illam idololatriam semel è medio tollant. Neque vllus extat hodie alicuius in Ecclesia no minis, qui non perinde sentiat. Cùm igitur Dominus te dignatus sit cognitione nominis sui, teque Euangelij sui veritate illuminauerit, fac vt cœlestem illam vocationem agnoscas. Neque enim alia de causa è nostris illis tenebris ad lucem suam admirabilem traftulit, quàm vt illi vni irretorto oculo adhæreamus: demùsque operam vt magis ac magis eruditi, continuum profectum in ipsius sapientia meditemur, vt illius rudimenta iam ab ipso accepimus. Imprimis vero cauédum, ne Spiritum ipsius extinguamus: vti illis accidit, qui & claudunt oculos, & aures ob struunt, illiusque rei vnam ignorationem affectant, quam Dominus omnibus patefactam voluit. Absit vero à nobis tantum scelus, ne ingratitudinem illam & contemptum seuerissime tandé vindicet. Quin potius eò vnicè studium applicemus, vt in optimi Magistri schola assiduè proficiendo, tandem ipsius doctrinæ scopum apud illum consequamur. Illud vero tum dabitur, cùm ex corporeo istius molis ergastulo ad illũ emigrabimus, vt perpetua hæc nostra cum Dauide schola sit. Doce me Domine fa- cere voluntatem tuam. Atque vbi illo affectu & zelo ducemur, non est dubitandum, quin ita ab ipso dirigendi simus, vt nihil in via nos sit remoraturum. Ad nostros vero defectus & ignorantiam subleuandam non deerit ipsius gratia, quç maiorem lucem afferat, quàm enus ipse nouit quid expediat. Summum est vt teneamus, qui legitimi sint nostræ vocationis fructus. Nimirum vt Dei verbo cor nostrum & mensetiam trásformentur, vt gloria Domini in nobis elucescat, quæ in integritate, innocentia,
units.tr: Let the Mass not even come under suspicion of idolatry, at least. Yet by our example they are led not to abstain from it, now that the scruple pricking their conscience about standing present has been torn away. The worst kind of scandal is this: weak consciences, not far from hope of healing, are turned aside by our example from every sense of piety and are snatched away once and for all into the pernicious argument of our own act. Finally, I hear that our good N. wants to lighten the seriousness of this scandal about attending Mass by appealing to the example of the German Churches, which, he says, leave it free to each person to attend Mass or not. But I ask who is the author of this fraud and insult against so many churches of God. The matter is plain, if you make even the slightest inquiry. For my part I assure you that this is so accepted not only among all the Churches here, but also among each one of the faithful: that the Mass is an abomination not to be tolerated. Even Capito himself, who was regarded as more devoted to moderation, wrote a book on this matter to the King of England, not at all early, in which he teaches that it is above all the duty of princes to set about performing their office and to remove that execrable idolatry once and for all from the midst. Nor is there anyone of name in the Church today who does not think the same. Since therefore the Lord has deigned to grant you knowledge of his name and has illumined you with the truth of his Gospel, see that you recognise that heavenly calling. For he brought us out of those darkness into his wonderful light for no other reason than that we should cling to him alone with unwavering eyes, and labour, being ever more and more taught, to pursue continual progress in his wisdom, since we have already received its first elements from him. Above all we must take care not to quench his Spirit, as those do who both close their eyes and stop their ears and affect ignorance of that one thing which the Lord wished to be made known to all. Far be such wickedness from us, lest he at last severely avenge that ingratitude and contempt. Rather let us apply our zeal wholly to this: that, making continual progress in the school of the best Master, we may at last attain with him the goal of his teaching. That will be given us when we emigrate from the prison-house of this bulky body to him, so that this school of ours with David may be perpetual: "Teach me, Lord, to do your will." And where we are led by that affection and zeal, there is no doubt that we shall be so directed by him that nothing will hold us back on the way. For relieving our defects and ignorance his grace will not be lacking, which will bring a greater light than we ourselves know to be expedient. The main thing is to hold fast to the lawful fruits of our calling: namely, that our heart and mind be transformed by the Word of God, so that the glory of the Lord may shine forth in us, which consists in integrity, innocence,

units.la: Psa.143.10 sanctitate consistit.Vbi ista non extant, vanum est Evangelij nomen & inanis illius professio.Quod igitur facere coepisti,ita deinceps persequere,ut opus Dei prouectius in te agnosci possit.Itaque vero huius mea liberæ & syncerę admonitionis veniam deprecor. De scandalis si quid amplius desideras, ut certam viam inter anfractus istos teneas,dabo operam,ut plenius etiam à me in posterum satisfiat. Ad eam rem pertinet,quam ad te mitto, epistola.Si vacabit legere,appositam ut spero,iudicabis. Scripsi etiam libellum de scandalis qui sua breuitate,ut spero, ad te con-solandum vsui esse poterit, cum doctrinam ipsam satis copiose illic me complexum esse existimem.Dominus te respiciat in ista tua infirmitate, & Spiritus sui virtutem tanto efficacius exerat, quæ te non minus in domo ipsius conspicuam reddat, quam in præsentis vitæ conditione supra multorum fortem communem cuectam voluit. Geneuæ.
units.tr: Psa. 143.10 holiness. Where these are not present, the name of the Gospel and its empty profession are vain. Therefore continue as you have begun, so that the work of God may be recognised in you ever more fully. I beg your pardon for this free and sincere admonition of mine. If you desire anything more on the subject of scandals, so that you may keep a sure course through those windings, I will take care that it is satisfied more fully by me in future. To this purpose belongs the letter which I send to you. If you have leisure to read it, I hope you will judge it apt. I have also written a little book on scandals which, by its brevity, I hope may be of use in consoling you, since I think I have covered the doctrine itself fully enough there. May the Lord look upon you in this your weakness, and exert the power of his Spirit all the more effectively, so as to make you no less conspicuous in his house than he willed you to be, in the condition of this present life, a common example of strength to many. Geneva.

units.la: Calvinus N. s. D.
units.tr: Calvin to N., greetings

units.la: CVM ex eo tempore quo Domino placuit probare fidę tuâ, nihil de te acceperim, nisi ex communi fama, non habeo nunc quidę N.quod ad te scribā: neqj tamen deesse voluj tam opportunæ occasioni. Dolet verò q, non ita pridem aliquis ex tuis hac præteriit me inconsulto, per quem ad te tutò poteram literas dare.Non videbam cui satis siderem ex quo tibi illæ molestiæ infliictæ sunt. Et quanuis de afflictionum tuarum exitu perplexus hærerem,ut idoneum ad te scribendi argumentum nondum suppeteret: laborabam tamen eo nomine,maximè q, nō haberem ad manum per quem scriberem. Nunc etiam quia non ita mihi constat de tuo statu,illud tantum perstringam, facile me existimare tibi fuisse de via recta deflectendum, ut hominibus morem gereres. Est enim triste illud indicium, quòd qui ante tibi tam acerbè instabant,ut te à Dei cultu auerterent, tibi nunc in otio agere per illos liceat.Ita enim res habet.Diabolus nepe ista occasione tibi s inflauit,ut coacti fuerimus capite deiecto ingemiscere, ab ampliori disquisitione abstinendo.Quod reliquum est, N. cum Dominus ille & clementiss. parens nunquam non paratus sit ad nos in gratiam recipiendos,cum lapsis porrigat manum,ne casus nostri letales euadant,peto à te vt animum colligas : neque si hostis semel aduersum te præualuit per infirmitatem tuam,solidâ tamen victoriam reportet:sentiat potius quos Dominus restituit,duplo confirmatiores redditos ad illius excipiendos insultus. Cum igitur cogitaueris ita solere Dominum suos humiliare,ut tamen cōfusos nūquam reddat,illud te ad spem certam eriget,qua te longè cordatius geras in posterum. rum.Noui enim eosdem impetus qui te deie cerunt,tibi denuo imminere. Sed expende,quaeso, quantum illi debeas qui & te tä charè redemit,& te quotidie ad cœlestem hæreditatem compel-lat. Absit vt pro tanto hæroicuiquam rei parcamus, maximè fi exitum ipsum intueamur,qui nostras afflictiones & probra manet,quæ illius nomine subeunda sunt nobis.Ille igitur inuocan-dus cum certa illa confidentia, vnum illum abundè esse nobis, qui noftr's infirmitatibus medeatur. Singulares illæ promissiones meditandæ, quæ nos ad beatam spem cœlestis gloriæ attollant,& vel ipso earum gustu nobis fatis est,ad nos à mundo plane abducendos,vt illum pedibus iam calcare audeamus.Vt vero omnino demonstres, quàm non emortuus fit affectus in te seruiendi gloriæ Dei,cura N.vt non solùm in te ipsa exemplum edas vti par est,sed etiam ita familiam tuam constituas,vt maledicentium ora prorsus obturentur.Dominus te præsidio suo tueatur & manu potenti fulciat, augeat in te sua dona ,atque ad suam vnius gloriam illa in te promoueat.Idus Febr.
units.tr: Since the time when the Lord was pleased to test your faith, I have heard nothing about you except through common report, so I have nothing particular to write to you now, N.; yet I did not want to let so opportune an occasion pass. It grieves me that not long ago someone from your circle passed by here without my knowledge, through whom I could have safely sent you a letter. I did not see whom I could trust since those troubles were inflicted on you. And although I was uncertain about the outcome of your afflictions and no suitable subject for writing to you yet presented itself, I was nonetheless troubled on that account, especially because I did not have anyone at hand through whom to write. Now too, since I am not so certain about your condition, I will touch only on this: I easily suppose that you were forced to turn aside from the straight way in order to please men. For that is a sad sign, that those who before pressed you so harshly to turn you away from the worship of God now let you live at ease through them. For so matters stand. The devil, no doubt, on that occasion puffed you up, so that we were compelled to groan with bowed heads, refraining from fuller discussion. As for the rest, N., since that Lord, most merciful and ever ready to receive us back into favour, stretches out his hand to the fallen so that our deadly falls do not come to nothing, I beg you to collect your spirit. Even if the enemy has once prevailed against you through your weakness, let him not carry off a solid victory; rather let him perceive that those whom the Lord has restored have been made twice as firm to meet his assaults. Therefore, when you have considered that the Lord is accustomed to humble his people in such a way that yet he never leaves them confounded, that will raise you to a sure hope, by which you will conduct yourself far more wisely in future. For I know that the same assaults which have cast you down are again hanging over you. But consider, I beg, how much you owe to him who both redeemed you at so dear a price and daily calls you to the heavenly inheritance. Let us by no means spare anything heroic for his sake, especially if we look to the outcome itself, which awaits our afflictions and reproaches that must be borne for his name. Therefore let us call upon him with that sure confidence, that he alone is enough for us to heal our weaknesses. Let us meditate on those singular promises which lift us to the blessed hope of heavenly glory; and their very taste is enough for us to lead us wholly away from the world, so that we may dare now to tread it underfoot. And so that you may fully show how far from dead is your zeal for serving the glory of God, take care not only to set an example in yourself, as is fitting, but also so to order your household that the mouths of slanderers are utterly stopped. May the Lord guard you with his protection, strengthen you with his mighty hand, increase his gifts in you and advance them in you to his glory alone. Ides of February.

units.la: P. MARTYR CALVINO s. D.
units.tr: Peter Martyr to Calvin, greetings

units.la: CVM veftratium qui Frácfordia redeunt copia detur,vt absque meis literis venirent, pati nolui.Res nostræ pro tépore ac loco sunt fatis tranquillæ. Doctori Marpachio redditæ fuerunt literæ quas ad eum scripseras, quid profecerint ignoro, siquidem nihil mihi de illis cómunicauit:sed vt antea tibi significaueram,spero turbas illas breui conquieturas.Satagunt huius Ecclesiæ Ministri ac multis modis conatur,vt sacrificuli,& Missa rursus hinc eiiciantur:nec tantum è suggestu causam egerunt fortiter , sed ad'erunt Senatum , eíque simul omnes testati sunt, nisi hoc effecerit,fe hinc migraturos:quod nequeant bona conscientia hic vlterius ministrare,vbi tanta domi feratur & defendatur idololatria.Hanc illorum actionem Senatus grauissimè tulit,& post aliquot dies ipsis duriter admodum respondit.Id præsertim obiicientes, quòd ante multos annos Vvittembergenfes consilium dederint,cui Lutherus, Ionas, Pomeranus & horum similes manu propria subscripserunt, quo sentiunt magistratus in rebus publicis, ius non habere, vel potestatem vllam in Ecclesias cathedrales , & collegia. Ideóque confultum esse vt pios Ministros sibi procurent,qui populo Euangelium pure docéant in aliis templis, ab illis abstineant, nec ibi quicquam conentur reformare,cùm tamen suos ciues queant iure prohibere, ne sese idololatria contaminent.Sui autem consilij hanc rationem fubiiciût,quòd Ecclesiæ cathedrales,& collegia huiusmodi, non à Rebuspublicis verùm à Procetibus Imperij vel ab ipsis Imperatoribus instituta ac dotata fuerint. Cumque Papae auctoritas in ciuitatibus Euangelicis reiecta sit, putant istarum Ecclesiarum arbitrium ad Imperatorem deuolutum: quare illi ratum potestatem immutandi, & repurgandi cultus Dei quoad illas faciunt. Illo itaque fretus cofilio noster magistratus repulsam dedit ministris, vt qui putet auctores eius consilij nostris ministris longe doctiores. Caeterum hi responsum hoc licet acceperint, nō sunt animo fracti, neque ab incepto destiterunt, sed rursus instant, ac de illo consilio à doctoribus Vvitbergensibus ante multos annos dato, satisfacere ac respondere conantur. Posteriori vero congressu lenius ac mitius à Senatu fuerunt accepti, qui te pus ad deliberandum sumpsit. Interea quid responsi dandum sit, ignoratur. Sed ego ariolor dum Caesar vixerit, rem non successuram, nec dubito nostrum Senatum cupere quidem impietate ac idololatria ciuitatem liberare, sed nollent occasionem grauioris offensionis Caesari praebere. Consiliis attamen caeterorum Ministrorum omnium in his actionibus, & Beatus & eius diaconus noluerunt se admiscere: imo potius dissenserunt, quòd ipsis aegre fuit & populo magnae admirationi. Quid sit successurum cum sciuero significabo. Sturmius non est hic, sed ante octo dies ex urbe proficiscebatur, spero non diu abfuturum. Zanchus te salutat, & ego. Symmyftis tuis meo nomine salutem dici velim. Historia Sleidani, vt spero, iam imprimetur. Diu te nobis diuina bonitas conseruet incolumem. Petrus Alexander, vt ad me scribit, est breui te inuisurus, quaeso illum aequo ac libenti animo videas. Nam licet hactenus de re sacramentaria sit nobis aduersatus, attamen in praesentia Deo monstrante, totus est noster, atque potest Ecclesiae nonnihil prodesse. Rursus vale ac me precibus apud Deum iuuato. Argentinae, XXIIII. Septembris.
units.tr: Since your countrymen who are returning to Frankfurt were to be given the chance to travel without a letter from me, I did not want to allow it. Our affairs are fairly calm for the time and place. Letters that you had written to Doctor Marpach were delivered to him, but I do not know what they have achieved, since he has told me nothing about them. But, as I had earlier indicated to you, I hope those disturbances will soon subside. The ministers of this church are working hard and by many means trying to have the priestlings and the Mass expelled from here again. They have not only pleaded their cause boldly from the pulpit, but have also appeared before the Senate and declared to it, all together, that unless this is achieved they will leave here, since they cannot in good conscience minister any longer where such idolatry is practised and defended at home. The Senate took this action of theirs very badly and after a few days answered them quite harshly. Above all, they objected that many years ago the Wittenberg theologians had given advice, and Luther, Jonas, Pomeranus and men like them had signed it with their own hands, to the effect that magistrates have no right or power in public affairs over cathedral churches and colleges. Therefore, it was advised that they should procure for themselves pious ministers who would teach the gospel purely to the people in other churches, and keep away from those, and not attempt to reform anything there; although they could rightly forbid their own citizens from defiling themselves with idolatry. They put forward this reason for their advice: that cathedral churches and colleges of this kind were established and endowed not by the public states but by the princes of the Empire, or by the emperors themselves. And since the authority of the Pope has been rejected in the Evangelical cities, they think the decision about these churches has passed to the emperor; and so they claim for him the authority to change and purge the worship of God in those places. Relying on that advice, our magistrate therefore rejected the ministers, since he thinks the authors of that counsel far more learned than our ministers. However, although they have received this answer, they have not been broken in spirit, nor have they desisted from their undertaking, but they press on again and try to satisfy and answer the advice given many years ago by the Wittenberg doctors. At their later meeting they were received by the Senate more gently and mildly, which took time to deliberate. Meanwhile, what answer is to be given is not known. But I, guessing, think that as long as Caesar lives the matter will not succeed; and I do not doubt that our Senate desires indeed to free the city from impiety and idolatry, but they would not want to give Caesar an occasion for greater offence. Yet Beatus and his deacon did not want to mix themselves in with the counsels of all the other ministers in these proceedings; rather, they dissented, because it was painful for them and caused great astonishment among the people. I will tell you what happens when I know. Sturm is not here, but eight days ago he was setting out from the city; I hope he will not be away long. Zanchius greets you, and so do I. I would like greetings to be given to your fellow Symmystae in my name. Sleidan's history, as I hope, will now be printed. May the divine goodness keep you safe for us for a long time. Peter Alexander, as he writes to me, is going to visit you shortly; I beg you to see him with a fair and willing mind. For although hitherto he has opposed us on the matter of the sacrament, nevertheless, now that God is showing the way, he is wholly ours and can be of some benefit to the Church. Again, farewell, and help me with your prayers to God. Strasbourg, 24 September.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS VINCTO CVIDAM. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to a certain prisoner, greetings

units.la: Charitas Dei Patris, Gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi tibi semper adsit per Spiritus sancti communicationem.
units.tr: May the love of God the Father and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be always with you through the communion of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quum plane de facie nobis ignotus sis Dilectiss. frater, quòd tamen ex quorundam nostrorum sermone accepimus, te istic laborare propter verbum Dei, abunde nobis illud non men esse existimauimus, quod vere Dei filios declarat, vt nostro hoc ad te scripto testaremur, quae nostra sit tecum in eiusdem causae assertione coniunctio, quòd ad te consolandum, & in fan-cto il-
units.tr: Although we have no acquaintance with you by face, most beloved brother, yet from what some of our people have told us, that you are labouring there for the word of God, we have thought it no small matter to bear witness, by this letter of ours, to the close fellowship we share with you in the defence of the same cause, since it truly declares you to be a son of God; and we hope it will carry no little weight in consoling you and confirming you in the holy purpose.

units.la: Epist.198, Ex Gall. &to illo proposito confirmandum non parum momenti habiturum speramus. Primùm igitur hoc apud te perpendas hortamur,ex quàm horrenda abyiso te Dominus eduxerit: & quo te honore affecerit,dum testem filij fui designauit,cui tam obstina te per ignorantiæ tempus reluctatus fis. Repete igitur memoria tot in te Domini beneficia. Atque vt cùm quæ te nunc coftringunt vincula merito peccatis rependi poffient, in illud nomen Testimonij Veritatis transcripta sint, vt imde elucescat Christi gloria & Euangelij quoque efficacia propagetur. Si te grauitas præfentium afflictionum vrget, oppone quod est ad earum leuationem præfentiffimum. Nimirum cùm Dominus illis etiam adfuturum fe receperit,qui propter delicta sua pœnis addicti,ipsum interea inuocauerint, quantò minus tibi defuturam ipsius manum,cùm pro ipsius nomine labores? Appositû & illud erit, fi expendas, vbi ita duriter haberis ab hostibus veritatis, quàm nomen ipsum Domini & Christi Regnum nò vnius tantùm hominis vita,sed omnibus etiam creaturis est pretiosius. Accedit & illa singularis cõmendatio dignitatis verè incomparabilis,cùm Dominus indit nobis stigmata illa Filij fui dilecti,quæ vtcunq; coram mundo probrosa sint,coram Deo tamé & Angelis ipsius nullis non Regum diadematis ac purpuris antecellunt. Interea verò vt ad ista feriò meditanda te compares,non aliter de te iu dicamus,quàm vt cùm homo fis,humani àte alienum quicquà non fit. Fieri enim non posse,quin acerbissimas in carne punctiones sentias. Atqui cùm audimus simul quàm hactenus adfue rit tibi Dominus,quámque sua in te dona in dies adaugeat,non est quòd dubites,quin suum in te opus cumulatum præstet:ipsáque adeò virtus Spiritus quam hucvsque experrus es,eandem tibi constantiam spondet etiam in posterum & productio illa afflictionum,non dissimilem gratiæ Domini erga te profequutionem habitura est,vt in legitima constantia perseueres. Summa in eo posita est, vt te totum verbo Domini resignando, exitum ab ipso qualem ipsi visum erit, æquo & pacato animo expectes. Quemadmodum enim comparatos esse nos oportet,ad glorificandum morte nostra nomen ipsius,ita etiam nos illi viuere ac languere ad tempus non minus conuenit,vtillius nos esse in fo lidum reipfa constet. Hoc autem ideo tibi proponimus,quia te à longo tempore detineri audimus. De exitu nondum liquet. Hinc occasione arrepta caro illa fui semper similis te ad defectionem impelleret, nisi continuò summum illum Dominum opponeres,& veluti oculis tuis subiiceres, à cuius nutu pendent vniuersa,& in cuius manu sunt tempora & opportunitates:quíque omnia dispensat in commodum suorum, prout ipse nouit quid possimus. Interea verò singulare gaudium allaturum est toti Ecclesiæ hoc constantiæ tuæ testimonium : cùm nulla vbe- rior exultâdi materia piis offerri possit,quàm vbi intelligunt,ita magnificè prædicari nomen Domini, per inuictam Martyrum ipsius fortitudinem,vt quæ etiam aduersus omnes impiorum furores ad extremum vsque insultet.Sed neque insigne illud gaudij argumentum angustiis huius mundi spatiis continetur,cùm ad Angelos ipsos bona illius pars etiam redundet.Piis quidé hic inde fructus peculiaris constat,quòd eò confirmatiores reddun- tur, & felicibus illis exemplis non mediocriter accenduntur. Cùm ex opposito inconstantia & vecordia quam infœlices quidam & verè miseri,in veritatis notæ abnegatione produnt,mul torum qui adhuc infirmi sunt, fidem concutit atque subuertit. Quòd ad nos attinet, qui ista extra telorum iactum nunc quidem positi ad te scribimus,perinde nos animatos esse oportet atque si in procinctu staremus:neque enim longè à communi incendio absumus,neque scit nostrum quisquam,quatenus.Quare hoc vnum coniunctis animis cogitandum nobis est,vt oculis in cœlum erectis,atque illic continuò hærentibus ad metam properemus. Dominus tibi manum illam suam potentem porrigat magis ac magis,vt ad victoriam propositam per interiectu certamen contendas:te etiam dirigat suo Spiritu, complecatur præsidio,ac verè paternum & solicitum de te studium ita tibi praestet,vt ferio ac solide in ipso vno acquiescas.x 11.Decemb. M. D. LIIII.
units.tr: Epist.198, Ex Gall. First, then, we urge you to consider from how dreadful an abyss the Lord has drawn you, and with what honour he has favoured you, in designating you a witness of his Son, though you had so stubbornly resisted him during the time of your ignorance. Recall, therefore, the many benefits of the Lord towards you; and so that these chains which now bind you, and which may rightly be repaid as the price of your sins, may be transcribed into that name of the Testimony of Truth, so that from them the glory of Christ may shine forth and the efficacy of the gospel be spread abroad. If the weight of your present afflictions presses upon you, set against them that which is most effective in relieving them. Surely, since the Lord has promised to be present with those who, condemned to punishment for their sins, have meanwhile called upon him, how much less will his hand be lacking to you, who suffer for his name? This will also be fitting, if you consider, where you are so harshly held by the enemies of the truth, how much more precious the name of the Lord and the kingdom of Christ are than the life of one man alone, indeed than all creatures. There is added also that singular commendation of a dignity truly incomparable, since the Lord imprints upon us those marks of his beloved Son, which, however shameful they may be before the world, before God and his angels surpass all the diadems and purples of kings. Meanwhile, that you may prepare yourself to meditate on these things earnestly, we would not judge you otherwise than this: that since you are a man, nothing human is foreign to you. For it cannot be that you do not feel the most bitter stabs in the flesh. Yet when we hear at the same time how present the Lord has been with you until now, and how he daily increases his gifts in you, there is no reason for you to doubt that he will bring his work in you to completion; and that very power of the Spirit which you have experienced until now promises you the same constancy in future, and that prolonging of afflictions will bring a grace of the Lord towards you not unlike the former, so that you may persevere in lawful constancy. The sum of the matter lies in this: that, resigning yourself wholly to the word of the Lord, you await with an equal and calm mind the outcome, of whatever kind it shall seem good to him. For just as we ought to be prepared to glorify his name by our death, so it is no less fitting that we live and languish for a time for him, so that it may be firmly established in fact that we belong to him. We set this before you because we hear that you have been detained for a long time. The outcome is not yet clear. On this occasion that flesh, always like itself, would drive you to despair, unless you constantly set against it that supreme Lord, and held him before your eyes, at whose nod all things depend, and in whose hand are times and opportunities, and who arranges all things for the good of his own, as he knows what we can bear. Meanwhile, this testimony of your constancy will bring singular joy to the whole Church: since no richer matter for rejoicing can be offered to the pious than when they perceive that the name of the Lord is so magnificently proclaimed through the unconquered courage of his martyrs, who even against all the rage of the impious stand firm to the end. Yet this notable cause of joy is not confined within the narrow bounds of this world, since a good part of it overflows even to the angels themselves. For the pious there is indeed a peculiar fruit from this, that they are made the more steadfast by it and are not a little inflamed by such happy examples; whereas, on the contrary, the inconstancy and frenzy by which certain unhappy and truly wretched men betray themselves in the denial of the mark of the truth shakes and overthrows the faith of many who are still weak. As far as we are concerned, who write these things to you now, placed outside the range of missiles, we ought to be as spirited as if we were standing in battle line: for we are not far from the common conflagration, nor does any of us know how far it will reach. Therefore this one thing must be considered by us with united minds: that, with our eyes lifted to heaven and fixed there continually, we hasten towards the goal. May the Lord stretch out his mighty hand to you more and more, so that you may strive towards the victory set before you through the intervening contest; may he also direct you by his Spirit, embrace you with his protection, and show you such a truly fatherly and solicitous care that you may rest firmly and solidly in him alone. 11 December 1554.

units.la: BVLINGERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BULLINGER TO CALVIN, GREETINGS.

units.la: Literas tuas,honorande Domine& frater,ad me peculiariter scriptas,tum easquas communes esse voluisti vnà cum defensione tua accepi iam iam,ideóque nondum exhibui fratribus,cras exhibiturus. Nihil tamen dubito illos omnia libenter lecturos non sine gratulationes & gratiarum actione.Commodè verò literas & libellos aliis destinatos Ecclesiis coniunxisti. Nam illa ipsa hora qua reddüntur,commodè transmittere potui Curiam in Rhetiam,Sangallum & Schaffusium.Singulis meas adiunxi literas,quibus ipsis sanctum opus commendo. Spero illos breui tibi gratias acturos.Et quando eo ipso die tabellio Berna profecturus erat,huic quoq; meas tradidi, quibus D.Hallero exposui quid facto opus putem,maximè si biliosi contentionis finem dare velint.Nostrates cum Locarnensibus cocordes per omnia, legatos ad se missos vti prioribus tibi indicaram,ita dimiserunt, vt ne pilum quidem de sua cesserint sententia , copioséque illis exposuerint,cur nō possint per omnia cōsentire in sequestrium cum ipsis sententiam:præterea miserunt legatos in omnia oppida sua, in omnes Comitatus & Præfecturas, habitis quoque in urbe & agro maximis coetibus, exposuerunt omnibus quid actum sit in causa Locarnensi, cur consentire noluerint, quid periculi sit. Et quod mirum est concordes veluti ex uno ore omnes, magnis interim à se itineribus distates, ut nemo quisquam de syncro-ismo vel suspicari posset, responderunt: Placere sibi ex animo, quod stabiles in vera Religione permanent, neque socios religionis ad defectionem solicitari sustineant, orareque ut sic pergant: se enim & facultates, & sanguinem, & vitam spönte, & liberaliter depositurös, si quis vi velit ad impia & cum vera Religione pugnantia adigere. Interea adsunt duo legati à Locarnen. missi. Doctor quidam medicus, & nobilis quidam. Referùt in Senatu Cal. Ian. convocatos in coetum fideles, & his ex charta recitata esse sequestrium capita, additam amicam abhortationem à Locumtenente (nam præfectus noster iussus est se non immiscere huic negotio) & Scriba ut in viam redeant. Indicatum præterea legatos brevi venturos qui totum absoluant negotium. Ceterum patresfamiliās circiter 8o. destinasse solum vertere vnà cum suis familiis, nisi clementiora audierint à legatis venturis à 7. Rebuspu. vel vndecim, ideoque ipsos iam missos legatos parādis hospitiis. Quando vero commodissima foret migrantibus vallis Tellina Rhetis subiectà, orabant Amplissimum Senatum, literas ad Rhetos scriberet, quibus ipsis peteret hospitium. Senatus hac postulatione & expositione prorsus commotus, cōsolatus est legatos, aperuitque urbem & agrum suum. Quia vero illi se Rhetiam incolere malle significabant, & ideo literas ad Rhetos commendatitias postulabat, Senatus duos illis adiunxit ex Senatu viros auctoritate & senio reuerendos, & Rhetis acceptos. Hi vnà cum legatis Curiam profecti sunt, paraturi fidelibus hospitia. Dominus bene vertat. Ego toto hoc anno de omnibus quae facta sunt, fideles Locarnenses frequentibus literis diligenter admonui, & adhuc consolari non cessō. Dominus adsit illis & roboret Spiritu suo, eorumque miserea tur. Angliam recepisse Papam & Papatum non nescis. Vsus est diabolus in illa recuperanda duobus eximiis organis: in regno quidem Vintoniensi episcopo, extra regnum Reginaldo Polo Cardinali, qui iam & Primas Regni & Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis creatus est. Receptus est solenni pompa Londini ad S. Crucem in ædePaulinā. Proiecerunt se ad eius pedes Magnates, & absolutionem benedictionémque Apostolicam supplices postularunt à bestia confitentes se x v. annis à Catholica Romanāq; Ecclesia abscissos, per vepreta haereticorum aberrauisse. Oratione habuit in exco illo coetu Vintoniensis, qui & ipsam revocauit orationem, quam olim sub rege Henrico de obedientia edidit. Cardinalis cum veniisset ad Reginam Mariam, destitueretúrque salutandi formula tanta reparatibne digna,placuit vti verbis Angeli,Aue Maria gratia plena,Dominus tecum.O cæcas hominum mentes,ô pectora cæca.Veni,Veni D.Iesu,& vindica contumeliam tuam,& assere gloriâ tuam. Fratres nostri episcopi & Nobiles adhuc incarcerati tenétur,bre ui forte tradédi iudicio spirituali quod iam reparatur,mox brachio seculari.In vincula coniiciuntur quotidie innumeri.Inhibetur sub poena capitis,ne cui exuli feratur auxilium.Iaét it Vintonienfis effecturum se, vt exules omnibus eiecti locis, cogantur tandem fame perire, adeoque proprios vngues rodere. Qui apud nos versantur Angli, valde trishntur,sed consolamur ipsos.Orandus est sedulò Dominus,vt affl dæ suæ Ecclesiæ dexter & propitius adsit. Vale.Salutát te & tuos fymmyftas nostri fymmyftæ omnes.D.Iesus feruet te nobis diu incolumem. Iterum vale D. honorande & frater in Christo chiriffime. Tiguri, XVIII.Ianuarij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: I have just received your letter, honoured lord and brother, written to me personally, together with the one you wished to be shared in common, along with your defence. I have not yet shown them to the brethren, and will do so tomorrow. Nevertheless I do not doubt that they will read everything gladly, and not without congratulation and thanksgiving. You have conveniently enclosed letters and booklets intended for other churches. At the very hour they were handed to me, I was able to send them on to Chur in Rhaetia, St Gallen and Schaffhausen. I added my own letters to each, in which I commend this holy work to them, and I hope they will soon thank you. Since the courier was to set out for Berne on the same day, I gave him letters for them too, in which I explained to Haller what I think should be done, especially if they wish to put an end to this bitter quarrel. Our people of Zurich, in complete agreement with the men of Locarno in everything, have dismissed the envoys sent to them, as I earlier told you, and have not given up a jot of their opinion. They have set out fully to the envoys why they cannot agree in every respect with the sequestration plan. Moreover, they have sent envoys to all their towns, to all their districts and prefectures, and in the city and countryside they have held very large assemblies, explaining to everyone what has been done in the Locarno affair, why they were unwilling to consent, and what danger there is. And, strange as it is, all of them, as though from one mouth, although living at a great distance from one another, so that no one could suspect any collusion, have replied that it pleases them wholeheartedly that the men of Locarno remain steadfast in the true religion, and that they cannot bear to see their fellow believers tempted to defection. They pray that they continue thus: for they will freely and willingly lay down their property, their blood and their lives, if anyone should try by force to compel them to what is impious and contrary to the true religion. Meanwhile two envoys sent from Locarno have arrived, a certain doctor of medicine and a certain nobleman. They report that in the Senate on 1 January the faithful were called together into an assembly, that the points of the sequestration were read out from a paper, that a friendly exhortation was added by the lieutenant (for our prefect was ordered not to interfere in this business), and that the town clerk urged them to return to the right path. They also indicated that envoys would soon come to settle the whole affair. Furthermore, about eighty heads of families have resolved to leave their land together with their households, unless they hear more merciful terms from the envoys who are to come on 7 or 11 February; and so they have already prepared lodgings for the envoys who have been sent. As to when it would be most convenient for them to migrate, the Valtellina, which lies under Rhaetia, they begged the most honourable Senate to write to the Rhaetians, asking them to receive them. The Senate, deeply moved by this request and explanation, consoled the envoys and opened up its city and territory to them. But since they signified that they preferred to dwell in Rhaetia, and therefore asked for letters of recommendation to the Rhaetians, the Senate attached to them two men from the Senate, reverend for their authority and age and acceptable to the Rhaetians. These men have set out for Chur together with the envoys, to arrange lodgings for the faithful. The Lord grant it goes well. For my part, throughout this whole year I have diligently and frequently admonished the faithful Locarnese about all that has happened, and I do not cease to comfort them still. May the Lord be with them, strengthen them by his Spirit, and have mercy on them. You are not unaware that England has received the Pope and the Papacy again. The devil used two outstanding instruments in recovering it: in the kingdom, the bishop of Winchester; outside the kingdom, Cardinal Reginald Pole, who has now been made both Primate of the realm and Archbishop of Canterbury. He was received with solemn pomp in London at St Paul's Cross, at the cathedral of St Paul. The nobles threw themselves at his feet and humbly asked the beast for absolution and the apostolic blessing, confessing that for fifteen years they had been cut off from the Catholic and Roman Church and had wandered through the thickets of heretics. The bishop of Winchester gave an oration in that assembly, and he also revoked that very oration which he had once published under King Henry concerning obedience. When the cardinal came to Queen Mary, and the formula of greeting was found wanting, worthy of such a restoration, it was decided to use the words of the angel: "Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." O blind minds of men, O blinded hearts! Come, come, Lord Jesus, avenge your insult and assert your glory! Our brothers, the bishops and nobles, are still held in prison, and they will soon perhaps be handed over to the spiritual judgement that is now being restored, and soon afterwards to the secular arm. Countless people are thrown into chains every day. It is forbidden, on pain of death, to give any help to the exiles. The bishop of Winchester boasts that he will bring it about that the exiles, driven from every place, will at last be forced to die of hunger, and so to gnaw their own fingernails. The English who live among us are deeply saddened, but we comfort them. The Lord must be earnestly prayed to, that he may be present to his afflicted Church, gracious and favourable. Farewell. All your fellow-initiates and ours greet you, and Jesus Christ keep you safe among us for a long time. Farewell again, honoured lord and most dear brother in Christ. Zurich, 18 January 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS ANGLIS FRANCFORDIENS. S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to the English at Frankfurt. Greetings.

units.la: HOc vero me grauiter excruciat, & valde absurdum est, inter fratres ob eandem fidem à patria exules ac profugos dissidium oriri:& quidem hac de causa,quæ vel sola debuerat in hac vestra dispersione quasi factum vinculum, vcs simul deuinctos tenere. Quid enim vobis in hac tristi & miseraclade potius agendum erat, quàm vt à patriæ visceribus auulsi,Ecclesiam vobis adoptaretis, quæ animis & linguis coniunctos, materno gremio excipéret,ac foueret? Nunc vero de precandi forma, & ceremoniis quasi in otio & delitiis litem à quibusdam moueri,idque obstare,quominus in vnum Ecclesiæ corpus istic coalescatis,nimis meo iudicio,intempestiuum est.Neque tamen eorum constantiam reprehendo , qui vt pro iusta causa depugnent,inuiti in contentionem trahuntur:sed pertinaciam,quæ sanctum formandæ Ecclesiæ studium moratur, & impedit, merito damno. Equidem vt in rebus mediis, vt sint externi ritus, facilem me ac flexibilem præbeo:ita non semper vtile esse iudi co,stultæ eorum morositati qui nihil de consuetudine sua remittunt,obsequi.In Anglicana liturgia,qualem describitis,multas video fuisse tolerabiles ineptias.His duobus verbis exprimo, non fuisse eam puritatem, quæ optanda fuerat: quæ tamen primo statim die corrigi non poterant vitia,cùm nulla subesset mala nisesta impietas,ferenda ad tempus fuisse. Sic ergo à talibus rudimentis incipere licuit, vt doctos tamen probosque & graues Christi Ministros vltrà eniti, & aliquid limaitius ac purius quæ-rere, consentaneum foret. Si hactenus in Anglia viguisset syncera religio, aliquid in melius correctum, multáque detracta esse oportuit. Nunc cum cuerfis illis principiis, alibi instituenda vobis sit Ecclesia, & liberum sit, formam, quæ ad vsum & ædificationem Ecclesiæ maximè apta videbitur, de integro componere: quid sibi velint nescio, quos facis Papistic reliquiæ tantopere delectant. Amant ea quibus assueti sunt. Hoc primò & nugatorium, & puerile est: deinde multum interest hæc noua institutio à mutatione. Ego verò si quorundam infirmitas ad summum gradum non conscendat, vt vos vltra modum rigidos esse nolimus, rursus alios monitos esse cupio, ne sibi in sua inscitia nimis placeant: deinde ne sua peruicacia sancti ædificij cursum retardent. Tertiò, ne stulta eos æmulatio abripiat. Nam quæ illis rixandi causa, nisi quia pudet melioribus cedere? Sed ego frustra ad eos sermonem conuerto, qui forte non tantum mihi tribuunt, vt consilium à tali auctore profectum admittere dignentur. Si metuunt sinistrum in Anglia rumorem, quasi ab ea quæ illis exilij causa fuit, religione desciuerint, longè falluntur. Potius enim fideles, qui illic reliquiæ sunt, hæc magis ingenua syncera professio expendere coget, in quàm profundam abyssum ceciderint. Nam eos grauius suum præcipium vulnerabit, vbi vos vltra medium cursum, vnde retrahi sunt, progredi viderint. Valete integerrimi fratres, & fideles Christi serui. Dominus vos tueri ac regere pergat. Geneuæ, x v. Calendas Februarij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: This troubles me greatly, and it is very absurd that a quarrel should arise among brothers who are exiles and fugitives from their homeland for the same faith. It is all the more absurd because this very cause ought, in your dispersion, to have bound you together like a bond, holding you tightly joined. For what should you have done in this sad and wretched calamity, rather than, torn from the bosom of your fatherland, adopt a church for yourselves, one which, joined in minds and tongues, would receive you into its maternal bosom and cherish you? But now for some to raise a dispute about the form of prayer and the ceremonies, as if they had leisure and luxury to spare, and for this to hinder you from coalescing into one body of the Church there, seems to me, in my judgment, far too untimely. Yet I do not blame the steadfastness of those who, to defend a just cause, are dragged unwillingly into contention; but I rightly condemn the obstinacy that delays and hinders the holy zeal for forming the Church. Indeed, in matters indifferent, such as external rites, I show myself easy and flexible. So I do not think it is always useful to yield to the foolish stubbornness of those who give up nothing of their custom. In the English liturgy, as you describe it, I see many tolerable absurdities. By these few words I mean that it was not the purity that was to be wished for. Yet the faults could not be corrected on the very first day, since there was no underlying evil except open impiety, and they had to be tolerated for a time. So it was permissible to begin from such rudiments; yet it would have been fitting for learned, upright and grave ministers of Christ to strive further and seek something more polished and purer. If sincere religion had flourished in England until now, something should have been corrected for the better and much removed.
