Now, since those principles have been overturned and you must establish a church elsewhere, and it is free to compose afresh the form that seems most apt for the use and edification of the Church, I do not know what they want, those remnants of Papistry which so delight some. They love what they are accustomed to. This first point is both trifling and childish. Second, this new institution differs greatly from a mere change. For my part, if the weakness of some does not rise to the highest degree, I do not want you to be excessively rigid; yet I wish others to be warned not to please themselves too much in their ignorance, and then not to delay the course of the holy building by their obstinacy. Third, let not foolish emulation carry them away. For what is the cause of their quarrelling, unless it is shame at yielding to the better? But I turn my words in vain to those who perhaps do not credit me so much as to deign to admit advice from such an author. If they fear an unfavourable rumour in England, as if they had deserted the religion which was the cause of their exile, they are greatly mistaken. Rather, the faithful who remain there will be compelled to weigh this more ingenuous and sincere profession, lest they fall into a deep abyss. For it will wound their leader more grievously when they see you advancing beyond the middle course, from which they were drawn back. Farewell, most upright brothers and faithful servants of Christ. May the Lord continue to guard and rule you. Geneva, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BULLINGER, GREETINGS

units.la: Quia in hoc præclaro humanitatis officio, quod amplissimi Senatus vester profugis & miseris fratribus præstitit, relucet singulare pietatis specimen: quanuis praua mundi ingratitudine sepeliatur, nunquam tamen coram Deo excidet eius memoria. Mihi quidem dubium nō est, quiin rara quædam Dei benedictio ciuitatem vestram maneat. Quod etiam laborantibus & perplexis neque tuum consilium, neque assidua hortandi consolandíque sedulitas vnquam defuit, quia nostras omnium vices obiisti, ego pro mea parte, ingentes tibi ago gratias. Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi semper obseruande frater. Symmystis & familiæ tuæ plurimam salutem. Dominus vos omnes regere ac tueri pergat. Geneuæ, 1 1 1. Nonas Febr. M. D. L V.
units.tr: Since in this distinguished act of humanity, which your most distinguished Senate has shown to exiled and wretched brothers, there shines a singular example of piety: although it is buried by the perverse ingratitude of the world, its memory will never perish before God. I have no doubt that some rare blessing of God remains upon your city. And since neither your counsel nor your constant diligence in exhorting and consoling those in distress and perplexity has ever failed, having taken upon yourself the duties of us all, I for my part give you immense thanks. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother always to be honoured by me. Convey my most hearty greetings to the members of your Symmystae and to your household. May the Lord continue to keep and guide you all. Geneva, 3 days before the Nones of February, 1555.

units.la: y.j.
units.tr: y.j.

units.la: Illustrissimo Principi, D. Nicolao Radziwil Duci in Olika et Nießin, Palatino Vilnensi, Magni Ducatus Lithuaniae supremo Marscalco, et Archicancellario Domino apprime obseruando.
units.tr: To the most illustrious Prince, Lord Nicholas Radziwiłł, Duke of Olyka and Nieśwież, Palatine of Vilnius, Supreme Marshal of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and Lord Chancellor, to be especially honoured.

units.la: Quod te illustrissime Princeps, in hoc tam excelso honoris gradu positum homo ignobilis, & nullius fere in mundo pretij literis meis compello: quanuis audacter id à me fieri non ignorem: quod tamen mihi per te licere nō humanitate solùm tua, sed maximè pietate fretus confido, longo verborū circuitu non petam vt mihi concedas. Nam vt obscura sit mea conditio: quia tamen vnum me agnoscis ex Christi seruis, pro tua in Magistratum ipsum reuerentia patebit aliquis mihi, vt spero, ad tuam Amplitudinem accessus. Iam vero studium meum quod sanctis tuis votis consentit, sic probatum iri confido, vt sine alia commendatione, satis mihi apud te gratiae conciliet. Cùm vbique florere cupiam Regnum Christi: nunc tamen me Polonia merito quidam peculiari cura solicitat. Nam ex quo illic emergere coepit lux purioris doctrinae, laetum hoc initium cum spe melioris progressus desiderium simul accendit. Porrò si tantùm auctoritate polleres, vt facis, ad promouendum veræ pietatis statum: mihi iusta hortandi tui incitandíque ratio esset, ne tua officia Domino subducés, praeclarae eius vocationi deesses. Sed cùm probè iam ad tuendam pietatem animatus sis: imò heroica animi magnitudine ostendas quàm serio ac fideliter illius abste susceptum sit patrocinium: merito hæc tua virtus & ad gratias tibi agendas me animat, & materiam mihi suppeditat amplioris fiduciae. Quare non te simpliciter obtestor, vt similis tui esse pergas: sed etiam vt tecum certando, ad victoriam omnium præstantissimam contendas. Multis experimentis non dubito, te quotidie fieri certiorem, quàm non superuacua sit haec mea admonitio. Vides proculdubio, quàm immensae sit molis opus, coeleste Dei regnum in terra constituere. Vides rursum quàm multis obstaculis conetur Satan impedire ac morari, imò quàm multis subinde machinis vel clàm labefactare tentet, vel palàm euertere, quicquid in hoc sacro aedificio inchoatum fuerit. Vides denique quàm frigidè curetur ista causa, quæ non modò primatum in nostris curis tenere, sed omnes sensus occupare debuerat. Hoc postremum vitium inde nascitur, quòd omnes fere, dum gratuitam operam se Christo nauare putant, alió se magis conuertunt, vnde vel spes lucri vel laboris merces ac pretium ostendi-tur. tur. Tuæ vero prudentiæ est, illustrissime Princeps, primum cogitare, nihil te præstare Deo, quod non iure vt sibi debitum repossit: nec solum quia totus es in aere ipsius, sed quo eo te sibi magis deuinxit, quo in altiorem extulit dignitatis gradum: deinde præmium tibi ab eo non vulgare proponi cum dicit, qui mihi honorem detulerint, eos ego vicissim honore prosequar. Ergo vt incolumem & diuturnum domus tuæ statum coseruet, quoad poteris ad illustrandum eius regnum enitere. Quanquam autem Serenissimum Regem intelligo satis esse voluntarium: vt tamen vides in rebus perplexis non adeo præoperare: hoc tibi oneris diuinitus impositum esse memineris, vt non comes solum & adiutor sis eius Maiestati, sed etiam cunctantem stimules, atque etiam vbi ita flagitabit necessitas, præcurras. Neque enim iniquè feret, opinor, ad quam adspirat metam, aliorum feruore incitari. Vale illustrissime Princeps, mihíque vera obseruantia colende. Dominus te regat Spiritu suo, virtute sustineat, tuámque dignitatem diu seruet incolumem. Geneuæ, Idibus Februarij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince, I, a man of humble birth and of almost no worth in the world, am addressing you, who stand in so lofty a rank of honour, with this letter. I know how boldly I do this. Yet I trust that I am allowed to do so through you, relying not only on your courtesy but above all on your piety, and so I will not seek with a long roundabout of words that you grant me this. For though my own condition is obscure, since you acknowledge me as one of Christ's servants, out of your reverence for the magistracy itself some access to your Excellency will, I hope, be open to me. Indeed, my zeal, which agrees with your holy wishes, I am confident will be so well proved that, even without any other recommendation, it will win me favour enough with you. I desire that the kingdom of Christ flourish everywhere, but at present Poland deservedly draws my special concern. For since the light of purer doctrine has begun to rise there, that happy beginning, together with the hope of better progress, kindles my desire all the more. Moreover, if you had only the authority to advance the state of true piety, as you do, I would have a just reason to urge and spur you on, so that you would not withdraw your services from the Lord and fall short of his splendid calling. But since you are already sufficiently inspired to defend piety, and indeed by the heroic greatness of your spirit you show how earnestly and faithfully you have taken up the patronage of that cause, this virtue of yours rightly both moves me to give you thanks and supplies me with matter for greater confidence. Therefore I do not simply entreat you to go on being like yourself, but also to strive with yourself towards the most excellent of victories. I do not doubt, from many experiences, that you are informed every day how not superfluous this admonition of mine is. Doubtless you see how immense a task it is to establish the heavenly kingdom of God on earth. You see again how many obstacles Satan tries to hinder and delay, and how often, with various machines, he tries either to overthrow secretly or to subvert openly whatever has been begun in this sacred building. Finally, you see how coldly this cause is cared for, a cause which ought not only to hold the first place in our concerns but to occupy all our senses. This last fault arises from the fact that almost everyone, while they think they are doing a free service for Christ, turn themselves rather to other things, where either the hope of gain or the reward and price of labour is shown. But it is the mark of your prudence, most illustrious Prince, first to consider that you can offer God nothing which he could not rightly demand as his due, not only because you are wholly bound to him, but the more so because he has bound you more closely to himself by raising you to a higher rank of dignity. Then consider that he proposes to you no ordinary reward, when he says: "Those who honour me, I will in turn honour." Therefore, that he may preserve the safe and lasting state of your house, strive as far as you can to advance his kingdom. Although I understand that the most serene King is willing enough, yet, as you see, in perplexing matters one should not rush ahead too much; remember that this burden has been laid on you by God, so that you may be not only his companion and helper but also spur him on when he hesitates, and even run ahead of him when necessity demands it. For I suppose he will not take it amiss to be urged on by the zeal of others towards the goal to which he aspires. Farewell, most illustrious Prince, and to me one to be honoured with true reverence. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, sustain you by his power, and keep your dignity safe for a long time. Geneva, on the Ides of February, 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuæ Amplitudinis studiosissimus.
units.tr: John Calvin, most devoted to your Excellency.

units.la: CAL. MELANCHTHONI S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON, greetings.

units.la: Literæ tuæ, clarissime vir, non hoc solum nomine mihi gratæ fuerunt, quia mihi charum est, quicquid abs te proficiscitur: deinde quia ex illis intelligo, fixum adhuc in animo tuo manere amorem illum, quo me ab initio complexus es. Sed maximè, quòd illic luculento elogio meum in expugnanda Serueti impietate studium commendas: unde etiam coniicio, te simplici mearum admonitionum libertate nó fuisse offensum. Hoc defuit, quòd pleniores esse optassem. Neque tamen importunius vrgeo: sed quoad pace tua licet, etiam atque etiam te rogatum velim, vt tecum de quibus scripsi, tacitus saltem expendas. Sic enim te operam daturum confido, vt de gratuita piorum electione syncerior quàm antehac docendi forma inter nos mutuo conueniat. Περὶ τῆς ἀρτολάτρείας pridem interioranimi tui sensus mihi cognitus est, quem etiā nó difficultas in tuis literis. Sed mihi displicet tua ista nimia tarditas, quia non tantum foeutur, sed etiā in dies augetur eorum dementia, quos tam petulanter ruere vides in totius Ecclesiæ perniciem. Atque vt tibi non ita facile sit, tales bestias frænare: quod tamen vanum esse arbitror, si modò auderes: scis tamē à spe successus officia nostra minime pendere, quin præstare nos etiam in summa desperatione oporteat,quod Deus exigit. Nec vero illa mihi excusatio satisfa-cit, maleuolos qui te oppressum cupiunt,hinc captare plausibi-lem materiam. Quid enim facturi sunt serui Christi,nisi spreta inuidia,contemptis sinistris rumoribus,posthabito etiam discri-minum metu, quæcunque obstacula ingerit Satan, victrice con-stantia superent?Certe quantumuis in te insaniant,nihil tibi du-rius ab illis impendet,quàm vt migrare istinc cogaris.Quod ti-bi meo iudicio complures ob causas spōte optandum foret. Ve-rum vt timenda sint extrema quæque,tibi semel statuere necef-se est, quid Christo debeas, ne ingenuam veritatis professionem supprimens,ad eam opprimendam quasi tacitum patrocinium improbis hominibus accommodes. Ego vt eorum tumultus co-pescerem ,summam doctrinæ nostræ rursus breui compendio complexus sum.Subscripserunt omnes Helueticæ Ecclesiæ. Ti-gurini etiam mirificè probarunt. Nðhc iudicium tuum auidis-simè expecto : quid etiam reliqui vestrates vel sentiant, vel lo-quantur,scire vehementer expeto.Quod si tumultuari non desi-nant,qui tam hostiliter nos trahucunt,nos operam dabimus,vt nostros clamores totus mundus exaudiat. Vale clarissime vir,& mihi semper imprimis obseruande.Dominus te Spiritu suo gu-bernet,præsidio tueatur,ac virtute sustineat, nósque simul con-tineat in sancto consensu,donec in cœlestc suum Regnum col-ligat.1 i 1.Nonas Martij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Your letter, most distinguished man, was welcome to me not only for this reason, that whatever comes from you is dear to me, but also because from it I understand that that love with which you embraced me from the beginning remains fixed in your mind. But chiefly because there you commend with a splendid eulogy my zeal in fighting the impiety of Servetus; from which I also gather that you were not offended by the plain freedom of my admonitions. One thing was lacking: I would have wished your letter to be fuller. Yet I do not press you too importunately, but, so far as your leave allows, I would again and again ask you at least to weigh silently in your own mind the things about which I have written. For I trust you will work so that a more sincere form of teaching on the free election of the godly is agreed upon between us than before. Your inner feeling about [Περὶ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας] has long been known to me, nor did your letter make it any less clear. But I am displeased by that excessive slowness of yours, because the madness of those men, whom you see rushing so wantonly to the ruin of the whole Church, not only persists but increases every day. And although it may not be easy for you to restrain such beasts (which I nevertheless think would be vain, if only you would dare), you know that our efforts do not depend at all on the hope of success, so that we ought to perform, even in utter despair, what God requires. Nor does that excuse satisfy me, that the ill-wishers who want you crushed are catching at a plausible material here. For what will the servants of Christ do, unless, despising envy, disregarding sinister rumours, and setting aside even the fear of dangers, they overcome by victorious constancy whatever obstacles Satan throws in their way? Certainly, however much they rage against you, nothing harsher can be threatened by them than that you be forced to leave there, which in my judgment would for many reasons be desirable in itself. But although all extreme things are to be feared, you must once for all decide what you owe to Christ, so that you do not, by suppressing a frank profession of the truth, lend to wicked men a kind of silent patronage for crushing it. As for me, to check their uproar I have again summed up the substance of our doctrine in a short compendium. All the churches of Helvetia have subscribed to it, and the Zurich churches have even approved it marvellously. I most eagerly await your judgment on this; I also very much want to know what the rest of your fellow countrymen either think or say. And if those who drag us so hostilely do not cease their tumult, we will take care that the whole world hears our cries. Farewell, most distinguished man, and always to be honoured by me above all. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, protect you with his help, sustain you with his power, and keep us together in holy agreement until he gathers us into his heavenly kingdom. Nones of March, 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS GADIO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO GADIUS.

units.la: Literas tuas, optime frater, tertio demum mense, postquam datæ fuerant, accepi: ne mireris serius respònsum à me ve-nire,quam optabas. Breuius autem vt in festinatione tibi rescribo:quia Bernam proficiscens iam ad iter accingor.In dan-do quod petis consilio nonnihil sum perplexus.Cuperem opti-mo viro, qui se expedire cupit à tyrannide Antichristi, manum porrigere. Et certè pium eius studium ab omnibus Christi seruis iuuari par est. Sed videndum , quid Dominus nobis permittat: quia nostrum non est,quicquam ex eius placitis laxare. Porrò, in quæstione,quam mihi proponis, duo scrupuli occurrunt : li-ceátne Christiano homini reiciffionem testamenti à Papa pete-re:deinde,an sub hic lege petere liceat, vt bonus vir sponte do-narij loco annuum prouentum alicui Ecclesiæ assignet? Atque in hoc secundo magis laboro.Etsi enim tantum auctoritatis Papæ deferre absurdum est, vt sua indulgentia nos ab aliquo vin-culo soluat,deteriustamen videtur,idolis offerre partem aliquâ reditus,vt maior pars salua maneat. Itaque non video,quomo-do pio homini fas esse possit,Papam hac in re implorare,& qui-dem dem sub illa forma. Alia ratio magis esset tolerabilis, si cum Collegio, cui bonorum successio legata est, tran-figeret. Quod nō pu-to fore difficile, si modo tertiae partis iactura non refugiat. Nam Canonici, vel quicunque sint, nō aegre cedent dubio iure, praesenti lucro adducti. Si viro bono graue est, tertiam reditus sui partem quasi abiicere, cogitet satius esse perdere totum prouentum, etiā si centuplo maior esset, quàm aliquid illicitū tentare. Etsi autem prouentū illum Canonici in sacrilegia conuertent, quia tamen respectu boni viri nō est superstitiosa oblatio, sed pretium, quo se ab astrictione redimet, hoc pactionis genus offensa carere existimo. Non enim dicet in cultus peruersos se dicare prouentum illum, vt conscientiam liberet: sed haec erit transfigendi ratio, cum trecentos aureos Canonicis obligatos nunc possideat, centum illis concedar, vt ducenti liberi maneant. Si verò necessaria erit Papae auctoritas, vt rapus sit contractus, eam petere Canonici suo nomine poterunt. Hac autem confirmatione in suum commodum vtetur pius vir: quia non de spirituali iure hic agetur, sed tantùm de tranquilla fundi possessione. Quòd si commoda non erit haec ratio, vendat ipse Canonicis totum fundum, vel ex eorum consensu cuilibet obuio, ita vt illis tertia pars in prædam cedat. Mallem aliter, hoc est, minore eius damno. Sed dabit veniam, si non audeo vltrà progredi. Praestat enim quouis modo cum Canonicis pacisci, modò id fiat pollicitè ad soluendū astrictionis vinculum, quàm religionis praetextu, assem vnum offerre. Quòd si placidè se pius vir bonorum parte exuet, vberior ei fluet Dei benedictio, quàm vt molestum illi esse debeat, minus latum fundū quàm antehac tenere. Tu verò mi frater, cum probè sis ad obeundum munus tuum animatus, nullis stimulis indiges. Antequam operam tuam addiceretis Ecclesiae, non ignorae tibi erat difficultates, & molestiae, quibuscum nunc tibi luctandū est. Nunc tantùm rogādus est Deus, vt infracta constantiam, nouāsq; subinde vires suppeditet, vt per omne genus obstacula in stadio tuo pergas vsque ad metam. Valde optime frater, & mihi charissime. Dominus tibi semper adsit, sanctis laboribus det prosperum successum, téque Spiritu suo regat. Saluta meo nomine pios fratres, qui istic sunt. III. Nonas Martij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Your letter, best of brothers, reached me only in the third month after it was dated; please do not wonder that my reply comes later than you wished. I am writing more briefly, since I am hurrying to reply: I am about to set out for Bern and am already getting ready for the journey. In giving the advice you ask for, I am somewhat perplexed. I would gladly extend a hand to this excellent man, who wishes to free himself from the tyranny of Antichrist, and it is surely right that all the servants of Christ should support his pious zeal. But we must consider what the Lord permits us, for it is not ours to relax anything of his decrees. Moreover, in the question you put to me, two doubts arise: first, whether it is lawful for a Christian man to seek from the Pope the revocation of a testament; and second, whether it is lawful to seek it under this condition, that the good man, as a kind of gift, assigns an annual income to some church. On this second point I am more troubled. For although it is absurd to grant the Pope so much authority that by his indulgence he could release us from any bond, it seems worse to offer part of one's income to idols so that the greater part may remain safe. So I do not see how it can be permitted to a pious man to implore the Pope in this matter, and in that particular form. Another plan would be more tolerable, if he came to terms with the college to which the succession of the goods has been bequeathed. I do not think this would be difficult, provided he does not shrink from losing a third part. For the canons, or whoever they may be, will not be slow to give up a doubtful right when drawn by present gain. If it is hard for a good man to cast away, as it were, a third part of his income, let him consider that it is better to lose the whole yield, even if it were a hundredfold greater, than to attempt something unlawful. Yet although the canons would turn that income to sacrilegious uses, this kind of agreement, I think, is free from offence, since, with regard to the good man, the payment is not a superstitious offering but a price by which he redeems himself from the obligation. He will not say that he dedicates that income to corrupt worship in order to free his conscience; rather, the manner of the transaction will be this: since he now holds three hundred gold pieces bound to the canons, he will concede one hundred to them, so that two hundred remain free. If, however, the authority of the Pope is necessary to make the arrangement valid, the canons may seek it in their own name. The pious man will benefit from this confirmation, because no spiritual right is at issue here, but only the peaceful possession of the estate. But if this plan is not advantageous, let him sell the whole estate to the canons himself, or, with their consent, to whoever offers, so that a third part goes to them as spoil. I would prefer another way, that is, one with less loss to him; but he will forgive me if I do not dare to go further. For it is better to come to terms with the canons in any way whatever, provided it is done honestly to loosen the bond of obligation, than to offer a single penny under the pretext of religion. But if the pious man willingly strips himself of part of his goods, God's blessing will flow to him more abundantly, so that it ought not to trouble him to hold a smaller estate than before. As for you, my brother, since you are sufficiently inspired to discharge your office, you need no spurs. Before you devoted your labour to the Church, you were not unaware of the difficulties and troubles with which you must now struggle. Now we need only pray to God that he may keep your constancy unbroken, and supply you with fresh strength from time to time, so that you may press on through every kind of obstacle in your race to the goal. Most excellent brother, and dearest to me: may the Lord always be with you, give prosperous success to your holy labours, and govern you by his Spirit. Greet on my behalf the pious brothers who are there. Given on the third of the Nones of March, 1555.

units.la: REVERENDO VIRO ERUDITIONE ET VIRTUTE Praestanti D. Iohanni Cailuino fratri suo charissimo. S. D.
units.tr: TO THE REVEREND MAN, DISTINGUISHED FOR LEARNING AND VIRTUE, MY DEAREST BROTHER, MR JOHN CALVIN. GREETINGS.

units.la: Reuerende vir, & charissime frater. Sicio te pro tua excellenti prudentia ex scriptis aduersariorum tuorum iudicare, quales sint eorum naturae, & quod initueantur theatrum. Ideq y.iij. nihil de eis scribam. Tantum oro Filium Dei, ut ipse suæ laceræ Ecclesiæ medeatur, velut Samaritanus ille saucio viatori. Audio nunc τὸν ὑπερφάλον καὶ τὸν ἀλεκτρυὼνα ἐν σχῆμα ἱστρου ἀπο-ταμόν, magnum volumen στηλιτευτικὸν contra me cudere: quod sic fiedetur, decreui respondere simpliciter & sine ambiguitate. Eúmque laborem debere me Deo & Ecclesiæ iudico. Nec in hac senecta pertimesco exilia & alia pericula. Bene & feliciter vale. Die x 11. Maij.
units.tr: Reverend sir and dearest brother, I know that from the writings of your opponents you can judge, with your excellent good sense, what their natures are and what kind of stage they are setting up (y.iij.). So I will write nothing about them. I pray only that the Son of God will himself heal his torn Church, as the Samaritan healed the wounded traveller. I hear that they are now forging a large defamatory volume against me [τὸν ὑπερφάλον καὶ τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα ἐν σχήματι ἰστροῦ ἀποταμόν]. Since it will be published in this way, I have decided to answer it plainly and without ambiguity. I judge that this labour is owed by me to God and to the Church. Even in this old age I do not dread exile or other dangers. Farewell, and may all go well. Given 11 May.

units.la: Philippus.
units.tr: Philippus.

units.la: CALVINVS CNOXO ET GRECA-LIBVS S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO CNOXO AND GREGALIBUS, GREETINGS.

units.la: LItteris vestris, eximij viri, & mihi verè colendi fratres, feriu̇ forte quàm spes & opinio vestra ferebat, respondeo. Sed quum sciatis vias à latrunculis aliquàdiu fuisse obsessas, ut nulli fere nuntij hinc ad vos cõmearent: facilis erit apud vos hu ius morae excusatio. De contentione illa, quæ inter vos parū feliciter mota fuerat, liberè optimo fratri nostro Thomæ Sapsoni exposui, quod ex quorundam literis didiceram. Conquesti enim apud me amici quidam fuerunt, vos ita præcisè ceremonias Anglicas vrgere, ut satis cōstaret, vos plus æquo esse patriæ addictos. Rationes quidem fateor audiebam in medium à vobis proferri, quæ à recepta forma discedere non sinerent, sed earum facilis erat promptáque refutatio. Sicuti autem eos qui à vobis dissentiebant, hortatus sum, ut se qua possent moderatione inflecterent, ita mihi displicuit, nihil vicifim à parte vestra concedi vel remitti. Quia vero nullius mihi nomen per scriptum fuerat, me interponere ausus non sum, ne in temeritatis notam incurreret mea fiducia. Nunc vos in ipsa disceptatione fuisse magis humanos ac tractabiles, & totum negotium placidè fuisse compositum, gaudeo. Certè luminaria, cruces, & eius farinæ nugas ex su perstitione manasse, nemo, ut arbitror, sano iudicio præditus negabit. Vnde constituo, qui eas in libera optione retinent, nimis cupidè ex sece haurire. Nec video, quorsum attineat Ecclesiam friuolis & inutilibus ceremoniis, n- proprio nomine noxias appellem, onerari, vbi puri & simplicis ordinis libertas nobis permittitur. Sed me cohibeo, ne de re, ut ex vobis audio, bene transacta nouum certamen mouere videar. Hoc quidem non dissimulo, nec pie, nec fraterne, meo iudicio, actum fuisse cum N. si clandestino quorundam instinctu in crimen vocatus est. Præstabat enim manere in patria, quàm iniustæ sævitiæ facem in longinquas regiones afferre, quæ nolentes quoque inflammet. Cæterum quoniam delicta, quorum memoriam perpetua obli-ione uione sepultam cupio, vel leuiter attingere piget, tantum vos hortabor, venerandi fratres, vt si quorundam animos sentitis iam re exulceratos esse, eorum offensioni placandae operam detis. Cum audirem partem aliquam velle istinc migrare, admonui diligenter, vt par erat, si non omnibus commodum esset eodem habitare in loco, ne locorum distantia, fraternum consensum dissiparet. Verebar enim, ne qua ex priori contentione occulta maneret simultas. Ac mihi nihil erit gratius, quàm hoc metu liberari. Nam si qui forte ad nos concederent, mihi tristis esset vel sola occulti inter vos dissidij suspicio. Ergo quod de reconciliata gratia scribitis, firmum stabileque esse magnopere cupio: vt si contigerit partem alio migrare, locis tamen distinctis sanctam amicitiam colatis. Nam vt non longius serpat discordia, iam plus satis peccatum fuit. Vestrae tamen prudentiae & aequitatis erit, vt benevolentia retineantur, quicquid alienationis erit residuum, sedulò purgare. Valete fratres obseruandi. Dominus vos praesidio suo tueatur, Spiritu suo regat, benedictione prosequatur, & exilij tristitiam mitiget. Collegae mei vos amanter salutant. Geneuae, ptidie Idus Iunij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: I reply to your letter, distinguished men and brothers whom I truly honour, later than your hope and expectation had allowed. But since you know the roads were for some time beset by brigands, so that hardly any messengers passed between here and you, the excuse for this delay will be easy for you to accept. About that dispute, which had unhappily been stirred up among you, I frankly set out to our excellent brother Thomas Sampson what I had learned from some letters. Certain friends complained to me that you press the English ceremonies so rigidly that it was clear enough you were more devoted to your country than was right. I admit I heard reasons put forward by you which would not allow departure from the received form, but their refutation was easy and ready. Just as I urged those who differed from you to bend as far as they could with moderation, so I was displeased that nothing was conceded or relaxed on your side in return. But since no one's name had been given to me in writing, I did not dare to interpose myself, lest my confidence incur the mark of rashness. Now I rejoice that you were more humane and tractable in the very debate, and that the whole business was calmly settled. Certainly, I think, no one endowed with sound judgment will deny that lights, crosses and trifles of that sort flowed from superstition. Hence I conclude that those who keep them as a matter of free choice draw them too eagerly from that source. Nor do I see why the Church should be burdened with frivolous and useless ceremonies, which I would call harmful by their very name, when the freedom of a pure and simple order is permitted to us. But I restrain myself, lest I seem to stir up a new quarrel over a matter which, as I hear from you, has been well concluded. This much I do not conceal: in my judgment it was neither pious nor brotherly to deal as they did with N., if he was called to account at the secret instigation of certain people. For it was better to remain in the homeland than to bring the torch of unjust cruelty into distant regions, where it would inflame even those who are unwilling. Moreover, since I am grieved even to touch lightly on offences whose memory I wish buried in perpetual oblivion, I will only exhort you, venerable brothers, that if you perceive the minds of some are already sore, you should take pains to appease their offence. When I heard that some part wished to migrate from there, I advised carefully, as was fitting, that if it were not convenient for all to live in the same place, the distance between places should not scatter fraternal agreement. For I feared some hidden rivalry might remain from the earlier contention. Nothing will be more welcome to me than to be freed from this fear, for if some should happen to come over to us, the mere suspicion of a hidden disagreement among you would grieve me. Therefore, as to what you write about reconciled good will, I earnestly desire it to be firm and stable, so that if part of you should move elsewhere, you still cultivate holy friendship in separate places. For, so that discord does not creep further, enough sin has already been committed. It will, however, be the task of your prudence and fairness to carefully wipe away whatever residue of estrangement remains, so that kindness is retained. Farewell, brothers worthy of respect. May the Lord keep you under his protection, rule you by his Spirit, bless you, and soften the sadness of your exile. My colleagues greet you warmly. Geneva, the day before the Ides of June, 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Bullinger, greetings.

units.la: Quod tuis literis rogasti, vt proximii tumultus historiam apertius tibi & plenius exponerem, eò libentius facio, quòd nostra valde interest, rem istic & apud vicinos probe cognosci. Sinistros enim rumores de nobis spargi plus satis notum est idque eorum artificio, qui suo commodo nos passim exosos reddere cupiunt. Itaque gratum nostris officium praestabis si summam eorum quae scripturus sum, curaueris apud Clarissimum Senatum vestrum recitandam. Quinetiam, si tibi graue non erit, hanc epistolae meae partem fratribus nostris Schaffusianae Ecclesiae Ministris descriptam mitti cupio, vt ipsi quoque apud suos vt bem hanc falsa infamia liberent. Res omnino sic habet. Duo fuerunt in Senatu improbi homines, atque audaces vsq; ad summam impudentiam. Ambo etiam inopes, & famelici. Alter Perrinus vocatus, alter Vandelius. Prior, quum Capitaneus esset vrbis, colluuiem improborum, propositi scelerum impunitate, sibi conciliauerat. Nam si quid nequiter, proterue, dissolute gestum fuerat, ne vigerent legum poenae, patrocinium suscipere mox paratus erat. Alter vero fidus erat in his omnibus adiutor. Partem Senatus blanditiis illectam tenebant. Quosdam sordidos, & qui gradu suum nisi eorum fauore retinere non poterant, timore percutiebat cogebat in suum obsequium. Cognati, propinquitatis gratia y.iiij.
units.tr: As you asked in your letter, that I set out the recent disturbance more clearly and fully for you, I do so all the more willingly, because it matters greatly to us that the matter be properly understood there and among our neighbours. It is well known that sinister rumours about us are being spread, by the contrivance of those who wish to make us hated everywhere for their own advantage. So you will do us a kindness if you see to it that a summary of what I am about to write is read out before your Most Illustrious Senate. Moreover, if it would not trouble you, I wish a copy of this part of my letter to be sent to our brothers, the ministers of the Church of Schaffhausen, so that they too may free us among their people from this false infamy. The matter stands entirely thus. There were two wicked men in the Senate, bold to the point of utter shamelessness. Both were also penniless and hungry: one called Perrin, the other Vandelius. The former, while he was captain of the city, had won over a rabble of wicked men by promising them impunity for their crimes. For if anything had been done wickedly, insolently or dissolutely, he was at once ready to take up their protection, so that the penalties of the laws would not take effect. The other was a faithful helper in all these things. They held part of the Senate enticed by flattery. Some base men, who could not keep their rank except by their favour, they terrified and forced into obedience. Relatives, bound by the ties of kinship, went along with them. Epist.207.

units.la: Epist.207. deuincti, assentiebantur. Itaque in minore Senatu eoúsque inualuerat eorum potentia, vt libidini resistere vix quisquam auderet. Certe iudicia pluribus annis fuerunt in eorum arbitrio: & nundinatio minimè obscura erat. Hoc non modò Ciuitas videbat, sed apud vicinos, & exteros, eorum culpa, pessimè audiebamus. Neque tacebant permulti: quia sæpe atrocibus probris vexati, & lacerati fuerunt. Si quis contemptior, eorum flagitia detexerat, illis in promptu erat vltio. Quicquid ab æqualibus dictum erat, facile vorabant. Interim tamen multi iam contraxerant callum seruitutis. Omnia edicta in chartis mortua iacebat. Nullus denique legum metus, vel pudor, si modo illi fauerent. Nam & iudices cum Vrbis Præfecto non nisi eorum voto quotannis creabantur: eoque tandem progressa est petulantia, vt populus ipse, postquàm suffragiis suis quisquilias nescio quas, imo turpissimas sordes elegerat, suum decus horreret. Hoc quidem proximo anno fatebantur omnes, si hostibus vrbis permissa fuisset electio, non potuisse maiore cum ludibrio nihili homines ad honorem vocare. Iam quum antea si quid peccaret minor Senatus, vitiis & corruptelis medicinâ afferre solerent Ducenti, multos illuc coniecerant ex fæce, partim clamosos iuuenes, & turbulentos, partim turpis & dissolutæ vitæ. Et ne copia eos deficeret, posthabita numeri ratione, in turbam intruserant, quoscunque sibi putabant fore appositos. Denique tam confusi fuit licentia, vt in Curiam irrumperent quidam, ne ab ipsis quidem lecti. Illa fuit factio, quæ vnum Ecclesiæ iudicium sibi obstare videns, quò minus effrænis impunitas vitiis omnibus expósita esset, ne quid disciplinæ reliduum maneret, de Excommunicatione nobis certamen mouit: nec destitit sursum ac deorsum omnia versare, do nec magna contentione obtinuimus, vt cõsilium saltem ab Ecclesiis Helueticis peterent. Quia autem respondum vestrum improbos spe, & voto deiecit, paulò quietior deinde status fuit: sic tamen vt intenti subinde ad nouos occasiones, excussō pudore, vincula omnia abrumpere tentarent. Caeterum, quum nobis molestum esset, assiduè fluctuari, tandem ausi sumus eos lacessere, vt certi aliquid decernerent. Quain re mirabiliter eos frustratus est Dominus. Nam in illa promiscua colluuie, suffragiis fuimus superiores. Sequuta sunt paulò post creandis Syndicis comitia, vbi inopinata conuersio apparuit. Hic verò improbi palàm furere: quia se videbant in ordinem coactos. Itaque petulanter coeperunt multa tentare ad labefactandum præsentem statum. Nostris fem per fatis fuit, compescere sine tumultu eorum conatus, vel salte frangere. Sed quia minimè obscurum erat, illos sine modo inhiare nouandis rebus, Senatus optimum remedium eorum libidini opponere statuit. Ex hospitibus Gallis, qui hic diu habitauerant, rant, & quorum nota erat probitas, quossdam adoptauit in ciuium ordinem, forte ad quinquaginta vsque. Séserunt improbi, quátò munitior hoc præsidio futura esset bonorum manus. Itaque omnem lapidem sibi mouendum duxerunt, vt consiliũ hoc eυerterent. Resinter eos per compita passim & in cauponis, & clàm in priuatis ædibus agitata fuit. Quum traxissent quosdam in suam sententiam, non modo fremitu, sed apertis minis insurgere cœperunt. Subornatus fuit Vrbis Præfectus, qui cum magna, sed turpi & pudenda caterua in Curiam ascendens, denuntiauit Senatui periculum, si pergeret. Magna pars ex nautis, piscatoribus, cupediariis, & cocis, similíque nobilitate cóflata erat. Multi Inquilini permixti. Quasi non nisi his vindicibus ius suũ Ciuitas tueri posset. Senatus grauiter respondit se nihil noui aggressum: sed quod antiquissimo vsu sempeꝛ in vrbe receptũ fuisset. Indignum vero esse, nunc & vetustum vrbis morem conuelli, & arceri à ciuium ordine, qui honestè longum tempus in vrbe transegerant: & sibi denique eripi poste statè ab vltima memoria per manus traditam. Quia autem nihil violento imperio Senatus agendum censebat, apertæ conspirationi veniam in præsentia dedit. Tantum obiurgatus fuit Præfectus, quòd proterηuis hominibus operam in causa tam iniusta locasset. Simul tamen factum fuit decretum de vocandis Ducetis: ad quos vbi vtn tum est, sancita fuit Senatus minoris auctoritas: & permissum, vt posthac suo arbitrio ex Gallis hospitibus ciues deligerent. Sed antequam hoc postremum statuerent Duccenti, repente longius erupit eorum furor, qui ad extrema quæque, vt in rebus desperatis, se proiicere in animum induxerant. Nam tumultu noctur no prope ad summam cladem addusta fuit Ciuitas. Pridie quàm id accideret, multis nebulonibus datum sfuerat gratuitum prandium. Duces alibi epulabantur: ex quibus alter, quem nominauì, Vandellius sumptum prandij sustinuit. Perrinus verò, cœnæ. Volitabant interea nuntij: multæ sinistræ notæ obseruabantur: vt non frustra boni sibi metuerent. Moriis autem est, postquam dispositæ sunt in portis excubiæ, Præfectum vigilum circumire, & dispicere stationes. Hoc munus singuli Senatores vicibus obeunt. Quum media in vrbe starent vigiles noctis eius, clamore non procul audiunt. Nam è regione post tabernas mercatorias quidam lapide percussus clamabat se occisum. Accurrunt igitur pro officio. Contrà insurgunt duo fratres germani, ex sodalibus Perrini & Vandellij, homines quidem infimæ sortis, cupediarij scilicet: sed qui in eadem mensa gratis cœnauerant. Rem ex co-pòsito agi deinde patuit, quòd duo soli pluresarmatos aggredi ausi fuerant. Atque hoc ambo confessi suint & iudicibus, & plu-ribus aliis, & mihi priuatim. Tametsi autem cùm ad supplicium traherentur, negarunt signo dato se tumultum mouisse, sic tamen multis indiciis conuicti erant, ut sua impudentia nihil profecerint. Hoc quidem minime negarunt, se eodem die inter prandium & coenam Perrino animi gratia in propinquam villam egressō fuisse comites: inter eundum de quingentis hominibus armatis ad urbis custodiam aliunde vocandis habitum fuisse sermonem. Cum in merenda renouaretur eius rei mentio, Perrinum opificum aduentu repressum, Germanice, Schvvig, Schvvig, silentium indixisse. Quia autem villa illa extra fines Geneuensis ditionis sita est, dixisse paratum illic fore Asylum & hospitium, si quis in urbe capitale facinus patrasset. Crescente tumultu unus ex Syndicis, qui non procul aberat, cum suo Scipione, quod est insigne Magistratus, & luminibus accensis, prodiit. Tanta autem semper in hoc populo fuit sacri illius baculi reuerentia, ut eius conspectu non modo sedatae fuerint maximae turbae, sed cum ad caedes ventum foret, vis cohibita fuerit.
units.tr: Epist.207. Thus in the Lesser Council their power had grown so strong that hardly anyone dared resist their lust. Certainly for many years the courts were at their disposal, and the selling of offices was not at all hidden. The city not only saw this, but among our neighbours and foreigners we were, through their fault, very badly spoken of. Nor were many silent, since they were often assailed and torn apart by savage abuse. If anyone of higher standing exposed their disgraceful conduct, revenge was ready at hand for them. Whatever was said by their equals, they readily swallowed up. Meanwhile many had by now grown calloused to slavery. All edicts lay dead on paper. In short there was no fear of the laws, nor any shame, provided those men favoured them. For the judges, together with the City Prefect, were chosen each year only by their vote; and at last their wantonness advanced so far that the people themselves, after they had chosen with their votes I know not what trifles, or rather the most disgraceful dregs, shuddered at their own dignity. Indeed, in the previous year everyone admitted that if the choice had been left to the enemies of the city, they could not have summoned men of no account to honour with greater mockery. Now, whereas formerly, if the Lesser Council did wrong, the Two Hundred used to bring a remedy to its vices and corruptions, they had brought in many from the dregs, some noisy and turbulent young men, some of disgraceful and dissolute life. And lest they lack numbers, disregarding any consideration of fitness, they had pushed into the crowd whomever they thought would be suited to them. In the end such confusion of licence arose that some men forced their way into the Council who had not even been chosen by them. That was the faction which, seeing that the one judgment of the Church stood in its way, so that its unbridled impunity could not be exposed to all vices, and that nothing of discipline might remain, began a contest with us over Excommunication. Nor did they desist from turning everything upside down, until with great effort we obtained that they at least seek counsel from the Swiss Churches. But since your reply cast down the wicked from their hope and wish, the state was somewhat quieter afterwards; yet they remained intent on new opportunities and, having cast off shame, tried to break every bond. However, since it was troublesome to us to be constantly tossed about, at last we dared to provoke them, so that they would decide something certain. In this matter the Lord frustrated them wonderfully. For in that mixed rabble we were the stronger in the votes. Shortly afterwards the elections for appointing the Syndics followed, where an unexpected change appeared. Here the wicked openly raged, because they saw themselves forced into order. Accordingly they began to attempt many things insolently, to shake the present state. It was enough for us to restrain their efforts without disturbance, or at least to break them. But since it was not at all hidden that they were immoderately eager for revolution, the Senate decided to oppose the best remedy to their lust. From the French guests who had lived here for a long time, and whose uprightness was well known, it adopted some, perhaps about fifty, into the order of citizens. The wicked took fright, lest the band of good men be made stronger by this guard. So they thought every stone must be moved to overturn this plan. Meanwhile it was discussed everywhere among them, at street corners, in the taverns, and secretly in private houses. When they had drawn some to their opinion, they began to rise up not only with murmuring but with open threats. The City Prefect was suborned, who, ascending to the Council with a great but base and shameful rabble, threatened the Senate with danger if it persisted. A large part of the mob was made up of sailors, fishermen, pastry-cooks and cooks, and people of like nobility. Many resident aliens were mixed in. As if the city could defend its right only with the help of these avengers! The Senate answered gravely that it had undertaken nothing new, but only what had always been received in the city by the most ancient custom. It was unworthy, it said, that now the old custom of the city should be overthrown, and that men who had honourably spent a long time in the city should be shut out from the order of citizens; and that finally what had been handed down from the earliest memory should be snatched from them. But since the Senate thought nothing should be done by violent command, for the present it granted pardon to the open conspiracy. The Prefect was rebuked only so far as he had hired shameless men in a cause so unjust. At the same time, however, a decree was passed to summon the Two Hundred. When they came together, the authority of the Lesser Council was confirmed, and it was permitted that from then on they should choose citizens from the French guests at their own discretion. But before the Two Hundred could settle this last point, their fury, which had resolved to throw itself headlong into every extreme, as men do in desperate affairs, suddenly broke out further. For by a night tumult the city was brought close to utter ruin. On the day before this happened, a free dinner had been given to many scoundrels. The Captains were feasting elsewhere: of these, the one I named, Vandelius, paid for the dinner; Perrin, however, for the supper. Meanwhile messengers flitted about, many sinister signs were noticed, so that the good had reason to fear. It was the custom, after the guards had been posted at the gates, for the Prefect of the watch to go round and inspect the stations. Each of the Senators takes this duty in turn. While the watchmen of that night were standing in the middle of the city, they heard a shout not far away. For from the direction behind the merchants' shops, a certain man, struck by a stone, was crying out that he had been killed. So they ran up, as their duty required. Against them rose two brothers german, companions of Perrin and Vandelius, men indeed of the lowest rank, pastry-cooks to be sure, but who had dined free at the same table. It later became clear that the affair had been arranged beforehand, because only two men had dared to attack several armed men. Both confessed this both to the judges, and to many others, and to me privately. Although, when they were being led to punishment, they denied that they had raised the tumult at a signal given, nevertheless they were convicted by so many indications that their shamelessness gained them nothing. Indeed they did not deny this: that on the same day, between dinner and supper, they had accompanied Perrin for amusement as he went out to a nearby country house; and that on the way there was talk of five hundred armed men to be summoned from elsewhere to guard the city. When the mention of this matter was renewed during the afternoon drink, Perrin, when a workman arrived, imposed silence in German: "Schwig, schwig." And since that country house lies outside the borders of the Genevan territory, he said that a refuge and shelter would be ready there for anyone who had committed a capital crime in the city. As the tumult grew, one of the Syndics, who was not far off, came out with his Scipio, which is the emblem of the magistracy, and with lights lit. And among this people there was always such reverence for that sacred staff that at the sight of it not only were the greatest tumults calmed, but when it came to slaughter, violence was checked.

units.la: Vnus ex fratribus illis, exerto gladio, obuius Syndico incurrit. Syndicus insigni potestatis fretus manum iniecit, ut in carcerem duceret. Aduolant complures ex factione. Quicquid lumini erat, extinguitur. Negant illi se passuros bonum sodalem in carcerem duci. Adest confestim Perrinus. Ac initio pacificandi studium simulans, Syndicalem baculum arripit, Syndico in aurem susurrans, Meus est, non tuus. Ille quanquam pusillae staturae homo, non tamen cedere, sed contra animose, & fortiter obniti. Passim interea per omnes urbis vicos clamor erat sublatus, & fere momento peruaserat, Gallos in armis esse, ac urbem insidiis proditam: domum Senatoris, qui nocte illa Praefectus vigilum erat, refertam esse hominibus armatis. Emissarii quos sibi fauere nouerant, eos tumultuose accersere. Perrinus cum minime dubitaret, cateruam suam iam satis validam esse, vociferari coepit, Noster est Syndicalis baculus: eum enim teneo. Ad hanc vocem nullum consensus signum datum est: & tamen undique cinctus erat coniuratis: ut facile apparet arcano Dei instinctu retentos fuisse. Pudore ergo confusus, & simul territus, paulum se recepit. Sed in alterum Syndicum affinem suum incidens, baculum vi violenter extorsit. Ille quiritari vim sibi esse factam, ius urbis esse violatum. Quia autem armorum potentia longe vincebant improbi, nemo ad Syndici querimoniam digitum sustulit, ut subsidio veniret. Sed pellimos quosque rursum quaedam religio tenuit, ut nullus eorum Perrino succineret. Ita metu coactus, baculum clam reddidit. Erant iam in armis plurimi nebulones. Vna vox vbique sonabat, Trucidandos esse Gallos, & urbem ab ipsis proditam esse. Dominus autem pro miseris suis exulibus incredibiles excubias agens, partim sopore eos persaperfudit, vt inter horrendos strepitus suauiter in lectis dormirent: partim continuit, vt minis & periculi terrore non fuerint perculsi. Nemo certe domo egressus est. Atque hoc vno Dei miraculo fractus fuit impiorum impetus, quod nullus ad conflictum se obtulit. Statuerant enim, vt postea facile innotuit, si qui aggressi essent, se defendere: occisis quibusdam, graviori in alios: quasi a nobis exorta esset seditio. Nec vero tantum hospitibus minitabantur, sed quidam etiam clamabant patronos esse occidendos, & poenas de Senatu sumendas esse. Atque hic vide Senatus nostri clementiam. Nam licet deprehensi fuerint tam nefariae vocis auctores, ac conuicti, non modo pepercit eorum vitae, sed etiam a mediocri castigatione abstinuit, vt ne virgis quidem caesi fuerint. Syndici dum Senatum cogi iubent, per urbem curiitate. Sed improbi suis copiis freti, non modo eludere eorum imperium, & spernere, sed etiam conuiciis obstrepere, vt spes esset remedij exigua. Hoc tamen praeter spem diuinitus effectum est, vt paulatim resideret tempestas. Postridie decretum est, vt quaestio haberetur de vi publica. Syndici triduo in testibus rogandis consumpto, ne quis diceret se falso premi, Ducentos vocant. Dum recitantur testimonia, inter alios iudices sedebat ipsi quoque coniurati. Vt quemque vel culpae obnoxium, vel sinistra suspicione grauari apparuit, tandem iussi sunt egredi ex Curia: quia integri ad dicendam sententiam esse non poterant. Sed Perrinus detectum scelus videns, cum tribus ali is fuga elapsus est. Maior Senatus, rei indignitate iniustam iracundiam accensus, decernit seuere vlcisci endum esse coispirationis scelus: & Minorem Senatu, penes quem sunt iudicia, ad poenas strenue exigendas hortatur.
units.tr: One of those brothers, with drawn sword, rushed at the Syndic who met him. The Syndic, relying on the power of his office, laid hands on him to lead him off to prison. Several of the faction flew at him. Whatever light there was was put out. They declared that they would not allow a good comrade to be led to prison. Perrin was at once present. Feigning at first a zeal for peace, he snatched the Syndic's staff, whispering in the other Syndic's ear, "It is mine, not yours." Though a man of small stature, the Syndic did not give way but resisted boldly and strongly. Meanwhile a cry had been raised through every street of the city, and within a moment it had spread that the French were under arms and the city had been betrayed by treachery: the house of the Senator who was that night prefect of the watch was full of armed men. They summoned by tumult those emissaries whom they knew to favour them. Perrin, not doubting that his band was now strong enough, began to shout, "Our staff is ours: I have it." At this call no sign of agreement was given, and yet he was surrounded on all sides by the conspirators; as is plain, they were held back by a hidden impulse of God. Confused by shame and at the same time terrified, he therefore withdrew a little. But meeting the other Syndic, his relative, he violently wrested the staff from him by force. That man cried out that violence had been done to him and the right of the city violated. Yet since the wicked were far stronger in arms, no one lifted a finger to bring help to the Syndic's complaint. But a certain religious scruple again held the worst of them back, so that none of them supported Perrin. Thus, compelled by fear, he secretly returned the staff. By now many ruffians were under arms. One cry sounded everywhere: that the French were to be slaughtered, and that the city had been betrayed by them. But the Lord, while acting incredibly as guardian over his wretched exiles, partly drenched them in sleep so that they slept sweetly in their beds amid the dreadful uproar, and partly restrained them so that they were not struck with terror by threats and danger. Certainly no one left his house. And by this one miracle of God the attack of the impious was broken, in that no one offered himself for the conflict. For they had resolved, as soon became known afterwards, that if any should attack them, they would defend themselves; with some killed, they would then go more fiercely against others, as though the sedition had been raised by us. Nor did they threaten only the guests; some even shouted that the patrons were to be killed and vengeance taken on the Senate. And here see the clemency of our Senate. For although the authors of so impious a cry were caught and convicted, it not only spared their lives but also refrained from even a moderate punishment, so that they were not even beaten with rods. While the Syndics ordered the Senate to be summoned, they ran through the city. But the wicked, relying on their forces, not only mocked and scorned their authority but also raised a clamour of insults, so that there was little hope of a remedy. Yet, contrary to expectation, it was brought about by God that the storm gradually subsided. The next day it was decreed that an inquiry should be held concerning public violence. The Syndics spent three days in summoning witnesses, lest anyone should say he was unjustly oppressed, and then they summoned two hundred. While the testimonies were read, among the other judges sat the conspirators themselves. As soon as it appeared that any one of them was either liable to blame or weighed down by a sinister suspicion, they were ordered to leave the Court, since those who were not untainted could not give a sentence. But Perrin, seeing his crime exposed, slipped away in flight with three others. The Greater Council, kindled to unjust anger by the outrageousness of the affair, decreed that the crime of conspiracy must be avenged severely, and urged the Lesser Council, in whose hands the judicial powers lie, to exact the penalties vigorously.

units.la: Citantur a primo Apparitore fugitiui, deinde a praecone publico, vt fieri solet: quod per quindecim dies praecinente tuba factum est. Illi missis chirographis, testari, se nisi data fide publica, minime venturos. Atqui absurdissimum fuisset, quos ex vinculis reos causam dicere oportuerat, tanquam beneficiarios legibus solui. Praescripta igitur die, quinque damnati sunt. Sed antequam iudices pronuntiarent, coram toto populo recitata sunt crimina, quorum conuictos teneri necesse fuit, qui se vocari in ius, non purgabat. Accessit postea eorum confessio, de quibus sumptum est supplicium, & qui adhuc in carcere tenentur. Unde constat magis esse noxios, & scelerates, quam vt effugium illum pateat. Et tamen vt sunt perfricta frontis, odiosos rumores spargere non desinunt: se falsa invidia fuisse oppressos, quod ciuium causam contra Gallos, & Senatum Gallis deditum, tutati sint. Quasi vero Ducenti, quorum praeiudicio confossi sunt, non sint rex ciuibus. Quasi colecto exercitu expulsi fuerint. Quasi plebs, si intelligeret libertatis suae patronos crudeliter opprimi, tantam iniuriam passura esset.
units.tr: The fugitives were summoned first by the chief usher and then by the public herald, as is customary; this was done over fifteen days with the trumpet sounding before them. They replied by sending written letters, declaring that they would not come unless a public guarantee were given. Yet it would have been most absurd that men who ought to have been brought from their chains to plead their cause should be released by the laws as if they were privileged persons. Therefore, on the appointed day, five were condemned. But before the judges pronounced sentence, the charges were read out before the whole people, the charges by which those who did not clear themselves when summoned to court were necessarily held convicted. Afterwards there was also added the confession of those on whom the punishment was inflicted, and of those who are still held in prison. From this it is evident that they are more guilty and wicked than that such an escape should be open to them. And yet, being brazen-faced, they do not cease to spread malicious rumours: that they were overwhelmed by unjust hatred because they defended the cause of the citizens against the French and against a Senate given over to the French. As if the Two Hundred, by whose judgment they were struck down, were not citizens! As if they had been driven out by an assembled army! As if the common people, if it understood that the defenders of its liberty were being cruelly oppressed, would have suffered so great an injury!

units.la: Quin potius eorum discessu cõpofitæ sunt omnes turbæ: difcuf- fa fuit quam induxerant, caligo: leges reuiguerunt: reddita fuit vrbi tranquillitas. Viderunt certè qui illorum rogatu addepre- candum venerant,non diuersis studiis vrbem scissam esse,nec vl lis contentionibus flagrare:sed placido omnium consensu pro- bari decretam in illos pœnâ. Vt summa impudentia prediti sunt, non modo extenuant admiffium facinus,sed futilibus cauillis cri men in fe de nihilo conflatum fuisse iactant. Quæ tamen dilue- re non difficile est. Probabile esse negant,quum sub manu ha- berent magnam turbam, temere ipsos fine valido præsidio ad arma prorupisse. Quasi verò rarum fit, vel infrequens exemplū, improbos amentia cæcos & præcipites ferr. Certè quicquid ob- tendant, man festa rabies vnum ex cohorte impulit, vt ictu la- pidis hominem deiiceret,vnde exortus est clamor. Eadem quo- que duorum fratrum cæcitas, dum gladiis nudatis in vigiles ar- matos impetum fecerunt. Iam verò Syndicorum imperi,quibus non parere semper capitale fuit,petulàter,& cum ludibrio fper- nere,non solùm repentini furoris, sed conceptæ prius audaciæ, diuque inter ipsos conc pt signum est minime ambiguum Cla mor adhæc inter ipsos omnes consonus, de vrbe à Gallis prodi- ta,vnde nisi ex coniuratione? Nisi enim ex compacto hanc tef- feram sibi mutuò dedissent,qui fieri potuit,vt statim in locis lö- ge inter fe distantibus, vox illa de nihilo confpicta congrueret? Nam & illius,quem dixi,Vandellij vxor,quoscunque fuę factio- nis fore sperabat,oftiatim acciuit, Gallos proditionis incusans. Verum hoc est scilicet, quod confessus est quidam Perrini asse- cla,& quo nemo illi magis familiaris erat,nempe duos illos fe- ditionis principes quatuor ante, vel paucis diebus sic inter fe lo- quutos:Quid cessimus,breui ignauiæ nostræ pœnas daturi?Iam triennium est, ex quo in eædem nostram confpirarunt hostes. (Porrò,mihi in illo catalogo primum locum dabant.)Ergo an- teuertamus necesse est.Speciosus autem nunc oblatus est color. Dicemus è Republica non esse,tam multos ciuitate donari.Ni- hil impetrabimus nec in minore Senatu,nec apud Ducetos. Ad populum prouocabimus. Aduolabit multitudo, etiam inuitis Syndicis. Partis nostræ homines subornabimus, vt tumultum concitent. In tollendis hostibus nihil erit negotij. Tantummo- do audendum est:quia de victoria securi fumus. Hoc ille Perri- no intimus,& fere indiuidua eius vmbra quater repetiuit.Negét fe iure damnatos esse,quibus in medio populi conuentu,& loco sancto,duos ex Syndicis,quosdam Senatores,ex ciuibus optimos quosque omnes innoxios trucidare propositum fuit. De me ta- ceo,quem sibi gratis inimicum sumpserunt. Nam quòd me cæ- dem moliri, obtendere ipsos non puduit, putidius est, quàm vt excuexcusatione indigeat. Et tamen nondum iudicio Vandellium perfequutus est Senatus. Sed eum mala conscientia urbe expulit: ut facile appareat, in maximo tumultu moderationem, qualis in rebus tranquillisseruari solet, fuisse retentam: nec callide vel festinanter quicquam actum esse contra improbos. Quin potius tu si adsis, Senatum nostrum lente progredi, ac remisse dicas. Sed in hanc partem satius est peccari, ne quis praeposterè, ut in iracundiae feruore accidit, saeuitum esse queratur. Faxit Dominus, ut tantae liberationis memoria nos assidue ad gratitudinem stimulet, semperque in officio contineat. Cum has literas dictare inciperem, non putabam ab Orthomano nostro perlatum iri. Nam etsi iam de suo itinere verba fecerat, quia tamen incertus erat, an recta istuc venturus foret, alio potius nuntio statueram uti. Nunc opportune accidit, quod non parum gaudeo, ut si quid propter breuitatem erit obscurius, sermone plenius confirmet atque explicet. Quod me ad patientiam bis hortatus es, ego vero tot indignitates placide tulisse mihi videor, & quasi vorasse, ut dum stomachum cohibeo, animus mihi quoque defuerit. Vtinam saltem meo silentio ac dissimulatione placassem, qui odio mei in omnes bonos furere non desinunt. Sed quanquam inde magis accenditur, quae pridem nimis grassata est rabies: mihi tamen fixum est nihil mouere. N. prouinciam obtigisse gaudeo, in qua se vtiliter exerceat. Det modo ei Dominus fideliter ea defungi. Eum cum N. saluere cupio. Symmystis etiam tuis omnibus, vxori & familiae plurima meo nomine salutem dices. Vale, ornatissime vir, & semper obseruande frater. Dominus te Spiritu suo regere & benedictione prosequi perrgat. Geneuae, xv. Iunij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Indeed, by their departure all the disturbances were calmed: the mist which they had brought on was dispersed; the laws revived; tranquillity was restored to the city. Certainly those who had come to intercede for them at their request saw that the city was not split by divided aims, nor burning with quarrels, but that the punishment decreed against them was approved by the unanimous consent of all. Endowed with the utmost impudence, they not only minimise the crime committed, but with trifling quibbles boast that the charge was fabricated out of nothing against them. Yet these things are not difficult to refute. They deny that it is credible that, having a large crowd at their disposal, they rashly burst into arms without a strong guard. As if it were rare, or an unusual example, for the wicked to be blinded and rushed headlong by madness! Certainly, whatever they put forward, open frenzy drove one of the band to knock a man down with a blow of a stone, from which a cry arose. The same blindness was shown by the two brothers, when with swords drawn they made an assault on the armed guards. Now, as for the commands of the Syndics, to disobey whom has always been a capital offence, they scorned them insolently and with derision: this is not only the sign of a sudden fury but of a boldness conceived beforehand, and devised for a long time among themselves. The cry, one in unison among them all, that the city had been betrayed by the French, is no ambiguous sign: whence did it come, unless from a conspiracy? For unless they had given this watchword to one another by agreement, how could it have happened that that voice, invented out of nothing, agreed at once in places far apart from one another? For also the wife of Vandelle, whom I mentioned, summoned from door to door all whom she hoped would be of her faction, accusing the French of treachery. But this is surely true, which a certain follower of Perrin confessed, and no one was more intimate with him than he: that those two leaders of the sedition, four or a few days before, had spoken among themselves thus: "Why have we given way? Soon we shall pay the penalty of our cowardice. It is now three years since our enemies conspired against us. (Moreover, they were putting me first on that list.) Therefore we must anticipate them. A specious pretext has now been offered. We shall say that it is not in the interest of the Republic that so many should be granted citizenship. We shall gain nothing either in the Lesser Council or before the Two Hundred. We shall appeal to the people. The crowd will fly to us, even against the wishes of the Syndics. We shall suborn men of our side to stir up a tumult. In removing our enemies there will be no trouble. We need only dare, since we are sure of victory." Perrin was intimate with this, and almost repeated this same thing, as an individual shadow, four times. They deny that they were justly condemned, when it was proposed in the middle of an assembly of the people, and in a holy place, to slaughter two of the Syndics, certain Senators, and all the best citizens, who were innocent. I say nothing of me, whom they took as an enemy for nothing. For that they were not ashamed to pretend to plot my murder is too foul to need an excuse. And yet the Senate has not yet proceeded against Vandelle by judgment; but his guilty conscience drove him from the city. So it is easily seen that in the greatest tumult the moderation which is usually kept in peaceful times was maintained, and that nothing was done against the wicked either craftily or hastily. Indeed, if you were present, you would say that our Senate advances slowly and with restraint. But it is better to err on this side, lest anyone complain that it raged excessively, as happens in the heat of anger. May the Lord grant that the memory of so great a deliverance may constantly stir us to gratitude and keep us always in duty. When I began to dictate this letter, I did not think it would be carried by our Orthomanus. For although he had already spoken of his journey, since he was uncertain whether he would come straight there, I had decided to use another messenger instead. Now it has happened opportunely, which I greatly rejoice in, that if anything is somewhat obscure because of brevity, he may confirm and explain it more fully in conversation. As for your twice urging me to patience: I seem to myself to have borne so many indignities calmly, and as if to have swallowed them, so that while I restrain my bile, my spirit has also failed me. Would that at least I had appeased by my silence and dissimulation those who do not cease to rage with hatred against me and all good men! But although the rage which has long been raging too widely is thereby kindled more, it is nonetheless settled with me to move nothing. I rejoice that N. has been assigned a province in which he may exercise himself usefully. May the Lord only grant him to discharge it faithfully. I desire to greet him with N. You will give my greetings, very many, in my name to all your fellow-members of the Company, to your wife and household. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother always to be honoured. May the Lord continue to rule you by his Spirit and accompany you with his blessing. Geneva, 15 June 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS MARTYRI S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MARTYR, GREETINGS

units.la: Quod de arcana, quae nobis cum Christo est, communicatione me scripturum pollicitus fueram, minus solide pręstabo, quàm sperasti: quia tametsi magni momenti res est, paucis tamen verbis inter nos commodè posse definiri arbitror. Quòd Filius Dei carnem nostram induit, ut frater noster fieret, eiusdem naturae particeps, de illa communicatione dicere supersedeo. Nam de ea tantum agendum est, quae à coelesti eius virtute manat, & nobis vitam inspirat, & facit ut in vnum cum ipso corpus coalescamus. Dico autem, simul ac fide Christum recipimus, qualiter se in Euangelio offert, vere nos fieri eius membra, & vitam ab eo non secus atque à capite in nos defluere. Neque enim aliter nos Deo mortis suæ sacrificio reconciliat, nisi quia noster est, ac nos vnum cum ipso. Sic illum Pauli locum interpretor, vbi fideles in eius κοινωνίαν vocatos esse dicit, 1. Corinth. 1.9. Neque vero nomen consortij, vel societatis mentem eius sa-tis exprimere videtur: sed mihi sacram illam vnitatem designat, quia Filius Dei nos in corpus suum inserit, vt nobiscum sua om-nia communicet. Ita a carne eius & sanguine vitam haurimus, vt non immerito vocentur nostra alimenta. Quomodo id fiat, intelligentiæ meæ modulo longe altius est: fateor. Itaque hoc mysterium magis suspicio, quàm comprehendere laborem, nisi quòd diuina Spiritus virtute vitam e cœlis in terram transfundi agnoscō: quia nec per se viuifica esset caro Christi, nec vis eius ad nos vsque nisi immensa Spiritus operatione peruenires. Ergo Spiritus est qui facit, vt in nobis habitet Christus, nos sustineat atque vegetet, omniaque capitis officia impleat. Crassis interea commentis de substantiæ commixtione aditum præcludo: quia mihi satis est, dum in cœlesti gloria manet Christi corpus, vi-tam ab eo ad nos defluere, non secus ac radix succum ad ramos transmittit. Quinquam autem veteres, ac Hilarium præsertim & Cyrillum longius quàm par fit prouectos fuisse video: tamen eorum hyperbolas non admodum insector: nisi quòd ingenuè semper me opponam, si errori patrocinium quæratur. Dum e-nim contendunt, Christum Patri ὁμοούσιον esse, quia scriptum sit, Ego & Pater vnum sumus, dum retorquet Arriani quod mox additum est, vt sint ipsi quoque vnum nobiscum, illi in sua in-scitia deprehensi ad miseram latebram suffugiunt, nos quoque eiusdem cum Christo esse essentiæ. Hoc autem confessio, multis absurdis innolui necesse fuit. Sed modò ne eorum auctoritatem nobis obtendant noui isti fufores, mihi satis erit non subscribere, ne vltrò eos in arenam protraham. Iam venio ad secundam communicationem, quæ illius prioris mihi fructus est ac effectus. Nam posteam Christus interiore Spiritus virtute sibi nos deuinxit atque vniuit in corpus suum, secundam Spiritus virtutem exerit, donis suis nos locupletando. Quòd ergo spe & patientia fortes sumus, quòd sobriè & temperanter nos continemus à mundi illecebris, quòd ad domandos carnis affectus strenuè incumbimus, quòd viget in nobis iustitiæ & pietatis studium, quòd ad preces sumus intenti, quòd nos futuræ vitæ meditatio sursum rapit, id ex secunda ista communicatione manare dico, dum Christus, ne otiosus in nobis habitet, vim Spiritus sui in manifestis donis profert. Nec verò absurdum est, Chri-stum, vbi in eius corpus coaluimus, Spiritum suum nobis communicare, cuius arcana operatione nostra prius effectus est: quando vtrásque ei partes Scriptura sæpe assignat. Etsi autem in hanc communionem primo vocationis suae die veniunt fideles: quatenus tamen in illis augescit Christi vita, quotidie se illis fruendum offert. Haec est communicatio, quam in sacra Coena percipiunt. Apud alium quempiam, qui mihi docendus esset, fusius prosequerer, quae breviter apud te hoc tantum consilio perstringo, ut nos idem prorsus sentire videas. De te, nisi quid noui acciderit, huc accersendo verbum amplius facere non audemus. Et certe ego ut hac in re timidus sum, nunquam adduci potui, ut tibi migrandi auctor essem, nisi ii missione impetrata. Fructum vero ex tuo labore provenire cupio, qui nobis absentiae tuae desiderium leniat. Ecclesiolae vero Gallicanae clades me non parum angit. N. quidem prospectum studebimus, ubi venerit. Sed collapsae Ecclesiae restitutio imprimis curanda est: ad quam rem si neruos intendas, multum, ut spero, proderis. Tu igitur in malo hoc sanando, ut facis, eniteris: qua in re, D. Sturmium & Sleidanum fidos tibi adiutores fore arbitror. De statu rerum nostrarum commodius referet hic frater & Symmysta meus, quam literis completi queam. Quare nebis idem, hac nar ratione abstineo. Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi in Domino semper obseruande. Saluta diligenter amicos D. Sturmium, Zankum & reliquos. Nunc antequam literas obsigno, admonitus sum N. literis, magna ex parte sedatas eius aduentui esse turbas. Vtinam ad eum iuuandum vsui esse posset mea opera. Verum si Ecclesiae suffragijs electus fuerit, sua moderatione tranquillam statim Ecclesiam, nisi fallor, reddet. Dominus te semper tueatur, Spiritu suo regat, & benedictione prosequatur. Geneuae, v I II. Augusti. M. D. L V.
units.tr: I promised to write to you about the secret communion that we have with Christ, but I will deliver it less thoroughly than you hoped. Although it is a matter of great importance, I think it can be settled between us properly in a few words. That the Son of God put on our flesh so that he might become our brother and share our nature, I leave aside; I am not discussing that communion. I am concerned only with the communion that flows from his heavenly power, breathes life into us, and causes us to grow together into one body with him. I say that, as soon as we receive Christ by faith in the way he offers himself in the gospel, we truly become his members, and life flows from him into us no differently than from the head. Indeed, he reconciles us to God by the sacrifice of his death in no other way than by being ours and our being one with him. I interpret in this way that passage of Paul where he says that the faithful are called into his κοινωνία (1 Cor. 1.9) [κοινωνία]. The word "partnership" or "fellowship" does not seem to express his meaning adequately; to me it designates that sacred unity, because the Son of God inserts us into his body so that he may share all his possessions with us. Thus we draw life from his flesh and blood, so that they are rightly called our food. How this happens is far above the measure of my understanding; I admit it. Therefore I rather venerate this mystery than labour to comprehend it, except that I acknowledge that life is poured from heaven into earth by the divine power of the Spirit. For the flesh of Christ would not be life-giving in itself, nor could his power reach us except through the immense working of the Spirit. Therefore it is the Spirit who causes Christ to dwell in us, sustains and quickens us, and fulfils all the offices of the head. Meanwhile I shut the door on crude fancies about a mingling of substances, since it is enough for me that, while the body of Christ remains in heavenly glory, life flows from him to us, just as a root sends sap to its branches. Although I see that the ancients, especially Hilary and Cyril, went further than is fitting, I do not greatly attack their hyperboles, except that I always openly oppose them if they are used to defend an error. For when they contend that Christ is ὁμοούσιος with the Father, because it is written, "I and the Father are one," and when they turn back against the Arians what was added immediately, that they also may be one with us, they, caught in their own ignorance, flee to a wretched hiding place and say that we too are of the same essence as Christ. But I had to put this in writing, lest these new scoffers should, in their absurdities, be wrapped in the authority of others. For now it will be enough for me not to subscribe to such things, so that I do not drag them unwillingly into the arena. Now I come to the second communion, which is the fruit and effect of that first. For afterwards, when Christ has bound us to himself by the inward power of the Spirit and united us into his body, he exerts a second power of the Spirit, enriching us with his gifts. Therefore, that we are strong in hope and patience, that we restrain ourselves soberly and temperately from the allurements of the world, that we apply ourselves vigorously to subduing the desires of the flesh, that the zeal for righteousness and godliness flourishes in us, that we are intent on prayer, and that the meditation of the future life lifts us upward: I say all this flows from that second communion, since Christ, so that he may not dwell idle in us, puts forth the power of his Spirit in manifest gifts. Nor is it absurd that Christ, once we have grown together into his body, communicates to us his Spirit, by whose secret working we were first made his. Scripture often assigns both parts to him. Although the faithful come into this communion on the first day of their calling, yet insofar as Christ's life grows in them, he offers himself to be enjoyed by them daily. This is the communion that they receive in the holy Supper. I would have explained these things more fully to someone else who needed to be taught; but I touch on them briefly with you, with this purpose only, that you may see that we think exactly the same. About you, unless something new has happened, we do not dare say more while summoning you here. And indeed, I am timid in this matter; I could never be brought to advise you to leave, unless they had obtained your release. I wish, however, that the fruit of your labour may come, which will soothe our longing for your absence. As for the little church in France, its ruin troubles me no little. We shall take care to provide for N. when he comes. But the restoration of the fallen Church must above all be attended to; if you strain your strength toward this, I hope you will be of great help. You, then, strive to heal this evil, as you are doing; in which matter I think Sturm and Sleidan will be faithful helpers to you. Concerning the state of our affairs, this brother and my fellow-minister will report more conveniently than I can fill a letter; so I abstain from repeating it here. Farewell, most distinguished man, and always to be honoured by me in the Lord. Greet diligently our friends Sturm, Zanchius, and the rest. Now, before I seal the letter, I have been informed by letters from N. that the disturbances there have, for the most part, been calmed by his coming.
