Would that my work could be of use in helping him. But if he is chosen by the votes of the Church, he will, unless I am mistaken, at once restore the Church to tranquillity by his moderation. May the Lord always keep you, rule you by his Spirit, and bless you. Geneva, 8 August 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS GARNERIO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO GARNIER.

units.la: QVanquam ex tuis literis iam prope mobis certum erat, te propediem affore, facit tamen haec conditio praeter spem repente oblata, vt consilium profectionis te mutasse non mirer. Nam vt eius captandae nunquam tibi fuissem auctor, ita cur tam commode ac tempestiue oblatam aspernari debueris, non video. Est enim honestum munus, in quo te vtiliter exerceas. Neque in reprehensionem cadit mutatio, quae voluntaria non est. Tibi sponte nunquam deserenda fuit statio. Nunc quando violenter ab ea deiectus es, quominus operam tuam priuatim adolescentibus illis docendis impendas, nulla ratio impedit. Aula, quandiu te Ecclesia tenebat obstrictum, non fuit appetenda: nunc vero alia est libertas. Quominus itaque a publico munere solutus, prouinciam & sanctam, & a qua sperandus est fructus, suscipias, minime dissuadeo. Nec Farellum &
units.tr: Although from your letter it was already almost certain to me that you would soon be here, this unexpected offer, which I had not hoped for, makes me not surprised that you have changed your plan of leaving. I never advised you to seek it, but I do not see why you ought to have rejected an offer so conveniently and opportunely made. It is an honourable post, in which you can serve usefully. A change is not to be blamed when it is not of your own choosing. You should never have given up your post of your own accord. Now that you have been forcibly removed from it, nothing stands in the way of your devoting your labour privately to teaching those young men. The court was not to be sought while the Church held you bound to it, but now your freedom is different. So, since you have been released from public office, I by no means dissuade you from taking up a task that is both holy and likely to bear fruit. Nor do I think Farel and Viret will feel otherwise, though if they give a different advice, I do not want you to obey me. But, if I judge rightly, they will not be too severe to recall you. Farewell, most upright brother. May the Lord guide you with the Spirit of counsel, strengthen you with virtue, and cherish you with his blessing. Amen. Greet your wife and friends. Geneva, 8th August 1555.

units.la: Epist.209. Virëtum aliud sensuros existimo: quanquam fi aliud consilium dederint,nolo mihi obtemperes. Verùm,fi recte duimo,non eruntiam austeri,vt te reuocent. Vale integerrim frater. Dominus te consilij Spiritu regat, virtute suffentet, lenedictione sua foueat.Amen. Saluta vxorem & amicos. Geneuæ, viii. Augusti. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Epist. 209. I think Farel and Viret will feel otherwise, though if they give a different advice, I do not want you to obey me. But, if I judge rightly, they will not be too severe to recall you. Farewell, most upright brother. May the Lord guide you with the Spirit of counsel, strengthen you with virtue, and cherish you with his blessing. Amen. Greet your wife and friends. Geneva, 8th August 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calunus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: CALVINVS MELANCHTHONI
units.tr: CALVIN TO MELANCHTHON

units.la: REcte quidem & prudenter admones,ornatissime vir,id sibi vnum nostros antagonistas proponere, vt se heatro venditent. Quanquam autem sua opinio longè eos,wt spero,& credibile est,frustrabitur: tamen vt totius mundi plausum refe-rant,eò nos maiore studio ad cœlestem ἀγωνοθέτην,sub cuius oculis certamus,intentos esse decet. Quid? An sacer Angelorum confessus, qui & suo fauore nos excitant & viam irenuè agendi præmonstrant suo exemplo, pigrescere vel cunctanter pedes mouere sinet? Quid totus sanctorum patrum chorus? an nullos addet stimulos? Quid porrò Dei Ecclesia quæ in mundo versatur? cum eam scimus & votis nobiscum pugnare,& exemplo no ftro animari,an nihil apud nos valebunt eius suffragia? Mcum verò sit hoc theatrum, cuius approbatione contentus, quanuis me totus mundus exfibilet, animo nunquam deficiam: tantum abest,vt insulsis clamatoribus inuideam,fi multa gloriola in obscuro angulo ad breue tempus fruantur. Quid plausibile sit mundo velodiosum,me non later.Sed mihi nihil pluris est,quà præscriptam à magistro normam sequi. Nec dubito quin hæc ingenuitas piis & fanis gratior tandem futura sit, quàm flexibilis & mollis docendi ratio, quæ inanem metum præ se ferat. Quod te Deo & Ecclesiæ debere agnoscis, obsecro te vt quam primum soluas. Neque in hanc rem insisto,quòd partem inuidiæ in te exonerans,tantundem me leuatum iri confidam.Quin potius,fi liceat,quicquid in te oneris iam incumbit, pro meo in te amore atq; obseruantia,paratus forem in meos humeros suscipere:sed tuum est expendere, vt ego monitor non accedâ, nisi dubitatione pios homines qui te respiciût,maturè liberes,te vix vnquam soluendo fore.Adde etiam quì nisi ferum hoc & vesper-tinum gallicinium te expergefaciat,pigrum merito omnes clamabunt. Vale præstantissime vir,& mihi ex animo venerande. Christus fidelis suorum custos tibi semper adsit,te regat & tueatur,Amen. D.Cametarius,& si qui præterea istic sunt amici,meo nomine saluta. Geneuæ,x.Calend.Septemb. M. D. LV.
units.tr: You rightly and wisely advise, most distinguished man, that our opponents have only one aim, to make a show of themselves in the theatre. Although their hopes will, I trust, and it is credible, be largely frustrated, yet, so that we may bring back the applause of the whole world, we ought to be all the more intent on the heavenly president of the games [ἀγωνοθέτην], under whose eyes we contend. What then? Will the holy assembly of angels, who both stir us up by their favour and show us by their example the way to act calmly, allow us to grow lazy or to move our feet hesitantly? What of the whole company of the holy Fathers? Will they add no spurs? And what of the Church of God, which lives in the world? Since we know that she fights with us in prayers and is encouraged by our example, will her prayers count for nothing among us? As for me, let this be my theatre, and let me be content with its approval; though the whole world hiss me, I shall never lose heart. I am so far from envying the foolish shouters, even if they enjoy a little empty glory for a short time in some obscure corner. I am not unaware of what is pleasing to the world and what is hateful to it. But nothing is more valuable to me than to follow the rule prescribed by the Master. Nor do I doubt that this frankness will in the end be more welcome to the pious and sound than a pliant and soft method of teaching, which displays an empty fear. As for your acknowledgement that you owe yourself to God and the Church, I beg you to discharge it as soon as possible. I do not press this point because I trust that, by unloading part of the odium onto you, I shall be relieved to the same extent. Rather, if it were permitted, I would gladly take upon my own shoulders whatever burden now lies on you, out of my love and regard for you. But it is for you to weigh this. Admonished as I am, I should not come forward unless you free the pious men who look to you from their doubt in good time; you will hardly ever be released from paying it. Add also that unless a harsh and late cock-crow wakes you, all will rightly call you a sluggard. Farewell, most excellent man, and one I venerate from my heart. May Christ, the faithful guardian of his own, always be with you, guide and protect you. Amen. Greet Camerarius on my behalf, and any other friends who are there. Geneva, 23rd September 1555.

units.la: FARELLVS
units.tr: FAREL

units.la: PLus satis habes vnde in horas crucifigaris & domi & foris, vt opus non sit me tibi grauiorem addere crucem. Habes quàm iustissimas quaerendi rationes. Ex multis pauca attigisti in tuis literis. Quid enim dici potest de iis qui vltrò in Christum insurgunt, vt cum prorsus perdant, vt iniquissimum, & Satanam iustificent, vt sanctissimum? Nō heri coeptum est, sed mox vbi tu nobis datus fuisti à D. perseueratum est magnis animis, vt progressus in omni iniquitate fuerint quam maximi. Sed gratias ago D. quòd nullus suor potuisset efficere ea, quae videre nos facit Christus noster & efficit in hac tâ grauì & intolerabili molestia, vt plura multò sint pro nobis & nobis accedant, quàm contra nos aut à nobis deficiant. Fiunt multa indignè & proscindimur, sed latent nos plura, & ea quibus D. commendamur. Tangi expedit mala & argui, sed in bonis & bene merendo, Christum nobis debemus proponere quàm patiés est, quàm est studiosus, vt de malè merentibus quàm optimè merentur, non seruili animo, sed plus quàm heroico, qui malis non frangitur. Voluit Christus in te insigne edere cùm turba tot hostium conuenisset, vt caedibus omnia impleret, non dubitasti te non modò ridendum, rostris foedandum, sed conculcandum, lacerandum, perdendum, omnium gladiis confodiendum vltrò obiicere. Fauit Dominus tibi & quod strenuè coepit triumphans quàm foelicissimè absoluit. Non tam impedita sunt quae abs te peto, nec tam indigna, si rationem consulas, etsi videntur indignissima, sed mi lo coràm agere, si D. dederit. Tantum peto vt gratias agens D. super ingenti misericordia & bonitate, qua te cinxit vndique, commendes hostes D. feras omnia aequiori animo, quaeraris tantùm apud D. qui medeatur, apud eos qui peccant, vt conuertantur. Et si qui velint & possint vnà hostes admonere, paucos audias, qui aliorum mala narrent, paucioribus credas. Vides in Paulo quem tu notiorem orbi omnibus fecisti, quid is tribuat toti coetui propter interdum paucos valde. Sed quis est qui me non rideat haec ad te scribentem, si intellexerit? An non merito sus Minerua dicar? Sed nostro hoc condona amori. Et interea audi in quibus versemur. Ego litem habeo cum plebano Crescentino. Peto vt sibi consulat & pleb, & quod me tangit sepeliatur, me id non curare. Ille agnoscit aliqua de quibus veniam petit: alia negat, mihi probandum est. Guilielmus Hobraquius, quem semel prohibuerunt Laudecomenses arreptis Bibliis sacris & deiectis in terram, litem quoque habet cum iis, qui contumeliis eâ afficerunt. Scripsit aliqua de Missa, vnde mitatur quidam Helvetios, qui Missam habent, ciere, vt agant quemadmodum contra Michaëlem. Interea bonus vir pergit fœlicius, quàm hactenus. Conciones habet liberas & vsum Sacramentorū. Præterea Ioannes Drogius pastor Beuacensis cuius vxor in lepram incidit, quanuis Synodo interfuerit, & subscripserit non solui coniugium lepra, & ita omnium calculis fuerit conclusum, præseċto & omnibus approbantibus ordinibus: tamen quia Germanis aliter videtur, licet fuerit cū vxore, & filium habuerit ex ea, non-dum est alter annus exactus, vult nihilominus alteram ducere. Misera vxor vocata fuerat me inscio, sed à collega cum aliquot conuocatis, vt suum daret assensum, sed noluit coràm compa-rere. Vrgetur à viro. Petit cùm parum supersit vitæ, expectet. Si nolit, videat an ex verbo D. possit. Si D. id probet, eam non improbare. Vides vt habet cum vxore. Nuper dicebat fratribus, Vvatteuillanum ex fratribus petere, vt ea daremus per quæ iudi camus nō licere per lepram, sano alium ducere sanam vxorem. Illic vidi non recte agi, sed obliquè nos impeti. Omnes mihi reclamanti hanc prouinciam iniunxerunt. Pernegaui me factu-rum. Sed nofti nostrorum ingenia, quò plus renuo, magis vrgent. Et ne aliis ansam prebeam omnium sententiis refragandi, coactus annui, si daretur alios rogare cùm non putem me idoneum ad id præstandū. Quanuis olfaciam collegam consilij autorem: hæreo tamen an ansa captetur committendi nos cum Germanis. Quicquid tandé fit, tuum opto consiliū. Vellem si pos set fieri, vt rationibus tum Buceri, tum aliorum fieret satis. Nam q; dicitur Paulum alias afferre diuortij rationes quàm eam, quæ vna à Christo adducta sit, vbi de desertore agit, mihi alium scopum habere videtur: & quid habet commune infidelis discedes, cum fideli quæ manere optat? Tu non modo nobis prospicies, verùm etiam aliis. Vellem pectus Germanis tam firmum in per ferenda in coniugibus lepra, quæ est laudandum in peste tolerada. Quòd ad Magistratum attinet, non probatim tantùm illi deferendum, vt indulgentior in eos quibus præest, annuat ob duritiem cordis, vt seiunčti & auulsi ab iis quibus per D. suntcoiunčti, moerchentur cum aliis, quibus non possunt iungi sine adultærio, Christus faxit, vt sacrofanča hæc coniunčtio pura, sine omni macula seruetur. D. Martinus nondum rediit à nuptiis Georgij. Vtinam aliquid efficiat, quod quantùm coniicere licet, non appareat. Tossanus callidè quod agit & egit non cogitauit vnquam: coactus à Principe & iussus, innocens, purus, calùniis impetitur. Eiečti cùm ferri non possent, dimissi clementer propter ministe rium, cùm receperint pacem Ecclesiarum illarum se non inter turbaturos, nec quiescunt, nec cessant omnia agere secus quàm promiserint. Triumphat iam serió Tossanus & innocentes omniū sunt nocentissimi. Dabit tandem Christus finem tot & tantis malis. Ego in ista causa supra omnes traducor,& quanuis bona mihi respondeat conscientia,& gestiam hæc mihi propter Christum contingere: tamen meæ mihi cõscius imprudentiæ & carnis,quæ spiritui semper aduersatur, tam infirmus,tam procul ab iis quæ adesse debent,cum Apostolo ingemisco,& veniam peto in hoc gaudio & expectata mercede,quam dat & dabit, qui pro nobis mortuus est. Commendo tibi miseros quos Satanas vrget in re. Bene preceris illis, & quantum fieri potest, bonorum memineris & malorum obliuiscaris. Vide quis veneris,& quotus,& nunc vbi sis,vt pergas semper strenuè magis, & vide quid Iacobus ille dicat ita stipatus rediens. Quid illa ad istam gratiam,vt merito ferre debeas furores Satanæ,imò ridere? Finem non faci tecum agens indignè, mihi arrogans quod non licet. Pueris vt datur ineptire,quid iam bis puero non dabitur aliquid, qui nũquam sapiens fuit? Vale igitur,& omnes vorato molestias propter Christum. Opto collegas saluos non præterito Gallasio,Budæo, Normandio,Fratre Trierio,omnibus. Collega & reliqui fratres te saluum optant. Neocomi, vi :.Septemb. M. D. LV.
units.tr: You already have more than enough to be crucified every hour, both at home and abroad, so there is no need for me to add a heavier cross to you. You have the most just grounds for complaint, and in your letters you have touched on only a few of many. For what can be said of those who rise up against Christ of their own accord, so that, as the most unjust, they utterly destroy themselves, and, as the most holy, they justify Satan? This did not begin yesterday; it has been persisted in with great spirit ever since you were given to us by the Lord, so that the progress in every wickedness has been very great indeed. But I thank the Lord that none of their people could bring about what Christ our Lord makes us see and accomplishes in this so grievous and intolerable trouble: that there are far more things on our side and coming to us than against us or failing us. Many things are done unworthily and we are torn apart, but there are more things hidden from us, and by these we are commended to the Lord. It is good to be touched and rebuked by evils, but we ought to set before ourselves Christ, who is so patient and so eager to do the best for those who deserve the worst, and to do it not in a servile spirit but in a more than heroic one, which is not broken by evils. Christ willed to show his distinction in you, when a crowd of so many enemies had gathered to fill everything with slaughter. You did not hesitate to offer yourself of your own accord, not only to be laughed at and disfigured with beaks, but to be trampled, torn, destroyed, and pierced by the swords of all. The Lord favoured you too, since he who bravely began has so happily finished in triumph. The things I ask of you are not so difficult, nor so unworthy, if you consider the matter, though they may seem most unworthy; but I hope to act with you face to face, if the Lord grants it. I ask only this: that, giving thanks to the Lord for his great mercy and goodness, which has surrounded you on every side, you commend your enemies to the Lord; that you bear everything with a calmer mind; that you seek only the Lord, who heals, and the wrongdoers, that they may be converted. And if there are some who are willing and able to admonish the enemies together with you, listen to a few who tell of the wrongs of others, and trust still fewer. You see in Paul, whom you have made known to the whole world, what he brings to the whole assembly on account of a few, at times very much so. But who is there who would not laugh at me for writing this to you, if he understood? Shall I not rightly be called a sow teaching Minerva? But forgive this to our affection. Meanwhile hear what we are engaged in. I have a lawsuit with the parish priest of Crescentino. I ask that he look to his own interest and that of the parish, and that, as it concerns me, he be buried, though I do not care about this. He acknowledges some points for which he asks pardon; others he denies, and these I must prove. Guillaume Houbraque, whom the people of Laon once forbade, seizing his sacred Bibles and throwing them to the ground, also has a lawsuit with those who inflicted these insults on him. He has written some things about the Mass, for which some Swiss who keep the Mass are stirring up a certain man, so that they may act as they did against Michael. Meanwhile the good man goes on more happily than hitherto. He has free sermons and the use of the sacraments. Moreover, John Drogius, minister of Beauvais, whose wife has fallen into leprosy, although he took part in the synod and subscribed that marriage is not dissolved by leprosy, and it was so concluded by the votes of all, with the governor and all the orders approving; nevertheless, because the Germans think otherwise, although he has been with his wife and has had a son by her, not yet a full year has passed, and he nonetheless wishes to take another wife. The poor wife had been summoned without my knowledge, but by a colleague, with some others called together, so that she might give her assent; but she was unwilling to appear in person. She is pressed by her husband. She asks that, since little of life remains, he wait. If he is unwilling, let him see whether it can be done from the word of the Lord. If the Lord approves this, let us not disapprove. You see how he stands with his wife. Recently he was saying to the brethren that Watteville asked of the brethren that we give those things by which we might judge that it is not lawful, because of leprosy, for a healthy man to take another healthy wife. There I saw that things were not being done rightly, but that we were attacked obliquely. All of them, though I objected, entrusted this task to me. I flatly refused to do it. But you know the temper of our people: the more I refuse, the more they press. And so that I may not give others an occasion to oppose everyone's opinion, I was compelled to consent, if it were granted that I should ask others, since I do not think I am fit for this. Although I smell that my colleague is the author of the counsel, I hesitate whether an opportunity is being sought to set us against the Germans. Whatever happens, I wish your counsel to be followed. I should like, if it could be done, that enough be done for the reasons both of Bucer and of others. For what is said, that Paul brings forward other grounds for divorce than that one, which is alone adduced by Christ, when he speaks of the deserter, seems to me to have another aim. And what has the departing unbeliever in common with the believer who wishes to remain? You will provide not only for us, but also for others. I wish the Germans had as firm a heart in enduring leprosy in spouses as is to be praised in enduring plague. As for the magistrate, it is not only to be approved that he, more indulgent towards those he governs, consents on account of hardness of heart, that those separated and torn away from those whom the Lord has joined together should mourn with others, with whom they cannot be united without adultery. May Christ grant that this most sacred union be preserved pure, without any stain. Master Martin has not yet returned from the wedding of George. Would that he might accomplish something, which, so far as one can guess, does not appear. Tossanus never thought at all about how cleverly he acts and has acted; compelled and ordered by the Prince, though innocent and pure, he is assailed with slanders. Since those who were cast out could not bear to be carried, they were released kindly on account of the ministry; but when they received peace for those churches, that they would not disturb them, they neither keep quiet nor cease to act in every way contrary to what they promised. Tossanus now triumphs in earnest, and the innocent are the most guilty of all. Christ will at last put an end to so many and such great evils. In this cause I am slandered above all others, and although my conscience answers well and I should delight that these things happen to me on account of Christ, yet, aware of my own imprudence and of the flesh, which always opposes the spirit, I groan with the Apostle, so weak and so far from what ought to be present, and I ask pardon, in this joy and in the expected reward, which he who died for us gives and will give. I commend to you the wretched men whom Satan presses in this matter. Pray well for them, and, as far as possible, remember the good and forget the evil. See who you have become, and how many, and where you now are, so that you may always go on more and more vigorously; and see what that James says, who returned so beset. What does that answer to this grace, that you should rightly bear the rage of Satan, indeed laugh at it? I make no end, dealing with you unworthily, presuming on myself what is not permitted. As it is given to boys to play the fool, why should not something be given to me, twice a boy, who never was wise? Farewell, then, and bear all troubles for Christ's sake. I wish the colleagues safe, and I do not pass over Gallasius, Budé, Normandy, Brother Trier, and all. My colleague and the other brethren wish you well. Neuchâtel, 6th September 1555.

units.la: Tuus totus Farellus.
units.tr: Yours wholly, Farellus.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO. s. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET, greetings.

units.la: Litteras ad vos Stephani nostri, ex quibus intelligetis, quantumuis insaniat Satan, Christum tamen sub cruce regnare. De ludimagistro quod postulat,curæ nobis esse debet. Si quis erit apud vos idoneus, qui alacriter onus suscipiat, mittite. Nihil enim hic tentare volui. Cameraco nihil allatum est,post literas à fratribus scriptas,quas vobis legêdas mitto. Vbi legeritis statim mihi reddendas curate: quia apud me hactenus continui,atque in fratrum meorum permissu. Quàm atrociter me tota factio laceret, non ignoro: ac quotidie ex meo sensu experior, quantum à bonis naturis alienasit tyrannica crudelitas, quam vetus poeta describit his verbis, Oderint dum metuant. Atqui, si optio daretur, mallem omnium esse contemptissimus. Sed quia Deo aliter placet,feramus. Aderit tandem suis. Interim optima est bonæ conscientiæ fultura. Hodie Bertellerius aliorum morefactionem suam purgare conatus est: ipse tamen confessus est se dignum tali supplicio. Pluribus coram omnia referam. Hoc enim excepto,visus est aliqua resipiscentia tangi. Valete optimi fratres. Dominus vobis adsit,vos gubernet ac tueatur. Genevæ, 1 x. Septembris. M. D. LV.
units.tr: We send you the letter from our Stephen, from which you will understand that, however much Satan rages, Christ nevertheless reigns under the cross. As to the schoolmaster, which he asks for, we ought to take care of it. If there is anyone among you who is suitable and willing to take up the burden cheerfully, send him. For I did not want to attempt anything here. Nothing has been brought from Cambrai, after the letters written by the brothers, which I am sending you to be read. When you have read them, see that they are returned to me at once, since I have kept them with me until now, with the permission of my brothers. I am not unaware how savagely the whole faction tears me to pieces, and every day I experience from my own feeling how far tyrannical cruelty, which an old poet describes in these words, "Let them hate, provided they fear," is alien to good natures. Yet, if the choice were given, I would rather be the most despised of all. But since it pleases God otherwise, let us bear it. He will come at last to his own. Meanwhile the best support is a good conscience. Today Bertellerius has tried to clear his faction, as the others did, but he himself confessed that he deserved such punishment. I will report everything more fully in person. Apart from this, he seems to have been touched by some repentance. Farewell, best brothers. May the Lord be with you, govern you and keep you. Geneva, 10 September 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: Epist.212.
units.tr: Epist. 212.

units.la: Illustri ac magnifico Domino, D. Spiteko Inrdan à Zaklicźin & in Melstin haeredi Castellano Sandecźensi, Regni Poloniae supremo thesaurario.
units.tr: To the illustrious and magnificent Lord, Lord Spiteko Inrdan of Zaklicźin and Melstin, heir, castellan of Sandecz, supreme treasurer of the Kingdom of Poland.

units.la: {*}QVum in hoc fortunae honorisque splendore praecipuum tibi decus statuas illustris ac magnifice Domine, inter fyn ceros Dei cultores censeri: idque tuis literis, quas mihi venerandus frater noster N. ad se scriptis ostendit, abunde testatus: imo priu itim quoque asperseris iucundam amoris erga nos tui mentionem: mihi superuacua esse videtur excusatio, fide ac humanitate tua fretus, datam abs te scribendi fiduciam mihi sumo. Itaque certò persuasus, non ingratum tibi fore hoc officium, tui quoque hortandi partes libere suscipiam. Neque enim eum te hominem esse existimo, quem delectent inanes vel blanditiis refertae literae, quales ad captandam gratiam a ventosis hominibus scribi solent: sed à Christi seruo magis cupis & expectas, quod pietatis tuae progressus iuuet. Egregias ergo istas vir tu:es, quibus te excellere audio, non alium in finem laudare mihi propositum est, nisi ut assiduè in melius eniti pergas. Si in Polonia rite ex voto nostro compositus foret Regni Christi status, quanquam tibi facilius esset in tranquillo stadio rectum cursum tenere: res tamen altior est, nos approbare fynceros Dei cultores, quàm ut centesima officij parte fungantur, qui strenuè labo rando alios omnes superant. Nunc rebus confusis, vbi obeunda sunt multa certamina, resistendum fortiter hominum potentiū odiis, negligendi sinistri rumores, multi insultus sustinendi, lu-ctandum cum multis obstaculis, tentanda etiam disciplina, quàm tibi vtile sit, tum ad feruorem subinde incitari, tum ad constantiam animari, referre necesse non est: quia ipse plus satis expericeris. Iam verò cùm in ista dignitate magnum tibi onus sit impositum: non tamen cedit Deus iuri suo, neque defínit, quò te in altiore honoris gradu locauit, eò magis fidem tuam obstrictam sibi tenere. Nā quò plus apud quemque deposuit, eò etiam plus exigere aequum est. Ergo cùm te non hominem ex medio vulgo, sed vnum ex primariis inter paucos delegerit, quem ex densis ignorantiae tenebris liberatum, coelesti Euangelij doctrina illustraret: si hocinaestimabile beneficium suo pretio çsimas, hac lege tibi collatum esse memineris, vt aliis praeluceas. Et certè vides quàm multorum in te coniecti sint oculi, vt eos tuum exemplum vel moretur, vel extimulet: ac simul cogites, si tuę desidiae mediocris esse nō potest iactura, culpam quoque non minorem
units.tr: Illustrious and magnificent Lord, since you rank it as your special distinction, amid the splendour of fortune and honour, to be counted among the sincere worshippers of God, and since you have amply shown this in the letter you wrote to our venerable brother N., which he showed me, and even earlier made pleasant mention of your affection towards us, an excuse seems superfluous to me. Relying on your good faith and courtesy, I take up the freedom you have given me to write. I am persuaded that this office will not be unwelcome to you, and so I will freely undertake also the part of exhorting you. For I do not think you are the sort of man who is pleased by empty letters, full of flattery, such as windy men usually write to win favour. Rather, as a servant of Christ, you desire and expect something that will help your progress in piety. My purpose in praising the outstanding qualities for which I hear you excel is no other than that you should keep striving constantly towards what is better. If the state of Christ's kingdom in Poland had been arranged according to our wish, it would be easier for you to keep a straight course on a tranquil racecourse. But the matter is too high for us to approve sincere worshippers of God who labour vigorously and surpass all others, as if they had performed even the hundredth part of their duty. Now that affairs are in confusion, where many struggles must be undertaken, the hatred of powerful men must be resisted bravely, unfavourable rumours must be disregarded, many assaults must be endured, many obstacles must be fought, and church discipline must be attempted, there is no need to relate how useful it is for you both to be stirred up to fervour from time to time and encouraged to constancy, because you yourself experience this more than enough. Now, since a great burden has been laid upon you in this dignity, God does not give up his right, nor does he limit the higher degree of honour to which he has raised you by holding your faith all the more bound to himself. For the more one has been entrusted with, the more it is fair to demand. Therefore, since he has chosen you, not a man from the common crowd but one of the few foremost men, and has freed you from the dense darkness of ignorance to illuminate you with the heavenly doctrine of the Gospel, if you value this inestimable benefit at its worth, remember that it was conferred on you on this condition: that you should shine light on others. And certainly you see how many eyes are fixed on you, so that your example may either restrain or spur them on; and at the same time consider that if the loss from your sloth cannot be small, the blame will be no less

units.la: {*} Epist. 213. norem fore.Hæc verò præclara bene agendi occasio & facultas, quòd Regia Maiestas adeò nò aduersabitur sanctis tuis studiis, vt potiùs manum porrigere sit parata, nisi animum tibi addat, excusationem adimet.Neque enim vsque ad sanguinem tibi certandum est:sicuti multi in Gallia nostra fideles,quos omnia adiumenta deficiunt, quotidie pro fidei suae confessione capita in sacrificium offerre coguntur. Quando longè mitius tecum agi vides, animosius ac magis strenuè exequi conuenit, quod tibi est ad manum, vt te Regi serenissimo in repurgandis Papatus sordibus fidum comitem ac ministrum exhibeas. Atque vtinam reipsa ostendere liceret,quo animo hæc scribo.Sed quia vereor, ne tuae in alienda Christi gloria fortitudinai diffidere videar, meipsum cohibeo.Hoc restat,vt pro beneuolentiae comitatisque testimonio, quod in tuis ad N.literis perspexi, vicissim mea tibi obsequia,méq; adeò totum,quantulus sum, deferam. Deum interea precabor vt te diu seruet incolumé,Spiritu suo regat,præsi lióque tueatur.Vale,magnifice & insignis Domine. Geneuæ, Idibus Septembris. M. D. LV.
units.tr: be no less. This is a splendid opportunity and means for acting well: the Royal Majesty will not so much oppose your holy endeavours, but rather is ready to extend his hand to you, unless you lack the courage, which would take away your excuse. For you do not have to contend to the point of bloodshed, as many faithful in our France do, who lack every aid and are forced daily to offer their heads in sacrifice for the confession of their faith. Since you see that you are being dealt with much more gently, it is fitting that you carry out with greater spirit and vigour what lies to hand, so that you may show yourself a faithful companion and minister to the most serene King in cleansing the filth of Papacy. Would that it were possible to show in fact with what spirit I write these things! But because I fear I may seem to distrust your courage in promoting the glory of Christ, I restrain myself. It remains only that, in return for the testimony of goodwill and courtesy which I have perceived in your letter to N., I offer you my services in turn, and myself entirely, such as I am. Meanwhile I shall pray God to keep you safe for a long time, to rule you by his Spirit, and to protect you. Farewell, magnificent and distinguished Lord. Geneva, the Ides of September, 1555.

units.la: PHILIPPVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: PHILIP TO BULLINGER, GREETING.

units.la: Eucrēde vir,& charissime frater, cum allata essent exempla tui scripti ... statim em i & legi, ac laetatus sum cōsensu vestrarum ac nostrarum Ecclesiarum.Postea tuas literas,& librum à te missum accepi Tibi igitur & pro beneuolentia erga me tua,& pro munere gratias ago.Legietiam quę de Scrueti blasphemiis respondistis, & pietatem ac iudicia vestra probo. Iudico etiam Senatum Geneuensem recte fecisse, ꝗ hominem pertinacem & non omisurum blasphemias sustulit. Ac miratus sum esse,qui seueritatem illam improbent. Mitto de ea quæstione breues pagellas,sed tamen sententiae nostrae testes, Quidā veteres amici mei minitātur mihi,se ... contra me scripturos est,si quid edent, nominatim contra me, decreui Deo iuuante respondere , etiamsi hoc certamen omitti malim. Pios & doctos de re tanta placidè colloqui vtilius esset. Oro autem Filium Dei, vt nos omnes gubernet, sanet Ecclesiae vulnera,Bene & felicitèr vale,charissime frater.Die x x.Augusti. Salutem opto vobis omnibus.
units.tr: Excellent man and most dear brother, when examples of your writing were brought to me, I at once read them and rejoiced at the agreement of your churches and ours. Afterwards I received your letter and the book you sent. So I thank you both for your goodwill towards me and for the gift. I have also read what you have replied about the blasphemies of Servetus, and I approve your piety and your judgments. I also judge that the Senate of Geneva acted rightly in removing a man who was obstinate and would not cease from blasphemy, and I am amazed that there are some who disapprove of that severity. I send brief pages on that question, which are at least witnesses of our opinion. Some of my old friends threaten that they will write against me by name if they publish anything. With God's help I have decided to reply, although I would rather this contest were avoided. It would be more useful for the pious and learned to discuss so great a matter calmly. I pray the Son of God to govern us all and to heal the wounds of the Church. Farewell well and happily, most dear brother. 20 August. I wish health to you all.

units.la: BVLINGERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: BULLINGER TO CALVIN, GREETINGS

units.la: Accipe charissime mi frater & D.colendissime,exempla epistolarum harum. Putaui in hisce esse, quae te omnino scire conueniat. Ideo per generum meum describi curaui. Copiofiores literas adferat D.Thomas Lenerus Anglus,cui heri tibi ferendas tradidi. Opportunè nunc aderat Dominus Crispinus noster,cui has dare volui. Vale. Tigùri,vltima Septembr. M. D. L V.
units.tr: Accept, dearest brother and most honoured Lord, copies of these letters. I thought there were in them things which it is fitting for you to know altogether. I therefore took care to have them copied through my son-in-law. Master Thomas Lever, an Englishman, who will bring fuller letters, to whom I handed yours yesterday to carry, is at hand just now; our Lord Crispin, to whom I wished to give these, has also arrived opportunely. Farewell. Zurich, the last day of September, 1555.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO s. d.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL, GREETINGS

units.la: EGo verò mi Farelle,etsi gloriari merito in his probris licet, quae in me congerunt virulentae ac petulantes linguae,quando nihil in me infamant nisi quod Deo & Angelis probari scio:cuperem tamen in recessu aliquo latere,si forte mitigaretur istorum furor, quem mea praefentia accendere videtur. Non de quisquam liis loquor,quas pridem floccifacere, vt merentur, didici.Sed à gigantibus caelum,odio mei,assiduè turbari,non absre mihi dolet.Feramus tamen,quando scimus non fortuito accidere,vt tantis procellis iactemur. Vvefphalus etiam librum in me truculentum edidit,cui nescio an respondere expediat. Rogant amici quidam:vbi perlegero, Dominus consilium suggeret. Tu verò,quasi libros momento gignerem simul ac parerem, velles à me plures exire commentarios,quàm scribendis sufficiat longae vitae cursus in summo otio.Mihi verò quantulum vacui tem poris restare putas?Vtinam alij has vices obeant potius. Philippo acerrimus ero hortator:sed quàm lentus sit,nō ignoras.Vale optime & integerrime frater.Dominus tibi semper adsit,te protegat ac sustentet. Fratres & amici te plurimùm salutant,atque in his Beza noster qui nunc mecum est. Geneuae, x.Octobris. M. D. L V.
units.tr: Indeed, my Farel, although I may rightly boast in these reproaches which the venomous and insolent tongues heap upon me, since they defame me in nothing except what I know is approved before God and the angels, I would still wish to lie hidden in some retreat, if perhaps the fury of those men, which my presence seems to inflame, might be softened. I am not speaking of any individuals, whom I have long learned to regard as worthless, as they deserve. But that heaven is constantly disturbed by giants hostile to me does not grieve me greatly. Let us bear it, since we know that it does not happen by chance that we are tossed about by such great storms. Westphal also has published a savage book against me, and I do not know whether it is expedient to answer it. Some friends ask: once I have read it through, the Lord will suggest a plan. As for you, you seem to think I beget books the moment I give birth to them, and would have me send out more commentaries than the course of a long life, even in great leisure, would suffice to write. Yet how much free time do you think I have left? Would that others would rather take up these duties. I would be a most eager urger on Philip, but you know how slow he is. Farewell, most excellent and upright brother. May the Lord always be with you and keep and sustain you. The brothers and friends salute you warmly, and among them our Beza, who is now with me. Geneva, 10th October, 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: CAL. PIPERINO s. d.
units.tr: CALVIN TO PIPERINUS, GREETINGS

units.la: EQuidem dum passim tam atrociter me proscindi audio,nō ita sum ferreus,mi Piperine,quin dolore pungar.Sed hoc mihi saltem nō leue solatium est,te & complures alios Christi seruos, & pios Dei cultores meis iniuriis condolescere. Quanquam mallem si fieri posset, solus tacitè vorare quicquid in me probrorū congeritur:ne qua inde pars molestiae in fratres meos redundaret.Itaque haec quoque ratio inter alias facit,vt silentio calumnias praeteream,quas aliàqui diluere nullo negotio promptum esset, & quas à me excutere cuperem. Cur enim mei purgandi studio probos homines obtunderem? Si maior necessitas vrgeret,petita venia, defensionem proponerem. Sed futilior est probrorum,quibus me improbi aspergunt, vanitas,quàm vt solicita licita refutatione opus habeat. Ipsi quoq; auctores me ambitionis notarent, ac si de tuenda mea existimatione nimis essem anxius. Exemplum est in illa ingenti quam commemoras pecuniæ summa. Sciunt omnes quàm frugaliter viuam domi meæ: vident in vestium splendore nullum sumptum fieri: palàm apparet, extrem meum vnicum nec valde esse locupletem, nec meis opibus adeptum esse quicquid habet. Vbinam ergo defossus iaceret the-saurus ille? Atqui me pauperibus furatum esse iactant. Hoc etiam improbissimi de nihilo fictum esse fateri cogentur. Si quid pauperibus erogant pij homines, nullum nummum attingo. Mortuus est apud me ante octo annos vir quidam nobilis, qui apud me supra duo coronatorum millia sine chirographo depositurat. Vbi mortis esse periculum intellexi, quum meo arbitrio permittere vellet, negaui me id suscepturum oneris. Curaui etiam vt Argentinam mitti iuberet octingentos, subleuandæ exulum inopiæ. Meo hortatu delegit homines minime suspectos, qui reliquâ summâm distribuerent. Mihi quum legare vellet quod alij non spreuisset, recusaui: sed video quid vrat meos aduersarios. Quia enim ex suo me ingenio metiuntur, non dubitant quin vndiq; accumulè, vbi tam opportuna suppetit facultas. Verùm, si viuus non effugio nomen diuitis, ab hac nota morstandem me vindicabit. Cæterùm, nullùs mihi esset scribendi finis, si ad meditandam apologiam animum adiecero. Multa iltic si iactantur, scito vix centesimam esse eorum partem, quibus assiduè obtundor. Er go nihil superesset, nisi vt paratus ad reddedam rationem nihilominus os præbeam colaphis. Pergamus mi Christophore, per in samiam & bonam famam, neq; sinistris rumoribus frangi nos sinamus. Quanquam si tu fontem terreas, mecum facilè agnoscet patientia vincendum esse. Nemini enim verbum facere in metem veniret, nisi quisquiliæ hominum videret se Proceribus officium præstare, ac paratam sibi esse maledicentiæ mercedem, subitòque euanescerent mendacia, rursus ab iisdem illis in quorum gratiam confecta sunt, foucrentur. Quia epistolam cogor abrum pere, finem hic faciam. Vale optime, & mihi amicissime frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit, te Spiritu suo gubernet, laboresque tuos benedicat. Geneuæ, x viii. Octob. M. D. LV.
units.tr: Indeed, while I hear myself torn to pieces so savagely on every side, my Piperinus, I am not so made of iron as not to be pricked with grief. Yet this is at least no small consolation to me, that you and many other servants of Christ and pious worshippers of God sympathise with my injuries. Although I would prefer, if it could be done, to swallow quietly alone whatever reproaches are heaped upon me, lest any part of the annoyance flow back upon my brothers. And so this consideration too, among others, leads me to pass over in silence the calumnies which I could otherwise refute with no trouble at all, and which I would wish to shake off. For why should I, in zeal to clear myself, wear out good men? If a greater necessity pressed, I would, with pardon sought, put forward a defence. But the emptiness of the reproaches with which the wicked besmirch me is too trivial to need a careful refutation. The very authors would brand me as ambitious, as if I were too anxious to guard my reputation. The case of that huge sum of money which you mention is an example. Everyone knows how frugally I live at home; they see that no extravagance is practised in the splendour of my clothing; it is plain that my only brother is not very wealthy, and that he has gained nothing he possesses through my resources. Where then would that treasure lie buried? Yet they boast that I have robbed the poor. The most wicked men will be forced to confess that this too was invented out of nothing. If godly men give anything to the poor, I do not touch a single coin. Eight years ago a certain noble man died in my house, who had deposited with me more than two thousand crowns without a written receipt. When he realised there was danger of death, and wished to entrust it to my judgment, I refused to take on that burden. I also took care that he ordered eight hundred to be sent to Strasbourg, to relieve the poverty of the exiles. At my urging he chose men least open to suspicion to distribute the remaining sum. When he wished to leave me something which the others had not scorned, I refused; but I see what burns my adversaries. For since they measure me by their own nature, they do not doubt that I would heap up wealth on every side, whenever so opportune an opportunity presents itself. But if while alive I do not escape the name of rich man, death will at last free me from this stain. Moreover, there would be no end to my writing if I were to apply my mind to composing an apology. If many things are bandied about there, know that they are scarcely the hundredth part of those with which I am constantly battered. Therefore nothing would remain but that, ready to give an account, I should nonetheless offer my face to the blows. Let us go on, my Christopher, and let us not allow ourselves to be broken by ill rumours, provided our good name and integrity remain. Although, if you fear the source, you will agree with me that it must be overcome by patience. For no one would think of making an accusation, unless he saw that these trifles of men render service to the great, and that a reward for slander is ready for them; and immediately the lies would vanish, and be cherished again by the very same people in whose favour they were concocted. Since I am compelled to break off the letter, I will make an end here. Farewell, most excellent, and my dearest brother. May the Lord always be with you, govern you by his Spirit, and bless your labours. Geneva, 18th October, 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: AD SERENISSIMVM REGEM POLONIÆ.
units.tr: TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF POLAND.

units.la: Etsi non miror, præstantissime Rex, nec dubito quo tempore Maiestas Vestra conuentum ordinum regni sui agebat, in tanta negotiorum mole, summis & variis curis fuisse distriḉtam, vt ne perlegendæ quidem meæ cohortationi otium suppeteret: tamen ex quo plus otij datum fuit, confido aliquid vacui & soluti temporis sumpsisse, vt meus labor tandem non fuerit inutilis. Nam ex literis quas M V. mittere dignata est, intelligo, meam sedulitatem gratam fuisse: nec fastidio vel contemptu reiectum fuisse meum illud scriptum, in quo breuiter ostendere conatus fueram quænam vera esset reformandæ Ecclesiæ ratio, & quisnam commodissimus ingressus. Imò quia M. V. illud & humaniter excepisse, & libenter se inspexisse testatur, & vbi li berius otium contigerit, sibi in animo esse attentius singulas eius partes meditari, plus inde fiduciæ ad iterandum scribendi officium offerri mihi visum est. Itaque si nunc rursus M. Vestram cohortari audeo, non videtur esse cur de venia petenda laborè, ac ne longior quidem excusatio necessaria est. Non sum equidem nescius, vel immemor quantum à Celsitudine in qua magnum Regem Deus locauit, distet humilis mea & abiecta condi-tio: sed quia probè tenet M. V. quid valeat illud cœleste edictū, quo iubentur omnes Regesterræ Filium Dei osculari, nec ignorat externo osculi ritu notari fidei obsequium, quod reuerenter sanctas admonitiones à Christi ore & Spiritu profestas ample-ctitur, mihi videtur eximi omnis metus & dubitatio. Ego igitur, quem summus Rex Euangelij sui præconem & Ecclesiæ suæ Ministrum constituit, eius nomine M V. appello, cum iam in Polonia ex funestis tenebris Papatus emergere cœperit vera religio, cum multi pij & cordati homines, abiectis impiis superstitionibus, ad purum Dei cultum vltrò aspirent, vt curam hanc aliis omnibus præferat. Et certè quanto æterna Dei gloria vmbratilem & caducum huius mundi statum præcellit, ita ad tuedam vel asserendum pietatis dostrinam, posthabitis aliis omnibus, præcipua nostra studia conferre decet. Quod hactenus Polonia Papatus corruptelis fœdata, & vitiato peruersóque Dei cultu, post humana figmenta vagata est: quòd denique sub errorum colluuie demersa, cœlestis lucis aspectu caruit, triste ac miserum fuit spectaculum. Nunc verò cùm illa communi amentia & stupore, quo percussus fuit totus orbis, eam Dominus liberare incipiat, summos quosque & infimos à suo tot pore expergefieri necesse est. An igitur Regibus cessandū, quos ideo in sublime Deus extulit, vt inde gentibus vniuersis præluceant? Iam verò quanti nobis esse debeat syncera religio, per quam Christo inter nos tribunal erigitur, quanti etiam legitimus Dei cultus, in quo symbolum præsentiæ eius, viuáque imago relucet, M. V. me tacente satis intelligit. Et sanè nisi ad nos hac in parte animandos, vel vnum Dauidis exemplum sufficit, minimè excusabilis est nostra segnities. Cùm enim tunc non nisi sub obscuris figuris in terre-stri
units.tr: Although I am not surprised, most excellent King, and I do not doubt that, while Your Majesty was holding the assembly of the orders of your realm, you were so occupied by the great weight of affairs, with their many and pressing cares, that you had no leisure even to read through my exhortation. Still, I trust that since more free time has been given to you, you have found some empty and unbound hours, so that my labour may not have been wasted in the end. For from the letter which Your Majesty has deigned to send, I understand that my diligence was welcome, and that my writing was not rejected with disdain or contempt. In that work I tried to show briefly what the true method of reforming the Church is, and what the most suitable way in is. Indeed, since Your Majesty has testified that you received it kindly and read it willingly, and that when you have more leisure you intend to consider each of its parts more carefully, I thought I had more reason to hope that I might venture to write again. So if I now dare to exhort Your Majesty once more, there seems to be no reason to ask pardon for it, and no lengthy excuse is needed. I am not unaware, nor forgetful, of how far my humble and lowly condition is from that exalted station in which God has placed a great King. But since Your Majesty understands well the force of that heavenly edict by which all the kings of the earth are commanded to kiss the Son of God, and since you know that by the outward rite of the kiss is signified the obedience of faith, which reverently embraces the holy admonitions that come from the mouth and Spirit of Christ, it seems to me that all fear and hesitation should be removed. I therefore, whom the highest King has appointed as herald of his Gospel and minister of his Church, appeal to Your Majesty in his name. Now that true religion has begun to emerge in Poland out of the deadly darkness of Papacy, and now that many pious and sensible men, having cast off impious superstitions, are eagerly striving for the pure worship of God, Your Majesty should give this concern precedence over all others. And certainly, just as the eternal glory of God surpasses the shadowy and fleeting state of this world, so it is fitting that our chief efforts be directed, above all else, to guarding and defending the doctrine of piety. Hitherto Poland, defiled by the corruptions of Papacy and by a corrupt and perverted worship of God, has wandered after human inventions; and that, sunk under the filth of errors and deprived of the sight of heavenly light, it has been a sad and miserable spectacle. But now, since the Lord is beginning to free it from that common madness and stupor by which the whole world has been struck, it is necessary that all, high and low alike, be roused from their sleep. Ought kings then to hold back, whom God has raised on high for this very purpose, that from them they may shine light upon all peoples? Indeed, how much sincere religion ought to mean to us, through which a tribunal for Christ is set up among us, and how much the lawful worship of God means, in which the symbol of his presence and his living image shine forth, Your Majesty understands well enough without my saying so. And indeed, unless the single example of David is enough to rouse us in this matter, our sloth is by no means excusable. For although the fathers worshipped God in the earthly sanctuary only under obscure figures, yet we read of the solemn oath that he swore: that he would not give sleep to his eyes, nor slumber to his eyelids, nor enter the doors of his house, until he had found a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. If the devout anxiety for the legal worship did not allow that King to rest, so that he was no less anxiously and constantly intent, night and day, on seeking a resting place for the ark of the covenant, how much more ought the zeal for the spiritual worship of God now to seize the heart of a Christian King, and inflame all his efforts more keenly, so that he may undertake this so honourable and splendid task, that Christ may be exalted? Moreover, although David was deprived of the honour of building the temple, he nevertheless did not cease, throughout the whole course of his life, to gather together stones, materials, silver and gold, so that his successor Solomon, furnished with every resource, might immediately and without delay set himself more eagerly to the work. All the more eagerly ought a Christian King to gather all his strength to restore the temple of God and to strive with the utmost effort, lest the worship of God lie neglected for longer amid shapeless ruins. Although obstacles never fail to delay this pious undertaking, the situation of Your Majesty is much easier than that of the pious kings Hezekiah and Josiah of old, for whom the struggle with a stubborn people was arduous and hard; whereas today the Polish nobility, for the most part, offers a ready and eager obedience in embracing the faith of Christ. With such help the wise King ought to rouse himself, so that he may himself no less vigorously stretch out his hand in return. Nor indeed should ears be given here to flatteries, by which Satan, sprinkling a deadly chill through profane men, pours an idle drowsiness over the senses of many. Rather, every sluggishness must be shaken off, and one must press on with hands and feet in so noble a work, especially when the opportunity for acting appears ripe; for if an occasion offered by God is neglected, one will afterwards stand in vain at a closed door. Meanwhile we will pray with constant vows that the Lord, by his incredible power, may bring to a happy conclusion the work he has begun, may furnish Your Majesty with a heroic spirit, and may keep you safe in a prosperous state. Geneva, the day before the Lord's Nativity, 1555. I desire that he who has been given by the Father to hold supreme dominion be received reverently in your palace, as is his right, and be honoured by all.

units.la: Psal. 2. 12. ftri Sanctuario Deum colerent Patres, refertur tamen folenne quod concepit iusiurandum, quòd non daturus effet somnum oculis suis, nec palpebris dormitatione, nec ingressurus postes domus suæ, donec inuenisset locum Domino, tabernaculum Deo Iacob.Si Regem illum pia folicitudo legalis cultus quiescere passa non est, quin noctes & dies ad quærendam arcæ fœderis stationem non minus anxiè quàm assidue intentus foret, quanto magis nunc Christiani Regis studium ad se rapere debet spiritualis Dei cultus, omnésque eius conatus acrius accendere, ad obeundum hoc tam honorificum & præclarum munus, vt Christus emineat? Accedit etiam quòd Dauid quanuis extruendi templi honore priuatus esset, non tamen cessauit toto vitæ suæ cursu lapides, materiam, argentum & aurum congerere, quò succeßor Solomo copiis omnibus instructus, statim sine mora ad opus se alacrius accingeret. Quò animosius Christianum Regem vires omnes suas ad restituendum Dei templum colligere ac summopere eniti decet, ne diutius inter deformes ruinas, cultus Dei obsoletus iaceat. Etsi autem nunquam desunt obstacula, quæ pium hoc studium morentur, longè tamen Maiestatis Vestræ expeditio est ratio, quàm olim piis Regibus Ezechiæ & Iosiæ, quibus arduum, & durum cum populi contumacia certamen fuit, cùm hodie Polonica nobilitas magna ex parte, promptum & alacre ad suscipiendam Christi fidem obsequium offerat. Quo adiumento sic expergefieri cordatum Regem decet, vt non minus strenuè manum ipse vicissim porrigat. Nec verò hîc blanditiis dandæ sunt aures, quibus Satan per homines profanos letale frigus aspergens, ignauo sopore multorum sensus perfundit. Quin potius excutlo omni torpore, manibus & pedibus in tam præclaro opere insistendum est, ac præsertim vbi apparet agendi maturitas: ne si oblata diuinitus occasio negligitur, frustra deinde standum sit ad clausam ianuam. Interea assiduis votis precabimur, vt Dominus pro sua incredibili potentia opus quod cœpit, fœliciter absoluat, Miestatem Vestram heroico spiritu instruat, & in statu prospero incolumem tueatur. Geneuæ, pridie natalis Domini, quem cupio sicuti summo imperio à Patre donatus est, ita reuerenter in Palatium vestrum excipi, vt iure suo ab omnibus colatur.

Moreover, although David was deprived of the honour of building the temple, he nevertheless did not cease, throughout the whole course of his life, to gather together stones, materials, silver and gold, so that his successor Solomon, furnished with every resource, might immediately and without delay set himself more eagerly to the work. All the more eagerly ought a Christian King to gather all his strength to restore the temple of God and to strive with the utmost effort, lest the worship of God lie neglected for longer amid shapeless ruins. Although obstacles never fail to delay this pious undertaking, the situation of Your Majesty is much easier than that of the pious kings Hezekiah and Josiah of old, for whom the struggle with a stubborn people was arduous and hard; whereas today the Polish nobility, for the most part, offers a ready and eager obedience in embracing the faith of Christ. With such help the wise King ought to rouse himself, so that he may himself no less vigorously stretch out his hand in return. Nor indeed should ears be given here to flatteries, by which Satan, sprinkling a deadly chill through profane men, pours an idle drowsiness over the senses of many. Rather, every sluggishness must be shaken off, and one must press on with hands and feet in so noble a work, especially when the opportunity for acting appears ripe; for if an occasion offered by God is neglected, one will afterwards stand in vain at a closed door. Meanwhile we will pray with constant vows that the Lord, by his incredible power, may bring to a happy conclusion the work he has begun, may furnish Your Majesty with a heroic spirit, and may keep you safe in a prosperous state. Geneva, the day before the Lord's Nativity, which I desire to be received reverently into your palace, as the Father has given him supreme dominion, so that by right he may be honoured by all.

units.la: M. D. LV.
units.tr: M. D. LV.

units.la: Tuæ Maiestatis studiosissimus Ioannes Calvinus.
units.tr: Your Majesty's most devoted servant, John Calvin.

units.la: MAGNIFICO DOMINO STANISLAO LAS-foczki Subcamerario Terrae Lankzcienfis.
units.tr: To the noble lord Stanislaus Las-foczki, Subchamberlain of the Land of Lankzcien.

units.la: EGo vero tibi eximie vir ex animo gratulor, q; rebus adhuc istic dubiis,omni simulatione deposita libere professus fis,te vnum esse ex eorum numero, quibus nihil potius est, quàm obedieter sequi quò nos Filius Dei vocat.Hæc fynceritas omnes Dei filios,vbi de legitimo agitur eius cultu,apprime decet,vt nō vacillent ad quamlibet auram flexibiles,neque aliunde pende-ant,sed fundati sint in firma illa rupe,quæ nec ventos vllos,nec tempestates,vel procellas extimescit.Tenenda enim est illa pro-missio,qua Efaias fideles ad fortitudinem animat, Dominum e-xercituum sanctificate, ipse quoque erit pauor vester & arx in-expugnabilis Nam hunc ipse sibi honorem merito vult haberi, vt eius virtute confisi,quod præcipit & mandat, fine mora am-plectamur.Tu vero,ornatissime vir,re ipsa testatus es de fugien-dis superstitionibus non obscurum tibi esse eius præceptum,qui sacrilegio Papalis Missę valere iusso,sacræ Cœnæ actionem quæ instituit Christus ac fanciuit, palam in vsum reuocare ausus es: ac fi erecto vexillo,ex misera Papatus dissipatione reliquias col-ligeres ad fidei vnitatem. Euge ergo, generose Christi miles,& quod semel ingressus es stadium, ad metam vsque percurre,nec vllis obstaculis cedas, nec aliorum torpore remittas animu.nec vllis difficultatibus fatigeris,donecChriftus,qui noster est in hoc certamine Agonothetes æterna gloriæ palma te dignetur.Idem vero e cœlo infractas ad perfeuerădum viresfuggeret.Vt homo ignotus literis te compellarem,factum est fratris nostri N.horta-tu:has tamen partes libenter suscepi,vt intelligeres esse etiam in longinquis regionibus:qui licet coram suppetias non ferant,vo-tis & precibus,iuuare te contendunt. Vale magnifice Domine. Dominus te Spiritu suo regere pergat, sanctosque tuos conatus benedicat. Geneuæ,I III.Calendas Ian. M. D. LV.
units.tr: I heartily congratulate you, distinguished sir, because, with the matters there still doubtful, you have laid aside all pretence and openly professed yourself to be one of those who think nothing more important than to follow obediently where the Son of God calls us. This sincerity especially befits all the sons of God, whenever the question concerns the lawful worship of Him, so that they do not waver, swayed by every breeze, nor depend on other things, but are founded on that firm rock which fears no winds, no storms, nor tempests. For that promise must be held fast, by which Isaiah encourages the faithful to courage: "Sanctify the Lord of hosts; He himself also shall be your fear and your impregnable fortress." For He rightly wishes this honour to be paid to Himself: that, trusting in His strength, we embrace without delay what He commands and orders. You, most distinguished sir, have in fact shown by your deeds that the precept of Him who forbids superstitions is not obscure to you: you have bidden farewell to the sacrilege of the Papal Mass and have dared to restore openly to use the action of the Holy Supper which Christ instituted and sanctioned, as though, with a banner raised, you were gathering the remnants out of the wretched scattering of Papacy into the unity of faith. Well done then, noble soldier of Christ! Having entered the race, run it to the goal; yield to no obstacles, and do not let your spirit slacken through the sluggishness of others. Let no difficulties weary you, until Christ, who is our Agonothetes in this contest, deems you worthy of the palm of eternal glory. May He also pour into you from heaven strength unbroken for persevering. I was prompted by our brother N. to write to you, an unknown man, by letter; yet I have gladly undertaken this role, so that you may understand that there are also, in distant regions, those who, though they do not bring help in person, strive to assist you with their wishes and prayers. Farewell, noble lord. May the Lord continue to rule you by His Spirit and bless your holy endeavours. Geneva, on the 29th of December, 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: ILLVSTRI VIRO AC EXIMIIS VIRTVTIBVS Præstantissimo D.Ioanni Comiti Tarnouio Castellano Cracouiensi,exercituum Regni Poloniæ supre-mo Duci.
units.tr: To the illustrious man, endowed with outstanding virtues, the most distinguished Lord John, Count Tarnow, Castellan of Kraków, Supreme Commander of the armies of the Kingdom of Poland.

units.la: VIde quantum mihi fiduciæ præbeat virtutis tuæ fama,Illu-ftriffime Domine, quam apud me non vulgaribus elogiis celebrauit fidus & idoneus testis N.nepe vt homo tibi for-te intè incognitos non modò literis meis te cópellare, sed de re quoque omnium maxima familiariter apud te disserere, & adsubeundas oneris huius de quo agitur, partes cohortari audeam. Primum de regno Poloniæ ad puram & genuinam Christi fidem revocando mediocris spes affulserat. Etsi autem obliquis Satanæ artibus iniectæ sunt multiplices remoræ, nunc demum ianuam filio suo Deus aperuit, ex qua vos omnes ad eum reuerenter excipiédum inuitat. Et multi quidem, vt audio, cupidè obuiam accurrunt, & quæ debent pietatis officia cœlesti regi offerunt: vt in ordine nobilium non minus ad recipiendam doctrinæ puritatem vigeat sancta conspiratio, quàm Christi hostes ad impediendum Euangelij cursum peruicaciter inter se coniurant. Te verò præstantissime vir, qui summa auctoritate polles, & in quê non minus Regis quàm aliorum coniecti sunt oculi, aliis strenuè festinantibus, vel quiescere, vel tardius progredi minimè consentaneum est. Nec verò Deus alia lege in hunc dignitatis gradum te extulit, nisi vt è sublimi vexillo aliis monstres, ex cuius conspectu crescat omnibus studij alacritas. Iam quum prudentia & consilio non minus excellas, quàm honore, minimè deceret tot præclaros antesignanos, qui in certamine liberè & intrepidè progressi sunt, à Duce suo deflexi. Etsi enim non ignoro præcipuas esse serenissimi Regis partes, quia tamen sponte iam ad recte agendum propensus, vbi te certû adiutorem & comitem nactus erit, multò confidentius vt spero, neruos suos intendet, merito hoc abs te Christus exigere videtur, vt tot generosis suis militibus Ducem te ostendas. Ac iam quidem eousque progressus es, vt de syncero animi tui affectu exempla sit omnis dubitatio. Tantum vereor ne cunctando, nimis longum tempus effluat. Et certè hactenus in tarditate plus satis culpæ fuit. Nunc verò ad ingenuam, & apertam doctrinæ suæ professionem & Regem ipsum, & Proceres omnes sonora voce inclamat idem ille, qui Euangelio suo ianuam aperit. Quare tibi præstantissime vir, in mentem veniat illa Prophetæ admonitio, Tempore beneplaciti audiui te, & die salutis adiuui te, quæ omnes Dei filios ad visitationis suæ tempus sedulò amplexandum solicitat, ne gratia semel oblata, si per ignauiam negligatur, tandem pereat. Quia sæpe accidere solet, vt læta exordia dum fœlicem exitum promittunt, segnitiem multis adducant, prudenter cauendum est, ne quis ad suffocandam hanc lucem quæ emergere cœpit, obrepat torpor. Modum quidem mihi tenendum esse non ignoro, ne acrius vrgendo pietati tuæ diffidere videar: sed rursum tam præstantia operis, quàm difficultas, ad stimulos addendos me cogit, ne quid in te desiderent fideles Christi serui, quod tantæ existimationis viro dignum sit. Summa tamen huc redit, quum vnicus nobis viuendi finis esse debeat,
units.tr: I see how much confidence the reputation of your virtue gives me, most illustrious Lord, since a faithful and reliable witness, N., has praised you to me in no ordinary terms. For this reason I dare not only to address you in my letter, but also to discuss with you, on familiar terms, a matter of the greatest importance, and to urge you to take up the part of the burden about which we are speaking. At first there had been a modest hope that the kingdom of Poland would be called back to the pure and genuine faith of Christ. Although many obstacles have been thrown in by the crafty arts of Satan, God has now at last opened to his Son the door through which he invites all of you to receive him reverently. Many, as I hear, eagerly run to meet him and offer the duties of piety that they owe to the heavenly King, so that among the nobility a holy alliance flourishes no less to receive the purity of doctrine than Christ's enemies stubbornly conspire together to hinder the course of the Gospel. But you, most distinguished man, who hold the highest authority, and upon whom the eyes of the King and of everyone else are fixed, it is in no way fitting that you should rest or advance more slowly while others are eager to press on. Nor has God raised you to this rank of dignity on any other condition than that you should show others the way from this lofty standard, from the sight of which zeal for the work may grow in everyone. Since you excel no less in prudence and counsel than in honour, it would scarcely be proper for you, as leader, to turn aside from so many distinguished standard-bearers who have advanced boldly and fearlessly into the struggle. For although I am not unaware that the principal role belongs to the most serene King, nevertheless, since he is already inclined of his own accord to act rightly, once he has you as a sure helper and companion, I hope he will stretch his sinews far more confidently. Christ seems rightly to require this of you: that you show yourself a leader to so many noble soldiers of his. Indeed, you have already advanced so far that there can be no doubt about the sincerity of your inclination. I only fear that by delaying too long a great deal of time will slip away. And certainly until now there has been more than enough blame for the slowness. Now, however, the same One who opens the door to his Gospel calls loudly, both to the King himself and to all the nobles, to make an open and honest profession of his doctrine. Therefore, most distinguished man, let the warning of the prophet come to your mind: "In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you," a word that urges all the sons of God to embrace eagerly the time of his visitation, lest a grace once offered, if it is neglected through sloth, should at last perish. Since it often happens that happy beginnings, while they promise a fortunate outcome, bring many into lethargy, we must take care prudently that no torpor creep in to smother this light which has begun to rise. I am well aware that I must observe moderation, lest by urging too sharply I seem to distrust your piety. Yet, on the other hand, both the excellence of the work and its difficulty compel me to add spurs, so that the faithful servants of Christ may not find in you anything unworthy of a man of such high esteem. The sum, however, comes to this: since our only end in living ought to be

units.la: vt pure Deum colamus, posthabitis omnibus curis hoc maximè agendum esse, vt superstitionibus euersis emineat vera religio. Iam vero quàm fœdis corruptelis propemodum extincta fuerit sub Papatu, vix vllis verbis exprimi potest, nec fine summo horrore cogitari. Imò quum nihil aliud sit totus Papatus, quàm sacri lega & innumeris ludibrijs referta nominis Dei profanatio, si in repurgandis istis sordibus frigemus vbi suppetit facultas, minime coram Deo eiusque Angelis excusabilis erit nostra cessatio. Adhæc, quum veritatis confessio gratissimum Deo sit & suauissimi odoris sacrificium, infracta quoque eius tuendæ constantia inter summa pietatis officia merito numeretur, nullum certè est officij genus, in quo & summam tuam virtutem exeras, & te exerceas maiori cum laude. Rursum quum videas ipsè coràm quàm animose Christi hostes pro sua tyrannide certent, & simul quàm furiosè oppugnent quàm Filius Dei sanguine suo asseruit doctrinam, mirum nisi te eorum improbitas ad piam æmulationem accendat: vt scilicet pro vindicanda Dei gloria nihilò segnius contendas, quàm illi in opprimenda laborant. Si verò tuam prudentiam non fugit, quàm honorifico titulo dignatus sit Spiritus sanctus, quos vocauit primitias Achaiæ, tibi certè dan da opera est, ne hodie inter patronos renascentis in Polonia Euangelij vel postremus sis, vel medius. Adde quòd nulla in re cerinus tuæ erga serenissimum Regem fidei documentum edere potes. Etsi enim tranquillo ille Regni statu potitur, vt tamen hæc fœlicitas diuturna maneat, non alia ratione melius obtinebit, quàm stabilito Christi Regno. Nam etsi Deus, quò se generis humani custodem ostendat, politicum ordinem etiam inter profanos homines pessum ire non patitur, multis tamen exemplis apparet, nusquam residere solidam eius benedictionem, nisi vbi pura colitur Religio. Ac quum Euangelium inestimabiles æternæ vitæ thesauros nobis aperiat, hæc secundæ gratiæ non poenitenda est accessio, quòd Deus Regna & Principatus, quibus prosidet, in suum præsidium fidemque recipit. Itaque ex quibus locis profligata est Papatus impietas, vt succederet integra pietatis restitutio, illic leges & iudicia florere, maiorem vigere reuerentiâ Magistratuum, populos sub placida modestia contineri passim videmus. Quò minus tolerabilis est eorum improbitas, qui doctrinæ formam quam tradimus, proterue infamant, ac si dissipatio esset politici ordinis, quem nullo meliore adminiculo fulciri, experientia vbique clamat. Pluribus coràm tecum aget frater noster, & commodius, quàm ferat epistolæ ratio. Vale præstantissime vir & illustris Domine. Christus, qui te præclaris dotibus ornauit, mentem tuam, omnésque sensus in legitimum eorum vsum dirigat, quò sacrum eius nomen per te illustretur, sufulineat {*}ineat te sua virtute, & omni benedictionis genere prosequatur vsque in finem. Geneuæ, IIII. Calendas Ianuarij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: that we worship God purely, and that, all other cares set aside, the chief concern should be to overthrow superstitions so that true religion may stand forth. Indeed, how foul the corruptions were by which true religion was almost extinguished under the Papacy can scarcely be expressed in any words, and cannot be thought of without the greatest horror. Indeed, since the whole Papacy is nothing other than a profanation of the name of God, filled with sacrilegious rites and countless mockeries, if we grow cold in cleansing these filths when the opportunity is at hand, our inactivity will by no means be excusable before God and his angels. Moreover, since the confession of the truth is most pleasing to God and a sacrifice of the sweetest fragrance, unwavering constancy in defending it is rightly counted among the highest duties of piety. Certainly there is no kind of duty in which you can display your great virtue and exercise yourself with greater praise. Again, since you yourself see how bravely the enemies of Christ fight for their tyranny, and at the same time how furiously they attack the doctrine which the Son of God asserted with his own blood, it would be strange if their wickedness did not kindle in you a pious rivalry, so that you contend no less eagerly for the defence of God's glory than they labour to suppress it. If your prudence does not escape your notice how honourable a title the Holy Spirit has bestowed upon those whom he called "the firstfruits of Achaia," then you must certainly take care that today you are not the last or the middling among the patrons of the Gospel reviving in Poland. Add to this that in no matter can you give a surer proof of your faith toward the most serene King. For although he enjoys a peaceful state of the realm, yet, so that this happiness may last long, he will not secure it better by any means than by the firmly established Kingdom of Christ. For although God, to show himself the guardian of the human race, does not suffer the political order to perish even among profane men, yet many examples make clear that his solid blessing never abides except where true religion is worshipped. And since the Gospel opens to us the inestimable treasures of eternal life, it is no small addition to this second grace that God receives into his protection and faithfulness the kingdoms and principalities over which he presides. Accordingly, in those places from which the impiety of the Papacy has been driven out, so that full restoration of piety might follow, we see everywhere that laws and courts flourish, reverence for the magistrates grows greater, and peoples are held in check with a calm moderation. All the less tolerable, then, is the wickedness of those who shamelessly defame the form of doctrine we hand down, as if it were the dissolution of the political order, which experience cries out everywhere can be supported by no better aid. Our brother will treat these matters with you in person, and more fully than the nature of a letter allows. Farewell, most distinguished man and illustrious Lord. May Christ, who has adorned you with excellent gifts, direct your mind and all your senses to their lawful use, so that his holy name may be made illustrious through you, may sustain you by his power, and may accompany you with every kind of blessing to the end. Geneva, the fourth day before the Kalends of January, 1555.

units.la: AD MAGNIFICVM DOMINVM NICOLAVM Miskovvoski à Mirovv, Castellanum Vvoniycensem.
units.tr: TO THE MAGNIFICENT LORD NICHOLAS Miskovvoski of Mirovv, Castellan of Vvoniycz.

units.la: QVum istuc profectionem instituisset optimus vir N. qui tuam apud me pietatem non vulgaribus elogiis celebrauit, committere nolui, vt sine meis literis ad te veniret, quæ saltem amoris erga te mei & obseruantiæ testes forent. Nam vt te vehementius ad præstandum quod Deo Patri, eiusque Filio officium debes, exhorter, opus esse non videtur, quando vitam tuam aliis regulæ instar esse audio. Quare nihil aliud restat, nisi vt tui similis esse ad extremum vsque pergas. Vides præstantissime vir, quàm indigne multi sacrum Dei nomen obtendat, qui futili tantùm iactantia Euangelium in ore habentes, maiori diffluunt vitiorum licentia, quàm miseri Papistæ, quos sub aliquo disciplinæ iugo superstitio retinet. Quòd autem erroribus Papatus valere iussis, ita magna pars hominum profanescit, hinc accidere certum est, quòd & paucis curæ est vera Religio, & omnibus fere ingenitum, carni suæ delitias facere. Te verò ex eorum esse numero, in quorum cordibus puram Euangelij doctrinam viuas egisse radices, qui inde nascuntur fructus ostendunt, tum ex animo tibi gratulor, tum permultos extare similes magnopere cupio, vel saltem quos tuum exemplû ad imitationem accendat. Sed quia nihil tibi afferent meæ literæ quod non vberius & luculentius suppeditent lucubrationes in publicū editæ, in quarum lectione libenter te exerces, non est cur te longius detineã. Nam & hoc, vt initio præfatus sum, mihi præcipuum scribendi consilium fuit, vt scires præclaras tuas virtutes, quæ Polonis in exemplum prælucent, procul etiam notas esse, & quo merentur in pretio haberi. Vale nobilissime vir, & mihi plurimùm obseruande. Dominus donis suis te augere pergat ad illustrandam nomitis fui gloriam, téque Spiritu suo semper gubernet. Geneuæ, IIII. Calendas Ian. M. D. LV.
units.tr: When the excellent man N., who has praised your piety towards me in no common terms, had decided to set out for there, I was unwilling to let him go without a letter from me, which would at least be witness of my love and esteem for you. For I do not think there is need to urge you more strongly to render the duty you owe to God the Father and to his Son, since I hear that your life serves others as a rule. What remains, therefore, is only that you continue to be such to the end. You see, most excellent sir, how unworthily many put forward the sacred name of God, who, having the Gospel only on their lips in empty boasting, indulge in a greater licence of vices than the wretched Papists, whom superstition holds under some yoke of discipline. That a great part of mankind grows profane once the errors of Papacy have been cast off happens, it is certain, because true religion is a concern of few, and almost all are born with the inclination to indulge their flesh. But that you belong to the number of those in whose hearts the pure doctrine of the Gospel has struck living roots, as the fruits that spring from them show, I congratulate you from my heart; and I greatly wish that many like you may exist, or at least that your example may kindle others to imitate you. But since my letter will offer you nothing that the publications I have issued, in whose reading you willingly occupy yourself, do not supply more fully and clearly, there is no reason for me to detain you longer. For this too, as I said at the beginning, was my chief purpose in writing: that you should know that your distinguished virtues, which shine as an example to the Poles, are known even at a distance, and that they deserve to be held in high esteem. Farewell, most noble sir, and most worthy of my regard. May the Lord go on increasing you with his gifts for the illustration of the glory of his name, and may he always govern you by his Spirit. Geneva, 29 December 1555.

units.la: AD GENEROSVM DOMINVM STANISLAVM Carninski Iuan hæredem in Alexandrowicze Equitem Polonum.
units.tr: TO THE NOBLE LORD STANISLAUS CARNINSKI, JAN'S HEIR IN ALEXANDROWICZE, A POLISH KNIGHT.
