units.la: EX tuis ad optimum fratrem nostrum N. literis, quas mihi reciauit, perspicere facile licuit, ornatissime vir, quàm verè te Christo addixeris. Nam illæ non modo serium pietatis asse{u}dum vbique spirant, sed etiam clarè ostendunt tibi nihil maiori esse curæ ac studio, quàm vt legitimo Dei cultu in suum ordinem restituto, pura & integra religio in Polonia floreat. In hoc sancto instituto vt constanter pergas, pluribus verbis te hortari superuacuum forte esset. Si tamen vltrò currenti calcar adderem, speraui hoc meum studium nec inutile, nec tibi molestum fore. Vide ergo generose vir, quando studium hoc tam fœliciter ingressus es, ne qua te difficultas terreat, vel moretur, nec mundi strepitus animum tuum debilitet, nec te fatiget temporis longitudo. Bene autem est, quod Filius Dei non otiosus certaminis nostri spectator in cœlo sedet, sed inuictum etiam suppeditat robur, quod par sit ad sustinendam laboris molem. De vestro cum Valdensibus consensu optima quæque spero: non modo quia sanctam vnitatem, in quam coaluerunt Christi membra, Deus semper benedicere solitus est, sed quod inter hæc rudimenta, fratrum Valdensium peritiam, quam longo vsu Dominus exercuit, non vulgari adiumento vobis fore spero. Quare sedulò à vobis omnibus danda opera est, vt hæc pia consensio magis ac magis sanciatur. Te verò vt priuatim horter ad suscipiendum hoc negotium, occasio mihi ex tuis literis oblata est. Vale nobilissime vir, & mihi ex animo colende. Dominus te diu feruet incolumem, Spiritu suo regat & suum nomen per te illustret. Genuæ, 1111. Calendas Ianuarij. M. D. LV.
units.tr: From your letter to our excellent brother N., which he passed on to me, it was easy to see, most distinguished sir, how truly you have devoted yourself to Christ. Your letter breathes not only a serious zeal for piety everywhere, but also shows clearly that nothing matters more to you than that, with the lawful worship of God restored to its proper order, pure and whole religion should flourish in Poland. It would perhaps be superfluous to urge you at length to persevere constantly in this holy undertaking. Yet if I were to spur on one who is already running willingly, I hoped that this zeal of mine would be neither useless nor unwelcome to you. See then, noble sir, that now that you have entered upon this undertaking so happily, no difficulty frightens or delays you, the noise of the world does not weaken your spirit, and the length of the time does not wear you out. It is well, moreover, that the Son of God is not an idle spectator of our struggle, sitting in heaven, but also supplies an unconquered strength sufficient to bear the weight of the labour. As for your agreement with the Waldenses, I hope for the very best: not only because God has always been wont to bless the holy unity into which the members of Christ have grown together, but because I hope that the skill of the Waldensian brethren, which the Lord has exercised through long practice, will be no ordinary help to you in these first beginnings. Therefore all of you must take pains, diligently, to see that this godly agreement is strengthened more and more. As for urging you personally to take up this business, the occasion was offered to me by your letter. Farewell, most noble sir, and one to be honoured by me from the heart. May the Lord keep you safe for many years, rule you by his Spirit, and make his name illustrious through you. Geneva, the fourth day before the Kalends of January, 1555.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: IOANNI CLAVBVRGO SENATORI FRANCOFORTENSI.
units.tr: TO JOHN CLAUBURGUS, SENATOR OF FRANKFURT.

units.la: Tsi literis tuis, ornatissime vir, renouatus mihi dolor fuit, quem ex optimi & præstantissimi hominis D. Adolphi morte conceperam: fieri tamen non potuit, quin mihi ob rarum ergà me amorem, quem omni ex parte spirant, suaues essent ac gratissimæ. Ereptus ille nobis fuit, si ex nostro desiderio iudicium facere liceret, parum tempestiuè: sed quia Dei arbitrio standum est, peracto vitæ legitimo cursu in beatam stationem, vbi nos quietus expectet, suo tempore receptus est. Quod vester ille concionator ex libro Iesu Filij Sirach de Iesu nptum eius personæ aptauit, diuinitus abreptum esse, ne n alitia cor eius mutaret: Fateor certè Deum optimè consulere eorum saluti, quos ex tot tâtisque corruptelis, quæ passim grassantur hodie in toto mundo, eripit. Sed quòd summa laude in cognato tuo dignum fuit vertere in vitium, maligni fuit prauíque ingenij. Omitto ingratitudinem, {q}hominem cui viuo blandiri coactus esset, multis scilicet cet beneficiis obstrictus, mortuû arrodere non erubuit.Sed quid facias cum istorum peruicacia, quibus hæreticum est, quicquid vel tantillum ab eorum figmentis discrepat? Quomodo hominibus parcerent, qui syncerâ pietatis doctrinam non minus proteruo saltu conculcant, quàm truculenta morositate respuunt? Cæterum vt tibi, eximie vir, pro tua moderatione placida hæc indignitas fuit deuoranda, sic te priuatç iniuriæ dolor admonet, ad cohibendam istam intemperiem maturè adhibenda esse remedia. Ego tempestiuam, vt putaui, occasionem nactus, Amplissimum Senatum per literas rogaui, vt intestinis istis dissidiis occurreret. Etsi autem aduentus ad vos meus non esset forte inutilis, & eum linguæ nostræ homines optarent, quia tamen me ingerere abfurdû erat, verecundè testatus sum, mihi non graue nec molestum fore iter, si qui ex vestris concionatoribus doctrina mea offensi, placidum colloquium admittant. Suppetunt enim rationes, quibus eos placare, quoad in me erit, & quoad patietur veritatis defensio, conabor. Tu verò præstantiss. vir, pro tua prudentia, quid factu vtile sit, statues, totúmque negotium moderaberis. Linguæ nostræ homines, licuti iam feci, ad colendâ inter se pacem hortari non desinam: si qui etiam duræ ceruicis erûr, eos monere, ne se peruersis dissidiis lacerent. Nam inter tuas virtutes hanc iure suspicio, quod antehac multa vitia toleraueris, quæ à gente nostra alienare tuum animum poterant: si ad perseuerandû tibi animos addere opus esset, has partes minimè detrectarem. Sed dum mecum reputo quid agas, téqi sponte occurrere mihi video, paternámque folicitudinem testari, ne quid accidat aliter quam vellemus, pudore impedior ne quid te rogem. Tantùm rogandus est Christus, vt semper ad hæc tædia deuorada, inuicta animi fortitudine constantiáque fulciat, & alibi piis suis exulibus similes excitet patronos. Quòd ad me priuatim spe stat, mihi mire gratum fuit, adhuc antiquæ nostræ consuetudinis apud te memoriam vigere. Ego vt tuæ erga me beneuolentiæ vicissim respondeam, quibusçunque potero officiis studebo. Vale præstantiss. vir, & mihi imprimis honorande. Dominus te semper tueatur cum sanctâ familia, tibíque benedicat. Genevæ, Pridie Calendas Martij. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Although your letter, most distinguished sir, renewed the grief I had conceived from the death of the excellent and outstanding man, Master Adolph, it could not help but be sweet and most welcome to me, because of your rare affection toward me, which breathes from every line. He was taken from us, if it were lawful to judge by our own longing, too early. But since we must abide by God's decision, he was received at his appointed time into a blessed station, having completed the lawful course of his life, where he waits for us in peace. Your preacher applied to his person what is said in the book of Jesus the son of Sirach, that he was snatched away by God so that wickedness might not change his mind. I certainly confess that God consults the salvation of those whom he rescues from the many great corruptions that rage everywhere in the whole world today. But to turn into a fault what deserves the highest praise in your kinsman was the mark of a malicious and perverse nature. I say nothing of his ingratitude: he was not ashamed to gnaw at a dead man, one whom, while he lived, he had been forced to flatter, being bound to him by so many benefits. But what can you do with the obstinacy of these people, for whom anything that differs even slightly from their inventions is heresy? How could they spare men whom they trample with no less shameless leaping, and reject with savage sullenness, the pure doctrine of piety? Yet just as you, most excellent sir, in your calm moderation, must swallow this indignity, so the pain of a private wrong reminds you that remedies must be applied promptly to check this intemperance. I seized what I thought was a timely opportunity and asked the most honourable Senate by letter to address these internal dissensions. Although my coming to you might perhaps not be useless, and the men of our language wished for it, yet since it would be absurd to force myself upon you, I modestly declared that the journey would not be burdensome or troublesome to me, if any of your preachers, offended by my teaching, would admit a peaceful conference. For there are arguments by which I will try to placate them, as far as lies in me and as far as the defence of the truth permits. You, most distinguished sir, will decide what is useful to do in your prudence, and you will manage the whole matter. As I have already done, I will not cease to exhort the men of our language to cultivate peace among themselves; and if some are stiff-necked, I will warn them not to tear themselves apart with perverse quarrels. For among your virtues I rightly observe this, that you have hitherto tolerated many faults which could have estranged your mind from our people. If it were necessary to add courage for perseverance, I would by no means refuse that role. But while I reflect on what you are doing, I see that your thoughts come to me of their own accord, and I am held back by shame from asking anything of you, though I bear witness to a fatherly anxiety lest anything happen otherwise than we wish. Christ alone must be asked that he may always uphold you in these weariness-bearing trials with an unconquered strength and constancy of spirit, and raise up elsewhere defenders like his pious exiles. As for me personally, it was wonderfully pleasing that the memory of our old friendship still flourishes with you. I, in turn, will strive to answer your goodwill toward me with whatever services I can. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and above all to be honoured by me. May the Lord always keep you and your holy household, and bless you. Geneva, the day before the Kalends of March, 1556.

units.la: MINISTRIS ECCLESIAE FRANCFVRTENSIS.
units.tr: To the Ministers of the Church of Frankfurt.

units.la: ETsi literis meis gratiam apud vos non modò nulla interior necessitudo, sed ne mediocris quidem notitia conciliat, venerandi & dilecti fratres, fraterna tamen coniunctio, quæ iure ministerij communis inter nos mutuò vigere debet, fatis ad scribendum fiduciæ dare visa est, ut minime dubitem apertam mihi fore ianuam, ut comiter vestra & qua optandum est, mansuetudine excipiar. Nuper quum sub Amplissimi Senatus vestri nomine mea in tres Euangelistas harmonia edita est, quominus vobis scripserim, quid præter pudorem obstiterit, nescio, Vix enim vnquam nisi necessitate coactus, ad ignotos scribere soleo. Ignotos autem voco, nec quem vestrum offendat verbi asperitas, quibuscum familiaris visus non intercedit. Certe cótemptu vel negligentia minime fuisse præteritos, sanctè vobis affirmo. Vbi autem reuersi sunt ex nundinis librarij, miratus sum fateor, Ioachimi cuiusdam Vveftphali non minus insulsum quàm virulentum librum, quo meam de Sacramentis doctrinam oppugnat, istic editum esse. Nam mihi persuaserám, optimum inter nos consensum esse: aut si docendi ratio non prorsus eadem fortet, tantum non esse discrepantiæ, quod vsque in odiosum contentionem erūperet: ac fieri quidem potest, vt insciis vobis exierit liber ille, quem certe vestris suffragiis fuisse probatum non arbitror. Neque vero hoc expostulandi causa commemoro: sed quia simul aliatus est rumor, quibusdã è collegio vestro minus placere, quæ de Sacramentis trado, anteuertere visum est, ne quid dissidij silentio meo vel dissimulatione foueerem. Certe vt non libenter me obtrudo, ita fi quispiam vestrum mea doctrina offenditur, nulla ad eum placandum satisfactionis ratio à me negligetur. Quòd si ad offensiones tollendas vtilis mea ad vos professio esse videbitur, quanuis longum & incommodum esse iter, nihil tamen molestiæ recuso. Nam cum hoc studium sincæ inter nos concordiæ mihi debere videor: tum vero quia Amplissimus Senatus summa humanitate oblata sibi dicatámq; Harmoniam amplexus est, literisque testatus sibi gratum munus fuisse ac iucundum, ita me sibi deuinxit, vt hoc suo merito à me officium exigere videatur. Neque tam mea causa laboro, quàm vt peregrinos fratres quibus hospitium D. in vrbe vestra concessit, syncera dilectione amplectamini. Audio enim, nescio quid litium & vexationis metuere quod eorum quietem perturbet. Porrò quum sciatis partem vi & tyrannide hostium Christi patria expulsam ad vos migraffe, partem verò, vt vobiscum puraté Christi fidem profiterétur, voluntario se exilio multasse, quantum aliis miseria sua conditio, aliis prompta ad sequendū Christum alacritas gratiam conciliare debeat, apud vos dissere rere superuacuum foret. Imò si qua in ipsis desideretis, vt forte cos suis vitiis laborare credibile est, venia tamen & facilitate sci tis ferendos esse. Potius verò quàm vt in certamen erumpat, si qua hactenus occulta fuit simultas, quæscunque mihi partes imponere voletis, suscipere paratus sum. Certe ad pacificationem vtrisque fidus semper ero & hortator & adiutor. Valete chariss. & ex animo verè colendi fratres. Dominus vos Spiritu prudentiæ, fortitudinis, & mansuetudinis gubernet, laboresque vestros benedicat, Amen. Geneuæ, VI. Nonas Martij. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Although no close acquaintance, and not even a slight familiarity, recommends me to you in my letter, venerable and beloved brothers, the fraternal bond that ought to exist between us by right of our common ministry seemed to me enough to give me confidence in writing. I have no doubt that the door will be opened to me, and that I will be received kindly and, as one could wish, gently. Recently, when my harmony of the three Evangelists was published under the name of your most distinguished Senate, what prevented me from writing to you, I do not know, except perhaps shame. For I hardly ever write to people I do not know unless compelled by necessity. I call them unknown, and I do not mean that any of you is offended by the harshness of my words, since we have no familiar acquaintance. I solemnly assure you that I did not omit you through contempt or carelessness. But when the booksellers returned from the fair, I confess I was amazed that a book by a certain Joachim Westphal, no less silly than it is virulent, in which he attacks my teaching on the sacraments, had been published there. For I had been persuaded that there was the best agreement among us, or that if our manner of teaching were not altogether the same, the difference was so slight that it would not break out into hateful contention. It is certainly possible that this book appeared without your knowledge, and I do not think it was approved by your votes. I mention this not to complain, but because at the same time a rumour has been spread that some in your college are less pleased with what I teach about the sacraments. I thought it right to anticipate this, so that by my silence or dissimulation I would not foster any discord. Indeed, although I do not willingly thrust myself upon anyone, if any of you is offended by my teaching, I will spare no effort to make amends and to give him satisfaction. And if my profession of faith to you seems useful for removing offences, then, although the journey is long and inconvenient, I refuse no trouble. For I feel I owe this endeavour to sincere concord among us. Moreover, since your most distinguished Senate received and embraced the Harmony with the greatest kindness, and testified in its letters that the gift was welcome and pleasing to it, it has bound me to itself so that this service seems to be demanded of me as its due. I labour not so much for my own cause as that you may embrace with sincere love the foreign brothers to whom God has granted refuge in your city. For I hear that they fear some quarrels and troubles that might disturb their peace. Moreover, since you know that some have been driven from their homeland by the violence and tyranny of Christ's enemies and have come to you, and others have voluntarily gone into exile to profess the pure faith of Christ with you, it would be superfluous for me to argue before you how far their misery should win favour for the one group, and their ready zeal to follow Christ for the other. Indeed, if there are any faults in them, as they are probably burdened with some, they should nevertheless be borne with indulgence and gentleness. Rather than let any hidden enmity, if there has been any so far, break out into open strife, I am ready to take on whatever role you wish to assign me. Certainly I will always be a faithful helper, encourager and assistant to both sides in making peace. Farewell, most dear brothers, whom I truly honour from my heart. May the Lord govern you with the Spirit of prudence, fortitude and gentleness, and bless your labours. Amen. Geneva, 6 Nones of March, 1556.

units.la: CALVINVS PETRO FABRO S. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Peter Fabre, greetings.

units.la: ETsi literæ tuæ duplici nomine gratæ mihi suauéfq; fuerunt, quòd in illis ingenij dexteritas, & elegantioris doctrinæ nitor emicat: deinde quòd tuæ erga me obseruantiæ testes esse voluisti: plus tamen illis apud me gratiæ addidit, quòd tuæ in Deum pietatis signum ac pignus esse interpretor. Etsi enim qui liberalibus doctrinis sunt exculti, me forte amant, quia ab illis existimant non prorsus alienum esse: scio tamen ea me inuidia flagrare apud totum fere mundum, quæ multos à mea amicitia abster reat. Itaque reuerétiam quam communi Magistro defers, causam esse non dubito, quæ tuum mihi animum conciliat, téqj ad scribendum impulit. Hoc verò pietatis semen vt sedulò fouere atque etiam excolere studeas, & assiduo progressu ad frugem vsque perducere, pluribus de causis hortari te cogor. Video ætatem tuam: video corruptionem totius nostri seculi: video quot te circunstent mundi illecebræ, quæ totidem sunt ad te inescandum hami: video denique innumeras Satanæ insidias, quibus cauendis nemo vnquam satis erit intentus. Dominus te iam forte virili Spiritu ornauit. Sed quum lubrica semper & flexibilis sit iuuentus, remedio isto, quod omnibus suis æqualibus præscripsit Dauid, opus tibi esse cogita, nempe vt Dei sermonem custodias. Quantus verò scelerum labyrinthus hodie mundum inuoluat, & quanta impietatis colluuies vbique exundet, verbis explicare nihil attinet. Te verò ne falsis blanditiis mundus deliniat, non frustra metuo. Nam vt reliqua taceam, me patris tui exemplum huius periculi plus satis admonet. Quum mihi ingenij sui mansuetudinem & candorem (quæ duæ sunt rarae virtutes) probasset, longè alia mihi de eo pollicitus fueram, quàm quæ boni omnes se comperisse narrant. Hoc si homini maturæ iam prudentiæ, & ad optima quæque longa iam peritia assuefacto accidere potuit, quid tibi periculi imminet, nisi attentissimè caueas? Qua in re opinionem meam fefellerit, si rogas, vno verbo accipito, quia mundi blanditiis irretitus, sese Christo subduxit. Eius itaq; memoria ad te acrius stimulandum, me non immerito excitat. Sed quia longius progredi non patitur vel temporis angustia, vel epistolæ modus, tantum velim hunc tibi scopum toto vitæ cursu proponas, quando nobis in regem à Patre datus est Christus, & pro omnibus mortuus est ac resurrexit, vt omnes ei viuant ac moriantur,te in eius obsequium prorsus addicas:quan-do vnicus etiam nobis datus est Magister, vt coelesti eius sapien-tiæ studia tua consecres. Nam vt te liberalibus doctrinis excul-tum esse gaudeo,ita tuum est videre,nisi eas in legitimum finem & vsum referas,totum peruerti naturæ ordinem : quicquid etiā splendoris & opulentiæ te manet,non inuideo,modo ab eorum illecebris non secus atque exitialibus venenis tibi caueas. Vale frater mihi charissime.Dominus te Spiritu suo ad extremum regat,præsidio tueatur,omni genere benedictionis locupletet.Idibus Aprilis. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Your letter was welcome and pleasing to me for two reasons: because the cleverness of your mind and the polish of your more refined learning shine through it, and because you wished to be a witness of your regard for me. Yet it gave me even more pleasure, because I take it as a sign and pledge of your piety towards God. For although those who are trained in the liberal arts may perhaps love me because they think I am not wholly alien to them, I know that I am hated by almost the whole world with a kind of envy that keeps many away from my friendship. Therefore I do not doubt that the reverence you show to our common Master is the reason that has won your mind to me and moved you to write. I am compelled to urge you to cherish this seed of piety diligently, to cultivate it, and by steady progress to bring it to maturity, for several reasons. I see your age; I see the corruption of our whole century; I see how many worldly allurements surround you, each a hook to entice you; I see at last the countless snares of Satan, against which no one can ever be watchful enough. The Lord perhaps has already endowed you with a manly spirit. But since youth is always slippery and pliable, consider that you need that remedy which David prescribed to all his peers, namely, that you keep God's word. How great a labyrinth of crimes now entangles the world, and how great a filth of impiety overflows everywhere, there is no need to explain in words. As for you, I fear not without reason that the world may soothe you with false flatteries. For, to pass over the rest, the example of your father warns me more than enough of this danger. When I had approved the gentleness and candour of his mind (which are two rare virtues), I had promised myself something quite different from what all good men report they have found out about him. If this could happen to a man of mature prudence, long practised in all that is best, what danger threatens you, unless you take the greatest care? If you ask in what respect my opinion of him has been mistaken, take it in one word: he was entangled in the allurements of the world and withdrew from Christ. His memory therefore rightly stirs me to urge you more sharply. But since neither the shortness of time nor the limits of a letter allow me to go further, I would only wish you to set before yourself this goal through the whole course of your life: since Christ has been given to us by the Father as king, and died and rose again for all, so that all may live and die to him, devote yourself wholly to his service; since also one Master has been given to us, dedicate your studies to his heavenly wisdom. For as I rejoice that you are trained in the liberal arts, so it is for you to see that, unless you direct them to their lawful end and use, you would entirely pervert the order of nature. As for whatever splendour and wealth awaits you, I do not begrudge it, provided that you guard yourself against its allurements no less than against deadly poisons. Farewell, dearest brother. May the Lord guide you by his Spirit to the end, protect you with his help, and enrich you with every kind of blessing. Ides of April, 1556.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: Calvin sends greetings.

units.la: Ad certa quædam capita.
units.tr: On certain points.

units.la: Dilectissime frater, quia accidit vt plurimum, vt in pecunia fœnori locanda incidant multa præter ius & æquum,satis tutum non est si ad tuam quæstionem simpliciter respon-deam : quis nempe modus legitimi fructus pecuniæ statuendus sit. Fiet enim nonnunquam vt vel minimus fructus ex pecunia percipi non possit sine Dei offensione,& proximi iniuria. Quare me excusatum apud te velim, si nihil hic certum vt expectas, præscripsero. Est quidem in hac civitate certus legibus modus constitutus.Sed non inde cōsequitur ad eum etiam modum fructum pecuniæ exigere creditori bona conscientia licere à pauper​e, vnde ille aliquo modo opprimatur. Accidit & illud quod me retinet,ne plenius tibi respondeam, quòd sciam te hoc à me rogare ea de causa tantum,vt alium quendam redarguas qui omnia hic in parte sibi permittit me in consilium non adhibi-to:quem etiam fortasse ne audire quidem dignaretur.Illi igitur pro me respondeat regula illa iuris ipsius naturalis,quam Dominus Iesus Christus partem summæ Legis & Prophetarum statuit: ne videlicet faciamus alteri, quod factum non vellemus nobis. Quòd ad viduam attinet,si poterit secum liberos abducere, nihil illi pretiosius illorum animabus esse debet.Quare si illi manum porrexerit Dominus,vt ex eo luto aut abysso potius emergat, parum humanè nedicam Christianè fecerit, si illos a tergo reliquerit.Sed quia mihi non liquet quæ sit ætas & quæ voluntas ac rationes ad illud conficiendum appositè,illi ea sigillatim expendenda relinquo. Quicquid sit,non poterit sponte illos ita relinquere,quin perpetuum inde mœrorem sibi conciliaturam nouerit.Maior est in nupta difficultas. Vt enim illa à viro secedat, nisi vi quadam maiore & ad extremum eò redacta, si illam nomine Religionis aut alia occasione intolerandū in modum habeat, auctor esse non possum. Neque modum illum intoleran dum definio, cum domi durius etiam tractari cōtigerit. Omnem enim tolerantiam exhibuerit oportet, antequam ad illud remedium confugiat. Si vero ab idololatria tuta esse non poterit nisi cum aperto vitæ periculo, adeóque vir illi instet vt eam persequatur ipsemet, licebit tum illi fuga sibi consulere, non animo diuertendi a viro & illius deserendi, vtcunque se illi durum & intolerabilem exhibuerit: sed tantum vt euitet apertum periculum. Ac tantisper fieri poterit faciete Domino, vt cor illud adeo efferatum viri mitescat & componatur: in vllius vero mortalis gratiam in Deum peccare nefas est. Te vero qui ita es de aliis solicitus, tanto magis cogitaturum spero de tuo ipsius officio erga magnum illum Patrem coelestem, a quo donatus es luce Evangelij Filij ipsius in qua nobis rapositā est salus. Ac si hactenus benè coepisti, tanto magis in posterum enitendum est tibi, atq; in diēs modis omnibus serio proficiendum. Cumque istic tot corruptelæ vigeant, caue existimes aliter officio te fungi posse, quā vt ipse studeas vnicè vt Dei nomen glorificetur & ipsius cultus & honor inter tuos, vt par est, vigeat. Faxit Dominus, vt quod a te peto illius nomine, ipse etiam meis tibi precibus exoratus repsa præstet. x x v i i. Aprilis. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Dearest brother, since it very often happens that many things contrary to right and fairness creep into the lending of money at interest, it would not be safe for me simply to answer your question: what is the proper rate of lawful return on money to be fixed? It will sometimes happen that even the smallest return on money cannot be taken without offence to God and injury to one's neighbour. So I would ask you to excuse me if, instead of the definite answer you expect, I lay down nothing certain here. There is indeed a fixed rate set by the laws of this city. But it does not follow from this that a creditor may in good conscience exact that rate from a poor man in a way that oppresses him. There is also something that holds me back from answering you more fully: I know that you ask this of me only so that you may refute a certain person who in this matter permits himself everything, and who did not consult me, and who perhaps would not even deign to hear me. Let that rule of the natural law itself, which the Lord Jesus Christ laid down as the sum of the Law and the Prophets, answer for me in his place: namely, that we should do to others what we would not want done to us. As for the widow, if she can take her children away with her, nothing should be more precious to her than their souls. Therefore, if the Lord has stretched out his hand to draw her out of that mire, or rather abyss, it would be a Christian act, if hardly a humane one, to leave the children behind her. But since it is not clear to me what their age is, what their wishes are, and what reasons bear on the matter, I leave her to weigh these things one by one. Whatever the case, she will not be able to leave them of her own accord without knowing that she will thereby win for herself lasting grief. The difficulty is greater in the case of the wife. For I cannot advise her to separate from her husband unless it is by some greater force, and driven to that extremity, if he treats her in an intolerable manner on account of religion or some other occasion. Nor do I define that treatment as intolerable when she has merely been treated more harshly at home. For she ought to have shown every patience before she takes refuge in that remedy. But if she cannot be safe from idolatry except at the evident risk of her life, and her husband presses her to take part in it himself, then she may consult her own safety by flight, not with the intention of turning away from her husband and deserting him, however harsh and intolerable he has shown himself to her, but only so that she may avoid the open danger. And in the meantime it may be that, with the Lord's help, that heart of the husband, so savagely hardened, will soften and be brought to order; but to sin against God for the favour of any mortal is wicked. As for you, who are so anxious about others, I hope you will all the more consider your own duty towards that great Father in heaven, from whom you have been given the light of the Gospel of his Son, in which salvation has been laid up for us. And if you have begun well until now, all the more must you strive in future and make progress in every way, day by day. And since there are so many corruptions flourishing there, take care not to think that you can discharge your office in any other way than by striving, above all, that the name of God be glorified and that his worship and honour flourish among your people, as is fitting. May the Lord grant that what I ask of you in his name, he himself, moved by my prayers, may also bring about in you. 27 April 1556.

units.la: VALERANDO POLLANO.
units.tr: TO VALERANDUS POLLANUS.

units.la: SI liber fuisset Olbracus, neque ipse qua est pietate, cum Ecclesiæ vestræ incommodo hucusque moram traxisset, neque etiam ad eum stimulandum defuisset assidua nostra sedulitas. Sed quia bona spes erat, posse tandem dimitti, & neminem repe riebamus tam idoneum, coacti sumus vos longius tenere suspensos. Spero eius aduentum multis modis fore vtilem. Est enim probè in Scripturis exercitatus, suppetit nō vulgaris docēdi dexteritas, syncerè & ex animo sese Christo addixit: cordatus est nō minus quàm ad moderationem propensus. Accedit etiā & prudentia & maturitas quæ non solùm homini auctoritatem conciliet, sed plurimū valeat ad sedandas turbas. Itaq; nec gratia nec ambitione vt spero, flectetur, quin Ecclesiæ ædificationem fideliter procuret. Sed vereor ne Ecclesiæ vestræ morbus curatu sit perquàm difficilis. Nā incurabile dicere nō audeo: nec male ante tēpus ominari libet. Nunquā certè de exitu infaustæ huius cōcertationis fui migis anxius. Nā communibus literis scribitis tranquillū esse statum, cū vulgari rumore nō conuenit. Video equidē nimia pertinacia quibusdā propositū esse digladiari vel ad vltimā vsq; Ecclesiæ cladē: sed vnde implacabile tui odiū cōtraxerunt, nescio. Si pauci essent nō mirarer, & censeret spernēdos esse.
units.tr: If Olbracus had been free, he would not, out of his own piety, have delayed so long to the inconvenience of your Church, and our constant diligence would not have been lacking in urging him on. But since there was good hope that he could at last be dismissed, and we could find no one so suitable, we have been forced to keep you in suspense for longer. I hope his coming will be useful in many ways. He is well trained in the Scriptures, has no ordinary skill in teaching, and has devoted himself sincerely and wholeheartedly to Christ. He is judicious and no less inclined to moderation. Added to this are prudence and maturity, which not only win a man authority but greatly help to calm disturbances. So, I hope, he will be moved neither by favour nor by ambition, but will faithfully work for the building up of the Church. But I fear the illness of your Church may be exceedingly difficult to cure. I do not dare call it incurable, nor do I like to foretell evil before its time. Certainly I was never more anxious about the outcome of this unhappy dispute. In your joint letters you write that the state of affairs is calm, but this does not agree with common report. I see that some men are resolved, with excessive obstinacy, to fight on even to the final ruin of the Church. But where they contracted their implacable hatred of you, I do not know. If they were few, I would not be surprised, and one might think them to be despised.

units.la: Epist. 227. Nunc quum multos esse audiam, & ex illis quosdam non aliqui improbos, hoc me non leuiter conturbat: fateor quidem in hac causa non uno modo eos peccare, neque ab illa sententia di moueor, ipsos proprio iudicio tribuere plusquam oportet, morositate impelli, & aliis vitiis laborare: sed quia tam grauium offensionum causae mihi no satis cognitae sunt, hic perplexus haereo. Itaque D. Clauburgo scripsi, postquam tentata fuerint omnia remedia, si magnae Ecclesiae partite non placere intelligas, cedendum potius esse, quam vt te ac tuum ministerium continuis probris exponas, quotidie excogitentur noua crimina, & exitiali dissidio Ecclesiam lacerari. Nollem hoc vel praue factioni paucorum hominum, vel in tumultu concedi, quia res pessimi exempli foret, importunis clamoribus quasi violenter deiici Pastorem. Verum si ita alienatos esse videas magnę partis animos, vt operam tuam respuant, & doctrinam minus reuerenter amplexentur, expende ipse, an non expediat Ecclesiae iudicium fremel potius subire, vt si fastidio es, te absque sinistra nota dimittat, quam apud inuitos gradum tenens, acerba ęgritudine & assiduis molestiis confici. Et hoc parce apud D. Clauburgum attigi, quem & tibi penitus esse amicum scio, & causae tuae patrocinari quoad potest. Nec vero tam cito deliberandum censeo, donec ultima necessitas id extorqueat. Nam forte Olbraci aduentu fiet aliqua mutatio in melius. Imo forte discussis nebulis orietur serenitas. Tu interea vide, ne animi plus satis iam exulceratino ua aliqua offensione pungantur. Nec vero ignoras, vbi semel efferbuit contentio, praesertim vbi progressu vires collegit, praeuas suspiciones regnare, & omnia fere in calumniam trahi. Alios porro nouum bellum vobis mouisse doleo: sed ira scilicet opportunitates suas captat Satan. Miror etiam quum apud me nu per pacem & fraternam beneuolentiam colere in animo sibi esse testati sunt, repente ad tantam atrocitatem sine causa impulsos fuisse. Hoc etiam magis absurdum quum blanditi fuerint tanquam homini de Ecclesia bene merito, nunc regnum vel tyrannidem odiose obiicere. Cuperem sane depositis lautitiis, eos succedere in regnum cui nunc inuident. Sed put idior est calumnia, quàm vt mihi existimem longa defensione opus esse. De causa ipsa scripsi ad Dominum Clauburgum: quo animo acceperit, tu me certiorem facies. Apud illos priuatim nihil profecerem. Nam istis fere hominibus hoc est propositum video, vt vo luntario stupore se oblectent. De muliere quam perfide maritus deferuit, sic breuiter accipe. Sicuti ad permittenda diuortia nos faciles esse non conuenit, temperandum esse rigorem, ne quis vbi extra culpam comperrus fuerit, iure suo cum animę exitio fraudetur. Itaque si certò constet castitatem honesteque vixisse, ac
units.tr: Epist. 227. Now, since I hear that there are many people opposed to you, and that some of them are not at all wicked, this troubles me considerably. I admit that in this matter they err in more than one way, and I am not moved from that opinion: they attribute too much to their own judgment, are driven by moroseness, and suffer from other faults. But because I do not know well enough the causes of such grave offences, I remain here in perplexity. So I wrote to Dominus Clauburgius that, once every remedy has been tried, if you understand that you do not please the greater part of the Church, it is better to yield than to expose yourself and your ministry to constant reproaches, to the daily invention of new charges, and to the Church being torn apart by a deadly dissension. I would not wish this to be conceded either to the perverse faction of a few men or in a tumult, because it would be a matter of very bad example, that a minister should be thrown out, as it were by force, by importunate shouts. But if you see that the minds of the greater part have been so alienated that they reject your labour and embrace your teaching less reverently, weigh for yourself whether it would not be better to submit once to the judgment of the Church, so that, if you are weary of the work, it may dismiss you without any mark of disgrace, rather than you holding your place among unwilling people and being worn down by bitter distress and constant troubles. I touched on this sparingly with Dominus Clauburgius, whom I know to be entirely your friend and to defend your cause as far as he can. Nor do I think you should deliberate so hastily, until the last necessity forces it upon you. For perhaps with the arrival of Olbracus some change for the better will come. Indeed, perhaps once the clouds are dispersed, calm will return. Meanwhile, take care that minds already sufficiently ulcerated are not pricked by some further offence. Nor do you fail to know that once contention has flared up, especially where it has gathered strength as it progressed, evil suspicions reign and almost everything is twisted into calumny. I grieve that others have stirred up a new war against you, but of course Satan seizes his opportunities in anger. I am also amazed that, when they recently declared to me that they intended to cultivate peace and brotherly goodwill, they were suddenly driven without cause to such atrocity. This is even more absurd, since they flattered you as a man who had deserved well of the Church, and now odiously charge you with lordship or tyranny. I would indeed wish, once their finery was laid aside, that they might succeed to the kingdom which they now envy. But the calumny is too childish for me to think it needs a long defence. About the matter itself I have written to Dominus Clauburgius; you will let me know with what spirit he received it. With those men privately I would achieve nothing, for I see that such people have this purpose: to delight themselves in wilful stupidity. About the woman whom her husband has treacherously deserted, take my brief answer. Just as it is not fitting for us to be easy in permitting divorces, so rigour must be tempered, lest anyone who is found to be free of fault be defrauded of his right, to the ruin of his soul.

units.la: functam fundam esse probae vxoris officio : maritum vero fracta & violata coniugij fide,cum scorto in locum incognitum abiisse,cau sa legitime cognita,nubendi libertatem quam Dominus permisit,ab hominibus negari fas non esse arbitror. Vale charissime frater.Vxorem tuam meo nomine plurimum saluta. Dominus vos gubernet suo Spiritu, virtute tueatur, vobisque benedicat xxiiii.Iunij. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Therefore, if it is clearly established that she has kept her chastity, lived honourably, and discharged the duty of a good wife, while her husband, having broken and violated the faith of marriage, has gone off with a whore to an unknown place, and the cause has been legitimately examined, then I think it is not right for men to deny her the freedom to marry which the Lord has permitted. Farewell, dearest brother. Greet your wife warmly on my behalf. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, defend you with his power, and bless you. 24 June 1556.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN SENDS GREETINGS IN THE LORD

units.la: Si tibi minus prolixe respondeo, quàm rerum de quibus ad me scripsisti, ferebat copia & varietas, epistolae breuitati tempo-ris angustiam obtendere non licet: satis enim superq; ad scribendum fuit ocij, si modo vsus forem. Quod te moneri cupis, si quid in te desiderem, & tibi rursum anxie cavet, ne delatoribus aurem praebeam, quid mihi agendum sit nescio. Nisi enim me fallit opinio, superuacua suspicione laborans, quibusuis monitionibus iinuam praecludis. Ego vero mi frater, syncere tibi affero, non fuisse periculum a quibus tibi metuis. Verum vt hunc vel illum repudiesteftem, vix vnquam efficies quin duo in te nominentur vitia: ostentatio & immodicus satagendi feruor. Quare si extinguere cupis hominum sermones: danda opera est, primum vt purgatus omni ambitione animus ad veram modestiam spiret : deinde ne qua in vultu & verbis appareant fastus & confidentiae signa. Hoc tibi non ex vnius amici mei sensu, vt tu suspicatus es, sed ex communi multorum iudicio familiariter denuntio: apud quos doleo minori in pretio esse tuas virtutes, quas istis maculis infici putant. Iam vero vt alteram notam effugias, quia inualuit opinio multorumque animos occupat, aliena negocia te non solum ampleSti, sed cupide accersere, reipsa ostendes nihil tibi esse optabilius, quàm intra officij tui metas incedere. Cogit nos saepe hominum importunitas longius progredi quàm vellemus (atque hoc ego nimium experior) nec vero fieri aliter potest, quin multis turbinibus inuoluar. Sed aequi iudices non tribuunt vitio molestias, ad quas me inuitum trahi constat. Nec vero mirum tibi videri debet, si queruntur boni quidam, te imperiose magis quàm iuste confessionem exigere à fidei probatae hominibus. Si quis eandem tibi legem imponat, negas te ductu rum pro iniuria. Vt ita sit, quod tamen mihi nondum persuades, ego mihi aliter sentire permitto. Nam vt al a taceam, hoc inter Ecclesias mutuum ius vigere debet, vt in probando grege alte-ra alterius iudicio acquiescat. Et certè si tuo loco essem, non sine rubore audirem qui ad examen nouum vocarentur, probatos
units.tr: I am replying to you less fully than your letter deserves, since the many and varied matters you raised would have allowed. But the brevity of a letter is no excuse for the shortness of time, for I would have had leisure enough to write, if only I had used it. As for your wish to be advised on what I would have you correct in yourself, and your anxious warning that I should not lend an ear to informers, I do not know what I ought to do. Unless I am mistaken, you are troubling yourself with a needless suspicion, and you shut off every kind of admonition. For my part, my brother, I tell you frankly that there was no danger from those whom you fear. But you will hardly ever manage to get rid of every man you call an enemy without two faults being charged against you: ostentation and an excessive zeal for busying yourself. So if you wish to silence people's talk, you must take pains, first, that your mind, purged of all ambition, breathes true modesty, and then that no signs of arrogance and self-confidence appear in your face and words. I say this to you as a friend, not on the feeling of one friend alone, as you suspected, but on the common judgment of many, among whom I regret that your virtues are held in lower esteem, because they think those virtues are stained by these blemishes. Now, to avoid the second charge, since the opinion has taken hold and occupies the minds of many, that you not only take up other men's business but eagerly seek it out, you will show by your deeds that nothing is more to be desired by you than to keep within the bounds of your office. Men's importunity often forces us to go further than we would wish (and I experience this too much myself), nor can it happen otherwise than that I am caught up in many whirlwinds. But fair judges do not attribute to fault the troubles into which it is plain I am dragged against my will. Nor should it seem strange to you if certain good men complain that you demand a confession from men of proven faith more imperiously than justly. If someone imposes the same rule on you, you deny that you would submit to it as an injury. Suppose it were so, though you have not yet persuaded me of it: I allow myself to think otherwise. For, to say nothing of other things, this mutual right ought to hold among the Churches, that in testing the flock each should rest on the judgment of the other. And certainly, if I were in your place, I would not hear without blushing that men already proved in a place where sincere piety is cultivated were being called to a new examination.

units.la: A.iij. iam fuisse in eo loco vbi fyncera pietas colitur. Hæc ego familiariter apud te:neque enim me alibi exagitare audies. Cæterum ea tacere quæ vulgò sparguntur,ingenuum non eflet. Non dico apud nos vulgari:quia paucissimi sunt qui te nouerunt:& studemus vestro exéplo nostros potius stimulare in melius, quàm præbere vel exigui offendiculi materiam. Sed quid conterranei & quidem in patria de te sentiant & loquantur,tibi incognitum esse nolo, nisi forte iam aliunde resciueris. Neque etiam dissimulabo quod pridem à multis animaduersum fuit: cùm fratrem nostrum N. sæpe Diaconum tuum vocares, nomen illud nescio quid inanis iactantiæ fpirafle. Plurima eiusdem generis eodem consilio omitto nunc, quo hactenus vel vnum attingere distuleram,parcere tibi cupiens,ne recte agendi alacritas minueretur:& simul quia forte sperabam,vt sponte melior quædam maturitas hos næuos deleret. Quòd recipiendos non putas qui ab aliis Ecclesiis fine testimonio ad nos veniunt, facile tibi assentior:quia & veteri vsu inter pios receptum est, idque flagitat seculi nostri malitia. Summam quoque prudentiam & æquitatem adhibendam esse concedo,ne quid de fratribus & fymmyftis in malam partem statim credatur. Sed modum tenendum censeo,ne syncretismus noster,quem tantopere commendas,ad fotenda vitia spectet.Neque fatis aflequor interea,quorsum toties repetas ne temere non solùm de te , sed etiam de aliis quid credam: fateor me esse minus circunfpectum quàm deceret,sed cur me leuitatis infimulcs,nescio. Adde quòd non minus precifedictas quid sentire debeam, quàm fi tuo vnius arbitrio standum foret. Nam de rebus incognitis sententiam proferens, me aliter sentire vetas. In Anglorum controuersia moderationem tenui, cuius me non pœnitet: fi N. nostro fuccenfuerim, mihi constat optima ratio, quam fanis iudicibus haud dubiè probabo. Et tamen illam indignationem fyncerus erga eum verèque fraternus amor expressit mihi,quia ipsum-sibi nocuisse non secus dolebam , quàm fi in me recideret calamitas. Ac nunc quantopere me excruciet infœlix quem semper timui euentus, verbis explicare nihil attinet. Hæc mea libertas sic animum tuum pungat velim,vt tamen non dubites quicquid scripsi,à vero amore profectum esse. Vtinam sermone potius coràm daretur quàm literis : sed multi claui trabales huic me loco nimis affixum tenent. Cæterum non aliud mihi propositum asperè scribendi fuit, nisi vt integra fama Domino solidè seruias.
units.tr: I say this to you in private, for you will not hear me inveighing against you elsewhere. Yet it would not be right for me to keep silent about what is commonly spread about. I do not say it is commonly talked of among us, since very few know you; and we strive, by your example, to spur our own people toward what is better, rather than to offer even the smallest occasion of stumbling. But I do not want you to be ignorant of what your fellow countrymen, in your own homeland, think and say of you, unless perhaps you have already learned it from elsewhere. Nor will I hide what was noticed long ago by many: that when you often called our brother N. your deacon, that name breathed some kind of empty boasting. I now leave out a great many things of the same kind, for the same reason that until now I had put off touching on even one, wishing to spare you, lest the eagerness to act rightly be diminished; and at the same time because I hoped that some maturity, arising of its own accord, would wipe away these blemishes. As for your view that those who come to us from other Churches without a testimonial should not be received, I readily agree with you, since this has been accepted among the godly from long practice, and the wickedness of our age demands it. I also grant that the greatest prudence and fairness must be applied, so that nothing about brethren and fellow-mystics is at once believed in a bad sense. But I think a measure must be kept, lest our syncretism, which you commend so highly, serve to nourish vices. Meanwhile I do not quite see why you so often repeat that I should not rashly believe anything, not only about you but also about others. I admit I am less wary than I ought to be, but why you accuse me of levity I do not know. Add that I must not state what I think about matters not known to me, any less than if I were bound to the judgment of you alone. For while you forbid me to think otherwise, you yourself pronounce opinions on things unknown to you. In the controversy over the English I kept to moderation, and I do not regret it; if I have offended our N., I am sure of my good reasons, which I will readily prove before sound judges. Yet that indignation was prompted in me by the sincere and truly brotherly love I bear him, because I grieved no less that he was harming himself than if the calamity fell upon me. As for how greatly the unhappy outcome, which I have always feared, now torments me, there is no need to explain in words. I would like this frankness of mine to sting your mind in such a way that you still do not doubt that whatever I have written has come from true love. I wish this could be done by speaking face to face rather than by letter; but many beams nail me too firmly to this place. Nor was it my purpose in writing harshly to do anything other than to make you serve the Lord with an unblemished reputation.

units.la: M. D. LVI.
CLARISSIMO VIRO D. IOANNI CLAVBVRGO Seniori Patritio & Senatori Francfor-diensi, D. apprime obseruando.
units.tr: To the most illustrious man, Master Johann Clauburg, senior patrician and senator of Frankfurt, my most highly esteemed lord.

units.la: QVum tot molestias susceperis pro paranda linguae nostrae Ecclesiola, quae istic sub fide & patrocinio tuo est, totque tædia deuorauerit Clarissime vir & magnifice Domine, nunc te fructum laborum non percipere qualis optandus erat, & qualem ego speraui, vehementer doleo. Haec tibi proposita erat mercès, videre sanctum inter eos consensum, qui se prius mutuis discordiis lacerauerant. Videre pace florentem Ecclesiam, quam intestinae contentiones centies perdidissent, nisi eam Dominus mirabiliter seruasset. Nunc quod odiis adhuc certatur, quod sussurri & obtrectationes non cessant, noua denique virulentia erumpit, nec finis est turbarum, sicuti quàm graue acerbumque tibi sit spectaculum, reputo, ita me non minus offendit eorum inhumanitas, qui se tibi morigeros prębere debuerant, quàm angit & discruciat funesti exitus timor. Et tamen vt nihil dissimulem, vereor etiam ne certi quidam illi victoria inflati, aduersæ partis animos iam plusfatis ad contentionem procliues, magis exasperent. Vt nihil apud te dissimulem, in sententia abstracta, cuius missum est ad me exemplar, caput vnum vellem fuisse omissum, quod tibi ab vno illo suggestum non dubito. Neque enim vltrò tibi in mentem venit vetus ministerium eius, acsi adhuc integrum statum in Anglia teneret, in petitua eiusdem iuris possessione apud vos locare. Nihil forte est quod magis ab initio ad creanda dissidia valuerit, vel saltem ad gignedas simultates, deinde magis certamina accenderit quàm ista æmulatio, quòd maior pars putabat se gradu æquali deiici, & contumeliosè à communi societate excludi, si Ecclesia quę apud vos hospitium inuenerat, leges ab vna parte acciperet. Vtilius ergo fuisset, verbum illud taceri, & illum demum statuere Pastorem, ex quo gregis dispersi rogatu locum in vrbe vestra impetrauerat, & exercuerat munus Pastoris. Quàm peruicaciter omnia sua tueri contendat Augustinus, videor sed eorum quoq; ratio habenda fuit, quos spes erat fore magis flexibiles. Hoc obiter attingere placuit, non qu iudicium tuum improbem, sed tamen vt pro tua prudentia apud te expedias, sitne de nihilo conceptus timor qui me nō parum solicitat. Hunc enim vides non modo peruicacibus vel morosis, sed nonnullis forte probis & simplicibus vel exosum esse vel minus gratum: quia se inæqualiter gerat, nec semper eundem teneat modum. Quanquam autem iniquis odiis grauatur, mag-nam tamen Ecclesiae partem ab eo alienatam esse scio, quæ nisi reconcilietur, impendet tristis dissipatio, nec aliud video remedium, nisi vt eos mansuefaciat, sicuti fe facturum mihi pollicitus est, multi autem facere negant. Tu vero praestantissime vir, in re praesenti melius cernis, quomodo res habeat. Quod si tandem im placabilis erit offensio, hominem alio traduci praestaret, quam suis esse contemptui, assiduis calumniis esse expositum, non sine officij quo fungitur probro & dedecore. Hoc quidem improbis nunquam dandum putarem, vt eorum proterviae cederet Pastor: quia & res esset noxij exempli, & nimia ista facilitas augeret eorum furorem vel audaciam. Verum si maior pars Ecclesiae, Ministri pertaesa vix eum audire sustinet, vt demus cœcum esse fastidium, cuius nulla appareat ratio, tentatis omnibus remediis superest hoc extremum quod nuper attigi. Vtinam tamen paulatim mitescant animi, vt eum retinere cupiant, quem sic nunc fastidiunt.
units.tr: Since you have undertaken so many troubles to build up our little church of French speakers, which is under your protection and patronage, and since you have endured so many vexations, most distinguished sir and honoured lord, I am deeply grieved that you are not reaping the fruit of your labours in the form that was to be wished for and that I had hoped for. The reward set before you was to see a holy agreement among those who had previously torn themselves apart in mutual quarrels, and to see a Church flourishing in peace, which internal strife would have destroyed a hundred times over had the Lord not preserved it in a wonderful way. Now the hatreds still go on, the whisperings and slanders do not stop, and a fresh bitterness is breaking out, and there is no end to the disturbances. As I consider how grievous and bitter a spectacle this must be for you, so I am no less offended by the inhumanity of those who ought to have shown themselves compliant to you, and I am tormented by the fear of a disastrous outcome. Yet, not to conceal anything, I fear that certain men, puffed up by their victory, will only further exasperate the other side, whose spirits are already far too inclined to contention. To be frank with you, in the sentence that was drawn up and of which a copy was sent to me, I would have wished one point to be left out, which I do not doubt was suggested to you by that one man. For he did not of his own accord think of this: that his former ministry, as if it still held its full standing in England, should be set against the other side by claiming the same right of possession among you. Perhaps nothing has done more from the beginning to create divisions, or at least to breed rivalries and then to inflame quarrels, than this emulation, since the greater part believed that they were being pushed down to an equal rank and shamefully excluded from the common fellowship, if the Church that had found a home among you were to receive laws from one side. It would therefore have been more useful to keep silent about that point, and to acknowledge as minister only the one from whom, at the request of the scattered flock, he had obtained a place in your city and had exercised the office of minister. I see how obstinately Augustine strives to defend all his own positions, but their reasoning too had to be taken into account, those whom there was hope would be more pliable. I have thought fit to touch on this in passing, not because I disapprove of your judgement, but so that, by your prudence, you may consider whether the fear that troubles me no little is conceived for no reason. For you see that he is disliked, or at least not welcome, not only by the obstinate and the peevish but perhaps by some honest and simple people too, because he behaves unevenly and does not always keep to the same course. Although he is burdened by unjust hatreds, I know that a large part of the Church has been alienated from him, and unless it is reconciled, a sad dispersal hangs over us. I see no remedy except that he should soften them, as he has promised me he will do, though many deny that he will. You, most excellent sir, see more clearly how matters stand in the present situation. But if the offence proves irreconcilable in the end, it would be better for the man to be transferred elsewhere than to be an object of contempt among his own people, exposed to constant calumnies, and not without disgrace and dishonour to the office he holds. I would never think this should be granted to the wicked, that the minister should give way to their insolence, for it would set a harmful example, and such excessive yielding would only increase their fury and audacity. But if the greater part of the Church, weary of the minister, can scarcely bear to hear him, then, granting that this disgust is blind and has no apparent reason, after all remedies have been tried, there remains that last resort which I lately touched on. Yet I hope that their minds will gradually grow milder, so that they may desire to keep him whom they now so despise.

units.la: Quod vestris concionatoribus, Ornatissime vir & mihi obscure uande, literas curasti per Magnificum vestrum Consulem reddendas, prudeter abs te factum est. Quod etiam ab itinere super sedendum putas, consilium tuum probo & amplector. Nec vero mihi in animo fuit vltra vrgere, modo constaret mutuae inter nos pacis fouendae non defuisse studium: ac si qua emergat contentio, imputandum esse eorum culpae quibus oblata conditio non placuerit. Et humaniter quidem testati sunt se fore tranquillos. Quanquis autem non dissimulent, in doctrina se à me discrepare, se tamen daturos operam promittunt, ne certaminibus tur bentur Ecclesiae. Cum vero illi me fidelem Christi seruum agnoscant, & de Ecclesia bene meritum, valde miratus sum, cum nuper contenderent, domi potius & à foeminis baptizandos esse infantes, quam vt è vita migrent absque Baptismo, me odiose in crimen traxisse. Si tantum reprehendissent quod doceo, ferendum erat: sed dum Gallos iactant meo exemplo leges aliis velle imponere, atque addunt etiam me hic tyrannidem exercere, hoc fraterne benevolentiae quam mihi per literas sunt polliciti, minime respondet. Ac de tyrannide quidem quam putida sit calumnia, iudicium collegis & fratribus meis defero, qui certe nunquam conquesti sunt se imperio meo premi. Saepe autem mecum expostulat quod nimis sim timidus, nec satis liberè, vbi opus est, auctoritate quam probarent omnes, vtar. Vtinam viderent quam duris legibus munus docendi obeam, & interea quam nihil mihi arrogem, certe vltro eos suae leuitatis puderet. Etsi autem hac modestia improborum hominum morsus non effugio, mihi tamen sufficit non modo conscientiae, sed rei ipsius & claritatis expetiae testimonium, quo abunde refellitur, quicquid procul maleuoli obstrepunt. Velim tamen ab ipsis scire, quibus tum procul
units.tr: That you took care to have the letters delivered to your preachers through your Magnificent Consul, most distinguished sir and, to me, honoured beyond measure, was wisely done. I also approve of your counsel and accept it, that one should hold back from the journey for the time being. Nor indeed did I intend to press the matter further, provided it is clear that there has been no lack of effort on both sides to foster peace between us; and if any contention arises, it is to be charged to those whose fault it is that they did not like the terms offered. They have indeed testified kindly that they will be peaceable. Although they do not conceal that they differ from me in doctrine, they promise that they will take care not to disturb the Church with quarrels. Yet since they acknowledge me as a faithful servant of Christ, and one who has deserved well of the Church, I was greatly astonished when, not long ago, they argued that infants should be baptized at home and even by women rather than depart from life without Baptism, and so they have hatefully brought me into a charge of this. If they had only found fault with what I teach, it would have been bearable; but while they boast that by my example they wish to impose laws on others, and add that I exercise tyranny here, this does not match the brotherly goodwill they promised me in their letters. As for tyranny, how foul a calumny it is, I leave the judgement to my colleagues and brothers, who have certainly never complained that they were oppressed by my rule. Indeed, they often reproach me with being too timid and not using, where needed, the authority that everyone would approve. Would that these men could see how harsh the burden of teaching is that I bear, and how little I arrogate to myself; surely they would of their own accord be ashamed of their own levity. And although by this modesty I do not escape the bites of wicked men, it is enough for me to have the testimony not only of my conscience but of the thing itself and of its clarity, by which whatever the ill-willed mutter from afar is amply refuted. I would still like to learn from those very men, who find my authority so troublesome at a distance, what they have detected in me that is tyrannical.

units.la: molesta est mea potestas, quid in me tyrannicum deprehenderint. An quia me ad rationem reddendam obtuli, iter longum & difficile paratus fui suscipere in eorum gratiam, & quum nemo vnquam verbulo me salutasset, eos anteuerti, ideo regnum appetere visus sum? Certè nimis stomachosi sunt, si tam amicas conditiones respuere non contenti, insuper exacerbantur. Neque tamen efficiet eorum inhumanitas vt me vnquam suscepti officij poeniteat. Sed mihi dolet tam inconsideratè ipsos ruere in fratrem innoxium, vt ne ab atroci quidem iniuria abstineant. Quod ad rem ipsam spectat, non ignoro quàm altè infixa sit multorum cordibus haec persuasio, qui sine Baptismo discedunt ex mundo infantes, eos à spe salutis excludi. Sed quàm leui praetextu inualuerit hic error, simul expendere conuenit. Citatur celebre illud Christi dictum, Nisi quis renatus fuerit aqua & Spiritu, non intrabit in regnum Dei. Sed nego primùm, Spiritus regeneratione illic coniungi externum aquae Baptismum, quia potius res eadem bis dicitur, & nomen Spiritus expositiuè additum est. Absurdum enim fuisset, quum Christus Nicodemum spoliare vellet carnis suae ingenio, vt depositâ superbia ad veram humilitatem instar pueri se demitteret, à Baptismo incipere. Caeterum vt concedam de Baptismo verba fieri, non tamen praecisè vrgetur necessitas, sed vitae nouitati externum signum additur tanquam accessio, ac si dictum esset, non patere ingressum in regnum Dei absque vitę nouitate, cuius symbolum est Baptismus. Certè Lutherus cuius nomen isti vbique obtendunt, scitè notauit, quum dicit Christus apud Marcum, Quisquis crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit, non repetere secundo mébro, Quisquis non fuerit baptizatus, condemnabitur. Nam si absque Baptismo nulla est salus, latronem qui in regnum Dei admissus est absque Baptismo, necesse erit inde retrahi. Atque vt melius tollatur omnis dubitatio, semper tenendum hoc principium est, non conferri Baptismum infantibus vt filij Dei fiant & haeredes: sed quia iam eo loco & gradu censentur apud Deum, adoptionis gratiam Baptismo obsignari in eorum carne. Alioqui recte eos à Baptismo arcerent Anabaptistae. Nisi enim in eos competat externi signi veritas, mera profanatio erit, in signi ipsius participationem eos vocare. Porrò si quis Baptismum illis neget, in promptu nobis est responsio, iam esse ex grege Christi & ex Dei familia, quoniam foedus salutis, quod Deus cum fidelibus pacisciter, filiis etiam commune est sicuti etiam verba sonant, Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui post te. Nisi praecederet haec promissio, qua Deus liberos fidelium nondum natos adoptat, perperam illis Baptismum conferri certum est. Iam quaero, an Dei verbum suapte virtute ad salutem sufficiat, an vero aliunde mutuerut subfidium,quo suppleatur defectus, vel infirmitas iuuetur? Si prō-missio hæc per se non creditur efficax,non modò virtus Dei,sed etiam gratia & veritas externo signo alligabitur.Ita isti homines dum ornare Baptismum contendunt,grauem Deo ignominiam irrogant.Iam verò quid tot locis fiet,vbi Christus sola fide contentus est?Negabunt fidem à Baptismo separari. Fateor qui-dem,vbi eius recipiendi datur opportunitas.Verum si quem vbi Christi Euangelium fuerit amplexus,subita mor- rapiat,an ideo addicent exitio,quia externa lotione caret?An non veteres histo-riæ exempla quædam martyrum suppeditat,qui prius tracti fuerunt ad supplicium à tyrannis, quàm se ad Baptismum obtulis-sent? Et propter aquæ defectum nihil fundo martyri proderit Christi sanguis,qui pro Euangelij fide,in qua posita est omnium communis salus,sanguinem fundere non dubitat? Certè modestiores fuerunt Papistæ ,qui saltem in hac necessitate, baptismi sanguinis aquæ lotioni subrogât.In summa nisi omnia religionis principia euertere libet,fateri necesse erit,non esse fundatam in Baptismo infantis salutem, sed Baptismo tantum obsignari. Unde sequitur,non præcisè nec simpliciter esse necessarium.Atque vt demus quod peruerse isti postulant,vbi instat mortis periculum, baptizandos esse infantes, erit tamen administrandus ex Christi institutione, & mandato.Iam ostendant vbi Christus priuatis hominibus præceperit baptizare. Certè nemo in Ecclesia honorem sibi vsurpat:& Christus teste Apostolo aliis omnibus præscripsit,ne se ad publicum munus ingerant. Speciale est Christi mandatum ad Apostolos,Ite,prædicate,baptizate. Quisquis idem suo arbitrio tentabit,temeritatis damnabitur. Quid ergo de mulieribus dicendum,quibus ne loqui quidem in cœtu publico conceditur? Atque hæc pluribus forte quàm opus fuit, vel quàm ferebat epistolæ ratio, apud te clarissime vir,disserui. Quanquam si vberior tractatio & plenior te oblectauerit,appe-dix quæ addita fuit libello cōtra Interim,tibi suggeret,quæ voto tuo satisfaciant.Vale nobilis & mihi venerande Domine.Christus te incolumem cum familia coseruet,virtute sustineat,Spiritu gubernet, omníque benedictione locupletet. Geneuæ, XXIIII.Iunij. M. D. LVI.
units.tr: Is it because I offered myself to give an account of my conduct, or because I was ready to undertake a long and difficult journey for their sake, or because, though no one had ever greeted me with a word, I anticipated them, that I seem to have aimed at dominion? Certainly they are too irritable, if, not content to reject such friendly terms, they become even more embittered. Yet their inhumanity will never make me regret the office I have undertaken. But it grieves me that they rush so thoughtlessly upon an innocent brother that they do not refrain even from atrocious injury. As to the matter itself, I am not unaware how deeply this belief has taken root in the hearts of many, that infants who depart from the world without Baptism are excluded from the hope of salvation. But it is worth considering at the same time on how slight a pretext this error has gained strength. The famous saying of Christ is cited: Unless anyone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God. But first I deny that the external baptism of water is here joined to regeneration by the Spirit, since rather the same thing is said twice, and the name of the Spirit is added by way of explanation. For it would have been absurd, when Christ wished to strip Nicodemus of the nature of his flesh, so that, laying aside his pride, he might humble himself like a child to true humility, to begin with Baptism. Moreover, even if I grant that Baptism is spoken of, the necessity is not strictly urged; rather an external sign is added as an accessory to newness of life, as if it had been said that there is no entrance into the kingdom of God without newness of life, of which Baptism is the sign. Certainly Luther, whose name these men everywhere put forward, rightly noted that when Christ says in Mark, Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, he does not repeat in the second clause, Whoever is not baptized will be condemned. For if there is no salvation without Baptism, then the thief who was admitted into the kingdom of God without Baptism would have to be dragged back out from there. And so that every doubt may be removed more fully, this principle must always be held: Baptism is not conferred on infants so that they may become sons and heirs of God, but because they are already reckoned by God to be in that place and rank, and the grace of adoption is sealed by Baptism in their flesh. Otherwise the Anabaptists would rightly keep them from Baptism. For unless the truth of the external sign applies to them, it will be mere profanation to call them to participate in the sign itself. Furthermore, if anyone denies them Baptism, we have a ready answer: they are already of the flock of Christ and of the household of God, since the covenant of salvation which God makes with the faithful is common also to their children, as the words themselves sound: I will be your God and the God of your seed after you. Unless this promise, by which God adopts the children of believers not yet born, went before, it is certain that Baptism would be conferred on them wrongly. Now I ask whether the Word of God is by its own power sufficient for salvation, or whether it must borrow help from elsewhere to supply its lack or to aid its weakness. If this promise is not believed to be effective in itself, then not only the power of God but also his grace and truth will be bound to an external sign. Thus these men, while they strive to adorn Baptism, inflict a grievous dishonour upon God. Now, what will happen in so many places where Christ is content with faith alone? They will deny that faith is separated from Baptism. I indeed grant this, where the opportunity of receiving it is given. But if someone who has embraced the Gospel of Christ is snatched away by sudden death, will they therefore condemn him to destruction because he lacks the external washing? Does not ancient history supply examples of martyrs who were dragged to punishment by tyrants before they could offer themselves for Baptism? And because of the lack of water, will the blood of Christ profit the martyr nothing, when for the faith of the Gospel, in which the common salvation of all lies, he does not hesitate to shed his blood? Certainly the Papists were more moderate, who at least in this necessity substitute the baptism of blood for the washing of water. In short, unless one wishes to overturn all the principles of religion, one must confess that the salvation of an infant is not founded on Baptism but is only sealed by Baptism. From this it follows that Baptism is not strictly and absolutely necessary. And even if we grant what these men perversely demand, that when danger of death is imminent infants must be baptized, it will still have to be administered on the basis of Christ's institution and command. Let them show, then, where Christ commanded private persons to baptize. Certainly no one in the Church arrogates this honour to himself, and Christ, as the Apostle testifies, has prescribed to all others that they should not thrust themselves into public office. The command given by Christ to the Apostles, Go, preach, baptize, is a special one. Whoever attempts the same on his own authority will be condemned for rashness. What then must be said of women, to whom it is not even permitted to speak in a public assembly? I have discussed these matters, most distinguished sir, perhaps at greater length than was needed, or than the nature of a letter bore. Yet if a fuller and more extended treatment has pleased you, the appendix that was added to the little book against the Interim will supply you with what may satisfy your wish. Farewell, noble sir and lord, to be honoured by me. May Christ keep you and your family safe, sustain you with strength, govern you with his Spirit, and enrich you with every blessing. Geneva, 24 June 1556.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS RICHARDO VALLEVIL-lio Pastori Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Franco-furti. s. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Richard Vallevil, pastor of the French Church at Frankfurt. Greetings.

units.la: QVàm acerbum tibi doloris vulnus inflixerit mors optimæ vxoris,ex meo ipsius sensu existimo. Memini enim quàm mihi difficile ante septem annos fuerit,simile luctum vincere. Sed quia probè nosti, quæ ad temperandum immodicum ardorem idonea sint remedia, nihil superest aliud, nisi vt te ad in vsum reuocem. Inter alia, hoc tibi non mediocre solatium est, quod tamen ad doloris irritamentū caro arripit, te cum ille vxore, ad cuius contubernium libenter redeas, dum e loco erit migrandum. Deinde à vitæ socia tibi ostensum fuisse moriendi exemplum. Si mihi priuatus quispiam hortandus foret, cum expendere iuberem, quid sibi tuo debeat. Nam a suo iure perperam fraudamus, nisi eius arbitrio viuat ac atur quisque nostrum. Tuum vero est simul reputare, quæ neas personam in Ecclesia Dei. Sed quia præcipuum consonis argumentum nobis in eo situm est, admirabili Dei prouidentia nobis in salutem verti quæ aduersa putamus, neque sefari nos in mundo, nisi vt semel colligamur in cœlestem eius regnum, hic pro tua pietate acquiescas. Quia feruorem contentionum in Ecclesia vestra vtcunque sedatum esse audio, dabis operam, ne obscuræ simultates in animis resideant. Momento id fieri non potest, scio. Ergo paulatim lenire animos exacerbatos studeas, donec penitus offensiones diluatur. Vale optime & charissime frater. Dominus tuæ viduitatis tristitiam Spiritus sui gratia leniat, te gubernet suo Spiritu, ac benedicat laboribus tuos.
units.tr: I can well imagine how bitter a wound of grief the death of your excellent wife has inflicted on you, for I remember how hard it was for me to overcome a similar sorrow seven years ago. But since you know well which remedies are suited to curbing excessive passion, nothing remains except that I recall you to their use. Among other things, this is no small comfort to you, though our flesh seizes on it as a spur to grief: that you will rejoin that wife, in whose company you would gladly return, when you must leave this place. Further, your wife set before you an example of how to die. If some private person were to be urged by me, I would bid him weigh what he owes to his own… [text garbled]. For we wrongly defraud God of his right unless each of us lives and is sustained at his will. It is for you to consider at the same time what part you play in the Church of God. But since the chief ground of consolation lies in this, that by God's wonderful providence what we think adverse turns to our salvation, and that we are only pilgrims in the world until we are gathered once into his heavenly kingdom, take comfort in this, as befits your piety. Since I hear that the heat of the contentions in your church has been somehow calmed, take care that no hidden hostilities linger in men's minds. I know this cannot be done in a moment. So gradually strive to soothe minds that have been exasperated, until the offences are wholly dissolved. Farewell, most excellent and dearest brother. May the Lord soften the sadness of your widowhood by the grace of his Spirit, govern you by his Spirit, and bless your labours.

units.la: M. D. LVI.
IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to N. S. Greetings.

units.la: NVnquam de te cogitare possum, quod subinde tamen facere soleo, quin pro meo erga te amore, & communi inter nos pietatis sensu magnopere tibi condoleam. Neq; enim mihi dubium est, quin tu inter opes ac delicias quæ tibi affluunt, dies noctesque anxius suspires. Quanquam hoc longè præstat, quàm si in tam periculosa statione securus quiesceres. Proinde sic te in molestissimis istis curis, quæ te angunt ac cruciant, solari cupio: vt eas tibi penitus eximere, neque audeam, neq; velim. Quò magis sortem tuam displicere tibi necesse est: in qua nihil reperis melius, quàm grauem acerbumque miseriæ tuæ sensum. Adeóque tibi expedit acriter vellicari, vt nihil magis timendum sit, quàm ne lentæ punctiones tibi callum obducant. Quoties ergo te solicitat & vrit conscientia, memineris tuas esse partes, stimulos istos acuere potius quàm retundere: scintillas accedere potius quàm suffocare. Aliter plurimi: qui vt omne tristitiæ materiam procul abigant, non modò facere iubent salubres Dei monitiones: sed mortiferam & Dei & sui obliuione inducere sibi conantur. Tibi verò, quèadmodum iam dixi, multò vtilius, assidua inquietudine vexari, quàm sub tali tamque exitiali
units.tr: I can never think of you, as I often do, without sympathising deeply with you, out of my affection for you and the common feeling of piety between us. For I have no doubt that, amid the wealth and pleasures that flow to you, you sigh anxiously day and night. Yet this is far better than if you were resting securely in so perilous a station. Accordingly I wish to console you in those most troubling cares that torment and rack you, but I neither dare nor wish to free you from them entirely. The more necessary it is that you should be displeased with your lot, in which you find nothing better than a grave and bitter sense of your wretchedness. And it is so useful for you to be sharply stung that nothing is to be feared more than that the gentle pricks should harden a callus over you. Therefore, whenever your conscience troubles and burns you, remember that it is your part to sharpen those goads rather than blunt them, to fan the sparks rather than smother them. Many people do otherwise: so that they may drive away every cause of sadness, they not only refuse to heed God's salutary warnings but try to bring on themselves a deadly forgetfulness of both God and themselves. For you, as I have already said, it is far more profitable to be vexed by constant restlessness than to lie sunk in such a deadly lethargy.

units.la: {y} ... veterno sopitum iacere. Caeterum malis tuis ita affici te oportet, ut scrio adspires ad remedium. Video quantae tibi difficultates obstent. Sed amanti nihil arduum. Deinde si ex animo laqueos istos exuere cupies, quibus nunc implicitus teneris, habes qui eos vel expediat, vel abrumpat. Si emergere appetes ex luto, in quo defixus haeres, habes qui tibi manum e coelo porrigat. Dominus certe viam inveniet: modo ne eius auxilio tu defis. Satis & super hactenus deliberando fluctuatus es. In re tam certa mature statuendum, quid facto sit opus: & quod statueris, strenue & celeriter exequendum. Paucos videmus, qui spote ac praesenti animo, quaecunque occurrunt obstacula, superent. Verum si pauci nos ad imitationem virtutis suae inuitant: terreant nos eorum exempla, qui tarditatis nimiae poenas dederunt. Quanquam ut nullus sit hominum respectus, vna coelestis magistri auctoritas sufficere nobis debet. Itaque hanc tibi solam obiicio: sicuti eam, vbi animum tuum excitaueris, tibi confido tanti fore, ut amplius nihil requiras. Et nunc quid restat, nisi ut vincat ille, cui nos omnes in obsequium, absque certamine, addici conuenit? Vale dilectissime frater. xxxi. Ian. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: {y} ... sunk in such a deadly lethargy. Moreover, you ought to be so affected by your troubles that you earnestly aspire to a remedy. I see how great the difficulties are that stand in your way. But nothing is hard for one who loves.
