Then, if you desire from your heart to cast off those snares in which you are now held entangled, you have One who can either untie them or break them. If you wish to rise out of the mire in which you stick fast, you have One who will stretch out his hand to you from heaven. The Lord will surely find a way, provided you do not fail him by his help. You have wavered long enough in deliberating. In a matter so certain, you must decide promptly what needs to be done, and what you have decided, carry out vigorously and quickly. We see few who by their own accord and with presence of mind overcome whatever obstacles meet them. But if few invite us to imitate their courage, let the examples of those who paid the penalty for excessive delay frighten us. Yet even though there is no regard for men, the sole authority of the heavenly Master ought to suffice for us. So I set this before you alone: once you have stirred up your spirit, I trust it will be enough for you so completely that you will seek nothing more. And now what remains, except that he should prevail, to whom we all ought to be surrendered in obedience, without contest? Farewell, most beloved brother. 31 January 1557.

units.la: CLARISSIMO VIRO VIRTVTE ET ERVDITIONE Praestanti, Ioanni Calvino, fratri ac Symmystae obseruando, Ecclesiae Genevensis Pastori.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, eminent in virtue and learning, John Calvin, to be honoured as a brother and fellow-Mystes, pastor of the Church of Geneva.

units.la: Gratia & Pax per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Grace and peace through Jesus Christ.

units.la: CLatissime vir ac frater in Domino plurimum obseruande, vbi viderunt Vvesalienses concionatores de nostra contro uersia factum esse compromissum in sententiam Philippi, ac suas suggestiones non magni fieri, aduocarunt quosdam e Frisia qui sua auctoritate senatum monerent. Quod non infeliciter eis succesit. Per eos enim effectum est, ut senatum facti compromissi poeniteret. Quare statim missus est Vvittembergam Thomas vnus ex concionatoribus, qui Philippo senatus sententiam indicaret. Vix Coloniam peruenerat tabellarius quae ad te misi, cum Thomas rediit Vvittemberga. Nihil ad meas literas respondit Philippus. Rescripserat quidem Domino Huberto Languetto, sed nostri literas suppresserunt, ut nobis omnium ignaris facilius imponerent, & nostri exilij culpam a se remouerent. Acceptis literis a Philippo, me & Trihernum Anglum virum doctum vocarunt in Senatum. Nos autem, ne iuxta morem suum actionem nostram calumniarentur, ex nostris Ecclesiis aliquot nobis adiunximus, qui essent loco testium. Non recitarunt integras
units.tr: Most illustrious sir and brother in the Lord, most worthy of my respect: when the preachers of Wesel saw that our controversy had been referred to the judgment of Philip, and that their own suggestions were not held in much esteem, they summoned certain men from Friesland to warn the council by their authority. This did not turn out badly for them. Through these men it was brought about that the council repented of the agreed compromise. Therefore Thomas, one of the preachers, was at once sent to Wittenberg to tell Philip the council's decision. The courier whom I sent to you had scarcely reached Cologne when Thomas returned from Wittenberg. Philip made no reply to my letter. He had indeed written to Lord Hubert Languet, but our opponents suppressed that letter, so that they could more easily deceive us, who knew nothing, and shift the blame for our exile from themselves. After receiving Philip's letter, they summoned me and Trihernus the Englishman, a learned man, before the council. We, however, lest they slander our conduct as is their custom, took with us some men from our congregations to serve as witnesses.

units.la: Epist.231. gras literas Philippi, sed tres tantùm versiculos ex iis decerptos, nimirum vnum de Coena Domini, alterù de Baptismo, tertium de cerimoniis. Iis auditis permissum est nobis secedere delibe-tandi causa. Inter deliberandum visum est omnibus approban-dam esse sententiam Philippi, quod & à nobis factum est. Nihil enim in ea continebatur, quod Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctri-næ aduersaretur. Audita nostra responsione, iusserunt nos iterû secedere, vt ipsi inter se deliberarent. Reuersis nobis dixit Con-ful, Cùm satis constet ex vestra cófessione, vos omnino dissen-tire à nobis in articulo de Coena Domini, nec Philippi, nec cu-iusquam hominis auctoritatem in ea remoramur: imò mira-mur vos tâ præfracte & pertinaciter audere dissentire à tot san-ctis & eruditis viris. Quare nisi velitis credere, fateri, & syngra-pha testari illa duo axiomata vera esse, videlicet in Coena Do-mini verum corpus Christi in pane contineri, Item nos illud corpus non tantùm mente, sed etiam ore sumere, iubemus vt o-mnes intra Calendas Martias hinc migretis. Audita sententia petiimus, vt saltem temporis spatium, quod nobis ad componé-das res nostras concedebatur, ad Calendas Maias prorogaretur, cùm non sit facile tot miseris hominibus intra illud tempus mi grare: cùm præsertim toto Februario adhuc sæuiat hyems in il-lis regionibus, & difficulter navigetur aduersus Rheno. Respon-dit Consul esse quòd illis ageremus gratias pro tanta erga nos humanitate, cùm si vellent vti iure suo, nos bonis omnibus e-xuere, & præterea à nobis pœnas exigere possent. Vbi resciuerût concionatores huiusmodi sententiam in nos latam esse, coepe-runt ex suggestu debacchari, & miris calumniis nos onerare, vt populum aduersus nos concitarent, & præcipuè quidam Her-manus primus auctor huius Tragœdiæ, cuius maiorne sit insci-tia an impudentia, non satis scio. Nam semel pro concione au-sus est dicere, nos nullam fidem verbis Christi habere, ac esse sce leratos Sacramentorum contaminatores, qui instar luporum in gregem Domini irrepserimus, vt veras eius oues deuorare-mus, ac virus in Anglia haustum in eas euomeremus. Nó periit illi sua opera, nam media luce à quodam ictus fui lapide. Alius me vesperi domum redeuntem pugno in pectore percussit. Nec defuerunt qui striàto gladio quosdam ex nostris inuaderent, in-clamantes eos esse sceleratos sacramentarios: & certè nisi sibi su ga consuluissent, periculum illis erat de vita. Talis fuit exitus no stræ contentionis, potius quàm disceptationis Vvefalien sis, de qua sanè longè aliam spem conceperam. Dum sic Vvefaliæ ac-cipimur, in hac Ecclesiæ Francfordiensi ingrauescebant conten-tiones, quæ eovsque progressæ sunt, vt patrum abfuerit quin ali-quoties in ipso templo ad manus venirent. Ingemiscebat pij,
units.tr: They did not read out Philip's whole letter (Epist. 231.), but only three short verses picked out of it: one about the Lord's Supper, a second about Baptism, and a third about ceremonies. After these were heard, we were allowed to withdraw to deliberate. While we deliberated, it seemed good to all of us to approve Philip's judgment, and this we did. For nothing in it contradicted the doctrine of our churches. When our answer had been heard, they ordered us to withdraw again, so that they might deliberate among themselves. When we returned, the consul said: "Since it is quite clear from your own confession that you entirely disagree with us on the article of the Lord's Supper, we pay no heed to the authority of Philip or of any other man on this point. Indeed we marvel that you dare to dissent so stubbornly and obstinately from so many holy and learned men. Therefore, unless you are willing to believe, confess, and attest in writing that those two axioms are true, namely that in the Lord's Supper the true body of Christ is contained in the bread, and that we receive that body not only in the mind but also with the mouth, we order you all to leave this place before the Kalends of March." When we heard this sentence, we asked that the period of time granted us to settle our affairs be extended to the Kalends of May, since it is not easy for so many wretched people to move within that time, especially as winter is still raging throughout February in those regions and it is difficult to sail against the Rhine. The consul replied that we ought to thank them for such kindness toward us, since if they wished to use their right, they could strip us of all our goods and besides exact penalties from us. When the preachers learned that such a sentence had been passed against us, they began to rage from the pulpit and to load us with monstrous slanders, in order to stir the people against us. Especially Hermann, the first author of this tragedy, whether his ignorance or his impudence is greater I do not well know. For once, in a sermon, he dared to say that we have no faith in the words of Christ, and that we are wicked defilers of the sacraments, who had crept into the flock of the Lord like wolves, so that we might devour its true sheep and vomit out on them the poison we had swallowed in England. His efforts were not wasted, for in broad daylight I was struck by a stone thrown by someone. Another struck me in the chest with his fist as I was returning home in the evening. Nor were there lacking men who attacked some of our people with drawn swords, crying out that they were wicked sacramentarians; and certainly, had they not looked to their own safety, they would have been in danger of their lives. Such was the outcome of our dispute, which was more a contention than a debate at Wesel, and of which I had certainly conceived a very different hope. While we were being treated in this way at Wesel, dissensions were growing worse in this church of Frankfurt, and they have gone so far that the fathers have on several occasions nearly come to blows in the church itself. The godly groaned,

units.la: nec fe petulanti audaciæ aduerfariorū audebant opponere, cum viderent eos hoc agere, vt grauem aliquem tumultum excitarent quo posset Ecclesia euerti. Optimus vir Dominus Guilliel-mus quantùm in fe erat, ruetes res sustinebat: sed aduersarij mul-tis calumniis effecerant, vt is apud N. non tantùm haberet fidei, quantùm perturbatus Ecclesiæ status postulabat. Interea hîc resciscunt nos esse dimissos Vvefalia. Deliberant de me aduo-cando. Hoc significant Clavvburgo, qui probat consilium, & iubet omnes lites in meum vsque aduentum sopiri. Mittitur ad me vnus ex Diaconis, qui circa brumam Vvefaliam venit cum literis ab Ecclesiâ, quibus obnixè à me petebatur, vt statim itine-ri me committerem. Conuocaui fere omnes ex nostra Eccle-fia, ostendi illis literas, & dixi me nihil nisi ex eorum consilio facturum. Suaserunt omnes ne in tam præsenti periculo Fran-cofordienfi Ecclesiæ deesse m. Constitui res meas, quanta potui celeritate: & licet effent sæuissimæ tempestates, huius Ecclesiæ precibus obsequutus sum. Calendis huius mensis huc veni. Quatriduo post rediit à vobis tabellarius cum tuis ad me lite-ris, in quibus beneuolentiâmne tuam, prudens consilium, an in-defessum studium iuuandi Ecclesias magis sum amplexatus, di-cere non possum. Ingentem certè consolationem ex iis perce-pi, cum viderem me habere quod calumniatoribus opponerem: & præterea liberari illa anxietate deligendi loci, in qua re nihil proifus nisi ex tuo consilio facere constitueram. Itaque ago ti-bi ingentes gratias, & te obtestor, cum tanto affectu hanc Ec-clefiam (malitiaeorum quos minimè decebat pene letaliter vul-neratam) fanandam susceperis, ne eidem suæ valetudini Dei be-neficio vtcunque restitutæ, consilio, exhortatione, ac sanctis pre-cibus adesse te pigeat. Idem etiam tota ipsa Ecclesia efflagitat. Vix dici potest quàm impedita hîc omnia inuenerim: quò ma-gis est nobis prædicandum Dei opus inter nos, quòd intra pau-cos dies res multò in meliorem statum præterfpem humanam restituta sunt: sublatæ verò occasiones mali, quantùm Dominus & videre, & posse, & præstare concessit. Perendie (Deo iuuante) aliquot mensibus intermissam Cœnam Domini celebrabimus. Angustia temporis cogit nos festinantius quàm cupieremus agere. Vvefaliam enim mihi properandum est, vt quantùm in me est miseris illis reliquiis consulam. Nam non ita multùm super-est ex tempore illis concesso ad res suas componendas. Vvefa-lia erit mihi eundum A. siquidem hoc à me flagitat Ecclesia. Vix potero huc redire ante mercatum. Vale Clarissime vir, & obser-uande frater, peto vt ignoscas mearum literarum prolixitati. Deus conferuet te, ac totam vestram Ecclesiam, cuius precibus afflictum hunc gregem commendamus. Francofordiæ, quar-
units.tr: and did not dare to oppose the shameless audacity of their adversaries, since they saw them aiming to stir up some serious tumult by which the church might be overthrown. The excellent man, Lord William, as far as he was able, upheld the falling affairs; but the adversaries, by many calumnies, had brought it about that he had among the people not as much trust as the disturbed state of the church required. Meanwhile here they learned that we had been dismissed from Wesel. They deliberated about calling me. They signified this to Clauburg, who approved the plan and ordered all quarrels to be put to rest until my arrival. A deacon was sent to me, who came to Wesel about the time of the winter solstice with letters from the church, in which I was earnestly asked to set out for the journey at once. I called together almost all of our congregation, showed them the letters, and said that I would do nothing except by their counsel. All of them advised that I should not fail the Frankfurt church in so pressing a danger. I settled my affairs with all the speed I could; and although the storms were most severe, I yielded to the prayers of this church. I came here on the Kalends of this month. Four days later a courier returned from you with your letter to me, in which I cannot say whether I embraced more your goodwill, your prudent counsel, or your tireless zeal for helping the churches. Certainly I received from it great consolation, since I saw that I had something to set against the slanderers; and moreover I was freed from that anxiety of choosing a place, in which I had resolved to do nothing at all except by your counsel. Therefore I give you immense thanks, and I entreat you: since you have undertaken with such affection to heal this church, which had been almost mortally wounded by the malice of those who ought least to have done it, do not be reluctant to be present to it, in counsel, exhortation, and holy prayers, now that it has by God's benefit been somehow restored to health. The whole church itself also earnestly asks the same. It can hardly be said how entangled I found everything here; all the more must we proclaim among ourselves the work of God, since within a few days affairs have been restored to a much better state than human hope allowed, and the occasions of evil have been removed as far as the Lord has granted us to see, to be able, and to accomplish. The day after tomorrow, God helping, we shall celebrate the Lord's Supper, which has been interrupted for some months. The shortness of time forces us to act more hastily than we would wish. For I must hasten to Wesel, so that I may, as far as lies in me, look after those miserable remnants. For not much of the time granted them for settling their affairs is left. I must go to Wesel on the ... since the church demands it of me. I can hardly return here before the market. Farewell, most illustrious sir and brother deserving of respect. I ask that you pardon the long-windedness of my letter. May God preserve you and your whole church, for whose prayers we commend this afflicted flock. Frankfurt, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, 1557.

units.la: NVnc demum vrget ipsa necessitas, fratres dilectissimi, vt oculos in coelum constanter attollatis. Exitus quis futurus sit, nondum tenemus. Sed quando plane videtur Dominus vocare ad martyrium designatis, ad obsignandam veritatem vti velle, vnum hoc est appositissimum, vt vos ad illud ipsum comparetis, rogando vt suo vos arbitrio ita obsequentes praestet, vt nihil quicquam ab eo abducat, quo vos ipsi vocare libuerit. Sic enim fratres, mortificationem nostram procedere oportere didicistis, vt in sacrificium ipsi offerri parati simus. Neque interea fieri poterit, quin duri insultus excipiendi sint, vt in vobis experiamini quod ita Dominus semel protulit: Ducent te, nempe quo no voles: sed & illud succurrat, cuius nomine & virtute nobis decertandum sit, qui illi vnquam innixi sunt, nunquam attonitos trepidasse, nedum vt iacuerint confusi. Confidite igitur fratres vos ipsos vbi ad extremum vetum erit, ipso etiam Domini Iesu Spiritu confirmatu iri, vt sub illo tentationum pondere, etiamsi virium vestrarum ad illud ratio nulla sit, no magis deficiatis quam Christus ipse, qui tam insignem ex illis victoriam retulit, vt ipsa nobis certissimum triumphi per medias mortes capessendi pignus & quasi vexillum sublatum extaret. Quare si ita feret ipsius voluntas, vt ad mortem vsque ius & causam ipsius propugnetis, manum illam auxiliarem porriget, vt strenue ad extremum perstetis, neque vel minimam vestri sanguinis guttam vacuam, & euanidam cadere in terram sinet. Atque vt fructus Martyrij ex vobis non ita statim emergat: tamen dubium non est, quin longe vberior extaturus tandem sit, quam quisquam existimet. Et quoniam eo vos honore affecit, vt vinculorum vestrorum fama exierit ad plurimos, & vndiquaque sparsa sit, tanto certius est mortem illam vestram vel frequente Satana latissime emanaturam, vt Dei nomen per illam exaltetur amplissime. Ego quidem sic statuo, si Domini haec mes erat, vt vos ad se vocaret, vestram illam diuturniorem detentionem ab ipso destinatam fuisse, vt illius occasione excitarentur plurimi, quos ipsos vestro exitu demum aedificandos sibi prouidit. Plura hic no addo quibus vos exhorter, aut consolari studeam, cum satis sciam Patrem ipsum Cœlestem suam ipsius consolationum efficaciam vobis per se testatam reddere: vósque etiam satis per vos ferri ad studium & meditationem eorum, quæ verbo Dominus suis ipse commonstrat. Et illa etiam quæ extant virtutis ipsius in vobis habitantis documenta, omnino confirmant, ipsum adeo ad extremum vsque opus illud suum profequuturum. Illud vobis cōstat, nos ex hac vita migrantes non in incertum ferri: tum quia de certissima illa post istam euanidam cœlesti vita abunde estis persuasi, tum imprimis quōd plenissima adoptionis Domini gratuitæ fide instructi, ad illam vitam, iam non secus atque ad vestram hæreditatem & patrimonium contenditis. Et quòd ordinati estis à Domino Filij ipsius testes, illud peculiarem & præcipuam quan dam tantæ veritatis notam vobis etiam apponit. Supererit lucta illa, in qua demum non incedere modo, sed etiam currendo eniti nos iubet Spiritus Domini. Est quidem illud grauissimum tentationis genus, ac lôgè acerbissimum, vbi instat nobis & obuersatur oculis hostium veritatis illè effrænis tumor, atque vbi eorum furor impotens ita despumat, dum nulla piis à Domino melior spes affulget. Atqui si illud non excidit nobis, vitam nostram absconditam esse, ac nos mortuos hic esse (vti perpetuus est sensus & vsus istius doctrinæ) perinde nouum non erit, quod afflictiones perdurent. Cùm enim ita Domino visum est, nos aduersariis nunc quidem permittere: nostrum est etiam, si tempus illud redemptionis nostræ moram trahit, placidènos tantis per continere. Porrò cùm idem ille iudicaturum se testetur gentem illam quæ populum ipsius iugo seruitutis oppressèrit, nolite dubitare, quin horribilis vindicta illos maneat qui tam impotenti audacia ipsius Maiestatis infultarint, atque illos crudelissimè insectati fuerint qui nomen ipsius inuocarent. Vos modò illud Dauidis vobis ipsis applicate, quod legem Domini non fitis obliti, etiamsi anima vestra per singula momenta fit in manibus vestris: cùmque Dominus ipse vita vestra in re tanti momenti vti statuerit, qualis est veritatis ipsius confirmatio, nolite dubitare, quin & ipsa futura sit illi quàm commendatissima. Infiat verò illud tempus quo terra deteget sanguinem quem absorptâ contegit, nos verò vbi caducis istis corporibus exuti fuerimus, in optatissimum statum reformabimur. Satis sit igitur quòd per nostrum opprobrium tantisper glorificetur Filij Dei nomen, atque in illo testimonio firmissimè acquiescamus, quòd verè nobis conscij simus, nobis ista non inferri alia de causa, quàm quia speremus in Deo viuo. Atque illo argumento fas sit nobis insul tare totius mundi ferociæ, dum ad illam spem contendimus, quæ nos demum in abfcôditæ nostræ vitæ plenissimam fruitionem intromittet. Valete fratres in Domino vnicè dilecti, ac vt nostri memoriam in vestris precibus vigere cupio ac postulo, ita etiam vestro nomine Dominum oro, ut suo illo sancto praesidio vos complectatur, sua virtute confirmet magis ac magis, vobis reipsa patefaciat studium illud suum de salute vestra impensum, atque imprimis Spiritus sui dona adaugeat, ut ad ipsius gloriam ad extremum usque vigeant & valeant in vobis. 1. Februarij.
units.tr: Now at last the very necessity presses upon you, dearest brothers, that you lift your eyes constantly toward heaven. We do not yet know what the outcome will be. But since the Lord plainly seems to be calling those he has designated to martyrdom, and to seal the truth with their blood, the one most fitting course is for you to prepare yourselves for that very thing, asking that he would so grant you a willing obedience to his will that nothing draws you away from whatever he has been pleased to call you to. For, brothers, you have learned that our mortification must proceed in such a way that we are ready to be offered to him as a sacrifice. Meanwhile it will not be possible but that harsh assaults must be endured, so that you may experience in yourselves what the Lord once said: "They will lead you where you do not wish to go." Yet let this also come to mind: that in whose name and power we must fight, those who have ever leaned upon him were never found terrified and dismayed, much less lying down in confusion. So be confident, brothers, that when the final test comes you will be strengthened by the Spirit of the Lord Jesus himself, so that under the weight of these temptations you will not fail any more than Christ himself did, who won such a remarkable victory over them that it stands as a most certain pledge for us of obtaining triumph through the midst of death, and as a raised banner. Therefore, if it is his will that you defend his cause and right even to death, he will stretch out that helping hand, so that you stand firm to the end, and he will not allow even the smallest drop of your blood to fall to the ground empty and vanished. And although the fruit of your martyrdom may not emerge from you immediately, there is no doubt that it will at last be far more abundant than anyone supposes. And since he has honoured you so far that the report of your chains has gone out to very many and been scattered on every side, it is all the more certain that your death, even with Satan's frequent opposition, will spread very widely, so that the name of God may be exalted through it most amply. I for my part hold this view: if this was the Lord's intention in calling you to himself, then that longer detention of yours was appointed by him so that through it very many would be stirred up, whom he foresaw would be edified by your departure. I add no more here by which I might exhort you or try to console you, since I know well that the Heavenly Father will himself make the efficacy of his consolations evident to you by his own testimony, and that you are sufficiently led, through yourselves, to the study and meditation of those things which the Lord shows his people in his Word. The evidences of his power dwelling in you, which are already present, altogether confirm that he will carry on that work of his even to the end. This much is certain to you: that we who depart from this life are not carried into uncertainty. This is so both because you are fully persuaded of that certain heavenly life after this one, which is fading, and above all because, being instructed in the full faith of the Lord's free adoption, you strive toward that life no less than toward your own inheritance and patrimony. And that you have been ordained by the Lord as witnesses of his Son, this too sets upon you a special and principal mark of so great a truth. There remains that struggle, in which the Spirit of the Lord bids us not merely to walk but to press on by running. Indeed this is the most grievous kind of temptation, and by far the most bitter, when that unbridled swelling of the enemies of the truth presses upon us and stands before our eyes, and when their impotent fury froths up so, while no better hope from the Lord shines upon the godly. Yet if it has not slipped from our minds that our life is hidden and that we are dead here (as the constant meaning and use of this teaching is), it will be no novelty that afflictions persist. For since it has seemed good to the Lord to permit us for now to our adversaries, it is ours also, if the time of our redemption delays, to bear calmly such great things. Moreover, since the same God testifies that he will judge the nation which has oppressed his people with the yoke of slavery, do not doubt that a dreadful vengeance awaits those who have insulted the majesty of God with such reckless audacity, and who have most cruelly persecuted those who called upon his name. Only apply to yourselves that saying of David, that you have not forgotten the law of the Lord, even though your soul is in your hands from moment to moment. And since the Lord himself has decided to use your life in a matter of such weight as the confirmation of his truth, do not doubt that it will be most acceptable to him. The time will come when the earth will reveal the blood which it has swallowed and covered; and we, once stripped of these perishable bodies, will be transformed into the most desired state. Let it be enough, then, that through our reproach the name of the Son of God is glorified for a while, and that we rest most firmly in this testimony: that we are truly conscious that these things are inflicted on us for no other reason than that we hope in the living God. And by that argument it is right for us to scorn the fierceness of the whole world, while we press toward that hope which will at last bring us into the full enjoyment of our hidden life. Farewell, brothers, dearly beloved in the Lord. As I desire and ask that the memory of us may flourish in your prayers, so also in your name I pray the Lord that he may embrace you with his holy protection, strengthen you more and more by his power, show you in fact the zeal he has shown for your salvation, and above all increase the gifts of his Spirit, so that they may flourish and prevail in you to the end, to his glory. 1 February.

units.la: VRENHONIVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Utenhonius to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: {a}CVM iam scribendis ad amicos passim literis operam dare, Caluine mihi obseruandissime, nolui committere quin te nunc certiorem facerem de successu rerum Magnifici Domini Ioannis à Lasco in Polonia. Cui sane non omnino infeliciter cessit hactenus (gratia Deo Optimo Maximo) tametsi non sine incredibili reluctatione Satanae, qui sibi suoque regno ab eo (quae eius admiranda hic multis nominibus est auctoritas) non parum metuit. Ac proinde omnes conatus, omniaque studia, per suos stipendiarios hactenus congessit ut eum perderet, aut saltem Regno pelleret. Cum enim ante duos, plus minus, menses, Episcopi nostri (qui omnes apud Regem Vvarsouiae in Regni comitiis erant) subolfecissent D. Ioannem à Lasco huc advenisse, mox conuenerunt apud Archiepiscopum Gnesnensem, vnà cum Lipomano Veronensi Episcopo Legato hic Pontificis, semotis atbitris (ut vocant) secularibus. Vbi totum diem consultarunt inter se, quid hic facto opus esset, ut Dominum à Lasco omnium commodissime Regno eiicerent: re enim eorum hoc esse. Nam ipsum si maneat eorum carnificem fore (quod ipsum dixisse Cracouiensem Episcopum, affirmauit Nicodemus quidam) ac proinde tempestuo opus fore remedio. Postridie vero Regem adeunt, primo Lipomanus: deinde etiam reliqui Episcopi turmatim omnes. Se compertum habere Ioannem à Lasco aduenisse, velleque Regem adire, ut cum ipso colloquatur. Quare supplicare se, ne eum ad colloquium admittat, eo quod maximus esset haereticus (qui nusquam gentium fertetur, ideoque nunc in patriam reuersum esse) ac talis hic olim pronunciatus esset. Quibus respondit Rex, qui adhuc est pusillanimior. Verum quidem est, ipsum olim à vobis in vestris synodis haereticum fuisse pronunciatum: sed non item à Regio, Regnique Senatu. Ioannemque à Lasco ac suos asseuerare & probare velle se non haereticos, sed catholicos esse. Non video itaque qua ratione hic vobis condescendam. Tum vero aiebant Episcopi, Regem hoc omnino facere
units.tr: Since I am already busy writing letters to friends everywhere, my most esteemed Calvin, I did not want to fail to inform you now of how matters have gone for the Magnificent Lord John à Lasco in Poland. Thus far (by the grace of God Most Good and Great) they have gone not unsuccessfully, though not without incredible resistance from Satan, who fears no little for himself and his kingdom from him (such is the remarkable authority he enjoys here in many respects). Accordingly, through his hired agents, he has so far devoted all his efforts and every endeavour to destroying him or at least driving him from the kingdom. For about two months ago, when our bishops (who were all at the court of the King at Warsaw for the assembly of the realm) got wind that Lord John à Lasco had come here, they soon met at the house of the Archbishop of Gniezno, together with Lipomano, the Bishop of Verona and the Pope's legate here, with the lay onlookers (as they call them) removed. There they spent the whole day conferring among themselves as to what should be done here so that they might most conveniently drive Lord à Lasco from the kingdom; for it was in their interest to do so. For if he remained, he would be their executioner (as Nicodemus, a certain man, affirmed that the Bishop of Kraków had himself said), and therefore a drastic remedy would be needed. The next day they approached the King: first Lipomano, then all the other bishops in a body. They said they had learned that John à Lasco had arrived and wished to go to the King to confer with him. Therefore they begged him not to admit him to an audience, since he was the greatest heretic (who is nowhere to be found in the world, and so is now said to have returned to his homeland), and had once been pronounced such here. To this the King, who is still rather timid, replied: It is true that he was once pronounced a heretic by you in your synods, but not by the King and the Senate of the realm. And John à Lasco and his followers assert and wish to prove that they are not heretics but Catholics. I therefore do not see on what grounds I should give in to you here. Then the bishops said that the King must absolutely do this, if he truly wished to provide for the tranquillity of the kingdom. For there was no doubt that many disturbances would arise here if John à Lasco were allowed to remain. But the King, since they made no end or limit to their demands here, ordered them to be silent: their request was unjust and contrary to the law of the kingdom. When they saw that they had accomplished nothing with that first battering-ram, from that day on they shamelessly devised a thousand lies, with which they burdened Lord à Lasco everywhere, and especially before the King himself. Among other things they asserted that Lord à Lasco had come into Poland to take up arms against the King, and that he would fill everything here with tumults and sedition: that with the help of the bishopric of Kraków, with a hundred or two hundred horsemen, he was already, since his arrival, pulling down everything in the churches at his own discretion, and many other things of this kind. They related and asserted all these things so consistently and firmly that the King began for some time to suspect something sinister about Lord à Lasco and to be more hostile to him, until he himself questioned a certain nobleman, a relative of Lord à Lasco, about this very matter. For he told the King that all these things were nothing but mere calumnies, most shamelessly devised and fabricated by his opponents.

units.la: B.j. debere, si modo vellet recte consulere tranquillitati Regni. Non enim dubium esse quin multæ turbæ hic oborituræ essent, si hic ferretur Ioannes à Lasco. Rex vero (dum illi nullum finem neq; modum hic facerent) iussit ut silerent. Iniquam enim & contra ius regni eorum esse postulationem. Quum vero illi iam videret se primo illo ariete nihil effecisse, mille mendacia ab eo die impudentissimè excogitarunt, quibus Dominum à Lasco passim & præsertim apud Regem ipsum grauarunt. Inter cætera asseuerantes ipsum D. à Lasco venisse in Poloniam, ut arma sumeret contra Regem: utque impleret hic omnia turbis & seditionibus: cum obequitate Episcopatum Cracouiensem centum aut ducentis equitibus, passimque iam sub ipsum eius aduentum demolirì in tèplis omnia pro suo arbitrio, & id genus alia multa: quæ omnia adeò constanter referebant, firmiterque asseuerabant, ut Rex cœperit aliquandiu sinisterius quippiam suspicari de Domino à Lasco, eique infensior esse, donec ipse cum Procere quodam, affine Domini à Lasco de hoc ipso expostulasset. Ille enim dixit Regi, ea omnia nihil esse quàm meras calumnias, multò impudentissimè excogitatas, & confictas ab ipsius aduersariis.
units.tr: B.j. ought to do so, if it truly wished to consult the tranquillity of the kingdom. For there is no doubt that many disturbances would arise here if John à Lasco were brought forward. The King, however, since they would make no end or limit to their demands, ordered them to be silent, for the request was unjust and contrary to the law of their kingdom. But when they saw that they had achieved nothing with that first battering-ram, they devised from that day on a thousand most shameless lies, with which they burdened the Lord à Lasco everywhere, and especially before the King himself. Among other things they asserted that the Lord à Lasco had come into Poland to take up arms against the King and to fill everything here with tumults and seditions; that with the help of the bishop of Kraków he had a hundred or two hundred horsemen; and that, from the time of his arrival, they were everywhere tearing down churches at his own discretion, and many other things of that kind. They related all these things so consistently and asserted them so firmly that the King began for some time to suspect something sinister about the Lord à Lasco and to be more hostile to him, until he himself questioned a certain nobleman, a relative of the Lord à Lasco, about this very matter. For that man told the King that all these things were nothing but mere calumnies, most shamelessly invented and fabricated by his adversaries.

units.la: Hócque Regem sibi persuadere debere: sese in veritatis stabilimentum hic fidem ac etiamnum vitam suam pignoris loco interponere velle. Ad cuius demum verba regius animus cœpit mitescere. Aitque illi Rex, Tu scis eiusmodi turbas ac motus magnorum regnorum excidij occasionem plerunque fuisse. Quare dic D à Lasco ut ipsi inter vos (qui sanguine & affinitate iuncti estis) Religionis negotium agatis, videbis & ipse breui me maiorem Dei quàm hominum rationem habituram esse. Quod ut det Deus Optimus Maximus ad incrementum regni sui etiam atque etiam obnixe oramus. Porrò comitia illa nuper Vvarsouiæ habita non omnino adhuc ex animi nostri successerunt sententia: adeò furiosè sese opponit Satan propagationi Regni Christi Domini. Illa autem propter bellum istud Liuonicum, ad quod se nunc accingit Rex, veluti abrupta fuerunt, ut tractatio de Religione ac Reformatione Ecclesiarum reiecta fuit in proxima Comitia, quibus nodum dictus est dies. Interim Nobilitas tota summa vtitur libertate, in quos nulla cadit Episcoporum inquisitio: qui etiam sibi ac suis Euangelicos concionatores alere possunt. Et sperandum est tandem, nos hic aliquando feliciores progressus habituros esse, nisi nos nostra ingratitudine irâ Dei in nos prouocemus. Turca nô ita pridem habuit suum Legatum apud Ioannem 11. Regem Vngariæ, dum comitiis illis regni celebrandis impediretur, misitque ei vexillum quoddam Turcicum, suo ipsius interfignio insignitum, iubens ut copias suas omnes quas cùm ex Polonis, tum ex Vngaris, colligere possit, sub eo vexillo xillo Viennam versus, proximo vere educeret aduersus Ferdinandum. Quid vero Ioannes respondebit aut facturus sit, adhuc ignoramus. Sed veremur ne Turcae addictior fiet quàm par sit, sicuti ipse nuper non obscurè declarauit, ad iussum Turcae mittendo ei quendam insignem capitaneum (quem detinebat) qui à Ferdinandi partibus fideliter semper steterat. Deus interim misereatur nostri ac Viennae, quae hactenus firmum aduersus Turcarum furorem & potentiam Christianis fuit propugnaculum. Vale mi Domine Caluine, mihi perpetuò colendissime in Christo Domino, cui ego te tuúmque ministerium commendo ex animo. Salutat te peramanter Dominus à Lasco, cui per otium non licuit nunc scribere. Saluta mihi D. à Sancto Andrea, Raymundum, D. Io. Budaeum ac reliquos fratres in Domino. Cracoiae, xix. Febr. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: And the King ought to be persuaded of this: that he himself was willing to pledge his faith, and even his life, here as a guarantee for the establishing of the truth. At these words the King's mind began to soften. And the King said to him: "You know that such disturbances and movements have very often been the occasion of the ruin of great kingdoms. Therefore tell Lord à Lasco that you, who are joined to him by blood and kinship, should handle the business of religion among yourselves; you will see that before long I myself shall have regard for God rather than for men. This we earnestly pray that God, the Best and Greatest, will grant, for the increase of his kingdom. Moreover, that recent assembly held at Warsaw has not turned out altogether according to our wishes, so furiously does Satan oppose the propagation of the kingdom of Christ the Lord. But because of that Livonian war, for which the King is now preparing himself, the assembly was as it were cut short, so that the discussion of religion and the reform of the churches was put off to the next assembly, for which a day has been set. Meanwhile the whole nobility enjoys the greatest liberty, against whom the bishops have no power of inquiry; they can also maintain evangelical preachers for themselves and their people. And we must hope that at last we shall make happier progress here some day, unless by our ingratitude we provoke the wrath of God upon ourselves. Not long ago the Turk had his envoy with John, King of Hungary, the second of that name, while the meeting of the kingdom was being held; and he sent him a certain Turkish standard, marked with his own seal, ordering him to lead all the troops he could gather, both Poles and Hungarians, under that standard towards Vienna against Ferdinand, in the coming spring. What John will reply or do, we do not yet know. But we fear he will become more devoted to the Turk than is right, as he himself lately made plain, when at the Turk's command he sent him a certain distinguished captain (whom he had been holding), who had always stood faithfully on Ferdinand's side. Meanwhile may God have mercy on us and on Vienna, which hitherto has been a firm bulwark for Christians against the rage and power of the Turks. Farewell, my Lord Calvin, ever most honoured by me in Christ the Lord, to whom I commend you and your ministry from my heart. The Lord à Lasco greets you most affectionately; he has not been able to write now, for lack of leisure. Greet for me Lord à Sancto Andrea, Raymund, Lord John Budaeus, and the rest of the brethren in the Lord. From Kraków, 19 February 1557.

units.la: Tuus ut suus multòque addictissimus Ioannes Vtenhonius.
units.tr: Yours as his own, and most devotedly, John Utenhove.

units.la: Ita nunc obruor curis ac negotiis, mi Caluine, vt nihil possim scribere. Hinc hostes, hinc falsi fratres nos adoriuntur, vt non sit quies vlla. Sed & pios multos habemus, sit Deo gratia, qui nobis sunt & adiumento & consolationi. Vtenhonius noster nouit omnia. Itaque quae is scripsit, à me scripta esse cogitabis. Vale. Saluere officiosissimè iubeo fratres in Domino omnes.
units.tr: I am so overwhelmed now with cares and business, my Calvin, that I can write nothing. Here enemies, here false brethren attack us, so that there is no rest at all. But we have many godly people, thanks be to God, who are both a help and a comfort to us. Our Utenhove knows everything; so whatever he has written, consider it written by me. Farewell. I bid all the brethren in the Lord greet you most dutifully.

units.la: Ioannes à Lasco manu propria.
units.tr: John à Lasco, in his own hand.

units.la: CALVINVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BULLINGER, GREETING.

units.la: Etsi in excusanda mearum literarum raritate facilem te mihi praebes: atque etiam, quae tua est aequitas, hoc mihi officium vltrò remittis: me tamen vel ignauiae, vel securitatis nimiae pudet, quòd ergo te minus quàm vulgares quosdam amicos sedulus sim. Verùm haec ratio est, quod alij importunè flagitando, mihi torporem excutiunt: tu qui liberalius indulges, tacere pateris. Et sanè ita assiduis scriptionibus fatigor, vt propemodum saepe, taedio fractus, literas ipsas oderim. Vtinam tua haec moderatio apud alios valeret, vt parcius scribendo amicitiam fideliter colere liceret. Sed Galli nostri hac in parte plusquà inconsiderate me vrgent. Ita fit, vt vulgò satisfaciens pigritiae me apud praecipuos amicos suspectum reddam. Adde, quòd nisi certa materia se offert, ineptire mihi videor, dum communia argumenta quasi procul accerso. Caeterum quòd vos pridem scripsisse commemoras, nec fuisse datum à me responsum, quid sibi velit,
units.tr: Although you make it easy for me to excuse the scarcity of my letters, and even, with your usual fairness, release me from this duty of my own accord, I am still ashamed of my laziness or my excessive complacency that I am not more diligent in writing to you than to certain ordinary friends. The reason is this: others, by their insistent demands, rouse me from my torpor, while you, who are more generous, let me keep silent. Indeed I am so worn out by constant correspondence that, broken by weariness, I have often come close to hating letters themselves. I wish your moderation had weight with others, so that I might be allowed to cultivate friendship faithfully by writing less. But our Frenchmen press me on this point more than is reasonable. So it happens that, by satisfying the common run of people, I make myself suspect to my closest friends. Add to this that, unless a definite subject presents itself, I feel I am being foolish when I fetch common topics from afar. As for your mention that you wrote to me some time ago and received no reply, I do not understand what you mean, except that I suspect something was sent by you that has not reached me. If anything of the kind has been sent, once I am informed I will not neglect what is my part to do.

units.la: B.ij. non assequêr: nisi quòd suspicatus sum profectum esse à vobis aliquid, quod ad me non peruenerit. Si quid tale fuerit, admonitus, quod mearum erit partium, non negligam. Quoniam non-nulli vel m, vel morosi, vel sinistri homines concordiæ nostræ obstrepunt, si ita visum fuerit vobis, editam esse cupere. Multa placide tuli, præterij, deuoraui: sed, crede mihi, multis modis animaduertit quantopere Satanæ disp1iceret. Si edita fuerit consensionis forma, Saxonicis Ecclesiis id valde profuturum spero. Vos tamen pro vestra prudentia, quid melius sit, statuite. Ego, cùm plurimi exemplaria peterent, nunquam eò me adduci passus sum, vt prelo daretur: donec permissu vestro fieret. Qua de re iam ante scripseram. Sed ex silentio conieci, nondum vobis maturum videri tempus. Velim tamen iudicium vestrum mihi significes. De bulla gratum fecisti. Maior vsus fuisset, si biduo citius eam recepissem. Iam enim excudi coeperat praefatio, qua argumentum illud tractaui. Eius exemplar hic habes, si forte legere vacabit. Rogo tamen, vt prima quaque occasione vnà cum literis mittendum N. curcs. Hoc boni est in bulla, quòd Papa absque vllo simulationis fuco meram tyrannidem spirat. Ad preces itaque, vt dicis, nobis confugiedum est. Germaniam dicunt hoc anno à bellis intestinis quietam fore: quoniam Turca Ferdinâ-dum vrget. Sed quia Domini est, sed ire omnes armorum tumultus, ille inuocandus est, vt indomitam alioqui hostium nostrorum rabiem compescat. Vale eximie vir, & frater mihi imprimis colende. Saluta meo & fratrum meorum nomine collegas tuos & familiam. Dominus vos tueatur, vobis adsit, vos gubernare pergat. Geneuæ, x iii. Calend. Martij. M. D. LI.
units.tr: B.ij. Since some men, either ill-natured, or peevish, or malicious, are hindering our harmony, I wish, if it seems good to you, that our agreement be published. I have borne many things calmly, passed them over, and swallowed them; but believe me, in many ways I have noticed how greatly it displeases Satan. If the form of our consensus is published, I hope it will be of great benefit to the Saxon Churches. Yet you must decide what is better, in accordance with your own prudence. I, although very many were asking for copies, never allowed myself to be persuaded to have it given to the press until it should be done with your permission. I had already written to you about this matter, but from your silence I gathered that the time did not yet seem ripe to you. Still, I would like you to tell me your judgement. You did me a kindness regarding the bull. It would have been more useful had I received it two days sooner, for the preface, in which I treated that subject, had already begun to be printed. You have a copy of it here, should you by chance have leisure to read it. I ask, however, that at the first opportunity it be sent along with the letters to N. Here is the good thing about the bull: the Pope breathes pure tyranny without any pretence or disguise. So, as you say, we must take refuge in prayers. They say Germany will be quiet this year from civil wars, since the Turk presses Ferdinand. But since all tumults of arms are in the Lord's hands, he must be called upon to restrain the otherwise unbridled rage of our enemies. Farewell, most excellent man, and brother especially to be honoured by me. Greet your colleagues and household in my name and in the name of my brothers. May the Lord keep you, be with you, and continue to govern you. Geneva, 13 days before the Kalends of March, 1551.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: IO. CAL. D. MARTINO SCHALINGIO Ratisb. Ecclesiæ Pastori.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO MARTIN SCHALLING, MINISTER OF THE CHURCH AT REGENSBURG

units.la: LIteræ tuæ eximie vir & frater ex animo mihi colede, serius quàm optandum foret, mihi fuerunt redditæ, quum iam ad nundinas profecti essent omnes nostri mercatores: etsi praeter spem oblata est noua scribendi opportunitas, nisi quòd tumultuarie respondere cogor, quia iam in procinctu erat nuntius, antequam de eius discessu admonitus fuerim. Alia certamina quibus à proteruis ingeniis scindi turbarique Ecclesiam merito deploras, nunc omitto. Dissensio quæ nos hodie quoque exercet, inter pios alioqui & sanctos viros commota, magis principiis, & nihilò feliciore progressu nos plus satis admonet, quàtopere expetenda sit inter nos pax & concordia. Atque vtinam quem tibi animum esse intelligo, idem alii is fuisset. Nam si quid adhuc restaret dissidij, saltem abfq; odio & acerbitate intra suos fines consisteret. Dolendum quidem est, quum nos pauci numero idem profiteamur Euangelium, sacrae Coenae occasione, quae praecipuum inter nos vnitatis vinculum esse debebat, in varias sententias distrahi. Sed hoc longe atrocius, non minus hostiliter confligere, quàm si nihil esset nobis cum Christo commune. Maior eorum pars qui à nobis dissident, nescio quo instinctu percita, non minus intemperanter in nos ebullit, quàm si prorsus diuersa esset Religio. Quum initio tanta esset discrepantia, Lutherum, vt erat vehementi ingenio, paulò acrius efferbuisse non miror. Nunc quando de praecipuis capitibus conuenit, quę in finem D. Sacramenta nobis instituerit, quisnam legitimus sit eorum vsus, qua e efficacia, quae dignitas, quae inde ad nos vtilitas perueniat: quicquid adhuc reliduum est controuersiae, moderatius tractari poterat. Ego vero quum totis quindecim annis optima fide conatus essem, quantum patiebatur ingenua veritatis confessio, meum docendi genus ad sedandas discordias accommodare, traxit me in odiosum certamen Vveltphali vestri importunitas. Et tamen quicquid extorsit amarulentia, diligenter continui, ne alios cum eo inuolueret: semperque dabo operam, ne mea culpa scindantur vel distrahantur Ecclesiae: nec quisquam à me lacesseretur, nisi qui ex professo bellum indixerit. Imò quanuis Snepphius & nescio quis somniator petulanter me lacessiuerint, malui, quàm de nihilo turbas mouere. Nam q; à paucis intelligi scribis, quid Ecclesiae vestrae sentiant, certè si absurda quae in multorum scriptis occurrunt, colligere & exagitare libeat, non vnam esse omnium sententiam ostendere difficile non esset. Hoc quidem ycs omnes vno consensu asserere videó, quicunque ad sacram mensam accedunt, siue impij sint, siue fideles, substantialiter comedere Christi carnem, & sanguinem bibere. Quin fideles carne & sanguine Christi vere & substantialiter in Coena alantur, non nego, sed interim definiatur modus arcana Spiritus virtute fieri, vt vim sanguinis & sanguis Christi in nos transfundant. Cur me longius trahere velis, non video: cur vero non aliam communicationem admittam, optima ratione impedior: quia & carnem Christi à nobis deglutiri, & cum carne nostra corruptibili misceri, nimis crassum commentum foret. Si tantum mysterium carnis sensu aestimandum esse neges, fateor: nec vero aliud respuo, nisi quod Christi gloriae non esse consentaneum fides ipsa dictat. Adde quòd non poterit Christi corpus hoc substantiali modo comedi, nisi fingamus esse immensum, quod non minus à tota Scripturae doctrina, quàm à veteris Ecclesiae testimoniis abhorret. Quòd enim quidam veštrum difpensationis nomen obtendunt,vt persuadeant corpus Christi si-mul fuisse in cruce mortale,& gloriosum in cœlis,inscitia labū-tur, neque vnquam assequuti sunt quid vetustis Ecclesiæ doɔto-ribusefset dispensatio.Tu quoque eximie vir,pace tua dixerim, dum nos cōfundere putas,quid nobis in Cœna detur, & ad quid ḳetur,aliquantum falleris.Pluribus enim locis diserte assero,bo na Christi non esse nostra,donec ipse noster sit.Et satis mihi di-stinɛte loquutus videor in mea institutione, vbi materiam Cœ-nç vel substantiam voco ipsum Christum crucifixum:virtutem, effeɛtum,vel fruɛtum esse doceo,quicquid ex eius morte conse-quimur,vt inde est gratuita reconciliatio, vitæ nouitas,& bea-titudo cœlestis. Nomé vero efficaciæ in hunc finem vsurpo,nō vt confundam quæ distinguí debent, sed vt transfusionem sub-stantiæ excludam. Dico igitur nos efficaciter substantia carnis & sanguinis Christi pasci,quia mirabili , & incomprehensibili Spiritus sui virtute efficit Christus,vt vnum simus cum ipso:viui sica sit nobis sua caro:vita denique sua in animas nostras pene-tret.Iam in secundo capite miror,vos non consideratius atten-dere ad tot absurda,quibus implicitum est hoc commentum,di gnos simul & indignos promiscue carnem Christi edere. Sicuti enim vestra de substantiali edendi modo opinio,Christi carnem à sanguine separat, ita hæc communis manducatio,corpus eius à spiritu diuulsum,vita & omni virtute priuat.Qualis vero recep-tio hæc erit,vt in ventre impij lateat mortuum Christi corpus? Quod obiicitur cōmuniter omnibus dici, Hoc est corpus meū, nullo negotio refellitur:nihil enim obstat,quominus verè om-nibus seipsum exhibeat Christus, neque tamen alij eum recipi-ant,nisi qui sunt capaces.Hanc me doɛtrinæ formam,non perti-nacia retinere,sed quia Scripturæ auɛtoritate obstrictus teneor, Deus mihi optimus est testis.Suffragatur & veteris Ecclesiæ con sensus:in quo probando,quia mihi longius insistere nō est pro-positum,nobis vnus ille Augustini locus sufficiat.Quum alij dis cipuli comederent panem Dominum , Iudam non nisi panem Domini comedisse.Ego itaque si quis alius,veram & synceram confentionem expeto,quam modoDeus ipse suo verbo sanciat. Nec vero Augustanam confessionem repudio,cui pridem volēs ac libens subscripsi,sicuti eam auɛtor ipse interpretatus est. Atq; vtinam Principes , vt decebat, maior dissipationis nostræ cura tangeret, vt conuentu piorum doɛtorum habito, studerent Ec-clesias colligere:sed quibus flabellis ad odium nostri incitentur, minimè dubium est.Hoc tibi coram Deo voluì testatum,vt sci-res religione & Dei metu ad amplexandum quod profiteor do-ɛtrinæ genus,ɹdduɛtum,non posse inde auelli.In quo tamen as serendo(quoad per vestros homines licebit) placidè me geram, ut ante Vvestphali intemperiem me fecisse satis notum est. Te vicissim hortabor, ornatissime vir, ut retota probe expesa, quod rectum est ampleeti non dubites. Vale. Dominus te Spiritu suo gubernet semper, praesidio suo tueatur, laboresque tuos benedicat in Ecclesiae suae aedificationem. Geneuae, v III. Calendas Aprilis. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Your letter, outstanding sir and brother whom I cherish from my heart, reached me later than I would have wished, when all our merchants had already set off for the fairs. Although a new opportunity for writing unexpectedly presented itself, I am forced to reply in haste, since the messenger was already preparing to leave before I was told of his departure. The other conflicts by which the Church is torn and disturbed by unruly minds, which you rightly lament, I now pass over. The dissension that still troubles us today, arisen among otherwise pious and holy men, warns us more by its principles, and by its progress, which has been no happier, how greatly peace and concord are to be desired among us. And would that the spirit I understand to be in you were also in the others! For if any disagreement remained, it would at least keep within its own bounds, without hatred and bitterness. It is indeed to be lamented that, since we few in number profess the same Gospel, on the occasion of the Holy Supper, which ought to have been the chief bond of our unity, we are drawn apart into different opinions. But this is far more atrocious: that we fight no less hostilely than if we had nothing in common with Christ. The greater part of those who dissent from us, stirred up by I know not what impulse, boil over against us no less intemperately than if their religion were entirely different. Since at the beginning the disagreement was so great, I am not surprised that Luther, being of a vehement temperament, grew somewhat more fierce. Now that agreement has been reached on the principal heads, namely what the Lord has instituted the Sacraments for us, what is their lawful use, what their efficacy, what their dignity, and what benefit comes to us from them, whatever controversy still remains could have been handled more moderately. For my part, although for fifteen whole years I have striven in the best faith, as far as an honest confession of the truth allowed, to adapt my manner of teaching to calming discords, the importunity of your Westphal drew me into a hateful contest. Yet whatever bitterness he extorted, I have carefully restrained, so that I would not involve others with him; and I will always take care that the Churches are not torn or divided through my fault. Nor has anyone been provoked by me, except one who has declared war openly. Indeed, although Schnepf and some dreamer or other have wantonly attacked me, I preferred not to stir up disturbances over nothing. For since you write that what your Churches think is understood by few, certainly, if one wishes to gather and tear apart the absurd statements that occur in the writings of many, it would not be difficult to show that their opinion is not one. This much, at least, all of them seem to me to assert with one voice: whoever approaches the holy table, whether impious or faithful, eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood substantially. Indeed, I do not deny that the faithful are truly and substantially nourished in the Supper by the flesh and blood of Christ, but meanwhile it should be settled that this happens by the secret power of the Spirit, so that they transfuse into us the power of the blood and the blood of Christ. I do not see why you wish to drag me further; but I am hindered for the best reason from admitting any other communication, because it would be too gross a fiction for the flesh of Christ to be swallowed by us and mixed with our corruptible flesh. If you deny that this great mystery is to be judged by the senses, I agree; nor do I reject anything else, except what faith itself declares is not consistent with the glory of Christ. Add that the body of Christ cannot be eaten in this substantial way unless we imagine it to be immense, which abhors no less from the whole doctrine of Scripture than from the testimonies of the ancient Church. For when some of you put forward the word "dispensation" to persuade people that the body of Christ was at the same time mortal on the cross and glorious in heaven, you slip into ignorance, and you never grasped what dispensation meant to the ancient teachers of the Church. You also, outstanding sir, with your leave I may say, are somewhat mistaken when you think that we are confusing what is given to us in the Supper and what it is given for. For in many places I plainly assert that the good things of Christ are not ours until he himself is ours. And I seem to myself to have spoken quite clearly in my Institutes, where I call Christ crucified himself the matter or substance of the Supper, and teach that its power, effect, or fruit is whatever we obtain from his death, such as free reconciliation, newness of life, and heavenly blessedness. I use the name of efficacy for this purpose, not to confuse things that ought to be distinguished, but to exclude the transfusion of substance. So I say that we are effectually fed on the substance of the flesh and blood of Christ, because Christ, by the wonderful and incomprehensible power of his Spirit, brings it about that we are one with him, that his flesh is made living for us, and that his life at last penetrates our souls. Now in the second chapter I am surprised that you do not attend more carefully to the many absurdities bound up with this fiction, namely that worthy and unworthy alike eat the flesh of Christ indiscriminately. For just as your opinion about the substantial mode of eating separates the flesh of Christ from the blood, so this common manducation, tearing his body from the Spirit, deprives it of life and of all power. And what kind of reception would this be, that the dead body of Christ should lie hidden in the belly of the impious? As for the objection that is commonly raised, that "This is my body" is said to all alike, it is refuted without difficulty: nothing prevents Christ from offering himself truly to all, yet others do not receive him unless they are capable of it. God is my best witness that I hold to this form of doctrine not out of obstinacy, but because I am bound and held by the authority of Scripture. The consensus of the ancient Church also supports it. In proving this I do not intend to dwell at length; let that single passage of Augustine suffice for us: when the other disciples were eating the bread of the Lord, Judas was eating nothing but the bread of the Lord. Therefore, if anyone else seeks a true and sincere agreement, I desire it too, one which God himself may now sanction by his word. Nor do I repudiate the Augsburg Confession, which I long ago subscribed willingly and gladly, as its author himself interpreted it. And would that the princes, as was fitting, were more concerned about our dissension, so that, once a meeting of pious and learned teachers had been held, they would strive to gather the Churches. But by what bellows people are stirred up against us is hardly in doubt. I wanted to testify this to you before God, so that you may know that, by religion and the fear of God, I am bound to the kind of doctrine I profess and cannot be torn away from it. In asserting it, however, I will conduct myself calmly (as far as your people allow), as it is well known I did before the Westphal storm. In turn I will urge you, outstanding sir, that, having weighed everything carefully, you not hesitate to embrace what is right. Farewell. May the Lord always govern you by his Spirit, keep you under his protection, and bless your labours for the building up of his Church. Geneva, 3rd day before the Calends of April, 1557.

units.la: RICHERIVS N. S. D.
units.tr: Richerius sends greetings

units.la: Gratia et Pax a Deo per Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Grace and peace from God through Jesus Christ.

units.la: NOlii oblatam occasionem praeterire, frater, quin tuam humanitatem de rebus nostris certiorem facerem: imprimis notum tibi esse velim beneficium, quod a Domino hactenus accepimus, ut eiusdem bonitati digneris nobiscum gratias referre. Idutique est quemadmodum optamus. Quandoquidem omnium ioftrum talem pro sua bonitate habuit curam, ut per tam variarum et maris discrimina, omnes nos ad portum sanos et incolumes perduxerit. Satan quidem ut est sui similis diuersis nos in itinere exposuit periculis; sed ut filij (etsi hoc nomine indigni) experti sumus semper tanti Patris manu auxiliatricem; quam etiam benigne exporrigit in dies magis ac magis erga nos. Altero die postquam appulimus, Villagagno voluit verbum Dei publice praedicari; deinde subsequenti hebdomada sacrosanctam Christi Coenam administrari expetiuit, quā & ipse cū aliquot e suis domesticis religiose adiit, reddita primum suae fidei ratione cū magna Ecclesiae quae aderat aedificatione. Quid commodius nostro instituto contingere poterat? Quid demum votis omnibus nostrum respondisset opportunius, quam ut his testeris apud nos vera appareret Ecclesia? Talibus beneficiis dignatus est nos prosequi benignus ille summus Pater. Regio haec autem quod fit inculta raróque habitatore, nil fere profert quod nostrates vel gustare vellent. Milium quidem, ficus syluestres, & quasdam radices quibus farinam ad viaticum conficiunt, suis gignit incolis. Panem vero non habet, nec vinum aut quid vino proximum profert. Imo nec fructum aliquem (quem nouerim) quoquando quaeque vsi fuerimus. Nihilo minus tamen nobis bene est, & recte valemus, imo ut me exemplum vice proferam, vegetior sum solito: sed & id omnibus aliis commune est. Beneficium aeri ascriberet physicus, qui adeo temperatus sit vt nostro respondeat Maio. Sed ne tanta summo illi Maximo & Optimo nimini irrogetur iniuria, dicam quod sentio. Hoc modo paternum suum affectum nobis aperit bonus ille caelestis Pater, qui hic in tam barbaro & agresti solo suum nobis ministrat
units.tr: I did not want to let pass the opportunity offered, brother, without informing you of our circumstances. Above all I want you to know the blessing we have so far received from the Lord, and I ask you to deign to give thanks with us for his goodness. Things are as we wish. Since the Lord of all has taken such care of us in his goodness, through so many varied dangers at sea he has brought us all safe and sound to harbour. Satan, true to his nature, has exposed us on our journey to various perils; but as sons (though unworthy of the name) we have always experienced the helping hand of so great a Father, which he also extends to us more kindly day by day. The day after we landed, he wished the word of God to be preached publicly at Villegagnon's; then the following week he asked that the most holy Supper of Christ be administered, which he himself attended devoutly with some of his household, first giving an account of his faith, to the great edification of the Church that was present. What could have happened more fittingly for our purpose? What could have answered all our prayers more opportunely than that through these things a true Church should appear among us? The gracious highest Father has deigned to favour us with such benefits. This region, however, being uncultivated and thinly inhabited, produces almost nothing that our countrymen would even want to taste. It bears millet, wild figs, and certain roots from which its inhabitants make flour for provisions. It has no bread, and it yields no wine or anything close to wine. Indeed, as far as I know, it has not produced any fruit at all in the whole time we have been here. Nevertheless we are well and in good health; indeed, to offer myself as an example, I am more vigorous than usual, but this is common to all the others as well. A natural philosopher might credit the benefit to the air, which is so temperate that it matches our May. But lest so great an injury be done to that supreme, greatest and best God, I will say what I think. In this way that good heavenly Father reveals his fatherly affection to us, who here, on such barbarous and rough soil, supplies us with his own

units.la: Bullingeri fauorem, adeo vt experiamur viaticum hominis pendere non é pane, sed é verbo Dei, cuius fauor hic nobis est omnium deli- ciarum loco. Vnum est quod nos non mediocriter vrget & an- git, populi scilicet barbaries quæ tanta est vt maior est: non pof sit. Non affero, quòd sint anthropophagi, quod tamen illis ideo vulgare est vt nil magis: sed doleo crassam mentis ipsorum he- betudinem, quæ mediis in tenebris tamen est palpabilis. De vir- tute Patris quanuis ethica, nihil norunt prorsus, bonum à ma- lo non secernunt, denique vitia quæ natura in cæteris gentibus naturaliter arguit, loco virtutis habent: saltem vitiorum turpitu- dinem non agnoscunt, adeo vt hac in re à brutis parum diffe- rant. Cæterum quod omnium perniciosissimum est latce os an sit Deus, tantùm habet vt legem eius obseruent, vel potestiam & bonitatem eius mirentur: quo fit vt prorsus sit nobis idempta spes lucrifaciendi eos Christo: quod vt omnium est grauissimù, ita inter cætera maximè ægreferimus. Audio quidemqui mox obiiciet eos tabulam rasam esse quæ facile suis possit dispingi co loribus, quòd natiuo huiusmodi colorum splendori nihil ha- beat contrarium. Sed norit ille quantùm impedimentum impedit idomatum diuersitas. Adde quòd desunt nobis interpretes, qui Domino sint fideles. Proposueramus quidem illorum ministerio & indu- stria vti: scilicet reperimus illos ipsissima esse Satanæ membra, quibus nihil magis inuisum quàm sanctum Christi Euangelium. Proinde hac in re nobis operæ pretium est sistere gradum patientérque expectare, donec adolescentuli, quos Dominus à Villagagnone barbaris huius patriæ tradidit erudiendos, norint naturalem ipsorum distinguere linguam. Ad hoc enim il- li apud eos degunt & versantur. Faxit Deus vt sic hoc illis citra aliquod animarum suarum periculum. Nam vbi hoc munere nos donarit Altissimus, speramus hanc Idumæam futuram Christo possessionem. Interim expectamus frequentiorem populum, cuius conuersatione & formetur hæc natio barbara, & nostra Ecclesia suum accipiat incrementum. Abundarimus virtique omni bonorum copia, si hic frequés adesset populus. Nam quòd tenuis & modica nostra sit annona, id efficit raris habitator, & somnolentus agricola. Sed iis omnibus profp ciet Altissimus. Nos verò nostratum omnium Ecclesiarum precibus commendari obnixè cupimus. Ex Gallia Antartica. Pridie Apri- lis. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: favour of Bullinger, so that we experience that man does not live by bread alone but by the word of God, whose favour here takes the place of all delights. There is one thing that presses and troubles us no little: the barbarity of the people, which is so great that it cannot be exceeded. I do not mention that they are cannibals, although that is so common among them as to be nothing unusual; but I grieve over the gross dullness of their minds, which is palpable even in the midst of darkness. Concerning the virtue of the Father, although they have a kind of ethics, they know absolutely nothing of it; they do not distinguish good from evil; and finally, the vices which nature in other peoples naturally condemns they hold in place of virtue. At least they do not recognise the baseness of vices, so that in this respect they differ little from brutes. Yet what is most destructive of all is that they hardly know whether there is a God; they only observe his law in so far as they have one, or marvel at his power and goodness. Hence it follows that we have utterly lost the hope of winning them to Christ, and as this is the most grievous thing of all, we take it most painfully among other things. I hear that someone will soon object that they are a blank slate, which can easily be painted over with any colours, since there is nothing in them contrary to the native brilliance of such colours. But let him know how great an obstacle the diversity of languages presents. Add to this that we lack interpreters who are faithful to the Lord. We had intended to use their ministry and diligence, but we found them to be the very members of Satan, to whom nothing is more hateful than the holy Gospel of Christ. Therefore in this matter it is worth our while to halt and wait patiently until the young lads, whom the Lord has handed over from Villegagnon to the barbarians of this land to be taught, learn to distinguish their native tongue. For to this end they live and mix among them. May God grant that this be done for them without any danger to their souls. For when the Most High grants us this task, we hope that this Idumaea will become a possession for Christ. Meanwhile we look for a more numerous people, by whose company this barbarous nation may be formed and our Church may receive its growth. We would have an abundance of every good thing if a numerous people were present here. That our supply is meagre and scanty is caused by the rare inhabitants and the sluggish farmer. But the Most High will provide for all these things. We earnestly desire to be commended to the prayers of all our Churches. From Antarctic France, the day before the Kalends of April, 1557.

units.la: Tuus P. Richerius.
units.tr: Yours, P. Richerius.
