units.la: ILlustrissime Princeps ac Domine, Quando Vestrae Celsitudini morem gerere summopere cupio, quòd non dignitati magis & generis excellentiae, quàm vestris praeclaris virtutibus rarae- que imprimis pietati debere me existimo, vtinam testandae huius obseruantiae probandiqúe officij aliquando laetior occasio mihi se offerat. Sed quia nunc de Matthaeo Gribaldo vobis scis- citari placuit, breuiter quomodo se hic gesserit, exponam. Ac primùm in hac vrbe itaeverfatus est, vt nũquam vel Senatui nostro operam suam addixerit, vel obstrictus etiam fuerit fide data: sed habitus semper fuerit inter hospites atque exteros. Atque vt fere quotannis solebat huc venire, forte hic erat quo tempore in carcerem coniectus est Seruetus. Ac tunc dissimulans sibi cum impiis illius erroribus quicquam esse commune, tantùm obliquos sermones ferebat, non esse de falsis dogmatibus exigendas poenas, quia libera cuique esset fides. Postea tamen aperuit, quod initio tegebat, se ideo conquieri de Senatus nostri seueritate, quia impunè sibi permitti cuperet impia sua delira vomere. Actunc quidem colloquium meum petiit, fateor: quod ideo negaui, quia ante expertus fueram quale esset hominis ingenium. Nec melior occurrebat ratio, quàm vt idonei adhiberentur testes nostris sermonibus, quod ipse fugitabat. Ita tunc discessit. Paulò post cùm reuersus esset, significaui per familiarem amicum, liberum ei fore si vellet, mecum fraterne conferre, modò id fieret coram Symmystis meis ac tribus Ecclesiasticis Senioribus. Denuntiaui etiam, ne quid periculi aut fraudis metueret. Affuit, ac venit quò vocatus erat. Sed ingressus in locum vbi cò sidebamus, quia primo ingressu manum ei porrigere nolui, tamen multuosè mox discessit: & tamen humaniter, imò etiam blandis verbis excusaui mihi id non licere, donec inter nos de fide principiis conueniret. Rem enim magis seriam agi, quàm vt fallacibus ceremoniis ludendum foret. Postquam vidimus hominem amicè non posse placari, dedimus operam, vt vocatus in Cuiriam, de sua fide respondere. Vbi non modò tergiuersatus est, sed palàm ostendit se nolle quid sentiret, illic profiteri. Paulò post tamen elapsae sunt ei voces, ex quibus colligere promptum fuit, quàm prauis erroribus esset implicitus. Cùm ad modestiam hortarer, vemosa sua obstetatione palàm fecit, nihil esse audacius infscitia. Itaque in tanta peruicacia, nihil profuit pia & vtilis admonitio. Interea hunc clypeum opposuit, nimij & iniusti esse rigoris, quia in doctrina fidei à nobis dissentiret, non ferri in vrbe. Quae eius obiectio vt par erat, refutata fuit. Senatus hominem axterum vlterius vrgendum non censuit. Et nobis etiam satis fuit curare, ne impietatis suae virus poštea hic spargeret. Hoc meum testimonium quid fidei mereatur, iudicabit Vestra Celsitudo. Certe ab odio proficisci non potest, quod nullum vnquam inter nos fuisse, Gribaldus quoque ipse fatebitur. Caeterum quanuis multa deliria simul misceat, specimen vnum proferre visum est: ex quo facile intelliget Vestra Celsitudo minus asperè me haftenus de homine loquutum esse, quàm ferebat detestabilis eius impietas, imò etiam postulabat. Neque enim de meo vel alterius cuiusquam relatu hic agitur: sed quia doctrinae genus quod in eo damnamus, manu sua scriptum prodidit, indicet Vestra Celsitudo, ferendùsne sit profanus homo, qui tam peruerse Dei essentiam lacerat, & Christum fingit nouitium Deum à Patre diuersum, & cui non eadem sit cum Patre essentia. Sed quia mihi nunc propositum non est eius sacrilegia refutare, ne taedio sit epistolae meae prolixitas, putaui non posse me ex animi vestri sententia melius officio defungi, quàm si confessionem manue iusscriptam & subscriptam, in qua se Italis fratribus purgare conatus est, Celsitudini Vestrae mitterem. Vnde illustrissimus Princeps nepos vestep satis superque cognoscet, quàm profanè & scelerate hic miser praecipuum fidei nostrae caput conuellat ac pruertat.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince and Lord, I very much wish to oblige Your Highness, since I believe I owe this more to your personal virtues, and above all to your rare piety, than to your rank and the distinction of your family. I only hope a happier occasion to show this respect and perform this duty may present itself to me at some point. But since you have wished to be informed about Matthew Gribaldi, I will briefly set out how he has behaved here. First, he has lived in this city in such a way that he never pledged his services to our Senate, nor did he bind himself by any promise of loyalty; he has always been regarded as a guest and a foreigner. He usually came here nearly every year, and it happened that he was here at the time when Servetus was thrown into prison. Then, pretending that he had nothing in common with that man's impious errors, he made only oblique remarks, to the effect that people should not be punished for false doctrines, since each person is free to hold his own faith. Afterwards, however, he revealed what he had at first concealed: that he was complaining about the severity of our Senate only because he wanted to be allowed to vomit forth his impious and deranged ideas with impunity. At that time, I admit, he asked for a private conference with me, but I refused, because I had already learned beforehand what sort of man he was. Nor did any better course suggest itself than to have competent witnesses present at our discussions, which he himself was avoiding. So he left at that time. A little later, when he returned, I informed him through a close friend that he would be free, if he wished, to confer with me as a brother, provided this took place in the presence of my colleagues and three ecclesiastical elders. I also assured him that he need fear no danger or trickery. He came, and appeared at the place to which he had been summoned. But when he entered the room where we were sitting, I did not want to give him my hand at the first meeting, and he at once withdrew in a great huff. Yet I politely, and even with gentle words, excused myself, saying that I could not proceed until we had agreed between ourselves on the principles of the faith, since the matter was too serious to be played with deceptive ceremonies. After we saw that the man could not be placated by friendly means, we took care that he should be summoned before the Consistory to give an account of his faith. There he not only evaded the question, but openly showed that he was unwilling to state there what he thought. A little later, however, some words escaped him from which it was easy to gather how entangled he was in depraved errors. When I urged him towards moderation, by his blustering obstinacy he made it clear that nothing is more reckless than ignorance. Thus, in such great stubbornness, pious and useful admonition was of no avail. Meanwhile he raised this shield: that it was a thing of excessive and unjust severity that he, because he dissented from us in matters of faith, should not be tolerated in the city. This objection was refuted, as it deserved to be. The Senate decided that the man should not be pressed any further, and it was enough for us to take care that he did not henceforth spread the poison of his impiety here. Your Highness will judge what credit my testimony deserves. Surely it cannot arise from hatred, since there never was any enmity between us, as Gribaldi himself will admit. Moreover, although he mixes many delusions together, I thought it fitting to set forth one specimen, from which Your Highness will readily understand that I have so far spoken of the man less harshly than his detestable impiety deserved, and indeed than it demanded. For this is not a matter of my report or that of anyone else; rather, since he has set forth in his own hand the kind of doctrine we condemn in him, let Your Highness judge whether a profane man is to be tolerated who so perversely tears apart the essence of God, and who invents a new Christ, distinct from the Father, and not of the same essence with the Father. But since it is not now my purpose to refute his sacrileges, and lest the length of my letter be tedious, I thought I could not discharge my duty more fittingly to your wishes than by sending to Your Highness the confession, written and signed by his own hand, in which he has tried to clear himself before the Italian brethren. From it, your most illustrious nephew the Prince will know well enough, and more than enough, how profanely and wickedly this wretched man overthrows and perverts the chief article of our faith.

units.la: Valete illustrissime Princeps, mihíque plurimum suf-ficiende Domine. Patrem coelestem supplicitér precabor, vt vos cum illustrissima coniuge fultentet, tueatur, omnisque bonorum genere locupletet. Geneuae, v i. Nonas Maij. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Farewell, most illustrious Prince, and Lord most worthy of my great respect. I will earnestly pray the heavenly Father to sustain and protect you and your most illustrious wife, and to enrich you with every kind of good. Geneva, 2 May 1557.

units.la: CAL. MATTHIAE PFARRO S.
units.tr: Calvin to Matthias Pfarro, greetings.

units.la: QVum mihi scripsisset doctor Othomanus te Consulem esse rursus electum, vir ornatissime, statueram pro mea in te obseruantia tibi gratulari, & quò esses ad munus obeundum alacrior, vota mea praecesque addere. Nunc igitur dum oblata mihi fuit noua scribendi occasio, eam libenter arripui. Frater enim meus, qui frumenti petendi causa isthuc profectus erat, mihi retulit, se ita fuisse humaniter acceptum, vt facilè prosperet, nomen meum commendationis loco apud te fuisse. Pro hoc amoris testimonio, nisi gratias agerem, me inhumanum fore putaui. Hinc etiam mihi creuit scribendi fiducia, quin mihi dubium non fuit, quin tibi gratae essent meae literae. Etsi autem sponte ad officium propensus vllis stimulis non indiges: si tamen pro vetere nostra amicitia ardorem, quo praeditus es, magis excitare liberè audeam, non molesta, vt spero, tibi erit haec sedulitas. At primò quidem, dum coniectos in te, ac tuum Consulatum bo-
units.tr: Since Doctor Othomanus wrote to me that you have been re-elected Consul, most distinguished sir, I had resolved, out of my regard for you, to congratulate you and to add my prayers and good wishes, so that you might take up the office with more eagerness. Now that a fresh opportunity to write has come my way, I have gladly seized it. My brother, who went there to seek grain, has told me that he was received so kindly and that his business is going so smoothly that my name must have served as a recommendation to you. For this proof of your affection, I would think myself unkind if I did not give thanks. This has also made me bolder in writing, since I had no doubt that your letters would be welcome to you. Although you are of your own accord inclined to duty and need no spur, I hope that this eagerness of mine will not be unwelcome to you, if I may freely dare to rouse further the warmth which you possess, out of our old friendship. But first, while you see the eyes of all turned upon you and your Consulship,

units.la: Epist. 229. horum omnium oculos vides, ac plus spei de hoc anno, quàm de aliis quinque proximis,concipere,hæc te expectatio sanctio-re vinculo obstrictum tenet,ne tua cessatione euentus ipsos fru-stretur.Sed altera cogitatio studia tua,piósquè conatus acriusex citare debet, quòd tibi admirabili Dei consilio præclara nunc oblata est opportunitas repurgandæ à sordibus Papatus vestræ vrbis:vbi quum per annos triginta vidisti veram pietatem,syn cerúmque Dei cultum florere,triste haud dubie acerbúmq; spe-staculum haußisti oculis, ex quo impius superstitionibus fœdata est.Hoc vero iam tibi inæstimabile solatium erit, si moriens re-linquas tua opera à superstitionibus purgatam: Imò si nunc se-nex Dei cultum,in quo erigendo fideliter olim & strenuè labo-rasti, restituas. Alterum à te peto etiam vt tuo patrocinio mise-ros exules tuendos recipias, & per sacrum Christi nomen obte-stor.Nam vt inter nos colatur hospitalitas,postulat misera tem-porum conditio.Vale præstantissime vir. Dominus tibi semper adsit,te Spiritu inuistæ fortitudinis, & sanctæ prudentiæ guber-net,Magistratum tuum benedicat.Amen. Geneuæ,x I x.Maij M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Epist. 229. and while you hope more from this year than from the five before it, this expectation holds you bound by a more sacred tie, so that by your delay you do not frustrate the outcome itself. But another consideration ought to stir up your zeal and your pious efforts more keenly: that, by the wonderful counsel of God, you now have the splendid opportunity of cleansing your city of the filth of Papacy. For during these thirty years you have seen true piety and the pure worship of God flourish there, and you have undoubtedly looked upon a sad and bitter spectacle since the city was defiled by impious superstitions. Indeed, it will be for you an inestimable comfort if, when you die, you leave behind a city purged of superstitions by your work; or even better, if now, as an old man, you restore the worship of God, which you once laboured faithfully and vigorously to set up. The second thing I ask of you is that, under your protection, you receive and defend the wretched exiles, and I entreat you by the holy name of Christ. For the wretched condition of the times demands that hospitality be practised among us. Farewell, most excellent sir. May the Lord always be with you, govern you with the Spirit of invincible courage and holy prudence, and bless your magistracy. Amen. Geneva, 19 May 1557.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus verè tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, truly yours.

units.la: CALVINVS DOCTORI IACOBO ANDRAEAE S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO THE DOCTOR JAMES ANDREAE, GREETINGS.

units.la: LIteræ tuæ hoc saltem nomine mihi non parum gratæ fuerunt,eximie vir & ex animo colende frater,quòd inter infaustas tristesq; dimicationes, quibus inuitus exerceor,eodem te semper erga me esse animo testantur. Vtinam pałlus fuisset Vvestphalus,qua coeperam moderatione sedandis contentionibus dare operam.Eius tamen furorem nunc superarunt vicini quidam Saxones:ac palàm iactant, non aliam sibi fuisse excandescendi causam,nisi quòd blandius quàm vellent,eos compellauerim.Nunc quando mihi mansuetudinem excussit eorum pertulantia,coactus sum aspetius cum ipsis agere.Nequè tamen impediet hæc vehementia, si quibus cordi erit pacificatio, quò minus sedatus accedâ.Et sanè quò magis exarsit incendium, eò maiore studio ad illud restinguendum accurrere decet eos omnes, quibus hastenus datum fuit quiescere. Librum tuum, quia linguæ Germanicæ sum ignarus, cuidam amico legendum dedi, qui mihi summam referret. Quantum intelligo, absque acerbitate,aut cuiusquam contumelia,quod oppugno defendis. Etsi autem tuam moderationem exosculor, & laudo:mihi tamen non parum dolet, plus esse in sententiis nostris dissidij, quàm
units.tr: Your letter was very welcome to me, at least for this reason, outstanding man and brother to be cherished from my heart: amid the unhappy and grievous conflicts in which I am involved against my will, it assures me that you have always had the same disposition towards me. Would that Westphal had been as gentle as I had begun by moderating my approach to calming the quarrels. But his fury has now been surpassed by certain neighbouring Saxons, who openly boast that the only cause of their anger was that I addressed them more gently than they wished. Now that their insolence has shaken off my gentleness, I have been compelled to deal with them more sharply. Yet this vehemence will not prevent me from coming to a calm settlement, if those for whom peace is a concern are willing. And indeed, the more the fire has blazed, the more eagerly should all those who have hitherto been allowed to stay quiet rush to put it out. Since I do not know German, I gave your book to a friend to read, so that he could report its substance to me. As far as I understand, you defend what I oppose without bitterness or insult to anyone. Although I embrace and praise your moderation, it grieves me not a little that there is more disagreement between our opinions than I had supposed. Otherwise, provided the dissension does not break out into hostile hatred, which is still hidden, the Lord will in the end bring it into the open. What I think about the promiscuous eating [of the wicked] I set out clearly before, and I repeat it more often in this latest work. So far am I from being moved by your arguments that I am surprised it has not occurred to you that the wicked, by rejecting Christ rather than receiving him, bring destruction upon themselves. But if you have any grounds for finding fault with my teaching, once you have weighed my reasons for a little while, let me know what you disapprove of in my doctrine. The outcome of the Worms assembly will be nothing other than God's will: the Papists, by prolonging the time, will mock the princes, the patrons of pure religion, in their old way. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother to be honoured by me. I wish D. Brenz much health. May the Lord continue to guide you by his Spirit, strengthen you with courage, and bless you with his favours. Geneva, the Kalends of August, 1557.

units.la: Epist.240. putaueram. Caeterum, modò ne ad hostile vsque odium erum-pat dissensio,quod adhuc occultum est,tandem patefaciet Dominus. Quid de promiscua manducatione sentiam,clarè ante-hac exposueram,& in hoc postremo opere saepius repeto. Tantumque abest,vt tuis argumetis dimouear,vt mirer tibi non vt nihil in mentem,impios Christum respuendo magis quàm reci-piendo,sibi accersere interitum.Quòd si tamen aliquid à me de sideras,vbi rationes meas paulisper expenderis,quid in mea doctrina improbes,fac me certiorem.Exitum conuentus Vvormaciensis non alium fore diuino, nisi vt Papistae tempus extrahendo,Principes syncerae religionis patronos,veteri more eludant. Vale ornatissime vir,& mihi obseruande frater.D.Brentio salutem plurimam opto.Dominus te Spiritu suo regere,virtute fulcire,& benedictionibus augere pergat.Geneuae,Calend.Augusti. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Epist.240. Meanwhile, provided the dissension does not burst out into hostile hatred, which is still hidden, the Lord will at last bring it to light. What I think about promiscuous eating I had clearly set out before, and in this latest work I return to it more often. And so far am I from being moved by your arguments that I marvel it has not come to your mind that the impious, by rejecting Christ rather than receiving him, bring destruction upon themselves. But if you have anything against me, once you have weighed my reasons for a little while, tell me what you find fault with in my teaching. The outcome of the Worms assembly will be nothing other than God's will: the Papists, by stalling for time, will mock the princes, the patrons of sincere religion, in their old fashion. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother to be honoured by me. I wish D. Brenz much health. May the Lord continue to rule you by his Spirit, uphold you with strength, and enrich you with blessings. Geneva, the Kalends of August, 1557.

units.la: CALVINVS BARTHOLOMAEO HAGENIO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BARTHOLOMEW HAGEN.

units.la: Quod doctor Iacobus Andreas libro suo rationem aliquam consensus quaesiuit,nec modò lenire exasperatos animos, sed etiam quod erat asperius in doctrina, mollire conatus est,etsi eius studium laudo:fructum tamen huius operae non tam uberem spero,quàm initiò putaueram. Miratus enim sum,non minus à nobis quàm ex professis hostibus quemlibet diffidere: cuius rei nullum hactenus signum dederat. Sic ex boni viri relatu intelligi, excepta amarulétia prorsus idem doctrinae genus ab eo defendi,quod nobis obtendunt Saxones,nos verò toto animo reiicere cogimur. Itaque non immeritò te retineri agnosco,quominus eius iudicio subscribas. Nec verò est quod te ab hac ingenuitate,& constantia deterreat vllus metus. Neque seruis Christi veldurum velinfolens videri debet,si pro defensione purae sanaeque doctrinae subeunda sint multorum odia. Apud vos caeca magis pertinacia,quàm errore certatur. Vtinam ne accederet voluntaria quoque caecitas in quibusdam,quos faustus nihil dispicere patitur.Si qua tamen spes erit pacificationis,libentissimè quocunque vocatus fuero,accurram:si repudior,non leue mihi solatium erit,quum mihi probè conscius sim, bonam causam me agere, quaesiisse tamen quod optimum erat sedandis turbis remedium.
units.tr: Doctor James Andreae has sought some basis for agreement in his book, and has tried not only to soothe exasperated minds but also to soften what was harsher in doctrine. I praise his zeal, yet I do not hope for as rich a fruit from this labour as I had first thought. For I was surprised that he should distrust anyone more than us, and more than open enemies, when he had given no sign of this so far. So, from the report of a good man, I understand that, apart from the bitterness, he defends exactly the kind of teaching which the Saxons put forward to us, and which we are forced to reject with our whole heart. Therefore I recognise that you are rightly held back from subscribing to his judgment. Nor should any fear turn you from this frankness and constancy. Nor should a servant of Christ wish to seem unwilling to bear hatred from many, if this must be endured in defence of pure and sound doctrine. Among you the contest is one of blind obstinacy rather than of error. Would that there were not added, in some, a wilful blindness, which a happy fortune does not allow them to see. Yet if there is any hope of reconciliation, I will hasten there most willingly, wherever I am called. If I am rejected, it will be no slight comfort to me that, being conscious of my own good cause, I have sought the best remedy for calming the troubles.

units.la: PHILIPPO
units.tr: TO PHILIP

units.la: QVi factum sit vt toto iam triennio nihil ad meas literas re-sponderis, nescio: quia tamen ex tam longo silentio con-iicere merito licebat non adeò tibi fuisse gratas, atque e-tiam meum studium abs te repudiari, nihil nunc scribere ausus essem, nisi ab hoc optimo sene certior factus essem eodé te semper erga me esse animo: quod alioqui creditu difficile erat. Nunc collecta noua fiducia, quia te hoc mense Vvormaciæ fore confido, quò literæ meæ & tutius & maturius ad te perue-nient, occasionem hanc prætermittere nolui. Tantum cuperem mihi lætius offerri argumentum. Et tamen si partem veteris erga me amoris retines, hoc quicquid est molestiæ facile vorabis, quòd curas & dolores meos familiariter in sinum tuū exonero. Vicinos tuos tanta in me intemperie bacchari, nō dubito quin pro modestia tua & humanitate valde tibi displiceat, imò cùm nō hominem vnum, sed pios omnes, nec priuatam vnius doctrinam, sed com-munem fidem oppugnent, tibi causæ societas non vulgare mœ-rorem afferre debet. Cæterum, quando semel in hanc arenam protracto, liberum non est pedem inde citò retrahere, truculen-tas verò bestias humano more tractare absurdum fuisset, dabis vehementiæ meæ veniam quæ in tanta indignitate à me cohi-beri non potuit. Si quid te priuatim offendet, non longa excu-satione opus fore arbitror. Quia subinde fallendis imperitis su-cum ex tuo nomine videbam facere aduersarios, ne viderer in re tam clara tergiuersari (quod minimè ingenuum erat) fidem tuo testimonio sæpius deferre non dubitaui. Hac in re culpam de qua me purgare operæprætium sit, adeo non agnosco, vt iure optimo conqueri de tua cunctatione liceat: etsi à turbulentis cer-taminibus abhorres, scis tamen quid suo exemplo Paulus om-nibus Christi seruis præscribat. Certè maior tibi, quàm in eo spe-ctata fuit, moderationis laus non est appetenda. Cùm ergo ille summa lenitate præditus, per seditiones intrepidè transierit, nec eadem nobis molesta sit hodie conditio. Ac tibi omnino iam videndum est quidem maturè, ne tibi apud posteros dedecori sit nimia taciturnitas. Quòd si, dum suis telis undique te confodiant hippocentauri isti, expectas, timendum rursus ne parum oppor-tuna censeatur confessio, quàm tanta necessitas extorserit. Quid si mors occupet? Nonne vt tibi decedat omnis auctoritas, fidés-que abrogetur, seruiliter timidum fuisse clamabunt? quam infa-miam vt abs te extergere festines, non es pluribus verbis monę-dus. Si pacificandi ratio quæritur, vna spes erat in colloquio, quod te quidem expetere non dubito: tantum cuperem animo-sius flagitari. Nam cum videas Principes non modò cessare, sed etiam alio à suis doctoribus retrahi, colligis haud dubiè clausos esse aditus omnes, nisi aliis inflat fraeni, aliis vice stimuli sit tua auctoritas. Nuper audiui, quod minime sperauerā, Ducem Vvirte bergensem spōte iam huc propēsum esse: imò si ea fuissęt, quæ es se debebat humanitas, oblata erat quā semper optauimus occasionem: sed quia multorū animis insidet praua suspicio, magis alienā tos esse à nobis animos Principū, quàm vt placide audiamur, cō gressus omnes formidant. Addunt etiā illud, nō nisi praestrictos homines te vno excepto vēturos, qui imperiosè praescribant ne à suis placitis discedatur. Neq; tamen eorū qui sic loquuntur tāta est morositas, quin libenter venturi sint si vocentur: hoc nunc in te onus recumbere existima, vt tua oratione persuasi Principes, nostros ad colloquium inuitent: vel Argentorati, vel Tubingæ, vel Hildelbergæ, vel etiam Francfurti commodus esset locus: tātum si hoc impetres, vt ad placidam disceptationem vtraq; pars descendere parata sit, meliorem fore spero exitum, quàm diuinent multi suspiciosi homines. Quòd si te hoc negotio infesto iterū in Saxoniam recipis, vereor ne serò te pœniteat, exitialibus istis turbis non allatum fuisse tua opera remedium. Ac nunc memineris non tam votis hic tibi esse agendum quàm strenua solicitudine, vt ad satagendū paulò feruentius quàm mores tui ferāt intentus sis. Iam vero si non tam flexibiles erunt Principes, non tamen negligendum erit, quod anno superiore amicis quibusdā scripsisti, te operam daturum, vt cum piis, integris, & moderatis hominibus ipse conuenires. Ex eorum numero si me vnum esse censes, quæcunque aliunde vrgeat necessitas, hoc tamen in præcipuis votis est mihi, antequam Dominus in Regnum suum coe lestè nos colligat, quò alacrius admorem properem, iucundissimo tuo cōspectu semel adhuc in terra frui, & mala quibus mederi non possumus, apud te deplorando aliquid leuationis sentire. Vale, præstantissime vir, & mihi ex animo semper obseruan-de. Dominus te semper suo Spiritu gubernet, prasfidio tueatur, & ad hanc actionem te sansta prudentia, inuictaque fortitudine instruat, tuósque pios conatus benedicat. I I I. Nonas Augusti.
units.tr: I do not know why you have answered my letters with nothing for a whole three years. Yet since from so long a silence I could reasonably conjecture that my letters were not much welcome to you, and that even my zeal was rejected by you, I would not have dared to write now, had I not been assured by this excellent old man that you have always had the same feeling towards me, which otherwise would have been hard to believe. Now, having gathered fresh confidence, since I trust you will be at Worms this month, so that my letter may reach you more safely and more promptly, I did not want to let this opportunity pass. I would wish to have a happier subject offered to me. Yet if you still keep some of your old affection for me, you will easily swallow whatever annoyance this brings, since I unburden my cares and sorrows familiarly into your bosom. I do not doubt that your neighbours raging against me with such intemperance displease you greatly, given your modesty and humanity. Indeed, since they attack not one man but all the godly, and not a private teaching of one man but the common faith, the shared cause should bring you no small grief. Moreover, since I have once been drawn into this arena, it is not allowed to withdraw my foot quickly from it, and it would have been absurd to treat savage beasts in a human manner. So you will pardon my vehemence, which could not be restrained by me in such great outrage. If anything offends you personally, I think there will be no need for a long apology. Since I saw my adversaries, in order to deceive the unlearned, repeatedly making use of your name as a mask, I did not hesitate to appeal more often to your testimony, so as not to seem to be evading a matter so clear (which would not have been ingenuous). In this matter I do not acknowledge any fault from which it would be worth clearing myself; so much so that one may rightly complain of your hesitation. Although you shrink from turbulent contests, you know what Paul, by his own example, prescribes to all the servants of Christ. Certainly no greater praise of moderation is to be sought than that which was looked for in him. Since he, endowed with the highest gentleness, passed fearlessly through seditions, and the same condition is not troublesome to us today. And you must indeed now see to it early, lest excessive silence bring you disgrace among posterity. But if, while those hippocentaurs pierce you on every side with their weapons, you are waiting, there is a fear again that the confession which such great necessity has forced from you may be judged untimely. What if death overtakes you? Will they not cry out that you were servilely fearful, so that all your authority would be lost and your trustworthiness abrogated? You need not be told at length how to hasten to wipe away this infamy. If a way of making peace is sought, the only hope lay in a colloquy, which I do not doubt you desire; I would only wish it to be demanded more spiritedly. For, since you see the princes not only holding back but even being drawn away from it by their own teachers, you rightly conclude that all approaches are closed, unless your authority bridles some and spurs others on. I lately heard, which I had hardly hoped, that Duke Wilhelm of Württemberg was already coming here of his own accord. Indeed, had he shown that humanity which he ought to have, the opportunity we have always desired would have been offered. But because a bad suspicion lodges in the minds of many, namely that the princes' minds are more estranged from us than that they will listen to us calmly, they fear all such approaches. They add also that men will come, not otherwise than tied up, excepting you alone, who dictate arrogantly that no one should depart from their opinions. Yet the morosity of those who speak thus is not so great that they would not gladly come if they were invited. Consider that the burden now lies on you: that, persuaded by your speech, the princes should invite our people to a colloquy. Whether at Strasbourg, Tübingen, Heidelberg, or even Frankfurt, a convenient place would be available. If you obtain only this, that both parties are prepared to come down to a calm disputation, I hope the outcome will be better than many suspicious men conjecture. But if you withdraw again into Saxony from this hostile business, I fear you may repent too late that no remedy was brought to these deadly troubles by your work. And now remember that you must act here not so much by wishes as by vigorous solicitude, and be intent on working somewhat more fervently than your habits bear. Indeed, if the princes are not so pliable, still you must not neglect what in the previous year you wrote to some friends: that you would make an effort to meet personally with godly, upright and moderate men. If you count me among their number, whatever necessity presses on you from elsewhere, this is among my chief wishes: before the Lord gathers us into his heavenly kingdom, that I may hasten there more eagerly, and enjoy once more on earth your most delightful presence, and feel some relief by lamenting with you the evils which we cannot cure. Farewell, most excellent man, and always to be honoured by me from my heart. May the Lord always govern you by his Spirit, guard you with his protection, and equip you for this undertaking with holy prudence and unconquered courage, and bless your pious endeavours. Nones of August, 1557.

units.la: Vantum mœroris nobis attulerint vestræ afflictiones & mi-serię, fratres dilectissimi, scripto testari non est necesse: nā & nostra vobiscum coniunćtio, & communis causa aliter nos
units.tr: How much grief your afflictions and miseries have caused us, most beloved brethren, there is no need to say in writing; for our fellowship with you and our common cause do not allow us to feel otherwise about your affairs.

units.la: Epist.243. Ex gallica. nos rerum vestrarum sensu affici non sinunt. Ac si ad manum esset ratio qua vobis adesse possemus, reipsa agnosceretis, quanto vestri iuuandi studio teneamur. Vna nobis in precibus ratio suppetit: si quid aliud in nobis fuit omissum etiam noluimus, etsi de eventu statuere nō audeamus. Enimuero quocunque res cadat, certò statuite oculos Domini super vos intentos esse, ac vestros gemitus & lacrymas ad ipsum peruenire. Atque nisi illa fides certissima paternae ipsius prouidentiae nos sustineret, ianos istius mundi voragines prorsus absorpsissent, ad quamuis aurā agitati circumferremur, neque mens neque animus nobis constaret, denique inextricabilis quidā error vita hic nostra habenda esset. Imprimis vero vbi Satanae & ipsius instrumentis habenae laxantur ad miseram Ecclesiam perseq uendam, illud demum nobis succurrat oportet, cum Dominus nullā ex rebus a se creatis a sua prouidentia alienam esse velit, ab ipso non derelinqui qui illum inuocant, cumque ne minimus quidem pusillus in terram cadat sine ipsius nutu ac prouidentia, paternum illud ipsius studium erga filios non defuturum. Est sane grauis illa & praedura tentatio, tantis fluctibus mersari quique certissimum naufragium portendunt, vt tantisper cunctetur Dominus, neque dum porrigat manum: sed non perperam illud ab Apostolo appositum est: Dominum nempe perinde atque aurum camino, fidem illam nostram probare velle. Quare etiamsi non ita praesentem opem adferat nostris malis, maneat illa tamen eius veritas in nobis, quod capilli etiam capitis nostri numerati sint: ac si sanguinem etiam suorum effundi sinat, ipsas etiam nunc illorum lacrymas esse in pretio apud illum, atque in vtre ipsius & libro sigillatim reponi, vt testatur Dauid Psal. 56. v. 9. Vnum constare debet: Dominum videlicet non permisisse, vt quod accidit eueniret, quin ita quodammodo designare statuerit magnum opus aliquod, quod nostrum omnium captum exuperet. Qui hactenus martyrium adierunt, fere obscuri & despecti erant apud homines, tum in sua ipsorum persona, tum quia non ita conferti & numerosi ducti sunt: quid igitur si aliquem istis angustiis suorum exitum Dominus destinat, qui amplissimum in ipso exultandi, atque ipsius concelebrandi argumentum proferat? Tantum, vt ita vere sapiamus, dum nos illi absolute submittemus: atque vt omnia sursum deorsum ferantur, placide liberationem illam quam pollicitus est expectemus. Vos vero fratres dilectissimi, dum ista ita se habent, illam coelestis Magistri vocem ad vsum vestrum referte, vt in patientia vestra posideatis animas vestras. Equidem quidam fit illud carni arduum, non ignoramus: sed nunc maxime succurrat oportet, hoc esse tempus certandi aduersus nos ipsos, ac nostros affectus. quum ita acerbè à nostris aduersariis impetimur. Neque verò exi/ftimate vobis malè ita confultum iri, cùm vt agni in faucibus luporum versamini, cùm illa promissio coniuncta fit, non defuturum nobis fidum pastorem, qui nos in suam curam recepit. Satis potens est Dominus, vt cun/que furant & rumpantur impij, ad illos coercendos vti ipsi videbitur, etiamsi nullis apparentibus mediis vtatur. Vestrum est autem vnicè videre, ne quid præter illud quod ex verbo ipsius licet audeatis. Sic enim nos continendo vt ipsi obediamus, certi fumus ipsum aut tela propulsaturum à nobis, aut idoneis viribus ad ipsa excipienda nos inftruturum: vt contrà fiultra ipsius voluntatem perrumpimus, timè dum est netandem metcedem temeritatis nostræ referamus. Neque verò sic loquimur vt de vestro periculo fecuriores: sed quia in extremis illis rebus extrema nonnulla suggeri posse putamus, quibus ita ansam præcidere non fit facile. Quare non aliud vobis consilium damus, quàm quod ipsi nobis dari vellemus, fi eifemus vestro loco. Præstat enim nos omnes nullam hic salutem sperare ac certæ morti occumbere, quàm vt nostra fraude & diffidentia Euangelio vlla inuratur nota. Fœcundi nempe cineres martyrũ à Domino, humana verò consilia & suggestiones stabilitatem & quasi vflionem potius inducunt. Illud igitur & sententiam in vobis & reipfa palàm facite, vos profecisse legitimè in illius schola, qui nos sibi in sacrificium offerri iubet: neque quic quam à nobis recipi patitur, sed nos nostràque in folidu pro suo nomine impendi vultis: sic tolerando peruincamus, donec impotentes illos aduersarios prorsus conterat, aut sibi obsequentes & morigeros Dominus reddat. Quòd autem vestræ Ecclesiæ ordo nunc conuulsus est, videte ne plane effluere sinatis. Nam & vos ipsos pro vestra trepidatione ad signum à Domino vtcunque ereætum intueri hoc tempus admonet, & nihil Satan magis vel-let, quàm vt huc & illuc dispersi, nunquam deinde coire & coalescere possetis. State igitur densi ac conferti prout tempus & res ferunt per Dominum, ac veluti vni humero compacti, vno ore Dominum inuocare, qui etiam pollicitus est interfuturum fe in cœtu & duorum vsque & trium congregatorum in nomine ipsius. Valete fratres dilectissimi. Dominus Deus & Pater protegat vos omnes sub præsidio Filij fui, inuicta constantia obarmet, Spiritu suo fanato dirigat in omnem prudentiam, rectitudinem, fynceritatem, humilitatem ac fortitudinem, ac vestros illos aduersarios tantisper infrænet ac cohibeat, donec in vestra illa obedientia ipsos ad meritã ignominiam & probrum perpetuum adducat. X V I. Sept. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Letter 243. From the French. If we had any means by which we could be present with you, you would know in fact how eagerly we are bound to help you. Our only resource is prayer. We have omitted nothing else that lay in our power, though we dare not determine the outcome. Whatever happens, be certain that the eyes of the Lord are fixed upon you, and that your groans and tears reach him. Had that most certain faith in his fatherly providence not sustained us, the whirlpools of this world would have swallowed us altogether; we would be tossed about by every breath of wind, our minds and spirits would have no steadiness, and our life here would be an inextricable confusion. Above all, when Satan and his instruments are given free rein to persecute the poor Church, this thought must come to our aid: the Lord wills that none of the things he has created be alien to his providence; he does not abandon those who call upon him; and since not even the smallest sparrow falls to the ground without his nod and providence, his fatherly care for his sons will not fail. It is indeed a grievous and harsh trial to be plunged into such waves, which threaten certain shipwreck, while the Lord delays and does not yet stretch out his hand. But the Apostle rightly applied the image: the Lord wishes to test our faith as gold is tested in the furnace. Therefore, even if he does not bring present help to our evils, let this truth remain in us, that even the hairs of our head are numbered; and if he allows the blood of his people to be poured out, their tears are still precious in his sight and are laid up one by one in his bottle and his book, as David testifies (Ps. 56:8). One thing must be certain: the Lord has not permitted what has happened to take place without having determined, in some way, to bring about a great work that surpasses the grasp of us all. Those who until now have gone to martyrdom were for the most part obscure and despised among men, both in their own persons and because they were not led forth in large and crowded numbers. What, then, if the Lord has appointed for some of you an outcome from these straits that brings forth a most ample cause for exultation and for celebrating him? Only let us be wise in this way: while we submit ourselves wholly to him, and though all things are tossed up and down, let us calmly await the deliverance he has promised. And you, most beloved brethren, while these things stand thus, apply to your own use that voice of the heavenly Master: in your patience possess your souls. Indeed we know that this is hard for the flesh; yet it is above all now that this must come to our aid: this is the time to fight against ourselves and our own affections, since you are so bitterly attacked by your adversaries. Do not think that it will go badly for you, though you live as sheep in the midst of wolves, since that promise is joined to it: that a faithful shepherd will not fail us, who has taken us into his care. The Lord is powerful enough, however much the wicked rage and burst, to restrain them in whatever way he sees fit, even without using any visible means. Your task is only to see that you do nothing beyond what is permitted by his word. For by thus restraining ourselves in order to obey him, we are sure that he will either ward off the weapons from us or equip us with suitable strength to receive them; whereas if we break through against his will, we shall reap at last the reward of our rashness. We do not say this as though we were more careless of your danger, but because we think that in these extreme matters some extreme counsels may be suggested, by which the occasion is not easily cut off. Therefore we give you no other advice than what we would wish to be given to ourselves if we were in your place. For it is better that all of us hope for no safety here and perish in a sure death, than that any stain be imprinted on the gospel through our deceit and distrust. The ashes of martyrs are fruitful, from the Lord; but human counsels and suggestions produce instability, and as it were a sort of vain show. Therefore, let your mind and your conduct make it plain that you have made progress lawfully in the school of him who bids us be offered to him in sacrifice, and who does not allow anything to be taken from us, but wishes us and our possessions to be spent wholly for his name. Thus, by enduring, let us overcome, until the Lord utterly crushes those powerless adversaries or makes them compliant and obedient to him. As for the fact that the order of your Church has now been shaken, take care that you do not allow it to dissolve altogether. For this time admonishes you, in your alarm, to look to the sign which the Lord has somehow raised up, and Satan would wish nothing more than for you, scattered here and there, never to be able to come together and cohere again. Stand therefore close and compact, as the time and circumstances allow, under the Lord; and as if joined on one shoulder, call upon the Lord with one mouth, who has also promised to be present in the assembly of two or three gathered in his name. Farewell, most beloved brethren. May the Lord God and Father protect you all under the shelter of his Son, arm you with unconquered constancy, direct you by his Holy Spirit into all prudence, uprightness, sincerity, humility and fortitude, and restrain and check those adversaries of yours for a time, until he brings them, in that obedience of yours, to deserved shame and perpetual reproach. On the 16th of September, 1557.
