units.la: nunc assequimur, enitamur saltem aduersus nostram illam de-iectionem, quæ beatæ illius exultationis sensum à nobis percipi non finit. Nam vestrame pericula non ita fugiunt, vt præcipiti aliquo zelo committam, quòd furétibus aduersariis occasionem vllam præbeat: Sed tamen ratio quædam hîcest adhibenda, vt qui noua confirmatione indigent, illi re tam necessaria nō destituantur. Vosipsi iudicate, annon iam vestrum plurimos occupet incredulitas, quæ afflictos humi tenet, quasi Deus iam nullus sit. Hinc illi colligant quæ mihi necessitas incumbat, vt quacunque ratione ad cor ipsos redire compellam, ne Dei in ipsis gratia penitus extinguatur. Sane nihil hoc noui est, si vt oues in mediis luporum faucibus, nūc multò magis exacerbatos aduersum vos sofores veritatis sustinetis. Non est hoc etiam vnius loci. Cogitate nimirum easdem quoq; afflictiones à vestra quæ in mundo est, fraternitate impleri. Nunc igitur reipsa testemur, an frustra in Domini schola edocti fuerimus. Certum esse enim debet illi vni & viuere & mori, qui pro nobis semel ipse est mortuus. Neque suo nomini respondet fides nostra, dum victoria aduersus mundum appellatur, si in vmbra tantùm, & extra telorum iactum lacertos intendimus: sed tum demum cum illa probè instructi, Satanam ipsum cum suis omnibus machinis despicimus atque pedibus conterimus. Ipsa etiam Euangelij doctrina non eò spectat, vt quis de illa in otio sermonem habeat, sed vt ipsa sectio imbuti, nihili fieri mundum à nobis & quæ in mundo sunt, præ cœlestis Regni gloria ostendamus. Proinde qui ita percellū-tur ad nomen persecutionum atque instantes motus, vt exanimes fere concidant, perquam tenuiter in Dei schola profecerūt. Sane quòd timore corripimur, humanū est, & à nobis alienum esse non potest. Cūmque ipse Dominus hoc in nobis tolerer, absit vt Domino erga alios duriores ipsius serui simus. Et qui se ita commotos sentiunt animum ne despondeant, quasi ad defectio nem vsque elapsi essent. Illud modò quod summum est propemus omnes, vt fomentis omnibus infirmitatis nostræ vale dicendo, ab illa ipsa sensim enatemus, auctore & ductore Domini Spiritu. Nihil enim est à Christianorum nomine magis alienū, quàm si Filio Dei exercitum lustrante, ac suos in prælium mi-suro, ita demum trepidi & metu quasi extincti deprehendimur, vt iam ex illo numero vt desertores expūgendi simus. Obluct in dum igitur carni vt spiritus perduelli: atque vt condonet nobis Dominus, ipsi nobis ne cōdonemus, sed rigidi iudices aduersum nos ipsos sedeamus. Addat sibi quisque etiam stimulos, pro suæ tarditatis conscientia: & qui nos ad officium tam male compara tos agnoscimus, exoptemus & boni consulamus, aliunde etiam ad officiū excitari: agnoscamus & illud Dei opus erga nos, quòd suis occasionibus aurem nobis vellicat, & somnolentos pungit ad viuu,vti nostram tarditatem sibi medicandam esse vnus nouit optime. Porrò si quid est in iis quæ pios Martyribus contingunt,quod nos omnium maxime percellat,acerbitas supplicio- rum est,quibus illi exquisitissimis addicun tur. Et sane terribilis quædam rerum facies illic existit, quæ non satis constantes cō- cutiat. Hoc verò vbi vel in oculos incurrit,vel in mentem venit,subeat & illa præsentissima cogitatio, de inuicta illorū constantia,animíque fortitudine,quas suos illos Dominus tum mini mè omnium destituere solet. Quicquid enim excogitent ofores veritatis,vt seruos Dei de gradu deiiciat, illa Spiritus Dei virtus quæ ipsis inditur,omnem pœnarum horrorem superuincit.Stet illic nempe Satan armatus,sefeq; totum excutiat,vt fidelibus pudorem incutiat,ad defectionem cogat,à salute auertat,eo denique numerosa illa furoris sui instrumenta conferat, ac nullum crudelitatis genus intentatu relinquat.Atqui in mediis illis cruciatibus quibus serui Dei secundum carnem excarnificantur,illa perpetua & constans nominis Christi confessio , quæ in ipsis tum longe ardentior sese ostendit, aperte clamat,potentiorem longe esse,qui ita tum suos fulcit atque confirmat,dum ex horribili illo congressu victrices tamen absumptis corporibus animas,cū inuictæ veritatis trophæo propugnatori cœlesti sistunt. Quid igitur!illa nempe aduersariorum immanitas,quæ vel ipsis frendentibus Martyrum constantiæ cedere cogitur,plus valebit ad nos deiiciendos, quàm ad excitandos virtus illa ex alto,qua Dominus in suis & luctatur,& vincit,& triumphat?Et vos agnoscitis manum Domini pro suis sese exerentem,vt in illa non acquiescatis? Ac fides Martyrum in media morte caput attollet,vt mortis illorum occasio fidem extinguat in vobis?Quare dilectif simi fratres,dum suos illos furoresin seruos Dei tyranni despumant , vos ipsi mentis oculos ad intuendam Dei opem & auxilium intendite: ac quum magnos illos athletas ab ipso nunquā deseri compertum habueritis,colligiteanimū,& inlucta illa aduersus carnem & sanguinem eousque progredi contendite, illámque vobis fiduciam comparate , vt beatos esse nos sentiatis siue in vita,siue in morte,qui modo Christi fumus Atqui nihilominus iusti illi crudelissime accipiuntur ab impiis,quorum fceleta dum inulta finit Dominus , tantò magis eorum in nos furor exardescit.Sic est nempe Domini voluntas,vt cùm hic nobis durandum sit,& subeundum quod ipse imponit,nostram vt Ecclesiæ ipsius forte agnoscamus.Nam & Ecclesia Domini nouali comparatur, per quod vltrò citróque protractis fulcis totū tandem in glebas comminuitur:sic inquam vt est in Psal.129.Ecclesiam Domini tergo obiecto impiorum sæuitiæ quasi vomere perducto exarati oportet. Ac si nobis illud durum est & contra animi sententiam, satis sit vero, q; Dominus ita nos quidem exponit morti, vt eandem simul in vitæ & salutis occasionem nobis cōuertat. Imo si rem ipsam vt est, expendimus, optabilius nobis illud erit, cum pro ipsius nomine constanter aliquid ferre debitur, quàm si veritatis professionem remota afflictione tenere mur. Neque enim percipimus tam bene quæ sit Spiritus Domini vis, nobis in portu nauigantibus, atque vbi in altum afflictionū delati, spei remigio tamen salui & erecti cōfiftimus. Facit autem nostra caecitas vt illud minus liquido percipiamus, quod Domi nus tamen cuius oculi certius multò intuentur, ita vt expedire nouit, reipfa etiam prospicit. Dubitādum igitur non est, quin ad suorum salutem Dominus dirigat, quod ipsos suo modo exerce ri finit: nobis vero statuendum, non aliud magis exoptandū nobis esse, quàm quod vnus ille pro suo arbitrio de nobis semel statuerit. Quod nisi primaria illa ratio, sic esse voluntatem Dei, veram in nobis acquiescentiam vt ita loquar, sola iam parit: ipsi demum & aliæ accedant, quæ nos eriam ad officij rationem agnoscendam ample ctendámque constringant. Nam & fides nostra cum auro vel argento sit pretiosior, non minus ferium examen subeat oportet: & mortificatio nostra quæ vocationis nostræ fcopus est, sensim ita in nobis progreditur: & affectus innati à rebus praefentibus auelluntur: & tot cupiditates prauæ nobis etiam incompertæ corriguntur: sic tandem perpetuus ille noster & natiuus tumor, quem nunquam bene exuimus, appositè omnino retunditur. Sic praeterea admonemur quàm incomparabile sit pretium verbi Dei, cum vbi gratis & sine sudore obtruditur, vilescere nobis soleat. Omnium porrò summum illud est, quod per afflictiones Euangelij, conformes efficimur imaginis Filij Dei, cùm æquius nihil sit, quàm extare istiusmodi inter caput & membra conuenientiam. Ex quibus manifeste efficitur, adeò nostras pro veritatis testimonio afflictiones non esse dcre lictionis à Deo argumenta, vt tum potius in salutem nostram omnibus modis promouendam illa à Domino disponi constare nobis oporteat. Quod vero sensus noster contrarium prorsus dictat, illud eo fit, quia natura hic nidum figere gestimus, Regni Dei & rerum verè nostrarum obliti. Et sane cum in cœlo demum nos triumphus manet, ad bellum accinctos esse oportet, quandiu in terra versamur. Ergo vbi vobis ferio istis de rebus cogitandum est, nolite dubitare quin Dominus ipse vos quantum opus erit, confirmaturus fit, vti idoneis exemplis non obscure testatus est. Nouit enim temperare ipsas tentationes ad illud virium, quod ad easdem excipiendas nobis ipse collaturus fit. Docet etiam Scriptura nominatim, nullam in nos fore tyranno: rannorum potestatem, nisi quantum Dominus ipse permiserit. Ipsum vero quidquam illis permiffuru in nos quin primam nostri rationem habeat, indubium esse debet: de exitu ergo ipse etiam prospiciet. Nempe illud nos exanimat, quod in infirmitatis nostrae sensu defixi haeremus. Quin igitur oculos tandem leuamus ad coeleste illud auxilium, quod neque temere ab ipso expectare, neque frustra implorare pollimus. Merito igitur abesse a nobis sentimus, quem sese nobis offerentem adire negligimus. Imo vero eousque etiam spes nostra porrigenda est, vt post statutum a Domino examen de Ecclesia sua habitum, Dominum ipsum tyrannorum impotentiam coercituruum expectemus, vt vel inuitiffimi Ecclesiam tamen respirare sinant. Hoc dum fiat a Domino, possideamus in patientia nostra animas nostras: sic tame vt extaturam illam promissionem quae subiicitur Pfal. illo 129, nouerimus, Praecidit Dominus funes illos aratorios, quibus trahae & tribulae in nos tandiu protractae fuerant. Et Pfal. 125. Virga iniquitatis non incumbet perpetuo haereditati iustorum, ne iusti malis fraudi ad malum ipsi declinent. Vtvt fit igitur, sic illa quae in fratribus sese exerit constantia, affici vos oportet, vt illius exemplo confirmati in eadem fide perfletis. Atque vt martyrum cineres proditum est femen esse Ecclesiae, non minus etiam illorum sanguis roris instar fit oportet, quo perfusi crescatis, & ad sanctum vitae exitum vos comparetis. Et qui apud Dominum adeo pretiosus reputatur, apud vos sterilis esse non debet. Sic testatur Apostolus sua vincula non parum valuisse ad Euangelij promotionem, & certa illa spe sese erigit, quod morte sua Chriftu non minus quam vita glorificandum statuat. Nec immerito sane, quando, qui pro Euangelio laborant, sistuntur illic a Domino vt iuris ipsius assertores, idque non quod idonei fimus, aut ipse nostra procuratione opus habeat, sed quatenus insigni illo honore nos dignari ipsi visum est, nostrum quoque laborem fructu apud Ecclesiam carere non finit. Quare detestanda est prorsus illa perditorum & hypocritarum hominum blasphemia, qua sanctis tot martyribus obstrepere audent, quasi inuicta illorum constantia ad mortem fubeúdam & pietatis professio nescio quid scandali afferrent. Scilicet isti audiendi, quibus Christus nihil sapit omnino, imo qui Christi loco idolum comminif cuntur, dum scandalum illic affingunt, vbi ampletenda nobis est certissima obfignatio fidei nostrae, cuius beneficio ipsa Euangelij veritas in nobis quasi rata firma que reddatur magis ac magis. Atqui dum eos non pudet, illa Dei seruos temeritatis nota aspergere, qui sese ad morte offerunt pro Christi iure propugnado, suo tandem summo cum opprobrio sentient, quato Deo fit acceptior ista qua suggillant temeritas, sua illa mudana sapientia aut mere diabolica versutia qua vt fe quouis periculo eximant, certam sibi Dei veritatem adulterare, adeoque eiurare non detrectant. Horrendum plane,quod qui fe Christianos appellant, statim atque Christus ipsis cum sua cruce occurrit, ita hebetes & dementati inueniantur, vt ipsum auersentur & ab omni affectus aut notitiae etiam specie seponant. Vos autem vestrorum illorum fratrum sanguinem, qui in testimonium veritatis effusus est, & Dei gloriae sacer ac dicatus manet, fanctacum reuerentia apud vosipfos agnoscite. Tum vero exemplum illic oblatum vobis statuite, ad quod insequendum piae illae animae vos iam ex portu compellant. Hoc fi vti parem est minus ab affectu comparatos mouet, qi ab officio praestando tantum abiitis videte, vt & quod deest vobis, requiratis apud Dominum, & vestrae illi vitiofitati quę ab officio vos adhuc reuocat, ferio ingem ficite. Illud enim est omnium peffimum, quum in suo metu quis sibi blanditur. Et fidesipfa diutius sopita esse non potest, quin tandem etiam plane suffocetur. Sic tes cedit nepe personatis illis qui tantum sapiunt, vt & cum Deo ludant ad tempus, vt cum sua illa simulatione horrendum in modum excidant a cognitione Euangelij ac fide eo ne per somnum quidem vnquam cogitaff nt. Quandiu vero grex Domini, ita a lupis dissipatus & tatum non discerptus iacebit, vos qui illius oues estis, adipsum summum pastorem accurrite, ac vobis & veftrę infirmitati gratiam & veniam orate. Orate etiam vt ipse exerat potentem manum aut ad ipsosmet aduer farios in ouile suum traducendos, aut vt immanes belluas profliget, obtuiret ora fanguinatia, vngulas feroces atteiat, ac semel impotentem illorum rabiem compressam teneat. Orate & vt Dominus ipse suam illam ad dexteram Patris sessionem dignissima occasione illustret, dum & Maiestatis suae gloriam & suorum salutem afferet. Sic nempe certa vobis a Domino leuatio malorum expectanda est, quu lachrymae & preces ferio vos illi humiliatos sistent. Absit enim a vobis q nonnullis accidit, cotra persecutores frendere, dum ab illo praesidio sese auertut, ad quod vnu summa visperfecutionum nos compellit. Vtinam vero mihi per Domi nu liceret, propius vobis manu porrigere quouis modo. Quod quando non datur, meas demu preces ad Dominum interpono ac supplex rogo, vt qui vos omnes semel Domino Iesu Christo cuftodiedos tradidit, reipfa patefaciat, quam certo loco salus vestra conftitua fit illo vos protegente, vt ipsius quoque arbitrio vos deducendos velitis & permittatis: vtq; vestri, ac omniu qui affliguntur misertus, ex impiorum faucibus vos eripiat: ad summum, vt qui vos ad participandam veritatis suae cognitione vo cauit primum, ita in vobis cumulata in dies praestet, vt eiusdem fructus in vobis extet ad perpetuam ipsius gloriam, Amen.
units.tr: Now that we have reached this point, let us at least struggle against that dejection of ours, which does not allow us to feel the joy of that blessed exultation. I do not mean to flee from your dangers in such a way as to commit myself, in some headlong zeal, to giving the raging adversaries any opportunity. Still, some method must be applied here, so that those who need fresh strengthening are not deprived of a thing so necessary. Judge for yourselves whether unbelief does not already seize most of you, keeping you prostrate in your affliction, as if God were no longer anywhere. Let them then infer what necessity lies on me, that by whatever means I might recall you to your hearts, lest the grace of God be utterly extinguished in you. Certainly this is nothing new: you endure it as sheep in the midst of the wolves' jaws, and now, much more fiercely provoked, you bear the assaults of the enemies of the truth against you. This is not confined to one place. Consider that these same afflictions are being borne by the brotherhood that is in the world. Now, therefore, let us prove by our deeds whether we have been taught in the Lord's school in vain. For it must be settled that he alone lives and dies, who once died for us. Our faith does not match its name, when it is called victory over the world, if we aim only at a shadow and stand outside the range of the missiles. Rather, only when we are well armed for this do we look down upon Satan himself with all his machines and trample him under our feet. Indeed, the very doctrine of the Gospel does not aim at our holding discussion about it at leisure, but at our showing, being instructed by its very teaching, that the world and what is in it are worth nothing compared with the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore those who are so struck down at the name of persecutions and at impending commotions that they almost collapse lifeless have made very poor progress in the school of God. Certainly that we are seized by fear is human, and it cannot be foreign to us. And since the Lord himself bears this in us, far be it that we be harsher than the Lord toward others. And those who feel themselves so disturbed should not despair, as if they had already slipped away into utter defection. Let us all strive above all for this, that, bidding farewell to all the fomentations of our weakness, we gradually work our way out of it, with the Spirit of the Lord as author and guide. For nothing is more alien to the name of Christians than that, when the Son of God is reviewing his army and sending his men into battle, we should be found so trembling and as it were extinguished by fear that we must be purged from that number as deserters. Therefore let us struggle against the flesh as against a hostile spirit; and so that the Lord may pardon us, let us not pardon ourselves, but sit as stern judges against ourselves. Let each one add spurs for himself, according to his awareness of his own sluggishness; and those of us who recognise that we are so ill prepared for duty should wish, and gladly accept, to be stirred up to duty from elsewhere as well. Let us also acknowledge that work of God toward us, that by his occasions he plucks our ear and pricks us, drowsy, to the quick, since he alone knows best how our sluggishness is to be cured. Moreover, if there is anything among the things that befall the godly martyrs which most of all shakes us, it is the bitterness of the punishments to which they are delivered in the most exquisite forms. And indeed a certain terrible aspect of things appears there, which does not sufficiently shake even the steadfast. But when this strikes our eyes or comes into our minds, let that most present thought also come to mind: of the unconquered constancy and strength of soul of those martyrs, which the Lord is accustomed to withhold from none of his own. For whatever the enemies of the truth may devise to throw the servants of God from their footing, that power of the Spirit of God which is implanted in them overcomes all the horror of punishments. Let Satan stand there armed, let him shake himself out entirely to put shame on the faithful, to force them to defection, to turn them from salvation; let him at last bring together all those numerous instruments of his fury and leave no kind of cruelty untried. Yet in the midst of those torments by which the servants of God are tortured in the flesh, that perpetual and constant confession of the name of Christ, which then shows itself far more ardent in them, cries out plainly that he is far more powerful who then upholds and confirms his own; for out of that dreadful conflict he presents to the heavenly champion souls that are victorious, though their bodies are consumed, bearing the trophy of unconquered truth. What then? Will that savagery of the adversaries, which is compelled to yield even to the constancy of the martyrs, though they gnash their teeth, prevail more to cast us down than that power from on high, by which the Lord both struggles in his own, and conquers, and triumphs, avails to rouse us? And do you recognise the hand of the Lord stretched out for his own, and yet do not rest in it? And will the faith of the martyrs raise its head in the midst of death, only for their death to extinguish faith in you? Therefore, most beloved brothers, while tyrants foam out their furies against the servants of God, turn the eyes of your mind to behold the help and assistance of God; and when you have found that he never deserts those great athletes, gather your courage, and strive to advance in that struggle against flesh and blood as far as you can, and acquire for yourselves such confidence that you may feel ourselves blessed, whether in life or in death, if only we are Christ's. Yet nonetheless those just men are most cruelly treated by the wicked, and while the Lord allows their blood to go unavenged, the rage of those men against us blazes all the more. Such is indeed the will of the Lord: that while we must endure here, and undergo what he lays upon us, we should recognise in ourselves the field of his own tillage. For the Church of the Lord is compared to a field newly broken, in which, after the furrows have been drawn to and fro, the whole is at last reduced to clods; so, I say, as it is in Psalm 129, the Church of the Lord must be ploughed, with its back laid open to the cruelty of the wicked as with a plough driven through it. And if this is hard for us and contrary to the inclination of our mind, it is enough to know this truth: the Lord so exposes us to death that at the same time he turns the very same thing into an occasion of life and salvation for us. Indeed, if we weigh the matter as it really is, it will be more desirable for us, when something must be borne constantly for his name, than if we held the profession of the truth free from affliction. For we do not perceive well enough what the power of the Spirit of the Lord is, while we are sailing into harbour, and when, having been carried into the deep of afflictions, we nevertheless stand firm, safe and upright, by the oar of hope. Our blindness, however, makes it that we perceive less clearly what the Lord, whose eyes see far more certainly, nevertheless foresees in fact, as he knows how to order it. There is therefore no need to doubt that the Lord directs to the salvation of his own what he allows them to be exercised in in his own way. But for us it must be decided that nothing is more to be desired by us than what he, by his own judgment, has once decided about us. Unless that primary reason, that such is the will of God, by itself brings forth in us a true acquiescence, so to speak, let other reasons come also, which constrain us to recognise and embrace the duty of our calling. For our faith, though more precious than gold or silver, must also undergo a fiery testing; our mortification, which is the goal of our calling, advances in us gradually in this way; the affections innate from present things are torn away; and so many depraved desires, unknown to us, are corrected; thus at last that perpetual and native swelling of ours, which we never fully shed, is blunted in a most fitting way. Furthermore, we are thus reminded how incomparable is the value of the Word of God, which we are accustomed to think little of when it is offered freely and without sweat. Moreover, the highest of all is this: that through the afflictions of the Gospel we are made conformed to the image of the Son of God, since nothing is more just than that such agreement should exist between head and members. From these things it is plainly shown that our afflictions for the testimony of the truth are by no means signs of God's rejection, but rather that we ought to be sure that they are then ordained by the Lord for promoting our salvation in every way. But that our feeling dictates the very opposite is because we are eager to make our nest here, forgetful of the Kingdom of God and of the things that are truly ours. And indeed, since our triumph awaits us only in heaven, we ought to be girded for battle as long as we dwell on earth. Therefore, when you must think seriously on these matters, do not doubt that the Lord himself will strengthen you as much as is needed, as he has testified by fitting examples. For he knows how to temper the very temptations to that measure of strength which he himself will bestow upon us to endure them. Scripture also teaches by name that tyrants have no power over us except as far as the Lord himself permits. That he will permit them to do nothing against us without first taking account of our good must be beyond doubt; therefore he will also look ahead to the outcome. What indeed dismays us is that we stick fixed in the sense of our weakness. Why then do we not at last lift our eyes to that heavenly help, which we are neither to expect rashly from him nor to implore in vain? Rightly, then, we feel that he is far from us, whom we neglect to approach when he offers himself to us. Indeed our hope must be stretched even so far that, after the examination of his Church which the Lord has determined, we should wait for the Lord himself to restrain the impotence of the tyrants, so that even the most unwilling allow the Church to breathe. While this is done by the Lord, let us possess our souls in our patience; yet so that we know that promise which follows in Psalm 129 will stand: "The Lord has cut through the cords of the ploughmen, by which the harrows and the traces had been drawn over us so long." And in Psalm 125: "The rod of wickedness shall not rest for ever upon the inheritance of the righteous, lest the righteous put forth their hands to iniquity." However it may be, you ought therefore to be affected in such a way that you are strengthened by the constancy that shows itself in your brothers, so that, following their example, you persevere in the same faith. And just as it is said that the ashes of the martyrs are the seed of the Church, so their blood must likewise be like dew, by which, being watered, you may grow and prepare yourselves for a holy end of life. And he who is accounted so precious before the Lord ought not to be barren among you. Thus the Apostle testifies that his chains had not a little helped the advance of the Gospel, and with that sure hope he lifts himself up, because he resolves that Christ is to be glorified no less by his death than by his life. And not undeservedly, since those who labour for the Gospel are set there by the Lord as asserters of his right; and this not because we are fit, or because he has any need of our management, but insofar as it has pleased him to honour us with that remarkable dignity, and so our labour too is not allowed to lack fruit in the Church. Therefore that blasphemy of lost and hypocritical men is utterly to be detested, by which they dare to clamour against so many holy martyrs, as if the unconquered constancy of those men in undergoing death and their profession of piety brought some sort of scandal. Surely those men ought to be heard, to whom Christ savours of nothing at all; indeed, who invent an idol in place of Christ, while they fasten scandal where we ought to embrace the most certain sealing of our faith, by whose benefit the very truth of the Gospel is made more and more firm and ratified in us. Yet while they are not ashamed to smear those servants of God with the mark of rashness, who offer themselves to death for defending the right of Christ, they will at last feel, to their own great disgrace, how much more acceptable to God is that rashness which they sneer at than that prudence of their own, or their purely diabolical cunning, by which, in order to free themselves from any danger, they do not hesitate to adulterate for themselves the sure truth of God and so to forswear it. It is truly horrible that those who call themselves Christians, as soon as Christ meets them with his cross, are found so dull and demented that they shrink from him and set themselves apart from all affection or even the appearance of knowledge. But as for you, acknowledge with holy reverence among yourselves the blood of those brothers of yours, which was poured out as a testimony to the truth and remains sacred and dedicated to the glory of God. Then, indeed, set before yourselves the example offered there, to follow which those pious souls now summon you from their harbour. If this, though comparable, moves you less because you are attached less to affection, see how far you have withdrawn from the performance of duty, so that you may seek from the Lord what is lacking in you, and seriously lament that vice of yours which still recalls you from duty. For it is the worst of all things when someone flatters himself in his fear. And faith itself cannot remain dormant for long without at last being utterly suffocated. Thus it happens to those masked men who are so wise that they play with God for a time, and who, with that pretence of theirs, fall out in a dreadful way from the knowledge of the Gospel and never even think, even in their sleep, about faith. But as long as the flock of the Lord lies thus scattered by the wolves and not wholly torn to pieces, you who are his sheep, run to the highest Shepherd himself, and pray for grace and pardon for yourselves and your weakness. Pray also that he stretch out his mighty hand either to lead the very adversaries themselves into his fold, or to strike down the savage beasts, to blunt their bloodied mouths and sharpen their fierce claws, and to hold their raging impotence once and for all in check. Pray too that the Lord himself may make illustrious that his seat at the right hand of the Father on a most fitting occasion, while he both brings about the glory of his majesty and the salvation of his own. For thus a sure relief from evils is to be expected from the Lord, when your tears and prayers set you before him in humility. Far be it from you, as has happened to some, to gnash your teeth against persecutors while you turn away from that protection to which the sum of the persecutions alone compels us. Would that I were permitted by the Lord to stretch out my hand to you more closely in some way! Since this is not granted, I put my prayers before the Lord, and humbly beg that he who once committed you all to the custody of the Lord Jesus Christ may in fact make clear in what certain place your salvation is established, with him protecting you, so that you are willing and allow yourselves to be led by his judgment too; and, having mercy on you and on all who are afflicted, may snatch you from the jaws of the wicked; and, in the end, that he who first called you to share in the knowledge of his truth may so heap his gifts upon you day by day that the fruit of the same may remain in you to his everlasting glory. Amen.

units.la: Ad coniugium minus recte instituturn
units.tr: On a marriage not rightly contracted

units.la: ETsi in tanto consultantium numero non semper omnium votis obsequi vacat: non sum tamen usque adeo morosus, ut piis eorum studiis offendar. De tuis autem literis veritissima fuit excusatio. Quum enim tumultuarie & concursim tantum inspexissem, iterum paulo attentius legere in animo esset: quod rarissime vel nunquam mihi accidit, eas perdidi. Respondere vero temerarium putavi, donec melius compertum mihi foret, non modo quid quaererès, sed quos tibi expediri velles nodos. Clandestina coniugia, quae occasionem praebent, imo ianuam aperiunt multis flagitiis, merito boni omnes improbant. Atque utinam iste quisquis est, aliam sibi uxorem potius sumpsisset, quam consobrinam. Etsi enim tam lege Moysis, quam communi Gentium iure id semper licuit: tenenda est Pauli admonitio, ne plus sibi permittant fideles, quam expediat. Certe in coniugiis gradus ille apud nos adhuc excipitur, ne probris obnoxium sit Evangelium Christi. Dum vero isti nimium carnis suae libidini indulgent, scortationis infamiam subire malunt, quam coniugium fateri. Atqui si ex duobus malis alterutrum eligere oportuit, praestabat libertatem pecunia redimere, quam se demergere in hunc labyrinthum. Nam inde factum est, ut mulier simulatque obrepsit fa stidium mariti, neglecta fide diuortium fecerit: eadem levitate maritus, causa incognita, ad novas nuptias transfuolaret. Digni ambo in quos seuere ani naduertatur, indigni in quorum gratiam tam laboriose de perplexa causa inquiras. Quis enim iam exitus reperietur? Vxor iugum mariti excutiendo, violauit datam fidem. Voluntarium ergo hoc diuortium non procul abfuit ab adulterij specie, siue eam morositas, siue libido impulit. Verum maritus, quia res adhuc manebat integra, licet frustra tentata reconciliatione, & quidem saepius debuit quotidiis potius subire dif crimen, ut eam ad praestandum officium cogeret, quam & privato consilio sacrum & insolubile vinculum abrumpere, & sibi iudicium sumere in propria causa. Itaque secundae vxoris inductio nihil aliud est, quam merum adulterium honesto coniugij titulo velatum. Neque enim illa vxoris dissensione liber erat, do nec legitime cognitum foret, suo iure eum priuari. Fefellit igitur secundam, cui fidem iam alibi obstrictam quasi solutus dedit. Mulieri quoque nihilo maior libertas, quae occasionem adulterio praebuit. Si lere enim, quum videret adulterinum coniugium tractari, quid aliud fuit quam subscribere? Certe turpissimi lenocinij rea tenetur, quae volens & sciens marito permisit se ita pro-
units.tr: Although in so large a number of consultants it is not always possible to comply with everyone's wishes, I am not so fussy that I take offence at their pious efforts. Your excuse for the delay in your letter was most true. When I had only glanced through it hurriedly and in a rush, I meant to read it again more carefully. This happens very rarely, or never, to me, but I lost it. I thought it rash to reply until I had learned more clearly not only what you were asking but which knots you wished to have untied. Clandestine marriages, which offer an occasion and indeed open a door to many crimes, are rightly condemned by all good people. And I wish that the man, whoever he is, had taken a wife other than his cousin. For although such a marriage was always permitted, both by the law of Moses and by the common law of the Gentiles, the warning of Paul must be observed, that the faithful should not presume more than is expedient. Certainly among us that degree is still excluded in marriages, so that the Gospel of Christ may not be exposed to reproach. But while these men indulge too much their carnal lust, they prefer to incur the infamy of fornication rather than to acknowledge a marriage. Yet if one of two evils had to be chosen, it would have been better to buy off freedom with money than to plunge oneself into this labyrinth. For from this it came about that, as soon as the wife's distaste for her husband crept in, she disregarded her faith and made a divorce; with the same levity the husband, without any inquiry into the cause, flew off to new nuptials. Both are worthy to be severely punished, and neither is worthy that you should investigate so laboriously a perplexed case in their favour. For what outcome will now be found? The wife, by shaking off her husband's yoke, violated the pledge she had given. This voluntary divorce therefore was not far removed from the appearance of adultery, whether moroseness or lust drove her to it. But the husband, since the matter still remained intact, even though reconciliation had been attempted in vain, and indeed more than once, ought daily rather to have endured the wrong, so as to compel her to perform her duty, than by private counsel to break a sacred and indissoluble bond and to take judgement into his own hands in his own cause. Therefore the induction of a second wife is nothing other than plain adultery veiled by the honourable title of marriage. For he was not free from the wife's refusal, and he could not be deprived of his right unless this was lawfully established. He therefore deceived the second woman, to whom he had already bound himself elsewhere, by giving her himself as if he were free. Nor is the wife's freedom any greater, since she gave occasion for adultery. For if she kept silent, while seeing an adulterous marriage being arranged, what else was it than to give her signature? Certainly she is held guilty of the most shameful procuring, who, willing and knowing, allowed her husband to be so...

units.la: D.j. stituere.Rogabis,quisnam ergo sit exitus. Certè nisi hominibus conceditur, vt peccando maiorem peccandi licentiam sibi acquirant, vterque prima fide manet deuinctus: neque alia solutionis ratio apparet, nisi vt vir se adulterum fuisse fateatur, vbi ad secundam vxorem præpostere transii : mulier se quoque sociam criminis agnoscat, imò primam culpæ originem in se residere.Nunc si ad priorem redire nolit ille,suberit non parua col lusionis suspicio,& res erit mali turpisque exempli.Mulieri quæ diuortium temere fecit,non video liberum esse ius nubendi,do nec se ad reconciliationem obtulerit.Quid faciet ille?nisi valde fallor,perplexum hærere necesse erit. Ego igitur quid pronuntiem,nisi perspectis melius circunstantiis,non reperio.Acte rogo,eximie vir,vt meæ dubitationi ignoscas,si de re adeò confusa inter homines ignotos iudicium ferre non audeo.Plus fortè aliquid à me expectasti:boni consules quod possum.Vale frater mihi honorande Dominus tibi semper adsit,te gubernet Spiritu prudentiæ & rectitudinis,præsidio tueatur,& virtute sustineat. III.Calendas Ianuarij. M. D. LVII.
units.tr: Pray to the Lord for us. The envoys of ours who returned a little while ago from Just bring such news that there is no remedy left except either to receive the whole Antichrist and restore everything to him, and to submit themselves to him in extreme servitude, thereby losing all their possessions both here and in the future; or immediately to bring all these things into present and extreme danger. May the Lord grant his people to see how much better it is to lose everything for Christ, so that they may find here a hundredfold with persecutions, and in the future eternal life, than to lose everything with Christ, here and in the future. Our colleagues stand firm, and with them many from all orders. Direct your prayers for us most ardently, together with your churches. Farewell, most excellent. 10 July.

units.la: BVCERVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Bucer to Calvin, greetings

units.la: ORa Dominum pro nobis. Legati adferunt nostri qui nuper iustertius redierunt, ea vt nihil supersit medij, quàm aut Antichristum totum recipere, & eidem cunctì restituere, seque ipsos ei in extremam seruitutem addicere: atque ita se & sua omnia perdere & hic & in futuro: aut statim cuncta ista in præsens extremum discrimen adducere.Dominus det suis videre,quanto præstet perdere omnia pro Christo,vt & hic inueniat centuplum cum persecutionibus, & in futuro vitam æternam, quàm perdere omnia cum Christo,hic & in futuro.Collegę sor titer perstant,multíque cum illis ex omnibus ordinibus.Vos intendite preces pro nobis cum Ecclesiis vestris ardentissimè. Optime vale. x. Iulij.
units.tr: Pray the Lord for us. The envoys whom our men sent back recently bring word that there is now no middle course left: either to receive the Antichrist entirely and restore all things to him, and to deliver themselves into his utmost slavery, thereby losing all they have both here and in the future; or to bring all these things at once to the immediate and extreme peril. May the Lord grant to his people to see how much better it is to lose everything for Christ, so that they may find here a hundredfold with persecutions, and in the future eternal life, than to lose everything with Christ, both here and in the future. Our colleagues stand firm, and with them many from all ranks. Bring your prayers to bear on our behalf, most earnestly, together with your Churches. Farewell, most well. 10th of July.

units.la: Tuus Bucerus.
units.tr: Yours, Bucer.

units.la: CALVINVS ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI D.Philippo Lantgrauio Hessiæ,&c.
units.tr: Calvin to the most illustrious Prince, Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, etc.

units.la: ILlustrissime Princeps ac Domine,Etsi mihi satis conscius sum meæ tenuitatis:quia tamen persuasus sum me à V.C.vnum ex fidelibus Christi seruis censeri,& eandem beneuolentiam quâ olim expertus sum, manere adhuc confido : non opus habet hæc mea commendatio longa excusatione, ac si plusquam par sit mihi arrogem: quia in tanta necessitate crudelis esset mea segnities vel cessatio. Nec vero antehac quum ad Vestram Celsitudinem profecti sunt duo isti fratres mei, alia de causa abstinui à scribendo, nisi quia verebar, ne mea sedulitas vt superuacua, ita & molesta foret: quum V.C.ad praestandum officium vltrò satis propensam nouis stimulis vrgendo, aliiquod diffidentiæ signum daturum mihi viderer. Nunc vt tertia profectio ab ipsis suscipitur, noua me ratio, vt meas preces adiungerem eorum postulationi, impulit, ne quà scilicet vobis suspicio obrepat, toties idem repetendo, eos intempestiuè satagere. Nam probabile est eosdem tumores qui per alias aulas vagati sunt, ad V. quoque C.delatos esse, nihil iam deprecatione opus esse apud Regem, quia sponte liberos dimitti iusserit, quicunque ob Euangelij testimonium in carcerem coniecti erant. Et verum quidem est, ex magna turba septem tantum fuisse exustos: sed longè fallitur qui putat modum sæuitiæ ideo fuisse impositum, quasi manfuef.cti fuerint hostes, vel saturati innoxio sanguine. Tantum inuicta Martyrum constantia ad breue tempus eorum rabiem vel fregit, vel cohibuit. Nam quum postremò pueros duos rapuissent ad supplicium, quos credibile erat ob teneram ætatem minus animosos & constantes fore, atque hoc modo tentassent aliquo defectionis exemplo infamiam & dedecus aspergere fyncerx fidei, vbi sua spes eos frustrata est, deflectere coeperunt ad nouas consilia. Examinatis omnibus quos viderunt ad mortem obeundam paratiores esse, & quibus in mumdi opibus, vel splendida cognatione nihil erat subsidij, in speluncas abdiderunt, vt prima quaque occasione illinc ad mortem trahantur, cui iam se adiudicatos esse non dubitant: & res etiam vulgò nota est. Hi autem plures sunt triginta, tam viri, quam mulieres. Alij in cœnobia distributi sunt, quibus monachi esse nt velut quotidiani tortores. Quod autem ex illo numero clam elapsi sunt multi, non clementia vel humanitate contigit, sed quòd monachis gratum fuit, quasi pestibus sua claustra purgari, ne serperet longius contagio. Interim tamen quantum dissplicuerit hæc media ratio Cardinali, qui solus in aula regnat, ex atrocibus Regis minis, & conuitiis apparuit, ac si curia Parisiensis non satis viriliter, aut strenuè ageret. Tandem supplicitr per legatum suum petiit ab Antichristo Romano, vt inquisitioni præficeret tres Cardinales, quibus permissa est effrænis perdendi & maclandi licentia. Nouum etiam edictu promulgauit ipse, quo datur episcopis summa vitæ necisque potestas: nec Regiis iudicibus aliud relinquitur, quàm vt sint illorum carnifices. Hinc omnibus nobis tacetibus, C. V. facile pro sua singulari prudetia colliget quid D.ij. futurum fit,nisi mature obuiam eatur.Pro sua aute pietate ftu-debit haud dubie,omni cunctatione abrupta,leuare miseros fratres,quorum suspiria & gemitus merito pias omnes mentes vulnerare,& ad opem feredam assidue stimulare debent. Nec enim de solis captiuis agitur,sed de trecentis millibus,quos singulis momentis noui terrores exagitant. Adhuc quidem non Parisiis modo,sed in aliis Galliae vrbibus ad preces & alia pietatis exercitia conueniunt nonnulli fideles. Verùm quum impendeat certum mortis discrimen,quominus vitae suae parcat,eò digniores sunt, quibus ferantur suppetiae,si qua ratio suppetat.Dominus V.C.Illustriss.princeps tueatur,omni bonorum genere exornet,Spiritúque inuictae fortitudinis confirmet in finem vsque. Geneuae, v i.Calend.Martias. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince and Lord, although I am well aware of my own insignificance, yet because I am persuaded that Your Excellency counts me among the faithful servants of Christ, and I trust that the same goodwill which I once experienced still remains, this recommendation of mine needs no long apology, as though I were claiming more than my due; for in so great a necessity my sloth or silence would be cruel. Indeed, I did not write before now, when these two brothers of mine set out for Your Highness, for any other reason than that I feared my zeal would be superfluous and also troublesome. Since Your Excellency is already quite willing of your own accord to perform this duty, I seemed to show a sign of distrust if I urged you with fresh goads. Now, since a third journey is being undertaken by them, a new consideration has moved me to add my prayers to their request, lest any suspicion should creep upon you that they are being unseasonably busy by repeating the same thing so often. For it is likely that the same rumours which have wandered through other courts have also been carried to Your Excellency, namely that there is no need for any intercession with the King, since he has of his own accord ordered free the men who were thrown into prison for the testimony of the Gospel. And it is true that, out of a large crowd, only seven were burned; but he is greatly mistaken who thinks that the limit of cruelty was therefore set, as though the enemies had been tamed or satisfied with innocent blood. Only the unconquered constancy of the Martyrs has for a short time broken or restrained their rage. For when at last they had seized two boys for execution, whom they believed would on account of their tender age be less spirited and steadfast, and so by this means they had tried to cast on sincere faith the infamy and disgrace of some example of apostasy, when their hope was frustrated, they began to turn to new plans. After examining all whom they saw to be more ready to meet death, and who had no help in worldly wealth or distinguished kinship, they shut them up in caves, so that at the first opportunity they may be dragged thence to death, to which they do not doubt these men are already condemned; and the matter is also commonly known. There are more than thirty of these, men as well as women. Others have been distributed among monasteries, where the monks are like daily torturers to them. That many have secretly escaped from that number, however, happened not through clemency or humanity, but because it pleased the monks, as though their cloisters were being purged of plague, lest the contagion creep further. Meanwhile, how much this middle course displeased the Cardinal, who alone reigns at court, has appeared from the savage threats and reproaches of the King, as though the Parisian court were not acting manfully or vigorously enough. At last he suppliantly asked through his legate that the Roman Antichrist would set three Cardinals over the inquisition, to whom an unbridled licence of destroying and slaughtering was granted. He himself also published a new edict by which the bishops are given the supreme power of life and death; nor is anything left to the royal judges except to be their executioners. Hence, while all of us keep silent, Your Excellency, by your singular prudence, will easily gather what is going to happen unless a remedy is applied in time. Out of your piety you will doubtless strive, every delay being cut off, to relieve our wretched brothers, whose sighs and groans rightly ought to wound all pious minds and constantly spur them to bring help. For it is not only the captives who are at stake, but three hundred thousand people, whom new terrors harass every moment. Even now, not only at Paris but also in other cities of France, some of the faithful assemble for prayers and other exercises of piety. But since a certain danger of death hangs over them, so that they spare not their own lives, they are all the more worthy to whom aid should be brought, if any means of doing so is available. May the Lord, most illustrious Prince, keep Your Excellency, adorn you with every kind of good, and strengthen you with the Spirit of invincible fortitude to the end. Geneva, 6th before the Calends of March, 1558.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS D. MICHAELI DILLERO.
units.tr: John Calvin to Master Michael Diller.

units.la: Literis quas ad optimum fratrem nostrum Bezam scripsisti liteteris,praestantissime vir,mixtum, vt par erat, dolore gaudiū accepi. Nam quòd de fratribus nostris,qui ob Euangelij testimonium tenentur in Gallia captiui,tâtopere folicitus es, quia inde colligo quàm sedulò causam eorum acturos sis apud Illustrissimum Principem,non parum laetor te nunc diuinitus oblatum esse fidum & cordatū adiutorem huic negotio. Interea cor meum grauiter vulnerauit eorum perfidia, qui nefarium quaestum facere non dubitant ex Martyrum sanguine. Ac eius quidem iam ante mensem non leuis mihi suspicio obrepserat: nūc verò non sine acerbissimo moerore palàm cognoui, miseros fratres in Aula quoque vestra scelerate esse proditos. Quum hac transfiret impius ille delator,qui persuasit Illustrissimo Principi legatione non esse opus, tale quiddam oblique apud me attigit. Sed quum singulis prope verbis eius mendacia refellere promptum esset, sperauì meis responsis nonnihil fuisse mutatum, vt saltem ad fingendum minus audax foret. Sed vt video, prorsus obdurauerat. Quia mihi ante annum nota fuerat eius futilitas, putaui initio inconsiderate eugarrire de rebus incognitis. Tandem in sermonis progressu animaduertere licuit proditorie ipsum agere:improbior tamen fuit quàm putaueram.Certè quod quinque tantùm dixit fuisse exustos,abiecto pudore sciens & volens fefellit. Nam quo tempore in Aula erat,duo adolescentes, quorum alter annum decimumsextum vix ingressus erat,pene in eius conspectu rapti sunt ad supplicium. Si qua pietatis gutta praeditus fuisset,hoc nescire turpe fuit. Quòd autem à me admonitus, & conuictus, eadem mendacia obtrudere non desistit, miniminime tolerabilis impudentiæ est. Cohibita quidem hostium sævitia fuit, quòd tam alieno tempore Germanos Principes offendere, non esse utile putabant. Neque tamen ita Rex placatus fuit, quin sæpius mollitiem exprobraverit Curiæ Parisiensi, quòd tam segniter exequeretur quod mandatum erat, de promiscua omnium cæde. Omnes enim optabat prius esse extinctos, quàm ad deprecandum venirent Principum lagueti. Et quanquam multi ex iudicibus plus satis ardebant ad fundendum sanguinem, terruit tamen eos constantia quatuor virorum, nobilis unius fœminæ & puerorum, à quibus initium fecerunt. Nam quum singulos blanditiis pellicere tentassent ad fidem abnegandam, viderunt eos alacriter ad mortem pergere. Hinc factum est, ut non ausi fuerint properare, sed quos videbant robustiores, & magis intrepidos tetris carceribus addixerint, unde pro sua commoditate eos ad mortem trahant, simul ac libuerit. Certè pij fratres non dubitant de sua vita iam esse transactum: & vulgò notum est, haberi pro damnatis. Alios monachis in custodiam dederunt, ut paulatim languefacerent ipsorum fidem: imò ut sacrilegis superstitionibus se polluentes Christum abnegarent. Itaque piis hæc durior fuit conditio, quàm si in profundo carcere iacuissent. Et tamen maior pars ex claustris illis aufugit monachorum coniuentia, vel quod molestum erat gratis eos alere, vel quòd sibi à contagione metuerent. Nemo quidem iudicium permisit hactenus exire, nisi cum turpi defectionis nota, ut statius fuerit recta eos ad ignem trahi. Nec est quod miremur dilatum fuisse supplicium, quum astutè hostes ad breue tempus declinata inuidia aliâ opportunitatem captauerint, quæ nisi mature illis eripitur, laxabit frena suæ truculentiæ. Unius etiam rei monendus es, quicunque damnatur, paulò ante supplicium grauissimis tormentis cruciari, ut socios prodant. Ita in singulis mortibus centenæ quæruntur. Nunc quid te, eximie vir, vel rogem, vel hortor, ut totum huic causæ te impendas, quum ipse anteuerteris, & voluntarius Bezæ nostro fueris hortator, nefratres indignè à mercenariis delatoribus proditos deserereret. Huic igitur tà piæ folicitudini vota mea adiunxisse satis est. Vtinam mihi liberum fuisset coràm gratias agere. Imò satagere etiam pro miseris fratribus, quorum gratia ne vitæ quidem parcerem. Sed quia iter meum, quasi aliud moliretur, sinistris quorundam sermonibus fuisset obnoxium, non ausus sum pedem movere. Bene autem habet, quòd duo in vnius vicem succedunt, qui mihi sunt veluti duæ animæ, & summa dexteritate peragent, quod ego pro mea virili conarer. Vale ornatissime vir, & frater mihi observande. Dominus semper tibi adsit, te gubernet, laborésque tuos benedicat. Geneuæ, v iii. Calendas Martij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I received with pain, as was fitting, and yet with joy, the letter you wrote to our excellent brother Beza, most distinguished man. For that you are so anxious about our brothers who are held captive in France for the testimony of the Gospel, from which I gather how diligently you will plead their cause before the most illustrious Prince, I rejoice not a little that you have now been divinely offered as a faithful and wise helper in this business. Meanwhile their perfidy has deeply wounded my heart, those men who do not hesitate to make a wicked profit from the blood of the Martyrs. Indeed, a suspicion of this had crept over me no slight time ago, a month since; but now I have openly learned, not without the bitterest grief, that our wretched brothers have also been wickedly betrayed in your court. When that impious informer passed through here, who persuaded the most illustrious Prince that an embassy was not needed, he touched on something of the kind to me in an indirect way. But since it was easy to refute his lies almost word by word, I hoped that my answers had changed him somewhat, so that he would at least be less bold in inventing. But, as I see, he had become utterly hardened. Because his frivolity had been known to me for a year, I at first thought he was chattering inconsiderately about matters unknown. At last, as the conversation went on, it was possible to notice that he was acting treacherously; yet he was more shameless than I had supposed. Certainly, in saying that only five had been burned, he knowingly and deliberately deceived, with his shame cast aside. For at the time when he was at court, two young men, one of whom had barely entered his sixteenth year, were seized for execution almost in his sight. If he had had any drop of piety, it would have been shameful for him not to know this. But that, when admonished and convicted by me, he does not cease to thrust forward the same lies, is hardly a tolerable impudence. The savagery of the enemies was indeed restrained, because they thought it not useful to offend the German Princes at a time so unsuitable for it. Yet the King was not so placated that he did not often reproach the Parisian court for its sluggishness, because it carried out so slackly what had been ordered, namely the indiscriminate slaughter of all. For he wished all to be killed before they came to plead with the Princes' ... Nor, though many of the judges burned all too eagerly to shed blood, were they frightened by the constancy of four men, one noble woman and the boys, with whom they began. For when they had tried to coax each one with flattery into denying the faith, they saw them go cheerfully to death. Hence it came about that they did not dare to hurry, but consigned to foul prisons those whom they saw to be more robust and more fearless, from which they may drag them to death whenever it suits them. Certainly the pious brothers do not doubt that their lives are already finished, and it is commonly known that they are held to be condemned. Others they have handed over to the monks for custody, so that they might gradually weaken their faith; indeed, so that by polluting themselves with sacrilegious superstitions they might deny Christ. Thus this condition is harder for the pious than if they had lain in a deep dungeon. And yet most of them escaped from those cloisters through the connivance of the monks, either because it was troublesome to feed them for nothing, or because they feared contagion for themselves. Indeed, no one has so far been allowed to leave the court except with the shameful mark of apostasy, so that it would have been better for them to be dragged straight to the fire. Nor is there any reason for us to wonder that the execution was postponed, since the enemies, having cleverly diverted odium for a short time, have sought an opportunity elsewhere, and unless it is snatched from them in time, they will loosen the reins of their savagery. You must also be warned of one thing: whoever is condemned is tortured with the most severe torments shortly before execution, so that he may betray his companions. Thus from each death a hundred more are sought. Now, distinguished man, what should I ask or urge you, since you have gone before and of your own accord have been an encourager of our Beza, so that you would not abandon the brothers unworthily betrayed by mercenary informers? It is enough, therefore, that I add my prayers to such pious concern. Would that it had been free for me to thank you in person. Indeed, I would even labour on behalf of our wretched brothers, for whose sake I would not spare even my life. But because my journey, as if it were aiming at something else, would have been exposed to the unfavourable talk of certain people, I did not dare to move a foot. It is well, however, that two men are taking the place of one, who are to me like two souls, and who will with the greatest skill accomplish what I would have attempted to the best of my strength. Farewell, most distinguished man, and brother to be honoured by me. May the Lord always be with you, govern you, and bless your labours. Geneva, 8th before the Calends of March, 1558.

units.la: IO. CAL. D. OTHONI HENRICO PRINCIPI Electori. s.
units.tr: Calvin to Otto Henry, Prince Elector. Greetings.

units.la: ILlustrissime Princeps ac Præstantissime Domine, quum ante hac ad Vestram Celsitudinem profecti sunt optimi fratres mei, Theodorus Beza & Ioannes Budæus: quanuis meo rogatu iter illud susciperent, vt causa illa piis omnibus communis erat, me verò inter alios patronum pro ratione mei officij postulabat, non ausus tamen sum quod maxime optassem, quidquam commendationis illis dare: quia verebar ne superbum videri posset, hominem Celsitudini Vestræ adhuc incognitum scribendi licentiam sibi sumere, ac si qua auctoritate vel gratia polleret. Sed iustior quàm vellem mihi oblata est excusatio: quia scilicet quod tunc facere vetuit pudor, nunc cogit & extorquet necessitas. Ex eorum quos dixi relatu, cognoui Celsitudinem Vestram ad miseros fratres iuuandos & leuandos magis propensam esse, quàm vt meo vel cuiusquam hortatu excitari opus sit. Sed vbi exposuerint, quomodo nunc res habeant in Gallia, plenâque & liquidam narrationis sidem fecerint: non modò san stum eorum studium in hac secunda expeditione laudabit Vestra Celsitudo: sed mihi facile concedet, vt adiutor ipse quoque accedam. Quum tam liberaliter & vno consensu nec minus syncero hauddubie cordis affectu vos, Illustrissimi Principes, afflictos fratres vobis fore curæ polliciti essetis, mirati sumus & illi etiam nobiscum, vnde iniecta est mora legationi, quæ iam decreta fuerat. Putauimus tamen vos interea minimè cunctatos esse, sed aliam rationem, quæ nobis esset incognita, vobis autem visa esset melior & vtilior, sequutos fuisse. Neque enim modestiæ nostræ fuit, & eius quam vobis deferimus obseruantiæ, aliter sentire, quàm in his turbulentis temporibus sic vos mutasse consilium, vt tamen consultum esset miseris fratribus. Dum ita hæremus suspensi, probabilis coniectura animos nostros pupugit, vanis rumoribus, vel vt liberius dicam, malitiosis quorundam artibus vos fuisse deceptos. Tandem nôn modò suspicati sumus, sed aperte vidimus, quosdam famelicos & conductitios homines lucri captandi causa sparsisse falsas blanditias, quæ vestram alacritatem tardarent. Ignoscat V.C. si ingenuè rem totam aperio. Nam quod relatum fuit, carceres nunc esse vacuos, vanissimum esse comperient legati vestri, si illuc venerint. Verum quidem est magnam partem fuisse distributam in liberas custodias, vnde quidam aufugerunt. Sed hoc vel puellis vel adolescentibus datum est, vel aliis quos propter familiæ splendorem cognati postularunt in cœnobia transferri. Quicunque verò se constantius gesserunt, quanuis ad vitæ vsque discrimen aliqui eorum ægrotauerint, adhuc in fœtidis cauëls tenentur inclusi, illícque & pedorem, & frigus, & asperrimas quasque contumelias perferuant. Si de numero interroget V. C. plures esse quàm triginta, oculatus testis de cuius fide non dubito, nuper mihi scripsit. Ac nemo eorum est, qui non se morti addictum certò cognoscat. Sicuti vulgò motum est obiurgatos fuisse iudices curiæ Parisiensis, quod nimis torperent, vel remissi essent. Ac si detur optio fidelibus illis Christi seruis, gratior esset mortis celeritas, quàm adeo miseræ vitæ prorogatio. Pedemontani & reliqui Alpini fratres non multò mitius tractantur, nisi quod difficiles aditus eos tuentur. Citati nullam vim opponunt, sed tantum excusant, quia sacro & insolubili pietatis vinculo Deus eos simul coniunxit, secorsim causam non dicturos. Verum vt trab osi est hostium crudelitas, si quis deprehendi potest, rapitur in carcerem: vt hodie Taurini vnus verbi minister compeditibus adstrictus est, quum per duos menses catenis ligatus fuerit. Curia quoque Graciopolitana cuiusdam vallis incolas diutiùs vexat. Omnes certè inter assiduos metus trepidant. Regem vero nō esse mitigatum, ex edictis nuper promulgatis palàm est. Quia mihi seueri errant iudices, quos tamen atrocibus minis ad seruitiam cogebaat, rogatu eius præfecti sunt ab Antichristo Romano tres Cardinales, qui suo arbitrio iurisdictionem hac, vel potius ex sua libidine, per suos satellites exerceant. Rex etiam episcopis & eorum ministris alteroedicto summam licentiam mastandi restituit, qua penes eos potestas erit vitæ & necis. Iudices autem totius regni, quibus adem pta est cognitio, illorum erunt carnifices. Quàm fœdis cótumeliis proscindat Rex puram Euangelij doctrinam ex edictis perspiciet V.C. Nam quòd Sacramentarios videtur petere, merum esse fucum experientia clamitat. Nec dubium est, quin aulici artifices ad fallendos Germanos Principes captiosè nomen hoc suggerant, quod putant multis esse odiosum. Ego autem sanctè coràm Deo & Angelis affirmo, Sacramentarios illic haberi, quicunque non satentur Christum in Missa Papali quotidie immolari. Ergo quibus nesandum illud Missæ sacrilegiū displicet, falsa ignominia aspergitur, ac si factam Christi Cœnam abrogarent. Neque tamen dissimulo Gallos fratres idem sentire quod publicè doceo, sicuti Ecclesiæ nostræ catechismo vtuntur. Nec verò hac de causa C.V. patrocinio spoliari merentur, quàdo & Christum veraciter in sua Cœna præstare, quod figurat, agnoscunt, & clarè fatentur non alitèr animas nostras in Cœna pasci Christi carne & sanguine, quàm pane & vino ad corpus alendum pascimur. Si de modo cōmunicationis non prosus conueniat, an deseredi sunt in vltimo discrimine, qui arcana Spiritus virtute Christum nobis vere communicari credunt, quanuis cœlum & terram cae ne sua non impleat? Quid enim aliud quaerendum est, cuàm vt coalescamus in corpus Christi? Quòd si aliter fieri non posse credimus, quàm si vbique sit secundum carnis naturam, certè eius potentiæ derogatur. Atque vtinam hæc infœlix disceptatio vestris auspiciis, prudentia, auctoritate aliquando sedari queat. Interim verò Christi martyres laniena expositos omni auxilio destitui, neque pium neque humanum esse V.C. cognoscit. Caeterū, nihil minus propositum est Euangelij hostibus, quàm discerne re alios ab aliis, quum promisceu Sacramentarios iudicent, quicunque; vnicum Christi sacrificium sufficere in æternam salutem fatentur: quia ipsorum nihil interest, quid de carnis & sanguinis Christi communicatione credatur, modò quæstus illis ex nefando Missæ sacrilegio integer maneat. Deinde, quum relapsos & pertinaces simili poenæ adiudicet edictum, minimè obscurum est destinari ad eædem, quicunque à syncera & ingenua Christi confessione non discedent. Nunc mihi non aliud restare video, nisi vt totius Gallicæ Ecclesiæ nomine suppliciter C.V. fidem implorem, vt non modò regem ipsum deprecari non graeatur, sed alios quoque Illustrissimos Principes sibi adiungat, vt Rex intelligat serio vos omnes in hanc curam incumbere. Modum aliquem præscribere neque meum est, neque eorum quis litteras meas perferent. Quod tamen maximè optandum esset, facere nequeo quin C.V. exponam, vt admonita secum expendat, annon hæc optima sit commendatio: Regi semel palàm ficere, quodnam doctrinæ genus impugnet. Quod si testandæ fidei consilium placuerit, parata erit in manibus fratrum meorum Bezæ & Budæi confessio, cui subscribent ad vnum omnes, qui hodie in Gallia pro hæreticis vexantur. Verùm ne tædio sit mea prolixitas, finem facio. Dominus V.C. Princeps Illustrissime perpetuò tueatur, omni benedictionum genere locupletet, Spiritu prudentiæ & inuictæ fortitudinis in finem vsque regere pergat. Geneuæ, VIII. Calendas Martij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince and most distinguished Lord, when my excellent brothers Theodore Beza and John Budé set out earlier to Your Highness, I did not dare to give them the recommendation I most wished to give, although they undertook that journey at my request, since this cause was common to all the godly and my office required me to act as advocate among the others. I feared it might seem presumptuous for a man yet unknown to Your Highness to take upon himself the liberty of writing, as if he had some authority or influence. But a more justified excuse than I wished has now been offered me: what shame forbade me to do then, necessity now compels and wrings from me. From the report of those I have named, I have learned that Your Highness is more inclined to relieve and help our unhappy brothers than needs any urging from me or anyone else. But when they have set out how matters now stand in France, and have given a full and clear account, Your Highness will not only praise their earnest zeal in this second mission, but will readily allow me also to join them as a helper. When you, most illustrious Princes, promised with such generosity and unanimity, and no less undoubtedly with a sincere feeling of heart, that you would take care of our afflicted brothers, we were astonished, and they with us, at the delay that was thrown in the way of the embassy, which had already been decided upon. Yet we supposed that in the meantime you had not hesitated at all, but had followed some other plan, unknown to us, which seemed to you better and more useful. For it was not becoming to our modesty, or to the respect we owe you, to think otherwise, that in these turbulent times you had changed your plan in such a way that the wretched brothers would nevertheless be cared for. While we hung in suspense, a probable conjecture pricked our minds: that you had been deceived by empty rumours or, to speak more freely, by the malicious tricks of certain men. At last we not only suspected but plainly saw that certain hungry, hired men, seeking gain, had spread false flatterers' tales which might slow your eagerness. May Your Highness forgive me if I lay the whole matter openly before you. For what has been reported, that the prisons are now empty, your envoys will find to be most untrue if they go there. It is indeed true that a large part of them has been distributed into free custody, from which some have escaped. But this has been granted either to girls and young men, or to others whom their relatives, on account of the splendour of their family, have asked to be transferred to monasteries. Yet those who have borne themselves more steadfastly, although some of them have fallen ill to the point of danger to life, are still kept shut up in foul dungeons, and there they endure both stench and cold and the harshest insults of every kind. If Your Highness asks how many there are, an eyewitness, whose good faith I do not doubt, wrote to me recently that there are more than thirty. And there is not one of them who does not know for certain that he is condemned to death. As has been commonly reported, the judges of the Parisian court have been rebuked because they were too slack and lenient. And if those faithful servants of Christ were given the choice, a swift death would be more welcome than a prolonged life of such misery. The Piedmontese and the other Alpine brothers are treated not much more gently, except that the difficult approaches protect them. Those summoned offer no resistance, but only excuse themselves, because God has joined them together in a sacred and indissoluble bond of piety, so that they will not plead their cause separately. Yet as the cruelty of the enemies is always at hand, if anyone can be caught he is dragged off to prison; thus today at Turin one minister of the Word has been bound in fetters, after being kept in chains for two months. The court of Grenoble also long harasses the inhabitants of a certain valley. Certainly all of them tremble amid constant fears. That the King has not been softened is plain from the edicts recently published. For, since the severe judges, whom he had compelled to cruelty by atrocious threats, are not enough for him, at his request three Cardinals have been set over this jurisdiction by the Roman Antichrist, who are to exercise it at their own will, or rather at their own lust, through their satellites. By another edict the King has also restored to the bishops and their ministers the fullest licence of punishing, by which they will have the power of life and death. Moreover, the judges of the whole kingdom, to whom the hearing of cases has been taken away, will be their executioners. How foully the King tears to pieces the pure doctrine of the Gospel, Your Highness will see from the edicts. For that he seems to be seeking out Sacramentarians, experience cries out is pure deception. Nor is there doubt that the court artisans, to deceive the German Princes, craftily throw up this name, which they think is hateful to many. But I solemnly affirm before God and the angels that those are held to be Sacramentarians there who do not confess that Christ is daily sacrificed in the Papal Mass. Therefore, those who dislike that unspeakable sacrilege of the Mass are smeared with false infamy, as if they denied that the Lord's Supper had been instituted by Christ. Nor do I hide that our French brothers think the same as I teach publicly, as they use the catechism of our Church. Nor for this reason do they deserve to be deprived of Your Highness's patronage, since they acknowledge that Christ truly exhibits in his Supper what it signifies, and they clearly confess that our souls are fed in the Supper by the flesh and blood of Christ no otherwise than we are fed by bread and wine to nourish the body. If they do not altogether agree about the manner of communion, are those abandoned in their final peril who believe that Christ is truly communicated to us by the secret power of the Spirit, although heaven and earth do not contain him? For what else is to be sought than that we be joined together into the body of Christ? But if we believe that this cannot happen unless he is everywhere according to the nature of his flesh, surely his power is diminished. And would that this unhappy dispute might at some time be settled under your auspices, your wisdom and your authority. Meanwhile, Your Highness knows that it is neither godly nor humane that the martyrs of Christ, exposed to slaughter, should be left without any help. Moreover, nothing is further from the purpose of the enemies of the Gospel than to distinguish one from another, since they judge all indiscriminately to be Sacramentarians who confess that the one sacrifice of Christ suffices for eternal salvation: for it is of no concern to them what is believed about the communion of Christ's flesh and blood, provided that their profit from the unspeakable sacrilege of the Mass remains intact. Then, since the edict condemns the relapsed and the obstinate to the same punishment, it is quite plain that all who do not depart from a sincere and open confession of Christ are destined for the same end. Now I see nothing left for me but to implore your faith suppliantly, in the name of the whole Church of France, that you not only be unwilling to plead with the King himself, but also join other most illustrious Princes to yourself, so that the King may understand that you all are seriously taking up this cause. It is neither my place, nor that of those who will carry my letters, to prescribe any particular course. Yet what would be most desirable I cannot refrain from setting before Your Highness, so that, once warned, you may consider whether this would not be the best recommendation: once to show the King plainly what kind of doctrine he is attacking. And if it pleases you to adopt the plan of bearing witness to the faith, the confession is ready in the hands of my brothers Beza and Budé, to which all who are today harassed in France as heretics will subscribe, every one of them. But lest my lengthiness be tedious, I make an end. May the Lord keep Your Highness, most illustrious Prince, enrich you with every kind of blessing, and continue to rule you with the Spirit of prudence and invincible fortitude to the end. Geneva, the eighth day before the Calends of March, 1558.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS D. GOSSNINO ZENELO. S.
units.tr: John Calvin to Gossninus Zenelus, greeting.

units.la: Licebat tibi & reliquis, quum hic essetis, ex me scisciscitari si qua vos dubitatio angeret. Paucis autem verbis coràm forte melius vobis satisfecissem, quàm nunc longiore scripto. Nec verò mihi nunc commodum est prolixè ad vos scribere, quin etiam pauca hæc vix dictare permisit lateris dolor, qui me toto iam mesc propè inutilem reddidit. Fide, quam fratri nostro Martino dedistis, vos coram Deo & Angelis eius, quum sciatis esse
units.tr: You and the others were free, while you were here, to ask me about any doubt that troubled you. A few words in person would perhaps have satisfied you better than a longer letter now. Nor is it convenient for me to write at length, and the pain in my side, which has left me almost useless for a long time, scarcely lets me dictate these few lines. You pledged your faith to our brother Martin before God and his Angels, and you know that you are

units.la: Epist.258. esse obstrictos merito soliciti estis, ne a vobis vlla in parte violetur: ac in ea sanctè colenda vobis omnino perseuerandum: quia simul ac tantillum à recto propòsito deflexeritis, nullus erit licetiæ modus: vt multas semper illecebras reperit carnis sensus, quibus nos deliniat. Nunc videndum quousque pateat quod polliciti estis. Martinum quidem nihil aliud stipulatu fuisse statuo, nisi vt abstineretis ab omnibus inquinamentis, quæcum syncera pietatis & fidei professione pugnant. Porrò si quis templum idolis dicatum ingreditur, non ideo protinus sordium aliquid contrahit: sicuti quum Paulus Athenis falsorum deorum aras lustraret, non se polluit ab spectu illo. Sed hic spectanda est consilij ratio: quia si Papistis gratificari propositum est, impia est & minime excusabilis simulatio. Quibus per templum Papale trafire religio fuit, facilè ignosco: quanuis plus æquò timidi fuerint. Ad legem verò tam austeram neque me neq; alios auderem astringere, quia mihi sufficit abesse omnes superstitionis species: & simul dari operam, ne quem iuste & merito offendat nostra libertas. Hæc principia modò teneamus, non video cur nimis anxiè fingamus nobis scrupulos, qui cursum nostrum in plana via morentur. Quòd ad conciones spectat, duo mala cauenda sunt, ne vbi plenis buccis veram pietatis doctrinam proscindunt illi rabulæ, silentium nostrum speciem consensus præbeat: deinde ne superstitiosis precibus communicemus. Si quem ergo mera curiositas ad audiendas blasphemias trahat, multum abest ab eo zeli feruore, quem Deus à filiis suis exigit. Quomodo enim verè & ex animo dicet, Zelus domus tuæ comedit me & opprobria exprobrantium tibi ceciderunt super me, si volens & sciens aurem accommodat sacrilegis doctrinis? Imò eas cupidè venatur? Si autem hoc modo colorem simulationis accepit declinandæ inuidiæ causa, hæc certè obliqua est pietatis abnegatio. Quisquis impius conciones audire se iactat ne videatur Dei contemptor, fucum obtendit, quo licet se & alios delu dat, non tamen oblinet Dei oculos. Qui verò eas se audire excusat, vt commodè instituat suos, videat iterum atque iterum, ne quid aliud tegat animo. Nam cùm omnes ad fugiendam crucem nimis propensi sint, qui sibi vltrò blandiuntur, intenti sunt ad captandos prætextus: sensus autem carnis ad eos excogitandos plus æquò ingeniosus est. Ergo nisi melior alia ratio, vel necessitas cogat, longè tutius est ab ingressu templi abstinere, dum illic ex professo corrumpitur & adulteratur Dei veritas. Et certè vix fieri potest, quin animi simul ac aures labis aliquid contrahant, vbi sponte audientia datur Satanæ mendacijs. Quòd ad reprehensiones attinet, quanuis optandum sit, eas inter nos magis vigere, & se quisque ad hoc officium errantibus præstädum strenuè animare debeat: certam tamen ac perpetuam lege figere non audeo, vt quicquid displicet, statim & fine exceptione reprehendatur. Hoc quidem nobis omnibus praeftandu esse non dubito, vt appareat nos moleste ferre, quicquid Dei gloriae & verbo repugnat: deinde fi detur occasio, studium nostrum clarius testari oportet: praesertim fi qua spes est profectus, minime negligenda est: imo fi grauius contingat violari sacrum Dei nomen, minime timenda est importunitas. Et hac ratione nihil hodie melius est, quam parce frequentare sodalitia in quibus pugnandu est, nisi velimus perfida segnitie prodere gloriam Dei. Certe vbi apertę probro afficitur Deus, vel fyncera Religio, vel vbi indigne non abfq; contumelia arripitur eius nomen, quauis assensum non simulemus: pudendum tamen corporem esse lua cu que conscientia didtat, nisi palam ostendimus nobis curae est Dei cultum & gloriam.
units.tr: Epist. 258. bound by it. You have rightly been anxious that it not be violated by you in any part, and you must persevere entirely in keeping it sacredly. As soon as you stray even a little from the right purpose, there will be no limit to license, since the sense of the flesh always finds many enticements by which it coaxes us. Now we must see how far what you promised extends. I hold that Martin stipulated nothing more than that you abstain from all defilements that are at odds with a sincere profession of piety and faith. Moreover, if someone enters a temple dedicated to idols, he does not at once contract any filth, just as Paul, when he walked about the altars of false gods at Athens, did not pollute himself by that sight. But here the reasoning behind the plan must be considered: if the aim is to humour the Papists, the pretence is impious and by no means excusable. For those who thought it right to pass through a Papal temple, I readily pardon, although they were more timid than was right. But I would not dare to bind either myself or others to so harsh a law, since it is enough for me that every form of superstition is absent, and that care is taken not to offend anyone justly by our liberty. If we hold to these principles, I do not see why we should anxiously invent scruples that delay our course on a level road. As for sermons, two evils must be guarded against: that, when those wranglers tear apart the true doctrine of piety with full mouths, our silence not give the appearance of consent; and that we not join in superstitious prayers. If mere curiosity draws anyone to hear blasphemies, he is far from that fervour of zeal which God demands from his sons. For how will he truly and sincerely say, "The zeal of your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen upon me," if he willingly and knowingly lends his ear to sacrilegious doctrines? Nay, if he eagerly hunts after them? And if he has taken on the colour of pretence in this way to avoid odium, this is certainly an oblique denial of piety. Whatever impious man boasts that he hears sermons lest he seem a despiser of God, he puts up a mask by which he deceives himself and others, yet he does not deceive God's eyes. But he who excuses himself from hearing them in order to instruct his own people properly should see again and again that nothing else is covering his mind. For since all men are too prone to flee the cross, those who flatter themselves are intent on seizing pretexts, and the sense of the flesh is far too ingenious in devising them. Therefore, unless a better reason or necessity compels, it is far safer to abstain from entering the temple while God's truth is deliberately corrupted and adulterated there. And certainly it can hardly happen that minds and ears do not at the same time contract some stain when hearing is willingly given to Satan's lies.
