As for rebukes, although it is to be wished that they flourish more among us, and each man ought to stir himself vigorously to perform this duty toward the erring, I do not dare to fix by a rigid and perpetual rule that whatever displeases must immediately and without exception be rebuked. This much I do not doubt must be shown by all of us: that we bear with displeasure whatever opposes God's glory and Word. Then, if an opportunity is given, our zeal ought to be attested more clearly, especially if there is any hope of progress, which must by no means be neglected. Indeed, if God's holy name is violated more gravely, importunity must by no means be feared. By this reasoning nothing is better today than to frequent sparingly those gatherings in which we must fight, unless we wish by faithless sloth to betray the glory of God. Certainly where God is openly disgraced, or pure Religion is attacked, or where his name is unworthily seized upon with insult, then even if we do not feign assent, conscience dictates that we should not be ashamed to be seen, unless we openly show that the worship and glory of God is our concern.

units.la: Non praescribo vt primo statim verbo pius vir ad obiurgationem prorumpat: sed vbi delicta alia aliis addita feruntur, tam su pina remissio extra noxam non est. Quod ad mensae ben edictio nem, precesque priuatas spectat, quisquis retecto capite eas audit, non obscure declarat illis fe subscribere. Ergo fi qua miscetur corruptela vel fupe rftitio, tali professione sese contaminat. Si alios aspicimus fe cruce signare, vel nugas suas agitare, aliquantum diuersa est ratio: & tamen hinc monemur non esse adunda loca, vbi occurrunt innumerae superstitiones, quarum aspectu fequuti Paulum nos incalescere conuenit: certe fi qua in no bis est pietatis gutta, saltem tacitos gemitus exprimet: qui vero tacitus gemet quae videre cogitur, loquiffime sub ducere fe cupiet, fi liberum fit. Ad nuptias qui accedit, modo a saltationibus, tri pudiis, alisque lasciuiis fe contineat, non erit forte ob solum aspectum damnandus: semper tamen danda opera est, vt modestia nostra pudorem aliis incutiat, fitque grauis quoddam cohibendae lasciuiae censura. Idem & de alea iudicium facere conuenit. Nam quum lufu illo pecunia male dilapidare non liceat, nihilo etiam minus lucrum facere. Qui sibi ab hac contagione non temperat, prorsus excusatione caret. Nec me latet quam vobis difficile fit hanc integritatem colere: sed mei arbitrij non est, vel tantillum laxare ex Dei praeceptis. Et quia fieri nullo modo potest, quin multorum animi in vos exacerbentur, donec ad subeundas offensas parati eritis, claudicare necesse erit ad dextram vel sinistram. Non disputo quam perplexa res fit, alienari a cognatis & amicis: tantum simpliciter ostendere mihi propositum est, quid vetet Deus, aut iubeat. Si te filij fui in Baptismo fideiuf forem aduocet quispiam, inhumanum videbitur negare: & ille repulsam passus, quasi accepta graui iniuria excandescet. Atqui infantem foetidis illis nugis, quae legitimum & genuinum Christi Baptismum non sine ludibrio confpurcant, offerte qui liceat, nemo vt opinor, ostendet: quandoquidem fideiussor sacrifico astipulans,impia societate fe inquinat. Quoties ergo nos huc vel illuc impellere tentant homines,unde arcemur verbo Dei amicitiis omnibus renuntiandum potius est, quam talibus obsequiis redimenda totius mundi gratia. Denique modo placidè, adhibita etiā prudentia, & quæsita opportunitate testemur nobis Dei pluris esse quàm homines, quomodo hoc accipiant veritatis hostes, non est in nobis situm: sed qualiscunque erit euentus, fatis fit studium nostrum Deo probari, & grattum esse. Ex hoc breui responso colligere vt spero, licebit, qualiter vos gerere deceat. Ecclesia N.inter hostium terrores statum suum retinet. Martinus noster in stadio suo constanter pergit, nec fatigatur. Et quâquam minacibus edictis fulminant hostes in Gallia, fœuitiam quoqde suam despumant: passim tamen crescit vigor & alacritas. Vale eximie vir & frater integerrime cum reliquis amicis, quibus has fore communes spero. Dominus vos omnes tueatur, Spiritu suo gubernet, inuictâque fortitudine sustineat. Geneuæ, Pridie Idus Martias. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I do not prescribe that a godly man should break out in rebuke at the very first word. But where one fault is added to another, such slack indifference is not free from guilt. As for the blessing of the table and private prayers, whoever hears them with bared head plainly declares that he subscribes to them. So if any corruption or superstition is mixed in, he contaminates himself by such an open profession. If we see others crossing themselves or performing their trifles, the case is somewhat different. Yet this warns us that we should not frequent places where countless superstitions occur, and at the sight of them we ought to burn as Paul did. Surely if there is any drop of piety in us, it will at least wring out silent groans; and whoever is forced to silently groan at what he sees will wish to lead the people far away, if that is permitted. Whoever attends a wedding, provided he refrains from dancing, indecent jests, and other wantonness, will perhaps not be condemned for his presence alone. Yet we must always take care that our modesty strike shame into others, and that there be a certain serious censure restraining wantonness. We should likewise judge gambling in the same way. For since it is not lawful to squander money wastefully in play, neither is it lawful to make a profit from it. Whoever does not restrain himself from this contagion has no excuse at all. Nor am I unaware how difficult it is for you to keep this integrity, but it is not for my judgement to relax even slightly the precepts of God. And since it is in no way possible that the minds of many will not be provoked against you, until you are prepared to endure offences, it will be necessary to limp to the right or to the left. I do not discuss how perplexing a matter it is to be estranged from kin and friends; I simply intend to show what God forbids or commands. If someone calls upon you to stand surety for a child in Baptism, it will seem inhuman to refuse; and he who has suffered the rejection will flare up as if he had received a grave injury. Yet no one, I think, will show how it is lawful to offer an infant with those foul trifles which defile, with mockery, the legitimate and genuine Baptism of Christ; since the surety who consents to a sacrilegious rite stains himself with an impious partnership. Therefore, whenever men try to push us here or there, from which the Word of God bars us, we ought rather to renounce all friendships than to purchase the favour of the whole world with such compliances. Finally, if we bear witness calmly, with prudence applied and a suitable opportunity sought, that God is to be valued above men, how the enemies of truth take it is not in our power. But whatever the outcome, it is enough that our zeal be approved by God and be pleasing to him. From this brief reply I hope it will be possible to gather how you ought to conduct yourselves. The Church of N. keeps its position amid the terrors of its enemies. Our Martin presses on constantly in his course and does not tire. And although the enemies in France thunder with threatening edicts and foam over their cruelty everywhere, vigour and eagerness nonetheless grow. Farewell, most excellent man and most upright brother, with the rest of our friends, to whom I hope this letter will also be common. May the Lord keep you all, govern you by his Spirit, and sustain you with unconquered fortitude. Geneva, the day before the Ides of March, 1558.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus subscripsit: quia epistolam dictare coegit lateris dolor.
units.tr: John Calvin, your friend, has signed this letter, since pain in his side has forced him to dictate it.

units.la: De ceremoniis Ecclesiae.
units.tr: On the ceremonies of the Church.

units.la: Vod ad ceremonias spectat, generalle hoc tenendum est axioma, quia immensa earum congeries onerata fuit Ecclesia, & feré obruta Euangelij claritas, prudentissimè facere, qui parco & sobrio earum vsu contenti sunt. Deinde in mysteriis quæ vocantur Sacramenta, sedulò esse cauendum, ne hominum commentis vitietur pura & genuina cœlestis magistri institutio: præsertim vbi libera est electio, nihil melius, quàm præscriptam a Christo formam simpliciter tenere, qualis ad nos per manus tradita est. Si obiicitur vetustas (quanquam hoc clypeo ad tegendas omnes corruptelas audacter vtuntur, qui consuetudini, & receptis moribus nimiū addicti sunt) facilis refutatio est: quia veteres quoq; ipsi grauibus querimoniis fatis testati sunt, sibi non probari quicquid hominum arbitrio excogitatum fuerat. Augustinus maximè ad Ianuarium deplorat iniusta & non tolerabili seruitute iam tunc oppressam fuisse Ecclesiam ob immodicos ritus: quum tamen vix decima pars eius labyrinthi, quo nūc tenetur orbis implicitus ad irretiedas animas, cōposita esset. Deinde vt silentio & tolerantia multæ ceremoniæ pridem recepta
units.tr: As for ceremonies, this general rule must be held: the Church has been burdened by an immense heap of them, and the clear light of the gospel was nearly buried under them, so those who are content with a sparing and sober use of them act very wisely. Further, in the rites called sacraments we must take care that the pure and genuine institution of the heavenly Master is not spoiled by human inventions, especially where there is freedom of choice. Here it is best simply to keep the form prescribed by Christ, as it has been handed down to us. If antiquity is raised as an objection (and those who are too devoted to custom and to accepted practices boldly use this shield to cover every corruption), the answer is easy, because the ancients themselves bore sufficient witness, with serious complaints, that whatever had been devised by human judgment did not please them. Augustine, especially in his letter to Januarius, laments that the Church was already then oppressed by an unjust and intolerable slavery because of excessive rites, although at that time the tenth part of that labyrinth, in which the world is now held entangled to ensnare souls, had hardly been put together. Next, as to how many ceremonies were long ago received through silence and toleration, we must hold to the distinction Paul laid down, that we must not allow the clear light of the gospel to be obscured by legal figures.

units.la: Epist.259. fuerint, tenendum est quod Paulus statuit discrimen, ne legalibus figuris sinamus claram Euangelij lucem obscurari. Si legis umbris locus non cōceditur, quanto minus hanc licentiam obtinere debent hominum figmenta? Iam si probè & penitus inspicitur quid homines tantopere solicitet ad fabricandas ceremonias, reperiemus ex hoc fonte omnes fluxisse, quia quisque nouū Dei cultum fingere ausus fuerit. Atqui fictitios omnes cultus nō modò repudiat Deus, sed etiam seuerè abominatur, apud quem obedientia plurimis est, quàm omnes victimæ. Et merito: quia eius imperio decedit quantum sibi homines hac in parte arrogant. Statuendum quidem est simulacro suo arbitrio Deum colere appetunt homines, fœtidam esse profanationem quicquid de suo afferunt: sed ne latissimam fyluam ingrediar, ad speciem descen do. Dixi legitimum Baptismi, & sacræ Cœnæ vsum non aliunde petendum esse, quàm ab institutione & mandato Christi. Aqua mysterium illud peragi volui tvnigenitus Dei Filius. Placuit hominibus Chrisma, & exsufflationem addere. Si nobis sancta & inuiolabilis est Christi auctoritas, & quam meretur reuerentiam obtinet, quis non videt aduentitiis illis nugis fœdatum fuisse Baptismum? Meris deinde ludibriis ita corruptus fuit, vt inquinet magis quàm purget eos omnes qui ablutioni crassa illa sacrilegia permisçet. Quorsum de mixtione aquæ & vini in sacra Cœna disceptatio moueri debuerit non video. Christus symbolis panis & vini testatus est carnem suum esse nobis cibum, & sanguinem suum potum. Si penuria sit vini, exiguum quod suppetet aqua diluere, vt toti Ecclesiæ sufficiat minimè absurdum erit. Si religio iniicitur, acsi necessaria foret mixtio, superstitione hoc non caret. Nam & noua lege præter Christi mandatum perperam non minus quàm temere obstringitur Ecclesia, & mysterium in re nihili puerili quæritur. Calicem ex aqua & vino mixtum habere volunt, quia è latere Domini fluxerunt aqua & sanguis. Quasi vero auctoris consilium fuerit tale quicquam docere: ac non magis pignus dare spiritualis potus. Nec vero recte huc tor quetur Cyprianus testimonium: quia nunquam diluendum in sacra Cœna vinum esse contendit, sed contra lymphaticos homines asseruit ex Christi mandato bibendum illic esse vinum. Erat enim qui abstinentiæ prætextu vinum quo intemperanter vulgus abutitur, arcebant à cœlesti mysterio. Quum ergo nō aqua, sed vino repræsentari in sacra Cœna Christi sanguinem tota disputatione doceat, quæ de mixtura obiter tradit, non recte ad aquæ patrocinium trahuntur. Adde q. in miscendi verbo, quod subinde vsurpat, falluntur imperiti, dum pro diluere semper accipiunt: quum potius fundere significet ex recepto apud veteres & idoneos Scriptores linguæ Latinæ vsu. Et sanè alibi ad vnitatem tem pios hortari volens, non ex multis aquæ guttis, sed ex plu-ribus acinis sacrum Calicem, sicut ex pluribus granis panè mysticum constare admonet. Neque tamen inficior ipsum mixtionem aquæ & vini afferere, sed euanido prætextu: quia vinum Christi sanguinem, aqua plebem significet. Hæc argutia si cui arridet, dignus est qui vento pascatur. Nos vero curiositate humani ingenij quæ semper nimium lasciuit, valere iussa, ab eius ore pendeamus, qui vnicus est Cœnæ auctor. Imò videmus vt Cyprianus ipse memorabili sententia nos à se ad Christum ableget, vbi vetat consuetudinem sequi in aqua sola offerenda: quia potius quærendum est, quem sequuti sint patres, quos alij imitari volunt. Nam si solus, inquit, Christus audiendus est, non debe mus attendere quid aliquis ante nos faciendum putauerit: sed quid qui ante omnes est, Christus prior fecerit. Neque enim hominis consuetudinem sequi oportet, sed Dei veritatem. Hæc certè apud modestos & placidos lectores plena est ac solida causæ definitio, vbi hominum placitis in ordinem coactis, & consuetudine quamlibet veteri abdicata, Christi auctoritas sola eminet. Vale, Nonis Aprilis. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Epist.259. If no place is granted to the shadows of the law, how much less should this licence be allowed to human inventions? Now, if we examine carefully and thoroughly what so greatly moves men to fabricate ceremonies, we will find that all of them have flowed from this one source: whoever has dared to devise a new worship of God. Yet God not only rejects all fictitious worship but also severely abominates it, he for whom obedience is worth more than all sacrifices. And rightly so, because by his command whatever men claim for themselves in this matter is abolished. It must indeed be stated that whatever they bring of their own, while they desire to worship God according to their own judgment, is a foul profanation. But, so as not to enter a very wide forest, I come down to the particular case. I have said that the lawful use of Baptism and of the holy Supper must be sought from nowhere else than from the institution and command of Christ. He willed that this mystery be performed with water, the only-begotten Son of God. Men have chosen to add chrism and exsufflation. If the authority of Christ is holy and inviolable for us, and holds the reverence it deserves, who does not see that Baptism has been defiled by those extraneous trifles? Then it was so corrupted by mere mockeries that it stains rather than cleanses all those who permit that gross sacrilege in the washing. I do not see why a dispute about mixing water with wine in the holy Supper should have arisen. Christ, by the signs of bread and wine, has testified that his flesh is our food and his blood our drink. If there is a shortage of wine, it will be by no means absurd to dilute the small amount that remains with water, so that it suffices for the whole Church. But if religion is brought in, as though the mixing were necessary, superstition is not lacking here. For the Church is bound, in a new law and against Christ's command, no less rashly than foolishly, and a mystery is sought in a thing of no importance, a childish one. They want the chalice to contain a mixture of water and wine because water and blood flowed from the side of the Lord. As if the Author's purpose had been to teach any such thing, and not rather to give a pledge of the spiritual drink! Nor is the testimony of Cyprian rightly brought forward here, because he never contended that the wine in the holy Supper should be diluted; on the contrary, against men who were watery, he asserted that by Christ's command wine must be drunk there. For there were some who, under the pretext of abstinence, kept from the heavenly mystery the wine which the common people abuse intemperately. Therefore, since his whole discussion teaches that in the holy Supper the blood of Christ is represented not by water but by wine, the things he hands down in passing about the mixture should not be dragged into support of water. Add that the unlearned are deceived by the word miscere, which he uses from time to time, while they always take it to mean diluere, whereas it rather means to pour, according to the usage of the Latin language accepted among the ancients and sound writers. Indeed, when he elsewhere wishes to exhort the faithful to unity, he reminds them that the sacred chalice is made up not of many drops of water but of many grapes, just as the mystical bread is made up of many grains. Nor do I deny that he himself asserts a mixture of water and wine, but with a vanishing pretext: that wine signifies the blood of Christ, and water the people. If anyone is pleased by this subtlety, he deserves to be fed on the wind. As for us, let us abandon the curiosity of the human mind, which has always been excessively wanton, and hang upon the lips of him who alone is the Author of the Supper. Indeed, we see how Cyprian himself, by a memorable saying, sends us away from himself to Christ, where he forbids following custom in offering water alone, because we ought rather to ask whom the Fathers followed, those whom others wish to imitate. For, he says, if Christ alone is to be heard, we must not consider what anyone before us thought ought to be done, but what Christ, who is before all, did first. For we ought not to follow human custom, but the truth of God. Surely, for modest and calm readers, this is a full and solid settlement of the cause: when human opinions have been brought into order and any custom, however old, has been set aside, the authority of Christ alone stands out. Farewell, on the Nones of April, 1558.

units.la: MARTYR CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Martyr to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: ACcepi, Vir Clarissime, superioribus diebus istas literas Vienna, vt eas ad te mitterem, quod antea non feci, quia commodum tabellarium prius non habui. Nunc verò partim ista occasione data scribo, partim quoniam videtur iam esse diu ex quo te non salutaui: quod officium etsi aliquantulum distuli, nihilominus intermori non patiar. Atque ad hanc meam voluntatem aliud accedit, nempe superioribus diebus me summa voluptate perlegisse, quum edidisti lucubrationem, pro tuenda æterna & saluifica Dei Optimi Maximi prædestinatione. Proinde cum ea lectione fuerim admodum recreatus, par & æquum existimaui gratias tibi agere: nec dubito laboris tuo quoad electos ac prædestinatos ad æternam vitam à Deo, ad cuius gloriam susceptus fuit, iustum vberémque fructum conceßum iri. Ego quoque in istam eandem sententiam permulta collegeram in commentario meo epistolæ ad Romanos, quem ante aliquot menses imprimendum Petro Pernæ Basileam miseram: qui tamen liber iis nundinis absolui non potuit. Quod idcirco nunc significo, quò tibi fidem faciam, ex animo & iusta de causa, me tuo scripto non vulgariter gauisum esse. Nos hic noui nihil fere habemus, quod ipse nescias. Inauguratio noui Imperatoris, forma & ratione insolita & hactenus inaudita, omnibus admiratione mirabilis incredibilé peperit. Hac enim (vt loquuntur) coronatione, Antichristi Romani auctoritas videtur deiecta,plus quàm hacte nus vnquam fuerit:& quo pacto Electores Archiepiscopi adduci potuerint,vt eiusmodi consenserint inaugurationi,nullum propemodum intelligit.Sed quicquid sit, expectabimus operam Dei. Huc venerunt duo Vienna,quorum alter est concionator: alter vero Comes,aetate quidem iuuenis, at in literis admodum exercitatus,& Religionis amatiss.Nouo Imperatori erat a consiliis. Caeterum agit modo cum Maximiliano Rege Bohemiae,conteplatur Ecclesias Euangelicas, nititurq; ostendere Lutheranos & nos dere Sacramentaria idem sentire, verum hucusq; id non potuit ad liquidum nonnullis probare.Tubyngam & Heyidesergà proficisicitur.Haec ad Philippum in Saxoniam,quem ait se coma pertissimum habere,coactum esse iam ad scribendum,acteftan dum quidnà de re Sacramentaria statuat.Vtinam illi Deus eam constantiam largiatur,quae illius eruditionem & pietatem decet. Vterqi vero istorum affirmat Regem Maximilianum totum ad Euangelicam Religionem s propensum , & Viennensem Ecclesiam cupere omnino reformatam. Haec habui quae scribere, vir clarissime,ac mihi multis nominibus plurimùm obseruàde. Precor Deum Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt Ecclesiae suae quàm diutissimè incolumem feruet Tyguri,x x 1.Aprilis.Rogo vt fymmyftas meo nomine saluere iubeas.
units.tr: I received these letters from Vienna in recent days, Most Distinguished Sir, to send on to you. I had not done so before because I had no convenient courier. Now I write partly because this opportunity has arisen, and partly because it seems a long time since I last greeted you. I have put off this duty somewhat, but I will not allow it to lapse altogether. To this wish of mine another reason is added: in the past few days I read with the greatest pleasure your recent work defending the eternal and saving predestination of God, most good and great. Having been greatly refreshed by that reading, I thought it right and fitting to thank you. I do not doubt that your labour, undertaken for the glory of God, will bring a just and rich reward for the elect and predestined to eternal life. I too had gathered a great deal to the same effect in my commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, which a few months ago I sent to Peter Perna at Basel to be printed. That book, however, could not be finished for the present fair. I mention this now so that you may be assured that I rejoiced in your writing not in an ordinary way, and for a just reason. Here we have almost no news that you do not already know. The inauguration of the new Emperor, in a form and manner unusual and hitherto unheard of, has caused wonder and astonishment in everyone. By this coronation, as people say, the authority of the Roman Antichrist seems to have been overthrown more than ever before. How the Electors and Archbishops were brought to consent to such an inauguration, almost no one understands. But whatever the case, we shall await God's work. Two men have come here from Vienna: one is a preacher, the other a count, young in years but well trained in letters and a lover of religion, who is a counsellor to the new Emperor. Moreover, he is now dealing with Maximilian, King of Bohemia, and is studying the Evangelical churches, and he strives to show that the Lutherans and we Sacramentarians think alike; but so far he has not been able to prove this clearly to some. He is setting out for Tübingen and Heidelberg. These things he reports to Philip in Saxony, whom he says he holds in the highest regard, and he says that Philip has already been compelled to write and testify what he thinks about the question of the Sacrament. May God grant him that steadfastness which befits his learning and piety. Both of these men affirm that King Maximilian is wholly inclined to the Evangelical religion, and that the Church of Vienna wishes to be entirely reformed. These are the things I had to write, Most Distinguished Sir, and most worthy of my esteem in many respects. I pray God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to keep his Church safe for as long as possible. From Zurich, 21 April. I ask you to bid the members of your congregation greet me in your name.

units.la: Tuus in Domino Petrus Martyr.
units.tr: Yours in the Lord, Peter Martyr.

units.la: BLAVRERVS CALVINO.
units.tr: Blaurer to Calvin.

units.la: DEillo negotio non visum est quicquam porrò ad te scribere,quòd sperem alioqui iam calorem istum defrbuisse. Ego nemini qui vocetur detrectandum puto, quòd omni petenti fidei nostrae rationem reddere iubeamur. Si aliud à nouo Imperatore colloquium impetrabunt imperij ordines, tum Magistratibus scribetur(si vera ab amicis accipio) vt Theologos suos adesse iubeant. Sunt certè ex Principibus nonnulli qui paci Ecclesiarum magnopere studeant, ac nullis parcerent sumptibus, modò hanc redimere vlla ratione possent. Atque vtinam in vnam hac rem,per bellicos istos motus,qui alij ex alijs idem oriuntur,incumbere illis liceret.Gallum cum Turca colludere infaustaque cum eo foedera meditari constantissimè ac publicè affirmatur. Deinde Roman. Pontific, sic iratum nouo Imperatori,vt omnia citius periclitari,quàm hanc inauguratio nem ratam habere velit,cùm praesertim sacramento adactus sit nouus Caesar,ne vel coronam,vel gladium, vel quicquam eiusmodi modi à Pontifice peteret, sed Principum Electorum, Ordinúmq; imperij consensu, solitisque ceremoniis, quæ absque superstitio-ne adhibitæ sunt, contentus esse velit. Sicque à tribus istis Potentiss. mundi Monarchis, Pontif. Gallo, & Turca summum Cæsari imminere periculum. Esse enim hos triplicem vixque nunquam rumpendum funiculum, quo velut laqueo, Cæsaris collum induendum pariter ac præsocandum fiet. Sed fortior est omnibus istis Dei veritas, à qua si steterit Cæsar, non est cur sibi suisque metuamus ab imbellibus omnibus terræ vermiculis. Nos perpetuis flagrantissimisque fidei votis cœlestem Patrem, cuius manus omnium Regum corda moderatur, supplices interpellemus, ut fractis frustratisque omnibus omnium hostium conatibus, regnum Iesu Christi Filij sui vsque propagare, ac seipso quotidie auctius, illustrius ac florulentius esse velit, nosque in illo æternùm fœlices ac beatos futuros conseruet. Scripseram Philippo per symmystam meum, sed non attigit is Saxoniam, ut animus erat, quandoquidem Principes quibuscum agendum erat, Francofurti inuenit. Tu si quid habes, vel ex Gallia, vel de Philippo, ne me celes. Meliora mihi de hoc promiseram, & valde miror, magnum hunc virum non perinde magno animo esse, verùm semper vbi ad rem vetum est, veterem recipere imbecillitatem.
units.tr: I did not think it worth writing anything further to you about that business, since I hope that the heat of it has by now cooled. I think no one who is called should be refused, since we are commanded to give an account of our faith to everyone who asks. If the Estates of the Empire obtain another colloquy from the new Emperor, then, if I hear the truth from friends, letters will be sent to the magistrates asking them to order their theologians to attend. Certainly some of the princes earnestly desire peace for the churches, and would spare no expense, provided they could somehow secure it. I wish that they might be allowed to concentrate on this one matter amid these warlike disturbances, which arise one after another from the same source. It is openly and constantly asserted that the French are conspiring with the Turk and planning disastrous treaties with him. Furthermore, the Roman Pontiff is so angry with the new Emperor that he would rather risk everything than allow this inauguration to stand, especially since the new Caesar has been bound by oath not to seek from the Pontiff either the crown, the sword, or anything of that kind, but to be content with the consent of the Electoral Princes and the Estates of the Empire and the customary ceremonies, which were observed without superstition. Thus the Emperor faces grave danger from these three most powerful monarchs of the world, the Pontiff, the Frenchman, and the Turk. They are, as it were, a threefold cord, hardly ever to be broken, by which the Caesar's neck is to be bound, as with a noose, and at the same time throttled. But God's truth is stronger than all of these. If Caesar stands by it, there is no reason for us to fear for him and his people from all the feeble little worms of the earth. Let us with constant and burning prayers of faith entreat the heavenly Father, whose hand guides the hearts of all kings, that, having broken and frustrated all the attempts of every enemy, he may wish the kingdom of his Son Jesus Christ to be ever more widely spread, and to grow daily more prosperous and glorious in itself, and may keep us to be happy and blessed in him for ever. I had written to Philip through my fellow-Symmystes, but he did not reach Saxony as he had intended, since he found the princes with whom he had to deal at Frankfurt. If you have anything, from France or about Philip, do not keep it from me. I had hoped for better things from him, and I am much surprised that this great man is not as high-spirited as he ought to be; but whenever a matter comes to the point of action, he always resumes his old weakness.

units.la: Dominus illi excelsos planéque heroicos, hoc est, sed dignos animos addat: quippe cuius auctoritas in pacificationis negotio tantum afferet momenti, quantum vix cuiusquam. Et profecto, vtut dissimulet, seipsum negare haudquaquam poterit. Ad multos multa modestissimè scripsit, quibus non obscurè testatur, quantùm absit ab illorum sententia, qui de Christi Cœna superstitiosius sentiunt, & loquuntur: quantumque sibi displiceant temerariæ istæ Saxonum quorundam aduersum nostros condemnationes, & inauspicata præiudicia. Seruator Iesus Christus electum organum hoc suum inexpugnabili Spiritus sui virtute semel exaltato induat, vt rem, & vitam & omnia periclitari citius, quàm suscepctum iamdudum veritatis patrocinium tanto cum suo dedecore indicibilíque Ecclesiarum Christi iactura deferere velit secum. Vale mi anime, ac omnium mihi longè colendissime charissimèque frater, mēque cœlesti Patri assiduis votis diligenter commenda, vt triumphatis Christi fui auspiciis à morte quà veteranus iam quotidie meditor ad vitalem illam vitam, quæ sola vita, vt verè est, sic rectè dici merito potest transfire mihi quàprimùm liceat. Iterum iterúmque vale præter cæteros veneran-de mihi semper Caluine, frater in Christo Iesu suauiter arctissimèque, complectende, qui tibi præsentissimus suo numine semper adsit. Linguam tuam ad dicendum, manum verò ad scribendum, ita Spiritu sancto suo regat, vt te loquente suam vocem, te scribente suam manum, quotquot sunt vere Christiani semper agnoscant, atque fidei obedientia strenue se ac feliciter parent. Salutant te nostri, praecipue symmysta cum reliquis tibi notis. Saluta fratres & amicos qui nos in Christo diligunt, cum primis administrostuos in opere Domini, cum Archigrammateo vestro. Bienae XIII I.Maij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: May the Lord give him lofty and truly heroic, that is, worthy, courage, since his authority in the business of pacification will bring as much weight as that of almost anyone. And indeed, however much he may dissemble, he will by no means be able to deny himself. He has written to many people, very modestly, in ways that make it not obscurely plain how far he is from the opinion of those who think and speak too superstitiously about the Lord's Supper, and how much he dislikes those rash condemnations and ill-omened prejudgments of certain Saxons against our side. May Jesus Christ, the Saviour, clothe this chosen instrument of his, once exalted, with the invincible power of his Spirit, so that he may wish to abandon the defence of the truth, long since undertaken, rather than risk his property, his life, and everything else, to his own great dishonour and the unspeakable loss of the Churches of Christ. Farewell, my soul, and, of all my friends by far the most to be cherished and most dearly loved brother. Commend me diligently in constant prayers to the heavenly Father, so that, with the auspices of Christ our victor, I may pass, as a veteran who every day meditates on death, as soon as I may, to that life which alone is truly life, and rightly and deservedly can be called so. Again and again, farewell, Calvin, to me always most venerable beyond the rest, brother in Christ Jesus, to be embraced sweetly and most closely; may he who is most present to you by his divine power always be with you. May he so guide your tongue for speaking and your hand for writing by his Holy Spirit, that all who are truly Christians may recognise his voice when you speak and his hand when you write, and may strenuously and happily prepare themselves for obedience to the faith. My people greet you, especially my fellow-Symmystes, along with the others known to you. Greet the brothers and friends who love us in Christ, and above all your fellow-workers in the Lord's work, and your Archgrammateus. From Biel, 13 May 1558.

units.la: Vere T. Ambr. Blaurerus.
units.tr: Truly yours, T. Ambr. Blaurer.

units.la: CAL. MARTYRI S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MARTYR, GREETINGS

units.la: BInas his paucis diebus abs te literas accepi, Clariss. vir. Ex prioribus intelligere gratum fuit, tuo iudicio probari breve scriptum, quo aeternam Dei prouidentiam contra impuras rabulae calumnias defendere volui. Causae quae tibi mecum est communis, sciebam te ex animo favere. Etsi vero satis agnosco non adeo fuisse qua par erat dexteritate & inductria: imo quod inuitus ad eam accessserim, fastidium quo tenebar, magno fuisse obstaculo scio mihi abunde sufficit, mea culpa nihil iactare pro sum esse. Hoc tamen longe mihi gratius iam sub prelo esse tuos commentarios, in quibus harum rerum fusa & dilucida explicatio tradetur. Quando tandem in Genesin quoque, & in Prophetas aliquid exibit? Cur non hic es, ut tibi de manibus vi extorqueantur, quae nimis diu premis? N. noster parua quidem in re expertus est, quantum testimonio tuo & commendationi defer rem: per me tamen non stetit, quominus me ad maiora officia prompto & parato vteretur. His diebus in Ecclesia Italica aliquid fuitturbarum. Gribaldus femina quaedam suorum errorum sparserat, quorum summa huc redit: vnicum Deum esse, qui Pater est Christi, vt Monarchia sit penes solum Patrem, Christus vero secundarius, & quasi primogenitus inter multos deos. Hoc non animaducrtebant simplices, qui tamen falsis principiis impliciti pertinaciter tuendo quod nunquam intellexerant, iam coeperant repudiare quae nihil controuersiae habent inter pios. Iam adhuc superstite optimo fratre nostro Martinengo, pullulabant haec dissidia. Itaque moriens summa vehementia & me & collegas hortatus fuerat, vt cauendo huic malo, & sanando intenti essemus. Me vero praesertim nominetur & quater appellans, Qui mihi & gregi, dicebat, hactenus fuisti Pater, nunc Pastore suo orbatum gregem in tuam fidem & curam suscipe: & quo notiores tibi sunt morbi, a quibus summum discrimen impendet, adhibendis maturè remediis sedulo aduigila. Post eius mortem Laetantio & mihi multum fuit negotij in pacandis turbulentis hominibus, qui dubitandi praetextu suis deliriis alios imbuebat. Quum omnia putarem composita, repente apparuit, clandestinis illorum artibus plures esse corruptos. Cuius mali sanádi non alia fuit ratio, quàm vt omnes certæ confessionis formulæ subscriberent: qua propositâ liberum singulis fuit contrà afferre si quid eos angeret: scrupulos omnes ita discussi, & nodos expediui, vt certò confidam nunc in sanctam vnitatem rursus Ecclesiam coaluisse. Horum te volui facere certiorem, vt si quis ad vos vsq; rumor perferatur, ne solicitus sis, quasi dubio adhuc euentu. Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi venerande frater. Dominus te sibi & Ecclesiæ suæ diu incolumem seruet, Spiritu suo gubernet ac benedicat. Geneuæ, x xii. Maij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Within these few days I have received a letter from you, most distinguished sir. From your earlier letter I learned, with pleasure, that the short treatise in which I wished to defend God's eternal providence against the foul slanders of a certain blusterer has met with your approval. I knew that you favour the cause we share, and I know you favour it from the heart. Although I acknowledge well enough that I did not handle it with the skill and diligence it required, and I know that my reluctance to take it up, and the distaste that held me back, were a great obstacle, it is enough for me that I am not boasting of anything, since the fault is my own. Still, I am much more pleased that your commentaries are now going to press, in which a full and clear explanation of these matters will be given. When at last will something on Genesis, and also on the Prophets, appear? Why are you not here, so that the pages you have pressed on for far too long may be wrested from your hands by force? Our friend N. has found, in a small matter, how much I would have deferred to your testimony and recommendation; yet it has not been my fault that he has not used me, ready and prepared, for greater services. In these days there has been some disturbance in the Italian Church. A certain Gribaldus had spread some of his errors, the sum of which comes to this: that there is one God, who is the Father of Christ, so that the monarchy belongs to the Father alone, while Christ is secondary, as it were the firstborn among many gods. Simple people did not notice this; yet, entangled in false principles and stubbornly defending what they had never understood, they had already begun to reject things that involve no controversy among the godly. Even while our excellent brother Martinengo was still alive, these dissensions were springing up. So when he was dying, he urged me and my colleagues most earnestly to take care to remedy and heal this evil. He called upon me in particular, naming me and calling my name four times: "You have been a father to me and to the flock until now," he said; "now take the flock, deprived of its minister, into your trust and care, and, the better you know the diseases that threaten the greatest danger, watch carefully to apply remedies in good time." After his death, Lattanzio and I had much trouble in calming the turbulent men who, under the pretext of doubt, were infecting others with their madness. When I thought everything had been settled, it suddenly appeared that many had been corrupted by their secret tricks. There was no other way of healing this evil than to have everyone subscribe to a formula of a certain confession; once this was proposed, each man was free to bring forward against it whatever troubled him. I have so thoroughly examined all the scruples and untied all the knots that I am confident the Church has now grown back together into holy unity. I wanted to make you aware of this, so that if any rumour reaches you there, you need not be anxious, as if the outcome were still in doubt. Farewell, most distinguished man and my venerable brother. May the Lord keep you safe for a long time for himself and his Church, govern you by his Spirit, and bless you. Geneva, 22nd May 1558.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO FAREL, GREETING

units.la: Quomodo Rochæus noster postridie quàm captus fuerat liberatus sit à Rege Nauarræ, fuisse recitare non vacat. Cognitum fuit, temere fuisse arreptum, & coniecturis magis quàm testimoniis grauatum. Ita priorum impulsu aufusus est homo pusilli animi eum repescere, ac si vnus esset ex domesticis. Ipse etiam carcerem adiit, vt captiuum eximeret. Hic nuntius per se laetus vti nos exhilarat, ita nos angit altera ex parte, quòd nouas tragedias paulò post esse exortas credibile est: quia omnibus Regis officiariis mandatum fuerat, vt Deum panaceum in pompa solenni comitarentur: quod non omnes videbuntur facturi. Quauis in eiusmodi hominibus insolubilis quidam laqueus à mundo deprehenditur. Paucissimi cum Abrahamo in Deum simpliciter respiciunt. Multi cum Lotho, vt Sodomam relinquant, quaerentur se non posse seruari in monte. Sed quò rarior est cordatorum numerus ex eo genere, eò illustrior est Dei manus, quæ duplici pelle quodammodo istos exuere dignatur: natiuo affectu nempe, tum aduentitio, ex fulgore suæ dignitatis. Sed progressus suum vlterius, ne vacua plane exiret epistola. Vale optime & integerrime frater cum reliquis symmystis. Dominus vos omnes gubernet, tueatur, benedicat vsq; in finem. Geneuæ, x v iii. Iunij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I have no time to recount how our Rochette was set free by the King of Navarre the day after he had been arrested. It became known that he had been seized rashly and burdened more by conjectures than by evidence. So the timid man was driven on by his predecessors' push to win him back, as if he were one of their own household. He himself even went to the prison to free the captive. This news cheers us in itself, as it delights us, but on the other side it troubles us, because it is likely that new tragedies arose soon after, since all the King's officers had been ordered to accompany the host in solemn procession. Not all of them will apparently do so. Indeed, an inextricable snare is set by the world for men of this kind. Very few look simply to God, as Abraham did. Many, like Lot, when they are leaving Sodom, complain that they cannot be saved on the mountain. But the rarer the number of the wise from that sort, the more illustrious is the hand of God, which deigns in a way to strip them of a double skin: namely, their natural feeling, and the other, drawn from the glare of their own dignity. But I shall proceed further, lest the letter go out entirely empty. Farewell, best and most upright brother, along with the rest of our fellow-initiates. May the Lord govern, protect and bless you all to the end. Geneva, 18 June 1558.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to our beloved in the Lord, greeting

units.la: Inuitus scribo, mi frater, quòd non libenter audiui dissidium esse ortum inter vos leui de causa, quòd magnas offensiones pariat. Tu forte excipies, & iustam fuisse causam, neque tam
units.tr: I write unwillingly, my brother, because I did not gladly hear that a quarrel has arisen between you over a slight matter, one that produces great offences. Perhaps you will object that the cause was just, and that the feelings were not so greatly stirred that the report ought to have reached this far.

units.la: E.j. graues fuisse motus,vt fama hucvfq; peruenire debuerit. Vtrunque vt tibi breuiter expediam: quanuis initiò disceptatio maximè feria videri potuerit, & quam priuato arbitrio finire vix liceret,patuit tamen ipso progressu, hominem vnum inconsiderato sermone mouisse inutiles turbas:alterum ne in crimen tra heretur,nimis feruidè tumultuatum esse.Quòd si publicam auctoritatem intercedere oportuit,atque hoc flagitabat causæ gratuitas,scire velim quo iure abstè & senioribus suscepta fuerit cognitio.Si respondeas, nondum maturum fuisse tempus, donec melius patefacta esset veritas,saltem lætari oportuit odiosò hoc molestóque onere leuatum te esse. Quid enim lætius vel magis optandum, quàm vt arbitris totam molem sustinentibus, ipse securus quiescerés? Ergo quòd te metu & cura exemerant,beneficij loco ducendum fuit tantùm abesse vt æquum fuerit excandescere,ac si tibi facta esset iniuria. Negas fas fuisse, litem apud vos pendentem ad arbitros deuolui. Quid si duo litigantes,nullo interposito arbitrio inter se vltrò fuissent reconciliati,an illa voluntaria in gratiam reditio tibi displiceret? Si te subpectum fuisse iudicas,quia non fueris adhibitus, vide ne tuis coniecturis plus æquo tribuas. Atque vt sinistro aliquo prærudicio iniuste fuisse grauatum & læsum concedam, an priuata iniuria in fugge stum vsque prorumpere debuit? Neque dissimulandum est,tibi hoc ab æquis & moderatis auditoribus vitio verti,quòd permul ta vel leuicula, vel quæ suppriimi essent vtilius, ad populum vulgare, & immodica vehementia exagitare soleas. Certè in hoc negotio cur tantopere excandescéres,si omnia melius expendéris, causam forte non reperies. Cur vero arbitros odiose apud plebem traduxeris,non video.Adde quòd in c-llegam tuum homiminem placidum,& modestum,& de Ecclesia bene meritū violenter insurgere, neque humanum fuit, neque tua persona dignum.Ac si tibi cordi est Ecclesiæ ædificatio, potius dada opera fuit,vt integra maneret eius auctoritas. Quid de aliis dicam? quorum si nulla apud te ratio habetur,Ecclesiam vestrâ ornamentis non poenitendis spolias. Quum igitur & tua priuatim & totius Ecclesiæ magnopere interfuit,tibi amicos esse & quidem coniunctissimos,qui hactenus fidelem operam præstiterunt, & animati sunt ad pergendum:si meo consilio obtemperas depositâ contentione,pacificationi te acquiescere ostendes. Memini te aliquando mihi dicere,si lapsus errore esses,nihil tibi gratius esse quàm moneri. Qua fiducia te liberius hortari non dubitaui, vt vehementiam quæ modum excedere visa est, maturè frænes ac temperes Si quid remedij ad placandos animos à me afferri posse existimas,non deero partibus meis. Vale frater mi colende,cum vxore & amicis, quibus salutem multam precor.
units.tr: ...that the disturbances were so serious that news of them ought to have reached this far. I will briefly deal with both points for you. Although at first the dispute may have seemed very trivial, and such that it could hardly be settled by private judgment, it became clear as it went on that one man, by a thoughtless remark, stirred up useless troubles, while the other, lest he be dragged into blame, had made too much noise in his anger. But if public authority had to step in, and the seriousness of the case demanded it, I would like to know by what right you and the elders took up the inquiry. If you reply that the time was not yet ripe, until the truth had been brought more fully to light, you should at least have been glad to be relieved of this hateful and troublesome burden. For what could be happier or more to be wished, than that others should bear the whole weight while you yourself rested untroubled? So, since they had freed you from fear and anxiety, you ought to have counted it a kindness, not something to be so angry about, as if you had been wronged. You say it was wrong for the suit pending among you to be referred to arbitrators. But what if two litigants, without any arbitration, had of their own accord been reconciled with each other: would that voluntary return to friendship displease you? If you judge that you were suspected because you were not called in, take care that you do not attribute more than is fair to your own conjectures. And even if I grant that you were unjustly burdened and harmed by some unfavourable prejudice, ought a private wrong to have burst out into fury? Nor should I hide that your fellow hearers, both fair and moderate men, find fault with you for often exposing to the common people, and attacking with immoderate vehemence, many matters that are trivial, or that would be better suppressed. Certainly in this affair, if you weighed everything more carefully, you would perhaps not find a reason for being so furious. Why you have held the arbitrators up to odium before the common people, I do not see. Add to this that to rise up violently against your colleague, a peaceable and modest man who has deserved well of the Church, was neither humane nor worthy of your character. And if the building up of the Church is dear to you, you should rather have taken pains that its authority remain whole. What shall I say of the others? If no account is taken of them by you, you are stripping your Church of ornaments that are not to be regretted. Since it is therefore of great importance both to you personally and to the whole Church that you have as friends, and indeed the closest of friends, those who have hitherto given faithful service and have been encouraged to persevere, you will show that you are willing to accept reconciliation if you obey my advice and lay down your contention. I remember that you once told me that if you had fallen into error, nothing would be more welcome to you than to be admonished. Trusting in that, I have not hesitated to urge you more freely to restrain and temper promptly the vehemence which seems to have gone beyond measure. If you think there is any remedy that I can bring to calm the minds of those concerned, I shall not fail in my part. Farewell, my dear and honoured brother, with your wife and friends, for whom I pray much health.

units.la: Dominus vos omnes tueatur, gubernet, benedicat. Vtinam brevi de vestra concordia nuntium audiam, qui me exhilaret. Genes. x, x x.Iunij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: May the Lord keep, govern and bless you all. I hope to hear soon of your harmony, which would cheer me. Geneva, x x June 1558.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin sends greetings.

units.la: Qui liceat participare cultui Romanæ Synagogæ.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to take part in the worship of the Roman Synagogue.

units.la: QVia de quæstionibus quas moues, iam decem fere annis ex variis partibus exhibita fuit molestia: neque hoc trecentis responsis adeptus sum, vt quiescere in posterum liceret, nihil melius esse duxi iusto tædio victus, quàm locum dare superioribus meis scriptis, ne implacabilis multorum curiositas frustra me conficeret. Quare si breuiter tibi & concisè respondeo, non solùm temporis angustiis, quibus tamen costringor, adscribas: sed conceptæ pridem deliberationi. Nà si quibus ita prurit aures, vt nouis quotidie responsis obleflare se cupiant, facile patiar aliunde petere. Nec mihi inter tot negotia, & assiduos propè morbos tantum suppetit otij, vt publicè & priuatim scribendo omnibus morem geram. Rogant quidam, Si Apostolis licuit ho ra precationis in templum ascendere: deinde etiam Paulo solennem ritum sanctificationis obire: cur non etiâ hodie nobis fas sit preces miscere cum Papistis? Primò tenen dum est, quæ tunc apud Iudæos preces vigebant, fuisse puras, & formatas ad præscriptum Legis. Nec verò, si Papistæ puram orandi formam conciperent, mihi religio esset templum cum ipsis ingredi. Atqui illos minimè decuit aggregare se ad eorum coetum, qui Christum crucifixerant. Respondeo actionem per se piam & sanctam non corrumpi vitio hominum: sicut dicere soleo, ne omnes quidem Angelos si Missæ intersint, posse eluere eius sordes sua sanctitate: nec rursum Diabolos omnes posse sua præsentia efficere, quò minus sacra Cœna dum celebratur ex Christi instituto, suam puritatem retineat. Certum tamen est, non omnibus precandi horis Apostolos venisse in templum, quia in ædibus priuatis agebant sacros conuentus: sed vt oblata illis fuit spes ædificandi, hac occasione fuisse vsos. Non ergo data opera frequentarunt templum, vt Gentis suæ in publicis & quotidianis precibus essent socij: sed quia probabile erat, loci reuerentia magis dociles ac morigeros fore ad excipiendam Euangelij doctrinam, qui in locis profanis minus fuissent attenti. Atque id in Paulo clarius perspicitur, qui certè nulla religione impulsus votum suscepit, sed tantùm vt purgata qua falso grauatus fuerat suspicione, ianuam sibi ad spargendum Euangelium patefaceret. Neque enim sponte hac ceremonia fuisset
units.tr: Since for nearly ten years I have been troubled by the questions you raise, put to me from various quarters, and since three hundred replies have not brought me the rest I hoped for, I have judged it best, overcome by a justified weariness, to give my earlier writings the place of an answer, lest the relentless curiosity of many wear me out for nothing. So if I answer you briefly and concisely, please attribute this not only to the shortness of time, by which I am nonetheless constrained, but to a decision I formed long ago. For if there are people whose ears itch so much that they want to be fed new replies every day, I will gladly let them seek them elsewhere. Nor, amid so many tasks and almost constant illness, do I have enough leisure to satisfy everyone by writing in public and in private. Some ask: if the Apostles were allowed to go up into the temple at the hour of prayer, and Paul was allowed to perform the solemn rite of purification, why should it not also be lawful for us today to join our prayers with the Papists? First, it must be held that the prayers then in use among the Jews were pure and shaped according to the prescription of the Law. Indeed, if the Papists were to devise a pure form of prayer, I would not scruple to enter the temple with them. But it was by no means fitting for those men to join the company of those who had crucified Christ. I answer that a pious and holy action is not in itself corrupted by the faults of men. As I am accustomed to say, even if all the Angels were present at the Mass, they could not wash away its filth by their holiness; nor again could all the Devils by their presence make the Lord's Supper, while it is celebrated according to Christ's institution, lose its purity. It is certain, however, that the Apostles did not come into the temple at every hour of prayer, since they held their sacred assemblies in private houses; but when the hope of building up was offered to them, they seized the occasion. So they did not frequent the temple on purpose, to share with their nation in its public and daily prayers, but because it was likely that people would be more teachable and compliant in receiving the doctrine of the Gospel out of reverence for the place, whereas in profane places they would have been less attentive. This is seen more clearly in Paul, who certainly, moved by no religious scruple, took up the vow, but only so that, once the suspicion falsely laid upon him was cleared, he might open for himself a door for spreading the Gospel. For he would not have undertaken this ceremony of his own accord

units.la: E.ij. defunctus:neque rogatus est ab Iocobo, vt ita Deum coleret,sed vt testatum faceret infirmis fratribus se non esse apostatam à Lege Mosis.Interea liberum illis fuit & templum ingredi,& sacta oblatione testari suam pietatem:quia nō alius erat finis,nisi vt profiterentur se Deum Israelis colere.Iam emergit altera quæstio,Si aduentu Christi abolitæ erant Legis vmbræ,cureas adhuc sectati fuerint?quæ facile soluitur,si tenemus quandiu stetit templum, fuisse sacrum domicilium cœlestis doctrinæ, & illic Deum ritè fuisse adoratum.Sic enim finem legalibus ceremoniis impo suit Christus, vt eas abrogando non prorsus statim damnauerit quasi impias & pollutas, donec per Euangelium clare innotuit. Si excipias,lucem Euangelij tunc satis fuisse conspicuam,res ipsa palam docet, multis adhuc incognitum fuisse Christum : alios vero sic fuisse illustratos eius radiis, vt tamen abesset à pleno fulgore. Hinc apparet inter legales ritus,& Papales ceremonias latum discrimen. Nam quum illi ab origine sua puri sanctique fuerint,has cōstat Satan artificio fabricatas esse ad extinguendam Christi lucem.Vnde colligere promptum est,à suo principio vitiosas esse. Itaque Legis abrogatio dextre intelligi debet, quia fidelibus Christi seruis templum,& ritus per se medios & in differentes nō ante deferere necesse fuit,quàm partibus suis defuncti essent in promulgando Euangelio. Interea certum est, quotties in templum venerunt,habitam ab illis fuisse rationem infirmæ plebis:sicuti quocunque venissent folenne fuit,adire sy nagogas non orandi causa, licet interpositæ quoq; fuerint preces: sed quia illic maior erat frequentia hominum, & animi ad discendum melius præparati,vt docendo prodesse ntur.Quod obiicitur,Nisi in nomine Messiæ orarent,peruersas fuisse eorū preces. Respondeo,vt erant à patribus instituti,in nomine Messiæ licet incogniti orasse.Et certè effectu ipso patuit,quum tam facile, & alacri animi promptitudine ad Christum transierint permulti,occultum in illis fuisse pietatis semen. Et probabile est,fidem à Paulo laudari in matre Timothei Eunicha,& auia Loidè, antequam Euangelio imbutæ essent, vt bonæ illius radicis fructus fuerit ad Christum conuersio. Vmbras Legis non simpliciter concedo veritati fuisse contrarias,nisi quatenus perpetam à superstitiosis, & præfractis Christo vel permixtæ vel oppositæ fuerunt. Qui verò more patrio sacrificabant Iudæi ante acceptâ Euangelij lucem, socij piorum omnium fuerunt in legitimo Dei cultu : quia fixum illud manere debet figuras legales veteri populo datas esse,donec illucesceret Christus:quod paulatim fa ctum est.Adde quòd plerique gustatis Euangelij rudimentis, vt cunque non aliunde iustitiam peterent, quàm à Christo, & in eius sacrificio locarentspem salutis: non tamen eovsque statim progressos
units.tr: E.ij. having been performed, nor was he asked by James to worship God in this way, but so that he might show his weak brothers that he had not apostatised from the Law of Moses. Meanwhile it was open to them to enter the temple and, by making an offering, to bear witness to their piety, since the only aim was that they should profess that they worshipped the God of Israel. Now another question arises: if the shadows of the Law were abolished at the coming of Christ, why did they still pursue them? This is easily resolved if we hold that, as long as the temple stood, it was the sacred dwelling of heavenly teaching, and God was duly worshipped there. For Christ set an end to the legal ceremonies in such a way that, by abrogating them, he did not at once condemn them outright as impious and polluted, until the Gospel made it clearly known. If you object that the light of the Gospel was then already sufficiently visible, the thing itself plainly shows that Christ was still unknown to many, while others were so illumined by his rays that they were nonetheless far from full brightness. Hence it appears that there is a wide difference between the legal rites and the Papal ceremonies. For while the former were pure and holy from their origin, it is established that the latter were fabricated by Satan's craft to extinguish the light of Christ. Whence it is easy to conclude that they were vicious from their beginning. Therefore the abrogation of the Law must be understood rightly: it was necessary for the faithful servants of Christ not to abandon the temple and rites, which in themselves were indifferent, until they had finished their part in proclaiming the Gospel. Meanwhile it is certain that whenever they came to the temple, they took account of the weakness of the common people; just as, wherever they came, it was customary to go to the synagogues not for the sake of praying, although prayers were also offered, but because there was a greater crowd of people there, and minds better prepared for learning, so that they might benefit them by teaching. As to the objection that, unless they prayed in the name of the Messiah, their prayers were perverse: I answer that, as they had been instituted by the fathers, they prayed in the name of the Messiah, though he was still unknown. And indeed the outcome itself showed this, since so many were turned to Christ so easily and with such eager readiness; this showed that a hidden seed of piety was in them. It is also probable that Paul praises the faith of Timothy's mother Eunice and grandmother Lois, before they were imbued with the Gospel, so that their conversion to Christ was the fruit of that good root. I do not simply concede that the shadows of the Law were contrary to the truth, except insofar as they were either mixed with Christ or set against him by superstitious and obstinate people. But those Jews who sacrificed in the manner of their fathers before the light of the Gospel was received were companions of all the pious in the lawful worship of God. For this should remain fixed: the legal figures were given to the ancient people until Christ should dawn, which happened gradually. Add that many, having tasted the rudiments of the Gospel, though they sought righteousness from no other source than Christ and placed their hope of salvation in his sacrifice, nevertheless did not in some measure progress so far as to free themselves from every doubt.

units.la: 2.Tim.15. progressos liquet, ut omni dubitatione se eximeret. Vitiosa quidem & reprehensione digna fuit illa infirmitas, sed quam ad tempus tolerabilem fuisse Paulus docet: quia minime propositum illis erat, Christo quidquam detrahere: sed durū erat & asperum, protinus discedere à consuetudine diu recepta. Iam quum de caeremoniis legalibus agitur, prudenter adhibendum est discrimen inter sacrificia ex quibus petēda erat expiatio, & alia exercitia, quorum liberior fuit usus: sicuti hodie à fraudulis quibusdam & leviculis caeremoniis longè distant aliae, in quibus apparet manifesta & crassa impietas. Nam in pacificis, & similibus primas olim tenuit gratiarum actio. Ut demus, Christo adhuc incognito, licitum figurae usum fuisse, vel non satis perspicue cognito, ex cusabilem: non ideo fidelibus ad Christum conuersis fas fuisset oblato sacrificio se expiare, ut voto Eucharistico (nec eo simpliciter ad testandum pietatem, sed praecipue charitatis respectu, & purgandae calumniae perniciosissimae causa) defungi, ut Paulo accidit auctore Iacobo Ierosolymis. Interea semper illud tenendum est, non eodem esse gradu ritus, qui puri ab initio, postea veritatis sole adeuniente obscurati & planè aboliti sunt. Vti Christianismus ita Iudaismo successit, vel qui ab vsu degenerarunt in vitium, ut idem Iudaismus superstitiosè & literaliter à Iudaeis vsurpabatur iam olim, & superstitiones meras, quae auctore Diabolo ad vitiandum Dei cultum fabricatae sint. Nam si quis Legis ablutiones cum lustrali Papistarum aqua comparet, grauem Deo facinus iniuriam, qui veterem populum vtiliter signo illo exercuit, quum hac foetida ablutione, Baptismum iterando quodammodo deleuerit mendacij pater. Vale optime & charissime frater. Nam epistolam hanc abrumpere me coegit aliae scriptiones. Dominus vos omnes protegat vmbra sua, gubernet Spiritu suo, virtute fulciat. x x i. die Iunij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: 2.Tim.15. It is clear that this weakness was faulty and deserving of rebuke, yet Paul teaches that it was tolerable for a time, because it was by no means their purpose to take anything away from Christ; but it was hard and bitter to depart at once from a custom long received. Now when legal ceremonies are under discussion, a prudent distinction must be drawn between sacrifices by which expiation was to be sought, and other exercises whose use was freer. Just so, today other practices, slight and trifling, are far removed from those in which manifest and gross impiety appears. For in the peace offerings and similar rites, thanksgiving once held the first place. Granted that, while Christ was still unknown, the use of the figure was lawful, or excusable where it was not yet clearly understood, it would not on that account have been permitted to the faithful converted to Christ to expiate themselves by an offering, or to discharge a eucharistic vow (and not simply to testify to their piety, but chiefly out of regard for charity and for the sake of clearing away a most pernicious calumny), as happened to Paul at Jerusalem on the advice of James. Meanwhile it must always be held that rites which were pure from the beginning, and afterwards obscured and utterly abolished when the sun of truth drew near, are not of the same rank as those which degenerated from their use into vice, as Judaism itself was already long ago used superstitiously and literally by the Jews, and as there are mere superstitions, fabricated at the instigation of the Devil to corrupt the worship of God. For if anyone compares the ablutions of the Law with the lustral water of the Papists, he charges God with a grave wrong, since God usefully exercised the ancient people with that sign; whereas the father of lies, by this foul ablution, has in a manner obliterated Baptism by repeating it. Farewell, best and dearest brother. Other writings compel me to break off this letter. May the Lord protect you all with his shadow, guide you by his Spirit, and strengthen you with his power. 21st of June, 1558.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS HENRYCO. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Henry Co., greetings

units.la: ANte duos menses scripserat Fracifcus noster, sibi inter magnas & arduas difficultates hoc non vulgari fuisse solatio, quòd fideli tua opera commodè & opportunè adiutus foret. Idem nobis iterum confirmans paucis abhinc diebus, magnopere & ingenuam in te synceritatem & perseverantiam laudauit. Etsi autem nihil narrabat, nisi quod praestandum fuit Christi seruo: quia tamen vbi periculosa est vel damnosa integritas, rara apparent eius exempla: ex animo, ut par erat, laetati sumus, te opprobrium crucis Christi mundi lautitiis praeferre, quae multos ita inebriant, ut Euangelij simplicitas, quasi insipida, sit illis fastidio. Quòd si eorum altitudinem esse simulatus, qui nimis ad fouendam suam quietem sunt prouidi:erat speciosus color,cur te à fratre nostro disiungeres. Hoc enim prætextu solent,qui priuatæ securitati consulere volunt,ab omni odio & molestia pro cul se subducere, quia nihil vtilius fit, quàm medio quodam & flexiloquo docendi genere mulcere populi aures. Quo maiori laude dignus es, qui molliter & extra omne certamen cum docere poss s,posthabita priuata vtilitate,ad dandam fratri nostro societatis dextram vltrò fuisti propensus. Et certè videmus hoc tandem consequi versutos illos artifices,qui pietatis doctrinam ad suum commodum infleꝗunt, vt discipuli eorum semper discendo nunquam peruenient ad veritatis scientiam. Porrò quanuis iam minus æquos ac propitios experiaris, qui ante hac suore te profequuti sunt, non est tamen cur syncerę confessionis te pœniteat. Neque enim ignoras,hac lege nos seruire Christo, vt non modò cum professis hostibus gerendum sit bellum,sed multis etiam domesticorum calumniis simus obnoxij. Fremunt multi,alij aperte clamabunt,te ad libertatem quæ apud vos tolerabilis non sit,inconsideratè progressum esse. Tibi non modò has voces spernere necesse erit,sed delicias quibus indulgent,seuerè illis excutere,vt intelligant claudicationem qua pugnas omnes declinant,exosam esse Deo. Pergendo quà cœpisti (quod factûrum certò confidimus) tandem sentiet puram coram Deo & Angelis conscientiam, centum theatris longè præstare : eiúsque pacem , totius mundi plausu magis esse expetendam. Addè quòd pij Dei cultores tibi iam merito gratulantur, atque vberem ex hac sanctâ tua alacritate fructum sibi promittunt. Tibi optimus frater noster Francifcus,quem & nos experti sumus vere Christo esse addictum, & tu eximiis ad ædificandam Ecclesiam doctibus possere vides, fidelis ac strenuus erit adiutor.Audimus reuersum esse concionatorem aulicum, qui vtinam ne suo more. Vtcunque verò se gerat, minime consentaneum esset ab homine flexibili,& ad quaslibet auras nutare soli-to,Christi seruos pendere. Tu pro tua moderatione,& prudentia, hauddubiè studebis eum tibi adiungere, ne rectum cursum impediat vel moretur. Sin metus & nimia cauendi solicitudo, vel etiam peruersa ætmulatio hominem in diuersas partes rapiat, contra hæc quoque obstacula fortiter eniti necesse erit.Vale eximie vir, & integerrime frater. Dominus te Spiritu suo regere, virtute fulcire & tueri, studiisque tuis & piis laboribus benedicere pergat.x xi.Iunij. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Two months ago our Francis wrote that, amid great and arduous difficulties, it had been no small comfort to him that you had helped him faithfully, conveniently and opportunely. Confirming this again a few days ago, he greatly praised your frank sincerity and perseverance. He reported nothing beyond what is owed to a servant of Christ. Yet where integrity is dangerous or costly, examples of it are rare, so we rejoiced, as was right, that you prefer the reproach of the cross of Christ to the luxuries of the world, which intoxicate many so that the simplicity of the gospel, seeming insipid, becomes distasteful to them. If you had pretended to be one of those who are too careful to protect their own ease, there would have been a plausible reason for you to separate yourself from our brother. Those who want to look after their private safety usually use this pretext to keep far away from all hatred and trouble, since nothing is more useful than soothing the ears of the people with a vague, equivocal way of teaching. You deserve all the more praise, since you could have taught smoothly and outside all conflict, yet, setting private advantage aside, you willingly offered our brother the right hand of fellowship. Indeed we see that those crafty artisans who bend the teaching of piety to their own convenience ultimately achieve this: their disciples are always learning but never reach the knowledge of the truth. Moreover, although you now find men less fair and well-disposed, men who once followed you with favour, you have no reason to regret your sincere confession. You know that we serve Christ on this condition: we must wage war not only against open enemies but also endure many slanders from our own people. Many will rage, and others will openly cry out that you have rashly advanced to a liberty that is not tolerable among you. You will have to despise these voices, and also sternly strip from them the pleasures they indulge in, so that they understand that the limping by which they avoid every battle is hateful to God. By continuing as you have begun, which we confidently expect you will do, you will at last feel that a conscience pure before God and the angels is far better than a hundred theatres, and that its peace is to be sought more than the applause of the whole world. Add that the pious worshippers of God already rightly congratulate you and promise themselves rich fruit from your holy eagerness. Our excellent brother Francis, whom we too have found truly devoted to Christ, and whom you see endowed with outstanding gifts for building up the Church, will be a faithful and vigorous helper to you. We hear that the court preacher has returned; would that he had not, as is his way. However he conducts himself, it would be quite inconsistent for Christ's servants to depend on a man who is pliable and, as usual, sways with every breeze. In your moderation and prudence you will no doubt take care to join him to yourself, lest he hinder or delay your straight course. But if fear, excessive anxiety to be cautious, or even a perverse rivalry drags him to different sides, you will have to strive bravely against these obstacles too. Farewell, excellent man and most upright brother. May the Lord continue to guide you with his Spirit, strengthen and defend you with his power, and bless your studies and pious labours. 21 June 1558.

units.la: IOAN.
units.tr: JOHN.

units.la: ETsi mihi Gaspar noster, quem ego idoneum & fidum testem esse duco, te satis ad synceritatem pietatis studium sponte animatu esse retulit, vt meae exhortationis stimulis minime indigeas: quia tamen te quotidie experiri non dubito, eximie vir, quâ variis modis conetur Satan cordatissimos quosque Christi seruos à recto cursu auertere, vel vbi id non poterit, quot obstaculis eorum celeritatem retardet ac moretur, hæc mea sedulitas, quâuis superuacua te minime offendet, si currenti calcar addere visum est. Nâ quia persuasus sum probari tibi, quos pro Ecclesia Christi suscipio labores, méq; hoc nomine fraterne absteadiligi, saltem grata tibi erit hæc cura, quæ me ad fereda subsidia impellit. Porrò non tantùm vt te priuatim Deo addicam hortari propositum est, sed vt ciuibus tuis ad purum cultum adducendis strenuè incumbas. Vides qua contumacia & quo feruore cæci veritatis hostes in perniciem suâ ruendo, alij alios mutuò impellant. Quare falsem eorum exemplo crescere nobis debet animus ad promouendum Christi regnum, quia turpe est tanto conatu eos pugnare aduersus Deum: nos vero in tam præclara causa vel sedere ignauos, vel cunctâter lenteque progredi. Difficile quidem & arduum tibi certamen paratum esse scio, si te apertum Papatus hostem profiteris: sed videndum est sub cuius ducis vexillo milites, ne vel laßitudine frangaris vel moleßiis succumbas, vel terreacalis vllo discrimine, vel præ desperatione concidis. Exordia regni Christi, vbiq; nostro seculo fere humilia contemptâque fuerunt: itaq; derisa fuit à profanis hominibus eorum simplicitas, qui tantam molem aggredi audeant, perinde ac si vellent lunã è cœlo deducere. Atqui felici successu patuit Deum opus suum non negligere, neq; spem eorum frustrari, qui ineftimabili eius virtute freti contra terrena omnia impedimenta niituntur, & contendunt. Et sane vtcunque vtatur hominum opera, non frustra tamen hoc sibi proprium vendicat, Ecclesiam mirabiliter erigere, & erectam ad extremum tueri. Meminerit quo maiori auctoritate polles in vrbe vestra, plus tibi impositum esse oneris à Deo, cuius manu in hoc gradu locatus es, vt minus excusabilis sit tua cessatio, quàm priuati cuiuslibet vel obscuri hominis. Sed quia spero quas ad ornatissimum virum Dominum Petrum Sirkiû literas scripsi, pro vestra coniunctione tibi fore communes, pluribus supersedeo, tantùm supplex precor cœlestem Patrem, vt te regat sancta prudentia, sustineat inuicta virtute, suá manu protegat, piósque tuos labores benedicat. Geneuæ, 1111. Calendas Septembris. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Although our Gaspar, whom I consider a suitable and trustworthy witness, has reported that you are already eager for sincere piety of your own accord, so that you need no spur from my exhortation, yet since I do not doubt that you daily experience the many ways in which Satan tries to turn the most sensible servants of Christ from the right course, or, where he cannot, how many obstacles he sets to slow and hold back their progress, this earnestness of mine will not offend you, though it may seem superfluous, if I add a spur to one who is already running. For since I am persuaded that you will approve the labours I undertake for the Church of Christ, and the brotherly anxiety I feel on this account, at least this concern, which drives me to write to you, will be welcome. Moreover, I am urging you not only to devote yourself privately to God, but to apply yourself vigorously to bringing your fellow citizens to pure worship. You see with what obstinacy and fervour the blind enemies of the truth rush headlong to their own destruction, urging one another on. Therefore our courage should grow from their example to advance the kingdom of Christ, since it is shameful that they fight against God with such effort while we sit idle or move forward slowly and hesitantly in so noble a cause. I know that a difficult and arduous struggle awaits you if you openly profess yourself an enemy of the Papacy. But you must see under whose leader's banner you serve, lest you be broken by weariness, overcome by troubles, struck down by fear of any danger, or cast down by despair. The beginnings of Christ's kingdom in our age were almost everywhere humble and despised, and the simplicity of those who dared to undertake so great a task was mocked by profane men, as if they wished to draw the moon from the sky. Yet by a happy outcome it has been shown that God does not neglect his work, nor disappoint the hope of those who, relying on his incomparable power, strive against all earthly obstacles. And certainly, however he uses human labour, he claims for himself the task of raising up the Church wonderfully, and having raised it, of preserving it to the end. Let him remember how great an authority he holds in your city, and how much more burden God has laid on you, by whose hand you have been placed in this rank, so that your inactivity is less excusable than that of any private or obscure person. But because I hope that the letters I wrote to the most distinguished man, Lord Peter Sirkius, will be common to you both on account of your fellowship, I will say no more, and only humbly pray the heavenly Father that holy prudence may guide you, invincible virtue sustain you, that he protect you with his own hand and bless your pious labours. Geneva, 29 August 1558.

units.la: Epist.267.
units.tr: Epist.267.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS D. PETRO SYRKIO, s. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Peter Syrkius, greetings.

units.la: QVod tibi nulla humana necessitudine coniunctus, Vir Clarissime, familiariter ad te scribo, neque tu vllam excusationem desideras, & Gaspar noster, qui fiduciam scribendi dedit, suggessit idem materiam. Cognoui ex eius sermone, non modo te vnum esse ex synceris Dei cultoribus, sed etiam propagando Christi regno fidelem acseriam operam dare. Sed ex turbido vel saltem nondum rectè composito vrbis vestræ statu, qualem mihi depinxit, facilè coniicio, & duros certaminum impetus tibi esse sustinendos, & cum multis illecebris luctandum, quæ ad impediendum pietatis cursum non minori obstaculo esse solent, quàm apertæ pugnæ. Ergo non minor tibi danda opera, vt intentus sis cauendis insidiis, quàm ad fortiter bellandum armatus, sicuti non abs re admonet Paulus fideles, vt à dextris & sinistris probè muniti sint contra omnes hostis incursus. Nomè Christo dare non potes, quin excidas à multorum gratia, quos retinere amicos vtile & iucundum esset: multarum commoditatum iacturam facias: forte etiam minuatur popularis fauor: minæ & terrores ab altera parte instabunt. Nam & totus Papalis clerus qui opibus & potentia excellit apud vos, imò tràquillum imperiù tenet, acerrimè ad turbanda omnia conspirabit, & multos secum trahet asseclas. Tibi cum aliis iurgari, aliorum probra refellere, aliorum insidiis occurrere, necesse erit. Multa tædia deuoranda, multæ ferendæ iniquitates, molestiæ ingentes sustinedæ. Forte etiam longius procedet eorum væsania, qui cœlum terræ miscere non dubitabunt potius, quàm aditum concedat sanæ doctrinæ. Verùm si te pugnare Christi auspiciis reputes, non modò solatium hoc sufficiet ad leuandas omnes acerbitates, sed inuictum tibi robur suggeret, quo ad frangendos insultus quoslibet obdurescas. Dura conditio piorum, nisi & causæ dignitas præualeret, & Agonotheta noster Christus, non tantùm suo conspectu nos animaret ad certandum, sed victoriam de manu, vt aiunt, in manum nobis porrigeret. Iam quem in locum te produxerit, non ignoras, quando & gradum obtines, ex quo te alios incitare conuenit: & eo vsque Spiritus cœlestis impulsu progressus es, vt retrocedere turpe sit ac nefas. Ergo non vocatio tantùm, quæ te satis arcto vinculo obstringit, sed principia hæc, in quibus se ducem ostendit Deus, animum tibi addant. Statuera m longè prolixius tecum agere: sed cùm morbus hactenus impedisset, sequuta sunt negotia, quæ abrumpere cogunt vix inchoatas literas. Vale igitur præstantissime vir, & mihi ex animo obseruande. Dominus tibi adsit, te gubernet Spiritu prudentiç dentiæ & rectitudinis, præsidio suo tueatur, & tuos sanctos conatus benedicat. Geneuæ, 11 11.Calendas Septembris. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I am writing to you familiarly, most distinguished sir, although no human ties bind me to you, and you do not ask for any excuse. Our friend Gaspar, who gave me the confidence to write, also supplied the subject. From his conversation I learned that you are not only one of the sincere worshippers of God, but also that you labour faithfully and earnestly to spread the kingdom of Christ. Yet from the troubled, or at least not yet settled, state of your city, as he described it to me, I readily conjecture that you must withstand hard assaults of conflict and struggle against many enticements, which are wont to hinder the course of piety with no less an obstacle than open battle.
