So you must take no less care to be watchful against snares than to fight bravely in arms, as Paul rightly warns the faithful to be well protected on the right and on the left against every assault of the enemy. You cannot confess Christ without falling out of the favour of many whom it would be useful and pleasant to keep as friends; you will suffer the loss of many advantages, and perhaps popular goodwill will be diminished. On the other side, threats and terrors will press upon you. For the whole Papist clergy, which excels in wealth and power among you, and indeed holds the peaceful government, will conspire most fiercely to throw everything into confusion, and will draw many followers along with it. You will have to quarrel with others, refute their insults, and meet their plots. Many weariness must be endured, many injustices borne, and great troubles sustained. Perhaps also the madness of those men will go further, who will not hesitate to stir heaven and earth rather than allow an entry to sound doctrine. Yet if you consider that you are fighting under the auspices of Christ, this consolation will not only suffice to lighten all the bitterness, but will also supply you with an unconquered strength, by which you may become hardened to break down whatever assaults. Hard is the condition of the godly, unless the dignity of the cause prevails, and unless Christ, our Agonothetes, not only encourages us to strive by his presence, but also, as they say, puts victory into our hands from his hand. Now you know to what place he has brought you, since you hold a rank from which it is fitting that you should spur others on; and by the impulse of the heavenly Spirit you have advanced so far that to turn back would be shameful and wicked. Therefore, it is not only the calling, which binds you by a fairly close chain, but these beginnings, in which God shows himself as your leader, that should give you courage. I had intended to deal with you at much greater length, but since illness has hitherto hindered me, and business has followed which compels me to break off a letter scarcely begun, farewell, most excellent man, who are dear to me from my heart. May the Lord be with you, guide you by the Spirit of prudence and uprightness, protect you by his defence, and bless your holy endeavours. Geneva, 11 days before the Kalends of September, 1558.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS D. ADMIRALIO. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to the Admiral, greeting.

units.la: CVM ex mearum ad te literarum lectione tibi constaturum sperem, quanto salutis tuæ studio tenear, meum hac in re consilium, vbi illas perlegeris a te improbatum non iri confido. Neque vero tandiu hoc facere distulissem, si apud te mihi aditus patuisset. Iam cum hoc mihi oblatum videam, non est diutius te detineam, cum plane mihi persuadeam opimam in partem a te acceptum iri, quod illius nomine tibi a me proponitur, cui me addictum esse scis, pro illa obseruatia quate illum prosequi compertum habeo. Non est etiam quod multis tecum agam, vt ad legitimam tolerantiam te compares, cum ita existimem & de te etiam audiam: te nempe ita ad illam esse confectum à D. vt magis habeam fere vnde illi eo nomine gratias agam, quàm vt ad illam te multis exhortari debeam. Hæc est nimirum solida illa magnanimitas, vbi affectus nostri ita domantur, vt non modò illos in potestate habere possimus, sed vt tanquam de triumphatis hostibus in nobilipsis, sacrificiū obedientiæ Deo offeramus. Parum est enim non deficere neque frangi animo in aduersis rebus, nisi eoque oculos intedamus, vt Dei voluntati nos submittamus, atque illic placidè acquiescamus. Cū igitur ita te per Dei gratiam comparatum audiam, illud superest quod te præterea cogitare serio velim: Deum nempe ista tibi immissa calamitate te tibi subductum voluisse, vt tato commodius illi te attentum præberes. Neque enim ignoras quandiu in mūdo versamur, vbi honores vel opum strepitus nos à Deo abducunt, quam difficile sit aurem illi præbere, dum fere in eiusmo di rerum iactatione extra nos rapimur, nisi suos ille respiciendo quasi ex turba ad se per calamitates reciperet. Non quod exist-mem honores aut alia illa bona per se repugnare cultui Dei & legitimo ipsius honori, cum potius quibus illa D. contulit, eosdem ad se ea ratione quodammodo compellare voluerit, vt ad ipsius cultum propensiores redderet: sed tamen experientia tibi constare credo, aliter ferè accidere solere, vt qui in mundo florent magis, illic ita distriçte teneantur, vt vix vnquam illis otium supetat quod ad præcipuam partem officij sui conferant, atque de Dei gloria procuranda, de ipsius cultu profitendo, de vita cœlesti meditanda serio cogitent. Quare à te peto vt quum hac tibi opportunitatem proficiendi in ipsius schola obtulerit Dominus, quasi ipse tecum familiarius adurús esset, teipsum plane attentu prabeas, ut perguftes plane quid valeat ipsius doctrina, quamque ea nobis & chara atque pretiosa esse debeat: hic etiam ut te diligenter sacro ipsius verbo legendo impendas, unde & erudiaris magis ac magis, & vnam radicem fidei percipias: qua nempe tibi in reliquam vitam confles, atque omnes tentationes eluderis. Non ignoras quam omnia passim corrupta sint: quo magis piis omnibus cauendum est, ne illis rebus implicetur, quae ipsos deinde inquinent. Illud plane constat nihil hodie non impune esse praeter unam Dei pure colendi professionem, ut ad illam ne mo se comparare possit, quin undique se impetitum iri statuere debeat, nisi forte verbis tantum & minis cum eo agatur ad tem pus. Atqui D. unius gloria tanti esse tibi debet, ut omnia pro illa calcare non dubites, cui una illius gratia infinitis modis omnem omnium mortalium gratiam & favorem exuperet. Suppetit etiam nobis illud singulare privilegium, quod pro nostra infirmitate tre pidamus ille se vires suffecturi virtute sua recepit: ut in eo uno omne nostrum praesidium situm est, ut ad illud nos conferamus, precemurque ut unus ipse sit robur nostrum atque invictum propugnaculum. Dominus tibi adsit Spiritu suo, teque in omni bono conservet, atque ita te respiciat, ut in te uno habeamus omnes, de quo illi gratias perpetuo agamus. IIII. Septembris.
units.tr: Since I hope that from reading my earlier letters you will understand how deep my concern for your salvation is, I am confident that you will not disapprove of my purpose in this matter once you have read them through. I would not have put this off so long had there been an opening to you. Now that I see this opportunity offered, I will not detain you any longer. I am fully persuaded that what is proposed to you on behalf of that man, to whom you know I am devoted and whom I know you have courted with such regard, will be received by you in good part. Nor is there need for me to say much to you about preparing yourself for lawful endurance. I think you are already so prepared, and I hear that you are, by God's grace, so far along that I have more reason to thank him for it than to urge you to it at length. This is surely that solid magnanimity, when our feelings are so tamed that we not only keep them under our control but, as over conquered enemies, offer them to God as a sacrifice of obedience. It is little to fail to give way or lose heart in adverse circumstances unless we also fix our eyes there, submit ourselves to God's will, and rest calmly in it. Since I hear that you have been so equipped by God's grace, there remains one thing more I would have you consider seriously: that God, by sending you this calamity, wanted to withdraw you from yourself so that you might be more attentive to him. You know how long we live in the world, where honours and the din of wealth draw us away from God, and how hard it is to lend him an ear while we are carried outside ourselves amid such a whirl of affairs. Unless he took back his own from the crowd, as it were, through calamities, they would hardly hear him. I do not mean that honours or those other goods are in themselves opposed to the worship of God and his lawful honour. Rather, God, who bestowed them, has wished in this way to draw to himself those upon whom he conferred them, so as to make them more inclined to his worship. But I believe experience has taught you that it usually happens otherwise: those who flourish most in the world are held so tightly there that they scarcely ever have leisure for the chief part of their duty, or think earnestly about promoting God's glory, professing his worship, and meditating on the heavenly life. Therefore I ask you, since the Lord has offered you this opportunity to make progress in his school, as if he himself wished to be more familiar with you, to give yourself fully to attention, so that you may thoroughly learn what his teaching is worth and how dear and precious it ought to be to us. Here too, devote yourself diligently to reading his holy Word, whereby you may be instructed more and more and grasp the one root of faith, which will hold you fast for the rest of your life and enable you to elude all temptations. You know how everything is corrupted on every side. All the more must all the pious take care not to be entangled in those things that will then defile them. This much is plain: today nothing is without its penalty except the one profession of the pure worship of God. No one can prepare himself for it without deciding that he must be attacked on all sides, unless perhaps the matter is dealt with for the time being only in words and threats. Yet the glory of the one God ought to be so great to you that you do not hesitate to trample everything underfoot for its sake, since his grace alone surpasses in countless ways all the grace and favour of all mortals. We also have that singular privilege: since we tremble at our weakness, he has taken it upon himself to supply strength by his power. All our protection lies in him alone, so let us betake ourselves to him and pray that he himself be our strength and unconquered bulwark. May the Lord be with you by his Spirit, keep you in every good thing, and so regard you that in you alone we all may have cause to give him thanks continually. 4 September.

units.la: M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: M. D. LVIII.

units.la: CALVINVS N. ABBATI. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO THE ABBOT, GREETING.

units.la: Advicram saepius, eximie vir, quum unus esses ex multis, qui syncerum pietatis doctrinam quae nobis a Deo tradita est, pro defensione Romani Papatus oppugnant, maiore tamen quam alios vehementia in nos excandescere. Et priuatim quoque in me asperius invehi. Neque vero mirabar, quum & superstitionibus quae maiorem orbis Christiani partem occupant, imbutus esses, atque errorum laqueis implicitus, simul inconsiderato zelo rapi ad me durius tractandum, atque etiam conuitiis vexandum. Ac iampridem ad eiusmodi probra, quibus & Prophetas, & Apostolos, & unigenitum Dei Filium obnoxios fuisse video, continuo vsu obdurui. Nam hoc nobis diu initus praescriptum est, neque aequum esset a communi lege me eximi, neque ferenda mea mollities, si molestę ferrem me violari, vbi ne Christo quidem summo omnium regi parcitur. Nunc vbi mihi narratum est, non modo te manuefactum esse, ut placide nos audire paratus sis, sed quam prius abominatus es doctrinam amplecti, vel saltem ita ad nos accedere, ut posthac inter aduersarios censeri non debeas: quam iucundus hic mihi nuntius fuerit, vix possum litteris exprimere: quia ex hac mutatione non vulgarem expecto fructum. Nam & multi quos auctoritas tua quasi deinde conflictosq; tenebat, ne ex labyrintho illo emergerent tuo exemplo adducti, incipient tandem attentius reputare quid agendum sit, multorum torpor expergefiet, multorum fragetur, aut molletur peruicacia deniq; multi, qui te errorum ducem fuerant sequuti, tecum resipiscent. Neque vereor (si tibi suauis est Dei miseri cordia) ne te libera erroru, a quibus te eripuit, reprehensio offendat. Ac sane non aliter gustare potes, quàm liberaliter tecum egerit Deus, nisi reputes quàm miserum fueritin profunda illa impietatis abyss demersum iacere: imò tua conuersio. vt scribendi materiam suppeditat, ita gratulationis mihi argumentum est. Iam superest vt te liberatori tuo, & officia tua addicas, & qui fallaci religionis praetextu obtenebrasti multorum mentes, nunc lucem praeferendo, discutiendis tenebris sedulò incumbas. Caeterum, quia plena exhortationem, & qualem res postulat, vix caperet epistola, vltrò tibi pro tua prudentia hortator eris, vt ingenium, eruditio, & facundia, quibus te Deus ornauit, illustrandae eius gloriae consecrentur. Vtinam, quia mihi praeclusum ad vos est iter, commodum tibi esset hucexcurrere lagnoscere profecto ex vultu & ser mone, quàm verè & ex animo cupiam fraternam beneuolentiā cum omnibus colere, quos sibi Deus reconciliauit. In hoc saltem melior erit tua quàm Pauli conditio, quòd ille ex praesenti vitae periculo elapsus ob fidei testimonium, vix idem à fratribus, quia suspectum habebant, admissus fuit. Ego verò ad te non comiter modò, sed etiam honorificè excipiedum non secus ero propensus, quàm sime nunquam verbulo vno laesisses. Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi in Christo venerande. Deum precor vt te gubernet Spiritu intelligentiae & prudentiae, sua virtute sustineat, & confirmet, donis omnibus locupletet, incolumem tueatur & benedicat. Geneuae, 1 x. Calend. Octob. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I have often heard, most distinguished sir, that although you were one of the many who attack the pure doctrine of piety handed down to us by God in defence of the Roman papacy, you have raged against us with greater vehemence than the others, and have attacked me more harshly in private as well. I was not surprised, since you were steeped in the superstitions that occupy the greater part of the Christian world and entangled in the snares of error, and at the same time carried away by an ill-considered zeal to treat me more severely and to harass me with insults. I have long since grown hardened to such abuse through constant practice, for I see that the Prophets, the Apostles, and the only-begotten Son of God himself were exposed to it. This has long been the lot prescribed for us; it would not be fair for me to be exempted from the common law, nor would my softness be tolerable if I were offended when not even Christ, the highest King of all, is spared. Now that I have been told not only that you have been brought round so as to be ready to hear us calmly, but that you have begun to embrace the doctrine you once abhorred, or at least to approach us in such a way that you ought no longer to be counted among our opponents, I can hardly express in a letter how welcome this news has been to me, for I expect no ordinary fruit from this change. Many whom your authority had held as if entangled, will, following your example, finally emerge from that labyrinth and begin to consider more attentively what must be done; the torpor of many will be roused, the obstinacy of many will be broken or softened; and at last many who had followed you as the leader of their errors will repent together with you. Nor do I fear (if the mercy of the God of the wretched is sweet to you) that the frank rebuke of the errors from which he has rescued you will offend you. Indeed, you cannot taste how generously God has dealt with you unless you consider how wretched it was for you to lie plunged in that deep abyss of impiety; your conversion, as it supplies me with matter for writing, is also for me a cause of rejoicing. It now remains for you to devote yourself to your deliverer, and, having darkened the minds of many under the deceptive pretext of religion, now to hold up the light and labour diligently to dispel the darkness. Moreover, since a letter could scarcely contain a full exhortation of the kind the matter requires, you will, by your own prudence, become your own exhorter, so that the talent, learning, and eloquence with which God has adorned you may be dedicated to illustrating his glory. Would that, since the way to you has been closed to me, it were convenient for you to come hither; you would surely recognise from my face and speech how truly and from my heart I desire to cultivate fraternal goodwill with all whom God has reconciled to himself. In this respect at least your condition will be better than that of Paul, who, escaping from danger to his present life for the testimony of the faith, was scarcely admitted by the brethren, because they regarded him with suspicion. For my part, I shall be no less inclined to receive you not only kindly but also with honour, as if you had never once injured me by a single word. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and venerable to me in Christ. I pray God to govern you with the Spirit of understanding and prudence, to sustain and strengthen you by his power, to enrich you with all gifts, and to keep you safe and bless you. Geneva, the 18th day before the Calends of October, 1558.

units.la: Tuus ex animo Ioannes Calvinus.
units.tr: Yours from the heart, John Calvin.

units.la: IOANNES CALVINVS D. STANISLAO ab Oftrorog Castellano Medzeucensi. S. D.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO LORD STANISLAUS OF OSTROROG, CASTELLAN OF MEDZEUC. GREETINGS.

units.la: HVnc pium fratrem nactus, qui meas ad te literas tutò perferret, Praestantissime vir & generose Domine, scribendi occasionem praetermittere noluinon tam vt amorem erga te meum, & obseruatiam testarer (etsi haec etiā vna fuit ratio) quàm vt tibi sponte & alacriter accensio ad asserendā quę nimis diu contempta iacuit, pietatem, animos si fieri posset adderem ad pergendum: non quòd stimulis meis indigeas, sed quia iucundum est gratulando hunc tuum vigorem fouere. Fuit hoc raræ virtutis, ex alto honoris gradu in humilem Christi scholam descendere, vt te Euangelij quod vulgò tot probris oneratur, mi nimè pudeat: ac palàm ingenuéque profitearis, te superstitionū, quibus indignè fœdata est vera Religio, ac errorum, quibus sceleste adulterata est Dei veritas, acerrimum esse hostem. Verùm tibi assiduè reputandum est, quàm multæ certaminum species te maneant: quia non desinet Satan omnia moliri, quibus sanctos tuos conatus vel frangat, vel moretur, vel quouis modo impediat. Et experientia docet, quàm pertinax sit in aduersariis pugnandi libido. Quare ita statuendum est, longæ militiæ te diuinitus esse addictum, in cuius medio cursu minimè fatigari decet. Cæterùm ne de animi tui magnitudine & perseuerantia dubitare videar, alió me conuertam. Minimè te fugit generosè Domine, nullum inter Satanæ artificia esse deterius, quàm vt dissidiis eos scindat, qui ad restituendum purè fidei consensum aspirant. Quò maiore prudentia cauendum erit, ne hoc quoque obstaculo vos retardet. Intelligis quid velim, & fuius hanc admonitionem prosequerer, nisi iam febris accessio literas abrumpere cogeret, quæ non modò vires corporis debilitat, sed etiā minuit ac languefacit animi vigorem. Sed bene est quòd his partibus probè fungetur venerandus mihi frater Dominus Ioannes à Lasco, excellentiæ tuæ affinis: cuius non dubito auctoritatem, vt meretur, magni esse apud te ponderis. Vale illustris & generose Domine, & mihi ex animo sufpiciéde. Patrem cœlestem supplex oro & precor, vt te incolumem diu conseruet, Spiritu suo dirigat, omnique benedictionum genere locupletet. Geneuæ, xiii. Calend. Decemb. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Having found this pious brother, who would safely carry my letter to you, most excellent and noble Sir, I did not want to let the chance of writing pass. I wished to bear witness not so much to my love and respect for you (though that was also one reason) as to add, if I could, spirit to you, who of your own accord and eagerly have taken fire to defend that piety which has lain neglected for far too long. This is the mark of rare virtue: to come down from a high place of honour into the humble school of Christ, so that you are not at all ashamed of the gospel, which is commonly burdened with so many reproaches, and that you openly and frankly declare yourself the fiercest enemy of the superstitions by which true religion has been shamefully defiled, and of the errors by which the truth of God has been wickedly corrupted. Yet you must constantly bear in mind how many kinds of conflict lie before you, for Satan will not cease to devise every means to break, delay, or somehow hinder your holy endeavours. Experience teaches how stubborn the appetite for fighting against adversaries can be. Therefore you must be resolved that you have been devoted by God to a long campaign, and in the middle of your course you ought by no means to grow weary. But, lest I seem to doubt the greatness of your spirit and your perseverance, I will turn to another point. Noble Sir, you are not unaware that among Satan's devices there is none worse than to split apart those who strive to restore a pure agreement in faith. All the more prudence must be used to guard against his letting this obstacle also hold you back. You understand what I mean, and I would pursue this warning further, were it not that an attack of fever now compels me to break off this letter, a fever which not only weakens the strength of the body but also diminishes and enfeebles the vigour of the mind. But it is well that the venerable brother Lord John à Lasco, your excellency's kinsman, will discharge this office well in these regions. I do not doubt that his authority, as he deserves, carries great weight with you. Farewell, illustrious and noble Sir, and think of me with affection. I humbly beseech and pray the heavenly Father that He keep you safe for a long time, direct you by His Spirit, and enrich you with every kind of blessing. Geneva, 19th November 1558.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS Illustri et reuerendo Domino Iacobo Ithauio Episcopo Vladislauiensi, mihi ob eximias virtutes obseruando. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to the illustrious and reverend Lord James Ithauius, Bishop of Vladislavia, who is to be honoured by me for his outstanding virtues. Greetings.

units.la: Quòd homo ignotus ad te, illustris & reuerende Domine, scribere ausus sum, si quid culpæ est in hac fiducia, reiicere in nuntium licet, qui pro singulari salutis tuæ studio & cura, has literas propè inuito extorsit. Quod verò breuiter, & quasi defunctorie scribo, iusta excusatio est in temporis angustiis: quia vix ante admonitus fui de eius aduētu, quàm se mox abiturum dixit, vt mihi diem vnum ad scribendum concederet: cuius tamen maior pars mihi eripitur à febre quartana,quæ me cubiculo inclusum,& ferè lecto affixum tenet,ex quo etiam hæc pauca dictare coactus sum. Scribendi autem hæc mihi ratio & materia est, vt Euangelij luce nunc apud vos exorta,quum tibi Deus oculos aperuerit, serió expergiscaris. Audio enim te non modò gustasse veram pietatis doctrinam, sed eius cognitione imbutum, quæ omnem erroris & ignorantiæ prætextum excutiat.Tu verò pro tua prudentia non ignoras,quàm intolerabilis sit cœlestis gratiæ profanatio,vbi eam quasi data opera suffocamus.Etsi autem plausum tibi in mundi theatro conciliat splendida hæc dignitas,cauendum tamen diligenter, ne te demulceant fallaces blanditiæ, quibus laqueis Satan multos hodie in exitialem labyrinthum trahit.Ita fit vt qui captandis effugiis fo lertiam suam exercent, tandem vbi vident colores suos euanescere,palàm se Deo opponant,imò erumpant in manifestum furorem.Huius rei exempla haud dubiè nimis multa ante oculos tuos versantur,dum alij violenter ferro & igni extinguere pertentant cœlestem doctrinam : alij vt in sordibus suis secure demersi iaceant, non modò indulgent torpori suo, sed pecudum more conscientias suas obstupefaciunt.Ab hac tam pestifera Epicureorum labe quisquis in deliciis sedulò & attente sibi non cauet,vix fieri potest quin profanescat,& abiecto Dei timore,in eandem cum illis lasciuiam se proiiciat. Quid ergo tibi agendum est? Feruent apud vos dissidia, pars vna restitui cupit integrum Dei cultum : altera impias superstitiones peruicaciter defendit. Te medium stare, quem Deus quasi porrecta manu ad causæ suæ patrocinium vocat, turpe ac nefas est. Cogita quem locum occupes,& quod onus tibi sit impositum.Adde quòd pietatis hostes,dum in densis tenebris exiguas pietatis tuæ scintillas ferre nequeunt, quodammodo te extruduint e sua factione,quæ vltrò fugienda tibi erat. Ignoscere mihi pro tua humanitate,si verno in verbo sim asperior (quia vt proficiam, liberè quod sentio dicendum est)vbi ad cœleste tribunal ventum fuerit,non posse elui proditionis crimen, nisi te mature subducas ab ea caterua, quæ aperte ad opprimendum Christi nomen conspirat. Iam verò si tibi molestum est minui, vt crescat in te Christus, in mentem veniat Mosis exemplum, qui sub vmbris obscuris, Christi opprobrium deliciis Ægyptiorum & opibus præferre nõ dubitauit. Quanquam autem plus forte mihi apud tuam excellentiam permisi quàm decebat: quia tamen propositum fuit salutis tuæ consulere, non odiosa, vt spero, tibi erit mea libertas. Vale præstantissime vir,illustris & reuerende Domine,cui à cœlesti Patre fausta omnia precor, præsertim vt te suo Spiritu gubernet, accendat in corde tuo ardentius pietatis studium, & in eius constantia te confirmet. Geneuæ, xiii. Calend. Decembris. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: That I, an unknown man, have dared to write to you, illustrious and reverend Lord, if there is any fault in this boldness, may be laid upon the messenger, who, out of a singular concern and care for your welfare, all but forced this letter from me. As for the fact that I write briefly and, as it were, perfunctorily, the reason is a fair excuse: the time was short, since I was scarcely warned of his arrival before he said he would leave at once, so that he granted me only one day to write. Even of that day most was taken from me by a quartan fever, which keeps me shut in my room and almost fixed to my bed; it is from there that I have been forced to dictate these few lines. My reason and purpose for writing is this: that now that the light of the Gospel has risen among you, you may, now that God has opened your eyes, rouse yourself earnestly. For I hear that you have not only tasted the true doctrine of godliness but are imbued with its knowledge, which strips away every pretext of error and ignorance. You yourself, in your wisdom, are not unaware how intolerable is the profanation of heavenly grace when we deliberately stifle it. Although this splendid dignity wins you applause in the theatre of the world, you must take care that deceitful flatteries do not soothe you, the snares with which Satan today draws many into a deadly labyrinth. So it happens that those who exercise their cunning in devising escapes, when at last they see their colours fading, openly set themselves against God, or even break out into manifest rage. Of this there are no doubt far too many examples before your eyes: some violently try to extinguish the heavenly doctrine with sword and fire; others lie sunk in their filth, carefree, not only indulging their sloth but, like cattle, dulling their consciences. Whoever does not carefully and attentively guard himself against this most pestilent fall into the pleasures of the Epicureans can hardly avoid becoming profane and, casting off the fear of God, throwing himself into the same wantonness as they. What, then, must you do? Dissensions burn among you: one party desires that the pure worship of God be restored; the other stubbornly defends impious superstitions. For you to stand in the middle, when God calls you, as it were with outstretched hand, to defend his cause, is shameful and wicked. Consider what place you occupy and what burden has been laid upon you. Add to this that the enemies of godliness, since they cannot bear the small sparks of your piety in their dense darkness, are in a manner thrusting you out of their faction, which you ought to have fled of your own accord. Forgive me, in your kindness, if I am rather harsh in my language, for to make progress I must speak freely what I feel: when we come before the heavenly tribunal, the crime of betrayal cannot be washed away unless you withdraw in good time from that band which openly conspires to crush the name of Christ. Now, if it is distasteful to you to be diminished so that Christ may increase in you, let the example of Moses come to mind, who, under obscure shadows, did not hesitate to prefer the reproach of Christ to the delights and riches of the Egyptians. Although perhaps I have taken more liberty with your excellency than was fitting, yet, since my purpose was to care for your salvation, I hope my frankness will not be unwelcome to you. Farewell, most excellent man, illustrious and reverend Lord; I pray the heavenly Father that every blessing may be yours, above all that he may govern you by his Spirit, kindle in your heart a more ardent zeal for godliness, and confirm you in its steadfastness. Geneva, 19th November 1558.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS D. COMITI IN TARNAVV. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to the Count of Tarnów, greetings.

units.la: ETsi literis meis superioribus, Amplissime vir & Illustris Principeps, quale optabam responsum non tuli, quia minus apud te quàm optandum esset profecerat mea exhortatio, singularis tamen humanitas qua exceptum fuisse meum officium cognoui, denuo me ad scribendum animat. Et cùm nos iubeat Paulus importune instare, vbi stimulandi sunt homines ad pietatis studium: non vereor tanto auctore & magistro fretus, etiamsi molesta tibi esset mea sedulitas, ne vitio mihi vertatur. Sed hoc quoque metu & solicitudine me liberat æquitatis tuæ fiduciamimo cùm hucusque sparsa fuerit fama, defensionem puræ Euangelij doctrinæ, à qua initio refugiebas vel eras paulò alienior, propensiore animo nunc te suscipere, eò alacrius exhortatione, quæ semel fructu carere visa fuerat, repetere ausus sum.
units.tr: Although, most distinguished sir and illustrious prince, my earlier letter did not bring the reply I hoped for, since my exhortation had made less headway with you than I could have wished, the singular courtesy with which I know my duty was received encourages me to write again. Paul bids us insist urgently when people must be stirred to zeal for godliness, and relying on so great an author and teacher, I do not fear that my persistence will be held against me, even if it is unwelcome to you. Your fairness also frees me from fear and anxiety on this point. Since the report has spread far and wide that you have now taken up, with a more favourable disposition, the defence of the pure teaching of the Gospel, which at first you shrank from or were somewhat more estranged from, I have dared to repeat the exhortation with greater eagerness, though it had once seemed to bear no fruit.

units.la: Cùm scriberes nihil tibi videri in statu regni movendum, quòd omnis nouitas graues motus & exitiales minitaretur, mihi quidem tristis nuntius fuit, Christi causam destitui à patrono tam idoneo: gratior tamen fuit ingenua illa profitio, quàm si quorundam more simulasses, quod tibi cordi non erat. Nunc quanquam te rectius sentire arbitrer, ignoscas tamen pro tua prudentia, si paucis vanum hunc timorem refutauero. Neque me latet quàm pro ingenij tui præstantia & acumine peritiam collegeris ex longo magnarum rerum vsu. Sed mirum non est hac in parte homine summo iudicio præditum potuisse illi, vbi humana omnis solertia euanescit. Laudatur apud Xenophontem quod ex tripode oraculum olim reddidit Apollo, colendos esse deos pro vetusto more cuiusque gentis: nempe quia nihil censetur vtilius vel magis consultum, quàm fouere publicam pacem. Unde etiam natum vulgare prouerbium: Mala bene posita non mouenda. At verò quicquid discriminum impendeat, caducos terræ Principatus, nobis tantum esse non cōuenit, vt in eorum gratiam neglectus iaceat cultus Dei & syncera Religio, à qua pendet æterna salus. Profanis hominibus hic scopus fuit, cauere modis omnibus, ne quid publicam quietem turbaret: nostra verò diuersa est ratio, apud quos Dei gloriæ & doctrinæ cœlesti merito cedere debet, quicquid in mundo est sublime ac pretiosum. Adde quòd superuacuus est ille timor: quia tumultus omnes quos Satan excitare conabitur, facile sedabit Christus Rex pacis, per quem Reges regnant. Fieri quidem vix poterit in tanta hominum pra-uitate, uitate, malitia, ingratitudine, & contumacia, quin strepitus, dissidia & turbæ comitentur puram Euangelii doctrinam: sed nostrum est reiecta in Deum huius mali cura, qui remedium inueniet, strenuè nihilominus in officio pergerē. Dandus enim est eius prouidentiæ hic honor, vt incommodis quæ non licet nostra industria effugere, occurrat. Si ita nos diuinitus gubernari patimur, latior semper erit exitus, quàm nobis sensus noster dictet: quia re ipsa probabit Deus verè fuisse de ipso prædicatum, quod legitur in Psalmo: Perfringit lanceas, gladios comminuit, currus absumit, igni bella componit vsquè ad fines terræ. Rursum memineris, nobilissime vir & Domine, vitia & corruptelas quibus polluitur vera Religio, totidem esse sacrilegia, quorum Deus acerrimus erit vindex: ac proinde odiosam illi esse hanc prudentiam, vbi externam quietem pietatis iactura redimere cupimus. Sed quia voluntarium vt spero, te literæ meæ reperient, pluribus hunc sermonem prosequi necesse non est: & me etiam febris quartana ad breuitatem cogit. Postremò cum istic sit eximius Christi minister & frater mihi venerandus Dominus Ioannes à Lasco, quem non dubito pro zeli sui feruore satagere, hac ei partes libenter resigno: quia etiam apud te valebit eius auctoritas, quantum meretur. Deum itaque precabor, vt Tuum Celsitudinem fauore suo tueatur, modisque omnibus augeat, Spiritu suo gubernet, virtute sustineat. Geneuæ, xii Calend. Decemb. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: When you wrote that nothing in the state of the kingdom seemed to you to need stirring, since every novelty threatened grave upheavals and ruin, the news saddened me, that the cause of Christ had been abandoned by so fit a patron. Yet that frank confession pleased me more than if you had pretended, as some do, to feel what was not in your heart. Now, although I think you judge more rightly, please pardon me, in keeping with your prudence, if I refute this vain fear in a few words. I am not unaware how much skill you have gathered, by your outstanding talent and acumen, from long experience of great affairs. Yet it is no wonder that a man of such high judgement could be at a loss in this matter, where all human skill vanishes. Xenophon praises the oracle that Apollo once gave from the tripod, that gods should be worshipped according to the ancient custom of each people, namely because nothing is judged more useful or more prudent than to foster public peace. Hence also the common proverb arose: things well settled should not be disturbed. But whatever dangers may threaten, it is not fitting for us to hold the fragile principalities of the earth in such regard that the worship of God and the pure Religion, on which eternal salvation depends, lie neglected for their sake. For profane men the aim was to take every precaution that nothing disturb public quiet; but our reasoning is different, for we, to whom the glory of God and heavenly doctrine rightly yield, must place everything in the world that is lofty and precious beneath them. Add that this fear is groundless, because Christ, the King of peace, through whom kings reign, will easily calm all the tumults that Satan tries to stir up. Indeed, in such great human wickedness, perversity, ingratitudine, and obstinacy, it will scarcely be possible for clamour, discord, and disturbances not to accompany the pure teaching of the Gospel. But it is our task to cast the care of this evil upon God, who will find a remedy, and meanwhile to press on vigorously in our duty. For this honour must be given to his providence: that it meets the troubles which our industry cannot avoid. If we allow ourselves to be governed by God in this way, the outcome will always be broader than our own feeling dictates, because God will in fact prove true what is said of him in the Psalm: he breaks the spears, shatters the swords, burns the chariots, and makes wars cease to the ends of the earth (Ps. 46). Again, remember, most noble sir and lord, that the vices and corruptions by which true Religion is polluted are so many sacrileges, of which God will be a most fierce avenger; and therefore this prudence, when we seek to buy outward quiet at the cost of the loss of godliness, is hateful to him. But since I hope that my letter will find you willing, there is no need to pursue this discourse at length, and a quartan fever also forces me to be brief. Finally, since the distinguished minister of Christ and my venerable brother, Lord John à Lasco, is there, whom I do not doubt is bestirring himself out of the fervour of his zeal, I gladly yield this part to him, because his authority will carry as much weight with you as it deserves. I will therefore pray God that he keep your Excellency under his favour, increase you in every way, govern you with his Spirit, and sustain you with his strength. Geneva, 12 days before the Calends of December, 1558.

units.la: MARTYR CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Martyr to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: Mlhi sane, vir clarissime, neque mirum neque graue fuit, quante paucos dies, cum literas ad Bullingerum nostrũ dicta ueris, nihil ad me (per illum excusare voluisti) tamen scripseris. Verum id me antea valde male habuit, quate morbo eoq; periculoso ægrotare audiueram: neq; nunc minus ægre est, quando febrim quartanam significas esse, qua laboras. Ego de istius morbi cõtumacia, & rebelli quadã aduersus pharmaea & medicos obstinatione multa possem narrare, vt qui iam bis cum eo sim conflictatus: summa est, magna, diuturnáq; patientia, eos qui sint isto loco, vti oportere, quàm vtendã foris, vti certo scio, non petes, cum in animo tuo, à Christi Spiritu sit abūdè insertas. Sed habeo vnà cum permultis aliis de ista tua ægrotatione duplicem dolendi causam. Vna quòd ipse doleas, frangaris, & debiliteris, id quod aliter fieri non potest, præsertim in corpusculo iã propemodum laboribus exhausto. Altera vero est laboresque tuos in agendo & in scribendo, magno Christi omnium detrimento interrumpi. Nihil enim est quod isti morbo æquè atque studiã, & curæ,aduersetur. Hæc sunt quæ non tantum me, fedomnes veré pios excruciant. Attamen quádo ita res habet,nostrum est officium,precibus contendere,quanta possumus instantia,vt pri ftinæ sanitati quamprimum restituaris.Tuum veró,vt ī noxiis omni cura,summáque diligentia tibi ipsi temperes,præsertim à ferio studio,& grauium curarum folicitudine,quibus humor atræ bilis,vnde ista febris accenditur, ita pulsatur atque percuti-tur,vt ad medullas ossium vsque infigat. Porrò multo expetibi-lius est, ad aliquot dies aut menses quiescere, quando ita Deo visum est,quam aut cum magno bonorum mœrore interire, quod auertat Deus, aut cum incredibili Ecclesiæ iactura, quantum vitæ superest,debilitato prorsus,& fracto corpore,atq; animo viuere.Videtoitaque vt neque in te,neque in Ecclefi Christi pecces. Venerunt huc certi nuntij heri, missi à nobilibus viris Anglis, qui Argentinæ agunt: significant verò suam Reginam. x. v 1.Nouembr s obiiiffe,acIlluftriffimam Elifabetham successi-fe in regnum idque summo consensu omnium ordinum : con-uenerant enim forte fortuna hoc tempore ab omnibus Angliæ partibus ad Comitia,vel,vt vulgo dicunt,ad Parlamentum. Nunc Deus rogandus est,vt hæc rerum commutatio, nomini Christi, & fanéto eius Euangelio bene vertat. Scio te tuámque sanctam Ecclesiam,officio non defuturos. Tempus fortasse iam est, vt in eo regno muri Ierusalem reædificentur, vt ne tot martyrū sanguis videatur in cassum tam largiter effusus.Nihil præterea novi habeo,nisi quòd meum librum sub prelo habeo,quo Stephani Gardineri olim Vinthonensis Episcopi omnia sophisma ta,& prœftigias de re Eucharistica retexi,& confutaui.Quod vti spero, valde tempestiuè cecidit : nam commodum erit hoc præsertim tempore, vt Papatus Anglicanus intelligat, librum illum non esse,quemadmodum hactenus iactitarunt, inuictum. Bene vale,atque Christo & eius Ecclesiæ quàm diutissime viuas.Symmy-stas omnes iubeo saluere,necnon Bezam & Marchionem. Tiguri 1.Decembris.
units.tr: To me, most distinguished sir, it was neither surprising nor troublesome that you wrote nothing to me in these few days, although you dictated letters to our Bullinger and asked him to excuse you to me. Still, I was very distressed to hear that you were ill with a serious and dangerous sickness, and I am no less distressed now that you tell me the fever you suffer from is quartan. I could say much about the stubbornness of this illness and its somewhat rebellious obstinacy against remedies and doctors, since I have already struggled with it twice. In short, those who are in your position must be patient, great and long-lasting, and I know for certain that you will not need to seek outside what the Spirit of Christ has already planted so abundantly in your mind. But, together with very many others, I have two causes for grief over your illness. The first is that you yourself are distressed, broken and weakened, as cannot fail to happen, especially in a body already almost worn out by labours. The second is that your work in teaching and writing is interrupted, to the great loss of all Christians. For nothing is more opposed to this illness than study and care. These are the things that torment not only me but truly all the godly. Nevertheless, since matters stand as they do, it is our duty to pray with all the urgency we can that you be restored to your former health as soon as possible. Yours is to spare yourself with all care and the greatest diligence, especially from intense study and from the anxiety of heavy cares, by which the humour of black bile, from which this fever is kindled, is so stirred and struck that it sinks into the very marrow of the bones. Moreover, it is far more desirable to rest for some days or months, since God has so willed, than either to perish, which God forbid, to the great sorrow of good people, or to live for whatever time remains with the body and spirit utterly weakened and broken, to the incredible loss of the Church. So see that you sin neither against yourself nor against the Church of Christ. Certain messengers came here yesterday, sent by English noblemen who are staying at Strasbourg. They report that their Queen died on the 17th of November and that the most illustrious Elizabeth has succeeded to the kingdom with the highest consent of all the estates, for by chance the representatives of all parts of England had gathered at this time for the assembly, or, as the common people say, for Parliament. Now God must be asked to turn this change of affairs to the good of the name of Christ and of his holy Gospel. I know that you and your holy Church will not be wanting in your duty. Perhaps the time has now come for the walls of Jerusalem to be rebuilt in that kingdom, so that the blood of so many martyrs may not seem to have been shed so freely in vain. I have no other news, except that my book is at the press, in which I have laid bare and refuted all the sophistries and tricks concerning the Eucharist of Stephen Gardiner, once Bishop of Winchester. As I hope, it has come out very opportunely, for it will be useful especially at this time for English Papism to understand that the book is not, as they have boasted until now, unconquered. Farewell, and may you live as long as possible for Christ and his Church. I bid all my fellow partakers in the mysteries farewell, and Beza and the Marquis as well. Zurich, 1 December.

units.la: Tuum quantus est Petrus Martyr.
units.tr: Yours, such as I am, Peter Martyr.

units.la: Io. Cal. D. Gvl. Cicellio Reginae Angl. Secretario.
units.tr: John Calvin to Master William Cecil, Secretary to the Queen of England.

units.la: Quod nunc ad te familiariter scribere instituì, vir ornatiss. homo de facie tibi ignotus, non longa excusatione vtar: quia testimonio quorundam piorum fretus, qui tuam humanitatem mihi prædicarunt, te ad literas meas comiter excipiendas piendas sponte propensum fore confido: ac præsertim vbi tibi ex lectione consilium meum perspectum fuerit. Ex quo discussa hor ribili caligine, quæ mètes plorum fere obstupefecerat, noua lux repente supra omnium spem affulsit, te pro gratia qua apud Serenissimam Reginam non vulgari pollles, sedulò incumbere fa-ma est, vt profligatis quæ per quadriennium isthic grassatæ sunt, superstitionibus Papatus, iterū vigeat syncera Euangelij doctrina, purúsque & integer Dei cultus. Quare vt incipias Christo li-bere & palàm militate, te hortari opus non est: sed alterum hoc mihi restat, vt quod agis, & maiori strenuitate, & inuicta constantia agere pergas: neque vllis molestiis, difficultatibus, pugnis, terroribus, non dico frangantur, sed vel minimum tardentur sancti tui conatus. Equidem obstacula tibi subinde occurrere, vel ante oculos versari discrimina nō dubito, quę fortissimos quos-que debilitent, nisi mirifica Spiritus sui virtute eos Deus sustineat: sed vna hæc causa est, pro cuius defensione, nullum laboris genus refugere nobis fas est. Quandiu maestandis Dei filiis aperta fuit carnificina, ipse quoque obmutueras cum aliis. Nunc saltem vbi nouo & incredibili Dei beneficio maior reddita est libertas, colligere animum decet, vt si antehac timidus fuisti, id studij ardore compenses. Equidem non ignoro, quantopere noceat interdum præposterā festinatio: atque vt multi inconsideratò zelo ac præcipiti retardent, quod volunt momento ad metam rapere. Sed ex adueꝛso probè reputandum tibi est, quia Dei opus est, puram Euangelij veritatem & totámque pietatem asserere, non segniter esse suscipiendum. Ex re præsenti melius iudicare potes, quos tenere progressus conuenit, & quænam adhibenda sit moderatio. Sed meminéris omnem cunctationem, quam-libet specioso colore tecta sit, debere tibi esse suspectam. Vnus, vt conijcio, motus est à populari metu, quum inter Proceres non desint multa flabella: & si inter se Angli tumultuarentur, præsto sunt vicini, qui occasionibus quibuslibet nimis cupidè immi-nent. Sed quòd Serenissima Regina mirabiliter Dei manu in sol-um euecta est, suam gratitudinem probare non aliter potest, quàm si prompta alacritate remoras omnes discuti at atque im-pedimenta magnanimitate superet. Quādo verò vix fieri potest, quin rebus adeo turbulentis & confusis, inter principia distrahatur, perplexa hæreat, sæpe etiam vacillet, eam hortari ausus sum, vt rectum cursum ingressa, constanter perseueret. Hoc verò prudenter necne fecerim, iudicium est penes alios. Si tua opera factum erit, vt mea admonitio fructum afferat, me consilij non pœnitebit. Tu quoque clarissimi viri, in eo quem obtines fauoris & dignitatis gradu, te diuinitus locatum esse cogita, vt in hanc curam totus his intentus, ad opus hoc peragendum neruos omnes F.j. intendas. Ac ne qua tarditas obrepat, subinde veni it tibi in men tem, quanti momenti sint haec duo, ut Religio quae miserè collapsa fuit, doctrina salutis quae execrandis medi ciis adulterata, cultus Dei qui fœdè inquinatus, nitorem suum recuperet & Ecclesia sordibus repurgetur: deinde ut filiis Dei apud vos liberum sit nomen eius pure invocare: & qui dispersi fuerunt, iterum colligantur. Vale ornatiss. vir, mihique ex animo observande Domi nus te Spiritu suo regat, tueatur, omnique bonorum genere locupletet. Geneuæ, 1111. Calend. Febr. M. D. LIX.
units.tr: Since I have now begun to write to you in a familiar way, most distinguished man, though I am a stranger to you by sight, I will not make a long apology. Relying on the testimony of certain godly men who have praised your kindness to me, I trust that you will willingly and courteously receive my letters, especially once you have seen my purpose from reading them. For a report has reached us that, after the dreadful darkness which had almost stunned the minds of most good people has been dispelled, a new light has suddenly risen beyond all hope, and that you, by the favour you enjoy with the most serene Queen, are working diligently so that, with the superstitions of Papism that have raged there for four years destroyed, the pure doctrine of the Gospel and the sincere and unblemished worship of God may flourish again. There is no need for me to urge you to begin to fight freely and openly for Christ. What remains for me is this: that you keep on doing what you are doing with greater energy and unshaken constancy, and that your holy efforts are not broken by any troubles, difficulties, struggles or terrors, or even slowed in the slightest. Indeed, I do not doubt that obstacles will from time to time meet you, and dangers will stand before your eyes, which weaken even the bravest, unless God sustains them by the wonderful power of his Spirit. But this is the one cause for whose defence we must shrink from no kind of labour. As long as the slaughter of the sons of God was open, you too kept silent with the others. Now at least, since by a new and incredible benefit of God a greater liberty has been restored, it is fitting that you gather your courage, so that, if you were timid before, you may make up for it with the fervour of your zeal. I am not unaware of how much hasty and ill-considered haste sometimes harms, and how many, through an imprudent and headlong zeal, delay what they want to seize in a moment. But you must weigh carefully, from the outcome, that it is God's work to assert the pure truth of the Gospel and the whole of godliness, and that it must not be undertaken sluggishly. From the present situation you can judge better which progress it is right to hold to and what moderation must be applied. But remember that every hesitation, however well it be covered with a specious colour, ought to be suspect to you. One such hesitation, as I suppose, arises from popular fear, since among the nobles there are not lacking many fans to stir the air, and if the English should riot among themselves, neighbours are at hand who are only too eager to threaten on any pretext. But since the most serene Queen has been raised up marvellously by God's hand alone, she cannot show her gratitude in any other way than by promptly removing all hindrances and overcoming obstacles with magnanimity. Since it can hardly happen that, amid such turbulent and confused affairs, she is not distracted at the outset, remains perplexed and often even wavers, I have ventured to exhort her to enter upon the right course and to persevere in it steadfastly. Whether I have done this wisely or not is for others to judge. If, through your efforts, my admonition brings forth fruit, I shall not regret my counsel. You too, most distinguished sir, should consider that, in the degree of favour and dignity which you hold, you have been placed there by God, so that, wholly intent on this care, you may bend all your sinews to carrying out this work. And lest any slowness creep in, let it often come to your mind how great are these two aims: that the Religion, which has fallen wretchedly, and the doctrine of salvation, which has been corrupted by accursed remedies, and the worship of God, which has been foully defiled, may recover their brightness, and the Church may be cleansed of its filth; and then that it may be free for the sons of God among you to call upon his name purely, and that those who have been scattered may be gathered together again. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and may the Lord, whom I sincerely honour, govern you by his Spirit, keep you safe, and enrich you with every kind of good. Geneva, 1 February 1559.

units.la: VTENHONIVS CALVINO s. D.
units.tr: JOHANNES UTENHOVIUS TO CALVIN, greetings

units.la: Quum istæc mihi nunc ad te scribendi daretur occasio, Vir Clarissime, fratérque observandissime, non potui eam praetermittere, quin te earum, quae hic geruntur, rerum facere certiorem. Hoc itaque habe: in Comitiis Petricouiensibus nunc tractari inter alia, de excludendis e Regni Senatu Episcopis. Illustris D. Comes Tarnouiensis rem in Senatu nunc recens proposuit, indicans contra rectam Politiae constitutionem esse, regni Senatores non tam Regi sane, quam Papae ipsi iuratos esse. Se quidem reliquosque Laicos, quos Seculares vocant, Regem ipsum, cui vni iurati essent, pro suo capite agnoscere: Episcopos vero non item, sed solum Papam, cui vni iurati essent pro suo capite, maximo cum & dignitatis Regiae & patriae totius praeiudicio, agnoscere. Ac proinde eos sibi amplius in Senatu ferendos non esse. Qua propositione facta conuenerunt mox Episcopi omnes apud Legatum Papalem. Ac postquam varie inter ipsos consultatum esset, ab ipsis respon sum est, (ie iam in possessione ef se per longissimi (vt loquuntur) temporis praescriptionem. Qua lisnam vero huius rei fuerit euentus, adhuc ignoramus. Quam autem facilis fit responsio, ad eam Episcoporum exceptionem, nemo non nouit. Nota est ipsiusmet iuris Canonici tristissima regula, ex sexto Decretal. libro: possessor malae fidei vllo tempore re non praescribit. Non habeo quod praeterea scribam de Comitiis, nisi quod res eo spectare videtur, vt toti Nobilitati libera reformandarum Ecclesiarum suarum facultas permitti debeat, vtque ea ab Episcoporum iurisdictione liberetur. An quid praeterea ex hisce Comitiis nobis sit expectandum, omnino nescio. Sed si quid euenial praeter expectationem cognitu dignum, non committam quin te eius faciam certiorem prima quaque occasione. Illustrissimus Princeps D. Palatinus Vilnen. venit ad Comitia, neque hinc vult ad sua redire, prius quam habeatur hic fratrum conuentus, ad quem nostri hic seniores ac etiam fui quidam, qui secum adduxit, accedant, quo paritas quaedam in ceremoniis Ecclesiasticis, quatenus fieri possit, inter utrosque inducatur ac seruetur. Sui enim hactenus vsi sunt ceremoniis impurioribus: spes tamen est, diuino beneficio, eas breui repurgatum iri. Spes est etiam ipsum Palatinum Vilnen. suas hic Ecclesias propediem reformaturum esse. Audio te nunc scripsisse literas exhortatorias ad Vchanium episcopum Cuyauiensem, quo nomine sane gaudeo, ac te precor, ut eum literis tuis subinde inuisas ad eius consolationem. Is enim tanta odiorum mole grauatur à sui ordinis hominibus, propter ipsius pietatem, raraque libertatem, qua in Comitiis etiam ipsis iam vtitur, ut eum sublatum cupiant, venenoque tollendum iudicent, ne quid amplius dicam. Gratiam autem tibi habeo pro eis ad Magnates hic nostros literis, quae non omnino importune nunc sunt redditae. Neque dubitamus eas fructus suos aliquado relaturas esse. Si qua ego vicissim tibi gratificari aut seruire possim, ut me libere vtaris in rebus omnibus rogo. Nihil enim est quod grauatè, ad tui postulationem, sim subiturus, in Domino: cui ego te tuumque ministerium, vir clarissime, fratrque obseruandissime ex animo commendo: vtque Vtenhonium tuum perg is amare, vti fecisti vehementer oro. Saluta mihi omnes ibi fratres. Clarissimus vereque Reuerendus vir D. Ioannes à Lasco te peramanter salutat. Ex Querceto, XXVII. Ianuarij. M. D. LIX.
units.tr: Since I now have an opportunity to write to you, most distinguished sir and most honoured brother, I could not let it pass without informing you of what is happening here. Take this, then: at the Diet of Piotrków, among other matters, the question of excluding bishops from the Senate of the kingdom is now under discussion. The illustrious Count of Tarnów recently raised the matter in the Senate, declaring that it is contrary to the proper constitution of the commonwealth that the senators of the kingdom are sworn not so much to the King as to the Pope himself. He and the other laymen, whom they call secular, acknowledge the King himself, to whom alone they are sworn, as their head; but the bishops, he said, do not do so, acknowledging only the Pope, to whom alone they are sworn as their head, to the very great prejudice both of the royal dignity and of the whole country. Therefore, he said, they should no longer be tolerated in the Senate. After this proposal was made, all the bishops at once met at the Papal Legate's. When they had deliberated on it in various ways among themselves, they replied that they were already in possession, by the prescription of a very long (as they put it) period of time. What the outcome of this matter will be, we still do not know. How easily an answer can be given to this objection of the bishops, everyone knows. The most damning rule of canon law itself is well known, from the sixth book of the Decretals: a possessor in bad faith never acquires a thing by prescription at any time. I have nothing further to write about the Diet, except that the matter seems to tend toward allowing the whole nobility the free power to reform their churches and toward freeing them from the jurisdiction of the bishops. Whether anything else is to be expected from this Diet, I simply do not know. But if anything worth knowing happens beyond expectation, I will not fail to inform you of it at the first opportunity. The most illustrious Prince, the Palatine of Vilnius, has come to the Diet, and does not wish to return home from here before the assembly of the brethren is held here, to which our elders here, and certain others whom he brought with him, will come, so that some parity in ecclesiastical ceremonies, as far as can be done, may be introduced and maintained between the two sides. Hitherto they have used rather impure ceremonies; yet there is hope, by God's blessing, that these will soon be purified. There is also hope that the Palatine of Vilnius himself will soon reform his churches here. I hear that you have now written a letter of exhortation to Bishop Uchański of Chełmno, for which I am certainly glad, and I beg you to visit him from time to time with your letters, for his consolation. For he is burdened with such a mass of hatred from men of his own order, on account of his piety and the rare freedom which he now exercises even in the Diet itself, that they wish him removed and judge that he must be got rid of by poison, not to say more. I am grateful to you for the letters to our magnates here, which have been delivered not altogether at an inopportune time. Nor do we doubt that they will at some point bear their fruit. If I can in turn do you any favour or service, I ask you to use me freely in all matters. For there is nothing I would undertake reluctantly at your request, in the Lord, to whom I commend you and your ministry from my heart, most distinguished sir and most honoured brother; and I earnestly beg you to keep loving your Utenhovius, as you have greatly done. Greet all the brethren there for me. The most distinguished and truly Reverend man, Lord John à Lasco, sends you his warmest greetings. From Querceto, 27 January 1559.

units.la: Tuus tibique addictissimus quantus est Ioannes Vtenhonius.
units.tr: Yours, and most devoted to you, however great he is, John Utenhovius.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS VINCTIS FIDELIBVS. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to the faithful prisoners, greeting.

units.la: Quod hactenus ad vos non scripsi, Dilectissimi fratres, per meum erga vos studium non stetit, si quid meae ad vos literae aut leuationis afferre potuissent, aut animi addere ad sanctam illam constantiam quam à Domino accepistis in vobis confirmandam. Cum enim hoc ab illis officium praestari non dubitem qui istic sunt, meum etiam hic in parte à vobis requirendum non putabam. Nunc cum profuturum hoc vobis commertu habeam, inhumanus sim, si vestro desiderio non satisfaciam. Et tamen hic etiam me excusare cogor, quod breuior sim quàm vellem, & res ferat. Sic enim à quartana nunc exercet iā a tribus mensibus, vt vix tertiae parti negotiorum possim, quae si bona valetudine vterer, mihi conficienda essent. Atqui vbi & meum hoc leuiusculum malum, cum illis quae vos constringunt, & quā Do minus offert leuatione, cum illis quae vobis inferuntur molestiis & aerumnis cófero, non tantum tolerā ut legē mihi prescribi, & nonnihil leuationis mihi adesse præ vobis agnosco : sed vester status ita me afficit,vt à meipso discedens vestris malis ingemiscam,& enixè orem pro vobis Dominum,vt vestros dolores alleuet,ac vos contra quosuis infultus sustineat atque confirmet. Quòd autem vestra nunc conditio dura & acerba vobis videri potest,non est quòd multùm hoc vos moueat,quasi fidei nostrę vis & efficacia nos præstaret sensus dolorum expertes, cùm ad natiuos affectus eluctandos tantùm nos instruat:adeóque Dominus ipse,Spiritussui præsentiam in nostris infirmitatibus à no-bis certius agnosci velit,vti Apostolus etiam hoc ab eo responsum retulit. Præsertim verò quia longioris custodiæ molestiæ, tædium non mediocre coniunctum habent: ita voscoram Domino demittite, vt non dubitetis vestram infirmitatem ab ipso hac etiam in parte, vobis modò aduersus illam enitentibus cò-donatum iri. Vt autem ita perstetis in certamine,vt tandem con sequamini foliidam victoriam, ille vobis est serìo inuocādus,vt iisdem armis instruat,quæ hæctenus ab illo idonea accepistis,ad Satanam ipsum cum instrumentis suis despiciendum. Quo nomine hoc vobis indictum sit bellum, nempe pro Dei gloria à vobis asserenda,pro veritate Euangelij approbanda,pro Christi regno in legitimum suum statum restituendo,ipsi nostis. Quàtò verò acriorեsse debet ille stimulus ad vos ad officium animâ dos, quàm quod plerique Principum mācipijs accidit,qui nescio quæ spe lucri & suâ ambitione abrepti, certissima pericula adire non dubitant? Et cùm isti cæco tātùm impetu ita animati ferantur, quantò nobis melius constare mens debet, vbi cœlestis heri vocem & mandatum audimus?Atq; illud maximè,cùm neque ad illas partes vocemur, nisi in salutem nostram: neque morte ipsa fiat conditio nostra deterior,cùm vbi eousq; venien-dum erit, illam ipsam in summum & cumulatissimū nostrum bonum sit ipse commutaturus?Nam quid ipsi nobis testibus vel procuratoribus opus est,nisi quòd illud omnino cedit in nostrā gloriam,vbi rei omniū dignißimæ instrumenta efficimur?Porrò illud sixum habete,vtcunque in aduersariorum potestate nūc sitis: vos tamen esse sub Dei tutela, penes quem vnum sint vitæ ac mortis exitus,vti Psal.68.testatur: ac proinde cui nulla ratio deesse possit vos eruendi,si ita tulerit eius voluntas. Atque illud ita vobis est cogitandum,vt quod ad vos interea attinet,compa retis vothers... ceptus est. Agnoscite & illud ex Psal.119.verf.41.42. Sint super me Domine misericordiæ tuæ secundum verbum tuum, & respondebo exprobrantibus mihi. Item verf.51. Superbi irriserunt me, à lege tua non declinavi. Item verf.110. Tetenderunt mihi impij rete, non declinavi à mandatis tuis. Item verf.161. Principes persecuti me sunt gratis, & ad verbum tuum tremuit cor meum. Item verf.23. Sederunt & contenderunt adversum me, seruus tuus autem meditabatur in statutis tuis. Discite item ab Esaia, Deum unum timere & sanctificare in cordibus vestris, ut furorem illum quem impij in cœlum euomunt, non formidetis. Atque interea illam apud ipsos mansuetudinem retinete, quapropter vos non fiat, quominus aliquid ab ipsis obtineatis: non solum ut moderatiores erga vos experiamini, sed impri-mis, ut ad Dei cognitionem aliquomodo pertrahiantur. Tantum ut quam viam ingressi estis, & instatis adhuc, in illa constanter incedatis. Intedite igitur in cœlum oculos, ut ad palmam supernæ vocationis vnice adspiretis. Hoc à Domino vobis precamur omnes, ut Dominus vestrum se protectorem testetur, quetiam vobis recipsa constet, dum eum vestris malis exitum dabit, qui nobis omnibus occasionem afferat glorificandi & benedicendi in vobis sancti ipsius nominis. x v. Febr. M. D. LIX.
units.tr: That I have not written to you until now, dearest brothers, has not been for want of goodwill toward you. I hoped that my letter might bring some comfort, or add courage to that holy constancy which you have received from the Lord to be strengthened in you. Since I do not doubt that those who are there perform this duty, I did not think my part should be required of you here. Now, since I have this to offer that will profit you, I would be inhuman if I did not satisfy your wish. Yet here too I am forced to excuse myself, because I am briefer than I would like, and my circumstances allow no more. For a quartan fever has troubled me for three months now, so that I can barely manage a third of the business I would otherwise have to complete in good health. But when I compare this slight illness of mine with the bonds that hold you, with the relief the Lord offers, and with the troubles and hardships inflicted on you, I not only bear it patiently to have the law prescribed to me, I also acknowledge that I have some relief compared with you. Your state so affects me that, setting myself aside, I groan at your evils and earnestly pray the Lord to lighten your sorrows and to uphold and strengthen you against every assault. As for the fact that your present condition may seem hard and bitter to you, there is no reason this should move you greatly, as if the power of our faith made us free from the sense of pain. It teaches us only to struggle against our natural feelings. Indeed, the Lord himself wishes us to recognise his presence in our weaknesses more certainly, as the Apostle also reports this answer from him. Especially since a long imprisonment brings considerable discomfort and weariness with it, submit yourselves humbly before the Lord. Do not doubt that he will pardon your weakness, in this respect too, as long as you strive against it. So that you may persevere in the contest and at last win a solid victory, you must earnestly call upon him to arm you with the same weapons you have hitherto received from him as suitable, so that you may despise Satan himself and his instruments. You yourselves know under what banner this war has been declared on you: namely, for the glory of God to be asserted by you, for the truth of the Gospel to be upheld, and for the kingdom of Christ to be restored to its lawful state. How much keener should that spur be to you to perform your duty bravely, than the spur that drives many men in the service of princes, who, carried away by I know not what hope of gain and by their own ambition, do not hesitate to face the most certain dangers? And when those men are borne along, moved by blind impulse alone, how much more settled should our minds be, when we hear the voice and command of the heavenly Master? And especially this: we are called to those regions only for our salvation, and death itself will not make our condition worse, since when we must go that far, he himself will turn that very thing into our highest and most abundant good. For what need has he of us as witnesses or advocates, except that it all redounds to our glory when we are made instruments of a most worthy cause? Moreover, keep this firmly fixed: however much you are now in the power of your adversaries, you are still under God's protection, in whose hand alone lie the outcomes of life and death, as Psalm 68 testifies; and so there can be no lack of means to deliver you, if his will so decides. Think of this in such a way that, as far as concerns you in the meantime, you prepare yourselves accordingly. Acknowledge this also from Psalm 119. Psal.119.verf.41.42. "Let your mercies come upon me, O Lord, according to your word, and I will answer those who reproach me." Likewise verse 51: "The proud have mocked me greatly, yet I have not turned aside from your law." Likewise verse 110: "The wicked have laid a snare for me, yet I have not strayed from your precepts." Likewise verse 161: "Princes have persecuted me without cause, but my heart trembled at your word." Likewise verse 23: "They sat and plotted against me, but your servant meditated on your statutes." Learn also from Isaiah to fear the one God and to sanctify him in your hearts, so that you do not dread the fury which the wicked vomit against heaven. Meanwhile, keep that gentleness toward them, so that nothing hinders you from obtaining something from them; not only so that they may deal more moderately with you, but chiefly so that they may in some way be drawn to the knowledge of God. Only continue steadfastly on the path you have entered and are still pursuing. Therefore lift your eyes to heaven, so that you may aspire to the prize of the heavenly calling alone. This we all pray the Lord for you: that he may prove himself your protector, and that this may become plain to you in fact, while he brings your troubles to an outcome that gives us all occasion to glorify and bless his holy name. Feb. 15, 1559.

units.la: CALVINVS MENSONI POPPIO S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO MENSONIUS POPPIUS, GREETING.

units.la: Ad disciplinam Ecclesiasticam responsa.
units.tr: Responses concerning church discipline.

units.la: SI meas occupationes cognoscere, optime frater, nō esset mihi petenda breuitatis venia, si forte votiis tuis non satisfacio. Vix enim credas, quàm onerosum sit ac negotiosum munus quod sustineo, & quàm multa aliunde publice & priuatim ad me distrahendum accedant. Iam vero quintum menseim febris quartana me in cubiculo captum tenet, maiori etiam temporis parte lecto affixum. Etsi enim paulatim mitescit, sic tamen debilitauit & animum, & corpus, vt multis laboribus non sufficiam.
units.tr: If you knew my occupations, best of brothers, I would not need to ask your pardon for brevity, should I perhaps fail to satisfy your wishes. You could hardly believe how burdensome and demanding the office I bear is, and how many other public and private matters crowd in on me from every side. Moreover, for five months now a quartan fever has held me confined to my room, for the greater part of the time fastened to my bed. Although it is gradually easing, it has so weakened both my mind and my body that I am not equal to many labours.

units.la: Quod quæris de indoctis Pastoribus, qui etiam ad discendum propter ignauiam adduci nequeunt, vel etiam qui impura vita contaminant Ecclesiam Dei, nec sæpius admonitri respiscunt, sintne excommunicandi: an quia conniuet Magistratus & cessat, tolerandi sint, ego ita sentio. Postquam frustra expertus es re media quæ extremam seueritatem debent præcedere, agendum esse cum aliis fratribus & Symmystis, quibus cordi est rectus ordo, ne diutius patiantur sordibus istis pollui Dei sanctuarium. Ad hanc rem conuentu opus esset, non Pastorum modo, sed
units.tr: As to what you ask about unlearned ministers, who cannot even be brought to study because of their laziness, or who defile the Church of God with an impure life and, when admonished again and again, do not repent: whether they should be excommunicated, or tolerated because the magistrate connives and does nothing, my view is this. Once you have tried in vain the remedies that ought to precede the extreme severity, you must act together with the other brothers and colleagues who care for good order, so that they do not suffer God's sanctuary to be polluted by these filths any longer. For this matter a meeting would be needed, not only of the ministers but also of those to whom the care of the Church has been entrusted by the prince, so that the deliberation may be shared.

units.la: eorum quibus à Principe mandata est Ecclesiæ cura, vt communis sit deliberatio. Si spes aliqua correctionis appareat, sperandum ad tempus erit cum gemitu: sin vero longius progredi vos coget eorum peruicacia, rogandi erunt discipli næ præfecti, quibus authoritas data erit vt vobiscum in paucorum abdicationem consentiant, quæ cæteris terrorem incutiat. Ac ne immodicus videri possit rigor, colligenda erunt crimina, ex quibus palàm fiat, vel insanabiles esse morbos, vel superioribus offensis non esse parcendum, quia non sint in Pastore tolerabiles. Hoc quoque si demum impetrari non poterit, hoc vnum restare arbitror, vt liberè denuntietis, etiamsi eos vel foueat, vel toleret Magistratus: vobis tamen nullam posthac coniunctionem cum ipsis fore, nec iam vobis esse loco fratrum. Hæc excommunicatio forte Magistratum expergefaciet, ne ita torpeat: saltem conscientia vestras pacabit, quia partibus vestris eritis defuncti.
units.tr: If some hope of correction appears, one must hope for it for a time, with groaning. But if their obstinacy forces you to go further, the prefects of discipline must be asked, those to whom authority has been given, to agree with you in cutting off a few, so that the rest may be struck with fear. And lest the rigour seem excessive, the crimes must be gathered, from which it will become plain either that the diseases are incurable or that earlier offences must not be spared, since they are not tolerable in a minister. If even this cannot be obtained, I think one thing remains: that you declare plainly, even if the magistrate favours or tolerates them, that there will be no further fellowship between you and them, and that they are no longer to be counted as brothers. This excommunication may perhaps rouse the magistrate from his torpor, so that he does not remain so inert. At the least it will calm your own consciences, because you will have discharged your part.

units.la: De secunda quæstione ita sentio: curandum esse imprimis, vt publica authoritate excommunicatio in Ecclesia vigeat. Atque in hanc rem strenuè incumbere cordatos Pastores necesse erit. Si ad hunc consensum adduci Magistratus non poterit, ficuri omnes fere à iugo abhorrent: non tamen frangantur repulsa pij Pastores, neque ab incepto cursu desistant: sed constanter profiteantur sibi fas non esse diutius profanare sacra mysteria. Porro indignam & minimè ferendam esse profanationem, dum promiscuè quoslibet admittunt: vt porcis etiam & canibus pateat Christi mensa.
units.tr: On the second question, I think as follows. Above all, care must be taken that excommunication flourishes in the Church by public authority. To bring this about, wise ministers will have to apply themselves vigorously. If the magistrate cannot be brought to agree, since nearly all of them shrink from the yoke, let the godly ministers nonetheless not be broken by the refusal, nor abandon the course they have begun, but steadfastly profess that it is not lawful for them to profane the holy mysteries any longer. Furthermore, the profanation is unworthy and not to be endured, while they admit anyone at all indiscriminately, so that the table of Christ lies open even to swine and dogs.

units.la: Quod ad filios improborum spectat, legitima Ecclesiæ gubernatio postulat, ne ad Cœnam accedant, nisi examinati. Erit autem in examine ratio, qua arceantur si indigni sunt, donec profectum aliquem offenderint.
units.tr: As for the children of the wicked, the lawful government of the Church requires that they not come to the Supper unless they have been examined. In the examination there will be a method by which, if they are unworthy, they are kept away until they have shown some progress.

units.la: Negligentiam in liberis instituendis excommunicatione punire, durum mihi videtur. Obiurganda quidem est parentum segnities: stimulandi sunt modis omnibus: adhibendæ etiam minæ: sed vbi neque manifesta impietas, neque contemptus, neque grauius crimen cernitur, lenitatem rigori præferri satius est. Atque hæc omnino regula in censuris Ecclesiasticis tenenda est, ne auctoritas humanitatem superet.
units.tr: It seems harsh to me to punish negligence in bringing up children with excommunication. The sloth of parents certainly deserves rebuke; they must be spurred on by every means, and threats must be applied too. But where neither open impiety, nor contempt, nor a more serious crime is evident, it is better to prefer gentleness to rigour. And this rule must by all means be kept in ecclesiastical censures, so that authority does not overcome humanity.

units.la: Quantum ad pueros attinet, si adoleuerint, asperius corrigen da erit eorum proteruia. Neque enim veniam meretur tam dissoluta intemperies, de qua narras. Cæterum vbi ducunt vxores, hoc tæno cohiberi expediet, non alia lege benedici eorum coniugium, nisi se ad bonam frugem reducturos promittat. Quòd si redierint ad ingenium, leuitas eorum & perfidia bis reos faciet.
units.tr: As for the sons, if they have grown up, their wantonness must be corrected more sharply. For such a dissolute wildness, of which you speak, does not deserve pardon. Moreover, when they take wives, it will be expedient to curb them with this bridle: that their marriage be blessed on no other condition than that they promise to return to a good way of life. But if they fall back into their old nature, their fickleness and treachery will make them guilty twice over.

units.la: Quoniam baptizandi licentia, quam sibi fœminæ arrogant, nihil aliud est quàm crassa superstitio, ut ulta illa & temere suscepta actio pro nihilo ducenda est. Pastorū ergo officium est eas compescere: interea legitimo Baptismo consecrare infantes, qui stulta & praepostera aemulatione nihil aliud quàm polluti fuerunt. Plura in libello quodam meo reperies, cui titulus est, Appendix ad rationem reformandae Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Since the license to baptize, which women arrogate to themselves, is nothing but gross superstition, that vain and rashly undertaken act must be counted as nothing. It is therefore the duty of ministers to restrain them, and meanwhile to consecrate the infants by lawful baptism, which, through foolish and perverse rivalry, have been polluted to no purpose. You will find more in a little book of mine, entitled Appendix to the Account of Reforming the Church.

units.la: Quod rogas an digni sint Ecclesiastica communione, qui eā colere negligunt alendis pauperibus, cùm suppetat facultas. Respondeo amicis monitionibus, non praecisο imperio hic esse locum. Videmus enim ut sibi temperet Paulus, nihil extorquens ab inuitis, sed tantùm blandè rogans, ut subveniant egenis fratribus: neque id ex necessitate, sed prout tulerit animi promptitudo, ut sit benedictio non tenacitas: quia hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Ergo hoc charitatis officium hortando quidem urgere conuenit, voluntaria tamen relinqui debet liberalitas. 2.Cor. 8.9. & deinceps.
units.tr: As to your question whether those are worthy of ecclesiastical communion who neglect to honour it by feeding the poor, although they have the means: I answer that friendly admonitions, not absolute command, have their place here. For we see that Paul moderates himself, extorting nothing from the unwilling, but only asking gently that they help their needy brothers; and not out of necessity, but as their readiness of mind prompts, so that it may be a blessing and not a grudging thing, because God loves a cheerful giver. Therefore this duty of charity should be pressed by exhortation, yet the liberality must be left voluntary. 2 Cor. 8.9. and following.

units.la: Quos intelligas resilire, vel rigore disciplinae, vel crucis ignominia offensos, non satis allequor. Nam si meticulosi tantùm sint ac frigidi, Christi exemplum ergà eos instar Legis nobis proponitur, dum ex Isaia 42.3 refert Matth. 12.20. Ellychnium fumigans non extinguet, calamum quassatum non confringet. Sin verò palàm discessionem ab Ecclesia faciunt, ac eos Euangelij pudet, vel taedet, nullo modo admittendi sunt ad sacram Coenam.
units.tr: I do not sufficiently grasp whom you mean by those who recoil, offended either by the rigour of discipline or by the shame of the cross. For if they are merely timid and cold, the example of Christ is set before us as a rule towards them, when He is quoted from Isaiah 42.3 in Matthew 12.20: a smoking wick He will not quench, a bruised reed He will not break. But if they openly withdraw from the Church, and are ashamed of, or weary of, the Gospel, they must by no means be admitted to the holy Supper.

units.la: Qui admoniti subinde ad eadem vitia relabuntur, nec finem peccādi faciunt, imò Ecclesiam ludunt vanis pollicitationibus, eos seuerius tractandos iudico, nec simplicibus verbis agedum, ubi verba dare non desinūt. Nam si haec lenitas impune feratur, ad obstinationem & impudentiam postea transiliet.
