Recordamini igitur dilecti, hocillud tempus esse, quo serio à vobis inuocetur Dominus, vt vos illi committatis sedulò: itemque vt in timore ac folicitudine ambulētis, ne incidatis in arrogantiam vel socordiam, quæ huic pesti vos obnoxios reddant. Rei ipsius confutationem hic omitto, quoniam certo tractatu hoc à me comprehensum habetis: quod etiam vsui erit ad perditorum hominum infultus repellendos, modò syncera fide admittatis, quæ ad vos legitimè instruendos ex Dei verbo illic vobis offeruntur. Quod ad priuatos cuiusque mores attinet, consideranda nobis est in genere incredibilis illa corruptio, quæ passim in mundo hodie grassatur: non sane vt ad illam accedatis & cum lupis lupi fitis: neque existimetis illorum malo veltrū eleuatum iri cum aliorum exemplo abducemini. Tantum vt vobis sit præcautionis loco, ne accidat malis vos exemplis abduci vel contaminari. Est enim inter spinas nobis iter faciendum, quando homines ita depravatos comperimus. Cesser illud igitur, quòd ita se omnes alii pridem gerant, vbi apertum scelerum diluuium iam mundo incumbere ipsi sentimus. Neque vero alii alios intueamur, vt ex malis exemplis certam regulam confingamus. Nempe hic & ille ita se gerunt, quia portabit vnusquisque onus suum. Neque etiam sic nos esse quisque ad excusationem obtendamus, quum
units.tr: Ioan.7.46 incomparable, and offered by the Lord. If we must prepare defences against the temptations that assail the body, we must think no less about those struggles which Satan tries to bring on us through deceptive teachings. It is not without reason that he is called both a murderer and the father of lies. You will learn this from your own experience. For now he is entirely bent on forcing you, through the persecution he is pursuing by the instruments suited to it, to renounce Christ. Now he is stirring up I know not what hucksters who overturn the whole purity of the Gospel in order to lead you astray and draw you completely away from the way. That first assault has the harshness of persecution, and against it the hand of God alone can strengthen us, so that we are not swept away by its violence and fall. But temptation is far more dangerous when the adversary sows tares among the wheat in order to corrupt it utterly. That is a kind of hidden warfare, carried on as if by mines beneath the ground, so that unless we give serious heed we are surrounded before we notice. Since no kind of teaching is not most poisonous, yet hardly anything can be compared with that by which Satan has breathed his poison into your region. I mean that infamous and accursed sect of the Libertines, who claim for themselves the name of Spirituals. That is most certainly a scourge of God's wrath overflowing upon the world, when he loosens the reins of Satan so far that he persuades Christians of things so detestable, which would strike horror even into profane men merely by being heard. Remember therefore, beloved, that this is the time when the Lord must be earnestly called upon by you, so that you commit yourselves diligently to him, and likewise that you walk in fear and anxiety, lest you fall into arrogance or carelessness, which would make you liable to this plague. I omit here the refutation of the matter itself, since you have it comprehended by me in a certain treatise. That will also serve to repel the assaults of wicked men, provided you receive with sincere faith the instruction which is offered there from the Word of God to equip you properly. As for the private morals of each person, we must consider in general that incredible corruption which rages everywhere in the world today. Certainly not so that you should approach it and become wolves with the wolves, nor think that you will be raised above their evil if you are led away by the example of others. Rather, let this be a precaution for you, lest you be led away or contaminated by evil examples. For we must make our way among thorns when we find men so depraved. Let it cease, then, that all others have long behaved in this way, when we feel the flood of open wickedness already bearing down on the world. Nor should we look at one another and fashion from bad examples a settled rule. Surely this man and that man behave thus because each shall bear his own burden. Nor should each of us put forward this as an excuse for himself, since

units.la: ca eâ sit prima lectio quam inculcat nobis Dominus ex ipso scho- le aditu, ut renuntiemus nobis ipsis: estque illud omnium fere in Scriptura frequentissimum, nimirum ut carnem mortificemus, & affectus nostros quasi captiuos mittamus sub iugum obedi- entiæ Domini. Auscultemus igitur appositas illas admonitio- nes Apostoli, Eratis olim tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domi- no, ut filij lucis incedite. Ne etiam secundum carnem ambu- lemus, sed secundum Spiritum. Christi sanguine loti sumus, ut in puritate perstemus. Ex vinculis peccati à Christo redempti su-mus, vt illi vni & eius gloriæ viuamus, adeoque ille viuat in no-bis. Ista passim extant apud Apostolum vt & illa ex opposito, frustra sibi Dei cognitionem tribuere qui concupiscentiis inser-uiant. Si quis, inquit, in Christo sit noua creatura. At tot hodie scè lerum facies in mundo grassantur, vt eas percensere sit infinitum. Sunt vero inter al a quæ consuetudinis prætexxu emolliuntur, cuiusmodi sunt iuramenta, blasphemiæ, aleæ, luxus vanissimi in saltationibus, cauponarum ordinariæ additiones, & de genere eo dem non pauca. Ne vero iis in rebus imponamus ipsi nobis vel ab aliis sinarus imponi. Neque enim iudicium Dei malis mo-ribus & consuetudini inueteratæ obnoxium est. Hoc ipse semel edixit, Non habiturum sepro innocentem, qui nomè ipsius in va-num assumpserit. Fixum igitur maneat oportet. Nam & ratione summam habet. Quis enim satis reuerenter agnoscat dignitatem sacratissimi nominis, ad quod vniuersæ creaturæ cõtremiscunt? Qui vero assumit in vanum, contemptum prodit. Quid igitur dicemus de blasphemo? Atqui meus sic est mos. Nempe vt tanto grauius reus sias. Hoc est igitur eradendum funditus ne Dei iram prouocemus, dum abutemur tolerantia. Quod ad lusus, caupo-nas, & gulæ illecebras, præter ipsam temporis iacturam, & me-ram in vitia inordinatione, videmus etiam quot mala existis conse quantur. Exhauriunt se, nempe qui ista sectantur, atque temere, imò etiam indigne omnino profundunt, quod meliori-bus visibus erat impendendum. Inde iræ, atque inimicitiæ. Atque vbi quis semel istis rebus sese addixit, ipsum animum quasi at-terit atque imminuit. Taceo tot alia incommoda, quæ quotidie ex eodem illo fonte nascuntur. De aliis illis rebus vanissimis quas verbo indicaui, non est quod vlterius contendam, quado & ipsæ per se suum probrum & turpitudinem deteguut, modo ne ocu-los aperire pigeat. Tadem vero illud etiam vobis succurrat, Di- lectiss. fratres, sieri non posse vt Dei Filij censeamur, nisi chari-tate fraterna inter nos mutuo colligemur. Inde illa vocari per-sectionis vinculû, quod in illa sita sit Christiani smi summa: atq; illa proinde vt hic nobis Dominus commendet. Vt vero vnanimes inter vos sitis, dãda est vobis opera, vt alij alios iuuetis mutuò: vt fidem & fynceritatem colatis inter vos,omnem simulationem, prauitatem, dolum auersemini. Cum pace benignitatem exhibeatis,alieni fitis à iurgiis & rixis,itémque à conuitiis & contumeliis.Demissi ac modesti fitis,omnem de vobis opinionem semel exuatis.Siquidem non aliud est præfentius venenum aduer sus charitatem,quàm arrogantia. Cauendum est omnibus modis,ne affectus ille adeò perturbatus in vobis hæreat,qui vos pe nitus excæcet,iram intelligo. In eo igitur incumbite,vt frænis coerceatis, ac vim ipsis vobis inferatis ad illud monstrum perdomandum.Nihil enim est quod minus compesci possit, quàm ira infrænis. Pluribus ad vos scripsissem ex meo & vestro voto, nisi alia me occuparent plus quàm optaffem,quod à vobis æqui & boni consulendum esse mihi facilè persuadeo. Dominus adaugeat vobis dona sua spiritualia,quæ vos in ipsius bona voluntate & eiusdem obedientia confirment, vt vita vestra ipsius honori cedat, plena vos constantia instruat, vt in fanéta ipsius vocatione ad extremum vsque perstetis. Cúmque tot vndique hostes vos circumcingant, suo vos præsidio compleétatur, suúmque de vobis studium reipfa, cùm opus erit,testificetur.
units.tr: the first lesson which the Lord urges upon us from the very threshold of his school is that we deny ourselves. This is almost the most frequent teaching of Scripture in its entirety: that we mortify the flesh and bring our affections, as captives, under the yoke of obedience to the Lord. Let us therefore heed those fitting admonitions of the Apostle: "You were once darkness, but now are light in the Lord; walk as children of light" (Eph. 5:8). "Let us not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit" (cf. Rom. 8:4). "We have been washed in the blood of Christ, so that we may persevere in purity." "We have been redeemed by Christ from the bonds of sin, so that we may live to him alone and to his glory, and so that he may live in us." These things are found throughout the Apostle, and so is their opposite: that those who serve their lusts claim in vain to know God. "If anyone," he says, "is in Christ, he is a new creature." Yet today so many kinds of wickedness rage in the world that to list them would be endless. Among the other things, some are softened under the pretext of custom, such as oaths, blasphemies, dice games, the most vain extravagances in dancing, the ordinary extras of taverns, and not a few of the same sort. Let us not impose these things on ourselves, nor allow others to impose them on us. For God's judgment is not subject to evil morals or to long-established custom. He himself has declared once for all that he will not hold him innocent who takes his name in vain. Let this therefore remain firmly fixed. For it is also most reasonable. Who would acknowledge with sufficient reverence the dignity of the most holy name, before which all creatures tremble? But whoever takes it in vain shows contempt for it. What then shall we say of the blasphemer? Surely that is his way, so that he may be all the more gravely guilty. This therefore must be rooted out utterly, lest we provoke God's anger while we abuse his patience. As for play, taverns, and the allurements of gluttony, we see, apart from the sheer waste of time and the plain disorder that leads to vices, how many evils also follow from them. Those who pursue these things exhaust themselves, and they squander rashly, indeed even wholly unworthily, what ought to be spent on better uses. From this come anger and enmities. And once a man has given himself over to these things, they wear down and diminish, as it were, the very mind. I pass over the many other inconveniences which arise every day from that same source. There is no need for me to dwell further on those other vain things I have named, since they themselves disclose their own disgrace and baseness, provided only that you are not too lazy to open your eyes. Finally, beloved brothers, let this also come to your mind: it cannot happen that we are counted sons of God unless we are bound together by mutual brotherly love. Hence love is called the bond of perfection, because the sum of Christian life lies in it; and therefore the Lord commends it to us here. So that you may be of one mind among yourselves, you must make it your business to help one another mutually, to cultivate faith and sincerity among yourselves, and to turn away from all pretence, perversity and deceit. Show kindness with peace; be far from quarrels and brawls, and likewise from reproaches and insults. Be humble and modest, and put off once for all every high opinion of yourselves. For there is no more deadly poison against love than arrogance. Above all, take care that that passion, so violently disturbed, does not cling to you and blind you utterly; I mean anger. Therefore strive to restrain it with bridles, and apply force to yourselves to tame that monster. For nothing can be less easily held in check than unbridled anger. I would have written to you at greater length, according to my wish and yours, had other concerns not occupied me more than I would have wished. I readily persuade myself that you will receive this fairly and kindly. May the Lord increase for you his spiritual gifts, which may confirm you in his good will and in obedience to him, so that your life may be to his honour, may furnish you with full constancy, and that you may persevere in his holy calling to the end. And since enemies surround you on every side, may he surround you with his protection, and may he show his care for you in deed when the need arises.

units.la: M. D. LIX.
units.tr: M. D. LIX.

units.la: MARTYR CALVINO.
units.tr: Martyr to Calvin.

units.la: Qvod literas,vir clarissime,rarius quàm ipse velis,& ego cu perem huc scribas , me non ita mouet vt vel abste minus diligi,vel minus curari suspicer.Nam vt afflicta valetudine haétenus fueris,& quàm grauibus atque multiplicibus nego tiis tantum non obruaris,compertiffimum habeo.Vtinâ quemadmodum id probè noui,sic te aliqua ex parte alleuare possem. At confido patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui fons opportuni auxilij atque solidæ consolationis est , ita denique tibi adfuturum, vt & corpore melius valeas, & molestiæ quibus vltra vires premeris nonnihil mitigentur. Quod Gallię res tàm malè habeant,çgerrimè quidem fero,quanuis ita euenturum antea iu dicaui.Nam intelligebam N.illos facilè rerū potituros,ad quorum manum imperii summa fi peruenif-set, facile diuinatu fuit, quò religionis fortuna effet casura.De Regina mirantur fortassis alii,ego non miror. Nam pietas eius erga religionem fynceraм vllam significationem haétenus nunquam sensi. At de Rege Nauarrę nouum admodum videtur,vt qui antea Euangelio Filij Dei tam pleno spiritu fauere videbatur, nunc quando maxime opus erat,fe pietate vacuum adeò præbeat. Quid hîc agamus?Qui Rex regum est,& Dominus dominantium,absque Re-gibus gibus & Dominis huius mundi, causam suam tuebitur, & promouebit: vestræ quoque vrbi defensor & propugnator, vti spero,aderit.Non enim fidelibus,quando suis temporibus vrgentur, solet deesse.Id autem cùm hactenus minime commiserit,vt nûc à vobis incipiat non est opinandû.Nos verò quando aliter non possumus, rem vestram contentissimis precibus apud Christum iuuamus,nec diffidimus quç illius bonitas est, ab ipso nos denique auditum iri.Bulingero & cæteris tuo nomine salutem dixi, qui te vicissim plurimum saluere inbent.Iuueni autem,quem tuis literis commendasti,quacunque in re potero,libentissimè gratificabor, Symmystas tuos mihi velim diligenter admodum salutari,præsertim Dominum Viretum atque Bezam,cuius nomine Lelius mihi dedit institu a vestri collegii:quod vos erexisse ve hementer gaudeo tum ea de causa Deo ingentes gratias ago, illum obsecrãs vt quod bene cœpistis,fœlicissime vertat. Bezę libenter modo scripsissem,nisi tabellarius nimium festinaret.Vale Domine colendissime ac frater in Christo plurimum obseruandæ x x v i.Septembris. Tiguri.
units.tr: Most distinguished sir, you write to me less often than you would like, and I, though I too have sent you letters here, am not so troubled by this that I suspect you of valuing me less or caring for me less. I know well how your health has been, and how you are all but overwhelmed by such heavy and manifold business. I wish that, as I know this well, I could in some measure relieve you. But I trust that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the fount of timely help and of solid consolation, will be with you so that you may recover your bodily strength and that the troubles that weigh on you beyond your strength may be somewhat eased. As for the state of affairs in France, I bear it very badly, although I had foretold that this would happen. For I understood that those men would easily gain control of affairs, into whose hands the supreme power of government had come, and it was not hard to foresee where the fortune of religion would fall. Others perhaps wonder at the Queen; I do not. For I have never yet perceived any sincere sign of piety in her towards religion. But about the King of Navarre it seems quite strange, since he seemed before to favour the Gospel of the Son of God with such a full spirit, and now, when he is most needed, he shows himself so utterly empty of piety. What are we to do here? He who is King of kings and Lord of lords will defend and advance his cause without the kings and lords of this world; and he will, I hope, also be the defender and champion of your city. For he is not wont to fail the faithful when they are pressed in their times. That he should begin now with you, since he has hitherto by no means failed to do so, is not to be supposed. As for us, since we cannot do otherwise, we help your cause with the most earnest prayers to Christ, and we do not doubt that we shall at last be heard by him, since his goodness is what it is. I have greeted Bullinger and the others in your name, and they in turn bid you very many greetings. As for the young man whom you commended in your letters, I shall most gladly oblige him in anything I can. I should like you to greet your colleagues diligently for me, especially Master Viret and Beza, in whose name Lelius gave me the institution of your college. I rejoice greatly that you have set it up, and for this reason I give immense thanks to God, beseeching him that what you have begun well may turn out most happily. I would gladly have written to Beza just now, had the courier not been in such a hurry. Farewell, most honoured sir and brother in Christ, whom I greatly esteem. 25 September. Zurich.

units.la: Tui studiosissimus Petrus Martyr.
units.tr: Your most devoted, Peter Martyr.

units.la: IOAN. ST. CALVINO. S. D.
units.tr: Johannes Sturm to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: Quid agas? homines sunt: atqui falsi sumus.Sed nos non vt de hominibus iudicauimus: verum vt de viris sapientibus sperauimus: neque cogitauimus nos de hominibus iudicare,qui in remotis ab hominũ celebritate atque iudicio montibus habitant,quibus nihil placet nisi patrium.N.omnino fesellit. Vsque adeò φιλολου Ξηροσεst, vt vel crepidas eius adorandas putet. Velim N.posse ab illis auocari, & ab omnibus ciuitatibus conferri,vt honesta conditione Basileæ aut apud vos viueret: aut etiam apud nos: quanquam etiam nostri pueri σοφίζονται ἐν τοῖς δεῖπνοις,ita vt senibus non permittant sapere. Euocatum tamen eum velim ex illis locis:quibus nullæ terræ sapere videantur: credo Sibillam Delphicam migraturam eò: ita omnes in illis locis saguntur. Ego ita non laudo istam N. μικροψυχίαν : φιλόψυχος mihi in hac ætate affecta atque affiicta esse videtur nimium: in re præsertim tali ac tanta. Te laudo, qui laudes,& qui contemnis ea, quæ si ab aliis spernerentur, minus laboraremus. Vale.
units.tr: What are you doing? They are men, and we are fallible. But we did not judge them as men; we hoped for them as wise men. Nor did we think we were judging men who live on mountains remote from the crowds and judgement of men, men who like nothing but their own country. N. has utterly deceived us. He is so fond of himself that he thinks even his sandals ought to be worshipped. I wish N. could be called away from those places and be invited from all cities, so that he might live in an honourable position either at Basel or with you, or even with us, although even our boys play the sophist at dinners [σοφίζονται ἐν τοῖς δεῖπνοις], so that they do not allow old men to be wise. Still, I should like him to be summoned out of those places, where no land seems to have any wisdom. I believe the Delphic Sibyl will migrate there, since everyone in those places is so bewitched. I do not praise that pettiness of spirit [μικροψυχίαν] of N.; a lover of life [φιλόψυχος] seems to me, at his age, too much affected and afflicted, especially in a matter so grave and so great. I praise you, who praise and despise those things which, if others despised them, we would be less troubled. Farewell.

units.la: Ad tria quaedam capita.
units.tr: On three certain heads.

units.la: Diligentior fuissem in respondendo, dilectissime frater, nisi me retinuisset illa difficultas, quae cum eo mihi coniuncta visa est, quod tuis literis a me requirit. Queris igitur ecquid liceat Ministris ex sua pecunia fructum aliquem stipulari & percipere. Si praecise non licere dixero, durior quam par sit, iudicari poterit mea responsio, & aduersus quam non desint quae etiam regerantur. Quare illud non licere, ipse quidem affirmare non ausim. Iam vero ubi expendo quam hoc obnoxium sit calumniis & scandalis, & quam plerique latissime extendant quod sub moderata conditione vsurpari poterat, vt modum hac in re legitimum excedere sibi permittat, multo lubentius subsisterem quam vt pleno responso hoc semel expediendum censerem. Consultissimum esset nempe, ab eiusmodi contractibus & reditiuum captationibus abstinere. Neque enim fructus ita de se restaturremissorum; Non faeneraui eis, neque ipsi faenerati sunt mihi: omnes maledicunt mihi. Quare cum ab eiusmodi quaestu se continere poterit Minister verbi, recte sibi consulit: & tamen quadam quaestus ille tolerabilior est, quam si ipse per se negotiaretur, aut aliquam artem faceret, quae ipsum a munere suo auocaret, non video cur factum in genere damnationem mereatur. Interea hanc moderationem adhiberi velim, ne videlicet certum reditum, vel summam sibi praescripsit pendi stipuletur: sed vt pecuniam ita apud probum virum colloc-t, vt in illius fide ac probitate acquiescat: ac proinde contentus sit aequo & honesto fructu pecuniae, pro ratione benedictionis Dei erga ipsum pecuniae exercitore. Quod ad iurisiurandi exactionem in Consistorio attinet, agendum est prudenter, vt detractionibus & susurris malorum obuiam eatur. Expedit igitur cum opus erit, adiurare qui vocati erunt, atque illos vel iti ad Dei tribunal sistere, quando ille ipse intali coetu prae fidei abstinendum est vero sedulo ab omni agendi ratione, quae iurisdictionis speciem habeat, aut aliquid etiam ab illa non diuersum. Ad vltimum vero, non video quid difficultatis subsit, quin admittantur ad Consistorium, qui iurisdictioni ordinariae & ciuili praesunt, modo ne inter-linit illic nomine & respectu suo illius iurisdictionis, sed vt diserime obseruetur semper inter mu nera illa duo plane distincta, ciuile nempe & Ecclesiasticum. Alioquin nulla ratio finit, excludi illos qui Magistratum gerunt ab inspectione & regimine spirituali. Summa est, vt cum idonei homines ad illud munus electi erunt, videant ipsi ne cum gladij potestate confundat, quod ab illa sui natura distinctum manere debet. Sic vilum est respondere ad tua postulata, quod & fratres approbarunt, quibuscum de istis nominatim contuli, neex meo vnius sensu ista prodiisse viderentur. Bene vale. x. Ianuarij. M. D. L X.
units.tr: I would have been more careful in replying, most beloved brother, had I not been held back by the difficulty that seems bound up with the question you put to me in your letter. You ask, then, whether ministers may stipulate for and receive some profit from their own money. If I were to say flatly that it is not lawful, my answer might be judged harsher than it ought to be, and there are not lacking those who would argue against it. For this reason I would not dare to affirm that it is unlawful. Yet when I consider how open this practice is to slander and scandal, and how most people extend very widely what could have been used under a moderate condition, so that a minister may allow himself to exceed the lawful measure in this matter, I would much rather hold back than think this should be settled once for all by a full reply. It would certainly be most prudent to abstain from such contracts and from the pursuit of returns. For profits of this kind are not in themselves safe: "I have not lent to them, nor have they lent to me; everyone curses me." So when a minister of the Word can keep himself from such gain, he consults his own good well. Yet since that kind of gain is more tolerable than if he himself traded or practised some craft that would draw him away from his office, I do not see why the practice, considered in its kind, should deserve condemnation. Meanwhile I would wish this moderation to be observed: that he should not stipulate for a fixed return or a fixed sum to be paid him, but should so place his money with an upright man that he rests on that man's faithfulness and integrity; and accordingly he should be content with a fair and honest profit from his money, in proportion to the blessing of God upon the one who puts out the money. As for requiring an oath in the Consistory, it must be done prudently, so that the slanders and whisperings of evil men may be prevented. It is therefore expedient, when need arises, to put those who are summoned on oath, and to bring them before the tribunal of God; but when that is done, the Consistory itself must, in such an assembly, carefully abstain from every mode of procedure that has the appearance of jurisdiction, or anything not different from it. Finally, I do not see what difficulty stands in the way of admitting to the Consistory those who preside over the ordinary and civil jurisdiction, provided they do not intrude there in their own name and with regard to that jurisdiction; rather, the distinction between those two offices, the civil and the ecclesiastical, which are plainly distinct, must always be carefully observed. Otherwise no reason permits those who hold the magistracy to be excluded from spiritual oversight and government. The sum is this: when suitable men have been chosen for that office, let them see to it that the power of the sword is not confused with what by its nature must remain distinct from it. This seemed to me the right way to answer your questions, which also the brethren approved, with whom I discussed these matters by name, so that they might not appear to have come forth from my own opinion alone. Farewell well. 10 January 1560.

units.la: DOMINO IO. CALVINO GASP. OLE-VIANVS. S. D.
units.tr: To the Lord John Calvin, Gaspar Olevianus, sends greeting.

units.la: Gratia & Pax a Deo Patre per Iesum Christum Filium suum fit sempertecum, servae Christi fidelissime.
units.tr: Grace and peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ his Son be with you always, most faithful servant of Christ.

units.la: QVod citius ad te non scripsi de rebus nostris Treuerefibus, in eo non excuso negligentiam: debebam enim vos citius liberasse dolore, quem mei causa proculdubio ex variis rumoribus conceperatis: quaquam e custodia in qua decem septimanis integris ad initium fere Ianuarij detentus fui, perdifficile mihi erat & plenum periculi: a Ianuario fortasse literas Argentinam potuissem mittere, si diligens fuissem occasionis inquisitor: quare segnitiem meam non excuso, sed veniam peto. Initiu a Sionis scio te ex iis literis cognouisse, quas superioribus nundinis a D. Martyre accepisti, epitomen totius progressus & eventus ab eodem breui accipies, nisi forte iam accepisti: cuius haec est summa. Cum populi maxima frequentia ad audiendum verbum Domini concurreret, egoque pergerem in templo publico docere adiutus a ministro quodam syncero ac pio misso ad nos e Biponto, eo permouit Senatores Papistas Episcopus, ut eum in urbem intromitterent stipatum ducentis sexaginta plus minus equitibus. Urbem ita ingressus Episcopo, nos postposita omni pro hibitione in vocatione nostra pergimus: et ita quidem ut populus contineretur, ne quidquam moueret aduersus Episcopum. Magnus erat zelus in plerisque omnibus, et ad disciplinam etiam recipiendam erant parati. Episcopus secum in comitatu habebat Latomum, et officialem Confluentinum, qui etiam suus est se a nostra Religione desciuisse. Vehebantur illi molli lectica: hac ostentatione, ac si me disputando erroris alicuius conuincendi causa adducerentur: sed vana tantum fuit ostentatio, neque enim vnquam publice me offerentem disputationem audire voluerunt: quae res multos confirmauit. Dum nos pergimus concionari, saepe per proditores quos habebant ex Senatoribus et aliis ciuibus, turbas excitare conabantur, sed frustra. Dominus enim mirabiliter nos protegebat. In capitulo dum in urbe adhuc esset Episcopus, cum equitatu oriebatur dissensio, aliquot Religionem approbantibus, reiicientibus aliis: quemadmodum
units.tr: I have not written to you sooner about our affairs at Trier, and I do not excuse my negligence in this. I ought to have relieved you sooner of the anxiety which you have doubtless felt on my account from various rumours. From the prison in which I was held for almost ten whole weeks, until about the beginning of January, writing was very difficult and full of danger for me. From January I might perhaps have sent a letter to Strasbourg, had I been a diligent seeker of an opportunity. So I do not excuse my sloth but beg your pardon. I know you have learned the beginning of the affair from the letters you received from Dr. Martyr at the last fair. You will soon receive from him an epitome of the whole course and outcome, unless perhaps you have already received it. Its substance is this. When a very large crowd was gathering to hear the word of the Lord, and I was continuing to teach in the public church, assisted by a certain sincere and pious minister sent to us from Zweibrücken, the bishop persuaded the Papist senators to admit him into the city, escorted by some two hundred and sixty horsemen, more or less. Having entered the city, the bishop and we, setting aside every prohibition, went on with our calling, and indeed in such a way that the people were restrained from stirring up anything against the bishop. There was great zeal in nearly all of them, and they were ready even to receive discipline. In his retinue the bishop had Latomus and the official of Koblenz, who is also said to have fallen away from our religion. They were carried in soft litters. This display was as though they were being brought to refute some error by disputation, but the display was empty, for they never wished to hear me publicly offer a disputation, and this strengthened many. While we went on preaching, they often tried to stir up tumults through the traitors they had among the senators and other citizens, but in vain, for the Lord protected us wonderfully. In the chapter, while the bishop was still in the city, a dissension arose among the horsemen, some approving our religion and others rejecting it, just as

units.la: Latomus ipse (qui crudelissimè se gessit in tota actione & plane fraudulenter) Principum Legatis postea est confessus: quæ causa fuit, cur Episcopus cum equitatu vrbe excesserit, in oppidulum vicinum quod dimidio milliari abest ab vrbe: Episcopus milite vias obsidet, vt nihil inferatur in vrbem, vastat etiam hortos cium. Nihil denique prætermittit, quod ad concitandos Papistas aduersus pios valere aliquo modo posset. Per proditores suos tribunos aliquot, iubet suos Papistas strenuè bibere, neque de annona esse sollicitos: Lutheranos omnia soluturos, qui patriæ suæ voluerunt esse proditores. Potatur noctu ac diu in hypocaustis publicis, aliquot septimanis diebus ac noctibus integris, nostris interim non exiguam penuriam patientibus: per proditores sub ornatos feminæ rumorem atque scripta, nostros emisisse legatos ad alios Principes, ad euocandum militem è Germania, & ad tradendam vrbem aliis Principibus: harum technarum sexcenta excogitabantur millia: deinde vt tota proditio succederet, selegerant proditores subornati ex plebe Papistica pessimosquosque & stupidissimos, vt hi quicquid statuissent cum Episcopo, ratum haberetur, tanquam à maiore parte plebis constitutum.
units.tr: Latomus himself (who behaved most cruelly in the whole affair and quite fraudulently) afterwards confessed this to the legates of the princes. This was the reason why the bishop left the city with his horsemen for a little town about half a mile away. The bishop blockades the roads with soldiers so that nothing is carried into the city, and he even lays waste the gardens around it. In short, he omits nothing that could in any way serve to rouse the Papists against the godly. Through some of his traitorous tribunes he orders his Papists to drink heartily and not to worry about the grain supply, since the Lutherans, who wished to be traitors to their fatherland, would pay for everything. They drink by night and by day in the public bathhouses, for several weeks, whole days and nights on end, while our people meanwhile suffer no small shortage. Through bribed traitors, women spread rumours and writings that our men had sent legates to other princes, to summon soldiers from Germany and to hand the city over to other princes. Six hundred thousand such schemes were devised. Then, so that the whole betrayal would succeed, the bribed traitors had picked out the worst and most stupid men from the Papist populace, so that whatever they decided with the bishop would be held valid, as if it had been determined by the greater part of the people.

units.la: Hi ad reliquos siue Papistas siue pios nihil referebāt, sed pro suo iure agebant omnia. Satanas rapiebat eos omnes plane transuersos, vt nihil vnquam visum sit horribilius: adeo vt qui antea fuissent pigerrimi & trunci, essent indefessi & vaferrimi, vt nocstu etiam vix paululum temporis somno darent, quin continenter concurrerent, & noua singulis fere horis inirent consilia. Tandem Episcopus per literas petiit à Papistis, quoniam sibi constaret nos & seditiosos esse & proditores patriæ, qui vellemus vrbem tradere aliis Principibus, vt defendendæ ipsorum libertatis causa, coniicerent omnes Senatores nostros cum Ministris in carcerem. Se enim velle iure nos convincere proditionis, & seditionis, & criminis læsæ Maiestatis: & vt tuto accusationem per suos cõsiliarios laicos constituere, & sententiam latam exequi mandare possit, petere vt non grauentur militem in vrbem intromittere, qui non ipsis sed seditiosis oneri sit futurus.
units.tr: These men paid no attention to the rest, whether Papists or pious, but did everything by their own right. Satan carried them all completely off course, so that nothing more horrible was ever seen. Those who had been the most sluggish and dull became tireless and very crafty; at night they hardly gave themselves a little time for sleep, but kept running together and devising new plans almost every hour. At last the bishop sought by letter from the Papists, since it was plain to him that we were both seditious and traitors to the fatherland, who wished to hand the city over to other princes, that in defence of their own liberty they should throw all our senators, together with the ministers, into prison. For he wished to convict us lawfully of treason, sedition and high treason; and so that he could safely bring the accusation through his lay counsellors and have the sentence passed carried out, he asked that they not hesitate to admit soldiers into the city, who would be a burden not to themselves but to the seditious.

units.la: Ita fafcinarat Papistas nostros Satan, vt nullas admonitiones Consulis pii aut aliorum audirent, sed plane surdi essent & cæci. Cum in Senatum ventum esset, Papistæ Senatores iubent nostros in custodiam, quæ in ædibus est Senatoris quo conuenerant, se recipere, alioqui furorem populi se cohibere non posse: subornarant autem aliquos qui seditionem mouerent, si nostri id recusassent. Itaque duodecim nostrum in custodiam imus, & nisi iuissemus, magna fuisset sequuta strages, vt plærisque ex nostris existimant. Cum essemus in custodia, Papistæ nobis plane insultabat, & augebatur prorsus ipsorum furor. Aliquot insignia peditum cum Episcopo rursus in vrbem intromittunt maxima cum lætitia, quantumcunque reclamarent præstantissimi ciues vrbis. Producimur per mediam vrbem inter medias turmas comitati centum armatis, ad audiendum accusationem quæ centum & vno constabat articulis, falsis plane & malitiose excogitatis. Inter hos præcipui erant de proditione, de accendenda vrbe, de occidendo Episcopo, de me concionatore Caluiniano. Petentibus nobis spatium deliberandi, vrgebat Latomus & reliqui accusatores, vt quæstioni statim subiiceremur, scilicet Cöful ipse senex, Ottho, Sirkig Proconsul, & nos reliqui. Iidé erant & proditores nostri, & iudices: Dominus tamen mirabiliter gubernabat actione, vt vnus ex ipsis syncerior politicus diceret, quatuordecim dies nobis concedendos esse ad respondendum. Sciebant Legatos sex Germaniæ Principū esse Vvormatiæ, propterea vrgebant condemnationem, & executionem. Antequam elapsum esset hoc spatium, veniunt Legati itaque rursus producti non fuimus, nec ad actionem responsum scripto vllo, sed per Legatos. Tantus erat furor nostrorum hostium, vt nullis fere Legatorum precibus possent sedari, adeo vt coacti fuerint consentire in nostrum exilium, & mulctam trium millium florenorum, pro sumptibus bellicis: petebat autem semel viginti millia, postea octodecim millia, tandem in tria millia est consensum. Reliqui cognoscēs ex communibus literis quas Tigurum misi, & qui inde fit rerum mearum status intelliges ex literis D. Petri collegæ mei. Magna certe hic est bonorum ministrorum penuria, vt fere felicem iudicem Gallliam præ Germania. Auocatus est hinc Petrus ad Ecclesiam Gallicam quæ est Argetinæ. Rogatum te velim, vt diligenter ponderes circunstantias omnes, ne pura doctrina hic deseratur, cum certo mihi constet Argentinensi Ecclesiæ melius prospectum esse vno Ministro quem habent, quàm nostræ multis quos describere tibi non est opus: ita vt existimem non sine summa iniuria Ecclesiæ totius Palatinatus mihi posse eripi Petrum. De hac re cuperem abste commonefieri Ecclesiam Argetinensem, ne cum huius Ecclesiæ maximo detrimento (quæ certe seminarium, vti spero, erit magnæ partis Germaniæ) sibi cupiant prospectum: quod etsi spero consideratuvos Seniores Ecclesiæ acceptis Petri literis, quoniam tamen sunt homines, vereor ne pergant vrgere: ego certe cuperem puram doctrinam modis omnibus hic promotam. Leges Consistorij vestri optarim tuto ad me trāsmitti per Cortæum nundinis proximis: communicarem eas cum aliquot in Senatu Ecclesiastico: quanquam inter omnes est cōsensus. Porro accepi heri literas e patria, quibus mirabilia narrantur Dei iudicia in nostros aduersarios. Multi ex plebe repentina morte obeunt, duo ex præcipuis apoplexia percussi iacent, tertius perfidiffimus (qui meam doctrinam se non improbare posse dixerat nostris Senatoribus, & si rogatus fuisset a nostris se vnà promoturum fuisse Euangelium, sed quoniam adeo strenuè voluerint progredi se non rogato, ideò se modis omnibus impe diturum, quod etiam fecit miris technis & maximis laboribus) is inquacùm manè optimè haberet, ante vespera. subitò mortuus concidit. Nunc & tempus & charta requirit, vt finem faciâ, commendans te ac fratres Seruatori meo Iesu Christo, quæ continenter pro me orate. x i i. Aprilis.
units.tr: Satan had so bewitched our Papists that they heeded no warnings from the godly consul or from others, but were utterly deaf and blind. When the matter came before the Senate, the Papist senators ordered our men to withdraw into custody in the house of the senator where they had gathered, otherwise they could not restrain the fury of the people. They had indeed bribed some men who would stir up sedition if ours refused. So twelve of us went into custody, and had we not gone, a great slaughter would have followed, as many of ours believe. While we were in custody the Papists openly insulted us, and their fury grew more and more. Some ensigns of foot soldiers, together with the bishop, were again let into the city with the greatest rejoicing, however much the most distinguished citizens protested. We were led through the middle of the city, between the troops, escorted by a hundred armed men, to hear the accusation, which consisted of 101 articles, plainly false and maliciously devised. Among these the chief charges concerned treason, setting fire to the city, killing the bishop, and me, the Calvinist preacher. When we asked for time to deliberate, Latomus and the other accusers pressed that we be subjected to examination at once: namely the aged consul himself, Otto, Sirkig the proconsul, and the rest of us. The same men were both our traitors and our judges. Yet the Lord governed the matter wonderfully, so that one of them, the more sincere politician, said that fourteen days should be granted to us to reply. They knew that the legates of six princes of Germany were at Worms, and therefore they pressed for condemnation and execution. Before this period had run out, the legates came. We were not brought out again, nor was any answer to the charges given in writing, but through the legates. The fury of our enemies was so great that it could hardly be calmed by any prayers of the legates, and they were forced to agree to our exile and a fine of three thousand florins for the cost of the war: at first they demanded twenty thousand, afterwards eighteen thousand, and at last they agreed on three thousand. The rest you will learn from the common letters which I sent to Zurich, and you will understand the state of my affairs from the letters of Dr. Peter, my colleague. Certainly there is a great scarcity of good ministers here, so that I judge France almost fortunate compared with Germany. Peter has been called from here to the French church at Strasbourg. I would have you weigh carefully all the circumstances, so that pure doctrine is not abandoned here, since I am certain that the Strasbourg church is better provided for with the one minister it has than ours would be with many, whom there is no need for me to list for you. So I think that Peter could not be taken from me without great injury to the whole church of the Palatinate. I would wish the Strasbourg church to be reminded of this matter, lest, to the great loss of that church (which I hope will certainly be a seminary for a large part of Germany), they wish to provide for themselves. I hope that the elders of your church, having received Peter's letters, will consider this; but since they are men, I fear they may go on pressing. For my part I would wish pure doctrine to be promoted here by every means. I would gladly have the rules of your consistory sent safely to me through Cortaeus at the next fair, so that I might share them with some in the ecclesiastical senate, although there is agreement among all of us. Furthermore, yesterday I received letters from home, which tell of wonderful judgments of God upon our adversaries. Many of the common people are dying of sudden death, two of the chief men lie struck by apoplexy, and a third, most treacherous (who had said to our senators that he could not disapprove of my teaching, and that if he had been asked by ours he would have promoted the gospel together with them; but since they wished to proceed so vigorously without asking him, he would therefore hinder it by every means, which he also did with wondrous devices and very great labours), while he was in very good health in the morning, suddenly fell dead before evening. Now both the time and the paper demand that I make an end, commending you and the brothers to my Saviour Jesus Christ, and pray constantly for me. 12 April.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: CALVIN TO N., SENDING GREETINGS

units.la: NThil de Saxonicis Doctoribus narras, Optime frater, quod non vbique plus satis tristi experientia notum sit. Quaf-cunque enim occupant Ecclesias, non stolida modo confidentia, sed truculento etiam fastu pessundant. Genuit, fateor, Viteberga pios quosdam & cordatos homines: sed maior pars genuinam Lutheri imaginem se referre putat, si pro animi magnitudine qua præditus fuit vir ille, flatu arrogantiæ turgeat. Idem & Ierosolymæ olim contigit, quum sub Apostolis illic maxime vigeret ac floreret pietas: quia nulli infestiores Ecclesiis Gentium hostes fuerunt, quàm qui inde profecti Iacobi & aliorum discipulos se iactabant. Non quòd immodico studio, vt sepe fieri solet, addicti foret magistris quorum nomine superbiebat, sed vt fallaci prætextu obruerent veros omnes & synceros doctores. Sic Lutheri simiæ (paucos enim reliquit imitatores) Vvittebergæ nomen crepando, nisi protinus deditio fiat in eorum ver ba, vbique ingentes mouent tumultus. Quum editus esset Ecclesiæ nostræ cum Tigurina consensus, nihil minus timebâ, quàm vt inde pugnandi materiam arriperet Vveftphalus. Tunc in certamen coactus descendi, vt bestiæ ferociam compesceret. Postea miratus sum plurimos similli rabie esse infectos. Sic tamen eorum non modò inscitiam, sed improbas calumnias detexisse mihi videor, vt eorum fastum & putidam vaniloquentiam merito despiciant, quicunque sunt mediocri iudicio præditi. Et sanè nō dissimulant sibi non nisi in tyrannica violentia residuam spem esse. Quod modestè bonam causam tueris, & sedulò caues, ne vestris dissidiis turbetur Ecclesia, laudo & tibi gratulor, modò vicissim cordatè sustineas eorum pertinaciam, vt maneat in suo gradu Dei veritas, quam stultorum vel amentiæ vel superbiæ tantillum cedere fas non est. Libenter, si daretur facultas, vel ita ferret occasio, tibi arma suggererem: verùm si institutionem proximè editam legere non graueris, reperies, nisi fallor, in 17.cap.lib.4. non pœnitendum subsidium. Porrò quòd me consulis, sulis,an tibi sacram Christi Cœnam ex eorum manibus sumere liceat quibus hæretici fumus,quia negamus Christi carnem dentibus atteri:quanquam mali exempli rem esse video,si quis à Cœna abstineat,peruerse tamen atque adeo perfidæ simulationis effet,accepto concordiæ symbolo falsum illud & absurdum commentum, quod exitialibus præstigiis fidei principia euertit, vel tacitè approbare, nisi clara & ingenua precedat sanæ doctrinæ confessio. Nihil igitur melius fore arbitror, quàm si liberè palámque tester s,te eorum culpa à Cœnæ participatione prohiberi, quia puram & genuinam Christi doctrinam non admittunt. Beza noster plurimùm salutat.Velim etiam ornatissimo viro Doctori N.eiúsque filio plurimam meis verbis salutem dicas.Vale eximie vir & integerrime frater.Dominus te Spiritu suo semper gubernet,præsidio tueatur,& labores tuos benedicat. Genevæ,xxii.Aprilis. M. D. LX.
units.tr: You tell me nothing about the Saxon teachers, my excellent brother, that is not already known well enough from experience almost everywhere. Whatever churches they seize, they ruin them with not only foolish overconfidence but also savage arrogance. I admit that Wittenberg produced some pious and sensible men, but most of its people think they reflect Luther's true image if they swell with the puffed-up arrogance that goes with the greatness of spirit that man possessed. The same thing once happened at Jerusalem, when piety flourished and thrived there under the apostles, because no enemies were more hostile to the churches of the Gentiles than those who went out from there boasting that they were disciples of James and others. Not that they were devoted with excessive zeal to the teachers in whose name they took pride, as often happens, but they used a deceitful pretext to crush all the true and sincere teachers. In the same way, Luther's apes (for he left few imitators) keep crying out the name of Wittenberg and, unless immediate surrender to their words follows, stir up huge tumults everywhere. When our Consensus with the Tigurines was published, I feared nothing so much as that Westphal would seize on it as material for a fight. Then I was forced to enter the contest, to tame the ferocity of that beast. Afterwards I was amazed that many were infected with a similar madness. Yet I think I have exposed not only their ignorance but also their dishonest calumnies, so that all who have even moderate judgment rightly despise their pride and their foul babbling. And indeed they do not conceal that their only remaining hope lies in tyrannical violence. That you defend your good cause modestly, and take care that the Church is not disturbed by your quarrels, I commend and congratulate you; provided that in turn you firmly resist their obstinacy, so that God's truth remains in its place, to which it is not right to yield even a little to the madness or the pride of fools. Gladly, if the opportunity were given or the occasion offered, I would supply you with weapons; but if you do not mind reading the Institutes recently published, you will find, unless I am mistaken, a help that is not to be despised in chapter 17 of book 4. Furthermore, as to your question whether you may receive the holy Supper of Christ from the hands of those by whom, although they regard us as heretics because we deny that Christ's flesh is ground by the teeth, it is permitted: although I see that it is an evil example if someone abstains from the Supper, nevertheless it would be a perverse and even faithless pretence to tacitly approve, by accepting the Formula of Concord, that false and absurd invention which overturns the principles of faith with deadly delusions, unless a clear and frank confession of sound doctrine goes before. I therefore think nothing better than that you should freely and openly testify that you are kept from participation in the Supper by their fault, because they do not admit the pure and genuine doctrine of Christ. Our Beza greets you warmly. I would also like you to give my most cordial greetings to the most distinguished man, Doctor N., and to his son. Farewell, outstanding man and most upright brother. May the Lord always govern you by his Spirit, protect you with his help, and bless your labours. Geneva, 22 April 1560.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS BVLINGERO.
units.tr: John Calvin to Bullinger.

units.la: Quod Gallici tumultus inuidiam à nobis depellere non dubitasti tutò id poteras.Quum ante octo menses agitari cœpisset hæc incipere rent,meâ auctoritatem interposui,ne longius progredi tentarent. Occultè id quidem & placidè, quia verebar ne si rei fama ad hostes manaret,ad carnificinam pios omnes traherem. Putabam tamen mea opera repressos atque sedatos impetus, dum ex Gallia venit quidam nullius apud me pretii,qui se creatum esse ducem apud me gloriatus est. Compescui statim eius iactantiam, nequeab hac conspiratione longè abhorrer profestus sum.Postridie homo famelicus,qui prædam vn dique aucupabatur, vt amicum diuitem illaqueaet ac sub collationis prætextu emungeretbonam pecuniæ summam, impudenter mentitus est, mihi non improbari conspirationem : sed me inuidiæ declinandæ causa nolle palàm fieri.Re audita subitò commotus adhibitis collegis vanitatem eius acriter refutaui. Imò testatus est se iam Lutetiæ certò comperisse ab eo consilio me remotissimum. Cæterùm quanuis plaßim sciretur,mihi esse suspeßu:quia tamè Laufannæ habitabat,propter vicinia,vt erat blandus & illecebris plenus,còciliauerat sibi apud nos multorum amicitiâ:unde factu est vt triduò hac vrbe mira cotagione infecerit.Multi tã nobiles quã gregarij & opifices clanculù consultare:sic tamen vt strepitus à me exaudiretur.Quantopere mihi diflicet conspiratio hæc,tum publicè, tum priuatim osteñi abs que dissimulatione. Quum nihil proficerem,conquestus sum in nobis tam parum esse authoritatis, vt in re maximè feria consilium nostrum spermeretur.Centies dixi,nouum esse fascini genus. De tristi eventu ita sum vaticinatus, ut sero multos poenituerit suae amentiae. Rogo igitur ut pro tua humanitate, & mutua nostra amicitia, in nobis excusandis secure pergas. Reliquas petes ex D. Petro Martyre. Capitis enim dolor longius extrahi sermonem non patitur. Itaque cogar ab optimo fratre nostro D. Volphio veniam petere, quod eius litteris non respondeo. Tu meo nomine gratias agesde labore in meam gratiam suscepto, eumque & reliquos Symmystas diligenter salutabis. Vale eximie vir, & mihi plurimum obseruande frater Dominus te gubernet, tueatur, sustentet, ac tum tota familia benedicat. Amen. Geneuae, v. Idus Maij. M. D. L X.
units.tr: That you did not hesitate to clear the odium of the French disturbances from us, you could certainly have done safely. When, eight months ago, this business had begun to stir and to take shape, I interposed my authority, so that they would not try to go further. I did so quietly and privately, because I feared that if word of the affair reached the enemy, I would drag all the godly to the slaughter. Nevertheless I believed that by my efforts the attacks had been checked and calmed, until a certain man came from France, of no account in my eyes, who boasted that he had been made their leader. I at once suppressed his boasting, and I withdrew from this conspiracy as far as possible. The next day, a starving fellow who was hunting for plunder on every side, intending to ensnare a rich friend and squeeze from him, under the pretext of a meeting, a good sum of money, shamelessly lied that I did not disapprove of the conspiracy, but that I was unwilling for it to be made public, in order to avoid odium. When I heard this I was suddenly roused, and with my colleagues present I sharply refuted his vanity. Indeed he testified that he had already learned for certain in Lyons that I was most remote from that plan. Moreover, although it was widely known that I was suspected, because he lived at Lausanne, close by, and as he was charming and full of allurements, he had won for himself many friends among us; hence it came about that for three days this city was infected with a wonderful contagion. Many, both nobles and common workmen, were consulting secretly, yet in such a way that the murmur reached my ears. How much this conspiracy displeases me, I have shown without dissimulation, both publicly and privately. Since I accomplished nothing, I complained that we had so little authority that in a matter of the greatest danger our counsel was held in no regard. A hundred times I said that it was a new kind of enchantment. I prophesied the sad outcome so accurately that many repented too late of their madness. I ask you therefore, out of your kindness and our mutual friendship, to continue with confidence in excusing us. The rest you will seek from Peter Martyr, for the pain in my head does not allow the letter to be drawn out any longer. Thus I shall be compelled to ask pardon from our excellent brother Volphius, because I do not reply to his letter. Give thanks in my name for the labour he has undertaken for my favour, and greet him and the other fellow ministers diligently. Farewell, excellent man and brother most worthy of my regard. May the Lord govern, protect, sustain you, and bless your whole family. Amen. Geneva, 11 May 1560.

units.la: VALDENSES CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: THE VALDENSES TO CALVIN, GREETINGS

units.la: Gratiam & Pacem per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Grace and peace through our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quoniam, vir venerande, ante annos circiter viginti, inter humanitatem tuam, tum Argentinae agentem, & fratres, qui falso Picardi vel Valdenses dicuntur, charissimos in Domino patres nostros, sancta intercessit notitia & familiaritas, visum est nunc nobis, qui loca patrum (quos iam fere omnes Dominus ex hac mortali vita eripuit) obtinemus, eandem notitiam, imo vinculum illud Christianae charitatis, quo omnes pios maxime Ecclesiae Ministros arctissime constrictos esse decet, renouare. Videmus enim hostes Domini nostri & totius Ecclesiae variè mutuas operas tradere, & ad opprimendam veritatem prorsus conspirare. Quibus cum nos strenuè resistere oporteat, omnino curandum est, ut omnes unum simus in Domino: quod si quae dissensiones & discordiae pullulare inciperent, in spiritu lenitatis, ut componerentur, ne quid per contentionem fieret, vel ij qui extra sunt, conqueri iuste possint. Eam ob causam hos duos in Domino fratres, ad humanitatem tuam, & Symmystas tuos mittimus, ex quibus & vos statum rerum nostrarum (ut & nos vicissim veltrarum) intelligere poterimus, eos ut h. t. amicè exciperedignetur, rogamus. Vale & nos, Ecclesiasque nostras veltris sanctis precibus commendare pergite, rogamus. Datum in Boemia ex Carmelo. xi. Maij. Anno M. D. L X.
units.tr: Venerable sir, about twenty years ago, while your kindness was living at Strasbourg, a holy acquaintance and friendship sprang up between you and the brothers, who are falsely called Picards or Valdenses, our most beloved fathers in the Lord. Now it seemed right to us, who occupy the places of those fathers (nearly all of whom the Lord has already snatched from this mortal life), to renew that same acquaintance, or rather that bond of Christian love by which all godly ministers of the Church ought to be most closely joined. For we see the enemies of our Lord and of the whole Church variously lending each other aid and conspiring altogether to crush the truth. Since we must resist them vigorously, every care must be taken that we all be one in the Lord; but if any dissensions and discords should begin to sprout, they must be settled in a spirit of gentleness, so that nothing is done through contention, and so that those outside cannot justly complain. For this reason we send these two brothers in the Lord to your kindness and to your fellow ministers, and through them you will be able to learn the state of our affairs, just as we in turn may learn of yours. We ask that you deign to receive them kindly at this time. Farewell; and continue, we beg you, to commend us and our churches in your holy prayers. Given in Bohemia, from Carmel, on 11 May, in the year 1560.

units.la: Seniores Vnitatis fratrum, qui vulgò Valdenses vocantur.
units.tr: The elders of the Unity of the Brethren, who are commonly called Valdenses.

units.la: IOANNES CALVINUS EPISCOPO LONDINENSI.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO THE BISHOP OF LONDON.

units.la: ETsi non expectas, Clarissime vir & Obseruande Domine, dum tibi pro pietatis officio, quod Ecclesiae Christi praestiti-sti, gratias agam, quod tamen curam popularium nostrorum qui in praecipua Episcopatus tui vrbe habitant, suscipere dignatus es, non solum vt libertas illis daretur Regine beneficio, Dei pure inuocandi, sed vt pastorem fidum hinc accerserent, nisi hac de causa me tibi obstrictum fatererr, stultitiae & inhumani tatis essem damnandus. Quando autem grauatus non es vltro me rogare atque hortari, vt Pastorem ipsis idoneum curarem de ligendum: non est cur eos fidei tuae patrocinioque commendem pro quorum salute ita solicitum esse video. Et sane vt hactenus tam liberaliter eos iuuando, rarum & singulare pietatis studium testatus: ita nunc constantiae tuae erit, beneficium tuum ad finem vsque tueri. Quod ad nos spectat, quia locus postulare visus est hominem eximiis dotibus instructum, & veltri hospites sibi ex coetu nostro aliquem dari maxime optabat, spoliare nos maluimus, quam non sancto eorum desiderio morem gerere. Ideoque fratrem nostrum Nicolaum Gallasium vnum ex tribus, quos initio nominauerant, ipsis concesserimus: qui etsi egre patie batur a nobis auelli, a quibus non vulgariter se diligi sciebat, & locum hunc, cui non minus fructuosam quam fidelem operam diu nauauit, inuitus relinquebat, nostris tamen obtestationibus victus prouinciam hanc suscepit: quia propagando Christi Regno non parum commodam fore sperabat. Certe vt a nobis dimitteremus, necessitas sola extorsit: quia veriti sumus, ne aliter quam eius aduentu, non satis probe consuli posset tenerae adhuc & incompositae Ecclesiae. Iactura enim eius discessu nō leuem facier hic locus, vbi & in pretio habitus fuit, & se gessit vt dignum erat Christi seruo. Ego priuatim, cui valde charus & familiaris fuit, non sine acerbo dolore, vt mihi eriperetur, assensus sum. Sed quiduis potius ferendum fuit, quam fratribus destitutis ac laborantibus, opem quam anxie flagitabant, negare. Quo maiore cura afficior, vt saltem gratam istic stationem inueniat, quae migrationis tristitiam leuet ac soletur. Vbi propius tibi innotuerit, quod pro tua humanitate fore confido, Reuerende Domine, satis abque aliena commendatione cognosces esse amabilem. Nunc si quem apud te obtineo gratiae locum, etiam atque etiam rogo, vt quem mihi tantopere deuinctum vides, fauore ac bene volentia prosequaris. Ecclesias totius Regni nondum ita compositas esse vt optarent boni omnes, & principio sperauerant, vehementer dolet. Verum ad vincenda obstacula, infatigabili co-
units.tr: Although you do not expect it, most distinguished sir and honoured lord, I will thank you for the service of piety you have rendered to the Church of Christ. You have deigned to take up the care of our fellow countrymen who live in the chief city of your bishopric, and you have done so not only by obtaining for them, through the Queen's kindness, the liberty to call upon God purely, but also by having them send for a faithful minister from here. Unless I acknowledged myself bound to you for this, I would deserve to be condemned for folly and inhumanity. Since you were not reluctant to ask and urge me yourself to find them a suitable minister, I need not commend them to your trust and protection, for I see how anxious you are for their salvation. Indeed, just as you have hitherto shown a rare and singular zeal for piety by helping them so generously, so it will be a mark of your constancy to maintain your kindness to the end. As for us, since the place seemed to require a man endowed with outstanding gifts, and since your guests especially wished that someone be given to them from our company, we preferred to be deprived ourselves rather than refuse to humour their holy desire. So we have granted them our brother Nicolas Gallasius, one of the three whom they first named. Although he was reluctant to be torn away from us, by whom he knew himself to be loved in no ordinary way, and although he unwillingly left this place, where for a long time he had laboured no less fruitfully than faithfully, he nevertheless, overcome by our entreaties, undertook this charge, because he hoped it would be no small help in spreading the kingdom of Christ. Indeed, only necessity wrung from us his release, for we feared that the still tender and unsettled Church could not be sufficiently provided for in any other way than by his coming. His departure will be no slight loss to this place, where he was held in high esteem and conducted himself as became a servant of Christ. I personally, to whom he was very dear and familiar, assented to his being taken from me, though not without bitter grief. But anything had to be endured rather than refuse help to brethren who were left destitute and struggling, and who begged for it so anxiously. For this reason I am the more concerned that he find a pleasant position there, one that may lighten and console the sadness of his migration. When he becomes better known to you, as I confidently expect from your kindness, Reverend Sir, you will recognise without any further recommendation from me that he is lovable. Now, if I have any place of favour with you, I beg you again and again to embrace with your goodwill and affection the man whom you see to be so closely bound to me. It grieves me greatly that the churches of the whole kingdom are not yet arranged as all good men wished and had at first hoped. But to overcome the obstacles, there is need of unwearied effort.

units.la: H.j. natu opus est.Iam vero expedit,atq; adeo necesse est Reginam cognoscere,sic vos libeter remittere,imo à vobis reiicere,quicquid terrenam dominationem sapit,vt ad exercendum spiritua le munus,legitima & quam Deus contulit,auctoritas vobis con stet. Hæc vera erit eius Celsitudo & Eminentia: tunc summum dignitatis gradum sub Christo capite tenebit, fi legitimis Pastoribus manum porrexerit, ad exequendas quæ vobis iniunctæ sunt partes. Sed quia neque consilio indiget tua prudentia,neq; magnanimitas stimulis: tantum ad vota confugiam, Deumque precabor, Præftantiff.vir, atque Obferu.Domine, vt te Spiritu suo gubernet, virtute sustineat, præsidio tueatur,sanctosque labores benedicat.Collegæ mei reuerenter omnes te salutant.Geneuæ,x v.Maij. M. D. L X.
units.tr: Now indeed it is expedient, and therefore necessary, that the Queen understand this: that she should gladly dismiss you, or rather reject from you, whatever savours of earthly lordship, so that the legitimate authority which God has conferred upon you for exercising the spiritual office may be secure. Her Majesty and Eminence will be this: she will hold the highest rank of dignity under Christ the head, if she extends her hand to the lawful ministers so that they may carry out the duties enjoined upon them. But since your prudence needs no counsel, nor your magnanimity any spur, I will only have recourse to prayers and beseech God, most excellent and honoured sir, to govern you by his Spirit, sustain you with his strength, protect you with his help, and bless your holy labours. All my colleagues greet you reverently. Geneva, 15 May 1560.

units.la: 10. CALVINVS BLAVRERO.
units.tr: 10. CALVIN TO BLAURER.

units.la: ETsi multa quæ scribam occurrunt,venerande frater,quia tamen in tam multiplici rerum copia vix vllum finem repe-rio, hæc mihi difficultas magis obstat quàm argumenti penuria:quia nescio vnde potius incipiam. Verum ne pigritia cessare prorsus videar,quæ maxime scire cupis breuiter perstringam. Gallis infœliciter cessisse inconsideratum suum ardorem ad vos perlatum esse non dubito. Ab initio vaticinatus sum quod accidit:sed nescio quo fafcini genere sic captæ erat multorum mentes,vt frustra impetu illum sedare conatus sim. Antea meis consiliis fe regi passi fuerant:sed cum intelligerent totâ hanc actionem mihi non placere, nullum putarunt esse melius compendium,quàm fi me fallerent. Quineti am quidam me vel inscio, vel palàm & fortiter reclamante,profecti sunt. Quanquâ rumor ille,quem dicis apud vos fuisse sparsum,de aliquot millibus,vaniffimus fuit. Non enim plures fuerut quàm septuaginta,& quidem ex dimidia parte infimæ fortis opifices. Sicut autem eorum expeditio nunquâ mihi probata fuit,quia plus meo iudicio tentabant,quàm Deus permitteret:ita consilio destituti,rem non legitimam stulte & puerliter aggressi sunt.Qui præ aliis erant innoxij,pœnam dederunt nimiæ facilitatis. Eodem fere tempore, in quibusdam Prouinciæ & Delphinatus vrbibus nostri homines templa occuparunt,acsi votorum iam effent compotes:verùm vt temeritas nunquam firma est, vel sibi constat, iniecto terrore statim conciderunt:ac zelus ille, quem frustra compescere ftuduer amus,primo armorum strepitu evanuit. Quoniam vero palàm & aperto marte non audebant congredi Guifiani, blandis & fallacibus edictis sub Regis nomine paulatim frege-runt eorum animos,quorum viribus erant impares.His insidiis plurimi illaqueati sunt, & dum sibi priuatim quisque consulit, dissipata fuit eorum societas. Nunc rebus aliquantum pacatis, atrociter saeuire incipiunt carnifices: ac nisi obstaret bellum Scoticum, longe deterior esset conditio piorum in Gallia. Nobis vero & huic vrbi praecipue minitantur: vbi existimant conflari quicquid est turbarum, vel potius captandi praetextus causa, sic ita sentire fingunt. Hoc fere toto mense putarunt omnes vicini de nobis esse actum: ego tamen vt timerem, nunquam adduci potui, nec sane videbam timendi causam. Si maiora pericula vrgeant, Dei praesidio freti eauentum placide expectabimus. Quicquid acciderit, in salutem nostram conuertet caelestis Pater: atque vt nostri misereatur, aliquid etiam valebit totius Ecclesiae respectus. Ignosce quod non propria manu, quia ex lecto dictaui, vbi pro more dimidia temporis parte decumbo, vt saltem horae aliquae mihi salubres maneant. Vale Praestantissime vir, & frater mihi ex animo Obseruande. Dominus tibi semper adsit, te gubernet, ac tuos sanctos labores benedicat. Viretus & Beza & reliqui Collegae mei te plurimum salutant. Geneuae, v. Calendas Iunij. M. D. L X.
units.tr: Although many things come to mind that I might write, venerable brother, I find hardly any end amid such a great abundance of matters, and this difficulty stands in my way more than any lack of subject. But so that I do not seem to be wholly idle, I will briefly touch on what you most wish to know. I do not doubt that the rash zeal of the French, which turned out unhappily for them, has been reported to you. From the beginning I foretold what happened, but I know not by what kind of enchantment the minds of many were so captivated that I tried in vain to restrain their impetus. Previously they had allowed themselves to be guided by my counsels, but when they understood that I did not approve of this whole undertaking, they thought there was no better expedient than to deceive me. Indeed some set out either without my knowledge or with me openly and vigorously protesting. Yet that rumour which you say was spread among you, about several thousand men, was most empty. There were no more than seventy, and of these half were workmen of the lowest class. But just as I never approved their expedition, because they attempted more than God would permit, so, being without counsel, they foolishly and childishly undertook an unlawful thing. Those who were among the others most innocent paid the penalty of their excessive credulity. At about the same time, in some towns of the Province and the Dauphiné, our people occupied the churches, as if they already had their wishes fulfilled. But since rashness is never firm, or consistent with itself, they quickly collapsed once terror was thrown among them, and that zeal, which we had in vain tried to check, vanished at the first clash of arms. Since the Guises did not dare to meet us openly and in the open field, they gradually broke the spirits of those whose strength they could not match, by smooth and deceitful edicts issued in the King's name. Many were ensnared by these traps, and while each looked out for himself in private, their fellowship was dissolved. Now that matters are somewhat quieted, the executioners begin to rage savagely; and unless the Scottish war stood in the way, the condition of the godly in France would be far worse. They threaten us especially and this city, where they think whatever disturbances there are will be stirred up, or rather they pretend to think so as a pretext for seizing us. For almost this whole month all our neighbours thought it was all over for us, yet I could never bring myself to fear, nor did I really see any cause for fear. If greater dangers press upon us, we will calmly await what may come, trusting in the protection of God. Whatever happens, the heavenly Father will turn it to our salvation, and so that he may have mercy on us, the regard for the whole Church will also count for something. Forgive me that I did not write with my own hand, since I dictated from my bed, where, as is my custom, I lie down for half the day, so that at least some hours may remain healthful for me. Farewell, most excellent man and brother whom I honour from my heart. May the Lord always be with you, govern you, and bless your holy labours. Viret, Beza and my other colleagues greet you warmly. Geneva, 25 May 1560.

units.la: Io. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin sends greeting in the Lord.

units.la: ETsi Dilectissima in Domino, non ea im te exiterit constantia & animi fortitudo vbi oportuit, quae debuerat, & quae a nobis spe concepta erat, vti a te Domiinus requirebat, viden dum est tamen vt & istius tui lapsus serio pertaedeat, & tamen animum non despondeas, vt deficias magis. Sane cum nullus color a te possit ad tam apertum malum eleuandum adduci, cauendum est interea, ne Satan pro suo ingenio ad desperationem te impellat, vt a Deo prorsus alienet. Quare ipsius machinae nobis tegendae sunt, vt & ipsis eamus obuiam. Modus autem ille expeditus erit, si ad peccata illa iam admissa cumulum deinde no addideris. Coram iudicibus non fuit a te respon sum vt oportuit. Marito vt satisfaceres, nimirum concessisti. Si ita deflectere pergis, periculum est ne quicquid in te contulitzeli & synceri affectus Domi nus, emoriatur. Non est vero mediocre malum cum infideli profiteris te ipsum Domino anteferre paratam esse. Quare cum ex eo quod non bene apud te constitutum habueris Deum syncere & simpliciter ducem sequi, ita tibi excideris, sic ingem fce tanto casui, vt te etiam in illo erigas, qui potens est te quoque aduersus omne genus tentationes victricem reddere. Optandum est quidem, vt virum quouis modo lucrifacias: atque vt Christi iugum detrectet, nulla ratio tamen finit, vt te ab illo auertas. Vt vero illi ita obsequaris, vt hoc cum sacrilegio coniunctum sit, vt te cum illo reconcilies, vt cum Deo diuortium facias: vt maledictam pacem foueas cum illo, coelestem aduersum te iudicem prouoces: ac in coniugij terreni & momentanei gratiam, sacrum illud ac perpe tuum vinculum quo cum Christo Dei Filio Seruatore nostro coniunctifumus, abrumpas: an vero vel centies potius adeunda mors non effet, tibi iudicandum relinquo. Quod si eousque Deum semel tentares, habet Satan horribiles laqueos, ad illos circuncipiendos, qui se ita perditum eunt. Vide igitur, vt cum te Dominus hactenus retinuerit, & retineat adhuc, ne tibi vlterius indulgeas. Hoc autem pro folicito in te meo studio praedico, etsi non diffido, quin Pater misericordiarum quod in te coepit, impleat. Sed nostro periculo tādem noros esse nobis & cautos reddi oportet, nisi quod absit, donum Dei temere negligimus in no stram perniciem. Quatenus autem marito morem gerere de beas, non est expeditum mihi consilium offerre, cum multa incidere possint, quae mihi perspecta non sunt. Tantum à te contendam, ne semel labyrinthum ingrediaris, ex quo nunquam exitus sperandus sit: sed in eo fixa maneas, quod Deo sit obediendum. Tu autem illum inuoca, cuius vnius ope contra quosuis infultus qui te cunque manent, firma statura sis: simul etiam precare vt Spiritu prudentiae & consilij te instruat, vt te qui bufuis difficultatibus expediat. Ego vero illum etiam tuo nomine orabo, vt reipsa ostendat te in ipsius praesidium & Spiritus sancti directionem & tutelam ab ipso receptam esse. x. Aprilis. M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: Although, beloved in the Lord, you did not show the steadfastness and courage of spirit that you ought to have shown, and that we had hoped for, and that the Lord required of you, nevertheless you must see to it that you are truly displeased with this lapse of yours, yet do not lose heart so as to fail all the more. Certainly, since no excuse can be offered to lessen so plain an evil, we must meanwhile take care that Satan, by his own cunning, does not drive you into despair and so alienate you utterly from God. Therefore his schemes must be exposed to us, so that we may also meet them head on. The way out will be easy if you do not add a further heap to the sins you have already committed. Before the judges you did not answer as you should have. You have indeed consented to satisfy your husband. If you keep giving way in this manner, there is a danger that whatever zeal and sincere affection the Lord has kindled in you will die out. And it is no small evil that you have professed, in a faithless way, that you are ready to put yourself before the Lord. Therefore, since you have not settled in your mind to follow God sincerely and simply as your leader, and have so fallen and collapsed under so great a fall, rise up again in him who is able to make you victorious against every kind of temptation. It is indeed to be wished that you win your husband by any means, but no reasoning permits you to turn away from Christ, who casts off his yoke. But to obey him in such a way that it is joined with sacrilege, to reconcile yourself with him, to make a divorce from God, to cherish a cursed peace with him, to provoke the heavenly judge against yourself, and for the favour of an earthly and momentary marriage to break that holy and perpetual bond by which we are joined to Christ the Son of God, our Saviour: whether it would not be better to face death a hundred times, I leave for you to judge. But if you were to test God in this way once more, Satan has dreadful snares with which to entangle those who go astray like this. See, therefore, that since the Lord has hitherto held you back, and still holds you, you do not indulge yourself any further. I say this out of my anxious concern for you, though I do not distrust that the Father of mercies will complete what he has begun in you. But at our own peril we must at last become wise and be made cautious, lest, which God forbid, we carelessly neglect the gift of God to our own destruction. As for whether you ought to comply with your husband, I have no ready counsel to offer, since many things may arise which are not clear to me. I only urge you not to enter a labyrinth once for all, from which no way out can be hoped for, but to remain fixed in the conviction that God must be obeyed. Call upon him, by whose help alone you may stand firm against whatever assaults await you, and at the same time pray that he will endow you with the Spirit of prudence and counsel, so that he may bring you through any difficulties. As for me, I will pray to him in your name as well, that he may show in fact that you are under his protection and under the direction and guardianship of the Holy Spirit. 10 April 1558.

units.la: Io. Calvinus Valdensibus s. d.
units.tr: John Calvin to the Waldensians, greeting.

units.la: Postquam mandata vestra mihi priuatim exposuit frater à quo literas vestras accepi, quia videbam non ad me solum, sed etiam ad Collegas simul meos missum esse, eadem vt in coetu nostro repeteret, hortatus sum. Itaque de communi omniū sententia respondebo. Ac primum gratias agimus non vulgares, quod fratres qui vestri erga nos amoris, fraternaeq; coniunctionis testes essent, & quasi sponsores, mittere grauati non estis: eoque libentius officium hoc vestrum sumus amplexi, quia ex syn cero pietatis studio manabat. Cupimus idem vicissim vobis de propenso nostro ad fouendam sanctam vnitatem affectu perfua sum esse. Et certe cum tam longis regionum spatiis inter nos distemus, & undique cinguntur hostibus qui totum fere orbem occupant, hoc saltem dispersionis nostrae solatio frui, dulce ac iucundum est. Testemur ergo mutuo consensu vnum esse nobis patrem in coelo, & nos sub Christo capite vnum esse corpus: quod certo speramus vos esse factuos: atque vt re ipsa sentiatis nobis
units.tr: When the brother from whom I received your letter laid out your instructions to me privately, I urged him to repeat the same things before our assembly, since I saw that the message had been sent not only to me but to my colleagues too. So I will reply with the common opinion of all of us. First, we give thanks, and no ordinary thanks, that you did not hesitate to send brethren who would be witnesses and, as it were, guarantors of your love towards us and of our fraternal bond. We took up this duty of yours all the more gladly because it flowed from a sincere zeal for piety. We wish, in return, to assure you of our inclination to foster that holy unity. Indeed, although we are separated by such long distances of lands, and are surrounded on every side by enemies who occupy almost the whole world, it is sweet and pleasant to enjoy at least this consolation of our scattering. Therefore we testify with one mutual consent that we have one Father in heaven, and that under Christ our head we are one body. We firmly hope that you too are of this mind, and we will take care that you actually perceive that we hold you dear.

units.la: Epist. 298. nobis cordi esse, operam dabimus. Porro alendæ & retinendæ in ter fratres concordiæ scimus hoc optimum esse vinculum, si alii de aliis sinistros rumores nimia crudelitate non admittant: nec vero putamus hac in parte quicquam à nobis fuisse peccatum. Nam quod de literis ad Polonos scriptis visus est frater vestro no mine oblique coqueri, nullius culpæ conscii nobis fumus: acvos ipsi rationibus probè expesis pro vestra æquitate reperietis, cum de causa illa essemus consulti, non potuisse dari responsu huma nius vel moderatius.
