Certè nec odiose de wobis loquuti sumus: & quoad licebat, curæ fuit mitigare offensiones quæ iam subortæ erant, occurrere peioribus dissidiis, & ita vos vltro citroque recon ciliare, vt inter exordia Polonis effectis adiutores ad Regnum Christi apud eos erigendum. Ad vos etiam scripturi eramus, si opportunitas dedisset. Verum minime vos latet, quam difficile sit in tanta locorum distantia communicandi ratio. Nunc quando oblata est melior facultas, ingenue sensu mostrum profitebimur.
units.tr: Epist. 298. Furthermore, we know that the best bond for keeping alive and preserving concord among brethren is this: that we do not admit unkind rumours about one another through excessive cruelty. Nor do we think that anything was sinned by us in this respect. For as to the letters written to the Poles, which our brother seemed to complain of obliquely in your name, we are conscious of no fault, and you yourselves, weighing the matter properly by your own sense of fairness, will find that when we were consulted on that question, no more humane or moderate answer could have been given. Certainly we did not speak hatefully of you; and as far as was permitted, we took care to soften the offences that had already arisen, to forestall worse dissensions, and so to reconcile you to one another in both directions, so that at the beginning of the work, helpers might be raised up among the Poles for the kingdom of Christ there. We were also going to write to you ourselves, had an opportunity been given. But you are not unaware how difficult it is to communicate across such a distance of places. Now that a better opportunity has been offered, we will openly state our mind.

units.la: Quantopere interfit vos Polonis manum porrigere, vt apud eos progressum faciat pura Euangelii doctrina, vosipsi nobis tacentibus pro vestra prudentia reputate. Neque enim dubium est, quin vestra dissensio, si ab hostibus animaduersa fuerit, aliquid remoræ initiat rebus bene & feliciter inceptis. Probabiles quidem causas nobis retulit frater, cur metuntis propius ad illos accedere: quia scilicet videtis eos scindi perruersis factionibus. Verum hæc necessitas vos magis vrgere debet, vt gliscentibus malis, vel pullulantibus, remedium afferat vestra coniunctio. Nam spiritus phreneticos, qui in dissipatione tumultuandi & omnia turbandi licentiam sibi sumunt, facile compescere tot Ecclesiarum auctoritas, si aliæ alias iuuarent. Nunc pii fratres vestro suf fragio destituti, grauius laborant. Si Stancari, Georgii Blandrate & aliorum turbulentos impetus, in Poloniam conuertit Satan, nonne vestrum est succurrere? Si negligitis, videte ne forte vobis aliquando desint fratrum subsidia. Neque enim semper in manu vestra erit, certamina effugere, à quibus vos hactenus immunes Deus præstitit. Quo minus alii ad alios accedant, impedit controuersia de communicatione carnis & sanguinis Christi: cuius obstaculi tollendi causa, cesuimus quærendam esse hinc inde commodam & dilucidam explicationem. Si consilium hoc vobis displicet, experientia tandem docebit rectum & salubre fuisse, quanquam non putamus vos adeo morosos esse, vt illud repudietis. Duo forte vos pupugerunt: quod scripsimus in vestra confessione breuitatem esse & obscuram & ambiguam, quæ cer tiore docendi forma indigeat: deinde in Apologia nimium esse vehementiæ & feruoris contra eos omnes, qui præcisè loquendi genere non contenti, lucem sanæ explicationis desiderant in voverbis,vbi asseritis panem esse Christi corpus.Scimusquâ plau-fibils fit eorum actio, qui sub vmbra cofeffionis Auguftanæ,pacem & otium captãdo,molestias,odia,,crucem denique fugiunt. Quid autem hac de re senserit author ipse D.Philippus Melâch thon,neque vos latet,& fortè palàm nos toti mudo facere coget eorum improbitas,qui claræ luci tenebras obducere conantur. Neque tamen quâuis Philippi memoriam reuerenter colamus, eius auctoritate nitimur ad grauandos aduersarios: sed tantùm ostendimus quàm iniquè cofeffionem Auguftanâ obtendât,qui alienissimi sunt ab auctoris mete.Nos quidè (quod bona vettra pace dictum fit) manemus in sententi, non posse simpliciter reci pi confessionis vestræ formulam absque periculo,ac fuscriptio-ne,nisi adhibita dextra interpretatione,Polonis multatu cóten-tionú originem & materiam fore. De vehementia facilis est ex-cufatio.Neque enim exagitare placet quæ vellemus sepulta esse. Hoc tantũ sufficiat,nō posse verecudè negari,quin auctor Apo-logiæ vestræ modu exceflerit. Quod retaliadi causa mihi obiecit nuntius vester,me etiam in quibusdam scriptis nimiu excádefce re,etsi in totũ non inficior, tempestiuè tamè non protulit. Nam fi quosdam impuros canes durius insector, lögè dissimilis est Apologiæ vestræ ratio,quæ promiscue & absque deleétu vllo,mul tos pios,doctos homines male sentientibus inuoluit. Nam fi vo bis propofitu erat quorundam errore impetere, distinctione opus fuit,ne in idem crimen traherentur innoxii.Veru vt omnis facessat contentio tantum vos rogamus & obtestamur, fi liberè oftedimus quæ nobis ad placandas omnes lites, purgandofq; fi-niftros affectus,probaretur ratio,ne id in vos côrumeliofu esse ducatis. Nec tam fumus nobis addicti,quin placide sustineamus nos moneri & reprehedi,fi quid minus circufpectè exciderit.Va-lete integerrimi fratres, & nobis colendi Patrem cœlestem pre camur,vt vos Spiritu suo semper gubernet,præsidio tueatur,do-nifque suis locupletet, ac benedicat sanctos labores vestros. Geneuæ,Pridie Calend.Iulij. M. D. LX.
units.tr: How much it matters that you stretch out your hand to the Poles, so that the pure doctrine of the Gospel may make progress among them, you yourselves, without our speaking, may consider in your wisdom. For there is no doubt that your dissension, if it were noticed by enemies, would bring some hindrance to affairs well and happily begun. Indeed, the brother has reported to us plausible reasons why you fear to draw closer to them, namely that you see them split by perverse factions. But this very necessity ought to press you the more, so that your union may bring a remedy against evils that are growing or sprouting up. For the authority of so many Churches could easily curb frenzied spirits, who take to themselves licence to stir up tumult and throw everything into confusion, if they helped one another. As it is, the godly brethren, deprived of your support, suffer more grievously. If Satan has turned the turbulent assaults of Stancari, Giorgio Biandrata and others upon Poland, is it not your duty to bring help? If you neglect it, see that the help of the brethren may at some time fail you too. For it will not always be in your power to escape conflicts, from which God has hitherto kept you free. What prevents the others from drawing close to one another is the controversy about the communication of the flesh and blood of Christ; to remove this obstacle, we have decided that a convenient and clear explanation should be sought on both sides. If this counsel displeases you, experience will at last teach that it was right and wholesome, although we do not think you are so headstrong as to reject it. Two things perhaps have pricked you: that we wrote that the brevity of your confession is both obscure and ambiguous, and needs a more certain form of teaching; and secondly that, in the Apology, there was too much vehemence and heat against all those who, not content with a precise manner of speaking, desire the light of a sound explanation in those words where you assert that the bread is the body of Christ. We know how plausible is the conduct of those who, under the shadow of the Augsburg Confession, seek peace and quiet, and flee troubles, hatred, and finally the cross. But what the author himself, Philip Melanchthon, thought about this matter is not unknown to you, and perhaps their wickedness, who try to cast darkness over clear light, will at length compel us to make it public to the whole world. Yet although we revere Philip's memory with respect, we do not rely on his authority to burden our adversaries; we only show how unfairly those who are most alien from the author's mind put the Augsburg Confession forward as a shield. For our part (with your good will be it said) we remain of the view that the formula of your confession cannot simply be received by the Poles without danger and a disturbance of sources and matter of quarrels, unless a right interpretation is applied. As for vehemence, there is an easy excuse. For we do not wish to stir up again things we would have had buried. It is enough to say this much: it cannot be shamefully denied that the author of your Apology exceeded the due measure. As for the charge your messenger brought against me, that I too have burst out a little too harshly in certain writings, I do not wholly deny it, but he did not bring it up at the right time. For if I attack some foul dogs more harshly, the method of your Apology is very different, which without distinction and without any selection involves many godly and learned men along with those who think ill. For if your purpose was to attack the error of certain people, a distinction was needed, lest the innocent be drawn into the same charge. But so that all contention may cease, we only ask and beseech you: if we frankly show what might, in our judgment, serve to calm all disputes and purge sinister feelings, do not take it as an insult to yourselves. Nor are we so attached to our own opinions that we cannot calmly bear being admonished and rebuked if anything has slipped from us less than cautiously. Farewell, most upright brethren, and to us to be honoured. We pray the heavenly Father that he may always govern you with his Spirit, protect you with his defence, enrich you with his gifts, and bless your holy labours. Geneva, the day before the Kalends of July, 1560.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus omnium nomine.
units.tr: John Calvin, on behalf of all.

units.la: RESPONSIO AD QVÆSTIONEM PROPOSI-tam de prouentu annuo Sacerdotij Papalis,& venditionis pretio.
units.tr: Answer to the question proposed about the annual income of a papal priesthood and the price of its sale.

units.la: SI de re adhuc integra dandum effet consilium, non licere e-xiftimo,quamlibet specioso prætextu,possidere vlla Sacerdo tia in Papatu: quia nullum assem colligere inde licet, qui non fit sacrilegio inquinatus. Verum si quis per inscitiam & errorem collectos inde fructus absumpserit, non video cur de restitutione anxie laboret. Distinguo alimenta a repositis thesaurus. Nam si quis ex ea pecunia fe ditauerit, donec restituat quod iniuste detinet, non est purus ab anathemate. Ergo sicuti Moses tranquilla conscientia aulam Pharaonis, & delicias reliquit, quia genus illud vitae non sponte appetiuerat: sic hodie quisquis maledictis illis opibus se abdicat, quibus se ad tempus sustinuit, quieto animo in posterum legitima ratione victum sibi acquirere poterit.
units.tr: If advice were still to be given on a matter that is not yet settled, I think it would not be lawful to hold any priesthood in the Papacy, whatever specious pretext is offered, because one cannot collect a single penny from it without being polluted by sacrilege. But if anyone, through ignorance and error, has consumed the fruits collected from it, I do not see why he should anxiously worry about restitution. I distinguish between what is spent on living and what is stored as treasure. For if anyone has grown rich from that money, he is not clear of the curse until he restores what he unjustly keeps. Therefore, just as Moses left the court and luxuries of Pharaoh with a quiet conscience, because he had not sought that way of life willingly, so today whoever renounces those accursed riches by which he has sustained himself for a time may, with a quiet mind, win his living in future by lawful means.

units.la: Quod ad pretium venditionis spectat, scelerata haud dubie fuit pactio. Sed emptore mortuo non aliud superest, nisi ut qui pecuniam iniuste accepit, studeat, quoad suppetet facultas, & occasio dabitur, lucrum illud quo se contaminauit, alio transferre. Itaque pro suo iudicio, quibus & quando videbitur eroget, quantum adhuc retinet, ne sit ex alieno locupletior.
units.tr: As for the price of the sale, the bargain was undoubtedly wicked. But since the buyer is dead, nothing remains except that the man who received the money unjustly should take care, as far as his means allow and an opportunity is given, to pass on that gain by which he has defiled himself. So, by his own judgment, let him give away, to whom and when it seems right, whatever he still retains, so that he is not made richer from what belongs to another.

units.la: Adolescens qui insciis parentibus vxorem duxit, agnoscat se iustas leuitatis poenas dare, si vxor est immorigera: nec miretur, quum Deo & parentibus non praestiterit quod debebat obsequium, sibi rependi iustam mercedem in vxoris contumacia. Et quia dissensio in Religione coniugium non dit imit, quandiu poterit absque periculo cum vxore habitare, matrimonio officio fungatur. Quod si maior vis & necessitas ipsum cogat ab ea discedere, in coelibatu maneat, donec vel resipiscat vxor, vel diuortij causam praebeat. Calendis Septembris. M. D. LX.
units.tr: A young man who married without his parents' knowledge should acknowledge that he pays a just penalty for his rashness if his wife is disobedient. Nor should he be surprised that, since he did not render to God and to his parents the obedience he owed, a just reward is paid back to him in his wife's stubbornness. And since a difference in religion does not dissolve marriage, as long as he can live with his wife without danger, let him fulfil the duties of marriage. But if greater force and necessity compel him to leave her, let him remain unmarried until either the wife repents or gives cause for divorce. Calends of September, 1560.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Bullinger, greeting.

units.la: Nvper ad Fõtem Bellae Aquae (qui locus vix itinere bidui distat Lutetia) vocati sunt omnes proceres. Adfuit Cardinalis quidam, qui aut cadus est aut lagena, ne hominis quidem figuram gestans. Putarunt Guisiani magnum fore splendorem conuentus, si equites conchiliatos (qui se venditant ordine sancti Michaelis) quàm plurimos vndique accerserent. Comparuerunt triginta, quum ante essent duodecim Illic Cacellarius magnifacere praeclarum Senatum, in quo resideret tota Regni autoritas. Praefatio adulationis putidae. Disseruit postea de Regni statu: & quoniam remediis opus erat ad sanandos morbos, malorum causam inuestigandam esse. Hic relationi suae finem imposuit, quasi medicos implorasset, consilij inops. Rex ex composito Episcopi Valentini, qui inter postremos consiliarios erat, sententiam rogauit. Volebant scilicet Guisiani excutere omnium arcanos affectus, & repente singulos, prout visum esset, aggredi.
units.tr: Lately all the nobles were summoned to Fontainebleau, a place scarcely two days' journey from Paris. A certain Cardinal was present, who is either a cask or a flagon, not even bearing the figure of a man. The Guises thought the gathering would have great splendour if they summoned from everywhere as many knights in purple as possible (who call themselves of the order of St Michael). Thirty appeared, whereas before there had been twelve. There the Chancellor made much of the distinguished Senate in which the whole authority of the kingdom rests. It was a preface of foul flattery. Afterwards he spoke about the state of the kingdom: since remedies were needed to heal the diseases, the cause of the evils had to be investigated. Here he brought his speech to an end, as if he had begged doctors for help, having no counsel of his own. The King, by arrangement with the Bishop of Valence, who was among the last of the councillors, asked for opinions. The Guises, of course, wished to probe the hidden feelings of everyone and then suddenly to attack each one, as seemed fit.
