Idem faciet vehemen tius Pontifex:idem conabitur Rex Philippus. Et sanè metuo ego insidiasDiaboli,& hominum fraudes. Atque hæc causa etiam est eadem cum superiore,vt ad C.V.scribam,non tam meum consilium explicans, quàm prudentium hominum sententiam atque voluntatem indicans.
units.tr: or Evangelists, or Apostles, or Fathers can they pronounce this man a heretic and condemn him, excommunicated on their own private authority? Especially since such absurd things are said by them, namely that the natural body of Christ, which is endowed with flesh and bones, is not everywhere, and yet is everywhere eaten together with its flesh and bones and truly eaten; and that this is said properly, that is, in the native sense of the word. Likewise that the bread is not transubstantiated, and yet the bread is the body; and in this they use the term synecdochically [συλσο-ματικῶς] and corporally, calling the body corporeal. Likewise that the body of Christ is not present locally, and yet is given and eaten in the bread, the very same body, namely with flesh and bones. And with this they descend so far that they tell the unlearned common people that Christ is taken just as he lay in the cradle wrapped in swaddling bands, that is, that he is eaten. Who can understand this jumble of words, this licence and impudence, whether of the common people or of the learned? Whence this new theology, these new schools, these new dogmas of Stoic apathy [ἀπαθείας δόγματα]? Luther abolished veneration and adoration, but those are pleasing to these men who do the contrary: they bare their heads, bend the knee, receive with the mouth and not with the hand, and would be still more pleasing if they adored. Just as among the Papists those are dear and welcome who worship statues, prostrate themselves in supplication before them, and set lights before them. But I have pursued these matters at greater length than I had intended. Yet grief has driven me, and still drives me, when I consider how confidently they write, so that they do not fear the judgment of learned men, nor dread the reputation of posterity. Both of these make a shameful example: for the living, who though able do not refute them; and for those to come, what great wretchedness and folly they will judge these men to deserve, in thinking it necessary that others must follow their folly. As for why I write to Your Clemency, the reason is this. They have great hopes that after this assembly of princes there will be a synod of theologians, and some seem to aim at this and to work for it, so that by the authority of that synod the Churches of Helvetia and France may be condemned on this article concerning the Lord's Supper. But if this is done with the cause unheard, the matter not debated between the two sides, and without the reasons of each party being known, by arbiters who are prudent and learned but not partisans of these disputes, how many and how great would be the inconveniences arising from it? The Papists would then be free to do the same, to exclude us from a general council and to condemn all our doctrine and religion. The most important and powerful nations would be offended: Italian, Spanish, French, English, Swiss, among whose peoples nearly all the learned are unwilling to be bound to these new verbal formulas. Yet they would gladly admit the words of the Fathers, if these men themselves felt and spoke modestly as Fathers do. The King of Navarre will take it very ill that he and his people are excommunicated by the Saxon Churches; the Queen of England too will grieve, who, although she approves the Augsburg Confession, cannot receive these carnal verbal formulas. Moreover, they seize upon Luther's pure doctrine on this sacrament, together with his hyperboles, and thrust them upon the people. Some say that Philip Melanchthon is raving in his old age; some say he is inconstant in his doctrines; some say he did not hold what he wrote to Your Clemency. As if that writing were the work of a raving old man, or as if he had not first communicated his opinion over the past twenty years, since the earlier colloquy at Worms, then at the Diet of Hagenau with John Calvin, then with Peter Martyr, and with many other friends, and as if he had not maintained a lasting friendship with them; or as if we did not know what he thought about Westphal's writings, or as if I were ignorant of what he said to me and what he wrote to me. These men, whom he loved, to whom he wrote with affection, with whom he kept up friendship, these men they dare to assail with abuse and to drive out of the Church. There is nothing in which the Papists boast more than in our present dissensions; there is nothing that alienates men's minds more than these same things. I also fear that these same charges will be daily thrown at the King of Navarre at the very beginning of his administration of the whole kingdom. It is written from Brabant that he promised filial obedience to the Pope through his legates in the council of Cardinals; the same is written from Lyon. I believe he is forced to do this by the importunity of the Cardinals and the slanders of his adversaries. Meanwhile, however, he recalls the provincial bishops to their country and their sees, frees prisoners held for their religion, and does not hinder private assemblies, the invocation of God, or the administration of the sacraments. Today Polwiler, from this neighbourhood of Scherwiller, is about to set out for France, sent there by the Emperor. These men too will pour cold water on it: they will strike fear, and they will try, if they can, to make him one of their party. The Pope will do the same, more vehemently; King Philip will try the same. Indeed I fear the snares of the Devil and the frauds of men. And this is also the same reason as before for writing to Your Clemency: not so much to set out my own counsel as to indicate the opinion and will of prudent men.

units.la: Hi summis votis expetunt constitui concilium & synodum Theologorum,in qua Princeps aliquis præses sit:& illi adsint aliorum Principum Legati,viri prudentes & boni,non implicati huiusmodi cotentionum dissidiis: & hæc eadem synodus pateat omnibus,qui causam suam cognosci volunt. Vocentur eò principes aduersariæ partis, Petrus Martyr, Bulingerus, Caluinus, Beza. Legitima cognitione de re disceptetur: tum deinum aliquid fiet,cum hac ratione fiet. Et si Principes hac sua synodo exemplum constituant Pontificiis, quomodo in generali concilio de controuersiis Religionis fieri debeat iudicium?
units.tr: These men most earnestly desire that a council and synod of theologians be set up, over which some prince presides, and that there be present the envoys of other princes, wise and good men not entangled in disputes of this kind of contention; and that this same synod be open to all who wish their cause to be heard. Let the leaders of the opposing side be summoned there: Peter Martyr, Bullinger, Calvin, Beza. Let the matter be disputed in a lawful hearing; only then will anything be done, and only if it is done in this way. And if the princes set this synod as an example for the Papists, how ought judgment be given on the controversies of religion in a general council?

units.la: Quòd si ratione agetur alia, præscribemus nos nostra ista ratione tione aduersariis, quid ipsi in suo tyrannico concilio instituere & sequi debeant. Et postrema mala primis deteriora erunt, & ingens in Ecclesia schisma excitabitur, cuius incendium nulla poterit extinguere posteritas. Quamobrem aut hac ratione synodus constituenda est, aut satius est nullam fieri. Vt enim nunc homines affecti aduersus sese animis sunt: & vt nunc libri scribuntur, qui semel auctori atis gladium arripuerit, nihil iudicare poterit, quod æquitati & moderationi fit consentaneum. Hæ sunt igitur bonorum voluntates, & hæc quotidiana vota, vt hu iufmodi synodus decernatur: hoc iudicium, vt fi fieri id non queat, neque ab iis impetrari qui cæteris mortalibus æquiores esse deberent, satius fit res suo cursu currere: vt quam partem Deus & melior pars hominum approbet, eidem ipse Deus & viri boni assistant. Qua in re Deus Pater noster & Dominus noster Iesus Christus non negligetbonorum virorum & piorum hominum quotidiana, diurna atque nocturna vota, preces atque suspiria.
units.tr: But if matters are handled by some other method, we shall prescribe to our adversaries, by this very method of ours, what they themselves ought to set up and follow in their tyrannical council. The last evils will be worse than the first, and a huge schism will be stirred up in the Church, whose fire no posterity will be able to extinguish. Therefore either a synod must be constituted in this way, or it is better that none be held at all. For as men are now disposed against one another in their minds, and as books are now written, whoever has once taken up the sword of authority will be able to judge nothing that is consonant with fairness and moderation. These, then, are the wishes of good men and their daily prayers: that a synod of this kind be decreed; but if this cannot be done, and cannot be obtained from those who ought to be fairer than other mortals, it is better to let things run their course, so that God and the better part of mankind may approve whichever side, and God himself and good men may stand by it. In this matter God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ will not neglect the daily, day and night prayers, entreaties and sighs of good and pious men.

units.la: Ad hanc autem synodi rationem vtilem esse iidem iudicant, qui superiora optant Legationem ad Regem Nauarræ mittere, quæ quoad aperte dici & peti possit, in Regio consilio exponat; quæ vero priuatim cum Rege Nauarræ & fratre & reliquis Principibus, qui Religioni veræ fauent, agenda sunt, illa priuatim etiam explicet, quemadmodum à Principibus in mandatis habitura. Hæc ratio has habet causas. Primùm maior erit auctoritas synodi: & quasi Nationale concilium habebitur trium Populorum, Germaniæ, Galliæ, Angliæ: non enim dubium est, quin libenter Regina Angliæ sese fit adiun&ura, fi ab ipsa & à Principibus Galliæ petetur, vt homines mittant ad eam synodum, pacis & concordiæ studiosos, pietate prædictos, doctrina eruditos.
units.tr: Those who desire the earlier embassy to the King of Navarre also judge that this plan of a synod is useful: that he should set out in the royal council, as far as can be openly said and asked, what is to be said; and what must be handled privately with the King of Navarre, his brother and the other princes who favour the true religion, let him explain privately as the princes will have instructed him. This plan has these grounds. First, the authority of the synod will be greater, and it will be regarded as a national council of three peoples, Germany, France and England; for there is no doubt that the Queen of England will gladly join herself to it, if she and the princes of France are asked to send men to that synod who are devoted to peace and concord, endowed with piety and learned in doctrine.

units.la: Deinde Rex Nauarræ opus habet hortatoribus in hac oppugnatione Cardinalium, Episcoporum, callidorum & experientium hominum. Et gratissimum illi erit intelligere, quam de fe Germaniæ Principes existimationem habeant: & quam habeant erga fe & Regnum Galliæ beneuolentiam: & quid sibi suis aliquando necessariis temporibus ab ipsis Principibus expectandum fit: & quod suum esse debeat officium, fi quando suis etiam necessariis temporibus atque periculis Principes Imperij, Regni Galliæ & Nauarræ consilio & opæ opus habeant.
units.tr: Next, the King of Navarre needs encouragers in this assault on the cardinals, bishops and shrewd and experienced men. It will be most welcome to him to understand what esteem the princes of Germany have for him, what goodwill they bear towards him and the kingdom of France, what he may expect from the princes themselves in his times of need, and what duty ought to be his if at some time the princes of the Empire, the kingdom of France and Navarre should need his counsel and help in their own times of need and danger.

units.la: Deinde fi honestum officium faciunt Imperator, Rex Philippus, Papa, Regina Angliæ, quod Legatos mittunt in hoc Principio Regis noui, & nouæ administrationis, cur non pernecessarium & perhoneftum officium faciant Principes, fi idem sibi vsurpent quod alij faciunt?
units.tr: Next, if the Emperor, King Philip, the Pope and the Queen of England perform an honourable office in sending envoys to this beginning of the new King and new administration, why should the princes not perform a most necessary and most honourable office, if they claim for themselves what others do?

units.la: Atq; eò istud Principes hoc tempore cómodiùs facere poterunt,
units.tr: And the princes will be able to do this more conveniently at this time,

units.la: I.iij. quod heri allatum est extribus ordinibus Regni, Nobilitatem, quæ præstantissima pars est, postulare, vt Rex Nauarræ gubernator nominetur, illius sit prima & summa auctoritas in omnibus negotiis: & Regina liberetur istis quotidianis Regni laboribus, & vt cum liberis viuat. Huius ordinis auctoritatem tertius ordo sequetur, qui est ciuitatum. Solum cum Ecclesiasticis erit contentio: inter quos tamen multi sunt quorum sententiæ cum Optimatium voluntatibus congruant.
units.tr: (I.iij.) because it was reported yesterday that from the three orders of the kingdom, the nobility, which is the most outstanding part, demands that the King of Navarre be named governor, that his authority be first and supreme in all affairs, and that the Queen be freed from these daily labours of the kingdom and live with her children. The third order, that of the cities, will follow the authority of this order. Only with the churchmen will there be contention; yet among them there are many whose opinions agree with the wishes of the nobles.

units.la: Illud etiam nos consolatur, quod Nauarræ Rex socium fidum habet tanquam fortem Achatem, in causa Religionis D. Admiraldum, quem pij viri optimum consiliarium, & constantissimum patronum nominare poterunt & debent.
units.tr: This also comforts us: the King of Navarre has as a faithful companion, like a brave Achates, in the cause of religion, Admiral Coligny, whom godly men can and should name the best counsellor and most constant patron.

units.la: Postremo ipse Rex Nauarrę aliquid huiusmodi de Principibus Germaniæ expectat & expetit quo ij confirmentur, quos socios habet consiliorum qui terrentur illis vocalis: Nullus Pontificis hostis vnquam pugnauit feliciter. Nullus fœlix Princeps qui à Romana defecit Ecclesia. Hunc Pontificę ea esse inducturia, vt facile queat Cæsarem & Regem Philippum, & totam Italiam, Venetos, Sabaudos, & illos vicinos Heluetiorum quinque pagos, Florentinos, Ferrarienses, in belli societatem pertrahere. Etiam à populi & ab Ecclesiasticorum in ipso Regno conspiratione esse metuendum & quidem vehementer.
units.tr: Finally, the King of Navarre himself expects and seeks something of this kind from the princes of Germany, by which those whom he has as allies in his counsels, and who are frightened by the outspoken voice of the other side, may be strengthened: "No enemy of the Pope has ever fought successfully; no prince who has revolted from the Roman Church has prospered." The Pope will bring these things about, so that he can easily draw the Emperor, King Philip, all Italy, the Venetians, the Savoyards, those neighbouring five cantons of the Swiss, the Florentines and the people of Ferrara into a league of war. Even a conspiracy of the people and of the churchmen within the kingdom itself is to be feared, and indeed greatly.

units.la: Visum mihi fuit ista Illustrissimæ Clementiæ Veštræ perscribere: qua in re primum Deum Patrem & Dominum nostrum le sum Christum oro, vt suo Spiritu mentem I.C.V. reliquorumque Principum illuminet, vt quid optimum factu futurum sit, decer natis. Deinde oro Celsitudinem Vestram, vt mihi veniam det si mea sponte hæc scribam, motus cum istis difficiis Ecclesiarum, tum etiam existimatione de Vestræ Celsitudinis prudentia atque humanitate. Postremo etiam hac perturbatione Heidelbergensis Academiæ: qua sentio ex literis ad Doctorem Bozemium Celsitudinem Vestram paterne comoueri. Postremo oro & obsecro Celsitudinem Vestram, vt ne mihi hæc fraudi sint, quæ diu no stúque in meis cogitationibus recondita, in Vestræ Illustrissimę & Clementissimæ Celsitudinis finum sim ausus deponere. Heri vesperi cum superiora magna ex parte descripta effent, ad me allata est Hefhuffij responsio ad prætiudicium Philippi Melanchthonis de cotrouersia Cænæ Domini: sic enim inscribitur. Plane Melanchthonem in hæreticis Zuinglianis & Caluinianis habet. Illum locum Philippi ex Pauli sententia de ξοιναvία refutat copiose: sed non vere... Adfert Augustinum contra hunc locum Philippi, cum tamen contra ipsum faciat. Origenis auctoritate contemnit, authoritate Lutheri & Epiphanii: cum tamen Epiphanius in refutandis erroribus Origenis, non faciat mentionem huius dogmatis de Coena Domini. Etiam Clementem contemnit: vtrunque tanquam ex tripode magna cum arrogantia: vehementer commotus sum. Scribam de illo libello, & de illo altero plenius sententiam meam, si intellexero hoc meum studium non ingratum esse Illustrissimæ Celsitudini Vestræ, & me tuto posse huiusmodi meas commentationes Optimi Principis fidei atque taciturnitati committere. Meum enim institutum est, conseruare mea studia ad concordiam, & ad compositionem discordiarum: propterea quod hæc ratio non obfutura est Ecclesiæ, & idonea meæ sententiæ. Coena Domini & Baptismus duo sunt postrema & sempiterna Ecclesiæ Christi Sacramenta, quibus hic orbis post Christum illiusque doctrinam nihil habuit salutarius. De his ego ita sentiendum & loquendum & docendum arbitror, ut nihil de illorum dignitate diminuatur: nihil tamen tradatur, quod naturæ sensibus horribile sit, & quod adversarium doctrinæ Christi & Apostolorum, aut quod horum doctrina demonstrari non poterit, neque expressum sit verbis Iesu Christi: cui potestas, potentia, imperium, honos, gloria in æuum sempiternum. Amen. Argentorati, xix. Ianuarij. Anno M. D. LXI.
units.tr: It seemed right to me to set these things down for Your Most Illustrious Clemency. In this matter I first pray God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ that by his Spirit he may enlighten the mind of Your Illustrious Highness and of the other princes, so that they may decide what will be best to do. Next I pray Your Highness to pardon me if I write these things of my own accord, moved both by these difficulties of the Churches and by my esteem for Your Highness's prudence and kindness. Lastly, I am also moved by the disturbance of the Heidelberg Academy, which I perceive from letters to Doctor Boze that Your Highness is paternally moved by. Finally I pray and beg Your Highness that these things, which I have long kept hidden in my own thoughts, not be a cause of blame to me, since I have dared to lay them in the bosom of Your Most Illustrious and Most Clement Highness. Yesterday evening, when the foregoing had been for the most part written out, there was brought to me Hesshus's reply to the preface of Philip Melanchthon on the controversy about the Lord's Supper; for so it is entitled. Plainly he holds Melanchthon to be a Zwinglian and Calvinist heretic. He refutes at length that passage of Philip, from Paul's saying about the [κοινωνία], but not truly... He cites Augustine against this passage of Philip, though he actually acts against him. He scorns Origen's authority, and the authority of Luther and Epiphanius; yet Epiphanius, in refuting the errors of Origen, makes no mention of this doctrine about the Lord's Supper. He also scorns Clement, and both as if from the tripod, with great arrogance; I am greatly stirred. I shall write fuller opinions on that little book and on that other one, if I understand that this zeal of mine is not unwelcome to Your Illustrious Highness, and that I can safely entrust such commentaries of mine to the faith and discretion of so good a prince. For it is my purpose to keep my labours directed to concord and to the settling of discords, since this course will not be harmful to the Church and suits my opinion. The Lord's Supper and Baptism are the two last and everlasting sacraments of Christ's Church, than which this world since Christ and his teaching has had nothing more wholesome. About these I think one must feel, speak and teach in such a way that nothing is taken from their dignity; yet nothing is to be handed down which is horrible to the senses of nature, or which is opposed to the teaching of Christ and the Apostles, or which cannot be shown by their teaching, nor is expressed in the words of Jesus Christ, to whom be power, might, dominion, honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen. Strasbourg, 19 January, in the year 1561.

units.la: Io. Cal. D. Ioanni Knoxo.
units.tr: John Calvin to Master John Knox.

units.la: QVatuor fere mensibus antequam postremæ tuæ literæ mihi redditæ sunt, alteras absque acceperam, quibus anxiete purgabas, quod cum amicis & conterraneis tuis responsum dedissem super certis quæstionibus, ægre tulisse me de his me iterum rogari. Sic autem res habet: nisi mihi polliciti fuissent literas tuto petilatum iri, saltem exemplar apud me seruassem. Sed cum eorum culpa & parum considerata spe fuissem nimis securus: dum aliquanto post tempore dixerunt responsum illud, de quo asseruerant nihil timendum esse periculi, intercidisse, flagitaruntque vt nouum laborem de integro suscipere: commotus sum fateor, & suspiciosum esse respondi quod petebant, acsi me insidiose tentarent. Ne autem mireris tam aspere me loquutum fuisse: certo cognoueram prius illud consilium non fuisse ex eorum sententia. Ergo cum scirem illis minime esse satisfactum, probabilis coniectura animum meum subiuit, supplicem cupere ipsos quod non placebat, & ad me redire, vt aliquid elicerent voto suo propius. Te vero dolose quicquam egisse, neque dixi, neque suspicatus sum. Et eodem momento euanuerat offensio illa, vt nihil excusatione opus fuerit. Ac mihi dolet, quod exciderat ex ore meo, sic in animum tuum penetrasse, vt putares malæ fidei aut altitudinis, a qua te remotum esse iudico, fuisse.
units.tr: About four months before your last letter reached me, I had received another from you, in which you cleared yourself of anxiety. You were troubled that, after I had given a reply on certain questions to your friends and fellow countrymen, I was being asked about these matters again. But the situation is this. Unless they had promised me that the letter would be safely carried to you, I would at least have kept a copy. Yet, through their fault and with too little thought, I had been overconfident in trusting them. Some time later they told me that the reply, which they had assured me carried no danger, had been lost, and they begged me to take up the work afresh. I admit I was moved, and I replied that I was suspicious of what they asked, as if they were trying to trap me. Do not be surprised that I spoke so sharply. I had already known for certain that the plan had not been their own. Since I knew they were not satisfied, it occurred to me as a plausible guess that they were eager, against their own wishes, to see me come back and draw something out of me closer to their desire. As for you, I neither said nor suspected that you had acted deceitfully. That offence vanished at once, so there was no need for an excuse. I am sorry that what slipped from my mouth reached your mind in such a way that you thought I was acting in bad faith or with a haughtiness from which I judge you are far removed.

units.la: Epist. 305 insimulatum.Facessat igitur metus ille vel cura. Nunc ad tuas vices nio,quas mihi nuper attulit pius frater, qui se huc contulit studiorum causa. Euangelium apud vos tam felices lætôsque progressus facere,vehementer,vt par est,lætor.Certa mima vobis moueri non nouum est:sed eo clarius refulget Dei virtus,quod hactenus nulli Satanæ & improborū conatus obstiterunt,quo minus victrice constantia pergeretis in recto cursu: quando ad resistendum nunquam fuissetis pares, nisi è cœlo vobis opem tulisset ille, qui superior est toto mundo. In ceremoniis consido tuum rigorem,quauis multis displiceat,moderatum tamen fore.Danda quidem opera est,vt Ecclesia sordibus omnibus purgetur,quæ ex errore & superstitione manarunt. Sedulò etiam emiti oportet, ne fœdentur Dei mysteria ludicris vel insipidis mixturis.Hac exceptione posita,quœdam etsi minus probentur,tolerandaesse nō ignoras. Intestinis dissidiis Proceres vestros scindi,grauiter doleo,vt par est: ac merito magis te angit ac torquet, quod intus molitur Satā, quàm turbatus antehac fueris ob motus Gallicos. Sed rogandus erit Deus,vt huic quoque malo medeatur.Hic vero samur inter multa discrimina. Vna tantum cœlestis præsidij fiducia nos à trepidatione eximit: quanuis non simus metu vacui. Vale eximie vir,& ex animo colende Frater. Dominus tibi semper adsit,re gubernet,tueatur,ac sustentet sua virtute.Viduitas tua mihi,vt debet,tristis & acerba est. Vxorem nactus eras, cui non reperiuntur passim similes.Sed vnde petendum sit tristi tiæ solatium,quia probè edoctus es, non dubito quin patienter hanc calamitatem feras. Salutabis meo nomine perquam officiosè pios fratres. Collegæ quoque mei vobis multum salutem precantur.Geneuæ,xxiii.Aprilis. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Let that fear or worry, then, be gone. Now I turn to the greetings which a godly brother recently brought me from you, and who came here for the sake of his studies. I rejoice greatly, as is right, that the Gospel is making such happy and prosperous progress among you. That you should be stirred by conflicts is nothing new; but God's power shines all the more brightly because, until now, the attempts of Satan and of the wicked have not prevented you from running your course with victorious constancy. You could never have resisted them had he not brought you help from heaven, he who is above the whole world. As for the ceremonies, I trust that your strictness, though it displeases many, will be moderate. Care must indeed be taken that the Church is purged of all the filth that has flowed from error and superstition. We must also take equal care that the mysteries of God are not defiled by trivial or insipid admixtures. With that proviso, you know that some things, even if less approved, must be tolerated. I grieve deeply, as is fitting, that your leaders are torn by internal dissensions. You are rightly more troubled and tormented by the fact that Satan is plotting within than you were earlier by the disturbances in France. But God must be asked to heal this evil too. We are here caught among many dangers. Our only release from trembling is the confidence in heavenly protection, though we are not free from fear. Farewell, distinguished sir and brother, to be honoured from the heart. May the Lord always be with you, govern you, protect you and sustain you by his power. Your widowhood is, as it should be, sad and bitter to me. You had a wife whose like is not to be found everywhere. But since you have been well taught where to seek consolation in sorrow, I do not doubt that you will bear this calamity patiently. Please greet the godly brethren on my behalf most courteously. My colleagues also send you many greetings. Geneva, 23 April 1561.

units.la: Io. Calvinus Christophoro Goodmanno.
units.tr: John Calvin to Christopher Goodman.

units.la: Literæ tuæ mihi variis nominibus gratissimæ fuerunt.Etsi autem superuacua fuit diuturni silentij excusatio, quia neque scribendi officium exigere soleo ab amicis,& certò persuasus sum fieri non posse, vt vnquam amor erga me tuus intereat: libenter tamen eam amplexus sum,quia piæ solicitudinis testimonium erat, ne putarem me fuisse neglectum. Fratrem nostrū Knoxum,etsi non parum doleo suauissima vxore fuisse priuatū: gaudeo tamen eius morte non ita fuisse afflictum, quin strenuè operam suam Christo & Ecclesiæ impendat. Non vulgare solatium est,quòd te adiutorem fidissimum & apprime idoneum natus est.Nec sane video quomodo in tāta penuria tibi fas sit hāc prouinciam deserere. Quin potiùs ista, quam merito deplorae paucitas,
units.tr: Your letter was very welcome to me for several reasons. Although your excuse for such a long silence was unnecessary, since I do not usually demand the duty of writing from my friends, and I am firmly convinced that your affection for me can never perish, I nonetheless gladly accepted it, because it was a sign of loving concern and showed that I had not been neglected. Our brother Knox, though I grieve not a little that he has been deprived of his most sweet wife, rejoices that he was not so crushed by her death that he does not vigorously devote his labour to Christ and the Church. It is no small comfort that he has found in you a most faithful and thoroughly suitable helper. Nor indeed do I see how, in such a scarcity of workers, it can be right for you to desert this province.

units.la: Epist.306. paucitas, teque reliquos excitare debet ad cordaterpergendum. Quod si necessitas acerrimus est stimulus ad alacritatem, hoc certe in opere Domini maxime valere debet, in quo scimus nunquam irritos fore nostros conatus, cum filios huius saeculi saepe frustre tur sua animositas. Pergendum igitur tibi censeo, integerrime frater, donec additis subsidiis Ecclesiam Scoticam melius stabilierit Deus. Vale eximie vir, & frater mihi colende. Dominus te gubernet Spiritu prudentiae & fortitudinis, laboresque tuos benedicat. Symmystae meae salutant. Genevae, xxiii. Aprilis. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Epist.306. Rather, this very scarcity, which you rightly lament, ought to rouse you and the others to press on steadfastly. If necessity is a very sharp spur to eagerness, this should certainly hold especially in the work of the Lord, in which we know that our efforts will never be in vain, whereas the sons of this age are often frustrated in their own ambitions. I think you should therefore press on, most upright brother, until God, by adding further help, establishes the Scottish Church more firmly. Farewell, distinguished man and brother deserving my respect. May the Lord govern you with the Spirit of prudence and fortitude, and bless your labours. My colleagues salute you. Geneva, 23 April 1561.

units.la: CAL. FRATRIBVS AQVENSIBVS.
units.tr: Calvin to the brethren of Aachen.

units.la: Dilectissimi Domini & fratres, hoc unum vobis persuasum imprimis volumus, non secus nos affici veritrarum calamitatum sensu, quam fraternae nostrae coniunctionis ius & ratio postulat. Ita enim apud vos testandum duximus, ne existime nos eo audacius vos ad tolerantiam cohortari, quod extra tolorum iactum nunc quidem sumus. Cum igitur communis sit nobis vobiscum doloris sensus, sic tamen nobis moderati decet & frenum iniicere, itaque inter nos consilia conferre, ut illi unicui ius omnes in nos est, summa ac simplex obedientia exhibeatur. Scimus non deesse praetextu speciosum, ubi vis a concitata plebe illata vi repellitur, cum hoc aliud sit quam Magistratui resistere: cum ad ò leges ipsae arma quibusuis aduersus latrones induant. Atqui, ut non desint eiusmodi praetextus, summa tamen sapientiae nostrae in eo sita est, ut regulam a coelesti magistro positam obseruemus, ut in patientia nostra possideamus animas nostras. Et sane illud unum appositum est asylum ac certissimum, ut sub ipsius umbraculo unico ab estu & turbine quarumuis tempestatum recepti delitescamus. Iam ubi vim vi repellimus, ipsius manum & auxilium a nobis auertimus. Ac proinde Apostolus, ut frenum iniiciat nostris motibus, exhortatur nos ut demus locum irae ipsius, atque innitamur ipsius promissioni, qua se protectum & alterum suos recepit postquam impij furorem suum in se ipsos despumauerint. Si vero quod accidit vos percellit, sperate Deum reipsa declaraturum, quod semper etiam constitit, sanguine piorum nempe non solum ad eum de terra clamaturum, ut illum requirat, sed eundem etiam semper loco futurum ad magnum Ecclesiae incrementum. Nec frustra scriptura tandiu in eo immoratur, ut praecipitatiam nostram peruincat, cum adeo aegre a nobis obtineri solet, ut futurum Deum sinamus operari pro suo arbitrio, non aute ad nostri affectus in emperiem. Quatumuis enim admoniti pridem sumus, sic eius voluntatem esse, ut Ecclesiae ipsius aedificium miro quodam modo assurgat: vix tamen sustinemus vt vel lapidem illic compingat, quin fere rupamur, vbi opus ex voto non procedit. Atqui hoc illud tempus est labo randi, & tempus tolerandi simul. Laborandi inquam, dum viriliter agemus ac superabimus quaeuis obstacula, vbi officij nostri ratio hoc feret. Nulla morsenim vel minima remissione hic nō tolerabilior ducenda est: & tamen hoc non impediet, quin labo rando simul tolerandum sit: vtq; Spiritu mansuetudinis praediti sine vllo motu nostro fluctus & tempestates aduersariorum frangamus. Si huic consilio manum dederitis, speramus auxiliarem Domini manum vobis quamprimum adfuturam. Ac proinde ipsum oramus, vt vos regat Spiritu prudentiae & fortitudinis, atque in omni bono prosperare donet, vt nomen ipsius glorificetur in vobis magis ac magis. I. Maij. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Most beloved lords and brethren, above all we want this one thing to be firmly fixed in your minds: we are affected by the sense of your grievous calamities no less than the right and reason of our brotherly bond demand. For we thought it right to bear witness to this among you, lest you think that we urge you to endurance more boldly because we are now, indeed, out of the reach of the missiles. Since, then, our sense of sorrow is shared with you, it nevertheless becomes us to moderate it and to put a bridle on it, and so to take counsel together among ourselves that a sum of simple obedience be shown to that authority which all have over us. We know that there is no lack of specious pretexts where force is repelled by force from an excited crowd, though this is something other than resisting the magistrate, since the laws themselves take up arms against any robbers whatever. Yet, however such pretexts are not lacking, the highest wisdom of ours lies in this: that we observe the rule laid down by the heavenly Teacher, that in our patience we may possess our souls. And indeed there is one fitting and most certain refuge, that, received under his single shelter from the heat and whirlwind of whatever storms, we may lie hidden. Now, when we repel force with force, we turn away from ourselves his hand and help. And therefore the Apostle, to put a bridle on our passions, exhorts us to give place to his wrath and to rely on his promise, by which he has received his own as his protector and defender after the wicked have foamed out their fury against themselves. But if what has happened strikes you down, hope that God will in fact declare, as has always been the case, that the blood of the godly will not only cry out to him from the earth, so that he may seek it out, but that he will also always serve for the great increase of the Church. Nor in vain does Scripture dwell so long on this, to overcome our haste, since it is so hard for us to bring ourselves to let God work at his own pleasure and not at the bidding of our feelings. For although we have long been taught that it is his will that the building of his Church rise up in a wonderful manner, we can scarcely bear that he should lay even a stone there without our almost breaking down where the work does not proceed as we wish. Yet this is the time for labouring, and at the same time the time for enduring. For labouring, I say, while we act manfully and overcome whatever obstacles, where the reason of our duty requires it. For no delay, however slight, is to be thought more tolerable here; and yet this will not prevent us from enduring while labouring, so that, endowed with a spirit of gentleness, we may break the waves and storms of our adversaries without any movement on our part. If you give your hand to this counsel, we hope that the helping hand of the Lord will be with you very soon. And therefore we pray him to govern you with the Spirit of prudence and fortitude, and to grant that you prosper in every good thing, so that his name may be glorified in you more and more. 1 May 1561.

units.la: Vobis addictiss. Calvinus.
units.tr: Your most devoted Calvin.

units.la: IOANNES CALVINVS PIIS OMNIBVS DEI cultoribus, qui regnum Christi in Gallia recte constituí cupiunt S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to all godly worshippers of God who desire the kingdom of Christ to be rightly established in France, greeting.

units.la: ETsi patria vobiscum mihi communi, cuius amoenitas multos adse exteros ex remotissimis plagis allicit, iam totos viginti sex annos non aegre carui: quin ea terra habitare mihi nime iucundum esset vel optabile, à qua exulabat Dei veritas, pura Religio & aeternae salutis doctrina, à qua etiam profligatu erat Christi regnum, nec mei eius desiderium hodie solicitat: gen tis tamen ex qua oriundus sum obliuisci, & curam abiicere, neq; humanum, neque fas esset. Ac me quidem illustribus documetis testatum esse arbitror, quàm serio & ardenter cuperem nostratibus prodesse: quibus etiā vtilis forte fuit mea absentia, quò vbe riores ex meo studio fructus perciperent. Cuius boni aestimatio non omnem solum molestiam mihi abstersit, sed suaue reddidit laetumq; exilium. Cum itaque continuo illo temporis progressu cona us fuerim publicè Gallis opitulari, necdesiterim priuatim quoque torpetes excitare, tardos stimulare, trepidates animare, dubios vel flexibiles hortari ad perseuerantiam: danda nunc fuit opera, ne in hoc tam necessario temporis articulo officium erga eos meum cessaret: cuius praestandi diuinitus optima data fuit opportunitas. Nam cum in lucem exirent meae Praelectiones quibus Danielis prophetias interpretatus sum, nihil accidere commodius potuit, quàm si in hoc speculo vobis demonstrarem, Fratres ex animo dilecti, cum hac aetate variis certaminibus probare vellet
units.tr: Although for the full twenty-six years I have not found it hard to be without my common homeland, whose pleasantness draws many foreigners to it from the most remote regions, it would not be pleasant or even desirable for me to live in a land from which God's truth, pure religion and the teaching of eternal salvation have been banished, and from which Christ's kingdom has been driven out. Nor does my longing for it trouble me today. Yet to forget the people from which I am descended, and to cast aside care for them, would be neither human nor right. I think I have shown by my illustrious proofs how earnestly and ardently I wished to help my countrymen, for whom my absence perhaps proved useful, so that they might gain richer fruits from my zeal. The appreciation of this benefit has not only wiped away all my distress but made my exile sweet and happy. Since, therefore, throughout that long passage of time I have tried to help the French publicly, and have not hesitated to stir up privately those who were sluggish, to spur on the slow, to encourage the fearful, and to exhort the doubtful and wavering to perseverance, I now had to take care that in this so necessary moment my duty towards them should not cease, and God gave me the best opportunity to perform it. For when my lectures, in which I have interpreted the prophecies of Daniel, were about to come out into the light, nothing could have happened more opportunely than that I should show you in this mirror, brethren dearly beloved in heart, how God, in his admirable wisdom, wished in this age to test the faith of his people by various conflicts.

units.la: Deus suorum fidē,pro admirabili sua sapientia,veteribus exemplis fulciendos curasse eorū animos,ne grauissimis quoque pro cellis aut tépest.tibus concussi vnquam labascant: vel saltem, si quando nutare contigerit,ne deficiant ad extremum. Quanuis enim stadiū feruis Dei propositum sit multis obstaculis impeditum,quisquis librū hunc diligenter euoluerit,quidquid voluntario nec ignauo curiori à carceribus ad metam vsque dirigēdo, aptū est,in eo cōprehensum reperiet:boni etiā ac strenui athletę experimento agnoscent se ad luctam satis esse instructos.Primū occurret historia tristis quidem, sed valde fructuosa, Danielem eúsque sodales,stante adhuc regno & sacerdotio,in exilio fuisse tractos:acsi Deus per ignominiam & probrum extremae calamitati addiceret præcipuum electi populi florem. Quid enim primo intuitu magis indignum,quàm pueros Angelicis ferè vir tutibus præditos superbo victori tanquam mancipia in prædam cedere,cùm domi incolumes manerent sceleratissimi quique&c perditi Dei contemptores?Hæccine pietatis & inoxiæ vitæ merces, impiis suauiter ob impunitatem sibi blandientibus,quam illi meriti erant pœnam,sanctos lucre? Verum hic quasi in viua imagine cernimus,Deū vbi pessimis quibusque ad tempus parcit,atq; etiam indulget,seruos suos instar auri & argenti examinare,ne durum nobis sit,dum placida quiete fruuntur profani homines, in fornacem probationis coniici. Accedet secundo loco exemplum plusquam virilis prudentiæ, & continentiæ singularis,cū animi magnitudine plane heroica,dum aulicis illecebris tetati pij adolescentes in tenera illa ætate,non modò temperantia superant oblatas sibi delicias, sed quia videbāt astutè se captari, vt paulatim à syncero Dei cultu descisceret:vt se à Diaboli laqueis extricent,honorem veneno illitum non absque præsenti mortis periculo fortiter liberèque aspernantur. Sequetur pugna fœuior & magis formidabilis,cum memorabili constantiæ incredibilis exemplo, dum neque atrocibus minis flectuntur Danielis socij, vt statuæ adoratione se polluant,ac tandem non suo tātum sanguine, sed horribili cruciatu, qui oculis erat propositus, parati sunt syncerum Dei cultum vindicare.Quę verò in huius tragoediæ exitu relucet Dei bonitas, ad nos inuicta fiducia armandos non parum valebit.Addetur nō absimilis Danielis ipsius pugna & victoria cadé,dum leonum truculentiæ obiici maluit,quàm triduo ab ingenua fidei professione abstinere, ne perfida simulatione sacrum Dei nomen proflitueret impiorum ludibriis, & mirabiliter è fouea non secus ac è sepulchro erutus , de Satana eiúsque factione triumphauit.Hic non prodeunt in medium philosophi ,qui subtiliter in umbra & ocio differant de virtutibus: sed infatigabilis sanctorum virorum in studio pietatis cōstantia ncs ad eorum imitationem clara voce inuitat. Ergo nisi profusus simus indociles, ab his magistris discere conuenit, siue blanditiarum laqueos tendat Satan, prudenter ne irretiamur, cauendum esse: siue nos violenter aggrediatur, intrepido mortis & maiorum omnium contemptu frangendos esse eiusmodi insultus. Si quis excipiat, rara esse quae retulimus vtriusq; liberationis exempla: fateor certe Deum non eodem semper modo ad suos servandos manum e coelis exerere, sed quod nobis satis esse debet, testatum fecit fidum se fore vitae nostrae custodem, quoties in aliquo discrimine versabitur: nec impiorum libidini nos esse expositos, quin eorum furorem & turbulentos conatus, si ita visum fuerit, compescat. Nec vero euentus tantum spectandus est: sed quam animo sefanđi viri pro afferenda Dei gloria, se morti devouerint: nec quia Dei beneficio erepti sunt, ideo minus laudis meretur prompta eorum voluntas, quum se victimas obtulerint. Iam inter quos agitationes iactatus fuerit Propheta annis septuaginta, quos in exilio transfegit, reputare operae pretium est. A nullo Rege aeque humaniter tractatus est, atque a Nabuchadnezar: quem tamen expertus est feram bestiam. Aliorum maior crudelitas: donec subito interitu Balfazar, & urbis expugnatione, ad nouos dominos Persas & Medos traductus est: quorum hostilis irruptio cum omnibus pauorem incuteret, minime dubium est quin perculerit eius animum. Etsi autem clementer a Dario fuit exceptus, vt seruitus illa quodam modo effet tolerabilis: Procerum tamen in uidia scelestaque conspiratione, tunc maxime periclitatus est. Verum vt de communi Ecclesiae salute magis erat solicitus, quam priuatae quieti studebat: in quanto moerore eum iacuisse probabile est, & quanta anxietate fuisse constrictum cum tam durae & miserae populi oppressioni nullum finem often deret rerum status? Acquiescebat quidem in Ieremiae vaticinio: sed eius spem tandiu suspensam non languescere, incomparabilis tolerantiae fuit: imo inter tempestuosos fluctus varie distractamnon submergi. Nunc ad prophetias venio: quarum priores destinatae fuerunt Babyloniis: partim quia Deus seruum suum certis insignibus ornare voluit, quae gentem superbissimam & victricem, ipsum reuereri cogerent: partim quia oportuit nomen eius apud prophanos veneratione dignum censeri, vt auctoritate praeditus apud suos munus propheticum liberius exercet. Postquam vero celebre apud Chaldaeos fuit eius nomen, prophetias maioris momenti Deus apud ipsum deposuit, quae pe culiares essent electo populo. Porro sic eas Deus accommodauit in vsum veteris populi, quae & dolorem lenirent opportunis remediis, vacillantes animos ad Christi vsque aduentum sustentarent: vt nostrae quoque aetatis nō minorem habuerit rationem. Nam quod de fluxo & euanido Monarcharum splédore & perpetuo regni Christi statu prædictum est, hodie non minus est vtile cognitu, quàm olim. Ostendit enim Deus omne terrenam potentiam, quæ in Christo fundata non est, caducam esse: regnis vero omnibus: quæ se nimium efferendo, Christi gloriam obscurant, breuem interitum minatus est. Qui nunc longè lateque dominantur Reges, nisi vltro se Christi imperio subiiciant, tristi experientia tandem sentient ad se quoque pertinere horribile illud iudicium. Et quid minus tolerabile, quàm eum fraudare iure suo, cuius præsidio salua manet eorum dignitas? Atqui videmus quàm pauci ex eorum numero, Dei Filium admittant: imò vt omnes moueant lapides, atque extrema quæque potiùs tententct, quàm sinant in suos fines penetrare: multi etiam consiliarij totam suam industriam & studia ad claudendos omnes aditus sedulò cõferunt. Quòd vero interea & nomen Christianum ob tendunt & se fidei Catholicæ optimos defensores s‑ctant, nullo negotio refellitur tam friuola vanitas, si tenetur vera & genuina regni Christi definitio. Non enim aliud est eius vel solium, vel sceptrum, quàm Euangelij doctrina: nec alibi refulget eius maiestas, nec aliter imperium suum obtinet, quâ vbi omnes à summis ad infimos placidâ docilitate, instar ouium vocem eius audiunt, & quocunque vocet, sequuntur. Doctrinam hanc, quæ con tinetur certa Religio atque legitimus Dei cultus, in qua æterna hominum salus & vera fœlicitas consistit, non modò passim rependiant: sed minis, terroribus, ferro, flammáque procul abigunt: nec quicquam omittùt violentiæ ad eam exterminandam. Quæ nam vero cæcitas, & quàm prodigiosa, vt quos ad se comi'er inuitat vnigenitus Dei Filius, non sustineant ipsum osculari? Sed multi pro sua superbia, scilicet, existimant se in ordinem cogi, si summo Regi fasces submittant: alij alias libidines fræn ari nolunt. Atque vt omnium sensus occupat hypocrisis, tenebras appetunt, & in lucem protrahi formidant. Nulla tamen pestis deteriôr, quàm Herodis metus: quasi terrena imperia raperet Monarchis, qui minimis quibusque & contemptissimis ex plebe hominibus cœleste offert. Adde quòd dum alij alios respiciunt, mutua colligatio exitiali nexu omnes deuinctos retinet sub impie tatis iugo. Nam si serió in animum induceret, quid verum sit ac rectum sciscitari: imò tantùm aperirent oculos, non obscura esset cognitio. Sed quia vsu fere compertum est, vbi emergit cum suo Euangelio Christus, simul graues motus oriri, honesto præ-textu reiiciunt cœlestem doctrinam, vt publicæ tranquillitati cõ sulant. Merito fateor, ostisa cestseri potest, quæ turbas gignit mutatio: sed grauis sit Deo iniuria, nisi hoc saltem defertur eius virtuti, vt qualescunque se rueant tumultus, illis sedatis, regnum Filii fui stabiliat. Quanuis cœlum terræ misceri contingat, pretiosior est Dei cultus, quàm vt vlla mercede pensetur minima eius diminutio. Sed falsa inuidia grauant Euangelium, qui pertur bationum materiam esse fingunt. Verùm quidem est, Deum illic oris sui vehementia tonare, quæ concutiat cœlum & terram; sed dum hoc elogio gratiam illius prædicationi conciliat Propheta, fœlix & optanda est illa concussio. Et certè si nó eminet in suo gradu Dei gloria, donec humilietur vniuersa caro super biam hominū, quæ se contrà attollit, nec vnquam cedit nisi inuita, forti & valida Dei ipsius manu prosterni necesse est. Quod si ad Legis promulgationem cótremuit terra, nihil m rum si vis & efficacia Euangelij splendidior appareat. Quare eò suauius decebat amplexari doctrinam, quæ dum mortuos ab infernis excitat, & indignis quos terra sustineat, cœlum aperit, insolitam virtutem exerit: acsi elementa omnia saluti nostræ subscriberent. Ecce autem ex alio fonte manant procellæ & tempestates: quia nunc Proceres & qui in mundo excellunt, non libenter subeunt Christi iugum: nunc imperitum vulgus, antequam gustum capiat, quidquid salutare est, respuit: pars etiam sordibus, porcorum instar, se obleætat: alii tanquâ à Furiis perciti, per cædes grassantur. Præci puo autem furore ad omnia turbâda diabolus instigat, quos habet sibi prorsus mancipatos. Hinc clangor tubarum: hinc conflictus & prælia, dum Heliogabalus Romanus sacerdos cum rubra sua & sanguinaria cohorte & cornutis bestiis præcipiti impetu contra Christum insanit, & vndiq; accersit suppetias ex fœtidi Cleri sui çolluuie, quæ tota, & si non paribus lautitiis, offas tamen quibus pascatur, ex eadé olla profectas sorbet: multi quoque famelici ad conducendas operas aduolant: magna pars ludicum, quæ dudum Saliaribus epulis ventrem farcire consueuit, pro culina & foco pugnat: præsertim vero rabulas ex claustris Monachalibus & Sorbonicis lustris emittit, qui tanquam flabella ignem accendat. Omitto clandestinas artes & nefandas conspirationes, quarum mihi testes optimi esse possent, qui infestissimi sunt pietatis hostes. Nem nem nomino: satis est digito monstrafle, qui satis superq; vobis noti sunt. In hac confusa tot bestiarum irruptione si perplexi hæreant, qui pendent à multiplici rerum euentu, nihil mirum est: sed diffidentiæ suæ culpam iniuste, & perperà reiiciunt in sacrum Christi Euangelium. Demus totum Acheronta cum suis Furiis iam ad prælium desc̈edere: an Deus in cœlis otiosus sedebit, vt causam suam deferat & prodat? atque vbi fe opposuerint: an eius victoriam impediet quamlibet versutæ hominum astutiæ, vel impetuofi conatus? Papa, inquiunt, longam factionem secum trahet. Iusta incredulitatis merces, trepidare ad strepitum folij cadentis! Quid vos autem tem 'male prouidi Consiliari? Faceflat Christus,ne quid turbet nouitas. Paulò pòst ergo fcitietis, quanto satius fuisset Deum habere propitium, & sprets nihili terroribus in eius præsidio cõquiefcere, quàm eum apeto bello lacessere,ne malos & sinistros genios ad iram prouoctis. Certè vbi omnia discussa fuerint,Papæ defensoribus,fuprftitio quæ hactenus regnauit,nihil aliud est quàm malum bene positum:quod mouendum esse non censent,quia sine iactu non posse fieri videtur. Quibus verò cordi est Dei gloria, & qui syncera pietate sunt præditi,longè aliud propositum esse debet nempe ita suam operam Deo im pendere vt euentus omnes eus prouidentiæ commendent. Qui si nihil nobis esset pollicitus, forte iusta esset timendi & assiduè vacillandi causa: sed cùm tutiessit testatus nunquam auxilium suum in asserendo Christi sui regno defore,in hac fiducia recumbere,vnicum est recteagend compendium. Porrò vestrum est, optimi fratres, quantum fert cuiusquefacultas,& vocatio postulabit,cordatè satagere vt vera Religio integrum statum recuperet. Quantopere hactenus conatusfim omnes tumultuandi an sis præcidere,referre necesse non est:modò coram summo Iudice,Angelos omnes habeant testes,per me non stetisse,quò mi nùs sedatos absque vlla noxa progressus ageret Christi regnum. Et aliquid mea sedulitate profectum esse arbitror, ne suas metas transilirent priuati homines. Nunc etsi admirabili virtute longiùs Ecclesiæ suæ restitutionem prouexit Deus, quàm ausus fuisset sperare, memoria amen repetere conuenit quid suis præcipiat Christus, nempe vt animas suas in tolerantia possideant. Quòcriam pertinet quæ à Daniele exposita fuit vi sio : Lapidem, à quo contra sunt quæcunque Deo bellum intulerant regna,non fuisse hominum manu formatum:& quanuis rudis esset ac impolitus creuisse tamen in magnum montem. Cuius rei vos monentes estis duxi,vt inter minarum toni trua placidè expectetis, dum inanes nebulæ cœlesti virtute dissipatæ euanescant. Nec verò me latet, vt de innumeris triginta annorum ignibus taceam quantas indignitates his postremis sex mensibus pertuleritis: quoties pluribus in locis à tumultuosa plebe facta in vos fuerit irruptio:quoties fueritis impetiti nuc lapidibus,nunc gladiis: vt infiniti fuerint hostes, quò pacatos vestros conuentus subita vi & inopinata opprimerent:vt occisi fuerint alij in ædibus suis,alij in compitis tracta per ludibrium mortuorum corpora,raptatæ mulieres,plurimi vulnerati,graui da etiam mulier cum suo fœtu transfossa fuerit, ædes effractæ ac dirutæ.Verùm quamuis ætatis adhuc instarent,vt vos pro betis Christi discipulos,probeque in eius schola formatos, dada opera est,ne vlla impiorum rabies,dum ita intemperanter feruntur,
units.tr: God, in his wonderful wisdom, has taken care to strengthen the faith of his people with examples from the past, so that their minds, shaken even by the most violent storms and tempests, never give way, or at least, if they chance to totter at any time, do not fail in the end. For although the race course set before God's servants is hindered by many obstacles, whoever reads this book carefully will find in it everything that suits a willing and eager runner, from the starting gates to the goal. Trained athletes will also recognise from their own experience that they are sufficiently equipped for the struggle. First comes a history sad indeed, but very fruitful: while the kingdom and the priesthood still stood, Daniel and his companions were dragged into exile, as if God, through shame and disgrace, were handing over the chief flower of his chosen people to the utmost calamity. For what could seem more unworthy at first sight than that boys, almost endowed with angelic virtues, should be surrendered as slaves and plunder to a proud conqueror, while the most wicked and abandoned despisers of God remained safe at home? Is this the reward of piety and of an innocent life, that the holy should be made to suffer, while the impious, flattering themselves with impunity, are spared the punishment they deserved? Yet here we see, as in a living image, that God, while for a time he spares and even indulges the worst of men, tests his servants as gold and silver are tested, so that the profane, enjoying a calm quiet, are not hard for us to bear, and yet are cast into the furnace of trial. In the second place comes an example of more than manly prudence and singular self-restraint, with a truly heroic greatness of spirit: the godly young men, at that tender age, not only rise above the pleasures offered them at court by their temperance, but, seeing that they were being cunningly enticed to turn gradually away from the pure worship of God, they bravely and freely scorn an honour smeared with poison, not without immediate danger of death, so that they might free themselves from the snares of the Devil. Then follows a fiercer and more formidable battle, with a remarkable example of incredible constancy: Daniel's companions are not moved by savage threats to defile themselves by worshipping the statue, and in the end they are ready to defend the pure worship of God not only with their own blood, but with the horrible torture that was set before their eyes. The goodness of God that shines forth in the outcome of this tragedy will go a long way toward arming us with unconquerable confidence. There is added a no less similar battle and victory of Daniel himself, when he preferred to be thrown to the fury of lions rather than abstain for three days from the open confession of faith, lest by a treacherous pretence he should prostitute the holy name of God to the mockery of the impious; and, drawn out of the pit as if out of a grave, he triumphed over Satan and his faction. Here no philosophers come forward who subtly debate about the virtues in the shade and at leisure; but the tireless constancy of holy men in the pursuit of godliness calls us with a clear voice to imitate them. Therefore, unless we are utterly unteachable, it is fitting to learn from these masters: whether Satan lays the snares of flattery, we must take care to be wise so that we are not caught; or whether he attacks us by force, such assaults must be broken by fearless contempt of death and of all greater evils. If someone objects that the examples of both deliverances that we have related are rare, I admit indeed that God does not always stretch out his hand from heaven in the same way to save his people; but what ought to be enough for us is that he has testified that he will be a faithful guardian of our life whenever we are in some danger, and that we are not exposed to the lust of the wicked without his restraining their fury and turbulent attempts, if it seems good to him. Nor indeed is the outcome alone to be regarded, but also how readily these holy men devoted themselves to death for the sake of bringing glory to God; nor, because they were snatched away by God's kindness, does their ready will deserve any less praise, since they offered themselves as victims. Now it is worth considering among what troubles the Prophet was tossed during the seventy years that he spent in exile. He was treated as humanely by no king as by Nebuchadnezzar, yet he experienced him as a wild beast. Others were more cruel; until, after Belshazzar's sudden death and the capture of the city, he was transferred to new masters, the Persians and Medes, whose hostile invasion, since it struck terror into everyone, certainly must have shaken his spirit. And although he was kindly received by Darius, so that his servitude was in some way bearable, yet, through the envy and wicked conspiracy of the nobles, he was then in the greatest danger. But since he was more anxious for the common safety of the Church than devoted to his private peace, how great the grief must have been in which he lay, and how great the anxiety that gripped him, when the state of affairs promised no end to the so harsh and wretched oppression of the people! He indeed acquiesced in Jeremiah's prophecy; but that his hope, held in suspense so long, did not grow faint was a matter of incomparable endurance; indeed, that amid the stormy waves, though variously tossed about, he was not submerged. Now I come to the prophecies: of which the earlier were directed to the Babylonians, partly because God wished to adorn his servant with certain distinctions that would compel that most proud and victorious nation to reverence him, and partly because it was fitting that his name should be considered worthy of veneration even among the profane, so that, invested with authority, he might exercise his prophetic office more freely among his own people. But after his name became famous among the Chaldeans, God committed to him more important prophecies, which were peculiar to the chosen people. Moreover, God so adapted these to the use of the old people that they both eased their sorrow with timely remedies and sustained their wavering minds until the coming of Christ; and he has likewise taken no smaller account of our own age. For what has been foretold about the fleeting and vanishing splendour of monarchs and the perpetual state of Christ's kingdom is today no less useful to know than it was formerly. For God shows that all earthly power that is not founded in Christ is frail; and he threatens a speedy ruin to all kingdoms which, by exalting themselves too much, obscure the glory of Christ. The kings who now rule far and wide, unless they willingly submit themselves to the rule of Christ, will at last learn by sad experience that that dreadful judgment applies to them too. And what is less tolerable than to deprive him of his right, by whose protection their own dignity remains safe? Yet we see how few of their number admit the Son of God; indeed, they move every stone and try every extreme measure rather than allow him to enter their borders; many counsellors also devote all their energy and zeal to closing every access. Meanwhile, though they boast of the Christian name and pose as the best defenders of the Catholic faith, such frivolous vanity is easily refuted if the true and genuine definition of Christ's kingdom is held. For his throne or sceptre is nothing other than the doctrine of the Gospel; nor does his majesty shine anywhere else, nor does he obtain his rule in any other way, than where all, from the highest to the lowest, with calm docility, like sheep, hear his voice and follow him wherever he calls. This doctrine, which contains the sure religion and the lawful worship of God, in which the eternal salvation and true happiness of men consist, not only do they everywhere refuse, but they drive it far away with threats, terrors, sword and flame, and omit no violence to exterminate it. And what blindness, and how monstrous, that they do not endure to kiss the only-begotten Son of God, whom he kindly invites to himself! But many, through their pride, think, of course, that they are being brought into subjection if they bow down to the supreme King; others do not want to restrain their various lusts. And as hypocrisy occupies everyone's senses, they seek darkness and fear to be dragged into the light. Yet no plague is worse than the fear of Herod, as if he were snatching earthly empires from monarchs, when he offers heavenly ones to the humblest and most despised men of the common people. Add that while some look at others, their mutual alliance keeps all bound in a deadly knot under the yoke of impiety. For if they were seriously to resolve to inquire what is true and right, indeed if they merely opened their eyes, the knowledge would not be obscure. But since experience has almost shown that wherever Christ arises with his Gospel, serious disturbances arise at the same time, they reject the heavenly doctrine under a specious pretext, in order to look after public tranquillity. I admit, rightly, that the disturbance that change produces cannot be easily checked; but it would be a grave wrong to God unless at least this is granted to his power: that however the tumults may rage, once they are calmed he will establish the kingdom of his Son. Even if heaven should happen to be mixed with earth, the worship of God is too precious to be weighed against any reward for even its smallest diminution. But false hatred burdens the Gospel, those who pretend that it is the cause of the disturbances. It is true that God thunders there with the force of his mouth, which shakes heaven and earth; but while the Prophet, by this description, recommends his grace to his preaching, that shaking is happy and to be desired. And certainly, if the glory of God does not stand out in its own degree until the whole flesh is humbled by the pride of men, which sets itself against him and never yields except unwillingly, it must needs be overthrown by his own strong and powerful hand. And if the earth trembled at the promulgation of the Law, it is no wonder if the power and efficacy of the Gospel appear more splendid. Therefore it was all the more fitting to embrace with sweetness the doctrine which, while it raises the dead from the depths and opens heaven to those unworthy of the earth that bears them, displays an unusual power, as if all the elements were subscribing to our salvation. But see, storms and tempests burst from another source: for now the nobles and those who are eminent in the world unwillingly submit to the yoke of Christ; now the ignorant crowd, before it has tasted anything, spits out whatever is wholesome; some also wallow in filth like pigs; others, as if driven on by the Furies, rage with slaughter. But the Devil incites to the disturbance of everything with a special fury those whom he holds wholly as his slaves. Hence the blare of trumpets, hence the clash and battles, while the Roman priest Heliogabalus, with his red and bloody cohort and horned beasts, rages against Christ with headlong assault, and summons help from every side from the filthy dregs of his clergy, which, though not with equal luxuries, all drink down the morsels to feed on, derived from the same pot; many hungry men also rush to hire themselves out; a great part of the judges, who have long been accustomed to stuff their bellies with Salian feasts, fights for the kitchen and the hearth; and above all he sends forth brawlers from the monastic cloisters and Sorbonne brothels, who, like bellows, fan the fire. I pass over the secret arts and wicked conspiracies, of which the best witnesses would be the most hostile enemies of godliness. I name no one; it is enough to point with the finger at those who are more than well known to you. If men who depend on the many chances of events hang in doubt amid this confused irruption of so many beasts, it is no wonder; but they unjustly and wrongly throw the blame for their own distrust upon the holy Gospel of Christ. Let us grant that all Acheron with its Furies is now setting out for battle: will God sit idle in the heavens, so that he betrays and abandons his own cause? And when they have arrayed themselves, will any cunning of men, however crafty, or any impetuous attempts, hinder his victory? The Pope, they say, will draw a long faction with him. A fair reward for unbelief, to tremble at the rustle of a falling leaf! But what of you, most shortsighted counsellors? Let Christ take care that novelty does not disturb anything. Soon, therefore, you will know how much better it would have been to have God propitious, and, scorning terrors, to rest in his protection, rather than to provoke him to a rash war, lest you stir up evil and sinister spirits against you. Surely, when everything has been examined, the superstition that has hitherto reigned for the Pope's defenders is nothing other than an evil that is well settled, which they do not think should be moved, because it seems that it cannot be done without a throw of the dice. But for those to whom the glory of God is dear, and who are endowed with sincere piety, a quite different purpose should be theirs: namely, to devote their effort to God in such a way that they commend all outcomes to his providence. If he had promised us nothing, perhaps there would be a just cause for fear and for constant wavering; but since he has testified most surely that he will never fail to give his help in defending the kingdom of his Christ, to rest in this confidence is the one right and short way of acting. Moreover, it is your duty, best brothers, to strive wisely, as far as the ability and calling of each one requires, that true religion may recover its full state. It is not necessary to recount how earnestly I have hitherto tried to cut off all tumults; only let all the angels be witnesses before the supreme Judge that it was not through me that the kingdom of Christ was prevented from advancing, calmed and without any harm. And I think something has been achieved by my diligence, so that private persons did not leap over their bounds. Now, although by his wonderful power God has advanced the restoration of his Church further than we had dared to hope, it is fitting to recall in memory what Christ commands his own, namely that they possess their souls in patience. To this pertains what was set forth by Daniel in his vision: that the stone against which all the kingdoms that had waged war on God were struck had not been formed by human hand, and that, although it was rough and unpolished, it grew into a great mountain. Since you are reminded of this, I have wished that, amid the thunder of threats, you should calmly wait until the empty clouds, scattered by heavenly power, vanish away. Nor am I unaware, to say nothing of the countless fires of the thirty years, what indignities you have endured in these last six months: how often you have been attacked by a tumultuous crowd in several places; how often you have been assailed, now with stones, now with swords; how many enemies there have been, so that they might overwhelm your peaceful assemblies by sudden and unexpected force; how some have been killed in their own houses, others in the streets, the bodies of the dead dragged about in mockery; women have been seized, very many wounded, a pregnant woman has been pierced through with her unborn child, and houses have been broken into and destroyed. But although they press on in years, so that you, as true disciples of Christ, well formed in his school, should be..., care has been taken that no rage of the impious, while they are carried on so intemperately,
Luke 21:19

units.la: Hæc autem tum erant præludia tantum eorum, quæ eo de modo ticulatim annis sequentibus accidernt puris viris ac mulieribus in Gallia. moderationem qua sola haetenus viti fraétíque fuerunt, excu-tiat. Quod si tædium vobis afferat diuturnitas, subinde in men-tem redeat celebre illud vaticinium, in quo ad viuum Ecclesiæ conditio depicta est. Ostendit quidem tunc Propheta suo Deus quæ certamina, anxietates, molestias, discrimina Iudæos manere à fine exilij, lætóque in patriam reditu, vsque ad Christi aduentum: sed facit temporum similitudo, vt nobis eadem conueniant, ac proinde aptanda sint in vsum nostrum. Miseræ Ecclesiæ, quæ diu profundo malorum diluuio submersa fuerat, gratulabatur Daniel, quum ex annorum supputatione colligeret, instare liberationis diem à Ieremia prædictum. Atqui respondum accipit, acerbiorem fore populi fortem ex quo reddita fuerit libertas, vt à continua ingentium malorum serie vix respiret. Nō sine summa doloris amaritudine & multis fastidiis spem suam protexerat annis septuaginta: nunc Deus tempus septuplicando, lethale quodammodo vulnus cordi eius penitus infligit. Nec verò tantum pronunciat populum, vbi politiminio reuersus vires collegerit, vrbémque & templum extruxerit, nouis postea molestiis fore obnoxium: sed inter ipsa lætitiæ primordia, vix dum gustata gratiæ suauitate, anxietati eum addicit. Iam calamitates quæ paulò post sequutæ sunt, quarum multiplex illic texitur catalogus, quum ad solum auditum nunc expauescamus, quàm pu-dimus rudi populo lugubres fuisse & acerbas? Templum videre profanatum sacrilegi tyranni audacia, sacra probrose mixta foedis inquinamentis, libros omnes Legis in ignem coniici, vt tota religio aboleretur, quàm horribile fuit spectaculum? Ad idem in cendium raptari quicunque ingenue constanterque profitebantur se perstare in Dei cultu, qui poterant teneri & debiles sine ingenti conflernatione aspicere? Et hoc erat consilium tyranni, vt immanitas ad defectionem minus cordatos adigeret. Sub Machabæis quædam visa est relaxatio offerri, sed quæ mox fœuillimis cladibus deformata, nunquam luctu & mœrore caruit. Nā cum hostis & copiis & omni bellico apparatu longè præcelleret, nihil potius fuit omnibus qui pro defensione Ecclesiæ, arma sumpserant, quàm se abdere in ferarum lustra, aut vagari per fyluas in summa egestate, rerumque omnium inopia. Acceßit aliud genus tentationis, quòd se improbi & perfidi, fallaci zeliia ëantia, vt dicit Daniel, Iudæ & eius fratribus adiunxerunt. Quo artificio Satan infamia aspersit, manum à Iuda colleçam, acti latrunculorum effet turba. Sed bonis nihil magis luctuosum, quàm dum Sacerdotes ipsi, prout quemq; rapiebat sua ambitio, nefariis pactis templum & Dei cultum prodiderunt. Nec modo venalis fuit sacra illa dignitas: sed empta mutuis cædibus, atque etiam parricidiis. Hinc factum, vt omnium ordinum homines, quanuis
units.tr: These, however, were only the first foretastes of what, in the years that followed, befell pure men and women in France, one by one, in that manner. Let it shake off that moderation by which alone they have hitherto been kept alive and unbroken. If the long duration wearies you, let that famous prophecy come back to your mind, in which the condition of the Church is depicted to the life. God indeed showed his prophet what struggles, anxieties, troubles and dangers awaited the Jews from the end of the exile until the coming of Christ, even after their joyful return to their homeland. But the similarity of the times makes these same things fit us, and therefore they are to be applied to our use. Daniel rejoiced for the wretched Church, which had long been submerged in the deep flood of evils, when from counting the years he gathered that the day of deliverance foretold by Jeremiah was at hand. Yet he receives the answer that the lot of the people after their liberty was restored would be harsher, so that they would hardly draw breath from a continuous series of great evils. For seventy years he had sustained his hope, not without the bitterest grief and many weariness; now God, by multiplying the time sevenfold, inflicts a wound on his heart that is in a sense deadly. Nor does he only declare that the people, once they had returned, gathered their strength, and built the city and the temple, would afterwards be exposed to new troubles; but even at the very beginnings of joy, scarcely having tasted the sweetness of grace, he hands him over to anxiety. Now the calamities that followed soon after, whose manifold catalogue is woven there, though we now shudder merely at hearing of them, how grievous and bitter must they have been to a rude people? To see the temple profaned by the audacity of a sacrilegious tyrant, sacred things shamefully mixed with foul defilements, and all the books of the Law thrown into the fire so that the whole religion might be abolished: how horrible a spectacle that was! To be dragged to the same fire whoever openly and steadfastly professed that they persevered in the worship of God: who, even the tender and weak, could look upon this without great dismay? And this was the tyrant's plan, that his savagery might drive the less steadfast to apostasy. Under the Maccabees a certain relaxation seemed to be offered, but it was soon disfigured by most cruel defeats, and never lacked mourning and grief. For since the enemy far surpassed them both in forces and in every warlike equipment, nothing was more to be expected by all who had taken up arms for the defence of the Church than to hide themselves in the dens of wild beasts, or to wander through the woods in the utmost poverty and lack of all things. Another kind of temptation was added, namely that wicked and treacherous men, pretending a deceitful zeal, as Daniel says, joined themselves to Judas and his brothers. By this artifice Satan cast infamy upon them, so that the band of Judas, deserted, became a mere troop of brigands. But nothing was more sorrowful for good men than when the priests themselves, as each was carried off by his own ambition, betrayed the temple and the worship of God by wicked bargains. Nor was that sacred dignity merely for sale; it was bought with mutual slaughter and even parricides. Hence it came about that men of all orders, although circumcision and sacrifices remained in use, and corruptions raged so freely and unpunished everywhere, at last became profane, so that it was a rare marvel, at the time when Christ appeared, to look for the kingdom of God. For very few are distinguished by this praise. Although
