units.la: Dan. 11.32, 33, 34, 35 quanuis Circuncifio & sacrificia in vsu manerent,& corruptelis ita passim & impunè grassantibus,tandem profanescerent: vt rarum fuerit miraculum,quo tempore apparuit Christus,regnum Dei expectare. Paucissimi enim hac laude insigniuntur.Si in illa indigna Ecclesiæ deformitate,in multis dissipationibus,inter diros terrores, agrorum vastationem, ædium direptiones, mortis pericula, pios animos sustinuit Danielis vaticinium, quum adhuc obscuris umbris implicita essET religio,&doctrina fere extincta,& sacerdotes ipsi, vt erant degeneres,sacra omnia pessundarent:quàm pudenda erit nostra mollities,nisi hæc Euangelij claritas,in qua Deus paternam faciem nobis ostendit, sursum nos supra omnia obstacula attollat, constantiáque infatigabili fulciat?Sicuti enim dubium non est quin ũc serui Dei,quæ de exilio Babylonico à Prophetis dicta erant, ad suam ætatem accomodarint leniendo præsentium malorum dolori: ita nostrum est oculos habere defixos in Patrum miserias, ne refugiamus ad eam Ecclesiam aggregati,cui dictum est, Paupercula,tempestate obruta,& solatio priuata,ecce ego te suscipio:& quæ alibi,postquam conquesta est dorsum suum fuisse laceratu ab impiis:non secus atq; ager sub fulci tractu proscinditur,gloriatur tamé continuò post,incisos fuisse illorum funes à Deo iusto, vt non prævaluerint. Nec verò illorum modò temporum exéplis ad spem & patientiam nos animauit Propheta:sed exhortationem à Spiritu dictatam,quæ ad totum Christi Regnum extenditur,nobisque propria est, adiunxit.Quare nobis durum non fit in eorum numero comprehendi, quos igni probatum iri denunciat vt dealbentur , cùm omnes crucis molestias fatis superque compensat inæstimabilis fœlicitas,& gloria quæ inde nascitur.Ac quâquam hæc plurimis sunt insipida,ne eorum socordia & stupor nos segnio res reddat,probè cordibus infixum sit quod mox denunciat Propheta,impios impiè quidem acturos,quia nihil intelligent:filios tamen Dei intelligentia fore prædictos,vt rectum diuinæ vocationis cursum teneant.Fontem quoque brutæ illius cæcitatis,quæ vulgò cernitur,tenere operæpretium est,vt nobis cœlestis doctrina sapiat.Neque enim aliunde fit vt Christum cum suo Euangelio maior pars vilipédat, nisi quò secure sibi indulgendo,neque timore vllo, nec malorum suorum sensu, nec iræ Dei horrore expergiscuntur ad ferìò ardenterque appetendam, quæ sola nos ab æterni interitus abysso eripit , redemptionem. Interea verò deliciis,voluptatibus,& aliis illecebris capti, vel potius fascinati,nulla tanguntur beatæ æternitatis cura. Etsi autem multiplices sunt eorum sectæ, à quibus Euangelij doctrina contemptim despicitur , ac in aliis magis eminet superbia, in aliis mollities, in aliis quàdam mentis cbrietas,in aliis somnolentus torpor:re-
units.tr: Dan. 11.32, 33, 34, 35 although circumcision and sacrifices remained in use, and corruptions raged so freely and unpunished everywhere, at last became profane, so that it was a rare marvel, at the time when Christ appeared, to look for the kingdom of God. For very few are distinguished by this praise. If, in that unworthy deformity of the Church, amid many dispersions, among dire terrors, the devastation of fields, the plundering of houses and dangers of death, the prophecy of Daniel sustained pious souls, when religion was still entangled in obscure shadows, doctrine was almost extinct, and the priests themselves, being as degenerate as they were, were ruining all sacred things, how shameful will our softness be, unless this clarity of the gospel, in which God shows us his fatherly face, lifts us up above all obstacles and strengthens us with unwearying constancy? For just as there is no doubt that the servants of God then applied what the prophets had said about the Babylonian exile to their own age, easing the pain of present evils, so it is ours to keep our eyes fixed on the miseries of the Fathers, lest we flee to that Church, gathered together, to which it was said, "Poor little one, overwhelmed by the storm and deprived of comfort, behold, I take you up." And elsewhere, after she complained that her back had been torn by the impious, as a field is ploughed by a long furrow, she nevertheless boasts soon after that their cords were cut by the just God so that they did not prevail. Nor has the prophet encouraged us to hope and patience only by the examples of those times; he has also added an exhortation dictated by the Spirit, which extends to the whole kingdom of Christ and belongs to us. Therefore it should not be hard for us to be counted among those whom he declares will be tried by fire so that they may be made white, since the inestimable happiness and the glory that springs from it fully compensate for all the troubles of the cross. And although these things are very insipid to most people, lest their sloth and stupor make us more sluggish, let it be fixed deeply in our hearts what the prophet goes on to declare: the wicked will act wickedly, indeed, because they understand nothing; but the sons of God will be endowed with understanding, so that they may keep to the straight course of their divine calling. It is also worth our while to grasp the source of that brutish blindness which is commonly seen, so that heavenly doctrine may taste sweet to us. For the greater part despise Christ and his gospel for no other reason than that, indulging themselves securely, they are roused neither by fear, nor by a sense of their own evils, nor by the horror of God's wrath, to seek eagerly and earnestly that redemption which alone snatches us from the abyss of eternal destruction. Meanwhile, caught by delights, pleasures and other allurements, or rather bewitched, they are touched by no concern for blessed eternity. Although there are many sects of those who contemptuously despise the doctrine of the gospel, and in some pride stands out more, in others softness, in others a certain drunkenness of mind, in others sleepy torpor,

units.la: K.j. periemus tamen ex prophana securitate manare contemptum, quia nemo in seipsum defcedit ad excutiendas suas miserias, vt illis remedium quærat. Prodigiosa quidem dementia est, vbi no bis incumbit Dei maledictio iustaque eius vindicta nos vrget, ex cuffa omni folicitudine, nobis adhuc placere, ac si nihil effet me tuendum. Atqui vitium plus quàm commune est, vt qui millies rei sunt, dignique mille æternis mortibus, friuolis ceremoniis er ga Deum leuiter defuncti, soporem vel potius veternum, sibi ob ducant. Porrò cùm denunciet Paulus mortiferum esse Euangelij odorem omnibus quorum mentes Satan fascinat, vt saporem eius in vitam gustemus, necesse est ad Dei tribunal nos sistere, & illuc subinde citare nostras cófcientias, quibus serio terrore vul neratis recóciliatio quam pretioso suo sanguine nobis Christus peperit, pro sua dignitate & pretio a nobis æstimetur. Itaque Angelus, vt Christi doctrinæ reuerentiam & auctoritatem concili-er, concionatur de æterna iustitia, quâ mortis suæ sacrificio obsignauit modum & rationem simul exprimens, quia deleta fue ritac expiata iniquitas. Nos ergo, dum mundus in suis lasciuiis bacchatur, damnationis quam meriti fumus cognitio expauefa ctos coram Deo humiliet ac dum se prophani homines terreris deliciis ingurgitant, cupide amplexemur hunc incomparabilem thesaurum, in quo recondita est solida beatitudo. Garriant hostes nostri vt libuerit, sibi quoque curæ esse vt Deum habeat pro pitium: cum non nisi dubitanter inuocandum esse sentiat, quod erat salutis fundamentum ab illis euerti constat. Fidem nostram qua volent petulantia insectentur, modo nobis liquido constet neminem nisi eius beneficio hanc prærogatiuam consequi, vt li bere pacataq; fiducia Christi patrocinio fretus Deu Patrem inuo cet. Verùm nunquam vigebit vt par est in nobis pietatis studiu, do nec mentes nostras, quæ alioqui in terram nimis propensæ sunt, sursum attollere discamus, eáque in continua cœlestis vitæ meditatione exercere. Qua in parte se prodit mira humani generis vanitas, quòd cum omnes de huius vitæ breuitate quasi Philo-sophi præclarè loquantur: nemo tamen ad illam perpetuam af pirat. Itaque non abs re Paulus Colossenfium fidem & charitatem commendans, eos perfpem animari dicit, quæ in cœlis repo sita est. Alibi verò de fine gratiæ differens, quæ nobis, in Christo patefacta est, dicit nos inde erudiri, vt abnegata omni impietate, mundanisq; desideriis, sobrie, iuste, & pie viuamus in hoc mundo expectantes beatam spem & aduentum gloriæ magni Dei & Saluatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Hæc igitur expectatio impedimentis omnibus solutos ad se nos rapiat: & quo magis Epicurea tabe refertus est orbis, ne ad nos vsque serpat contagio, eò acrius eniti nos decet, donec ad metam pertigerimus. Porrò etsi dolendum lendum est, tantam turbam vltrò perire, quòd tamen in suum exitium quasi devoti ruunt, ne nos conturbet væsanus eorum furor, succurrat altera Danielis admonitio, salutem certam omnibus repositam esse qui inuenti fuerint scripti in libro. Quanuis autem in arcano Dei consilio, quæ prima est salutis nostræ cau sa, electio abscondita sit, quando tamen omnium qui in Christi corpus fidei Euangelij inserti sunt, minime dubia est adoptio: hoc testimonio contenti, strenuè in cursu fœliciter incœpto pergite. Quòd si diutius adhuc dimicādum erit (vt vobis denuntio restare duriores quàm putatis pugnas) quocunq; impetu ebulliat imperorum rabies, atque vt totos inferos concitent, memineritis finitum vobis esse stadium à cœlesti Agonotheta, cuius legibus eò alacrius parendum est, quia suis vires ad finem vsque suppeditat. Quando autem mihi fas non est stationem in qua me Deus manere voluit, deserere, hic meus labor vobis dicatus, mei ad vos adiuuandos studij pignus sit, donec completa mea peregrinatione, cœlestis Pater pro immensa sua misericordia in æternā hæreditatem simul vobiscum me colligat. Dominus vos gubernet Spiritu suo, fratres ex animo mihi charissimi, tueatur suo præsidio contra omnes hostium machinas, inuictáque virtute sustineat.
units.tr: K.j. we shall nevertheless find that this contempt springs from profane security, because no one goes down into himself to shake out his miseries and so seek a remedy for them. It is a monstrous madness that, when God's curse and just vengeance press upon us, we should be free of all anxiety and still wish to please ourselves, as if there were nothing for us to guard against. Yet it is more than a common vice that those who are a thousand times guilty, and deserving a thousand eternal deaths, having lightly discharged their duty to God with frivolous ceremonies, should count for themselves a drowsiness, or rather a lethargy. Moreover, since Paul declares that the gospel is a deadly odour to all whose minds Satan has bewitched, so that we may taste its savour unto life, we must stand before God's judgment seat and summon our consciences there from time to time, so that, once seriously wounded by terror, we may value the reconciliation that Christ won for us by his precious blood according to its dignity and price. Therefore the angel, in order to win reverence and authority for the doctrine of Christ, preaches of eternal righteousness, by which he sealed the sacrifice of his death, expressing at the same time the manner and the reason, namely that iniquity has been blotted out and expiated. Let us therefore, while the world revels in its wantonness, be humbled before God and struck with dread at the knowledge of the damnation we deserved; and while profane men gorge themselves on earthly delights, let us eagerly embrace this incomparable treasure, in which true blessedness is laid up. Let our enemies chatter as they please; let them also be concerned that they have God propitious, since it is clear that they think he must be called upon only doubtfully, which was the foundation of salvation and is plainly overturned by them. Let them assail our faith with whatever wantonness they choose, provided it is clear to us that no one obtains this privilege except through his benefit, so that, relying on Christ's patronage with a free and peaceful confidence, we may call upon God the Father. But the zeal for piety will never flourish in us as it should, unless we learn to lift up our minds, which are otherwise too prone to the earth, and to exercise them in continual meditation on the heavenly life. In this respect the marvellous vanity of the human race shows itself: although all speak most eloquently, like philosophers, of the brevity of this life, yet no one aspires to that which is perpetual. Therefore it is not without reason that Paul, commending to the Colossians their faith and love, says that they are sustained by the hope laid up for them in heaven. Elsewhere, speaking of the purpose of the grace that has been revealed to us in Christ, he says that we are taught by it to renounce all impiety and worldly desires, and to live soberly, justly and piously in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. This expectation, therefore, should draw us to itself, freed from all hindrances; and the more the world is filled with Epicurean corruption, the more keenly we ought to strive, lest the contagion creep even to us, until we reach the goal. Moreover, although it must be lamented that so great a crowd perishes of its own accord, yet since they rush headlong to their own destruction as if devoted to it, let not their frenzied fury disturb us; let us recall the other admonition of Daniel, that salvation is laid up for all who are found written in the book. Although election, which is the first cause of our salvation, lies hidden in the secret counsel of God, yet since adoption is by no means doubtful for all who have been grafted by faith in the gospel into the body of Christ, be content with this testimony and press on vigorously in the race happily begun. But if you must still struggle for longer (for I warn you that harder battles remain than you think), whatever the force with which the rage of tyrants boils up, and though they stir up all the depths of hell, remember that the course has been set for you by the heavenly Agonothete, whose laws must be obeyed all the more eagerly because he supplies strength to the very end. Since it is not right for me to desert the post where God wished me to remain, let this my labour, dedicated to you, be a pledge of my zeal to help you, until, my pilgrimage being completed, the heavenly Father, in his immense mercy, gathers me together with you into the eternal inheritance. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, brothers most dear to me from my heart, defend you by his protection against all the devices of your enemies, and sustain you with unconquered strength.

units.la: APpuli in aulam ante biduum, tanto Procerum nostrorum exceptus studio, vt vix mihi respirandi spatium daretur, vt singulis me sisterem. Primum Admiralium offendi, quem vix salutaram, cum Nauarrenus & Condensis in me sese ita effudderunt, vt ad summam eorum beneuolentiā desiderari nihil posset. Atque illic cōtinuò sum suspicatus Cardinales Borbonium & Castilionæum vtrumque mihi dexteram prætendentem, cùm sigillatim omnia persequi nō possim illud indicasse sufficiet, protestatum me esse apud Borbonium, nullo modo ab illo mutatū me esse, quem aliàs alloqui dedignatus esset, ne excommunicationem subiret. Regessit ille sibi iam esse in animo de re tota amplius audire: Ego vicissim meam operam ita obtuli, vt eandem illi mentē simul precarer in posterum. Atque tum fere vlterius gliscebat sermo, nisi bonus ille vir paucis egisset, quem & ipse in eo secutus sum. Quòd ad Nauarrenū, summa orationis meæ ad illum fuit: vereri me vt aduentus iste meus illi tam gratus breui futurus sit: quod vbi illum subridentem audire animaduerti, atqui inquam, quod per iocum ita accipis, scrib tibi à me dictū pu ta. Totū istud semihorā circiter abstulit. Et nox instabat. Illi ad Reginā: ego maiore multo turba cinctus quā putarā adDominā Cond.Principem & Admiraliam deducor, in quibus singulare omnino pietatis studium deprehendi.Postridie, qui fuit hesternus dies, concionem habui in Principis aedibus, frequenti caetu & perquam honorato. Ille aberat,distractus nimirum certo suo negotio cum altero illo quem ignoras,quod eodem die voti confectum est,ipse mihi priuatim communicauit, atque acta illius rei exhibuit,quorum haec summa erat:Aduersarium ipsius testatum coram ipsa Regina & Regio consilio,nullo modo se in causa fuisse cur Princeps in custodia haberetur:Ipsum excepisse, habere se pro improbis ad quoscunque eius rei nota pertineret: Ego sic credo, respondit ille,& hoc ad me non spectat ullo modo.Rogatus quid sentirem, verba illa ambiguitatem prae se ferre respondi:sed quod illas res attingeret, relinquere me illis eorum cognitionem,qui melius tenerent quid esset ex ipsius honore& dignitate. Quod ad priuatam ipsius iniuriam, non ignorare ipsum,cui vni vindicta omnis committenda esset. Interea nemi-nem inter Dei amicos censeri posse, qui sese inimicum oso-rum Dei & Ecclesiae ipsius eo vno nomine non profiteretur.
units.tr: I arrived at court two days ago, and our nobles received me with such eagerness that I hardly had a moment to breathe, since I had to present myself to each of them in turn. First I met the Admiral, whom I had barely greeted when the King of Navarre and Condé poured out their goodwill towards me so warmly that nothing more could be wished for. There too I at once noticed both Cardinals, Bourbon and Châtillon, each holding out his right hand to me. I cannot go through everything one by one, so it will suffice to report this: I protested to Bourbon that he had in no way changed me, although he had at other times disdained to speak to me, lest he incur excommunication. He replied that he had already decided to hear more about the whole matter. I in turn offered my services, praying that he might have the same disposition in future. The conversation would have gone on further, had that good man not brought it to a close after a few words, and I followed his lead. As for Navarre, the sum of my speech to him was that I feared my visit might soon cease to be so welcome to him. When I saw him smiling at this, I said, "You take it as a joke, but I assure you I said it in earnest." That took up about half an hour, and night was coming on. They went on to the Queen, and I was escorted to the Princess of Condé and the Admiral's wife, with a much larger crowd than I had expected, and in them I found a quite singular zeal for godliness. On the next day, which was yesterday, I preached in the Prince's house to a crowded and most honoured gathering. He was absent, no doubt distracted by his own business with that other man whom you do not know, which was settled on the same day. He himself told me about it privately and showed me the record of the proceedings. The substance was this: his opponent declared, before the Queen herself and the royal council, that he had in no way been responsible for the Prince being held in custody; the Prince had accepted this, and held that those who had done such things were wicked, whoever the matter concerned. "I believe so," he replied, "and this does not concern me in any way." Asked what I thought, I replied that his words carried an ambiguity; but as for those public matters, I left their consideration to those who better understood what was due to his honour and dignity. As for the private injury done to himself, I said he should not be unaware that vengeance belongs to him alone to exact. Meanwhile, I said, no one could be counted among the friends of God who does not profess himself, on that ground alone, an enemy of the enemies of God and of the Church itself.

units.la: Respondit non defuturam nobis ex ista conciliatione Dei laudandi occasionem, modo firma staret. Ac re ipsa magnę turbę nascituręrant ex illis priuatis affectibus:ac modo occasio vlti-rius pergendi semel praecisa fit, dolendum non est quod illa iur-giaita sopita sint,vt cum eo de quo nunc agitur a nobis,nihil in de permisceatur.Atque is fuit rei illius exitus,a qua non parum metuebamus,modo ne caudam aliam trahat in posterum. Eo-dem die ad supplicem libellum nostrum responsum est àRege, nos auditum in, aduersarios etiam iudices nobis non sefluros: non deesttamen quod nos adhuc impeditos teneat, vt absolu-tum responsum non obtinuerimus:quod tamé in audientia pu-blica solenniter nobis datum iri audimus. Saltem breuis & opta-ti exitus spes non deest. Post coenam, adeoque sub nonam vo-catus in cubiculum Nauarreni, praeter illum ex insperato offen-di ibidem Reginam matrem,Condensem,Stampensem,Borbo-nium & Lotharingum Cardinales, Curfoliam cum altera qua-dam.Sic fere interceptus,mihi tamen Dei beneficio non defui, quin Reginae causam aduenius mei studiumque in patriam pro-pensum significarem: quod illa perhumano isto responso acce-pit:Maximae sibi laetitiae futurum,si re ipsa hoc ita constaret,vn-de Regno pax & quies procuraretur. Tū Cardinalis Lotharenus subiecit, sibi me ante ex scriptis meis tatum cognitū fuisse, hor-tari autem praesentem,vt paci & concordiae studerem,additis in super his verbis,quas absens scriptis Regno turbas dedisse,eafdé meo aduentu fortasse sedatu iri.Hic ego iterū de meo ergaRege & patriam seçudum Deum intento studio testatus,cum ea sit in quam,mea tenuitas vt tanto Regno ab illa turbæ nullę vnquam metuendæ sint:tum vero ab eiusmodi cogitatione sæpe alenifimum fuisse me,& scriptis ante abunde docuisse, & in mutua porro collatione parefacturum esse. Rogat me tum Regina,ecquid Gallicè scripsisset Psalm.ac respondsum quoddam ad confessionem Ducis Northumbriæ. Occasio sermonis erat, quòd ad illa delatus esse vt auctor probrosi cuiusdam carminis, quod anno superiore per Galliam circunferebatur: quod à me nullo modo profectu esse aperte & diserte coram illa testatus sum. Rogatus de tua ætate & habitu, respondi quod res erat.Cœpit tum Cardinalis mentionem iniicere libri cuiusdam quem Possiaci haberet,de re Sacramentaria, qui liber meum nomen præferret:In eo,inquit,legi aliquid quod mihi perabsurdum videtur,Perinde nempe quærendum esse nunc Christū in Cœna, atque antequam ex Virginis utero prodiisset. Præterea, inquit,in altero quodam libro tuo sic te scripsisse audio(nam librum ipse non vidi)nempe quòd Christus sit in Cœna sicut in cœno.Hoc cum Reginam & qui aderant,commouisset, excepi, si libri ipsi coram offerretur,certius multò pro meis agniturum,siquidem mei essent. Quòd ad primam illam positionem,possi illam aliquantum absurdam videri, vti nudè à Cardinali prolata esset.Speculandū igitur quid præcederet quidque sub sequeretur:quia illius positionis sensus appositus facilè constare posset. Quòd ad alteram vero,ita mihi non indignā modò, sed etiam blasphemam videri, vt non modò non extare in meis scriptis,sed neque in alterius vllius,qui doctrinam Ecclesiarū reformatarū amplecteretur,affirmarem. Tum Cardinalis omissa secunda illa criminatione vt quā impudentissimam calumniā esse liqueat,vndecunque primum suggesta sit,illum alterum sermonem multis exagitauit,quòd Christus in Cœna perinde quærendus esset atque ante quam ex Virginis vtero prodiret. Summa orationis fuit,si res ita haberet, nihil amplius in Cœna dari nobis, quàm illis qui Christi aduentū præcessissent: eò accedere quòd caro ipsa dari non potuisset,cum necdum extaret. Hic ego petij à Cardinali,Num aliqua semper Ecclesia extitisset ab orbe condito?Maximè inquit Num verò,inquā,Ecclesia fuit Ecclesia pro pter mediatorem inter Deum & homines?Et illud admisit,Num etiam, inquam,Christus verus Deus & homo extitit semper ille mediator? Omnino inquit. Ergo(subinde tuli)comunicatio fidelium cū Christo nō est restringeda ad tépus illud,quo Christus naturā suam diuinam nostræ coniunxit: quin potius illud ipsum quod per ordinem naturæ nondum extabat,præsens adfuit sæper fidelibus virtute & efficacia:vti de Abrahamo scriptum est, vidisse il lum die D.atque viso exultasse. Et quod est apud Paulū ad Cor.
units.tr: He replied that there would not be lacking for us, from this reconciliation, an occasion to praise God, provided it held firm. In fact, great disturbances had arisen from those private feelings, and now that the opportunity for pressing further has been cut off, we need not regret that those quarrels have been laid to rest, so that nothing of that kind will be mixed up with the man of whom we now speak. And this was the outcome of that affair, which had caused us no small fear, provided it does not drag some other tail after it in future. On the same day the King replied to our humble petition: he said that we would not fail to find the judges favourable to us, though we were not yet holding a full answer, which we hear will be given to us solemnly at a public hearing. At least there is hope of a brief outcome, and of the one we desire. After supper, and so about nine o'clock, I was summoned to the bedchamber of the King of Navarre, where, to my surprise, I found besides him the Queen Mother, the Cardinals of Condé, Estampes, Bourbon and Lorraine, and Curfoliam with some other woman. Though caught somewhat off guard, by God's favour I did not fail to tell the Queen of my coming and of my zeal for my homeland. She received this with a most courteous reply: it would be a great joy to her if it were shown in fact that this would bring peace and quiet to the kingdom. Then Cardinal Lorraine added that he had known me only from my writings, but urged me, now that I was present, to pursue peace and harmony, adding these words: that the disturbances my absent writings had caused in the kingdom might perhaps be calmed by my coming. Here again I professed, with my usual devoted zeal under God, my loyalty to the King and to my country. As for the realm, I said, my own slightness is such that no disturbances from it are ever to be feared by so great a kingdom. Indeed, I said, I had often been very far from such thoughts, and had already amply shown this in my writings, and I would make it plain in our further conference. Then the Queen asked whether I had written anything in French, and the Psalms, and a certain reply to the confession of the Duke of Northumberland. The occasion for this talk was that I had been reported to them as the author of a disgraceful song which had been circulating through France the year before. I openly and clearly declared before her that this had in no way come from me. Asked about your age and bearing, I answered as the facts were. Then the Cardinal began to bring up a certain book, which he said was in the hands of someone at Poissy, on the sacramentarian question, bearing my name. "In it," he said, "I read something that seems to me utterly absurd: namely, that Christ is now to be sought in the Supper just as before he came forth from the Virgin's womb. Moreover," he said, "I hear that in another of your books you have written thus (for I have not seen the book myself): that Christ is in the Supper as in a mire." When this stirred the Queen and those present, I replied that if the books themselves were produced, they would be recognised as mine far more certainly, if indeed they were mine. As for the first statement, it might seem somewhat absurd as the Cardinal had put it bare, so one must look at what preceded and what followed, since the sense of that statement could easily be established in context. As for the second, I said, it seemed to me not only unworthy of me but even blasphemous, so that I would affirm it did not exist not only in my writings but in those of anyone who embraced the teaching of the reformed Churches. Then the Cardinal, dropping that second accusation as a most shameless calumny, whatever its origin, pressed the first statement at length: that Christ was to be sought in the Supper just as before he came forth from the Virgin's womb. The gist of his argument was that if things were so, we would receive nothing more in the Supper than those who had preceded Christ's coming; and, moreover, the flesh itself could not be given, since it did not yet exist. At this I asked the Cardinal: had there always been some Church since the world began? "Certainly," he said. "Then," I said, "was there a Church for the sake of the Mediator between God and men?" He admitted this too. "And," I said, "did Christ, the true God and man, always exist as that Mediator?" "Altogether," he said. "Therefore," I went on at once, "the communion of the faithful with Christ is not to be restricted to that time when Christ joined his divine nature to ours. Rather, that very thing which, in the order of nature, did not yet exist, was always present to the faithful by virtue and efficacy, as is written of Abraham: that he saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced when he saw it. And what Paul has in 1 Cor.

units.la: 1.10. Patres eandem escă edifle, eundem potum spiritualem bibisse, nempe Christum. Et illud agnouit Cardinalis, & vicissim locum illum ex Apocalypsi suggessit appositè, Agnus qui occisus est à creatione mundi. Inde igitur ingressus sum in plenio rem tractationem, vt ostenderem in quo vetus testamentum à no uo differret. Illa vero decisio, cui visus est Cardinalis acquiescere, aliam quæstionem statim peperit: Quis esset nepe sensus horum verborum, Hoc est corpus meum: In hoc articulo inquit, qui tan ti est momenti, inter nos & vos non conuenit. Agnosco hoc in quam, neque sine magno meo mœrore quòd inter nos qui Christiano nomine censemur, maior consensus non fit: sed tamen quando aliter res se habere non potest, malo hoc ita ex te audire quàm si in tanta sententiarum repugnantia merum consensum & coueneintiâ fingi audirem. Ego sane, inquit Cardinalis, sic pue ros meæ diocœsis doceo, vt cum rogantur: Quid sit panis Cœnæ? respondeant esse corpus Christi: An tu hoc improbas? Imò ve rò, inquam, quid enim Christi verba non approbem? Sed de eo quæritur, quomodo panis vocetur corpo Christi. Quicquid enim aliquid est, non est tamen illud eodem modo. Ingressus in locutionum Sacramentalium disquisitione, audiuas ab illo sum qui dem: sed cum locum illum proferrem, Petra erat Christus, oppo suit alterum, Verbum caro factum est. Sed locus ille statim illi è manibus effluxit. Tandem igitur totum hunc tractatu in quatuor ista capita sumatim ita conferri posse subieci. Primū vt con staret de signis. Tum de re significata. Tertium de coniunctione signorum cum re significata. Quartum de participatione tum signorum tum rei significatæ. In primo igitur non conuenit nobis vobiscum, quia inquam, vos non alia signa in Cœna statuitis, quàm nuda accidentia: nos retinemus ipsa substantiam panis & vini iuxta naturam Sacramentorum & totâ Scriptura. Tum ille. Atqui, inquit, sperem etiam me tueri posse ipsamet transubstantiationem, sed poterat illa tamen omitti à Theologis: & ipse quidem propter transubstan Ecclesias scindi noluerim. Ad secundum vero, non ponimus inquam, pro re significata in Sacramentis, ipsum tantum meritum passionis Christi, sed ipsissimi corpus cruci affixum, sanguinem ipsissimū in cruce effusum pro nobis. In summa Christus ipsemet verus Deus & homo nobis significatur per illa signa, vt attollamus corda nostra ad illum contemplandum spiritualiter fide in cœlis vbi nunc est: atque ita comunicemus cum omnibus ipsius bonis ac thesauris in vitam æternam: siδque tam vere, tamq; certo, quà verum ac certum est, nos naturaliter videre, accipere, edere, bibere signa illa quæ videntur à nobis & sunt corporea. Acquieuit & huic doctrinæ Cardinalis, addito, valde gaudere se quòd ita nos sentire audiret, cùm aliū esse sensum ensum noftrũ ipse accepisset. Adtertiddeinde: Agnoscimus in- quam magnum esse discrimen inter aquâ cõmune & aquâ Baptismi: inter etiam panem communem & vinum cõmune,& panem ac vinum Coenæ Aquam enim Baptismi,panê etiam ac vinum Coenæ D. signa esse ac testimonia visibilia corporis & sanguinis D.sed nos hoc ita exaudire,vt mutatione ipsam nõ statu- amus in ipsa signorũ substãtia,qu̇ in sese semper integra manet: sed in eo demũ,quod illa signa ad aliũ vsum referatur,quâ qui naturalis sit,& ad solũ vsum corporis pertineat:ex quo enim Sacramêta fiunt,tum nobis repræsentare illud quod nutriat spiritualiter.Porrò mutatione illâ Sacramentale acceptam non ferre aut certis verbis prolatis & cõceptis, aut cõcipiêtis intẽtioni:sed vnius Dei virtuti & potétiæ, cuius voluntas & institutio nobis verbo ipsius constet.Cum igitur resipsa signisicata tã vere nobis offeratur & conferatur à D.quam signa ipsa visibilia,eo refpeƈu demũ accipiendâ agnoscendãque esse signorũ cum re significata coniunctione,non autẽ alio modo.Proinde corpus & sanguinẽ Christi,quatenus vere nobis dantur & cõmunicatur, vere in Coenæ vsu adesse:nõ vt existimetur esse sub vel in vel cũ pane aut alibi vspiã,quâ in cœlo vbi afcedit Christus, vt illic reideat quod ad naturâ humanâ ipsius attinet,donec redeat iudicaturus vivos & mortuos.Hic etiã Card.testatus iterũ nõ vrgere se trãsubst.rect pödit, Christũ vere in cœlo quærendũ esse,interiectis simul quibusdã de locali præsentia & de quorundã Germanorũ sententiâ: sed illud totũ ita cõpleƈtebatur, vt satis ostenderet penitus se nõ tenere quid hoc rei esset.Agnoscebat enim se aliis studiis tẽpus impendisse. Inde mihi oblata occasione, agnosco inquâ,nobis non cõuenire cum Germanis quibusdã in tertio isto capite de ratione cõiunctionis signorũ cum re significata:sed tamen Dei beneficio cõsentimus tum in transubst.reiectione,& quæ eã consequuntur,tũ agnoscimus omnes verâ cõmunicationem corporis & sanguinis D.An vero inquit Card. profitemini nos cõmunicare realiter & substantialiter vero Christi corpori & sanguini?Illud est inquâ,vltimũ caput quod mihi attinget ndũ est.In summa igitur dicimus,naturaliter percipi manu,edi,bibi signa visibilia: quad rem significatã,corpus nempe & sanguiné Christi, omnibus quidé offerri,sed non posse percipi, nisi spiritualiter & fide,non manu,non ore.Tam certã esse verò illam cõmunicationem,vt nõ magis certa sint ipsa illa signa quæ manibus palpamus: quâ- uis arcanũ istius cõmunicationis & efficacitatis Spiritus sancti & fidei nostræ incõprehensibile sit mentibus ac sensibus nostris. Tandem Card.ego, inquit,sum rudis in istis tractãdis,tu tamen audisti quid vellem.Et tu ex me perinde,respõdi,quæ tibi satisfacere debeãt.In summa enim sic colligo,Panis est corpus Christi
units.tr: 1.10. The Fathers ate the same food and drank the same spiritual drink, namely Christ. The Cardinal acknowledged this, and in turn aptly cited that passage from the Apocalypse: "The Lamb who was slain from the creation of the world." From there I went on to treat the subject more fully, to show in what the Old Testament differs from the New. But that settlement, to which the Cardinal seemed to agree, immediately gave rise to another question: what is the meaning of these words, "This is my body"? "On this article," he said, "which is of such importance, we do not agree between you and us." I acknowledge it, and not without great sorrow of my own, that among us who are called by the Christian name there is no greater agreement. Still, since things cannot be otherwise, I prefer to hear this from you than to hear a feigned full consent and harmony in such a great conflict of opinions. "For my part," said the Cardinal, "I teach the children of my diocese in this way: when they are asked, What is the bread of the Supper? they answer that it is the body of Christ. Do you disapprove of this?" "Not at all," I said. "Why should I not approve the words of Christ? But the question is how bread is called the body of Christ. For whatever a thing is, it is not therefore in the same way that it is." When I entered into the inquiry about sacramental expressions, he did listen to me; but when I cited that passage, "The rock was Christ," he set against it another, "The Word was made flesh." That passage, however, immediately slipped out of his hands. At last, therefore, I suggested that this whole discussion could be summarily arranged under four heads: first, that we agree about the signs; second, about the thing signified; third, about the conjunction of the signs with the thing signified; fourth, about the participation both in the signs and in the thing signified. On the first point, then, I said, we do not agree with you, because you set up no other signs in the Supper than bare accidents, whereas we retain the very substance of bread and wine, according to the nature of the sacraments and the whole of Scripture. Then he said: "Yet I hope I can defend transubstantiation itself as well, but the theologians could have omitted it; and I myself would not wish the Churches to be torn apart over transubstantiation." On the second point I said: "We do not set forth as the thing signified in the sacraments only the merit of Christ's passion, but the very body of Christ fixed to the cross and the very blood poured out for us on the cross." In sum, Christ himself, true God and man, is signified to us by those signs, so that we may lift up our hearts to contemplate him spiritually by faith in heaven, where he now is; and thus we communicate in all his goods and treasures unto eternal life. This is as true and as certain as it is true and certain that we naturally see, receive, eat and drink those signs, which are seen by us and are corporeal. The Cardinal also assented to this doctrine, adding that he rejoiced greatly to hear that we thought thus, since he had understood our opinion to be otherwise. Next, I added on the third point: "We acknowledge that there is a great difference between common water and the water of Baptism, and likewise between common bread and wine and the bread and wine of the Supper. For the water of Baptism, and the bread and wine of the Supper, are signs and visible testimonies of the body and blood of God. But we understand this so that we do not place the change in the substance of the signs themselves, which always remains whole in itself, but only in this: that those signs are referred to another use, which is natural and pertains only to the use of the body; for from the time the sacraments come into being, they represent to us that which nourishes spiritually. Moreover, we do not ascribe that sacramental change either to certain words spoken and understood, or to the intention of the one who understands them, but to the power and virtue of God alone, whose will and institution is established for us by his Word. Since, therefore, the very things signified are offered and conferred on us by God as truly as the visible signs themselves, we acknowledge that the conjunction of the signs with the thing signified is to be understood and recognised only in that respect, and in no other way. Accordingly, the body and blood of Christ, insofar as they are truly given and communicated to us, are truly present in the use of the Supper; not that they are thought to be under, in, or with the bread, or anywhere else in space, as if Christ, who ascended into heaven, were there with respect to his human nature, until he returns to judge the living and the dead." Here too the Cardinal again testified that he did not press transubstantiation. He said that Christ must truly be sought in heaven, adding meanwhile some remarks about local presence and the opinion of certain Germans; but he wrapped the whole matter up in such a way as to show plainly that he did not in the least grasp what it was about, for he acknowledged that he had devoted his time to other studies. Then, the occasion being offered to me, I said: "I acknowledge that we do not agree with certain Germans on this third point, concerning the manner of the conjunction of the signs with the thing signified; but still, by God's favour, we agree both in rejecting transubstantiation and in what follows from it, and we all acknowledge a true communication of the body and blood of God." "But do you profess," asked the Cardinal, "that we communicate really and substantially with the true body and blood of Christ?" "That," I said, "is the last point that concerns me, and it needs no discussion. In sum, then, we say that the visible signs are naturally perceived by hand, eaten and drunk; but the thing signified, namely the body and blood of Christ, is indeed offered to all, yet cannot be perceived except spiritually and by faith, not by hand or by mouth. That communication is as certain as the signs themselves, which we touch with our hands, are certain, although the secret of that communication and of the efficacy of the Holy Spirit and of our faith is incomprehensible to our minds and senses." Finally the Cardinal said: "I am unskilled in handling these matters, but you have heard what I wanted." "And you," I replied, "may take from me answers of the same kind, which ought to satisfy you. For in sum I conclude thus: Bread is the body of Christ"

units.la: Sacramentaliter, id est, quanuis corpus illud hodie fit in cœlo nec alibi, signa vero nobisci̇cum in terra: tam vere tamen nobis dari, & à nobis percipi corpus ipsum per fidem, idque in vitam æternam propter Dei promissionem, quàm vere signum naturaliter nobis in manus porrigitur. Sic credo Domina, inquit, ille ad Reginam conuersus, hoc mihi satisfecit. Tum ego ad illam.
units.tr: Sacramentally, that is, although that body today is in heaven and nowhere else, while the signs are with us on earth, nonetheless the body itself is given to us and received by us through faith, and that unto eternal life, on account of God's promise, as truly as the sign is naturally placed in our hands. "So I believe," said the Cardinal, turning to the Queen; "this has satisfied me." Then I said to her:

units.la: En ergo miseros illos Sacramentarios tandiu vexatos & omnibus calumniis oppressos. Audis ne, inquit illa, D. Cardinalis, non aliam esse Sacramentariorum opinionem, quàm eam ipsam quam nunc ipse approbasti? Atque hic nonnulla interiecta sunt de vnione & conciliatione. Hic demum Regina & qui aderant sese inde receperunt. Card. porrò mihi gratulabundus, D. Beza, inquit, (ipsissima enim illius verba proferam) valde gauisus sum, quod te videri m & audierim. Adiuro te in Dei nomine, vt intelligam rationes tuas, ac tu etiam meas. Et reperies me non tam nigrum esse quam me quidam faciant. Ego vero gratiis illi actis eo nomine, petij vicissim, vt in hac conciliationis ratione pergeret: neque me ei rei tam sanctæ támque necessariæ pro domo sua Deo in me collatis defuturum. Sic valde fero discessum est cum optima spe quadam, nisi quod D. Curfolia quasi præsagies quid crastino accideret, prehensa Cardinalis manu ita illum etiam aperte (nofti mulieris ingenium) palam accepit. Hodie, inquit, Vir bonus, Cras vero quid? Sic nempe accidit. Sparsus est enim rumor non per aulam modò, sed Pofliacum vsque, & vlterius, Cardinalem conuertisse Bezam ad fidem Catholicam, atque induxisse ad palinodiam, & ad agnoscendum augustum illud altaris Sacramentum, cum aliis eiufcemodi abfurdiffimis, quæ longe lateque disseminata sunt. Illa vero mendacia vel ipsius Reginæ testimonio confutata & tantorum Principum, qui contrarium prorsus ipsimet audierant, tandem per fe ita conciderunt, vt certam auctoribus suis impudentiæ notam inustam relinquerent. En quis exitus fuerit vespertini illius occursus.
units.tr: Behold, then, those wretched Sacramentarians, so long harassed and overwhelmed by every calumny! "Do you hear, Lord Cardinal," said she, "that the opinion of the Sacramentarians is no other than that very one which you have now approved?" Here some things were interposed about union and reconciliation. At last the Queen and those present withdrew from there. The Cardinal, rejoicing, said to me: "Beza, (for I will give his very words) I was very glad that I saw and heard you. I adjure you in the name of God, that I may understand your reasons, and you mine. And you will find me not as black as some make me out to be." I gave thanks to him for this, and in turn asked him to persevere in this plan of reconciliation, promising that I would not be wanting to him in a matter so holy and so necessary, with whatever gifts God had bestowed on me for his house. Thus we parted with a certain good hope, except that Madame de Curfolia, as if foreseeing what would happen the next day, took the Cardinal's hand and received him openly in this way (you know the woman's temper): "Today, good man; but tomorrow, what?" And so it indeed happened. For a rumour was spread not only through the court but as far as Poissy and further, that the Cardinal had converted Beza to the Catholic faith, had brought him to a recantation, and to acknowledging that august sacrament of the altar, together with other utterly absurd things of this kind, which have been spread far and wide. But those lies, refuted even by the testimony of the Queen herself and of such great princes, who had heard the contrary directly from me, at last fell apart of their own accord, so that they left a sure mark of shamelessness branded on their authors. Such was the outcome of that evening encounter.

units.la: A te vero peto mi pater, vt quòd hic ita prolixè & incondite ad te scribo mihi condones. Senatui imprimis, ac etiam fratribus plurimam salutem adscribo. Cùm vero Domini placuerit isto tam infirmo & inutili instrumento, meipfo nempe vtiad tantum opus, confido neque mihi preces tuas, neque consilium à quibus vnice post Deum pendeo defutura. Dominus te confirmet, benedicat tibi, réque magis ac magis sustineat. Ex Sangermano, x x v. Auguft. sub vesperam. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: And from you, my father, I ask that you forgive me for writing to you here at such length and in such a disorderly way. I send my most hearty greetings first to the Senate, and also to the brothers. Since it has pleased the Lord to use me, so weak and useless an instrument, for so great a work, I trust that neither your prayers nor your counsel, on which I depend solely after God, will fail me. May the Lord strengthen you, bless you, and sustain you more and more. From Saint-Germain, 25 August, in the evening, 1561.

units.la: Filius in Domino & addictissimus tibi Th. Beza.
units.tr: Your son in the Lord and most devoted to you, Th. Beza.

units.la: BEZA
units.tr: BEZA

units.la: EX quo ad te scripsi, nihil fere novi incidit, quod non possis ex aliis copiosius intelligere. Nam quia domi nos continemus, nihil illorum nisi ex aliorum sermonibus accipimus. Ego quotidie conciones habui in Principis aedibus, tanto hominum concursu, ut penè opprimeretur. Heri N.cum Pr.& A.expeditis quis obuiam ierunt Reginae Nauarrenae, quam intra triduum suidissimè expectamus, ut torpentes excitet. De nostro negotio nondum audiuimus quid sit constitutum, id est, quando & quibus conditionibus liceat audiendi. Aduersarios alij aiunt esse ad disputationem paratos, alij negant. Nos interea Deum precamur assiduè, ut, quantum fieri potest, ad omnem occasionem simus intenti. Et profectò inanes non erunt absentis preces, quandoquidem eo sum redactus, ut tam necessario tempore frui praesente non possum. Si Martyr noster venerit in tempore, id est, si valde festinarit, magnopere nos recreabit ipsius aduentus. Erit enim nobis negotium cum veteranis sophistis: & quanuis confidamus fore, ut vincat simplex verbi veritas, tamen non cuiusuis est illorum strophas statim diluere, & Patrum dicta regerere: & ita illis respondendum erit, ut si nulcircunstanti Principum & aliorum Ordinum coronae appareat, nos nullo modo tergiuersari. Denique quum in istas difficultates intueor, valde sum anxius, & magnopere in eo peccatum conqueror, quòd negletis excellentibus Dei organis, quodammodo videamur eius bonitatem tentare. Interea tamen decreuimus pedem non referre, & in eo confidimus qui nobis sapientiam promisit, cui mundus resistere non possit. Ex Episcopis audimus nonnullos nobis iniquos non fore. De quibusdam Theologis idem nobis pollicemur, sed enim fortasse nobiscum non committentur. Card. fortiter iactat me primo statim congressu à se superatum, sed à grauissimis testibus refellitur. Augustanam confessionem habet in ore, de qua etiam seorsim rogatus à Doctore Botellerio, an eam possemus admittere, plane respondi non posse in quibusdam, nisi plana & perspicua addita interpretatione. Si non vrserimus, tergiuersari videbimur & congressum defugere: vel, si quid remiserimus, videndum ne praecipites eò ruamus, unde non possimus nos extricare. Denique, mi pater, quandoquidem praesens nondum potes, absens, ut pueros & consiliis & modis omnibus nos regito. Nos vero plane pueros esse quotidie video & sentio, ex quorum ore vtinam Dominus ille noster admirabilis sapientiae suae laude perficiat. Bene vale, mi obseruande pater, vnà cum fratribus & amicis omnibus, quos vnà tecum cupio magis ac magis à Domino benedici & incolumes coseruari. Iterum vale. Priuilegium Psal-
units.tr: Since I last wrote to you, almost nothing new has happened that you could not learn more fully from others. As we keep ourselves at home, we hear of such things only from what others tell us. Every day I have preached in the Prince's house, to such a crowd of people that I was almost crushed. Yesterday N., Pr., and A., having been dispatched, went to meet the Queen of Navarre, whom we eagerly expect within three days, so that she may rouse the sluggish. We have not yet heard what has been decided about our business, that is, when and on what conditions we may be heard. Some say the adversaries are ready for disputation, others deny it. Meanwhile we pray to God constantly that, as far as possible, we may be alert to every opportunity. Indeed the prayers of the absent will not be in vain, since I am reduced to such a state that I cannot enjoy your presence at so necessary a time. If our Martyr comes in time, that is, if he hurries greatly, his arrival will greatly refresh us. For we shall have a contest with the veteran sophists. Although we trust that the simple truth of the Word will prevail, it is not for just anyone to dissolve their tricks at once and to answer the sayings of the Fathers. We must reply in such a way that, if the princes and the other orders of the court are standing by, it does not appear that we are evading the issue in any way. Finally, when I look at these difficulties, I am very anxious, and I greatly lament that, while the excellent organs of God are neglected, we seem in some way to tempt his goodness. Meanwhile, however, we have decided not to give ground, and we trust in him who has promised us a wisdom that the world cannot withstand. We hear from some bishops that they will not be hostile to us. We promise the same about certain theologians, but perhaps they will not engage with us. The Cardinal boasts loudly that he defeated me at the first encounter, but he is refuted by most serious witnesses. He always has the Augsburg Confession on his lips. When Doctor Botellerius asked me privately whether we could admit it, I plainly replied that we could not in certain points, unless a clear and perspicuous interpretation were added. If we do not press it, we shall seem to be evasive and to avoid the meeting; or if we yield anything, we must take care that we do not rush headlong into a place from which we cannot extricate ourselves. Finally, my father, since you cannot yet be present, you guide us like children in all counsels and by every means. Indeed I see and feel every day that we are children; would that our wonderful Lord would perfect his praise of his wisdom from their mouths. Farewell, my revered father, together with the brothers and all our friends, whom I wish, along with you, to be blessed more and more by the Lord and kept safe. Farewell again. Privilege for the Psalm-

units.la: Epist.310 morum breuime habituruim spero, quod statim ad hanc mittam. Totus fratrum coetus te salutat, id est, Marlor.Merl.Colon.Virellus.Galaf.Ex Sangermano,x x x.Augusti.
units.tr: Epist. 310: I hope to have a brief copy of the Psalms, which I shall send to you at once with this letter. The whole company of brothers greets you, namely Marlorat, Merlin, Colladon, Virellus, Galaf. From Saint-Germain, 30 August.

units.la: Tuus B.
units.tr: Yours, B.

units.la: FOELIX CRVCIGER Io. CAL. ET ALIIS FRATRIBVS.
units.tr: Felix Cruciger to John Calvin and the other brethren.

units.la: Gratiam & Pacem a Deo Patre Domini nostri Iesu Christi fratres veltri, qui manent per vniuersam minorem Poloniam.
units.tr: Grace and peace from God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to your brethren who dwell throughout Lesser Poland.

units.la: INtelleximus, viri clarissimi, & ex testibus fide dignis, & ex litteris aliquorum, quoad nostros ex vestris regionibus adferutur, nostros coetus aliquo modo istic sufpitione laborare, acsi peregrinorum dogmatū,& potissimum Arianae, Seruetianaeve im pietatis defensores, aut salte fautores esse debeaemus. Quae sane res, vbi ad nos perlata est, grauiter animos nostros percelluit & sauciauit, ita vt nunc cogamur denuo in hoc articulo coram vobis fratribus amantissimis explicare rationem fidei nostrae. Nolite igitur de nobis addubitare. Credimus & confitemur vnum Deum iuxta Canonicas Scripturas, & hunc agnoscimus & colimus ita sicuti se patefecit in tribus personis, ad illam ripam Iordanis. Credimus Patrem Omnipotentem, Filium ei per omnia aequalem quoad naturam, essentiam, vel Deitatem. Minorem eo tantum, qui cum esset in forma Dei semetipsum exinaniuit, seu vt vno verbo complectamur, ratione officij Mediationis. Sic & in Spiritum sanctum credimus verum Deum, qui a Patre & Filio procedit. Quid multa? amplectimur reuerenter tria illa symbola, Apostolicum, Nicenum, & diui Athanasij. Nec volumus a consensu vestrarum Ecclesiarum discedere. Et abhorremus omnia dogmata noua & exotica, memores dicti: Depositum custodi o Timothee. Haec est fides & confessio nostra. Quod si igitur Stan carus deinceps, aut quisquam alter nostrae famae insidiabitur apud vos, ne credatis, per nomen Iesu vos obtestamur. Id enim vobis viris pietate & grauitate Christiana praeditis congruit. Georgius Blandrata ante aliquot hebdomadas nostrae confessioni videbatur ferio subscripsisse. Cuius causam oramus vt diligenter & prudenter discipiatis, & nos de omnibus certiores reddatis. Sed quod attinet nostras Ecclesias, coram Deo testamur, quod hactenus per Dei gratiam in ea fide perstitimus, & perstare Deo volente cupimus, sicuti supra recitatum est. Valete fratres in Domino perpetua obseruantia colendissimi. Datum ex magna Kxiaefl.in Synodo nostra, III. die Septemb. Anno M. D. LXI.
units.tr: We have learned, most distinguished men, both from trustworthy witnesses and from letters of certain persons, as far as they are brought to us from your regions, that our congregations there are in some way under suspicion, as though we were defenders, or at least supporters, of foreign doctrines, and especially of the Arian or Servetian impiety. When this report reached us, it struck and wounded our spirits severely, so that we are now compelled once more, on this article, to set out for you, our most beloved brethren, the grounds of our faith. Do not therefore doubt concerning us. We believe and confess one God according to the canonical Scriptures, and we acknowledge and worship him as he revealed himself in three persons at the bank of the Jordan. We believe in the Almighty Father, and in the Son, equal to him in all things as to nature, essence and Godhead; he is less only in that he, being in the form of God, emptied himself, or, to sum it up in one word, in respect of the office of Mediation. So also we believe in the Holy Spirit as the true God, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. Why say more? We reverently embrace those three creeds, the Apostles', the Nicene, and that of the holy Athanasius. Nor do we wish to depart from the agreement of your Churches. And we abhor all new and strange doctrines, mindful of the saying: "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust." This is our faith and confession. But if Stancarus henceforth, or anyone else, should lay snares for our reputation with you, do not believe him; we beseech you by the name of Jesus. For this befits you, men endowed with piety and Christian gravity. Georgius Blandrata seemed, a few weeks ago, to have readily subscribed to our confession. We ask that you examine his case diligently and prudently, and that you inform us of all matters. But as for our Churches, we testify before God that until now, by the grace of God, we have persisted in that faith, and we desire to persist in it, God willing, just as has been recited above. Farewell, brethren, most worthy of constant esteem in the Lord. Given at our synod at Kxiaefl, the 3rd day of September, in the year 1561.

units.la: CAL.
units.tr: CAL.

units.la: Io. Calvinvs N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to N., greeting

units.la: Neme vnius tantum hominis mors simplici ludu afflige-ret, Varennium meum triduo post sequutus est Antesigna-nus. De vita Baduelli nulla spes residua est. Heri Quaestoris nostri vxor dum foeliciter peperisse visa est, repente ex neruo-rum conuulsionibus est mortua. Nicolaum Igneum, vt plura su-nera accumulem, catarrhus intra nouem horas suffocauit. Ali-quid solatij, quod Beraldus paulatim cum vxore puerpera con-ualescit. Prope immaturo partu extincta fuit: nunc tamen foetu saluo, vires colligit. Quod nuper rogaui, vt alter e duobus ve-stris collegis redirct, quam celerrime fieri poterit, curate. Si in-tegrum eiset Gallo fio, & quidem Ecclesia cui praeest, incolumi, nobis restitui, vellemus. Verum re incerta quiescendum censui-mus. Tempus docebit quid rectum sit ac vtile. Caeterum ne te a-micitia Lotaringi cautum nimis reddat: te in tempore admo-neo, me quoque esse fratrem Ferrariensis. Nam quum me hic ante annos tredecim amplectetur, promisit se mihi semper fo-re optimum fratrem. Caue igitur ne in me superbias, quia facul-tas retaliandi in manu esset: praesertim quum Legatus omnes Cardinales superet. Vale optime & integerrime frater. Dominus tibi adsit, te gubernet, tueatur, donis omnibus locupletet, in-struat ad omnes pugnas, contra insidias prudentia, contra terro-res fortitudine muniat. Salutem plurimam fratribus nostris pre-cor. Salutant te fratres & amici. Iterum vale. III. Nonas Sep-tembris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: If the death of only one man were not to grieve me with such simple sorrow, my Varennius followed me three days later, and Antesignanus too. For Baduellus there is no hope left. Yesterday our Quaestor's wife seemed to have given birth happily, but suddenly she died in convulsions of the nerves. Nicolaus Igneus, to add more funerals, was suffocated by catarrh within nine hours. Some comfort is that Beraldus is slowly recovering along with his wife, who has just given birth. She was nearly lost to a premature delivery, but now, with the child safe, she is gathering her strength. As I asked recently, please see to it that one of your two colleagues returns to us as quickly as possible. If it were whole, we would wish Gallo to be restored to us, and indeed the Church he presides over, unharmed. But since the matter is uncertain, I have judged that we should wait. Time will show what is right and useful. Meanwhile, let not the friendship of the Lotharingian make you overly wary. I remind you in good time that I too am a brother of the Ferrarese. For when he embraced me here thirteen years ago, he promised that he would always be a very good brother to me. Beware, then, of showing pride towards me, since he would have the power to repay you in kind, especially since the Legate surpasses all the Cardinals. Farewell, most excellent and upright brother. May the Lord be with you, guide and protect you, enrich you with all his gifts, equip you for every battle, arm you with prudence against snares and with courage against terrors. I pray that you pass many greetings to our brothers. The brothers and friends greet you. Farewell again. Written on the third day before the Nones of September, 1561.

units.la: Io. Calvinvs Bezae.
units.tr: Io. Calvinus Bezae.

units.la: Heri tuae mihi redditae sunt quinque penultima Augusti scripse-ras. Dum alij nos iucundis rumoribus tam liberaliter pas-cut, mirum nisi te eius parsimoniae pudeat, quae nos prope ieiunos relinquit. Si multis cupias satisfacere, profice in schola in qua nomen tuum ita celebratur, & disce paulo audacius me-tiri. Cum enim mirifica alij narrent, tu solus vix mediocrem no-bis spem ostendis. Sed nunc extra iocum: meminerit e iste mihi scribe-re, qui nihil malo, quam simplici relatu in rem praesente deduci. Quicquid alij sentiant, semel mihi persuasi euanidum esse, quic-quid de Colloquio iactatur. Crede mihi, nunquam venient Epi-scopi ad feriam disputationem. Nec tamen dubito esse inter eos qui bene cupiant & sperent. Verum qui gubernacula tenent, re-digenter potius ad extrema, quam sustineant hoc modo se in or-dinem cogi. Itaque quos secum Theologos trahit Legatus in magna caterua, & qui ab Hispania venerunt, productum iri in theatrum arbitror,vt qui olim fercula in pompa gestabant. Denique si mi hi credis,Colloquij nulla te cura tanget.Si liberum illis esset conditiones dare,aliqua forte esset vmbratilis velitatio. Nunc cum videant leges sibi imponi, palam omne certamen detrectabunt. Inflabit etiam spiritus eorum aduentus Legati : cuius terrores si discussi fuerint,vt confido,prorsus actu est.Ante quam ad te perueniant hæ literæ,audita erunt tonitrua.Fulmen,nisi admodum fallor,non vibrabit,sed arrociter minabitur ante quam discedat. Hoc erit viuum examen. Quod si fallendi causa fe ad certamen offerant Episcopi,iam habetis P.Martyrem: quem ex dictu suppu tatione tempestiue appulilse colligo.De me ne verbum facere quanquam vehementer te rogaui, non definis tamen, vt video,aliquid tentare:quod meo iudicio non expedit. Ac mihi data opera aditum præcludere volui mea in Danielem Præfatione:non quod me pigeat laboris,aut vlla pericula defugium: sed quia vbi adsunt fatis idonei & probe instructi, non magnum præsentiæ meæ vsum arbitror.Et certe omnes,te & Merlino exceptis,fatis sunt animosi. De conditionibus quid sentirem,non scripsi, partim quia putabam ferum fore conlilium re iam transacta, partim quia mihi summopere placebat vobis cocedi quod fratres nostri potulauerant. Ego tamen si fuissem eorum loco, veritus fuissem tam duras leges præscribere. De successu gratuloraliqua ex parte:finem auidè expecto. Existimo te memoriate nerc quid tibi prædixerim, non esse metuendum,quin maximo cum illorum probro e conclaui in quo delitescunt ad vos erum peret præclara victoria,quanuise sublimi vos despicerent. Ideo cauendum esse,ne si in æquo iure tuendo effetis nimium pertina ces,culpa in vos reiceretur. Aug.Confessio,vt scis,fax est vestræ furiæ ad excitandum incendium,quo conflagrettota Gallia.Sed quærendum est quorsum obtrudatur:cum semper eius mollities cordatis displicuerit, auctorem eius pœnituerit, & in plerisque locis accommodata fit ad peculiarem vsum Germaniæ.Omitto quod eius breuitas & obscura, & præteritis quibusdam maximi momenti capitibus mutila est. Cæterum absurdum esset,neglecta Confessione Gallorum,illam arripere.Quid quòd in futurum tempus paratur hoc modo dimicandi materia? quia nunquam maior pars à Confessione semel recepta discedet. Perinde nunc disputo, acsi fyncerè Confessionem illam ampleterentur Cardinalis & eius affectæ.Sed insidiæ vobis tenduntur,vt discussa prę senti actione omnia conturbent.In eum finem editus fuit libel lus Bafileæ:cuius auctorem suspicor Balduinum,& pene pro certo habeo.Nebulonem excipere cupterem pro merito:sed priuatis literis obruor:& si quid alacritatis restabat,elanguit.Pergam tamen quoad licebit.Audio etiam nescio quod σὐν τάγμα Lutetiæ tiæ fuisse excusum, de historiæ coniunctione cum Iurisprudentia: vbi odiose perstringeris. Nunc cum suo Cassandro venenum aliquod coquere dicitur. Iam vobis curæ fuisse arbitror, vt vestro subsidio leuaremur. Si cessatum fuit, properet, quisquis venturus est. Vale integerrime frater, cum tota cohorte. Dominus vos Spiritu prudentiæ & fortitudinis gubernet, tueatur, & benedicat labores vestros. Collegæ nostri plurimum vobis omnibus salutem precantur. Amici etiam quos recensere longum esset. Vtinam vnus quē mihi mors eripuit, esset in numero. x. Septemb. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Yesterday your letter, dated the penultimate day of August, was delivered to me. While others feed us so generously with pleasant rumours, it would be no wonder if you were ashamed of that stinginess of yours which leaves us almost starving. If you wish to satisfy many, go to the school where your name is so celebrated, and learn to measure a little more boldly. For while others report marvellous things, you alone show us scarcely a moderate hope. But now, to be serious: remember that you are to write to me, who prefer nothing to a plain account of a matter as it happens. Whatever others think, I have persuaded myself once and for all that all the talk about the Colloquy is empty. Believe me, the bishops will never come to a fair disputation. Yet I do not doubt that there are some among them who wish well and hope for the best. But those who hold the reins would rather go to extremes than submit to being forced into line in this way. So I suppose the theologians whom the Legate drags along with him in his great troop, and those who have come from Spain, will be brought out onto the stage, like those who once carried the dishes in a procession. In short, if you believe me, the Colloquy will not trouble you at all. If it were open to them to lay down conditions, there might perhaps be some shadow-skirmish. Now, since they see that laws are being imposed on them, they will openly refuse every contest. The arrival of the Legate will also puff up their spirit; but if his terrors have been dispersed, as I trust they have, it is utterly finished. Before this letter reaches you, the thunders will have been heard. The lightning, unless I am much mistaken, will not be hurled, but will threaten fiercely before it departs. This will be a living trial. But if the bishops offer themselves for combat with the intent to deceive, you already have Peter Martyr, whom I gather from your report has arrived in good time. As for me, although I earnestly asked you not to mention me, you do not cease, as I see, to attempt something of the kind, which in my judgment is not expedient. Indeed, I deliberately wished to close the way to this in my Preface to Daniel: not that I shrink from labour or flee any dangers, but because where there are men sufficiently fit and well prepared, I think my presence is of little use. And certainly all of you, except you and Merlin, are spirited enough. As to what I thought about the conditions, I did not write, partly because I thought it would be fruitless to advise on a matter already settled, partly because I was very pleased that you should yield what our brethren had demanded. Yet if I had been in their place, I would have feared to prescribe such harsh laws. I await eagerly, though in part I congratulate you on the outcome. I believe you remember what I predicted to you: that there was no need to fear that they would, with great disgrace to themselves, peer out from the room in which they lie hidden, while you won a splendid victory, and that they would look down on you from a lofty height. Therefore one must take care that, if you are too stubborn in defending a fair right, the blame is not thrown back upon you. The Augsburg Confession, as you know, is a torch for kindling the fire by which all Gaul will be set ablaze. But we must ask where it is being thrust: since its mildness has always displeased men of sound judgment, its author has repented, and in many places it is adapted to the particular use of Germany. I pass over that its brevity is obscure, and that, with certain chapters of the greatest importance left out, it is maimed. Moreover, it would be absurd, with the Confession of the French neglected, to snatch up that one. And what of this, that material for fighting is being prepared for a future time in this way? For never will the greater part depart from a Confession once received. I argue now as if the Cardinal and his supporters embraced that Confession sincerely. But snares are being laid for you, so that, once the present action is broken off, they may throw everything into confusion. To that end a little book was published at Basel, whose author I suspect is Balduin, and I almost hold it for certain. I would gladly take vengeance on that scoundrel as he deserves, but I am overwhelmed by private letters, and whatever liveliness remained has grown faint. Still, I shall continue as long as I am able. I also hear that some ... was printed at Paris, concerning the connection of history with jurisprudence, in which you are odiously pilloried. Now they say he is brewing some poison together with his Cassander. I suppose it has been your concern that we should be relieved by your help. If there has been delay, let whoever is coming hasten. Farewell, most upright brother, with your whole company. May the Lord govern you with the Spirit of prudence and fortitude, guard you, and bless your labours. Our colleagues send you all very many greetings. Friends also, whom it would be long to list. Would that the one whom death has snatched from me were among the number. 10 September 1561.

units.la: CALVINVS. BEZAE.
units.tr: CALVINUS. BEZAE.

units.la: QVod binæ simul literæ tibi redditæ sunt, causam moræ vides fuisse in pigritia amici qui curam hanc suscepit. Certe cum tertio quoque die nuntij sint ad manum, culpam eluere non potest, quin differendo in nonum diem officij sui fuerit oblitus. Quæcunque de præclara actione scribis, aliunde iam innotuerant. Longe tamen gratius fuit rem quasi ante oculos positam perspicere, & fieri testimonio tuo certiores, quam narrationes aliorum audire, qui vt plurimum suo ornatu historiç syn ceritatem corrumpunt. Fœlicissimus dies ille, quo parta fuit Ecclesiis libertas, quam concedere necesse erit, difficilimum vero eripere. Oratio tua apud nos est, in qua Deus mirificè mentem & linguam tuam gubernauit. Quod bilem commouit sanctis Patribus omnino testatum oportuit, nisi turpiter velles tergiuer sari, ac te obiicere eorum probris, quos miror ea tantum de causa tumultuatos esse cum aliis locis non minus grauiter vulnerati esient. Hac vero offensione abruptum fuisse Colloquium stulte iactatur. Reperiffent enim centu alias, qui nunc vna mordicus arrepta, quodammodo reliquæ doctrinæ subscribunt. Ergo & hoc feliciter cecidit. Acanthium nomen Christo ingenuè pa lamq; dedisse gaudeo: quem propriis literis hortor ad pergendū. Expecto quàm dextrè suos centones contexuerit Lotharingus. Etsi verò finem velitationi impositum esse conijcio, scrium certamen nullū fore arbitror. Etsi autem admonui ne propere missionem peteres, iucundum tamen officium mihi præstabit Legatus, si te breui expediat. Verè reliquias amicorum nominas: quia in residua copia mihi fere solus videor. Collegæ nostri omnes te plurimum salutant. Vale integerrime frater. D. te semper gubernet, inuicta constantia & virtute confirmet, tibi adsit in sanctis laboribus, faluúmq; & incolumè tueatur. Tuos omnes comites salutare cupio. Quoties supra dies decem silebis, quod nunc rursus factum est, pigrum te esse dicam. x x i i i i. Sept. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: That two letters were delivered to you together, you see the cause of the delay lay in the laziness of the friend who undertook this task. Certainly, since messengers are at hand every third day, he cannot wash away the blame, for by postponing his duty to the ninth day he must have forgotten it. Whatever you write about the splendid action was already known to us from elsewhere. Yet it was far more pleasing to see the matter laid out as if before our eyes, and to be made more certain by your testimony, than to hear the accounts of others, who for the most part corrupt the truth of the history with their own embellishments. That most happy day on which liberty was won for the Churches, which they will have to concede, but which would be most difficult to snatch away. Your speech is with us, in which God has wonderfully governed your mind and tongue. That it stirred the bile of the holy Fathers had to be stated plainly, unless you wished to shamefully draw back and expose yourself to the reproaches of those whom I marvel to have been roused to tumult for this reason alone, since in other places they were no less gravely wounded. It is foolishly bruited that the Colloquy was broken off by this offence. For they would have found a hundred others who, now clinging stubbornly to this one point, in some measure subscribe to the rest of the doctrine. So this too has turned out well. I rejoice that you have openly and frankly given the name of Christ to Acanthius, whom I urge by my own letters to persevere. I await how skilfully the Lotharingian has stitched together his patchwork. And although I conjecture that an end has been put to the skirmishing, I think there will be no serious contest. Although I advised you not to seek your dismissal hastily, the Legate will nevertheless do me a pleasant service if he dispatches you soon. You truly name the remnants of friends, since in the remaining crowd I seem almost alone. All our colleagues salute you very warmly. Farewell, most upright brother. May the Lord always govern you, strengthen you with unconquered constancy and virtue, be present with you in holy labours, and keep you safe and sound. I desire to greet all your companions. As often as you keep silent for more than ten days, as has now happened again, I shall call you lazy. 24 September 1561.

units.la: VLtimis tuis breuiter responderam : quia sperabam te huc propediem venturum. Nunc vero hac spe me fuifle deceptum apprime gaudeo:t̀bíq; ex animo gratulor,eo te fuif fe sponte conuersum, quo cunctantem impellere modis omnibus fuissem conatus.Omnino sic agendum fuit,vt temporis preteriti moram,& tarditatem ex piorum omnium animis deleres: quia nisi in tanta certandi opportunitate apparuisses inter Christi athletas,communi omnium iudicio,vel astutiæ, vel ignauiç damnatus effes.Nunc tuæ fynceritatis specimen dedisti,quo fatis fuperq; purgata est sinistra omnis suspicio. Nec dubito quin maxima eorum lætitia fueris exceptus, qui tibi minimè parce-bant,quantifper tergiuersari vifuses. Superest vt ab hoc confli-ctu ad continuam militiam te accingas:multisque molestiis ac laboribus subeundis, qui manent veros Christi seruos, strenuè te compares. Etsi enim quamprimùm te videre optabam,mihi tamen gratius erit Ecclesiam, quæ tanta penuria laborat, tuo subsidio iuuari, & ex tua opera præsentem fructū maturius colligere,quàm fi hucte contulisses.Vale eximie vir,& mihi ex animo dilecte & colende frater.Dominus te Spiritu suo semper gubernet, virtute sustineat ac tueatur. xxiiii. Septembris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: I had briefly answered your last letter, because I hoped you would come here shortly. But now I rejoice most heartily that I was deceived in this hope, and I congratulate you from my heart that you have turned yourself of your own accord to the very course which I had tried in every way to urge upon you while you hesitated. It was altogether necessary to act so that you would remove from the minds of all the godly the delay and slowness of the past time; for unless in so great an opportunity for fighting you had appeared among the athletes of Christ, you would, by the common judgment of all, have been condemned either for cunning or for cowardice. Now you have given a sample of your sincerity, by which every sinister suspicion has been more than sufficiently purged. Nor do I doubt that you were received with the greatest joy by those who spared you not at all, as long as you were seen to be shifting. It remains that you gird yourself from this conflict for continual service, and that you prepare yourself vigorously for the many troubles and labours which await the true servants of Christ. For although I wished to see you as soon as possible, it will be more pleasing to me that the Church, which labours under such great scarcity, be aided by your help, and that I gather the present fruit more quickly from your work, than if you had betaken yourself hither. Farewell, excellent man, and brother dear and esteemed to me from my heart. May the Lord always govern you with his Spirit, sustain and guard you with virtue. 24 September 1561.

units.la: BEZA CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Beza to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: SEnas minimum literas ad te dedi,neque vnquam prætermisi iustam scribendi occasionem.Si quæ sunt intercepta,accidit præter expectationem. Omnes enim fidis amicis commisi, qui per expeditiss.curarent perferendas, quoniam hæc via mihi semper visa est tutissima & breuissima. Neque dubito,quin iam acceperis, quæ ad te scripsi de duabus primis nostris actionibus. Iam accipe cætera.Post splendidam illam nostri purpurati orationem, quam nulla ratione potuimus obtinere, totos nouem dies consumi nobis inuitis oportuit,vt de agendis rebus statue-retur. Quàm multa , & quàm varia nobis hic occurrerint, aliquando,vt spero,cognos es.Certè nullum non lapidem moue-runtilli,vt cœlum terræ miscerent:sed Dominus mirificè nobis adfuit. Tandem igitur vigesimoquarto die huius mensis, licuit nobis respondere ad duo capita quæ ille proposuerat, de Ecclesia nimirum,& de Cœna Domini.Disserui ad sesquihoram,magna omnium attentione, ac ne mireris nos esse tam verbosos, scito nos studio id facere,quoniam ex hoc colloquio nullū maiorem iorem fructum speramus, quàm vt cognita ac perspecta nostra causa,qui per ignorantiam nos damnabant,saltem æquiores no bis fiant:neque est Dei gratia, cur nos laboris pœniteat.Oratio- nem meam excepit conductitius Balaam,qui tibi aliquando du- ctum obtulit, vt chartam & pennas tibi comparares. Præfatus est, sibi nunquam placuisse seueritatem,qua nonnulli in nos v- fi effent,& hoc quidem inepte:quia neque conquesti eramus,ne quequemquam poterat videri magis accusare,quàm eum ipsum cui acceffrat aduocatus.Postea fassus est fe mihi assentiri de iis quæ de Ecclesia diff-ruissem,tàta vis est veritatis! & certè quan- tùm postea intelligi potuit ex eorum etiam Procerum sermone qui nobis alioqui minimè faucbat, vix eum tulissent aperte no- bis dissentientem. Tandem tamen dixit sibi non satisfactum in nostræ vocationis explicatione,quam modis omnibus exagita- uit,cùm ego nihil nisi in genere & δεπικῶς dixissem:& de hypo thesi hoc vnum addidissem,fi vellent ipsi,quod minimè optare- mus,ad nos ista transferre quæ de vocatione dixeram,paratos ef fe nos & vocationem nostram,& nostras Ecclesias exDei verbo tueri,sed rogare vt ad nostræ doctrinę disceptationem potiùs de fcenderent.Obiecit ergo suspectas esse vocationes extraordina- rias,nisi miraculis vel prophetiis expressis probarentur. Obiter etiam perstrinxit quædam quę ἀπαρίβῳρ adduxeram de Paphnu tio,& ex Tertulliano,& suo more multa verba consumpsit in ci tandis historiis & testimoniis, vt omnia edidicisse videretur. Quum vellem respondere, ecce infacetiffimus cucullio prodit, qui nos cum Anabaptistis compararet.Addidit vulgata teftimo nia de traditionibus & consuetudinibus.Tandè adiecit blafphe- miam,scriptum fuisse verbum præter Dei consilium,& eludens certa testimonia Chrifoftomi & Basilii, quæ citaram, hortatus est,vt semel atque iterum legerem Patrum testimonia quæ pro- ferrem. Hæc ferè sesquihoram abstulerunt. Tum ego præfa- tus, non esse hanc legitimam agendi rationem, cùm neque cer tis argumentis ageretur, neque libri, neque notarii adessent, & tam confuse prolixéque propositis rationibus, vix posset figil- latim responderi: tamen summam rationum complexus, dixi quæ sufficere arbitrabar. Monacho paucis respondi, & ita qui- dem, vt eo ipso die testatus fit ipsius magister, nunquam post- hac eum producturum in lucem.
units.tr: I have sent you very few letters, and I have never let slip a fair opportunity to write. If some have been intercepted, it happened against my expectation.
