I entrusted them all to trusty friends, who would see that they were delivered as quickly as possible, since this route has always seemed to me the safest and quickest. Nor do I doubt that you have already received what I wrote about our first two sessions. Now take the rest. After that splendid speech of our purpled one, which we could by no means prevent, we were forced against our will to spend a full nine days settling the business. How many and how varied the difficulties that arose for us here, you will learn at some point, I hope. They certainly moved every stone to mix heaven with earth, but the Lord stood by us wonderfully. At last, then, on the twenty-fourth day of this month, we were allowed to answer the two heads he had proposed, namely concerning the Church and the Lord's Supper. I spoke for an hour and a half, with everyone listening closely. Do not be surprised that we were so wordy; know that we did this on purpose, since we hope for no greater fruit from this conference than that, once our cause is known and clearly understood, those who condemned us out of ignorance may at least become fairer to us. And there is no thanks to God for which we should regret the labour. My speech was followed by the hired Balaam, who once offered you a ducat so that you could buy paper and pens. He began by saying that he had never liked the harshness with which some had attacked us, and he said this foolishly, since we had not complained, and no one could seem to accuse more than the man himself whose advocate he had become. Afterwards he admitted that he agreed with me on what I had said about the Church, so great is the power of truth! And indeed, as could be understood from the speech of the grandees themselves, who were otherwise by no means favourable to us, they would hardly have borne his openly disagreeing with us. Finally, however, he said that he was not satisfied with the explanation of our calling, which he attacked in every way, since I had said nothing except in general and popularly [δημοτικῶς]. And on the hypothesis I had added only this: if they themselves wished (which we would by no means desire) to apply to us what I had said about the calling, we were ready to defend both our calling and our Churches from the Word of God; but we asked them rather to come down to a discussion of our doctrine. He therefore objected that extraordinary callings are suspect unless they are proved by express miracles or prophecies. In passing he also touched on some things I had cited accurately [ἀκριβῶς] about Paphnutius and from Tertullian, and in his usual way he spent many words in citing histories and testimonies, as if he had learned them all by heart. When I wanted to reply, behold, the most unwitty hooded monk came forward, who compared us with the Anabaptists. He added the commonplace testimonies about traditions and customs. Finally he added a blasphemy, that the Word was written beyond God's counsel, and, mocking the sure testimonies of Chrysostom and Basil that I had cited, he urged me to read through the testimonies of the Fathers that I offered, once or twice. These things took up nearly an hour and a half. Then I began by saying that this was not a legitimate way of proceeding, since the matter was not being conducted by certain arguments, and neither books nor notaries were present, and since the reasons were put forward so confusedly and at such length that it was hardly possible to answer point by point. Nevertheless, I gathered up the sum of the arguments and said what I thought sufficient. I answered the monk briefly, and in such a way that on that very day his own master bore witness that he would never bring him forward again.

units.la: Excepit rursus Balaam, quæ voluit : postea,cùm de industria nihil dixissem de Cœna Domini (quoniam sciebam quid il- li captarent)ille idem multa garrire cœpit de pace & concor- dia,& cùm diuersas quæstiones imperitiffimè confunderet,scio, inquit,fore vt à voce fubftătialiter non abhorreatis,fi vobis pro duxero magni cuiufdam viri testimonium. Deinde suppresso tuo nomine tria loca mutilata ex vltimo tuo in Heshufiũ libello recitauit. Ego sum interfatus me agnoscere præceptoris verba. Quum responsum pararem non passus est purpuratus αὐτο-κράτωρ (sed nonnisi interfuos,idque admodum ægre imperium suum retinens) & de traditionum auctoritate præfatus ad Cœnā descendit,ac tandem aliquot chartas proferens, ecce,inquit,quæ recèns accepi ex Germania, partim à Palatino, partim ab alio Principe,quibus subscripserunt 42.Ministri,tibi ipsi Beza,vt opi nor non ignoti.An & vos illis atque adeò præceptori vestro nō subscribetis?facite hoc obsecro. Nam alioqui nulla coniunctionis spes est.Subscribite,inquam,alioqui colloqui non possumus. Nec tamen postulo,vt omnia comprobetis.Scio enim vos nũquam id facturos. Tantum particulam habetc & subscribite, vt fit concordiæ initium : deinde pauca quædam plane Brentiana recitauit.Ad hæc ego vicifim Reginam precari,vt potius de cō sessione nostra dispiceretur,quam ipsa à nobis accepisset,vtque legitima collatio institueretur. Non rectè fieri à Cœna Domini initium, cum tam multa præire oporteret Sacramentorum tractationi. Denique rogaui Cardinalem,an ipse vellet iis subscribere,quæ nobis exhiberet,quod alioqui nullus eflet nostræ fubfcriptionis fructus futurus. Ibi deprehensus ille tergiuersari,sed in summa dicere fieri non posse,quin abrumperetur spes omnis concordiæ,nisi subscriberemus. Nox instabat,omnes vrgebant vt paci consuleremus,alij quidem per simplicitatem, alij ex copofito. Itaque non potuimus alia ratione elabi,quàm fi teftarc-mur nihil nos habere fecundum veritatem antiquius regni pace,& scriptum illud cum tuo libro nobis tradi peteremus,vt po ftero die daremus responsum, cuiusmodi ferre conscientia no-ftra posset.Ita igitur discessum est,illis quidem, suo more,victo-riam sibi promittentibus,nobis verò,Dei gratia,& verbis & vul tu testantibus eam fiduciam,qua consueuit Dominus nostèr fer-uos suos implere.
units.tr: Balaam spoke again, saying what he wished. Afterwards, since I had deliberately said nothing about the Lord's Supper (because I knew what they were aiming at), he began to chatter at length about peace and concord, and while he very ineptly confused different questions, he said: "I know that you will not substantially dissent from the word, if I put before you the testimony of a great man." Then, with your name suppressed, he recited three mutilated passages from your last little book against Heshusius. I interrupted him, saying that I recognised my teacher's words. When I was preparing a reply, the purpled one, the autocrat [αὐτοκράτωρ], did not allow it (he only interrupted, and even then he kept his authority with great difficulty), and after speaking about the authority of traditions he came down to the Supper. Finally, producing some papers, he said: "Behold, these are what I have lately received from Germany, partly from the Palatine and partly from another prince, and they have been signed by 42 ministers, including yourself, Beza, as I believe you are not unknown. Will you and your teacher not sign them as well? Please do so. For otherwise there is no hope of union. Sign, I say, or we cannot talk. Nor do I ask you to approve everything, for I know you will never do that. Only take the little part and sign, so that there may be a beginning of concord." Then he recited a few things that were plainly Brenzian. In reply I begged the Queen in turn that the confession we had made should be examined first, rather than what she had received from us, and that a lawful comparison should be set up. It was not right to begin with the Lord's Supper, when so many things ought to come before the treatment of the sacraments. Finally I asked the Cardinal whether he himself would be willing to sign the documents he was presenting to us, since otherwise our signature would have no fruit at all. There, caught out, he tried to evade, but in sum he said that it could not be avoided that all hope of concord would be broken off unless we signed. Night was approaching, and everyone urged us to consult for peace, some indeed out of simplicity, others on purpose. So we could not slip away in any other way than by declaring that we held nothing more important, according to truth, than the peace of the kingdom, and by asking that the written document be handed over to us along with your book, so that we could give an answer the next day, of such a kind as our conscience could bear. And so we parted: they, in their usual way, promising themselves victory, but we, by the grace of God, with both our words and our faces witnessing that confidence which our Lord is accustomed to fill his servants with.

units.la: Postridie quum nos ad iter accingeremus,nobis nuntiatum fuit dilatum esse colloquium in alterum diem, qui hesternus fuit,quod etsi initiò moleste culimus,tamen sensimus Dei proui dentia factum. Fuimus enim ab amicis,quos & multos & fidos ac constantes Dei beneficio habemus,de multis rebus admoniti, quas etsi coniecturis non erat difficile consequi,tamen gratum fuit certis testimoniis confirmari, vt firmum consilium capere-mus. Consilium Cardinalis erat, fi differremus fubfcriptionem, colloquij statim abrumpendi culpam in nos maxima cum om-nium ordinum inuidia transferre:fi nos aperte negaremus sub-scripturos statim vniuerfamGermaniam in nos concitare,quasi patratus ipse fuerit Auguftanam confessionem saltem aliqua ex parte concordiæ causa recipere:sin vero subscriberemus,postea vel nobis eiectis abEcclefiis,quas prodidissemus,vel scissis nostris in diuersas partes, triumphare. Has technas ita euasimus. Quum eo ventum effet,grauissimam querelam ex scripto recitaui,ut fi forte abruptum effet colloquium,nos extra culpam esse consta-ret. Ostendimus nos non addicendum causam coram aduersa-riis, sed ad reddendam ex Dei verbo rationem nostræ fidei coram toto mundo: neque ad fubfcribédum quod illis liberet,sed ad pacificam collocutionem venisse. Satis apparere nihil aliud illos captare quàm fubterfugia, promisisse Cardinalem,fe nobis ex verbo Dei & orthodoxis Patribus, qui proximis à Christo quingentis annis vixissent, sua probaturum, nostra confutatu-rum. Eundem vero nunc nobis pro collatione ista damnatione præscribere, nisi suis placitis subscriberemus: nec tamen nobis constare an hoc ipse sua vnius auctoritate, an vero omnibus Collegis approbantibus faceret. Præterea quàm iniquum esse, non de nostris controuersiis sed de alienis quæri, quasi isti inter nos & Germanos arbitri sederent. Quòd si illis placeret illud quorundam Theologorum scriptum, quod nobis tradiderant, age subscriberent ipsi non mutilatis propositionibus,sed toti Augustanæ confessioni:quòd si facerent,tum vero nos non procul abfore à concordia,vnico excepto articulo, de quo parati essemus sanctè & amicè colloqui. Sin autem id ipsi facere recusarent,iniquè à nobis peti,vt iis subscribamus,quæ ne ipsi quidem probent.Cæterum quod ad quæstionem de nostra vocatione attineret,satis illam nobis defensam videri, nec recusare quin suo loco iterum de illa quæratur ad satietatem vsque. Sed imprimis de doctrina ipsa agendum fuisse, & quidem certo ordine,si disputatio legitima quæreretur.Nos igitur petere à Regina & omnibus Principibus,vt vel audiremur,vel si abrumperetur collo-quium,nos excusatos haberent.
units.tr: The next day, when we were preparing for the journey, we were told that the conference had been put off until the following day, which was yesterday. Although at first we took this badly, we came to feel that it had happened by the providence of God. For we were warned by friends, whom by God's favour we have many, trusty, and steadfast, about many matters, which, though it was not difficult to guess them from conjecture, it was nevertheless pleasing to have confirmed by sure testimonies, so that we could take a firm decision. The Cardinal's plan was this: if we postponed signing, to lay the greatest blame for breaking off the conference on us, to the great resentment of all orders; if we openly refused to sign, to stir up the whole of Germany against us, as if we had brought about the Augsburg Confession for the sake of concord at least in some part; but if we did sign, then afterwards, either by expelling us from the Churches we had betrayed, or by splitting us into different parties, to triumph. We escaped these tricks in this way. When we arrived there, I read out from a written text a very grave complaint, so that, if by chance the conference was broken off, it would be plain that we were free of blame. We showed that we had not come to hand over our cause to our adversaries for judgement, but to give an account of our faith from the Word of God before the whole world; nor had we come to sign whatever pleased them, but for a peaceful discussion. It was clear enough that they were aiming at nothing but evasions: the Cardinal had promised that he would prove his own positions from the Word of God and from the orthodox Fathers, who had lived within five hundred years of Christ, and that he would refute ours. Yet now he was prescribing for us, as the condition of this conference, condemnation unless we signed his positions; and it was not clear to us whether he did this on his own authority alone or with the approval of all his colleagues. Moreover, how unfair it was to inquire not into our controversies but into those of others, as if these men were sitting as arbiters between us and the Germans. But if they were pleased by that writing of certain theologians which they had handed over to us, let them sign it themselves, not with the propositions mutilated, but in its entirety, the whole Augsburg Confession; and if they did so, then indeed we would not be far from concord, apart from a single article, on which we were ready to talk holily and in a friendly way. But if they refused to do this, it was unfair for us to be asked to sign things they themselves did not approve. Besides, as for the question of our calling, we thought it had been sufficiently defended for us, and we did not refuse that it be asked again in its own place, to satiety. But above all the doctrine itself ought to have been dealt with, and indeed in a fixed order, if a lawful disputation were sought. We therefore asked the Queen and all the Princes that either we be heard, or, if the conference were broken off, that they hold us excused.

units.la: Subiecimus deinde breuem & perspicuam confessionem de Cœna Domini,ne calumniarentur nos extra oleas vagari: quæ si non satisfaceret, iustam & plenam disceptationem petiimus. Quid si verò,inquam,de vestra vocatione quæratur?vbi illa doctrinæ & morum inquisitio,vbi electio,vbi iusta ordinatio,imò quomodo vos à Simonia excusabitis?Conclusio fuit,vel vt confessionem à nobis exhibitam oppugnarent, vel suam traderent à nobis oppugnandam:sin minus,nos esse officio nostro defun-ctos, & Regni concordiæ omnem nostram operam, atque adeò nos ipsos ex animo consecrare. Ad hæc Cardinalis æstuans,vt qui nihil eiusmodi de nobis per suos exploratores cognouisset, ex tempore tamen satis diserte in tam mala causa respon-dit. Nos ipsos causam præbuisse quæstioni de nostra vocatione:
units.tr: We then submitted a brief and clear statement on the Lord's Supper, so that they could not slander us as wandering outside the paths; and if that did not satisfy them, we asked for a full and proper disputation. What if, I said, the question were raised about your own calling? Where is that inquiry into doctrine and morals, where is the election, where is the lawful ordination? Indeed, how will you excuse yourselves from simony? The conclusion was that they should either attack the confession we had presented, or hand over their own to be attacked by us; otherwise we had failed in our duty and should devote all our effort, and indeed ourselves, wholeheartedly to the harmony of the kingdom. To this the Cardinal, who was seething, since he had learned nothing of this kind about us through his spies, nevertheless answered quite fluently on the spur of the moment, in so bad a cause. He said that we ourselves had given occasion for the question about our calling.

units.la: L.j. Iure fe cum suis conqueri de iis, qui in suos greges inuasissent: non posse nos melius ostendere quàm fimus à pace alieni, quàm duos simul conuellendo Gallici Regni cardines, Ecclesiasticam videlicet & Regiam auctoritatem: deinde in hunc campum ingressus, tentauit modis omnibus non aliter quàm publicos hostes obiicere statim ad supplicium trahendos, perinde acsi Regè ac ipsius maiores dixissem tyrannicè Ecclesiam Dei populatos. Postea de suo statu multa praedicare, nescire nos quales eflent Episcoporum ordinationes, in quibus nihil vetusti moris praetermittetur. Tandem ad quaestionem de Coena Domini delapsus, vertit sese in omnis facies vt ostenderet fe, quod fecisset de fubfcriptione, pacis studio fecifle, cuius spem omnem re ipsa praecideremus.
units.tr: He complained, with good reason, that he and his people had been attacked by those who had invaded their flocks; that we could show ourselves no better aliens from peace than by overturning the two hinges of the kingdom of France at once, namely ecclesiastical and royal authority. Then, having entered this field, he tried by every means, as if he were dealing with public enemies to be dragged off to punishment at once, to make out that I had called the King and his ancestors tyrants who had ravaged the Church of God. Afterwards he proclaimed many things about his own position, saying that we did not know what the ordinations of bishops were like, in which nothing of ancient custom is omitted. At last, slipping into the question of the Lord's Supper, he turned himself into every shape, to show that what he had done about the subscription he had done for the sake of peace, the hope of which we had cut off by our deeds.

units.la: Ad haec quoque ego ex tempore ita me puto respondisse, Dei beneficio, vt & Reginae & Proceribus certò sciam defensionem meam multò magis, quàm illius accusationem placuisse.
units.tr: I think I answered these points too on the spur of the moment, by God's blessing, so that I know for certain my defence pleased both the Queen and the nobles far more than his accusation did.

units.la: Tum verò noster Balaam multa partim ex ante habita difpu tatione iterum odiose repetere, multa innoluere, denique multa dicendo nihil dicere. At noster Martyr tum primum loqui exorsus Italico sermone, vt à Regina intelligi posset, rem totam ab ouo vsque explicauit, & vel inuitos ad rem ipsam descendere coegit. Respondit Balaam, & testimonia vicissim suo more coacernauit, vt tropum negaret in Coenae verbis subesse. Dum haec geruntur, ecce prodit Iesuita Hispanus, Catholicae Ecclesiae columen. Alloquutus est Reginam hora ferme integra, sed ita ineptè, ita stulte, vt nemo posset risum continere, quum ille histrio inter caetera in extremo fabulae actu lacrymaretur. Rogabat in summa Reginam, ne audiret haereticos toties damnatos, sed ad concilium relegaret, crepans illud. Tu es Petrus, &, roga ii pro te Petre. Disputauit postea de corpore fine dimensione, & Eucharistiam docuit esse instar ludicrae pugnae, in qua Rex ipse interesset. Tum ego, petita à Regina venia paucis dixi me Hispano illi omnia concedere, quae dixisset, fi probaret. Quòd nos vulpes, & serpentes, & simias diceret, non magis nos credere, quàm transubstantiationem. Satis illam pro sua prudentia intelligere quid isti fit credendum, quiCoenam Domini profabula, Christum pro histrione haberet. Deinde quum aduersus Balaamum agere coepissem, ecce nouus hostis prodit sophista quidam Sorbonicus planeconfidens, qui primo loco me docuit, quid effet pronomen, quae propositio identica, & adipulante ac pertinacifsime consentiente Cardinali, docuit per pronomen (hoc) non designari panem, sed vagum, quod vocant, indiuiduum. Quàm mul tis, & quàm planis argumentis absurdum hoc commentum potuerit dilui, quis ignorat? Sed tamen nunquam potuit Sophistae perpersuaderi, vt se victum fateretur. Itaque cum iam pene nox effet, omnes vtrinque assurrexerunt. Ibi me Regina in medium cum Cardinali aduocat, & per Deum obtestatur, vt pacis rationem ineamus. Confluit caetera turba. Iterum instauratur disputatio, sed omnibus tumultuose perstrepentibus. Tandem igitur nox clamoribus finem imposuit. Aiût nos intra triduum reuersuros: sed nisi certus ordo instituatur, quorsum istos labores? Itaque nunc toti in eo sumus. Hesterno tamen die sumus duo praeclara consequuti. Fregimus enim illorum consilia, & certo scimus nos obtinuisse, vt & nostros firmiores etiam quam antea, & eos qui nobis erant infensissimi, multo habeamus aequiores. Habes duorum dierum actionem. Vtinam vel isto labore breui defungar, vel alius mihi substitui posset, quo vobis iniquissimo onere pressis possim aliquando, vt antea, subuenire. Nam mihi crede hic mihi sordent omnia praeclarissima mea Geneua, cuius vnius memoria refic-ior. Eram aliqua praeterea scripturus, sed ita sum defessus, vt prorsus cogar in crastinum diem caetera differre. Bene vale, mi plurimum obseruande pater, vna cum caeteris fratribus & amicis, quos vtinam Dominus saluos & incolumes conseruet, ac modis omnibus tueatur. Ex Sangermano, xxvi i. Septembris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Then indeed our Balaam repeated many things, partly from the disputation held earlier, in a hateful way, entangled many matters, and finally, while speaking much, said nothing. But our Martyr then first began to speak in Italian, so that the Queen could understand, and explained the whole matter from the very beginning, and forced even unwilling men to come down to the point itself. Balaam replied, and in his usual way heaped up testimonies in turn, to deny that any trope lies in the words of the Supper. While these things were going on, behold, there came forward a Spanish Jesuit, the pillar of the Catholic Church. He addressed the Queen for almost a whole hour, but so clumsily and so foolishly that no one could keep from laughing, since that actor, among other things, wept at the end of the play. In sum, he begged the Queen not to listen to heretics so often condemned, but to refer them back to the council, repeating that phrase: "You are Peter, and, pray for them, Peter." Afterwards he disputed about a body without dimension, and taught that the Eucharist is like a mock battle in which the King himself takes part. Then I, having asked the Queen's pardon, said briefly that I would concede to that Spaniard everything he had said, if he could prove it. As for his calling us foxes, serpents and apes, I said we believed that no more than transubstantiation. The Queen, in her wisdom, understood well enough what such men are to be believed, who make the Lord's Supper a fable and regard Christ as an actor. Then, when I had begun to deal with Balaam, behold, a new enemy appeared, a certain Sorbonne sophist, very self-confident, who first taught me what a pronoun is and what an identical proposition is; and with the Cardinal assisting and most stubbornly agreeing, he taught that the pronoun "this" designates not the bread but what they call a vague individual. Who does not know how many and how plain arguments could refute this absurd invention? Yet the sophist could never be thoroughly persuaded to admit that he was beaten. So, when it was now almost night, everyone on both sides rose. Then the Queen summoned me into the middle with the Cardinal, and by God she entreated us to enter upon a way of peace. The rest of the crowd flocked in. The disputation was resumed, but with everyone shouting tumultuously. At last the night put an end to the clamour. They say we shall return within three days; but unless a fixed order is established, what is the point of these labours? So for now we are wholly intent on that. Yet yesterday we achieved two notable things. For we have broken their plans, and we know for certain that we have won over both our own people, who are firmer even than before, and those who were most hostile to us, whom we now have much more favourable. You have the account of two days. I wish I could finish this labour quickly, or that someone else could be substituted for me, so that I could sometime, as before, help you who are crushed by a most unfair burden. For believe me, here all things, even my most splendid Geneva, seem worthless to me, and I am refreshed by the memory of that city alone. I was going to write some other things as well, but I am so worn out that I am forced to put the rest off until tomorrow. Farewell, my most honoured father, together with the other brothers and friends, whom I pray the Lord will keep safe and sound, and protect in every way. From Saint-Germain, 26 September 1561.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS BEZAE.
units.tr: John Calvin to Beza.

units.la: HOdie literas tuas accepi, die scilicet nostro, vberrimas, & peraeque suaues. Vnde cognosces in dolore articulari adhuc me deliciis vacare. Non semper tantum otij fuit, toto enim biduo passus sum acerrimos cruciatus in pede dextro. Coepit morbus mitigari quidem nudiustertius: sed non ita remisit, quin pedem teneat deuinctum. Atque vt scias me nihil fingere, odor olei mihi prope est amabilis, quanuis saepe nausea citet. Ita nō est cur aulicis tuis lautitiis inuidea bene & pinguiter vnctus. Crede mihi, iocando non ita me oblecto, vt tibi abstergere cupio omne molestiam: nec si forte obscurus rumor ad te aliunde perueniat, anxietatem aliquā concipias. Video enim, nisi te mirabiliter sustineret Deus, non esse tibi vigorem decimae partiferendae. Tu post dimidiam noctem mihi respondes. Ego ex lecto post horam septimam, dum commode licet. Ita prouidi sunt senes podagrici. Sed extra iocum: nullis verbis exprimere queo, quam mihi iucundae fuerint tuae literae, quibus in rem presente sum adductus. Quae etsi non omni ex parte arridet, plus tamen laetitiae continet, quam indignationis aut fastidij. Ter & quater benedictus sit Deus noster, qui nos videtur supra nubes attollere:
units.tr: Today I received your letters, that is, on our day. They are very full and equally pleasant. From them you will learn that, even in my joint pain, I am still given over to pleasures. I have not always had so much leisure, for for two whole days I have suffered the most severe torments in my right foot. The illness began to ease the day before yesterday, but it has not let go so completely that it does not still hold my foot bound. So that you know I am not making things up, the smell of the oil is nearly pleasing to me, although it often makes me queasy. There is therefore no reason for you to envy your courtiers their fine fare, since I am well and thickly anointed. Believe me, I do not amuse myself with jokes so as to wipe away all your worry. Nor, if some vague rumour reaches you from elsewhere, should you feel any anxiety. For I see that, unless God sustained you wonderfully, you would not have the strength to bear even a tenth part of it. You answer me after midnight; I write from bed after seven o'clock, as far as it is convenient. So prudent are old men with gout. But seriously: I cannot express in words how pleasing your letters were to me, by which I was drawn into the matter at hand. Though they do not please me in every respect, they contain more joy than indignation or disgust. Three and four times blessed be our God, who seems to lift us above the clouds, so that, embracing the feet of the triumphant Christ, we may look down from on high upon all our enemies.

units.la: L.ij. vtamplexi Christi triumphantis pedes, ex alto despiciamus omneseius hoftesac nostros. Non habeo quam tibi mercedem referam,ne fi aere quidem loco auri contentus eftes.Porro vt intelligas,dum vos in astu & arena ferio certatis, me hic in vmbra velitari,mitto quod Balduini libello respondi. Caue ne improbes: quia dicam eiusdem te effefactionis, ficum eo sentias cui maxime displicebit.Merlinus operam non perdidit fcriben do, quanuis paria cum eo non faciam: quia debitorem habet qui aufugere non potest.Fratres nostri te & reliquos plurimum salutant. Valete iterum atque iterum omnes. Nonis Octobris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: I have no way to repay you for this kindness, since I would not be content even with gold in place of bronze. Furthermore, so that you understand that while you struggle in the heat and sand, I skirmish here in the shade, I say nothing of having answered Balduin's little book. Take care not to take offence, for I shall say that you belong to the same faction, so that you will feel the sting most in the one who will be most displeased. Merlin has not wasted his labour in writing, although I shall not match him in kind, because he has a debtor who cannot escape. Our brothers greet you and the rest most warmly. Farewell, all of you, again and again. On the Nones of October, 1561.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO N. S., GREETING

units.la: QVod mecum expostulas quod Georgium Blandratam fingulatem tuum amicum, & compatrem chariffimu durius perstrinxerim: de hac priuata offensione facilis & prompta est excusatio,me nihil talefuiffe suspicatum. Certe nunquam diuinaffem tanto in pretio apud te fore hominem nihili.Et quo niam te non minus praeclara apud omnes existimatione, quam dignitate & potentia florere cupio,mihi non parum dolet obliquis fuisartibus ita eum obrepsisse in tuam gratiam.Si mihi cre dibile fuisset,hominem,cuius mihi compertaerat impietas,tibi esse familiarem, certe priuata admonitione fuissem contentus, idque nomini tuo dedissem. Sed aliorum potius causa publice traducendum esse censui,vt sibi omnes a peste tam noxia cauerent.Ergo praecipua indignationis causa euanuit: quia mihi nihil minus fuit propositum, quam famam tuam oblique laedere, quum verba me facere putarem de homine vobis incognito,vel saltem qui nullo amicitiae vel necessitudinis gradu te attingeret: fedtibi est amicus. An maiore in gradu quam Iudasapud Christum? Si non parcimus Christi discipulo,quin ob sua perfidiam omnibus fiat detestabilis,non plus indulgentiae merentur cuiusquam amici. Sed ne taedio fit epistolae prolixitas,breue historiae compendium descripsi,ex quo facile cognoscas,meritone an iniuste detexerim occultum venenum, ne diutius clam graf fando multos in Polonia inficeret. Neque enim odio, vel aemulatione, vel inuidia ad publicandum obscuri hominis dedecus impulsus sum:sed quia fratresmihi charissimos silentio & dissimulatione prodere nefas esse duxi. Quod fi resipiscat, nulla in me erit mora, quin praeteriti temporis memoria sepeliatur. Si autem pertinaciter contendit sibi factam esse iniuriam, quasnam mihi relinquit partes, nisi vt mihi fit pro obstinato haeretico? Sicuti
units.tr: As for your complaint that I dealt too harshly with Georgius Blandrata, your singular friend and very dear co-parent, the excuse for this private offence is easy and ready at hand: I had suspected nothing of the sort. Certainly I never imagined that a man of no account would be held in such high esteem by you. Since I wish you to flourish in the highest reputation with everyone as much as in your dignity and power, it grieves me not a little that he has crept into your favour by these oblique arts. If I had found it credible that a man whose impiety I had come to know was familiar with you, I would certainly have been content with a private admonition, and would have spared your name. But I judged that he should be exposed publicly for the sake of others, so that everyone might guard against a pest so harmful. So the main cause of my indignation has disappeared, because my purpose was by no means to wound your reputation obliquely. I thought I was speaking of a man unknown to you, or at least one who had no degree of friendship or connection with you. But he is your friend. Is he any closer than Judas was to Christ? If we spare no one in Christ's own disciple, on account of his treachery, the friends of anyone deserve no more indulgence. But so that my letter may not become tedious through length, I have written a brief summary of the history, from which you can easily see whether I have exposed this hidden poison rightly or unjustly, lest it secretly infect many in Poland for longer. For I was not driven to publish the disgrace of an obscure man by hatred, rivalry, or envy, but because I thought it wrong to betray my dearest brothers by silence and concealment. If he comes to his senses, there will be no delay on my part, and the memory of the past will be buried. But if he stubbornly insists that a wrong has been done to him, what role does he leave me, except to regard him as an obstinate heretic?

units.la: Epist.318. Sicuti mihi optabile est pro mea erga te obseruantia studiose vo tis tuis obsequi, ita te rogatum esse velim, vt imprimis caueas ne sibi ianuam aperiat Blandrata ipse, vestra auctoritate addu- ctus.Aliud remedium non video.Sed fortasse vbi de re tota red- diti fueritis certiores,mutare iudicium non pigebit.Quod fi mi hi nihil tribuitis,saltem fidem meretur testimonium Italicæ Ec- clefiæ,quæ apud nos est,& D.Petri Martyris.Hac de re plus fatis. Toti Poloniæ, & priuatim Lithuaniæ gratulor, quod maiores subinde illic progressus faciat purior Religio,& nouis increme tis longe lateque dilatetur Christi Regnum.Hæc etiam non pœ- nitenda gaudij accessio, cum audio disciplinam cum Euangelij professione coniungi.Et certe non immerito vocare soleo disci- plinam neruos Ecclesiæ: quia vt propensi sunt hominum mo- res ad lasciuiam,delicias,& licentiam quamlibet,nisi continea- mur sub fræno, maior pars libertatis prætexru luxuriabitur & insolescet. Vnum defidero,vt in posterum tempus prospiciatur Ecclesiis ne Pastoribus orbatæ & nudatæ breui intereant.Scho- læ autem,seminaria sunt pastorum:& apte censeri possunt tan- quam cœlestis doctrinæ gazophylacia.Quo maior danda est o- pera,vt quamplurimi instituantur tam in pietate,quàm bonis li teris.Hæc vero nobilissima erit vobis liberalitatis materia,vt ve ftro exemplo reliqui ad imitationem incitentur. Ergo vt finem faciam Deum suppliciter precabor, vt te Spiritu suo gubernet, incolumem tueatur, magisque ac magis suis donis illustret ac locupletet.Genevæ,1 x.Octob. M. D. L X I.
units.tr: Just as it is my wish, out of my regard for you, to comply eagerly with your wishes, so I would ask you to take special care that Blandrata himself, led on by your authority, does not open a door for himself to them. I see no other remedy. But perhaps, once you have been fully informed about the whole matter, you will not be reluctant to change your judgement (Epist. 318). If you give me no credit, at least the testimony of the Italian Church, which is among us, and of Master Peter Martyr deserves belief. Enough on this matter. I congratulate all Poland, and Lithuania in particular, that the purer religion makes ever greater progress there, and that the kingdom of Christ is spreading far and wide by new increases. This is also an addition to my joy, which I do not regret, when I hear that discipline is joined to the profession of the Gospel. And indeed I am accustomed, not without reason, to call discipline the sinews of the Church. For human morals are so prone to wantonness, pleasure, and unrestrained licence that, unless we are held under the bridle, the greater part of men will indulge in luxury under the pretext of liberty and grow insolent. I have one wish: that provision be made for the future, so that the Churches, deprived and stripped of ministers, do not soon perish. But schools are the seminaries of ministers, and may fitly be regarded as the treasuries of heavenly doctrine. Therefore all the more effort must be given so that as many as possible are trained both in piety and in good literature. This will be a most noble matter for your generosity, so that others may be stirred to imitate your example. So, to make an end, I will humbly pray God that he may govern you by his Spirit, keep you safe, and enrich and adorn you more and more with his gifts. Geneva, 10 October 1561.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS STANISLAO.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO STANISLAUS

units.la: QVod mihi per literas innotescere voluisti, eximie vir, vt posthac te inter amicos meos censeam, gratissimum mihi su t:ac sicuti libenter amplector hoc beneuolentiæ tuæ ftu dium,ita vicissim polliceor me fraterno erga te fore animo,ficu ti & tua pietas & eruditio merentur:cuius vtriufq; in literis il- luftre specimen apparet.Nam cum omnes in Blandrata hallucinentur,tanquam eius præstigiis fascinati,vnus prudenter fubol facis non temere esse credendum. Sed ne coniecturis tantum agamus,scito Valentinum Gentilem, cuius delirla breuiter refutaui,ex eadem fuisse factione:adeoque alterum Blandratā, quāuis neuter alteri cederet. Non fuisse deprehensas eius fraudes in Polonia,nec adhuc perspici quàm insidiosus fit & fallax,tolerabile forsan effet.Sed valde miror hominē, quem sola ostentatio & fastuosus vultus commendat,tanti apud vos fieri,vt quasi nouus Atlas Ecclesiam sustineat suis humeris.Certe tā inconsidera tæ credulitatis nisi me puderet, gentem vestram nou amarem,
units.tr: Your letter, distinguished sir, which made known to me that you wish to be counted among my friends from now on, was most welcome to me. Just as I gladly embrace this zeal for goodwill of yours, so in turn I promise that I will feel toward you the affection of a brother, as both your piety and your learning deserve. Both appear clearly in your letter. For while everyone else is deluded about Blandrata, as though bewitched by his tricks, you alone have prudently realised that he should not be believed rashly. But lest we proceed by conjecture alone, know that Valentinus Gentilis, whose ravings I have briefly refuted, belonged to the same faction, so that one Blandrata would yield nothing to the other, though neither gives way to the other. That his frauds were not detected in Poland, and that even now it is not clearly seen how insidious and deceitful he is, might perhaps be tolerable. But I am greatly surprised that a man whom only show and a haughty countenance recommend is held in such high regard among you that, like a new Atlas, he supports the Church on his shoulders. Certainly, if I were not ashamed of such thoughtless credulity, I would not love your nation.

units.la: L.iij. Cæterum ex communibus literis, quas Ecclesiis scribo, plane ad facietatem, imò ad fastidium usque, perspicies quid hominis sit, vel bestiæ, vel monstri. Vale eximie vir, & mihi ex animo colendè frater. Dominus te Spiritu suo semper gubernet, sustineat invicta virtute, & donis suis in dies locupletet. Geneuæ, v II. Idus Octobris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Moreover, from the common letters which I write to the Churches, you will see plainly, even to the point of satiety and disgust, what sort of man he is, or rather what beast or monster. Farewell, distinguished sir, and brother whom I must honour from my heart. May the Lord always govern you by his Spirit, sustain you with unconquered virtue, and enrich you with his gifts day by day. Geneva, 7 October 1561.

units.la: Io. Cal. D. Foelici Crucigero, Eivsqve Collegis, Ecclesiarum minoris Poloniæ fidis Pastoribus & Ministris.
units.tr: Io. Cal. To Felix Crucigerus and his colleagues, the faithful pastors and ministers of the churches of Lesser Poland.

units.la: QUid Stacarus profecerit, quibus vos grauare tentauit calumniis, ex responso nostro apparet. Nobis certè nunquam fuit suspecti. Sed quia vobis visum est purgare, si quid conceptum esset suspicionis, libenter confessionem à vobis scriptam amplectimur, quia eius breuitas nihil habet obscurum vel ambiguum. Nec vero timendum fuit, ne vllis sinistris rumoribus à vobis alienaremur. Sacta igitur manet inter nos coniunctio, eamque vltro citróque fraterna beneuolentia colamus. Vnum tamen non dissimulo, eos qui tam humaniter Georgium Blandratâ exceperunt, parum fuisse cautos & prouidos, & male cofuluisse vestræ existimationi. Magis etiam miror quosdam primarias avcto ritatis viros grauiter offendi, quòd libere hominem detexerim, vt necesse erat. Ac ne putetis temerè fuisse quicquam à me creditu, historicam narrationem dictaui, quæ vos omnium certiores faceret. Tacere verò in tanto vestro discrimine fas non fuit, cùm intelligerem non modò lupum in ouile admissum fuisse, sed ouibus datum esse custodem. Nunc tamen si resipiscere in animo habeat Blandrata, te ipsa de monstret. Quod si mihi reconciliari velit, ignoscere paratus sum, simul ac mutatum fuisse in melius cognouero. Sed profecto vobis illudit dum se indignè traductu fuisse conqueritur. Quid? cùm scirem impiis deliriis imbutum, an non fuisset proditorium de tanto periculo vos non commonefacere? Syncere ergo de salute vestra solicitudinis officiu præstiti, cuius nunquam me pœnitebit. Valete integerrimi fratres, & ex animo mihi charissimi. Dominus vobis adsit, vos gubernet, ac tueatur perpetuò 1 x. Octob. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: How much Stancarus has achieved, and with what calumnies he has tried to burden you, is clear from our reply. We never had any suspicion of you. But since you thought it right to clear yourselves of any suspicion that had arisen, we gladly accept the confession you have written, because its brevity leaves nothing obscure or ambiguous. Nor indeed was there any need to fear that we would be estranged from you by any sinister rumours. So the fellowship between us remains intact, and let us cultivate it with mutual brotherly goodwill. I do not, however, conceal one thing: those who so warmly received Giorgio Blandrata were rather incautious and unforeseeing, and they did ill in consulting your reputation. I am even more surprised that certain leading men of the highest authority were gravely offended because I exposed the man openly, as was necessary. And lest you think I have written anything rashly, I have dictated a historical account, which will make you all aware of the facts. But in so grave a danger to you, it was not right to keep silent, since I understood that not only had a wolf been admitted into the fold, but the sheep had been given him as their guardian. Yet if Blandrata now intends to repent, let him show it by his conduct. If he wishes to be reconciled with me, I am ready to forgive him, as soon as I learn that he has changed for the better. But he is certainly mocking you while he complains that he has been unworthily slandered. What? Since I knew he was steeped in impious delusions, would it not have been treacherous not to warn you of so great a danger? I have therefore performed the duty of sincere concern for your welfare, and I shall never regret it. Farewell, most upright brothers, and dearest to me from my heart. May the Lord be with you, guide you, and keep you for ever. 1 October 1561.

units.la: Io. Cal. Ministris Et Senioribus Ecclesiæ Vilnensis.
units.tr: Io. Cal. To the Ministers and Elders of the Church of Vilnius.

units.la: QVod de charitatis mutuo inter nos colendæ studio scribitis, libenter ampletor: ac piæ vestræ admonitioni morem gerere paratus essem, si mihi iusta ratio à vobis præscribere-retur, retur, quomodo reconciliari me oporteat cum Georgio Blan-drata.Quod dum sub persona Illustrissimi Ducis & Palatini Vil-nensis,vos omnes hortatus sum ad cauendam illam pestem,gra-uiter fuistis offensi:mihi certe dolet officium a syncero veストri amore profectum, & pia salutis vestrae cura, non placuisse. Sed quid facerem?saltem defunctus sum:nec me vnquam poenitebit eius offensionis,quam mihi summa necessitas iniunxit. Magni vobis est exi stimatio Blandratae: quia integerrimum virum esse cognoscitis, nec vllus erroris suspectum. Quid autem de ipso publice testatus sim, ostendit praefatio, de qua mecum expostulatis. Et si vobis non est suspectus, plane apud me conuictus est, imo coram hac Ecclesia. Mihi non creditis, cur ego potius vobis credam? Multum scilicet vobis otii est, vt synodos cogatis ob tales quisquilias. Sed Blandratae excellentia vos mouet: quia horribile scandalum nasceretur, si confligere mecum incipiat. Ergo non vulgare fecit operaepretium longo itinere, quod tantum sibi nomen acquisierit. Nullus est apud alias gentes: vos admiramini non secus atque Angelum e coelo delapsum. Vestras delicias minime vobis inuideo. Summo etiam vt in pretio sit apud vos per me licet: modo vicissim pro vestra aequitate mihi permittatis non nescire quod apud nos omnibus satis superque compertum est. Si asperius loquor, vos me coegistis. Caeterum vt scias tis immodicas quorundam facilitate male Ecclesiis vestris fuisse consultum, quibus praefectus fuit, mitto breve historiae totius compendium: ex quo perspicuum vobis fiet, nisi infideliter & proditorie vobiscum agere vellem, tacendum non fuisse in tanto vestro periculo. Si nihil fidei obtineo, aliquid tamen & Italicae quae apud nos est Ecclesiae seniioribus, & eximio Christi seruo Doctori Petro Martyri tribuite. Valete fratres ex animo dilecti, & colendi. Dominus vos Spiritu suo gubernet, virtute inuicta sustineat, donisque omnibus locupletet. Geneuae, 1 x. Octobris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: As for your writing about cultivating mutual charity between us, I gladly embrace it, and I would be ready to comply with your pious admonition, if you had set out for me a just reason why I ought to be reconciled with Giorgio Blandrata. When I exhorted you all to beware of that pest, speaking in the person of the most illustrious Duke and Palatine of Vilnius, you were gravely offended. I am truly sorry that my duty, which arose from sincere love for you and from pious care for your salvation, did not please you. But what was I to do? At least I have discharged my obligation, and I shall never regret that offence, which the greatest necessity laid upon me. Blandrata is of great value in your estimation, because you know him to be a most upright man, and no one suspects him of error. But what I have publicly testified about him is shown by the preface, about which you complain to me. And if he is not suspect to you, he has certainly been convicted in my eyes, and indeed before this church. You do not believe me; why should I rather believe you? You surely have a great deal of leisure, to call synods over such trifles. But it is Blandrata's eminence that moves you, because a dreadful scandal would arise if he were to begin to contend with me. It was therefore no ordinary achievement for him to have made such a name for himself after a long journey. He has no equal among other peoples; you marvel at him as though he were an angel fallen from heaven. I do not begrudge you your darling. I also allow that he be held in the highest esteem among you, through me: only, in return for your fairness, allow me not to be ignorant of what is known to all among us, more than enough. If I speak more harshly, you have forced me to it. Moreover, so that you may know how ill your churches, over which he was placed, were served by the excessive ease of certain men, I am sending a short summary of the whole history. From it you will see clearly that, unless I meant to deal unfaithfully and treacherously with you, I could not have kept silent in so great a danger to you. If I carry no weight of trust with you, nevertheless attribute some credit to the elders of the Italian church that is among us, and to the distinguished servant of Christ, Doctor Peter Martyr. Farewell, brothers, beloved and to be cherished from my heart. May the Lord guide you by his Spirit, sustain you with unconquered strength, and enrich you with all his gifts. Geneva, 1 October 1561.

units.la: BLANDRATA.
units.tr: BLANDRATA.

units.la: Georgius Blandrata medicus vixit apud nos quiete & placide ad tempus, & Christianae docilitatis signa dedit. An opinione deceptus fuerit, quia non reperit quod sperabat, nescimus. Exceptus enim fuit pro nostra simplicitate tanquam vnus ex aliorum numero. Coepit deinde per ambages in quaestionem trahere fidei nostrae articulum de Christi Deitate: & sua somnia sparsit clanculum apud imperitos. Sed quo impunitate sibi acquireret, suas quaestiones depositit apud Pastorē Italicū Maximiliā-num ex celebri Comitum familia natum (Martinengues vocant L. iii). Itali)qui etsi acuto erat ac perspicaci ingenio, oderat tamen fri-uolas speculationes. Itaque quàuis Blandrata sedulò officia Me-dici obtruderet in curanda illius valetudine & vxoris, hominis tamen importunitate offensus, eum repudiabat. Quod clarius sub mortem suam patefecit. Eodem tempore suis quaestionibus fatigabat Caluinum: eoque magis quòd cum subinde fingeret se placatum esse, & acquiesceret responsis, postridie redibat quasi nouus, nec desinebat ea ipsa, de quibus saepe audierat, sciscitari. Itaque coactus est ei Caluinus in faciem dicere, vultus tuus detestabile monstrum mihi ostendit, quod in corde occultum foues: ac saepius eum asperè obiurgauit, vt si fieri posset, corrigeret perfidiam, & fallacias dolosque tortuosos, quorum fallido erat quodammodo defessus. Nec tamen destitit Blandratamcomiter salutare, & admittere ad sermonem. Imo huc vsque obtempera-uit improbi hominis votis, vt breui scripto dissoluerét omnes scrupulos, quibus fingebat ille nequam se impediri. Notare autem operaepretium est prauum eius consilium. Neque enim tam optauit expediri sibi dubitationes, in quibus dicebat se perplexum haerere, quàm contendit à Caluino, vt damnaret omnium aliorum sententias. Ac saepius asseruit ab omnibus Germanis se turbari: vnius autem Caluini doctrina se reddi tranquillū. Cùm identidem vrgeret vt sedandis multorum conscientiis Caluinus reiiceret quaecunque ab aliis erant prodita, sibi fidem omnem detraxit. Ex eo tempore desiit Caluinus eum admittere quia tantùm dissidia & turbas quaerebat. Serpebat interea virus impiorum dogmatum apud Italos. Itaque seniores Caluinum rogarunt, vt manum auxiliarem porrigeret. Condicta est hora plebi. Missi sunt duo ex Senatoribus, Caluinus verba fecit. Horatus est nomine Senatus, vt quisque liberè proferret, quid sentiret. Ac Senatus nomine promisit impunitatem, si quid perperam & inconsidera te elapsum esset. Illic non dubitauit Blādrata obiicere Caluino, quod salsissimum erat, iactareque illud esse scriptum manu Caluini. Coactus proferre, tergiuersari coepit. Pertinaciter tamen asseruit Caluinum ita scripsisse, donec charta allata fuit in templum. Deprehensus in manifesta calunnia miserrimus, non tamen erubuit cùm omnes fuste dignum censerent. Etsi autem nō protulit ipse horribilem blasphemiam, quae mox sequetur: totam tamen eius culpam sustinet. Dixit enim intimus eius sodalis Ioannes Paulus Alciatus, qui adhuc pro anima sua habet, tres Diabolos à nobis adorari peiores omnibus idolis Papatus: quia statueremus tres personas. Si execrabile illud sacrilegium, vt decebat exhorruit, cur ab eius familiaritate non discessit? Imo cùm eo paulò post profectus est: & eo comite, sodali, & socio molitus est scinderePcclesias. Pepercit tamen Caluinus, ac deprecatus est est,ne quid accideret molestiæ.Exorta est rursus nova querimonia Italicæ Ecclesiæ quòd clandestinis artibus,,simplices e vulgo imbuerentur peruersis illis deliriis.Vocati igitur sunt ad Consistorium Blandrata,& alij quidam.Satis habere debet,quod fuerit abstinue ignominia dimissus. Calvinus etiam ore suo iussit ipsum esse securum:ac promisit se daturum operam, ne fraudi essent quæcunque antea peccassent.Aliquato post tempore cùm in auditorium Calvini ingressus esset vnus ex quatuor præsidibus Senatus(quos vocant Syndicos)id quod vt tum legentem Calvinū audiret, Blandrata qui lectioni interesset mox fugario naribus opposito, acii sanguis fluxeret, se in fugam proripuit, nec postea in urbem reuersus est. Hæc est Calvini crudelitas,qui peruersum homines & turbulentum,fouere tamen studuit. Hæc est innocentia Blandratæ quem præcipitem egit mala conscientia: fuitque illi carnifex,cùm nemo esset inimicus.Concessit Tigurum:an illic se rectius gesserit,testantur D Petri Martyris literæ.Ex Polonia multas faces iaculatus est ad renouandum incendium. Conatus est modis omnibus labefactare simplicium fidem. Et cuidam amico scripsit, vadum se reperisse in illis profundis aquis, vbi ante dubius natabat.
units.tr: Georgius Blandrata, a physician, lived among us for a time quietly and peacefully, and gave signs of Christian docility. Whether he was deceived in his expectation, because he did not find what he hoped for, we do not know. For he was received, because of our simplicity, as one of the rest. Then he began, by roundabout ways, to call into question our article of faith concerning the Deity of Christ, and he secretly spread his dreams among the unlearned. But so that he might acquire impunity for himself, he deposited his questions with the Italian minister Maximilian, born of the famous family of the Counts (they call him Martinengo, Book 3). The Italian, although he had a keen and perceptive mind, hated frivolous speculations. And so, although Blandrata zealously forced on him the services of a physician in treating his own health and that of his wife, he rejected him, offended by the man's importunity. This he made clearer at the time of his own death. At the same time Blandrata was wearing out Calvin with his questions, and all the more so because, whenever he pretended to be satisfied and accepted the answers, the next day he came back as if he were new, and did not stop asking about the very things he had often heard about. So Calvin was compelled to say to his face: "Your countenance shows me a detestable monster, which you cherish hidden in your heart"; and he rebuked him rather harshly many times, so that, if it were possible, he might correct his treachery and his tortuous deceits and trickery, by which he was in some measure wearied out. Yet he did not cease to greet Blandrata courteously and to admit him to conversation. Indeed, up to this point he had yielded to the wishes of the wicked man, so that he would dissolve in a short writing all the scruples by which that worthless fellow pretended he was hindered. It is worth noting, however, his perverse purpose. For he did not so much wish his doubts, in which he said he hung perplexed, to be resolved, as he insisted that Calvin should condemn the opinions of all others. And he often asserted that he was troubled by all the Germans, but was made calm by the teaching of Calvin alone. Since he kept urging that Calvin, to calm the consciences of many, should reject whatever had been put forward by others, he withdrew all trust from himself. From that time Calvin ceased to admit him, because he sought only quarrels and disturbances. Meanwhile the poison of impious doctrines was creeping among the Italians. So the elders asked Calvin to stretch out a helping hand. An hour was set for the common people. Two of the Senators were sent; Calvin spoke. In the name of the Senate he was asked that each might freely state what he thought. And in the name of the Senate he promised impunity, if anything had slipped out wrongly and thoughtlessly. There Blandrata did not hesitate to object to Calvin something most absurd, and to boast that it was written in Calvin's own hand. Compelled to produce it, he began to equivocate. Nevertheless he stubbornly maintained that Calvin had written thus, until a paper was brought into the church. Caught in a plain calumny, the wretched man nevertheless did not blush, though everyone judged him worthy of the cudgel. Although he did not himself put forward the horrible blasphemy which follows, he nonetheless bears the whole blame for it. For his intimate companion, Giovanni Paolo Alciati, who still holds it for his soul, said that three Devils are worshipped by us, worse than all the idols of Papacy, because we posit three persons. If he shuddered at that execrable sacrilege, as was fitting, why did he not withdraw from his intimacy with the man? Indeed, shortly afterwards he set out with him, and with that companion, comrade and partner, he undertook to tear the churches apart. Calvin nevertheless spared him, and begged that nothing unpleasant should happen to him. Then a new complaint arose from the Italian Church, because by secret arts simple people from the common crowd were being imbued with those perverse delusions. Blandrata and certain others were therefore summoned to the Consistory. He ought to be content that he was dismissed without the disgrace of punishment. Calvin also bade him by his own mouth to be secure, and promised that he would take care that whatever he had earlier sinned would not be held against him.

units.la: En cur debuerit quisquam suscipere hominis patrocinium,& priuatas meas monitiones procul reiicere,quibus malum placide sanari poterat.1 x.Octob. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Here is why anyone should take up the man's defence, and cast aside my private admonitions, by which the evil could have been calmly healed. 1 October 1561.

units.la: CALVINVS BEZAE.
units.tr: CALVIN TO BEZA.

units.la: POstridie quàm tibi nuper scripsi correptus fui cholicis dolor ibus,qui absque vllaremissione fuerunt toto biduo.Postea interdiu nonnihil fuerunt mitigatiores tamen postea non etsi adhuc infestæ Nedum audeo mihi multum promittere de leutione quæ à clysteribus pendet,semperque vnctionibus mixta est. Tantum autem ex vomitionibus, peruigiliis, & doloris vehementia,similisque inedia,& siti palati & gutturis ariditas,vt nunc hæc etiam pauca dictare molestum sit. Mandassem alteri scribendi partes,nisi veritus essem,ne plus inde metus & solicitudinis conciperes Colloquium ab aduersariis quouis modo abrumpi non ægre feram.Nondum enim res maturuit, vt eorum consensu vigeat pura Religio. Partem verò aliquam concedi nihil aliud esset,quia veritatis cursum abrumpere. Velim igitur hac in parte vos esse faciles. Vale integerrime frater vna cum D. Martyre & reliquis.Deus vos omnes tueatur,gubernetque benedicat in omnibus. x v. Octobris, M. D. LXI.
units.tr: The day after I last wrote to you, I was seized by a painful attack of colic, which lasted for two whole days without any remission. Afterwards, during the day, it was somewhat milder, though still troublesome, and I do not yet dare to promise myself much relief from the purging, which depends on enemas and is always combined with ointments. Such is the extent of the vomiting, sleeplessness and severity of the pain, together with the fasting and thirst, and the dryness of my palate and throat, that it is now troublesome even to dictate these few lines. I would have handed the writing over to another, had I not feared that it would give you more anxiety and worry. I shall not take it hard if the rivals break off the colloquy in any way at all. For the matter has not yet ripened so that pure religion may flourish with their consent. To concede any part of it would be nothing else than to cut short the course of truth. I would therefore have you be accommodating on this point. Farewell, most upright brother, together with Master Martyr and the rest. May God keep you all, guide you and bless you in all things. 15 October 1561.

units.la: Calvinus suus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: EX quo cessarunt termina, vel aliquatulum laxata sunt, gravedo me inuasit, quae tamen minus acriter me infestat. Pes nondum conualuit. Nudiu stertius concionatus sum, sed delatus sella in templum vsque. Quanquam haec melius ex Normandio nostro intelliges, qui forte has praeueniet. Colloquium mature abrumpi mihi nunquam displicuit: modo abfq; vestra culpa fiat. Nolim tamen dum sinistros rumores fugitis, vos esse nimis verecundos, qui semper vereor ne vobis & causae noceat facilitas. Ergo a fraude cauendum. Vna in re insi lere oportet, vt fidelibus tolerabilis sit libertas. Seuere tamen obiurgandus erit eorum feruor, qui metas transiliunt: ac de eo frenando consultandum vobis erit, vt quod statueritis, omnes prouinciae sequantur. Si qui parere nolint, fero agnoscent quanto potior moderatio sit, quam temeritas. Vtinam foli poenas luerent. Sed nisi eorum intemperantiam compescat Deus, omnia pessundabunt. Vide quam acre sit telum necessitas, quae prodigos facit in maxima inopia. Si Merlinus huc se receperit ante finem mensis nobiscum, bene actum putabimus. Colongius ne reuocaretur, accurate me rogavit D. Ducillas: cuius de te spem etiam frustrari vix fas esset. Ea enim cupide expectat te & D. Martyrem: quos sibi promissos esse asserit. Tot remorae plus aequo tempus producent, vt longius non abscedas. Martyrem quoque relinquere non esset humanum. Sed in primis vide, vt scholae desertae cito succurras. Ego enim, cum obeundae erant tuae vices, iam toto fere mense decubuisti: quia paulo post quam has acceperis, ad iter, vt opinor, te accingesposthac a scribendo desistam: nisi forte consilium te mutasse cognouero. Vale eximie vir, & integerrime frater cum D. Martyre & reliquis fratribus, apud quos excusa quod non scribam. Dominus vos omnes tueatur, gubernet, studiaque vestra benedicat. XXI. Octob. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Since the fever has ceased, or eased a little, a heaviness has come over me, which nonetheless troubles me less sharply. My foot has not yet recovered its strength. Three days ago I preached, but I was carried in a chair as far as the church. You will understand these things better from our Normandy friend, who will perhaps forestall this letter. I have never been displeased that the colloquy should be broken off early, provided it happens without your fault. Yet I would not have you, while you flee sinister rumours, be too over-scrupulous; I am always afraid that your readiness may harm the cause itself. Therefore caution must be taken against deceit. In one matter you must be unbending, so that liberty may be tolerable to the faithful. Yet the zeal of those who overstep the limits must be sharply rebuked, and you will have to consider how to curb it, so that all the provinces may follow whatever you decide. If some are unwilling to obey, they will in time recognise how much better moderation is than rashness. Would that only they paid the penalty! But unless God restrains their intemperance, they will overturn everything. See how sharp a weapon necessity is, which makes spendthrifts of those in the greatest want. If Merlin withdraws here to us before the end of the month, we shall think the business well done. Lord Ducillas earnestly asked me that Colongius not be recalled; it would hardly be right to disappoint his hope of you, for he eagerly awaits you and Master Martyr, whom he claims were promised to him. So many delays will prolong the time beyond what is right, so that you will not go far away. Nor would it be human to leave Martyr behind either. But above all see that you hasten to help the deserted school. For when your duties had to be discharged, you have now lain ill for almost the whole month; so, shortly after you receive this, I think you will be girding yourself for the journey. I shall stop writing hereafter, unless perhaps I learn that you have changed your plan. Farewell, most distinguished man and most upright brother, with Master Martyr and the other brethren, to whom please excuse me for not writing. May the Lord keep you all, guide you, and bless your studies. 21 October 1561.

units.la: Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: Your Calvin.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS BVLINGERO S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Bullinger, greeting.

units.la: SEro admonitus fui de nuntij discessu, quum me ad legendum traherem. Sic enim loquendum est: quia nunc pedis, nunc totius cruris dolor vix me lente reptare patitur. Imo aegre me sustineo, nisi alterius brachio innixus. Nunc fere hora quarta est post meridiem, & cras etiam proficiscitur nuntius, qui meas ad Bezam & quosdam alios expectat. Peto igitur, venerande frater, vt mea breuitati des veniam. Quanquam si plus esset otij, & ad scribendum essem alacrior, nescio an operæpretium factu-rus essem, res Galliæ narrando. Mitto enim à Martyre nostro li-teras, quæ te, opinor, totius summæ certiorem reddent: ac ipse breui coram vobis exponet quicquid actum fuit. Pridem subol-feci Diabolum in Germania clandestinis artibus moliri quod nunc tandem apparuit: & ante tres menses diligenter hortatus fueram Regem Nauarræ, vt sibi ab insidiis caveret. Quàm parùm verò profecerim, quia chartæ mandare piget, malo ex D Mar-tyre cognoscas, vbi istuc reuersus fuerit. Promiserat mira, & quò plus fidei acquireret, non dissimulabat se fuisse tentatum: sed si-lentio repudiasse eius pollulata. Atqui ex Germania mihi scri-ptum est eius rogatu missos fuisse quinque Theologos, qui nùc sunt in aula: nisi forte dimissi fuerint, quia sero aduenerant, to-ta actione abrupta. Quid si Deus perfidiam miseri illius frustre-tur, qui nefariis obsequiis Papæ se venditat, qui tamen eum ludi-brio habet? Sed propediem aliquid sciemus. Valeornatissime vir, & frater ex animo colende. Dominus tibi semper adsit, te gubernet, ac benedicat tuos labores. Symmystis omnibus, vxori, totíque familiæ multam salutem precor. Geneuæ, v. Nouemb. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: I was reminded late of the messenger's departure, just as I was forcing myself to read. I must put it that way, since pain now in my foot, now in my whole leg, scarcely lets me creep about slowly. Indeed I can barely hold myself up unless I lean on another's arm. It is now about the fourth hour after noon, and the messenger, who is waiting for my letters to Beza and some others, sets out tomorrow too. I ask you, venerable brother, to forgive my brevity. Even if I had more leisure and were keener to write, I doubt I would have made the effort worthwhile by recounting the affairs of France. I am sending letters from our Martyr, which will, I think, inform you of the whole matter, and he himself will soon explain to you in person whatever has happened. Some time ago I suspected that the Devil was working in Germany by secret arts, and that has now at last come to light. Three months ago I earnestly urged the King of Navarre to beware of snares. How little I achieved, I would rather you learn from Master Martyr when he returns there, since I am loath to commit it to paper. He had promised marvels, and to win more trust he did not hide that he had been tempted, but he rejected his budding schemes in silence. Yet I have been written to from Germany that at his request five theologians were sent, who are now at court, unless perhaps they were dismissed because they arrived late and the whole business was broken off. What if God frustrates the treachery of that wretch who sells himself to the Pope's wicked service, and who nonetheless mocks him? But we shall soon know something. Farewell, most distinguished man and brother to be cherished from my heart. May the Lord always be with you, guide you, and bless your labours. To all your fellow ministers, your wife, and your whole household I wish many greetings. Geneva, 5 November 1561.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N.N. S. D. Ad Baptismum minus legitimè administratum.
units.tr: John Calvin to N.N., greeting. On a baptism less lawfully administered.

units.la: LIteræ vestræ perquâ nobis iucundæ fuerunt, optimi fratres, quòd tandem vobis concessus sit in vrbe locus, & data con-cionandi libertas. Hoc singulare beneficium aliis maiori-bus Deus cumulabit. Etsi autem vos manent noui & assidui cō-flictus, & breui forte erumpet Diaboli furor, strenuè pergendum erit. Superioribus vestris literis hucusque non respondimus: quia nemo se obtulerat, qui nostras tuto perferret. De quæstione au-tem propositâ sic sentimus. Quia nemo priuatus Baptismi legiti-mus est Minister, huic malo seuerè occurrendum esse: quia ma-nifesta Baptismi est profanatio. Et quoniam hic mos peruersus ex superstitione traxit originem, dum salutis necessitas signo af-fixa fuit: eò minus suendum est duplex malum. Dubitanter hac de re loquitur Augustinus: Si quispiam priuatus baptizet, v-bi cogit necessitas, aut nullum est, aut veniale delictum. Atqui nobis longè pluris est debet inuiolabile Christi mandatum: Ite, docete, baptizate. Hic nexus absque sacrilegio solui non potest. Accedit Apostoli sententia: Nemo vsurpat sibi honorem, sed qui vocatus est. Adulterinum ergo Baptismum censemus, qui admi-nistratus est à priuato homine. Ac in Ecclesia recte composita tolerabilis non effet hæc temeritas. Sed quid id apud vos inter principia contigit, ante restitutum Ecclesiæ ordinem, & rebus adhuc confusis, non tantum errori danda est venia, sed feredus est qualiscunque Baptismus: modò ne in exemplum trahatur, quod semel perperam gestum est. Nam in Ecclesiæ dissipatione multa Deus condonat, quæ nullo modo admittere fas esset in Ecclesiâ bene ordinatam. Olim quum vitiata esset Religio, haud dubiè multis vitiis ac corruptelis implicita Circuncisio fuit: quâ tamen iteratam fuisse non legimus, quum reuocaretur populus ad purum cultum. Ergo anxiè d·squirere necesse non est, ac ne expedit quidem in omnes circunstantias, quæ innumeros scrupulos gignerent. Proinde quod ignouit Deus sub Papatu, nos quoque sepeliamus. Nunc vbi de vero Baptismi vsu admonita fuerit Ecclesia, quòd pugnaret cum Christi instituto pro nihilo ducendum esset, ac de integro baptizandus qui pollutus fuerit profana aspersione. De mulierum Baptismo, aliud est nostrum iudicium. Nam quia prodigiosa fuit audacia, vt se præter naturæ legem mulieres ad hoc munus ingererent, minimè dubitamus quin secure tale flagitium repudiandum sit. Interea periculum non est, ne vulnerentur infirmæ conscientiæ: nisi quis nimia cum riositate frustra sibi molestus sit: quia nemo est qui sciat se à muliere fuisse baptizatum: deinde quia veteri decreto Concilij Carthaginensis prohibitæ sunt fœminæ ab officio baptizandi, neminem offendet nouitas, quæ metuenda esset in viris. Valete optimi & integerrimi fratres. Dominus vos gubernet spiritali prudentia, virtute sustineat, & omnibus donis locupleret. Multâ salutem precamur Senioribus, & toti Ecclesiæ. Geneuæ, XIII. Nouemb. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Your letter gave us great pleasure, best brothers, because a place in the city has at last been granted to you, and freedom to preach. God will heap still greater benefits upon you. Although new and constant conflicts remain for you, and perhaps the Devil's fury will soon break out, you must press on vigorously. We have not answered your earlier letters until now, because no one had offered himself who could carry ours safely. On the question you raised, we think as follows. Since no private person is a lawful minister of baptism, this evil must be dealt with severely, for it is a manifest profanation of baptism. And since this perverse custom arose from superstition, when the necessity of salvation was attached to the sign, the double evil must all the more be avoided. Augustine speaks doubtfully on this matter: if a private person baptizes where necessity compels, it is either no sin or a venial one. But for us the inviolable command of Christ carries far more weight: "Go, teach, baptize." This bond cannot be loosed without sacrilege. Add the saying of the Apostle: "No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called." Therefore we judge a baptism administered by a private man to be spurious. In a Church rightly constituted this rashness would not be tolerable. But what happened there among you at the beginning, before the order of the Church was restored and affairs were still confused, must be pardoned as an error, and whatever baptism it was must be tolerated, provided only that what was done wrongly once is not drawn into an example. For in the dissipation of the Church God pardons many things which it would in no way be right to admit in a well-ordered Church. Formerly, when religion was corrupted, circumcision was doubtless entangled in many vices and corruptions, yet we do not read that it was repeated when the people were called back to pure worship. Therefore it is not necessary to inquire anxiously into every circumstance, nor is it even expedient, since that would beget countless scruples. Accordingly, let us also bury what God pardoned under the Papacy. Now, where the Church has been instructed about the true use of baptism, whatever conflicts with Christ's institution must be counted as nothing, and whoever was polluted by profane sprinkling must be baptized afresh. Concerning baptism by women, our judgement is different. Since it was a monstrous audacity for women to thrust themselves into this office against the law of nature, we have no doubt that such a crime may be rejected without hesitation. Meanwhile there is no danger that weak consciences will be wounded, unless someone, through excessive curiosity, troubles himself needlessly; for no one knows that he was baptized by a woman. Further, since by the old decree of the Council of Carthage women are forbidden the office of baptizing, the novelty, which would be feared in men, will offend no one. Farewell, best and most upright brothers. May the Lord guide you with spiritual prudence, sustain you with strength, and enrich you with all his gifts. We wish many greetings to the elders and to the whole Church. Geneva, 13 November 1561.

units.la: CALVINVS SALINIACO.
units.tr: CALVIN TO SALINIACUS.

units.la: QVod aliena manu tibi scribo, ornatiss. vir, & mihi in Christo venerande, non minoris, vt opinor, abs te fient meæ literæ, vbi ex intimo animi sensu dictatas fuisse cognoueris. Et certè ita est: nec vnquam adeo familiariter tecum agere ausus essem, nisi fiducia dedisset amor erga te meus, & quæ inde nascitur salutis tuæ cura, quæ me non solicitum modò, sed anxium quoque pridem reddidit, quoties de tuo statu cogitabam. Vnum te ex eorum esse numero memini, quos Deus Euangelij fui luce ante annos triginta dignatus est. Non vulgaris honor, quòd inter primitias delectus es: cui accessit liberalis doctrina, & eximia Scripturæ sacræ cognitio: vt aliis omnibus facem præferre merito debueris. Porrò quàm indignè sepultus fuerit incomparabilis ille thesaurus, quem Deus apud te depositum fuerit, vtinam potius sis ipse iudex, quàm expectes dum coram coelesti iudice reddenda sit otij ratio. Quid dico otium? Neque enim sine fructu solum iacuerunt tot praeclarae dotes: sed in sordibus demersae, in probrum & dedecus syncerae fidei quodammodo cessarunt. Quanuis enim laude digna fuerit vitae integritas, & castitas: scis tamen, & non sine maximo dolore viderunt pij & cordati homines, impios & sceleratos de te triumphum agere, cum metu constrictus obmutescerent. Praeteriit nimis longum tempus, quo misera illa non minus quàm turpis servitus mentis tuae vigore oppressit. Detur venia communi malo: quia obiectis undique terroribus, pauci ingenue Christi se discipulos profiteri audebat. Nunc vero ex quo melior affulsit conditio filiis Dei, vt à pericu lo immunis sit eorum libertas, erumpere in vocem cogor. Quousque tandem sponte libebit tergiuersando Christum iure suo fraudare? Hactenus indulgenter tibi Deus pepercit, dum rectae intelligentiae lumen quod cunctatione tua suffocasti, prorsus ex tinguipassus non est. Sed obsecro per hanc indulgentiam, qua te ad hunc vsque diem sustinuit, quo tot hominum millia sub vexillum se colligendo, te ad eandem studij alacritatem inuitant, vt diligenter tecum reputes quàm pretiosum Deo sacrificium sit pura fidei confessio. Vt quod residuum est vitae, vbi simpliciter Christo dicatum fuerit, tarditatem anteacti temporis compensfer. Nihil certe iucundius mihi accidere poterit, quàm si audiero, te excusssa mollitie, & timiditate victa, Christo palàm, & ex professo nomen dedisse. Quanquam vt hoc mihi priuatim dispon postulo, sed vt Ecclesias omnes quas mirabiliter Deus in Gallia erexit, exhilarses: quae certatim sibi & tibi gratulabuntur, si reliquis hostium castris te in Christi ouile contuleris. Nec paruus eorum, qui adhuc vacillant, numerus se ad imitationem protinus accinget. Ac si prudenter expendas quàm multi abste pendeant, & quàm multorum in te conuersi sint oculi, facile agnosces, vt excusabilis sit aliorum torpor, cessationi tuae nullo modo posse ignosci. Forte iam satis te animatum reperient meae literae, vt superuacua sit exhortatio. Partibus tamen meis deesse nolui. Vale praestantissime vir, & mihi ex animo colende. Dominus te Spiritu suo gubernet, fortitudine instruat, & incolumem tueatur. XIII. Calendas Decembris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Because I write to you through another's hand, most distinguished sir and venerable brother in Christ, my letter will, I think, be no less valued by you when you learn that it was dictated from the depths of my heart. And indeed it is so: I would never have dared to deal with you so familiarly had not my love for you, and the care for your salvation that springs from it, moved me. That care has for some time made me not merely anxious but troubled whenever I think of your condition. I remember that you are one of those whom God, some thirty years ago, deigned to bring into the light of the Gospel. It is no common honour that you were chosen among the first-fruits; to this was added a liberal learning and an outstanding knowledge of Holy Scripture, so that you ought rightly to have carried a torch before all the others. But how unworthily that incomparable treasure, which God committed to your keeping, has been buried! Would that you yourself might be its judge rather than wait until an account of your idleness must be rendered before the heavenly Judge. Why do I speak of idleness? Those many splendid gifts have not merely lain fruitless; they have sunk into filth and, to the shame and disgrace of sincere faith, have in a sense ceased to be of service. For though the integrity and chastity of your life deserve praise, you know, and godly and wise men have seen with great grief, that the impious and wicked have triumphed over you while you stood silent, hemmed in by fear. Too long a time has passed in which that wretched servitude, no less shameful than miserable, has oppressed the vigour of your mind. Let pardon be granted to a common evil, since, with terrors thrown up on every side, few dared frankly to profess themselves disciples of Christ. But now that a better condition has dawned for the sons of God, so that their liberty is free from danger, I am compelled to break out into speech. How long will you of your own accord choose to defraud Christ of his right by evasion? Hitherto God has spared you with indulgence, while the light of right understanding, which you have smothered by your delay, has not utterly been extinguished. But I beseech you, by this indulgence with which he has sustained you to this day, and by the great numbers of men who are gathering under his banner and invite you to the same zeal, consider carefully how precious to God is the sacrifice of a pure confession of faith. Let what remains of your life, once it has been simply dedicated to Christ, make up for the sluggishness of the time gone by. Nothing could happen that would please me more than to hear that, having shaken off your softness and conquered your timidity, you have openly and deliberately given your name to Christ. Yet I ask this not only for my own private satisfaction, but that you may gladden all the churches which God has raised up wonderfully in France; they will eagerly rejoice for themselves and for you if you transfer yourself from the enemy's camp into the fold of Christ. Nor will a small number of those who still waver at once set themselves to follow your example. And if you weigh prudently how many depend on you, and how many eyes are turned upon you, you will easily see that the sluggishness of others may be excused, but your inactivity can in no way be pardoned. Perhaps my letter will find you already sufficiently roused, so that exhortation is superfluous. Still, I did not wish to fail in my part. Farewell, most excellent sir, and one I hold in sincere esteem. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, strengthen you with courage, and keep you unharmed. 19 November 1561.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: SALINIACVS CALVINO. S. D.
units.tr: SALINIACUS TO CALVIN. GREETINGS.
