units.la: MEritò te amo, vir clarissime, de ista tua erga me humanitate, qui me, vt pium ac cordatum virum decet, officij mei, tuis ad me literis admoneas. Quae ista tua erga me voluntas, non minus profecto mihi grata esse debet atque iucunda, quàm à summa tua erga me benevolentia (qui enim ego aliter de te existimem?) eam esse profecta certò scio. Sed illud profecto permirum mihi accidit, quòd non secus de me sentire videare, ac de eo statuas, qui omnino à Christo sit alienus, & perpetuam propugnationem pro veritate suscipere nolit: cùm nemo adhuc me in aduersariorum castris signa sequentem videat: neque promissis, quæ minimum apud me valent, sed ne periculis quidé vllis, quibus tamen mouentur fortissimi viri, adduci vnquam potuerim, vt ipse à me deficerem, & deserto Imperatore Christo, ac in acie, ordine meo, ad hostium castra turpissimè atque flagitiosissimè transfugerem. Quod si tu eò fortasse me nomine, iure reprehendendum esse putes, non quòd ipse quidé Religionem oppugnauerim (neque enim id vere de me dici posse puto) sed eam cùm possem, non defenderim, equidem id hoc loco quod res est paucis respondebo: me in tanta animorum de Religione contentione, & opinionum dissensione, cui simpliciter me dederem adhuc constituere non potuisse. Cupiam ego vehementer eam nos Reip. Christianæ formam habere, quam tu ipse spiras, & Apostolicam fuisse legimus. Sed quanto molis sit Christianam denuo condere gentem, aut potius recudere, quæ tot iam annos à recta virtutis & veritatis via deflexerit: & præsertim apud nostros, qui οὐ δὲ κατ' ὀναρ, id quod rectum est & verum viderint, tu vel me tacente, qui apud nos sis natus & educatus, & in Gallia nostra, prima virtutis tuæ fundamenta iecceris, quique & polito & literis exculto sis ingenio, & acri iudicio præditus, optimè potes intelligere. Expeditissima igitur mihi quædam ad hanc rem via esse videtur, si non Scripturæ tantùm quæ plurimum apud pios valere debeat, sed veterum etiam auctoritate, quæ maximi ab ad vulgus à male sanis hominibus docentur, quantùm à veritate ipsa diiudicant, planum faciamus. Quia sanè in re (vt otij etiá nostri ratio tibi cóste) succisiuis quidem horis (nam meliorem, vt æquum est, diei parte literarum sacrarum studi tribuimus) libenter me quantum per occupationes alias, & valetudinem licet, exerceo. Quod vt aliquando è re Ecclesiæ nostræ esse possit, Psalmos Dauidicos Hebraïcè, & reliquos deinceps veteris fœderis libros, Kimhianis ad eosdem adiunctis commentariis incunte Ianuario, in nostra hac Academia publicè explicandos (si Deus Opt. Max me, vt spero, seruauerit ac iuuerit) suscepi: vt dum cæteri Sanctam vi & impressione euertere, bonis omnibus approbatibus conantur, ego pro virili, vt leuis armaturæ miles, subsidio veniam Miles vero Christi ego sum, cuius nunquam me pudeat. Ec-quo
units.tr: I rightly love you, most distinguished sir, for your kindness toward me, since as a pious and judicious man you remind me by your letter of my duty. This goodwill of yours ought to be no less welcome and pleasing to me than I am sure it springs from your great affection for me (for how else could I think of you?). But something truly strange has happened to me: you seem to judge me no differently than someone entirely alien to Christ, who refuses to take up a constant defence of the truth. No one has yet seen me following the standards in the enemy's camp. I could never be brought, not by promises, which count for very little with me, nor by any dangers, which nonetheless move the bravest men, to desert myself, to abandon Christ my commander, and in the battle line, in my own rank, to defect shamefully and disgracefully to the enemy's camp. But if you perhaps think I deserve rebuke on this account, not because I have attacked religion myself (for I do not think that can truly be said of me), but because I have not defended it when I could, I will answer briefly and as the matter stands: in such a great contention of minds and dissension of opinions about religion, I have not yet been able to settle on a position to which I could simply give myself. I greatly desire that we have that form of the Christian commonwealth which you yourself aspire to, and which we read was Apostolic. But how great a labour it is to found afresh a Christian people, or rather to reshape one that for so many years has turned aside from the right path of virtue and truth, especially among our people, who have not seen what is right and true as in a dream [οὐ κατ' ὄναρ]. You, even without my saying so, who were born and brought up among us and laid the first foundations of your virtue in our France, and who have a polished, literary and cultivated mind and a keen judgement, can understand very well. So a rather convenient way to this end seems to me to be, if we make plain not only Scripture, which ought to carry the greatest weight with the pious, but also the authority of the ancients, which men of unsound mind teach to the common people, and to show how far they depart from the truth itself. How then

units.la: quo quæso modo eius me pudeat,pro cuius decretis vitam profundere non dubitem,idque summæ mihi laudi esse ducam, atque omnium triumphis anteponam? Ego nempe ante menses octo, aut eo etiam amplius, Prophetas aliquot cum Kimhianis commentariis publicè sum interpretatus, eademque illa quæ vos proponere soletis, docui: auditores meos ab externis,& asp(e)ctabilibus ad veram Religionem,Christo vno,per quem seruemur, propositio, reuocaui, & quo ad eius fieri potuit,ad pietatem semper erudiui. Fateor equidem(nec causa est cur negem) falsam illam doctrinam,non tam fortasse aperte, quàm ipsi facere soletis, confutasse : Babylonem tamen tum cuniculis, tum aperto etiam marte, vt res & tempus ferebat, ita semper oppugnaui, vt nolter ille in eo genere conatus, optimo cuique semper probaretur.Plura in hanc sententiam non scribam.Quo enim ego sim, semperque fuerim animo, quid item spectem, mihique proponam,& quàm longè lateque Dominum regnare cupiam,ipsa dies,vt spe sum optima,docebit. Neque eo certè con fi.io hæc commemoro,atque ad te scribo, quo mihi quicquam laudis tribui postulem, sed vt me Dei beneficio, non omnino in propagandis illius Regni finibus cessatorem fuisse intelligas. Vale, & me vt te in Christo veneror & amo,redama. Lutetiæ, Idibus Decembris. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: by what means, I ask, could I be ashamed of him for whose decrees I would not hesitate to pour out my life, and whom I count the highest honour, placing him above all triumphs? In fact, eight months ago or even more, I publicly expounded several Prophets with the Kimhi commentaries, and taught the same things that you are accustomed to propose. I called my hearers away from outward and showy things toward true religion, toward Christ alone, through whom we are saved, and as far as possible I always trained them in piety. I admit (nor is there any reason I should deny it) that I did not perhaps refute that false doctrine as openly as you are wont to do; yet I have always attacked Babylon, sometimes by mines underground and sometimes by open warfare, as the matter and the time required, and that kind of effort of our friend was always approved by the best men. I will not write more to this effect. The day itself, as I hope most fervently, will show what my mind is, and always has been, what I aim at and propose to myself, and how far and wide I desire the Lord to reign. I do not mention these things and write to you with the aim of claiming any praise for myself, but so that you may understand that, by God's blessing, I have not been wholly idle in extending the borders of his kingdom. Farewell, and love me in return, as I revere and love you in Christ. From Paris, on the Ides of December 1561.

units.tr: Ioannes S., yours.

units.la: BEZA CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Beza to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: ACcipe quid noui acciderit,ex quo postremas ad te dedi,Pridi Natalis Domini discedens Nauarrena,Parisiensi Ecclesiæ me concessit ad triduum. Natali ipso quieuimus. Postridie,copia nobis tum primum facta publicè diebus festis cocionandi, duas conciones habui frequentissimas, vnam in D. Antonij alteram in D.Marcelli suburbio, idque sine vlla profusfpecie tumultus.Interfuerunt ex omnibus ciuium ordinibus plurimi, & quidem inter cæteros D. Andelotius, qui me cum honestissimo & firmissimo comitatu per mediam vrbem deduxit,obstupescentibus aduersariis, & summa cum bonorum gratulatione, quorum multitudine ita oppletos vicos conspexisses, vt numerus facile iniri non posset. Altero post die mane concionem tertiam habui, in qua multo etiam plures affuerunt, quàm vnquam antea. A prandio itum est ad Marcelli suburbium,me quidem repugnante,quoniam præmoniti eramus sacrificos nescio quid moliri.Sed fieri aliter non potuit,quoniam sua
units.tr: Learn what has happened since I last wrote to you. On the day before Christmas, leaving Navarre, I was granted by the Parisian church three days' leave. We rested on Christmas Day itself. The next day, being then for the first time granted public permission to preach on festival days, I gave two very crowded sermons, one in the suburb of St Antoine and the other in the suburb of St Marcel, and this without any appearance of tumult. Many people from every rank of citizens were present, and among the rest M. d'Andelot, who escorted me through the middle of the city with a most honourable and steadfast company, while our opponents stood amazed and the good rejoiced greatly. You would have seen the streets so packed with people that their number could not easily be counted. On the following morning I preached a third sermon, at which far more people were present than ever before. After dinner we went to the suburb of St Marcel, though I was reluctant, since we had been warned that the priests were plotting something or other. But it could not be otherwise, since of its own accord an immense crowd was flocking there, which we would otherwise have betrayed to our enemies.

units.la: Epist.329. sponte infinita turba eo confluebat,quam alioqui inimicis pro-didiffemus.Accessi à prandio.Aderat autem nobiscum ex Regi-næ mandato vigilum Præfectuscum suis apparitoribus, ita vt Regia auctoritas vbique nobis præiret.Concionatus est Maloti-us.Ecce igitur quum vix concionem auspicatus coeperunt sacri-fici in proximo atque adeo contiguo Medardi templo campa-nas suas omnesquam vehementissime pulsare, quasi suas, quas vocant Vesperas canturi, ita vt Malotius audiri vix poterat. Ibi ex nostris aliquis,nullius tamen iniuriæ,illos adit,& blande rogat, vt obstrependi finem faciant. Illi quasi occasionem nacti quam caprabant, vt qui vna cum aliquot sicariis ad hoc ipsum egregie sese comparasset,impetum in illum faciunt,& inermem contotraiiciunt,quem Pertuisanam vocamus.Hoc fecerunt nostri simulatque conspexerunt, eo recta feruntur. Hostes & ipsi occurrunt, simulque ex turri templi & vicinis ædibus & sudes, quasi signo dato deiici coeperunt. Ad hunc tumultum qui concionem audiebant ingenti murmure exorto statim prouolant, omnia maximo tumultu miscentur. Interea nostri ad ipsas vsque templi fores aduersarios repellunt. Ego forte in cubiculo adstabam,quod ex vno latere locum ipsum vbi coactus erat coetus,ex altero plateamspectabat,qua transeundum erat omnibus ad certamen properantibus.Conatus sum quantum potui & voce & manu mulieres & turbam confirmare:& Malotius ipse minime perturbatus, signo dato vt Psalmum decimum sextum canneremus,populum vtcunque retinuit.Iam igitur pene compota erant omnia, quum repente sacrificii cum sua cohorte,quum sese & a vigilum Præfecto & a nostris ita cernerent obsessos, vt euadendi spes non esset, campanarum pulsu, quem Toxinum vocant,omnes ad arma conuocat.Tum vero nostri eo ferri præcipites. Ego quum iam cernerem nullum esse remedio locum, in plateam accurro,inermes procurrentes verbis & opposito obstio impedio,ne in periculum manifestum ruant: quod quidem ita commode mihi suggessit Dominus,vt magna pars turbæ fuerit periculi ignara,&Malotius per dimidiam horam quasi rebus tranquillis perrexerit concionari, quanuis ille Toxini sonitus auditorum animos subinde percelleret. Si qui interea prodibat, eis fiebat exeundi potestas,sed cum conditione, vt consisterent tantisper,dum a nostris fi ita opus esset, euocarentur. Dum hæc intus geruntur, nostri, præeunte & iubente vigilum Præfecto, imperu facto Templi fores cum repagulis summa vi perfringuntur. Hostes balistis,ensibus,contis,faxis,& sudibus(hæc enim omnia summo studio compararat) fortiter quidem se tueri,sed frustra. Nam accurrentes adfubfidium nostri subuibanos interea ita repulerant,vt eorum nulli postea appruerint.Id vnum igitur superetur, pererat,vt opprɛssi omnes obtruncarentur:sed, quod mirum est in tanto impetu nemo interemptus,omnes,acceptis tamen aliquot vulneribus,in deditionem receptí,& Præfecto vigilum traditi in manus. Inde in turrim templi perreatum est, vbi rursus effractis valuis omnes ad vnum capti, qui Toxinum pulsarant. Itaque plus valuit in mediis etiam armis,regij Præfecti auctoritas quàm ira.Sed qui hostibus armatis pepercerant,idolis & panaceo illi deo parcere non potuerunt:frustra reclamatibus,quibus ista non placebant. His peractis, absoluta concione,gratiis solenibus Deo actis,& admonitis omnibus,vt moderatos se præberent,si quid in itinere occurreret,ita reditum instituimus. Ita & suburbium & vrbem totam,sine vllo prorsus tumultu,transiuimus,& domum quisque rediit.Imò,quod magis mireris,capti ui hostes triginta sex,ita vt erant ferè omnes vulnerati,& in iis decem ad minimum sacrifici,funibus vincti, spectantibus & ne mutilentibus quidem aduersariis,non aliter transuecti sunt,& mi noris Castelli carceribus inclusi,quàm olim nostri illi fratres in D.Iacobi vico deprehensi.Vtinam verò nihil eiusmodi incidisset,ac tranquille potius Deum nobis colere liceret. Sed quando id nulla nostra culpa accidit, gratiæ Deo agendæ pro insigni victoria,quæ vt spero, barbaros istos & immanes Cyclopas docebit suis saltem,quod aiunt,sumptibus sapere. Postridie,id est 28. huius mensis bene mane huc accurri, vt calumniis maleuolorum occurrerem,&,quantùm possum coniicere,non male res cedet. Missus est latim,N.homo probus & à nobis nō alienus,qui causa cognita in seditiosos ex edictorum formula animaduertat. Sed audi etiam alia.Heri eo ipso loco iterum concio habita est, sine vllo tumultu. Sed ecce vix digressi multitudine, quidam ad hoc comparati,in ædes vacuas quæ illi plateæ imminet, ignem iniiciunt. Nostri repente recurrentes,flammam extinguunt,& frustra repugnantes incendiarios,vi ex suis ædibus extractos,evocatis liboribus tradunt in carcerem deducendos.In eo confli ctu feruntur aliquot ex hostibus interempti. Ex nostris duntaxat vnus priore illo certamine trucidatus in ipso templi limine,aliquot sunt lapidibus vulnerati.Habes nostri statushistoria, qui vtinam minus esset turbulentus, aut mihi impositæ non essent necessitas,ita nō audiendi tātum sed etiā aspiciendi,à quibus nā tura ipsa a horreo.Precibus opus est,si quādo aliās,quoniā adversarios certum est omnia experturos,& firmitatem in multis requiro. Sed Deus proculdubio Ecclesiam suam, tam necessario tempore rō deferet. Bene vale,mi pater cum Collegis & amicis omnibus. D.Iesus te incolumem seruet,& sanctis tuis laboribus magis ac magis benedicat.Ex Sangermano,11 i.Calend.Ian.
units.tr: Epist.329. of its own accord an endless crowd was flocking there, which we would otherwise have betrayed to our enemies. I came after dinner. The captain of the watch was with us by the Queen's command, with his attendants, so that royal authority went before us everywhere. Malotius preached. But scarcely had he begun the sermon when the priests of the nearby and adjoining church of St Medard began to ring all their bells as hard as they could, as if they were about to sing what they call Vespers, so that Malotius could hardly be heard. One of our people, who had done no wrong, went up to them and politely asked them to stop the din. They, as if they had found the opening they were looking for, since their leader had equipped himself well with some hired thugs for this very purpose, attacked him, unarmed, and ran him through with pole-arms, what we call pertuisans. Our men, as soon as they saw this, rushed straight there. The enemy also came to meet them, and at the same time, as if at a signal, stakes began to be hurled down from the church tower and the neighbouring houses. At this uproar those who were listening to the sermon broke out in a great murmur and immediately rushed out, and everything was thrown into the greatest confusion. Meanwhile our men drove the adversaries back as far as the very doors of the church. I happened to be standing in a small room which looked on one side onto the place where the assembly was gathered, and on the other onto the square, across which everyone hurrying to the fight had to pass. I tried as hard as I could, by voice and gesture, to steady the women and the crowd. Malotius himself, not at all disturbed, at a signal given for us to sing Psalm 16, somehow held the people. Now almost everything was settled, when suddenly the priests with their band, seeing themselves so beset by the captain of the watch and by our men that there was no hope of escape, summoned everyone to arms by a peal of the bells, which they call the tocsin. Then indeed our men rushed headlong there. Since I now saw there was no room for a remedy, I ran into the square and, by words and by placing myself in their way, stopped the unarmed men who were rushing forward from plunging into obvious danger. The Lord so conveniently suggested this to me that a large part of the crowd was unaware of the danger, and Malotius continued preaching for half an hour as if all were calm, although the sound of the tocsin repeatedly struck fear into the hearers' minds. Meanwhile, if anyone went out, they were allowed to leave, but on condition that they stay put for a while until, if need be, they were called back by our men. While these things were going on inside, our men, led and ordered by the captain of the watch, made an assault and broke down the church doors with their bars by main force. The enemy defended themselves bravely, with crossbows, swords, pikes, stones and stakes (for they had gathered all of these with great zeal), but in vain. For our men who had run up to help had meanwhile driven back the suburban men so thoroughly that none of them appeared afterwards. The only thing left, then, was for all of them, once overpowered, to be cut down; but, remarkably, in so fierce an attack no one was killed. All were taken into surrender, though wounded in several places, and handed over into the hands of the captain of the watch. From there they made their way into the church tower, where, with the doors broken open again, every one of those who had rung the tocsin was taken. So even in the midst of arms the royal captain's authority prevailed over anger. But those who had spared armed enemies could not spare the idols and that god Panaceus, though those who disliked this protested in vain. With these things done, the sermon finished, solemn thanks given to God, and everyone admonished to behave with moderation should anything happen on the way, we arranged our return. So we passed through both the suburb and the whole city without any tumult at all, and each went home. Indeed, what is more remarkable, thirty-six of the enemy were taken, nearly all of them wounded as they were, and among them at least ten priests, bound with ropes. Without the adversaries so much as mutilating them while they looked on, they were carried off in this way and shut up in the prison of the Petit Châtelet, just as those brethren of ours once caught in the street of St James had been. Would that nothing of this kind had happened, and that we might rather worship God in peace. But since this came about through no fault of ours, thanks are to be given to God for a notable victory, which, I hope, will teach those barbarians and savage Cyclopes at least to be wise at their own expense, as they say. On the next day, that is the 28th of this month, I hurried here very early in the morning to meet the slanders of the ill-disposed; and, as far as I can judge, the matter will turn out not badly. Latim has been sent, an upright man, N., and not unfriendly to us, who, once the case has been heard, is to punish the seditious according to the wording of the edicts. But hear also another matter. Yesterday a sermon was again preached in that very place, without any uproar. But look: scarcely had the crowd dispersed when certain men, prepared for this purpose, set fire to an empty house overlooking that square. Our men, running back suddenly, put out the flames, and forcibly dragged the arsonists, who resisted in vain, out of their own houses. Calling the officers, they handed them over to be led off to prison. In this clash some of the enemy are reported killed. Of our people, only one was slain in the earlier fight, on the very threshold of the church, and several were wounded by stones. You have the history of our present state. Would that it were less turbulent, or that the duty laid upon me did not require me not only to hear but also to see things from which nature itself recoils. There is need of prayers, if ever at any other time, since it is certain the adversaries will try everything, and I look for steadfastness in many. But God, without doubt, will not forsake his Church in so critical a time. Farewell, my father, with your colleagues and all friends. May the Lord Jesus keep you safe and bless your holy labours more and more. From Saint-Germain, 11 i. Calend. Ian.

units.la: Tuus Bez.
units.tr: Your Beza.

units.la: M.j.

units.la: LIteras tuas, integerrime frater, sero tandem accepi post messem elapsum ex quo scripta fuerant. Etsi autem mihi gratum fuit, ex te ipso intelligere quomodo valeres, ac multo magis quàm strenuè cordatèque pergeres in obeundo munere: vehementer tamen dolui, certamina tibi moueri a quibus minimè decebat: imò quos par erat fidos tibi esse adiutores. A professis hostibus oppugnari Christi seruos, neque novum est neque mirum. Cum intestinis aduersariis configere, molestius est atque acerbius. Quanquam ad hoc quoque pugnae genus nos assuefactos esse oportet: quia nunquam in Ecclesia res adeo bene fuerunt compositae, quin e medio eius sinu prodirent remorae & obstaculà, quibuscum nobis luctandum est. Optimè verò factum, quòd inexpugnabili Christi virtute fretus, hactenus perrumpere non dubitasti. Malo, quod mihi incognitum erat, citius mederi non potui. N. aliquid de nimia D. erga suos indulgentia retulerat. Serio eum admonui. Quia nihil respondit, suspicatus sum non fuisse iucundum meum rigorem. Nunc quum & stulta credulitate, & aliis modis eovisque progressum legerem, fere obstupui. Etsi autem remedium quod utile & opportunum censui, afferre conatus sum, prolixèque de praecipuis capitibus disserui: verumtamen ne vulpes aulici diuturno taedio te macerrent ac conficiant, nisi Deus mirabiliter occurrat. Locum deseri nullo modo placet, nisi obtigerit pius successor: praesertim donec tibi liberum erit manere. Nam si pro imperio te expelleret, tibi patienter ferenda vis esset. Nec vero a statione discedit, qui cedit inuitus. Quòd si Ecclesiae prospectum mediocriter fuerit, & eius permissu resignatus fueris alteri Ecclesiae, forte nec publicè nec priuatim improbanda esset mutatio. Vtinam cum te RR. postularunt, probus vir ad manum fuisset tuis partibus obeundis: modo sua populo relicta esset libertas. Vnius enim arbitrio deligi pastores vel moueri, prorsus barbarum est. Interea te ad perseuerantiam, quicquid acciderit, confirma: ac memineris non frustra admonitos esse à Christo discipulos, vt sibi cauerent à fermento Pharisaeorum & Herodis: quia semper aulicis solenne fuit, suis corruptelis simplicem Euangelij doctrinam infice-re. Ignosce si tam ampla materia mihi suggesta, breuiter & succinctè tibi rescribo. Quanquam verè tibi affirmo, indignatione factum esse magis quàm pigritia, vt sim ita restrictus. Vale.M. D. LXI.
units.tr: I received your letter, most upright brother, only late, after the harvest had passed since it was written. Although it was pleasing to me to learn from you yourself how you are, and how much more vigorously and wisely you persist in discharging your office, I was nonetheless deeply grieved that you have been stirred up into conflicts which were by no means fitting, indeed with those who ought rather to be faithful helpers to you. That Christ's servants should be attacked by open enemies is neither new nor surprising. To contend with enemies within is more troublesome and bitter. Yet we ought to be accustomed to this kind of struggle too, since affairs in the Church have never been so well settled that hindrances and obstacles, with which we must wrestle, do not spring forth from her very bosom. You have done very well, in that, relying on the invincible power of Christ, you have not hesitated to press on thus far. I could not heal the evil sooner, since it was unknown to me. N. had reported something of the excessive indulgence of D. towards his people. I admonished him seriously. Since he made no answer, I suspected that my severity was not welcome. Now, when I read that he has gone so far through foolish credulity and in other ways, I was nearly astonished. Although I have tried to offer the remedy which I judged useful and fitting, and have discussed at length the principal points, nevertheless the courtiers' foxes will wear you out and wear you down with long weariness, unless God meets it with wonderful help. I do not at all approve of leaving the post unless a godly successor has been found, especially while it is still open to you to remain. For if he were to expel you by authority, you would have to bear the violence patiently. Nor does he who yields unwillingly abandon his post. But if the welfare of the Church is moderately provided for, and with its permission you are released and transferred to another church, perhaps the change would be open to neither public nor private objection. Would that when the reverend brethren asked for you, there had been an upright man at hand to take up your duties, provided only the people were left their freedom. For for pastors to be chosen or removed by the decision of one man is utterly barbarous. Meanwhile, whatever happens, strengthen yourself to perseverance, and remember that Christ rightly warned his disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, since it has always been the custom of courtiers to taint the simple doctrine of the Gospel with their corruptions. Forgive me if, with so ample a subject put before me, I reply to you briefly and concisely. Yet I truly assure you that I have been so restrained more from indignation than from laziness. Farewell. 1561.

units.la: BEZA
units.tr: BEZA

units.la: Mirarii imirum tam altum & diuturnum silentium. Cum parum sustineant oportet, qui diem de die ducunt. Aduersarios habemus partim Sorbonicos omnis generis, partim Italos Iesuitas, Franciscanos, Dominicanos, & crescit quotidie eorum numerus. Nos quatuor omnino sumus, Marloratus, Perofcelius, Barbastus bonus & integer homo, Nauarrenae Minister, & ego. Conditiones colloquij nullae. Tantum constituit Regina ad Pontificem mittere, quae vltro citroque dicta fuerint. Vides quam multa causificari licuerit. Tamen satis nobis fuit testari ne fratribus & Ecclesiis fraudi esset, quodcunque facturi aut dicturi essemus. Addidimus de Concilio, nos liberum Concilium non detrectare, sed cuiusmodi illud est, quod nunc instituitur pro nullo a nobis existimari. Tandem igitur ventum est ad Colloquium in magna huius arcis basilica, 28. superioris mensis. Interest Regina cum Cardinalibus & reliquis priuati Concilij consiliariis. Adsunt etiam Episcopi aliquot, sed vt priuati. Assident quoque ex Parlamentis selecti duodecim. Praescripta sunt quinque capita, De imaginibus, de forma Baptismi, de forma Communionis, de sacrificio Missae, de ministerio, de doctrinae capitibus. Non placet forte ullis neque ordo, neque diuisio, ac ne mihi quidem, sed ita visum est iis qui possunt omnia. Rogatus quia ob causam ab Ecclesia Romana dissensionem fecisse mus, exor-sus sum ab illis protestationibus, deinde ad duas horas de imaginibus dixi, quae mihi suggessit Dominus, tum ex ipsius verbo, tum ex veteris illius Ecclesiae testimoniis. Aduersarij tempus sibi ad respondendum postularunt. Conuenimus ergo vltimo die huius mensis. Habuit orationem Pelletarius, sed prorsus vulgarem. Sequutus est lesuita ille histrio qui in conuentu quoque Possiacensi interuenerat, nec minus se lepidum praestitit quam antea. Tertio loco dixit Salignacus, & vere profecto & fortiter, non contentus dicere quod res erat, nisi etiam quae ab illis erant alla ta palam confutaret. Vbi animaduertit Turnonius quorsum tenderet eius oratio, primum murmurare, deinde querulari, postremo relicta sede ad focum pergere, tandem vero etiam in extremum angulum se recipere, vnde cospici non posset. Salignacus ex aduerso pergere, & eousque progredi vt diceret idololatras, sicut petierat Dauid, in stipites & saxa conuerti, ac proinde veritatis vocem non exaudire. Vbi ille desiit accurrens Benedictus ille Dominicanus vt ruentia idola fulciret, multa blateravit, sed salsissima & ineptissima. Tandem igitur respondi, & Salignaco assensus, singula aliorum argumenta, ita vt potui, diluere studui. Ita discessum est, aduersariis Dei gratia eo adductis, vt nisi nox intercunisset, prorsus superati videri potuerint. Hodie reditum est in campum. Longam orationem habuit Corcyrensis quidam Francifcanus, vt aiunt, legati assess cla, satis acutus sophista, nec prorsus imperitus. Sequutus est Spensa qui copiosissimè causam nostram defendit, ita tamen vt multò minus neruorum haberet quàm Salignacus, nec tam syncerè, quin nonnulla per miscuerit quæ aduersarios placarent. Conclusit nullo nec externo nec interno cultu dignas esse imagines: sed de cruce multa protulit, re in dubio relicta, & ex templis penitus tollenda idola non censuit. Denique quod recte censuerat conatus est vtcunq; emollire. Iussus est postea prodire minimus ille Parisiensium seditionum sax, quo nihil ineptius & indoctius audire memini. Eram responsurus, si per tempus licuisset. Nox igitur hanc tertiâ actionem diremit, quam ego, vt spero, cras excipiam. Rogas quid sperem? hoc vnum, vt magis elucescat veritas, & aliquos semper lucrifaciamus, aliud præterea nihil. Inquirunt diligenter quibus conditionibus liberum, & Christianum Concilium definiamus. Hic ergo nobis erit laborandum, & rogo vt nostro consilio, primo quoque tempore adiuues. Edictum Rotomagi promulgatum est. Parisienses adhuc resistunt, neque dubium est quin alicunde in hac pertinacia cõfirmentur. Miser ille iam prorsus est perditus, & omnia secum perdere constituit. Vxorem amandat. Possidonium, cui omnia debet, vix sustinet intueri. Accersuntur Lothaingi. Denique extrema omnia in nos comparantur. Ita placet Domino gaudium nostrũ temperare. Vtcunque sit, Deum spero victorem fore, & nos interea, illo fauente, pergemus. Interea tibi cogitandum relinquo, quibus curis & laboribus & doloribus excrucier, vt Deum precari non desinas, donec vobis restituat. Quàm diuturnum sit futurum hoc colloquium, & quæ sint subsecutura nescio, sed me totum Deo committo. Condensem morbus repentinus pene nobis abstulit Lutetiæ. Heri lectica huc perlatus, incipit melius habere, & affirmant medici extra periculum esse. Ego neque prorsus valeo, neque etiam ægroto, sed medius pendeo. Bene vale, mi pater, & tuum Bezam, si vnquam alias, Domino commenda. Amplissimum Senatum cum Collegis & amicis omnibus rogo, vt meo nomine salutes. Dominus Iesus vos incolumes seruet. Ex Sangermano primo die Februarij.
units.tr: Indeed, you will be surprised at so long and so deep a silence. Those who put off each day from day to day must be hard pressed. We have adversaries, partly Sorbonnists of every kind and partly Italian Jesuits, Franciscans and Dominicans, and their number grows daily. There are only four of us: Marlorat, Perocel, Barbastus, a good and upright man and minister of Navarre, and I. No conditions for the colloquy have been set. The Queen has only arranged to send to the Pope what is said on each side. You see how many matters it has been possible to discuss. Still, it was enough for us to make a statement, so that it would not bring discredit on our brethren and churches, whatever we might do or say. We added that we do not reject a free council, but that the kind of council now being set up we regard as no council at all. At last we came to the colloquy in the great basilica of this citadel on the 28th of last month. The Queen attended, with the Cardinals and the other councillors of the private council. Some bishops were also present, but only as private persons. Twelve men selected from the Parlements sat as well. Five heads were laid down: on images, on the form of baptism, on the form of the Communion, on the sacrifice of the Mass, and on the ministry; and on the heads of doctrine. Perhaps neither the order nor the division pleases anyone, not even me, but it seemed right to those who can do everything. When asked why we had caused a schism from the Roman Church, I began with those protestations, and then for two hours I spoke on images, as the Lord suggested to me, both from his own Word and from the testimonies of that ancient Church. Our opponents asked for time to reply, so we met again on the last day of this month. Pelletier gave the speech, but a thoroughly commonplace one. Then came that Jesuit buffoon who had also taken part at the Poissy assembly, and he showed himself no less witty than before. Third, Salignac spoke, truly and boldly, not content to say what the matter was but also openly refuting what had been advanced by them. When Turnon noticed where his speech was heading, he first muttered, then complained, and finally, leaving his seat, went to the fireplace, and at last withdrew into the farthest corner, where he could not be seen. Salignac went on from there and proceeded so far as to say that the idolaters, as David had prayed, had been turned into stocks and stones, and therefore did not hear the voice of truth. When he stopped, that Dominican Benedictus ran up to prop up the falling idols, and he babbled a great deal, but very witty and very silly things. At last I replied, and, agreeing with Salignac, I took care to refute the individual arguments of the others as well as I could. We broke off thus, with our opponents, by God's grace, brought to a point where, had the night not intervened, they might have seemed utterly defeated. Today we returned to the field. A certain Franciscan from Corfu, as they say, the legate's assessor, gave a long speech, a fairly shrewd sophist and not altogether unskilled. Then came Spenser, who defended our cause very fully, though he had far less muscle than Salignac, and not so sincerely that he did not mix in some points that would placate our opponents. He concluded that images deserve no worship, external or internal, but on the cross he put forward much that left the matter in doubt, and he did not judge that idols should be wholly removed from the churches. Finally he tried in some way to soften what he had rightly concluded. Afterwards that little man, the rabble-rouser of the Parisians, was ordered to come forward, and I remember hearing nothing more silly or more ignorant. I would have replied, if time had allowed. Night therefore broke off this third session, which, I hope, I shall take up tomorrow. You ask what I hope for? This one thing: that the truth may shine more clearly, and that we may always win over some, and nothing else besides. They are diligently inquiring on what conditions we would define a free and Christian council. So here we shall have to labour, and I ask you to help us with your counsel at the earliest opportunity. The edict was published at Rouen. The Parisians still resist, and there is no doubt that they are being strengthened in this obstinacy from somewhere. That wretched man [the Cardinal of Lorraine?] is now utterly ruined, and he has resolved to lose everything with himself. He is sending away his wife. He can hardly bear to look at Possidonius, to whom he owes everything. The Lorrainers are being summoned. In short, every extreme measure is being prepared against us. So the Lord is pleased to temper our joy. However it turns out, I hope God will be victorious, and meanwhile, with his favour, we shall press on. In the meantime I leave it to you to consider with what cares and labours and sorrows I am tormented, so that you may not cease to pray to God until he restores us to you. How long this colloquy will last, and what will follow, I do not know, but I commit myself wholly to God. A sudden illness nearly took me from us at Paris. Yesterday, carried here in a litter, I am beginning to feel better, and the doctors affirm that I am out of danger. I am neither altogether well nor altogether ill, but I hang in the balance. Farewell, my father, and commend your Beza to the Lord, if ever before. I ask you to greet the most distinguished Senate, with your colleagues and all friends, in my name. May the Lord Jesus keep you safe. From Saint-Germain, 1 February.

units.la: BEZA CALVINO S.
units.tr: BEZA TO CALVIN, GREETING.

units.la: DIv & obstinatè tacui, ne tibi solicitudinem & dolores auge rem: sed ne nunc quidem possum aliud quàm turbas & tumultus nuntiare. Primas actiones nostri congressus dili-genter
units.tr: Though I have stubbornly kept silent so as not to add to your worry and distress, even now I can report nothing but disturbances and tumults. I have described the first proceedings of our conference diligently

units.la: Epist.332. genter ad te perscripsi: postremæ dissimiles non fuerunt. Audiuimus infinita, & incredibiles ineptias. Ita illis respondum est, Dei gratia, vt miserer aduersarios præ pudore, & ignominia non corruisse. Perstiterunt tamen suo more, & omnes contumelias fortiter deuorarunt. Vbi ventum est ad primi capitis de imaginibus conclusionem, tres inuentæ sunt sententiæ. Nos enim petiimus semel eci imagines, aduersarij cum omni suo cultu retinere. Medij (id est Valentinus Episcopus Salignacus, Spensa, Botellerius, Pichetellus, à quibus alioqui miserrimè & acerbissimè vexati sunt hoscs) cultum duntaxat sustulerunt. Tum Regina, cuius patientiam tibi satis connotare non possum, nos ad concordiam multis verbis cohortata, tandem imperauit vt singulæ factiones suam sententiam perscriberent. Hostium opinione nec describere, nec mittere placuit. Ex nostra cognoscescere nos de indu stria studuisse, vt abrupti colloquij culpa omnis in illos transferretur. Id enim callidè captabant, vt quoniam primi eramus sententiam nostram recitaturi, si præcisè negaremus nos nunquam nec vllis conditionibus coituros nisi omnibus imaginibus statim profligatis, responderent sibi cum tam præfractis hominibus nihil fore negotij, & alioqui fuisse de iure suo deceßuros. Neque verò nos hæc expectatio fefellit. Nam simulatque viderunt nos de veritate quidem nihil concedere, sed tamen, oblata quadam conditionis specie, illis eripere quod quærebant, apte cœperunt per suos dicere omnia hæc ad Concilium Tridentinum esse remittenda. Nos autem contenti fuimus de nostra promptitudine testari, & manifestas rationes proferre, cur illius conciliabuli decretis stare non possemus. Regina initio in ea erat sententia, vt omnino vellet illos ad finem usque pergere, sed cum animaduerteret factiosos quosdam hac occasione arrepta interea per cuniculos aliud moliri, tandem per Cancellarium significauit, sibi non videri vt procederet colloquium, quandoquidem in primo capite quod maxime videbatur perspicuum, tanta appareret differentia. Nihil hoc consilio gratius accidere potuit nostris aduersariis, quibus iste ludus minimè placebat, adeò vt ipse Democrates (asinus omnium quadrupedum, Mallario excepto, infacetissimus) pene sui oblitus in meos amplexus ruit, & eius sodales honorificè me salutarent. Relinquo tibi cogitandum quàm bellè mihi cum illis beatiis conuenerit. Certè non fine risu ipsius Reginæ illos à me dimisi. Interea iussi fumus nostram dereliquis etiam capitibus sententiam paucis perscribere. Sed hoc fiet, opinor, ad Calendas græcas. Interea dum hæc fabula peragitur, non credas quas nobis Tragœdias excitarit illeque minimè omnium oportuit, de quo si deinceps scripsero, Iulianu vocabo. Dicá vno verbo, opus est Domini, iusta sua iudicia exercere.
units.tr: Epist.332. in full to you, and the last ones were not unlike them. We heard endless and incredible nonsense. We answered them, by God's grace, so that I pity our opponents for not having collapsed in shame and humiliation. Yet they persisted in their usual way and bravely swallowed every insult. When we came to the conclusion of the first head, concerning images, three opinions emerged. We asked that images be removed at once, while our opponents wished to keep them together with all their worship. The moderates (that is, Valentinus the Bishop, Salignac, Spensa, Botellier and Pichetel, by whom our enemies were otherwise treated very wretchedly and harshly) removed only the worship. Then the Queen, whose patience I cannot adequately convey to you, urged us to concord with many words, and at last ordered each faction to put its opinion in writing. Our enemies decided not to write it out or send it. You should know that we deliberately took care that the whole blame for the broken colloquy would be shifted onto them. They were cunningly hoping that, since we were the first to recite our opinion, if we flatly stated that we would never come to terms under any conditions unless all images were immediately abolished, they could reply that there was no business to be done with such obstinate men, and that otherwise they would have given up some of their right. Nor did this expectation deceive us. For as soon as they saw that we conceded nothing of the truth, yet, with some appearance of a condition offered, we were taking from them what they wanted, they promptly began to say through their own people that all these matters must be referred to the Council of Trent. We, however, were content to attest our readiness and to set forth clear reasons why we could not abide by the decrees of that conventicle. At first the Queen was of the mind to let them go on to the end, but when she noticed that some factious men, seizing this opportunity, were meanwhile contriving something else through underground channels, she finally signified through the Chancellor that it did not seem right to her for the colloquy to proceed, since on the first head, which seemed most clear, so great a difference appeared. Nothing could have been more welcome to our opponents than this decision, for they did not at all like this game, so much so that Democrates himself (the most unwitty ass of all quadrupeds, Mallarius excepted) nearly forgetting himself rushed into my embrace, and his companions greeted me with honour. You may consider for yourself how pleasantly I got on with those blessed men. I certainly dismissed them not without the Queen's own laughter. Meanwhile we were ordered to set out briefly our opinion on the remaining heads as well. But this will be done, I suppose, at the Greek calends. Meanwhile, while this farce is being played out, you would not believe what tragedies it has stirred up for us, and least of all from the person from whom it least ought to have come; if I write about him further, I will call him Julian. To say it in one word: it is the Lord's work to carry out his just judgments.

units.la: M.iij. centis,& vix vllum extat similis leuitatis, perfidiæ, celeris exem-plum. Neque puduit illum quo die sum eum in aulo alloquu-tus,non aliter mecum agere,quàm fi ignorare quæ vel ipsis pue-ris nota sunt.Ab eo tempore odium in me tuum non iam fimu-lare,sed aperte prodere coepit,& spiritu malo pa'am agitatus in-fanire. Sed bene habet quod Deus omnem illi mentem ademit, adeo vt ne insanus quidem videatur magno pere formidabilis. Vxorem autem tibi affirmo duplo fortiorem fuisse, quàm vn-quàm antea. In Poffidonio & al'ero eius fratre nihil est,quod requiras. Vterq; cessit illius insani furoribus, sed certo consilio, quod nobis vtile fore spero, quanuis maluissem ad extremum inuictos sese opponere.Sed aliter iudicant faciendum fuisse,qui bus arcana ista notiora sunt quàm mihi.Hoc quidem scio & Re gi & Reginæ gratissimos difceffiffe, & spero aliis ad exeundum ianuam patefecifle qui minimè hoc fperarat. Terr us frater in au la remansit,homo fi quisquam in eo ordine alius,plane integer, adeo effusa est Dei benedictio in totam illam familiam.Hac oc cafione arrepta,cupidè & ipse ex aula difcefli ad patre profectu-rus,simúlque me ad reditum comparans. Sed ecce nuæ turbæ in quibus nefas fuit hanc Ecclesiam (cuius gubernationem no-fti) deferere.Senatus neque precibus, neque minis potuit exora-ri, vt iniquissima etiam addita duorum capitum declaratione, Edictum promulgaret.Hinc igitur infiniti tumultus,conspirati-ones apertæ,mutuæ cædes,& quid non?& hæc omnia debemus accepta referre Iuliani furoribus. Interea grex crescit infinitis modis, quæ vna res me hic retinet, quoniam video Dominum huic qualicunque meo labori benedicere.Ab hinc quatriduum Regina huc venit, vt Edicti promulgationem extorqueret.Eius consilium infœlix ille impediit.Edictum igitur illa,vnà cum ea quam dixi declaratione,secum abstulit,& Senatu monuit vt sal tem meliusaliquod confil um daret.Eodem die qui tamen festus non erat,conuenimus in cœcione pomeridiana ad vigi nti quin-que hominum millia, in quibus erant plurimi omnium ordinum huius ciuitatis, non alio habitu, quàm fi in curiam fuissent ingressuri,& ex nobilitate quamplurimi. Hoc fpectaculu alios ad rabiem & desperationem adegit,alios fregit,alios coegit fufpen fos hærere,& sane in his turbis quiduis experiendum video.Con filium eorum qui in senatu nobis aduersantur, id est partis ali-quanto maioris,eiusmodi est in summa.Obseruandum esse Iulij mensis Edictum,non quale habetur, sed ita vt perscriptum erat in Curiæ regiftro,id est,multò crudelius. Nõ deesse Principe(is est Aumallæus)qui paratus fit intra mensem omnes istos extra Regni limites profligare.Sorbonam scripturam esse breue Cate chifmum,qui à Catholicis doctoribus,in omnibus oppidis expli-cetur tetur, itémque fidei capita, quibus Rex ipse primus, deinde omnes sine exceptione subscribant. Qui hoc facere recusarit, si quo munere fungatur, ab eius functione per annum abstineat: nisi intra annum resipuerit, exilio & fortunis multetur. Sin priuatus fuerit, intra mensem excedet Regni finibus Ministri intra diem decimum quintum, addita reuertentibus capitali poena, pellantur. Nostrarum Eccl. fiarum matrimonia irrita habeantur, & ex iis prognati mares vel foeminae inter spurios numeretur. Quid amplius? vt quos baptizauimus, alieni ab Ecclesia censeatur. Hæc illi, & sane gaudeo quod nullum medium consilium coeperint. Neque enim arbitror vllum prosus fore qui non eos vt stultos rideat, & vt insanos reiiciat. Interea exitum aliquem praestolamur. De mea valetudine, videor quidem mihi melius habere, sed tamen quotidiani labores, vix sinunt me respirare. Interea millies mori malim, quàm in tanta tempestate quiescere, laboriosus omnibus. Preces tantum peto, & rogo, mi pater, vt quod ad rem iltam attinet, caetera arbitrio meo relin quas. Nam scitutc hic est, piger tibi videret, in tanta, necessitate, quantum hic conspicio, in ea vrbe quam aduersarii praecipuè petunt. De meo reditu idem est mihi animus. Quid multi cupiant, atque etiam importuniffimè flagitent, partim iam admonui, partim deinceps cognoscetis. Nam etsi ita restiti, vt millies praedixerim nihil tale esse ipsis cogitandum, tamen video ipsos omnia tentaturos. Quid expediat, si requiris, puto de hoc constitui non posse in ista rerum perturbatione. Coniicio Iulianū, qui omnibus bonis semel bellum minatur, nunquam passuru vt diutius in hoc Regno maneam. Sed in omnem, vt, aiunt, euentum, proderit publicis literis me ad Calendas Maij, ad summum renocari. Si interea eiiciar, certe solus non ero. Sed hoc vt spero, Deus auertet. Sin minus, tamen omnes intelligent merito me de reditu cogitare, & hoc fortassis obstabit, quominus ad vos mittantur qui vobis, atque etiam mihi sint molesti. Hæc tamen ita dicta & scripta sunto, vt me existimetis nihil aliud decreuisse, quàm quod censueritis ex visu esse Ecclesiæ, siue hic mihi sit manendum, siue redeundum. Iam ad postremas tuas venio. Quod de Hispani & aliorum foedere istic f. rtur, iampridem hic volitat, & facit aduersariorum confidentia, vt non penitus vanum esse rumorem coniiciamus. Sed nihil certi possumus adhuc affirmare, quanuis Poffidonius quitum hic erat, cùm literæ tuæ & illi & mihi redderentur, omnia sedulò fit expiscatus. Nam commodè euenerat, vt tu quoq; Regina hic esset. Puto igitur neque contemnendū esse hunc rumorē neque nimium reformidādum. Diligenter omnia scrutabor, & statim perscribam. Et hūc necesse est, mi pater, vt tibi aliquid tot laboribus
units.tr: Nor was he ashamed, on the day I spoke with him at court, to treat me as though I were ignorant of things known even to boys. From that time he began to show his hatred of you not by pretence but openly, and, driven by an evil spirit, to rage in public. But it is well that God has taken away all his judgment, so that even when mad he does not seem very formidable. I assure you that his wife is twice as brave as she was before. Concerning Possidonius and his other brother there is nothing you need ask. Both yielded to that madman's fury, but by a deliberate plan, which I hope will prove useful to us, although I would have preferred that they stood unconquered to the end. But those who know these secrets better than I do judge that they had to act so. This much I know: they left, very welcome to both the King and the Queen, and I hope they have opened the door for others to leave too, who scarcely hoped for it. Their brother Terrus remained at court, a man, if anyone in that order is, altogether upright, so richly is God's blessing poured out on that whole family. Seizing this opportunity, I too eagerly left the court, intending to set out for my father, and at the same time preparing for my return. But behold, new tumults have arisen, in which it was wrong to desert this church (whose governance you know). The Senate could be moved neither by prayers nor by threats to promulgate the edict, even with the most unjust declaration of two chapters added. Hence endless tumults, open conspiracies, mutual slaughters, and what not, and all of this we must put down to the furies of Julian. Meanwhile the flock grows in countless ways, and this is the one thing that keeps me here, since I see the Lord blessing my labour here, such as it is. Four days ago the Queen came here to extract the promulgation of the edict. That unhappy man hindered her plan. So she took the edict away with her, together with the declaration I mentioned, and warned the Senate that it should at least devise something more moderate. On the same day, which was not a festival, we gathered in the afternoon assembly, some twenty-five thousand men, among them very many of every rank of this city, dressed no differently than if they were about to enter the council chamber, and a great number of the nobility. This spectacle drove some to rage and despair, broke others, and forced others to hang back in suspense; and indeed in these tumults I see that anything may be tried. The plan of those in the Senate who oppose us, that is, the considerably larger part, is in summary this: that the edict of July must be observed, not as it is held, but as it was written in the register of the court, that is, much more cruelly. That there should be no lack of a prince (this is Aumallaeus) who is ready within a month to drive all those people beyond the boundaries of the kingdom. That the Sorbonne is to write a short catechism, to be expounded by Catholic teachers in all the towns, and likewise articles of faith, which the King himself shall subscribe first, and then all without exception. Whoever refuses to do so, if he holds any office, shall abstain from its duties for a year; unless within the year he comes to his senses, he shall be punished with exile and the loss of his property. If he is a private person, he shall leave the boundaries of the kingdom within a month. The ministers shall be expelled within fifteen days, with capital punishment added for those who return. The marriages of our churches are to be held void, and the sons and daughters born of them are to be counted among the bastards. What more? Those whom we have baptized are to be regarded as alien to the Church. Those are their proposals, and I am indeed glad that they have not begun with any middle course. For I do not think there will be anyone at all who will not laugh at them as fools and reject them as madmen. Meanwhile we await some outcome. As for my health, I seem to myself to be getting better, but my daily labours scarcely allow me to draw breath. Meanwhile I would rather die a thousand times than rest in such a storm, labouring at everything. I ask only for prayers, and I beg you, my father, that as far as that matter is concerned you leave the rest to my judgment. For you should know that here, in such great necessity as I see here, he would seem idle to you, in the city which our adversaries especially attack. About my return my mind is the same. What many want, and even demand most importunately, I have partly already mentioned, and partly you will learn hereafter. For although I have resisted so firmly that I have a thousand times declared that nothing of the kind is to be thought of, still I see they will try everything. What is expedient, if you ask, I think cannot be decided in this upheaval of affairs. I conjecture that Julian, who has once threatened war on all good men, will never allow me to remain in this kingdom for long. But to be prepared, as they say, for any outcome, it will help if I am recalled, at the latest, by public letters at the Calends of May. If in the meantime I am cast out, I shall certainly not be alone. But this, as I hope, God will avert. If not, yet everyone will understand that I am rightly thinking of returning, and perhaps this will stand in the way of those being sent to you who would be troublesome to you and even to me. Yet let these things be said and written in such a way that you think I have decided nothing other than what you judge to be in the interest of the Church, whether I should remain here or return. Now I come to your last letter. What is being rumoured there about a covenant between the Spaniards and others has been flying about here for some time, and the confidence of our adversaries makes us suspect that the rumour is not entirely empty. But we can as yet affirm nothing certain, although Possidonius, who was here when your letters were delivered to him and to me, has sifted everything diligently. For it happened conveniently that you too, Queen, were here. I think, therefore, that this rumour is neither to be despised nor greatly feared. I shall examine everything carefully and write at once. And it is necessary, my father, that I impose on you, though unwillingly, something more to add to so many labours, namely that you inform Martyr and our friends there, as often as it is possible, of what is done here; and although I shall gladly relieve you of this trouble myself, as far as that can be done. You have a letter somewhat longer than if I had written only briefly, but still I beg you not to...

units.la: M.iiij. oppresso, hoc onus inuitus imponam, vt Martyrem &nostros illos quoties licebit, certiores facias eorum, quæ hic geruntur, quanuis hac molestia, quoad eius fieri poterit, ipse te libenter liberabo. Habes literas aliquanto longiores, quàm si scripissem: sed tamen rogo ne vlla negligentia factum putes vt tandiu tacuerim. Bene vale, mi pater, cum fratribus, Collegis & amicis omnibus. D.Iesus te magis ac magis in opere suo confirmet, & ad extremum vsque tibi benedicat. Lutetiæ, xxvi. Februarij.
units.tr: M.iiij. Though I am overwhelmed, I will reluctantly lay this burden on myself: whenever it is possible, keep Martyr and our other friends informed of what is happening here, though I will gladly spare you this trouble as far as I can. You have a letter somewhat longer than I would have written, but please do not think that my silence has been due to any negligence. Farewell, my father, with the brothers, colleagues and all friends. May the Lord confirm you more and more in his work and bless you to the end. Paris, 26 February.

units.la: ORATIO LEGATORVM PONTIFICIS AD Principes Germanos habita Naumburgi die v. Februarij, M. D. LXI.
units.tr: ORATION OF THE PAPAL LEGATES delivered to the German Princes at Naumburg on the 5th of February, 1561.

units.la: Alter Legatus.
units.tr: The First Legate.

units.la: CVM summus Pontifex ad sacrosanctæ regimen Ecclesiæ vt catus esset, in eam statim curam pro suscepto munere Pastoralis incumbere coepit, quomodo corrupti mores emendarentur, vt esset tandem pax Ecclesiæ, & idem sentirent omnes Nationes. Cùmque tam ad mala sananda, quàm ad bona consequenda, nullum aliud remedium quàm sacri Oecumenici Concilij celebratione superesset, habita matura deliberatione cum ordine Cardinalium, Sacrum tandem Tridenti ad festum Pascatis Concilium celebrandum, auctoritate diuinitus sibi tradita decreuit. Vt verò ad notitiam omnium Principum id peruenire, & ipsi eandem curam susciperent, suáque studia ad consulendum Germaniæ tráquillitati Pontificiæ solicitudini coniungerent, ablegauit hos nuntios suos, qui pro amore & studio, quo inclytam Germaniæ nationem semper profequuutus est, eiúsque vnitatem dilexit, Pij Pontificis nomine singulos conuenire-mus, rogaremus, hortaremur, & obsecraremus vt ad Concilium hoc accederent, cum plena mansuetudinis ac pacis omnia ibi sint futura, omnes ibi auditos, ac in rebus iustis benignè exauditos iri. Petántque vt iidem Principes piam hanc solicitudinem, progressum habere velint, cùm Pontifex nihil aliud studeat, nisi vt concordia & pax Ecclesiæ restituantur. Paratus est idem Pontifex saluum conductum Principibus in amplissima & tali forma dare, qualis vnquam data fuit, aut excogitari potest. Petit quapropter Pontifex ac hortatur vt singuli Principes Legatos suos cum plenis mandatis eò mittant, vt Principum studio sedatis Ecclesiæ dissidiis (tot enim de Religione opiniones, quot capita: & tot Euangelia, quot doctores) Ecclesiæ suum decus restituatur, vna fides vbique seruetur, & vnus Deus ab omnibus colatur. Caetera Principes ex Collega audituros.
units.tr: Since the supreme Pontiff, so that he might be a careful governor of the most holy Church, straightway began to apply himself to the care that comes with the pastoral office he had undertaken: how corrupt morals might be amended, so that at last there might be peace in the Church and all nations might think alike. And since, both for healing evils and for obtaining goods, no other remedy remained than the celebration of the holy Ecumenical Council, he decided, after mature deliberation with the college of Cardinals, to hold the holy Council at Trent at the feast of Easter, by the authority divinely committed to him. And so that this might come to the knowledge of all the Princes, and that they might take up the same care and join their zeal to the Pontiff's concern for the peace of Germany, he sent these envoys of his, who, out of the love and zeal with which he has always pursued the illustrious German nation and cherished its unity, were to meet each of you in the name of the pious Pontiff, to ask, urge and beseech you to come to this Council, since everything there will be conducted with full gentleness and peace, all will be heard there, and in just matters they will be kindly granted a hearing. And they ask that the same Princes be willing to let this pious solicitude make progress, since the Pontiff desires nothing else than that the concord and peace of the Church be restored. The same Pontiff is ready to give the Princes a safe conduct in the fullest form, such as was ever given or can be imagined. Therefore the Pontiff asks and urges that each Prince send his Legates thither with full powers, so that, through the zeal of the Princes, the dissensions of the Church being calmed (for there are as many opinions about religion as there are heads, and as many gospels as there are teachers), the Church's dignity may be restored, one faith be kept everywhere, and one God be worshipped by all. The Princes will hear the rest from my colleague.

units.la: ALTER LEGATVS.
units.tr: The Second Legate.

units.la: ILlustrissimi Principes cum eadem mandata vtrique nostrum summus Pontifex dederit, non arbitror repetenda quae a Collega iam apposita sunt, ac explicandas censeo Ecclesiae calamitates. Nemo est enim qui ignoret, quo res deducta sit, & quo relabatur. Aliud ex alio malum exoritur, hostibus Christiani nominis ad perniciem Reipub. aditus datur. Huic obuiam vt cautur, opus est. Postulant haec pericula, suadet temporis opportunitas, Pij Pontificis benignitas, & studium vt nulla vnquam pacis conciliandae commodior occasio oblata, aut dari posse videatur, pacata Repub. Christiana, ac Pontifice diu initus dato, cuius studium singulare est erga Principes, solicite de animarum salute, & vt Ecclesiae pax & tranquillitas restituatur. Haec sunt quae paucis exponenda censuimus.
units.tr: Most illustrious Princes, since the supreme Pontiff has given the same instructions to each of us, I do not think what has already been set forth by my colleague need be repeated, and I judge that the calamities of the Church should be explained. For there is no one who does not know to what state affairs have been brought and into what they are sliding back. One evil arises from another, and an opening is given to the enemies of the Christian name for the ruin of the commonwealth. Care must be taken to meet this. These dangers demand it, the opportunity of the times urges it, and the kindness of the pious Pontiff, and his zeal, so that no more convenient occasion for reconciling peace has ever been offered or seems capable of being given: a Christian commonwealth at peace, and a Council long since granted by the Pontiff, whose zeal toward the Princes is singular, anxious for the salvation of souls and that the peace and tranquillity of the Church may be restored. These are the things we have thought should be set out briefly.

units.la: IOAN. CALVINVS GIBOTIO TOLOSANO.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN TO GIBOTIUS OF TOULOUSE.

units.la: SIcuti cum antehac audirem, eximie vir, te istic pro defensione salutis doctrinę strenuē pugnare, & hac de causa vexari ab hostibus pietatis, de salute tua solicitus fui, & coram Deo gratulatus sum tuae constantiae: ita nunc miratus sum, vbi maior affulsit libertas filiis Dei te adhuc desidere in eo coeno, vnde pridem emergere debueras. Nam cum de laetiore vrbis vestrae statu verba fierent, mox scisciscatus sum quomodo te gereres. Vbi vero mihi narratum est te in eadem manere professione, libere tibi fatebor, huius parum ingenuae tuae tarditatis me puduit. Etsi enim non dubito Satanam & mundum multa obiicere, quae te impediant ac morentur: omnia tamen obstacula perrumpere te decebat. Nam cum in te multorum conjecti sint oculi, nisi exemplo tuo praeluceas omnibus, quicquid coloris obtendes ad excusationem nullius erit momenti. Adhaec in eo te gradu locauit Deus, qui te arctiore vinculo ad reliquos excitandos obstringat. Nec tibi venia dabitur, nisi te certamina, quibus Deus pridem te exercuit, animo sum reddant. Iam quasi sublato vexillo suos omnes Deus ad pugnandum inuitat. Quanuis aliorum ignauiae parcatur, tibi omnium minime cessare licet. Quid enim absurdius vel minus decorum, quam puero duce colligi Christo Ecclesiam, certatim confluere multas turmas, vulgus hominum acri ter se impietati opponere, omnium ordinum homines vno consensu purum Dei cultum profiteri: veteranu autem Theologum qui luculentum recti animi specimen edidit, de quo tanta concepta fuit expectatio, non modo quietum stare, sed permixtum esse manifestis & professis Christi hostibus? Negabis te prorsus silere, vel esse medium, sed multa signa dare synceri ergo Religionem studij. Sed mutum abest quin haec obscura & ambigua significatio ad placandos piorum animos sufficiat, qui merito aliquid maius abs te flagitant. Nisi ergo in apertum prodeas ad dandum Christo nomen, adeoque primus in acie appareas tanquam Antesignanus, culpam nimium mollis inertiae neque coram Deo, neque coram Ecclesia vnquam effugies: quando res eo prouestæ sunt, vt iam non supersit tergiuersandi locus. Ignosce mea vehementia, quam mihi verus erga te amor suggessit. Nam dona quibus te ornauit Deus, sic amplexus sum, vt non possim non tibi esse amicus. Vale ornatissime vir, & mihi ex animo colende. D. te Spiritu suo gubernet, virtute fulciat, praesidio tueatur. Geneuae, xiiii. Martij. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Since I formerly heard, distinguished sir, that you there were vigorously fighting in defence of the saving doctrine, and that for this cause you were being harassed by the enemies of piety, I was anxious for your safety, and before God I rejoiced at your constancy. So now I am astonished that, when greater liberty has shone upon the sons of God, you still linger in that mire from which you ought long since to have emerged. For when talk was made of the happier state of your city, I at once inquired how you were faring. But when I was told that you remained in the same profession, I will frankly confess to you that I was ashamed of this rather ungenerous slowness of yours. For although I do not doubt that Satan and the world throw many obstacles in your way and delay you, it was fitting that you should break through all hindrances. For since the eyes of many are fixed upon you, unless you give light to all by your example, whatever colour you put forward as an excuse will be of no weight whatever. Moreover, God has placed you in a rank which binds you by a closer tie to rouse the rest. Nor will pardon be given you unless the struggles with which God long since exercised you restore your spirit. Now, as if the banner had been raised, God invites all his people to fight. Although the cowardice of others is forgiven, it is by no means permitted you to cease. For what could be more absurd or less becoming than that, with a boy as leader, the Church be gathered to Christ, great companies flock together eagerly, the common people oppose themselves fiercely to impiety, and men of every rank with one accord profess the pure worship of God, while a veteran theologian, who gave a brilliant specimen of an upright mind, about whom such great expectation was conceived, should not only stand quietly but be mixed up with the open and avowed enemies of Christ? You will say that you do not keep silent altogether, or that you are in the middle, but that you give many signs of a sincere zeal for religion. But this vague and ambiguous indication is far from sufficient to satisfy the hearts of the pious, who rightly demand something more from you. Therefore, unless you come forward openly to confess the name of Christ, and so appear first in the battle line as a standard-bearer, you will never escape the blame of excessive soft inertia, either before God or before the Church, since matters have advanced to the point where there is no room left for shifting evasions. Pardon my vehemence, which true affection for you has prompted. For the gifts with which God has adorned you I have so embraced that I cannot but be your friend. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and one to be honoured by me from my heart. May the Lord govern you by his Spirit, strengthen you with virtue, and keep you under his protection. Geneva, 14th March, 1561.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N.N. S. D.
units.tr: JOHN CALVIN to N.N., greeting

units.la: VTinam, Dilectissimi fratres, laetius ad vos scribedi argumentum fecisset offerret, vt meae etiam literae plus gaudij vobis afferrent, Peto igitur a vobis ne moleste feratis, si vos ad tem pus tristitia affecero, cum ea vna sit ratio, qua vere in Domino gaudium capti renouari possit. Optarem vero hoc potius scripto praedicari a me vestram fidem, charitatem, tolerantiam, vt vos etiam ad perstandum ac proficiendo in melius exhortarer. Cum autem vestra salus mihi chara atque pretiosa sit, ad aliud argumentum me conferre cogor, vt vos serio commonefaciam quae ad me de vobis perferuntur, non respondere Euangelij cognitioni, vti illam a Domino semel accepistis. Quare necessitas quae me huc adducit, excusationis vicem satis apud vos supplere debet. Sic enim Paulus ipse, cuius tanta erat spiritus mansuetudo ac singularis humanitas, Corinthios ipsos in causa esse dicit, q aduesus ipsos vehementia & asperitate vti cogeretur. Et tamen vbi itaillos tractauit, testatur eius rei se non poenitere, dummodo tristitia illa quam ipsis scribendo intulit, eos ad ingemiscendum suis malis adducat, vt serio respiscant. Sic etiam ipse colligo, quod ita me geram erga vos, a vobis acerbum ad primum motum iudicatum iri: atqui si in vos vti par est, descendetis, vt vestros morbos persentiatis, agnoscetis non aliud ad illos medicandos leniusremedium adferri potuisse. Sic autem de vobis sentio, ex iis quae audiui a fide dignis, & qui bene in vos affecti sunt. Ac ne vos pluribus moror, sic accipite. Vitam illam vestram ma gnę gno esse probis offendiculo: ac vicissim ea occasione os impiis à vobis aperiri, vt nomen Domini & sanctam doctrinam blasphe ment Sic enim ista connotanda sunt vt se habent, vt malum vo bis retegatur, quod tandem quale sit agnoscatis, vt remedio lo cus esse possit. Enimuero sat scio gratioresse multò illos medi cos, qui malum emplastris & vnctionibus linendo leniunt, vt vl cus intimum non fodiant, quàm qui vt ægrotum probè curet, serió lancinando pus ipsum exprimunt. Ac si ad vestram salu tem ita expediret, nihil magis optarem, quàm mollius & blan dius omnino vob scum agere. Sed quid agam, si quæ nimis no ta sunt dissimulauero, ac tam inordinatis modum aliquem affin xero, cùm res nullo modo iam ferat? Hæc sunt igitur quæ de vo bis audiuntur, vt & à vobis audiantur placidè, vt remedium malis quætamus, quæ nimis iam diu apud vos obtinuerunt. Primum igitur hoc fertur, vos plurimùm refrixisse ab affectu qui extabat olim in vobis ad audiendum verbum Dei: illud ex eo colligi, q nullum sit apud vos in illo proficiendi studium: item vos effu sos esse ad blasphemias, luxus, scortationes, eásque eiusmodi, vt ad illarum auditum exhorrescam. Item strepere intervos omnia dicteriis & falsis conuitiis, quibus vos ipsos mutuò admorderis, quasi certatim & perpetuò, tantùm mutuæ ædificationis studiosi estis: itè odia, detractiones, inuidiam, ita regnare apud vos, iurgia manifesta atque rixas, vt à verbis tandem ad pugnas etiam deue niatur. En verò natiuos plane fructus contemptus doctrinæ il lius, quæ fræni instar esse debuit, vt in vera sanctitate & honesta te contineret, Atque illè fons est mali, reftixit nempe zelus au diendi verbi & in illo proficiendi, qui olim vigebat. Est verò il lud infausti ominis: cùm qui optimè verbum Dei concoquunt, nunquam illo tamen se satis expleri posse sentiant. Vt contrà qui Dei verbo quasi saturum grauari se ostendit, iam fastidium illius prodit, vt tandem cuomat quicquid ante percepit. Equidem me non latet, non ita vos ipsa auditione verbi institutos pridem fuisse, vti optandum esset. Sed tamen vel minima portio tati bo ni optabilior erat, quàm si nihil omnino accepissetis. Iam audi mus de vobis, non valde à vobis requiri publicam priuatámve institutionem Sane etiam si centies vberior vobis intelligentia veritatis inesset, ea tamè est immensitas sapientiæ Christi, vt nú quam non illic reperturi siis, quod vobis maximo vsui esse de beat: adeóque prouectissimos quosque doctores perpetuum disci pulorum locum in hac vita retinere statuédum est. Vt verò ipsa simplici doctrina non ita vobis opus esset, an verò qui cum illa coniunctı sunt exhortationum stimuli parum necessarij iudicà di sunt, vt tot illa mala quæ inter vos emergunt salté indicent, atq; vos vobis ipsis exhibeant? Si nullu aliud peccatum inter vos extaret,illudtamen est non mediocre,quòd non in melius, sed in deteriustenditis.Infigne, inquam est peccatum,& ingratitu-do omni deprecatione maior, vbi cordis aures obuiæ non pa-tent,Domino sacrum illud os suu apud nos aperiente.Imò cùm non sit hoc vnius diei,sed quotidianû ipsius beneficiû,nostrum erat quotidie etiam illi audientiâ præstare:quò pertinet illa Pau-li admonitio,vt Dei verbum copiosè in nobis inhabitet.Agno-scite igitur vt summum inter vos malum, cùm non alio affectu proficiendi magis ac magis ducamini,vt teneatis quæ sit volun-tas Domini: cumque remittitis omne studium & diligentiam ad vos siue per lectionem,siue alia ratione in cœlesti illa cogita-tione confirmandos.Quemadmodum enim fastidium cibi ma-lam corporis habitudinem declarat, ita longè peius habere li-quet ipsam animam,vbi gustus ille & sapor verbi Dei plane de-perditur. Porrò ex ipsis fructibus malietiam magnitudo æsti-mâda est.Neque hoc dico vt vnguem vlceri apponam,sed vt in quo versemini periculo,commonstrem, vt tanto melius appo-situm remedium amplecti possitis.Nam quis illud credat, quòd nomen ipsum Dei,quod satis pretiosum apud nos esse non pos-sit,ira apud vos indignè profanatur? Neque enim temeritas iu-randi istic tantùm vsurpatur,sed & blasphemiæ,quæ passim per ora volitant,audiuntur. Ecquid verò in Deum creditis,qui tam secure hoc illius quasi fulmen non expauescitis?Dominus non habebit pro innocente qui assumpserit nomé ipsius in vanum. Iam si non ferendum à se iuramentum temerè conceptum pro-nuntiat,scilicet illi perinde erit quòd sacrum ipsius nomen blas-phemiis etiam magis per vos vilescat, quin horrenda vindicta tantum scelus secutura sit? Tantine scilicet vobis esse corpus ip-sum Christi Domini,ipsúmque sanguinem,vt eorum mentio si-ue per insultationem,siue per ludibrium à vobis etiam fiat? At-qui nisi ista propius expenditis,satis ostendet vestro malo,quàm alio in pretio illa ipsa habeat,quæ vos ita fœdè proculcatis.Ne-que verò hoc etiam dissimulauit haftenus.Quæ enim nobis pro-bra incubunt,certa sunt ipsius flagella, quæ eo nomine ab ipso immittuntur, quòd non eam quam parerat nominis ipsius ra-tionem habuistis.Auditis Apostolum nempe,vbi de illis agit qui cùm Deum cognouerint,ipsum tamen legitimè non glorificaue runt,ideo,inquit,tradidit illos in mentem reprobam, vt in om-nem fœditatem proiecti essent. Atque ita loquitur Apostolus de profanis ipsis,quibus lux illa Dei non perinde atque vobis affulsisset. Cùm igitur Euangelij lucem vobis obtulerit,quòd ita nùc vehementer in vos excàdescat,apud quos nomen ipsius ita pro scinditur,ipse quidem mirari non possum.Hinc omnino illa in-ter vos pudenda confusio:ac nominatim scortationes:eaque ad-eò eò fœdæ,vt ipsis infidelibus horrorem incutiant.Equidem non vt causæ cognitione præmissa sententiam fero:sed tamen scandalum ipsum adeo vulgare est,vt plusfatis malifubesse clamet: sed tamen si illa Pauli admonitio memoriæ saltem hæreret, vt abstineamus etiam ab eo quod mali speciem habeat, attentius vt exististimo,à malo ipso caueretis.Contrà verò non desunt quos hoc vnum quærere credibile sit, vt famam illam quæ de seipsis circunferrtur,& malum simul exemplum confirment.Optadum vero esset,fama ipsam quæ passim volitat,extinctam esse omnino. Sed nihil agitur, nisi factum male purgetur. Sic enim finit Dominus ipsam fœditatem detegi,vt qui libentius in tenebris sibi in vitiis indulgerent atque blandirentur, ipsi demum vbi se detectos sentient,pudore suffundatur.Sic solet ad resipiscentiam compellere.Porro quid cõtineat Scriptura quòd ad promiscuas & vulgares scortationes, non ignoratis. Illas nempe à Deo mapedici,propter illas Dei vindictam rebellibus impendere,ad eos qui illas sectantur,Regnum Dei non pertinere,illas adeo sacrilegij instar habere,quando nostra ipsorum corpora,quæ Spiritus sanctus sibi templa sacrauerat, illis demum polluantur:qui se illis addicunt,à Christi corpore abscindi. Scortatoré denique sibi ipsi peculiarem quandā maculam, quæ aliis sceleribus non iuncta sit,inurere.Atqui non in scortatione istiusmodi stetit apud vos malum. Quis enim est iam vester pudor,quòd ad eam vsque licentiam progressi estis, quam profani ipsi detestati sint, cum ipse naturæ sensus hoc omnes doceret, crimen esse intolerandum.Incestum nempe toleraftis,& approbastis. Quare date operam imprimis,vt quòd ad istud attinet, conscientiâ vestram coram Deo imprimis aperiatis, atque vos ita syncere hic gerite in posterum, vt nulla inde macula apud alios in vobis hæreat. Testabatur Paulus,si quos scortatores aut profusos & inordinatos apud Corinthios offenderet, quos mali non pœnituisset, sibi hoc nouum luctum allaturum, atque ipsorum in se opprobrium deriuatum iri. Quanto magis ipsis mali auctoribus ad lacrymas & extremam demissionem confugiendum erat?Quum autem vos omnes etiam vt eiusdem corporis membra partem etiam mali sustineatis, illa tam horrendi peccati agnitio vos quoque afficiet atque serió deiiciet, vt in posterum studiosius quàm hactenus fecistis, enitamini,vt vos mutuò ædificetis,tum verbo, tum ipso vitæ exemplo. Nam & eo male auditis, quòd nonnulli quasi artem quandam sannionum factitent, toti diuersis referti sint ad pungendos quosliber. Paulus verò nominatim etiam dicacitatem,& facetias illas scurriles à Christianis alienas esse iubet.Hoc igitur à vobis remoueite : ídque eo magis quòd mali illi & insulsi sermones afferunt secum male agendi licentiam,quoniam in illis proferendis iam modus omnis reli-citur. Sequuntur deinde odia & inuidentiæ,quæ nimis produnt, Regnum Dei non extare apud vos,cum ipse sit Deus concordiæ & pacis. Adiunctæ sunt etiam detractiones,quæ nullum charitatis esse locum indicant, quando Charitas tegere dicitur multitudinem peccatorum. Atque hic satis mirari non possum,unde vobis ad ista otium dari possit, cum tot hostes undique immineant,qui hoc vnum quærunt, vt aliquâ vobis noceant. Etiam Guelphis cum Gibellinis conuenit, vbi tertius hostis emergit. Inter vos autem ita paucos,atque undique adlatrantibus hosti busfubiectos, ita tamen odia & rixas feruere quàm absurdum est! Instant circumcirca qui ad vos deuorandos intenti sunt: & à vobis ipsis occasio obtruditur, dum ita vos mutuo mordetis, quasi nempe cotem ad exacuendos ipsorum mucrones data operâ subministraretis. Agnoscite verò quòd ita præcise vobis-cum egi,me ad vos expergefaciendos necessitate adactum fuisse. Nisi enim lethargo grandi laboratis hactenus, non ita & tamdiu,inque tam crassis vitiis vobis indulsisse, Vt enim perpetua cum omnibus coniuncta sit infirmitas,tamen quod in vobis notaui,mera est prauitas & contemptus. Atqui nolim vos hac mea reprehensione ad animum despondendum impelli, cùm illud mihi potius proposuerim,vt in spe misericordiæ Domini vos adducerem,quæ omnibus obuia est, qui modo ad ipsum se conuertunt. Et quòd ad illa ipsa mala,quæ vobis digito commonstraui, cùm non possint vobis aliter quàm probro & ignominiæ cedere,illud vnum vos erigat,quod Dei gloria ita etiam illustretur: vt in illius misericordia quæ vos vna sustinet, merito gloriam vestram repositam statuatis,cùm nomen beni-gniffimi patris erga vos ita à vobis non frustra inuocari con-stet. Excitate vos ipsos interea, vt à Domino ipso edocti,ferio tandem resipiscatis. Adhibete meliorem diligentiam tum ad lectionem Scripturæ,tum ad reliqua pietatis exercitia. Pollutiones illas omnes & fœditates semel e medio vestri tollite. Sic nomen Domini reueremini, vt nunquam à vobis nisi ad ipsius honorem proferatur.
