Sic quisque vitam domi instituat,vt nemini vlius impudicitiæ suspicio suboriri possit. Facite etiam vt omnis luxus & insolentia,quæ non decet Christianos,semel reuellatur à vobis. Atque vt odia & rixæ à primis fundamentis eruantur, ipsas causas ferio excutite. Ablegate nempe à vobis infidelitate & nequitiam:neque porrò locum retineat apud vos superbia,vt quisque sibi omnes velit esse obnoxios. Præcipuè verò à Domino petite vt vos respiciat, atque ita admiffiorum malorum memoriam sepeliat, vt vos etiâ syncere reformatos ad se reducat. Hic enim ipsius opus extare oportet singulari aliquo modo: cum alioquin periculum fit ne in exemplum statuamini, vt per vos alij discant quàm intutum fit cum tanto hero quasi per lusum agere. Attendite denique ne ad istam admonitionem obdu refcatis,ne in eorum condemnationem incidatis,qui postquam ipsius gratiam reiecerunt, ignem aduersum semetipsos excitat, qui tandem ipsos absumat. Atqui meliora de vobis spero,atque de vobis aliquid audire exopto, quod præsentem tristitiam abstergat.Faxit Dominus vt quæ in vos contulit dona euanida nō sint:vt vestros lapsus restituat, vt in vobis omnes certissimè ipsius infinitam misericordiam conspicuam,habeant, ac proinde in vobis etiam exaltetur fœlicius quàm antea sanctum nomen eius,Amen. M. D. LXII.
units.tr: Would that, most beloved brothers, the subject I have to write about gave me more cause for joy, so that my letter might bring you more gladness. I ask you, therefore, not to take it badly if for a while I cause you sadness, since sorrow is the only way by which joy in the Lord can truly be restored. I would rather have used this letter to commend your faith, love and endurance, so that I might exhort you to persevere and to make progress for the better. But since your salvation is dear and precious to me, I am compelled to turn to another subject, so that I may seriously warn you about what is reported to me concerning you: that your conduct does not correspond to the knowledge of the Gospel which you received once from the Lord. The necessity that brings me to this should therefore serve as a sufficient excuse before you. For Paul himself, whose spirit was so gentle and whose kindness was so singular, says that the Corinthians were the cause why he was forced to use vehemence and harshness against them. Yet when he dealt with them in that way, he testifies that he did not regret it, provided that the sorrow he caused them by writing led them to lament their evils and so to repent in earnest. So I too reason: if I deal with you in this manner, you will at first judge me harsh; but if you consider the matter as you ought, you will feel your diseases and acknowledge that no gentler remedy could have been applied to heal them. This is my judgement of you, formed from what I have heard from trustworthy men who are well disposed towards you. And not to delay you further, take it as follows. Your way of life is a great stumbling block to good people; and conversely, through that occasion the mouths of the impious are opened against you, so that they blaspheme the name of the Lord and his holy doctrine. These things must be set side by side as they actually stand, so that the evil may be laid bare to you, and you may at last recognise what sort of evil it is, so that there may be room for a remedy. Indeed I know well that those physicians are more welcome who soothe an evil by smearing it with plasters and ointments, so as not to cut into the ulcer, than those who, to cure the sick man properly, lance it in earnest and squeeze out the pus itself. And if it were expedient for your salvation, I would wish for nothing more than to deal with you more softly and kindly in every way. But what am I to do, if I pass over what is too well known and do not apply some limit to such disorders, since the situation by no means allows it now? These, then, are the things that are heard about you, and they are set before you calmly, so that we may seek a remedy for the evils that have held sway among you for far too long. First, it is reported that you have grown much cold in that zeal which once burned in you for hearing the word of God; this is gathered from the fact that there is no eagerness among you to make progress in it. Likewise, that you have given yourselves over to blasphemies, luxury and fornications, and to such things that I shudder to hear of them. Likewise, that everything among you resounds with taunts and false insults, with which you bite one another, as if eagerly and without ceasing; you are zealous only for mutual injury, not for mutual edification. Likewise, hatreds, slanders and envy reign among you, open quarrels and brawls, so that from words you finally come to blows. Behold the plainly natural fruits of contempt for that doctrine which ought to have been a bridle to keep you in true holiness and honest living. And that is the source of the evil: the zeal for hearing the word and for progressing in it, which once flourished, has cooled. This is of ill omen indeed: those who digest God's word best always feel that they can never be fully satisfied by it, whereas the one who shows himself burdened by God's word, as if already sated, betrays his distaste for it, until at last he vomits up whatever he had received before. I am not unaware that you were not, by hearing the word, instructed as thoroughly as would be desirable; yet even the smallest portion of so great a good was more to be desired than if you had received nothing at all. Now we hear that you do not much demand public or private instruction. Even if your understanding of the truth were a hundred times richer, the immensity of Christ's wisdom is such that you would never find there nothing that would be of greatest use to you; so it must be held that even the most advanced teachers keep the place of perpetual disciples in this life. But even if you did not need plain doctrine so much, are the goads of exhortation that accompany it to be judged of little necessity, when all those evils that arise among you at least point them out and set them before you? If there were no other sin among you, that one alone would be considerable: you are advancing not for the better, but for the worse. It is a notable sin, I say, and an ingratitude greater than any entreaty can express, when the ears of the heart are not open while the Lord opens his holy mouth among us. Indeed, since this is not a benefit of one day but a daily gift of his, it was our duty to give him daily attention as well; to this belongs Paul's admonition that the word of God should dwell richly in us. Recognise, therefore, as the greatest evil among you, that you are not led by any desire other than to go on making greater and greater progress, so that you may hold what the will of the Lord is; and that you give up all zeal and diligence to be confirmed in that heavenly thought, whether by reading or by some other means. For just as loss of appetite reveals a bad bodily condition, so it is clear that the soul is far worse off when that relish and taste for the word of God is utterly lost. Moreover, the magnitude of the evil must also be judged from its fruits. I do not say this to apply salt to the wound, but to show you the danger in which you stand, so that you may embrace the remedy all the more readily. For who would believe that the name of God itself, which can never be precious enough among us, is so unworthily profaned among you? Not only is rash swearing practised there, but blasphemies, which fly from mouth to mouth everywhere, are heard. What, then, do you believe about God, that you are not so terrified by his thunderbolt? The Lord will not hold him innocent who takes his name in vain. If he declares that an oath rashly sworn by him is not to be borne, will it be a matter of indifference to him that his holy name is made cheap by you through blasphemies, and that no dreadful vengeance will follow so great a crime? Is the body of Christ our Lord, and his very blood, so little to you that you mention them even by way of insult or mockery? But unless you weigh these things more closely, your evil will show well enough how highly those very things are valued by you, which you trample so foully. Nor has this been overlooked until now. For the reproaches that press upon you are certain scourges, sent by him for this very reason: that you have not shown the regard for his name that it deserved. You hear the Apostle, namely, where he speaks of those who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as they ought; therefore, he says, God gave them up to a reprobate mind, so that they were cast into every filthiness. The Apostle speaks thus of profane men, on whom the light of God had not shone as it has on you. Since, therefore, he has offered you the light of the Gospel, I cannot wonder that he is now so vehemently angry with you, among whom his name is so torn apart. Hence comes that shameful confusion among you, and especially the fornications, so foul that they strike horror even into unbelievers. I do not pass sentence as one who has first examined the case; but the scandal itself is so common that it cries out that it is more than enough evil. If only that admonition of Paul stayed in your memory, that we should abstain even from what has the appearance of evil, you would, I think, guard yourselves far more carefully against evil itself. On the contrary, there are not lacking those who, it is credible, seek only this: to confirm the reputation that circulates about themselves and, at the same time, the bad example. It would be desirable that the rumour which flies about everywhere were quite extinguished. But nothing is achieved unless the deed itself is cleansed of its evil. For the Lord so permits the foulness to be uncovered that those who indulged in vices more willingly in darkness, and flattered themselves, may at last, when they feel themselves exposed, be suffused with shame. Thus he is wont to drive men to repentance. What Scripture contains about promiscuous and common fornications, you are not ignorant of: namely, that God forbids them; that God's vengeance hangs over rebels on account of them; that the kingdom of God does not belong to those who pursue them; that they are held to be like sacrilege, since our bodies, which the Holy Spirit has consecrated as his temples, are polluted by them; that those who give themselves to them are cut off from the body of Christ; and finally, that the fornicator brands upon himself a peculiar stain, not joined with other crimes. Yet the evil among you has not stood in fornication of that sort. For what shame have you left, since you have advanced to that license which even the profane detested, when the sense of nature itself taught everyone that such a crime was intolerable? You have indeed tolerated and approved incest. Therefore, take pains first of all, so far as that matter goes, to open your consciences before God, and so conduct yourselves sincerely in future that no stain from it remains in you in the eyes of others. Paul testified that if he had offended any fornicators or wasteful and disorderly persons among the Corinthians, who had not repented of their evil, this would bring him fresh grief, and their reproach would be transferred upon him. How much more, then, should the authors of the evil themselves have fled to tears and the deepest humiliation! Since, however, you are all members of the same body and bear a part of the evil, that acknowledgement of so dreadful a sin will also affect you and cast you down in earnest, so that in future you strive more zealously than you have hitherto done to edify one another, both by word and by the example of your lives. You are also ill spoken of, for some practise a kind of art of mockery and are all full of barbs to sting whomever they please. Paul, however, commands by name that buffoonery and scurrilous jests be kept far from Christians. Remove this from among you, all the more because such evil and foolish talk brings with it a licence for wrongdoing, since in uttering it every restraint is cast aside. Next come hatreds and envyings, which reveal too clearly that the kingdom of God does not exist among you, since he is the God of concord and peace. Slanders are added, which indicate that there is no room for charity, since charity is said to cover a multitude of sins. Here I cannot sufficiently wonder where you find the leisure for these things, when so many enemies threaten on every side, who seek only this: to harm you in some way. Even the Guelphs make common cause with the Ghibellines when a third enemy emerges. But among you, so few and subject on every side to enemies barking at you, hatreds and quarrels seethe! How absurd it is! Those who are intent on devouring you press in from all around, and you yourselves offer them the opportunity, while you bite one another as if you were deliberately supplying a whetstone for sharpening their points. Now acknowledge that I have spoken so bluntly to you because I was compelled by necessity to rouse you. For unless you have been suffering from a great lethargy until now, you would not have indulged so long and so freely in such gross vices. Although weakness is bound up with all men perpetually, what I have noticed among you is sheer depravity and contempt. Yet I would not wish you to be driven to despair by this rebuke of mine, since I have rather aimed to lead you to hope in the mercy of the Lord, which is open to all who simply turn to him. As for those very evils which I have pointed out to you with my finger, since they can yield nothing but reproach and shame, let this one thing raise you up: that the glory of God is thereby also made manifest, so that in that mercy alone which sustains you, you may rightly hold your glory laid up, since it is clear that the name of the most kind Father is not invoked by you in vain. Meanwhile rouse yourselves, that, taught by the Lord himself, you may at last repent in earnest. Apply better diligence both to the reading of Scripture and to the other exercises of piety. Remove all those pollutions and foulnesses from among you once for all. Revere the name of the Lord, so that it is never uttered by you except to his honour. Let each man order his household so that no suspicion of unchastity can arise against anyone. See also that all luxury and insolence, which does not befit Christians, is plucked out from you. And so that hatreds and quarrels may be uprooted from their first foundations, examine their causes earnestly. Drive out from among you unbelief and wickedness; and let not pride keep its place among you, so that each wishes all others to be subject to him. Above all, ask the Lord to look upon you, and so bury the memory of the sins committed that he may restore you to himself, once you have been sincerely reformed. For his work ought to be evident among you in some singular way; otherwise there is a danger that you will be set up as an example, so that through you others may learn how unsafe it is to trifle with so great a Master. Finally, take heed lest you harden yourselves against this admonition and fall into the condemnation of those who, after rejecting his grace, kindle against themselves a fire that at last consumes them. Yet I hope better things of you, and I long to hear something of you that may wipe away the present sorrow. May the Lord grant that the gifts he has bestowed upon you are not vain; that he restore your lapses; that in you all may behold his infinite mercy made plain; and that thus his holy name may be exalted among you more happily than before. Amen. 1562.

units.la: VIRETVS CALVINO S. D.
units.tr: Viret to Calvin, greetings.

units.la: DVo sunt quæ me hîc adhuc detinent.Primùm medici quibuscum mihi res est: deinde motus variis in locis excitati ab hostibus, & cædes crudelissimæ ab iisdem perpetratæ. Audiuisti de motibus & seditionibus Prouincialium.Paucis ante diebus Narbonenses ficti duelli prætextu inter duos Hispanos, ciues & incolas penè omnes ad fictum illud spectaculum vrbe ex traxerunt. Postquam egressi sunt, fraus prodita est & patefacta proditio.Quum enim nuntiatum esset in alium diem reiectum duellum,ac omnes qui egressi fuerant, in vrbem regredérentur, iis solis patuerunt portæ qui Papisticam tuentur & sequuntur religionem,alij sunt exclusi.Sub idem pene tempus,cùm Ecclesia Carcassonensis Regio parens edicto, vrbe egressa esset ad sacrum conuentum, clausæ sunt vrbis portæ, ne in vrbem reuerteretur. Fratres cùm se viderent exclusos, vrbis portas obsederunt,ne quis vrbe egrederetur,aut in eam ingrederetur. Interea tormento bellico ex vrbe tres ex nostris occisos fuisse audiuimus.Sed longè grauius est & atrocius,quod eodem pene tempore accidit in vrbe,cui nomen est Castelnau, quæ non ita procul à Tholosa abest.Nã pari sœuitia & crudelitate in nostros hostes grassati sunt,qua iam ante menses aliquot Cadurci.Nam quum nostri ad sacrum coetum conuenissent,incensa prius domo hostes in eos irruerunt tanta crudelitate, vt magnus fuerit occisorum numerus. In his primus cæsus est minister,qui suum caput hostibus pro cæteris omnibus obtulit.Sed ne hac quidem ratione compesci potuit hostium rabies: deinde diaconus pari fato sublatus, & vnus Regius procurator vir Opt.& Consiliarij aliquot, præter vulgus promiscuè.Interea Tholosani hucadueniunt,cùm multorum literis,Tholosam si possunt me deducturi,quanuis disertis verbis admonuissent ne pedem mouerent,an equâ à me intellexissent
units.tr: Two things still keep me here: first, the physicians I am dealing with; second, the disturbances stirred up by our enemies in various places, and the most savage slaughters they have carried out. You have heard about the riots and seditions in the province. A few days ago the people of Narbonne drew almost all the citizens and inhabitants out of the city, under the pretext of a mock duel between two Spaniards, to watch that sham spectacle. When they had gone out, the trick was discovered and the treachery exposed. For when it was announced that the duel had been put off to another day and that everyone who had gone out was returning to the city, the gates were opened only to those who uphold and follow the Papist religion; the rest were shut out. About the same time, when the church of Carcassonne had left the city for a sacred assembly, in obedience to the royal edict, the city gates were closed so that they could not return. Seeing themselves shut out, the brethren besieged the city gates, so that no one could leave or enter the city. Meanwhile we heard that three of our people had been killed from the city by artillery. But what is far more grievous and atrocious is what happened at about the same time in a town called Castelnau, not far from Toulouse. For there they raged against our people with the same savagery and cruelty that had been shown some months earlier at Cahors. When our people had gathered for the sacred assembly, the enemy first set fire to a house and then rushed upon them with such cruelty that the number of those killed was large. Among them the first to be slain was the minister, who offered his own head to the enemy in place of all the others. But even in this way the rage of the enemy could not be checked: then a deacon was struck down by the same fate, and a royal procurator, a worthy man, and several councillors, along with the common people, indiscriminately. Meanwhile the men of Toulouse have come here with letters from many people, intending to take me to Toulouse if they can, although they had warned me in plain words not to move. I wonder whether they understood from me what would be allowed me, given the time, my health, and the church of Geneva, to which alone I am bound.

units.la: Epist.337. quid mihi pet tempus,per valetudinem,& per Ecclesiam cui vni obstructus sum,Geneuensem,liceret. Montpesullani vero etsi spe fructus quem ex meo Tholosam aduentu sperant,eo adducuntur, vt hanc a me suscipi professionem optent: non sunt tamen in ea sententia, vt eo iter arripiam his turbulentis temporibus, donec tota regio paulo sit pacatior. Vt res modo habent, nescio plane vtra ex parte tutius sit iter aggredi. Sed spero fore vt breui D. viam tutiorem aperiat, aut vt ad vos reuertar ad tempus mihi prescriptum, aut vt longius progrediar si coegerit necessitas. Interea Ecclesiae augentur, quae pergunt magis atque magis ministros postulare. Hic tabellarius, quum neque hic neque Nemaui, neque alibi ministrum inuenire potuerit, cogitur ad vos se recipere. Valde cupio qua sis nunc valetudine cognoscere, quam vt diligenter cures, iterum atque iterum precor, vt qui magis omnibus sis Ecclesiis necessarius, quàm hactenus vnquam. Salutem multam dico collegis & amicis omnibus. Vale opt. ac diutiflì. E Montepelio, xxiii. Martij. M. D. LXI.
units.tr: Although the people of Montpellier are led, by hope of the benefit they expect from my coming to Toulouse, to wish that I would accept this professorship, they are not of the opinion that I should set out on the journey in these turbulent times, until the whole region has become somewhat more peaceful. As things now stand, I cannot clearly tell which way it is safer to undertake the journey. But I hope that God will soon open a safer way, either so that I may return to you at the time set for me, or so that I may go further if necessity compels. Meanwhile the churches are growing, and they keep demanding more and more ministers. This messenger, since he could find no minister here, nor at Nîmes, nor anywhere else, is forced to return to you. I very much wish to know how you are now in health, and I urge you again and again to take care of yourself, since you are more necessary to all the churches than ever before. I send many greetings to all my colleagues and friends. Farewell, most excellent and long-lived friend. From Montpellier, 23 March 1561.

units.la: Tuus Petrus Viretus.
units.tr: Your Peter Viret.

units.la: BLAVRERVS CALVINO.
units.tr: Blaurer to Calvin.

units.la: GAllicarum Ecclesiarum fidem inter tot potentium aduersariorum praesturas, & immensos conatus eminere, tum & in dies magis atque magis assurgere, magna animorum gratulatione audiunt, quotquot sunt in nostra Germania, qui Christi regnum apud omnes gentes propagatum cupiunt. Guisianorum cum nostris aliquot Principibus collusio vereor, ne monstrum alat, quod Galliae regno magnum malum daturum sit. Quandoquidem illorum simulatum Religionis studium, quo Augustanam confessionem probare sibi videri volunt, horum simplicitatem, qui alioqui plus satis infensi sunt nunc quidem Sacramentariis quos vocant, facile circumueniet. Quanquam solatur interim, quod Dominus est, qui sapientes mundi huius in sua ipsorum astutia comprehendit, quem serio perpetuoque precemur, vt Spiritu sui consilij suorum omnium actiones ad Christi aedificationem feliciter dirigat, & magnum suum nomen in ea vsque sanctificet.
units.tr: The churches of France, standing out amid so many schemes of powerful adversaries and their immense efforts, and rising higher day by day, are heard of with great joy by all who are in our Germany and who desire the kingdom of Christ to be spread among all nations. I fear the collusion of the Guise faction with some of our princes, which may nurse a monster that will bring great harm to the kingdom of France. For their feigned zeal for religion, by which they wish to seem to approve the Augsburg Confession, will easily deceive the simplicity of those who are otherwise all too hostile now to the so-called Sacramentarians. Yet this is some comfort, that the Lord is the one who catches the wise of this world in their own cunning. We earnestly and constantly pray that by the Spirit of his counsel he will happily direct all the actions of his people to the building up of Christ, and sanctify his great name among them always.

units.la: De aliis Germaniae nostrae rebus, Linerus hic noster omnia tibi coràm melius exposuerit. Dubia profecto sunt omnia, nisi quod grauissimi motus, & hostiles vastitates omnino nobis imminere videntur. Quandoquidem nullam hactenus legationem sacrarum precationum, fidelium lachrymarum & omnino scriptis respisicentiae ad illum mittimus paulo adhuc longius agentem,qui tot millibus contra nos venit, ea quæ pacis sunt,petentes,quum iamdudum missis Prophetis suis velut certif.fidei fecialibus,bellum nobis extrema commeritis indixerit:quos ipsos etiam, & contemptim sæpe risimus, & non raro quoque sumus persequuti, magis atque magis iram nobisipsis in die iræ colligentes.
units.tr: Concerning the other affairs of our Germany, our Linerus here will set everything out for you better in person. Everything is indeed uncertain, except that the gravest disturbances and hostile devastations seem altogether to hang over us. Since we have so far sent no embassy of sacred prayers, faithful tears, and in writing, repentance, to him who, though he is going a little further off, came against us with so many thousands, we have been asking for the things of peace, while he, long ago, sending his prophets as heralds of certain faith, has declared war upon us, who deserve the utmost punishment. These same prophets we have often laughed at with contempt, and not rarely also persecuted, thus gathering for ourselves more and more wrath on the day of wrath.

units.la: Bezæ nostri duram prouinciam & ter miseram fortem vehementer etiam atque etiam dolemus, quum optimi & doctissimi viri non æstimandos labores,sudores, vigilias,tædia, perturbationes,& præsentissima pericula paulo diligentius nobiscum re putamus : verum vbi ad illum cui vni militat, animos attollimus,tum vero térque,quatérque fœlicem iudicamus,quòd cum sancto Apostolo electum Domini organum destinatus, Christi nomen coram gentibus & regibus portat; cui etiam post decertatum bonum certamen & consummatum cursum , seruatámque fidem, iustitiæ corona ab eo qui iustus est iudex in illo die haud dubiè reddetur.Faxit autem Christus,vt & ipsi Bezam nostrum superatis aliquando omnibus istis difficultatibus,& fœliciter confectis in Gallia negotiis,reducem videre & saluum nobis redditum gratulari possimus.
units.tr: We grieve greatly, again and again, over the hard task and thrice-wretched lot of our Beza, when we consider, with some care, the labours, sweat, watches, weariness, troubles, and most pressing dangers, which the best and most learned men must not undervalue. But when we lift our minds to him whom alone he serves, then indeed we judge him thrice and four times happy: appointed as the chosen instrument of the Lord, he bears the name of Christ before nations and kings, as the holy Apostle did. For him, too, after he has fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith, the crown of righteousness will undoubtedly be rendered on that day by the righteous Judge. May Christ grant that, once all these difficulties are overcome and the affairs in France have been happily completed, we may one day see our Beza return and rejoice in his safe homecoming.

units.la: Tu mi colendissime Caluine , vbi ad eum scribis mea etiam vice quàm potes amanter, officiosè, reuerenterque ipsum salu-ta , cuius nunquam non mentionem in precibus nostris apud Dominum facimus,vt sermo Christi currat & glorificetur: quód-que ipsius ministerio plantatur & rigatur , cœleste ac copiosissimum accipiat incrementum , vtque eripiatur ab absurdis & peruersis hominibus, vt quod facit,in tanta fidelium & prudentium Ministrorum Christi penuria,quàm diutissimè faciat. Bene vale amice mihi obseruandissime in Domino, & charissime frater. Christus Iesus te nobis à febribus istis medica sua & fœlicissima manu curatum ac plane sanum & incolumem restituat, ac præsentissimo suo numine semper tibi in sua vinea strenuè laboranti adsit,æternúmque te seruet. Saluëant quotquot istic sunt fidelis in Domino amantes,Symmystæ imprimis cum Cof. Roseto. Commendo me piis ac fidelibus vestris apud Dominum patrociniis. Iterum vale. Vituduri,iii.Aprilis,quo die in hanc mundi lucem anno 1492. editus sum , iam septuaginta annos natus, quod reliquum est vitæ mihi hic transmittendæ, verè vitalis vitæ auctor Christus sic moderetur & dirigat, vt ad hanc me propediem propitius recipiat. Anno M. D. LXII.
units.tr: You, my most honoured Calvin, when you write to him, greet him for me as lovingly, dutifully, and reverently as you can. We never fail to mention him in our prayers before the Lord, that the word of Christ may run and be glorified, and that, being planted and watered through his ministry, it may receive heavenly and most abundant increase, and be rescued from absurd and perverse men; and that he may continue to do so for as long as possible, in such a scarcity of faithful and prudent ministers of Christ. Farewell, my dear friend and brother, whom I greatly esteem in the Lord. May Christ Jesus restore you to us, cured of these fevers by his healing and most fortunate hand, and entirely sound and well. May he always be present to you with his most immediate divine power, as you labour vigorously in his vineyard, and keep you for ever. Greetings to all who are there, faithful lovers in the Lord, especially the fellow Symmystae and Cof. Roset. I commend myself to your pious and faithful protection before the Lord. Farewell again. Vituduri, 3 April, the day on which I was born into this light of the world, in 1492, now seventy years old. As for the rest of the life that I am to spend here, may Christ, the true author of living life, so guide and direct it that he may soon graciously receive me to himself. 1562.

units.la: N.j.
units.tr: N.j.

units.la: Io. Calvinus N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin sends greetings in the Lord.

units.la: NVdiustertiustibi scripsi, venerande frater, per Italiam mihi familiarem & vicinum. Heri tuas accepi cum Sarnicij sasciculo, vbi literas Thretio scriptas inueni, quas remitto. Tamētsi autem multa Sarnicius putabat me ex illis cognoturū, nolui tamen resignare: ac præstabit vt intactas recipiat. Simul autem recuperaui responsum illud, quod mihi perierat, in quo nō parum placuit Thretii sedulitas. Nescio an expediat noxam lucubrationem aggredi contra discipulos Blandratæ, donec audierimus quomodo excepta fuerit admonitio iam olim edita cū sua explicatione. Breuitas enim ad quam me testrinxi, obscura esse non videtur. Nec vero nebulones illi quidquam obiectant, quod non ante fuerit à me refutatum. Forte vnum desiderari potest, vt patrocinium quod sibi asciscunt ex veteribus scriptoribus excu tiā. Etsi autem certa hac quoq; in parte est, labor tamen erit plenus tædij & molestiæ. Ac Diabolus per has salebras se iactare, & in his latebris se volutare ipsos docuit, vt sine magno fructu per longos certaminum circuitus nos traherent. Scis quàm durus sit & asper sermo Tertulliani. Certè stridet magis, quàm loquitur. Atqui longum inde volumen contexere necesse foret. In Hilario non tam difficilis ratio, cuius tamen sermo valde spinosus est ac perplexus. Siquid adhuc scribendum censeas, consilium tu um hac in parte expecto. De rebus Galliæ nihil assertur: vnde colligimus omnia sic esse turbata, vt inter spem & metum tam nostri, quàm hostes pendeant. Extra Aulam animos colligunt fratres, nec hostium superbiæ succumbunt, vel insultationibus fraguntur. Vale clarissime vir, & mihi honorande frater vnà cum Symmystis omnibus, quos plurimum saluto. Idem faciunt Collegæ mei & amici. Dominus te incolumem nobis seruet, laborēsque tuos semper benedicat. Geneuæ, v i. Iunij. M. D. LXIII.
units.tr: I wrote to you only the day before yesterday, venerable brother, by way of a man who is a friend of mine and lives nearby in Italy. Yesterday I received your letter with the bundle from Sarnicius, where I found the letter written to Thretius, which I am returning. Although Sarnicius thought I would learn many things from it, I did not want to open it, and he will see that it reaches him intact. At the same time I recovered that reply which had gone missing for me, and I was not a little pleased by Thretius's diligence. I am not sure it is advisable to undertake a harmful treatise against the disciples of Blandrata until we have heard how the admonition already published long ago, with its explanation, has been received. For the brevity to which I confined myself does not seem to be obscure. Nor do those scoundrels raise any objection that has not already been refuted by me. Perhaps one thing might be wanted: that I examine the support they claim for themselves from the early writers. Even on this point the matter is certain, but the labour will be full of weariness and trouble. The devil has taught them to hurl themselves through these rough places and to wallow in these hiding places, so that they could drag us through long circuits of dispute without any great profit. You know how harsh and rough Tertullian's style is; it certainly grates more than it speaks. Yet to weave a long volume out of it would be necessary. In Hilary the method is not so difficult, though his style is very thorny and intricate. If you think anything more should be written, I await your advice on this point. Nothing is reported about affairs in France, from which we gather that everything is so disturbed that our people and their enemies alike hang between hope and fear. The brothers are gathering their spirits outside the Court, and they do not give way to the arrogance of their enemies or break down under their taunts. Farewell, most distinguished man and honoured brother, together with all the fellow-ministers, whom I greet most warmly. My colleagues and friends do the same. May the Lord keep you safe for us and always bless your labours. Geneva, 6 June 1563.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS D. CVRSOLIO.
units.tr: CALVIN to CURSOLIUS.

units.la: QVod certo homini mandasti, vt quid conscientiam tuam vrgeret, mihi aperiret, meúmque ad eam rem consilium exquireret, bona fide ab illo præstitum esse scio. Antequam autem respondeam, est quod Deo gratias agam cùm ita te affectum video, vt conscientiæ habenas laxiores non permittas multorum exemplo: qui nimirum vtcunque sese apud homines excusent, tādem tamen sese coram Deo damnare coguntur.
units.tr: That you entrusted to a certain man the task of disclosing to me what was troubling your conscience, and of seeking my counsel on the matter, I know he carried out in good faith. Before I answer, however, I must give thanks to God that I see you so disposed that you do not allow the reins of conscience to be loosened, as many have done. Such men, however much they excuse themselves before people, are at last compelled to condemn themselves before God.

units.la: Iaia Iam vt ad rem veniam, non eorum te loco habeo, qui medios sc profitentur: sed te à me simplicit[?] r quærere mihi persuadeo, an cum Christiană Religionem pr[?] f[?]sus sis, fas ne sit tibi prosequi. N.ad supplicationes & cætera id genus idololatriæ exempla. Hic autem ista tibi expendenda sunt. Primum ne exemplo illo tristi tiam piis aut scandalum, aut infirmis vel ignorantibus adhuc fa stidium aliquod afferas. Alterum est, ne des occasionem impiis Dei & veritatis hostibus se efferendi: adeóque os impurum a- periendi, quò veram Religionem traducant. Sunt enim illa duo tanti momenti, vt non fatis à nobis attendi possint, vt diserte ita nobis inculcantur. Cum igitur Dei Spiritus vetet nominatim ne fratribus tristitiæ ausam afferamus, seriò illud tibi in mentem veniat, oportet: si contingat pios aliquo apud se ingemiscere, cum te in media illa turma conspicuum viderint, quę ad Deum contumelia afficiendum prodeat. Scandalum vero quale futurum sit, quàmq; late emanaturum satisetiam vides. Plerique enim e- xemplo tuo ducentur, adeoque hypocritæ illi quos suæ væcor- diæ h[?]ctenus pudui, sub v[?]nbra tua secure latebūt. Altera ex par te cothurnos indues aduersariis, non modò vt despiciant Euan- gelium, sed vt indurentur in sua immanitate aduersus illos, qui de pietatis ingenua professione nihil remiserant. Quò magis de nique singula expendes, grauissimè in Deum ate peccatū iri iu- dicabis. Superest vnum Naamani exemplū, Sed santa est diuersi- tas inter illius & cuam personam, vt ad vsum tuum referri illud factum nō possit. Vnus erat ille in tota Syria qui Deum coleret, vnde nemini ab eo potuit afferri scandalum. Nemo ex iis cōtri- stari potuit, quasi facto suo verā Religionem probro exponeret. Nemo potuit à recta via abduci, aut ne illam ingrederetur impe diri. Quin potius ille exemplo suo insultabat genti suæ, cùm altare sibi haberet, in quo Deum Israelis adorare. In summa nō est vr- gendū quod illic speciale notari potest, sed potiùs quod ad ædi- ficationem pertinet sequendum. Nunc dispiciendum an illi mi- litiæ renuntiare debeas potius, quàm vt N. minus ea in re obtem peres. Atque hic tenenda est Pauli regula, nō esse facienda mala, vt eueniant bona: satis video quantum commodi ad Ecclesiam rediturū sit, si eum locū retineas: quātum verò damni si deseras. Sed in isiufmodi angustiis illud dandum est Deo, vt in eum re- cumbamus, qui vnus idoneè omnibus prospeċturus sit. Neq; in- terea tibi decrit excusatio honesta, q̃ cum N. non ignoret, quam Religionem profiteaŕis, illam te ab omnibus illis rebus auocare, non posse integra conscientia illic stare, vbi in Deum peccatu- rum te noueris. Imò etiā constātiam illam tuā magis ei accepta fore cōsido, quā si quicquā de officio remitteres. Etsi absentiam tuam tulit satis diuturnā, non erit illi graue si triduum in anno, vti per valetudinem te subduxeris. Atque hoc quidé per iocum. Morbum enim te obtendere nihil aliud esset, quàm quod puderet te Euangelij. Vbi ergo ista apud te expenderis, non dubito quin cum Paulo colligas, non posse te fieri participe Coenæ Christi, atque interea inter idololatras conspici, maxime vbi res habet coniunctum scandalum. Peto igitur à te vt tibi instes atque Deum enixè ores, qui tibi vires suppeditet, & arma illa tibi induat, quibus te ad Domini militiam tanto animosiùs accingas. Dominus tibi atque coniugi adsit magis ac magis, vt semper omnia in melius succedant. x x x i. Iulij. M. D. L x i i i.
units.tr: Now to come to the matter. I do not count you among those who profess to be neutral; rather, I am persuaded that you are asking me plainly whether, since you have openly professed the Christian religion, it is lawful for you to continue in the processions and other examples of that kind of idolatry. Here these things must be weighed by you. First, take care that by that sad example you do not bring either offence to the godly or some loathing to the weak and the ignorant who are still unskilled. The second is that you do not give the impious and the enemies of God and the truth an occasion to exalt themselves, and so to open their foul mouths to slander the true religion. For these two considerations are of such weight that they cannot be sufficiently attended to, as they are impressed upon us so clearly. Since, then, the Spirit of God forbids us by name to cause sorrow to the brothers, it ought to come seriously to your mind: if the godly should see you conspicuous in the midst of that crowd which goes forth to do insult to God, they will groan inwardly. How great the scandal would be, and how widely it would spread, you yourself see well enough. For most people will be led by your example, and those hypocrites whom the shame of their own cowardice has hitherto restrained will hide securely under your shadow. On the other hand, you would put buskins on your adversaries, so that they not only despise the Gospel but are hardened in their savagery against those who had relaxed nothing of the open profession of piety. The more finally you weigh each point, the more you will judge that a very grave sin against God would be committed. There remains one example, that of Naaman; but the difference between that man's position and yours is so great that the deed cannot be referred to your practice. He alone in all Syria worshipped God, so no offence could be given by him to anyone. None of them could be saddened, as though by his act he were exposing the true religion to reproach. None could be drawn away from the right way, or hindered from entering it. Indeed, by his example he was rather taunting his own nation, since he had an altar on which he could worship the God of Israel. In sum, what can be noted there as special is not to be urged, but rather what pertains to edification is to be followed. Now we must consider whether you ought rather to renounce that service, than not to comply with N. less in this matter. And here the rule of Paul must be kept: evil is not to be done that good may come of it. I see well enough how much advantage would return to the Church if you kept that place, and how much harm if you abandoned it. But in such straits the matter must be left to God, so that we may rest upon him alone, who can provide for all things properly. Meanwhile an honest excuse will not be lacking to you, since N. is not unaware what religion you profess; he will know that you cannot, with a clear conscience, stand where you know you would sin against God by taking part in those things. Indeed I trust that your constancy will be more acceptable to him than if you yielded anything of your duty. Although he has borne your absence for quite a long time, it will not be a burden to him if you withdraw for three days in the year, under the pretext of ill health. Yet this I say in jest; for to pretend sickness would be nothing other than to be ashamed of the Gospel. When therefore you have weighed these things in yourself, I do not doubt that with Paul you will conclude that you cannot become a partaker of the Lord's Supper, and yet be seen meanwhile among the idolaters, especially where the matter carries a scandal along with it. I ask you therefore to press on with yourself and to pray to God earnestly, that he may supply you with strength and clothe you with those arms by which you may gird yourself the more boldly for the warfare of the Lord. May the Lord be with you and your wife more and more, so that all things may always turn out for the better. 31 July 1563.

units.la: Tibi addictissimus Ioannes Calvinus.
units.tr: Most devotedly yours, John Calvin.

units.la: IOANNES CALVINVS DELPHINATIBVS FRATRIBVS. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to the brethren of the Dauphiné. Greetings.

units.la: HActenus ad vos non scripsi, dilectissimi fratres, quod expectare vt res inter vos paulo melius se haberent: quádo aliter fieri non poterat, quàm vt bellorum exitus plurima satis perturbata, & inordinata relinquat. Nec tamen eam omnium restitutionem sperabam, in qua nihil desideraretur: cùm nihil tu meis literis opus fuisset. Sed quoniam in mediis illis feruoribus, non ita me à vobis commodè auditum iri iudicabam, meliorem oc casionem quæ nunc videtur offerri, mihi opperiedam duxi. Habeo igitur duo summa capita, quæ vobis proponam. Vnum est ne valde illorum exemplo sinatis vos duci, qui sibi persuadent sese quàm optimè de Deo meritos esse, quòd pro Ecclesiæ iure ad uersus tyrannicam audaciam secundum Edicta principalia asse-rendo, arma tulerint, pericula adierint, facultatum detrimentū sustinuerint. Imò eovsque insolescunt nonnulli, vt sibi deberi ia ctitent, quòd in Euangelij possessionem alij missi sint. Atqui si ita Domino visum est, vt tam honorato vsui vos impenderet, non est quòd eo nomine vobis placeatis, aut remittatis manus, quasi opere ad finem vsque perducto: sed potius vt inde sumatis animum pergendi in melius, quod reliquum est longioris viæ. Cùm si postquam tam bene coepistis, cessare contingeret, effetis tanto minus excusabiles. Alterum sequitur, quòd cùm belli occasio eâ licentiam inuehere soleat, vt optimi etiam tum sibi excidant, vi dendum esse ne profusiones illæ & insolentiæ quibus multi addicti fuerunt, à vobis deinceps retineantur. Cùm potius malum ipsum quod ita iam inhæsit, stimulare vos debeat, ad remedium tanto studiosius requirendum. Eorum verò quæ tam inordinatè gesta sunt, omnis apud vos sepelienda est memoria, nisi vt illis ingemiscendo à Deo veniam precemini, atque ab eiusmodi rebus scrib pedem referatis. Cum vero facultas a Deo item oblata sit, ut cum aliqua pace conueniatis in nomine ipsius, ad ipsius verbum audiendum, ad promouendâ vestram fidem, ad vos in ipsis timore confirmandos per illa media quae in Ecclesia ipse in statuit, sic ad tanti beneficij vsum legitime praestandu incumbite, ut aliquatenus etiam quae secus ante acciderunt, compensare studeatis. Optandum erat sane, ut omnes sese iisdem animis ad Filium Dei agnoscendum adiungi paterentur: sed cum sit illud decretum Patris, ut extet inter medios hostes Filii Regnum, sustinete patienter quod non sine moerore a vobis audiri potest. Interea vero ne puderet adhaerere Domino cum perpetua demissione, & humilitate, dum impii quasi victores passim exultant. Ac si illud vos angit, quod ipsa coelestis veritas, quam omni rerum praesentium comparatione superiorem nobis esse oportet, ita despecta iaceat inter illos, vos ipsi operam date, ut errantes reducantur in viam. Ut eo peruenianis, vestro imprimis exemplo illos afficite, ut quod ad vos non accedunt, pudorem ipsis afferat. Nominatim ut rectus ille ordo, qui soliditatis vestrae in Christum fidei fructus sit, extet apud vos, cuius testimonio agno scere cogantur, Deum inter vos praesidere. Scitis hoc ipsos in ore habere, quod nihil aliud quam vagantem & effrenem licentiam inuehere quaeramus. Ergo ipsis re ipsa commonstrandu est, nos non alio animo excusasse Antichristi iugum, quam ut Christi iugum admitteremus. Atqui res longe aliter se habet. Qui enim in tolerabiles illius conscientiarum fidiculas in Papatu sustinuerunt, quique horribilem illam animarum carnificinam tolerarunt tandiu, nunc Euangelium obtendunt ut anormes & exleges viuat. Sic istis accedit quod de falsis Apostolis ad Corinthios quercabantur Apostolus. Nempe, inquit omnia illorum placide admittitis, & tantumnon deosculamini, cum interrera ad paternam obiurgationem seruorum Dei ita refractarii sitis. Plerique autem hoc magis probarent, ut se quisque pro arbitrio gererent, quibus satis esse videretur, quod verbum Dei publice doceretur. Quod si vero perperam instituta sit a Domino in ipsius Ecclesia disciplina, quae omnes in officio contineat. Atque ut similiari exemplo hoc constet, quarnam esset vita nostra & vigor, si anima ita corpori inesset, ut vel deesset nervi interea, vel officium non facerent? Sic omnino anima Ecclesiae verbi auditione constat, ita ut etiam neruorum locum obtineat ordo & politia constituta appositae, ad bonum corporis illius habitum conseruandum. Atque eo spectat illud Apostoli, quod Deus noster non sit auctor seditionis sed pacis. Illud praeterea vel vnum abunde esse oportuerat, ut nihil aliud obstaret nobis ne dissueremus ad malum, vnum inquam Ecclesiae Reformatae nomen quod gerimus.
units.tr: Until now I have not written to you, most beloved brethren, because I hoped that matters among you would settle somewhat better. Since that cannot be done otherwise, the outcome of wars leaves many things rather disturbed and disordered. Yet I did not expect a full restoration in which nothing was lacking, and you did not need my letter in any case. But since, in the midst of those heated passions, I judged that I would not be heard by you in a fitting way, I thought I should wait for a better opportunity, which now seems to be offered. I have therefore two main points to set before you. The first is that you must not allow yourselves to be led by the example of those who persuade themselves that they have deserved very well of God because they took up arms, faced dangers and suffered loss of property in defending the rights of the Church against tyrannical audacity, in accordance with the principal edicts. Indeed some grow so arrogant that they claim to be owed something because others were sent into possession of the Gospel. But if it has pleased the Lord to employ you in so honourable a service, there is no reason for you to be pleased with yourselves on that account, or to relax your hands as if the work had been brought to completion. Rather you should take from it courage to press on towards better things, for the rest of the road is long. For if, after having begun so well, you were to cease, you would be so much the less excusable. The second point follows: since the occasion of war is accustomed to bring in such licence that even the best men lose their footing, you must take care that those excesses and insolences to which many have been given over are not kept up among you in future. Rather, the evil which has already taken such hold should spur you on to seek a remedy all the more eagerly. As for those things which have been done so disorderly, all memory of them must be buried among you, unless you groan over them, ask God for pardon, and withdraw your feet from such deeds. Now that God has also offered you the opportunity to come together in some peace, in His name, to hear His Word, to promote your faith, and to strengthen one another in the fear of Him through those means which He has established in the Church, apply yourselves lawfully to the proper use of so great a benefit, and strive to make up in some measure for what went wrong before. It was certainly to be wished that all would allow themselves to be joined in the same spirit to acknowledge the Son of God; but since it is the Father's decree that the kingdom of the Son should stand in the midst of enemies, bear patiently what cannot be heard by you without grief. Meanwhile, do not be ashamed to cling to the Lord with constant lowliness and humility, while the impious everywhere exult as if they were victors. And if this troubles you, that the heavenly truth itself, which ought to be above all present circumstances for us, lies so despised among them, then you yourselves should labour that those who err may be brought back into the way. In order to attain this, move them above all by your own example, so that the fact that they do not come over to you may bring them shame. Especially let that orderly arrangement, which is the fruit of the steadfastness of your faith in Christ, stand among you, so that by its testimony they may be compelled to acknowledge that God presides among you. You know that they have this on their lips: that we are seeking nothing other than to introduce a wandering and unbridled licence. Therefore it must be shown to them by the fact itself that we did not cast off the yoke of Antichrist with any other intention than to take up the yoke of Christ. Yet the matter stands very differently. For those who endured in Popery the tolerable snares of conscience, and who bore for so long that dreadful butchery of souls, now put forward the Gospel so that they may live lawless and without law. So what the Apostle complained of concerning the false apostles among the Corinthians applies to them: namely, that you calmly tolerate all their doings, and almost kiss them, while towards the fatherly rebuke of the servants of God you are so stubborn. Most of them, however, would approve this more, that each should conduct himself at will, for it would seem enough to them that the Word of God is taught publicly. But if discipline in the Church of the Lord, which keeps all in their duty, has been established amiss... And that this may be made plain by a similar example: what would our life and vigour be if the soul were in the body in such a way that the sinews were either lacking meanwhile or did not perform their function? Thus the Church truly subsists by the hearing of the Word, and order and a fitting polity likewise take the place of the sinews, to preserve the good condition of that body. To this end belongs the Apostle's saying that our God is not the author of sedition but of peace. Moreover, that one thing ought surely to have been enough, so that nothing else would hinder us from being accustomed to what is good: I mean the one name which we bear, the Reformed Church.

units.la: 1 Cor. 14, 33 Quòd si quis hìc timendum putat, ne sub regiminis spiritualis titulo, species aliqua dominationis inuehatur, aut ne ministri sibi plus quàm licet tribuant, & sua potestate abutantur, vestrum est ei rei prospicere, atque eam moderationem adhibere in iis quæ apud vos his de rebus statuenda sunt, vt neque constringatur quisquam in sua vocatione, neque etiam fines legitimi transiliantur. Adeóque vt illi ipsi, qui regendis aliis præerunt, arctioribus etiam disciplinæ vinculis, quàm alij ex medio coetu contineantur. Summum igitur hoc est, quod à vobis per Dominum vnicè contendo, quantùm & vos Patris cœlestis præsidio fouendos, & ouium natiuam docilitatem illi exhibendam à vobis exoptatis, vt mansueto animo admittatis quicquid ipse præscribit, tum in vestram salutem, tum præsertim vt obstruatur os impiis, ne per illos vestra vlla occasione nomen ipsius blasphemetur. Dominus & Pater misericordiarum complectatur vosfuo præsidio, Spiritu regat, atque omnibus suis bonis locupletet. Geneuæ, xxxi. Iulij. M. D. LXIII.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 14, 33 But if anyone thinks that here we must fear lest under the title of spiritual government some appearance of domination be introduced, or lest the ministers attribute to themselves more than is allowed and abuse their power, it is your business to provide against this and to apply such moderation in those matters which must be decided among you on these questions, that no one is constrained beyond his calling, nor are the lawful limits overstepped; and indeed that those who are set over others to rule them are held by even stricter bonds of discipline than the rest of the assembly. This, then, is the chief thing I earnestly press upon you through the Lord: that you desire to be cherished by the protection of the heavenly Father, and that you show to Him the native docility of sheep, so that you admit with a gentle spirit whatever He prescribes, both for your salvation and especially so that the mouths of the impious may be stopped, lest through them your name, in any occasion, be blasphemed of Him. May the Lord and Father of mercies embrace you with His protection, rule you by His Spirit, and enrich you with all His good gifts. Geneva, 31 July 1563.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS D. CHRISTOPHORO THRETIO. S.
units.tr: John Calvin to Christopher Thretius, greeting.

units.la: SI mea admonitio profuit tuis popularibus, eximie vir, & mihi colende frater, Deo gratias ago, qui tàtillum laboris, quod illic insumpsi, passus non est fructu carere. Nec verò nunc me pigeret, plus operæ ponere in tractando illo argumento, si otium suppeteret. Sed ex quo hinc abiisti, continuum mihi negotium fuit cum variis morbis, vt ne ordinario quidem muneri obeundo sufficiam. Quòd si maior daretur relaxatio: sunt tamè alia nunc in manibus quæ mihi non permittunt, in refutandis illis duobus errorum monstris operam impendere. Commentarios meos in Moysem Gallica lingua vertendos suscepi, non tantùm vt noftratibus communis esset huius libri lectio, sed quòd opus al oqui non pœnitendum, innumeris quibus scatebat mendis, repurgare necesse fuit. Fratres me hortati fuerant, vt librum Iosuæ explicarem: hactenus vix ad tertium vsque capur progredi licuit, quum tamen breuitati maximè studeam. Vrgeor etiam aliunde, vt tibi nihil polliceri audeam. Si quando tamen melior dabitur opportunitas, eam non omittam. Sed tanta congerie me obruere minimè expedit. Quòd si patriæ tuæ studio prospicis, studium tuum laudo. Sed cogita nostram quoque Galliam multis morbis laborare, quibus maturè succurrere oportet. Quanquam per Ionuilæum non stabit, quominus tibi gratificer, quia & strenuus est exactor: nec verò cessabit, si contigerit melior opportunitas: quòd si quid vigoris recuperem, libenter bentet ipse quoque defungar eo munere. Sed nunc tam corporis quàm animi vires magis sunt collapsæ, quàm vt studium meum applicare possim ad nouos labores. Quod apud D.Hyperiū hyemare in animo tibi est, nusquam, fateor, commodius hospitium reperies. Nam præter raram pietatem & eruditionem, quæ in eius scriptis relucet, aiunt hominem esse mansueto ingenio, magna synceritate præditum. Sed tardior in patriam tuus reditus mihi non placet. Nam cùm alios tantopere incites ad manum genti tuæ porrigendam, quid sibi velit hoc cunctandi & otiandi consilium non assequor. Quanquam frustra hæc disputo, quia antequam ad te perueniant meæ literæ, hyems feré trásfacta erit.
units.tr: If my admonition has helped your fellow countrymen, distinguished sir and my esteemed brother, I thank God, who has not allowed the little labour I spent there to go without fruit. Indeed, I would not now grudge spending more effort on that subject, if I had leisure. But since you left here, I have been in constant struggle with various illnesses, so that I can hardly manage even my ordinary duties. Even if more relaxation were granted, I have other work in hand which does not allow me to devote effort to refuting those two monsters of error. I have undertaken to have my commentaries on Moses translated into French, not only so that our own people may have common access to this book, but because the work, which is otherwise not to be regretted, needed to be cleansed of the countless errors with which it was teeming. The brothers had urged me to expound the book of Joshua; so far I have scarcely been able to get as far as the third chapter, although I am especially eager for brevity. I am also pressed from elsewhere, so that I dare not promise you anything. If a better opportunity is offered at some time, I will not let it pass. But it is in no way advisable for me to overwhelm myself with such a heap of work. If you look out for the good of your homeland, I commend your zeal. But consider that our France too is suffering from many ills, which must be remedied promptly. Yet Ionuilaeus will not stand in the way of my pleasing you, for he is also a vigorous taskmaster; nor will I cease, should a better opportunity arise; and if I recover some strength, I would gladly discharge that duty myself too. But now my bodily and mental powers have collapsed too far for me to apply my zeal to new labours. As for your intention to winter at the house of Hyperius, I confess that you will find no more suitable lodging anywhere. For apart from his rare piety and learning, which shine forth in his writings, they say he is a man of gentle disposition, endowed with great sincerity. But I am not pleased that your return to your homeland is delayed. For since you so greatly urge others to stretch out a hand to your people, I do not understand what this policy of delay and idleness means. Yet I argue this in vain, since by the time my letter reaches you, the winter will almost be over.

units.la: Vale ornatissime vir, mihi ex animo colende frater. Dominus te Spiritu suo semper gubernet, virtute sustineat, & manus suę protectione incolumem tueatur. Geneuæ, Pridie Galend. Decemb. M. D. LXIII.
units.tr: Farewell, most distinguished sir, my brother, esteemed from my heart. May the Lord always guide you by his Spirit, sustain you with strength, and keep you safe under the protection of his hand. Geneva, the day before the Kalends of December, 1563.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: Medicis Monspessvlanis S. D.
units.tr: To the Physicians of Montpellier, greetings.

units.la: Qvum nuper Saracenus Medicis qui valetudini meæ curandæ præest, mihi obtulisset quæ mihi præscripsistis ad morbos meos leuandos remedia, quis hanc curam me inscio fusce pisset, quæsiui Respondit se collegæ nostri qui apud vos est rogatu, summam eorum co nplexum quæ facere visa sunt, vt mihi vtile consilium daretis. Ego vero ex accurata vestra responsione agnosco, quàm vobis chara sit mea vita, de qua prorogada spon te adeo fuistis solliciti: si postulanti id laboris cōcedere graue non fuisset, officium fuisset minimè spernendum. Nunc quia anteuer tistis, eò magis sum vobis obstrictus. Cæterùm non alia testādæ gratitudinis ratio vel facultas suppetit, nisi vt ex meis scriptis vi ciffim fumatis, quæ spiritualem vobis medicinam afferant. Eadem ante annos viginti humanitate vsi erga me fuerat eximij medici Acatius, Tagautius & Gallus Parisienses. Verùm neq; tunc infesti mihi erat podagrici dolores, neq; cū calculo & arena mihi erat negotiū, neq; vexabat cholicis torminibus, neque molestiā exhibebat dolor ani, neq; sanguinis excreatio minitabatur. Tum matim quasi vno impetu in me irruptione fecerūt tot hostes. Simul atq; cōualui à febre quartana, excepit me grauis & acerbus in furis dolor, qui paulisper mi igatus iterū ac tertiò me repetiit. Tādem versus est in morbum articulare, qui à pedibus ad genua excurrit. Diu me in venis hæmorrhoicis cruciauit vlceratis, cūm me titillassent afcarides quibus nunc sum liberatus: hac occasione corripuit me proxima æstate nephritis. Nam quia equi agitatione non fereb, lectica in agrū delatus sum. Volui in reditu
units.tr: Recently the Saracen, who looks after my health, brought me the remedies you had prescribed to relieve my illnesses, and when I asked who had arranged this treatment without my knowledge, he replied that it was done at the request of our colleague who is with you, and that he had summarised the substance of what you thought best, so that you might give me useful advice. From your careful reply I see how dear my life is to you, since you were so anxious about prolonging it of your own accord. Had it not been a burden to grant the request, your kindness would not have been spurned in any way. Now that you have anticipated me, I am all the more bound to you. I have no other way or means of showing my gratitude than to take in return from my writings what may bring you a spiritual medicine. Some twenty years ago the distinguished physicians Acatius, Tagautius and Gallus of Paris had shown me the same kindness. But at that time I did not yet suffer from gout, nor had I any trouble with stone and gravel, nor was I troubled by colic pains, nor did the pain in my anus cause me difficulty, nor did a discharge of blood threaten me. Then, as if in a single assault, so many enemies burst in upon me. As soon as I recovered from a quartan fever, a severe and bitter pain in the loins seized me; it abated for a while, then returned a second and a third time. At last it turned into a joint disease, which runs from the feet up to the knees. For a long time haemorrhoids, now ulcerated, tormented me, and when the ascarids, from which I am now free, began to irritate me, on that occasion nephritis seized me last summer. Since I could not bear the jolting of a horse, I was carried into the countryside in a litter. On the way back I wanted to complete part of the journey on foot.

units.la: Epist. 343. partem itineris pedibus conficere. Vix ad milliare perueneram, quum me subsistere coegit renum lassitudo. Atque tum sanguinem pro vrina mitti à me miratus sum. Domum reuersus decubui. Nephritis me acerrime vrgere, cui modica tantum ex remediis leuatio. Tandem calculus eiectus non absque molestissimo nixu malum illud mitigauit. Sed ea erat magnitudine vt venas laeserit, nec cohibitum fuerit sanguinis profluuium, nisi iniecto per firyngem mulieris lacte. Ab eo tempore plurimos enixus fuit, & grauedo quae in renes incumbit, satis indicat esse illic lapidicinam. Bene tamen est quod minuti vel saltem mediocres exeant. Spem sanationis eripit desidia, ad quam me constringunt aegri pedes. Ab equitatione etiam prohibeor sedis doloribus. Aliud praeterea malum, quod cibus male in ventriculo cococtus in phlegmata vertitur, quae sua densitate tanquam glutino exitum impediunt. Verum ego parum consideraté, qui pro laboris mercede laborem vobis duplico, non iterum consuluandi, sed nugas meas legendi. Valete ornatissime viri & mihi syncera ob seruantia colendi. Dominus vos semper gubernet suo Spiritu, virtute sustineat, ac donis suis vos magis ac magis locupletet.
units.tr: Epist. 343. I had scarcely reached a mile when weariness in my kidneys forced me to stop. Then I was amazed to see blood passed in my urine. I returned home and took to my bed. The nephritis pressed on me most severely, and the remedies gave only slight relief. At last a stone was expelled, not without the most painful straining, and this eased the trouble. But it was so large that it had injured the veins, and the flow of blood could not be stopped until a woman's milk was injected through a syringe. Since then I have strained many times, and the heaviness that settles in my kidneys clearly shows that there is a quarry of stones there. It is well, however, that the stones that come out are small, or at least of moderate size. Inactivity, to which my lame feet confine me, takes away my hope of recovery. I am also forbidden to ride because of pain in the seat. There is another trouble besides: food badly digested in the stomach turns into phlegm, which by its thickness, as if by glue, blocks the way out. But I am being thoughtless, since I, who should be paid for my labour, add to your labour by asking you not to advise me again, but to read my trifles. Farewell, most distinguished gentlemen, and accept my sincere respect and goodwill. May the Lord always govern you by his Spirit, sustain you by his strength, and enrich you more and more with his gifts.

units.la: Geneuae, VIII. Febr. M. D. LXIIII.
units.tr: Geneva, 8 February 1564.

units.la: CALVINVS FARELLO s. D.
units.tr: Calvin to Farel, greeting

units.la: VALE mi optime & integerr. frater: & quando te Deus superstitem manere vult, in mundo, viue memor nostrae coniunctionis: quae vt Ecclesiae Dei fuit vtilis, ita nos eius fructus in coelo manet. Nolo te fatiges mea causa. Aegre spiritum traho, & assidue expecto, dum me anhelitus deficiat. Satis est quod Christo viuo & morior, qui suis lucrum est in vita & morte. Iterum vale cum fratribus. Geneuae, 2 Maij. M. D. LXIIII.
units.tr: Farewell, my dearest and most upright brother. And since God wills that you remain alive in the world, live mindful of our fellowship, which has been useful to the Church of God and whose fruit remains for us in heaven. I do not want you to tire yourself on my account. I draw breath with difficulty and wait constantly until my breathing fails. It is enough that I live and die for Christ, who is gain to his own both in life and in death. Farewell again, and give my greetings to the brothers. Geneva, 2 May 1564.

units.la: RESPONSIO PRINCIPVM AD LEGATOS PONTIFICIOS.
units.tr: The Princes' Reply to the Papal Legates

units.la: REuerendi viri: Illustrissimi Sacri Romani Imperij Electores & Principes, Illustrissimorum Electorum & Principum Legati ac Consiliarij, ad orationem vestram, qua Pontificis Romani mandata Celsitudinibus ipsorum expositis, hoc responsi vobis dari iusserunt. Non dubitare se quin multi omnium gentium in toto orbe terrarum, viri docti, sapientes & pij iamdudum meliorem Ecclesiae statum optarint, & nunc quoq; anxia ad Deum vota faciant, vt tandem doctrinae puritas restituatur, & terri in Ecclesiam abusus inuecti pia emendatione tollantur. Quod ipsum Pontificibus Romanis in sua iurisdictione prispræcipuè curæ esse debet, qui Ecclesiæ titulum tam longo annorum spatio magnificè sibi arrogarunt. Verùm quibus ipsi potissimum rebus semper occupati fuerint, nimirum regni cupiditate, regnisque committendis, & superstitionibus in Ecclesia cumulandis, magis quàm illustrandæ gloriæ Dei, fanandisque Ecclesiæ morbis, obscurum bonis omnibus non est, & multos Pontificio nomini addictos viros sapientes fateri necesse est. Mirantur autem Illustrissimi Electores ac Principes reliquorum quoque Legati, qua vel opinione persuasus vel spe fretus Pius Papa, missa hac Legatione, Celsitudinibus suis Concilij indictione obtrudere, eòsque Tridentum vocare ausus fuerit. Neque enim Pontifice & vos ignorare quam Religionem statuS Augustanæ Confessionis amplectantur, quibúsq; de causis Ecclesias suas, iuxta synceram Euangelij doctrinam repurgare, & se ab eo cœtu, qui oppressæ doctrinæ cœlestis veritate, suam potius quàm Christi gloriam quæsit, sequungere coacti sunt. Sic igitur Pontificem ac vos statuè Illustrissimi Principes voluntnon agnoscere se Romanæ sedis auctoritatem, certisque Diuini ac Humani Iuris indubitatis testimoniis Celsitudinibus suis persuasum esse, Concilij indicen di ius Pontificem Romanum non habere. Iudicis enim officio fungi, & controuersias dirimere, cum à quo differentiones & distractiones in Eccl. sia ortæ sunt, quíque manifestam veritatem crudeliter oppugnat, fas non esse & humana dictat ratio, nec nõ Diuini humanísque iuris scripta testantur. Iniuste etiam oratione vestra sese taxari Illustrissimi Principes affirmant, quòd nullam fidei certitudinem habeant, sed tot nunc sunt Euangelia quot doctores. Extat enim non solum de omnibus fidei articulis, perspicua ipsorum Confessio Imperatori Carolo V. Augustæ anno XXX exhibita: verùm etiam variis hactenus editis scriptis cœlestis doctrinæ veritas illustrata ac propagata est. Quibus autem erroribus Romana nunc Ecclesia imbuta, quamque tetris abusibus & superstitionibus vera Euangelij doctrina oppressa sit, ut Ethnicæ quàm Christianæ Religioni similior esse videatur, vniuersi orbis terrarum querelæ testantur. Cumque non errore lapsi nec temeritate, curiositate aut prauis cupiditatibus, sed seueris simo Dei mandato, quo præcipitur idola fugienda esse, impulsi Germaniæ Principes, discesserint à Romana Ecclesia, constaret in ea sententia perseveraturi, nullas sibi à Romano Pontifice leges præscribi patientur. Nullus enim auctoritatem, vel iurisdictionem quàm Imperatoris sui Ferdinandi Cæsaris agnoscunt: cuius Legatis quam ipsi de Concilio Oecumenico ac generali celebrado sperm ac sententiam habeant, coram hic exposuerunt. Quòd verò ad vos attinet, ita vobis omnino persuadeatis, Celsitudines ipsorum volunt nisi Pontificiæ legationis munus obiiss setis, omnia ipsorum clementiæ & beneuolentiæ studia & obse-quia vobis ex clarissimis Venetorum familiis ortis præstituros fuisse, tum quòd erga Amplissimam Venetorum Rempublicam animo affecti sunt beneuolo, tum vero etiam quòd vos ob generis nobilitatem, doctrinæ ac sapientiæ laudem fauore suo dignos esse ipsi profitentur.
units.tr: Reverend sirs: the most illustrious Electors and Princes of the Holy Roman Empire, and the legates and counsellors of the most illustrious Electors and Princes, have ordered us to give you this reply to your speech, in which you set out the commands of the Roman Pontiff. They do not doubt that many learned, wise and pious men of every nation throughout the whole world have long desired a better state of the Church, and that they now also make anxious prayers to God that the purity of doctrine may at last be restored and the abuses introduced into the Church by wicked men may be removed by pious reform. This ought to be the chief concern of the Roman Pontiffs in their jurisdiction, since for so long a span of years they have proudly arrogated to themselves the title of the Church. But that they themselves have always been occupied chiefly with other matters, namely the desire for power, the handing over of kingdoms, and the piling up of superstitions in the Church, rather than with setting forth the glory of God and healing the diseases of the Church, is not unclear to all good men, and it is necessary to admit that many wise men devoted to the Papal name confess as much. The most illustrious Electors and Princes, and the legates of the others too, are amazed that Pope Pius, persuaded by some opinion or relying on some hope, dared, by sending this legation, to impose on their Highnesses an indiction of a Council and to summon them to Trent. For you too cannot be unaware what religion the states of the Augsburg Confession embrace, and for what reasons they were compelled to purify their churches according to the sincere doctrine of the gospel, and to separate themselves from that assembly which, having suppressed the truth of heavenly doctrine, sought its own glory rather than Christ's. So the Pontiff and you, most illustrious Princes, must know that they do not acknowledge the authority of the Roman see, and that their Highnesses are persuaded by certain and indubitable testimonies of divine and human law that the Roman Pontiff does not have the right to indict a Council. For to exercise the office of judge and settle controversies, when he is the one from whom the disagreements and divisions in the Church have arisen, and who cruelly assails manifest truth, is not permitted, as human reason dictates and the writings of divine and human law also attest. The most illustrious Princes also declare that they are unjustly taxed in your speech for having no certainty of faith, and that there are now as many gospels as teachers. For there exists not only a clear confession of all the articles of faith, presented to the Emperor Charles V at Augsburg in the year 1530, but also the truth of heavenly doctrine has been made clear and spread by the various writings published so far. As for the errors with which the Roman Church is now imbued, and the foul abuses and superstitions by which the true doctrine of the gospel has been suppressed, so that it seems more like the heathen religion than the Christian, the complaints of the whole world bear witness. And since the German Princes departed from the Roman Church not having fallen into error, nor through rashness, curiosity or wicked desires, but impelled by the most severe command of God, by which idols are commanded to be fled, and since it is established that they will persevere in that opinion, they will not allow any laws to be prescribed to them by the Roman Pontiff. For they acknowledge no authority or jurisdiction other than that of their Emperor Ferdinand Caesar, to whose legates they have set out here, in person, what hopes and opinions they hold concerning the holding of an ecumenical and general Council. As for you, you must be fully persuaded that their Highnesses wished, had you not discharged the office of the papal legation, to show you all their kindness, benevolence and courtesy, you who are sprung from the most distinguished families of the Venetians; both because they are well disposed toward the most renowned Venetian Republic, and also because they themselves declare that you, on account of the nobility of your birth and your praise for learning and wisdom, deserve their favour.

units.la: QVAE DEINCEPS SEQUUNTUR, Theologica fere sunt, & ad Responsa magis pertinent.
units.tr: The matters that follow are mostly theological and pertain more to the Answers.

units.la: DE DEI NOMINE ET ILLIVS RECTA acceptione, propter Inuocationis vsum maximè.
units.tr: On the Name of God and Its Correct Understanding, Chiefly on Account of the Use of Invocation

units.la: Quum de Deo tantum loquimur sine vlla notæ appositione, quum nobis considerandus est in sua simplici essentia, vt Deus vnus.
units.tr: When we speak of God without any added qualification, we must consider him in his simple essence, as the one God.

units.la: Quum de Iesu Christo tantum loquimur non adiecta Patris mentione, tum ille agnoscendus nobis est, vt Deus manifestatus in carne. Hoc autem sic habet: Deum assumpsisse naturam nostram, vt in illa habitet, tanquam in templo Maiestatis suæ: atqj hocita procedit, vt vnio naturarum diuinæ atque humanæ con-stet, quæ etiam vnitatem personæ constituat.
units.tr: When we speak of Jesus Christ without any mention of the Father being added, we must acknowledge him as God manifested in the flesh. This holds as follows: God assumed our nature so that he might dwell in it as in the temple of his majesty; and this proceeds in such a way that the union of the divine and human natures is established, which also constitutes the unity of the person.

units.la: Quum de Deo & de Iesu Christo simul loquimur, tu sub Dei nomine intelligendus est nobis Pater: Christus autem statuen-dus est, vt Caput ac Dominus, qui nobis à Patre ordinatus sit, vt nobis dominetur atque omne ius in nos habeat.
units.tr: When we speak of God and Jesus Christ together, by the name of God we must understand the Father; Christ, however, is to be regarded as Head and Lord, who has been ordained for us by the Father, so that he may rule over us and have all right over us.

units.la: In summa siue de Deo cogitemus siue loquamur, non est hæ-rendum nobis in nuda infinitæ ipsius essentiæ consideratione. Periculosi enim est eiusmodi cogitatio, quia mens humana illa hebetatur. Ad Christum igitur nos totum conuertere oportet, in quo Pater se revelauit & aperuit nobis.
units.tr: In sum, whether we think of God or speak of him, we must not cling to the bare consideration of his infinite essence. For such a thought is dangerous, because the human mind is dulled by it. We must therefore turn ourselves wholly to Christ, in whom the Father has revealed and opened himself to us.

units.la: Quum de Scriptura loquimur, distinguendum est inter Vetus & Nouum Testamentum. Quanquam enim Lex & Prophetæ à Christo emanarint, quatenus ille semper fuit Angelus, ille magni consilij, & summus Patris legatus, per quem sese Deus communicauit hominibus: vsus tamen non obtinet, vt dicamus Christum hoc vel illud dixisse per Mosen aut per Dauidem, sed simpliciter pliciter Deum id dixisse, quia nempe Christus eo tempore manifestatus nondum fuerit. Tenendum est igitur ex Petri doctrina,sanctos omnes Prophetas per os Christi locutos esse:itémque ex Paulo,Christum ducem populi extitisse in deserto,ac per eius manum legem datam fuisse: sed tamen ex vsu recepto Scripturæ,cùm aliquid ex Veteri Testamento proferendū erit, non dicemus,Christus hoc dixit per Isaiam vel per Mosen : sed potius Deus dixit,aut Spiritus Dei. Noui Testamenti alia est ratio,quia Christus veniens in mundum ordinatus est nobis à Patre magister ac doctor,à quo omnem veritatem accipieremus. Atque ita à nobis habeti & nominari debet auctor totius doctrinæ Apostolorum, vt Paulus testatur in sese loqui Christum.
units.tr: When we speak of Scripture, we must distinguish between the Old and the New Testament. For although the Law and the Prophets proceeded from Christ, inasmuch as he always was the Angel, the Angel of great counsel, and the highest envoy of the Father, through whom God communicated himself to men, yet the established usage does not allow us to say that Christ said this or that through Moses or through David, but simply that God said it, namely because Christ had not yet been manifested in that time. It must therefore be held, from the teaching of Peter, that all the holy Prophets spoke through the mouth of Christ; and likewise from Paul, that Christ was the leader of the people in the wilderness and that the law was given through his hand. Nevertheless, by the received usage of Scripture, when something from the Old Testament is to be brought forward, we shall not say, "Christ said this through Isaiah or through Moses," but rather, "God said it," or "the Spirit of God." The case of the New Testament is different, because Christ, coming into the world, was ordained for us by the Father as teacher and doctor, from whom we should receive all truth. And thus the author of all the doctrine of the Apostles must be held and named by us, as Paul testifies that Christ speaks in him.

units.la: Quòdad inuocationem attinet, aut Dei tantum nomen edimus, non expressi Christi mentione, aut addimus,vt Deus Pater nos exaudiat Christi nomine, quem ipsi Mediatorem proponimus.Si nomen Christi ore quidem non exprimimus,animo tamen & intelligentia supplendum illud nobis est.
