Non quòd illa nobis cogitatio etiam obuersari debeat, semper nos Patrem implorare per illum nostrum intercessorem, sed quia illud pro fundamento & principio constitutum nobis semper esse debet, non aliter esse nobis aditum ad Deum,quàm si ad illius maiestatem ille aditum faciat,qui sese adeo demisit,vt humilitati nostrę sese accommodaret.
units.tr: As for invocation, we either utter the name of God alone, without expressly mentioning Christ, or we add, "that God the Father may hear us in the name of Christ, whom we set forth as our Mediator." If we do not express the name of Christ with our mouth, it must nevertheless be supplied by us in mind and understanding. Not that this thought ought always to be present to us, that we always implore the Father through that our intercessor, but because it must always remain fixed for us as the foundation and principle, that there is no access to God for us except if he who has so humbled himself as to accommodate himself to our lowliness makes that access to his majesty.

units.la: Si Patrem nominatim imploramus,vt nos exaudiat Filij nomine, sic nobis cogitandum est:ita nempe Christum sacrificio illo mortis suæ aditum nobis ad Patrem patefecisse ad nos illi sistendos cum fiducia, vt nunc etiam illius eiusdem sacrificij vitute intercedat pro nobis , orationibus nostris gratiam conciliet,atque illarum effectum nobis impetret.Neque verò imaginādus nobis ille quidem Christi genibus Patris aduoluti status, vt inter homines fieri solet , sed eo vno satis nobis sit quòd habeamus ipsum patronum ,qui nostro nomine Patrem interpellet,qui nostras orationes admittat & Patri offerat , nobisque & audientiam impetret & gratiam. Audientiam dico vt illius nomine sit nobis facultas inuocandi Patrem vt & ab illo audiamur: fuoré verò,vt ita quæ à Patre petierimus ipsius gratia obtineamus. Ac proinde hic esse debet pij viri sensus, cum Deum precatur Christi nomine:si mihi ad Deum accedendum esset sine vllo deductore vel medio,nunquam ad præcelsam illam maiestatem pro mea humilitate peruenirem. Iam verò vbi constat mihi seruatoris mei sponsio,qua mihi manum porrigit,non erit mihi difficilis accessus.
units.tr: If we invoke the Father by name, that he may hear us in the name of the Son, we must think of it thus: namely, that Christ by that sacrifice of his death has opened to us the way to the Father, so that we may present ourselves to him with confidence; and that now also, by the power of that same sacrifice, he intercedes for us, wins grace for our prayers, and obtains for us their effect. Nor must we imagine that picture of Christ kneeling before the Father's knees, as is usually done among men; it is enough for us that we have him as our patron, who on our behalf pleads with the Father, who admits our prayers and offers them to the Father, and who obtains for us both a hearing and grace. I say a hearing, so that through his name we may have the freedom to invoke the Father and be heard by him; and grace, so that we may obtain by his favour the things we have asked from the Father. And accordingly this must be the sentiment of the godly man when he prays to God in the name of Christ: if I had to approach God without any guide or mediator, I would never, by reason of my lowliness, come to that most lofty majesty. But now that the promise of my Saviour is established for me, by which he holds out his hand to me, access will not be difficult for me.

units.la: Si hæc cogitatio veniat in mente,quomodo Christus Deus cum sit, intercedat apud Patrem : quum idem eundem precari videti posset, quod à ratione est alienissimum, hæ duæ consideraciones adhibendæ sunt, quibus illi difficultati obuiam eatur. Prima est, sic vnum esse Deum verum, vt tamen in vna illa Deitate distinctio personarum tenenda sit: Patris nimirum, Filij & Spiritus sancti. Ita nihil est absurdi, si ad personam Patris nos conuertimus inter precandum. Altera vero, quòd Christus assumens nostram naturam, vt in ea redemptionem nostram impleret, hoc Media toris munus suscepit, quod exerceret demum intercedendo pro nobis in ea natura, quam assumpsit à nobis.
units.tr: If the thought comes to mind of how Christ, being God, can intercede with the Father, since it might seem that the same one is asking, which is most alien to reason, two considerations must be applied to meet that difficulty. The first is that there is one true God, yet within that one Deity the distinction of persons must be maintained: namely, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. So there is nothing absurd if, in prayer, we turn to the person of the Father. The second is that Christ, assuming our nature in order to accomplish our redemption in it, undertook the office of Mediator, which he finally exercises by interceding for us in that nature which he took from us.

units.la: Quum ad Christum orationem dirigimus, aut petimus vt ad Patrem nos ipse, vt Mediator, deducat, atq; illud præparationis instar habet, vt ad Patrem perueniamus: aut sic illum oramus vt propria virtute nobis adsit, vt is in quem omnis potestas col lata sit, in quo habitet omnis plenitudo Deitatis, quíque adeo sit Deus noster æternus manifestatus in carne. Atque vtraque inuo candi Christi ratio & legitima & sancta est.
units.tr: When we direct our prayer to Christ, we either ask that he, as Mediator, lead us to the Father, which serves as a preparation for us to come to the Father; or we so pray to him that by his own power he may be present to us, as the one to whom all power has been given, in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead, and who is thus our eternal God manifested in the flesh. Both ways of invoking Christ are lawful and holy.

units.la: CONFESSIO CALVINI DE TRINITATE propter calumnias P. Caroli.
units.tr: Calvin's Confession concerning the Trinity, occasioned by the calumnies of P. Carolus.

units.la: CUm in Dei Maiestate consideranda mens humana per se omnino cæcutiat, neque quicquam possit, quàm & infinitis erroribus sese inuoluere, & ministricis implicare & altissimis demum tenebris immergere, si iuxta captus sui tenuitatem Deum imaginari conetur: iliud bonorum omnium pace ac venia facturos confidimus, si Deum nusquam quæramus nisi in eius verbo, nihil de ipso cogitemus nisi cum eius verbo, de ipso nihil loquamur nisi per eius verbum. Hæc vero sobrietas & reuerentia si in familiari sermone commendatur, in quo multa effutiri solent non ante præmeditata: vbi quis publicam edere fidei suæ confessionem hac de re instituit, nulla adhiberi satis di ligentia potest, & in sententiis concipiendis & in delectu verbo rum habendo vt nihil in ea deprehendatur, quàm ipsissima scriptura veritas exquisitis ac folennibus verbis religiose comprehensa. Nemo ergo nobis succensebit, si Confessionem quam piis omnibus volumus approbatam ita moderamur, vt nō ex variis hominum placitis consarcinata, sed ad rectam scripturæ normā diligenter exacta sit. Siquidem hic nobis succurrere debet, quod tradit Apostolus, fidem esse ex auditu, auditū verò per verbum Dei. Iam si Religionis Confessio nihil est, quàm conceptæ intus fidei testificatio, vt solida sit & syncera, ex puris Scripturæ fontibus petitam esse oportet: neque verò Confessionem duntaxat eâ recipimus, quæ ex solis scripturæ verbis superstitiose cotexta sit & confuta: sed iis verbis conscribendam esse contendimus, quæ & sensum habeant intra Scripturæ veritatem limitatû, & quàm minimè habeant asperitatis, qua piæ aures offendi queant, nec Deo quidpiam affingant sua maiestate indignum. Quem modum in ista nostra Confessione, quia tenere studuimus, bonis omnibus ac cordatis viris non dubitamus studium nostrum probatum iri.
units.tr: Although the human mind, in contemplating the majesty of God, is utterly blind by itself, and can do nothing but entangle itself in endless errors, get lost in vanities and sink at last into the deepest darkness, if it tries to imagine God according to the narrowness of its own capacity, we trust that all good people will grant us pardon if we seek God nowhere except in his Word, think of him nothing except in agreement with his Word, and speak of him nothing except through his Word. If this sobriety and reverence is commended in familiar conversation, where many things are commonly blurted out without prior thought, then when someone undertakes to publish a public confession of his faith on this matter, no diligence can be too great, both in framing the statements and in choosing the words, so that nothing is found in it but the very truth of Scripture, faithfully expressed in carefully chosen and solemn words. No one, therefore, will take offence with us if we have so shaped the Confession which we wish to be approved by all the pious, that it is not patched together from the various opinions of men, but has been carefully drawn up according to the right rule of Scripture. For here the saying of the Apostle should come to our aid, that faith is from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. Now if a confession of religion is nothing other than the testimony of faith conceived within, then in order for it to be solid and sincere it must be drawn from the pure sources of Scripture. Nor do we accept only that confession which has been superstitiously woven and stitched together from the bare words of Scripture; we maintain that it must be written in words which have a sense limited within the truth of Scripture, which have no harshness that might offend pious ears, and which ascribe nothing to God unworthy of his majesty. Since we have striven to keep this measure in our present Confession, we do not doubt that our endeavour will be approved by all good and sensible men.

units.la: DEVM VNVM quem nobis Scripturæ prædicant credimus & adoramus: talem etiam concipimus, qualis illic nobis describitur: nempe essentiæ æternæ, infinitæ & Spiritualis, qui & solus in seipso vim subsistendi, à seque ipso habeat & eam creaturis omnibus largiatur. Anthropomorphitas cum suo corpore Deo, Manichæos item, cum duobus principiis explodimus: in una tamen Dei essentia Patrem cum æterno suo Verbo & Spiritu agnoscimus: qua nominû distinctione dum vtimur, neque tres imaginamur Deos, perinde ac si aliud quidda esset Pater quàm Verbum: neque rursum nuda esse epitheta intelligimus, quibus à suis operibus varie designetur Deus, sed vna cum Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus in simplicissima Dei vnitate sentimus has esse tres hypostases, id est subsistentias: quæ tametsi vna essentia constant, nô tamen inter se confunduntur. Itaque tametsi vnus Deus est, Pater cum Verbo & Spiritu suo, non tamen aut Pater Verbum est, aut Verbum ipsum Spiritus. Atque in hanc sententiam confirmandam extant solida Scripturæ testimonia. Filius enim ille & Iehoua nominatur, & Deus fortis, & Deus in sæcula laudandus, quem adorant omnes Angeli Dei, cuius thronus in sæculum sæculi est stabilitus. Tum omnia illi deferuntur, quæ nisi in vnum verum æternum Deum nullo modo competere possunt. Nam vt nuncupatur salus, iustitia, sanctificatio nostra: ta fiduciâ speque omnem in ipso reponere & eius nomen invocare docemur, quæ practica notitia certior haud dubiè est qualibet otiosa speculatione. Illic enim pius animus Deum præsentissimum conspicit & pene attrectat, vbi se viuificari, illuminari, saluari, iustificari ac sanctificari sentit. Quare iisdem etiam è fontibus ad confirmandam Spiritus sancti diuinitate probatio petenda est. Logê enim à creaturis alienum est quòd illi Scripturæ tribuûr, & nos ipsi certa pietatis experientia discimus. Ille enim est, qui vbique diffusus omnia sustinet, vegetat & viuificat, qui in fidelibus habitans ducit eos in omnem veritatem, regenerat, sanctificat, & olim ad plenum viuificabit. Nec vero cùm de ipso Scriptura loquitur, à Dei appellatione abstinet. Paulus enim nos esse templum Dei ex eo colligit, quia Spiritus eius habitat in nobis. Petrus verò Ananiam reprehendens quòd Spiritui sancto mentitus esset non hominibus mentitum esse dicebat, sed Deo. Iam cum fixum illud maneat Deum vnum esse, non plures, Verbum &
units.tr: We believe in and worship the one God whom the Scriptures proclaim to us, and we conceive of him as he is described there: of eternal, infinite and spiritual essence, who alone has in himself the power of subsisting, from himself, and bestows it on all creatures. We reject the Anthropomorphites, with their notion of a bodily God, and likewise the Manichaeans, with their two principles. Yet in the one essence of God we acknowledge the Father together with his eternal Word and Spirit. While we use this distinction of names, we do not imagine three Gods, as if the Father were something other than the Word; nor again do we understand these names to be bare epithets by which God is variously designated from his works. Rather, with the ecclesiastical writers, we hold in the most simple unity of God that these are three hypostases, that is, subsistences, which, although they consist in one essence, are nonetheless not confused with one another. Thus, although God is one, the Father with his Word and Spirit, the Father is not the Word, nor the Word the Spirit itself. And to confirm this opinion there exist solid testimonies of Scripture. For that Son is named Jehovah, and mighty God, and God to be praised for ever, whom all the angels of God adore, and whose throne is established for ever and ever. Then all things are ascribed to him which can in no way belong except to the one true and eternal God. For as he is called our salvation, our righteousness and our sanctification, so we are taught to place in him all our trust and hope, and to invoke his name; and this practical knowledge is surely more certain than any idle speculation. For there the pious soul beholds God most present and almost handles him, when it feels itself quickened, enlightened, saved, justified and sanctified. Wherefore from these same sources the proof for confirming the divinity of the Holy Spirit is also to be sought. For what Scripture attributes to him is far from creatures, and we ourselves learn it by the sure experience of piety. For he is the one who, diffused everywhere, sustains, nourishes and quickens all things; who, dwelling in believers, leads them into all truth, regenerates and sanctifies them, and at last will quicken them fully. Nor, when Scripture speaks of him, does it refrain from calling him God. For Paul gathers from this that we are the temple of God, because his Spirit dwells in us. Peter, rebuking Ananias because he had lied to the Holy Spirit, said that he had lied not to men but to God. Now since it remains fixed that God is one, not many, we hold that the Word and

units.la: Spiritum non aliud esse, quàm ipsam Dei essentiam constituimus. Et sane si in vnius Dei fidem ac Religionem baptizamur, eum nos profiteamur Deum habere, in cuius nomen baptizamur. Ex quo Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum in vna Dei essentia contineri plane constat. Quindoquidem in nomen Patris & Filij, & Spiritus sancti baptizamur. Rursum & quædam Patris à Verbo, Verbi à Spiritu distinctio Scripturis demonstratur. Perspicuum enim est quod dicitur, Patrem per Filium omnia creasse, eundem in hunc mundum misisse, in mortem exposuisse, à mortuis excitasse, dedisse nomen quod est supra omne nomen: vt nisi quis Dei verbo repugnare ex profesto velit, non aufert tergiuersari. Nam nec in terram descendit Pater, nec carnem induit, nec mortem subiit, nec excitatus est. Iam & se à Spiritu differre significabat Christus, cum alium Consolatorem se missurum pollicebatur. Porrò simplicissimam Dei vnitatem adeò non impedit illa distinctio, vt Filium inde probare liceat vnum esse cum Patre Deum, quia vno simul cum eo Spiritu constet. Spiritum autem non aliud esse à Patre, & Filio diuersum, quia Patris & Filij sit Spiritus. Summa haec sit, Nos in illa quam super cœlestì fumus æterna spirituali infinita Dei essentia Patrem cum Verbo, aut Verbum cum Spiritu non confundimus. Arrij dementiam, qui æternam Filium diuinitate spoliabat, simul & Macedonij qui per Spiritum dona gratiæ duntaxat in hominibus effusa intelligebat, improbamus & execramur, nihilo magis Sabellij errori assentimur, qui nullam in Patre, & Filio, & Spiritu distinctionem admittebat. Quod ad Christum peculiariter attinet, duabus ipsum naturis constare affirmamus. Nam antequam c rnem induerat, Verbum illud æternum fuit ex Patre ante fæcula genitum, verus Deus vnius cum Patre essentiæ, potentiæ, maiestatis, adeoque Iehoua, qui à se ipso semper habuit, vt ef set, & aliis subsistendi virtutem inspirauit. Siquidem ipse de se te statu est gloriam quam in carne illustratus est, se ab initio apud Patrem possedisse, an equam mundi iacerentur fundamenta. Quod ipsum & Paulus docet dum in forma Dei fuisse scribit per formæ vocabulum maiestatem intelligens. Potentiam verò suam his verbis asserit, Ego & Pater operamur huc vsque Scripturæ etiam passim idem docent, per eum creatum esse orbem, in ipso vitam fuisse, & eiusmodi plurima. Neque opera pretium est hic pluribus immorari. Nam si Deus est, omnia in se continet quæ Dei sunt. Proinde stolidissimè mentiebantur Arriani, qui cum Deum faterentur, Dei substantiam illi admebant. Verbi quoque appellatione non intelligimus fluxam & euanidam vocem quæ in aere emittatur, cuiusmodi & oraculi Patribus edita, & Prophetiæ fuerunt: sed perpetuam sapientiam apud Deum residentem, vnde oracula & prophetiæ omnes prodierunt. Non enim minùs Spiritu Christi loquuti sunt veteres Prophetæ, quàm Apostoli,& quicunque veritatem Dei hominibus administrarunt. Iam verò secundum tempus redemptionis no ftræ manifestationi definitum, verbum caro factum est,non quòd in carnem versum fuerit,sed quia ex virgine carnem assumpsit, vt verum esset ac germanum Dauidis semen,& qui Filius erat Dei,filius hominis factus est. Sic autem coniunctam humanitati diuinitatem asserimus,vt sua vtrique naturæ solida proprietas maneat :tamen ex illis duabus vnus Christus constituatur. Itaque Scripturæ tamen proprietates illas distinctè nobis considerandas proponunt,dum Christo interdum, quod filius est Dei,interdum quod hominis est,tribuunt:earum tamen coniunctionem quæ in Christo subest, tanta Religione exprimunt,vt eas quà indoque inter se communicent: vt cùm sanguine Dei acquisitam Ecclesiam, & Filium hominis in cœlo fuisse dicunt,quo tempore adhuc in terris agebat (qui tropus veteribus ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία dictus est) verum mnium clarissimæ veram Christi essentiam enarrant illi loci, qui simul vtramque naturam complectuntur, quales in Euangelio Ioannis extant quamplurimi. Christum ergo verum Deum, & verum hominem Dei Filium esse asserimus,etiam secundum humanitatem, etsi non ratione humanitatis. Istud enim & scripturis diserte consignatum,& veteris Ecclesiæ consensu receptum est. Eos omnes, qui diuinæ in Christo maiestatis veritatem aut euertere, aut imminuere aut obscurare conati sunt, vt sacrilegos detestamur. Marcionitas qui spectrum illi pro corpore affingebant: Manichæos item qui cœlesti carne præditum somniabant, procul reiicimus. Nec Apollinarianos assentimur,qui dimidiam humanitatis partem illi detrahebat. Nestorij deniq; errorem damnamus,qui ab humanitate Diuinitatem distrahens, duplicem Christum comminuscebatur.
units.tr: Spirit are nothing other than the very essence of God. And indeed, if we are baptized into the faith and religion of the one God, we profess that we have that God in whose name we are baptized; from which it plainly follows that the Father, Son and Spirit are contained in the one essence of God, since we are baptized into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Again, a certain distinction of the Father from the Word, and of the Word from the Spirit, is demonstrated in the Scriptures. For it is clear what is said: that the Father created all things through the Son, sent him into this world, delivered him to death, raised him from the dead, and gave him the name which is above every name. Unless someone wishes to openly contradict the Word of God, he cannot evade this. For the Father neither descended to earth, nor put on flesh, nor underwent death, nor was he raised. Christ also indicated that he differs from the Spirit when he promised to send another Comforter. Moreover, that distinction does not so hinder the most simple unity of God that one cannot from it prove that the Son is one God with the Father, since the Spirit exists in one together with him at the same time. But the Spirit is not other than the Father, and different from the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. The sum is this: we do not confuse the Father with the Word, or the Word with the Spirit, within that eternal, spiritual, infinite essence of God which we confess to be above heaven. We condemn and execrate the madness of Arius, who stripped the eternal Son of divinity, and likewise that of Macedonius, who understood the gifts of grace poured out upon men through the Spirit as mere gifts. Nor do we assent in any way to the error of Sabellius, who admitted no distinction in Father, Son and Spirit. As for Christ in particular, we affirm that he consists of two natures. For before he put on flesh, that eternal Word was begotten of the Father before all ages, a true God of one essence with the Father, in power and majesty, and thus Jehovah, who has always had being from himself, and breathed into others the power of subsisting. For he himself testified that the glory with which he was illumined in the flesh he had possessed with the Father from the beginning, before the foundations of the world were laid. Paul also teaches this when he writes that he was in the form of God, understanding by the word "form" majesty. He asserts his power in these words: "I and the Father work until now." The Scriptures everywhere teach the same thing: that the world was created through him, that life was in him, and many such things. Nor is it worth lingering here at greater length. For if he is God, he contains in himself all that belongs to God. Therefore the Arians spoke most foolishly, who, while confessing him to be God, attributed to him a substance other than God's. Nor by the name Word do we understand a fleeting and vanishing voice emitted into the air, such as the oracles and prophecies delivered to the Fathers were; but the perpetual wisdom residing with God, from which all oracles and prophecies have proceeded. For the ancient prophets spoke no less by the Spirit of Christ than the apostles and all who administered the truth of God to men. Now, according to the time of our redemption, determined for its manifestation, "the Word was made flesh"; not because it was turned into flesh, but because it assumed flesh from the virgin, so that it might be the true and genuine seed of David, and he who was the Son of God became the Son of man. We assert that divinity is so joined to humanity that the solid property of each nature remains, and yet from those two one Christ is constituted. Thus the Scriptures set forth those properties for us to consider distinctly, ascribing to Christ at one time what is his as Son of God, and at another what is his as man; yet they express the union which underlies Christ with such reverence that they communicate those things to one another in turn. So when they say that the Church was acquired with the blood of God, and that the Son of man was in heaven at a time when he was still on earth (a figure which the ancients called [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία]), the passages which embrace both natures together, of which there are very many in the Gospel of John, most clearly set forth the true essence of Christ. Therefore we assert that Christ is true God and true man, the Son of God also according to his humanity, though not by reason of his humanity. For this is both expressly recorded in the Scriptures and received by the consent of the ancient Church. We detest as sacrilegious all who have tried either to overturn, or to diminish, or to obscure the truth of the divine majesty in Christ. We reject far away the Marcionites, who ascribed to him a phantom in place of a body; likewise the Manichaeans, who dreamed that he had a heavenly flesh. Nor do we assent to the Apollinarians, who took away half of his humanity. Finally, we condemn the error of Nestorius, who, separating divinity from humanity, cut Christ into two.

units.la: CONFESSIO FIDEI DE EVCHARISTIA quam obtulerunt Farellus,Caluinus, & Viretus,cui subscripserunt Bucerus & Capito.
units.tr: CONFESSION OF FAITH CONCERNING THE EUCHARIST, which was offered by Farel, Calvin and Viret, and subscribed by Bucer and Capito.

units.la: Vitam spiritualem quam nobis Christus largitur, non in eo duntaxat sitam esse confitemur, quòd Spiritu suo nos viuificat, sed quòd Spiritus etiam sui virtute, carnis suæ viuificæ nos facit participes, qua participatione in vitam æternam pascamur. Itaque cùm de communione quam cum Christi fideles habent, loquimur, non minus carni & sanguini eius com municare ipsos intelligimus quàm Spiritui, vt ita totum Christum possideant. Siquidem cùm aperte testetur Scriptura, carnē Christi verè nobis esse cibū, & sanguinem eius verè potum: ipsis verò nos educari oportere constat, si vita in Christo quaerimus. Iam nec exiguum quiddam, aut vulgare docet Apostolus, cùm nos carnē de Christi carne, & ossa ex ossibus eius esse asserit: sed eximium noštræ cum ipsius corpore communionis mysterium ita designat, quod nullus verbis satis pro dignitate explicare queat. Cæterum istis nihil repugnat, quòd Dominus noster in cœlum sublatus, localem corporis sui præsentiam nobis abstulit, quæ hic minimè exigitur. Nam vtcunque nos in hac mortalitate peregrinantes in eodem loco cum ipso non includimur, aut continemur, nullis tamen finibus limitata est eius Spiritus efficacia, quin verè copulare, & in vnum colligere possit, quæ lo corum spatiis sunt disiuncta. Ergo Spiritum eius vinculum esse nostræ cum ipso participationis agnoscimus, sed ita vt nos ille carnis & sanguinis Domini substantia verè ad immortalitatem pascat & eorum participatione viuificet. Hanc autem carnis & sanguinis sui communionem Christus sub panis & vini symbolis, in sacrosancta sua Cœna offert, & exhibet omnibus, qui eam rite celebrant iuxta legitimum eius institutum.
units.tr: We confess that the spiritual life which Christ bestows on us does not lie merely in this, that he quickens us by his Spirit, but that by the power of his Spirit he also makes us partakers of his life-giving flesh, by which participation we are fed unto eternal life. Therefore, when we speak of the communion which the faithful have with Christ, we understand that they partake of his flesh and blood no less than of his Spirit, so that they possess the whole Christ. For since Scripture plainly testifies that the flesh of Christ is truly food for us and his blood truly drink, it is certain that we must be nourished by these very things, if we seek life in Christ. Nor does the Apostle teach something small or common when he asserts that we are flesh of Christ's flesh and bones of his bones; rather he indicates a remarkable mystery of our communion with his body, which no one can explain in words worthy of its dignity. Moreover, nothing in these things is opposed by the fact that our Lord, taken up into heaven, has removed from us the local presence of his body, which is not required here. For however we, wandering in this mortality, are not enclosed or contained in the same place with him, yet the efficacy of his Spirit is not limited by any bounds, so that it cannot truly join together and gather into one those things which are separated by spaces of place. Therefore we acknowledge his Spirit to be the bond of our participation with him, but in such a way that by the substance of the flesh and blood of the Lord he truly feeds us unto immortality and quickens us by their participation. This communion of his flesh and blood, however, Christ offers and exhibits to all who celebrate his most holy Supper duly and according to its lawful institution, under the symbols of bread and wine.

units.la: SVBSCRIPTIO BVCERI, CAPITONIS ET ALIORVM.
units.tr: SUBSCRIPTION OF BUCER, CAPITO AND OTHERS.

units.la: HAnc sententiam optimorum fratrum & Symmyftarū notrorum G. Farelli, Io. Caluini, atque P. Vireti, vt orthodoxam amplectimur, neque vnquam sensi Christum Dominum in sacra Cœna præsente localiter aut vbique diffusum: verum & finitum habet corpus & in gloria minet cœlesti. In hac autem nihilominus est per verbum suum atque symbola: hic sistit se nobis cum ipso iam in cœlestia per fidem subleuatis, vt panis quem frangimus, & calix per quem Christum prædicamus, fit nobis verè corporis & sanguinis eius communicatio. Praeterea vt errorem in Ecclesia non ferendum agnoscimus, nuda & inania Christum statuere in sacra sua Cœna symbola, & non credere hic ipsum quoque corpus, & ipsum sanguinem Domini percipi, hoc est ipsum Dominum verum Deum & hominem.
units.tr: We embrace this opinion of our best brothers and fellow-ministers G. Farel, John Calvin and P. Viret as orthodox, and we have never held that Christ the Lord is present locally in the holy Supper, or diffused everywhere; rather he has a finite body and dwells in heavenly glory. Nevertheless, he is present in this Supper through his Word and the symbols; here he presents himself to us, we being raised with him now into heavenly things through faith, so that the bread which we break and the cup through which we proclaim Christ becomes for us a true communion of his body and blood. Moreover, we acknowledge that it is an error not to be tolerated in the Church to hold that Christ sets forth bare and empty symbols in his holy Supper, and not to believe that here the very body and the very blood of the Lord are also received, that is, the Lord himself, true God and man.

units.tr: ON THE WORD TRINITY AND THE WORD PERSON.

units.la: QVoniam voces istas Trinitatis & personarū plurimū Ecclesiae Christi commodare intelligimus, vt & vera Patris, Filij,& Spiritus S.distinctio clarius exprimatur, & contentiosis controuersiis melius occurratur ab his vsque adeo nō abhorremus, vt libenter eas amplexemur, siue ex aliis audiedae, siue à nobis vsurpandae sint: Itaque quod antea à nobis factum est, in posterum quoque operam daturos, quoad licebit recipimus, ne earum vsus in Ecclesiis nostris aboleatur. Nā neque ab iis, inter scribendum vel in Scripturae enarrationibus, in concionibus ad populum, abstinebimus ipsi, & alios docebimus ne superstitiose refugiant. Si quis autem praepostera religione teneatur, quominus eas vsurpare libenter audit, quanquam eiusmodi superstitionem nobis non probari testamur, cui corrigendae non sit defuturum nostrum studium: quia tamen non videtur nobis haec satis firma causa, cur vir alioqui pius & in eandem religionem nobis sensu consentiens repudietur, eius imperitiam hac in parte eatenus feremus, ne abiiciamus ipsum ab Ecclesia, aut tanquam male sentientem de fide notemus. Neque interim maligne inter pretabimur, si Bernensis Ecclesiae Pastores eos ad verbi ministerium admittere non sustineant, quos compererint voces istas aspernari.
units.tr: Since we understand that these words of the Trinity and of the persons are of great use to the Church of Christ, both so that the true distinction of Father, Son and Holy Spirit may be expressed more clearly and so that contentious disputes may be better met, we are so far from disliking them that we gladly embrace them, whether they are to be heard from others or to be used by ourselves. Accordingly, we accept, as far as it is permitted, that what we have done before we shall also continue to do in future, so that their use is not abolished in our churches. For we ourselves will not abstain from them in writing, in the explanation of Scripture, or in sermons to the people, and we will teach others not to shun them superstitiously. If anyone, however, is held back by a misguided scruple from gladly using them, although we testify that we do not approve of such superstition, and our zeal will not be lacking to correct it, nevertheless, since this does not seem to us a sufficiently firm reason why a man otherwise pious and agreeing with us in sentiment on the same religion should be rejected, we will bear with his lack of skill in this respect, so far as this goes, so that we do not cast him out of the Church or mark him as holding wrong opinions about the faith. Nor in the meantime will we interpret it maliciously if the pastors of the Church of Bern do not allow to the ministry of the Word those whom they have found to despise these words.

units.la: QVOD CALVINVS IN CONFESSIONE oblata Laufannae Christum Iehoua appellarit, declaratur.
units.tr: Why Calvin, in the confession presented at Lausanne, called Christ Jehovah, is explained.

units.la: QVod Christū esse Iehoua asserimus, qui à seipso semper habuit vt esset: ea particula quoniam non nihil obscura quibusdam visa est, ne quis offendatur quo sensu à nobis posita sit, breuiter indicabimus. Cum de Christi diuinitate sermo est, quae Dei propria sunt iure etiam illi deferuntur, quia tum in vnius Dei essentiam respicitur, praeterita distinctionis mentione: quae est inter Patrem & Filium, qua ratione vera dicitur Christū esse Deum vnicum & aeternum à seipso existentem. Neque huic sententiae stud obstat quod vere quoque ab Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus est traditum: Verbum seu Filium Dei à Patre esse etiam secundum aeternam suam essentiam. Quin haec personarum notatio locum habet vbi Patris & Filij distinctio commemoratur. Nomen autem Iehoua est diuinitatis elogium, quod non minus Patrem, Spiritum, quàm Filium complectitur. Sic Cyrillus qui sapiens Patrem Filij principium vocare solet, pro ingenti tamen
units.tr: That we assert Christ to be Jehovah, who has always had from himself that he is, we will briefly explain, so that no one is offended by the sense in which we have put it, since this particle has seemed somewhat obscure to some people. When we speak of Christ's divinity, those things that are proper to God are rightly ascribed to him as well, because the reference then is to the one essence of God, with no mention of the distinction between the Father and the Son. In this sense it is truly said that Christ is the one and eternal God, existing from himself. Nor does it stand in the way of this view that the ecclesiastical writers have also truly handed down that the Word or Son of God is from the Father even according to his eternal essence. Indeed, this designation of the persons applies where the distinction between Father and Son is mentioned. But the name Jehovah is a designation of divinity, which embraces the Father and the Spirit no less than the Son.

units.la: O.j absurdo ducit dialogo 3. de Trinitate, nisi Filius à seipso vitam & immortalitatem habere credatur. Idem docet, si ineffabili natu ræ proprium est vt ex seipsa sit, in Filium id iure cōpetere. Quin etiam lib. 1 hesauri 19. ratiocinatur Patrem à seipso nihil habere, nisi Filius etiam à seipso habeat. Nec quæquam mouere debet, quod paulo ante personarum notitiam explicado diximus nos illic tradituros, quæ ad Christum peculiariter attineant. Satis enim constat non aliò spectare illam distinctionem quàm ad in carnationis mysterium, cuius specialis est ratio à Trinitatis discretione. Alioqui nec Iehoua ipsidem dicendus fuisset, cùm diuinitatem seorsum à Patre non habeat.
units.tr: Thus Cyril, who is accustomed to call the Father the principle of the Son, nevertheless, in his third dialogue on the Trinity, regards it as a great absurdity unless the Son is believed to have life and immortality from himself. He teaches the same thing: if it is proper to the ineffable nature that it is from itself, this rightly belongs to the Son. Indeed, in the first book of his Thesaurus, chapter 19, he reasons that the Father has nothing from himself unless the Son also has it from himself. Nor should anything disturb us because, a little earlier, when explaining the knowledge of the persons, we said that we would there set out what pertains particularly to Christ. For it is well established that that distinction looks only to the mystery of the incarnation, whose particular reason differs from the distinction within the Trinity. Otherwise, he would not even have been rightly called Jehovah, since he does not have divinity apart from the Father.

units.la: RESPONSVM GENEVENSIS ECCLESIAE contra Stancarum.
units.tr: THE RESPONSE OF THE CHURCH OF GENEVA against Stancarus.

units.la: ANtehac rogati à fratribus Polonis, quomodo sit Christus Mediator, an scilicet, vt est Deus & homo, an vero humanę tantum naturæ respectu, breuiter & tamen dilucide senten tiam nostram exposuimus, in quo veritas ipsa nos coegit damnare & refutare Stancari commentum. Postea impulit nos iusta necessitas ad edendum illud responsum, non tam odio Stancari, vel vt eum grauaremus inuidia, quàm vt effugeremus sinistros quosdam rumores: vt facile est in rebus turbatis lucem tenebris inuolui. Porrò nullam querimoniæ causam habet Stancarus, si secum expendit, quàm atrociter vexauerit Philippum Melanchthonem, cuius memoria in pretio & honore esse debet apud omnes bonos. Cerre omni s modestiæ & humanitatis oblitus est, cū hominem tam probatæ pietatis, quàm de Ecclesia bene meriti atrocibus contumiis lacerauit: vt subinde Arrianos & hæreticum vocare non dubitet. Hæc inteperies nisi grauiter nos offenderet, ingrati essemus & Deo, & fideli eius seruo. Si pergat Stacarus sui esse similis, eadem expectanda est nobis merces, neque tamen cōui tiando quicquam noslædet: quin potius sibi plus asperget decoris. Deum tamen supplicitèr rogamus, vt Spiritu mansuetudinis tandem ipsum flectat ac frænet ad piam docilitatem. Ipsum quę horramur, vt seipsum colligere incipiat neque ita posthac indulgeat suæ iracundiæ & violentiæ. Quòd si tantopere eum oblestant paradoxa, quæ ædificationem Ecclesiæ peruertunt, sal tem ingenio suo temperare discat, & vehementiam illam, in qua nimius est frænare. Quòd ad rem ipsam spectat, videndum primum quid significet nomen Mediatoris. Nam certè λόγος æternus iam ab initio ante lapsum Adæ, & alienationem ac dissidium humani generis à Deo, fuit Mediator. Atque hoc sen-su, nisi fallimur, vocatur à Paulo primogenitus omnis creaturę. Et Ioannes cùm asserit in ipso fuisse vitam, modum communicationis otendit, quo ex fonte alioquin abscondito manauit ad homines Dei gratia. Ergo quatenus integro adhuc rerum statu caput Angelorum & hominum fuit Christus, iure censetur Mediator, qualem nunc quoque electi Angeli experiuntur & agnoscunt. Defectio autem hominis fecit, vt expiatione opus esset ad nos Deo reconciliandos. Itaque considerandus est Christus Mediator cum sacrificio suo, quo placauit iram Dei, vt in spem nos beatæ vitæ, à qua excideramus, restitueret. Mediatore vero esse docemus, non vnius tantùm naturæ respectu, sed quatenus Deus est manifestatus in carne. Quæ fides in rationibus firmis & validis fundata est, quas etsi aliqua ex parte explicuimus in prio te nostro responso, hic tamen iterum summam colligere expedit.
units.tr: Earlier, when the brothers from Poland asked us how Christ is Mediator, namely whether as he is God and man, or only with respect to his human nature, we briefly but clearly set out our view. In doing so, truth itself compelled us to condemn and refute the fiction of Stancarus. Afterwards, a just necessity drove us to publish this response, not so much out of hatred for Stancarus, or to load him with odium, but in order to escape certain sinister rumours, since in troubled times it is easy for light to be wrapped in darkness. Moreover, Stancarus has no cause for complaint if he considers how savagely he has assailed Philip Melanchthon, whose memory ought to be held in honour by all good people. He has entirely forgotten all moderation and humanity in tearing with savage insults a man of such proven piety, who has deserved so well of the Church, so that he does not hesitate from time to time to call him an Arian and a heretic. Had this intemperance not gravely offended us, we would be ungrateful both to God and to his faithful servant. If Stancarus continues to be like himself, we must expect the same reward, yet by reviling us he will harm us in nothing; rather, he will only heap more disgrace upon himself. Nevertheless, we earnestly beseech God to bend him at last, by the Spirit of gentleness, and to curb him into pious teachableness. We also pray that he may begin to gather himself together and no longer give way so readily to his anger and violence. But if the paradoxes which overturn the building up of the Church so greatly delight him, at least let him learn to temper his talent and to restrain that vehemence in which he is excessive. As to the matter itself, we must first consider what the name Mediator signifies. For certainly the eternal Word [λόγος] was already Mediator from the beginning, before the fall of Adam and the alienation and estrangement of the human race from God. And in this sense, unless we are mistaken, he is called by Paul the firstborn of every creature. And when John asserts that life was in him, he shows the manner of communication by which the grace of God otherwise flowed from a hidden source to men. Therefore, insofar as Christ was still the head of angels and men in the unimpaired state of things, he is rightly regarded as Mediator, such as the elect angels now also experience and acknowledge him to be. But the defection of man made it necessary for us to be reconciled to God by expiation. Thus Christ is to be considered as Mediator with his sacrifice, by which he appeased the wrath of God, so as to restore us to the hope of the blessed life from which we had fallen. We teach, moreover, that he is Mediator not only with respect to one nature, but insofar as God has been manifested in the flesh. This faith is founded on firm and solid reasons, which, although we explained them in part in our previous response, it is nevertheless useful to gather up again here in summary.

units.la: Primò constat non esse credendum nisi in Deum. Atqui iubet Christus discipulis, in se credere, quomodo? vel qua ratione? Nempe, vt continuò post sequitur, non modo quia est veritas & vita, sed quia est via ad Patrem. Quòd si in Christum Mediatorem credendum est, certè munus hoc completitur duas naturas: deinde cùm Christus summum imperium obtineat & in cælo & in terra, vt est Mediator, quod minimè quadraret soli humanæ naturæ, colligimus nomen Mediatoris, non proprie nisi toti personæ tribui. Nam certè omnes sicti ad eius tribunal (quia scriptum est: mihi flectetur omne genu) non cadit in humanam naturam, & tamen accommodatur à Paulo ad personam Mediatoris. Si excipitur Regnum fuisse eidatum à Patre, respondemus quanuis nihil in diuinitatem nouû conferri possit, nihil tamen esse absurdi, si Christus totius personæ respectu augeri & ornari dicitur. Et certè idem Deus qui iurat coram se flectendum esse omne genu, negat etiam se daturum gloriam suam alteri. Separatum igitur hoc accipere homo non potuit, vt esset mundi iudex, idque aperte sonant Pauli verba. Cui enim dicit esse datum illud summum nomen, nisi Dei Filio, qui cùm esset Patri æqualis, scipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accepta? videmus vt totam personam, quæ constat duabus naturis, Paulus nobis statuit ante oculos. Tertia ratio. Proprium est Mediatoris Deo nos coniungere, cùm id nemo præstare queat, nisi qui vnum est cum Deo; nemo etiam idoneus est ad obeundum munus Mediatoris, nisi qui homo est, ac simul Deus. Minor autem probatur ex Christi verbis: vt vnum sint nobiscum, sicut tu Pater & ego vnum sumus. Eodem pertinet quod alibi dicit: sicut Pater habet vitam in semetipso, ita & Filio dedit vitam habere in semetipso. Nec repugnat Dei nomen, quominus toti personæ hoc rite applicetur, quia nihil minus consentaneum est quàm in carne residere vitâ, quæ non nisi in Deo quærenda est. Quarta ratio. Sicuti verò ratiocinatur Apostolus Christum vt nobis esset frater, oportuisse fieri partici pem carnis nostrae & sanguinis: ita ex opposito recte colligitur, vt nos ad Patrem vsque reuocheret, oportuit prius Deum esse. Quis enim finis est nostrae adoptionis quam per ipsum consequi mur, nisi tandem participes simus diuinae naturae, sicut testatur Petrus? Id autem quomodo praestaret, si subsisteret infra ordinem Angelorum? Nec vero in ipsum insiti efficimur Filij Dei alia ratione, nisi quatenus nobis datus est Mediator. Atqui hinc pendet adoptionis gratia, quia in nos transfert, quod habet ipse naturaliter. Itaque ad implendas Mediatoris partes non sufficeret, nisi esset vnigenitus Dei Filius. Ac proinde Apostolus ad probandum eius Sacerdotium, testimonio hoc vtitur: Tu es Filius meus, ego hodie genui te. Vnde probe conficitur, si inseparabilis est Filij dignitas a Sacerdotio, non aliter idoneum esse Mediatorem, nisi quia ex Deo genitus. Nec vero absque Diuinitatis respectu, censeri potest Dei Filius. Ideoque in Sacerdotij honore comprehenditur & diuina natura. Quod ipsum confirmat Paulus, vbi dicit fuisse de claratum Filium Dei in virtute. Nam cum elogio illo, definiat Mediatoris personam, duas certe simul naturas comprehendit. Iam quod asserit alibi Christus, Ego in Patre, & Pater in me, non potest de sola natura humana praedicari. Atqui illic ad viuum exprimitur imago Mediatoris. Imo totum Ioannis Euangelium eiusmodi est sententiis refertum, vbi quae sibi vendicat Christus, alteri naturae non conueniunt, sed respiciunt in totam personam. Ac se omnibus nodis expediet quisquis tenebit Christi mentem, quia videbit, nefas esse, quae vtrique naturae communia sunt elogia, separatim vel distincte ad alteram trahere. Neque tamen interea quaecunque annexa sunt Mediatoris officio, vel eius sunt partes, vtrique naturae communia facimus. Quando enim sine morte & sanguinis effusione non peragitur expiatio, Mediatorem oportuit mori. Hoc fatemur peculiare esse humanitati: sed quoniam aliud est mors, aliud effectus mortis, recociliatio quae morte peracta est, perperam tribuitur soli humanae naturae. Ideo qui dicit Apostolus, Christum per Spiritum obtulisse seipsum, qua voce admonet non considerandum esse simpliciter, vt homine, vt efficacia & fructus mortis eius nobis pateat. Similiter iustitia nobis acquirere sua obedientia, & ita fieri Patris seruum, Mediatoris proprium fuit: quamen perperam ascriberetur diuinae naturae, sed ipsa iustitiae acquisitio, vim sua nihilominus a diuina natura mutuatur. Vtrunque vero aperte coniungitur in ipso complexu, cum dicit Christus, pro his sanctifico meipsum. Nam cum sanctificari carni conueniat, sanctificare autem Deo, vtrunque membrum, non nisi in tota persona reperitur. Ex opposito etiam fatemur quaedam sic esse diuinitati propria in ipso Mediatore, vt ad
units.tr: First, it is established that one must believe only in God. But Christ bids his disciples to believe in himself: how, or on what ground? Namely, as follows immediately after, not only because he is the truth and the life, but because he is the way to the Father. If we must believe in Christ as Mediator, then certainly this office is fulfilled in both natures. Next, since Christ holds supreme authority both in heaven and on earth, as Mediator, which would by no means fit the human nature alone, we conclude that the name of Mediator is not properly ascribed except to the whole person. For certainly every knee shall bow before his tribunal (because it is written: to me every knee shall bow), which does not fall to the human nature, and yet Paul applies it to the person of the Mediator. If it is objected that the kingdom was given to him by the Father, we reply that although nothing new can be conferred upon the divinity, there is nothing absurd in saying that Christ is increased and adorned with respect to the whole person. And certainly the same God who swears that every knee shall bow before him also declares that he will not give his glory to another. Man therefore could not understand this as separate, that he should be judge of the world, and Paul's words plainly sound this. For to whom does he say that that supreme name was given, except to the Son of God, who, being equal to the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? We see that Paul sets before our eyes the whole person, which consists of two natures. A third reason: it is proper to the Mediator to join us to God, since no one can do this except one who is one with God; nor is anyone fit to discharge the office of Mediator except one who is man and at the same time God. The minor premise is proved from the words of Christ: that they may be one in us, as you, Father, and I are one. To the same point belongs what he says elsewhere: as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself. Nor does the name of God stand in the way of this being rightly applied to the whole person, because nothing is less consistent than that life should reside in the flesh, which is only to be sought in God. A fourth reason: just as the Apostle reasons that Christ, to be our brother, had to become a partaker of our flesh and blood, so conversely it is rightly concluded that, to bring us back to the Father, he had first to be God. For what is the end of our adoption, which we obtain through him, if not that at last we become partakers of the divine nature, as Peter testifies? But how would he accomplish this if he stood below the order of the angels? Nor are we engrafted into him and made sons of God by any other way than insofar as the Mediator has been given to us. Yet the grace of adoption depends on this, because he transfers to us what he has by nature. Therefore, to fulfil the parts of the Mediator it would not suffice unless he were the only-begotten Son of God. And accordingly the Apostle, to prove his priesthood, uses this testimony: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Hence it is clearly established that, since the dignity of the Son is inseparable from the priesthood, he is a fit Mediator in no other way than because he is begotten of God. Nor indeed can he be regarded as the Son of God without regard to his divinity. Therefore the divine nature is also included in the honour of the priesthood. Paul confirms this very thing when he says that the Son of God was declared in power. For with that designation he defines the person of the Mediator, and so he certainly comprehends both natures at once. Now, what Christ asserts elsewhere, I am in the Father and the Father in me, cannot be said of the human nature alone. Yet there the image of the Mediator is expressed to the life. Indeed, the whole Gospel of John is filled with such sayings, in which the things Christ claims for himself do not belong to the other nature but refer to the whole person. And whoever holds to the mind of Christ will untie all these knots, because he will see that it is wrong to draw separately or distinctly to one nature those attributes which are common to both. Yet meanwhile we do not make common to both natures whatever is attached to the office of Mediator or is part of it. For since expiation is not accomplished without death and the shedding of blood, the Mediator had to die. We confess that this is peculiar to the humanity; but since death is one thing and the effect of death another, the reconciliation which was accomplished by death is wrongly ascribed to the human nature alone. Therefore when the Apostle says that Christ offered himself through the Spirit, by this word he warns that we are not to consider him simply as man, so that the efficacy and fruit of his death may be laid open to us. Similarly, to acquire righteousness for us by his obedience, and so to become the servant of the Father, was proper to the Mediator; yet this would be wrongly ascribed to the divine nature, but the very acquisition of righteousness nonetheless borrows its power from the divine nature. Both, moreover, are plainly joined together in the one complex when Christ says: for them I sanctify myself. For since to be sanctified belongs to the flesh, and to sanctify belongs to God, both members are found only in the whole person. Conversely, we also confess that some things are so proper to the divinity in the Mediator himself, that

units.la: Heb.9.14 vt ad humanam naturam transferri non debeant, nisi per idiomatum communicationem. Dicit alibi Christus, Ego animam meam à me ipso pono, loquitur vt mediator: neque tamen vt homo, quia arbitrium vitæ & mortis nullus à seipso habet, præter vnū Deum, & hoc est satis perspicuum. Longè etiam fallitur in illo Pauli loco, Vnus est Deus, & vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, Homo Iesus Christus, quia non alio consilio positum est hominis nomen, quàm vt nobis familiaris esset ad Patrem accessus: neque tamen negamus sub Patre totam Deitatem comprehendi & Deum vnius essentiæ. Nūc apparet ad officium Mediatoris requiri, vtriusque naturæ coniunctionem: neque tamen quæcunque ad Mediatoris personam spectant, promiscuè ad vtrancque naturam trahenda esse: quod argumentum plenius exequitur Caluinus libro 2. Institutionum cap. 14. Quod ab aduersa parte obiicitur absurdum, nullum est: Nempe cùm Mediator sit inter Deum & homines, Christum fore Deo inferiorem respectu Deitatis, si ad cum Mediatoris nomen extenditur. Nam dum ita locatur Christus in medio gradu, non agitur de eius essentia, nec subtiliter disputatur quid sit, sed ad Dei consilium, quod veteres œconomiam aut dispensationem vocarunt, attendere cōuenit. Si quæratur de essētia, scimus in Deo nihil esse minus & maius. Sed quia pro infirmitatis nostræ captu, apparuit æternus Dei Filius, vt medius esset inter nos & Deum, in ipsa Mediatoris persona & officio, appositè ad regulam pietatis dicitur Patre inferior. Hoc sensu non dubitant Prophetæ conuerrere nomen Iehouæ cum titulo Angeli, quemadmodum apud Ofeam dicitur cap. 12. Præualuit Iacob Angelo: mox subiicitur, Iehoua Deus exercituum, Iehoua memoriale eius. Apud Malachiam paulò aliter, Veniet Adonai, quem quæritis in templum suum, & Angelus fœderis, quem expetitis. Eodem tamen recidit sensus, quando Dei legato & Mediatori non modò defertur summum imperium, sed asseritur etiam diuina Maiestas, vbi dicitur in templum suū venturus. Quod deinde obiicitur, si commune est diuinitati Mediatoris officium, necesse est fore, vt apud seipsum Christus intercedat, facile diluitur: quia etsi roget Christus in Mediatoris persona, id tamen peculiari modo respicit humanam naturam. Quanquam hic rursus sensus nostros ad Dei consilium dirigere necesse est. Non insectamur quidem neque præcisè reiicimus illud Augustini, Mediatorem apud Filiū & Spiritū sanctum intercedere, vt cum Deo redeamus in gratiam, à quo sumus alienati. Nam certè vnica & simplex Dei essentia in tribus personis cōsistit. Sed merito apud nos pluris est ratio loquendi, quam dictauit cœlestis ille Magister. Multis quidem locis Deitatem suam Christus extollit, nusquam tamen docet se à secunda persona na vel tertia fuisse missum. Nihilo etiam magis fe apud Spiritu intercedere, sed apud Patrem. Itaque nihil tutius est, quam prophanis argutiis & speculationibus valere iussis, mentes nostras defixas tenere in illa admirabili dispensatione, in qua dicitur Patrem Filium vnigenitum miffife, vt in eo nobis effet propitius, & eius Aduocati patrocinio exorabilis. Imo cum barbaries grassata est in toto mundo, vulgare tamen illud dictum, opera Trinitatis esse indiuisa, quia per fe ducius erat, interposita restrictione correctum vel mitigatum fuit: nempe cum addita fuit particula intrinsecus. Nos vero ruditatis nostrae conscij, extrinseca operatione contenti fumus, qua fe Deus ad exiguum intelligentiae modulum attemperat. Ita fine offensione Christus medius locabitur inter nos & Patrem. Neque tamen quicquam decedit ex immen fa eius gloria, tametsi sub velo humanitatis (obscurius autem) cernatur, donec completo Mediatoris cursu, Patri subiiciatur Christus in natura humana, & liquido in fe vel immediate refulgeat diuina eius effentia & maiestas. Haec sobrietas, fi non arrideat curiosis hominibus, sedandis tamen modestis & piis moribus satis superque erit. Nemo quidem quantuuis proteruus rixator, aliud nobis exprobrare poterit, qua ob mysterij reuerentia, quae laudi ducebat est potius quam vitio, simplicitati nos studere. Nunc discutere promptum est, quae obtendit Stancarus, in sententiae fuq confirmationem. Definitione fumi posse dicit ex loco Pauli, Mediator vnius non est, Deus autem vnus est. Atqui fi prudenter expenderet contextu, videret illic conferri Gentes cu Iudaeis, quod scilicet Christus non tantu olim Iudaeos reconciliarit Deo, sed nuc quoq; Getes vocet in focitate eiusdem gratiae. Expositio enim qua adducit, frigida est, atque insipida, sicut nec firmu est, quod adiungit, no opus esse Mediatore nisi vbi est diffidiu. Ostendimus enim nuper electos Angelos Deo per Christu vniri, qui tamen nunqua discordes fuerunt. Sed quia in eo non vertitur cardo quaestionis: fateor Christum nobis proponi, & debere a nobis suscipi Mediatorem, quatenus Deum nobis suo sacrificio placauit. Caeterum quod nomen Deitatis accipit Stancarus, vt probet tres personas fuisse offensas, iterum regero, male & inscite ab eo negligi dispensationis mysterium, quod Scriptura vbique commendat. Ac mirum est eum non attendere ad manifesta quae citatteftimonia. Quod fi proprie loquedo, & vsitato Scripturae more, Mediator est Christus inter nos & Deum Patrem, arguta illa speculatio nihil aliud qua inuoluit, & obscurat, quod effet aliofqui perspicuum. Longe etiam fallitur in illo Pauli loco, Vnus est Deus, & vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, Homo Iesus Christus, quia non alio consilio positu est hominis nomen, quam vt nobis familiaris effet ad Patrem accessus: neq; tamen negamus sub
units.tr: Heb.9.14 ought not to be transferred to the human nature, except through the communication of properties. Christ says elsewhere, "I lay down my life of myself" (John 10:18). He speaks here as Mediator, and not as man, since no one has the power of life and death from himself except the one God. This is clear enough. Those who cite Paul's words, "There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. 2:5), are also badly mistaken, because the name of man was given for no other purpose than to make access to the Father familiar to us. Yet we do not deny that the whole Deity is comprehended under the Father, and that God is of one essence. It now appears that the office of Mediator requires the joining of both natures. Yet not everything that belongs to the person of the Mediator is to be drawn indiscriminately to either nature. Calvin works out this argument more fully in book 2 of the Institutes, chapter 14. The absurdity that the opposing side objects is no absurdity at all. Since the Mediator stands between God and men, Christ would be inferior to God with respect to his Deity, if the name of Mediator were extended to him in that sense. For when Christ is placed in the middle rank in this way, the question is not about his essence, nor is it subtly debated what he is. Rather, we should attend to the counsel of God, which the ancients called the economy or dispensation. If we ask about essence, we know that in God there is nothing less or greater. But because, according to the measure of our weakness, the eternal Son of God appeared to be the mediator between us and God, in the very person and office of the Mediator he is rightly called inferior to the Father, as the rule of godliness requires. In this sense the prophets do not hesitate to join the name Jehovah with the title of Angel, as in Hosea, chapter 12: "He prevailed over the Angel; and soon after it is added, Jehovah God of hosts, Jehovah is his memorial" (Hos. 12:4–5). In Malachi the wording is somewhat different: "The Lord (Adonai), whom you seek, will come into his temple, and the Angel of the covenant, whom you desire" (Mal. 3:1). Yet the sense comes to the same thing, when not only the supreme power is granted to the envoy of God and Mediator, but also the divine Majesty is asserted, where it is said that he will come into his temple. As for the further objection that, if the office of Mediator is common to the Deity, it must follow that Christ intercedes before himself, this is easily answered. Although Christ asks as Mediator in his person, he nevertheless looks to his human nature in a peculiar way. Yet here again we must direct our senses to the counsel of God. We do not indeed attack, nor do we strictly reject, Augustine's saying that the Mediator intercedes before the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that we may return into favour with God, from whom we have been alienated. For certainly the one and simple essence of God subsists in three persons. But among us the manner of speaking that the heavenly Teacher has dictated carries more weight. In many places Christ exalts his own Deity, yet nowhere does he teach that he was sent by the second or third person. Nor does he intercede before the Spirit, but before the Father. Therefore nothing is safer than to dismiss profane subtleties and speculations, and to keep our minds fixed on that admirable dispensation in which the Father is said to have sent his only-begotten Son, so that in him he might be propitious to us and be placated by the patronage of his Advocate. Indeed, although barbarism has spread through the whole world, the common saying that the works of the Trinity are undivided, because it was taken too absolutely, was corrected or softened by an added restriction, namely by the addition of the particle "inwardly." But we, aware of our own rudeness, are content with the outward operation, by which God adapts himself to the small measure of our understanding. Thus Christ will be placed without offence as the middle between us and the Father. Nor does anything detract from his immense glory, although he is seen under the veil of humanity (and somewhat obscurely), until, when the course of the Mediator is complete, Christ in his human nature is made subject to the Father, and his divine essence and majesty shine forth clearly in himself, immediately. This sobriety, if it does not please curious men, will nevertheless be more than enough to calm modest and pious minds. No stubborn wrangler, however contentious, will be able to reproach us with anything other than that we strive for simplicity out of reverence for the mystery, which is a matter for praise rather than blame. Now it is easy to examine what Stancarus puts forward to confirm his opinion. He says that a definition can be drawn from Paul's text: "The Mediator is not of one, but God is one" (Gal. 3:20). Yet if he weighed the context more carefully, he would see that Paul there compares the Gentiles with the Jews, since Christ not only once reconciled the Jews to God but now also calls the Gentiles into fellowship of the same grace. For the exposition he adduces is cold and insipid, just as what he adds is not firm, namely that there is no need for a Mediator except where there is discord. For we have shown recently that the elect angels are united to God through Christ, although they were never at odds. But since the hinge of the question does not turn on this, I grant that Christ is set before us, and that we must receive him as Mediator, insofar as by his sacrifice he has placated God for us. As for the fact that Stancarus takes the name of Deity so as to prove that three persons were offended, I repeat again that he has badly and unskilfully neglected the mystery of the dispensation, which Scripture everywhere commends. And it is strange that he does not attend to the plain testimonies that are cited. But if, speaking properly and in the customary manner of Scripture, Christ is the Mediator between us and God the Father, that subtle speculation accomplishes nothing except to wrap up and obscure what would otherwise be plain. Those who cite Paul's words, "There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus," are also greatly mistaken, because the name of man was given for no other purpose than to make access to the Father familiar to us. Yet we do not deny that under the Father

units.la: Patrs Patre comprehendi totam Deitatem, & Deum vnius essentiae in tribus personis, fuisse placatum. Sed profundo illo & incomprehensibili arcano omisso, tantum reputamus illud quod didicimus ex Scriptura & sacro Christi ore. Neque enim haec magis inter se pugnant, λόγος & aeternum Dei Filium Patri esse aequalem & Mediatorem esse thirlotem Patre, quàm altera duo, λόγος per se & seorsum efficere personam in diuinis, & tamen vnam Christi & Mediatoris personam constitui ex duabus naturis. Ac inscite argumentatur Stancarus. Si Christus in duabus naturis Mediator, est minor Patre, ergo secundum vtramque naturam, quando paulo antea docuimus, quòd vere atque apte competit in totum complexum non debere distrahi ad naturas, sicut medius hic gradus, quem tenet Christus redemptor, nihil derogat prorsus diuinae eius essentiae. Rationes quas adducit ex officio Mediatoris, nihilo plus habent momenti, quia ducuntur à parte ad totum. Dedit se Christus pretium redemptionis: reconciliauit omnia in cruce carnis suae: Agnus est, qui tollit peccata mundi: Datus est propitiator per fidem in sanguine eius. Nempe etiam haec omnia praestitit secundum humanam naturam, non tamen inde conficitur, eius tantum respectu esse Mediatore, quia expiatione & sacrificio non absoluit Christus omnes officij sui numeros. Quid enim est mortem vincere? quid est resurgere in virtute Spiritus, & vitam recipere à seipso? quid est nos Deo vnire? & vnum esse cum Deo? Haec certe extra Deitatem non reperiuntur in humana Christi natura. Et tamen in rationem veniunt, vbi de Mediatoris officio agitur. Atque vtinam animaduertat Stancarus ad verba, quae recitat, Deum non pepercisse vnigenito Filio. Neque enim si in vtraque natura Filius est, id habet à sua humanitate. Iam si Dei nomen tres personas signat, & nimis pertinacit er vrget, sequitur Christum tam suum quam Spiritus sancti Filium. Haec sola antithesis, si eam referenter exdendere non grauetur Stancarus, cum à multis nodis expediet: Nempe duin Mediator se cum patre confert, à quo missus est, atque etiam vbi Paulus Deum in carne manifestatum vocat, cò filium eius est, Mediatorem nobis statuere: quem & mox subiicit iustificatum esse in Spiritu, apparuisse Angelis, praedicatum fuisse Gentibus & receptum in gloriam. Hinc magis petenda erat simplex & genuina definitio. Ide n plane elicitur ex 3. ad Colossenses capite, vbi reconciliatio per carnem ita describitur, vt Diuinitas locum suum retineat in primatu & plenitudine. Aut ergo probet Stancarus Christum sedere ad Patris dexteram, vt nos Spiritus virtute defendat ac tueatur, Angelis commendet salutis nostrae custodiam, Diabolum & totum mundum subiicit, non esse ex officio Mediatoris, aut agnoscat ex sacrificio ... & intercessione se perperam inferre, Mediatorem non esse Dei Filium, nisi quatenus homo est. Ante ostendimus cur Paulus de Mediatore disserens, diserte adscribat nomen hominis, nempe vt excusso metu, blandè nos ad eum inuitet. Neque enim subtiliter disputat de essentia, sed fiduciæ materiam suppeditat, ne dubitemus ad eum confugere, qui frater noster est. Miramur autem quo prætextu in sensum suum torqueat quod ante demon strauimus optime nobis suffragari, Christum cum in forma Dei esset, seipsum exinaniuisse. Hæc, inquit, Regula est soluendæ quæstionis: sit sane ita, nam libenter amplectimur. Sed si vnigenitus Dei Filius, qui Patri æqualis erat seipsum exinaniuit, certe in duabus naturis est Mediator: ac ille idem, qui factus est obediens vsque ad mortem, quæ ctus est accepto nomine super omne nomen, vbi omnis lingua confiteatur, quod sit in gloria Dei Patris. Porrò qualis hæc sit gloria & quomodo intelligi debeat, potius respondeat ipse Christus quàm nos. Pater, inquit, glorifica Filium ea gloria quam habui apud te ab initio, ante mundi creationem. Fatebitur profecto Stancarus præposterum fore votum, si carnem solam postulet, Christus ornari & illustrari æterna Dei gloria: quod si hoc nonnisi toti persona aptatur, hinc rite colligere licet, quum citauit locum, non alio referri posse. Dum ad Patres ventum est, speciosos quidem colores inducit, vt eos habeat caussæ suæ patronos ac suffragatores. Verum si extra contentionem quæritur, quid senserit Augustinus, nulla nobis cum eo est dissensio. Fatemur quidem compluribus locis, Christum ab hoc pio Doctore fieri Mediatorem, quatenus homo. Agnoscimus etiam eius verba, tam ex libro 10. de Ciuit. Dei, quàm ex aliis. In forma serui est sacerdos & idem sacrificium, in hac se obtulit, in hac oblatus est, secundum hanc Mediator est. Sed interea non dissimulat necessario requiri ad munus Mediatoris, vt sit etiam Deus, vt libro 1. Confessionum cap. penultimo, vt Mediator esset, oportuit aliquid simile habere Deo, aliquid hominibus, ne in vtroque hominibus similis, longe abesset à Deo, aut in vtroque Deo similis, longe abesset ab hominibus: atque ita Mediator non esset. Similiter lib. 9. de Ciuit. Dei cap. 10. Si omnes homines miseri, quarendus est medius, qui non solum homo, verum & Deus sit, vt homines ex mortali miseria ad beatam immortalitatem traducat beata eius mortalitas. Item in Psal. 134, In illa magna separatione missus est Mediator. Non poteras ad Deum homo, Deus factus est homo. Si homo solum esset, hoc sequendo quod es, nunquam peruenires: si Deus solum esset, non comprehendendo, quod non es, nunquam peruenires. Libro autem de ouibus, Non Mediator homo præter Deitatem, nec Mediator Deus præter humanitatem. Ecce Mediator, Diuinitas sine humanitate non est mediatrix, Humanitas sine diuinitate non est mediatrix. Sed inter Diuinitatem solam & Humanitatem solam, Mediatrix est Diuina humanitas Christi, & humana Christi Diuinitas. Non negamus etiam Cyrillum saepe ad naturam humanam referre, quod Christus sit Mediator, ne scilicet obnoxiam Deitatem faciat subiectioni, quod Arriani vigebant. Verum alibi dexter est ac fidus dictorum suorum interpres Dialogo 2 de Trinitate, Mediator hac ratione intelligitur, quia ostendit in seipso collatas & vnitas Deitatem, & humanitatem. Nam Deo est cognatus, quandoquidem ex eo est, ac in eo, nobis quoque cognatus, quia ex nobis & in nobis. Vides vt ex duabus naturis constituat Mediatorem, & earum vnionem ad hoc munus necessario flagitet. Nec diuersa est Chrysostomi ratio. Etsi enim Mediatorem quaeri vult in humana natura, negat tamen intercessionem fore legitimam, nisi accedat & diuinitas. Ita in 2. cap. prioris ad Timot. Mediator vtrisque debet coniungi, quorum Mediator est. Id quippe Mediatoris proprium, fieri amborum participem inter quos se interponit. Nisi igitur consors sit paternae naturae Christus, Mediator profecto non est. Ideo in Homilia de Ascensione tradit, non Angelum vel Archangelum, sed ipsum Dei Filium deprecari. Et statim additur expositio, quod se medium iniecerit Christus, vtran que sonando naturam. In eandem quoque sententiam Ambrosius locum Pauli enarrans, Quia vnus est Pater, non persona, sed indifferenti natura, vt arbiter esset Dei & hominum Filius Dei, assumpta carne homo natus est, vt Mediator esset Dei & hominum, homo & hiiius. Id non est fine Diuinitate, quia in Deo homo erat, & Deus in homine: & vt ex vtroque esset Mediator, & vtrunque reconciliaret. In se primum haec fecit, neque enim poterat, vnitate fructi Mediator fernari. Pluribus id persequi necesse non est, modo semel admoniti sint lectores, quoties occurrit apud veteres hoc loquendi genus, Christum in carne esse Mediatorem, si exclusive accipitur, depravari eorum germanum sensum. De quaestione proposita liberè & clarè ita respondendum censuimus. Ac maluimus quidem omisso Stancaro, rei summam placidè explicare, sed refutationem inuitis ipse extorsit. Interea tamen in responso nostro nulla amarulentia, nulla contentio, vel pugnandi cupiditas pios, & humanos lectores offendet.
units.tr: Stancarus claims that the whole Deity is comprehended in the Father, and that God, one in essence in three persons, was appeased. But setting aside that deep and incomprehensible mystery, we consider only what we have learned from Scripture and from Christ's own mouth. For these things no more conflict with each other than the other two do: that the Word [λόγος], the eternal Son of God, is equal to the Father, and yet is the Mediator who is inferior to the Father; and that the Word by itself and apart constitutes a person in the divine nature, and yet one person of Christ the Mediator is constituted from two natures. Stancarus argues badly. If Christ is Mediator in two natures, he is less than the Father, therefore according to both natures. But we taught a little earlier that what fits the whole complex should not be distributed to the natures. This middle rank, which Christ the Redeemer holds, takes nothing at all from his divine essence. The reasons he adduces from the office of Mediator have no more weight, because they are drawn from the part to the whole. Christ gave himself as the price of redemption; he reconciled all things by the cross of his flesh; he is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world; he was set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. Certainly he accomplished all these things according to his human nature. Yet it does not follow from this that he is Mediator only in respect of that nature, since Christ does not complete all the parts of his office by expiation and sacrifice. For what is it to overcome death? What is it to rise again in the power of the Spirit, and to receive life from himself? What is it to unite us to God, and to be one with God? Surely these are not found in the human nature of Christ apart from the Deity. Yet they come into account when the office of Mediator is discussed. Would that Stancarus would notice the words he quotes, that God did not spare his only Son. For if the Son is Son in both natures, he does not have this from his humanity. Moreover, if the name God signifies three persons, and he insists on it too stubbornly, it follows that Christ is the Son of the Spirit no less than of the Father. This single antithesis, if Stancarus would not grudge to weigh it properly, would untie many knots: namely, that while the Mediator compares himself with the Father by whom he was sent, and where Paul calls God manifested in the flesh, it is the Son of God who is set before us as Mediator; of whom Paul soon adds that he was justified in the Spirit, appeared to the angels, was preached to the Gentiles, and was received up into glory. From here a simple and genuine definition ought rather to have been sought. This is plainly drawn out of Colossians 3, where reconciliation through the flesh is so described that the Deity keeps its place in primacy and fullness. So either let Stancarus prove that Christ sits at the Father's right hand in order to defend and protect us by the power of the Spirit, commends the guardianship of our salvation to the angels, and subjects the Devil and the whole world, that these are not part of the office of Mediator; or let him acknowledge that he is wrongly inferring, from the sacrifice and intercession, that the Son of God is not Mediator except insofar as he is man. Earlier we showed why Paul, discussing the Mediator, expressly ascribes to him the name of man: namely, so that, fear being cast out, he might gently invite us to him. For he is not disputing subtly about essence, but supplying the matter of trust, so that we do not hesitate to flee to him who is our brother. We wonder, however, under what pretext he twists to his own meaning what we demonstrated earlier very well in our favour, that Christ, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself. "This," he says, "is the rule for solving the question." Let it be so, for we gladly embrace it. But if the only-begotten Son of God, who was equal to the Father, emptied himself, then certainly he is Mediator in two natures; and he is the same one who became obedient unto death, and was given the name above every name, so that every tongue should confess that he is in the glory of God the Father. Moreover, what kind of glory this is, and how it ought to be understood, Christ himself should answer rather than we: "Father," he says, "glorify the Son with the glory which I had with you from the beginning, before the creation of the world." Stancarus will surely admit that it would be an absurd prayer if he asked that only the flesh of Christ be adorned and illustrated with the eternal glory of God; and if this fits only the whole person, it may rightly be concluded from this that, since he cited the passage, it cannot be referred to anything else. When we come to the Fathers, he brings forward specious colours, so as to have them as the patrons and supporters of his cause. But if we inquire beyond the dispute what Augustine thought, we have no disagreement with him. We indeed concede that in many places this godly teacher makes Christ Mediator insofar as he is man. We also acknowledge his words, both from book 10 of the City of God and from elsewhere: "In the form of a servant he is priest, and the same offering; in this he offered himself, in this he was offered, according to this he is Mediator." But meanwhile he does not hide that, for the office of Mediator, it is necessarily required that he be also God, as in book 1 of the Confessions, last chapter but one: "That he might be Mediator, it was necessary that he have something like God and something like men; lest, being like men in everything, he be far from God, or, being like God in everything, he be far from men; and so he would not be Mediator." Similarly in book 9 of the City of God, chapter 10: "If all men are wretched, a mediator must be sought who is not only man but also God, so that his blessed mortality may lead men from mortal misery to blessed immortality." Likewise on Psalm 134: "In that great separation the Mediator was sent. You could not go to God as man; God became man. If he were only man, by following what you are you would never arrive; if he were only God, by not grasping what you are not, you would never arrive." But in the book on sheep: "Not a Mediator who is man apart from the Deity, nor a Mediator who is God apart from the humanity. Behold the Mediator: the Deity without the humanity is not a mediator; the humanity without the Deity is not a mediator. But between the Deity alone and the humanity alone, the Mediator is the divine humanity of Christ and the human Deity of Christ." We do not deny that Cyril also often refers to the human nature the fact that Christ is Mediator, namely lest he make the Deity subject to subjection, which the Arians upheld. Yet elsewhere, in the second dialogue on the Trinity, he is a sound and faithful interpreter of his own words: "The Mediator is understood in this way, because he shows in himself the Deity and the humanity brought together and united. For he is akin to God, since he is from him and in him; and he is also akin to us, since he is from us and in us." You see how he constitutes the Mediator from two natures, and necessarily requires their union for this office. Nor is Chrysostom's reasoning different. For although he wishes the Mediator to be sought in the human nature, he nevertheless denies that intercession would be lawful unless the Deity also comes in. So in chapter 2 of the first epistle to Timothy: "The Mediator must be joined to both parties of whom he is Mediator. For it is the peculiar property of a mediator to become a partaker of both between whom he places himself. Unless, therefore, Christ shares the Father's nature, he is certainly not Mediator." Therefore in the homily on the Ascension he teaches that it is not an angel or archangel, but the Son of God himself, who intercedes. And immediately an explanation is added: that Christ placed himself in the middle, touching both natures.
