As to the fitness both of pastors and of presbyters or overseers: just as no one can discharge his office so exactly that something better could not still be wanted even in the best man, so likewise, unless those are admitted who have been lawfully chosen and who perform what they are able to do, there will be no end of disturbances and contentions in the Church. To lay down, however, that the wealthier men, and those conspicuous for rank and name, be chosen for ecclesiastical offices clearly conflicts with the order and rule of Christ. Indeed, we are especially shown to be true disciples of Christ by this one thing: when we are not ashamed to submit ourselves to the administration of those whose worth and esteem in the world are slight. The function of the Consistory has its own ends and limits, within which those who are called to exercise it should confine themselves. It is their task, therefore, to watch over the flock of the Lord, so that God may be purely worshipped; likewise to admonish, both privately and publicly; and further to excommunicate as well, when the matter requires it. When the Consistory keeps itself within these bounds, and does not extend itself further than the Lord permits, no occasion for clamour will be given. Now, however, apart from that ecclesiastical assembly which is held in the Consistory, we do not see how it accords with the institution of the Lord Himself to set up some ecclesiastical council, as they call it. Rather, it must be recognised and denounced as a wholly new undertaking, lest by various changes a window be opened for further alterations. And this in particular can bring nothing but certain ruin, since those who oppose the truth will seize upon it as an occasion for insulting us, as though something were being done against the political state under that pretext. Nor, however, do we disapprove of it when necessity arises that men learned and endowed with experience be chosen, who may see what the state of the Church requires; yet in such a way that this office too is for a time and extraordinary, and in no way ordinary.

units.la: CALVINVS N. S. D. Vt se pius homo a Papatus superstitionibus subducat.
units.tr: Calvin to N.N., greeting in the Lord. How a godly man may withdraw himself from the superstitions of the Papacy.

units.la: GRatias ago Domino, fratet charissime, te ad synceram ve ritatis suae cognitionem perduxit, teque ab illis erroribus eripuit, in quos incidere suos etiam nonnunquam sinit, vt ita ipsos humiliet. Vide igitur vtvt in isti fidei simplicitate incedas, vt Dominus in ipsa te confirmet magis ac magis: cumque iam ex hoc mundo cum Domino nostro Iesu Christo vnitus sis, ac membrum ipsius existas, quatenus ipse carnem nostram induit, vt plenam fraternitatem nobiscum iniret, ex Euangelij ipsius præscripto vitam instituas: cuius summa est, vt in ipso vno solidâ salutē quæramus, atq; ita tandem ad vitam illâ peruenianus, quae fidelibus est reposita in cœlis, sub spe & expectatione resurrectio nis ad gloriā æternam. Fixa enim etiā illa nobis spes hærere debet, quandiu corpora nostra in terra quiescunt, animas apud illum vicituras in cœlis. Quod ad illud quod à me quæris liceatne Christiano homini participare Cœnæ Domini quæ istic administratur, respôsio aperta est, licere omnino, modo Cœna Christi ea sit de qua agitur. Atqui vbi rem vti par est expedieris, inuenies nō magis couenire inter Cœnam Domini, ac Missam Papisticâ, quàm inter lucem ac tenebras. Constat quidem ordinatione Domini deteriorem fieri non posse prauitate hominum vel ignorantia, sed illud pernego, Missam ad Christū auctorē referri posse:
units.tr: I give thanks to the Lord, most beloved brother, that he has brought you to a sincere knowledge of his truth and has delivered you from those errors into which he sometimes allows his own people to fall, so that he may humble them. See to it, therefore, that you walk in the simplicity of this faith, so that the Lord may confirm you in it more and more. Since you are now united with our Lord Jesus Christ out of this world and are his member, inasmuch as he put on our flesh in order to enter into full fellowship with us, order your life according to the prescript of his Gospel. Its sum is that we seek salvation solidly in him alone, and so at last come to that life which is laid up for the faithful in heaven, under the hope and expectation of resurrection to eternal glory. For that hope must also remain fixed in us, while our bodies rest in the earth, that our souls will live with him in heaven. As for your question whether a Christian may take part in the Lord's Supper which is administered there, my answer is plain: it is altogether lawful, provided the Supper is the Supper of Christ of which we speak. But when you examine the matter as it ought to be examined, you will find that the Lord's Supper and the Papist Mass agree no more than light and darkness. It is certain that by the ordinance of the Lord it cannot be made worse by the wickedness or ignorance of men; but I flatly deny that the Mass can be referred to Christ as its author.

units.la: T.J. quin potius in ipsius contumelia ab ipso Satana fabricatam affec-tio ad sanctæ Cœnæ euersionem certissimâ. Planè enim ex dia-metro illi repugnat, vbi sacrificij nomine censetur atq; in actio-ne tenere inuenta, vis & efficacia passionis Domini transcribi-tur. Extat illic præterea apertissima idololatria, non tantum vbi panis adoratur, sed quia & oratur pro defunctis, & merita atque intercessiones sanctorum implorantur, & pleraque eiusmodi illic fiunt, quæ Dominus nominatim condemnat. Quare non magis licet si lebibus communicare illi superstitioni, quā olim licebat sa-crificare in Bethel. Illud enim omnino repugnat confessioni fi-dei, quā à nobis Dominus requirit. Sed quia hoc argumentū per-tractatū est fusius in libris ea de re editis, àte peto, vt illos dili-gen-ter euoluas. Te interea gratiæ Domini comendo, vt ipse suā vo-luntatem te edoceat, & aperiat oculos, vt nigrum à candido dis-cernas: sic enim tibi non defuturum confido, in quo acquisescas. Tibi verò omnem licentiam præcidas simulandi interea impie-tatem à te vllo modo approbari. Dominus sua in te dona adau-geat, atque vbi quod rectum est ostenderit, det etiam animū con-stantem, vt in eo agnito vt par est, adhæreas. Geneuæ, x v. Iunij.
units.tr: Rather, it was devised by Satan himself to insult Christ, and the disposition toward the overthrow of the holy Supper is most certain. For it is wholly opposed to the Supper where it is regarded as a sacrifice, and where the force and efficacy of the Lord's passion are transferred to an action invented by men. Moreover, there is most manifest idolatry there, not only where bread is adored, but also because prayers are offered for the dead, the merits and intercessions of the saints are implored, and many things of this kind are done there which the Lord expressly condemns. Therefore it is no more lawful to communicate in that superstition than it was once lawful to sacrifice at Bethel. For it is wholly contrary to the confession of faith which the Lord requires from us. But since this matter has been treated more fully in books published on the subject, I ask you to read them carefully. Meanwhile I commend you to the grace of the Lord, that he himself may teach you his will and open your eyes so that you may distinguish black from white; for thus I trust that he will not fail you, in whom you may rest. As for yourself, cut off for yourself all license of pretending in the meantime that impiety is in any way approved by you. May the Lord increase his gifts in you, and when he has shown what is right, may he also give you a steadfast mind so that, having recognised it as is fitting, you may cling to it. Geneva, 15 June.

units.la: Tuus Calvinus.
units.tr: Yours, Calvin.

units.la: RESPONSIO AD DVO CERTA CAPITA.
units.tr: REPLY TO TWO DEFINITE QUESTIONS.

units.la: QVod ad dies festos & certas alias ceremonias attinet: vt il-los Dei iudicio obnoxios existimo, qui sub specie nescio cuius conformitatis & conueniētię inter Ecclesias statuēn dæ, & fouerunt malum, & remedium auerterunt: piis verò fratri-bus durum est subiicere se rebus illis, quas nec rectas esse nec v-tiles animaduertunt: ita etiā def. ćus multos tolerandos iudico, vbi emendari non possunt. Quare non censeo vt quisquam fra-trum ea de causa instet, vt ab Ecclesia cui addictus est recedat, si maior pars gregis feratur in contrariū: quia in eiusmodi casibus satis esse mihi videtur, si quod rectum esse nouimus, à nobis pro curatum fit. Quanuis enim quod obtruditur, & scandalum asse-rat, & malâ causam trahat: quia tamen per se Dei verbo non re-pugnat, concedi potest: maxime vbi maior numerus peruincit, quando ei qui membrum est tantum illius corporis, nulla ratio suppetit vlterius pergendi. Ad alterum de Ministris non legiti-mè vocatis, non video vt eorum vocatio pro legitima approbā-da fit. Quare duorum alterum sequendum mihi videtur, nempe vt vel tolerantia in suo statu & functione sustineantur: vel vt culpam agnoscant, atque ita admittantur. Prima ratio hones-tum præsextum habet, quia nullus aperte cogitur ad approban-dum, quod rectū initium non habuit: vt si Princeps ipse induxit MiniMinístrum populo non ad consentiendum, sed ad testimonium præbendum tātūm vocato. Res igitur propter temporis lapsum suo loco ita relinquatur. Posterior ratio est expeditior, & magis ad ædificationem pertinet, & ad Ecclesiæ ordinem etiam magis accedit: vbi nempe qui sine vocatione inducti sunt, testabuntur displicere sibi quòd se ipsi ingesserint, ac quòd meliore vocationis testimonio destituantur: ac simul declaratio subiiciatur, neque vtile esse, neque ferendum vllo modo, vt rebus in ordinem redactis, illa ad ministerium introductio præter ordinem & merè confusa locum habeat in posterum. Videndum autem ante omnia, vt dum ista quæ ad ordinem pertinent pro merito suo disquiruntur, vt par est: tum ipsius veritatis doctrina solida & aperta constet, & agnoscatur apud omnes, tum si qui illam in quocunque capite proscindunt, aut illi detrahunt, illis nisi alij esse discant fraternitas, quam primi conuellunt, renuncietur.
units.tr: As for the feast days and certain other ceremonies: I judge that those who, under the appearance of I know not what conformity and agreement among the Churches to be established, have both fostered the evil and turned away the remedy, are liable to the judgment of God. But it is hard for godly brothers to submit themselves to those things which they perceive to be neither right nor useful. Thus, too, I judge that many things must be tolerated where they cannot be amended. Therefore I do not think that any of the brothers should press for this reason that he withdraw from the Church to which he belongs, if the greater part of the flock is carried in the contrary direction; for in cases of this kind it seems to me sufficient if what we know to be right is taken care of by us. For although what is forced upon us both gives offence and draws an evil cause after it, yet, because in itself it is not contrary to the Word of God, it may be conceded, especially where the greater number prevails, since for one who is only a member of that body there is no reason left for going further. As to the second point, concerning ministers who were not lawfully called, I do not see how their calling should be approved as lawful. Therefore it seems to me that one of two courses must be followed: either that they be sustained in their present state and function by toleration, or that they acknowledge their fault and so be admitted. The first course has an honourable pretext, because no one is openly compelled to approve what did not have a right beginning, as when a prince himself has introduced a minister to the people, called not to consent but only to bear witness. Let the matter therefore be left as it is, owing to the lapse of time. The second course is more expeditious, pertains more to edification, and comes closer to the order of the Church: namely, where those who were introduced without a calling testify that they are displeased that they forced themselves in, and that they lack the better testimony of a calling; and at the same time a declaration is added that it is neither useful nor to be tolerated in any way that, once things have been restored to order, that introduction to the ministry, outside order and purely confused, should have a place in future. But above all it must be seen to, while those matters which pertain to order are examined as their merit requires, as is fitting, that the doctrine of the truth itself be established solidly and openly, and acknowledged by all; and that, if any persons tear it apart in any article or detract from it, fellowship be renounced with them, unless they learn to be others, whom the first ones overthrow.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N.N. S. D. Cùm à ministerio quis indicta causa abdicatus esset.
units.tr: John Calvin to N.N., greeting. When someone has been removed from the ministry without a hearing.

units.la: CVm & de turbis quæ vestră Ecclesiam vexarunt, & de muta tione Pastoris subsequuta audiuisemus: testatus sit etiam apud nos N. non constare sibi, quamobrem ministerio à vobis abdicatus esset, cōmodissimum duximus paucis vos ea de re commonefacere, quod eodem animo quo scribitur à nobis, acceptum iri cōfisi sumus. Et quemadmodū zelo Christiano ac syncritate & vero amore fraterno eò adducimur, ita etiam facite, vt Spiritum illum mansuetudinis quem Scriptura vnicè commendat, nobis audiendis accommodetis. Non est verò ꝗ multum disceptemus, quam illa ἀταξία propinquam Ecclesiæ ruinam minitetur, vbi res eò redierunt, vt Magistratus ipse absolutè ac per se Ministros vel abdicet, vel instituat. Quia tamen eò quandoque redigitur, vbi feruent contentiones ac turbæ, neque remedia ordinaria locum amplius habere possunt, experientia edoctos esse oportebit in posterum, ne ita vos proscindatis mutuò, vt inuertendi ordinis causam ipsi præbeatis. Pluribus agere vobiscum non est necesse, cùm nemo sit qui & mali magnitudinē, & quid illud consequatur, non percipiant. Cùmque non nunc primùm vestra Ecclesia ruinā illam duxerit, eò minus sunt excusabiles, qui mali ciusdam dederunt. Quare à vobis petimus, vt seriò vobis attendatis in posterum, vt Satanæ artes præcaueatis. Dum enim vi & fulgore veritatis, quam Dominus mundo restituit, premi se sentit, totus in eo est, vt ordinem Ecclesiæ cōuellendo, pios omnes probro & ignominiæ exponat. Quod ad istam ministerij abdicationem, secundum ea quæ ad nos frater scripto detulit ipsi nempe cum a nemine accusatus sit, suggestum interdictum esse, non expressa vlla ratione, alienissima nobis hæc agendi ratio vti reipsa est, planè etiā videtur. Neque vero quod ab illo accepimus, dissimulandū apud vos duximus, vt si quid hic in agedi modo peccatum est, emendaretur, tam vt illi iusta querimoniæ causa, quàm vt scandalum simul communctum tolli possit. Et tamen hanc nostra admonitionem præiudicium vobis afferre nolumus, sed illa tantum eò spectat, vt nostro officio defungamur. Hoc tantum habuimus quod vobis scriberemus ea de re, de quæ nobis non satis liquet: non quòd vestra nobis integritas in dubium veniat, sed ne leuitatis alicuius nota nobis impingatur, si re minus explorata viterius progrederemur. Neque rursum vos vrgere volumus vt quid res sit, amplius nobis significetis: nisi q eam hic locum afferri optaremus, quæ noxios omnes rumores statim profligaret. Illud penes vos esto. Nobis satis erit, quòd vos fraterne exhortati simus, vt vid retis ne quid Ecclesiæ vobis credita ab vnitate & concordia alienum admitteret: ac proinde ne sacer ille ordo qui obtinere debet, iurgiis & rixis pessundaretur. Noftis enim vt Dei filios Spiritu mansuetudinis in vera mo deratione contineri oporteat. Nos interea Deum precamur, vt sublatis illis litibus & plane extinctis, quæ vobis distrahendis tum valuerunt, suos vos præsidio protegat, in omni bono prosperare donet, sua in vobis dona adaugeat, vt tanto magis glorificetur in vobis. Geneuæ, x. Decembris.
units.tr: Since we have heard both of the disturbances that have troubled your Church and of the change of minister that followed, and since N. has also assured us that he does not know why he was removed from the ministry by you, we thought it most fitting to remind you of a few points on this matter, trusting that they will be received in the same spirit in which we write. Just as we are moved by Christian zeal, sincerity and true brotherly love, so please also accommodate yourselves to hearing us in that spirit of gentleness which Scripture alone commends. There is no need for us to argue at length how close to ruin the Church is threatened by that disorder [ἀταξία], when things have come to the point where the magistrate himself absolutely and of his own accord dismisses or installs ministers. Yet since it sometimes comes to this, where contentions and tumults rage and the ordinary remedies can no longer have effect, you will need to be taught by experience in future, so that you do not tear each other apart in such a way as to furnish the very cause of overturning the order. We need not say more, since there is no one who does not perceive both the greatness of the evil and what it leads to. And since your Church has not now for the first time been brought to that ruin, those who have given occasion for this evil are all the less excusable. We therefore ask you to pay serious attention in future, so that you may guard against the arts of Satan. For while he feels himself pressed by the force and brightness of the truth which the Lord has restored to the world, he is wholly intent on overturning the order of the Church and exposing all the godly to disgrace and shame. As for this dismissal from the ministry: according to what our brother has reported to us in writing, namely that he was accused by no one, yet was forbidden to preach without any stated reason, this way of acting is wholly alien to us and clearly seems so in fact. Nor have we thought we should conceal from you what we have heard from him, so that if any wrong has been committed here in the manner of proceeding, it may be corrected, both so that he may have a just cause for complaint and so that the scandal arising from it may be removed. Yet we do not want this admonition of ours to prejudice you; it aims only at discharging our duty. We have only this reason for writing to you about a matter that is not sufficiently clear to us: not that your integrity is in doubt with us, but lest a mark of levity be fixed on us if we proceeded further with a matter not sufficiently examined. Nor again do we wish to press you to tell us more of what the case is, unless we would wish it brought forward here, which would at once put an end to all harmful rumours. That is for you to decide. It will be enough for us that we have exhorted you as brothers to take care that nothing admitted in the Church committed to you is alien to unity and concord, and therefore that that sacred order which ought to prevail is not destroyed by quarrels and brawls. For you know that the sons of God must be held in true moderation by the Spirit of gentleness. Meanwhile we pray God that, once those strifes which have prevailed to divide you are removed and wholly extinguished, he may protect you with his defence, grant you to prosper in every good thing, and increase his gifts in you, so that he may be glorified all the more in you. Geneva, 10 December.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. Si omnis disciplinæ statu tolerabilis negabitur.
units.tr: John Calvin to N. If a tolerable state of all discipline is denied.

units.la: ETiamsi hactenus tolerabilis fuisset ἀταξία, quæ tibi mouit hoc certamen: iam tamen eò deducta res est, vt liberum tibi non sit meo iudicio, ea lege manere, vt tam grauibus malis nullum adhibeatur remedium. Sed quia in re perplexa adhuc ambigis quænam moderatio tenenda sit, meaque sententiam audire cupis, sic accipe: Si sacra mysteria profanare nefas est, certè quæcunque occurrant offendicula, ad excusandum sacrilegium non sufficient. Quæreda igitur definitio est, ex qua certò statuere liceat quoufq; pateat ista profanatio. Porrò in re clara & obuia non est tantopere laborandum. Nam qui passim, nullóque delectu, vel discrimine quoslibet admittit ad Sacramenta, quin ea profanet non dubito. Fateor quidem nunquam ita purum esse vsum in Ecclesia, qui eorum sanctitati omni ex parte respondeat: nos plus satis experimur quàm procul absit nostra ratio à mun- ditie quę optanda effet: sed aliud est sacros thesauros alienissimis quibufq; profituere, quàm ind gnis permittere, qui arceri legi- timo iudicio nequeunt. Nimia fuit auftueritas in veteribus. Atqui minus reuerentiæ deferri sacris nostris, quàm scimus olim ha- bitum fuisse impuris superstitionibus, plufquam indignum est. Ergo nisi inter nos vigeat discrimen aliquod, vt prohibeantur qui fine ciaffi Dei iniuria admitti nequeunt, pro confesso fumo tam Baptismum quàm Cœnam profanari. Fideiussor enim qui recipiendus fit ab Ecclesia alienus, non video. Sed pios malorum culpa priuari iniustum est. Scio vt à publica excommunicatio- ne abhorruerit Augustinus. Nam quum vulgò regnaret tunc in Africa ebrietas, quadam ad Valerium Epistola morbum hunc lentis remediis fanandum potius esse existimat, quàm excom- municatione, quæ totam Ecclesiam conuellat ac dissipet. Sem- per tamen videndum est, ne frœno laxato foueatur peccandi li- centia. Ego vt concedam nimium rigorem esse temperandum: impunitas tamen nullo modo ferenda est. Nullam ergo esse le- gem, quæ Cœnæ & Baptismi sanctitatem custodiat, ne vtrunque myste- i m contemptui & ludibrio expositum fit, remissio est minime excusabilis. Quod excipis nihil priuatim tentandum esse: neque etiam hoc mihi probatur, vt Pastor re nondum co- gnita, fe officio abdicet, sponte ue deferat stationem suam: ve- rum qui funcero ædificandi studio præditus erit, hoc saltem te- stabitur sibi fas non esse, ad sacram Christi Cœnam promiscue admittere qui palam fe canes esse ostendunt, & excusso pudore, quasi ex professo contumeliam irrogant Dei mysteriis. Nec vero paucorum hominum arbitrio acquiescet, donec populum ipsum cognouerit iugo nolle subiici: tunc sequetur deliberatio, quo iure obstrictum teneant Christi seruum, qui ordinem Diuinitus præscriptum palam recusant. Certe vbi rogando, & hortando nihil proficiuntur, ac frustra etiam conquesti fumus nos Religione constringi, ne pergamus scientes & volentes sacra Dei mysteria profanare: in tam cofufa ordinis perturbatione quomodo stare nobis liceat nescio. Erfi autem cunctatio reprehensione non ca ret, ingenuéque fatendum, serius quàm deceba h inccaufam fusce ptam esse, vel non fatis strenue, & viliter fuisse defensam: non alia tamen quàm nimiæ lenitatis culpa obiici poterit, quæ om- nium qui contumaciter obftiunt, crimen duplicat potius, quàm inuidia oneret Christi seruum, qui sua tarditate ostendit, vt po- puli salutī consuleret, fe n m s fuisse timidum. Nec vero feruo- ris & præcipitantiæ calumniam vllo argumento meliùs diluere optarem fi tuo effem loco, quàm ingenua ista confessione: vidisse quidē ab initio quàm turpis & pudenda effet ista profanatio facrorum:sed fperaffe quû adoleuissent,correctione aliquâm:atq; hanc fuisse tolerantiæ caúam,quia malebas profectu sensim ad docilitate formari,quàm eos repente cogere in ordinem:iaterea non tacuisse quales te angútiæ premerent donec videres melio re rerum statû:nunc serius & vehementius vrgere,quia hoc tibi necessitas extorquet. Hoc fi nunc liberè testeris , constanterque postea insistas,nec finem vrgedi facias, vel remedium malis istis insanabilibus inueniet Deus:vel te expediet,vt certò tibi fis con scius quicquid alij obstrepant, nihil temerè abs te fuisse tentatû. Quòd fi tibi elapsa fuerit hæc occasio,timendum est,ne posthac sentias alio te quâ sanctæ vocationis vinculo teneri conftrictû.
units.tr: Even if the disorder [ἀταξία] which has stirred this contest had so far been tolerable, the matter has now been carried to such a point that, in my judgment, you are not free to remain on those terms while no remedy is applied to such grave evils. But since in a perplexing matter you are still uncertain what moderation should be observed, and you wish to hear my opinion, take it thus: if it is wrong to profane the holy mysteries, then certainly whatever obstacles occur will not suffice to excuse the sacrilege. A definition must therefore be sought from which one can determine with certainty how far this profanation extends. Moreover, in a clear and obvious matter one need not labour so much. I do not doubt that whoever admits anyone at all, without discrimination or distinction, to the sacraments profanes them. I confess indeed that the practice in the Church has never been so pure as to correspond in every respect to their holiness: we experience more than enough how far our practice is from the purity that ought to be desired. But it is one thing to expose the sacred treasures to altogether alien persons, and another to allow the unworthy, who cannot be kept away by a lawful judgment. There was excessive severity among the ancients. Yet that less reverence should be shown to our sacred things than we know was once shown them by impure superstitions is more than shameful. Therefore, unless some distinction prevails among us, so that those who cannot be admitted without injury to God's glory are forbidden, it must be taken as granted that both Baptism and the Supper are profaned. For I do not see who the surety is who should be received by the Church if he is alien to it. But it is unjust for the godly to be deprived on account of the fault of the wicked. I know that Augustine shrank from public excommunication. For when drunkenness then reigned commonly in Africa, in a letter to Valerius he thinks this disease should be healed by slow remedies rather than by excommunication, which would overturn and scatter the whole Church. Yet one must always take care that the reins are not loosened and the licence of sinning fostered. Though I concede that excessive rigour must be tempered, impunity must nonetheless by no means be tolerated. Therefore, that there is no law which guards the holiness of the Supper and of Baptism, so that both mysteries are not exposed to contempt and mockery, is a most inexcusable remissness. As for your objection that nothing should be attempted privately: this also does not please me, that a minister, with the matter not yet known, should abdicate his office or of his own accord relinquish his post. Rather, one who is endowed with zeal for building up the flock will at least testify that it is not lawful for him to admit promiscuously to the holy Supper of Christ those who openly show themselves to be dogs, and who, casting off all modesty, as it were deliberately offer insult to the mysteries of God. Nor will he acquiesce in the judgment of a few men until he has come to know that the people itself is unwilling to submit to the yoke; then will follow deliberation as to by what right they may hold bound the servant of Christ, when they openly refuse the order prescribed by God. Certainly, where nothing is gained by asking and exhorting, and we have complained in vain that we are bound by religion not to go on knowingly and willingly profaning the holy mysteries of God, I do not know how we can stand in such a confused disturbance of order. But if the delay is not free from blame, and it must be frankly confessed that the cause was taken up later than it should have been, or was defended not vigorously enough and too meanly, yet it can be objected only as a fault of excessive gentleness. That fault doubles the crime of all who obstinately resist, rather than burdening with odium the servant of Christ, who by his slowness showed that he was concerned for the salvation of the people, not that he was timid. Nor indeed would I wish to refute the charge of heat and precipitancy better by any argument, if I were in your place, than by this ingenuous confession: that you saw from the beginning how shameful and disgraceful this profanation of the sacred things was, but hoped that when they had grown up they would be corrected in some measure, and that this was the reason for your tolerance, since you preferred to form them gradually to docility by progress rather than to compel them suddenly into order; meanwhile you did not conceal what anguish troubled you until you saw a better state of affairs; now you press more urgently and vehemently, because necessity extorts this from you. If you now testify this freely, and afterwards persist steadfastly, and do not make an end of pressing, God will either find a remedy for these incurable evils or will bring it about that you are certain in your own conscience, whatever others may clamour, that nothing was rashly attempted by you. But if this opportunity has slipped from you, it is to be feared that you will afterwards find yourself bound by another chain than that of your holy calling.

units.la: DE CERTORVM MINISTRORVM ἀταξία.
units.tr: On the disorder of certain ministers.

units.la: Dilectio Dei Patris nostri, & Gratia D. nostri Iesu Christi vobis semper adsit, per Spiritus sancti communicationem.
units.tr: May the love of God our Father, and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, always be with you, through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: QVod ad nos perlatum est, dilecti fratres, verbum Dei ita expositum esse apud vos probro, idque illorum culpa qui exemplo aliis præire debuerant, perquam moleste accepimus: audimus enim illos ipsos quorum partes erant quemuis ex plebe ad pacem & concordiam fraternam exhortari,eovsq; continentionis vi efferbuisse,vt ad arma ipsimet cóclamauerint. Quàm vero indignum facinus & quàm enorme! quantum etiam exillius fama passim sparsum erit scandalû, ex quo non tantum contemptus verbi Dei enascatur,quando ad verbi Ministros scandalum referendum fit, sed etiam occasio offeratur Satanæ atque ipsius instrumentis, ad vos demum conuellendos atque ita dispergendos,vt vix deinde inflicto malo remedium adferri possit? Sane quod ad Ecclesiam Dei attinet, illam passim hode ab hostibus circunfideri omnes vident: sed tamen vestræ rationes omnino vobis indicunt,vt pacem & concordia retineatis omnibus modis. Satis enim constat ab vna Dei prouidentia quæ aduer farios constrictos tenet,stare,ne qui vestrum exitium toties iam defignarût,vel leuissima occasione oblata in illud ferantur præcipites. Quamobrem aliter de N.& N.iudicare quàm de abfeptiis non possumus,quibus ita simul ac semel exciderit cum ipsorum ministerij ratione illa etiam consideratio,quod ipsorum audacia extremam omnibus istic Ecclesiis pernicie aliatum effet. Ac primum quidem probari à nobis illud non potest, quòd Ministri verbi ita ad gerenda ipsi arma & eiusmodi rerum tractationem sese applicent. Scimus aliquâdo vrgente necessitate accidere, vt intra officij metas non ita præcisè sese singuli contineant.
units.tr: We were very distressed to hear, dear brothers, that the word of God has been brought into disrepute among you, and that through the fault of men who ought to have gone before others as examples. For we have heard that those very men, whose task it was to urge every ordinary person toward peace and brotherly harmony, have been so inflamed by a spirit of contention that they themselves have shouted for arms. What an unworthy and monstrous deed this is! How much scandal will have spread on every side from its report! From it not only does contempt for the word of God arise, since the scandal must be charged to the ministers of the word, but also an opportunity is offered to Satan and his instruments to tear you apart and scatter you, so that once the harm is inflicted, scarcely any remedy can be applied. Indeed, as far as the Church of God is concerned, everyone sees that it is now surrounded on all sides by enemies. Yet your own circumstances plainly show you that you must keep peace and harmony by every means. For it is well established that only the providence of God, which holds the adversaries bound, keeps them from rushing headlong into your ruin, which they have so often plotted; should even the slightest opportunity be offered, they would be carried into it. Therefore we cannot judge of N. and N. otherwise than of men who have fallen away, since, once that consideration has at once and altogether dropped out, together with the character of their ministry, namely that their recklessness would bring the utmost ruin upon all the churches there. And first of all, we cannot approve that the ministers of the word apply themselves in this way to bearing arms and handling such matters. We know that sometimes, under pressing necessity, it happens that individuals do not keep strictly within the limits of their office.

units.la: Scimus etiam eovsque inualuisse pericula, vt cuiq; pro virili adversum illa enitendum fuerit. Atqui illud videre nō possumus, qui tolerari posiit vt verbi Ministri agminum duces cuadant, ac proinde & copias ipsi cogant, & coactas iidem perducant. Ita fit enim vt ab officio quisque tantundem recedat, ac prorsus à vocatione sua degenerer, quod & illis accidit nominatim. Ex eo enim accidit vt ad mores stratioticos occalluerint, vtque exuta penitus illa ministerij persona, in licentiam militarem prorupe-rint. Sic nos loqui res ipsa cogit: plane enim confusi hisce audi-tis iacuimus: etsi ex literis vestris vnius prae altero grauius est ma-lum, quod ab vtroq; admissum est. Nunc vero cū quid nobis videatur expectatis, sic ipsi in Domino congregati vobis respon-dendum duximus. Ac primū omniū nisi omnia sursum ac deor-sum ferri volumus, non potest tam indignum scelus & enorme dissimulatione ac conniuentia sepeliri. Si quaeratur à N. cur ex Comitatu Mosbelgardensi abierit, parata erit respofio, quia nepe omnia illic essent confusa cum nullus disciplinae statu extaret. Atqui si nos ipsi aliis disciplinā prescribimus, quātō ardtioribus vinculis ipsimet nobis adstringi debemus? Ita vt huic malo reme-diū afferatur, satis videmus quid incommodi secuturū sit, vbi qui sunt in culpa nō admittenr reprehensione, sed iugū excutere co-nabūtur: sed tamen quicquid accidat, ferendū non est, vt nostra timiditate foueatur malum. Proinde vbi hoc agitur, vt & rectus ordo retineatur & scadala coprimantur, qualescunq; immineat procellae & tempestates: non est comittendum tamen vt de con-stantia & legitima fortitudine quicquā remittatur, maximè vbi con-trahendū est frenum. Quamobrem videre non possumus vt quod ifis accidit, silentio trāsmitti possit, quin ea occasione ma-ledictio Domini inhaereat vobis, & incumbat perpetuo. Locus Pauli 1.Tim.5.quo sese tueri cupit N.eū nullo modo iuuat: illic enim earenus voluit Paulus rationem haberi feruorum Dei, vt iporum innocentiae consulatur, quando vt plurimum obno-xij esse solent multorum calumniis. Atqui N.conuictus iam sa-tis tenetur bis (displosi in N. bombardula ex qua fecunda vice ignis emicarit) tentatae caedis. Accedit quiam antea parum ex of-ficio sese gessit inter ves, vt mirum sit tandiu tolerari potuisse. Vt igitur eam prouinciam deinceps retineat, qua sese plane indi-gnum praebuit, nobis quidem nullo modo probari potest. Nō-minatim quita praefracte detrectauit acquiescere piissimae exhor-tationi vestrae: ita hoc exaggerat hominis factū, vt abdicandum plane iam constet. In modo autem agendi hoc consilium damus, vt deligatis ex vestro coetu qui totius coetus nomine aperiat fra-tribus N vti rationibus idoneis mature ac legitime expensis pro numeratū fuerit N. ferendū non esse amplius in ministerio quod
units.tr: We also know that dangers have grown so great that each person must strive against them as best he can. Yet we cannot see how it can be tolerated that ministers of the Word should lead the companies of soldiers, forcing troops together and then leading them once gathered. In this way each man departs from his duty to the same extent and wholly degenerates from his calling, which has happened to them by name. For from this they have become hardened to military habits and, with the ministerial character utterly cast off, have burst out into soldierly license. The matter itself compels us to speak in this way. We were utterly dismayed on hearing these things, although from your letter one wrong is graver than the other, and both were committed by each side. Now, since you ask what seems right to us, we, gathered together in the Lord, have thought it right to answer you as follows. First of all, unless we want everything turned upside down, so great a crime cannot be buried by dissimulation and connivance. If N. is asked why he left the county of Mömpelgard, the answer is ready: because everything there was in confusion, since no state of discipline existed. But if we ourselves prescribe discipline to others, with how much tighter bonds ought we to be bound ourselves? As for applying a remedy to this evil, we see well enough what trouble will follow when those at fault refuse reproof and try to shake off the yoke. Yet whatever happens, it must not be endured that the evil be nourished by our timidity. Therefore, where the aim is both to keep right order and to suppress scandals, whatever storms and tempests threaten, nothing must be surrendered of constancy and lawful fortitude, especially where a bridle must be applied. Wherefore we cannot see how what has happened among you can be passed over in silence without the curse of the Lord clinging to you on that account and pressing upon you forever. The passage of Paul, 1 Tim. 5, by which N. wishes to defend himself, does not help him at all. For there Paul wished the servants of God to be considered only so far as their innocence is safeguarded, since they are usually exposed to the slanders of many. But N. is already sufficiently convicted of having twice attempted murder (a small bomb was set off against N., and fire burst out of it the second time). Add that before this he conducted himself among you with little regard for his office, so that it is surprising he was tolerated for so long. Therefore, that he should now keep the post in which he has shown himself plainly unworthy cannot in any way be approved by us. Especially since he stubbornly refused to comply with your most pious exhortation, and he so magnifies the man's deed that it is now clear he must be deposed. As to the manner of proceeding, we advise this: that some be chosen from your assembly who, in the name of the whole assembly, shall declare to brother N. that, once the reasons have been weighed in good time and lawfully, it has been decided that N. can no longer be tolerated in the ministry, which he has exercised badly. They should therefore ask that the church of that place also dismiss him from itself and approve that another be chosen in his place, whom they themselves acknowledge and approve.

units.la: T.iiij. male exercuerit: proinde rogare vt illius loci Ecclesia ipsum etiam à se emittat, ac probet vt in eius locum submittendus alius eligatur, quê & ipsi agnoscant & approbent. Si Ecclesia requiret rationes iudicij, vt plenius de re tota ipsis liqueat, tum demùm expediet eadem illa ipsis articulatim proponere, quæ à vobis accepimus. Quòd si ita ille populum loci pellexerit atque irretierit suis artibus, vt ipsi non acquiescant vestro consilio & exhortationi, tum demum admonendi erunt serio, videant vti hoc admissuri sint: cùm si in eo obstinatè perstent, schismaticos se ex hibituri sint, vnde & ipsos à vestri corporis vnitate separandi iniiciendi sit vobis necessitas. Quòd ad Alterum attinet, quia plus in illo est imprudentiæ & impetus quàm certæ improbitatis, fatis fore videtur, si Ecclesiæ etiam ipsius significetur suspendi illu à ministerio: cum vt ipse sese ita humiliet, tum etiam vt scandalum farciatur: atque illud ita demum, vt quoties ipsis videbitur, ipsum liceat repetere & recipere in Ministrum. Monendi autem erunt nominatim si de illo repetendo agetur, nõ aliter hoc posse procedere, quàm vt ipsi etiam omnem culpæ ipsius memoriâ sepeliant, neque ipsi vllo modo quod acciderit, exprobret, neve hæc temporalis castigatio illi sit fraudi, quominus ipsi integrum sit alios deinceps reprehendere ex Ministerij ratione, adeoque vt doctrina ipsius plenum ius & auctoritatem quâ meretur, obtineat. Optaßemus quidem in mitiorem sententiam inclinare si fieri potuisset, sed veriti sumus ne parcedo illis, Dominus interea tanto minus parceret. Valete fratres dilectissimi. Dominus suo vos præsidio tueatur, Spiritu confirmet, atque sua in vobis dona semper adaugeat. Geneuæ in nostro cœtu.
units.tr: T.iiij. If the Church asks for the grounds of the judgement, so that the whole matter may be made fully clear to them, then at last it will be expedient to set before them, point by point, the very things we have received from you. But if that man has so enticed and ensnared the people of the place by his arts that they do not agree with your counsel and exhortation, then at last they must be seriously warned to consider what they are undertaking. For if they obstinately persist in it, they will show themselves to be schismatics, and so you will be under the necessity of separating them also from the unity of your body. As for the other man, since there is more imprudence and impetuosity in him than settled wickedness, it will seem enough if it is signified to the Church itself that he is suspended from the ministry: partly so that he may humble himself, and partly so that the scandal may be made good. And this should be done in such a way that, whenever it seems good to them, he may be allowed to be taken back and received as minister. Those who are concerned about his restoration must be admonished by name that this cannot proceed otherwise than by their burying all memory of his fault, by their not reproaching him in any way for what has happened, and by this temporary chastisement not being to his disadvantage, so that it remains open to him in future to rebuke others on the basis of his ministry, and so that his teaching obtains the full right and authority it deserves. We would indeed have wished to incline to a milder sentence, if that could have been done, but we feared that if we spared them, the Lord would spare them so much the less. Farewell, most beloved brothers. May the Lord keep you under his protection, strengthen you by his Spirit, and always increase his gifts in you. Geneva, in our assembly.

units.la: Vester Io. Calvinus omnium nomine.
units.tr: Your John Calvin, on behalf of all of us.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D. De vsuris respondsum.
units.tr: John Calvin sends greeting. A response on usury.

units.la: NOndum ipse quidem tentaui quid appositè responderi possit ad quæstionem propositam: sed aliorum exemplo didici, quanto res ea cum periculo coniuncta sit. Si enim omnino vsuras damnamus, induimus strictiorem laqueum conscientiis, quàm Dominus ipse voluerit. Si vel minimum concedimus, stim sub illo pretextu plurimi effrenè licentiâ arripient, quæ nulla deinde moderatione vel exceptione coerceri possit. Si ad te tantùm scriberem, minus id vererer. Nora est enim mihi tua prudentia atque moderatio: sed quoniam alterius nomine consilium rogas, metuo, ne ille verbulo quodam arrepto plus sibi multo perpermittat quàm vellem. Confisus tamen te recte prospecturum quod sit illius ingenium, atque ex re ipsa qua de re agitur expenſurum quid expediat & quatenus, meam tibi mente aperiam.
units.tr: I have not yet tried myself to find what could be fittingly answered to the question put to me, but from the example of others I have learned how dangerous a matter this is. For if we condemn usury altogether, we tighten the noose on consciences more than the Lord himself wished. If we concede even the smallest amount, many will at once seize on that pretext and take liberties without restraint, which no moderation or exception could then check. If I were writing only to you, I would fear this less. For your prudence and moderation are known to me. But since you ask for advice on another's behalf, I fear he may seize on some small word and allow himself far more than I would wish. Yet, trusting that you will rightly judge what sort of man he is, and will weigh from the matter itself what is expedient and how far, I will open my mind to you.

units.la: Ac primùm nullo testimonio Scripturæ mihi constat vsuras omnino damnatas esse. Illa enim Christi sententia, quæ maximè obuia & aperta haberi solet: Mutuum date nihil inde sperantes, male huc detorta est. Quemadmodum alio loco notans splendida conuiuia, & diutium illam ad sese mutuò excipiendos ambitionem, vocari potiùs ad suam illa epula ab iis iubet cæcos, claudos atque alios egentes homines, qui in compitis iacerent, quibus non esset par pari referendi facultas: sic etiam notato illo loco, Christus correcturus illum hominum abusum in dando mutuo, præscribit nominatim illis dandi mutuò àquibus nulla spes sit quidquam receptum recuperatúmve iri. Solemus autè primum omnium videre satisfactam futura sit nostra pecunia apud illum qui mutuum rogat, cùm tamen egentibus maximè succurrendum fuerit, apud quos minus tuta esse pecunia solet. Eò igitur referuntur Christi verba, ac si egenis potius quàm diuitibus mutuum dare iuberet. Nondum igitur constat vsuram omnem esse prohibitam. Lex verò Mosis politica cùm sit, non tenemur illa vltra quâ æquitas ferat atque humanitas. Optandum quidem esset omnes vsuras, ipsúmque adeo nomen à mundo prorsùs exulare. Hoc vbi obtineri non poterit, quid bono publico fieri possit, videndum est. Supersunt certa loca Scripturæ in Prophetis & Psalmis, in quibus Spiritus S. inuehitur aduersus vsuras. Sic enim vrbem impia describit, qu vsuræ viguerint in foro & in plateis ipsius. Sed quando vocabulum Hebraeum significat in genere fraudes, nô ita strictè accipi hic quidem posse videretur. Sed vt concedamus agere illic Prophetam de vsuris nominatim, mirum non est quòd inter ingétia quæ grassantur mala, vsuras quoque attigerit. Fere enim vbi ad vsuram pecuniæ elocantur, comites indiuiduæ accedunt crudelitas atque innumerae aliæ fraudes & circunuentiones. Vt ex oppósito inter pii & sancti viri encomia illud traditur, qu non decerit pecuniam suâ ad vsuram. Adeo plusquam rarum est, eundem esse hominem probum atque fœneratorem. Ezechiel verò vlterius procedit. Dú enim ea scelera recenset propter quæ accensa sit vindicta Dei aduersum Iudæos, duo quædam vocabula vsurpat, quorum vnû significat vsuram atque à themate quodâ deductum est, quod etiam significat rodere, alterum significat incrementum seu augmentû: quia nempe priuato quisquê lucro addictus, quæstum ex proximi damno captabat, aut potius extorquebat: quanquâ certum est duriùs etiam locutos esse Prophetas de vsuris, quia nominatim inter Iudæos illæ interdictæ essent. Cùm igitur apertû Dei mandatum prætergrederentur, grauior im etiam reprehensionem merebātur. Quod adducitur noc loco eandem esse nostræ inter nos coniunctionis rationem, vt eadem quoque vsurarū prohibitio retineatur, respōdeo q₃ ad cōiuctionem ciuilē attinet, aliquod esse discrimen. Quia nempe circumstantia loci ipsius in quo Iudæos collocauerat Dominus, vt & saliæ circumstantiæ etiā eō pertinebat, vt facile illis esset negotiari inter se sine vsuris Nostra cōiunctio hodie per omnia nō respon det. Nō videmus igitur ita nobis interdictas simpliciter vsuras, nisi quatenus repugnant tum æquitati, tum charitati. Ratio Ambrosii quam etiam affert Chrisostomus, nō est magni momēti. Pecunia nō parit pecuniā. Quid mare? quid domus ex cuius locatione pensione percipio, an ex tectis & parietibus argentū pro prie n̄ scitur? Sed & terra producit & mari aduehitur quod pecuniam deinde producat, & habitationis commoditas cū certa pecuniā parari commutative solet. Quid si igitur plus ex negotiatione lucri percipi possit, quām ex fundi cuiusvis prouētu, an senetur qui fundum sterile fortasse colono locauerit ex quo mercedem vel prouentum recipiat sibi, qui ex pecunia fructū aliquē perceperit, non feretur? & qui pecunia fundū acquirit, annon pecunia illa generatim alterā annuam pecuniam? Vnde vero mercatoris lucrū? ex ipsius, inquiēs, diligentia atque industria. Quis dubitat pecuniam vacuam nutilem omnino esse? neque qui à me mutuam rogat, vacuam apud se habere à me cogitat. Non ergo ex pecunia illa lucrum accedit, sed ex prouētu. Illæ igitur rationes subtiles ⁊ uidem sunt, & speciē quandā habent, sed vbi propiùs expenduntur re ipsa cōcidunt. Nunc igitur cōcludo, iudicā dum de vsuris esse, non ex particulari aliquo Scripturæ loco, sed tantum ex æquitatis regula. Hoc exemplo clarius fiet. Sit aliquis diues & amplis fundis ac reditibus prædictus, & minus numatus tamen. Sit alius mediocriter diues, & non quidē ad alterius illius opes accedens, sed cui tamen amplior fit præsens pecunia. Hic igitur cum sua pecunia lubenter fundum ipse emptarus sit sibi: rogetur ab illo d tiore, vt mutuam det illi pecuniam. Posset qui dem cui mutuū dat ita stipulari sibi reditum pecuniæ suæ, vt fundus ex illa emptus ipsi in hypothecam subiiceretur, donec sua ipsi pecunia redd retur (atque ita sibi melius consuleret) sed fructu pecuniæ siue vsura contentus erit. Cur igitur primus ille cōtractus sine hypotheca ad pecuniæ fructū tantū damnabitur, alter sub hypotheca fundi emptī & cum reditu annuo longe asperior prohibitur? & quid aliud est quām puerorum instar ludere cum Deo, cū de rebus ex verbis nudis, ac non ex eo quod intest in re ipsa iudicatur? Quasi ex formā ipsa verborū, virtutes vitiāve discerni debeant. Non est verò animus rem ipsam hic excutere, indicare tantū m volui, quod tu exactius apud re perpendere s.
units.tr: First, I am certain from no testimony of Scripture that usury is altogether condemned. That saying of Christ, which is usually held to be the most obvious and plain, "Lend, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6), has been wrongly twisted. Elsewhere, when he rebukes lavish banquets and that ambition of repaying one another in turn, he bids those who give such feasts to invite instead the blind, the lame and other needy people who lie in the streets, who have no means of repaying in kind. So too, in that passage, Christ, about to correct that abuse in lending, names precisely those to whom one should lend, those from whom no hope exists of getting anything back or recovering it. We usually look first to see whether our money will be safe with the one who asks for the loan, whereas help should be given chiefly to the needy, among whom money is usually less safe. Christ's words therefore refer to this: as if he were bidding us lend to the poor rather than to the rich. It is not yet established, then, that all usury is forbidden. The law of Moses is a political law, and we are not bound by it beyond what fairness and humanity require. Indeed it would be desirable that all usury, and the very name of it, should be banished from the world altogether. Where this cannot be obtained, we must consider what can be done for the public good. There are definite passages of Scripture in the Prophets and Psalms in which the Holy Spirit inveighs against usury. For thus he describes a wicked city in which usury flourished in its marketplace and its streets. But since the Hebrew word generally signifies frauds, it might seem that it cannot be taken so strictly here. But even if we grant that the Prophet is speaking of usury by name there, it is no wonder that, among the huge evils that were rife, he also touched on usury. For generally, where people are drawn to usury on money, cruelty and countless other frauds and deceptions inseparably accompany it. Hence, by contrast, the praise of a pious and holy man is given as this: that he has not put out his money at usury. So rare is it for the same man to be both upright and a moneylender. Ezekiel goes further. For, in listing the crimes for which the vengeance of God was kindled against the Jews, he uses two words, one of which signifies usury and is derived from a root that also means to gnaw, and the other signifies increase or interest. This is because each man, given over to private gain, sought, or rather extorted, profit from his neighbour's loss. Yet it is certain that the Prophets spoke more harshly of usury because it was expressly forbidden among the Jews. Since they were transgressing a plain command of God, they deserved a graver rebuke. As for the argument that our union among ourselves here is of the same kind, so that the same prohibition of usury should be kept, I answer that as far as civil union is concerned there is some difference. For the circumstances of the place in which the Lord had settled the Jews, and other circumstances too, made it easy for them to trade among themselves without usury. Our union today does not correspond in all respects. Therefore we do not see usury as simply forbidden to us, except insofar as it conflicts with both fairness and charity. The argument of Ambrose, which Chrysostom also cites, is of no great weight: "Money does not give birth to money." What of the sea? What of a house, from whose letting I receive rent? Is silver actually produced from its roofs and walls? But the earth also yields, and goods are brought by sea, which then produce money; and the convenience of a dwelling is usually bought with a set sum of money. So if more profit can be made from trade than from the yield of any estate, will he who has let out a field, perhaps barren, to a tenant, and from it receives rent or yield, be blamed? And will the one who has gained some fruit from money not be allowed the same? And does one who acquires an estate with money not, as a rule, get another yearly sum of money from that money? Whence, then, comes the merchant's profit? "From his own diligence and industry," you say. Who doubts that idle money is entirely useless? Nor does one who asks me for a loan think of keeping idle money with himself from me. The profit therefore comes not from that money but from the yield. Those subtle arguments, then, are indeed clever and have a certain appearance, but when they are weighed more closely in the matter itself, they fall apart. So now I conclude that we must judge about usury not from any particular passage of Scripture, but only from the rule of fairness. This will become clearer by an example. Let there be someone rich, endowed with ample estates and revenues, and yet short of ready money. And let there be another, moderately rich, who does not match the wealth of the first, but who nonetheless has more ready money than he. This man, wishing to buy an estate for himself with his money, is asked by the richer man to lend him money. He who lends could indeed stipulate that his money be repaid with interest on condition that the estate bought with it be pledged to him as security until his money is returned to him (and thus he would look after his own interests better). But he will be content with the fruit or interest of his money. Why, then, should that first contract, without security, be condemned only as a return on money, while the second, under security of a purchased estate and with a yearly return, is forbidden as far harsher? And what else is it than playing like children with God, when things are judged by bare words and not by what is within the thing itself? As if virtues and vices could be distinguished by the form of words alone. I do not intend to examine the matter itself here; I have only wished to indicate it, so that you may weigh it more exactly yourself.

units.la: Tantùm Tantum illud memineris, non hic in vocabulis, sed in re ipsa momentum quæstionis versari. Nunc igitur posito fundamento, veniam ad exceptiones. Exactè enim attendere hic oportet, cùm plerique ex verbulo temere arrepto sibi deinde quiduis audendi suprà quàm par sit, licentiam præripiunt.
units.tr: Only let this be remembered: the weight of the question lies not in words but in the thing itself. Now, with this foundation laid, I will come to the exceptions. For here one must attend closely, since most people, having rashly seized on a little word, then grant themselves a licence to dare whatever goes beyond what is fitting.

units.la: Primum igitur illud esto, me, cum vsuras in genere non damno, non omnes etiam promiscuè probare posse, neque etiam mihi probari si quis vsurariam quasi artem aliam quæstuariam faciteт. Postremò sub istis semper exceptionibus vsuram pecuniæ legitimè percipi posse tantùm, non fœnus.
units.tr: Let this, then, be the first point: although I do not condemn usury in general, I cannot approve all of it indiscriminately, nor would I approve it if anyone practised it as a kind of other money-making trade. Finally, under these exceptions always, money may lawfully be received only as interest on a loan, not as usury (fenus).

units.la: Prima est, ne exigatur vsura ab egentibus hominibus, neque ab iis qui necessitate aut alia calamitate premuntur, ad pensionem vsuræ cogi fas esse.
units.tr: The first is that usury must not be exacted from needy people, nor from those oppressed by poverty or some other calamity; it is not right to compel them to pay interest.

units.la: Secunda, vt qui mutuum dat, non ita addictus sit lucro & commodo suo, vt interea omittat quod ex mera necessitate tenetur procurare: nempe ne dum cautum vult pecuniæ suæ, pauperum fratrum nullam rationem in ea apud illos etiam collocada habeat.
units.tr: The second is that the lender should not be so devoted to his own profit and advantage that he neglects what he is bound, by plain necessity, to provide for. Namely, while he wants his money secured, he should not take no account of his poor brothers in the investment of it.

units.la: Tertia est, ne quid mutuo illo inferatur, quod non conueniat cum æquitate naturali, si expendatur ad illud Christi mandatum: quicquid vultis facere homines vestri causa, vos quoq; perinde illorum causa facite.
units.tr: The third is that nothing should be imposed through that loan which does not agree with natural equity, when weighed against Christ's command: whatever you want men to do for you, do so for them in the same way.

units.la: Quarta, vt qui mutuo accipit, lucretur tantundem, aut plus etiam ex ea pecunia, quàm qui illi mutuò dat, siue indultiam siue operam conferat.
units.tr: The fourth is that the borrower should gain as much from that money, or even more, than the lender does, whether he contributes his industry or his labour.

units.la: Quinta, ne ex eo quod in vsu est, quid vis & æquum sit æstimemus, neque ęquum ipsum ex hominum iniquitate, sed ex Dei verbo metiamur.
units.tr: The fifth is that we should not judge what is right and fair from what is customary, nor measure equity by human iniquity, but by God's Word.

units.la: Sexta, ne tantùm rationem habeamus commodi illius vnius cuiusque res nobis erit, sed etiam attendamus quid expediat Reipublicæ. Vsura enim quam pendunt mercatores, est publicu vetigal. Videndum igitur, vt contractus etiam magis sit ad vtilitatem Reipub. quàm ad illius detrimentum.
units.tr: The sixth is that we should consider not only the advantage that the matter will bring to each person, but also what is expedient for the commonwealth. For the interest that merchants pay is a public tax. We must therefore see that the contract serves the public good more than it harms it.

units.la: Septima est, ne excedatur certus modus constitutus in quauis regione vel Reipub. et si neque eo vsque exigere etiam semper oportuerit. Sæpe enim permitritur quod non potest corrigi vel coerceri edicto ciuili. Imprimis igitur æquitas vna intuenda est, quæ vna præcidat si quid hic nimium erit. Tantum abest verò vt id ad te pro edicto vel axiomatis haberi velim: vt nihil magis exoptem, quàm vt ea humanitate sint omnes, vt mihi necessitas ion sit, argumentum istud deinceps attingere. Quare sic ista complexus sum magis vt gratum facerem tibi, quàm quod vellem te in eo plane acquiescere. Tu pro tua beneuolentia meum istud officium boni consulesac fratrem mihi salutabis. Domi nus e & familiam tucatur.
units.tr: The seventh is that a fixed limit set in any region or commonwealth should not be exceeded, even though one need not always demand the full amount. For often something is allowed which cannot be corrected or restrained by civil edict. Above all, then, the single principle of equity must be kept in view, which alone will cut away whatever is excessive here. I do not, however, wish you to take this as an edict or axiom. I desire nothing more than that all men be so humane that it would not be necessary for me to touch on this subject again. I have set these things out in this way more to please you than because I wanted you to acquiesce in them entirely. In your goodwill, you will take this service of mine in good part, and you will greet my brother for me. May the Lord keep you and your household. ## An liceat fratris mortui viduam ducere in uxorem.

units.la: An liceat fratris mortui vidluam ducere in uxorem.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to take a dead brother's widow as wife.

units.la: QVid hac de re pronuntiauerit Deus in Lege sua, obscurum non est. Mali enim sunt interpretes qui exponunt non esse rapiendam ethoro prioris mariti: vel si repudiata fuerit, id licitum esse illius coniugium viuente adhuc marito. Neque enim conuenit torquere in diuersos sensus, quae vno in loco iisdem verbis pronuntiantur. Vetat Deus retegere turpitudinem vxoris patris & patrui, & filij, & nepotis. Cum de fratris vxore eandem sententiam totidem verbis profert, absurdum est diuersos sensus fingere. Itaque si filius non est patris, vel filij, patrui vel nepotis vxorem habere in matrimonio, vnum & idem de fratris vxore sentire conuenit: de qua similis prorsus lex vno contextu & tenore pergit. Nec ignoro vnde errandi occasionem sumpserint, qui ita sentiunt. Nam quia alio loco iubet Deus, Si quis absque liberis decesserit, fratrem qui superstes erit, viduam accipere, vt ex ea semen mortuo suscitet, hoc perperam & insciè restrinxerunt ad germanos fratres: cum Deus alios cognationis gradus potius designet. Nota est phrasis lingua Hebraica, quae in genere consanguineos omnes fratrum nomine complectitur. Quinetiam Latini olim sic vocarunt patrueles & amitinos. Lex ergo, cuius nunc fit mentio, de vxore fratris mortui ducenda ad eos tantum cognatos dirigitur, qui alioqui non impediuntur a tali coniugio: quia Deo propositum non fuit, ne intercidat nomen mortui, incestuosa coniugii permittere, quae alibi damnauerat. Quare haec duo simul probe conueniunt, germanum fratrem prohiberi a coniugio viduae fratris: & tamen propinquos iure cognationis obstringi ad semen mortuis suscitandum, vbi liberum alioqui ex praescripto Legis coniugium est. Hac ratione Booz vxorem duxit Ruth, quae ante nupta fuerat eius consanguineo. Et ex historia satis patet, lege ad omnes consanguineos spectasse. Quod si quis adhuc contendat fratres germanos in hoc numero comprehendi, eadem ratione ducenda socero in vxorem fuisset nurus, & vxor nepotis patruo, imo & priuigno nouerca: quod dictu pudendum est. Si quis obiiciat, filios Iudae Her & Onan, & Sela fuisse germanos: Thamar tamen duobus nupsisse: solutio in promptu est, Iudam ex communi & recepto gentium more hac licentia non recte fuisse vsum. Satis patet ex omnium temporum historiis apud gentes Orientales foedas mixturas neglecto pudore fuisse in coniugiis. Mala igitur consuetudine, vt fieri solet, tractus fuit Iuda, vt eandem daret vxorem filio secundo, quae ante fuerat vxor primogeniti. Et hoc etiam flagitium inter gentes graßatu esse exprimit Deus, vbi incestus damnat. Hoc igitur tanquam indubium retineo. Lege Moses vetitum esse coniugium cum vidua fratris germani.
units.tr: What God has pronounced on this matter in his Law is not obscure. Those are bad interpreters who explain that it is not to be taken, the bed of the former husband, or that if she has been divorced, it is lawful for her to marry while her husband is still alive. For it is not right to twist into different senses things that are stated in one place in the same words. God forbids uncovering the nakedness of a father's wife, of a father's brother, of a son, and of a grandson. When he gives the same judgment in the same words about a brother's wife, it is absurd to invent different meanings. So if it is not lawful to have as wife a son's, a father's, an uncle's or a grandson's wife, the same must be felt about a brother's wife, about whom the law proceeds in exactly the same context and tenor. Nor am I unaware how those who think otherwise came to err. Because in another place God commands that if anyone dies without children, the surviving brother shall take the widow so that he may raise up seed for the dead, they have wrongly and unwittingly restricted this to full brothers, whereas God rather designates other degrees of kinship. The Hebrew idiom is well known, which in general embraces all blood relations under the name of brothers. Indeed the Latins of old also called paternal cousins and paternal aunts' children by this name. The law now mentioned, about taking the wife of a dead brother, is therefore directed only to those kinsmen who are not otherwise hindered from such a marriage. For it was not God's purpose, lest the name of the dead perish, to permit incestuous marriages which he had condemned elsewhere. Hence these two things agree well together: a full brother is forbidden marriage with his brother's widow, and yet relatives are bound by right of kinship to raise up seed for the dead, where marriage is otherwise free under the prescription of the Law. In this way Boaz took Ruth as wife, who had previously been married to his kinsman. And from the history it is quite plain that the law looked to all kinsmen. But if anyone still contends that full brothers are included in this number, by the same reasoning a daughter-in-law would have been taken as wife by her father-in-law, a wife of a grandson by a paternal uncle, and a stepmother by a stepson, which is shameful even to say. If someone objects that Judah's sons Er and Onan and Shelah were full brothers, and yet Tamar was married to two of them, the answer is ready: Judah did not rightly use this licence, following the common and accepted custom of the nations. It is plain enough from the histories of all ages that among the Eastern peoples foul mixtures in marriage were practised with shame set aside. So Judah, as usually happens through bad custom, was led to give to his second son the wife who had earlier been the wife of the firstborn. God also indicates that this shameful practice was widespread among the nations, where he condemns incest. Therefore I hold this as beyond doubt: by the Law Moses forbade marriage with the widow of a full brother.

units.la: Qui volunt hac lege soluros hodie esse Christianos, obiiciūt illud Pauli, standum esse in libertate ad quam vocati sumus, & quæ nobis à Christo parta est: sed insciè trahunt ad præsentem, quod longè alio fine & consilio protulit Paulus. Agitur enim illic de ceremoniis, quarum obseruatione seruiliter premebant conscientias falsi doctores, qui necessariæ essent ad Dei cultum.
units.tr: Those who want Christians today to be released from this law object to that saying of Paul, that we must stand in the liberty to which we are called and which Christ has won for us. But without realising it, they apply to the present case what Paul put forward with a quite different aim and purpose. For there he is speaking of ceremonies, by whose observance false teachers, who held them necessary for the worship of God, were servilely burdening consciences.

units.la: In hac autem quæstione nihil simile. Quòd rursum excipiunt, nos politicis legibus non subiici, facile diluitur. Neque enim lex de qua nunc agitur, simpliciter numeranda est inter politicas, quia sumpta non est à communi iure gentium, & naturæ honestate: quod ex præfatione colligitur. Quoniam enim omnes vicinas gentes abripuerat libido ad incestus, ut Deus pudicitiam populo suo commendet, ita præfatur, Ego sum Iehoua Deus vester: secundum consuetudinem terræ Ægypti, & secundum morem regionis Chanaan ne ambuletis. Postea subiicit, quinam & quot gradus cognationis vel affinitatis viros & fœminas arceat à coniugio. Si quis rursus excipiat, Legem Israelitis peculiariter latam censeri non debere in parte iurisgentium, præsertim quæ apud alios populos contemneretur: respondeo corruptelam quæ grassati fuit passim in Oriente, nō mereri nomen iurisgentium, quum barbaries fuerit, & castitatis verecundiæque obliuio. Porrò quod naturale est, nullo consensu vel more deleri potest. Tenendum igitur, prohibitione de qua nunc vertitur quæstio, non esse ex earum numero, quæ pro temporum & locorum circumstantiis abrogari queant: sed fluere ab ipso fonte naturæ, & fundatam esse in generali omnium legum principio, quod perpetuum est ac inuiolabile. Deus quidem morem qui apud Ægyptios & profanas gentes inualuerat, sibi displicere testatur. Vnde idem nisi quòd fœditatem licet hominum suffragiis probatam, repudiat ipsę naturæ sensus atque aspernatur? Olim quum Claudius Imperator vxorem sibi sumpsisset Agrippinam neptem suam, tollendi probri causa, senatusconsultum fieri curauit, quo dabatur talibus coniugiis libertas. Nemo tamen repertus est, qui exemplum imitari vellet, excepto duntaxat liberto vno. Dissimilis causa, fateor. Verùm id retuli, vt appareat apud gentes profanas insolubile fuisse ius naturæ: atque inde colligant æqui & moderati homines, inter leges politicas & ius naturæ, quasi ingenitum humano generi & omnium cordibus infixum statui debere magnum discrimen. Huc facit solennis illa admonitio, qua Deus populum suum à profanis gentibus separat, nempe Ægyptiis & Chananæis. In terra enim Chanaan sese miscebant fratres sororibus, posthabito honesti respectu. In Ægyptiis autem nihilo plus fuisse verecundiæ ex veteribus scriptis cōstat. Lex ergo politica censeri non debet, quia Deus clarè populum suum retrahit ab inquinamentis gentium. Vt res clarius innotescat, Paulus in re minima nobis proponit ipsam naturæ legem. Nam vbi docet turpe esse ac indecorum mulieres in publicum prodire, nisi velatas, consulere naturam iubet, an deceat mulieres tonso capite in publico versari: & tandem subiicit, Natura id non patitur. Non video igitur, cur præterita legis politicæ aboleri debeat, quod est ex iure naturæ, ideoque mutari nequit.
units.tr: In this question, however, there is nothing similar. That they again object that we are not subject to political laws is easily refuted. For the law now under discussion is not simply to be counted among the political laws, because it is not taken from the common law of nations and from natural decency, as is gathered from the preface. Since lust had carried all the neighbouring nations away into incest, God, in order to commend chastity to his people, prefaces it thus: "I am Jehovah your God: do not walk according to the custom of the land of Egypt, or the manner of the region of Canaan." Afterwards he sets out which and how many degrees of kinship or affinity bar men and women from marriage. If someone again objects that a law given peculiarly to the Israelites should not be regarded as part of the law of nations, especially since it would be despised among other peoples, I answer that the corruption which was widespread throughout the East does not deserve the name of law of nations, since it was barbarism and a forgetting of chastity and modesty. Moreover, what is natural can be destroyed by no consent or custom. We must hold, therefore, that the prohibition now in question is not among those which may be abrogated according to the circumstances of times and places. It flows from the very fountain of nature and is founded on the general principle of all laws, which is perpetual and inviolable. God indeed testifies that the custom which had prevailed among the Egyptians and profane nations displeases him. Is it not the same thing that the very instincts of nature repudiate and spurn that foulness, though it is approved by the votes of men? When the Emperor Claudius had taken as his wife Agrippina, his own niece, to remove the reproach, he had a decree of the senate passed by which liberty was granted for such marriages. Yet no one was found who wished to imitate the example, except one freedman only. The cause is dissimilar, I admit. But I have related this so that it may appear that among profane nations the law of nature was held inviolable. From this let fair and moderate men conclude that a great distinction ought to be drawn between political laws and the law of nature, which is, as it were, born in the human race and fixed in all hearts. That solemn admonition, by which God separates his people from the profane nations, namely the Egyptians and Canaanites, points to this. For in the land of Canaan brothers mixed with sisters, with regard for decency set aside; and among the Egyptians, it is clear from ancient writings, there was no more modesty. Therefore this law should not be counted as political, because God clearly withdraws his people from the defilements of the nations. To make the matter clearer, Paul sets before us the very law of nature in a very small matter. For where he teaches that it is shameful and unseemly for women to come out in public unless veiled, he bids us consult nature, whether it is fitting for women to appear in public with shaven heads; and finally he adds, "Nature does not allow it." I do not see, therefore, why the prohibition found in the political law should be abolished, when it arises from the law of nature and so cannot be changed.

units.la: Venio nunc ad leges Romanas, quæ eiusmodi coniugia repudiant. Si earum ratio vel in vnius populi utilitate, vel in vsu certi temporis, vel in præsenti necessitate, vel in aliis circunstantiis fundata esset: abrogari possent nouis de causis, aut solui possent earum obseruatio in certis personis priuilegio singulari. Verum quia in illis ferendis tantum spectata fuit perpetua naturæ honestas, ne dispensatio quidem esset tolerabilis. Impune vt liceat statui potest: sicuti in arbitrio principis est pœnas remittere: verum vt vitiosum non fit quod vitiosum esse natura dictat, nullus legislator efficiet.
units.tr: I come now to the Roman laws, which reject such marriages. If their rationale were founded on the advantage of one people, on the custom of a certain age, on present necessity, or on other circumstances, they could be repealed for new reasons, or their observance could be relaxed for certain persons by a special privilege. But since in enacting them only the perpetual honour of nature was considered, not even a dispensation would be tolerable. It may be decreed that something goes unpunished, just as it is in the prince's power to remit penalties; but no lawgiver will make what nature declares to be wrong not wrong.

units.la: Si obiicitur non prohiberi nos in nouo Testamento à talibus coniugiis: respondeo neque inter patrem & filiam coniugiū vetari, neque matri interdici, ne filio suo nubat. An ideo promiscue licebit consanguineis inter se coire? Sed hoc obiectum Pauli testimonio facile diluitur. Nam Corinthium reprehendens, quife nouercæ coniugio polluerat, facinus, inquit, tolerandum ne inter gentes quidem auditur. Si quis excipiat, non agit nunc de coniugio priuigni & nouercæ, solutio intempestiua erit. Nihil enim aliud volo, quam dedecus nobis proponi in exemplo gentium: vt saltem nos pudeat, si plus in illis verecundiæ & modestiæ cernitur. Et sane ad hanc rem vna mihi Pauli admonitio sufficit: qui ad Philippenses scribens, Quæcunque, inquit, sunt vera, quæcunque honesta quæcunque accommoda, quæcúq; boni nominis, si qua virtus, & si qua laus, hæc cogitate.
units.tr: If it is objected that the New Testament does not forbid us such marriages, I reply that marriage between father and daughter is not forbidden there either, nor is a mother forbidden to marry her son. Will it therefore be lawful for blood relatives to unite with one another indiscriminately? But this objection is easily refuted by the testimony of Paul. For in rebuking the Corinthian who had defiled himself with his stepmother, he says that such a crime is not even heard of among the Gentiles. If someone objects that he is not now dealing with the marriage of stepson and stepmother, the objection is beside the point. For I want nothing more than that our shame be set before us by the example of the Gentiles, so that at least we may be ashamed if more modesty and restraint are seen among them. And indeed, for this matter one admonition of Paul's is enough for me, who, writing to the Philippians, says: "Whatever things are true, whatever honourable, whatever just, whatever pure, whatever lovely, whatever of good report; if there is any virtue, and if any praise, think on these things."

units.la: Postquam de quæstione ipsa in genere & ςεπτικῶς disserui: nunc ad Illustrissimum Principem verba mea dirigam, eiusque Ecclesiæ dinem & suppliciter rogabo, & sancte obsecrabo, vt se af sectúsque omnes suos Dei verbo penitus addicat. Equidem persuasus sum hoc desiderium à probabili ratione ortum esse: siue vtriusque partis virtutes mutuum amorem conciliarint, siue etiam spectata fuerit publica utilitas. Superest tamen vt affectum hunc qualemcunque licet originem ducat à bono principio, Illustrissimus Princeps téperet ac moderetur ne in progressu impingat. Multa licere admonet Paulus, quæ tamen non expediunt. Verum omnibus placidi & compositá mente expendis liquebit in hac causa etiam non licere, quod non expedit.
units.tr: Having discussed the question itself in general terms and in a sceptical manner, I now direct my words to the most illustrious Prince, and to his Church, and I will humbly ask and solemnly beseech him that he commit himself and all his people wholly to the Word of God. Indeed, I am persuaded that this desire arose from a reasonable motive, whether the virtues of both parties brought about mutual affection, or whether the public advantage was also considered. Nevertheless, however this feeling may have originated, let the most illustrious Prince take care to temper and moderate it, so that it does not stumble as it goes forward. Paul warns that many things are lawful which nonetheless are not expedient. But if you weigh the matter with a calm and composed mind, it will become clear that in this case too, what is not expedient is not lawful.

units.la: Ad
units.tr: To

units.la: IN quibus gradibus consanguinitatis non permittat Deus Lege sua coniugium contrahere, satis notum est. Fratri sororem patruo vel avunculo neptem, aut etiam proneptem ducere non licet: sicuti nec amita, vel matertera nepoti suo, vel pronepoti nubere potest. Frater autem patruelis, aut consobrinus sororem suam in gradu oppositο ducere non vetatur. Quod Lege Dei mandatum est, vocare in quæstionem fas non est, quantum ad prohibitiones spectat: ut incestuosa coniugia censeri debeant quæ illic damnantur. Sed quia longo usu receptum est, ne consobrinus, vel patruelis sororem suam ducat, offensionis habita fuit apud nos ratio, ne talibus coniugiis libertas concederetur. Si quis ergo interroget de summo iure, non respondebimus sine pliciter peccare, qui suam consobrinam uxorem accipiet. Verum quia hæc licentia exponeret Christi Euangelium multis probris, tenenda est Pauli admonitio, ne libertas nostra cuiquam cedat in offendiculum: deinde vt abstinea nus etiam a licitis, nisi ita expediat. Nec vero seruitus, qua inter se mutuo astricti sunt fideles pro charitatis officio, metuenda est: qu a liberæ manent conscientiæ coram Deo. Quatum ad gradus affinitatis spectat, similis est ratio. Disputant quidam, vel potius litigant, annon viro cœlibi liceat accipere sororem uxoris mortuæ: ac prætextum arripiunt ex verbis Mosis. Uxorem cum sorore eius non accipies in mœrorem vel angustiam, vt reueles turpitudinem eius ea viuente.
