Sed refellitur iisdem verbis eorum error, quia Mo ses illic non tam incestum damnat, quàm crudelitatem mariti, qui vellet cognatam uxoris suæ superducere. Est igitur illic exceptio polygamiæ: quia cum ob duritiem cordis concessum esset Iudæis plures simul uxores habere, excipere voluit Deus, ne duæ sorores, vel cognatæ, quod idem est, in certamen vel æmulationem committerentur.
units.tr: It is well known in which degrees of consanguinity God, by His Law, does not permit marriage. A man may not take his sister, his brother's daughter, or his sister's daughter, nor a granddaughter or great-granddaughter; and likewise an aunt on the father's or mother's side cannot marry her nephew or great-nephew. But a first cousin, whether paternal or maternal, is not forbidden to marry his cousin on the other side. Since God's Law has commanded these prohibitions, it is not right to call into question, so far as the prohibitions go, that the marriages condemned there should be deemed incestuous. But because it has long been the custom among us that a cousin should not marry his cousin, we have taken account of the offence it would cause, so that such marriages were not granted freedom. If anyone therefore asks about the highest right, we will not answer that one who marries his cousin sins without qualification. But since this licence would expose the Gospel of Christ to many reproaches, Paul's admonition must be observed, that our liberty should not become a stumbling block to anyone, and that we should abstain even from things that are lawful, unless it is expedient. Nor indeed is the bondage by which the faithful are bound to one another in the duty of love to be feared, since their consciences remain free before God. As regards degrees of affinity, the reasoning is similar. Some dispute, or rather quarrel, whether a single man may take his dead wife's sister, and they seize on a pretext from the words of Moses: "You shall not take a woman together with her sister, to vex her or distress her, to uncover her nakedness while she is alive" (Lev. 18). But their error is refuted by these same words, because Moses there condemns not so much incest as the cruelty of a husband who would wish to add his wife's kinswoman to her. There is therefore an exception here for polygamy: since, because of the hardness of their hearts, the Jews were allowed to have several wives at once, God wished to except two sisters, or two kinswomen (which amounts to the same), from being set in conflict or rivalry.

units.la: 2. Quia hactenus non tam seuerè, vt decebat, animaduersum fuit in adulteria, vt eorum vitæ parcatur, qui violant fidem coniugij, durum esset virum quocum diuortium fecit uxor adulterii causa, aut mulierem à marito repudiatam, si incontinentia laborent, in totam vitam à coniugio arcere. Itaque necesse est, vt indulgentia vna aliam trahat. Consultum tamen non videtur, in eius partis quæ damnata est, arbitrio ponere, vt statim ad alias nuptias transfuolet. Ideoque libertas ad tempus differenda est, siue prescribere liceat certum tempus, siue expectare dum pars innoxia ad aliud coniugium transeat.
units.tr: 2. Since hitherto adultery has not been punished as severely as it ought to have been, so that the lives of those who violate the faith of marriage are spared, it would be harsh to bar from marriage for life a husband from whom his wife has been divorced on account of adultery, or a wife repudiated by her husband, if they suffer from incontinence. Thus it is necessary that one indulgence should draw another after it. Yet it does not seem advisable to leave to the discretion of the guilty party, the one who has been condemned, to fly at once to another marriage. Therefore the liberty to remarry must be deferred for a time, whether it is possible to prescribe a fixed period, or to wait until the innocent party has passed to another marriage.

units.la: 3. Frigidos & eunuchos quibus negata est virilitas, diserte à matrimonio excludit Christus. Et certè cum nihil magis consensui repugnet quàm error,nō potest obstricta esse mulieris fides qu̧ viro se nubere putauit. Adde ꝑ hæc: frustratio coiugij natutam & finem prorsus euertit Nam matrimonium quid aliud est,quâ maris & fœminæ coniunctio? Quorsum vero institutum est,nisi ob duos fines,nempe vel ab sobolem procreandam,vel vt reme dium sit incontinentiæ? Ergo dubium non est,quin mulier quæ decepta fuit,causa cognita, & bene probata, diuortium impe trare debeat. Nec vero opus est rescindere coniugium,quod ab initio nullum fuit: sed pronuntiare sufficiet eum qui ad coniu gium idoneus non erat, perperam & malo dolo fœminam de cepisse,cui maritus esse non poterat: atque ita stipulationem in qua nihil erat mutuum,irritam fuisse ac prorsus nullam.
units.tr: 3. Christ expressly excludes from marriage the impotent and eunuchs who have been denied virility. And certainly, since nothing is more contrary to consent than error, the faith of a woman who thought she was marrying a man cannot be bound. Add to this that the frustration of marriage utterly overturns its nature and purpose. For what is marriage but the joining of a man and a woman? Why was it instituted, unless for two ends, namely either to produce offspring or to be a remedy for incontinence? Therefore there is no doubt that a woman who has been deceived, once the case has been examined and well proved, ought to obtain a divorce. Nor indeed is there any need to annul a marriage which from the beginning was no marriage; it will suffice to declare that the man who was not fit for marriage has wrongly and by evil deceit deceived a woman to whom he could not be a husband, and so that the stipulation, in which there was nothing mutual, was void and altogether null.

units.la: 4. Matrimonium nonnisi inter puberes legitimum esse,meri tò semper iudicatum fuit. Itaque lusus puerilis est,& simul ta men leuitas castigatione digna,si puer sibi vxorem despondeat. Ac primò statuendum est,quicunque sub parentum vel tutorū sunt potestate,hac maximè in parte non esse liberos nec sui iu ris. Verum quanuis accedat parentum vel tutorum consensus, vel ipsi sunt præcipui auctores: stipulationes tamé ante ætatem factæ impuberes non obstringunt, nisi põlt quàm adoleuerint, maneant in sententia, spontéque testentur,se ratū habere quod priùs intempestiuè gestū fuerat. Si qui vero liberos suos despon deant ante tempus,vt se & sua obligent,non possunt tamen pue ris nondum ad coniugium maturis laqueum iniicere. Et quan quam eiusmodi contractus profanatio quædam est coniugij, si quis tamen temerè multam sibi imposuerit,sustineat quam me ritus est pœnam: coniugij tamen nulla est actio: quia liberū est pueris, vbi ad pubertatem venerint, retractare quicquid paren tes de ipsis malè transegerant.
units.tr: 4. It has always been rightly judged that marriage is valid only between those who have reached puberty. Therefore it is a childish game, and at the same time a levity deserving of rebuke, if a boy betroths a wife to himself. And first it must be established that all who are under the power of parents or guardians are, especially in this matter, not free and not their own masters. But although the consent of parents or guardians may be added, or they are themselves the chief instigators, agreements made before the age of consent do not bind those who are still below puberty, unless afterwards, when they have grown up, they remain of the same mind and freely testify that they ratify what was done untimely before. If parents betroth their children before the proper time, in order to bind themselves and their property, they still cannot cast a snare upon boys not yet ripe for marriage. And although such a contract is a kind of profanation of marriage, if anyone has rashly imposed a heavy penalty on himself, let him bear the punishment he deserves; yet there is no action for marriage, because it is free for the boys, when they have come to puberty, to call back whatever their parents have transacted badly on their behalf.

units.la: Io. Calvinus Vireto S.D.
units.tr: John Calvin to Viret, greetings.

units.la: Ego vero nihil fore melius arbitror,quàm à Nicolao vestro coràm verbis exponi, quæ literis compleƈti iussus fueram. Nam & oratio testis oculati plus fidei ac ponderis,meo iudi cio,habitura est: & multas calumnias diluere poterit,quas illic spargi quotidie à Regiis credibile est. Nam cùm adhuc illic esse- mus, non credas quàm variis criminibus grauarentur pij fra tres. Ego,tametsi facilè poteram suspicari ex quo fonte oriebantur,suppressa auctorum mētione,simpliciter respondebã. Quin etiam Aroniam nonnulli ex legatis imbuti falsis rumoribus ve- nerât,quos difficile fuit ex animis reuellere. Omnino igitur co- sulo,vt Bernā concedat Nicolaus, & ea explicāda curet Senatui, quæ cognosci expediat. Ego literis sidem cius cōmendo,ac rogo ve covt cognoscere velint ex illius ore, quæ ego scribere debuerã. Tu quoque priuatim aliquod verbum ad Consulem addere poteris, si videbitur. Iterum dico, ne refrigescant animi, vtile est ab ipso Nicolao calefieri. Ipsum quoq; in Zebedçi locum subrogari, non displicet. Erit enim, meo iudicio, valde appositus. Vnum dolet, q nunquam hic se retineri passus est. Quanquam enim non palam recusabat: videbam tamen quorsum magis propenderet. Farellus mecum de Roberto quodã graui & moderato senc, facili tamen & placido, locutus erat. Quod ideo tibi in memoriam reuoco, ne prorsus nulla sui consilij rationem habitam putet, sinon illi quoq; satisfacere aliqua excusatione studeas. Erit autē non difficilis excusatio, cum tam idoneus successor nunc vobis sit ad manum. Ego hic valde sum anxius de duobus eligendis. Nam Ioannes Dralliani ministet ad Dominum migrauit. Clusanus vero, vt quotidiana petendi molestia creditores liberaret, nescio quo profugit. En quid faciant cauponæ. Ita enim propter gulæ intemperiem se ære alieno immerserat, vt non alio remedio emergere potuerit. Vereor ne & alij quidam sequantur hoc exemplū. Duos enim habemus, qui biennij stipendio, si interea ieiunent, nequeant se extricare: nec tamen propterea desinunt furtim se abdere sæpe in cauponas, & prandio vno plus absumere, quàm in diarium totius familiæ alimentū habeant. Verum redeo ad electionem. Trollietus quidam, q natione sit Geneuensis, nobis obtrudit: in quo multa signa apparent nobis omnibus parū grata. Nescio autem quid ministro dignum habeat: nisi quod simile amant suos catulos. Vtinam hic nobis adesset proximo veneris die, quo de ea re consultabimus. Sin minus: fac tamen vt ad Nicolai Galasij nuptias te sistas, quę futurę sunt die Dominico, hinc ad 12. diem. Quoniam certo te venturum confido, hæc causa est, cur sim breuior. Nicolao plurimam salutem dices, Imberto, Ribitto & vxori tuæ. Dominus vos conseruet omnes. Vbi veneris, audies quid Vvitebergæ agatur. Geneuæ, 1111. Nonas Iunias.
units.tr: I think nothing would be better than for Nicolas, your man, to explain in person what I was asked to put in writing. His account, given by an eyewitness, will carry more trust and weight, in my judgment, and it will be able to refute many slanders that, as is likely, are spread daily there by the King's men. While we were still there, you would not believe how many charges were laid against the godly brothers. I could easily guess where these came from, but I answered them plainly and without naming the authors. Indeed, some of the envoys came back from Aarau steeped in false rumours, which were hard to drive out of their minds. So my advice, all in all, is that Nicolas should go to Berne and take care to explain to the Senate whatever it is useful for them to know. I commend him to them by letter, and I ask them to hear from his own mouth what I ought to have written. You too may add a word privately to the Consul, if you think fit. Again I say: so that hearts do not cool, it is useful for them to be warmed by Nicolas himself. It also pleases me that he should be substituted in Zebedee's place. In my judgment he will be a very suitable choice. There is one thing I regret: he never allowed himself to be held back here. Although he did not openly refuse, I could see which way he leaned more. Farel had spoken with me about a certain Robert, a grave and moderate elder, yet easy-going and calm. I recall this to you so that he does not think no account was taken of his wishes at all, unless you also take care to satisfy him with some excuse. The excuse will not be difficult, since so suitable a successor is now at hand for you. Here I am very anxious about the choice of two men. John Dralliani has migrated to the Lord. Clusanus, to free himself from the daily nuisance of creditors, has fled I know not where. See what the innkeepers do! For he had so plunged himself into debt through intemperate gluttony that he could find no other remedy to climb out. I fear that some others will follow this example. For we have two men who, if they fast meanwhile, cannot extricate themselves from their two years' stipend; yet they do not stop slipping away secretly into inns, and spending more on one lunch than would feed their whole household for a day. But to return to the election. A certain Trollietus, a native of Geneva, is being thrust upon us, and in him many signs appear that are not at all pleasing to all of us. I do not know what he has that makes him worthy of the ministry, except that people love their own puppies alike. I wish he were here with us next Friday, when we shall consult about this matter. If not, please nevertheless make sure you present yourself at the wedding of Nicolas Galasius, which is to take place on Sunday, twelve days from now. Since I am confident that you will come, this is why I am briefer. Give my warmest greetings to Nicolas, Imbert, Ribit and your wife. May the Lord keep you all. When you come, you will hear what is going on at Wittenberg. Geneva, 2 June.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: Your John Calvin.

units.la: Io. Calvinvs Vireto s. d.
units.tr: John Calvin to Viret, greetings.

units.la: Iam pridem ad te scripturus eram, nisi quod sciebam literas meas nihilo citius ad te venturas esse, quàm si in reditum vsque tuum differrem. Nunc quia ex temporis supputatione rediisse te coniicio, accipe quæ in mentem nunc veniunt. Simul atque abiisti, mira certamina inter Sebastianum & eius sororios exciterunt, quæ me exercuerunt diu & sæpe, dum volo amico arbitrio ea componere. Has autem partes ideo suscipiebam, ne ad contentionem adhuc defenderent, cuius rumor cum
units.tr: I had meant to write to you long ago, but I knew my letters would reach you no sooner than if I postponed them until your return. Now that I reckon from the timing that you have come back, here is what comes to mind. As soon as you had left, remarkable quarrels broke out between Sebastian and his brothers-in-law, which have troubled me for a long time and often, as I have tried to settle them by friendly arbitration. I took on this role so that they would not carry the dispute further, since rumour of it was spreading far and wide and damaging the reputation of the school. Yet despite great zeal and diligence I could not prevent each of them from slandering the other, so that everywhere many people were circulating stories.

units.la: Epist.387. infamia scholæ longius manaret. Neque tamen id consequi potui magno studio ac diligentia, quin alius alium traduceret: atque ita passim fierent multorum fabulæ. Vbi communis controuersia de solutione dotalis pecuniæ sedata fuit, ecce novæ litis inter Sebastianum & Petrum, partim de administratione rei familiaris, partim de habitatione. Nihil unquam vidi tam implicitum. Postquam multum inter se iurgati sunt, facta est qualiscunque transactio: sed quæ mox novam controversiam peperit. Itaque sic exulcerati fuerunt hinc inde animi, ut vix solidam amicitiam unquam inter eos fore sperem, qualis inter fratres esse debet. Nunc quidem quieuerunt turbæ illæ, sed vereor ne leui occasione subito rursum excitentur. Ecce tibi scholæ nostræ statum, ne nobis invideas. Rursum Nicolaus Iuffiacus novam modestiam nobis ante paucos dies peperit, sua superbia. Cum enim nescio quem commendasset, cui putabat iniuriam fieri, cum optimo iure in carcerem coniiceretur: quia non acquiescebant eius postulato Assessores, in eos acerbi oratione invectus est. Res delata ad Senatum, qui larus hanc occasionem eius expellendi arripuit. Nos intercessimus: non in hominis gratiam, qui non multis abhinc diebus mihi nimium deferri conquerebatur: sed ne peruersum exemplum in Ecclesia ederetur tam facili vel præcipiti potius Ministri eiectione. Nunc amplius inquiunt: deinde, nobis adhibitis, pronuntiabunt. Si video esse fatis iustam causam, cur abdicetur, non vlterius pugnabo. Mirum quàm fortiter philosophetur Henricus noster de afferendo mi-nisterij honore: quia scilicet tam præclarum huius constantiæ exemplum nobis edidit. Quod ego minime tacui. Et tamen satisfeci meo officio, testatus palàm coram omnibus, me non respicere quid mihi factum sit: sed quid fieri debeat. Collegæ nostri toleranter pergunt in concionibus: verum in duobus unimeo nonnihil ξενοδοξίαν. Quis horum alter sit, intelligis: quàm quàm certè opinione nostra moderatiorem se præbet. Petrus autem aliqua signa iam dedit, quæ mihi displicent: siquidem verum est quod mihi retulit Geniftonius. Quoniam nondum satis id compertum habemus, decreui propius iam obseruare. Si in eo falsi fuerimus, vbinam erit fides? Ludouicus, quod semper verebar, plus leuitatis & inconstantiæ habet in verbis & actione, quàm ministerium nostrum deceat. Sed tempore, ut spero, vitium hoc corrigetur: modò non desint reliqua magis necessaria. Quia Neocomo transfuli cum Bernam ires, non dubito quin tibi ad plenum exposuerint fratres de Farelli professione, quod tibi ex eius literis indicare possum. Proinde super sedeo: literas tamen ipsas mitto, ne quid desideres. Frumentus nuper Lugdu-no rediit. Refert Reginam Nauarræ meliore nunc esse animo, quàm
units.tr: Epist.387. Once the common dispute over the repayment of the dowry money had been settled, a new lawsuit arose between Sebastian and Peter, partly over the management of the household property and partly over where they should live. I have never seen anything so tangled. After they had quarrelled bitterly with each other, some kind of settlement was reached, but it soon gave birth to a new controversy. So their feelings have been so inflamed on both sides that I can hardly hope for a solid friendship between them, such as ought to exist between brothers. For now those disturbances have quietened, but I fear they will be stirred up again suddenly on some slight occasion. There is the state of our school for you, so you need not envy us. Again, Nicolas Iuffiacus has given us fresh trouble a few days ago, through his own arrogance. When he had recommended someone whom he thought was being wronged, and who was being thrown into prison quite rightly, he attacked the assessors in a bitter speech because they would not agree to his demand. The matter was referred to the Senate, which eagerly seized this chance of getting rid of him. We interceded, not out of regard for the man, who only a few days ago complained to me that he was being treated too harshly, but so that no perverse precedent would be set in the Church by the hasty, or rather headlong, dismissal of a minister. They now say they will go further, and that afterwards they will pronounce judgment with us present. If I see that there is a sufficiently just cause for his removal, I will not fight on further. It is remarkable how bravely our Henry philosophises about maintaining the honour of the ministry, since he has shown us such a splendid example of constancy. I have not been silent about this. Yet I have discharged my duty, having testified openly before everyone that I am not looking at what has been done to me, but at what ought to be done. Our colleagues continue patiently in their sermons, but in two of them there is something of a touch of vanity [ξενοδοξίαν]. You understand who the second of these is, although he presents himself in a more moderate way than we thought. Peter, however, has already given some signs which displease me, if what Geniston told me is true. Since we do not yet have sufficient proof of this, I have decided to watch him more closely. If we are mistaken in this, whom can we trust? Ludovicus, as I always feared, has more lightness and inconstancy in his words and conduct than our ministry ought to have. But, as I hope, this fault will be corrected in time, provided the remaining and more necessary things are not lacking. Since you passed through Neuchâtel on your way to Bern, I do not doubt that the brothers have fully explained to you the profession of Farel, which I can also tell you from his letters. Therefore I will say no more about it, but I am sending the letters themselves so that you lack nothing. Frument recently returned from Lyon. He reports that the Queen of Navarre is now in better spirits than ever before. But this is according to her own words, for he spoke with her familiarly. Yet you know that one should not readily trust even a messenger's words on everything. He is so drunk with this glory, because he was admitted to the Queen's company, that he seems to me to have entirely lost the small part of sound sense that remained to him. For, among other absurdities, when she said she wanted my letters, he wanted to dictate the subject to me, and, as if my talent were not enough, he forbade me to send anything unless it had first been read and approved by him. He spread a rumour through the whole city that he had nearly preached before the King. There are a thousand things of this kind. Still, so that you do not think he is lying about everything, he has some of what he tells from the Queen or from her servants. But the courtiers, seeing that the man was credulous, took advantage of his easygoing nature for their own ends, so that this report would reach Germany, to reconcile the hearts of the pious to the King, whom they know are now deeply alienated. Among other things, they persuaded him that the Chancellor was held in prison for no other reason than that he had, without the King's command, arranged for that edict about books to be published and had ordered the godly to be burned. What more is there to say? He not only believed everything, but invented even more for himself than he had heard. The King of France is sending an army into Spain, and they say the Turk is threatening from the other side. The Duke of Orléans has so far achieved nothing notable, except that he burned two towns. Yet that is old news; perhaps much has happened since then. Our business is now a knot hard to untie, and all the more so because, even if everything were conceded on our side, the other party still holds out an uncertain hope. Nevertheless, I have won a smaller victory before the Senate. Pray the Lord that the matter may be brought to a happy outcome. For there is a danger that, when it comes to the sermon, those few men you know to be old and practised stirrers of trouble [ἡμαγοὺς] may throw everything into confusion. But I hope the Lord will steer things, provided we pray to him diligently. Farewell, most excellent brother and dearest to me. Greet all the brothers, and your aunt and your wife as well, to whom my wife gives thanks for such a friendly and holy consolation. For she cannot write back except through a secretary, and she would be greatly hindered in dictating. The Lord has certainly dealt us a severe and bitter blow in the death of our little son. But he is a Father; he knows what is good for his children. Farewell again, may the Lord be with you. I wish I could hurry over there. I would gladly talk with you for half a day. Geneva, 19 August.

units.la: ξενοδοξίαν [?] quàm vnquam fuerit. Verùm refert ex eius verbis. Nam cum ea familiariter est colloquutus. Tametsi non omnibus etiam nuntij verbis fidem temerè habendam nofti. Sic enim hac gloria inebriatus est, quòd in colloquium Reginæ admissus fit, vt particulam fani cerebri, quæ illi restabat, mihi videatur prorsus amisisse. Nam præter cæteras ineptias, cùm diceret Reginam meas literas desiderare, mihi volebat dictare argumentum: & quasi pa-rum ingenio meo sideret, vetabat ne quid mitterem, nisi ante à se lectum ac recognitum. Rumorem in tota vrbe dissipauit, minimum abfuisse, quin coram Rege concionatus fuerit. Mille sunt eius generis. Ne tamen putes ipsum omnia mentiri, partem eorum, quæ narrat, habet vel à Regina, vel ab eius ministris. Sed artifices aulici cùm viderent hominem credulum, eius facilitate abusi sunt in suum commodum, vt hæc fama in Germaniam perueniret, quæ reconciliaret piorum animos Regi, quos sciunt nunc vehementer alienatos esse. Inter alia, persuaserunt Cancellarium nõ alia magis de causa teneri in carcere, quàm quod iniussu Regis edictum illud de libris promulgandum curauerit, piosque exuri iusserit. Quid plura? non modò omnia credidit: sed sibi ipse plura confinxit, quàm audierat. Rex Galliæ exercitum traiicit in Hispaniam, cui aiunt Turcam altera ex parte imminere. Dux Aureliensis nihil adhuc egit memorabile, nisi quòd oppida duo exusit. Quanquam illud vetus est. Fortassis ab eo tempore multa contigerunt. Nostris nunc nodus est difficilis ad soluendum: eòque magis, quòd etiam si hinc omnia fuerint concessa, ambiguam spem adhuc altera pars facit. Euici tamen apud Senatum minorem. Precare Dominum, vt ad fœlicem exitum res perducatur. Est enim periculum, ne cùm in concionem ventum fuerit, omnia conturbent pauci illi, quos nosti esse veteres & exercitatos ἡμαγοὺς. Sed Dominus spero, gubernabit, modò nos diligenter eum precemur. Vale optime & mihi charissime frater. Saluta fratres omnes, materteram tuam quoque ac vxorem: cui mea gratias agit de tam amica & sancta consolatione. Rescribere enim non potest, nisi per amanuensem. Et in dictando non parum esset impedita. Dominus certè nobis vulnus inflixit graue & acerbum in morte filioli. Sed pater est; nouit quid filius suis expediat. Vale iterum, Dominus tibi adsit. Vtinam iceret istuc vsque accurrere. Libenter tecum dimidium diem confabularer. Geneuæ, x i x. Augusti.

units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: V.ij.
units.tr: V.ij.

units.la: HIcfrater accurátiore apud te testimonio non habet opus. Scire potes aliquá ex parte, qualiter apud nos fe gesserit. Cer-te insignis patientiæ testimonium reddere illi possumus. Nam cum extremam egestatem toto anno pertulerit, ita deuo-ratuit hanc acerbitatem, ut vix pauci querelam unam ex e us ore audierint. Animo est recto & syncero. In tota eius vita nihil ani-maduertimus non dignū pio, & Christiano homine. Quod prae-teritus a nobis fuit, cum aliquos ministros eligeremus, loga ex-cusatione apud te non indiget. Nosti enim nostrorum hominū delicias. Tantum cos linguae Prouincialis taedium cepit, ut haec sola aptissimos alioqui homines ingratos illis reddat. Deinde si reputes quos illi praetulerimus, nihil hoc imminuet ex illius exi-stimatione. Quanquam hoc totum melius est taceri, nisi forte quispiam mentionem iniiciat. Qua de causa voluit te monitum, ut occurras eiusmodi obiectationibus. Ego vix audebā illi con-silium dare, antequam tecum communicassem. Quoniā tamen ita censuerunt fratres, repugnare noluī, quin ad vos proficiscere-tur. Literas illi ad vos breves dedi: si a vobis obtinebit aliquam commendationem, spero aliquid Bernae effecturum. Nam id no-bis persuasit Nicolaus. Habet etiam meas literas ad Consulē Ne-gliuni. Verum tu totum hoc negotium meliustuo consilio mo-deraberis. Gaudeo vehementer, quod te brevi venturum promit-tas. Ego cum aliis desiderem, ut par est, uxorem tuā unitati suae restitui: tum haec etiam causa accedit, ne te aduersa eius valetu-do diutius moretur. Vale. Dominus tibi adsit, uxorem tuam bre-ui liberet a morbo, totam domum conseruet. Salutabis omnes tuos diligenter.
units.tr: Brother, there is no need for a more detailed testimony about him from me. You can know to some extent how he has conducted himself among us. Certainly we can give him a testimony of remarkable patience. For although he endured extreme want through the whole year, he swallowed down this bitterness so that scarcely a few heard a single complaint from his mouth. His mind is upright and sincere. In his whole life we have noticed nothing unworthy of a godly and Christian man. The fact that he was passed over by us when we were choosing some ministers does not need a long excuse before you. You know the delicacies of our people. The distaste for the provincial language has taken hold of them so strongly that this alone makes men otherwise most suitable unwelcome to them. Moreover, if you consider whom we preferred to him, this will not diminish his reputation in any way. Yet it would be better for all this to be passed over in silence, unless perhaps someone raises the matter. For this reason I wanted to warn you, so that you may meet objections of this kind. I hardly dared to give him advice before I had shared it with you. Since the brothers, however, were of this opinion, I did not resist his going to you. I gave him a brief letter to you; if he obtains some recommendation from you, I hope he will accomplish something at Berne, for Nicolas persuaded us of this. He also has my letter to the Syndic Negliunus. But you will manage this whole business better by your own counsel. I rejoice greatly that you promise to come soon. Like the others, I desire, as is fitting, that your wife be restored to her health; and this reason also adds weight, that her adverse state of health may not keep you away any longer. Farewell. May the Lord be with you, free your wife from her illness soon, and keep your whole household safe. Greet all your people diligently.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO s.
units.tr: CALVINVS VIRETO s.

units.la: MItto ad te literas Pellicani, ut ipse quoque mecum cógites, quorsū vergat, quod scribit. De libris, quos petit, nihil cer-ti habeo: expectabo donec e nundinis redierit Guillelmus. Antonius, ut scis, receptus est: idque sine vlla controuersia. Sic sa-piunt fratres, ut nihil melius iud cauerint, quàm tot flagitia si-lentio abolere. Fieri non potest, quin Dominus ad hac nostram socordiam vindicandam breui tribunal conscendat. Mihi per Matthaeum indicauit, se hortatu Sulceri, redire mecum in gratiā cupere, sed qua lege ad hanc reconciliationem descenderem? Caeterum si colloquium semel petierit, Dominus viam aperiet. Nuper disceptationem habuimus cum Senatu: sed quae statim fuit composita. Renuntiauerat nobis Syndicus in Consistorio, Senatum ius excommunicandi sibi retinuisse. Continuò excepi, decretum hoc aut morte mea, aut exilio sinciri oportere. Postridie vocaui fratres ex eorum consilio postulaui à Syndicis, vt Senatum nobis extra ordinem darent: annuerunt, etsi non libenter, illic longa & graui oratione de tota re disserui: obtinui nullo negotio quod petebam: quantum intelligo, acriter increpiti auctores, quos si nescias, diuinare tamen potes. Bene vale. Dominus te custodiat, & semper gubernet suo Spiritu, frater mihi dilestissime. Saluta mihi Ribittum, Imbertum, & reliquos. Pridie Paschatis.
units.tr: I am sending you a letter from Pellicanus, so that you too may consider with me where what he writes is leading. About the books he asks for I have nothing certain: I shall wait until Guillelmus returns from the fair. Antonius, as you know, has been received, and that without any dispute. The brothers have judged so wisely that they could not have decided better than to bury such scandals in silence. It cannot be but that the Lord will soon mount his judgment seat to avenge our negligence. He has told me through Matthew that, at Sulcer's urging, he wishes to return to favour with me; but on what terms would I come down to this reconciliation? Moreover, if he seeks a conference only once, the Lord will open the way. Lately we had a dispute with the Council, but it was settled at once. The Syndic had reported to us in the Consistory that the Council had kept for itself the right of excommunication. I immediately objected that this decree must be resisted even at the cost of my death or exile. The next day I summoned the brothers, and at their advice I asked the Syndics to give us an extraordinary hearing before the Council. They agreed, though not willingly. There I spoke at length, in a weighty speech, about the whole matter, and I obtained without difficulty what I was asking for. As far as I understand, the authors of the trouble were sharply rebuked; if you do not know who they are, you can nevertheless guess. Farewell well. May the Lord keep you and always guide you by his Spirit, my most beloved brother. Greet Ribittus, Imbert and the rest for me. On the day before Easter.

units.la: Ioannes Caluinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO S.
units.tr: CALVIN TO VIRET, GREETING.

units.la: HEri mihi sub cœnam allatæ sunt tuæ literæ, quibus binas Farelli incluseras, quas remitto. Hodie quoque alias àFa-rello accepi. Quoniam prioribus videbatur à te & à me pri-uatim petere consilium: non ausus sum in cœtu nostro facere mentionem. Nunc amplius hoc postulat, vt omnes simul respō-deamus. Verùm serius quàm oportuit, redditæ mihi literæ suo-rum. Quanquam non video, quid profuturum fuerit, si etiam ve-nissent in tempore. Quàm enim ridiculum fuerit, aliis dare con-silium, quo ipsi indigemus? Negabimus id ferendum esse, vt tē-runcius minuatur ex Ecclesiæ bonis? Quid auctoritatis habitu-ræ sunt nostræ literæ apud Neocomenses, cùm id apud nos pa-tiamur fieri? Dicemus per nos minimè stare. Sit sanè ita. Sed quia non admittunt nostri medicinâ contenti improbare quod pec-cant, non vltrà tendimus. Si quid sentiamus, habere volunt, non est difficile eorum voto satisfacere. Sed quantulum illud prodes-se rit? Consultabo tamen cum tribus aut quatuor, num aliqua pos-sit inueniri speciosa ratio. Ex Germania nihil habemus noui, nisi vulgi rumores. Nam Alexander, cui datæ sunt ad me literæ, suo more vagatur. Schola nostra perplexos nos habet. Nemo enim aptus ad id munus nunc occurrit. Nos quidem merito pœnas damus. Sed dolendum est, nulla in strictâ disciplina contineri pueros: & sp m quæ perquam exigua erat, omnino pessum ire. Ego me consolor, quod nulla mali huius portio culpæ meæ as-signari potest. Sed misera consolatio, quæ malo nihil assert le-uationis. Francisco consilium dedi, quale restabat in rebus des-peratis. Tu si quod habes melius, nobis commodes. Camperellus, vt auuc, discursur. Sed, nisi omnem pudorem abiecerint fratres, nihil proficiet. Quanquam à fratribus iam timere desij. Queritur
units.tr: Your letter reached me in the evening, at supper, enclosing two from Farel, which I am sending back. I also received another from Farel today. Since the earlier ones seemed to ask for counsel from you and me privately, I did not dare mention them in our assembly. Now the matter requires more, that we all reply together. But the letters from your people were delivered to me later than they should have been. Still, I do not see what good it would have done even if they had arrived in time. For how ridiculous it would be to give advice to others when we ourselves need it! Shall we say that it must not be tolerated that even a farthing be cut from the church's goods? What authority will our letters carry with the Neuchâtelois, when we allow this to happen among ourselves? We will say that the fault is not ours. So be it. But since our people, content with a mere reproof of their faults, will not admit them, we go no further. If they want us to state an opinion, it is not hard to satisfy their wish. But how much good will that do? I will nonetheless consult three or four others, to see whether some plausible plan can be found. From Germany we have no news except common rumours. Alexander, to whom the letters for me were entrusted, is wandering about as usual. Our school keeps us perplexed, for no one suitable for that post presents himself now. We indeed justly pay the penalty. But it is lamentable that the boys are kept under no strict discipline, and that the hope, which was already very slight, is utterly going to ruin. I console myself that no part of this evil can be assigned to my fault. But it is a wretched consolation, which brings no relief to the evil. I gave Francis the advice that was left in desperate matters. If you have anything better, lend it to us. Camperell, as I guess, is running about. But unless the brothers cast off all shame, it will achieve nothing. Though I have now ceased to fear the brothers.

units.la: V.iij. enim me sibi & sodali suo Macrino esse infestum, quod paro-chiæ Monien-sis agros emerint. Vides quibus cuniculis nos a-doriantur. Nisi velimus omnia perire, necesse est illum cæteris esse exemplo. Fuimus enim hactenus nimis remissi. Vale frater, & amice integerrime, vna cum vxore & familia, quam meo & vxoris meæ nomine salutabis, quæ ipsa se precibus vestris commendat. Ita enim subacta est morbi magnitudine, vt ægrè se recipiat. Interdum videtur convalescere. Mox recidit. Collegæ mei te omnes diligenter salutant. Copus te suis nuptiis interesse cupetet, si esset commodum. Scis enim, opinor, nos Gurini viduam illi dedisse vxorem. Dominus vos istic conseruet. Geneuæ, x iii. Octobris.
units.tr: For he complains that I am hostile to him and to his companion Macrinus, because they have bought fields in the parish of Monnaz. You see with what mines they assail us. Unless we want everything to perish, it is necessary to make him an example to the rest, for we have been too lax until now. Farewell, brother, most upright friend, together with your wife and household, whom you will greet in my name and my wife's; she commends herself to your prayers. For she has been so overcome by the severity of her illness that she recovers with difficulty. At times she seems to be getting better, but soon she relapses. All my colleagues greet you warmly. Copus would have liked you to attend his wedding, if it were convenient. For you know, I think, that we gave him as wife the widow of Gurin. May the Lord keep you there. Geneva, 13 October.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS VIRETO S.
units.tr: Calvin to Viret, greetings.

units.la: DE Combaudo sic respondent Fratres, hominem hic cogni-tum esse quieti ingenij, honestę vitæ, non improbum alio-qui, nec vllius notæ deterioris, nisi quòd supramodum est tenax: etiam vsque ad maximas sordes. Quandiu apud nos vixit, aliis negabat sibi esse pecuniam: aliis fatebatur, aliquantulum se habere, quo posset tenuiter se alere ad tres menses: apud alios augebat summam triplo amplius. Sed cùm vxorem duxit, tunc patuit crumenam habere satis bene refertam. Saltem non mi-nus sexaginta coronatis attulit ad vxorem. Si querulus est, sci-to eum esse ex animo. Æstuat enim mira diffidentia. Verùm se-rió monendus est, vt discat reposita in Dominum cura excute-re ista tormenta animi, quibus se frustra cruciat. Hoc, vt dixi, vi-tio excepto, virum probum & syncerum iudicamus Perrerio cer-tè non multum exhibuit humanitatis: cùm ille tamen valde in-digeret. Sex tantum quadrantes huius monetæ illi dedit commo-dato: idque maligne. Date operam, vt corrigatur tanta diffiden-tia, & quæ inde nascitur tenacitas, & reliqua, sperɑmus, bene ha-bebunt. Omnes nostri diligenter te salutant, vxorem tuam cum matertera totaque familia. Dominus vos conseruet. De vxore quia nihil dudum scribis, eam meliuscule habere iam confido. Mea paulatim reualescet, gratia Domino: nisi quòd tussis illi plurimùm molesta est, dolorésque ordinarios exacerbat. Vale frater & amice integerrime, iterum atque iterum. Geneuæ, x vii i. Octobris.
units.tr: The brothers reply about Combaud as follows. He is known here as a man of quiet temperament and upright life, not otherwise dishonest, and of no worse reputation, except that he is excessively tight-fisted, even to the point of the basest meanness. While he lived among us, he would tell some people that he had no money; to others he admitted that he had a little, enough to keep himself modestly for three months; with others he inflated the sum threefold. But when he took a wife, it became plain that he had a purse well stocked. He brought at least sixty crowns to his wife. If he is querulous, know that it comes from his disposition, for a remarkable distrust seethes within him. Yet he must be advised earnestly to learn to cast all his care upon the Lord, and so to shake off those torments of mind with which he vainly torments himself. Apart from this fault, as I have said, we judge him an honest and sincere man. Certainly he showed Perrerius little kindness, though Perrerius was in great need. He gave him only six farthings of this coin on loan, and that grudgingly. See to it that such great distrust is corrected, and the tightfistedness that springs from it, and the rest, we hope, will turn out well. All our people greet you warmly, along with your wife, her aunt, and the whole household. May the Lord keep you. Since you have written nothing lately about your wife, I trust she is now doing rather better. Mine will gradually recover, by the grace of the Lord, except that her cough is very troublesome to her and aggravates her usual pains. Farewell, brother and most upright friend, again and again. Geneva, 18 October.

units.la: Ioannes Calvinus tuus.
units.tr: John Calvin, yours.

units.la: CALVINVS
units.tr: CALVIN

units.la: ERgo perinde acsi in proximum mensem indictus esset habendi Concilij dies, copias vestras adornaris. Sed hoc ipsum argumento est, quàm temerè omnia & fortuitò apud vos, nihil prudenter, nec confultò agatur, quòd cùm ex toto regno deligendi essent idonei homines, talibus mandatum sit negotium: nisi forte, quòd alioqui inertissimi omnium, semper ad nocendum plus satis sunt instructi. Cæterum Concilij expectationem, quæ apud vos summa esse fertur, de nihilo conceptam arbitror. Conuentus Imperij Februario agetur. Verùm ante Martium nulla feria consultatio haberi incipiet. Noui Germaniæ morem. Hoc tibi tam certò possum asserere, acsi præsens interessem. Instabùt nostri, vt Antichristo exclu so, tandem ordinis inter se aliquid constituant: negabunt hoc sibi licere, qui adhuc voluntaria seruitute idolo sunt obnoxij. Cæsar, vt nostris ex parte satisfaciat, paratum se ad omnia fore pollicebitur. Forsan & aliquam actionis speciem ostentabit: sed quam statim ab initio abrumpet inuenta aliqua occasione, quæ nunquam istis hominibus deest. Hic certè seritexitus, non licere nisi ex Papæ auctoritate quicquam in Religionis causa decerni. De cogenda Synodo vbi cœptum fuerit agitari, nostri mox reclamabunt, indignum esse vt hæc Religionis cognitio, professis Dei hostibus deferatur. Antichristum postulabunt reum ad causam dicendam, iudicem certè nullo modo admittent. Quibus autem conditionibus Tridentum perтrahi posse existimas? verù n vt à nostris nihil sit remotæ, cùm nihil libentius sacturus sit Cæsar, quàm vt conuenire ad bellum Turcicum omnium animis suspensum Ecclesiæ statum ad tempus relinquit: annon in ea re, ad quam expectendam spontè alioqui propensus erit, facile idolo gratificabitur? Quanquam fingamus iam indictum esse Concilium: iam omnia esse comparata, putamúsne artem idolo defuturam, quà rem totam disturbet? Quid ergo Religioni horrendum in modum laceræ ac dissipatæ, quid miserę Ecclesiæ, quæ iam iam videtur ad interitum ruere, quid nomini Christiano, quid Dei gloriæ fiet? Petendum certè ab eo, vt horum omnium curam suscipiat ipse solusac sustineat. Nostri torpent, nec spes est cordate strenuéque scuros, nisi Dominus alicunde eos expergefaciat. Quanquam impij satis illis occasionis præbent, vt sibi incipiant cauere. Omnia tentarunt Colonienses Canonici, cum tota Clericorum sacre, vt Archiepiscopum deiicerent suo loco. Conuocarunt omnium ordinum Comitia, vt sibi permitteretur alium subro-gate. Negatum est. Idem à Cæsare postularunt, respondit se non. V.iiij.
units.tr: So you are making ready your forces as though the day for holding a council had been fixed for next month. But this very thing shows how rashly and by chance everything is done among you, and nothing prudently or deliberately, since when suitable men had to be chosen from the whole kingdom, the business was entrusted to such people. Unless perhaps, being the most inactive of all men otherwise, they are always sufficiently equipped for doing harm. As for the expectation of a council, which is said to be great among you, I think it has been conceived out of nothing. The assembly of the Empire will meet in February, but no formal deliberation can begin before March. I know the custom of Germany. I can assert this to you as surely as if I were present. Our people will press, so that once the Antichrist is shut out, they may at last settle some order among themselves; those who are still bound by voluntary servitude to the idol will deny that this is permitted to them. Caesar, to satisfy our side in part, will promise that he will be ready for everything. Perhaps he will even show some appearance of action, but he will break it off at the very start, as soon as some pretext is found, which these men never lack. Here they will certainly sow the claim that nothing in the cause of religion may be decided except by the authority of the Pope. When the summoning of a synod begins to be discussed, our people will at once protest that it is unworthy for this examination of religion to be handed over to the professed enemies of God. They will demand that the Antichrist be called to answer the charge, but they will by no means admit him as judge. On what conditions do you think Trent could be brought about? Surely, not without our side's objection, since Caesar will do nothing more willingly than leave the state of the Church for a time, while a war against the Turks holds all minds in suspense. Will he not readily gratify the idol in that matter, which he is otherwise naturally inclined to wait for? Even if we imagine that the council has now been summoned and that everything has been prepared, do we think the idol will lack a device by which to throw the whole business into confusion? What then will become of religion, dreadfully torn and scattered, of the wretched Church, which now seems ready to fall to ruin, of the Christian name, of the glory of God? Surely we must ask that he himself take up and sustain the care of all these things alone. Our people are sluggish, and there is no hope that they will bestir themselves with courage and vigour, unless the Lord rouses them from somewhere. Yet the impious give them plenty of opportunity to begin taking precautions. The Cologne canons tried every means, with the whole clergy of the diocese, to depose the archbishop from his place. They summoned assemblies of all the orders, so that they might be allowed to elect another in his place. It was refused. They demanded the same from Caesar; he replied that he would not, provided they did their duty. He did not wish to concede it openly to them. But from those circumlocutions one may guess that he would by no means oppose it if they stirred up disturbances; if they went further, there would certainly be war, by which the whole state of Germany will either be weakened or seriously shaken. But the Lord will also see to these things. This is my only consolation: that death cannot be a misfortune for a Christian man. Meanwhile I shall lament, as I ought, the calamities of the Church and share the lot of the pious, but in such a way that I do not give way to despair. If we agreed well among ourselves, I would be less anxious; but among those men, the preparations of enemies, and a leisure enough for going mad, is something like a portent. Look, on the other side, someone or other has provoked Oliander with an elegy, a man whose brain is hardly sound himself. Since he puffs himself up in purple, he has filled his pamphlet with black bile in his anger, so that I am greatly ashamed of him. But nothing torments me more than that in every third word he insults the Zwinglians. So, as if we had handed our tongues and hands over to the impious, we provide them with a pleasant and sweet spectacle, while we tear one another apart. Someone will say: who would not lose heart at so many obstacles? I confess that there is no spirit so iron that it would not be broken, unless it looked to the Lord. And so I interpret it thus: the Lord wishes in every way to test whether we depend upon men. But far from being weakened by this, I receive from it no ordinary confirmation. For while I see the Church being marvellously governed by the Lord amid these waves, so that it is not overwhelmed, and while I see the storms themselves, when everything seems about to be thrown into confusion, settle and grow calm in a moment, why should I not conceive good hope from this? Let us therefore press on in the course of our calling, supported by this confidence, that the Church will emerge, since it has God as the perpetual guardian of its salvation. But since not everyone has the same strength of mind, the more intimately I lay all things in your bosom, the fewer people you will share them with.

units.la: Epist.391. defuturum, modò officium suum facerent. Palam illis concedere noluit. Verùm ex illis ambagibus diuinare licet, cum minimè refragaturum, si quid turbarum mouerent: si vltrà progressi fuerint, certum bellum: quò totus Germaniæ status, aut labefactabitur, aut grauiter concutietur: sed hæc quoque videbit Dominus. Hæc mihi vnica consolatio est, quòd mors miseri esse non potest homini Christiano. Interea gemam, vt debeo, Ecclesiæ calamitates & afficiar piorum sorte: sed ita vt non examinem. Si inter nos bene conueniret, minus esset anxius: sed inter illos hostium apparatus, satis ad insaniendum otij quibusdam esse portento simile est. Ecce ex altera parte, nescio quis elegia Oliandri laceßiuit, parum & ipsum sani cerebri hominem. Cum se purpuret, ira libellum inspersit atra bile, vt me vehementer eius pudeat, sed nihil me peius torquet, quàm quod tertio quoque verbo, Zuinglianis insultat. Ita quasi impiis linguam & manus locauerimus, ipsis præbemus iucundum luaueque spectaculum, mutuò nos lacerando. Quis non animum despondeat, inquies, tot obiectis offendiculis? Fateor certè nullum esse tam ferreum animum, qui non frangatur, nisi in Dominum respexerit. Itaque sic interpretor, velle Dominum modis omnibus experiri, nunquid ab hominibus pendeamus: sed tantùm abest quin debiliter, vt non vulgaris inde confirmatio mihi accedat. Nam dum Ecclesiam inter istos fluctus, mirabiliter regi à Domino video, ne obruatur, dum ipsas tempestates, cùm omnia iam iam permixtu-ræ videntur, momento residere ac quiescere cerno, cur non bonam inde spem concipiam? Pergamus igitur in vocationis nostræ cursu, hac fiducia subnixi, emersuram Ecclesiam, quæ Deum habeat perpetuum salutis suæ custodem: sed quia non omnibus eadem est animi fortitudo, quò familiarius omnia depono in tuum finum, eò paucioribus communicabis.
units.tr: Epist. 391. He would be lacking, provided only they did their duty. He was unwilling to concede this openly. Yet from those ambiguous words one may guess that he would not object if they stirred up any disturbances; if they went further, war would be certain, by which the whole state of Germany would either be overthrown or gravely shaken. But the Lord will see to these things too. This is my only consolation: that death cannot be an evil for a Christian man. Meanwhile I groan, as I ought, over the calamities of the Church and I share the lot of the godly, yet not so as to be undone by it. If we were in good agreement among ourselves, I would be less anxious; but with the preparations of enemies on their side, it is almost a portent that some men have leisure enough to go mad. Look, on the other side, someone (I know not who) has attacked Oliander's elegy, a man himself not entirely sound in mind. Though he struts in purple, he has poured out a little book full of black bile, so that I am heartily ashamed of him; yet nothing troubles me more than that at every third word he insults the Zwinglians. So, as if we had handed our tongues and hands over to the impious, we provide them with a pleasant and sweet spectacle, while we tear one another apart. "Who would not lose heart," you will say, "amid so many obstacles?" I confess indeed that there is no spirit so iron-hard that it will not be broken, unless it looks to the Lord. So I interpret it thus: the Lord wishes in every way to test whether we depend on men; but far from being weakened by this, I gain from it no ordinary confirmation. For while I see the Church being wonderfully governed by the Lord amid these waves, so that it is not overwhelmed, and while I see the storms, when all things seem on the point of being thrown into confusion, subside and grow calm in a moment, why should I not conceive good hope from this? Let us therefore press on in the course of our calling, supported by this confidence, that the Church will emerge, since it has God as the perpetual guardian of its salvation. But because not all have the same strength of spirit, the more intimately I lay all things in your bosom, the fewer you will share with others.

units.la: Quod postremis tuis literis postulabas, an exequi deberem, aliquantisper hæsitaui. Longum enim est iter, asperum & difficile. Non ante diem vicesimum nuntius illuc equo peruenient. Quamlibet autem mittere sine delectu, periculosum erat. Erronibus aut leuibus, nulla fides, pauci autem alij reperiuntur. Linguæ imperito molestissima esset via, summa etiam vbique propter anni sterilitatem caritas. Ego à pecunia nequaquam instructus. Etiam quum tempus non est incommodum, oneribus quæ mihi incumbunt, suffinendis par esse nequeo, quin totus exhauriar. In hac verò annonæ penuria, cum qua iam biennium conflictamur, me ære alieno implicari necesse fuit. Quanquam hæc non dico conquerendi causa. Benignè enim mecum agit Deus, quòd habeo quantum animo meo satis est. Sed vt intelligas mihi hic non facilè esse inuenire, à quibus pecuniam mutuo sumam. Sunt enim omnes mercatores, & quidem famelici. Huc accedebat, quod iam dixi, Tempus consulendi Lutheri esse adhuc alienum, quia animus vixdum bene à contentionis feruore resedisset. Verum cum tam vehementer instares totque obiectationibus me urgeres ut facerem, nihil mihi prius fuit, quam votis tuis morem gererem. Ab honesto & non indocto adolescente impetratui, ut hinc molestiam subiret mea causa. Libellos meos ad verbum in linguam Latinam verti, quos adiunxi meis literis, ut inde iudicarent. Nec aliud petij meis literis, nisi ut liberè simpliciterque quod sentiant, proferant: nisi quod adiunxi nequaquam mihi gratum facturos, si quam mei haberet rationem. Vix ante duos menses redibit nuntius. Quadraginta enim dierum viam habet conficiendam. Quatriduum ad interquiescendum assigno. Reliquum temporis consultationi cedet. Vale.
units.tr: As to your request in your last letter, whether I ought to carry it out, I hesitated for some time. For the journey is long, rough and difficult. A messenger could not arrive there on horseback before the twentieth day. Yet to send someone without discrimination was dangerous. Vagabonds and light fellows cannot be trusted, and other men are hard to find. The journey would be most troublesome for one unskilled in the language, and everywhere there is great dearness of provisions because of the barrenness of the year. I am by no means supplied with money. Even when the time is not inconvenient, I am unable to bear the burdens that fall upon me without being utterly drained. Indeed, in this scarcity of provisions, with which we have now been struggling for two years, I was bound to become entangled in debt. Yet I do not say this in order to complain: God deals kindly with me, since I have as much as is enough for my mind. But so that you may understand that it is not easy for me here to find people from whom I might borrow money, they are all merchants, and indeed starving ones. To this was added what I have already mentioned: the time for consulting Luther is still unsuitable, since my mind has scarcely yet settled down from the heat of the controversy. Yet since you pressed me so vehemently and urged me with so many objections to do it, nothing was more important to me than to comply with your wishes. I obtained from an honest and not unlearned young man that he should undertake this trouble on my account. I have translated my little books word for word into Latin, and have enclosed them with my letter, so that they may judge from them. Nor have I asked anything else in my letter, except that they state freely and plainly what they think; except that I added they would by no means do me a favour if they took my position into account. The messenger will return in barely two months, for he has forty days' journey to complete. I allow four days for rest; the remaining time will be given to the consultation. Farewell.

units.la: IO. CALVINVS N. S. D.
units.tr: John Calvin to N., greeting

units.la: Literae tuae, eximie vir, non eo tantum nomine mihi gratae fuerunt, quod testes sunt priuati erga me tui amoris, sed quia non vulgare suendae in Ecclesia pacis & concordiae studium declarant. Quod diu intermissum utrinque fuit scribendi officium, id forte mihi adscribi debet. Neque certe inficior, ideo me libenter tacuisse, ne ad inutiles conflictus me provocarem. Quia ad eundem tendamus scopum, natura tamen & moribus magis fumus dissimiles, quam optarem. Quid de me sentias, & quid interdum loquaris, non ignoro. Neque vero ita sum mihi addictus, quin nonnulla quae in me reprehendis vitia, mihi quoque displicent: cuius rei satis multos habeo idoneos testes. Sed alia sunt, quae mutata nolim. Quanquam non natura tantum differimus, sed consilio rationem prorsus à tuis moribus diuersam sequor. Si te delectat mansuetudo, neque ego ab ea sum alienus. Quod autem seuerus nimium tibi videor, hanc mihi crede, personam imposuit necessitas. Interea non expendis, quantopere Ecclesiae noceat remissa tua facilitas, per quam improbis quiduis impune licet: & quae virtutem vitiis permiscens nigrum ab albo non distinguit. Dum praecipuum salutis nostrae caput labefactare conatur ille bonus vir, non pudet eum in detestabiles blasphemias prorumpere, Deum Calvini esse mendacem, hypocritam, duplicem, scelerum omnium auctorem, recti & honesti inimicum, ac deteriorem ipso diabolo. Quid te mecum inhumaniter agere conquerar? Scio enim nihil tibi minus esse propositum, quam approbare tam foedos ac detestabiles obscoenii canis latratus. Verum millies potius terra me absorbeat, quam no exaudiam quid mihi dictet ac praescribat Spiritus Dei per os Prophetæ,vt probra scilicet quibus laceratur Dei maiestas, in caput meum recidāt. Et tu dum pro fide officij causam defendo,quam deserere fas non est, quin proditor sim ac perfidus, me altercari dices? Vtinam tibi tam inconsiderata vox,cuius me pudet,sicuti indigna est homine Christiano,nunquam elapsa esset. Si qua in nobis est pietatis gutta, tanta certè indignitas nos ad summam indignationem accendet. Quòd ad me spectat,malim hic furere, quàm non irasci. Tu quomodo tibi olim reddenda ratio sit coram summo iudice,videris.Meliori quidem iure ac syncerio- re quoque affectu apud te familiariter depono hanc querimoniam,quàm ante biennium apud alios me traducens,Ciceronis potius quàm Christi discipulum esse iocose dixisti. Nunc redeo ad tuas literas. De N.discessu pridem admonitifuimus:at contemptissimus hominem,vt dignus erat.Causæ tamen habenda erit ratio,&d in tempore Si qua Synodis erit auctoritas.turpiter eiectus ad vos redibit. Si hoc modo saluum fore exi-stimas, te voti compotem fore promitto. Et facile recipietur, vt alij similes. Restitutionem nuper obtinuit bonus vir quidam periurij convictus & damnatus tantum quia innocenti maledicere non dedistitit. Cur non parceretur homini, qui tam strenuè labefactare conatus est æternam Dei electionem? Ac vide quos & quales habeat patronos Pelagianum delirium. Hic de quo agitur homo est indoctissimus ac prorsus nihili. N. fuore obrepsit ad ministerium. Frater enim eius insipidus scurra & circulator sodalis erat N.Insipidum voco, quia me cum suis facetiis nequiter fraudavit,quum tres aureos scutatos quos debebat, abstulit. Reuersus,pro sua canina impudentia blaterabit. Hæc est salus,si quid reliquum est salui perdere. Ego verò cū Propheta dicam,Quod perit,pereat Tam secure? inquies.Ego certè non minus anxie laboro de eius salute,&miseriæ ingemisco,quàm si blanda indulgentia cum mulcerem. Verùm sæpius audisti,non minus odiosam esse Deo crudelem misericordiam, quàm Ecclesiæ pestiferi est.Atque vt ingenuè fatear,si mihi omnia præstares,minus grata essent tua officia: quia prodigi non liberalis esse duco,quoslibet promisceuè & absque delectu iuuare. Video quàm amarulenta sit epistola: & certè parum abfuit, quin decies eam considerim.Sed quæ miseri animum meum prænebant,dissimulare nō fuit ingenuum. Noles hoc modo me tibi esse familiarem. Non igitur scribendum fuit: quia vt blandien do mentiar,adduci nequeo. Adde quod ex negotiorum mole plus morosi atis contraxi.Quò magis vereor,ne tibi qui curarum & laborum tedio obruerit,importunè sim molestus. IOAN.
units.tr: Your letter, distinguished sir, pleased me not only because it bears witness to your personal affection for me, but because it shows no common zeal for fostering peace and concord in the Church. The exchange of letters has lapsed on both sides for a long time; perhaps this should be laid to my account. I do not deny that I kept silent gladly, so as not to provoke myself into useless quarrels. We aim at the same goal, yet we differ more in nature and manners than I would wish. I am not unaware what you think of me or what you sometimes say. Nor am I so attached to myself that some of the faults you find in me do not also displease me; I have plenty of competent witnesses to that. But there are other things I would not want changed. We differ not only by nature: I follow, by deliberate choice, a method quite different from your manner. If you delight in gentleness, I am not a stranger to it either. As for my seeming too severe to you, believe me, necessity has imposed this mask on me. Meanwhile you do not weigh how greatly your lax easiness harms the Church, since through it wicked men may do anything with impunity, and since it mixes virtue with vice and does not distinguish black from white. While that good man tries to undermine the chief foundation of our salvation, he is not ashamed to break out into detestable blasphemies, calling the God of Calvin a liar, a hypocrite, double-faced, the author of all crimes, an enemy of right and honesty, and worse than the devil himself. Why should I complain that you treat me inhumanely? For I know nothing was less your intention than to approve such foul and detestable barkings of a filthy dog. Yet I would rather the earth swallow me a thousand times than fail to hear what the Spirit of God dictates and prescribes through the mouth of the Prophet, namely that the insults by which the majesty of God is torn should fall back on my own head. And will you say, while I defend with the faithfulness of my office a cause I must not desert without becoming a traitor and faithless, that I am quarrelling? I wish that such thoughtless words, of which I am ashamed, had never escaped you, as they are unworthy of a Christian man. If there is any drop of piety in us, such great indignity will surely kindle us to the highest indignation. As for me, I would rather rage here than not be angry. How you will have to render account one day before the supreme judge is for you to consider. Indeed, with better right and a more sincere feeling, I lay this complaint before you in familiar terms, rather than as I did two years ago, when you, slandering me before others, jokingly said that I was a disciple of Cicero rather than of Christ. Now I return to your letter. We were warned earlier about N.'s departure; but he is utterly despised, as he deserves. Nevertheless his case must be considered at the proper time, if the Synod has any authority; he will return to you shamefully ejected. If you think things will be safe in this way, I promise you will get your wish. And he will easily be received, like others of his kind. Recently a certain good man, convicted and condemned for perjury, obtained restitution, only because he did not cease to slander an innocent man. Why should a man be spared who has so vigorously tried to undermine God's eternal election? And see what sort of patrons the Pelagian madness has. The man we are discussing is most unlearned and utterly worthless. N. crept into the ministry through favour. For his brother, a dull buffoon and mountebank, was a companion of N. I call him dull because, with his jokes, he wickedly cheated me when he took away the three gold crowns he owed. When he returns, he will babble with his dog-like impudence. This is salvation: to lose what little salvation remains. But I, with the Prophet, will say: what perishes, let it perish. So carelessly, you will say? I am certainly no less anxiously concerned for his salvation, and no less grieved at his misery, than if I were soothing him with a flattering indulgence. Yet you have often heard that cruel mercy is no less hateful to God, and no less pestilential to the Church. And, to be frank, even if you did everything for me, your services would be less welcome to me; for I think it is not generosity but prodigality to help anyone indiscriminately and without choice. I see how bitter the letter is, and I came close to reconsidering it ten times. But it would not have been honourable to conceal what was weighing on my troubled mind. You would not want me to be so frank with you, I suppose. So I ought not to have written at all, since I cannot be brought to lie by flattering. Add that from the burden of business I have acquired more peevishness. The more I fear that I, overwhelmed with cares and toil, may be an importunate nuisance to you. John.

units.la: DE tuis scriptis duplicem habeo tibi gratiam: & quòd mihi priuatim exemplar misisti, & quòd hunc laborem quem fru-ctuosum esse iudico, dedisti Christi Ecclesiæ. Interea tristis nuntius hic spargitur, vetari fratres, ne ad Scripturam tractandā ex more conueniant. Ne quid dissimulēs, cùm hæc agendi ratio minimè sit Ecclesiastica, te & nostrum N. eius auctorem, vel approbatores fuisse valde miror & molestius fero. Magno hactenus cum fructu celebrati fuerunt isti conuentus, à quibus nunc Edictum fratres indicta causa prohibet. Vt nihil momenti apud nos habeat vsus, qui tamen optimus magisterr esse solet, rem vobiscum expendite. Certè non vtilem modò hunc morem esse reperietis, qui nunc abrogatur, sed prope necessarium. Quoniam singulis fratribus sunt suæ vices, perspicitur eorum diligentia: si negligentes deprehensi fuerint, admonentur. Illic cognoscitur an dextrè & appositè Scripturam in populi vsum accommodare nouerint. Optimum quoque hoc retinendæ in doctrina consensionis vinculum est, quia dum in communi non conferunt, licet cuique seorsum docere quicquid libuerit. Magnam licentiam dat solitudo. Qui tertio duntaxat mense in fratrum coetum prodibit, quidvis in reliquum anni tempus audebit nullius iudicium aut conscientiam reformidans. Denique nullum est melius corrigendæ ignauiæ remedium, nulla fouendæ in doctrina vnitatis aptior ratio: adhæc omnes & loquendo & tacendo proficiunt, neque solis ministris vtile est eiusmodi exercitium, sed plurimi ex plebe qui singulari intelligedæ Scripturæ studio ducuntur, partem vtilitatis sentiunt. Pauci forsan tales sunt, sed quia vniuersale est edictum, totam regionem comprehendo. Scio hic esse pios homines, & eruditionis non pœnitendæ: qui sibi duas conciones adimi malint, quàm vnam Scripturæ tractatione, quales audiuntur. Si hunc vsum non habent quendam Ecclesiæ, tantundem illis deesse fatendum est. Sed exortæ inde contentiones vos mouerunt. Id verò non alienum modò vestra æquitate, sed prorsus inhumanum fuit, si quid peccauit vnus homo, culpam in fratres innoxios coniicere. N. præfractum hominem & rixosum, adeòque importunum animal est notum est: ipse quibuscunque potuit modis turbauit bene stantem Ecclesiam. Cùm finem contentionibus nullum faceret, amotus est. Nunc verò ne culpam sustineat, quam meritus est, nota infamiæ aspergitur fratribus. Vt dissimulem fratrum iniuriam, pium, sanctum, & vtile institutum vbique abrogatur. Vetantur fratres agere ordinarios conuentus, quorū necessitas ipsa desuetudine melius patefiet. Quisquis huius cōsilij primus fuit auctor, quam Deo rationem sit reddituru*s*, videat. Graue certè Ecclesiis vulnus inflixit. Fuit tempus cùm istic quotidie audiebantur pro suggestu atroces inuectiuæ aliorum in alios: cur non à concionibus prohibiti fuerunt, qui sic petulanter suo munere abutebantur? Pudet me certè, cùm video quosdam in tatis deliciis habere N. vt præ ipso Ecclesiam Dei contemnant, & graui damno afficere non dubitent. Nam quid aliud iudicem, nō habeo. Fieri tamen potest vt errem: sed tu meæ libertati ignosces, quòd frustus amicitiæ nostræ fiducia, familiariter in tuum & fratris nostri sinum depono, quicquid in animo habeo. Ego de studiĭ vestri rectitudine ita sum persuasus, vt vos Ecclesiæ pacem & ædificationem quærere, pro certo habeam. Verùm quia nos hic me lius in re præsenti cernimus quid expediat, nō putaui mihi esse cessandum, quin vos ad medicinam in tempore adhibendā hortarer. Vale eximie vir & frater mihi colende. D. fratrem diligen ter meo nomine saluta & alios collegas, quibus gratum hoc officium esse agnosces. Geneuæ.
units.tr: I owe you a twofold thanks: both that you sent me a copy of your writings privately, and that you have given to Christ's Church this labour, which I judge to be fruitful. Meanwhile a sad report is spreading here that the brothers are forbidden to gather as usual for the study of Scripture. Not to dissemble, since this way of proceeding is by no means ecclesiastical, I am much surprised that you, and our N. its author or approvers, were involved, and I take it the more grievously. Until now these gatherings have been held with great profit, and now the brothers are forbidden them by an edict, the cause not having been heard. Though the practice, which is usually the best teacher, may seem of no weight among us, consider the matter with us. Certainly you will find that this custom, which is now being abolished, is not only useful but nearly necessary. Since each brother has his turn, his diligence is evident; if they are found negligent, they are admonished. There it is discovered whether they know how to apply Scripture rightly and fittingly to the use of the people. It is also the best bond for keeping agreement in doctrine, because when they do not confer in common, each may teach whatever he pleases in private. Solitude gives great licence. A man who appears in the company of the brethren only once in three months will dare anything for the rest of the year, fearing no one's judgement or conscience. In short, there is no better remedy for correcting laziness, and no more suitable means of fostering unity in doctrine; moreover, everyone profits both by speaking and by keeping silent, and such exercise is useful not only to the ministers but also to many of the common people, who are drawn by a special zeal for understanding Scripture and feel some part of the benefit. Perhaps few are such, but because the edict is universal, I include the whole region. I know there are pious men here, and men of learning not to be despised, who would rather have two sermons taken from them than one devoted to the study of Scripture such as they now hear. If they have no such practice in the Church, it must be admitted that just as much is lacking to them. But quarrels arising from it have moved you. That, however, was not only foreign to your fairness but altogether inhuman: if one man has sinned, to throw the blame on innocent brothers. N. is known to be a headstrong, quarrelsome and, indeed, unmanageable creature; by every means he could, he disturbed a Church that was standing well. Since he would make no end to the quarrels, he was removed. Now, so that he may not bear the blame he deserves, a mark of infamy is spattered on the brothers. To say nothing of the injury to the brothers, a pious, holy and useful institution is being abolished everywhere. The brothers are forbidden to hold their regular meetings, whose necessity will be made clearer by their disuse. Whoever was the first author of this plan, let him see to what account he must render to God. It has certainly inflicted a grave wound on the Churches. There was a time when there were daily heard there, from the pulpit, savage invectives of some against others; why were not those forbidden to preach who so wantonly abused their office? I am certainly ashamed when I see some holding N. in such esteem that, for his sake, they despise the Church of God, and do not hesitate to inflict grave damage on it. For I can judge it no other way. It may nevertheless be that I am wrong; but you will forgive my freedom, since, trusting in the confidence of our friendship, I familiarly lay before the bosom of you and our brother whatever is in my mind. I am so persuaded of the rectitude of your zeal that I hold it as certain that you seek the peace and building up of the Church. Yet since we here see more clearly what is expedient in the present situation, I did not think I should refrain from urging you to apply the remedy in time. Farewell, distinguished sir and brother to be cherished by me. Greet our brother D. diligently in my name, and the other colleagues, who you know will find this kindness welcome. Geneva.
