units.la: Responsio Io. Calvini ad quendam Curatum.
units.tr: Answer of John Calvin to a certain Curate.

units.la: EST ita vt dicis Domine Curate: Dei nempe flagellum est pestis qua hic laboramus, atque hoc etiam merito imputamus peccatis nostris, propter quæ Dominus ita nos castigat. Sed neque dubitamus nos ista ratione expergefieri vt in nos defcē damus, atque de resipiscentia seriò cogitemus. Accipimus igitur quod adscribis, instare tempus quo ad Deum cōuertamur, vt ab illo veniam & misericordiam obtineamus. Illud etiam perspicimus, vix vllum esse angulum orbis Christiani, vbi Dominus manum non exerat suo modo: ex quo omnino constat, ira Dei in miseros homines passim & valde accensam esse. Nec mirum quidem: obuiæ enim sunt causæ, nec procul requirendæ. Grassatur nempe vbique corruptio, & nullus est vspiam scelerum modus. Neque sic loquimur vt prætendamus excusatione, dum nos accensemus reliquis, cùm eò nobis esse debeat magis stupenda manus Domini, cùm ita vbique extensa est, atque diluuij instar omnia inundat. Atque vbi ista abunde perpendimus aliter senti re non possumus, nisi quòd præter illa vitia quæ vbique obtinēt, duo quædā summa notari possunt inter Christianos ipsos, quæ Domini iram plane accendant. Vnum est, quòd alij Deum cōtu melia afficiunt suis idolis & superstitionibus, ac non modò non admittunt sanctum ipsius verbum quo in viam reducantur, sed illud etiam despiciunt, aperte, adeòque oderunt, horrent, perse quuntur. Nos verò qui ex ipsius Euangelio legitimum ipsius cultum discimus,officium plane negligimus,vt Verbum illud vitæ fereotiofum & emortuum iaceat inter nos. Absit enim vt alios iudicado nobis parcamus. Quatenus enim Dominus eripuit nos ex horrendis illis tenebris, nofq; sua luce donauit ad tenendam rectum salutis viam, eatenus sane minime omnium excusabiles fumus, fi officio desumus iuxta illud Domini: Seruus qui nouit voluntatem Domini,neque illam præstitit,vapulabit durius. Mirum igitur videri non debet, fi pro nostra ingratitudine duplo etiam nos castigat Dominus, dum non ambulamus vt filij lucis, neque fructus edimus dignos fanctaipfius vocatione. Præterea ipse etiam denuntiat, iudicium ipsius incœpturum à sua domo, ac proinde admouendam ab ipso manum primum domeftic s ipsis castigandis.Neq; tamen hoc ita facit vt non oculos etiam alibi intendat,vt cum gloriam suam longe charissimam habeat, ac peculiari odio prosequatur & exhorrescat idololatriam cum quibus vis superstitionibus, quibus ipsius maiestas lædituf, quin inde etiam supra omnia alia peccata offenda ur quàm grauissime. Agnosce modo quid fiat inter vos. Ligna & lapides adorantur, mortui inuocantur, fides collocatur in rebus nihili, Dei cultus præscribitur in ceremoniis temere inuentis.&abfq; verbo ipsius veritatis doctrina fepultaiacet:ac fi quis illiâ restituere cogitat,a-cerbiffime tractatur.Et posse fieri censes vt Deus sinat tot modis pollui acblafphemari nomen suum! Testatur Paulus immissam Corinthiis pestem à Domino,q; sacra ipsius Cœna non fatis reue renter apud ipsos tum celebraretur. Et quid igitur sperandum est, vbi sacrum illud epulum tam lõgo tepore transformatum est in execrandum illud facrilegiu:vestram inquâ Missam!Neque hoc longa probatione indiget.Expendatur enim ipsa Domini institutio,& ineatur illius cum Missa vestra collatio:atqui cœlû terræ facilius comittas, quàm illa duo tam aperte repugnantia coeuenire possint.Nostrum igitur effet omnium dare omnes gloriâ Deo vno cofenfu,dum sua fingulimala,& peccata,vltrò citróq; profiteremur. Sic enim sentimus de nobis.grauissimum esse illud Icelus,dum oblatam ipsius gratiam nô vti par est admittimus:dû etiam pro ea notitia Euangelij ipsius,& ordinariis exhortationibus quasipfius mandato audimus,non dimus operam,vt mores nostri ad perfectam ipsius regulam meliuς exigantur. Sic etiam aliis faciendû esse qui pro Dei verbo,aut fuasipfi opiniones,aut traditiones hominû sectantur, quibus cultus Dei manifestè cor rupitur,vt& ipsi agnoscerent quàm illa fit ipsi abominatio into lerabilis,cuius ipsi rei sint.Quid enim potest istis prætexiquòd falsæ doctrinæ adhæreatur, fides salutis collocetur in creaturis, inuertatur rectus Sacramentorû vsus,non è Dei manifesto abusu cotaminetur:ac super hisomnibus,ipsos Domini testes fi vel minimum verbum contra tantos abusus protulerint, non mo- do non ferri, sed omnibus modis plecti vt e medio tollantur? Ne- que illud ad rem facit, si qui infidelium prosperis rebus vtantur, quasi habeant in quo acquiescant. Sic enim accidit hypocritis, & idololatris praesertim, vt glorientur, dum manus Dei ipsis non incumbit, quasi ea sit merces cultus quem Deo exhibuerint dum in ipsum suis idolis tum graviter peccarunt. Sic sese in sua impie tate indurant, sic blandiuntur sibi, & in alios sententiam ferunt. Quid autem ad ista Dominus? En, inquit, nullam illis benefaci- endi rationem praetermisi, atque ipsi hoc imputarunt pro mer- cede fornicationum suarum cum idolis suis: propterea inquit, tol- lam ab eis, quicquid in ipsos contuli, vt detegam turpitudinem ipsorum & cogam redire ad me.
units.tr: It is so, as you say, Lord Curate. The plague by which we are suffering here is indeed God's scourge, and we rightly impute it to our sins, on account of which the Lord so chastises us. Yet we do not doubt that this affliction rouses us to humble ourselves and to think seriously about repentance. We accept, therefore, what you add: the time has come when we should turn to God, that we may obtain pardon and mercy from him. We also see that there is hardly any corner of the Christian world where the Lord does not stretch out his hand in his own way. From this it is entirely clear that God's wrath is kindled far and wide and very fiercely against wretched men. Nor is this surprising, for the causes lie close at hand and need not be sought far off. Corruption rages everywhere, and nowhere is there any limit to wickedness. Nor do we speak thus to offer an excuse, by counting ourselves among the rest. Rather, the hand of the Lord ought to astonish us all the more, since it is stretched out everywhere and floods all things like a deluge. And when we weigh these matters carefully, we cannot judge otherwise: besides the vices that prevail everywhere, two especially grave faults can be noted among Christians themselves, which plainly inflame the wrath of the Lord. The first is that others provoke God by their idols and superstitions. Not only do they refuse to admit his holy Word, by which they might be brought back to the right way, but they openly despise it, and so hate, abhor and persecute it. We, however, who learn from his own Gospel the lawful worship of him, plainly neglect our duty, so that that living Word lies idle and dead among us. Far be it from us, however, to spare ourselves while judging others. For insofar as the Lord has snatched us out of those horrible darknesses and given us his light to hold to the right path of salvation, so far are we least of all excusable if we fail in our duty, according to the Lord's words: "The servant who knew his master's will and did not perform it shall be beaten more severely." It should not seem strange, then, if on account of our ingratitude the Lord chastises us twice over, since we do not walk as children of the light, nor bear fruit worthy of our holy calling. Moreover, he himself declares that his judgment will begin at his own house, and therefore he lays his hand first on his own household to chastise them. Yet he does not do this without also turning his eyes elsewhere. Since he holds his glory most dear, he pursues with peculiar hatred and abhors idolatry with whatever superstitions, by which his majesty is injured; and on account of this he is offended more gravely than by all other sins. Only acknowledge what goes on among you. Wood and stones are adored, the dead are invoked, faith is placed in things of nothing, the worship of God is prescribed in ceremonies rashly invented, and the doctrine of the truth of his Word lies buried. And if anyone thinks of restoring it, he is treated most bitterly. And do you think God will allow his name to be polluted and blasphemed in so many ways? Paul testifies that a plague was sent upon the Corinthians by the Lord, because his holy Supper was then celebrated among them without sufficient reverence. What, then, is to be hoped for, where that sacred feast has over so long a time been transformed into that accursed sacrilege, your Mass! Nor does this need a long proof. Let the institution of the Lord himself be weighed, and let a comparison be made between it and your Mass. You could sooner join heaven to earth than make those two things, so plainly opposed, agree. It would therefore be the duty of us all to give all glory to God with one accord, while we freely confess our individual faults and sins to one another. For this is how we judge of ourselves: that it is a most grievous thing that we accept his offered grace not as we ought; that although we hear the Gospel and its ordinary exhortations, as it were at his command, we do not take pains to bring our morals closer to his perfect rule. The same must be done with others who, in place of God's Word, follow either their own opinions or the traditions of men, by which the worship of God is manifestly corrupted; so that they too might recognise how intolerable an abomination it is to him, and of what they are guilty. For what can they put forward in their defence: that they cling to false doctrine, place the faith of salvation in creatures, pervert the right use of the sacraments, and pollute them with manifest abuse? And that, if the witnesses of the Lord bring forward even the slightest word against such great abuses, they are not only not tolerated, but are punished in every way so that they may be removed from the midst? Nor does it bear on the matter if some unbelievers enjoy prosperous circumstances, as if they had something to rest in. For this happens to hypocrites, and especially to idolaters: they boast because the hand of God does not press upon them, as if that were the reward of the worship they have offered God, while they have so gravely sinned against him by their idols. Thus they harden themselves in their impiety, thus they flatter themselves and pass judgment on others. What, however, does the Lord say to these things? "Behold," he says, "I have withheld from them no means of doing them good, and they have attributed it to the wages of their fornications with their idols. Therefore," he says, "I will take away from them whatever I have bestowed upon them, that I may expose their shame and compel them to return to me."

units.la: Atqui quod ad nos attinet, cum requiritur quae sint illa no- stra peccata quibus Deum provocaverimus, & quorum nomi- ne ab ipso nunc corripimur, imputatur illud imprimis, quod immutatus sit a nobis cultus Dei & ordo Ecclesiae, qui tam re- cte institutus esset, & observaretur prius inter nos. Non est vero inaudita ista exprobratio. Ita enim Ieremias ipse exceptus est olim, vt ipse testatur cap. 44. querebantur nimirum hypocritae, ex quo desierat coli Regina caeli, nullum non malorum genus populo incubuisse. Docent etiam Lactantius & Augustinus, suis temporibus imputari solita Evangelio omnia quae acciderent adversa: quod per Evangelium superstitiones Gentium abolitae fuissent, quae pro Dei cultu habebantur. Regeritur, non esse nunc perinde nos vero rem perinde se habere, contendimus. Quid igitur? Hic de re ipsa serio inquirendum sit, vt recta sententia proferatur.
units.tr: But as far as we are concerned, when it is asked what those sins of ours are by which we have provoked God, and for which he now rebukes us, the charge laid first and foremost against us is that the worship of God and the order of the Church, which were once rightly instituted and observed among us, have been changed by us. Nor is this reproach unheard of. Jeremiah himself was once met with it, as he testifies in chap. 44: the hypocrites complained that, since they had ceased to worship the Queen of heaven, every kind of evil had fallen upon the people. Lactantius and Augustine also teach that in their own times it was customary to blame the Gospel for all the adversities that befell, because through the Gospel the superstitions of the Gentiles, which had been held to be the worship of God, had been abolished. It is objected that the situation is not the same now; but we contend that the matter stands in exactly the same way. What then? Here the matter itself must be examined seriously, so that a right judgment may be reached.

units.la: Praeterquam autem quod conscientiae nostrae testimonio hac in parte stamus coram Domino, respondet. Hactenus enim nemo prodiit, qui eiuciet, immutatum esse quidquam a nobis, quod a Deo mandatum erat, aut effecta nobis institutum aliquid novi con- tra verbum ipsius: aut a nobis declinatum esse a veritate ad prae- uum aliquod dogma sectandum. Contra vero palam est, nostra a nobis Ecclesiam reformatam esse ex mero ipsius verbo: quod unum est pro regula, ad quam & instituenda illa sit, & tuenda le- gitime. Odiosum est quidem mutare quod obtinuerit ante: nisi sane unus ille ordo a Domino positus semel nobis esse deberet sacer & inviolatus: vt quum ille ad tempus abolitus fuit, restitui postliminio necesse fuerit, vt coelum & terra misceri debuerint.
units.tr: Apart from the testimony of our conscience, by which we stand before the Lord on this point, the facts themselves also answer. For so far no one has come forward who can show that anything has been changed by us which God had commanded, or that we have introduced anything new contrary to his Word, or that we have turned aside from the truth to follow some perverse doctrine. On the contrary, it is plain that our Church has been reformed by us solely from the Word of God, which is the one rule by which it must both be established and lawfully maintained. It is indeed odious to change what had prevailed before, unless that one order set by the Lord ought to have been sacred and inviolable for us once and for all, so that when it had been abolished for a time it would have had to be restored by right of return, as if heaven and earth would have had to be mixed together.

units.la: Nulla antiquitas aut usus praescriptio his obesse poterit, quin ad- ministratio Ecclesiae quae Deus ipsum auctorem habet, perpetua exstare debeat, quando ita illam Dominus semel positam fixamq; voluit. Plusquam idoneae vero sunt rationes quae ad mutationem illam nos adegerunt, cuius praeiudicio falso vrgemur. Primum nem̄ que caput Christianismi est, vt Deus recte colatur. Animi vertimus vero formā illam adorationis quae in vsu erat, falsam & peruersam esse, quia non erat in spiritu & veritate, sed in exteriis caeremoniis, & ritibus etiam superstitiosis. Quinuis etiā non iam vnus Deus adoraretur: sed loco ipsius ligna & lapides, pictur, mortuorum reliquiae, & caetera id genus. Cùm Dei adoratione cohaereret ipsius rectè inuocandi regula. Et qualis est Dei inuocatio in toto Papatu, nisi cum dubitatione & diffidentia coniuncta, quatenus non tenetur Christi munus, quod in eo positum est, vt intercedat pro nobis, vt eius nomine à Deo exaudiamur? Porrò quid sunt aliud publicae illae preces, quàm strepitus ignoti, & veluti exotici vlulatus? Postremò quot blasphemiae illic cēfende sunt, vbi virtus Mediatoris transfertur ad sanctos & sanctas, vt eorum nomine & meritis gratia impetretur? Tertio loco & inuocatio proximo est ipse Dei cultus. Docebamur autem Deum colere ex vanis hominum traditionibus: Ille suam vnam voluntate pro omni regula hac in parte, praescripsit. Quòd ad salutis fiduciam attinet quę vna est omnium veluti basis & fundamentum, cùm in vna Dei misericordia ea sita esse debeat, vt & ipsius gloriae & conscientiarum paci consulatur: docebamur etiam cum reliquo mundo fiduciam illam partim in nobis ipsis, partim in aliis creaturis reponere. Caetera percensere neque valde opus est, neque vllus esset modus. In summa, Christi gratia nobis planè sepulta erat. Cùm igitur percepimus & liquido nobis constitit, istiusmodi omnia meram esse abominationem coram Deo, quo nos vertere debuimus? An nostrū erat Deo resistere & ipsius veritati? Quòd ad ordinem & statum Ecclesiae attinet, si quid in eo fuisset tolerabile, lubenter & ipsi illum retinuisse mus. Atqui adeo erant omnia confusa, vt mera Babylon illic extaret, adeo vt nō aliud remedium quàm in certa renouatione sese proferret. Quid de Sacramentis? quorum vsus planè inuersus erat, & planè alius quàm vti ipsum à Domino primùm acceperamus? quantùm nugarum erat in Baptismo quęab hominibus introducta erat sine Domini mandato? Et quod grauissimum erat, pura illa ac natiua institutio Domini illis additionibus fere erat abolita. Hoc ita esse vel vnum Christi testatur, quod aquae elemento in Baptismo lō gissimē praeferetur. Vnde fit vt nosfer hodie Baptismus vix pro Baptismo habeatur, quū in eo illud tātūm vsurpemus, quod Dominus ipse instituit, atqui ipsius Apostoli tenuerunt & in vsu habuerunt. Coena porro longe grauius profanata erat. Illa nimirum institutio est à Domino vt sit perpetuum pignus alimenti animi nostrar in ipsius tum corpore tum sanguine, vt tum ipsius bonorum omnium participes sumus, tum nominatim mortis ipsius.
units.tr: No antiquity or prescription of custom can stand in the way of this, so that the administration of the Church, which has God himself as its author, must remain perpetual, since the Lord willed it to be once established and fixed. Indeed, the reasons which compelled us to that change, and by whose supposed prejudice we are falsely pressed, are more than sufficient. First, since the chief point of Christianity is that God be rightly worshipped, we judged that the form of adoration then in use was false and perverse, because it was not in spirit and truth but in outward ceremonies and even superstitious rites. Indeed, God alone was no longer adored; in his place were wood and stones, pictures, relics of the dead, and things of that kind. Connected with the worship of God is the rule for rightly invoking him. And what sort of invocation of God is there throughout the whole Papacy, except one joined with doubt and diffidence, inasmuch as the office of Christ, which consists in his interceding for us so that we may be heard by God in his name, is not held fast? Moreover, what are those public prayers but the noise of an unknown and, as it were, foreign howling? Lastly, how many blasphemies must be condemned there, where the power of the Mediator is transferred to saints, men and women, so that grace may be obtained in their name and by their merits? Third, closest to invocation is the worship of God itself. We were taught to worship God by the empty traditions of men, whereas he alone prescribed the one rule in this matter by his will. As for the confidence of salvation, which is the one foundation and basis of all, since it ought to rest in God's mercy alone, so that both his glory and the peace of consciences may be served, we were taught along with the rest of the world to place that confidence partly in ourselves and partly in other creatures. It is neither necessary nor possible to enumerate the rest. In sum, the grace of Christ was utterly buried for us. Since, therefore, we perceived, and it became clear to us, that all such things are mere abomination before God, to what should we have turned? Was it our place to resist God and his truth? As for the order and state of the Church, if anything in it had been tolerable, we would gladly have retained it too. But everything was so confused that mere Babylon stood there, so that no remedy appeared except a definite renewal. What of the sacraments? Their use was wholly inverted, and entirely different from the way we had first received it from the Lord! How much trifling there was in Baptism, which had been introduced by men without the Lord's command! And what was most serious, the pure and native institution of the Lord had been almost abolished by those additions. That this is so is attested by the single fact that in Baptism the element of water is pushed far into the background. Hence it comes that our Baptism today is scarcely regarded as Baptism, since we use in it only what the Lord himself instituted, and what the Apostles also kept and practised. The Supper, moreover, had been profaned far more gravely. That institution of the Lord is meant to be a perpetual pledge of the nourishment of our souls in his body and blood, so that we are partakers both of all his good things and, especially, of his death.

units.la: Ioan. 4. — 1 Tim. 2. — 1 Ioan. 2. — Heb. 2. — Deut. 12. — 1 Sam. 15. Ad illud praestandum forma ipsa distributionis a Domino primum mandata retinenda erat, adiuncta simul doctrina quo vim & vsum tanti mysterii complecteretur. Contra prorsus illa transformata erat in sacrificium, ad peragendam apud Deum reconciliationem certo illo hominis opere & ipso facto. Neque illud ad vivos tantum, sed & ad mortuos pertinebat. Sacerdos peractus mysteria & Sacramenta participaturus segregabat se ab Ecclesia. Omnia lingua ignota expediebantur, ut inter magos & sortilegos fieri solet. Vbi ad Pascha ventum erat, Sacramentum non nisi mutilatum exhibebatur plebi, atque ita a calicis communione aliena esse iubebatur contra mandatum ipsius Magistri. Eiusmodi facta legia approbare nulla sinebat ratio: & tamen imputatur nobis quasi Sacramentum illud euerterimus scilicet. Atqui res ipsa loquitur, illud a nobis restitutum esse integritati suo, cum tot modis corrupti ante pollutumq; esset. Paulus refotur maturus apud Cor. abusum qui Caenae Domini irrepserat, illos revocat ad primam institutionem Domini, tanquam ad statutum irrefixum. Quid igitur melius quam tale exemplum sequi nos praestitit, ad tollendos infinitos illos abusus quibus tantum Sacramentum contaminatissimum euaserat? Doceatur vero ecquid in nostra forma & vsu extet alienum aut ab institutione Domini, aut ab vsu Apostolorum, atque tum erit emendationis locus. Si vero praeter ius & aequum impetimur, nihil illud efficiet, ut a certa veritate ita temere dimoveamur. Proinde quod tu nobis summae culpae adscribis, illud contra pro singulari Dei opere accipimus, quo vix aliud eo gratius a nobis edi potuisse statuimus. Neque interea inficiamur, non uno modo peccatum esse a nobis, unde & a Domino castigamur merito, nempe quia non respondeant mores nostri, doctrinae ipsius quam profitemur. Perinde etiam est quod tu nobis praescribis eos modos qui bus ad Deum reuertamur, & iam illius placemus apud nos, quibus modis eum aduersum nos accensum & pro uocatum iri multo magis, ipsi plane sentimus. Iubes enim primo loco nos offerre pretiosum corpus & sanguinem Domini Iesu Christi. Sic nempe solet apud vos fieri. Atqui ut confiter, an Deo gratum illud opus futurum sit, de ipsius voluntate certos esse imprimis oportuit. Iam vero ille non est auctor nobis ut corpus ipsius offeramus, sed ut pro nobis oblatum accipiamus. Accipite, inquit, edite. Quare si acceptionis loco uti nobis praescripta est, oblationem ipsi obtrudemus, unde nobis legitima inventionis nostrae appetito? Petimus igitur, ut istam rationem serio expendas. Confutatio: lis fiquid [?] ut curemus offerri corpus per sacerdotem, ad obtinendam gratiam. Respondemus, Sacramentum illud non esse in eum finem institutum a Domino, sed potius ut illud accipiendo
units.tr: Ioan. 4. — 1 Tim. 2. — 1 Ioan. 2. — Heb. 2. — Deut. 12. — 1 Sam. 15. To accomplish that, the very form of distribution first commanded by the Lord had to be kept, together with the teaching that would embrace the force and use of so great a mystery. Instead, that form had been completely transformed into a sacrifice, to effect reconciliation with God by that human work and the deed itself. Nor did this pertain only to the living but also to the dead. The priest, having performed the mysteries and about to take part in the sacraments, separated himself from the Church. Everything was carried out in an unknown tongue, as usually happens among magicians and fortune-tellers. When they came to the Passover, the sacrament was offered to the common people only in mutilated form, and so they were told to abstain from communion in the cup, contrary to the Master's own command. Reason allows no one to approve such illegal practices; and yet it is imputed to us, as if we had overturned the sacrament. But the thing itself speaks: it was restored by us to its integrity, when it had been corrupted and polluted in so many ways before. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, calls back those who had crept into the abuse of the Lord's Supper to the Lord's first institution, as to a settled statute. What better then can we do than to follow such an example, in order to remove the countless abuses by which so great a sacrament had become most defiled? Let it be shown whether anything in our form and use is foreign either to the institution of the Lord or to the practice of the apostles, and then there will be room for correction. But if we are attacked contrary to right and equity, that will accomplish nothing, so that we are rashly moved away from certain truth. Therefore what you ascribe to us as the greatest fault, we on the contrary receive as a singular work of God, and we judge that scarcely anything more pleasing could have been done by us. Meanwhile we do not deny that we have sinned in more than one way, for which the Lord rightly chastises us, namely because our morals do not correspond to the teaching of him that we profess. Likewise, as to what you prescribe to us, the ways by which we should return to God and be reconciled to him, we ourselves plainly feel that by these ways, if we follow them, he would be far more kindled against us and provoked. For you bid us first of all to offer the precious body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ; and thus, of course, it is customarily done among you. Yet, as you yourself confess, we ought above all to be certain of God's will as to whether this work will be pleasing to him. Now he is not the author for us of offering his body, but of receiving it as offered for us. "Take," he says, "eat." Therefore, if we use it in the place of receiving, we would be thrusting an offering upon him; whence would we have any lawful warrant for our invention? We ask you, then, to weigh this reasoning seriously. Objection: that we should take care that the body be offered through a priest, in order to obtain grace. We reply that this sacrament was not instituted by the Lord for that end; rather, by receiving it we are to become partakers of the singular and eternal sacrifice which he alone offered in the discharge of his office.

units.la: Matth. 26. Mar. 14. Luc. 22. 1. Cor. 11. (marginal references, left) piedo participes fiamus singularis & æterni sacrificii, quod unus ipse oblulit pro officij sui ratione. Addimus insuper, illud pla ne derogare dignitati, quaten ipse constitut est Sacerdos absq; vllo vel socio, vel successore, vt offerret semetipsum: quù extaret nemo qui tã insigni illo opere præter illu perfungi posset. Sacrificandi liquidé munus eò pertinet, vt mediator sit qui sacrificat inter Deum & homines, Cui vero fides erit adhibeda, Christo am vobis, vbi ita ex opposito consistitis? Indicis nobis etiam supplicationes illas, quas vocatis processiones generales, Et quid illic operis extare potest, nisi fortasse magna illa pompa & ceremoniis ad ostentationem comparatis Deum à nobis placatum iri cogitaremus? Respondebis tibi in animo esse, vt ista cum certo animi affectu & deuotione peragantur. Scilicet illa erit legitima deuotio, vbi fidem affigemus cereis, funalibus, vestibus superbis & profusis, imaginibus & mortuorum reliquiis. Illud quidem in vsu fuit apud idololatras ex gentibus vt historiæ testantur: vt autem hoc Christiano cultui respondeat, primùm docendi est mus. Non disceptamus, an expediat coetum cogere, vbi folennes ad Deum preces concipiantur, illud quæritur in istiusmodi supplicationibus, quid extet præter illam pompam in vestibus, funalibus, reliquiis & cæterisid genus. Atqui illud totum mere Iudaicum est, ne dicam Paganicum prorsus, nedum vt in Christianis probandum fit. Auditur illic clamor & canatus, lingua vero incognita: ac proinde cotra disertum manda tum Spiritus sancti, quo iubet preces publicas concipi lingua communi, ea videlicet quæ omnibus promiscua fit, vt quicunque sunt rudiores & ex plebe, illorum participes fiant, & ad exitum Amen respondeant ex suæ conscientiæ & affectus testimonio. Hortaris deinde, vt imploremus Mariam Virginem, & sanctos, ac Petrum nominatim designas vt nostrum hic patronum. Atqui Deus nos ad fe vnum ita vocat, vt ad alium quemuis confugere vetet. Atque illud optimo iure, quando summa ei is gloriæ pars in eo sita est, vt ipsum invocemus vnum in Christi nomine. Et vt illa vna ratio non subsit, extant passim tot Scripturæ loca, quæ iubent nos ad Deum recipere cum oratione & precibus, fiue peft, fiue bello, fiue fame vrgeamur. De implorandis sanctis ne minimus quidem vspiam extat apex. Quàm igitur temere & perperam à nobis fieret te audientibus, vt simul Dei doctrinæ tergum à nobis obuerteretur. Quod Petrum nobis patronum vocas, nihil hoc aliud est, quàm quod est apud Prophetam: Israel Dij tui sunt iuxta numerum vrbium tuarum: cum tamen iis temporibus non hoc sibi populus proponeret, vt Deo vero abolito, plures illius loco submitterentur: sed quatenus vna iuxque vrbs sibi patronum certum eligebat in quo fiduciam collocaret. Exprobrat illis Propheta eo nómine, quòd singulæ vrbes singulos deos sibi haberent. Perinde nos facere etiā nunc iubes. Absit verò vt alium patronum optemus nobis præter vnum Iesum Christū, qui nos recepit in fidem suam, quos etiam Patri cōmendaret. Si in illa caecitate olim ipsi viximus, præterierunt illæ tenebræ: neq; iam errandi tempus est, vbi semel oculos nostros lux tanta circunfulsit. Atqui experientia edoctus es, inquis, quantum hæc valeant. Non est verò res nova, vbi Dei beneficia attribuuntur operibus nostris vanis & perversis, quasi idola colendo beneficia ipsius erga nos eliceremus, Sic se iactant sacrilegi, magi, diuini & cæteri eiusmodi. Est, autem nobis longè certior illa regula, nempe vt præeat ratio experientiæ. Hoc vbi sequemur, non feremur extra viā, itaq; extra Domini mandatum. Sic competemus denique reipsa & absque villa illusione, nunquam illis deesse opem ipsius qui solidè in eo fiduciam collocāt. Contrà verò, si quæ alibi præsidia requiremus, vt illa nos iuuare nobis persuadeamus, exitus tandem ostendet, nos ipsos ita plane fuisse deceptos.
units.tr: Matth. 26. Mar. 14. Luc. 22. 1. Cor. 11. (marginal references, left) We add moreover that this plainly detracts from the dignity of him who, as Priest, was constituted without any companion or successor, so that he might offer himself; since there was no one who could perform that remarkable work in his place. The office of sacrificing clearly pertains to this: that the one who sacrifices be a mediator between God and men. In whom, then, is faith to be placed, if you thus set yourselves over against Christ? You also point out to us those supplications which you call general processions. And what work can there be in them, unless perhaps we are to think that God will be appeased by us through that great pomp and ceremonies prepared for display? You will reply that you intend these to be carried out with a sure disposition of mind and with devotion. Surely that will be lawful devotion, where we place our faith in candles, torches, proud and lavish vestments, images and relics of the dead! Indeed that was the practice among idolaters of the Gentiles, as histories attest; but that it should correspond to Christian worship must first be taught us. We do not dispute whether it is expedient to gather an assembly where solemn prayers are offered to God; what is asked about in such supplications is what exists beyond that pomp of vestments, torches, relics and the like. Yet all of that is purely Jewish, not to say altogether pagan, and much less to be approved in Christians. There is heard there a clamour and singing, but in an unknown tongue; and so it runs against the clear command of the Holy Spirit, by which he bids public prayers to be offered in a common tongue, namely one shared by all, so that whoever are more untutored and of the common people may take part in them and respond "Amen" at the end, from the testimony of their conscience and affection. You urge us next to implore the Virgin Mary and the saints, and you name Peter specifically as our patron here. Yet God calls us to himself alone in such a way that he forbids us to flee to any other. And he does so with the best right, since the greater part of his glory lies in this: that we invoke him alone in the name of Christ. And lest that one reason alone should seem to stand, there are everywhere so many passages of Scripture that bid us turn to God with prayer and supplication, whether we are pressed by plague, war or famine. Of invoking the saints, not even the smallest iota is to be found anywhere. How rashly and perversely would it be done by us, with you listening, if at the same time we turned our backs on the teaching of God! As for your calling Peter our patron, this is nothing other than what is found in the Prophet: "Israel, your gods are according to the number of your cities." Yet in those times the people did not propose to themselves that, the true God being abandoned, several gods should be substituted in his place; rather, each city chose for itself a certain patron in whom to place its trust. The Prophet rebukes them on this account, because each single city had its own god. You bid us do the same even now. Far be it that we should wish for any other patron besides the one Jesus Christ, who received us into his faith and whom he also commended to the Father. If we once lived in that blindness, those darknesses have passed away; nor is it now the time to go astray, since such great light has shone around our eyes. But you say you have been taught by experience how much these things are worth. Yet it is no new thing when God's benefits are attributed to our vain and perverse works, as if by worshipping idols we were drawing his benefits toward us. So boast sacrilegious people, magicians, diviners and others of that kind. The rule we hold is far more certain, namely that reason should go before experience. If we follow this, we shall not be carried outside the way, and so outside the Lord's command. Thus we shall at last attain in fact, and without any illusion, that help is never lacking from him to those who place their trust firmly in him. On the contrary, if we seek protections elsewhere and persuade ourselves that they help us, the outcome will at last show that we ourselves have been thoroughly deceived.

units.la: Dominus Iesus dignetur tibi aperire oculos, vt agnoscas quid sibi velit, cùm se vnam vocat salutem, vitam, sanctificationem, sapientiam, fiduciam deniq; omnium hominum, vt & ab omnibus talis agnoscatur, & agnitus vno animo glorificetur & ore, & corde, & omnibus operibus nostris: ac proinde vt quemadmodum vnum baptisma suscepimus ipsius nomine, ita etiam vnum Christianismum omnes profiteamur.
units.tr: May the Lord Jesus deign to open your eyes, so that you may recognise what he means when he calls himself the one salvation, life, sanctification, wisdom and, in short, the trust of all people; so that he may be acknowledged as such by all, and, once acknowledged, may be glorified with one mind, with mouth and heart, and in all our works. And so, just as we have received one baptism in his name, we may all likewise profess one Christianity.

units.la: DE VTILITATE ET RECTA RATIONE lectionis sacræ Scripturæ.
units.tr: On the Usefulness and Right Method of Reading Holy Scripture.

units.la: SI longa aliqua præfatione hoc loco vtedum esset, tria omnino mihi pertractanda iudicarem. Ac primùm quidè demonstrarem quantus sit thesaurus Scriptura Sacra, quàm excellēs ipsius dignitas, fructus verò incomparabilis. Et sanè summum illa bonum vitæ iustius vti est, ita etiam merito prædicari debet. Scriptura clauis est quæ nobis patefit Regnum Dei, vt in illud intromittat, per eam nobis cōstet qui Deus adorandus, & quæ spes vocationis ipsius. Hic certū iter & expeditū nobis æternitatur, cui inhærendo à perpetua illa fluctuatione & incertitudine nobis caveamus, quæ nunquā nos certo loco stare permitteret. Hic verū discrimen boni & mali. Hic vera cultus Dei norma constat, ne illic temerè feramur, atq; nobis aliorū exemplo imponamus, dum nugis ac rebus nihili implicatur. Ac ne etiā Religionis studiū iis in rebus cōstituamus, quas vt merè impias Dominus reicit atq; condemnat. Scriptura lucerna illa est quæ nos dirigit, quæ illumi nat per medias præsentis vitæ tenebras, ne ad obiecta vndique scādala, vt cæci impingamus, ac ne multò magis ad singula monita. menta corruamus:Ipsa est totius fapietiæ schola, fapietiæ inquâ, quę omnē humanū captum exuperat, & quæ fit ipsius etiā Angelis admirationi:Ipsa speculū est in quo vultum illum Dei contuemur, vt in gloriā ipsius trāsformemur. Ipsa est sceptrū Regis nostri, quo nos tanquā subditos regit:ipsa pastorale pedū, quo se nobis Pastore vnicè præsignat. Ipsa etiā est documentū scripto cōprehensum fœderis ipsius nobiscum initi, quo sese mera gratia obstrinxit nobis ad perpetuæ nobiscū coniunctionis irruptū vinculum. Ipsa testimoniū bonæ illius voluntatis Domini, quo stat conscientiarū pax, quà certò persuasi sumus vbinam reposita sit nostra salus. Ipsa singulare animarū pabulum, quo aguntur in vitam æternā. Deniq; vnius Scripturæ beneficio à profanis & incredulis differimus, quatenus constat nobis certa Religio, cōfirmata & innixa indubitatæ Dei veritati:cùm alij omnes vagis & incertis opinionibus circunducì se sinât:aut ipsi sese sine vlla certitudine ac firmitate in impia obstinatione indurât. Hæc inquâ, pertractanda primùm essent, cum iis etiā quæ ad hūc locum pertinēt, Scopus autē esset ad exhortādū quenq;, vt tantū illud bonum singulari etiam in pretio haberet, vt omnes summi atq; infimi inuitarētur ad tāti muneris omnibus sine discrimine oblati à Domino participatione:ostēdendum etiā quātæ ingratitudinis foret Deo nos alloquenti aures claudere, retrocedere cum ad se vocat, neque sanctæ isti doctrinæ audientiā facere, in qua seipsum nobis reuelat in nostrā salutem, Hic etiā perstringenda esset mihi diabolica illorū audacia, qui ptomiscuā plebem hoc tā apposito Domini beneficio defraudare audent, dum Scripturæ sanctæ lectione interdicunt: quasi Dominus cōsilium ipse suū satis non aperuerit, quod Scripturam suam apud omnes cuiuscunq; cōditionis & linguæ extare vellet. Commōstrarem inquam, quàm nō ferenda sit crudelitas, vbi miseræ animæ cibo illo suo destituūtur, vt aut vento deinde pascātur, aut pabuli loco senenū ipsis propinetur. Hæc igitur esset summa primi illius capitis, quod tamē lōgè vberiore tractatione requireret. Alterū autē spectaret ad cōparādos lectoꝛes ad lectionē Scripturæ, vt ex illa sructū caperent. Huius vērō capitis essent duæ partes. Vna, vt idoneè præparati accederemus, altera vt teneremus, ad quem scopum nobis collimandū esser. Nemo enim vnquā idoneus erit discipulus Domini, nisi qui sese sistet ipsi cū animo illo prolixo ac propenso, vt admittat syncerè quid quid à Domino acceperit; nisi qui iudicio suo renuntiauerit & rationi simul, vt vnam sapientiam in summa docilitate statuat: nisi etiā affectus natiuos infrænet, vt arbitrio Magistri submittat: nisi deniq; seipsum quasi si custodiā sponte cōcludat, vt sub illius iugo cōtineatur, cui inseruire longē optabilius sit, quàm non modò liberū aliàs esse, sed vel latissime etiam dominari: nisi & omnis arrogatiæ obli-tus,sese ipsum deiiciat ad veram humilitate, & imminutionem illam quam in suis discipulis Dominus requirit:nisi cor aperiat, vt quid audierit, admittat:nisi timorem & reuerentia legitimam afferat,quæ creatoris Maiestati respondeat:nisi zelo puro & recto prædirus sit ad inquirendā voluntatem Dei, vt ad ipsam vitam omnem,opera,cogitationes, sermones exigatnisi seipsum expe diat terrenis negotiis, nisi corde sit vacuo & purgato ab omnibus carnis folicitudinibus & cocup fcentiis, vt totum sese conferat, ac sine ulla interpellatione ad coelestium rerū meditationem. Et quoniā naturalis nostra propensio istiusmodi præparationi ex diametro repugnat,inprimis hoc est cófultissimum,vt à Domino imploremus, vt agamur ipsius Spiritu : cum sine illo quidquid operæ ac laboris insumptum à nobis esset, nihil hic prorsus ageremus, Vt contra etiā vbi Spiritum directorem accepe-rimus,nihil erit nobis timendū, dum illum appositum dedu-ctorem sequemur.Constat vero Dominū non denegaturū Spiri-tum S.si qui sine simulatione postularint. Quare nos ita cōpara-re discamus,vt supra traditū esset,vt deinde orationē ad Domi-num serio præmissa cum fructu in Scripturæ lectione versemur. Altera secūdi capitis pars est, vt præmoneremur vagādum non esse in Scriptura, vt huc & illuc circumeundo nunquā ad veræ scientiæ scopū pertingamus. Quod ne accidat,cauendæ sunt otiosæ speculationes,neq; etiā hærendum in quæstionibus friuolis, quæ tantum cōtentiones & rixas pariant vt notat Paulus:aut meræ sunt ingeniorū cruces, aut sub specie subtilitatē in nebulas attollūt,atq; à solo & solido fundamēto abducūt. Neq; enim ideo Scriptura data nobis est,vt sultam curiositatem pascat,aut ambitioni inseruiat,sed vtilis ipsa est,inquit Paulus,nēpe vt erudiat in recta doctrina,consoletur, exhortetur,atq; ad omne opus bonū perfectos reddat.Ad illum vsum igitur ipsa nobis applicanda est. Atq; hæc legitimæ ædificationis ex illa nobis colligendæ summa' starui potest, vt ex Scriptura fidem collocare in Deo,tū in ipsius timore ambulare discamus.Et quoniā finis Legis & Prophetarū,ipsaq; adeo Euāgelij substātia Christ° ipse est, ne alium scopū nobis proponamus,quām qui ad Christi cognitionem perducat:cū m illud constituerit nō posse à Christo vel mi nimum deflecti,quin statim extra via erretur.Atq; istud secundum caput parcius attingo , quia præstitione etiā tradi hoc non posset,quod diffusiore tractatione requireret,ad rem ipsam plenius exponendā. Satiserit igitur indicasse quātum hic locus tulit,vt interea apud lectorē excusatam breuitatē velim,cum hoc tantum mihi proposuerim, vt admonerem quid in ipso Scriptu-ra scitu scire maxime expediret. Postremū est de ipso Scriptu-ra ia ræ in linguam nostram vernaculam interprëte. Nam inter eos qui huic operi nauarunt operam, Petrus Robertus Oliueta-nus plæ memoriæ, atq; olim fi.lelis Ecclesiæ Christi seruus se ita gessit, vt ipsius labor perpetuam apud bonos omnes commenda-tionem mereatur. Hactenus Quæ enim pauca supererant ad Galli-cam translationem tantum pertinebant.
units.tr: If a long preface were appropriate here, I would think three things must be treated. First, I would show how great a treasure Holy Scripture is, how excellent its dignity and how incomparable its fruit. Indeed, it is rightly to be proclaimed as the highest good of life, and it deserves to be preached as such. Scripture is the key that opens the Kingdom of God to us and lets us enter it. Through it we learn which God is to be worshipped and what hope belongs to his calling. Here a sure and open way is laid out for us. By keeping to it we are guarded against that perpetual wavering and uncertainty which would never let us stand firm in any place. Here is the true distinction between good and evil. Here the true rule of the worship of God is established, so that we are not carried rashly in there, nor led by the example of others while we are entangled in trifles and things of no account. Nor should we place the zeal of religion in those things which the Lord rejects and condemns as purely impious. Scripture is the lamp that guides us, that lights up the midst of the darkness of this present life, so that we do not stumble blind against the obstacles of scandal on every side, much less fall headlong at each single warning. It is the school of all wisdom, a wisdom that surpasses all human capacity and that even the Angels admire. It is the mirror in which we behold the face of God, so that we are transformed into his glory. It is the sceptre of our King, by which he rules us as his subjects. It is the shepherd's staff, by which he presents himself to us as our one Shepherd. It is also the written record of the covenant made with us, by which he bound himself to us by pure grace, to the unbreakable bond of perpetual union with us. It is the testimony of the Lord's good will, by which the peace of consciences stands, and by which we are firmly persuaded where our salvation is laid up. It is the unique food of souls, by which we are led into eternal life. Finally, it is by the benefit of Scripture alone that we differ from the profane and the unbelieving, inasmuch as we possess a certain religion, confirmed and resting on the indubitable truth of God, whereas all others let themselves be led about by vague and uncertain opinions, or harden themselves in impious obstinacy without any certainty or firmness. These things, I say, would have to be treated first, together with those matters that pertain to this place. The aim would be to exhort each person to hold this great good in such high esteem that all, high and low alike, would be invited without distinction to share in so great a gift, offered by the Lord to all. It would also have to be shown how great an ingratitude it is to close our ears when God speaks to us, to draw back when he calls us, and not to give heed to that holy teaching in which he reveals himself to us for our salvation. Here too I would have to expose the diabolical audacity of those who dare to deprive the common people of this so fitting benefit of the Lord, by forbidding them to read Holy Scripture, as if the Lord had not sufficiently declared his own counsel, since he wished his Scripture to be available to all of every condition and language. I would show, I say, how intolerable the cruelty is when wretched souls are deprived of that food, so that they are fed on wind instead, or are given hemlock to drink in place of nourishment. This, then, would be the sum of the first head, which would nonetheless require a much fuller treatment. The second concerns preparing readers to read Scripture, so that they may derive fruit from it. This head would have two parts. The first is that we approach it properly prepared; the second is that we keep in view the goal at which we must aim. For no one will ever be a fit disciple of the Lord unless he presents himself to him with that open and ready mind, so that he sincerely accepts whatever he has received from the Lord; unless he renounces his own judgment and reason alike, so as to hold one wisdom in the utmost docility; unless he also restrains his natural affections, so as to submit to the will of the Master; unless, finally, he willingly shuts himself up as if in a prison, so that he is kept under the yoke of the one whom it is far more desirable to serve than to be free or even to rule most widely. Unless he also, forgetting all arrogance, casts himself down into true humility and that diminishing which the Lord requires in his disciples; unless he opens his heart so as to admit what he has heard; unless he brings fear and a reverence fitting to the majesty of the Creator; unless he is equipped with a pure and upright zeal to inquire into the will of God, so that he directs his whole life, works, thoughts and words by it; unless he frees himself from earthly business; unless he is empty of heart and cleansed of all the anxieties and lusts of the flesh, so that he gives himself entirely, without any distraction, to the meditation of heavenly things. And since our natural inclination runs directly counter to this kind of preparation, it is above all most advisable that we beg the Lord that we may be moved by his Spirit, since without him whatever labour and effort we expend will achieve nothing at all here. Conversely, once we have received the Spirit as our guide, we need fear nothing, provided we follow the guide given to us. It is certain that the Lord will not deny his Holy Spirit to those who ask for him without pretence. Therefore let us learn to prepare ourselves as has been said above, so that, after a prayer to the Lord offered earnestly beforehand, we may then engage in the reading of Scripture with profit. The other part of the second head is that we should be warned not to wander about in Scripture, running here and there, so that we never reach the goal of true knowledge. To prevent this, idle speculations must be avoided, and we must not linger over frivolous questions, which, as Paul observes, produce nothing but contentions and quarrels. Such questions are either mere torments of the intellect or, under the appearance of subtlety, raise men into clouds and lead them away from the sole and solid foundation. For Scripture was not given to us so that it might feed idle curiosity or serve ambition, but, as Paul says, it is profitable, namely to teach in sound doctrine, to comfort, to exhort, and to make us perfect for every good work. It is to that use, then, that we must apply it. And the sum of the proper edification to be gathered from it can be put this way: that from Scripture we learn to place our faith in God and to walk in his fear. And since the end of the Law and the Prophets, and indeed the very substance of the Gospel, is Christ himself, we should not set before ourselves any other goal than the one that leads to the knowledge of Christ, since it is established that one cannot turn aside even a little from Christ without straightaway going astray outside the way. I touch on this second head more sparingly, because it could not be handled in brief compass, and it would require a fuller discussion to set the matter out properly. It will suffice, therefore, to have indicated as much as this place allowed, and in the meantime I would ask the reader to excuse the brevity, since I have proposed to myself only this: to point out what in Scripture it is most useful to know. The last matter concerns the translation of Scripture into our vernacular tongue. Among those who have laboured at this work, Pierre Robert Olivétan, of blessed memory, once a faithful servant of the Church of Christ, conducted himself in such a way that his labour deserves lasting commendation from all good people. Thus far. For what few things remained were concerned only with the French translation.

units.la: Binas abs te literas paucis abhinc diebus accepi. Priores attu-lit hic noster Raymondus, alteræ mihi à fratre meo sant redditæ. Verùm iâ ante Raymondi aduentu abierat Viretus. Ad eū igitur vtrafq; misi, vt ipse quoq; ad eas quod visum fuerit, respondeat. Fratres sicut dicis, commendemus Domino, quando aliud restat nihil. Cæterum hoc tempore de impetranda fratribus illinc aliqua leuatione frustra cogitarem: nisi forte noui quidpiam acciderit: quod nondum despero. Itaq; imminere occasioni statui. Sed adduci nequeo, vt satagam ante tempus. Ecce etiâ de eo qui Grariànopoli tenebatur, tristem nuntiù à fratre tuo Claudio audies: cuius literas ad te mitto. Quòd me tantopere hortaris, vt istuc cū Vireto quàm primùm veniâ: tgo verò tibi nō cōcedam, hoc tibi magis esse in votis quàm mihi. Sed vna est suscipiendæ perfectionis ratio, si Viretū Bernā vsq; comiter: quod facere tentabo. Sin verò hæc spes me & illū frustrabitur: dimidium saltem eius quod optas assequeris. Imò plus dimidio. Nam me aliqua ex parte secum ferei. Consilii interea fratribus nō possum aliud dare, nisi vt collegā tuum coram Magistratu admoneat, vt se patia-tur in ordinē redigi. Quòd si peruicaciter recusare instituerit, de-nunciet sibi nō esse loco fratris, qui cōmunem disciplinam con-tumacia sua perturbet: semper hoc in Ecclesia valuit, quod vete-ribus Synodis fuit decretū, vt qui subiici cōmunis disciplinę le-gibus noluerit, munere abdicetur. Neq; hic quæ tæda est hominū authoritas: cùm Spiritus S. de talibus pronunciauerit, Ecclesiam nō habere morem cōtendendi. Valere ergo ipsum iubeant, qui cōmunis sociétatis iura respuit. Nō puto eò vsq; Satanā istic aut aut alibi vsquā ualituru, vt tantæ vnius hominis proteruiæ in-dulgeatur, contépto fratrū omniū iubicio: q; importunitate sua vobis ipse tandē extorserit. Cæterū euentū gubernabit Deus. Vt-cunq; cadat, vestrarū tamē partiū omnino est, grauiter hāc mi-nimè tolerabilē insolentiā seueris remediis cohibere. Proderi tamē simul cōmemorare, q; improbē hasten patientia lenitateq; vestra abusus fuerit: ne ad cōtentione subito prosiliisse videami ni. Vale frater integerrimē & amice optime. Fratres omnes cum tuâ familia peramanter salutabis nomine meo. Dominus vos omnes cōseruet.
units.tr: I received two letters from you a few days ago. The first was brought by our friend Raymond here; the second was handed to me by my brother. But Viret had already left before Raymond arrived. So I have sent both to him, so that he too may reply to them as he thinks fit. As you say, we will commend the brethren to the Lord, since nothing else remains. For the present, however, I would be wasting my thoughts if I hoped to obtain some relief for the brethren there, unless some new development should arise, which I do not yet despair of. So I have decided to wait for the opportunity. But I cannot bring myself to hurry ahead of time. See also: you will hear from your brother Claude the sad news about the man who was being held at Grenoble; I am sending you his letter. As for your urging me so strongly to come to you there with Viret as soon as possible, I will not grant it to you: you wish this more than I do. But there is only one way to accomplish the task you undertake, if I can persuade Viret to come to Berne; I will try to do this. But if this hope fails me and him, you will at least obtain half of what you desire. Indeed, more than half; for I would bring myself along in some measure. Meanwhile I can give the brethren no other counsel than that your colleague be warned before the magistrate to allow himself to be brought into order. And if he persists in refusing stubbornly, let him be told that he is not in the place of a brother, since by his obstinacy he disturbs the common discipline. This has always held good in the Church, as the ancient Synods decreed, that whoever refuses to submit to the laws of common discipline should be removed from office. Nor is the authority of men at issue here, since the Holy Spirit has pronounced that the Church should not have the custom of contending in such cases. Let those who reject the rights of common fellowship bid him farewell. I do not think that Satan will prevail there or anywhere else to such an extent that the obstinacy of one man should be indulged, with the judgment of all the brethren set aside, which he has at last wrung from you by his importunity. But God will govern the outcome. Whichever way it falls, it is certainly your duty to restrain this altogether intolerable insolence with severe remedies. Yet at the same time it should be pointed out how wickedly his arrogance has abused your patience and gentleness, lest you seem to have leapt into contention suddenly. Farewell, most upright brother and best of friends. Greet all the brethren, together with your family, most affectionately in my name. May the Lord keep you all.

units.la: Indicem nouum libenter contexuimus, quia propemodum necesse erat, si satis otij dedissent proximæ & instantes nostris operis Francofordienses nundinæ. Cæterum, quia consultius ita visum est multis de causis, numeri non paginas designant, sed quota sit, & quo ordine quæque reperiatur Epistola, in qua hoc vel illud notatum requiris. Hoc enim etiam habet editio nostra, quod suis cuique præfigitur numerus, ut quot toto in volumine extent Epistolæ, constet omnibus, & facile quamque suo numero sic prænotatam reperire liceat. Vale benevole Lector, & omnia boni consule.
units.tr: We have gladly compiled a new index, which was nearly necessary, had the coming Frankfurt fair, close at hand, left us enough leisure. However, since it seemed more advisable for many reasons, the numbers indicate not pages but which Letter it is and in what order each item is found, in which you look for this or that noted matter. For our edition also has this feature, that each Letter is prefixed with its own number, so that everyone knows how many Letters there are in the whole volume, and it is easy to find each one so marked by its number. Farewell, kindly reader, and take everything in good part.
